units.la: Quisquis hoc legit, ubi pariter certus est, pergat mecum; ubi pariter hæsitat, quærat mecum; ubi errorem suum cognoscit, redeat ad me; ubi meum, revocet me. Ita ingrediamur simul charitatis viam, tendentes ad Eum, de quo dictum est; Quærite faciem ejus semper. -- Utile est, plures (libros) à pluribus fieri diverso stylo, non diversâ fide, etiam de quæstionibus eisdem; ut ad plurimos res ipsa perveniat, ad alios sic, ad alios autem sic.
units.tr: Whoever reads this, where he is equally certain, let him go on with me; where he equally hesitates, let him seek with me; where he recognises his own error, let him return to me; where it is mine, let him call me back. Thus let us enter together upon the way of love, striving toward Him of whom it is said: Seek His face always. -- It is useful that many books be written by many authors in different styles, but not with a different faith, and even on the same questions; so that the matter itself may reach many people in one way, others in another way, and others in yet another way.

units.la: multùmque diduétis : verùm frequenter, si non eadem omnia, saltem præstantissima quæque, iidem exiguâ & valdè contractâ formâ exprimunt; qui posterior modus, ut spectantium oculos oblectare ac blandè pascere solet, siç u-sum quoque multiplicem habet procul dubio. Similiter in Facultatibus, Scientiis, atque Artibus tradendis, interdùm prolixiores & locupletiores sunt earum Auctores; alias etiàm sunt breviores. Ubi verò sic brevitati litatur, ut sedulò evitetur obscuritas ; atque adeò paucis quàm plurima dicantur, & aptè; Compendia minimè sunt Dispendia: sed, Margaritarum instar, in minori corpore majus pretium habent. Nunc de instituti nostri ratione clariùs dicam. Antehàc tùm publicis Disputationibus, tùm aliter, tribus tomis edidi Systema Theologiæ dogmaticæ: ubi initiò quidem majorem mihi proposueram brevitatem ; posteà tamen in progressù, specialibus quibusdam de causis, quæ subindè digressiunculam, aut pleniorem explicationem requirebant, aut suadebant, præter opinionem prolixior factus sum. Multi interim isto opere feliciter usi sunt, atque ex eo se plurimum (Deo benedicente) profecisse agnoverunt. Sed in subsidium memoriæ suæ aliqui etiàm Compendium inde sibi confecerunt. Quin & non neminem in animo habuisse, talem quem conatum suum publici juris facere, per alios rescivi. Accessit, quod Exemplaria primi tomi illius Systematis sic ferè distracta essent, & vix apud Bibliopolas comparari amplius possent; unde minus commodè ad istud opus haberi deinceps potuerunt privata nostra Collegia dogmatica. Sed &, ratione prolixitatis & copiæ, nonnulla passim istic omitti debuerunt; ne nimis diù protraherentur dicta exercitia. Animum propterea induxi, ex diligentioribus atque exercitatioribus nostris Discipulis quatuor deligere, eosque adhortari, ut operam suam hâc in re mihi, & communi aliorum utilitati commodantes, singuli quinque Systematis illius capita contra herent: quod cum illi fecissent strenuè, ego deinde mutanda mutavi, superflua resecui, & omissa supplevi. Ità consectum est hoc Compendium Theologiæ dogmaticum: quod sic facilius absolvetur in Collegiis explicatoriis & examinatoriis, vel etiàm disputatoriis; & Studiosi ex eo commodius se præparabunt ad interroganda. Perspicuitati autem in omnibus, quoad ejus fieri potuit, operam dedi: sic præcipua, & utilissima quæque, hic exhibui. In Controversiis vèram sententiam distinctis aliquot Argumentorum classibus probatam dedi: Exceptiones vero & Objectiones Adversariorum, quibus per Occupationem crypticam, indicatis tantum Fontibus solutionum, prius obviàm ibatur, nunc etiam propositui distinctè; iisque Responsiones suas subjeci: quemadmodum Usus practicos suis identidem locis quoque annotavi. Indicem petierunt nonnulli, aut lemmata saltem marginalia: sed eorum vicem præstabunt satis Argumenta, quæ singulis Capitibus præponuntur. Interim qui prolixiorem ac pleniorem alicubi tractationem à me requirunt, dictos illos Systematis tomos
units.tr: and spread out widely. But often, if not all the same things, at least the most outstanding points, the same authors set forth in a small and greatly condensed form. This second method, as it usually delights the eyes of those who look at it and pleasantly feeds them, undoubtedly has many uses as well. Similarly, in teaching the faculties, sciences and arts, their authors are sometimes fuller and more detailed, and at other times briefer. But where brevity is pursued in such a way that obscurity is carefully avoided, and so much is said in few words, and aptly, compendia are by no means losses: like pearls, they have greater worth in a smaller body. Now I will explain more clearly the plan of my undertaking. Previously I published, both in public disputations and otherwise, the System of Dogmatic Theology in three volumes. At the start I had indeed intended a greater brevity for myself; afterwards, however, as the work went on, for certain special reasons which from time to time called for or suggested a digression or a fuller explanation, I became more lengthy than I had expected. Meanwhile many have used that work with success, and have acknowledged (God blessing) that they profited greatly from it. But some, as an aid to their memory, have also made a compendium of it for themselves. Indeed, I have learned from others that someone had in mind to make such an attempt of his own public. Moreover, the copies of the first volume of that System had sold out so thoroughly that they could hardly be obtained any more from the booksellers, so our private dogmatic colleges could less conveniently use that work from then on. But also, on account of its length and abundance, some things had to be omitted here and there, so that the said exercises would not be drawn out for too long. I therefore resolved to choose four of our more diligent and experienced students, and to urge them to lend their labour in this matter to me and to the common benefit of others, each to reduce five chapters of that System into a compendious form. When they had done this vigorously, I then changed what needed changing, cut away what was superfluous, and supplied what had been omitted. Thus this Compendium of Dogmatic Theology has been completed, which will be more easily gone through in explanatory, examining, or even disputatory colleges, and students will prepare themselves more conveniently from it for answering questions. I have, however, taken pains with clarity in all things as far as that could be done, and so I have set out here the chief and most useful points. In the Controversies I have given the true opinion, proved by several classes of arguments set out distinctly. The Exceptions and Objections of opponents, which were previously met by a cryptic allusion, with only the sources of the solutions indicated, I have now also set out distinctly, and I have added their Responses to them, just as I have from time to time noted the practical uses in their places. Some asked for an Index, or at least marginal headings; but the Arguments placed before each chapter will sufficiently take their place. Meanwhile, those who require from me a fuller and more complete treatment somewhere should consult the said volumes of the System.

units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: tomos cum hoc Compendio utiliter conserent privatim. Imo neque cuiquam quorumvis Theologorum Clariff. Institutiones, Systemata, Synopfes, Medullas, Ideas, &c. è manibus excuti velim. Bonum bono additum,facit majus bonum. Incipientibus quidem utile est, non distrahi per nimis multa & varia: sed provectiores, quibus nostra in usû etiàm sunt, ferio exhortor, ut ea ex aliis supplere, atque, ubi forte opus erit, corrigere annitantur sedulò. Ego interea temporis, adspirante clementer DEI gratiâ, pergam κατὰ δύναμιν in elaborando Systemate practico; quod publicis etiàm Disputationibus proponi cœptum est : & partem Systematis dogmatici priorem ad iteratam editionem præparare conabor; aliaque, quæ vobis publicè profutura spero, pro infirmitate meâ (sed potentia Domini per infirmitatem quoque consummatur) aggrediar, ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θέλῃ καὶ ζήσωμεν. Magnus autem ille Pater luminum, fons omnis sapientiæ falutaris, DEUS, & Dominus noster JESUS CHRISTUS, vera illa Lux & Vita, idem
units.tr: together with this Compendium usefully consult privately. Indeed I would not wish any of the famous theologians' Institutions, Systems, Synopses, Marrows, Ideas, and so on, to be taken out of anyone's hands. A good thing added to a good thing makes a greater good. For beginners it is indeed useful not to be distracted by too many and varied things; but to more advanced readers, for whom our works are also in use, I earnestly urge that they diligently strive to supplement them from other sources and, where perhaps it is needed, to correct them. Meanwhile, with the gracious grace of God breathing upon me, I shall continue according to my strength [κατὰ δύναμιν] in working out the Practical System, which has already begun to be proposed even in public disputations; and I shall endeavour to prepare the first part of the Dogmatic System for a second edition; and I shall undertake other things, which I hope will be publicly profitable to you, according to my weakness (but the power of the Lord is also made perfect in weakness), if the Lord wills and we live [ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θέλῃ καὶ ζήσωμεν]. But may that great Father of lights, the fountain of all saving wisdom, God, and our Lord Jesus Christ, that true Light and Life, the same...

units.tr: On the origin and use of the word. (1) Description of the thing. (2) Distinction according to subjects. (3) The theology of God himself. (4) Its objects, and how many kinds follow from them. (5) The theology of intellectual creatures: its cause of constitution and its first acquisition. (6) How many kinds of ectypal theology there are. (7) The theology of union. (8) The theology of vision. (9) What is opposed to these. (10) The theology of revelation: what it is, and how many kinds. (11) Natural theology. (12) What it was before the Fall. (13) What it is after the Fall, and how many kinds. (14) Congenital theology. (15) Proved against the Socinians. (20) In itself it does not oppose the supernatural. (21) How far it reaches, or does not. (22) That it is not sufficient for obtaining salvation, and so there is no common religion. units.la: I. Theologia Grammaticè deducitur à voce paronymâ Theologus.
units.tr: I. Theology is derived grammatically from the paronymous word Theologus.

units.la: Ista, aliaque vocabula similia, Gentilibus olim usurpata, Doctores Christiani jure in usum suum traduxerunt; rei significatæ veri ac justi, Deo dante, possessores. Hùc pertinet Inscriptio; Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννου Θεολόγου: quoniam ipse Apostolus de Deo accuratissimè disseruit; ὡς Θεότητος καὶ Λόγου, contra Ebionem, Cerinthum, eorumque sequaces singulari zelo asseruit.
units.tr: These and other similar words were once used by the Gentiles, and Christian Doctors rightly took them over for their own use, God granting them possession of the true and just thing signified. To this belongs the title "The Revelation of John the Theologian" [Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννου Θεολόγου], since the Apostle himself discoursed most accurately about God, and with singular zeal asserted the divinity of God and of the Word against Ebion, Cerinthus, and their followers.

units.la: Simplicia, Θεὸς, & Λόγος, vel τὸ Λόγιον, etiàm conjunctim in SS. Literis occurrunt sæpiùs: Joh. 1, 1. Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος. Apoc. XIX. 13. ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, de ipso Filio Dei. Sed & & I Thess. II, 13. Hebr. IV, 12. ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. Rom. III, 2. Hebr. V, 12. 1 Petr. IV, 11. τὰ Λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ. προφορικὸς, de Verbo, aut Sermonibus Dei ad homines.
units.tr: The simple terms, God [Θεὸς] and Word [Λόγος], or the Oracle [τὸ Λόγιον], also occur often together in the Holy Scriptures: John 1:1, "The Word was God" [Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος]; Revelation 19:13, "the Word of God" [ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ], of the Son of God himself. Also 1 Thess. 2:13; Heb. 4:12, "the word of God" [ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ]; Rom. 3:2; Heb. 5:12; 1 Pet. 4:11, "the oracles of God" [τὰ Λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ]. The word is used of the spoken Word, or of God's sermons to men.

units.la: II. Ut cognoscatur quid rei sit, Theologia in universum describitur, Sapientia de Deo.
units.tr: II. So that we may know what the thing is, theology is described in general as wisdom concerning God.

units.la: Generis instar dicitur Sapientia: hæc enim habitum intellectualem augustissimum notat; eumque non modo theoreticum, sed etiam practicum. Ita quæ nunc Philosophia appellatur, & ex parte practica est, olim Σοφία, h. e. Sapientia, vocatur. Et præit S. Pagina, Deut. IV, 6. „Custodite ergo, & facite; quia ea est sapientia vestra, &c. Col. III, 16. „Sermo Christi in habitet in vobis copiosè, cum omni sapientia. Vide etiam Psal. XIX, 8. Luc. XXI. 15. 2 Tim. III, 15. Jac. III, 13, 17.
units.tr: Wisdom is named as the genus, for it signifies the most excellent intellectual habit, and one that is not only theoretical but also practical. So too what is now called philosophy, and is partly practical, was formerly called Sophia, that is, wisdom [Σοφία]. Holy Scripture leads the way: Deut. 4:6, "Keep therefore and do them, for this is your wisdom," etc.; Col. 3:16, "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom." See also Ps. 19:8; Luke 21:15; 2 Tim. 3:15; James 3:13, 17.

units.la: Differentiæ locum obtinet ipsum objectum: Deus: sic tamen, ut omnia, quæ ad Deum spectant, quatenus talia sunt, comprehendantur. Joh. XVII, 3. „Hæc est autem vita æterna, ut Te cognoscant, illum solum verum Deum; &, quem misisti, Jesum Christum. Rom. XI, 33–36. „O profundas divitias, tum sapientiæ, tum cognitionis, Dei! Quàm imperscrutabilia sunt ejus judicia: & ejus viæ impervestigabiles! Quis enim cognovit mentem Domini? – Nam ex Eo, & per Eum, & in Ipsum (sunt) omnia. Ipsi (sit) gloria in sæcula! Amen.
units.tr: The difference is supplied by the object itself, God, yet in such a way that all things which pertain to God, insofar as they are such, are included. John 17:3, "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ." Romans 11:33–36, "O the depth of the riches, both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? … For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things. To him be glory for ever. Amen."

Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur; etiam profunditates Dei. – „Etiàm ea, quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei. Pfal. xciv, 9, 10. ,,An, qui plantavit aurem, non au- ,,diet? An, qui finxit oculum, non videbit? - An, qui ,,docet hominem scientiam (non cognoscet?)
units.tr: III. According to the subjects, or as it were, theology is called both the theology of God himself and that of intellectual creatures. Matt. 11:27, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him." 1 Cor. 2:10–11, "But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. … So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." Ps. 94:9–10, "He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see? He who teaches man knowledge, shall he not know?"

units.la: IV. Theologia ipsius Dei est, quâ Deus seipsum cognoscit convenienter Naturæ suæ.
units.tr: IV. The theology of God himself is that by which God knows himself in a manner fitting to his nature.

units.la: Hoc est, 1. Independenter; per Essentiam suam: ut hæc fit ἀδίδακτος.
units.tr: That is: (1) independently, through his own essence, so that this knowledge is untaught [ἀδίδακτος];

units.la: 2. Simplicissimè; actû purissimo: ut sit ipse idem ὁ Θεολόγος, τὸ Θεολογούμενον, καὶ ἡ Θεολογία.
units.tr: (2) most simply, in a most pure act, so that he himself is the theologian [ὁ Θεολόγος], the thing theologized [τὸ Θεολογούμενον], and the theology [ἡ Θεολογία].

units.la: 3. Infinitè, & adæquatè, ipse igitur sese cognoscit, ut absolutè cognosci potest.
units.tr: (3) Infinitely and adequately; therefore he knows himself as fully as he can be known absolutely.

units.la: 1 Tim. i, 17. ,,Soli sapienti Deo honor (sit). &c. Psal. cxlvii, 5. ,,Intelligentiæ Ejus non est numerus. Confer allegata th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 1:17, "To the only wise God be honour," etc. Ps. 147:5, "His understanding is without number." Compare the passages cited under thesis 3.

units.la: V. Deus autem cognoscit primò Essentiam suam, cum Attributis, & Personis: atque in Attributis nominatim Sufficientiam & Potentiam; quæ est principium Possibilitatis omnium Rerum Possibilium, cum Affectionibus Possibilibus. Hactenus est Theologia Dei naturalis & necessaria.
units.tr: V. God, however, first knows his own essence, together with its attributes and persons; and among the attributes he knows by name his sufficiency and power, which is the principle of the possibility of all possible things, together with their possible affections. So far this is the natural and necessary theology of God.

units.la: Deinde sibi conscius est Decreti sui; atque omnium eorum, quæ ipse Decreto suo constituit, tùm de aliis, tùm speciatim de Creaturis intellectualibus: imò etiam, quibus modis ac gradibus communicare iis velit notitiam Sui. Sapientissimè enim operatur τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς; Hebr. xi, 10. Unde Actor. xv, 18. ,,Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua. Hæc dicitur Theologia Dei libera; ratione objectorum.
units.tr: Then he is conscious of his own decree, and of all those things which he has established by his decree, both concerning others and specifically concerning intellectual creatures; indeed also of the ways and degrees in which he wills to communicate to them the knowledge of himself. For God works most wisely as craftsman and maker [τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς]; Heb. 11:10. Hence Acts 15:18, "All his works are known to God from eternity." This is called the free theology of God, with respect to its objects.

units.la: Ex dictis patet, quòd speciatim in Deo sit Theologia αρχέτυπος; prima & verissima idea omnis Theologiæ in Creaturis intellectualibus.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clear that in God there is especially an archetypal theology [αρχέτυπος], the first and most true idea of all theology in intellectual creatures.

units.la: VI. Omnis Theologia Creaturarum intellectualium est ἐκτυπος; ad ideam istam, juxta Dei decretum, in tempore expressa, & Creaturis illis imprimendo communicata. Col. iii, 10. ,,Renovatur in agnitionem con-gra„gruentem imagini Ejus, qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: VI. Every theology of intellectual creatures is ectypal [ἐκτυπος]: it is expressed in time according to God's decree, in accordance with that idea, and imparted to those creatures by being impressed upon them. Col. 3:10, "renewed in the knowledge according to the image of him who created him."

units.la: Ejus igitur universæ causa constitutionis principalis unica, & acquisitionis prima ac suprema, est ipse Deus: alias Theologia Ψευδώνυμος, & superstitio emergit. Deut. iv. 2. „Non addetis ad verbum, quod Ego præcipio vobis; neque diminuetis (quicquam) ex eo, &c. „Isai. viii, 20. „Ad Legem, & ad Testimonium. Si non „dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit eis aurora. Vide etiam Deut. xii, 32. Matth. xv, 9. Galat. i, 8, 9. Col. ii, 4, 8, 22, 23. Apoc. xxii, 18, 19. Item Iac. i, 5. „Quod si cui vestrum deest sapientia, petito à Deo, qui „dat (eam) omnibus benignè, &c. 17. „Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum munus, est superne descendens à Patre luminum, &c.
units.tr: Its only principal cause of constitution, and its first and highest acquisition, is therefore God himself; otherwise a theology that is falsely named, and superstition, arises. Deut. 4:2, "You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take away anything from it," etc. Isa. 8:20, "To the law and to the testimony. If they do not speak according to this word, there is no dawn for them." See also Deut. 12:32; Matt. 15:9; Gal. 1:8–9; Col. 2:4, 8, 22–23; Rev. 22:18–19. Likewise James 1:5, "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously," etc.; 17, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," etc.

units.la: VII. Theologia ectypa trifariàm dispescitur: vel enim Unionis est, vel Visionis, vel Revelationis.
units.tr: VII. Ectypal theology is divided in three ways: for it is either that of union, or of vision, or of revelation.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Theologia Unionis appellatur, quæ in Domino nostro Jesû Christo, secundùm humanam ipsius naturam, ex Unione hypostaticâ fluit; atque sic ipsi per Spiritum S. singulari modo communicata est. Psal. XLV, 8. „Unxit Te, Deus, Deus Tuus oleo gaudii „præ Consortibus Tuis. Ioh. iii, 34. — „Deus non dat „Ipsi Spiritum ad mensuram. Adde Isai. xi, 1, 2. LXI, 1. Ioh. vii. 29. Col. ii, 3, 9.
units.tr: The theology of union is the name given to that which flows into our Lord Jesus Christ, according to his human nature, from the hypostatic union; and in this way it has been communicated to him in a singular manner through the Holy Spirit. Psal. 45:8: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." John 3:34: "God does not give him the Spirit by measure." Add Isaiah 11:1, 2; 61:1; John 7:29; Col. 2:3, 9.

units.la: IX. Theologia Visionis est Beatorum cœlitum, Angelorum & Hominum. De Angelis diserte, Matth. xviii, 10. „Angeli eorum (parvulorum) in cœlis per „omne tempus vident faciem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Sed & Homines plenè glorificati in beatâ resurrectione, erunt ἰσάγγελοι. Luc. xx, 36. Interim verò Animæ fidelium separatæ pro sua parte ejusdem beatitudinis fiunt participes. 2 Cor. v, 7, 8. „Per fidem enim „ambulamus: non per aspectum. Confidente autem „animo sumus; & gratius est nobis abesse potius e corpore, & adesse apud Dominum. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Vide Psal. XCIV, 9, 10. „An, qui plantavit aurem, non au- „diet? An, qui finxit oculum, non videbit? - An, qui „docet hominem scientiam (non cognoscet?)
units.tr: IX. The theology of vision belongs to the blessed inhabitants of heaven, both angels and men. Concerning the angels, plainly, Matt. 18:10: "Their angels (of these little ones) in heaven always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven." But men also, fully glorified in the blessed resurrection, will be equal to the angels [ἰσάγγελοι] (Luke 20:36). Meanwhile the souls of the faithful, when separated from the body, become partakers of the same blessedness in their own measure (2 Cor. 5:7, 8): "For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, and we prefer to be away from the body and to be at home with the Lord." 1 Cor. 13:12. See Psal. 94:9, 10: "Does he who planted the ear not hear? Does he who formed the eye not see? Does he who teaches man knowledge (not know?)"

units.la: I V. Theologia ipsius Dei est, quâ Deus seipsum cognoscit convenienter Naturæ suæ.
units.tr: IV. The theology of God himself is that by which God knows himself in a manner befitting his nature.

units.la: Hoc est, 1. Independenter; per Essentiam suam : ut hæc sit ἀδιάδαχτος.
units.tr: That is, 1. Independently, through his essence, so that it is not taught by another [ἀδίδακτος].

units.la: 2. Simplicissimè; actû purissimo: ut sit ipse idem ὁ Θεολόγος, τὸ Θεολογούμενον, καὶ ἡ Θεολογία.
units.tr: 2. Most simply, in purest act, so that he himself is the theologian [ὁ Θεολόγος], the thing theologized [τὸ Θεολογούμενον], and the theology [ἡ Θεολογία].

units.la: 3. Infinitè, & adæquatè, ipse igitur sese cognoscit, ut absolutè cognosci potest.
units.tr: 3. Infinitely and adequately; he therefore knows himself as he can be absolutely known.

units.la: 1 Tim. i, 17. „Soli sapienti Deo honor (sit). &c. Psal. CXLVII, 5. „ Intelligentiæ Ejus non est numerus. Confer allegata th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 1:17: "To the only wise God be honour," etc. Psal. 147:5: "Of his understanding there is no number." Compare the passages cited under th. 3.

units.la: V. Deus autem cognoscit primò Essentiam suam, cum Attributis, & Personis : atque in Attributis nominatim Sufficientiam & Potentiam; quæ est principium Possibilitatis omnium Rerum Possibilium, cum Affectionibus Possibilibus. Hactenus est Theologia Dei naturalis & necessaria.
units.tr: V. God, however, first knows his essence, together with the attributes and persons; and among the attributes, namely his sufficiency and power, which is the principle of the possibility of all possible things, together with their possible affections. So far extends the natural and necessary theology of God.

units.la: Deinde sibi conscius est Decreti sui; atque omnium eorum, quæ ipse Decreto suo constituit, tùm de aliis, tùm speciatim de Creaturis intellectualibus : imò etiàm, quibus modis ac gradibus communicare iis velit notitiam Sui. Sapientissimè enim operatur τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς; Hebr. xi, 10. Unde Actor. xv, 18. „Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua. Hæc dicitur Theologia Dei libera; ratione objectorum.
units.tr: Then he is conscious of his decree, and of all those things which he has established by his decree, both concerning others and specifically concerning intellectual creatures; indeed, also of the modes and degrees by which he wishes to communicate to them the knowledge of himself. For God works most wisely as craftsman and maker [τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς] (Heb. 11:10). Hence Acts 15:18: "All his works are known to God from the beginning of the world." This is called the free theology of God, with respect to its objects.

units.la: Ex dictis patet, quòd speciatim in Deo sit Theologia αὐτοέχτυπος; prima & verissima idea omnis Theologiæ in Creaturis intellectualibus.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clear that in God there is, specifically, the archetypal theology [αὐτοέχτυπος]: the first and truest idea of all theology in intellectual creatures.

units.la: V I. Omnis Theologia Creaturarum intellectualium est ἐκτυπος; ad ideam istam, juxta Dei decretum, in tempore expressa, & Creaturis illis imprimendo communicata. Col. iii, 10. „ Renovatur in agnitionem congruentem imagini Ejus, qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: VI. All theology of intellectual creatures is ectypal [ἐκτυπος]: expressed in time, according to God's decree, to that idea, and communicated by being imprinted on those creatures. Col. 3:10: "It is renewed into knowledge in accordance with the image of him who created it."

units.la: Ejus igitur universæ causa constitutionis principalis unica, & acquisitionis prima ac suprema, est ipse Deus: alias Theologia Pseudɔ̀wvμ@, & superstitio emergit. Deut.iv. 2. Non addetis ad verbum, quod Ego præcipio vobis; neque diminuetis (quicquam) ex eo, &c. Isef. viii, 20. Ad Legem, & ad Testimonium. Si non dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit eis aurora. Vide etiam Deut.xii, 32. Matth. xv, 9. Galat. 1, 8, 9. Col. 11, 4, 8, 22. 23. Apoc. xxii, 18, 19. Item Jac. 1, 5. Quod si cui vestrum deest sapientia, petito à Deo, qui dat (eam) omnibus benignè, &c. 17. Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum munus, est superne descendens à Patre luminum, &c.
units.tr: Therefore the single principal cause of its establishment, and the first and supreme cause of its acquisition, is God himself; otherwise a pseudo-theology and superstition emerge. Deut. 4:2: "You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor shall you take away anything from it," etc. Isa. 8:20: "To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, there will be no dawn for them." See also Deut. 12:32; Matt. 15:9; Gal. 1:8, 9; Col. 2:4, 8, 22, 23; Rev. 22:18, 19. Likewise James 1:5: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously," etc. 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," etc.

units.la: VII. Theologia ectypa trifariàm dispescitur: vel enim Unionis est, vel Visionis, vel Revelationis.
units.tr: VII. Ectypal theology is divided in three ways: for it is either the theology of union, or of vision, or of revelation.

units.la: VIII. Theologia Unionis appellatur, quæ in Domino nostro Jesu Christo, secundùm humanam ipsius naturam, ex Unione hypostaticâ fluit; atque sic ipsi per Spiritum S. singulari modo communicata est. Psal. XLV, 8. Unxit Te, Deus, Deus Tuus oleo gaudii præ Consortibus Tuis. Ioh. iii, 34. Deus non dat Ipsi Spiritum ad mensuram. Adde Isef. xi, 1, 2. LXI, 1. Ioh. vii. 29. Col. 11, 3, 9.
units.tr: VIII. The theology of union is the name given to that which flows into our Lord Jesus Christ, according to his human nature, from the hypostatic union; and in this way it has been communicated to him in a singular manner through the Holy Spirit. Psal. 45:8: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." John 3:34: "God does not give him the Spirit by measure." Add Isai. 11:1, 2; 61:1; John 7:29; Col. 2:3, 9.

units.la: IX. Theologia Visionis est Beatorum cœlitum, Angelorum & Hominum. De Angelis diserte, Matth. xviii, 10. Angeli eorum (parvulorum) in cœlis per omne tempus vident faciem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Sed & Homines plenè glorificati in beatâ resurrectione, erunt ἰσάγγελοι. Luc. xx, 36. Interim verò Animæ fidelium separatæ pro sua parte ejusdem beatitudinis fiunt participes. 2 Cor. v, 7, 8. Per fidem enim ambulamus: non per aspectum. Confidente autem animo sumus; & gratius est nobis abesse potius ex corpore, & adesse apud Dominum. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. „ Videmus enim nunc per speculum, & per aenigma ; „ tunc autem coram (cernemus) ; &c. Vide etiam Hebr. XII, 23. Phil. 1, 23. cum Matth. v, 8. 1 Joh. III, 2.
units.tr: IX. The theology of vision belongs to the blessed inhabitants of heaven, both angels and men. Concerning the angels, plainly, Matt. 18:10: "Their angels (of these little ones) in heaven always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven." But men also, fully glorified in the blessed resurrection, will be equal to the angels (Luke 20:36). Meanwhile the souls of the faithful, when separated from the body, become partakers of the same blessedness in their own measure (2 Cor. 5:7, 8): "For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, and we prefer to be away from the body and to be at home with the Lord." 1 Cor. 13:12: "For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face (we shall see)," etc. See also Heb. 12:23; Phil. 1:23, together with Matt. 5:8; 1 John 3:2.

units.la: X. Ab hac longissime distat impura illa & terribilis cognitio Dei ac rerum Divinarum in Diabolis & Hominibus damnatis. Jac. II, 19. „ Daemonia quoque credunt (Deum unum esse) ; & horrescunt. Adde Matth. VIII, 29. Act. XVI, 17. Marc. IX, 44. cum Apoc. XVI, 10, 11.
units.tr: X. Far removed from this is that impure and terrible knowledge of God and of divine things found in the devils and in damned men. James 2:19: "The demons also believe that God is one, and shudder." Add Matt. 8:29; Acts 16:17; Mark 9:44, together with Rev. 16:10, 11.

units.la: XI. Theologia Revelationis speciatim dicitur, quae Hominibus in stadio hujus vitae communicatur. Joh. I, 9. Illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. Estque Naturalis ; vel Supernaturalis.
units.tr: XI. The theology of revelation is specifically that which is communicated to men in the course of this life. John 1:9: He enlightens every man coming into the world. It is either natural or supernatural.

units.la: XII. Naturalis, Naturam Hominis rationalem comitatur in hac vita: potestque spectari qualis extitit ante lapsum ; ac porro qualis existit post lapsum.
units.tr: XII. Natural theology accompanies the rational nature of man in this life, and it may be considered as it was before the fall, and further as it is after the fall.

units.la: XIII. Ante lapsum Hominis connaturalis fuit persecta Dei cognitio, mentem illius sufficienter imbuens ad vitam caelestem & gloriam aeternam consequendam, juxta Foedus Legale. Gen. I, 26, 27. Faciamus Hominem ad imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram, &c. Col. III. 10. in agnitionem congruentem imagini ejus, qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: XIII. Before the fall the perfect knowledge of God was connatural to man, sufficiently imbuing his mind to attain heavenly life and eternal glory, according to the legal covenant. Gen. 1:26, 27: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, etc. Col. 3:10: in knowledge in accordance with the image of him who created him.

units.la: XIV. Per lapsum amissa est integritas & puritas: remansit tamen Theologia naturalis ex parte. Haec occurrit tum congenita, sive innata; tum acquisita, sive adventitia. Utraque excolenda adversus Atheorum portenta & defendenda contra Socinianorum errores.
units.tr: XIV. Through the fall integrity and purity were lost, yet natural theology remained in part. This occurs both innate or inborn, and acquired or adventitious. Each is to be cultivated against the monsters of atheists and defended against the errors of the Socinians.

units.la: XV. Congenita vocatur, quatenus adhuc Scintillae quaedam Lucis illius primaevae, Imaginis Dei, menti humanae increantur & connascuntur ; Archetypum interim & Auctorem suum sic satis demonstrantes, quidque Ipsi debeatur, & quid nobis ac proximo nostro propter Ipsum, indicantes.
units.tr: XV. It is called innate insofar as certain sparks of that primeval light, the image of God, are still created and born together with the human mind; thus sufficiently demonstrating its archetype and author, and indicating what is owed to him, and what to us and to our neighbour on account of him.

units.la: XVI. Hanc probant, 1. ipsae reliquiae Imaginis Dei in homine ; atque adeo Synderesis, & naturalia Principia cipia honesti ac decori: per quæ aperte innotescit Ens primum ac perfectissimum, Divina majesta, Lex sancta, Justitia tremenda. Gen. v, 1, 3. „Creavit Deus „hominem; ad similitudinem Dei fecit illum. – Adam genuit ad similitudinem suam, ad imaginem suam (filium.) ix, 6. Sanxit Deus homicidium morte multandum; „quia ad imaginem Dei fecit hominem, Jac. iii, 9. „Excramur homines ad similitudinem Dei factos.
units.tr: XVI. These things prove this: 1. the very remnants of the image of God in man; and thus synderesis and the natural principles of honour and decency, through which the first and most perfect being, the divine majesty, the holy law and awful justice are plainly made known. Gen. 5:1, 3: "God created man; he made him in the likeness of God. – Adam begot (a son) in his own likeness, after his own image." Gen. 9:6: God decreed that murder be punished by death, "because he made man in the image of God." James 3:9: "We curse men, who have been made in the likeness of God."

units.la: 2. Loca alia satis diserta: Job. i, 9. Vide th. ii. Rom. i, 19. „Id quod de Deo cognoscipotest, manifestum est in- „tra ipsos: Deus enim eis manifestum fecit. 32. „Dei jure „agnito; eos qui talia faciunt dignos esse morte. ii, 14, 15. „Cum Gentes, quæ Legem non habent, na- „turâ quæ Legis sunt faciunt; isti Legem non habentes, „sibi ipsis sunt Lex: Ut qui ostendant opus Legis scri„ptum in cordibus suis; una testimonium reddente ipsorum “conscientiâ; & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, „aut etiam excusantibus.
units.tr: 2. Other passages are quite plain: Job 1:9. See thesis 2. Rom. 1:19: "What may be known of God is manifest in them, for God has shown it to them." 1:32: "Knowing the righteous judgment of God," that those who do such things are worthy of death. 2:14, 15: "When the Gentiles, who have not the Law, by nature do the things of the Law, these, not having the Law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another."

units.la: 3. Quòd Deus sit, exterminis constat: quia Prædicatum est de essentia Subjecti; & quidem itâ necessario, ut nulli præter Ipsum conveniat, aut convenire posset nisi ab ipso communicatum. Nemo igitur mentis compos, & ad veritatem animum advertens, serio & constanter existentiam Dei negare, aut ignorare, potest.
units.tr: 3. That God exists is clear from the terms themselves: existence is predicated of the essence of the subject, and so necessarily that it belongs to no one except Himself, or could belong to anyone except as communicated by Him. Therefore no one in his right mind who attends to the truth can seriously and steadily deny or be ignorant of the existence of God.

units.la: 4. Accedit Experientia, & Consensus omnium Gentium.
units.tr: 4. To this are added experience and the consensus of all nations.

units.la: XVII. Acquisita obtinent, tum Argumentatione propriâ, tum Institutione alienâ.
units.tr: XVII. Acquired knowledge is obtained both by one's own reasoning and by instruction from others.

units.la: Argumentatio ista institui potest, 1. ex Scintillis modo indicatis, & opere illo Conscientiæ; Auctorem inde colligendo.
units.tr: This reasoning can be set up: (1) from the sparks just indicated and from that work of conscience, gathering from them the Author.

units.la: 2. Ex naturâ Hominis, verè μικροκόσμος: ubi tum Animæ rationalis essentia, facultates, operationes, consideranda, tum admiranda Corporis fabrica. Zach. XII, 1. „JEHOVAH formans spiritum Hominis {in medio eius}. Psal. cxxxix, 14, 15, 16. „Terribilibus (modis) mirificatus sum, mirabilibus operibus tuis. Et anima mea cognoscit valde. Non fuit occultatum corpus meum à Te, quando factus fui in occulto: (quando) variis membris decoratus fui in inferioribus terræ; „Imperfectum meum viderunt oculi tui. Act. XVII, 25, 28. „Cùm ipse dat omnibus vitam & halitum, & omnia. „Fecitque ex uno sanguine totam gentem hominum. -Non „longè abest ab unoquoque nostrûm. In ipso enim vivimus „& movemur, & sumus, &c.
units.tr: (2) From the nature of man, truly a microcosm [μικροκόσμος]: here one must consider both the essence, faculties and operations of the rational soul and the wonderful structure of the body. Zech. 12:1: "JEHOVAH, who forms the spirit of man {in the midst of him}." Ps. 139:14–16: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, and my soul knows it very well. My frame was not hidden from you when I was made in secret, and intricately wrought in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance." Acts 17:25, 28: "Since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. And he made from one blood every nation of men. He is not far from each one of us. For in him we live and move and have our being," etc.

units.la: 3. Ex reliquis Creaturis, ubi spectanda communiter opera Creationis, & Providentiæ Divinæ, speciatim vero Miracula naturæ, nec non Miracula proprie dicta, variaque Judicia, &c. ascendendo ab Effectis ad Causam efficientem primam supremam, à Motû ad Motorem primum immobilem. Psal. xix. 2, 3, 4. „Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum Ejus annunciat Firmamentum. Dies diei eloquitur sermonem, & „nox nocti indicat scientiam. Non (est) sermo, nec (sunt) „verba, ubi non audiatur vox eorum. Ies. xl, 26. Levate „in excelsum oculos vestros; & videte, quis creaverit ista: Rom. 1, 20. „Ipsius enim invisibilia, jàm indè à creatione mundi, ex iis quæ fecit animadversa, pervidentur: „æterna (videlicet) ejus tùm potentia, tùm Divinitas. Adde Ioh. XII, 7, -10. Act. xiv. 17.
units.tr: (3) From the other creatures, where we consider in general the works of creation and divine providence, and in particular the miracles of nature, as well as miracles properly so called, and the various judgments of God, etc., ascending from effects to the first and supreme efficient cause, and from motion to the first immovable mover. Ps. 19:2–4: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows his handiwork. Day to day pours forth speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard." Isa. 40:26: "Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these things." Rom. 1:20: "For his invisible attributes, namely his eternal power and divinity, have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through what he has made." Add John 12:7–10; Acts 14:17.

units.la: 4. Ex is iusmodi Argumentis ac testimoniis illustribus: quæ in Scriptis ipsorum Gentilium satis obvia siunt.
units.tr: 4. From arguments and illustrious testimonies of this kind, which are quite readily found in the writings of the Gentiles themselves.

units.la: XVIII. Institutio hic ea intelligitur, quâ sagacio- res ac provectiores Naturæ rufpatores, quæ rectè ra- tiocinando de Deo cognoverunt, alios etiàm docent.
units.tr: XVIII. Here "instruction" is understood as that by which the keener and more advanced investigators of nature, who have rightly reasoned and come to know God, also teach others.

units.la: XIX. Obj. 1. Deum esse Credimus: Hebr. xi, 6. Non ergò per Naturam cognoscimus: quia Fides supra Naturam est. Resp. Prima illa veritas per Naturam cognoscitur imperfectiore modo: Fide tenetur persectiore ac salutari modo: prout se Deus ipse Verbo suo revelavit familiariter, & remunerator est secundùm Fœdus gratiæ. Talis autem cognitio necessaria est, ut quis accedat ad Deum, ipsíque placeat.
units.tr: XIX. Objection 1: We believe that God exists. Heb. 11:6. Therefore we do not know him through nature, because faith is above nature. Answer: That first truth is known through nature in a more imperfect manner, but is held by faith in a more perfect and saving manner, insofar as God has revealed himself familiarly through his Word, and is the rewarder according to the covenant of grace. Moreover, such knowledge is necessary so that a man may draw near to God and please him.

units.la: Obj. 2. Quod homini naturale est, omni inest, & semper: atqui Deum negant nonnulli: Psal. x, 4. xiv, 1. Eph. 11, 12. Et gentes repertæ in America, quæ nullum Numen agnoscerent. Resp. 1. Athei nimis multi sunt vitâ & conatû: nulli tranquillâ & constanti animi sententiâ. 2. Unum verum Deum ignorant plures Gentes; non tamen existunt sine omni Numinis conscientiâ.
units.tr: Objection 2: What is natural to man is present in every man and always. But some deny God: Ps. 10:4; 14:1; Eph. 2:12. And peoples have been found in America who acknowledged no deity. Answer: 1. Atheists are many in their life and striving, but none holds the opinion with a calm and steady mind. 2. Many nations are ignorant of the one true God, yet they do not exist without some consciousness of a divinity.

units.la: XX. Theologia naturalis objectivè, in se, bona est: scintilla bona in tenebris adhùc splendens, omnesque & singulos homines illuminans; donatio bona à Patre luminum descendens. Vide Joh. 1, 5, 9. cum Jac. 1, 17. Sed subjectivè, in homine irregenito, vitiata est & impura. Tit. 1, 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum; sed polluta est eorum & mens & conscientia. Adde Joh. 111, 6. Rom. viii, 7. Attamen in Regenitis per Gratiam iterum corrigitur & sanctificatur. Tit. 1, 15. Omnia quidem munda mundis. 1 Thess. v, 23. Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos, &c.
units.tr: XX. Natural theology is good objectively, in itself: a good spark still shining in darkness, illuminating all and each of men, a good gift descending from the Father of lights. See John 1:5, 9 with James 1:17. But subjectively, in the unregenerate man, it is corrupted and impure. Titus 1:15: "To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and conscience are defiled." Add John 3:6; Rom. 8:7. Yet in the regenerate it is corrected and sanctified again through grace. Titus 1:15: "To the pure all things are pure." 1 Thess. 5:23: "May the God of peace sanctify you wholly," etc.

units.la: XXI. Consequenter eadem Theologia naturalis, aut Philosophia, per se, & in subjecto sanctificato, non adversatur Theologiæ supernaturali. Nam 1. Veritas veritati non potest esse contraria; prout idem non potest simul esse, & non esse.
units.tr: XXI. Consequently the same natural theology, or philosophy, taken in itself and in a sanctified subject, does not oppose supernatural theology. For: 1. Truth cannot be contrary to truth, just as the same thing cannot at once be and not be.

units.la: 2. Utriusque idea est in mente Divinâ: cum verò hæc contrarietatem non admittat; etiàm in utroque ideato, contrarietas admitti non debet.
units.tr: 2. The idea of each is in the divine mind; since this mind admits no contrariety, there ought not to be any contrariety in either of the things conceived.

units.la: 3. Ipse Christus, Prophetæ, & Apostoli rectâ ratione etiàm usi sunt; atque indè argumenta varia depromserunt. Præter ea, quæ th. 17. allegata sunt, vide inter alia Matth. xvi, 2, 3. Luc. xxiv, 39, 40. 1 Cor. v, 1. xi, 14, 15.
units.tr: 3. Christ himself, the prophets and the apostles also used right reason, and drew various arguments from it. Besides those cited in thesis 17, see among others Matt. 16:2, 3; Luke 24:39, 40; 1 Cor. 5:1; 11:14, 15.

units.la: 4. Experientia comprobat, illam huic utilissimam operam stitutionis instrumentalis. 30. Objectum ejus, tum primarium, tum subordinatum. 31. Quomodo Deus agnoscendus. Elementa doctrinæ Christianæ. Articuli, tum Catholici, tum Theologici. 32. Quomodo Deus colendus. 33. Quibus partibus Religionem complectantur Sociniani; quibus Remonstrantes. Theologiam nostram non esse merè speculativam. 34. Objectum ejus secundarium, sive directionis. 35. Subjectum quo; & quod. 36. Finis summus. Subordinatus. Eventus per accidens. 37. Beatitudinis nostræ in hac vita caput. 38. Quæ inde scaturiant. 39. Theologia vere Θεοζοία, καὶ Θεωρία. 40. Beatitudo consummata post hanc vitam. 41. Media Theologiæ feliciter consequendæ. 42. Repugnantia. 43. Distributio. 44. Praxis. 45.
units.tr: 4. Experience confirms that this natural theology is most useful for this work of instrumental instruction. 30. Its object, both primary and subordinate. 31. How God is to be acknowledged. The elements of Christian doctrine. The articles, both Catholic and theological. 32. How God is to be worshipped. 33. By what parts the Socinians embrace religion, and the Remonstrants likewise; that our theology is not merely speculative. 34. Its secondary object, that is, of direction. 35. The subject by which and the subject in which. 36. The highest end. Subordinate. The incidental outcome. 37. The head of our blessedness in this life. 38. What springs from this. 39. Theology truly as wisdom of God and contemplation [Θεοζοία, καὶ Θεωρία]. 40. The perfected blessedness after this life. 41. The means of successfully attaining theology. 42. Opposing views. 43. Distribution. 44. Practice. 45.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Theologia Grammaticè deducitur à voce paronyma Theologus.
units.tr: Theology is derived grammatically from the paronym Theologus.

units.la: Ista, aliaque vocabula similia, Gentilibus olim usurpata, Doctores Christiani jure in usum suum traduxerunt; rei significatæ veri ac justi, Deo dante, possessores. Huc pertinet Inscriptio; Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννου καὶ Θεολόγου: quoniam ipse Apostolus de Deo accuratissimè disseruit, ὡς Θεότητος καὶ Λόγου, contra Ebionem, Cerinthum, eorumque sequaces singulari zelo asseruit.
units.tr: These words and others like them were once used by the Gentiles, and Christian teachers have rightly taken them into their own use, since God has given them the possession of the true and just thing they signify. To this belongs the title, The Revelation of John the Theologian [Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννου καὶ Θεολόγου], since the Apostle himself discoursed most accurately about God, as of the Godhead and the Word [ὡς Θεότητος καὶ Λόγου], and with singular zeal asserted this against Ebion, Cerinthus and their followers.

units.la: Simplicia, Θεὸς, & Λόγος, vel τὸ Λόγιον, etiam conjunctim in SS. Literis occurrunt sæpius: Joh. 1, 1. Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος. Apoc. XIX. 13. ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. et διαφέρει καὶ ὑπαρχικῶς, de ipso Filio Dei. Sed &c
units.tr: The simple terms Θεὸς and Λόγος, or τὸ Λόγιον, also occur often together in Holy Scripture: John 1:1, "The Word was God" [Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος]; Rev. 19:13, "the Word of God" [ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ]; and they are distinguished [διαφέρει καὶ ὑπαρχικῶς], said of the Son of God himself. But &c.

units.la: CAP. I. De Theologiâ.
units.tr: CAP. I. On Theology.

units.la: & 1 Thess.11,13. Hebr. 1V,12. ὁ Λόγος ℥ Θε�of. Rom. III,2. Hebr.V,12. 1 Petr. IV,11. τὰ Λόγια ℥ Θεοῦ. προφορικῶς, de Verbo, aut Sermonibus Dei ad homines.
units.tr: and 1 Thess. 2:13; Heb. 4:12: the word of God [ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ]. Rom. 3:2; Heb. 5:12; 1 Pet. 4:11: the oracles of God [τὰ Λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ]. Spoken, that is, concerning the Word, or the sermons of God to men.

units.la: II. Ut cognoscatur quid rei sit, Theologia in universum describitur, Sapientia de Deo.
units.tr: II. That it may be known what it is, theology is described in general terms as wisdom concerning God.

units.la: Generis instar dicitur Sapientia: hæc enim habitum intellectualem augustissimum notat; eumque non modò theoreticum, sed etiàm practicum. Itâ quæ nunc Philosophia appellatur, & ex parte practica est, olim Σοφία, h. e. Sapientia, vocatur. Et præit S. Pagina, Deut.IV,6. Custodite ergò, & facite; quia ea est sapientia vestra, &c. Col.III,16. Sermo Christi in habitet in vobis copiosè, cum omni sapientiâ. Vide etiàm Psal. XIX,8. Luc.XXI. 15. 2 Tim.III,15. Jac. III,13,17.
units.tr: Wisdom is spoken of as the genus, since it denotes a most excellent intellectual habit, and one that is not only theoretical but also practical. Thus what is now called philosophy, and which is partly practical, was formerly called Σοφία, that is, wisdom. Holy Scripture goes before us in this: Deut. 4:6, "Keep therefore and do them, for this is your wisdom, etc."; Col. 3:16, "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom." See also Ps. 19:8; Luke 21:15; 2 Tim. 3:15; James 3:13, 17.

units.la: Differentiæ locum obtinet ipsum objectum: Deus: sic tamen, ut omnia, quæ ad Deum spectant, quatenus talia sunt, comprehendantur. Joh. XVII,3. Hæc est autem vita æterna, ut Te cognoscant, illum solum verum Deum; &, quem misisti, Jesum Christum. Rom. XI,33–36. O profundas divitias, tum sapientiæ, tùm cognitionis, Dei! Quàm imperscrutabilia sunt ejus judicia: & ejus viæ impervestigabiles! Quis enim cognovit mentem Domini? – Nam ex Eo, & per Eum, & in Ipsum (sunt) omnia. Ipsi (sit) gloria in sæcula! Amen.
units.tr: The object itself, God, holds the place of the difference; yet in such a way that all things which relate to God, insofar as they are such, are included. John 17:3: "And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent." Rom. 11:33–36: "O the depth of the riches, both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? ... For of Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things. To Him be glory for ever. Amen."

units.la: III. Ratione subjectorum, vel quasi, dicitur, tùm Theologia ipsius Dei; tùm Creaturarum intellectualium. Matth.XI,27. Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater: neque Patrem quisquam novit, nisi Filius; & cuicunque voluerit Filius Eum retegere. 1 Cor. II,10. 11. Nobis autem Deus (ea) revelavit per Spiritum suum. Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur; etiàm profunditates Dei. – Etiàm ea, quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei. Pfal. XCIV, 9, 10. „An, qui plantavit aurem, non au„diet? An, qui finxit oculum, non videbit? - An, qui „docet hominem scientiam (non cognoscet?)
units.tr: III. By reason of its subjects, or as it were, theology is said to be either the theology of God Himself or that of intellectual creatures. Matt. 11:27: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." 1 Cor. 2:10–11: "But God has revealed these things to us through His Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. ... Even the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God." Ps. 94:9–10: "He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? He who formed the eye, shall He not see? He who teaches man knowledge, shall He not know?"

units.la: I V. Theologia ipsius Dei est, quâ Deus seipsum cognoscit convenienter Naturæ suæ.
units.tr: IV. The theology of God Himself is that by which God knows Himself in a manner agreeing with His nature.

units.la: Hoc est, 1. Independenter; per Essentiam suam: ut hæc sit αὐτοδακτ@.
units.tr: That is, (1) independently, through His own essence, so that this knowledge is self-taught [αὐτοδίδακτος].

units.la: 2. Simplicissime; actû purissimo: ut sit ipse idem ὁ Θεολόγ@, τὸ Θεολογούμενον, καὶ ἡ Θεολογία.
units.tr: (2) most simply, in the purest act, so that He Himself is at once the theologian [ὁ Θεολόγος], the thing theologized [τὸ Θεολογούμενον], and the theology [ἡ Θεολογία].

units.la: 3. Infinitè, & adæquatè, ipse igitur seipsum cognoscit, ut absolutè cognosci potest.
units.tr: (3) infinitely and adequately; therefore He knows Himself as fully as He can be fully known.

units.la: 1 Tim. 1, 17. „Soli sapienti Deo honor (sit). &c. Pfal. CXLVII, 5. „Intelligentiæ Ejus non est numerus. Confer allegata th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 1:17: "To the only wise God be honour, etc." Ps. 147:5: "There is no number to His understanding." Compare the passages cited under thesis 3.

units.la: V. Deus autem cognoscit primò Essentiam suam, cum Attributis, & Personis: atque in Attributis nominatim Sufficientiam & Potentiam; quæ est principium Possibilitatis omnium Rerum Possibilium, cum Affectionibus Possibilibus. Hactenus est Theologia Dei naturalis & necessaria.
units.tr: V. God knows first His own essence, with its attributes and persons; and among the attributes, especially His sufficiency and power, which is the principle of the possibility of all possible things, with their possible affections. So far this is the natural and necessary theology of God.

units.la: Deinde sibi conscius est Decreti sui; atque omnium eorum, quæ ipse Decreto suo constituit, tùm de aliis, tùm speciatim de Creaturis intellectualibus: imò etiam, quibus modis ac gradibus communicare iis velit notitiam Sui. Sapientissime enim operatur τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς; Hebr. XI, 10. Unde Actor. XV, 18. „Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua. Hæc dicitur Theologia Dei libera; ratione objectorum.
units.tr: Next, He is conscious of His decree and of all those things which He has established by His decree, both of other things and especially of intellectual creatures; indeed also of the means and degrees by which He wishes to communicate to them the knowledge of Himself. For God works most wisely, as craftsman and creator [τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεός]; Heb. 11:10. Hence Acts 15:18: "All His works are known to God from eternity." This is called the free theology of God, with respect to its objects.

units.la: Ex dictis patet, quòd speciatim in Deo sit Theologia ἀρχέτυπος; prima & verissima idea omnis Theologiæ in Creaturis intellectualibus.
units.tr: From what has been said it is plain that in God, specifically, there is archetypal theology: the first and most true idea of all theology in intellectual creatures.

units.la: VI. Omnis Theologia Creaturarum intellectualium est ἐκτυπος; ad ideam istam, juxta Dei decretum, in tempore expressa, & Creaturis illis imprimendo com- municata.
units.tr: VI. All theology of intellectual creatures is ectypal [ἔκτυπος]: it is expressed in time according to this idea, in accordance with God's decree, and is communicated by being impressed upon those creatures.

units.la: Col. III, 10. „Renovatur in agnitionem con-gra„gruentem imagini Ejus, qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: Col. 3:10: "Renewed in knowledge after the image of Him who created him."

units.la: Ejus igitur universæ causa constitutionis principalis unica, & acquisitionis prima ac suprema, est ipse Deus: aliàs Theologia ψευδώνυμος, & superstitio emergit. Deut. iv. 2. „Non addetis ad verbum, quod Ego praecipio vobis; neque diminuetis (quicquam) ex eo, &c. „Isa. viii, 20. „Ad Legem, & ad Testimonium. Si non „dixerint juxta verbum hoc, non erit eis aurora. Vide etiam Deut. xii, 32. Matth. xv, 9. Galat. i, 8, 9. Col. ii, 4, 8, 22. 23. Apoc. xxii, 18, 19. Item Jac. i, 5. „Quod si cui vestrum deest sapientia, petito à Deo, qui „dat (eam) omnibus benignè, &c. 17. „Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum munus, est supernè descendens à Patre luminum, &c.
units.tr: Therefore God alone is the principal and sole cause of its constitution, and the first and highest source of its acquisition; otherwise a falsely named theology [ψευδώνυμος] and superstition would arise. Deut. 4:2: "You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take away from it, etc." Isa. 8:20: "To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, there is no dawn for them." See also Deut. 12:32; Matt. 15:9; Gal. 1:8–9; Col. 2:4, 8, 22–23; Rev. 22:18–19. Likewise James 1:5: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously, etc." v. 17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, etc."

units.la: VII. Theologia ectypa trifariàm dispescitur: vel enim Unionis est, vel Visionis, vel Revelationis.
units.tr: VII. Ectypal theology is divided in three ways: for it is either of union, or of vision, or of revelation.

units.la: VIII. Theologia Unionis appellatur, quae in Domino nostro Jesù Christo, secundùm humanam ipsius naturam, ex Unione hypostaticâ fluit; atque sic ipsi per Spiritum S. singulari modo communicata est. Psal. XLV, 8. „Unxit Te, Deus, Deus Tuus oleo gaudii „præ Consortibus Tuis. Ioh. iii, 34. -- „Deus non dat „Ipsi Spiritum ad mensuram. Adde Isa. xi, 1, 2. LXI, 1. Ioh. vii. 29. Col. ii, 3, 9.
units.tr: VIII. The theology of union is that which in our Lord Jesus Christ flows, according to His human nature, from the hypostatic union, and so has been communicated to Him in a singular manner through the Holy Spirit. Ps. 45:8: "God, Your God, has anointed You with the oil of gladness above Your fellows." John 3:34: "God does not give the Spirit to Him by measure." Add Isa. 11:1–2; 61:1; John 7:29; Col. 2:3, 9.

units.la: IX. Theologia Visionis est Beatorum cœlitum, Angelorum & Hominum. De Angelis diserte, Matth. xviii, 10. „Angeli eorum (parvulorum) in cœlis per „omne tempus vident faciem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Sed & Homines plenè glorificati in beatâ resurrectione, erunt ἰσάγγελοι. Luc. xx, 36. Interim verò Animæ fidelium separatæ pro sua parte ejusdem beatitudinis fiunt participes. 2 Cor. v, 7, 8. „Per fidem enim „ambulamus: non per aspectum. Confidente autem „animo sumus; & gratius est nobis abesse potiùs ex „corpore, & adesse apud Dominum. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. „Videmus enim nunc per speculum, & per ænigma; “tunc autem coràm (cernemus); &c. Vide etiàm Hebr. XII, 23. Phil. 1, 23. cum Matth. v, 8. 1 Joh. III, 2.
units.tr: IX. The theology of vision belongs to the blessed in heaven, to angels and to men. Of the angels it is expressly said, Matt. 18:10: "Their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father who is in heaven." But also men fully glorified in the blessed resurrection will be equal to the angels. Luke 20:36. Meanwhile the souls of the faithful, when separated from the body, become partakers of the same blessedness in their own measure. 2 Cor. 5:7–8: "For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, and we would rather be absent from the body and present with the Lord." 1 Cor. 13:12: "For now we see through a mirror, dimly, but then face to face; etc." See also Heb. 12:23; Phil. 1:23, together with Matt. 5:8 and 1 John 3:2.

units.la: X. Ab hâc longissimè distat impura illa & terribilis cognitio Dei ac rerum Divinarum in Diabolis & Hominibus damnatis. Jac. II, 19. „Dæmonia quoque credunt (Deum unum esse); & horrescunt. Adde Matth. VIII, 29. Act. XVI, 17. Marc. IX, 44. cum Apoc. XVI, 10, 11.
units.tr: X. Far removed from this is that impure and terrifying knowledge of God and of divine things which the devils and the damned men have. James 2:19: "The demons also believe that God is one, and tremble." Add Matt. 8:29; Acts 16:17; Mark 9:44, together with Rev. 16:10–11.

units.la: XI. Theologia Revelationis speciatim dicitur, quæ Hominibus in stadio hujus vitæ communicatur. Joh. I, 9. Illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. Estque Naturalis; vel Supernaturalis.
units.tr: XI. The theology of revelation is specifically that which is communicated to men in the state of this life. John 1:9: "He enlightens every man coming into the world." It is either natural or supernatural.

units.la: XII. Naturalis, Naturam Hominis rationalem comitatur in hâc vitâ: potestque spectari qualis extitit ante lapsum; ac porrò qualis existit post lapsum.
units.tr: XII. Natural theology accompanies the rational nature of man in this life; and it can be considered as it was before the fall, and further as it is after the fall.

units.la: XIII. Ante lapsum Homini connaturalis fuit persecta Dei cognitio, mentem illius sufficienter imbuens ad vitam cœlestem & gloriam æternam consequendam, juxta Fœdus Legale. Gen. 1, 26, 27. Faciamus Hominem ad imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram, &c. Col. III. 10. in agnitionem congruentem imagini ejus, qui ipsum condidit.
units.tr: XIII. Before the fall, a perfect knowledge of God was connatural to man, sufficiently imbuing his mind to attain heavenly life and eternal glory, according to the legal covenant. Gen. 1:26–27: "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, etc." Col. 3:10: "in knowledge agreeing with the image of Him who created him."

units.la: XIV. Per lapsum amissa est integritas & puritas: remansit tamen Theologia naturalis ex parte. Hæc occurrit tùm congenita, sive innata; tùm acquisita, sive adventitia. Utraque excolenda adversùs Atheorum portenta & defendenda contra Socinianorum errores.
units.tr: XIV. Through the fall integrity and purity were lost; yet natural theology remained in part. This occurs both innate, or inborn, and acquired, or adventitious. Both are to be cultivated against the monstrosities of atheists and to be defended against the errors of the Socinians.

units.la: XV. Congenita vocatur, quatenùs adhùc Scintillæ quædam Lucis illius primævæ, Imaginis Dei, menti humanæ increantur & connascuntur; Archetypum interim & Auctorem suum sic fatis demonstrantes, quidque Ipsi debeatur, & quid nobis ac proximo nostro propter Ipsum, indicantes.
units.tr: XV. It is called innate insofar as certain sparks of that primeval light, the image of God, are still innate and connate in the human mind; thus showing their archetype and author, and indicating what is owed to Him, and what to us and to our neighbour on His account.

units.la: XVI. Hanc probant, 1. ipsæ reliquiæ Imaginis Dei in homine; atque adeo Synteresis, & naturalia Principia cipia cipia honesti ac decori: per quæ apertè innotescit Ens primum ac perfectissimum, Divina majesta, Lex sanĉta, Justitia tremenda. Gen. v, 1, 3. „Creavit Deus „hominem; ad similitudinem Dei fecit illum. – Adam genuit ad similitudinem suam, ad imaginem suam (filium.) ix, 6. Sanxit Deus homicidium morte multandum; „quia ad imaginem Dei fecit hominem, Jae. iii, 9. „Execramur homines ad similitudinem Dei factos.
units.tr: XVI. They prove this, first, by the very remnants of the image of God in man, and thus by synteresis and the natural principles of what is right and fitting. Through these there is plainly made known the first and most perfect Being, the divine majesty, the holy Law, and the dread Justice. Gen. 5:1, 3: "God created man; he made him in the likeness of God." "Adam begat [a son] in his own likeness, after his image." Gen. 9:6: God decreed that murder be punished by death, "because God made man in his own image." James 3:9: "We curse men, who are made after the similitude of God."

units.la: 2. Loca alia satis diserta: Joh. i, 9. Vide th. ii. Rom. i, 19. „Id quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in„tra ipsos: Deus enim eis manifestum fecit. 32. „Dei jure „agnito; eos qui talia faciunt dignos esse morte. ii, 14, 15. „Cum Gentes, quæ Legem non habent, na„turâ quæ Legis sunt faciunt; isti Legem non habentes, „sibi ipsis sunt Lex: Ut qui ostendant opus Legis scri„ptum in cordibus suis; una testimonium reddente ipsorum „conscientiâ; & cogitationibus sese mutuo accusantibus, „aut etiàm excusantibus.
units.tr: 2. Other passages are clear enough: John 1:9, see thesis 2. Rom. 1:19: "What may be known of God is manifest in them, for God has shown it to them." 1:32: "Knowing the righteous judgment of God, that those who do such things are worthy of death." 2:14, 15: "When the Gentiles, who have not the Law, do by nature the things contained in the Law, these, not having the Law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts accusing or even excusing one another."

units.la: 3. Quod Deus sit, exterminis constat: quia Prædicatum est de essentia Subjecti; & quidem itâ necessario, ut nulli præter Ipsum conveniat, aut convenire possit nisi ab ipso communicatum. Nemo igitur mentis compos, & ad veritatem animum advertens, serio & constanter existentiam Dei negare, aut ignorare, potest.
units.tr: 3. That God exists is evident from the terms themselves: existence is predicated of the essence of the subject, and indeed so necessarily that it belongs to no one but Him, or could belong to anyone except as communicated by Him. Therefore no one in his right mind, who attends to the truth, can seriously and consistently deny or be ignorant of the existence of God.

units.la: 4. Accedit Experientia, & Consensus omnium Gentium.
units.tr: 4. Add experience and the consensus of all nations.

units.la: XVII. Acquisita obtinent, tùm Argumentatione propriâ, tùm Institutione alienâ.
units.tr: XVII. Acquired knowledge is obtained both by one's own reasoning and by instruction from others.

units.la: Argumentatio ista institui potest, 1. ex Scintillis modo indicatis, & opere illo Conscientiæ; Auctorem indè colligendo.
units.tr: This argumentation can be developed, 1. from the sparks just indicated and that work of conscience, inferring from them the Author.

units.la: 2. Ex naturâ Hominis, verè μικροκόσμος: ubi tùm Animæ rationalis essentia, facultates, operationes, considerandæ, tum admiranda Corporis fabrica.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of man, truly a microcosm [μικροκόσμος]: here one must consider the essence, faculties and operations of the rational soul, and the wonderful structure of the body.

units.la: Zach. XII, 1. „JEHOVAH formans spiritum Hominis in medio eius. Psal. cxxxix, 14, 15, 16. „ Terribilibus (modis) mirificatus sum, mirabilibus operibus tuis. Et „ anima mea cognoscit valde. Non fuit occultatum corpus meum à Te, quando factus fui in occulto: (quando) variis membris decoratus fui in inferioribus terræ; „ Imperfectum meum viderunt oculi tui. Act. XVII, 25, 28. „ Cum ipse det omnibus vitam & halitum, & omnia. „ Fecitque ex uno sanguine totam gentem hominum. - Non „ longè abest ab unoquoque nostrum. In ipso enim vivimus „ & movemur, & jumus, &c.
units.tr: Zech. 12:1: "The LORD, who forms the spirit of man within him." Ps. 139:14, 15, 16: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made; marvellous are your works, and my soul knows it very well. My body was not hidden from you when I was made in secret, when I was woven with various members in the depths of the earth; your eyes saw my unformed substance." Acts 17:25, 28: "Since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. And he made from one blood every nation of men. … He is not far from each one of us, for in him we live and move and have our being."

units.la: 3. Ex reliquis Creaturis, ubi spectanda communiter opera Creationis, & Providentiæ Divinæ, specialiter vero Miracula naturæ, nec non Miracula proprie dicti, variaque Judicia, &c. ascendendo ab Effectis ad Causam efficientem primam supremam, à Motu ad Motorem primum immobilem. Psal. xix. 2, 3, 4. „ Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum Ejus annunciat Firmamentum. Dies diei eloquitur sermonem, & nox nocti indicat scientiam. Non (est) sermo, nec (sunt) verba, ubi non audiatur vox eorum. Isf. xl, 26. Levate in excelsum oculos vestros; & videte, quis creaverit ista: Rom. 1, 20. „ Ipsius enim invisibilia, jam inde à creatione mundi, ex iis quæ fecit animadversa, pervidentur: æterna (videlicet) ejus tum potentia, tum Divinitas, Adde Job XII, 7, - 10. Act. xiv. 17.
units.tr: 3. From the other creatures, where we should look at the works of creation and divine providence in general, and especially at the miracles of nature, as well as at what are properly called miracles, and the various judgments, and so on, ascending from effects to the first and supreme efficient cause, and from motion to the first immovable Mover. Ps. 19:2, 3, 4: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows his handiwork. Day to day pours forth speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard." Isa. 40:26: "Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these things." Rom. 1:20: "For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen through the things that have been made, namely his eternal power and divinity." Add Job 12:7–10; Acts 14:17.

units.la: 4. Ex ii iusmodi Argumentis ac testimoniis illustribus: quæ in Scriptis ipsorum Gentilium satis obvia sunt.
units.tr: 4. From arguments and testimonies of this kind, which are plentiful enough in the writings of the Gentiles themselves.

units.la: XVIII. Institutio hic ea intelligitur, quà fagaciores ac provectiores Naturæ rufpatores, quæ rectè ratiocinando de Deo cognoverunt, alios etiam docent.
units.tr: XVIII. By instruction here is meant that by which the keener and more advanced investigators of nature, who have rightly come to know God by reasoning, also teach others.

units.la: XIX. Obj. 1. Deum esse Credimus: Hebr. xi, 6. Non ergo per Naturam cognoscimus: quia Fides supra Naturam est. Resp. Prima illa veritas per Naturam cognoscitur imperfectiore modo: Fide tenetur persectiore ac salutari modo: prout se Deus ipse Verbo suo revelavit familiariter, & remunerator est secundùm Fœdus gratiæ. Talis autem cognitio necessaria est, ut quis accedat ad Deum, ipsique placeat.
units.tr: XIX. Objection 1. We believe that God exists (Heb. 11:6). Therefore we do not know him through nature, since faith is above nature. Reply: That first truth is known through nature in a more imperfect manner, but is held by faith in a more perfect and saving manner, insofar as God himself has revealed himself familiarly by his Word, and is a rewarder according to the covenant of grace. Such knowledge, moreover, is necessary for anyone to draw near to God and please him.

units.la: Obj. 2. Quod homini naturale est, omni inest, & semper: atqui Deum negant nonnulli: Psal. x, 4. xiv, 1. Eph. ii, 12. Et gentes repertæ in America, quæ nullum Numen agnoscerent. Resp. 1. Athei nimis multi sunt vitâ & conatû: nulli tranquillâ & constanti animi sententiâ. 2. Unum verum Deum ignorant plures Gentes; non tamen exsistunt sine omni Numinis consci-entiâ.
units.tr: Objection 2. What is natural to man is in every man, and always; but some deny God (Ps. 10:4; 14:1; Eph. 2:12), and peoples have been found in America who acknowledged no deity. Reply 1. Atheists are very many in their life and effort, but none in a calm and steady conviction of mind. 2. Many nations are ignorant of the one true God, yet they do not exist without any awareness of a divinity.

units.la: XX. Theologia naturalis objectivè, in se, bona est: scintilla bona in tenebris adhùc splendens, omnesque & singulos homines illuminans; donatio bona à Patre luminum descendens. Vide Joh. 1, 5, 9. cum Jac. 1, 17. Sed subjectivè, in homine irregenito, vitiata est & impura. Tit. 1, 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum; sed polluta est eorum & mens & conscientia. Adde Joh. iii, 6. Rom. viii, 7. Attamen in Regenitis per Gratiam iterùm corrigitur & sanctificatur. Tit. 1, 15. Omnia quidem munda mundis. 1 Thess. v, 23. Deus pacis sanctificet vos totos, &c.
units.tr: XX. Natural theology, objectively, in itself, is good: a good spark still shining in the darkness, illuminating all and each of men, a good gift descending from the Father of lights. See John 1:5, 9 with James 1:17. But subjectively, in the unregenerate man, it is corrupted and impure: Titus 1:15: "To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled." Add John 3:6; Rom. 8:7. Yet in the regenerate it is corrected and sanctified again through grace. Titus 1:15: "To the pure all things are pure." 1 Thess. 5:23: "May the God of peace sanctify you wholly," etc.

units.la: XXI. Consequenter eadem Theologia naturalis, aut Philosophia, per se, & in subjecto sanctificato, non adversatur Theologiæ supernaturali. Nam 1. Veritas veritati non potest esse contraria; prout idem non potest simul esse, & non esse.
units.tr: XXI. Consequently this same natural theology, or philosophy, considered in itself and in a sanctified subject, does not oppose supernatural theology. For, 1. truth cannot be contrary to truth, just as the same thing cannot at once be and not be.

units.la: 2. Utriusque idea est in mente Divinâ: cum verò hæc contrarietatem non admittat; etiam in utroque ideato, contrarietas admitti non debet.
units.tr: 2. The idea of each is in the divine mind; since this does not admit contrariety, neither should contrariety be admitted in either of the things conceived.

units.la: 3. Ipse Christus, Prophetæ, & Apostoli rectâ ratione etiam usi sunt; atque indè argumenta varia depromserunt. Præter ea, quæ th. 17. allegata sunt, vide inter alia Matth. xvi, 2, 3. Luc. xxiv, 39, 40. 1 Cor. v, 1. xi, 14, 15.
units.tr: 3. Christ himself, the prophets and the apostles also used right reason, and drew various arguments from it. Besides those cited in thesis 17, see among others Matt. 16:2, 3; Luke 24:39, 40; 1 Cor. 5:1; 11:14, 15.

units.la: 4. Experientia comprobat, illam huic utilissimam operi operam præstare, ubi sobria est, & supernaturali revelationi concedit, ac rite obsequitur.
units.tr: 4. Experience confirms that it renders very useful service in this work when it is sober, and yields to supernatural revelation and duly obeys it.

units.la: Aliter autem se habet Philosophiæ ac Rationis naturalis abusus: unde Col. 11,8: „Videte, nequis sit, „qui vos deprædetur per Philosophiam & inanem deceptionem, &c. ubi vel omnino falsa producuntur, vel non servantur leges veræ oppositionis, secundum idem, &c.
units.tr: The abuse of philosophy and of natural reason, however, is otherwise: whence Col. 2:8: "See to it that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deceit," etc., where either things altogether false are put forward, or the true laws of opposition, "in the same respect," are not observed.

units.la: XXII. Pertingit Theologia naturalis 1. ad cognoscendam Dei existentiam, & attributa essentialia.
units.tr: XXII. Natural theology extends 1. to knowing the existence of God and his essential attributes.

units.la: 2. Ad Decretum de rebus futuris, in genere: & opera Creationis ac Providentiæ, tùm in Homine, tùm in aliis creaturis contemplationi nostræ obviis.
units.tr: 2. To the decree concerning future things in general, and to the works of creation and providence, both in man and in other creatures that meet our contemplation.

units.la: 3. Ad jus Divinum, quatenùs id hominibus naturale est. De quibus satis constat ex citatis th. 16, 17. & 21.
units.tr: 3. To divine law, insofar as it is natural to men. Concerning these things enough is established from the cited theses 16, 17 and 21.

units.la: 4. Ad Fœdus Legale. Rom. 111,9. „Ante crimi„nati sumus, & Iudæos & Græcos omnes esse sub peccato. 19. Scimus autem, quæcunque Lex dicit, iis qui in „Lege sunt dicere; ut omnes os obturetur, & obnoxius fi„at totus mundus condemnationi Dei. Ista sic naturaliter cognoscuntur, non quidem perfectè; attamen verè, & quantum sufficit ad ἀναγωλογήσιν eorum, quibus sublimior ac perfectior revelatio non obtingit: Rom. 1,20.
units.tr: 4. To the legal covenant. Rom. 3:9: "We have already charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin." 3:19: "We know that whatever the Law says, it says to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become liable to the condemnation of God." These things are known naturally in this way, not indeed perfectly, yet truly, and as far as is sufficient for the ascent [ἀναγωγήν] of those to whom a higher and more perfect revelation does not come: Rom. 1:20.

units.la: Sed non pertingit 1. ad personam & officia Christi Mediatoris, salutem per ipsum partam, ac Fœdus Evangelicum: quæ homini in statu primævæ integritatis non fuerunt revelata, nedùm ex tenuibus illius reliquiis post lapsum colligi possint.
units.tr: But it does not extend 1. to the person and offices of Christ the Mediator, the salvation obtained through him, and the Gospel covenant. These were not revealed to man in the state of original integrity, much less can they be gathered from the slight remnants of that state after the fall.

units.la: 2. Neque penetrat ad mysterium S. Trinitatis, cujus cognoscendæ aut demonstrandæ principia solida non reperiuntur in naturâ; quamvis ibi occurrant nonnulla, per quæ mysterium illud, postquàm supernaturali revelatione innotuit, utcunque illustrari ac defendi potest.
units.tr: 2. Nor does it reach the mystery of the Holy Trinity, whose principles for knowing or demonstrating it are not found in nature, although some things occur there through which that mystery, once it has become known by supernatural revelation, can in some measure be illustrated and defended.

units.la: XXIII. Hinc colligimus, contra Pelagianos, eo-
units.tr: XXIII. From this we conclude, against the Pelagians, and their followers and supporters,

units.la: runquè sequaces ac fautores, Theologiam naturalem nunc non sufficere ad æternam salutem consequendam: sive, non dari communem aliquam & naturalem Religionem, per quam omnes omnino homines servari possint.
units.tr: that natural theology is now not sufficient for attaining eternal salvation; that is, that there is no common and natural religion through which all men without exception can be saved.

units.la: Patet hoc 1. ex necessitate Fidei; sine quâ nemo potest placere Deo: Hebr. xi, 6, quæ est ex auditu Verbi supernaturaliter revelati: Rom. x, 17. & quidem una; ut Deus unus; Eph. iv, 6. non autem omnium: 2 Thess. iii. 2. sed electorum Dei: Tit. 1, 1.
units.tr: This is shown first from the necessity of faith, without which no one can please God (Heb. xi. 6). Faith comes from hearing the Word supernaturally revealed (Rom. x. 17), and it is one faith, as God is one (Eph. iv. 6); it is not the faith of all (2 Thess. iii. 2), but the faith of the elect of God (Tit. i. 1).

units.la: 2. Ex consideratione Christi Mediatoris, Redemptoris, ac Salvatoris; cujus cognitio ad salutem consequendam necessaria est: Joh. xiv. 6. "Ego sum via illa, & veritas illa, & vita illa: nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Act. iv, 12. "Nec est in alio quoquam salus: nec enim aliud nomen est sub cœlo quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos salvari. Vide etiam Joh. xvii, 1, 3. 1 Cor. iii, 11. 1 Tim. ii, 5. Gal. i. 6-9. Sed istam cognitionem Ratio naturalis per se non assequitur.
units.tr: Second, from consideration of Christ the Mediator, Redeemer and Saviour, whose knowledge is necessary for attaining salvation (John xiv. 6): "I am that way, and that truth, and that life; no one comes to the Father except through me."
