Hinc diserte Fides electorum Dei appellatur; Tit. 1, 1. & credidisse dicuntur, quotquot ad vitam æternam erant ordinati; Act. xiii, 48. atque item prædestinati ad conformitatem imaginis Christi, & sic porro vocati; Rom. viii, 29, 30.
units.tr: XVI. The subject which of saving faith is men elect and effectually called. Hence it is expressly called "the faith of God's elect" (Titus 1:1), and they are said to have believed, "as many as were ordained to eternal life" (Acts 13:48); likewise they are "predestined to be conformed to the image of Christ" and so, in turn, called (Rom. 8:29, 30).

units.la: Sed fides merè historica, temporaria, ut & miraculorum, reprobis quibusdam obtingunt: Ac talis ex consequenti agnoscenda est in omnibus, qui deficiunt ad æternam perniciem: 1 Joh. 11, 19. „E nobis egressi „sunt; sed non erant ex nobis: nam si fuissent ex nobis, „permansissent utique nobiscum: sed (egressi sunt ex nobis „ut patefieret, non omnes esse ex nobis.
units.tr: But merely historical, temporary faith, as also the faith of miracles, falls to certain reprobate; and such faith must consequently be recognised in all who fall away to eternal destruction: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have remained with us; but they went out that it might be made plain that not all are of us" (1 John 2:19).

units.la: XVII. Subjectum quo proprie & formaliter est Intellectus: ad hunc enim pertinet veritatem percipere, discernere, eique assentiri, etiam cum speciali applicatione. Intellectus tamen sine Voluntate non existit, neque operatur: atque adeo dum Intellectus in hoc negotio occupatur circa verum, quatenus tale est, quod idem interim etiam bonum est; Voluntas per Fidem excitata, in illud etiam fertur; quatenus bonum est, expetendo, diligendo, obedientiam imperando; & praestando, &c. qui tamen imperati actus Fidei sunt; non elicti.
units.tr: XVII. The subject by which is properly and formally the intellect, for it belongs to the intellect to perceive truth, to discern it, and to assent to it, even with special application. Yet the intellect neither exists nor operates without the will. So while the intellect is occupied in this business with the true, as such, which at the same time is also good, the will, stirred up by faith, is carried toward that good as well, in so far as it is good: by desiring, loving, commanding obedience, and performing, etc. Yet these are commanded acts of faith, not elicited ones.

units.la: Obj. 1. Corde creditur; Rom. x, 10. Cor autem voluntatem designat; non intellectum: ergo, &c. Resp. Cor metonymicè & synecdochicè notat facultates interiores; etiàm intellectum. 1 Reg. 111,9. Psal. xiv, 1. cum x,4.
units.tr: Objection 1. "With the heart one believes" (Rom. 10:10). But the heart designates the will, not the intellect; therefore, etc. Answer: "Heart" by metonymy and synecdoche denotes the inner faculties, including the intellect (1 Kings 3:9; Ps. 14:1 with 10:4).

units.la: Obj. 2. Fides est receptio boni sub ratione boni, & intima unio cum eodem: Ioh. 1,12. Quotquot exceperunt eum, qui credunt. Resp. 1. Imò est perceptio, vel apprehensio veri, sub ratione veri, propter auctoritatem Divinam; ad quam sequitur receptio boni, ut talis, in voluntate: quatenus istud verum, simul quoque bonum est. 2. Intima unio cum bono non est ipsa fides formaliter; sed ejus effectus. 3. Ioh. 1,12. dicuntur credentes, Christum excipere; sed per intellectus assensum testimonio Divino habitum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Faith is the reception of good under the aspect of good, and an intimate union with it (John 1:12, "As many as received him, who believe"). Answer 1. Indeed it is a perception or apprehension of truth under the aspect of truth, on account of divine authority, and to this there follows the reception of good, as such, in the will, insofar as that truth is at the same time also good. 2. Intimate union with good is not faith itself formally, but its effect. 3. In John 1:12 believers are said to receive Christ, but this is by the assent of the intellect, held on the testimony of God.

units.la: Obj. 3. Fides est actus electionis; & sic fertur in bonum, quod distâ ratione fit nostrum: Ioh. vi, 35. Qui venit ad me: qui credit in me. Ergo ad Voluntatem pertinet. Resp. 1. Non est formaliter actus electionis; sed assensus: licet hunc etiam sequatur electio voluntatis. 2. Credendo quod Christus sit nobis causa salutis æternæ, intellectu formaliter in ipsum feriimur, & circa ipsum occupamur, ut vere talem; quanquam porro etiam voluntate & affectibus in ipsum ferimur, ut bonum: verum isti sunt imperati actus fidei.
units.tr: Objection 3. Faith is an act of choice, and so is directed towards the good which, under a different aspect, becomes ours (John 6:35, "He who comes to me", "who believes in me"). Therefore it belongs to the will. Answer 1. It is not formally an act of choice but of assent, although the choice of the will also follows it. 2. By believing that Christ is the cause of eternal salvation for us, we are formally borne by the intellect towards him and occupied with him as truly such; although we are also further carried towards him by the will and the affections, as good. But these are the commanded acts of faith.

units.la: Obj. 4. Fides, quâ credimus non tantùm Deum, aut Deo, sed in Deum, est vera & propria fiducia; quæ significat electionem & apprehensionem sufficientis ac idonei medii, in quo fundatur persuasio & expectatio boni futuri. Psal. lxxviii,22. non crediderunt in Deum, neque confisi erant in salute ejus. Sic credere in Deum, est credendo adhærere Deo, ipsi inniti, in ipso acquiescere, tanquam in vitâ ac salute nostra omnisufficiente. Deut. xxx. 20. adhærendo ei: nam ipse est vita tua. Resp. 1. Fateor, quod credere in Deum aliquando saltem idem notet ac assentiri testimonio Divino speciali, de salutari communione cum ipso: attamen ista fides non est formaliter fiducia, sed est ejus causa: Eph. 1. 11, 12. 2. Fides quidem est apprehensio sufficientis & idonei medii, in quo fundatur certissima expectatio boni futuri: at tunc medium illud spectatur sub ratione veri, testimonio Divino nobis confirmati. Sed non est proprie electio. 3. Fiducia recte Fidei adjungitur, ut effectus suae causae: non vero ut ejus ratio formalis. 4. Adhaerere Deo per voluntatem, sic ipsi inniti, & in ipso acquiescere, tanquam in vita & salute nostra, sunt etiam fructus fidei, & actus imperati.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Faith, by which we believe not only God, or what God says, but in God, is true and proper trust. Trust signifies the choosing and grasping of a sufficient and suitable means, on which the persuasion and expectation of future good rests. Ps. 78:22 they did not believe in God, nor trust in his salvation. To believe in God is thus, by believing, to cleave to God, to lean on him and rest in him, as in our life and all-sufficient salvation. Deut. 30:20 by cleaving to him, for he is your life. Reply: 1. I grant that to believe in God at least sometimes means the same as to assent to a special divine testimony concerning saving communion with him. Yet this faith is not formally trust, but its cause: Eph. 1:11, 12. 2. Faith is indeed the apprehension of a sufficient and suitable means, on which most certain expectation of future good is founded. But then that means is regarded under the aspect of truth, confirmed to us by divine testimony. It is not properly choice. 3. Trust is rightly joined to faith as its effect to its cause, not as its formal reason. 4. To cleave to God by the will, to lean on him and rest in him as in our life and salvation, are also fruits of faith and commanded acts.

units.la: Obj. 5. Crediturus, ex miseriae sensu, & omnimodae liberationis, cum in se, tum in aliis, defectu, necesse habet, se dedere Deo in Christo, tanquam Servatori sufficienti, & fideli: hoc autem fieri non potest, nisi per consensum voluntatis: ergo, &c. Resp. Deditio ista non est formalis actus fidei; sed consequens, & imperatus.
units.tr: Obj. 5. One who is about to believe, from a sense of misery and of the lack of every kind of deliverance, both in himself and in others, must necessarily surrender himself to God in Christ as a sufficient and faithful Saviour. But this cannot happen except by consent of the will. Therefore, etc. Reply: This surrender is not a formal act of faith, but a consequence and a commanded act.

units.la: Obj. 6. Particularis ista certioratio intellectus, in quibusdam deest ad tempus: qui tamen fidem veram in cordibus suis habent interim latentem. Resp. 1. Ubi in vere fidelibus actualis illa certioratio deest ad tempus, non tamen deest habitualis certitudo. 2. Ut quandoque deest actualis illa certioratio, ita non minus interdum deest actualis fiducia, & cordis acquiescentia in Deo per Christum, tanquam in vita ac salute nostra omnisufficiente.
units.tr: Obj. 6. That particular certainty of the intellect is lacking for a time in some people, who nevertheless have true faith hidden in their hearts meanwhile. Reply: 1. Where that actual certainty is lacking for a time in truly believing people, habitual certainty is not lacking. 2. Just as actual certainty is sometimes lacking, so at times actual trust is no less lacking, and the heart's resting in God through Christ, as in our life and all-sufficient salvation.

units.la: XVIII. Ad Fidei illius originem quod attinet, probatur Dei efficientia in hoc negotio, eaque realis hyperphysica; 1. ex eo, quod non alii quam docti a Deo & tracti, qui audiverunt a Patre, & didicerunt, veniant ad Christum, & credant: Joh. VI, 44, 45. Audidiverunt videl. sermonem Dei vivi, qui verè est incorruptibile semen regenerationis nostræ: 1 Petr. I, 23.
units.tr: XVIII. As far as the origin of that faith is concerned, God's efficiency in this matter is proved, and it is a real, hyperphysical efficiency. 1. From the fact that those who are taught and drawn by God, who have heard from the Father and learned, come to Christ and believe: John 6:44, 45. Namely, they have heard the word of the living God, which truly is the incorruptible seed of our regeneration: 1 Pet. 1:23.

units.la: 2. In prædicatione Euangelii, neque is qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat; sed Deus qui dat crescendi vim: 1 Cor, III, 7. qui adaperit cor, ad attendendum iis, quæ per Ministros dicuntur; exemplo Lydiæ: Act. XVI, 14.
units.tr: 2. In the preaching of the gospel, neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase: 1 Cor. 3:7. He opens the heart to attend to those things which are said through the ministers, as in the example of Lydia: Acts 16:14.

units.la: 3. Ex nobis ipsis non sumus idonei ad cogitandum quicquam; ac proinde neque ad credendum: sed omnis aptitudo nostra à Deo est: 2 Cor. III, 5, 6. qui nos discernit; & à quo accepimus, quicquid habemus:
units.tr: 3. We of ourselves are not sufficient to think anything, and so neither to believe. But all our fitness is from God: 2 Cor. 3:5, 6. He makes us sufficient, and from him we have received whatever we have.

units.la: 1 Cor. IV. 7. qui nobis dat, etiam credere in Christum: Phil. I, 29. Eph. II, 8. revelatus mysteria Regni cælorum & communicans beneficia salutaria, quibus ipsi secundum electionem placet: Matth. XI, 26, XIII, 11. Act. XIII, 48. Rom. VIII, 30.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 4:7. He gives us also to believe in Christ: Phil. 1:29; Eph. 2:8. He reveals the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and communicates the saving benefits, as it pleases him according to election: Matt. 11:26, 13:11; Acts 13:48; Rom. 8:30.

units.la: 4. Speciali appropriatione appellatur propterea Spiritus fidei; 2 Cor. IV, 13, sine quo nemo potest dicere Jesum Dominum: 1 Cor. XII. 3. Atque hoc contra Pelagianos, eorumque sequaces, tenendum. Sed pluribus eandem veritatem astruemus ac defendemus infrà in cap. de Vocatione & regeneratione.
units.tr: 4. By a special appropriation he is therefore called the Spirit of faith: 2 Cor. 4:13, without whom no one can say Jesus is Lord: 1 Cor. 12:3. This is to be held against the Pelagians and their followers. But we shall establish and defend the same truth at greater length below, in the chapter on vocation and regeneration.

units.la: XIX. Interim neque Verbi Divini, aut Euangelii prædicati, efficacia hic omittenda est.
units.tr: XIX. Meanwhile the efficacy of the Word of God, or of the preached gospel, is not to be omitted here either.

units.la: Diserte Paulus, Rom. 1, 16. „Non me pudet Euangelii Christi, potentia siquidem est Dei ad salutem cuivis credenti. Et cap. X. 17. Vide sup. th. 5. §. 3. Verùm ista efficientia proprie moralis est, per modum signi ad auditum ordinati, & signative nobis repræsentantis veritates credendas: Attamen necesse est, ut efficacia realis hyperphysica Spiritûs Sancti ad moralem illam accedat; cæteroquin ea effectum suum non sortiretur. 1 Cor. III, 7. Quod probè distinguendum, propter Swenkfeldianos, & Lutheranos. Verbum quidem aptitudine non suam moralem & signativam habet procul dubio; sed majori virtute opus est, ut homo prorsùs corruptus, ptus, & spiritualiter mortuus, illi credat ad salutem. Hinc Spiritus Sanctus dicitur nobis indere cor novum, Ezech. xxxvi. 26. nos iterum creare; 2 Cor. v, 17. resuscitare; Eph. ii. 5. & regenerare. Joh. iii, 5. Atque ita non solùm præstat, ut homo credere pollit, si velit; sed etiàm, ut actu credat: quod contra Jesuitas, & Remonstrantes, observandum.
units.tr: Paul says plainly, Rom. 1:16: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." And ch. 10:17; see above, th. 5, §3. But this efficacy is properly moral, by way of a sign ordained for hearing, and representing to us the truths to be believed. Nevertheless, the real hyperphysical efficacy of the Holy Spirit must accompany that moral efficacy; otherwise the Word would not produce its effect. 1 Cor. 3:7. This must be carefully distinguished, on account of the Swenkfeldians and the Lutherans. The Word undoubtedly has in its own nature a moral and signifying aptitude; but a greater power is needed so that a man who is utterly corrupt and spiritually dead may believe unto salvation. Hence the Holy Spirit is said to put in us a new heart, Ezek. 36:26; to create us again, 2 Cor. 5:17; to raise up, Eph. 2:5; and to regenerate, John 3:5. And thus he not only makes it possible for a man to believe, if he wishes, but also brings it about that he actually believes. This is to be observed against the Jesuits and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Obj. Sic videbitur Deus in nobis credere; non nos ipsi: quod absurdum. Resp. Neg. Deus in nobis efficit & ipsum Velle, & ipsum Agere; Phil. ii, 13. interim nos formaliter Volumus, & Agimus. Similiter nos per gratiam Dei, & ex Spiritu fidei, Credimus: & consequenter etiàm Loquimur: 2 Cor. iv, 13.
units.tr: Objection. Thus God would seem to believe in us, and not we ourselves, which is absurd. Reply. I deny it. God in us effects both the willing itself and the acting itself, Phil. 2:13; yet we formally will and act. Similarly, through the grace of God and from the Spirit of faith, we believe, and consequently we also speak: 2 Cor. 4:13.

units.la: XX. Ex superioribus sequitur, quid dicendum sit de Analysi Fidei.
units.tr: XX. From what has been said above, it follows what must be said about the analysis of faith.

units.la: Si enim objectivè spectentur veritates credendæ, analysis erit in Verbum Dei, quo veritates istæ nobis innotuerunt, & quod supremam atque infallibilem auctoritatem habet, ut ipsi assentiamur in omnibus sic propositis, & confirmatis. Vide sup. th. 2. Verùm si subjectivè spectetur actus credendi in nobis; quâ scil. virtute effectum sit, ut nos non solùm credere potuerimus, sed reipsa etiàm credamus; cùm alii multi, quibus idem Verbum quoque fuit propositum, non credant tamen; analysis erit in Deum aut Spiritum Sanctum, cujus reali & hyperphysicâ virtute hoc in nobis effectum est: ut jàm probatum, th. 18. & 19.
units.tr: If the truths to be believed are regarded objectively, the analysis will lead to the Word of God, by which those truths have become known to us, and which has supreme and infallible authority, so that we assent to everything so proposed and confirmed. See above, th. 2. But if the act of believing is regarded subjectively, that is, by what power it has been brought about in us that we not only could believe but actually do believe, since many others to whom the same Word was also proposed do not believe, the analysis will lead to God or the Holy Spirit, by whose real and supernatural power this has been effected in us, as has already been proved in th. 18 and 19.

units.la: XXI. Methodus autem potissimùm est hujusmodi:
units.tr: XXI. The method is chiefly as follows:

units.la: Spiritus Fidei in nobis operans, ipsumque habituale donum Fidei sese in actus secundos exerens, efficit ut peccata, corruptionem, vilitatem, turpitudinem, & universam miseriam nostram cum displicentiâ ac dolore agnoscamus; humiliter de nobis ipsis sentiamus, nos ipsos judicemus, atque in nobis, quantum ad nos ipsos & nostra, attinet, desperemus: Matth. ix, 13. xi, 28. Jerem. ii, 19. 1 Petr. v, 5. 6. 1 Cor. xi, 31. Jerem. xvii, 5, 6. Quod est antecedens & prærequisitum necessf necessarium ad formales actus Fidei salvificæ.
units.tr: (1) The Spirit of faith working in us, and the habitual gift of faith itself, stirring up its active acts, brings it about that we recognise our sins, our corruption, our baseness, our filthiness and all our wretchedness with displeasure and sorrow; that we think humbly of ourselves, judge ourselves, and despair of ourselves as far as we and our own things are concerned: Matt. 9:13; 11:28; Jer. 2:19; 1 Pet. 5:5, 6; 1 Cor. 11:31; Jer. 17:5, 6. This is the antecedent and prerequisite necessary for the formal acts of saving faith.

units.la: 2. Ut agnoscamus supremam, eamque salutarem veritatem universæ doctrinæ Scripturarum: & speciatim Promissionum Euangelicarum, atque adeo plenitudinem gratiæ & salutis in Christo, ac admirandam Dei misericordiam in isto Mediatore: Act. xxiv, 14. Rom. 1, 16, 17. iii, 25. Joh. 1, 16, 17. 1 Tim. ii, 5, 6. 1 Joh. i, 1, 2. Hoc autem pertinet ad Fidem generalem & Euangelicam.
units.tr: (2) That we acknowledge the supreme and saving truth of the whole doctrine of the Scriptures, and especially of the evangelical promises, and so the fullness of grace and salvation in Christ, and the wonderful mercy of God in this Mediator: Acts 24:14; Rom. 1:16, 17; 3:25; John 1:16, 17; 1 Tim. 2:5, 6; 1 John 1:1, 2. This belongs to general and evangelical faith.

units.la: 3. Ut serio nobis expetamus unionem & communionem Christi, hoc bonum desideremus, hanc justitiam esuriamus & sitiamus; Isa. i, 19. iv, 1. Psal. xlii, 1, 2, 3. Apoc. xxii, 17. Matth. v, 6. Phil. iii, 9. Qui est actus imperatus fidei generalis Euangelicæ, & necessarium prærequisitum specialis fidei salvificæ.
units.tr: (3) That we earnestly desire the union and communion of Christ, that we long for this good, hunger and thirst for this righteousness: Isa. 1:19; 4:1; Ps. 42:1, 2, 3; Rev. 22:17; Matt. 5:6; Phil. 3:9. This is the commanded act of general evangelical faith, and the necessary prerequisite of special saving faith.

units.la: 4. Ut juxta promissiones Euangelicas, ex desiderio isto spirituali, attestante etiam Spiritu Sancto in nobis, agnoscamus Christum esse nostrum Servatorem; sic eum singuli recipiamus, ac nobis applicemus, viciissim apprehendentes eum, qui nos apprehendit prior: 2 Cor. iv, 13. Rom. viii, 16. Joh. i, 12. 2 Tim. i, 12. Gal. ii, 20. Phil. iii, 12. Qui est formalis actus fidei salvificæ.
units.tr: (4) That, according to the evangelical promises, from this spiritual desire, with the Holy Spirit also bearing witness in us, we acknowledge Christ to be our Saviour; and so each of us receives him and applies him to ourselves, laying hold on him in turn, who first laid hold on us: 2 Cor. 4:13; Rom. 8:16; John 1:12; 2 Tim. 1:12; Gal. 2:20; Phil. 3:12. This is the formal act of saving faith.

units.la: 5. Ut porro agnoscamus, nos in communione Christi participes esse omnium & singulorum ejus beneficiorum; sic habere remissionem peccatorum, & jus vitæ æternæ: 1 Joh. i, 3. 1 Cor. i, 30. Act. x, 43. Joh. iii, 16, 36. v, 24. Qui est posterior actus, attamen etiam proprius, & elicitus, fidei salvificæ; cum quadam consequentia.
units.tr: (5) That we further acknowledge that we are partakers in the communion of Christ of all and each of his benefits, and so have the forgiveness of sins and the right to eternal life: 1 John 1:3; 1 Cor. 1:30; Acts 10:43; John 3:16, 36; 5:24. This is a later act, yet also a proper and elicited act of saving faith, with a certain consequence.

units.la: 6. Ut Patrem illum cœlestem, adeo misericordem ac beneficum, & Servatorem unicum perfectissimum, qui nos prior tantopere dilexit, viciissim diligamus, & sincera gratitudine ac nova obedientia prosequamur jugiter: 1 Joh. iv, 19. 2 Cor. v, 14, 15. Psal. cxvi, 1, 12, 13. Rom. XII, 1, 2. Tit. II, 11, 12, 14. Qui est actus imperatus fidei salvificæ.
units.tr: (6) That we in turn love that heavenly Father, so merciful and beneficent, and that most perfect single Saviour, who first loved us so greatly, and that we continually follow him with sincere gratitude and new obedience: 1 John 4:19; 2 Cor. 5:14, 15; Ps. 116:1, 12, 13; Rom. 12:1, 2; Titus 2:11, 12, 14. This is the commanded act of saving faith.

units.la: 7. Ut observemus omnes actūs jām commemoratos, eorumque sinceritatem in nobis: indè colligamus, nos esse verè fideles, translatos in statum gratiæ & regnum lucis, ac verè consortes bonorum modò recensitorum: atque adeò confidamus fore, ut potenter custodiamur, ac perficiamur amplius, virtute Dei & Christi; & suo tempore transferamur etiàm in statum gloriæ: 2 Cor, XIII, 5. 1 Petr. II, 9. Eph. v, 8. Rom, v, 1-11. VIII, 17. 23, 24, 25; 31-39. 1 Petr. I, 5, 9. 1 Thes. v, 23, 24. 2 Tim. IV, 7, 8.
units.tr: (7) That we observe all the acts already mentioned, and their sincerity in us; from this we conclude that we are truly believers, transferred into the state of grace and the kingdom of light, and truly partakers of the goods just now enumerated; and so we trust that we shall be powerfully kept and further perfected, by the power of God and of Christ, and in due time be transferred also into the state of glory: 2 Cor. 13:5; 1 Pet. 2:9; Eph. 5:8; Rom. 5:1-11; 8:17, 23, 24, 25, 31-39; 1 Pet. 1:5, 9; 1 Thess. 5:23, 24; 2 Tim. 4:7, 8.

units.la: XXII. Fructus fidei sunt saluberrimi, in quibus maximè capitalis est, 1 unio & communio nostra cum Christo, vitæ ac salutis æternæ causâ verissimâ; quem Verbo & Spiritū sic nobis propositum atque oblatum, credentes recipimus, amplectimur, tenemus; ut ipso, cum omnibus suis beneficiis, deinceps beati fruamur: Joh. 1, 12. cum Hebr. XI, 11. ac porrò, Joh. XV, 4. XVII, 20, 21. Gal. II, 20. Cant. II, 16.
units.tr: XXII. The fruits of faith are most salutary, of which the chief is (1) our union and communion with Christ, the most true cause of life and eternal salvation; whom, so offered and presented to us by the Word and the Spirit, we, believing, receive, embrace and hold, so that with him and all his benefits we may henceforth enjoy blessedness: John 1:12, with Heb. 11:11; and further, John 15:4; 17:20, 21; Gal. 2:20; Song 2:16.

units.la: Undè statim resultant, 2 Justitia coram Deo; immunitas à reatū, & jus vitæ æternæ, in isto Servatore nostro: Rom. 1, 16, 17. III, 21, -28. VIII, 30. &c. X, 9, 10.
units.tr: Hence there immediately result (2) righteousness before God, and freedom from guilt and the right to eternal life, in this our Saviour: Rom. 1:16, 17; 3:21-28; 8:30, etc.; 10:9, 10.

units.la: 3. Pax & Amicitia cum Deo, quæ omnem mentem exsuperat: Rom. V, 1, 10, 11. Phil. IV, 7. Coloss. 1, 19, 20, 21.
units.tr: (3) Peace and friendship with God, which surpasses every mind: Rom. 5:1, 10, 11; Phil. 4:7; Col. 1:19, 20, 21.

units.la: 4. Dignitas Filiorum Dei; ex Adoptione, in illo verè unigenito & ὁμοούσιῳ: Joh. 1, 12. Gal. III, 26.
units.tr: (4) The dignity of the sons of God, through adoption, in that truly only-begotten and homoousios [ὁμοούσιῳ] Son: John 1:12; Gal. 3:26.

units.la: Porrò autem hinc amplius promanant, 1. Filialis libertas & fiducia accedendi ad Patrem illum cœlestem: Rom. V, 2, VIII, 15, 16. cum certâ persuasione, quòd orationes nostræ exaudiendæ sint: 1 Joh. V, 14, 15. Matth. V, 5, -11. XXI, 22. Johan. XIV. 13, XV, 7, XVI, 34. Jac. I, 5.
units.tr: Moreover, from these there further flow: (1) filial freedom and confidence in approaching that heavenly Father, Rom. 5:2; 8:15, 16, with the firm persuasion that our prayers are to be heard: 1 John 5:14, 15; Matt. 5:5-11; 21:22; John 14:13; 15:7; 16:34; James 1:5.

units.la: 2. Jus civitatis, familiæ, & hæreditatis cœlestis; quæ nobilißima & gloriosißima sunt privilegia: Eph. 11, 18, 19. Hebr. xi, 9, 10, 13, 14, 16. Phil. iii, 20, 21. Rom. viii, 17.
units.tr: (2) The right of citizenship, of the family and of the heavenly inheritance, which are the most noble and most glorious privileges: Eph. 2:18, 19; Heb. 11:9, 10, 13, 14, 16; Phil. 3:20, 21; Rom. 8:17.

units.la: 3. Victoria mundi, aliorumque hostium & adversorum, in Duce & Capite nostro, qui prior vicit, & nos vincere facit: 1 Joh. v, 4, 5. Rom. viii, 37. Joh. xvi, 31, 33.
units.tr: (3) Victory over the world and other enemies and adversaries, in our Leader and Head, who has conquered first and makes us conquer: 1 John 5:4, 5; Rom. 8:37; John 16:31, 33.

units.la: 4. Exultatio pia, & Gloriatio humilis, in tanta illa salute, & tam admiranda Dei gratia: Rom. v, 2, 3, 11. Jac. 1, 2, 9.
units.tr: (4) Pious exultation and humble glorying in so great a salvation and so wonderful a grace of God: Rom. 5:2, 3, 11; James 1:2, 9.

units.la: Imo insuper, arctissimo nexu beneficiis illis gloriosis implicata sunt haec honesta & sancta, 1. Inhabitatio & vita ipsius Christi in nobis; qui manifeste ostendit, qualis ipse sit; & nos imagini suae similes reddit: Ephes. iii, 17. Gal. ii, 20. Joh. xv, 4, 5. Rom. viii, 29. 2 Cor. iii, 18.
units.tr: Indeed, moreover, bound by the closest tie to those glorious benefits are these honourable and holy things: (1) the indwelling and life of Christ himself in us, who clearly shows what he himself is like and makes us like his image: Eph. 3:17; Gal. 2:20; John 15:4, 5; Rom. 8:29; 2 Cor. 3:18.

units.la: 2. Cordis & conscientiae nostrae intima purificatio; quatenus hunc sanguinis Christi effectum & hanc Spiritus Sancti virtutem, fide etiam recipimus: Act. xv, 9. Tit. 1, 15. Joh. xv, 3. Hebr. ix, 14. 1 Cor. vi, 11.
units.tr: (2) The inner purification of our heart and conscience, insofar as we also receive by faith this effect of the blood of Christ and this power of the Holy Spirit: Acts 15:9; Titus 1:15; John 15:3; Heb. 9:14; 1 Cor. 6:11.

units.la: 3. Efficacia per charitatem; dum in veritate etiam observamus bonitatem Dei & Christi, ejusque imaginis in proximo nostro; atque adeo fides actus charitatis imperat: Gal. v, 6. 1 Joh. iv, 19. 2 Cor. v, 14, 15.
units.tr: (3) Efficacy through love, while in truth we also observe the goodness of God and of Christ, and his image in our neighbour; and so faith commands the act of love: Gal. 5:6; 1 John 4:19; 2 Cor. 5:14, 15.

units.la: 4. Sancta totius vitae, & omnium actionum nostrarum, gubernatio: adeo ut, quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum fit: Rom. xiv, 23. & fides cooperetur operibus bonis, atque ex illis perficiatur; h. e. significative vera ac viva declaretur, seu probetur, demonstratione τῷ ὅτι: Jac. ii, 22. confer 2 Cor. xii, 9. Non vero formaliter iis perficiatur, quasi charitas esset forma fidei, quod perperam contendunt Pontificii; cum virtutes illae specie differant: 1 Cor. xiii, 13. Quin & opus fidei celebratur, 1 Thes. 1, 3. Joh. vi, 29, 30. re-spectu spectu praxios perpetuae, quam requirit; & actuum tum elicitorum, tum imperatorum.
units.tr: (4) The holy government of the whole of life and of all our actions, so that whatever is not from faith is sin: Rom. 14:23; and faith cooperates with good works and is perfected by them, that is, it is significantly declared or proved to be true and living, by demonstration that [τῷ ὅτι]: James 2:22; compare 2 Cor. 12:9. But it is not formally perfected by them, as if charity were the form of faith, which the Papists wrongly contend; since those virtues differ in kind: 1 Cor. 13:13. Indeed the work of faith is also praised, 1 Thess. 1:3; John 6:29, 30, with respect to the continual practice which it requires, and to acts both elicited and commanded.

units.la: XXIII. Quo clarius patet fidei efficacia ad praxin pietatis promovendam, paucis adhuc notamus ista sequentia. 1. Per fidem ex Christo, & Spiritu Sancto, accipimus vires operandi spiritualiter.
units.tr: XXIII. That the efficacy of faith in promoting the practice of piety may be seen more clearly, we note the following points briefly. 1. Through faith, from Christ and the Holy Spirit, we receive strength to act spiritually.

units.la: 2. Agnoscimus normam nobis praescriptam, tam accurate nos obligantem; atque adeo necessitatem praecepti.
units.tr: 2. We recognise the rule prescribed to us, which binds us so strictly; and so the necessity of the precept.

units.la: 3. Praxin istam Deo gloriosam, atque in Christo gratam esse; simulque nobis salutarem, tum ut hic truamur pace conscientiae ac beatitudine inchoata, tum ut eâdem viâ ac methodo adeamus possessionem & fruitionem haereditatis ac gloriae coelestis.
units.tr: 3. That this practice is glorious to God and pleasing in Christ; and at the same time salutary for us, both so that here we may enjoy the peace of conscience and the inchoate blessedness, and so that by the same way and method we may come to the possession and enjoyment of the heavenly inheritance and glory.

units.la: 4. Universa Theologia nostra, & potissimum doctrina gratiae Euangelicae, multis modis praxin accuratissimam, sinceram, ac perpetuam, postulat: dum enim credimus Sanctitatem Jehovae, & voluntatem ipsius esse sanctificationem nostram; facile intelligimus, quid amicos & filios ipsius deceat: dum credimus Christum, caput nostrum sanctissimum, vitamque, & mortem, ac resurrectionem ejusdem; omnia talem immutationem & conformationem requirunt, dum credimus, nos justificatione absolvi a priori miseria, & vitam aeternam nobis adjudicari; quomodo peccatis serviemus amplius? quomodo non omni studio incumbemus sanctitati, quae in vita aeterna non minus comprehenditur, quam ipsa gloria? &c.
units.tr: 4. Our whole theology, and especially the doctrine of the Gospel grace, demands in many ways a most exact, sincere and perpetual practice. For while we believe that the holiness of Jehovah, and his will, is our sanctification, we easily understand what befits his friends and sons. While we believe that Christ is our most holy head, and of his life, death and resurrection, all these things require such a change and conformity. While we believe that by justification we are absolved from our former misery and that eternal life is adjudged to us, how shall we still serve sins? How shall we not devote every effort to holiness, which is comprehended in eternal life no less than glory itself? etc.

units.la: XXIV. Superest dubium, An fides Euangelica, & salvifica, recte dicatur virtus, aut actus obedientialis Lege Divina praescriptus? Resp. Aff. quatenus primo Decalogi praecepto obligamur ad unius veri Dei rectam agnitionem; ac proinde etiam ad fidem omnium, ipsius auctoritate nobis propositorum & confirmatorum: quod ad veritates Euangelicas quoque extendi debet, ex hypothesi istius revelationis,
units.tr: XXIV. There remains the doubt: whether evangelical and saving faith may rightly be called a virtue, or an act of obedience prescribed by the Divine Law? Answer: Yes, insofar as we are first bound by the precept of the Decalogue to the right acknowledgement of the one true God; and consequently also to faith in all things proposed and confirmed to us by his authority; which must also be extended to the Evangelical truths, given the hypothesis of that revelation.

units.la: Obj. 1. Omnis obedientia debet esse voluntaria: atqui Fides ad intellectum pertinet: ergo. Resp. Non credimus tamen actu, nisi concomitante voluntate: atque hactenus fides nostra etiam voluntaria est.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Every obedience ought to be voluntary; but faith pertains to the intellect; therefore. Resp. Yet we do not believe in act unless the will accompanies it; and so far our faith is also voluntary.

units.la: Obj. 2. Fides ad Evangelium pertinet; cujus non est, actum obedientialem praescribere. Resp. Evangelium objecta sic credenda proponit; & promissiones addit, ut alacrius credamus: sed obligatio formaliter, quod credere debeamus, ad Legem pertinet.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Faith pertains to the Gospel, and it is not the Gospel's business to prescribe an act of obedience. Resp. The Gospel sets forth the objects to be believed in this way, and adds promises so that we may believe more eagerly; but the obligation, formally, that we ought to believe, belongs to the Law.

units.la: Obj. 3. Theologi admodum solicite Fidem a bonis operibus distinguunt. Resp. Fidei peculiaris est ratio, & valde distincta a reliquis actibus obedientiae, seu bonis operibus: quod satis manifestum evadit, si spectetur, 1. ejus subjectum quo; 2. objectum formale; 3. specialis usus ac respectus in negotio justificationis nostrae; & 4. ratio principii ad alios actus obedientiae. Atque hoc observandum contra Socinianos & Remonstrantes.
units.tr: Obj. 3. The theologians distinguish faith from good works very carefully. Resp. Faith has a distinctive character, and is quite distinct from the other acts of obedience, or good works; which becomes sufficiently plain if we consider (1) its subject, the faculty by which; (2) its formal object; (3) its special use and bearing in the business of our justification; and (4) the manner of its principle in relation to the other acts of obedience. And this is to be observed against the Socinians and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sic Fides erit species Observantiae; a qua tamen in Divisione Theologiae cap. 1. th. 44. contradistinguebatur. Resp. Contradistinguitur tantum ratione objectorum, quae traduntur in priori parte Theologiae; & a nobis creduntur, non aguntur, aut fiunt: ad posteriorem vero partem referuntur agenda.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Thus faith will be a species of observance; from which, however, in the Division of Theology, chapter 1, thesis 44, it was distinguished. Resp. It is distinguished only by reason of the objects, which are delivered in the first part of Theology, and which we believe rather than do or perform; whereas the things to be done are referred to the latter part.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Ad praxin interim 1. revocetur Methodus jam indicata & confirmata th. 21.
units.tr: For practice, meanwhile, (1) let the method already indicated and confirmed in thesis 21 be recalled.

units.la: 2. Animum addant Fructus illi praestantissimi, de quibus th. 22.
units.tr: (2) Let those most excellent fruits, concerning which thesis 22, add courage.

units.la: 3. Sinceritatem vero exploremus potissimum, juxta quatuor postremos Fructus ibidem propositos; collatis etiam iis, quae th. 23. breviter notata sunt.
units.tr: (3) Let us examine our sincerity especially according to the last four fruits proposed there, comparing also those things which were briefly noted in thesis 23.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De Sacrâ Scripturâ.
units.tr: Concerning Holy Scripture.

units.la: Verbum Dei duobus modis consideratur. 1. Scriptu-ra, quid hoc loco: Quomodo à Deo inchoata; & perfecta. 2. Ejus definitio. Genus. 3. Causa efficiens princeps; & ministra. Subjectum receptivum. Finis proximus: ulterior: ultimus. 4. Partes S. Scripturæ: Libri Canonici. 5. Libri V. T. Eorum distributio. 6. Apocrypbi, perperàm illis adjecti à Pontificiis: Conditiones, quæ libros Canonicos faciunt. Signa, unde tales cognoscuntur. 7. Libri N. T. Eorum distributio. 8. Editio S. Scripturæ: Primaria. 9. Librorum V. T. Lingua Hebraica. 10. Particula Chaldaicæ. De Proselytis. 11. Librorum N. T. Lingua Græca. Quare: Evangelium Matthæi; Marci. Epistola ad Hebræos. 12. Editio secundaria. Translationum necessitas probatur, contra Pontif. 13. Attributa. Auctoritas. 14. Hæc ab auctore Deo. Non ab Ecclesiâ; contra Pontif. 15. Solvuntur Objectiones. 16. Ejus cognoscendæ Causa externa ministeriale adjuvans. 17. Principalior. 18. Causa interior. Non Enthusiasmus. 19. Αὐθεντία norma: Historia tantum. 20. Auctoritas Divina convenit toti S. Scripturæ, & singulis ejus partibus, &c. 21. SS. Scriptores nusquam erràrunt. Nulla vera differentia. Non loquuntur secundum erroneam hominum opinionem. 22. Apogragraphorum fideliter factorum similis est ratio. Quomodo in iis cognoscatur Divina auctoritas. 23. Cur Deus Autographa interire siverit. Objectio de Apographis solvitur. 24. Versionibus non convenit formalis ἀυθεντία. Nec speciatim Vulgata Latina; contra Pontif. Nec Graeca, quae dicitur LXX. Interpretum. 25. Translationibus fideliter factis quomodo conveniat Divina & Canonica Auctoritas. Objectio solvitur. 26. Quomodo ista auctoritas cognoscatur. 27. Perfectio S. Scripturae, quae. Perfectio integralis, quae. Asseritur contra Muhamm. Pontif. Socin. & Criticos qu. 28. Objectiones solvuntur. 29. Perfectio essentialis quae; & quomodo intelligenda. 30. Ea probatur 31. Adversantur Traditiones non scriptae, Iudaeorum Kabbalah, & Mischnajoth. 32. Pontificiorum Traditiones non scriptae. 33. Objectiones solvuntur, 34. Perspicuitas illius. Objective spectata probatur. 35. Objectiones solvuntur. 36. Subjective in hominibus, quomodo recipiatur, 37. Subjectiva imperitia. Quid hinc agendum. 38. Necessitas. Ea probatur. 39. Sententiae Pontif. Enthus. & Liberi. explicantur. Objectiones solvuntur. 40. Adjuncta consequentia. Lectio. Omnibus necessaria. Probatur c. Pontif. 41. Objectiones solvuntur. 42. Etiam Librorum V. T. c. Socin. & Anabapt. 43. Objectiones solvuntur, 44. Interpretatio realis; Sensus genuinus: cujusque loci unicus. 47. Pontificiorum quadruplex refutatur. tur. 46. Sensus alicubi compositus. Quædam virtualiter comprehensa. 47. Stylus. Communiter spectatus. In consideratione Grammatica. Rhetorica. 48. Verus modus interpretandi. 49. Ius interpretandi summum. 50. Subordinatum: Antecessorium. 51. Privatum. 52. Auctoritas interpretationis. 53. Iudicium controversiarum Theologicarum. Dei. Christi. Spiritūs S. Quomodò ipsius S. Scriptura. 54. Quomodò Antecessoribus Eccles. conveniat. Et quibusvis fidelibus. Probatur. Quomodò Magistratui Christiano. 55. Judicium ἀνυπεύθυνον non convenit Ecclesiæ Romanæ. neque Concilio generali, neque Papæ Romano. 56. Objectiones solvuntur. 57. Ratio humana non judex, aut norma, controversiarum Theolog. c. Socin. 58. Objectiones solvuntur. 59. Usus Rationis in his rebus. 60. Theologia nostra argumentativa: c.qu. Pontif. & Anabapt. 61. Catechesis. Confessio nostra. Conciliorum decreta. Canones Synodi Nat. Dordr. Constitutiones Ecclesiastic. Symbolum Apostolicum. Athanasianum, &c. 62. Revelationes Divinæ. Gentilium Prophetæ. Sibyllæ. Mercurius Trismegistus. 63. Jud. Talmud. Muhamm. Koran & Suna. 64. Praxis 65.
units.tr: The Word of God is considered in two ways. 1. Scripture, here, as to how it was begun by God and perfected. 2. Its definition: genus. 3. The principal efficient cause and the ministering causes. Receptive subject. Proximate end: further end: last end. 4. The parts of Holy Scripture: the canonical books. 5. The books of the Old Testament and their distribution. 6. The Apocrypha, wrongly added to them by the Papists: the conditions which make books canonical. The signs by which such books are recognized. 7. The books of the New Testament and their distribution. 8. Edition of Holy Scripture: the primary. 9. The language of the books of the Old Testament: Hebrew. 10. A Chaldee portion. On proselytes. 11. The language of the books of the New Testament: Greek. Why: the Gospel of Matthew; of Mark. The Epistle to the Hebrews. 12. Secondary edition. The necessity of translations is proved, against the Papists. 13. Attributes. Authority. 14. These come from God as author, not from the Church, against the Papists. 15. Objections are answered. 16. The external ministerial aid for knowing it. 17. The principal one. 18. Internal cause. Not enthusiasm. 19. Self-authentication, the norm: history only. 20. Divine authority belongs to all of Holy Scripture and to each of its parts, etc. 21. The holy writers never erred. No true difference. They do not speak according to the erroneous opinion of men. 22. The same reasoning applies to faithfully made copies. How divine authority is recognized in them. 23. Why God allowed the autographs to perish. The objection about the copies is answered. 24. Formal authority does not belong to versions, nor specifically to the Latin Vulgate, against the Papists; nor to the Greek version called that of the Seventy Translators [αὐθεντία]. 25. How divine and canonical authority belongs to faithful translations. An objection is answered. 26. How this authority is recognized. 27. Perfection of Holy Scripture: what it is. Integral perfection: what it is. It is asserted against Muhammad, the Papists, the Socinians and critics. 28. Objections are answered. 29. Essential perfection: what it is and how it is to be understood. 30. It is proved. 31. Unwritten traditions are opposed, as well as the Kabbalah of the Jews and the Mishnayoth. 32. The unwritten traditions of the Papists. 33. Objections are answered. 34. Its perspicuity. Considered objectively, it is proved. 35. Objections are answered. 36. How it is received subjectively in men. 37. Subjective ignorance. What follows from this. 38. Necessity. It is proved. 39. The views of the Papists, Enthusiasts and Libertines are explained. Objections are answered. 40. Attached consequence. Reading. Necessary for all. Proved against the Papists. 41. Objections are answered. 42. Likewise of the books of the Old Testament, against the Socinians and Anabaptists. 43. Objections are answered. 44. Real interpretation; genuine sense: of each passage, the single one. 47. The fourfold sense of the Papists is refuted. 46. Sense is sometimes compound. Some things are virtually included. 47. Style. Commonly considered. In the consideration of grammar and rhetoric. 48. The true manner of interpreting. 49. The supreme right of interpreting. 50. Subordinate: the teachers of the Church. 51. Private. 52. Authority of interpretation. 53. Judgement of theological controversies. God. Christ. The Holy Spirit. How this belongs to Holy Scripture itself. 54. How it belongs to the teachers of the Church and to any faithful believers. Proved. How it belongs to the Christian magistrate. 55. The judgement which is accountable to no one does not belong to the Roman Church, neither to a general council nor to the Roman Pope. 56. Objections are answered. 57. Human reason is neither judge nor norm of theological controversies, against the Socinians. 58. Objections are answered. 59. The use of reason in these matters. 60. Our theology is argumentative, against the Papists and Anabaptists. 61. Catechism. Our confession. The decrees of councils. Canons of the Synod of Dort. Church constitutions. The Apostles' Creed, the Athanasian, etc. 62. Divine revelations. Prophets of the Gentiles. Sibyls. Hermes Trismegistus. 63. Jewish Talmud. Muhammad's Koran and Sunna. 64. Practice. 65.

units.la: I. DIncipium doctrinale universæ Theologiæ, atque adeo primò credendorum; est Verbum Dei; seu Revelatio Divinitus nobis facta. Vide supra, cap. 2. th. 2. & 4.
units.tr: I. The doctrinal beginning of the whole of theology, and therefore of what is to be believed first, is the Word of God, or the revelation made to us by God. See above, ch. 2, th. 2 and 4.

units.la: Consideratur illud, tum absolutè, & per se: tum modaliter, & restrictè, quatenus scriptum est; unde Scripturam appellamus.
units.tr: This is considered both absolutely and in itself, and modally and in a restricted sense, insofar as it has been written; whence we call it Scripture.

units.la: Ἀγγεφον autem fuit ante Mosen: interim sic etiam tunc Verbo Dei fidem habuerunt electi & vocati illorum temporum; ut ejus analysis esset in illam infallibilem Dei veritatem. Vide cap. 2. th. 4. & 20. Postea datum est ἔγγραφον.
units.tr: The unwritten word [ἄγραφον] existed before Moses; yet the elect and called of those times also had faith in the Word of God, so that its analysis lay in that infallible truth of God. See ch. 2, th. 4 and 20. Afterwards the written word [ἔγγραφον] was given.

units.la: II. Scriptura hic non actum scribendi designat; sed ipsum opus scriptum. Hoc Deus immediatè inchoavit in decalogo: Exod xxxi,18, xxxii,16. Deut. ix,10, x,4. sed perfecit mediatè; intercedente operâ hominum Θεοπνευστων, Mosis & reliquorum Prophetarum, nec non Apostolorum & Evangelistarum. 2 Tim. iii,16.
units.tr: II. "Scripture" here designates not the act of writing but the written work itself. God began this immediately in the Decalogue: Exod. 31:18, 32:16; Deut. 9:10, 10:4; but he completed it mediately, through the work of men inspired by God [θεόπνευστοι], Moses and the other prophets, as well as the apostles and evangelists. 2 Tim. 3:16.

units.la: Tota Scriptura Divinitus (est) inspirata. 2 Petr. i,19, 20, 21. Habemus firmissimum sermonem Propheticum.
units.tr: All Scripture is divinely inspired. 2 Pet. 1:19, 20, 21. We have the most sure prophetic word.

units.la: Illud primum noveritis; nullam Prophetiam Scripturæ esse propriæ explicationis. Non enim libitu hominis allata est olim Prophetia: sed acti à Spiritu Sancto locuti sunt sancti Dei homines.
units.tr: Know this first: no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For prophecy never came by the will of man; but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: III. Definitur propterea; Syntagma librorum Θεοπνευστως per viros Dei extraordinarios conscriptorum, atque Ecclesiæ traditorum, in communem ac perpetuum canonem fidei ac morum, ad salutarem ejus instructionem, & Dei ipsius gloriam.
units.tr: III. It is therefore defined as a collection of books written by divinely inspired [θεοπνεύστως] extraordinary men of God and handed down by the Church, forming a common and perpetual canon of faith and morals, for its salutary instruction and for the glory of God himself.

units.la: Pro genere constituimus Syntagma librorum: ubi libros dicimus numero multitudinis; prout similiter Scripturæ appellantur, Luc. xxiv, 27. Joh. v,39. Act. xviii,24., Rom. i,2. xv,4. quemadmodum etiam singulares libri indicantur, Marc. xii, 26. Luc. iii, 4. iv, 17. xx, 42. Ioh. xx, 30. Act. i, 20, vii, 42. Vulgo κατ' ἐξοχὴν Biblia, vel SS. Biblia dicuntur.
units.tr: For the genus we set up "a collection of books", where we say "books" in the plural, just as they are called "Scriptures", Luke 24:27; John 5:39; Acts 18:24; Rom. 1:2, 15:4; just as single books are also indicated, Mark 12:26; Luke 3:4, 4:17, 20:42; John 20:30; Acts 1:20, 7:42. Commonly they are called, by preeminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], the Bible, or the Holy Bible.

units.la: Syntagma autem, sicut collectivè omnis, vel tota Scriptura nuncupatur, 2 Tim. iii, 16. & singulari notione Scriptura, Joh. ii, 22. xx, 9. 2 Petr. i, 20.
units.tr: The collection, however, is named collectively "all" or "the whole of Scripture", 2 Tim. 3:16, and in the singular sense "Scripture", John 2:22, 20:9; 2 Pet. 1:20.

units.la: Differentia sumta est à causis efficientibus, subjecto recipiente, & causis finalibus.
units.tr: The difference is taken from the efficient causes, the receiving subject, and the final causes.

units.la: IV. Causa efficiens princeps est ipse Deus Opt. Max. Causae vero ministrae fuerunt homines sancti, ad hoc opus extraordinarie efficaciter vocati, & infallibili Spiritus Sancti inspiratione ac directione instructi: 2 Tim. iii, 16. 2 Petr. i, 19, 20, 21. Vide sup. th. 1. Adde 2 Sam. xxiii, 1, 2. Joh. xvi, 13. Rom. iii, 2. 1 Petr. i, 11.
units.tr: IV. The principal efficient cause is God himself, Best and Greatest. The ministering causes, however, were holy men, extraordinarily and effectively called to this work and instructed by the infallible inspiration and direction of the Holy Spirit: 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:19, 20, 21. See above th. 1. Add 2 Sam. 23:1, 2; John 16:13; Rom. 3:2; 1 Pet. 1:11.

units.la: Subjectum recipiens est Ecclesia, cui traditi sunt isti libri: Psal. CXLVII, 19. „Annunciat Verbum suum ipsi Jacob; Statuta sua, & Judicia sua, Israeli. Rom. iii, 2. Eis credita sunt Eloquia Dei. 2 Petr. i, 19. Luc. xvi, 29.
units.tr: The receiving subject is the Church, to which these books were entrusted: Ps. 147:19, "He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and his judgements to Israel." Rom. 3:2, To them the oracles of God were entrusted. 2 Pet. 1:19; Luke 16:29.

units.la: Finis proximus, ut sit communis & perpetuus canon Fidei ac morum: Deut. iv, 2. Vide sup. cap. i. th. 6. Rom. xv, 4. „Quae ante scripta sunt, ad nos docendos „ante scripta sunt: ut per tolerantiam & consolationem „Scripturarum, spem retineamus. 2 Tim. iii, 16, 17. „Tota Scriptura Divinitus (est) inspirata, & utilis ad „doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, disciplinam „quae (est) in justitia: Ut perfectus sit homo Dei, „ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Vide etiam 2 Reg. xxiii, 2, 3, 24. Psal. CXIX, 5, 9, 105, 153. „Jes. viii, 20. 2 Petr. i, 19. Confer Phil. iii, 16. „(In eo) ad quo usque pervenimus, eădem incedamus regulă (κανόνι) Gal. vi, 16. „Et quicunque secundum hanc regulam incedent, pax (erit) super eos, & misericordia, „& super Israelem Dei. Finis ulterior est Ecclesiæ salutaris instructio; & consequenter beatitudo æterna: Ioh. xx. 31. „Hæc scripta sunt, ut credatis Jesum esse Christum illum, Filium ejus. Vide etiam Psal. xix, 8, 9. Ioh. v, 39. 2 Petr. 1, 19.
units.tr: The proximate end is that it be the common and perpetual canon of faith and morals: Deut. 4:2. See above ch. 1, th. 6. Rom. 15:4, "For whatever was written before was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope." 2 Tim. 3:16, 17, "All Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." See also 2 Kings 23:2, 3, 24; Ps. 119:5, 9, 105, 153; Isa. 8:20; 2 Pet. 1:19. Compare Phil. 3:16, "(In that) to which we have attained, let us walk by the same rule [κανόνι]." Gal. 6:16, "And as many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God." The further end is the salutary instruction of the Church and, consequently, eternal blessedness: John 20:31, "These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God." See also Ps. 19:8, 9; John 5:39; 2 Pet. 1:19.

units.la: Ultimus vero est ipsius Dei Opt. Max. gloria: Deut. iv, 6, 7. „Ea est sapientia vestra, & intelligentia vestra, in oculis populorum, qui audient omnia statuta ista; & dicent: Utique populus sapiens & intelligens, gens magna ista! Quæ enim est gens (ita) magna, cui sint Dii propinqui, sicut est Iehovah Deus noster in cunctis, pro quibus invocaverimus eum? Vide etiam Psal. cxlvii, 12, 19, 20.
units.tr: Lastly, the ultimate end is the glory of God himself, Most Good and Greatest: Deut. 4:6-7: "This is your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who shall hear all these statutes and say: Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people! For what great nation is there that has its gods near to it, as the LORD our God is in all things, whenever we call upon him?" See also Psal. 147:12, 19-20.

units.la: Sed præcipuè agendum nunc erit specialius de Partibus S. Scripturæ, Editione, Attributis, & Adjunctis consequentibus.
units.tr: But now we must treat more specifically of the parts of Holy Scripture, its edition, its attributes, and its consequent adjuncts.

units.la: V. Partes S. Scriptura sunt Libri tùm V. tùm N. T. non omnes simul conscripti; sed prout Auctori supremo placuit eos successivè exarari, atque ita salutaris doctrinæ promulgationem dispensari: Hebr. i, 1.
units.tr: 1. The parts of Holy Scripture are the books of both the Old and the New Testament. They were not all written at once, but were composed one after another as it pleased the supreme Author, and so the proclamation of saving doctrine was dispensed in stages: Heb. 1:1.

units.la: Quoniam verò omnes isti libri sunt communis & perpetuus canon fidei ac morum, Canonici appellari solent: Phil. iii, 16. Gal. vi, 16.
units.tr: Since all these books are the common and perpetual canon of faith and morals, they are usually called Canonical: Phil. 3:16; Gal. 6:16.

units.la: VI. Libri V. T. à Mose & Prophetis θεόπνευστος sunt conscripti, & Ecclesiæ V. T. primùm traditi: Psal. CXLVII, 19, 20. Rom. iii, 2.
units.tr: VI. The books of the Old Testament were written by Moses and the Prophets, God-breathed [θεόπνευστος], and were first handed down to the Old Testament Church: Psal. 147:19-20; Rom. 3:2.

units.la: Hi minus accuratè à Iudæis distribuuntur, in Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa: melius ab aliis in Legales, Historicos, Poëticos & Prophcticos; & Prophetici iterum in majores & minores. Sunt autem Legales; Gen. Exod., Levit., Num. cum Deuteronomio Historici; Josua, Iudic., Ruth, duo Sam., duo Reg. et duo Chronic. Esra, Nehem, Esther. Poëtici; — Iob., Psal., Prov. Ecclesiast., Cant. Prophet. maj. Jes. Jerem., Thren., Ezech., Dan. mini. min. ----- ----- Hoseah, Joel, Amos, Obad, Ion, Michah, Nahumque Habakuk, Zephaniah, Restant Haggæus, Zachariah, cum Malachia.
units.tr: The Jews distribute these less accurately into the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings; others distribute them better into Legal, Historical, Poetical and Prophetical books, and the Prophetical again into the greater and the lesser. The Legal books are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, with Deuteronomy. The Historical are Joshua, Judges, Ruth, the two books of Samuel, the two of Kings, the two of Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther. The Poetical are Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs. The greater Prophets are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel. The lesser Prophets are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

units.la: VII. Istis vero non debent cum Papali Concilio Tridentino accenseri, Liber Tobiæ, Historia Iudithæ, Sapientia Salomonis, Ecclesiasticus Iesu Siracidæ; Prophetia Baruchi, Additamentum ad librum Esthera; ut & Additamenta ad librum Danielis, scil. Precatio Azariæ, Hymnus trium juvenum in fornace, Historia Sufannæ, itemque de Bele & Dracone; ac tandem duo Libri Maccabæorum: non magis quàm Liber tertius & quartus Ezræ, Precatio Manassis, tertius Maccabæorum; &c. quorum priores quidem in Vulgata Editione Pontificiorum comparent; & tamen à dicto Concilio extra Canonem relinquuntur.
units.tr: VII. Nor should the following be counted among these with the Papal Council of Trent: the Book of Tobit, the History of Judith, the Wisdom of Solomon, the Ecclesiasticus of Jesus the son of Sirach, the Prophecy of Baruch, the Additions to the Book of Esther, and likewise the Additions to the Book of Daniel, namely the Prayer of Azariah, the Hymn of the three young men in the furnace, the History of Susanna, and also that of Bel and the Dragon; and finally the two Books of the Maccabees. Still less should the third and fourth books of Ezra, the Prayer of Manasseh, and the third book of the Maccabees be so counted, etc. The former of these indeed appear in the Vulgate edition of the Papists, and yet they are left outside the canon by the said Council.

units.la: Verùm istis pariter desunt conditiones, quæ à prioribus libros Canonicos faciunt: videl. ut 1. scripti sint Divinâ inspiratione per Ministros extraordinarios: ac porrò 2. Divinitùs ordinati in Canonem fidei ac morum; & 3. Ecclesiæ eo fine ac modo Divinâ auctoritate traditi & commissi: 2 Tim. iii, 15, 16, 17. 2 Petr. 1, 19, 20, 21. Deut. iv, 1, 2. xxxi, 9, 24, 26. Rom. iv, 23, 24. xv, 4.
units.tr: But these likewise lack the conditions which make the former books canonical, namely that 1. they were written by divine inspiration through extraordinary ministers; further, 2. they were divinely ordained into the canon of faith and morals; and 3. they were handed down and committed to the Church by divine authority, for that purpose and in that manner: 2 Tim. 3:15-17; 2 Pet. 1:19-21; Deut. 4:1-2; 31:9, 24, 26; Rom. 4:23-24; 15:4.

units.la: Neque consequenter adsunt signa quibus libri Canonici à posteriori cognoscuntur: scil. 1. ut sic olim ab Ecclesiâ fide Divinâ recepti sint; 2. sic usurpati; & 3. tali testimonio deinceps constanter commendati; atque interim 4. characteres Divinitatis fidelibus iniis manifesti sint, attestante unà Spir. S. in animis ipsorum: Prov. 1; 2; 3. Ies. lix, 21, 1 Thess. ii, 13. Iob. iv; 42. xvii, 8.
units.tr: Nor, consequently, are the signs present by which canonical books are recognized a posteriori: namely, 1. that they were thus received by the Church of old as divinely given; 2. that they were thus used; and 3. that they were thereafter constantly commended by such testimony; and meanwhile 4. the marks of their divinity have been made manifest to the faithful, the Holy Spirit together attesting in their hearts: Prov. 1; 2; 3; Isa. 59:21; 1 Thess. 2:13; John 4:42; 17:8.

units.la: Imò contrarium de istis libris perhibent monumenta Ecclesiæ V. T.: ad extremum usque terminum; & Ecclesiæ N. T.: per quatuor prima sæcula; atque amplius. Quò etiam pertinent confessiones Bellarmini, Melchioris Cani, Sixti Senensis, Cardinalis Cajetani, &c.
units.tr: On the contrary, the monuments of the Church of the Old Testament, down to its final term, and of the Church of the New Testament, through the first four centuries and beyond, bear witness to the opposite about these books. To this also belong the admissions of Bellarmine, Melchior Cano, Sixtus of Siena, Cardinal Cajetan, etc.

units.la: Pi8 Propterea libri illi appellantur Apocryphi, h.e. occulti; quòd clam haberentur, ad usús tantùm privatos; non autem publicè ad communem Ecclesiæ instructionem ac directionem. Confer Præfationem in Translatione Belgicâ iis præfixam.
units.tr: For this reason those books are called Apocryphal, that is, hidden, because they were kept privately, for private use only, and not publicly for the common instruction and direction of the Church. Compare the Preface prefixed to the Belgic translation.

units.la: VIII. Libri N. T. Divinâ etiam inspiratione per Apostolos & Euangelistas postea conscripti, atque Ecclesiæ Christianæ una cum Libris V. T. traditi sunt. Hi dispescuntur in Historicos, Dogmaticos, & unum Propheticum.
units.tr: VIII. The books of the New Testament were also afterwards written by divine inspiration through the Apostles and Evangelists, and were handed down to the Christian Church together with the books of the Old Testament. These are divided into Historical, Doctrinal, and one Prophetical book.

units.la: Historici sunt, Matthæus, Marcus, Lucas, Iohan. Atque Apostol. Dogmatici, Rom., bis Cor., Gal., Eph., Phil., Col., bis Thess., deinde Binæ ad Timotheum, Tit., Philem, Hebr.; Iacobi: Tunc binæ Petre; tres Iohan.; Iud. Propheticus, ---- ---- ---- Apocalypsis.
units.tr: The Historical books are Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and the Acts of the Apostles. The Doctrinal are Romans, two to the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, then two to Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James; then two of Peter; three of John; Jude. The Prophetical is the Apocalypse.

units.la: IX. Editio S. Scripturæ, intelligitur, quâ Verbum Dei scripto exhibitum est Ecclesiæ, in communem fidei morumque regulam.
units.tr: IX. The edition of Holy Scripture is understood as that by which the Word of God is presented in writing to the Church as the common rule of faith and morals.

units.la: Estque tum primaria, sic formaliter authentica; tum secundaria, metaphrastica, sive per translationem.
units.tr: And it is both primary, and so formally authentic, and secondary, metaphrastic, or by translation.

units.la: Primaria, non solùm materialiter secundùm Rem contentam, ejusque methodicam dispositionem, Θεόπνευστος est, Divinâque auctoritate pollet; sed etiam formaliter, ratione Idiomatis, sive Linguæ.
units.tr: The primary edition is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος] and possesses divine authority, not only materially with respect to the content and its methodical arrangement, but also formally, by reason of its idiom or language.

units.la: Alia interim est librorum V. T. alia N. T.
units.tr: The language is one thing for the books of the Old Testament, and another for the New.

units.la: X. Editio primaria librorum V. T. facta est Lingua Hebraïca; quæ Judaica appellatur, 2 Reg. xviii, 26, 28. Nehem. xiii, 24. communis enim fuit, & vernacula Ecclesiæ V. T. Sic igitur Deus tunc uni isti populo sibi fœderato familiariter tabulas fœderis sui salutaris tradidit. Psal. cxlvii, 19, 20. lxxxvi, 2, 3. Rom. iii, 2. ix, 4. Gentiles verò isto tempore, ut erant alienati à civili statu Israëlis; sic etiam extranei quod ad pactorum promissiones attinet, spem non habentes, &c. &c. Eph. 11, 12. Populo Dei & Prophetis barbari: Ezech. 11,16. suis ipsorum viis incedentes: Act. xiv, 16.
units.tr: X. The primary edition of the books of the Old Testament was made in the Hebrew language, which is called Jewish: 2 Kings 18:26, 28; Neh. 13:24. For it was the common and vernacular language of the Old Testament Church. Thus God then delivered the tables of his saving covenant familiarly to that one people bound to him: Psal. 147:19-20; 86:2-3; Rom. 3:2; 9:4. But the Gentiles at that time, since they were alienated from the civil state of Israel, and likewise strangers to the promises of the covenants, having no hope, etc.: Eph. 2:11-12; to the people of God and the Prophets they were barbarians (Ezek. 3:6); walking in their own ways (Acts 14:16).

units.la: XI. Aramicè interim, seu Chaldaicè, conscriptæ sunt quædam particulæ Biblicæ, sub captivitate scil. Babylonicâ, aut circa eam; & quidem iltæ propius spectantes res Babylonicas: ut Ezr. iv, 8. - ad vi, 19. atque iterum vii, 12, - 26. Dan. ii, 4. - ad viii. & Jerem. x, 11. Verum ista Lingua, sive potius Dialectus, non ita multum differt ab Hebraicâ; eamque Judæi per istam captivitatem magis etiam cognoverunt, & usurpârunt.
units.tr: XI. Meanwhile, certain portions of the Bible were written in Aramaic, or Chaldee, during the Babylonian captivity or around it; and indeed those which relate more closely to Babylonian matters: Ezra 4:8 to 6:19; again 7:12-26; Dan. 2:4 to the end of chapter 7; and Jer. 10:11. This language, or rather dialect, does not differ very much from Hebrew; and the Jews came to know and use it more, through that captivity.

units.la: Ad Proselytos quod attinet, illi deserto Gentilismo ad Judæorum sacra non solum, sed etiam ad Politiam Judaicam, transfibant eâdem operâ; vel saltem ad Festa celebranda quotannis se Hierosolymam conserebant. Act. ii, 10. viii, 27. cum Deut. xvi, 16. xxxi, 11, 12. Ac proindè eâdem quoque Editione Biblicâ utebantur; donec magno eorum commodo conficerentur Translationes in alias Linguas, sive ipsis vernaculas, sive saltem magis notas.
units.tr: As for proselytes, they, having abandoned Gentilism, passed over at the same time not only to the sacred rites of the Jews but also to the Jewish polity; or at least they betook themselves to Jerusalem each year to celebrate the feasts: Acts 2:10; 8:27 with Deut. 16:16; 31:11-12. And accordingly they also used the same Biblical edition, until translations into other languages were made, to their great advantage, either in their own vernacular or at least in more widely known tongues.

units.la: XII. Librorum N. T. editio primaria, facta est Linguâ Græcâ. Ecclesia enim N. T. colligebatur ex Judæis, & Gentilibus cujuscunque nationis. Idcirco potissimum deligenda erat Lingua, tunc maximè communis & nota; utpotè Græca; quoniam Græcorum Monarchia præcesserat: unde etiam Spiritus S. homines istius sæculi dispescit in Judæos, & Græcos; Act. vi, 1. Rom. 1, 16. 11, 9, 10. 111, 9. 1 Cor. 1, 24. Gal. 111, 28.
units.tr: XII. The primary edition of the books of the New Testament was made in the Greek language. For the Church of the New Testament was gathered from Jews and Gentiles of every nation. Therefore the language chosen had to be especially that which was then most common and known, namely Greek, since the monarchy of the Greeks had preceded; whence also the Holy Spirit divides the men of that age into Jews and Greeks: Acts 6:1; Rom. 1:16; 2:9-10; 3:9; 1 Cor. 1:24; Gal. 3:28.

units.la: Euangelium Matthæi Hebraïcè primitus conscriptum fuisse, (quod aliqui contendunt,) non admittimus: Deus enim ad ἰῶτα & apicem unum conservat, quod vult auctoritatem normalem in Ecclesiâ suâ obtinere; Matth. v, 18. atque eadem in usum fidelium, qui postremis sæculis vivent; etiam conscripta sunt, Rom. iv, 23, 24.
units.tr: We do not admit that the Gospel of Matthew was first written in Hebrew, as some contend. For God preserves even to the iota [ἰῶτα] and one tittle, since he wills that it obtain normative authority in his Church, Matt. 5:18; and these same things were also written for the use of the faithful who would live in the last ages: Rom. 15:4; 1 Cor. 10:11.

units.la: { } D 2 {z}23, 24. XV, 4. 1 Cor. X, 11. At vero non Hebraicam sed Græcam, istius Euangelii editionem Deus conservavit: & quidem talem, ubi non solùm voces quædam, sed etiàm sententiæ Hebraicæ, aut Syriacæ, formaliter citantur, ac porrò in Græcum sermonem transferuntur: Matth. 1, 23. XXVII, 46. quæ sic Hebraicè conscribi non potuerunt.
units.tr: Rom. 4:23-24; 15:4; 1 Cor. 10:11. But God has preserved not the Hebrew but the Greek edition of this Gospel; and indeed such an edition, in which not only certain words but also Hebrew or Syriac sentences are formally cited and then translated into Greek: Matt. 1:23; 27:46, which could not have been written in this way in Hebrew.

units.la: Similiter neque admittimus, Euangelium Marci Latinè, vel Epistolam ad Hebræos Hebraicè primùm exaratam fuisse.
units.tr: Likewise, we do not admit that the Gospel of Mark was first written in Latin, or the Epistle to the Hebrews first written in Hebrew. ## XIII. The secondary edition

units.la: XIII. Editio secundaria
est, quâ SS. Literæ, ex Linguis originalibus, in aliam qualemcunque translatæ, sic exhibentur, ut ab harum ignaris ad inftructionem ac demonstrationem Theologicam intelligi & usurpari possint.
units.tr: is that in which the Holy Scriptures, translated from the original languages into some other language, are presented in such a way that those who are ignorant of the originals can understand and use them for theological instruction and proof.

units.la: Istiusmodi Translationes non solùm ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem utiliter institui posse, sed etiàm ex voluntate Dei sub hâc œconomiâ necessariò institui debere, probatur contra Pontificios Scripturarum lucifugas; 1. Quia Deus omninò vult, ut Verbum suum scriptum familiariter legatur atque intelligatur ab omnibus, qui ad communionem istius Fœderis vocantur: patet hoc ex ipsis Editionibus primariis. At vero gentes quatuvis Linguarum sub hâc œconomiâ vocatæ sunt, atque amplius vocandæ: Matth. XXVIII, 19. Profecti docete omnes gentes, &c. Confer Rom. III, 29. Eph. II, 19, 20. Phil. II, 11. Apoc. V, 8.
units.tr: That such translations can not only be usefully undertaken for the edification of the Church, but must even necessarily be undertaken under this dispensation by the will of God, is proved against the Papists, the enemies of Scripture, as follows. (1) Because God wills absolutely that his written Word be read and understood familiarly by all who are called to communion in this covenant; this is evident from the primary editions themselves. Now people of every language have been called under this dispensation, and more are yet to be called: Go and teach all nations, etc. (Matt. 28:19). Compare Rom. 3:29, Eph. 2:19-20, Phil. 2:11, Rev. 5:8.

units.la: 2. Christus Apostolos non dimisit ad Euangelium omnibus gentibus prædicandum, nisi prius omnium Linguarum notitiâ instructos; ut unusquisque audiret eos suâ propria lingua loquentes, & magnifica Dei facta prædicantes: Act. 1, 4, 8. II, 4, 6, 8, 11. Quali dono variarum linguarum tunc etiàm plures fuerunt instructi; addito insuper in quibusdam aliis dono interpretationis verbalis: 1 Cor. XIV, 6, 13, 27, 28. unde conficitur, in quolibet cœtu etiàm Scripta Propheticæ
units.tr: (2) Christ did not send the apostles to preach the Gospel to all nations unless they had first been instructed in the knowledge of all languages, so that each one might hear them speaking in his own tongue and proclaiming the mighty works of God (Acts 1:4, 8; 2:4, 6, 8, 11). By this gift of various tongues many were then also instructed; moreover, in some cases the gift of verbal interpretation was added (1 Cor. 14:6, 13, 27-28), whence it follows that in every assembly the prophetic writings also...

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: tica & Apostolica alleganda, explicanda, & applicanda esse linguâ istic notâ.
units.tr: prophetic and apostolic, to be cited, explained, and applied in the language known there.

units.la: 3. Idem evincunt præcepta & exhortationes de Verbo Dei legendo, meditando, & aliis inculcando: Deut. vi, 6, -9. xvii, 18, 19. xxxi, 11, 12, 13. Psal. 1, 2. xix, 9, -12. cxix, 1, &c. Jes. viii, 20. Luc. xvi, 29. Joh. v, 39. xx, 31. Act. xvii, 11. Rom. iv, 23, 24. xv, 4. 1 Cor. x, 11. 2 Tim. iii, 14, -17. 2 Petr. i, 19. 1 Joh. i, 4. Judæ, 3. Apoc. i, 3. xxii, 18, 19. Ista enim fieri non possunt ab hominibus linguarum originalium ignaris, nisi per translationem.
units.tr: 3. The same is shown by the precepts and exhortations to read, meditate on, and teach others the Word of God: Deut. vi, 6, -9. xvii, 18, 19. xxxi, 11, 12, 13. Psal. 1, 2. xix, 9, -12. cxix, 1, &c. Jes. viii, 20. Luc. xvi, 29. Joh. v, 39. xx, 31. Act. xvii, 11. Rom. iv, 23, 24. xv, 4. 1 Cor. x, 11. 2 Tim. iii, 14, -17. 2 Petr. i, 19. 1 Joh. i, 4. Judæ, 3. Apoc. i, 3. xxii, 18, 19. For these things cannot be done by people ignorant of the original languages, except through translation.

units.la: 4. Ex praxi, eventu, & saluta-ri successu istius negotii, olim atque etiamnum.
units.tr: 4. From the practice, outcome, and successful results of this work, both formerly and still today.

units.la: XIV. Succedunt Attributa; & quidem potissi- mum Auctoritas, Perfectio, Perspicuitas, & Necessitas.
units.tr: XIV. The attributes follow; and chiefly authority, perfection, perspicuity, and necessity.

units.la: Auctoritas S. Scripturæ, est Divina ejus potestas, ad fidem & observantiam Deo debitam nos obligans.
units.tr: The authority of Holy Scripture is its divine power, binding us to the faith and obedience owed to God.

units.la: Quoniam Auctor ejus est ipse Deus Opt. Max. ut ostensum th. 4. inde manifesta est ejus in se Divinitas; atque in ordine ad homines, quibus tradita est, Auctoritas, & quidem Divina; ut ei fides haberi debeat, tanquam vere Verbo Dei; & obedientia religiosa præstari debeat, juxta voluntatem mandati Divini istic expressam. Vide 1 Thess. ii, 13. 1 Joh. v, 9, 10.
units.tr: Since its author is God himself, the best and greatest, his divinity is clear in itself; and in relation to the men to whom it has been delivered, it has authority, and indeed divine authority, so that it ought to be believed as truly the Word of God, and religious obedience ought to be rendered according to the divine will of the command expressed there. See 1 Thess. ii, 13. 1 Joh. v, 9, 10.

units.la: XV. Manifestum est, omnis testimonii, mandati, legis, diplomatis, &c. Auctoritatem, ab Auctore suo proprie pendere, & arcessendam esse: atque adeo Auctoritatem S. Scripturæ, ab Auctore Deo.
units.tr: XV. It is evident that the authority of every testimony, command, law, charter, and so on, depends properly on its author and must be sought from him; and therefore the authority of Holy Scripture depends on its author, God.

units.la: Absurdè vero & impiè Pontificii Auctoritatem S. Scripturæ, in ordine ad nos, suspendunt ab Ecclesiâ, & quidem Romanâ, ejusque Pontifice.
units.tr: But the Papists absurdly and impiously make the authority of Holy Scripture, in relation to us, depend on the Church, and indeed on the Roman Church and its Pope.

units.la: Nam 1. omnis Auctoritas est relativa; & in ordine ad alios, qui eâ obligantur: si ergo S. Scriptura, tanquam ipsius Dei Verbum scriptum, ab ipso Deo Auctoritatem in se habet, necessariò eandem sic habere debet in ordine ad homines, quibus S. Scriptura ptura data est in normam fidei ac morum.
units.tr: For first, all authority is relative, and is binding in relation to others who are bound by it. If therefore Holy Scripture, as the written Word of God himself, has authority in itself from God himself, it must necessarily have the same authority in relation to the men to whom Holy Scripture was given as the rule of faith and conduct.

units.la: 2. Christus, tanquam αὐτόπιστος, negat, se testimonium ab homine accipere; cum de se aliud majus habeat; idem ergo tenendum de Deo, aut Christo, loquente in Verbo suo scripto, Ioh. v, 34, 36. cum 1 Ioh. v, 9. Tit. 1, 1. 2 Tim. 11, 13. Hebr. VI, 13, 18.
units.tr: Second, Christ, as αὐτόπιστος [self-credible], denies that he receives testimony from a man, since he has something greater concerning himself; the same must therefore be held of God, or of Christ speaking in his written Word. John v, 34, 36, with 1 John v, 9. Titus i, 1. 2 Tim. ii, 13. Heb. vi, 13, 18.

units.la: 3. Vera Ecclesia exstructa est super fundamento Apostolorum & Prophetarum: Eph. 11, 20. & sanctificata in veritate Dei, quae est Verbum ipsius: Ioh. XVII, 17. Ipsa igitur in fide sua nititur Verbo Dei, per Prophetas & Apostolos exhibito; atque in obedientia sua similiter conformatur ad istam normam: non vero contra Verbum Dei scriptum, ejusque Auctoritas obligatoria, nititur Ecclesia, tanquam fundamento.
units.tr: Third, the true Church has been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Eph. ii, 20, and has been sanctified in the truth of God, which is his Word, John xvii, 17. Therefore the Church in its faith rests on the Word of God, delivered through the Prophets and Apostles, and in its obedience is likewise conformed to that rule. The Church does not rest, as on its foundation, against the written Word of God, whose binding authority it is.

units.la: 4. Absurde, & non sine crimine laesae majestatis, subditi arrogarent sibi dignitatem, ex qua penderet potestas obligatoria Legis a Principe latae, in ordine ad hos vel illos. Similiter autem hic agunt Adversarii.
units.tr: Fourth, it would be absurd, and not without the crime of treason, for subjects to claim for themselves a dignity on which the binding power of a law enacted by a prince would depend, in relation to these or those people. Yet the adversaries act in just this way.

units.la: XVI. Obj. 1.
units.tr: XVI. Obj. 1.

units.la: Ecclesia est columna & stabilimentum veritatis; 1 Tim. III, 15. Ergo. Resp. 1. Itaque ut 1. Ecclesia, tanquam columna, erecta & stabilita sit super isto fundamento, Verbo Dei; sic coagmentata & confirmata in veritate, pallive: non vero contra ut Verbum Dei scriptum nitatur Ecclesia; sicut tectum aliquod columna ipsum sustentante, architectonice. 2. Ut veritatem Verbi Divini aliis exhibeat, indicet, & suo modo attestetur: cujusmodi columnarum quarundam usus politicus est. 3. Nihil ibi speciatim de Ecclesia Romana.
units.tr: The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth, 1 Tim. iii, 15. Therefore... Reply: First, the Church, as a pillar, is erected and established upon that foundation, the Word of God, and so is joined together and confirmed in the truth, or the like; but the Church does not rest against the written Word of God, as a roof rests on a pillar that supports it architecturally. Second, it displays, points out, and in its own way attests the truth of the divine Word to others; this is the political use of certain pillars. Third, nothing there is said specifically about the Roman Church.

units.la: Obj. 2. Augustinus alibi: Non crederem S. Scripturae, nisi me auctoritas Ecclesiae Catholicae moveret. Resp. Non quicquid Augustinus dixit, aut credidit, verum est; neque ab ipsis Pontificiis, ut tale, admittitur: ex, gr. de Eucharistia danda infantibus. 2. Augustinus isto dicto offendit, qua methodo ipse perductus fuerit ad Divinitatem S. Scripturæ agnoscendam; interveniente scilicet ministeriali testimonio Ecclesiæ, aut Antecessorum ejus.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Augustine elsewhere: I would not believe Holy Scripture unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me. Reply: First, not everything Augustine said or believed is true, nor is it accepted as such even by the Papists themselves; for example, on giving the Eucharist to infants. Second, by that saying Augustine means the method by which he himself was led to acknowledge the divinity of Holy Scripture, namely through the ministerial testimony of the Church or of its predecessors.

units.la: XVII. Si quæratur, quomodo aliis innotescat Auctoritas S. Scripturæ? Hic etiam Ecclesiæ sunt suæ partes; Antecessorum scil. Ecclesiasticorum, quin & singulorum fidelium, suo modo. De luce quippe testantur, ut alii quoque credant; non tamen sunt ipsa lux, aut lucis causa, vel ἀξιοπιστίας in eâ; sed luce illâ collustrati, testimonium ei apud alios perhibent. Vide Joh. 1, 7, 8. Confer exemplum Samaritanorum, & mulieris de Christo apud illos testantis; Joh. 4, 28, 29, 30, 39. -42. Apparitor, vel etiam quivis ex plebe, advenæ alicui, aliive ignaro, indicium facere potest, dicens; Iste est Consul civitatis; ille Prætor; Hoc Diploma Senatus urbani, &c. Verùm istâ ratione nequaquam confert in Consulem, Prætorem, &c. talem dignitatem aut potestatem, &c. Non est causa rei constitutiva, vel effectiva; sed medium ejus cognoscendæ, quæ ante & citra istam cognitionem etiam verè talis est. Similiter indicatur, docetur, quòd fit, & qualis sit Auctoritas S.Scripturæ; ac suadetur, ut ei fides habeatur: ubi sic solùm occurrit externa ministerialiter adjuvans causa Auctoritatis istius cognoscendæ.
units.tr: XVII. If it is asked how the authority of Holy Scripture becomes known to others? Here too the Church has its part, namely that of its ecclesiastical predecessors, and indeed of individual faithful persons, each in his own way. They bear witness to the light, so that others may believe too; yet they are not the light itself, nor the cause of the light, nor of its ἀξιοπιστίας [trustworthiness]; but illuminated by that light, they bear testimony to it before others. See John i, 7, 8. Compare the example of the Samaritans, and of the woman testifying about Christ among them, John iv, 28, 29, 30, 39-42. An attendant, or even any man from the common people, can point out to some stranger or other ignorant person, saying: "This is the consul of the city; that one is the praetor; this is the decree of the city senate," and so on. Yet by such an indication he in no way confers on the consul, praetor, and so on, such a dignity or power. It is not a constitutive or effective cause of the thing, but a means of knowing it, which is truly such even before and apart from that knowledge.
