units.tr: 1. by that famous testimony, 2 Tim. iii, 14, 17. But you, remain in the things you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them; and that from childhood you have known the sacred letters, which can make you wise unto salvation through the faith that is in Christ. All Scripture is divinely inspired, etc. See above, th. 4. The Apostle dissuades the Evangelist from false doctrines and teaches in what things he must persevere after his departure; that is, that he should recall him to the Holy Scriptures. Concerning these he asserts (α.) that they can make him wise unto salvation, etc. Wisdom denotes a perfect habit, and this wisdom unto salvation is ascribed, in the faith of Christ, to the Holy Scriptures as the one doctrinal principle. (β.) He teaches that all Holy Scripture is divinely inspired, deriving its authority and perfection from its Author, in accordance with Jas. i, 17. Moreover, (γ.) he works this out part by part: profitable for doctrine, etc. For thus he shows its use, not in one kind only but in every kind necessary for salvation, whether truth is to be taught, or falsehood refuted, or evil morals corrected, or discipline in righteousness inculcated. Indeed (δ.) he completes the whole business and plainly ends the dispute, concluding: that the man of God (that is, a teacher of the Church by the ordination of God; 1 Reg. xvii, 24. 1 Tim. vi, 11.) may be perfect, namely in all those parts; and briefly, thoroughly furnished unto every good work. From the perfection of the effect, the perfection of the cause is evident.

units.la: 2. Locis quibusdam V. T. Exod. xxiv, 3, 4. "Venit ergo Moseh, & narravit populo omnia Verba Jehovae, omniaque judicia: & respondit totus populus voce unâ, ac dixerunt; Omnia Verba, quae locutus est Jehovah, faciemus. Et scripsit Moseh omnia verba Jehovae. Moses, quae à Deo audivit, omnia populo narravit; eademque omnia scripto consignavit: ne ea oblivioni traderentur, imo ut etiam posterorum usibus servirent; cum quibus Deus idem foedus pepigit. Exod. xxxiv, 27. Deut. xxix, 14, 15. xxxi, 9, 21.
units.tr: 2. In certain places of the Old Testament, Exod. 24:3, 4: "Moses therefore came and told the people all the words of Jehovah, and all the judgments; and all the people answered with one voice and said, All the words which Jehovah has spoken we will do." And Moses wrote all the words of Jehovah." Moses told the people everything he heard from God and committed all of it to writing, so that it would not be lost to oblivion but would even serve the use of posterity, with whom God made the same covenant. Exod. 34:27; Deut. 29:14, 15; 31:9, 21.

units.la: Iterùm Deut. xxxi, 24, -27. "Cùm autem finem fecisset Moseh scribendi verba Legis istius in libro, donec ea complerentur: Praecepit Moseh Levitis portantibus arcam foederis Jehovae dicendo; Capite librum istum, &c. Vide sup. th. 28. Legis ergo scripturam absolvit Moses; omnesque ejus partes complevit: & pro posteris exemplar illud, tanquàm depositum ac testimonium, diligentissimè confervandum mandavit. Ita quidem ut nemini quicquam addere, vel detrahere liceret; sed praescriptum illud accuratissimè omnes sequi deberent, non recedendo dextrorsum vel sinistrorsum; Deut. iv, 1, 2. v, 38, 39. xii, 32. Jos. 1, 7. xxiii, 6. Prov. xxx, 5, 6.
units.tr: Again, Deut. 31:24–27: "When Moses had finished writing the words of this Law in a book, until they were completed, Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of Jehovah, saying: Take this book, etc." See above, thesis 28. Moses therefore completed the writing of the Law and finished all its parts, and he commanded that this copy, as a deposit and testimony, be most carefully preserved for posterity. Indeed no one was permitted to add anything or take away, but all were bound to follow that prescription most exactly, not turning aside to the right hand or to the left; Deut. 4:1, 2; 5:38, 39; 12:32; Josh. 1:7; 23:6; Prov. 30:5, 6.

units.la: Infigne etiam est testimonium Psal. xix, 8, 9. Vide sup. th. 22. Ubi disertè perfectio laudatur, & quidem ad convertendam animam, sapientiam efficiendam, cor laetificandum, &c.
units.tr: The testimony of Psalm 19:8, 9 is also remarkable. See above, thesis 22. There the perfection is plainly praised, and that indeed for converting the soul, making wise, rejoicing the heart, etc.

units.la: 3. Similia sunt testimonia N. T. Luc. xvi, 29. ubi de evitandâ condemnatione: Habent Mosen & Prophetas. tas ; audiant illos. Ac porrò de consequendâ vitâ æternâ, Joh. v, 39. „Scrutamini Scripturas: quia vos vi„demini vobis in ipsis vitam æternam habere: & illæ sunt „quæ testificantur de Me. Confer verf. 46, 47. & xx, 31. Vide sup. th. 4. Item Luc. xxiv, 25, 26, 27, 44.
units.tr: 3. The New Testament testimonies are similar. Luke 16:29, where it concerns avoiding condemnation: They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them. And further, concerning attaining eternal life, John 5:39: "Search the Scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life, and they are the ones that testify of Me." Compare verses 46, 47, and 20:31. See above, thesis 4. Likewise Luke 24:25, 26, 27, 44.

units.la: Unde etiàm Paulus, Actor. xx, 27. „Non subter„fugi, quominùs annunciarem vobis omne Dei consilium: cum xxvi, 22. „Perstiti in hunc usque diem, testifi„cans (ista) tùm parvis, tùm magnis ; nec quicquam di„cens extra ea, quæ Prophetæ ac Moses futura prædixerunt. Confer xvii, 11. 1 Cor. iv, 6. Rom. xv, 4, 5. Jac. i, 21, 25.
units.tr: Hence also Paul, Acts 20:27: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God"; compare 26:22: "I have continued to this day, testifying (these things) both to small and great, and saying nothing beyond those things which the Prophets and Moses foretold would come to pass." Compare 17:11; 1 Cor. 4:6; Rom. 15:4, 5; James 1:21, 25.

units.la: Iterùm Gal. i, 8, 9. „Etiamsi nos, aut Angelus è „cœlo euangelizet vobis præter (id) quod vobis euangelizavimus, anathema esto. Ut antè diximus, etiàm nunc „iterùm dico ; Si quis vobis euangelizaverit præter (id) quod accepistis, anathema esto. Sicut etiàm ultimus liber N. T. atque adeò universus Canon, obsignatus est Apoc. xxii, 18, 19. „Enimverò unà testor cuivis au„dienti Verba Prophetiæ libri hujus ; Si quis adjecerit „ad hæc, imponet ei Deus plagas scriptas in libro isto: Et „si quis abstulerit (aliquid) ex verbis libri Prophetiæ hu„ius, auferet Deus partem ejus è libro vitæ, & ex urbe illâ „sanctâ, & ex iis quæ scripta sunt in libro isto.
units.tr: Again, Gal. 1:8, 9: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you beyond what we have preached to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so now I say again: If anyone preaches to you beyond what you have received, let him be accursed." Just as the last book of the New Testament, and indeed the whole canon, was sealed, Rev. 22:18, 19: "For I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these things, God will lay upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away (anything) from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the book of life, and from that holy city, and from those things which are written in this book."

units.la: 4. Idem probamus ex ratione Regulæ, seu Normæ, ad quam fides & vita nostra exigenda: Phil. iii, 16. Gal. vi, 16. Vide sup. th. 4. Item Jef. viii, 20. sup. cap. i. th. 6. Atqui Regulam perfectam esse oportet. S. Scriptura etiam Testamentum complectitur, & quidem confirmatum: cui nihil adjiciendum: Gal. iii, 15. Et passim usitatissima est appellatio tùm Veteris, tùm Novi Testamenti. Nihil ergò ad Perfectionem S. Scripturæ deest.
units.tr: 4. We prove the same from the reasoning of the Rule, or Norm, by which our faith and life must be regulated: Phil. 3:16; Gal. 6:16. See above, thesis 4. Likewise Isa. 8:20, see above, chapter 1, thesis 6. But the Rule must be perfect. Holy Scripture also comprises the Testament, and indeed a confirmed one, to which nothing is to be added: Gal. 3:15. And the appellation of both the Old and the New Testament is everywhere in most common use. Nothing therefore is lacking to the perfection of Holy Scripture.

units.la: XXXII. Adversantur huic veritati Traditiones non scriptæ ; seu Verbum Dei non scriptum ; ubi hoc jactatur, tanquàm ad fidem ac mores vivendi etiàm necessarium, ut salutem consequamur.
units.tr: XXXII. Against this truth stand the unwritten traditions, or the unwritten Word of God, where this is boasted of as necessary also for faith and for the conduct of life, in order that we may attain salvation.

units.la: Tradere proprie de rebus dicitur, quæ de manû in manum dando transferuntur: metaphoricè significat docere; sive id fiat viva voce, sive scripto. Correlata autem sunt Tradere, & Accipere: 1 Cor. XI, 32 „Ego accepi a Domino, quod & tradidi vobis &c. XV, 3. „Tradidi enim vobis inprimis, quod & accepi, Christum „videlicet mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundum Scripturas, &c.
units.tr: To hand down is properly said of things that are transferred by giving from hand to hand; metaphorically it means to teach, whether this is done by word of mouth or in writing. To hand down and to receive are correlatives: 1 Cor. 11:23: "I received from the Lord what I also handed down to you," etc. 15:3: "For I handed down to you first of all what I also received, namely that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures," etc.

units.la: Judæi præter Legem Dei scriptam, תורה שבכתב jactant etiam oralem, תורה שבעל פה: hanc autem contendunt, Mosi Divinitus quoque revelatam fuisse, sive traditam, viva voce tantum; ejusdemque cum scriptura Divinæ auctoritatis. Suntque Kabbalah, & Mishnah.
units.tr: The Jews, besides the written Law of God [תורה שבכתב], also boast of an oral one [תורה שבעל פה]. They contend that this too was revealed or handed down by God to Moses, by word of mouth only, and that it has the same divine authority as the Scripture. These are the Kabbalah and the Mishnah.

units.la: קבלה (à קבל accepit,) partim practica est, quæ ferè Magica; partim theoretica, cujus tredecim species, seu modos, recensent: atque istis artibus ex literis transpositis, aut in numerum resolutis, vel aliter mutatis, itemque ex punctis & accentibus S. Scripturæ, innumera mysteria elici temerè ac superstitiosè dicunt.
units.tr: The Kabbalah [קבלה] (from [קבל], he received) is partly practical, *which is almost magical; partly theoretical, of which they list thirteen species or modes. By these arts, with letters transposed, or reduced to numbers, or otherwise changed, and likewise from the points and accents of Holy Scripture, they rashly and superstitiously claim that countless mysteries are drawn out.

units.la: משנה, διδασκαλίαι, juxta eosdem, sunt penitiores cerimoniarum ac præceptorum Legalium explicationes, dubiorum solutiones, & variæ constitutiones: quæ tandem satis diu post adventum Christi scripto comprehensæ, ac deinceps prolixis Rabbinorum commentariis (nomine גמרא, h. e. complementi) auctæ & gravatæ, sic pariter constituunt corpus Talmudicum; quasi Jus illorum, tam Canonicum, quam Civile.
units.tr: The Mishnah [משנה], teachings [διδασκαλίαι], according to the same writers, are the more inward explanations of ceremonies and legal precepts, solutions of doubtful points, and various constitutions. These, committed to writing only a good while after the coming of Christ, and afterwards enlarged and burdened by lengthy commentaries of the Rabbis (called [גמרא], that is, completion), similarly form the Talmudic corpus, as it were their law, both canonical and civil.

units.la: Opponenda autem illis argumenta ex V. T. etiam modo producta, pro Perfectione S. Scripturæ.
units.tr: The arguments from the Old Testament, which have just been produced for the perfection of Holy Scripture, are to be set against these.

units.la: Observandum item; quómodò Servator noster ad
units.tr: It is also to be observed how our Saviour

units.la: Scripta Mosis ac Prophetarum semper provocaverit: Traditiones vero non scriptas nunquam commendaverit, neque approbaverit; imo diserte perstrinxerit, ut quibus illi mandata Dei facerent irrita, & frustra Deum colérent; Matth. xv, 3, 6, 9. ex Isef. xxix, 13. Quin & inter ipsos Iudaeos rectius hac saltem parte sensisse eos, qui שמרים h. e. Scripturarii appellabantur; quod rejectis omnibus istis Traditionibus, solo Verbo Dei niterentur.
units.tr: always appealed to the writings of Moses and the Prophets, but never commended or approved unwritten traditions; indeed he plainly censured them, as those by which men made the commandments of God void and worshipped God in vain: Matt. 15:3, 6, 9, from Isa. 29:13. Moreover, among the Jews themselves, those who were called [שמרים], that is, Scripturists, *judged more rightly at least in this respect; for, rejecting all those traditions, they relied on the Word of God alone.

units.la: XXXIII. Papale Concilium Tridentinum etiam defi- nivit,
units.tr: XXXIII. The Papal Council of Trent also defined:

units.la: „Salutarem veritatem & morum disciplinam „contineri in Libris scriptis, & sine scripto Traditionibus; quae ex ipsius Christi ore ab Apostolis acceptae, „aut ab ipsis Apostolis, Spiritu Sancto dictante, quasi „per manus traditae, ad nos usque pervenerint. Ac porro, „omnes Libros, tam V. quam N. T. nec non Traditiones ipsas, pari pietatis affectu ac reverentia suscipit „veneratur. Quam sententiam plenius exequuntur Doctores Pontificii.
units.tr: "The saving truth and the discipline of morals are contained in written books and in unwritten traditions, which, received by the Apostles from the very mouth of Christ, or handed down by the Apostles themselves as if by hand, under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, have come down to us. Moreover, all the books, both of the Old and New Testament, and the traditions themselves, it receives and venerates with an equal feeling of piety and reverence." The Papist teachers carry out this opinion more fully.

units.la: Sic Becanus Traditiones etiam V.T. Mosaicas praeter S. Scripturam agnoscit, & a Pharisaicis distinguit. Idem Traditiones N.T. statuit tum Divinas & Apostolicas, partim de Dogmatibus fidei, partim de Moribus & Ritibus externis; quae parem cum Scripturâ auctoritatem habeant: tum Ecclesiasticas, quae post tempora Apostolorum a Praelatis Ecclesiae introductae sint, & merito à Christianis servari debeant.
units.tr: Thus Becanus acknowledges traditions also of the Mosaic Old Testament, apart from Holy Scripture, and distinguishes them from the Pharisaic ones. He likewise lays down traditions of the New Testament: on the one hand divine and apostolic, partly concerning the dogmas of faith and partly concerning morals and external rites, which have equal authority with Scripture; on the other hand ecclesiastical, which were introduced after the times of the Apostles by the prelates of the Church and ought rightly to be kept by Christians.

units.la: Verum per Argumenta nuper exhibita patet, dogmata qualiacunque, SS. Literis prorsus non comprehensa, vel necessaria non esse, aut etiam incerta; vel erronea & falsa.
units.tr: But from the arguments set out recently it is plain that any dogmas whatever that are not at all contained in the Holy Scriptures are either unnecessary, or else uncertain, or else erroneous and false.

units.la: Quin & Traditionum non scriptarum levitas atque incertitudo facilè etiam demonstratur ex Historiis Ecclesiasticis, antiquis Partibus, ipsisque Scriptoribus Pontificiis.
units.tr: Indeed, the lightness and uncertainty of unwritten traditions is also easily demonstrated from ecclesiastical histories, the ancient Fathers, and the Papist writers themselves.

units.la: Sicut in antiquis Ecclesiae Doctoribus pro Perse-ctione stione & Sufficientiâ S. Scripturæ satis luculenta quoque exstant testimonia.
units.tr: Just as, in the ancient teachers of the Church, there also exist quite clear testimonies to the perfection and sufficiency of Holy Scripture.

units.la: XXXIV. Obj. 1. In Festorum solennibus, Sacrificiis, &c. multa per S. Scripturam determinata non sunt: in illis ergo observari debuerunt Traditiones non scriptæ. Resp. Quæcunque in illis erant necessaria, per S. Scripturam sufficienter determinata sunt: circumstantiæ quædam, de quibus istic nihil determinatum est, libertati ac prudentiæ Sacerdotum relinquebantur.
units.tr: XXXIV. Objection 1. In the solemn festivals, the sacrifices, etc., many things are not determined by Holy Scripture; therefore unwritten traditions ought to have been observed in them. Answer: Whatever was necessary in them has been sufficiently determined by Holy Scripture; certain circumstances, about which nothing has been determined there, were left to the freedom and prudence of the priests.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ecclesia Judaïca instituit dies Purim; Esth. ix, 21, 22, 26. itémque Encænia; 1 Maccab. iv, 59. cum Ioh. x, 22. Ergo etiàm nunc admitti debent instituta, & traditiones Ecclesiasticæ. Resp. In Mardochæo circa dies Purim videtur agnoscendus Spiritus Propheticus; & sic Divina auctoritas. Alioqui, sicut etiam in Encæniis, generatim spectari deberet officium gratitudinis, & quidem juxta istam œconomiam, dùm festa obtinebant, & sacrificia, &c. unde processerit institutio istiusmodi; sed citra necessitatem universalem ac perpetuam: atque sic non valet consequentia ad instituta, vel traditiones Ecclesiasticas, quæ omnes & semper obligarent necessariò.
units.tr: Objection 2. The Jewish Church instituted the feast of Purim (Esth. 9:21, 22, 26), and likewise the feast of Dedication (1 Macc. 4:59; compare John 10:22). Therefore institutions and ecclesiastical traditions ought still to be admitted now. Answer: In Mordecai, with regard to the days of Purim, a prophetic Spirit seems to be acknowledged, and so a divine authority. Otherwise, as also in the case of the Dedication, the duty of thankfulness should be regarded in general, and indeed according to that economy, while the festivals and sacrifices etc. were in force, from which such an institution arose; but it was without universal and perpetual necessity. And so the inference does not hold for ecclesiastical institutions or traditions, which would all and always bind necessarily.

units.la: Obj. 3. Cultus Leviticus sub N. T. abrogatus est; & nova Sacramenta instituta: ergo non eadem essentialis perfectio est librorum V. T. quæ librorum N. T. Resp. 1. Cultus Leviticus sub V. T. completebatur adjuncta signa Euangelii promissionis, & Christi venturi: terminari propterea debuit, quantum ad observantiam attinet, cum istâ œconomiâ: Hebr. vii, 1-x. manente tamen eâdem doctrinâ, quantum ad ipsam essentiam. 2. Sacramenta nostra sunt sacra sigilla, pro N. Test. Divinâ auctoritate institura: sic tamen, ut res eadem signata sub V. T. quoque obtinuerit: (quamvis aliæ tunc fuerint circumstantiæ;) & signis isti œconomiæ convenientibus obsignata etiàm fuerit. Quin hæc ipsa insuper signa, aliis quibusdam signis, atque etiam phrasibus, sic insinuata fuerunt; ut nova doctrina censeri prorsus non debeat. Vide inter alia, 1 Cor. x, 1-4. Ezech. xxxvi, 25. Zach. xiii, 1. Psal. xxxiii, 5. Prov. ix, 1, 5. Jes. lv, 1, 2.
units.tr: Objection 3. The Levitical worship was abrogated under the New Testament, and new sacraments were instituted; therefore the books of the Old Testament do not have the same essential perfection as the books of the New Testament. Answer 1: The Levitical worship under the Old Testament was completed with the added signs of the promise of the Gospel and of the coming Christ; therefore, as far as its observance is concerned, it had to come to an end with that economy (Heb. 7:1–10:...), while the same doctrine remained as to its very essence. 2. Our sacraments are holy seals instituted by divine authority for the New Testament; yet in such a way that the same thing signified was also in force under the Old Testament (although the circumstances were then different), and was also sealed by signs suited to that economy. Indeed these very signs were further insinuated by certain other signs and even by phrases, so that the doctrine ought not to be considered new at all. See among other places 1 Cor. 10:1–4; Ezek. 36:25; Zech. 13:1; Ps. 33:5; Prov. 9:1, 5; Isa. 55:1, 2.

units.la: Obj. 4. Non constat ex S. Scriptura, quodnam ante institutam Circumcisionem, quin etiam deinceps in feminis, fuerit remedium adversus peccatum originale. Resp. Imo satis constat, remedium adversus omnia electorum salvandorum peccata, semper fuisse gratiam Dei in Christo; sicut etiam nunc est: quam Circumcisio suo tempore non contulit proprie; sed collatam obsignavit, juxta foedus & promissionem Divinam. Vide Gen. iii, 15. xvii, 7, 11. Rom. iv, 11. Act. x, 43. xv, 11. Hebr. xiii, 8.
units.tr: Objection 4. It is not established from Holy Scripture what was the remedy against original sin before circumcision was instituted, and indeed afterwards in women. Answer: Indeed it is sufficiently established that the remedy against all the sins of the elect who are to be saved has always been the grace of God in Christ, just as it is now; which circumcision did not properly confer in its time, but sealed when conferred, according to the covenant and divine promise. See Gen. 3:15; 17:7, 11; Rom. 4:11; Acts 10:43; 15:11; Heb. 13:8.

units.la: Obj. 5. Joh. xvi, 12. "Adhuc multa habeo, quae vobis dicam; sed nunc non potestis portare. Ista ergo scripta non sunt; sed aliter postmodum tradita. Resp. Quae Apostoli tunc capere non poterant, & Christus isto tempore iis non dixit, quousque nobis ad salutem consequendam necessaria sunt, omnino SS. Literis continentur.
units.tr: Objection 5. John 16:12: "I still have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now." Therefore those things were not written, but were handed down otherwise afterwards. Answer: The things which the Apostles then could not grasp, and which Christ at that time did not tell them, are, in so far as they are necessary for us to obtain salvation, entirely contained in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Obj. 6. 2 Thess. ii, 15. Nempe igitur, fratres, "perstate, & retinete traditiones, quas edocti estis, tum per "sermonem, tum per epistolam nostram. Ergo necessariae etiam sunt Traditiones non scriptae. Resp. Thessalonicenses retinere debuerunt Traditiones, quas ab Apostolo acceperant: tum viva voce, per sermonem; tum per epistolam ad eos scriptam: unde nequaquam sequitur, Apostolum quaedam ad salutem necessaria Thessalonicensibus tradidisse solum viva voce; ut ea nec epistolis ad ipsos datis, nec aliis etiam scriptis Θεοπνεύστοις, comprehensa fuerint.
units.tr: Objection 6. 2 Thess. 2:15: "So then, brethren, stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our letter." Therefore unwritten traditions are also necessary. Answer: The Thessalonians ought to hold the traditions which they had received from the Apostle, both by word of mouth, in the spoken message, and by the letter written to them. From this it by no means follows that the Apostle handed down to the Thessalonians, solely by word of mouth, some things necessary for salvation, so that they were not included either in the letters given to them or in other writings [θεοπνεύστοις] divinely inspired.

units.la: Obj. 7. Hebr. xiii, 17. Obedite Ductoribus vestris, & obsecundate: ergo recipi & observari debent, quae a Praelatis Ecclesiae constituuntur. Resp. Obediendum est Antecessoribus Ecclesiasticis, dum excubantes pro animabus singulorum, tanquam rationem reddituri, ea docent, explicant, applicant, quae ipse Dominus praescripsit; cujus illi Ministri solum sunt. In applicatione ista fit quidem particularium circumstantiarum prudens determinatio, boni ordinis & communis aedificationis causa; sic tamen, ut rebus ita exigentibus determinatio illa variari possit ac debeat: 1 Cor. xiv, 40. Gal. v, 1. Col. ii, 18.
units.tr: Objection 7. Heb. 13:17: "Obey your leaders and submit to them." Therefore what is laid down by the prelates of the Church ought to be received and observed. Answer: One must obey the ecclesiastical leaders while, watching over the souls of individuals as those who must give an account, they teach, explain and apply what the Lord himself has prescribed, of which they are only the ministers. In this application there is indeed a prudent determination of particular circumstances, for the sake of good order and common edification; yet in such a way that this determination can and ought to vary as things require: 1 Cor. 14:40; Gal. 5:1; Col. 2:18.

units.la: XXXV. Perspicuitas, sive Claritas, est ea S. Scripturae virtus, per quam omnia istic ad salutem necessaria intelligi idonea sunt; quin & reipsa, per gratiam Dei, intelliguntur a subjectis capacibus, attente & accurate legentibus.
units.tr: XXXV. Perspicuity, or clarity, is that virtue of Holy Scripture by which all things there necessary for salvation are fit to be understood; and indeed they are actually understood, through the grace of God, by capable subjects who read attentively and carefully.

units.la: Ista autem virtus spectanda, tum objective in se; tum quomodo subjective in hominibus recipiatur.
units.tr: This virtue, however, is to be considered both objectively in itself, and as it is received subjectively in human beings.

units.la: Objective, in se, sive in suo systemate, Verbum Dei esse clarum ac perspicuum, vel aptum intelligi, probamus 1. disertis quibusdam testimoniis: Psal. xix, 8, 9. Praeceptum Jehovae purum: illuminans oculos. cxix, 105. Lucerna pedi meo Verbum tuum; & lumen semitae meae. 130. Ostium verborum tuorum illuminat, 2 Petr. i, 19. - Quem (sermonem Propheticum) bene facitis quod attendatis, velut lucernam splendentem in obscuro loco. Adde Prov. vi, 23. 2 Cor. iii, 8, 9. ii. iv, 4. Deut. xxx, 11, 14. cum Rom. x, 6, 7. & Actor. xxvi, 22. Ergo Verbum Dei, SS. Literis expressum, lucis instar, per se, suis radiis, fulget, conspicitur, intelligitur.
units.tr: Objectively, that is in itself, or in its own system, we prove that the Word of God is clear and perspicuous, or fit to be understood, first by certain explicit testimonies: Ps. 19:8, 9: "The commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes." Ps. 119:105: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." 130: "The opening of your words gives light." 2 Pet. 1:19: "which you do well to heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place." Add Prov. 6:23; 2 Cor. 3:8, 9; 4:4; Deut. 30:11, 14 with Rom. 10:6, 7; and Acts 26:22. Therefore the Word of God, expressed in the Holy Scriptures, like light, shines by itself, by its own rays, is seen and is understood.

units.la: 2. Ex fine & effectis: S. Scriptura ex ordinatione Dei; non solum Antecessores Ecclesiarum, aut adultos; sed adolescentes etiam, & pueros, potest sapientes reddere ad salutem. 2 Tim. iii, 15. Te a puero sacras Literas novisse, quae te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, &c. Psal. cxix, 130. - Intelligere facit simplices. Prov. i, 4. Ad dandum simplicibus calliditatem; puero scientiam & cogitationem. 1 Ioh. ii, 13, 14. Scrip,,bo vobis, patres, - adolescentes, - pueruli, &c. Adde Ioh. v, 39. xx, 31. Act. xvii, 11. Ergo S. Scriptura ex ista Dei ordinatione, & juxta talem usum, in se clara est atque apta intelligi.
units.tr: 2. From its end and effects: Holy Scripture, by the ordinance of God, can make wise unto salvation not only the teachers of the Churches or adults, but also youths and children. 2 Tim. 3:15: "from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise unto salvation." Ps. 119:130: "It gives understanding to the simple." Prov. 1:4: "to give prudence to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion." 1 John 2:13, 14: "I write to you, fathers... young men... little children," etc. Add John 5:39; 20:31; Acts 17:11. Therefore Holy Scripture, by this ordinance of God and according to such a use, is in itself clear and fit to be understood.

units.la: 3. Ex consideratione Auctoris; qui Lux est: 1 Ioh. 1, 5. & Pater Luminum: Iac. 1, 17. ac proinde potuit Literas suas dare satis claras: imo etiam voluit, juxta 1 Tim. 11, 4. Quosvis homines vult servari, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Psal. xxv, 14. Secretum Iehovae timentibus eum: & pactum ejus, ut scire faciat eos. Ipse promisit, Matth. vii, 7. 11. se petentibus daturum liberaliter; non pro pane lapidem, &c. adeoque nec libros. γεγραπται αγεγραπται. Ergo Scriptura, qua Deus doctrinam salutarem comprehendit, objective clara est.
units.tr: 3. From consideration of the Author, who is Light (1 John 1:5) and the Father of lights (James 1:17), and who therefore could give his writings clear enough. Indeed, he also willed to do so, according to 1 Tim. 11, 4: he wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Psalm 25:14: "The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will make them know his covenant." He himself promised, Matt. 7:7, 11, to give liberally to those who ask; he will not give a stone for bread, and so on, and therefore not books either. It is written; it has been written down [γέγραπται, ἀναγέγραπται]. Therefore Scripture, in which God has comprehended the saving doctrine, is clear objectively.

units.la: 4. A conditione subjectorum recipientium: quibus Deus dedit, ut est Ephes. 1, 18. illuminatos oculos mentis, ad sciendum, quae sit spes illa vocationis. Et 2 Cor. 11, 10, 12. revelavit per Spiritum suum; ut sciamus, quae Deus est nobis gratificatus. Consequenter, verf. 15. Spiritualis homo judicat omnia. Item Ioh. vi, 45. Scriptum est in Prophetis; Erunt omnes docti a Deo. vii, 17. Siquis voluerit voluntatem ejus facere, cognoscet de doctrina, utrum ex Deo sit. 1 Ioh. 11, 27. Ipsa unctio docet vos de omnibus. Cum Ioh. xx, 31. Rom. xv, 4.
units.tr: 4. From the condition of the subjects who receive it, to whom God gives, as in Eph. 1:18, the eyes of the mind enlightened, so that they may know what is the hope of his calling; and in 2 Cor. 11, 10, 12, he has revealed through his Spirit that we may know what God has freely given us. Consequently, v. 15: "The spiritual man judges all things." Likewise John 6:45: "It is written in the Prophets, They shall all be taught by God." John 7:17: "If anyone wills to do his will, he will know concerning the teaching whether it is from God." 1 John 2:27: "The anointing itself teaches you about all things." Compare John 20:31 and Rom. 15:4.

units.la: 2 Tim. iii, 16. Ista autem subjectorum dispositio, & elevatio ad illum actum, objecti aptitudinem & claritatem omnino supponit.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3:16. Now this disposition of the subjects, and their being raised to that act, presupposes entirely the fitness and clarity of the object.

units.la: XXXVI. Obj. 1. 2 Petr. iii, 16.
units.tr: XXXVI. Objection 1. 2 Peter 3:16.

units.la: ,,In quibus (descriptis a Paulo in suis epistolis) sunt nonnulla dissicilia intellectu; quae indocti, parumque stabiles, detorquent, ut & reliquas Scripturas, suo ipsorum exitio. Ergo Scriptura est obscura, & hominibus indoctis lectu periculosa. Resp. 1. Concedimus, in SS. Literis occurrere etiam quaedam intellectu difficilia; utpote mysteria, sublimitate sua captum humanum (si hominem mere ineré naturalem spectes, vel etiàm cognitionem adæquatam, & ϧ δἰάλ, ) excedentia: attamen ista sic accommodatè proponuntur, ut per gratiam Dei cognoscere, & credere possimus, saltem τὰ ὃσα, quantum quidem ad salutem consequendam opus est, quoniàm ex ordinatione Dei ista est proprius S. Scripturæ finis. Vide sup. th. 4. Quæ interim alicubi breviter & minùs clarè expressa sunt; alibi magis aperte, distinctè, & fusè traduntur in eodem syntagmate. 2. Quod homines indocti, parumque stabiles, quædam, vel etiàm plura SS. Literis comprehensa, detorqueant suo ipsorum exitio; id vitio istorum subjectorum evenit: sicut etiàm Euangelii prædicatio nonnullis ex accidenti est odor mortis ad mortem; 2 Corinth. 11, 16. Confer Hos. xiv, 10.
units.tr: "In these letters (described by Paul in his epistles) there are some things hard to understand, which the unlearned and the unstable twist, to their own destruction, as they do the rest of the Scriptures. Therefore Scripture is obscure, and dangerous for uneducated men to read." Answer 1. We concede that in the holy Writings there also occur some things difficult to understand, namely mysteries which, by their sublimity, exceed the human capacity (if you regard man as a mere natural man, or even adequate knowledge, and per se). Yet these things are so suitably set forth that by the grace of God we can know and believe them, at least τὰ ὅσα [the things necessary], as far as is needed for obtaining salvation, since by God's ordinance this is the proper end of Holy Scripture. See above, thesis 4. Those things which are at some places briefly and less clearly expressed are elsewhere set out more openly, distinctly and fully in the same system. 2. That unlearned and unstable men twist certain things, or even many things, comprehended in the Holy Writings, to their own destruction, happens through the fault of those subjects; just as also the preaching of the gospel is, by accident, to some "a fragrance from death to death," 2 Cor. 2:16. Compare Hos. 14:10.

units.la: Obj. 2. Eunuchus Æthiops Jesaiam legens, & interrogatus num etiàm intelligeret; respondit: „Quomodo enim possim, nisi mihi quispiam dux viæ fuerit? Act. viii, 30, 31. Quin & David, ipse Propheta, Deum rogavit, Psal. cxix, 18. „Revela oculos meos; & aspiciam mirabilia de Lege tua. Ergo, &c. Resp. 1. Eunuchus ille, Religionis Christianæ vixdùm catechumenus, non satis intellexit prophetiam, Isa. LIII. quod per ipsius imperitiam factum est. Nec valet consequentia à capite aliquo Prophetico, ad totum systema Biblicum. 2. David non petiit, ut S. Scriptura magis lucida redderetur; sed ut oculi sui revelarentur. Sic vitium subjectivè in se agnovit; non objectivè in S. Scripturâ.
units.tr: Objection 2. The Ethiopian eunuch, reading Isaiah and asked whether he even understood, replied: "How can I, unless someone guides me?" Acts 8:30, 31. Indeed David, the prophet himself, asked God, Ps. 119:18: "Open my eyes, that I may behold wonderful things from your law." Therefore, etc. Answer 1. That eunuch, scarcely yet a catechumen of the Christian religion, did not understand the prophecy of Isa. 53 well enough, which happened through his own inexperience. Nor does the inference from one prophetic chapter hold for the whole biblical system. 2. David did not ask that Scripture be made clearer, but that his eyes be opened. Thus he recognised the fault subjectively in himself, not objectively in Scripture.

units.la: XXXVII. Subjectivè claritas ista varie recipitur in hominibus. 1. Irregeniti, omnis gratiæ supernaturalis expertes, atque adeo solâ naturali facultate intellectivâ præditi, si S. Scripturam attente legant, plurima quidem grammatice & historice possunt intelligere; sed Divinam, spiritualem, vivificam, & salutarem lutarem eorum veritatem percipere non possunt; quin etiam contrario animo affecti sunt: Rom. viii, 7. 1 Cor. ii, 14. Tit. i, 15.
units.tr: XXXVII. This subjective clarity is received variously by men. 1. The unregenerate, lacking all supernatural grace and so endowed only with the natural faculty of understanding, if they read Scripture attentively, can indeed understand many things grammatically and historically; but they cannot perceive its divine, spiritual, life-giving and saving truth; indeed they are disposed in a contrary spirit: Rom. 8:7; 1 Cor. 2:14; Tit. 1:15.

units.la: 2. Quibus vero gratia saltem illuminans, refrenans, persuadens, & convincens obtigit, hi ulterius procedunt; & veritatem Divinam cum gaudio accipiunt, ac multa faciunt: Matth. xiii, 20, 21. Marc. vi, 20. Confer Hebr. vi, 4, 5. x, 26, 17. 2 Petr. ii, 20, 21, 22. Matth. xii, 31, 32. Verum salutaris intellectus Verbi Divini subjecta capacia non sunt, propter suam indispositionem, Hos. xiv, 10. Rom. viii, 7. 1 Cor. ii, 14. 2, 11, 16. Eph. ii, 1, 5. iv, 18. Tit. i, 15. 2 Petr. iii, 16. Quam subjectivam eorum impotentiam, nihil obstante objectiva Verbi Divini claritate, asserimus contra Socinianos & Remonstrantes.
units.tr: 2. Those, however, to whom grace has come at least as enlightening, restraining, persuading and convicting, proceed further; they receive the divine truth with joy and do many things: Matt. 13:20, 21; Mark 6:20. Compare Heb. 6:4, 5; 10:26, 27; 2 Pet. 2:20, 21, 22; Matt. 12:31, 32. Yet the subjects are not capable of saving understanding of the divine Word, because of their indisposition: Hos. 14:10; Rom. 8:7; 1 Cor. 2:14; 2, 11, 16; Eph. 2:1, 5; 4:18; Tit. 1:15; 2 Pet. 3:16. We assert this subjective impotence of theirs, notwithstanding the objective clarity of the divine Word, against the Socinians and the Remonstrants.

units.la: 3. Regeniti vero, ex Spiritu regenerante spirituales nati; Joh. iii, 6. Spiritus vivificantis participes; vi, 63. sic novae creaturae, quibus omnia nova; 2 Cor. v, 17. ac speciatim oculi mentis illuminati; Eph. i, 18. ut mentem Christi habeant; 1 Cor. ii, 16. & per fidem ejus vivant; Gal. ii, 20. hi veritatem salutarem vivide, & cum sensu spirituali, percipiunt. 1 Cor. ii, 15. Spiritualis homo omnia dijudicat. Confer Psal. xxxiv, 9. xxxvi, 9.
units.tr: 3. The regenerate, however, born spiritual from the regenerating Spirit: John 3:6; sharers in the life-giving Spirit: 6:63; thus new creatures, to whom all things are new: 2 Cor. 5:17; and especially with the eyes of the mind enlightened: Eph. 1:18; that they may have the mind of Christ: 1 Cor. 2:16; and live by his faith: Gal. 2:20; these perceive the saving truth vividly and with a spiritual sense. 1 Cor. 2:15: "The spiritual man judges all things." Compare Ps. 34:9; 36:9.

units.la: Observandum interim, jam sub N.T. magis plenam & distinctam dari notitiam, quam fuit sub V.T. ubi doctrina de Christo venturo prophetica erat & typica: Matth. xi, 11, xiii, 16, 17. Talis tamen ac tanta etiam nunc obtinuit, quanta sub ista foederis oeconomia ad salutem erat necessaria.
units.tr: It is to be observed meanwhile that under the New Testament there is now a fuller and more distinct knowledge than there was under the Old, where the doctrine of the coming Christ was prophetic and typical: Matt. 11:11; 13:16, 17. Yet such and so great a knowledge as is necessary for salvation under this dispensation of the covenant is also now attainable.

units.la: Praeterea infantes, seu incipientes, distinguendi sunt ab adolescentibus; atque etiam adultis & perfectis; qui sic comparate appellantur: Hebr. v, 12, 13, 14. 1 Cor. iii, 1, 2, 3. 1 Joh. ii, 12, 13, 14.
units.tr: Moreover, infants, or beginners, are to be distinguished from young men, and also from adults and the perfect, who are so called by comparison: Heb. 5:12, 13, 14; 1 Cor. 3:1, 2, 3; 1 John 2:12, 13, 14.

units.la: XXXVIII. Respectu subjectivae imperitiae, minus profecti quaedam adhuc intelligere nequeunt absque ductore:
units.tr: XXXVIII. With respect to subjective ignorance, those who are less advanced cannot yet understand some things without a guide:

units.la: ductore: Act. viii, 31. Confer Luc. xxiv, 25. Quin & provectiores constitentur, se ex parte cognoscere: 1Cor. xiii, 9. & Deum precantur, ut major sibi detur illuminatio: Psal. cxix, 18, 34. 135.
units.tr: a guide: Acts 8:31. Compare Luke 24:25. Indeed, even those who are more advanced confess that they know only in part: 1 Cor. 13:9. And they pray that greater illumination may be given to them: Ps. 119:18, 34, 135.

units.la: Hinc profectui studendum est, in hac vita jugiter: quo magis distinctè & profundè mysteria Divina intelligamus, veritatem illam firmiter credamus, bona Evangelica nobis applicemus, & sancta præcepta constanter ac sincerè observemus. Sic instandum est lectioni, meditationi, collationi; audiendæ sunt explicationes & applicationes Pastorum ac Doctorum: Joh. v, 39. 1 Tim. iv, 13. Col. iii, 16. Act. xvii, 11. Eph. iv, 12. ità videl, ut omnes explicationes & applicationes non aliunde, quam ex ipsis SS. Literis hauriantur; & ad easdem, tanquam ad lapidem Lydium, referantur: Nehem. viii, 8, 9. Isf. viii, 20. 2 Tim. iii, 16, 17. Act. xvii, 11. Rom. xii, 7. Unde patet, dum nihil necesse est lucem aliunde inferri S. Scripturæ, constare ei in suo syntagmate suam Claritatem, seu Perspicuitatem.
units.tr: Therefore we must strive for progress continually in this life, so that we may understand the divine mysteries more distinctly and more deeply, believe that truth firmly, apply the Gospel blessings to ourselves, and observe the holy precepts constantly and sincerely. We must press on in reading, meditation and conference; we ought to hear the explanations and applications of ministers and teachers: John 5:39; 1 Tim. 4:13; Col. 3:16; Acts 17:11; Eph. 4:12. But this must be done in such a way that all explanations and applications are drawn from no other source than Holy Scripture itself, and are referred back to it as to a touchstone: Neh. 8:8, 9; Isa. 8:20; 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; Acts 17:11; Rom. 12:7. Hence it is clear that, while there is no need for light to be brought to Holy Scripture from elsewhere, its clarity, or perspicuity, belongs to it in its own system.

units.la: XXXIX. Necessitas hic non absoluta, sed ex hypothesi voluntatis Divinæ intelligitur: juxta quam Ecclesia jam nunc S. Scriptura carere non debet, aut poteft, ob Divinam ordinationem hujus medii ad salutarem instructionem ac demonstrationem Theologicam.
units.tr: XXXIX. The necessity here is not absolute but is understood on the hypothesis of the divine will: according to this, the Church ought not, and cannot, now be without Holy Scripture, because of the divine ordinance of this means for salutary instruction and theological demonstration.

units.la: Hæc astruitur 1. diserto testimonio, Jude, 3. Necesse habui vobis scribere, &c.
units.tr: This is established, first, by the explicit testimony of Jude 3: I felt it necessary to write to you, etc.

units.la: 2. Ex mandatis scribendi. Hæc autem occurrunt primò generalia, in vocationibus Prophetarum, Apostolorum, & Euangelistarum; ubi jussi sunt docere non tantum vivâ voce, sed pro re nata etiam scripto: Matth. xxviii, 19. Docete omnes gentes, &c. quod citra scriptionem sic fieri non potuit, ut ipsorum doctrina pertingeret usque ad consummationem sæculi. Vide etiam 2 Tim. iii, 16. 2 Petr. i, 21. sup. th. 2. quæ Divina inspiratio fatis manifestum mandatum infert.
units.tr: Second, from the commands to write. These occur first in general form, in the callings of the prophets, apostles and evangelists, where they were ordered to teach not only by the living voice but, as occasion required, also in writing: Matt. 28:19, Go and teach all nations, etc. This could not have been done without writing, so that their teaching would reach to the end of the age. See also 2 Tim. 3:16 and 2 Pet. 1:21, cited above in thesis 2, where divine inspiration clearly implies a command.

units.la: Accedunt specialia mandata: Exod. xvii, 14. „Di„xit Jehovah ad Moseh, Scribe istud (pro) memoriali „in libro, &c. xxxiv, 27. Scribe tibi verba hæc. &c. Adde Deut. xxxi, 18. Jerem. xxx, 2. xxxvi, 2. Apoc. i, 11. Imo ipse Deus scribendo præivit, suamque doctrinam scripto conservari voluit. Vide sup. th. 2. & 28.
units.tr: There are also special commands: Exod. 17:14, "The LORD said to Moses, Write this as a memorial in a book," etc.; 34:27, Write these words for yourself, etc. Add Deut. 31:18; Jer. 30:2; 36:2; Rev. 1:11. Indeed God himself went before in writing, and willed that his doctrine be preserved in writing. See above, theses 2 and 28.

units.la: Ac porro mandata describendi, legendi, & meditandi S. Scripturam: Deut. xvii, 18, 19. xxxi, 6,-13. Luc. xvi, 30, 31, Joh. v, 39. 1 Tim. iv, 13. quæ quidem supponunt necessitatem ipsius S. Scripturæ.
units.tr: Furthermore, there are the commands to copy, read and meditate on Holy Scripture: Deut. 17:18, 19; 31:6, 13; Luke 16:30, 31; John 5:39; 1 Tim. 4:13. These presuppose the necessity of Holy Scripture itself.

units.la: 3. Ex consideratione finium: Deus S. Scripturam ordinavit ad salutarem Ecclesiæ instructionem, ac demonstrationem Theologicam: Joh. xx, 31. Rom. xv, 4.
units.tr: Third, from the consideration of its ends: God ordained Holy Scripture for the salutary instruction of the Church and for theological demonstration: John 20:31; Rom. 15:4.

units.la: 2 Tim. iii, 15, 16, 17. Vide sup. th. 4. Adde Luc. xvi, 28, 29. Joh. v, 39. 1 Joh. i, 4.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3:15, 16, 17. See above, thesis 4. Add Luke 16:28, 29; John 5:39; 1 John 1:4.

units.la: 4. Denique, Deus hoc modo nobis prospectum voluit adversus oblivionem hominum, fraudes Diaboli, & seductiones hæreticorum. Deut. xxxi, 26, 27. Vide sup. th. 28. Ief. viii, 19, 20. „Cum autem dixe„rint ad vos: Quærite à Pythonibus, & a Divinis, qui „garriunt, & loquuntur: (dicite illis;) Num popu„lus à Deo suo requiret? pro vivis à mortuis? Ad legem, „& ad testimonium &c. Luc. I, 1,-4. Quoniam multi „aggressi sunt componere narrationem rerum quarum „plena fides nobis sacta est:-Visum etiam est mihi, omnia „alte (repetita) penitus assecuto, ordine illa ad te scribere, præstantissime Theophile: Ut agnoscas, cer„tas esse res, quas auditione accepisti. 2 Pet. I, 16, - 19. „Non enim arte compositas fabulas secuti, &c. Et habemus firmissimum illum sermonem Propheticum, &c. Adde 2 Cor. xi. 3, 13, 14, 15. cum Gal. I, 6, 9. Phil. iii, 16. - 19.
units.tr: Fourth, in this way God wished to provide for us against the forgetfulness of men, the frauds of the devil and the seductions of heretics. Deut. 31:26, 27; see above, thesis 28. Isa. 8:19, 20: "But when they say to you: Seek of the mediums and of the wizards, who chirp and mutter, (say to them:) Should not a people seek its God? Should the living seek the dead? To the law and to the testimony," etc. Luke 1:1–4: "Since many have undertaken to compile an account of the things of which we have been fully assured, it seemed good to me, having traced everything carefully from the beginning, to write them out in order for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the things you have been taught are certain." 2 Pet. 1:16–19: "For we did not follow cleverly devised myths," etc., and "we have that most sure prophetic word," etc. Add 2 Cor. 11:3, 13–15, with Gal. 1:6–9; Phil. 3:16–19.

units.la: XL. Pontificii mirum in modum extollunt Verbum scriptum in corde Ecclesiæ & Papæ: sed S. Scripturæ necessitatem extenuant, vel negant, temere interdum jactantes, eam fortuitis solùm occasionibus conscriptam esse, sine speciali mandato Divino, &c. contrà quam modò ostensum est.
units.tr: XL. The Papists wonderfully exalt the Word written in the heart of the Church and of the Pope; but they minimise or deny the necessity of Holy Scripture, sometimes rashly asserting that it was written only on chance occasions, without a special divine command, etc. This is contrary to what has been shown just now.

units.la: Pseudo-Enthusiastæ vero, & Libertini, infantibus quidem usum S.S. Literarum concedunt; sed viris cum minimè convenire contendunt.
units.tr: The pseudo-enthusiasts and the Libertines, indeed, grant the use of the Holy Scriptures to infants, but they contend that it is by no means suitable for grown men.

units.la: Alia omninò mens fuit Regio Prophetæ : Psal. XIX, 12. CXIX. 18, 96. 99, 100. cum Deut. XVII. 18, 19. Josh. I, 7, 8. Apostolo Paulo, Timotheum Euangelistam ad electionem remittenti; 1. IV, 13. 2, III, 14, -17.
units.tr: The mind of the royal prophet was altogether different: Ps. 19:12; 119:18, 96, 99, 100; compare Deut. 17:18, 19; Josh. 1:7, 8; and the apostle Paul, sending Timothy, the evangelist, back to the Scriptures: 1 Tim. 4:13; 2 Tim. 3:14–17.

units.la: Obj. 1. Ecclesia est antiquior S. Scripturâ: ergo hæc non necessaria. Resp. Inepta est consequentia: Noah diù ante arcam extitit: hæc tamen necessaria fuit; postquam Deus eam ordinavit ac mandavit ad ipsius conservationem. Ecclesia etiam fuit ante Baptismum, imo & ante Circumcisionem; multòque magis (ad hominem argumentamur) ante Pontificem Romanum. Confer sup. th. 1.
units.tr: Objection 1. The Church is older than Holy Scripture; therefore Scripture is not necessary. Answer: The inference is invalid. Noah existed long before the ark, yet the ark was necessary once God had ordained and commanded it for the preservation of Noah. The Church also existed before baptism, indeed before circumcision; and much more (to argue ad hominem) before the Roman Pontiff. See above, thesis 1.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ipsa veritas salutaris, fide recepta, facit Ecclesiam: ergo. Resp. Sed veritati illi docendæ ac probandæ, ex ordinatione Divinâ, nunc S. Scriptura inservit, tanquam regula certissima & constantissima.
units.tr: Objection 2. The saving truth itself, received by faith, makes the Church; therefore... Answer: But by divine ordinance, that truth, to be taught and proved, is now served by Holy Scripture, as the most certain and constant rule.

units.la: Obj. 3. Litera occidit; Spiritus vivificat: 2 Cor. 11 3, 6. Ergo. Resp. Non ipsa S. Scriptura, ejusque usus apud fideles, istic litera occidens dicitur; (confer Joh. v, 39. XX, 31. 1 Joh. 1, 4.) sed Lex ejusque ministerium condemnans; oppositè ad Euangelium, & gratiam vivificantem ac justificantem per Spiritum comitem. Vide Prov. I. 23. Jes. LIX, 21. Gal. II. 2. 5. 1 Thess. II. 13.
units.tr: Objection 3. "The letter kills; the Spirit gives life," 2 Cor. 3:6; therefore... Answer: It is not Holy Scripture itself, nor its use among the faithful, that is called "the killing letter" there (compare John 5:39; 20:31; 1 John 1:4), but the Law and its ministry, which condemns, as opposed to the Gospel and to grace, which gives life and justifies through the accompanying Spirit. See Prov. 1:23; Isa. 59:21; Gal. 2:2, 5; 1 Thess. 2:13.

units.la: Obj. 4. 1 Joh. II, 27. „Unctio, quam vos accepistis, „manet in vobis: nec necesse habetis, ut quisquam vos doceat. Verùm eadem unctio docet vos de omnibus, &c. Ergo S. Scriptura aut Verbum externum, non est necessarium. Resp. Locus iste non ita accipi debet, quasi Spiritus intùs doceat, absque Verbo S. Scripturæ lecto, vel prædicato: aut quasi intus docti facile illo carere possint. Apostolus enim reipsâ scripsit ad eos, quos in hunc modum alloquitur: nec minus ad patres, quam ad pueriulos & adolescentes, verf. 13. 14. Sed uegat, necessum fuisse, ut docerentur tanquam ignari aut plane rudes; ipsi omnia ad salutem necessaria jam edocti, deque eorum veritate per Spiritum S. plene persuasi: adeo quidem, ut in iisdem manere deberent; non vero aliam aliquam doctrinam, sive in se novam, sive ipsis novam, accipere. Vide ibid. verf. 24. & 26. Confer etiam locum valde similem, Gal. 1, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: Objection 4. 1 John 2:27: "The anointing which you have received remains in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But the same anointing teaches you about all things," etc. Therefore Holy Scripture, or the external Word, is not necessary. Answer: This passage must not be taken as if the Spirit teaches inwardly without the Word of Scripture being read or preached, or as if those taught inwardly could easily do without it. For the apostle really wrote to those whom he addresses in this way, and no less to the fathers than to the little children and young men, vv. 13, 14. But he means that it was not necessary for them to be taught as if they were ignorant or utterly raw; they had already been taught everything necessary for salvation, and were fully persuaded of its truth through the Holy Spirit, so that they ought to remain in it, and not receive any other doctrine, whether new in itself or new to them. See the same chapter, vv. 24 and 26. Compare also the very similar passage, Gal. 1:6–8.

units.la: Obj. 5. Qui legere nesciunt; aut corporaliter caeci sunt, non tamen propterea, quod S. Scripturâ uti non possint, à salute aeternâ excludi debent. Idem dicendum de iis, qui forte in insulâ; vel apud infideles, per aliquem infidelem eodem delatum, ore tenus, sine exemplari Biblico, veritatem salutarem docerentur: ergo. Resp. 1. Priores non omnino destituuntur S. Scriptura: nam ex isto principio doctrinali salutaria dogmata iis depromuntur, praeleguntur, illustrantur, & confirmantur; quod ipsi etiam per gratiam Spiritûs Sancti, omnibus verè fidelibus communem, agnoscere possunt & debent. 2. Posteriores, si verè crederent, aeternum quoque salvandi forent; tanquam habentes veritatem salutarem, ex eodem hoc principio doctrinali quoque depromtam. Ipsa salus à praesentiâ S. Codicis quidem suspensa non est; sed à gratiâ Dei in Christo, quae isto Codice descripta, eoque mediante aliis ex ordine constituto tradi solet. Quare etiam existimandum est, siquidem Deo placeret Ecclesiam sibi illic stabilire, & conservare, futurum, ut SS. Biblia ad eos quoque deferrentur; utpote per ordinationem Divinam necessaria ad bene esse, ad successivam instructionem, & ad stabilitatem Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Objection 5. Those who cannot read, or who are physically blind, should not for that reason be excluded from eternal salvation, though they cannot use Holy Scripture. The same must be said of those who, perhaps on an island, or among unbelievers, were taught the saving truth by word of mouth from someone who had been brought there, without a Biblical copy; therefore... Answer 1. The former are not wholly deprived of Holy Scripture: for from this doctrinal principle the saving doctrines are drawn for them, read to them, illustrated and confirmed; and they too, by the grace of the Holy Spirit common to all truly faithful, can and should recognise this. 2. The latter, if they truly believed, would also be saved eternally, as having the saving truth, drawn from this same doctrinal principle. Salvation is not indeed bound to the presence of the sacred Codex; it depends on the grace of God in Christ, which is described in this Codex, and which is usually conveyed, through this Codex, to others by a settled order. Hence it must also be thought that, if it pleased God to establish and preserve his Church there, the Holy Bible would be brought to them too, since by divine ordinance it is necessary for well-being, for successive instruction, and for the stability of the Church.

units.la: XLI. Sequuntur Adjuncta consequentia S. Scriptu- rae; quae potissimum sunt ejus Lectio, & Interpretatio, itemque Judicium ex eâ de Controversiis Theologicis.
units.tr: XLI. The consequences that follow from Scripture: chiefly its reading and interpretation, and the judgment on theological controversies drawn from it.

units.la: Lectio S. Scripturæ, est Verbi Divini scripti, quatenùs scriptum est, usurpatio propria, ut sapientia salutaris indè hauriatur. Quod quidem non peculiare Antecessorum, sed omnium salutis suæ ac spiritualis instructionis avidorum commune officium esse, contra Pontificios probatur; 1. ex generalibus præceptis de familiari usu S. Scripturæ: Deut. vi, 6, -9. ,,Erunt verba ista, quæ Ego præcipio tibi, super corde tuo; & repetes ea filiis tuis: &c. Similiter xi, 18, -21. Joh.v, 39. Scrutamini Scripturas; &c. Col. iii, 16. Vide sup. cap.i.th.2. Adde Deut. xvii, 18, 19. Josf. i, 8.
units.tr: The reading of Scripture is the proper use of the written Word of God, as it is written, so that saving wisdom may be drawn from it. That this is the common duty not only of teachers but of all who long for their salvation and spiritual instruction is proved against the Papists: (1) from the general precepts on the familiar use of Scripture: Deut. 6:6–9, "These words which I command you shall be upon your heart, and you shall teach them to your sons," etc.; similarly 11:18–21; John 5:39, "Search the Scriptures," etc.; Col. 3:16. See above, ch. 1, th. 2. Add Deut. 17:18, 19; Josh. 1:8.

units.la: 2. Exemplis laudatis: 2 Timoth. iii, 15. ,,Te à ,,puero sacras Literas novisse, &c. Actor. xvii, 11. de Beræensibus. ,,Iis autem, qui erant Thessalonicæ, fuerunt isti generosiores; ut qui receperint sermonem cum ,,omni alacritate, quotidiè scrutantes Scripturas, an hæc ità se haberent. viii, 28, &c. de Eunucho Æthiope legente Jesaiam. 2 Petr. i, 19. Vide sup. th. 35.
units.tr: (2) From the examples cited: 2 Tim. 3:15, "that from childhood you have known the sacred letters," etc.; Acts 17:11, concerning the Bereans: "Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily, whether these things were so." Acts 8:28, etc., concerning the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah; 2 Pet. 1:19. See above, th. 35.

units.la: 3. Ex Divinâ ejus ordinatione ad communem instructionem & consolationem: Deut. xvii, 19. Ut discat Jehovam Deum suum revereri, ad observandum, &c. Psal. xix, 8, 9. Prov. i, 2, -6. Joh. xx, 31. Rom. iv, 23, 24. xv, 4.
units.tr: (3) From God's ordaining of Scripture for common instruction and consolation: Deut. 17:19, "that he may learn to fear Jehovah his God, to observe," etc.; Ps. 19:8, 9; Prov. 1:2–6; John 20:31; Rom. 4:23, 24; 15:4.
1 Cor. 10:11; 2 Tim. 3:16; 1 John 1:12–14. See above, th. 4 and 28, §2.

units.la: 4. Ex adjectâ salutis promissione: Psal. i, 1, 2. Vide sup. cap. i. th. 37. Apoc. i. 3. Beatus, qui legit --,,verba ,,Prophetiæ hujus. Joh. v, 39. xx, 31. 2 Tim. iii, 15. Vide sup. th. 31. §. 1. & 3.
units.tr: (4) From the promise of salvation attached to it: Ps. 1:1, 2; see above, ch. 1, th. 37; Rev. 1:3, "Blessed is he who reads" the words of this prophecy; John 5:39; 20:31; 2 Tim. 3:15. See above, th. 31, §§1 and 3.

units.la: Eandem veritatem confirmant in orthodoxâ antiquitate testimonia Chrysostomi, Gregorii M. aliorumque.
units.tr: The testimonies of Chrysostom, Gregory the Great and others in orthodox antiquity confirm the same truth.

units.la: XLII. Obj. 1. Multa in SS. Literis occurrunt ob- scura, difficilia, ἀναντιωφανῆ: ergo.
units.tr: XLII. Objection 1. Many things in the Holy Scriptures occur that are obscure, difficult, and [ἀναντιωφανῆ]; therefore...

units.la: Resp. Nos perspicuitatem & veritatem modo probavimus. Quædam interim difficiliora, & sublimiora agnoscimus: verùm iis nausea abstergitur, & fastus deprimitur; sedulitas vero ac piæ preces in lectoribus excitantut.
units.tr: Answer: We have just proved the perspicuity and truth of Scripture. We acknowledge that some passages are more difficult and sublime; yet these cure disgust and humble pride, and they rouse diligence and devout prayers in readers.

units.la: Obj. 2. Intercurrunt exempla peccatorum, etiam valde gravium, à viris sanctis commissorum; quæ scandalo futura plebi ea legenti: ergo. Resp. 1. Purissima est Lex Jehovæ; ad cujus normam vivendum est, & facta aliorum examinanda. 2. Saepissime etiam commemoratur, quàm graviter Deus illa castigaverit, & quomodo pii poenitentiam egerint, &c.
units.tr: Objection 2. Examples of sins, even very grave ones, committed by holy men, occur, which will be a scandal to the common people who read them; therefore... Answer 1. The law of Jehovah is most pure; by its norm one must live and examine the deeds of others. 2. It is also very often recorded how severely God punished those sins, and how the godly repented, etc.

units.la: Obj. 3. Periculum est, ne haereses oriantur ex istâ lectione: ergo. Resp. Saepius quidem homines profani & impuri rebus optimis, sanctissimis, ac salubberrimis abutuntur suo vitio, & suo damno: nec tamen usus idcirco prohibendus est. Deus sapientissimus abusum illum providit absque dubio; attamen usum instituit, laudavit, &c. Filii alimentis, pharmacis, armis necessariis, &c. privandi non sunt; quod servi nequam iis forte abutuntur.
units.tr: Objection 3. There is a danger that heresies may arise from this reading; therefore... Answer: Indeed, profane and impure men often abuse the best, most holy and most wholesome things to their own fault and loss; yet use is not on that account to be forbidden. God, most wise, undoubtedly foresaw that abuse; nevertheless he instituted, approved and commended the use, etc. Children are not to be deprived of food, medicine or necessary arms, because wicked servants may perhaps abuse them.

units.la: XLIII. Lectionem istam non restringimus ad libros N. T. quasi lectio librorum V. T. sub hâc oeconomiâ non esset necessaria, magnique adeò momenti; quod perperàm contendunt Socinciani, & Anabaptistæ aliqui.
units.tr: XLIII. We do not restrict this reading to the books of the New Testament, as if the reading of the books of the Old Testament were not necessary under this economy, and of such great importance; this is wrongly contended by the Socinians and certain Anabaptists.

units.la: Contrarium patet, 1. ex praecepto illo, Joh. v, 39. cum 46.
units.tr: The contrary is plain: 1. from that precept, John 5:39, compared with verse 46.

units.la: 2. Ex Laudatâ praxi Beroeensium; Act. xvii. 11.
units.tr: 2. From the praised practice of the Bereans, Acts 17:11.

units.la: 3. Ex manifestâ utilitate, & quidem per tempora N. T. Rom. iv, 23, 24. xv. 4. 1 Cor. x, 11. 2 Tim. iii, 16, 17. 2 Pet. I, 19. Jac. 10. 11.
units.tr: 3. From the manifest usefulness, and indeed in New Testament times: Rom. 4:23, 24; 15:4; 1 Cor. 10:11; 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; 2 Pet. 1:19; James 1:10, 11.

units.la: 4. Speciatim etiam ad convincendos Judaeos, juxta exemplum Apollo: Act. xviii. 28. ficet etiam Paulus intra limites Mosis & Prophetarum sese continuit: Act. xxvi, 22, 23.
units.tr: 4. Especially also for convincing the Jews, following the example of Apollos, Acts 18:28; and Paul too kept himself within the limits of Moses and the Prophets, Acts 26:22, 23.

units.la: XLIV. Obj. 1. Salutaris veritas clarius & plenius proponitur in libris N. T. Ergo. Resp. Imo major est claritas & plenitudo cognitionis, quae hauritur ex libris V. T. & N. T. simul inter se collatis: bonum bono additum, facit majus bonum. Obj. 2. Cerimoniae V. T. abrogatae sunt; Prophetiae de Messiâ venturo impletae, atque adeo cessant. Lex & Prophetae usque ad Johannem: Matth. xi, 13. Ergo. Resp. 1. Cerimoniae illae, quoniam abrogatae sunt, nunc à nobis observari non debent: utilissima tamen est ad veritatem illustrandam & confirmandam veterum typorum collatio cum suo archetypo & complemento. 2. Quia Messias modò venit in carnem, iste ejus adventus non debet amplius expectari: attamen ipsa veritas accuratius etiam cognoscenda est, ex Prophetiis priscinis. 3. In libris V. T. exstant quoque Prophetiae nondum prorsus completae: utpote de iis, quae pertinent ad Ecclesiam N. T. quin imò de judicio extremo, coelesti beatitudine, &c. Atque item doctrinae plures, tum ad fidem, tum ad mores vivendi spectantes. 4. Ministerium Evangelii promissionis, de Christo in carnem venturo, terminum suum habuit in Johanne Baptistâ; qui Christum coram praesentem demonstravit. Verùm indè nequaquam sequitur, quod volunt Adversarii.
units.tr: XLIV. Objection 1. The saving truth is set forth more clearly and fully in the books of the New Testament; therefore... Answer: Indeed, the clarity and fullness of knowledge drawn from the books of the Old and New Testaments taken together and compared with one another is greater: good added to good makes a greater good. Objection 2. The ceremonies of the Old Testament have been abrogated, the prophecies of the coming Messiah have been fulfilled, and so they cease. "The Law and the Prophets until John," Matt. 11:13; therefore... Answer 1. Those ceremonies, since they have been abrogated, ought not now to be observed by us; nevertheless the comparison of the old types with their archetype and fulfilment is most useful for illustrating and confirming the truth. 2. Because the Messiah has now come in the flesh, that coming of his ought no longer to be awaited; yet the truth itself is to be known more accurately also from the earlier prophecies. 3. In the books of the Old Testament there also exist prophecies not yet wholly fulfilled: namely those that pertain to the Church of the New Testament, and indeed concerning the last judgment, heavenly blessedness, etc.; and likewise several doctrines pertaining both to faith and to the conduct of life. 4. The ministry of the promise of the Gospel, concerning Christ who was to come in the flesh, had its end in John the Baptist, who showed Christ present before them. But it by no means follows from this what our opponents want.

units.la: XLV. Interpretatio S. Scripturae, (realis scil. sive exegetica: nam de verbali, sive metaphrastica, diximus sup. th. 13.) est Sensûs genuini, S. S. literis expreßi, accommodata ad intellectum explicatio.
units.tr: XLV. The interpretation of Scripture (namely the real or exegetical kind; for we spoke of the verbal or metaphrastic kind above, th. 13) is the explanation, adapted to the understanding, of the genuine sense expressed in the letters of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Sensus, qui hic eruitur, est quasi anima S. Scripturae: illa scil. realis veritas, quam Spiritus S. per talia verba ac tales sententias, significatam voluit. Hoc recte percepto, habemus mentem Christi; 1 Cor. xi. 16. & quidem ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam justitiae, ad consolationem: 2 Tim. iii, 16. Rom. xv, 4.
units.tr: The sense that is drawn out here is, as it were, the soul of Scripture: namely that real truth which the Holy Spirit wished to be signified by such words and such statements. Once this is rightly perceived, we have the mind of Christ, 1 Cor. 2:16; and indeed for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for discipline in righteousness, for consolation, 2 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 15:4.

units.la: Genuinus est ille sensus, quem Spiritus Sanctus revera intendit; sequeque intendisse, tali contextu ostendit. Contextus enim verborum, est signum; sensus verò res signata.
units.tr: The genuine sense is that which the Holy Spirit truly intends, and the context shows that he has intended it. For the context of the words is the sign, but the sense is the thing signified.

units.la: Signum autem satis idoneum atque evidens procul dubio adhibuit Sp. veritatis, nos ad salutem sapientes reddere volens: Ioh.xvi, 13. 2 Tim.iii,15. Psal.xix. 8, 9. 10.
units.tr: Moreover, the Spirit of truth, wishing to make us wise unto salvation, undoubtedly employed a sign that is sufficiently suitable and evident: John 16:13; 2 Tim. 3:15; Ps. 19:8, 9, 10.

units.la: Imo quoniam unum & verum convertuntur; sensusverus ac genuinus cujusque loci, unicus proprie est: qui, cum ex ipso verborum contextu colligatur, litera-lis, five grammaticus, appellari solet.
units.tr: Indeed, since one and true are convertible, the true and genuine sense of each passage is properly single; and since it is gathered from the very context of the words, it is usually called the literal, or grammatical, sense.

units.la: XLVI. Pontificii, praeter sensum literalem, fingunt alium insuper mysticum: eumque porro faciunt triplicem, convenienter tribus virtutibus Theologicis, Fidei, Spei, & Charitati. Vocant autem Allegoricum: quando verba Scripturae, praeter sensum literalem, ut loquuntur, significant aliquid pertinens ad fidem, vel ad Ecclesiam militantem: Anagogicum; quando praeter sensum literalem, significant aliquid pertinens ad spem, sive vitam aeternam, vel ad Ecclesiam triumphantem: & Tropologicum, sive Moralem; quando praeter sensum literalem, significant aliquid pertinens ad officia charitatis.
units.tr: XLVI. The Papists, besides the literal sense, invent another, the mystical, and they further make it threefold, in agreement with the three theological virtues, Faith, Hope, and Charity. They call it Allegorical when the words of Scripture, besides the literal sense, as they say, signify something pertaining to faith or to the militant Church; Anagogical when, besides the literal sense, they signify something pertaining to hope, that is eternal life, or to the triumphant Church; and Tropological, or Moral, when, besides the literal sense, they signify something pertaining to the duties of charity.

units.la: Absurde: sapientissimus enim doctor veritatis, docet veritatem perspicue, distincte, & pure: unde etiam Adversarii concedere coguntur, Argumenta Theologica formari non posse, nisi ex sensu literali.
units.tr: Absurd: for the most wise teacher of truth teaches truth clearly, distinctly and purely; whence even our opponents are compelled to concede that theological arguments cannot be formed except from the literal sense.

units.la: XLVII. Interim etiam nos fatemur, Veritatem illam a Spiritu Sancto intentam, aliquando directe & immediate proponi; aliquando mediate, & interveniente signo aliquo reali. Verba semper sunt signa rerum sic ad cognoscendum propositarum: sed res illae immediate & proxime significatae, quandoque sunt signa aliarum rerum sublimiorum. Atque hoc observandum in Typis, Parabolis, & Allegoriis: in quibus sensus unus compositus recte agnoscitur.
units.tr: XLVII. Yet we too acknowledge that the truth intended by the Holy Spirit is sometimes set forth directly and immediately, and sometimes mediately, through the intervention of some real sign. Words are always signs of things thus proposed for knowing; but those things, immediately and proximately signified, are sometimes signs of other, more sublime things. This must be observed in types, parables and allegories, in which a single compound sense is rightly recognised.

units.la: Tenendum insuper ea, quae ἀλληγορῶς & formaliter in SS. Literis expressa sunt, alia κατὰ διάνοιαν & virtualiter in se complecti; quae inde per legitimam consequentiam deducenda sunt.
units.tr: We must hold that those things which are expressed allegorically [ἀλληγορῶς] and formally in Holy Scripture also embrace, in themselves, other things according to the inner meaning [κατὰ διάνοιαν] and virtually, which are to be deduced from them by legitimate consequence.

units.la: XLVIII. Occurrit interim etiam Stylus SS. Scripturæ; h. e. ille dictionum & sententiarum modus, quo Spiritus S. veritatès expressas voluit.
units.tr: XLVIII. There is also the style of Holy Scripture, that is, the manner of words and sentences by which the Holy Spirit wished the truths to be expressed.

units.la: Ubi communiter quidem tenendum; prout unusquisque Scriptor suum habuit stylum, per naturam gratiam, curam; sic eum convenienter à Spiritu Sancto affumtum & infallibiliter ductum fuisse. Hinc manifesta est in Scriptoribus sacris Styli varietas; ut & methodus arbitraria.
units.tr: In general this must be held: each writer had his own style, shaped by his nature, grace and care, and the Holy Spirit took him up suitably and led him infallibly. Hence there is clear variety of style among the sacred writers, as well as a varied method.

units.la: Specialius autem in consideratione Grammatica, stylus subinde variat; nec tamen minus purus est, quam in aliorum etiam Auctorum scriptis observari solet: agnoscendæ interim alicubi Ellipses, Enallagæ, Hyperbata, &c.
units.tr: More particularly, when grammar is considered, the style sometimes varies, yet it is no less pure than is customarily observed in the writings of other authors. Meanwhile, ellipses, enallages, hyperbata and the like are to be recognised in places.

units.la: In consideratione item Rhetorica, Stylus alibi nudus & proprius; alibi improprius occurrit, & per Tropos ac Figuras coloratus.
units.tr: Likewise, when rhetoric is considered, the style is at one place plain and proper, at another improper and adorned with tropes and figures.

units.la: Attamen Spiritui S. sua ubique constat veracitas, gravitas, ac majestas.
units.tr: Yet the veracity, gravity and majesty of the Holy Spirit are everywhere evident.

units.la: XLIX. Verus modus interpretandi S. Scripturam ille est, quem ipse Spiritus S. in SS. Literis ostendit. Requiritur autem attenta ipsius contextus, antecedentium item & consequentium, nec non locorum parallelorum consideratio; modesto studio, accurata analysi, ac piis precibus in subsidium adhibitis. Sic per ipsam S. Scripturam, secundum analogiam fidei, instituenda est omnis ejus explicatio.
units.tr: XLIX. The true way of interpreting Holy Scripture is the one which the Holy Spirit himself shows in the Holy Scriptures. Careful attention is required to its context, both preceding and following, and also to the consideration of parallel passages, with modest study, accurate analysis and pious prayers brought in as aids. Thus every explanation of Scripture is to be carried out through Scripture itself, according to the analogy of faith.

units.la: Interim propria verborum significatio, quantum fieri potest, servanda est: neque ab eâ recedendum; nisi scopus & circumstantiæ textus, vel analogia fidei, vel denique recta ratio ad evitandam veram ac manifestam contradictionem, id omnino requirat.
units.tr: Meanwhile the proper signification of the words is to be kept as far as possible, and one must not depart from it unless the scope and circumstances of the text, or the analogy of faith, or finally right reason, in order to avoid a true and manifest contradiction, absolutely require it.

units.la: L. Jus interpretandi summum & αὐτοπεγθέχκον competit ipsi Deo: Gen. XVIII, 25. - Judex totius terræ, Psal. IX, 3, 5. Altissimus - Judex justitiæ. L. 6 Deus ipse Judex. Hic solus est omniscius, infallibilis, & S. Scripturæ auctor, ac proinde optimus interpres.
units.tr: L. The right of interpreting in the highest degree and self-existent [αὐτοπεγθέχκον] belongs to God himself: Gen. XVIII, 25: the Judge of all the earth; Psal. IX, 3, 5: the Most High, the Judge of righteousness; Psal. L, 6: God himself is judge. He alone is omniscient, infallible, and the author of Holy Scripture, and therefore the best interpreter.

units.la: 1 Joh. 111, 20. Deus novit omnia. Rom. 111, 4. Deus verax; omnis autem homo mendax. Iob. XXXVI, 22. Quis est Doctor, sicut ipse?
units.tr: 1 Joh. III, 20: God knows all things. Rom. III, 4: God is true, but every man is a liar. Job XXXVI, 22: Who is a teacher like him?

units.la: Attamen speciali quâdam appropriatione Jus istud competit Filio; τῷ Λόγῳ, Ioh. i, 1, 14. Sapientiæ hypostaticæ; Prov. VIII, 1, 12, 22, -31. Summo Prophetæ ac Doctori nostro; Deut. XVIII. 15, 18, 19. Act. III, 20, -23. In quo, ut plenitudo Deitatis inhabitat corporaliter, sic omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis sunt reconditi: Col. II. 3. 9. Vide etiam Matth. XXIII, 8, 10. XI, 27. Hebr. III, 1, 3, 4. Ioh. I. 17. 18. 1 Cor. I, 3 0. Apoc. III, 7.
units.tr: Yet by a special appropriation this right belongs to the Son, the Word [τῷ Λόγῳ], John I, 1, 14; the hypostatic Wisdom, Prov. VIII, 1, 12, 22–31; our supreme Prophet and Teacher, Deut. XVIII, 15, 18, 19; Acts III, 20–23. In him, as the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, so all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden: Col. II, 3, 9. See also Matt. XXIII, 8, 10; XI, 27; Heb. III, 1, 3, 4; John I, 17, 18; 1 Cor. I, 30; Rev. III, 7.

units.la: Aliter idem jus tribuitur Spiritui Sancto: per quem proximè datur verbum sapientiæ, & cognitionis, atque adeo fides, & reliqua dona spiritualia: 1 Cor. XII. 3, 8, 9. Jef. XI, 2. XL. 13. Ioh. XVI, 7, 8. 13. 2 Cor. III. 18. Hic audiendus: Apoc. II, 7. II. &c. Sed minimè ei resistendum: Act. VII. 51.
units.tr: Otherwise the same right is attributed to the Holy Spirit, through whom the word of wisdom and knowledge is immediately given, and so faith and the other spiritual gifts: 1 Cor. XII, 3, 8, 9; Isa. XI, 2; XL, 13; John XVI, 7, 8, 13; 2 Cor. III, 18. Here he is to be heard: Rev. II, 7, etc. But by no means is he to be resisted: Acts VII, 51.

units.la: Spiritus autem interpretationem suam pronunciat, tum externè in SS. Literis: ubi observanda textuum ἀσυγκρίτα καὶ συμβαλλόμενα; accedente etiam paflim Ministrorum, aliorumque fidelium, auxilio & indicio: tum interrè, secundùm easdem SS. Literas, per se efficaciter docens, persuadens, obsignans: 1 Ioh. II, 27. 2 Cor. IV, 13. 1 Cor. II, 12, 15, 16. XII, 11. Rom. VIII, 9, 14, 15, 16. Eph. IV, 30.
units.tr: The Spirit pronounces his interpretation, both outwardly in the Holy Scriptures, where the passages which are to be compared and set side by side [ἀσυγκρίτα καὶ συμβαλλόμενα] must be observed, with the help and indication of ministers and other faithful people also added where needed; both inwardly, according to the same Holy Scriptures, teaching, persuading and sealing effectively through himself: 1 Joh. II, 27; 2 Cor. IV, 13; 1 Cor. II, 12, 15, 16; XII, 11; Rom. VIII, 9, 14, 15, 16; Eph. IV, 30.

units.la: LI. Ius verò subordinatum, idque publicum & antecessorium, convenit publicis in Ecclesiâ Antecessoribus. Ubi non solùm spectantur Ministri extraordinarii, iisque infallibiles: Eph. IV, 11, 12. 2 Petr. I, 21. Matth. X, 20. Joh. XVI, 13. Act. I, 4. sed etiam ordinarii, fallibiles; Pastores, & Doctores: Eph. IV, 11. 1 Tim. V, 17. 2 Tim. III, 17. Hebr. XIII, 17. Act. XX, 28. tum tùm singuli in Verbo laborantes, & minis\terium apud Ecclesiam suam implentes: 1 Petr. v, 2. Tit. 1, 5. Col. iii, 17. tum in Synodo congregati, & in commune Ecclesiæ bonum dona atque consilia sua conferentes: Act. xv, 6. &c.
units.tr: LI. The subordinate right, which is public and antecessory, belongs to the public teachers in the Church. Here are considered not only the extraordinary ministers, who are infallible (Eph. IV, 11, 12; 2 Petr. I, 21; Matt. X, 20; John XVI, 13; Acts I, 4), but also the ordinary, fallible ones: pastors and teachers (Eph. IV, 11; 1 Tim. V, 17; 2 Tim. III, 17; Heb. XIII, 17; Acts XX, 28); then the individual men labouring in the Word and fulfilling their ministry in their own congregation (1 Petr. V, 2; Tit. I, 5; Col. III, 17); and then those gathered in synod, contributing their gifts and counsels for the common good of the Church (Acts XV, 6, etc.).

units.la: Vocamus illud antecessiorium, in ordine ad gregem, cujus sunt Pastores & Antecessores: Hebr. xiii, 17.
units.tr: We call it antecessory with respect to the flock, over which they are the pastors and leaders: Heb. XIII, 17.

units.la: 1 Thess. v, 12. Idem interim subsequens est respectu Dei, Christi, Spiritus Sancti, ac S. Scripturæ. Et ministeriale; quatenus sunt Ministri Christi ac Dispensatores mysteriorum Dei; à quibus fidelitas requiritur: 1 Cor. iv, 1, 2. quoniam rationem reddituri sunt. Hebr. xiii, 17. ac proinde isti nec magisterium, nec dominium, sibi arrogare debent: Matth. xxiii, 8, 9, 10. xx, 25, 26, 27.
units.tr: 1 Thess. V, 12. The same men are subsequent with respect to God, Christ, the Holy Spirit and Holy Scripture, and ministerial, in so far as they are ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, from whom faithfulness is required (1 Cor. IV, 1, 2), since they will have to give an account (Heb. XIII, 17). Therefore they ought not to arrogate to themselves either teaching authority or dominion: Matt. XXIII, 8, 9, 10; XX, 25, 26, 27.

units.la: LII. Privatum & omninò subsequens jus interpretationis qualiscunque, competit omnibus & singulis, quibus Verbum Dei proponitur: ut ipsi quoque SS. Literas legant, meditentur, conferant: Joh. v, 39. Psal. i, 2. Act. xvii, 11. sic de veritate doctrinæ persuasi, credant: 1 Thess. ii, 13. v, 21. 1 Joh. iv, 1. eandemque coràm aliis, cum instructione & exhortatione charitativâ profiteantur: Rom. x, 10. 1 Petr. iii, 15. Col. iii, 16. 1 Thess. v, 11.
units.tr: LII. The private and altogether subsequent right of interpretation, of whatever kind, belongs to all and each to whom the Word of God is set forth, so that they too may read the Holy Scriptures, meditate on them and compare them (John V, 39; Psal. I, 2; Acts XVII, 11), and so, persuaded of the truth of the doctrine, may believe it (1 Thess. II, 13; V, 21; 1 Joh. IV, 1), and may profess the same before others with charitable instruction and exhortation (Rom. X, 10; 1 Petr. III, 15; Col. III, 16; 1 Thess. V, 11).
