units.la: LIII. Quantum attinet ad Auctoritatem interpretationis; in hâc spectandus est genuinus sensus S. Scripturæ, qui sic colligitur & proponitur. Ille autem, quatenus talis est, habet procul dubio auctoritatem Divinam; & ad fidem Divinam nos obligat. Formalis vero collectio, ac propositio, per homines fallibiles, absolute quidem fallibilis est; sed in hypothesi, quando & quatenus est collectio ac propositio genuini sensus, quem Spiritus S. iltic expressit, vera est; nec sallere potest: ac per istam veritatem Divinam omnino habet auctoritatem. Divinam decisivam, & obligatoriam ad fidem & observantiam. Nec in re ipsâ materialiter refert, sive per unum aliquem privatum, sive per Antecessorem Ecclesiasticum, sive per plures in Concilio congregatos, ista veritas proponatur: Auctoritas enim Divina gradus non admittit. Sed formaliter tamen, in ministeriali illo indicio ac testimonio, discrimen satis insigne est: neque solum major, vel minor, pro re natâ, probabilitas; sed etiam auscultandi necessitas, ex ordinatione Divinâ: Eph. iv, 11, 12. Hebr. xiii, 17. 1 Thess. v, 12. 1 Tim. v. 17. 1 Cor. iv, 1. Luc. x, 16.
units.tr: LIII. As far as concerns the authority of interpretation, what is to be considered is the genuine sense of Holy Scripture, which is thus gathered and set forth. That sense, insofar as it is such, undoubtedly has divine authority and binds us to divine faith. But the formal gathering and proposing of it through fallible men is in itself fallible; yet under the supposition that, when and insofar as it is a gathering and proposing of the genuine sense which the Holy Spirit expressed there, it is true and cannot deceive, and through that divine truth it fully has authority, divine, decisive and binding to faith and obedience. Nor does it matter in the thing itself, materially, whether this truth is proposed through one private person, or through an ecclesiastical teacher, or through several gathered in a council, for divine authority admits no degrees. But formally, in that ministerial judgement and testimony, the difference is quite striking: there is not only a greater or lesser probability, according to the circumstances, but also a necessity of listening, from divine ordinance (Eph. IV, 11, 12; Heb. XIII, 17; 1 Thess. V, 12; 1 Tim. V, 17; 1 Cor. IV, 1; Luke X, 16).

units.la: LIV. Superest ut dicamus de Iudicio controversiarum Theologicarum.
units.tr: LIV. It remains to speak of the judgment of theological controversies.

units.la: Ex iis quae praecesserunt th. 50. patet, primò Judicium supremum, autocratorice decisivum, idemque solum absolute infallibile, competere ipsi Deo; & oeconomice Christo; atque iterum peculiari appropriatione, Spiritui Sancto: ob supremam & independentem sapientiam, veracitatem, ac potestatem judicialem, ipsamque S. Scripturae inspirationem; quae in tali Judicio maxime requiruntur.
units.tr: From what was said under thesis 50, it is clear, first, that the supreme judgment, decisive in an authoritative way and alone absolutely infallible, belongs to God himself; in the economy of salvation to Christ; and again, by a special appropriation, to the Holy Spirit. This is because of his supreme and independent wisdom, truthfulness and judicial power, and because of the very inspiration of Holy Scripture, which are chiefly required in such a judgment.

units.la: Sic igitur ipse 1. absolute sapientissimus est.
units.tr: Thus, first, he is absolutely most wise.

units.la: 2. Nec talli potest, nec fallere.
units.tr: Second, he can neither deceive nor be deceived.

units.la: 3. Intus animum hominis convincere potest efficaciter; judiciumque aeternum ferre.
units.tr: Third, he can effectively convince the mind of a person from within, and pronounce an eternal judgment.

units.la: 4. Sensum S. Scripturae, tanquam ejus Auctor princeps, optime novit; ipsique quam maxime curae est, ut ea ad fines suos certissime dirigatur.
units.tr: Fourth, as the chief author of Scripture, he best knows its sense, and it is his greatest concern that it be most certainly directed to its ends.

units.la: Secundò, Expressa judicii formula, eaque perfectissima, continetur in ipsis SS. Literis: unde iis etiam metonymice judicium tribuitur. Hebr. iv, 12. „Vivus est sermo Dei, - & dijudicat cogitationes & conceptus cordis. scil. quatenus est utilis & efficax ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, &c. 2 Timoth. iii, 16, 17. Rom. xv, 4. Neque solum adhortatio dicitur loqui fidelibus, tanquam filius; Hebr. xii. 5. sed etiam Moses, (h. e. Scriptura Mosaica) accusare Judaeos infideles; Joh. v, 45. & Lex eos condemnare; vii, 51. quod idem de verbis Christi asseritur, xii, 48. Adde Rom. iii, 19. cum i, 16.
units.tr: Second, the explicit form of judgment, and that the most perfect, is contained in the Sacred Letters themselves; hence judgment is also attributed to them by metonymy. Heb. 4:12: "The word of God is living… and judges the thoughts and intents of the heart", that is, insofar as it is useful and effective for teaching, for reproof, etc. 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; Rom. 15:4. Nor is it only that exhortation is said to speak to believers as to sons (Heb. 12:5), but also that Moses (that is, the Mosaic Scripture) accuses the unbelieving Jews (John 5:45), and the Law condemns them (John 7:51); the same is asserted of the words of Christ (John 12:48). Add Rom. 3:19 with 1:16.

units.la: LV. Tertiò, Antecessoribus Ecclesiasticis suum quoque competit judicium; respectu Dei, & S. Scripturæ, quidem subsequens, & discretivum; attamen respectu gregis, cui sunt præpositi, antecessorium, & ministerialiter decisivum. Vide sup. th. 51.
units.tr: LV. Third, the judgment of the ecclesiastical predecessors (elders) also belongs to them: with respect to God and Holy Scripture it is subsequent and discriminating, but with respect to the flock over which they are set it is antecedent and ministerially decisive. See above, thesis 51.

units.la: Quartò, Judicium quoque subsequens, discretivum credendorum & faciendorum, competit omnibus ac singulis fidelibus ad ea agnoscenda, observanda, sincereque ac prudenter applicanda, tum sibi, tum aliis ex charitate, & pro ratione donorum suorum.
units.tr: Fourth, the judgment that follows and discriminates between what is to be believed and what is to be done belongs also to all and each of the faithful, to recognise these, to observe them, and to apply them sincerely and prudently, both to themselves and to others, out of charity and according to the measure of their gifts.

units.la: Patet hoc etiam 1. ex diserto testimonio. 1 Cor. ii. 15. Spiritualis homo (h. e. à Spiritû S. illuminatus & regenitus) dijudicat omnia.
units.tr: This is evident, first, from the explicit testimony: 1 Cor. 2:15: "The spiritual man (that is, one enlightened and regenerated by the Holy Spirit) judges all things."

units.la: 2. Ex mandatis: 1 Cor. x, 15. „Tanquàm intelli„gentibus loquor, ipsi judicate. 1 Thess. v, 21. Omnia „probate: quod bonum est, tenete. 1 Ioh. iv, 1. Proba„te spiritus, an ex Deo sint.
units.tr: Second, from the commands: 1 Cor. 10:15: "I speak as to intelligent people; judge for yourselves." 1 Thess. 5:21: "Test all things; hold fast to what is good." 1 John 4:1: "Test the spirits, whether they are from God."

units.la: 3. Ex officio conscientiæ, sub Deo judicantis; quæque ipse præscripsit, agnoscentis, & nobis applicantis: Rom. ii, 14, 15. Vide sup. cap. i. th. 16. §. 2. Ioh. iii, 19, 20, 21! „Per hoc cognoscimus, nos ex veritate esse: & „coram ipso secura reddemus corda nostra. Nam si nos condemnet cor nostrum, potentior est Deus corde nostro; „& novit omnia. Dilecti, si cor nostrum nos non condemnet, libertatem loquendi habemus apud Deum. Prius ergo discernuntur & agnoscuntur ea, secundùm quæ judicium illud de statû nostro formari debet. Unde etiàm Phil. i, 10. „Ut exploretis, quæ discrepant.
units.tr: Third, from the office of conscience, which judges under God, recognises what he has prescribed, and applies it to us: Rom. 2:14, 15. See above, chapter 1, thesis 16, §2. John 3:19–21: "By this we know that we are of the truth, and shall reassure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God." Therefore those things are first discerned and recognised, according to which that judgment about our state ought to be formed. Hence also Phil. 1:10: "that you may test what is different."

units.la: 4. Exemplo Beræensium: Act. xvii, 11. Vide sup. th. 41. §. 2.
units.tr: Fourth, by the example of the Bereans: Acts 17:11. See above, thesis 41, §2.

units.la: Sed & Magistratus Christianus, non tantùm quatenùs Christianus est, commune cum aliis fidelibus officium habet: verùm etiàm quatenùs Magistratus est, de veritate Divinâ ac salutari sibi propositâ cognoscere debet. bet, eamque in districtu suo admittere, fovere, defendere, & quantum potest promovere. Hoc enim est Nutriciorum Ecclesiæ ; Jes. xlix, 23. & Ministrorum Dei ; Rom. xiii, 1, -4. Confer exempla Asæ, 1 Reg. xv, 11, -15. Josaphati, xxii, 42, 43, 44. Joasi, 2 Reg. xii, 2, 3, 6, -. Ezechiæ, xviii, 3, 4. Josiæ, xxii, 2.
units.tr: But also the Christian magistrate, not only insofar as he is a Christian, has a duty in common with other believers; but also insofar as he is a magistrate, he ought to know the divine truth set before him for salvation, and to admit it, foster it, defend it within his jurisdiction, and promote it as far as he can. For this is to be nursing fathers of the Church (Isa. 49:23) and ministers of God (Rom. 13:1–4). Compare the examples of Asa (1 Kings 15:11–15), Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 17), Joash (2 Kings 12:2, 3, 6), Hezekiah (2 Chron. 29:3, 4), and Josiah (2 Chron. 34:2).

units.la: LVI. Negamus ergo contra Pontificios, Judicium, illud supremum & infallibile, ἀναμάρτητον, tribuendum esse Ecclesiæ Romanæ, aut Concilio etiam generali, aut denique Pontifici Romano.
units.tr: LVI. We therefore deny, against the Papists, that that supreme and infallible judgment, sinless [ἀναμάρτητον], is to be attributed to the Roman Church, or to a general council, or finally to the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Nam 1. soli Deo, in SS. Literis loquenti, id competere, probatum est satis.
units.tr: For, first, it has been sufficiently proved that this belongs to God alone, speaking in the Sacred Letters.

units.la: 2. Consentit Orthodoxa antiquitas: in promptu sunt testimonia Augustini, Optati Milevitani, Chrysostomi, Basilii Magni, &c.
units.tr: Second, the orthodox antiquity agrees: testimonies of Augustine, Optatus of Milevis, Chrysostom, Basil the Great, and others are at hand.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Concilio qualicunque, Pontifici denique, nusquàm in SS. Literis tribuitur infallibilis veracitas, aut suprema illa & ἀναμάρτητος potestas. Aliter plane sonat ista comminatio, Rom. xi. 21. „Si Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, (vide) „ne tibi quoque non parcat!
units.tr: Third, nowhere in the Sacred Letters is infallible truthfulness, or that supreme and sinless power, attributed to the Roman Church, to some council of whatever kind, or finally to the Pontiff. That warning in Rom. 11:21 sounds quite otherwise: "If God did not spare the natural branches, take care lest he not spare you either!"

units.la: 4. Accedunt Confessiones ipsorum Pontificiorum; utpote Bellarmini, de Conciliis, etiam generalibus: Adriani Florentii Ultrajectensis, de Ecclesia Romana, ejusque capite Pontifice; qui diserte: Plures enim fuerunt Pontifices Romani hæretici, allegato exemplo Iohannis xxii. &c. Addi possunt Liberius ad Arianismum prolapsus, & Honorius Monothelita factus, &c.
units.tr: Fourth, there are the confessions of the Papists themselves: for example, Bellarmine, on councils, even general ones; Adrian Florent of Utrecht, on the Roman Church and its head the Pontiff, who states plainly: For there have been many heretical Roman Pontiffs, citing the example of John XXII, etc. Liberius, who fell into Arianism, and Honorius, who became a Monothelite, etc., may also be added.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Obj. 1. Scriptura est litera mortua, judex mutus, &c. Ergo. Resp. Falsum & blasphemum est antecedens. Vide sup. th. 54.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Scripture is a dead letter and a mute judge, etc. Therefore (it cannot decide controversies). Resp. The antecedent is false and blasphemous. See above, th. 54.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus in Scriptura testatur de seipso, & in propria sua causa: id vero absurdum est: Resp. Cum Deus sit prima & summa veritas, ipse de se testari potest; ipsique credendum est propter se : sicut, etiàm jurat per se ipsum: Hebr. vi, 13. Confer Ioh. v, 34. 1 Ioh. v, 9, 10. Sed Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ejusque Pontificis testimonium in propria causa, merito rejicitur.
units.tr: Obj. 2. God bears witness of himself in Scripture and in his own cause, which is absurd. Resp. Since God is the first and highest truth, he can bear witness of himself, and he is to be believed on his own authority, just as he swears by himself (Heb. 6:13). Compare John 5:34; 1 John 5:9, 10. But the testimony of the Church of Rome and of its Pope in their own cause is rightly rejected.

units.la: Obj. 3. Istâ methodo probabitur ex.gr. Deitas Spiritûs Sancti ex S. Scriptură; & vicißim auctoritas S. Scripturæ per Spiritum Sanctum: atqui iste est Circulus; absurdus probandi modus. Ergo. Resp. Nos Circulum in argumentationibus Theologicis nequaquam committimus. Diversæ sunt quæstiones; & propterea etiàm diversæ probationes. Quod ad veritates credendas objectivè attinet, unicè fidem resolvimus in Scripturas Canonicas; sed quod ad actum credendi subjectivè, solummodo analysin facimus in Spiritum fidei. Vide sup. cap. 2. th. 20. Verum ipsi Pontificij auctoritatem S. Scripturæ ab Ecclesiâ suspendentes, Ecclesiam iterum ex Scripturâ probantes, sese hinc expedire non possunt.
units.tr: Obj. 3. By this method, for example, the deity of the Holy Spirit would be proved from Holy Scripture, and conversely the authority of Holy Scripture through the Holy Spirit. But this is a circle, an absurd way of proving. Therefore (the objection stands). Resp. We never commit a circle in theological arguments. The questions are different, and so are the proofs. As regards the truths to be believed, objectively considered, we resolve faith solely into the canonical Scriptures; but as regards the act of believing, subjectively considered, we make the analysis only into the Spirit of faith. See above, ch. 2, th. 20. Indeed the Papists themselves, who make the authority of Holy Scripture depend on the Church and then prove the Church again from Scripture, cannot extricate themselves from this.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sub V. T. Judicium istiusmodi competebat summo Pontifici, & Concilio magno: ergo non minus nunc sub N. T. Resp. 1. Judices, & Sacetdotes Israëlitici, quin & ipse Moses, juxta formulam Legis Divinæ judicare debuerunt: Deut. xvii, 11. Ies. viii, 20. Hebr. iii, 2, -5. Ergo judicium illud non fuit absolutè summum, sed ministeriale. 2. A Mose, aliisque Ministris extraordinariis infallibilibus, non valet consequentia ad ordinarios, etiàm sub N. T. quasi his propterea infallibilitas quoque competeret.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Under the Old Testament such judgment belonged to the high priest and the great council; therefore it belongs no less now under the New Testament. Resp. 1. The Israelite judges and priests, and Moses himself, were bound to judge according to the form of the divine Law (Deut. 17:11; Isa. 8:20; Heb. 3:2, 5). Therefore that judgment was not absolutely supreme but ministerial. 2. The inference from Moses and other extraordinary, infallible ministers to the ordinary ministers does not hold, even under the New Testament, as if infallibility belonged to these as well.

units.la: Obj. 5. Nemo nunc audit vocem Spiritus Sancti, aut S. Scripturæ, sententiam ferentis: nec partes utrimque acquiescunt isti judicio, quòd pro unâ parte & contra alteram latum fit. Resp. Quoniam sententia quandoque rescripto pronunciatur; & per ignorantiam, vel malitiam alicujus partis, sæpè post latam sententiam protenditur contentio; non est necessarium JuJudicis requisitum, viva voce sententiam sic pronunciare, ut partes litigantes pariter audiant, & statim in eâ acquiescant. 2. Si hoc obtineat, nec ipse Papa Romanus Judex erit agnoscendus: ipsum enim sententiam sic non pronunciare; manifestissimum est. Viva ejus vox hîc non auditur; & plurimi ejus placitis non acquiescunt.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Nobody now hears the voice of the Holy Spirit or of Holy Scripture pronouncing sentence, nor do the parties on either side acquiesce in a judgment given for one side and against the other. Resp. 1. Since a sentence is sometimes pronounced by written rescript, and since through the ignorance or malice of one party the dispute often goes on long after the sentence has been given, it is not necessary for the judge to pronounce sentence aloud, so that both litigants hear it together and at once acquiesce. 2. If this objection held, the Roman Pope himself would have to be acknowledged as no judge, for it is perfectly clear that he does not pronounce sentence in this way. His living voice is not heard here, and very many do not acquiesce in his decisions.

units.la: LVIII. Neque admittendum, cum Socinianis, eorumque sequacibus, Rationem humanam esse Judicem & Normam controversiarum Theologicarum; vel etiàm, quod affine est, & aliquis contendere nuper ausus fuit, Philosophiam esse Normam infallibilem interpretandi S. Scripturam.
units.tr: LVIII. Nor is it to be admitted, with the Socinians and their followers, that human reason is the judge and rule of theological controversies; or, what is akin to this, that philosophy is the infallible rule for interpreting Holy Scripture, as someone recently dared to maintain.

units.la: Nam 1. veritates Theologicæ sunt supra rationem, mysteria diserte vocantur, &c. 1 Cor. 11, 6, - 10. IV, 1, Eph. 111, 3, 5. 1 Tim. 111, 16.
units.tr: For, 1. theological truths are above reason; they are expressly called mysteries (1 Cor. 2:6–10; 4:1; Eph. 3:3, 5; 1 Tim. 3:16).

units.la: 2. Eorum notitia ac fides datur, quibus Deo placet; & quidem ex gratiâ speciali ac supernaturali: Matth. XI, 25, 26. XIII, 11. XVI, 17.
units.tr: 2. The knowledge and faith of them are given to those whom God pleases, and that by special and supernatural grace (Matt. 11:25, 26; 13:11; 16:17).

units.la: 3. Ratio nostra nunc per naturam inepta & corrupta est, imò inimica adversus illas veritates; eòque minus judicialis ista auctoritas ei deferenda: Gen. VI, 5. VIII, 21. Rom. III, 10, 11, 12. Job. III, 6. XV, 5. 2 Cor. III, 5. Tit. I, 15. Eph. II, 1, 5. Rom. VIII, 7. 1 Cor. II, 14.
units.tr: 3. Our reason is now by nature unfit and corrupt, indeed hostile to those truths, and therefore all the less is this judicial authority to be conceded to it (Gen. 6:5; 8:21; Rom. 3:10–12; Job 3:6; 15:5; 2 Cor. 3:5; Titus 1:15; Eph. 2:1, 5; Rom. 8:7; 1 Cor. 2:14).

units.la: 4. Rationem hîc captivare debemus, & auctoritati Divinæ subjicere: 2 Cor. X, 5. Matth. XVI, 24.
units.tr: 4. We must take our reason captive here and subject it to the divine authority (2 Cor. 10:5; Matt. 16:24).

units.la: LIX. Ob. 1. Cultus noster vocatur rationalis; Rom. XII. 1. ergò ad rationem naturalem debet exigi. Resp. Vocatur rationalis; quia non consistit proprie in exercitatione corporali: 1 Tim. IV, 8. Sed rationem, cujus hîc usus est, gratiâ supernaturali corrigi & sanctificari necesse est, ac dirigi juxta normam à Deo in SS. Literis præscriptam.
units.tr: LIX. Obj. 1. Our worship is called reasonable (Rom. 12:1); therefore it must be measured by natural reason. Resp. It is called reasonable because it does not consist properly in bodily exercise (1 Tim. 4:8). But the reason whose use is in question here must needs be corrected and sanctified by supernatural grace, and directed according to the rule prescribed by God in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Obj. 2. Judicium demandatur ipsis hypocritis; Isf. v. 3. Resp. Non judicium quarumvis controversiarum TheoTheologicarum, aut mysteriorum fidei; & quidem ex iis, quæ nunc post lapsum homini naturaliter insunt: sed justæ rejectionis & ἀναπολογήσιας[?] carnalium ac pertinacium Judæorum; ubi causa Dei justa erat satis manifeste.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Judgment is committed to the hypocrites themselves (Isa. 5:3). Resp. It is not judgment of any theological controversies whatever, or of the mysteries of faith, and certainly not of those matters which now naturally belong to man after the fall; it is the just rejection and condemnation of carnal and obstinate Jews, in which the cause of God was sufficiently plainly just. [inexcusableness: ἀναπολογησίας]

units.la: Obj. 3. Philosophia est vera, certa, ac indubitata Rerum notitia, ex Principiis naturæ lumine cognitis deducta, atque apodictice demonstrata: ergo illa tàm SS. Literas interpretandi, quàm interpretationes explorandi, certa est atque infallibilis Norma. Resp. Transeat antecedens: nego consequentiam: Philosophia enim sphæram veritatum naturalium non excedit; sed in SS. Literis plurimæ occurrunt veritates supernaturales, quarum illa idcirco norma esse non potest.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Philosophy is the true, certain and indubitable knowledge of things, deduced from principles known by the light of nature and demonstrated apodictically; therefore it is a certain and infallible rule both for interpreting Holy Scripture and for testing interpretations. Resp. I grant the antecedent; I deny the consequence. For philosophy does not exceed the sphere of natural truths, but in Holy Scripture very many supernatural truths occur, and philosophy therefore cannot be a rule for them.

units.la: Obj. 4. Philosophia, cùm vera sit, ab omni errandi periculo libera est; cùm fallere nequeat, quodvis interpretamentum ad hanc exploratum, ad aliam deindè normam examinari prorsus non erit opus; neque, cùm immotis ac flecti nescius nitatur fundamentis, partium studio ducetur; ac denique hominum animis, cùm certa sit atque indubitata, assensum extorquere, ac firmam adferre cognitionem poterit: habet ergo omnia requisita, quæ in interpretandi normâ desiderantur, &c. Resp. 1. Interim Philosophia, ut in subjecto existit, non est ab omni errandi periculo libera. 2. Continetur intra limites rationis naturalis: ac proinde veritas supernaturalis ad istam explorari non potest; nedùm sic, ut ad aliam normam examinari prorsus opus non sit. 3. Fundamentis naturalibus, quantumvis certis, niti tamen non potest veritas supernaturalis; utpote sublimioris ordinis. 4. Consequenter Philosophia nullo modo ex suis principiis afferere potest veritates supernaturales; nedùm animis hominum circa illas assensum extorquere, ac firmam adferre cognitionem.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Philosophy, since it is true, is free from all danger of error; since it cannot deceive, there will be no need to examine any interpretation tested by it against some other rule; nor, since it rests on unmoving and immovable foundations, will it be led by partisan zeal; and finally, since it is certain and indubitable, it can extort assent from men's minds and bring firm knowledge. It therefore has all the requisites that are wanted in a rule of interpretation, etc. Resp. 1. Meanwhile philosophy, as it exists in its subject, is not free from all danger of error. 2. It is confined within the limits of natural reason, and therefore supernatural truth cannot be tested by it, much less so that there is no need to examine it against another rule. 3. Supernatural truth cannot, however, rest on natural foundations, however certain, since it belongs to a higher order. 4. Consequently philosophy can in no way from its own principles assert supernatural truths, much less extort assent to them from men's minds or bring firm knowledge of them.

units.la: Obj. 5. Unusquisque optimus verbotum suorum interpres est, quapropter, cum Deus Philosophiae auctor sit, ipsi etiam adscribenda erit omnis interpretatio, quae, Philosophiâ dirigente atque approbante, in medium adducitur. Resp. Verba Dei de veritatibus supernaturalibus exstant in S. Scriptura fatis plenè ac perspicuè; sed in Philosophiâ nullo modo; nedum in hac Deus illas interpretari voluerit:
units.tr: Obj. 5. Everyone is the best interpreter of his own words; therefore, since God is the author of philosophy, every interpretation that is brought forward under philosophy's direction and approval must also be ascribed to him. Resp. God's words concerning supernatural truths are found in Holy Scripture fully and clearly enough, but in philosophy in no way; much less has God wished to interpret them through philosophy.

units.la: LX. Interim tamen aliquis usus in his rebus concedendus est Rationi, per gratiam Spiritus S. illuminatae & sanctificatae: sic enim 1. est subjectum & instrumentum recipiens, atque agnoscens, veritates Theologicas.
units.tr: LX. Meanwhile, however, some use in these matters must be granted to reason, illuminated and sanctified by the grace of the Holy Spirit. For thus it is 1. the subject and receiving instrument which acknowledges theological truths.

units.la: 2. Conferens inter se varia SS. Literarum testimonia, typos cum veritate, parallela cum parallelis, &c.
units.tr: 2. It compares the various testimonies of Holy Scripture with one another: types with the truth, parallel passages with parallel passages, etc.

units.la: 3. Illustrans ex debitâ Verbi Divini consideratione, analysi, collatione.
units.tr: 3. It illustrates them by due consideration, analysis and collation of the divine Word.

units.la: 4. Inferens conclusiones Theologicas ex praemissis, tum meré Scripturariis, tum etiam lumine naturali ex parte aliquâ cognitis: in quibus conclusio dici debet supernaturalis, quia sphaeram naturae ipsa superat; & non nisi ope principii supernaturalis collecta est.
units.tr: 4. It draws theological conclusions from premises, both purely scriptural and partly known by the natural light; and a conclusion of this kind must be called supernatural, because it surpasses the sphere of nature itself and is gathered only by the aid of a supernatural principle.

units.la: LXI. Omnino etiam tenendum, contra Pontificios quosdam, & rudes Anabaptistas, Theologiam nostram esse argumentativam.
units.tr: 61. It must also be held, against certain Papists and crude Anabaptists, that our theology is argumentative.

units.la: Nam 1. sapientia est, ex principio suo conclusiones deducens: 2 Tim. iii, 15. & cultus noster rationalis: Rom. xii, 1.
units.tr: For, first, it is wisdom, deducing conclusions from its principle: 2 Tim. 3:15. And our worship is rational: Rom. 12:1.

units.la: 2. Idem evincunt phrases argumentativae; Act. iv, 19. xviii, 28. Rom. iii, 28. vi, 11. 1 Cor. ii, 14, 15. x, 15. xi, 13. xiv, 29. Phil. i, 10. 1 Thess. v, 21. Tit. i, 9, 11. Hebr. iv, 12. v, 14.
units.tr: Second, argumentative phrases prove the same: Acts 4:19; 18:28. Rom. 3:28; 6:11. 1 Cor. 2:14, 15; 10:15; 11:13; 14:29. Phil. 1:10. 1 Thess. 5:21. Titus 1:9, 11. Heb. 4:12; 5:14.

units.la: 3. Quia ipse Christus, & Apostoli, per consequentias tias difputarunt: Matth. xxii, 29, 31, 32. de refurrectione mortuorum. Vide etiàm Luc. xxiv, 25, -. Joh. v, 17, -. x, 24, -. Act. ii, 15. -. xv, 8, -. Rom. iv, 5, -8.
units.tr: Third, because Christ himself and the Apostles reasoned by consequences: Matt. 22:29, 31, 32, concerning the resurrection of the dead. See also Luke 24:25; John 5:17; 10:24; Acts 2:15; 15:8; Rom. 4:5-8.
1 Cor. 15:13, etc.

units.la: Speciatim huc faciunt istæ illationes Matth. xxviii, 6. Non est hîc; surrexit enim. Joh. viii, 55. Si dixero me non novisse Patrem, ero vobis similis, videlicet mendax. Gal. ii, 21. Si justitia est per Legem Christus frustrà mortuus est. Adde Hebr. vii, 7. x, 9.
units.tr: In particular, these inferences bear on this point: Matt. 28:6, "He is not here, for he has risen." John 8:55, "If I say that I do not know the Father, I shall be like you," that is, a liar. Gal. 2:21, "If righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died in vain." Add Heb. 7:7; 10:9.

units.la: 4. Cæteroquin nulla posset fieri applicatio, five in rebus fidei, five in moribus vivendi.
units.tr: Fourth, otherwise no application could be made, whether in matters of faith or in the conduct of life.

units.la: Obj. Quod ratiocinando colligitur, non habet certitudinem infallibilem; atque adeò non est fidei Divinæ; quia ratio nostra est fallibilis. Resp. 1. Absoluta infallibilitas foli Deo propria est: sic ergo ratio nostra fallibilis. Quando tamen & quatenùs ex Verbo Dei legitimè procedit, quanquam etiam collatis principiis quibusdam naturalibus necessariæ veritatis, ex hypothesi nec fallitur, nec falli potest. 2. Quatenus ista ratiocinatio Divinâ revelatione potissimùm nititur, atque ex ea conclusionem colligit, quæ ex principiis naturalibus solis colligi nunquàm potuisset; talis conclusio etiàm verè supernaturalis est, & fidei Divinæ.
units.tr: Objection: What is gathered by reasoning does not have infallible certainty, and so is not of divine faith, because our reason is fallible. Answer: (1) Absolute infallibility belongs to God alone; so our reason is fallible. Yet when and insofar as it legitimately proceeds from the Word of God, although certain principles of necessary truth from nature are also brought together, it on that supposition neither errs nor can err. (2) Insofar as such reasoning rests chiefly on divine revelation, and from it draws a conclusion which could never have been drawn from natural principles alone, such a conclusion is truly supernatural and is of divine faith.

units.la: LXII. Sic explicata est veritas de S. Scripturâ, Theo- logiæ nostræ supernaturalis principio doctrinali, & fi- dei morumque Canone unico.
units.tr: 62. In this way the truth concerning Holy Scripture has been explained: it is the supernatural doctrinal principle of our theology and the single canon of faith and morals.

units.la: Catechesis, aut Confessio nostra, (quicquid cavillentur Remonstrantes) talis Principii, aut Canonis, rationem non habet; licet materialiter præcipua saltem dogmata, & conclusiones Theologicas, ex unico illo Principio elicitas, fideliter exhibeat. Eadem medium quidem esse potest, quo novitates & heterodoxiæ facilius observentur ac dignoscantur, per modum indicis; sic tamen, ut analysis in ipsam S. Scripturam omnino facienda fit.
units.tr: Our Catechism or Confession (whatever the Remonstrants may quibble) does not have the character of such a principle or canon, although it faithfully sets forth, in material terms, at least the chief doctrines and theological conclusions drawn from that one principle. It may indeed serve as a means by which novelties and heterodoxies may be more easily observed and recognized, in the manner of an index; yet in such a way that the analysis must altogether be made into Holy Scripture itself.

units.la: Idem dicimus de Orthodoxorum Conciliorum Decretis, ac nominatim de Canonibus Synodi Nationalis Dordracenæ: nec non de Constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis ubi ea, quæ ad Ecclesiarum ordinem & regimen spectant, sive agenda, sive toleranda, secundum Verbum Dei, ad communem ædificationem, & scandalorum evitationem, prudenter applicata, proponuntur.
units.tr: We say the same of the decrees of the orthodox councils, and especially of the canons of the National Synod of Dort; and likewise of ecclesiastical constitutions, where those things which pertain to the order and government of the churches, whether to be done or to be tolerated, are proposed, prudently applied according to the Word of God, for common edification and the avoiding of scandals.

units.la: Quin & Symbolum, quod Apostolicum vocari solet non nisi materialiter tale est: at si formalem illam collectionem ac dispositionem spectes, ea nec ab Apostolis, nec à viris Apostolicis sic facta est; neque illud ab universâ Ecclesiâ sic antiquitus usurpatum. Consequenter non est αὐτόπιστον: sed tantum ἀξιόπιστον, propter S. Scripturam, unde desumtum & congestum est: quemadmodum & Symbolum Athanasianum, Nicenum, Constantinopolitanum, aliaque orthodoxographa.
units.tr: Indeed, the Creed commonly called Apostolic is such only in material terms; but if you look at that formal collection and arrangement, it was made neither by the Apostles nor by men of Apostolic times, nor was it so used in antiquity by the whole Church. Consequently it is not αὐτόπιστον [self-credible], but only ἀξιόπιστον [worthy of belief], on account of Holy Scripture, from which it was derived and put together; as also the Athanasian Creed, the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, and other collections of orthodox creeds.

units.la: LXIII. Revelationes Divinæ, post obsignatum Canonem S. Scripturæ pro Ecclesiâ N. T. fidelibus quibusdam extra ordinem factæ, illis quidem objecta fidei suæ Divinæ etiam fuerunt; non tamen Principium doctrinale Canonicum & commune.
units.tr: LXIII. Divine revelations made to certain faithful persons of the New Testament Church outside the ordinary way, after the canon of Holy Scripture was sealed, were indeed objects of their divine faith; yet they are not the canonical and common doctrinal principle.

units.la: Quæ vero Pythonici Gentilium Prophetæ aliquando dixerunt, aut scripserunt, quamvis interdum veritati consentanea, à Spiritu Sancto tamen profecta non sunt: Psal. cxlvii, 19, 20. Rom. iii, 2. ix, 4. Eph. ii, 12. Act. xiv, 15, 16, 17. sed à patre mendaciorum: Joh. viii, 44. 1 Cor. x, 20. 2, iv, 4. Qui quidem simium Dei agens, cultum partibus quibusdam similem Patriarchali, aut Levitico, instituit: nec non arcana quædam revelavit; & futura prædicere conatus est, aut videri voluit; sed plerumque ambiguè. Nonnulla interim ex Prophetiis Divinis transtulit: ac veritatem aliquam de Christo interdum dixit; sed ut falleret: quapropter ipse Christus, & Apostoli, testimonium istiusmodi non admiserunt; Matth. viii, 29. Marc. iii, 12. Act. xvi, 16, 17, 18. Sibyllas aliquandò extitisse, & carmina quædam conscripsisse, minimè negamus: sed quæ intercurrunt de Christo, aliisque mysteriis, tàm clara & plana, ut similia non reperiantur in veris Prophetiis V. T. ab aliis postmodùm composita, & Sibyllinis permixta, potiùs existimamus.
units.tr: But what the Pythonic prophets of the Gentiles sometimes said or wrote, although at times consonant with the truth, did not proceed from the Holy Spirit: Ps. 147:19, 20; Rom. 3:2; 9:4; Eph. 2:12; Acts 14:15-17. They proceeded from the father of lies: John 8:44; 1 Cor. 10:20; 2 Cor. 4:4. He, indeed, acting the ape of God, instituted a worship somewhat like the Patriarchal or the Levitical; he also revealed certain secrets, and tried, or wished to seem, to foretell the future, but mostly in an ambiguous way. Meanwhile he took some things from the divine prophecies, and sometimes spoke some truth about Christ, but in order to deceive; therefore Christ himself and the Apostles did not admit such testimony: Matt. 8:29; Mark 3:12; Acts 16:16-18. That Sibyls existed at some time and wrote certain poems we by no means deny; but what they say about Christ and other mysteries is so clear and plain that, rather, we judge that such passages were composed later by others and mixed in with the Sibylline verses, since similar things are not found in the true prophecies of the Old Testament.

units.la: Idem dicimus de Scriptis Mercurii Trifmegifti, aliorumque similium.
units.tr: We say the same of the writings of Mercurius Trismegistus and other such works.

units.la: LXIV. De Judæorum Talmude diximus fup. th. 32.
units.tr: LXIV. We have spoken of the Talmud of the Jews above, in thesis 32.

units.la: Muhammedanorum Korani mentio quoque facta est th. 28. Est autem insulsa & impia rhapfodia, ex particulis quibusdam SS. Scripturæ, plærumque tamen depravatis, fabulis item Talmudicis, Judaicis ac Gentilibus superstitionibus, & pfeudo-Christianorum quorundam hæresibus, per Muhammedem Arabicis rhytmis collecta, & SS. Literis perperàm subftituta.
units.tr: The Koran of the Muhammadans was also mentioned in thesis 28. It is, however, a silly and impious rhapsody, gathered by Muhammad into Arabic rhymes from certain fragments of Holy Scripture, mostly corrupted, along with Talmudic fables, Jewish and Gentile superstitions, and the heresies of certain pseudo-Christians, and wrongly substituted for the Sacred Writings.

units.la: Ejusdem furfuris est Suna ; Muhammedis lex ἀγεφ ; sed à fectatoribus ejus postmodùm in Scripturam redacta.
units.tr: Of the same chaff is the Sunna, the law of Muhammad, an unwritten law [ἄγραφος]; but it was later reduced to writing by his followers.

units.la: Usque adeò illa distant à Principiis veræ Theologiæ ac fidei Divinæ.
units.tr: To such an extent do these things differ from the principles of true theology and divine faith.

units.la: LXV. Pro praxi autem hæc erunt: 1. Omnes & singulos S. Scripturæ libros hoc animo, & scopo, & modo legamus ac meditemur jugiter, ut fidem & mores juxta canonem illum ἀκριβῶς instituamus: Psal. xl, 9. cxix, 4, 5, 9. 10, 11. 1 Sam. iii, 10. Phil. iii. 16. Apoc. ii. 7.
units.tr: LXV. As for practice, these shall be the rules: (1) Let us read and meditate continually on all and each of the books of Holy Scripture, with this mind, aim, and method, that we may shape our faith and morals exactly [ἀκριβῶς] according to that canon: Ps. 40:9; 119:4, 5, 9, 10, 11; 1 Sam. 3:10; Phil. 3:16; Rev. 2:7.

units.la: 2. Universam S. Scripturam, tanquàm verissimum Verbum ipsius Dei, solius sapientis, infallibilis, omnipotentis, agnoscamus & recipiamus: 1 Thess. ii. 13. Psal. cxix, 86, 89. 141, 142. Ne quis corrumpat, aut pervertat, vel minimam ejus particulam: Matth. v, 18, 19. Hof. xiv, 10. 2 Pet. iii. 16. Nemo contemnat. temnat, aut negligat: Psal cxix, 21, 118, 119. 155.
units.tr: (2) Let us acknowledge and receive the whole of Holy Scripture as the most true Word of God himself, the only wise, infallible, almighty one: 1 Thess. 2:13; Ps. 119:86, 89, 141, 142. Let no one corrupt or pervert even the smallest part of it: Matt. 5:18, 19; Hos. 14:10; 2 Pet. 3:16. Let no one despise, disregard, or neglect it: Ps. 119:21, 118, 119, 155.

units.la: 3. Illius vero intuitu contemnamus ac rejiciamus qualiacunque contraria dogmata, ratiocinationes, & revelationes: Matth.xv, 6, 9. 2 Cor.x, 5. Col. ii, 8, Luc.xvi, 29, 31. Gal. i, 8, -12.
units.tr: (3) Let us, with respect to it, despise and reject all contrary doctrines, reasonings, and revelations of whatever kind: Matt. 15:6, 9; 2 Cor. 10:5; Col. 2:8; Luke 16:29, 31; Gal. 1:8, 12.

units.la: 4. Grato animo agnoscamus instructissimum illum salutis thesaurum, apothecam locupletissimam, donum perfectissimum: Psal.cxix, 96. religiosè observantes istam αὐτάρκειαν; intra illas lineas continentes nos ipsos, & ad easdem revocantes alios, quantum in nobis: Col. iii, 16. Phil. iii, 16. 1 Joh. 1. 3, 4.
units.tr: (4) Let us gratefully acknowledge that most fully equipped treasury of salvation, that most abundant storehouse, that most perfect gift: Ps. 119:96; religiously observing that self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν]; confining ourselves within those lines and calling others back to them, as far as lies in us: Col. 3:16; Phil. 3:16; 1 John 1:3, 4.

units.la: 5. Istâ luce nos oblectemus, in eâ ambulemus, donec merus dies illucescat: 2 Petr. i, 19. cum Joh. v, 35. viii, 56. Psal.xxxv i, 9, 10. xix, 12. cxix, 103. In obscuris & dubiis huc confugiamus: Psal.cxix, 98, 99, 100. 104, 105. Actor. xvii, 11. 2 Tim. iii. 15, 16. Hoc pio studio peregrinationem nostram consolemur, Psal. cxix, 25, 28, 50, -56. Rom.xv, 4.
units.tr: (5) Let us delight ourselves in this light, walk in it, until the perfect day dawns: 2 Pet. 1:19, with John 5:35; 8:56; Ps. 36:9, 10; 19:12; 119:103. In obscure and doubtful matters let us take refuge here: Ps. 119:98-100, 104, 105; Acts 17:11; 2 Tim. 3:15, 16. Let us console our pilgrimage with this devout study: Ps. 119:25, 28, 50, 56; Rom. 15:4.

units.la: 6. Sic rationem nostram moderemur, atque in SS. Literis nos pie exerceamus, ut genuinum sensum assequamur: 1 Cor.x, 15. Matth.xvi, 24. xi, 25, 26, 27. xiii, ii, -1 Cor.xiv, 9, 12, 20. Præ aliis autem hoc agant Antecessores: 2 Tim. iii, 17. Ii, 15. i, iv, 16. Tit. i, 9, 10, 11. Quæ vero recte percepta sunt, teneamus constanter: Apoc. iii, 3, 11. in opera convertamus: Joh.xiii, 17. & ad aliorum ædificationem pro virili nostra conferamus: 1 Thes.v, 11.
units.tr: (6) Let us so govern our reason, and so devoutly exercise ourselves in the Sacred Writings, that we may attain the genuine sense: 1 Cor. 10:15; Matt. 16:24; 11:25-27; 13:11; 1 Cor. 14:9, 12, 20. Let the teachers especially do this: 2 Tim. 3:17; 2:15; 4:16; Titus 1:9, 10, 11. Let us hold constantly to what has been rightly understood: Rev. 3:3, 11; let us turn it into works: John 13:17; and let us contribute it, as far as our strength allows, to the edification of others: 1 Thess. 5:11.

units.la: CAPUT IV. DE DEO.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. CONCERNING GOD.

units.la: Terminus Deus. Existentia Dei probatur c. Atheos 1. Quomodò ad salutem cognoscendus. Effentia. 2. Vivens. Spiritus. Descriptio. 3. Nomina. 4. Deus non nomen officii, sed naturae: c. Socin. probatur, & defenditur. 5. Non appellativum; sed proprium. Obj. solv. 6. אלהים notat pluralitatem personarum. Obj. solv. 7. Epitheta. Tituli. אהיה, יהוה, יה. Κύριος. 8. Nomen יהוה non fictitium. c. Remonstr. Non habet virtutem patrandi miracula. Non est. ἀνεγκφώνητον. c. Jud. 9. Soli vero Deo proprium. c. Socin & Remonstr. Obj. solv. 10. Tituli, vel Attributa, loco Nominum. Nomina usurpata tum ἀγιωδῶς, tum ὑποσατικῶς. 11. Attributa Dei. Quomodò per naturam investiganda. 12. Attributa primi generis. 13. Primitas. 14. Deus à se. 15. Simplicitas. Quid Compositio. Illa in Deo probatur, c. Socin. & Remonstr. 16. Objectiones solvuntur. 17. Consectaria Simplicitatis. 18. Dei unitas. 19. Immutabilitas c. Socin. &c. 20. Objectiones solv. 21. Invisibilitas: c. Vorst 22. Impalpabilitas. 23. Ineffigiabilitas: c. Pontif. 24. Infinitas: primò Essentiae. 25. Aeternitas: & quidem Successione carens. 26. Objectiones solvuntur. 27. Immensitas: c. Socin. Anabapt.
units.tr: The term God. The existence of God is proved against the atheists (1). How he is to be known for salvation (2). His essence (3). Living. Spirit. Description (4). Names (5). God is a name not of office but of nature: this is proved and defended against Socinus (6). It is not a common noun but a proper name; objections answered (7). The Hebrew אלהים signifies a plurality of persons; objections answered (8). Epithets. Titles: אהיה, יהוה, יה. Κύριος (9). The name יהוה is not fictitious; against the Remonstrants. It does not have the power to work miracles. It is not ineffable; against the Jews (10). But it belongs to God alone; against Socinus and the Remonstrants; objections answered (11). Titles or attributes in place of names. Names used both ἀγιωδῶς and ὑποσατικῶς (12). The attributes of God, and how they are to be investigated through nature (13). Attributes of the first kind (14). Primacy (15). God is from himself (16). Simplicity. What composition is. That simplicity is proved in God, against Socinus and the Remonstrants (17). Objections answered (18). Consequences of simplicity (19). The unity of God (20). Immutability; against Socinus, etc. (21). Objections answered (22). Invisibility; against Vorstius (23). Impalpability (24). Incomprehensibility of image; against the Papists (25). Infinity: first of his essence (26). Eternity, indeed lacking succession (27). Objections answered (28). Immensity; against Socinus and the Anabaptists (29).

units.la: Remonstr. 28. Etiam extra mundum. 29. Speciales modi praesentiae Divinae. 30. Objectiones solv. 31. Incomprehensibilitas prob. & defend. 32. Attributa secundi generis. 33. Intellectus Dei. 34. Scientia simplicis intelligentia. Idea possibilium. Scientia visionis. Quaestio. 35. Deus definite novit omnia. Contingentia, & libera, &c. Obj. solv. 36. Scientia media refut. 39. Objectiones solv. 40. Intellectus Dei simplicissimus, & immutabilis. 41. Independens. 42. Voluntas Dei. Ejus objectum. Sanctitas Jehovae. 43. Objectum prajacens. Terminans. In genere entis. 44. Amor Dei. Amor benevolentiae. Complacentia. 45. Gratia. gratis dans Gratum faciens. Gratia Gratis data. 46. Misericordia Dei. Generalis. Specialis. 47. Patientia. Longanimitas. 48. Bonitas Dei in genere moris. Iustitia. 49. In dictis. Veracitas. Fides. Constantia. 50. In factis. Regimine. Jurisdictione. 51. Remuneratio bonorum operum. 52. Punitio peccatorum. 53. Poenarum exactio pertinet ad Justitiam: c. Socin. 54. Justitia punitiva perpetuo exstitit in Deo, ipsique essentialis est. 55. Ejus exercitium positis peccatis est necessarium. 56. Objectiones solv. 57. Iustitia distributiva praemiorum ex debito: itemque commutativa, non in Deo. Malum per se non objicitur Voluntati Divinae. 58. Voluntatis Div. infinitas. Non Velleitas. Obj. solv. 59. Ejusdem simplicitas. Distinctio in realem, & moralem: Occultam, & revelatam. Beneplaciti, & signi. Mandati. dati. 60. Sine intrinseca diversitate. 61. Independentia. Obj. solv. 62. Male distinguitur in absolutam & conditionatam. Antecedentem, & consequentem. Libertas complacentia: exercitii: specificationis. 63. Potentia Dei. 64. Infinita. Obj. solv. 65. Simplicissima. Distinguitur tamen in absolutam; & ordinatam. Impossibilia. 66. Independens. Radix possibilitatis & impossibilitatis. 67 Potestas, seu Dominium Dei. Circa possibilia. 68. Circa creaturas existentes. Rationales. 69. Independens. Non fundatur proprie in beneficio creationis, aut maleficio creaturae peccantis, aut contractu cum creatura rationali. c. Remonstr. 70. Objectiones solv. 71. Sic incommunicabilis. Potestas Magistratuum. Christi Mediatoris. 72. Gloria Dei. Unde innotescat Dei excellentia. Qualem cultum inferat. 73. Cultus religiosus Deo proprius. 74. Ex eo recte probatur vera Deitas, contra Arianos, & Socin. Exc. & Obj. solv. 75. Beatitudo Dei. 76. Usus practici. 77.
units.tr: Against the Remonstrants: (30) God is also present outside the world. (31) Special modes of the divine presence. (32) Objections answered. (33) Incomprehensibility is proved and defended. (34) Attributes of the second kind. (35) The understanding of God. (36) Knowledge of simple understanding; the idea of possibles; knowledge of vision; a question. (37) God knows all things definitely; contingent and free things, etc.; objections answered. (38) Middle knowledge is refuted. (39) Objections answered. (40) The understanding of God is most simple and immutable. (41) Independence. (42) The will of God: its object; the holiness of Jehovah. (43) The object lying beneath: the terminating object; in the genus of being. (44) The love of God: love of benevolence; complacency. (45) Grace: grace bestowing freely; grace making pleasing; grace given freely. (46) The mercy of God: general; special. (47) Patience; longsuffering. (48) The goodness of God in the genus of morals; justice. (49) In words: truthfulness; faithfulness; constancy. (50) In deeds: in governing; in jurisdiction. (51) The reward of good works. (52) The punishment of sins. (53) The exacting of penalties pertains to justice; against Socinus. (54) Punitive justice has always existed in God and is essential to him. (55) Its exercise, once sins are posited, is necessary. (56) Objections answered. (57) Distributive justice of rewards owed; likewise commutative justice, is not in God. Evil as such is not opposed to the divine will. (58) The infinity of the divine will. Not velleity. Objections answered. (59) Its simplicity. Distinction into real and moral; hidden and revealed; of good pleasure and of sign; of command; given. (60) Without intrinsic diversity. (61) Independence. Objections answered. (62) It is wrongly distinguished into absolute and conditional, antecedent and consequent. Freedom of complacency, of exercise, of specification. (63) The power of God. (64) Infinite. Objections answered. (65) Most simple. Yet it is distinguished into absolute and ordained. Impossibilities. (66) Independent. The root of possibility and impossibility. (67) The power, or dominion, of God, concerning possibles. (68) Concerning existing creatures, rational ones. (69) Independent. It is not properly founded on the benefit of creation, or on the wrongdoing of a sinning creature, or on a contract with a rational creature; against the Remonstrants. (70) Objections answered. (71) So also incommunicable. The power of magistrates; of Christ the Mediator. (72) The glory of God. Whence the excellence of God is made known; what worship it entails. (73) Religious worship is proper to God. (74) From this the true Deity is rightly proved, against the Arians and Socinus; excursus and objections answered. (75) The blessedness of God. (76) Practical uses. (77)

units.la: I. Rogredimur ad objectum primarium Theologiae nostrae, Deum: qui termi- nus animum nostrum elevat ad conce- ptum & contemplationem entis primi, summi ac perfectissimi.
units.tr: I. We proceed to the primary object of our theology, God, which term lifts our mind to the concept and contemplation of the first, highest and most perfect being.

units.la: Deum esse, contra Atheorum monstra, satis probat Natura: per ipsam conscientiam omnibus hominibus ingenitam, quae dictat numen aliquod religiose agnoscendum & colendum esse; honesti & turpis discrimen; justam eorum, quae hic aguntur, retributionem expectandam: unde animorum stimuli, heroici quorunrundam impetus, aliorum terrores, communis consensus, & qualiacunq; Religionis ubiq; gentium exercitia.
units.tr: That God exists, against the monstrosities of the atheists, is sufficiently proved by nature: through the conscience implanted in all men, which dictates that some divinity is to be acknowledged and worshipped religiously; the distinction between honourable and base; that a just retribution for what is done here is to be expected. Hence come the goads of souls, the heroic impulses of some, the terrors of others, the common consensus, and the practices of religion, of whatever kind, found among all nations everywhere.

units.la: 2. Ex reliquis creaturis, per demonstrationem a posteriori. Spectantur autem essentia, facultates, operationes; omnia dependentia, mutabilia, mutanda: unde adscenditur ad causam primam, immutabilem, persectissimam; in causarum enim subordinatione non datur progressus in infinitum; sed necessario subsistendum in primâ:
units.tr: 2. From the remaining creatures, by demonstration a posteriori. We observe their essence, faculties and operations: all of them dependent, changeable, and liable to change. Hence we ascend to a first cause, unchangeable and most perfect; for in the subordination of causes there is no progress to infinity, but we must necessarily stop at a first one.

units.la: 3. Speciatim ex judiciis, eventis quibusdam insolitis, portentis, prophetiis, ac miraculis: quae mentem nostram evehunt supra causas omnes naturales, ad Judicem supremum, & Auctorem naturae universae, qui legibus ejus non tenetur.
units.tr: 3. Especially from judgments, certain unusual events, portents, prophecies and miracles, which lift our mind above all natural causes to the supreme Judge and Author of all nature, who is not bound by its laws.

units.la: 4. Ex concordi discordia, & tendentia omnium rerum ad certum aliquem finem; cujus directionis analysis in causas creatas fieri nequit. Confer. sup. cap. 1. th. 14, -19.
units.tr: 4. From the concordant discord and tendency of all things towards a certain end; the analysis of this direction cannot be carried out into created causes. See above, chapter 1, theses 14–19.

units.la: II. Verùm cùm Theologia naturalis ad salutem nunc non sufficiat, & fide opus fit. (Hebr. xi. 6. Vide cap. 1. th. 22, 23, 24.) Deum fide magistrâ, & ratione utcunque ministrâ, contemplabimur tùm in se, scil. in essentia, & in personis, tum in actionibus suis.
units.tr: II. But since natural theology is now not sufficient for salvation, and faith is needed (Hebr. xi. 6; see chapter 1, theses 22, 23, 24), we shall contemplate God, with faith as our teacher and reason in whatever ministerial role it may play, both in himself, namely in his essence and in his persons, and in his actions.

units.la: Essentiam Dei rectè appellari probatur contra Antitrinitarios; 1. Quia S. Scriptura aiserte praeit: Prov. viii, 14.
units.tr: That the essence of God is rightly so called is proved against the Antitrinitarians. 1. Because Holy Scripture expressly says so: Prov. viii. 14.

units.la: 2. Ex paronymis: Deus se vocat אהיה אשר אהיה, Exod. iii, 14. Item Apoc. i, 4. 8. dicitur, ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος.
units.tr: 2. From paronyms: God calls himself אהיה אשר אהיה [I am that I am], Exod. iii. 14. Likewise in Rev. i. 4, 8 he is called ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [who is, who was, and who is to come].

units.la: 3. Occurrunt etiàm synonyma: utpotè φύσις Θεοῦ, Gal. iv, 8. 2 Petr. i, 4. μορφὴ Θεοῦ, Phil. ii, 6. Qui termini non physicè, sed prorsus hyperphysicè sumendi sunt.
units.tr: 3. Synonyms also occur, namely φύσις Θεοῦ [nature of God], Gal. iv. 8; 2 Pet. i. 4; μορφὴ Θεοῦ [form of God], Phil. ii. 6. These terms are not to be taken physically, but altogether hyperphysically.

units.la: 4. Appellatur denique Θεότης, Col. ii, 9. & Θειότης Rom. i, 20.
units.tr: 4. Finally, he is called Θεότης [Godhead], Col. ii. 9, and Θειότης [divinity], Rom. i. 20.

units.la: III. Essentia Dei vivens est: Deut. v. 26. xxxi. 40.
units.tr: III. The essence of God is living: Deut. v. 26; xxxi. 40.

units.la: 1 Sam. xvii, 36. Jerem. v. 2. 1Joh. 4, v, 20. Joh. 4. v. 26 Psal. xxxvi, 10. 1 Tim. vi, 16.
units.tr: 1 Sam. xvii. 36; Jer. v. 2; 1 John v. 20; John v. 26; Ps. xxxvi. 10; 1 Tim. vi. 16.

units.la: Sed vita illa spiritualis: Joh. iv, 24. Deus est spiritus. Hoc est, vera substantia, aut potiùs ὑπερουσία, molis corporeæ expers, sed intellectù & efficaciâ præcellens. Isef. xxxi, 3. Rom. xi, 33, 36. ix, 19. Eph. I, 11. Act. xvii, 25, 28. Psal. xciv, 9, 10.
units.tr: But that life is spiritual: John iv. 24, God is spirit. That is, he is a true substance, or rather a supersubstance [ὑπερουσία], free from corporeal mass, but excelling in understanding and efficacy. Isa. xxxi. 3; Rom. xi. 33, 36; ix. 19; Eph. i. 11; Acts xvii. 25, 28; Ps. xciv. 9, 10.

units.la: Verùm hæc ἁπλᾶ ὑπερούσια non habet genus supra se; ut nec species, vel individua, æquali secùm gradù: neque differentiam constitutivam; ipse actus primus ac purissimus. Consequenter proprie definiri non potest Deus infinitus. Interim describitur pro nostro modulo, Essentia spiritualis seipsa vivens. Nisi quis addi malit; tribus personis subsistens, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: Yet this simple supersubstance [ἁπλᾶ ὑπερούσια] has no genus above it, nor species or individuals of equal rank with it, nor a constitutive difference; he is the first and purest act. Consequently God, being infinite, cannot properly be defined. Meanwhile he is described, according to our measure, as an essence, spiritual and living of itself. Unless someone prefers to add: subsisting in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: IV. Deus, cùm per essentiam suam unicus sit, nomine discretivo non indiget; quo ab aliis ejusdem speciei, vel generis, distingueretur. Ipse tamen, ut nos propriùs in sui notitiam adduceret, seque à creaturis ac idolis clariùs discerneret, nomina quædam adhiberi voluit. Nomen diverse appellatur, Gen. xxxii, 29. Jud. xiii, 18. Prov. xxx, 4. Exod. iii, 13, 14. vi, 2. Jes. xlii, 8. &c. Imò metonymice Nomen Dei, aut καὶ ἐξοχὴν Nomen, quandóque usurpatur pro ipso Deo, aut ejus voluntate, potentiâ, auctoritate, vel gloriâ: Lev. xxiv, 11, 15, 16. 1 Sam. xvii, 45. Psal. lxxxvi, 9, 11. lxxxix, 17, 25. cxvi, 13, 17. Mich. vi, 9. Matth. xviii, 20. xxviii, 19. Phil. II, 10.
units.tr: IV. Since God, by his essence, is unique, he has no need of a distinguishing name by which he would be set apart from others of the same species or genus. Yet he himself, so that he might bring us nearer to the knowledge of himself, and that he might distinguish himself more clearly from creatures and idols, willed that certain names be used. The name is variously expressed: Gen. xxxii. 29; Judg. xiii. 18; Prov. xxx. 4; Exod. iii. 13, 14; vi. 2; Isa. xlii. 8, etc. Indeed, by metonymy, the name of God, or pre-eminently the Name [καὶ ἐξοχὴν], is sometimes used for God himself, or for his will, power, authority or glory: Lev. xxiv. 11, 15, 16; 1 Sam. xvii. 45; Ps. lxxxvi. 9, 11; lxxxix. 17, 25; cxvi. 13, 17; Mic. vi. 9; Matt. xviii. 20; xxviii. 19; Phil. ii. 10.

units.la: Frequentissimum est Hebraïcum nomen אֱלֹהִים, sicut Græcum Θεός, & Latinum Deus.
units.tr: The Hebrew name Elohim [אֱלֹהִים], like the Greek Theos [Θεός] and the Latin Deus, is extremely frequent.

units.la: V. Hîc autem primò contra Socinianos asserimus, quòd nomen Deus, sicut & ejus synonyma, in usû proprio, non sit nomen officii; sed essentiæ, vel naturæ.
units.tr: Here, first, we assert against the Socinians that the name God, like its synonyms, in its proper use is not a name of office but of essence or nature.

units.la: 1. Nam non deducitur ab alio Nomine, aut verbo, muneris alicujus functionem significante: ut quidem
units.tr: (1) For it is not derived from another name or verb signifying the performance of some function,

units.la: InImperator ab imperando; Rex, à regendo; &c.
units.tr: as Imperator (emperor) is from imperare (to command), Rex (king) from regere (to rule), and so on.

units.la: 2. Nec abstractum ejus Deitas formaliter officium exprimit; sed ipsam naturam entis perfectissimi: nam procul dubio synonyma sunt Deitas, & Natura vel Forma Dei.
units.tr: (2) Nor does its abstract form, Deity, express an office formally; it expresses the very nature of the most perfect being. For Deity and Nature or Form of God are without doubt synonyms.

units.la: 3. Neque supponitur aliud nomen ipsam naturam significans, cui deinceps superaddatur hoc nomen Deus, tanquam denotans ejus officium. Sic homo aliquis, puta Carolus, &c. est Rex, &c.
units.tr: (3) Nor is there any other name presupposed that signifies the nature itself, to which this name God is then added as denoting an office, as when some man, say Charles, is called king and so on.

units.la: Obj. Magistratus appellantur אלהים, ratione officii ac potestatis; non ratione naturae: ergo, &c. Resp. Nego consequentiam: Magistratus isto nomine non appellantur proprie; sed propter qualemcunque similitudinem analogicam. Vulpes metaphorice dicitur de homine vafro; atque tunc qualitatem notat, non naturam: verum inde nequaquam sequitur, etiam in usu proprio non significare naturam, sed qualitatem.
units.tr: Objection. Magistrates are called elohim, by reason of office and power, not by reason of nature; therefore, and so on. Reply. I deny the inference: magistrates are not properly called by this name, but on account of some analogical likeness, whatever it may be. The fox is spoken of metaphorically of a crafty man, and then it denotes a quality, not a nature. But it by no means follows from this that the name does not signify nature, but quality, even in its proper use.

units.la: VI. Deinde, quod idem hoc nomen non sit appellativum, sed proprium: significat enim ens natura sua singularissimum: Job. XVII, 3.
units.tr: VI. Next, this same name is not an appellative but a proper name, for it signifies a being that is by its nature most singular: John 17:3.

units.la: Obj. 1. Angeli, & Magistratus, Dii appellantur: Psal. VIII, 6. cum Hebr. II, 7. Item Psal. LXXXII, 6. Exod. IV, 15, 16. VII, 1, 2. XXII, 8, 9. Job. X, 35. Resp. Non usu nativo istius nominis; sed metaphorice & analogice.
units.tr: Objection 1. Angels and magistrates are called gods: Psalm 8:6, compared with Hebrews 2:7; likewise Psalm 82:6; Exodus 4:15, 16; 7:1, 2; 22:8, 9; Job 10:35. Reply. Not in the native use of this name, but metaphorically and analogically.

units.la: Obj. 2. Etiam idola. Resp. Hoc fit abusive, & μιμητικῶς. Vide Jud. XI, 24. Am. V, 26. cum Jerem. XVI, 20. Hos. VIII, 6. Psal. XCVI, 5. Confer etiam. 1 Cor. VIII, 5. 2 Thess. II, 4. cum Job. XVII, 3. 1 Job. V, 20.
units.tr: Objection 2. Idols too. Reply. This happens abusively and mimetically [μιμητικῶς]. See Judges 11:24; Amos 5:26, compared with Jeremiah 16:20; Hosea 8:6; Psalm 96:5. Compare also 1 Corinthians 8:5; 2 Thessalonians 2:4, with John 17:3 and 1 John 5:20.

units.la: VII. Caeterum nomen אלוה singulari numero occurrit, Deut. XXXII, 17. Job. III, 4, 23. XII, 4. XXXVI, 2 Psal. L, 22. Hab. III, 2. sed alibi saepissime pluraliter אלהים: & cum eo nomina adjectiva, & verba, tum pluraliter, tum singulariter, construuntur. Vide Gen. XX, 13. Deut. V, 26. Jos. XXIV, 19. Jer. X, 10. Etiam plu pluraliter in prima persona. Gen. I, 26. iii, 22. xi, 7. Isef. vi, 8. Scilicet ad exprimendam essentiam in se quidem unicam, pluribus interim personis subsistentem.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, the name eloah [אלוה] occurs in the singular, Deuteronomy 32:17; Job 3:4, 23; 12:4; 36:2; Psalm 50:22; Habakkuk 3:2, but elsewhere very often the plural elohim [אלהים] is used. With it, both adjectives and verbs are construed, sometimes in the plural and sometimes in the singular. See Genesis 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:26; Joshua 24:19; Jeremiah 10:10. Also the plural is used in the first person plural: Genesis 1:26; 3:22; 11:7; Isaiah 6:8. Evidently this is to express an essence which is indeed one in itself, yet subsists in several persons.

units.la: Obj. 1. Uni idolo idem nomen plurale tribuitur; neque tamen ibi notat pluralitatem personarum, Ergo neque in vero Deo. Resp. Idolum sic appellatur abusive; quatenus triuni vero Deo substituitur.
units.tr: Objection 1. The same plural name is attributed to one idol, and yet there it does not signify a plurality of persons; therefore neither does it in the true God. Reply. An idol is so called abusively, inasmuch as it is set up in place of the true triune God.

units.la: Obj. 2. Idem etiam usurpatur de una persona Divina: ut Psal. xlv, 8. Resp. Nimirum, quatenus ei competit essentia pluribus personis subsistens, per ἐμφανχώρησιν.
units.tr: Objection 2. The same is also used of one divine person, as in Psalm 45:8. Reply. Namely, inasmuch as the essence, subsisting in several persons, belongs to that person by coinherence [ἐμφανχώρησιν].

units.la: VIII. Ut autem a Diis nuncupatitiis planius se discerneret verus Deus, Nomen suum insignibus quibusdam epithetis circumscripsit; ut Deus Abrami, Isaaci, & Jacobi: Exod. iii, 6. Deus magnus: Tit. II, 13. Unus verus Deus: Joh. xvii, 3. Verus Deus & vita aeterna:
units.tr: VIII. So that the true God might be more clearly distinguished from the so-called gods, he surrounded his name with certain distinguishing epithets, such as God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: Exodus 3:6; the great God: Titus 2:13; the only true God: John 17:3; the true God and eternal life:

units.la: 1 Joh. v, 20. Supra omnes Deus benedictus in saecula: Rom. ix, 5. Imo & Nomina quaedam sibi prorsus peculiaria reservavit; atque ita revelavit: ut יהוה, Exod. iii, 14. essentiam illam eminentissimam denotans; ut & cognatum ei יהו, Exod. iv, 30. alias יה, Ezech. ii, 4. ante contracte י, Psal. cxxxv, 4. cujus periphrasis est, ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, Apoc. I, 4, 8.
units.tr: 1 John 5:20; God over all, blessed for ever: Romans 9:5. Indeed he also reserved for himself certain names that are wholly peculiar to him, and so revealed them: such as יהוה [Jehovah], Exodus 3:14, denoting that most eminent essence; and its kindred form יהו [Jehu], Exodus 4:30, elsewhere יה [Jah], Ezekiel 2:4, and before a vowel contracted to י [Jah], Psalm 135:4. Its periphrasis is ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [who is, who was, and who is to come], Revelation 1:4, 8.

units.la: LXX. Interpretes illud per Κύριος reddiderunt; quod in libris N.T. etiam servatum; tum quod propter literarum necessarium defectum, illud ipsum materialiter Graece exprimi non posset; tum quod fortasse verbum κυρῶ (sum) respexerint, & sic satis convenire exististimaverint.
units.tr: The Septuagint translators rendered it by Κύριος [Lord]; this is also retained in the books of the New Testament. This was partly because, owing to the necessary lack of letters, the name itself could not be expressed materially in Greek; partly because they perhaps had in view the verb κυρῶ (to be valid), and thought that it agreed sufficiently well in this way.

units.la: IX. Nomen illud יהוה, a numero literarum, quibus constat, appellari solet τετραγράμματον.
units.tr: IX. That name יהוה [Jehovah] is commonly called the Tetragrammaton [τετραγράμματον], from the number of letters of which it consists.

units.la: Sed porro observandum contra Remonstrantes, id non esse fictitium; sed ab ipso Deo sic revelatum, ac in S. Scriptura a viris Θεοπνευστοις consignatum, & quidem plurimis vicibus ac locis.
units.tr: But, further, it must be observed against the Remonstrants that this name is not fictitious, but was revealed thus by God himself, and was recorded in Holy Scripture by men inspired by God [Θεοπνεύστοις], and indeed on very many occasions and in many places.

units.la: Item contra Judæos, illud nomen, aut ejus interpretationem, non habere peculiarem virtutem aliquam patrandi miracula: nam omnia nomina sunt tantùm moraliter significativa rerum; nec possunt miracula patrari, nisi virtute ipsius Dei, qui isto nomine indicatur.
units.tr: Likewise, against the Jews: that name, or its interpretation, does not have any peculiar power of working miracles. For all names are only morally significant of things, and miracles cannot be wrought except by the power of God himself, who is indicated by that name.

units.la: Atque iterùm contra eosdem, & quosdam alios, illud nomen non esse materialiter, ἀνεκφώνητον: sed legendum & pronunciandum secundùm proprias suas literas & vocales. Nam i proprius finis scriptorum est, sic legi & pronunciari.
units.tr: And again, against the same and some others: that name is not materially unpronounceable [ἀνεκφώνητον], but must be read and pronounced according to its own letters and vowels. For the proper purpose of writings is that they be read and pronounced in this way.

units.la: 2. Hoc memoriali Deus ab omnibus aliis, & nominatim à λεγομένοις Θεοῖς, emphaticè discerni voluit: Psal. lxxx, iii, 19. Sed usus iste nullus est, nisi illud nomen sic legatur & pronuncietur.
units.tr: (2) By this memorial God wished to be emphatically distinguished from all others, and especially from the so-called gods [λεγομένοις Θεοῖς]: Psalm 83:18, 19. But this use is nothing unless the name is read and pronounced thus.

units.la: 3. In compositis pronunciatur ab iis ipsis, qui contrarium statuunt: ut in <bl>יהוה</bl>, <bl>יהוצדק</bl>, <bl>יהונתן</bl>, <bl>יהושפט</bl> &c.
units.tr: (3) In compounds it is pronounced even by those who hold the contrary, as in Jehovah, Jehozadak, Jonathan, Jehoshaphat, and so on.

units.la: 4. Satis etiam probabile est, ex famâ illius nominis Gentiles Jovem appellasse: &c.
units.tr: (4) It is also fairly probable that the Gentiles, from the fame of that name, called Jupiter by it, and so on.

units.la: X. Afferimus insuper contra Socinianos, eorumque sequaces Remonstrantes, idem hoc nomen soli vero Deo esse omninò proprium; adeò ut nulli unquàm creaturæ communicetur in casu recto: & consequenter, ex ejus attributione veram Deitatem rectè colligi. Ideò 1. toties & tàm emphaticè Deus hoc suum nomen dixit, quo maximè dignosci voluit.
units.tr: X. We further assert, against the Socinians and their followers the Remonstrants, that this same name is wholly proper to the true God alone, so that it is never communicated to any creature in the nominative case; and consequently, from its ascription, true Deity may rightly be inferred. Therefore (1) God called this his name so often and so emphatically, by which he most wished to be known.

units.la: Et 2. suum memoriale appellavit; Exod. iii, 13. vi, 3, 2. Psal. lxxxiii, 19. Hos. xii, 6.
units.tr: And (2) he called it his memorial: Exodus 3:13; 6:3, 2; Psalm 83:19; Hosea 12:6.

units.la: 3. Negavit se id aliis communicaturum: Jes. xlii, 8.
units.tr: (3) He denied that he would communicate it to others: Isaiah 42:8.

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Angelus aliquis interdum appellatur יהוה: at Gen. xviii, 1, 13, 14, & alibi. Resp. Intelligendus tunc Angelus increatus, qui Angelus fœderis dicitur. Mal. iii, 1. & faciei i Jes. lxiii, 9. Filius Dei, in consideratione œconomicâ.
units.tr: Objection 1. Yet some angel is sometimes called יהוה [Jehovah]: as in Genesis 18:1, 13, 14, and elsewhere. Reply. The angel must then be understood as the uncreated angel, who is called the angel of the covenant, Malachi 3:1, and the angel of his face, Isaiah 63:9: the Son of God, considered in his economic role.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ad Arcam fœderis dicebatur, Surge, Iehovah, &c. Num.x, 35, 36. Resp. Imo oratio ista dirigebatur ad ipsum Deum, per occasionem Arcæ fœderis, quæ erat singulare symbolum præsentiæ Divinæ.
units.tr: Objection 2. Over the ark of the covenant it was said, Arise, Jehovah, and so on: Numbers 10:35, 36. Reply. Indeed that prayer was directed to God himself, on the occasion of the ark of the covenant, which was the unique sign of the divine presence.

units.la: Obj. 3. Hierosolyma vocatur Iehovah ibi, Ezech. xlviii, 35. Resp. Sic urbs ipsa non vocatur Iehovah; sed de urbe prædicatur singularis præsentia gratiæ Divinæ.
units.tr: Objection 3. Jerusalem is called Jehovah is there, Ezekiel 48:35. Reply. In this way the city itself is not called Jehovah; rather, a unique presence of divine grace is predicated of the city.

units.la: XI. Accedunt insuper Tituli, aut Attributa, quæ instar Nominum de Deo in SS. Literis quandoque usurpantur: utpote יְהוָה Omnisufficiens: Exod. vi, 2, Ezech. i, 24, אֵל Potens; Isf. xliii, 10. אֲדֹנָי, Dominus; Isf. iii. 17. Vide etiam Jef. ix, 5. Act. xvii, 14. 1 Tim. vi, 15. Apoc. xv, 3. Item קָדוֹשׁ, Sanctus; Job. vi, 10. עֶלְיוֹן, Excelsus; Gen. xiv, 18. Vide etiam Isef. lvii. 15. Luc. 1, 32. Nec non metonymicè שָׁמַיִם, οὐρανὸς, Cœlum, Dan. iv, 26. Matth. xxi, 25. Luc. xv, 18. & metaphorice צוּר, Rupes; Deuteron. xxii, 18, 30. &c.
units.tr: XI. In addition, there are titles or attributes which, in the manner of names, are sometimes used of God in the holy Scriptures: for example, יְהוָה [Jehovah] meaning all-sufficient, Exodus 6:2; Ezekiel 1:24; אֵל [El], powerful, Isaiah 43:10; אֲדֹנָי [Adonai], Lord, Isaiah 3:17. See also Isaiah 9:5; Acts 17:24; 1 Timothy 6:15; Revelation 15:3. Likewise קָדוֹשׁ [Qadosh], holy, Job 6:10; עֶלְיוֹן [Elyon], most high, Genesis 14:18; see also Isaiah 57:15; Luke 1:32. Nor is it lacking that by metonymy שָׁמַיִם [shamayim], οὐρανὸς [ouranos], heaven, is used, Daniel 4:26; Matthew 21:25; Luke 15:18; and metaphorically צוּר [Tsur], rock, Deuteronomy 32:18, 30, and so on.

units.la: Porro autem Nomina de Deo usurpantur vel ὑπωστικῶς, essentialiter, ut significent ipsam essentiam, tribus personis communem: Gen. i, 1. Exod. iii, 6. Deut. x, 17. vel ἰδιοπροσωπικῶς; personaliter, ut hanc, vel illam personam distincte designent, Joh. iii, 16. xvii, 3. Act. xx 28. Rom. ix, 5. 1 Cor. 11, 8. xii, 6.
units.tr: Moreover, names of God are used either hypostatically, that is, substantially [ὑπωστικῶς], essentially, so as to signify the very essence common to the three persons: Genesis 1:1; Exodus 3:6; Deuteronomy 10:17; or personally [ἰδιοπροσωπικῶς], so as to designate distinctly this or that person: John 3:16; 17:3; Acts 20:28; Romans 9:5; 1 Corinthians 2:8; 12:6.

units.la: XII. Amplius vero cognoscitur essentia Dei per Attributa.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, the essence of God is known through the Attributes.

units.la: Hæc sunt perfectiones, quæ de essentiâ Dei verè prædicantur, & distincte explicant qualis ea sit.
units.tr: These are the perfections that are truly predicated of the essence of God, and that distinctly explain what it is like.

units.la: Iis investigandis ancillatur quodammodo Natura, 1. Per viam negationis; ubi dum creaturas contemplamur, ut Creatorem ex iis cognoscamus, omnem imperfectionem in creaturis obviam à Deo interim removemus.
units.tr: In investigating them, Nature serves as a kind of handmaid: (1.) by the way of negation, where, while we contemplate creatures in order to know their Creator from them, we meanwhile remove from God every imperfection found in creatures.

units.la: 2. Per viam causalitatis, cùm omnes rerum creaturum perfectiones Deo, tanquàm causæ primæ, acceptas referimus, atque adeo virtualiter eosdem ipsi tribuimus.
units.tr: (2.) By the way of causality, when we refer all the perfections of created things to God as first cause, and so attribute them to him virtually.

units.la: 3. Per viam eminentiæ; ubi quidquid perfectionis in creaturis, id longe eminentius Deo inesse colligimus; tanquàm causæ omnis illius, citrà ullam sui diminutionem, aut mutationem.
units.tr: (3.) By the way of eminence*, where we gather that whatever perfection is in creatures inheres in God far more eminently, as the cause of all of it, without any diminution or change in himself.

units.la: XIII. Sunt autem Attributa, vel Primi generis, sive essentiæ ut sic; vel Secundi generis, sive vitæ.
units.tr: XIII. The Attributes are either of the first kind, or of the essence as such, or of the second kind, or of life.

units.la: Attributa primi generis, incommunicabilia dici solent; quia itâ Deo propria sunt, ut nulli creaturæ competere possint. Suntque potissimùm Primitas, Simplicitas, & Infinitas.
units.tr: Attributes of the first kind are usually called incommunicable, because they belong to God in such a way that they cannot belong to any creature. The chief of them are Primacy, Simplicity, and Infinity.

units.la: XIV. Primitas, sive Independentia vocatur, quâ Deus absque causâ, absque principio sui, seipso est sufficientissimè id quod est. Hinc 1. ipse primus, principium, Ἀλφα, summus, vocatur; Apoc. 1, 4, 8. Isai. xliv, 6.
units.tr: XIV. Primacy, or Independence, is the attribute by which God, without cause and without a beginning of himself, is most fully by himself what he is. Hence (1.) he is called the first, the beginning, Alpha [Ἀλφα], the highest: Rev. 1:4, 8; Isa. 44:6.

units.la: 2. אל שדי Gen. xvii, 1. in quo fons vitæ: Psal. xxxvi, 10. Pater spirituum: Hebr. xii, 9. Pater luminum: Jac. 1, 17. ex quo omnia sunt: Rom. xi, 36. Joh. I, 3. Nehem. ix, 6.
units.tr: (2.) El Shaddai [אל שדי], Gen. 17:1; in him is the fountain of life, Ps. 36:10; the Father of spirits, Heb. 12:9; the Father of lights, Jas. 1:17; from whom are all things, Rom. 11:36; John 1:3; Neh. 9:6.

units.la: 3. Ex causarum subordinatione; in quâ non datur progressus in infinitum, sed in primâ subsistendum est necessariò.
units.tr: (3.) From the subordination of causes, in which there is no progress to infinity, but one must necessarily stop at the first.

units.la: XV. Cùm ergò Deus dicitur esse à se, phrasis ista sumitur 1. negativè; quòd non sit ab alio. 2. Improprie, ut significetur, Deum esse, per naturam suam, & per sufficientiam suam, ens primum, & actum purissimum. Eo ipso autem, quod essentia Dei prima sit, & actus primus, existentia est de Dei essentiâ; unde statim apparet absoluta Dei necessitas ad existendum, & actualitas purissima, cui nulla competit potentia passiva; propter sibi-sufficientiam primam, καὶ ἀνάιτιον, καὶ ἀνάρχον. Sim-
units.tr: XV. Therefore, when God is said to be from himself, this phrase is taken (1.) negatively, that he is not from another; (2.) improperly, to signify that God is, by his own nature and by his own sufficiency, the first being and most pure act. Indeed, from the very fact that the essence of God is first and is first act, existence belongs to the essence of God; whence it at once becomes apparent God's absolute necessity to exist and most pure actuality, to which no passive potency belongs, on account of his first self-sufficiency, and [καὶ ἀνάιτιον, καὶ ἀνάρχον], uncaused and without beginning. Sim-

units.la: CAP. IV. De Deo, 107
units.tr: CHAP. IV. Of God, 107

units.la: XVI. Simplicitas à Deo omnem compositionem removet; & simul asserit in ipso omnem omnino persectionem inesse actû purissimo.
units.tr: XVI. Simplicity removes from God all composition, and at the same time asserts that in him there is wholly every perfection, in most pure act.

units.la: Est autem compositio, plurium, quæ se habent ut potentia & actus, unio.
units.tr: Now composition is the union of several things which relate to one another as potency and act.

units.la: Simplicitatem contrà Socinianos & Remonstrantes probamus; 1. ex Dei Primitate, & Independentiâ modo assertâ: quæ omnem in Deo potentiam passivam, omnem perfectibilitatem excludit; & omnem causam unientem, perficientem, mutantem ipsius Dei omnino removet.
units.tr: We prove simplicity against the Socinians and the Remonstrants: (1.) from the Primacy and Independence of God just asserted, which excludes from God every passive potency and every perfectibility, and wholly removes from God himself every cause that unites, perfects, or changes him.

units.la: 2. Ex terminis simplicibus & abstractis, de Deo in S. Scripturâ usurpari solitis: quod sit principium; Apoc. 1,8. Lux; Joh. 1,9. 1 Joh.1,5. charitas; 1 Joh.iv,8,16. vita æterna: 1 Joh. v,20.
units.tr: (2.) From the simple and abstract terms commonly used of God in Holy Scripture: that he is the beginning, Rev. 1:8; light, John 1:9; 1 John 1:5; love, 1 John 4:8, 16; eternal life, 1 John 5:20.

units.la: 3. Nulla in Deo datur Compositio realis, imo nec rationis: utpote, non ex partibus quantitativis & integrantibus: est enim essentia spiritualis, non habens partem extra partem; sed omnia intime penetrans, &c. Joh. iv, 24. cum Jes. xxxi,3. Luc. xxiv,39. cum Act. xvii,27, 28. 1 Reg. viii, 27. Jer. xxiii,23,24.
units.tr: (3.) In God there is no real composition, nor even of reason: namely, not from quantitative and integral parts, for he is a spiritual essence, not having part outside part, but penetrating all things intimately, etc. John 4:24, compared with Isa. 31:3; Luke 24:39, compared with Acts 17:27, 28; 1 Kings 8:27; Jer. 23:23, 24.

units.la: Non ex materia & forma: nam istæ corporum partes essentiales sunt.
units.tr: Nor is he composed of matter and form, for these are the essential parts of bodies.

units.la: Neque ex substantia & accidentibus: accidentia enim substantiæ sic accidunt, eique tanquàm subjecto inhærent, ut eam perficiant, aut mutent: quod ab ipsâ causâ primâ ac summâ prorsus alienum est; ubi etiàm nulla mutatio, nec conversionis obumbratio: Jac. I, 17.
units.tr: Nor of substance and accidents, for accidents befall a substance and inhere in it as in a subject so as to perfect or change it; which is wholly alien to the first and highest cause, in whom there is no change nor shadow of turning: Jas. 1:17.

units.la: Imo neque ex subjecto & modo: quia nunquàm fuit in potentiâ ad modum aliquem recipiendum.
units.tr: Nor indeed of subject and mode, because he never was in potency to receive any mode.

units.la: Neque ex essentiâ & esse: quia ipsum esse omnino est de ejus essentiâ, tanquam actû purissimo.
units.tr: Nor of essence and existence, because existence itself belongs wholly to his essence, as to most pure act.

units.la: Nec denique ex genere & differentiâ: quæ Deo etiàm non convenire, ostensum est sup. th. 3.
units.tr: Nor finally of genus and difference, which, as has been shown above, do not apply to God either: see above, th. 3.

units.la: XVII. Obj. 1. Deo membra corporea tribuuntur in
units.tr: XVII. Objection 1. Bodily members are attributed to God in

units.la: in Sacris. Resp. 1. Illa improprie, metaphorice & metonymice de Deo dicta, Θεοπρεπῶς intelligenda sunt.
