units.tr: in the Sacred Writings. Reply 1. Those things said of God improperly, metaphorically and metonymically, are to be understood in a manner befitting God [θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: Obj. 2. In Deo sunt intelligere, velle, & posse; item justitia & misericordia; quæ compositionem arguunt. Resp. Ista intrinsece in Deo omnino unum idemque sunt; quamvis respectu objectorum & effectorum ratione distinguantur.
units.tr: Objection 2. In God there are understanding, will, and power; likewise justice and mercy; which argue composition. Reply: These are, intrinsically, altogether one and the same in God, although they are distinguished by reason with respect to their objects and effects.

units.la: Obj. 3. Actiones Dei externæ obstant Simplicitati. Resp. Istæ, si activè spectentur, sunt ipsa simplicissima Dei essentia; actuans extrà se in tempore, quæ ab æterno futura decrevit: passivè autem, sunt ipsæ creaturæ: unde jam nulla compositio in Deo colligi potest.
units.tr: Objection 3. The external actions of God are an obstacle to simplicity. Reply: These, if viewed actively, are the most simple essence of God himself, acting outside himself in time, which he decreed from eternity to come; but viewed passively, they are the creatures themselves. Hence no composition can now be inferred in God.

units.la: Obj. 4. Actiones Dei internæ, utpote decretum, &c. Resp. Decretum, si consideretur ut actus vitalis ipsius Dei, est ipsissima Dei essentia: si autem cogitemus de actus istius tendentia & terminatione ad talia objecta, habemus tantùm respectum; qui non componit, &c.
units.tr: Objection 4. The internal actions of God, such as decree, etc. Reply: The decree, if it is considered as the vital act of God himself, is the very essence of God; but if we think of the tendency and termination of that act toward such objects, we have only a relation, which does not compose, etc.

units.la: Obj. 5. In Deo datur personarum pluralitas & distinctio: ergo, &c. Resp. Nulla tamen hinc inferri potest compositio in Dei essentiâ: ibi enim nunquàm fuit aliqua potentia passiva, aut perfectibilitas; sed æternus actus purissimus.
units.tr: Objection 5. In God there is a plurality and distinction of persons; therefore, etc. Reply: Nevertheless no composition in the essence of God can be inferred from this, for there was never in him any passive potency or perfectibility, but an eternal, most pure act.

units.la: Obj. 6. In Christo saltem insignis est compositio, non tantum humanæ naturæ ex partibus suis essentialibus, & integrantibus, &c. sed etiàm personæ ℨ Λόγῳ cum istâ humanâ naturâ. Resp. 1. Non agimus nunc de humanâ naturâ Christi; sed de essentiâ, vel naturâ Divinâ absolutè. 2. Filius Dei assumendo humanam naturam, non accepit proprie aliquam perfectionem: sed naturæ isti contulit modum subsistendi; ac proinde Christus Θεάνθρωπος, totum quidem extraordinarium est; non tamen sic, ut essentia Divina censeri debeat pars componens, ad totum aliquod perfectius constituendum; aut quasi illa prius fuissent in potentiâ passivâ perfectibili-
units.tr: Objection 6. In Christ at least there is a notable composition, not only of his human nature from its essential and integral parts, etc., but also of the person of the Word [Λόγῳ] with that human nature. Reply 1. We are not now treating of the human nature of Christ, but of the Divine essence or nature absolutely. 2. The Son of God, by assuming human nature, did not properly receive any perfection, but conferred upon that nature a mode of subsisting; and accordingly Christ, the God-man, is indeed wholly extraordinary; yet not in such a way that the Divine essence should be considered a component part, to constitute some more perfect whole, or as if that essence had previously been in a perfectible passive potency...

units.la: XVIII. Ex Simplicitate sequitur de Attributis Dei in
units.tr: XVIII. From simplicity there follows, concerning the attributes of God in general:

units.la: in genere;1. quod non differant ab effentiâ Divinâ, & à se invicem, realiter: sed tantum ratione ratiocinatâ, sive ex naturâ rei virtualiter; ratione objectorum & efsectorum.
units.tr: 1. that they do not differ from the divine essence, or from one another, really; but only by a reason that is reasoned out (ratione ratiocinatâ), or virtually, from the nature of the thing, by reason of their objects and effects.

units.la: 2. Quod vere prædicentur de Deo, tàm in abstracto, quam in concreto; & consequenter etiam de se invicem.
units.tr: 2. that they are truly predicated of God, both in the abstract and in the concrete, and consequently also of one another.

units.la: 3. Quod nullam intrinsecam intensionem, aut remissionem, admittant.
units.tr: 3. that they admit no intrinsic intension or remission.

units.la: 4. Quod nullum eorum, ut in Deo est, ab aliis possit separari; propter realem identitatem.
units.tr: 4. that none of them, as it is in God, can be separated from the others, on account of their real identity.

units.la: XIX. Specialius ex Simplicitate patefecit Unitas; quâ Deus sic est distinctus a quolibet alio, ut nullus alius istius naturæ, aut conditionis, præter ipsum agnosci debeat, vel esse possit.
units.tr: XIX. More specifically, the Unity reveals itself from simplicity: by it God is so distinguished from every other being that no other of this nature or condition ought to be acknowledged, or can exist, besides him.

units.la: Evincitur hæc 1. testimoniis S. Scripturæ: utpote Deut. vi, 4. „Audi Israël; Jehovah Deus noster, Je„hovah unus est. Jes. xliv, 6. „Ego primus, & ego „novissimus; & præter me non est Deus. 8. Itaque vos testes mei, an sit Deus præter me, &c. Marc. xii, 32. Joh. xvii, 3. Rom. xvii, 29, 30. 1 Cor. viii, 5, 6. Eph. iv, 6. 1 Tim. ii, 5.
units.tr: This is proved 1. by the testimonies of Holy Scripture, such as Deut. vi, 4: "Hear, O Israel: Jehovah our God, Jehovah is one." Isa. xliv, 6: "I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God besides me." 8: "You are therefore my witnesses, whether there is a God besides me," etc. Mark xii, 32. John xvii, 3. Rom. iii, 29, 30. 1 Cor. viii, 5, 6. Eph. iv, 6. 1 Tim. ii, 5.

units.la: 2. Ex Dei Primitate, & Infinitate: qui enim est Ante omnia, & per quem omnia consistunt, (Col. i, 17.) is necessario unicus est: infinitum autem non est commensurabile alteri; sed omnia alia excedit: ac proinde Unicum est necessario. Speciatim duæ potentiæ activæ infinitæ sine manifestâ contradictione statui non possunt: vel enim una alteri poterit resistere, vel non poterit; &c.
units.tr: 2. from God's primacy and infinity: for he who is before all things, and by whom all things consist (Col. i, 17), is necessarily one. The infinite, moreover, cannot be measured against another, but exceeds all others; therefore it is necessarily one. In particular, two infinite active powers cannot be posited without a plain contradiction: for either one will be able to resist the other, or it will not be able to; etc.

units.la: 3. Nihil est quod pluralitatem Deorum inferre possit in creatione, conservatione, aut gubernatione; sed omnia unitatem spirant.
units.tr: 3. Nothing can bring in a plurality of gods in creation, preservation, or government; rather, all things breathe unity.

units.la: 4. Speciatim Deorum generationes, & contentiones mutuæ, à Gentilibus olim descriptæ ac traditæ prorsus prorsùs adversatur verae Deitati: ita πολυθεότης ἐστὶν ἀθεότης; unde Gentiles dicuntur fuisse absque Deo in mundo, Eph.II, 12.
units.tr: 4. In particular, the generations of gods and their mutual conflicts, once described and handed down by the Gentiles, are wholly opposed to true Deity: thus polytheism is atheism [πολυθεότης ἐστὶν ἀθεότης]. Hence the Gentiles are said to have been without God in the world (Eph. ii, 12).

units.la: XX. Ex Simplicitate Dei porrò deducimus, tùm ipsius in se Immutabilitatem; tum relate ad sensùs nostros, Invisibilitatem, atque Impalpabilitatem; & in ordine ad artem εἰκαστικῷ, Ineffigiabilitatem.
units.tr: XX. From the simplicity of God we further deduce both his immutability in himself, and, in relation to our senses, his invisibility and impalpability; and, with respect to the art of image-making (εἰκαστικῇ), his unfigurability.

units.la: Immutabilitas est, quâ Deus in se prorsùs idem, sibique semper similis manet.
units.tr: Immutability is that by which God remains entirely the same in himself and always like himself.

units.la: Haec veritas contra Socinianos, Vorstium, aliosque, probatur; primo disertis Scripturae testimoniis: tum generaliter, & quidem positive: Psal. cii, 27. 28. Hebr. 1. 11, 12. „(Coeli) peribunt; Tu stabis. Omnes ipsi „mutabuntur; Tu autem idem es. Exod. iii, 14. Ero qui ero. Apoc. 1. 8. Rom. I, 20. Ac porro negative: Mal. iii, 6. Ego Jehovah non mutor. Jac. I, 17. „Apud „quem non est transmutatio, aut conversionis obumbratio. Tum specialius: 1 Tim. I, 17. „Regi saeculorum immortali -- gloria in saecula saeculorum. vi, 16. Rom. i, 23. Item Psal. cii, 28. Hebr. i, 12. Anni tui non deficiunt. Num. xxiii, 19. „Non est vir Deus, ut mentiatur: & „filius hominis, ut poeniteat eum: An ipse dixit, & non „facit: & locutus est, & non stabiliet illud? Prov. xix, 21. Psal. cxvii, 2. 2 Tim. II; 13, 19.
units.tr: This truth is proved against the Socinians, Vorstius, and others: first by plain testimonies of Scripture; then generally, and indeed positively: Ps. cii, 27, 28; Heb. i, 11, 12: "(The heavens) shall perish; but you remain. All of them shall grow old; but you are the same." Exod. iii, 14: "I am who I am." Rev. i, 8. Rom. i, 20. And then negatively: Mal. iii, 6: "I, the LORD, do not change." James i, 17: "with whom there is no variation, or shadow of turning." Then more specifically: 1 Tim. i, 17: "To the King of ages, immortal ... glory for ever and ever." vi, 16. Rom. i, 23. Likewise Ps. cii, 28; Heb. i, 12: your years do not fail. Num. xxiii, 19: "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it stand?" Prov. xix, 21. Ps. cxvii, 2. 2 Tim. ii, 13, 19.

units.la: Accedunt Rationes: 1. à Simplicitate: nam actus ille purissimus excludit omnem mutabilitatem.
units.tr: Reasons also agree: 1. from simplicity, for that most pure act excludes all mutability.

units.la: 2. Ab Independentiâ: quae removet omnem causam mutationis in Deo.
units.tr: 2. from independence, which removes every cause of change in God.

units.la: 3. Ab Infinitate: sic enim nihil addi, vel etiàm adimi potest.
units.tr: 3. from infinity: for thus nothing can be added to him, or even taken away.

units.la: 4. Speciatim respectu Volitionis: ubi summa Sapientia, conjuncta cum Omnipotentiâ, nullam mutationem admittit.
units.tr: 4. Especially with respect to the will: where supreme wisdom, joined with omnipotence, admits no change.

units.la: XXI. Obj. 1. Incarnatio Filii Dei satis manifestam mutationem arguit; ac porro ejus passiones, mors, &c. Ergo. Resp. Θεὸς ὁ λόγος factus est homo ἀτρέπτως: activè naturam humanam assumfit, sine mutatione Deitatis. Idem ὑποστατικῶς dicitur passus, mortuus, &c. sed proprie secundum humanitatem.
units.tr: XXI. Objection 1. The incarnation of the Son of God indicates a sufficiently clear change; and moreover his sufferings, death, etc. Therefore. Answer: The Word of God [ὁ λόγος] became man unchangeably [ἀτρέπτως]: actively he assumed human nature without any change in the Deity. In the same way he is said, by a personal union [ὑποστατικῶς], to have suffered, died, etc., but properly according to the humanity.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus ex non creatore aliquando factus est creator: ergo. Resp. Creatio activè spectata, est aeterna Dei efficientia, per quam mundus in principio temporis productus est: unde nulla mutatio in ipso creatore colligi potest.
units.tr: Objection 2. God at some time became creator who was not previously creator: therefore. Answer: Creation, considered actively, is the eternal efficacy of God, by which the world was produced at the beginning of time: hence no change in the Creator himself can be inferred from it.

units.la: Obj. 3. Nunc existunt alia objecta, quàm olim: alia ergo nunc Deus cognoscit: & sic mutata est ipsius scientia. Resp. Objectorum mutatio non mutat ipsam Dei scientiam.
units.tr: Objection 3. Now there exist other objects than there were formerly: therefore God now knows other things, and so his knowledge has been changed. Answer: A change in the objects does not change God's own knowledge.

units.la: Obj. 4. Volitio Divina libera est: alia ergo esse poteft: & sic mutabilis est. Resp. Volitionis terminatio alia esse posset absolute, & in sensu divisô; non autem ex hypothesi, & in sensu composito.
units.tr: Objection 4. The divine will is free: it could therefore be otherwise, and so it is changeable. Answer: The terminus of the will could be otherwise absolutely and in the divided sense; but not on the hypothesis, and in the composite sense.

units.la: Obj. 5. Deo tribuitur poenitentia: Gen. xi, 6. &c. Ergo. Resp. Tribuitur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς; sed intelligenda est Θεοπρεπῶς, ut notet mutationem effectûs, non affectûs.
units.tr: Objection 5. Repentance is ascribed to God: Gen. 6, etc. Therefore. Answer: It is ascribed in a human manner [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]; but it is to be understood in a manner worthy of God [Θεοπρεπῶς], so as to denote a change of effect, not of affection.

units.la: XXII. Relate ad Aspectum oculareм, Deum Invisibilem dicimus: non solùm hoc, sed etiam in futuro saeculo. Et probamus contra Vorstium; 1. Ex eo, quòd Deus diserte ἀόρατος appelletur, 1 Tim. 1, 17. Hebr. xi, 27. Adde 1 Tim. vi, 16. Ioh. 1, 18: Exod. xxxiii, 20.
units.tr: XXII. With respect to the ocular sight, we say that God is invisible: not only in this present age, but also in the age to come. And we prove this against Vorstius; 1. From the fact that God is expressly called invisible [ἀόρατος], 1 Tim. 1:17; Heb. 11:27. Add 1 Tim. 6:16; John 1:18; Exod. 33:20.

units.la: 2. Ex omnimodâ Dei Simplicitate & Infinitate, quae emanantes radios, & oculorum corporalium receptivitatem, prorsus à Deo removent.
units.tr: 2. from God's entire simplicity and infinity, which wholly remove from God the emanating rays and the receptivity of the bodily eyes.

units.la: Obj. At nonnulli Deum vidisse, aut visuri dicuntur: Gen. xviii, 1, 2. xxxii, 30. Exod. xxiv, 10. Jud. xiii, 22. 1 Reg. xxii, 19. Psal. xvii, 15. Matth. v, 8. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Hebr. xii, 14. 1 Joh. iii, 2. Resp. Ista intelligenda, non de oculari visione ipsius essentiae Divinae in se: sed partim de symbolo aliquo extraordinario, ad gloriam & voluntatem aliquam Dei sic manifestandam; sicut etiam quodammodo fit per omnes res creatas: Rom. 1, 20. sed propius in humana Christi natura: unde Joh. xiv, 9. Qui Me vidit, vidit Patrem. Partim de visione prophetica qualicunque: partim etiam de visione illa mentali, seu notitia, quae familiarem gratiae, vel etiam gloriae fruitionem involvit, juxta Matth. xviii, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 9.
units.tr: Objection: Yet some are said to have seen God, or to be going to see him: Gen. xviii, 1, 2; xxxii, 30; Exod. xxiv, 10; Judg. xiii, 22; 1 Kings xxii, 19; Ps. xvii, 15; Matt. v, 8; 1 Cor. xiii, 12; Heb. xii, 14; 1 John iii, 2. Answer: These passages are to be understood not of ocular vision of the divine essence in itself, but partly of some extraordinary symbol, so as to make manifest in this way some glory and will of God; as also, in a certain way, happens through all created things (Rom. i, 20), but more closely in the human nature of Christ: hence John xiv, 9: He who has seen me has seen the Father. Partly it refers to prophetic vision of whatever kind; partly also to that mental vision, or knowledge, which involves a familiar enjoyment of grace or even of glory, according to Matt. xviii, 10. See above, chapter 1, thesis 9.

units.la: XXIII. Ratione Tactus Deo competit Impalpabi- litas, & quidem propter suam Simplicitatem: nam
units.tr: XXIII. By reason of touch, impalpability belongs to God, and indeed on account of his simplicity, for

units.la: Tangere, vel tangi, nisi corpus, nulla potest res.
units.tr: Nothing can touch or be touched except a body.

units.la: Unde Christus Luc. xxiv, 39. de se refusitato: Palpate Me; & videte: quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere: cum Joh. iv, 24. Deus est spiritus.
units.tr: Hence Christ, speaking of himself after the resurrection, says in Luke 24:39: Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have; and John 4:24: God is spirit.

units.la: Obj. Act. xvii, 27. Ut quaerant Dominum, si forte palpando cum invenirent: Ergo saltem palpari potest. Resp. Istud metaphorice ad mentem pertinet.
units.tr: Objection: Acts 17:27: that they might seek the Lord, if perhaps they might feel after him by groping and find him. Therefore he can at least be felt. Answer: this is said metaphorically, and pertains to the mind.

units.la: XXIV. Respectu artis εἰκαστικῆς, Deus est Ineffigiabilis.
units.tr: XXIV. With respect to the art of making images (εἰκαστική [eikastikē]), God cannot be portrayed.

units.la: Unde etiam Jes. xl, 18. Cui assimilabitis Deum, & quid similitudinis ornabitis ei? Scil. per Simplicitatem suam Deus lineamentorum, terminationum, & figurationum expers est. Item Deut. iv, 15. Non vidistis ullam imaginem in die, qua locutus est Jehovah ad vos in Choreb, e medio ignis. Ne forte corrumpamini, & faciatis vobis sculptile, imaginem alicujus similitudinis. Confer Act. xvii, 29. Rom. 1. 22, 23.
units.tr: Hence also Isaiah 40:18: To what will you liken God, or what likeness will you set beside him? That is, because of his simplicity God is without lines, boundaries, and figures. Likewise Deut. 4:15: You saw no image on the day when Jehovah spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, lest perhaps you should corrupt yourselves and make for yourselves a carved image, the likeness of any figure. Compare Acts 17:29; Rom. 1:22, 23.

units.la: Contra hanc veritatem, & disertum secundum Decalogi praeceptum, gravissime peccant Pontificii, practice Anthropomorphitae.
units.tr: Against this truth and the express precept of the Decalogue the Papists sin most gravely, and in practice the Anthropomorphites do too.

units.la: XXV. Sequitur Infinitas; quae talem ac tantam in Deo perfectionem designat, ut nullos terminos aut fines habeat; sed eos omnes conceptibiles excedat. Haec autem confidetanda est, tum respectu ipsius Essentiae; tum respectu Durationis & Spatii ubicalis; tum denique in ordine ad Intellectum.
units.tr: XXV. There follows infinity, which designates such and so great a perfection in God that it has no bounds or ends but exceeds all that can be conceived. This must be acknowledged both with respect to the essence itself, and with respect to duration and ubiquitous space, and finally in relation to the intellect.

units.la: Respectu Essentiæ, Deus infinitus est modo persectissimo, & quàm maximè positivo; ut omnes persectionum modos & gradus, qui in creaturis reperiuntur in Divinâ essentiâ sint eminenter; omnesque fines conceptibiles ipse excedat actû simplicissimo & sufficientissimo. Hinc Col. 1, 9. Omnis plenitudo Deitatis, Psal. cxlv, 3. - Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Job. xi, 7, 8, 9. Num investigatione Deum invenies? Num usque ad perfectionem Omnisufficientis (שדי) invenies, &c.
units.tr: With respect to essence, God is infinite in a most perfect and most positive mode, so that all the modes and degrees of perfection found in creatures are eminently in the divine essence, and he himself exceeds all conceivable limits by his most simple and most sufficient act. Hence Col. 1:9: all the fullness of the Deity; Ps. 145:3: his greatness is unsearchable. Job 11:7–9: Can you find out God by searching? Can you find out the Almighty (שדי [Shaddai]) unto perfection? etc.

units.la: Hæc Infinitas etiam facilè deducitur ex Independenti essentiæ Divinæ sufficientiâ superius assertâ th. 14. Qui enim tanquam causa absolute prima & Dominus supremus, reliquis entibus fines suarum perfectionum assignavit; adeò ut nec ulli fines absolutè possibiles dici, aut concipi possint, nisi dependenter ab ipso: is omnem imperfectionem, non solum privativam, sed & negativam, excludit; omnemque perfectionem conceptibilem includit eminenter; & omnes limites suâ naturâ excedit.
units.tr: This infinity is also easily deduced from the independent sufficiency of the divine essence, asserted above in thesis 14. For he who, as the absolutely first cause and supreme Lord, has assigned to the other beings the limits of their perfections, so that no limits can be called or conceived as absolutely possible except as dependent on him, excludes every imperfection, not only privative but also negative; he includes eminently every conceivable perfection, and exceeds all limits by his nature.

units.la: Non intelligitur autem hoc loco Infinitas mathematica, potentialis, aut syncategorematica; sed metaphysica, actualis, & categorematica, quam sic satis explicuimus modò.
units.tr: Here, however, infinity is not understood as mathematical, potential, or syncategorematic, but as metaphysical, actual, and categorematic, which we have sufficiently explained just now.

units.la: Obj. Omnia entia habent essentiam suam certam, distinctam, definitam; ac proindè etiàm Deus. Essentiæ rerum consistunt in indivisibili. Resp. Deus habet essentiam certam, & ab omnibus distinctam, hoc ipso quòd ea infinita sit. Atque illud indivisibile essentiæ Divinæ, intrinsecâ suâ perfectione infinitum est.
units.tr: Objection: All beings have their own certain, distinct, and defined essence, and therefore God too. The essences of things consist in what is indivisible. Answer: God has a certain essence, distinct from all others, by the very fact that it is infinite. And that indivisible thing, the divine essence, is infinite by its intrinsic perfection.

units.la: Creaturarum distantia à Divinâ perfectione, denominari solet infinita: quia nulla est earum ad hanc affinitas, aut proportio æqualitatis, vel commensurationis: finiti enim ad infinitum nulla est proportio. Interim illa à se invicem distinguuntur propriis suis perfectionibus, eâdemque gradibus, vel etiam speciebus.
units.tr: The distance of creatures from divine perfection is commonly called infinite, because there is no affinity between them and it, nor any proportion of equality or commensurability; for there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. Meanwhile they are distinguished from one another by their own perfections, and by degrees or even species.

units.la: XXVI. Infinitas Durationis est æternitas stricte dicta.
units.tr: XXVI. Infinity of duration is eternity, strictly so called.

units.la: sta; quæ non tantum principium & finem, sed etiam successionem prioris & posterioris excludit. Unde recte à Boëthio describitur, interminabilis vitæ totâ simul ac perfectâ possessio. Differt autem à Tempore strictè dicto, quod hoc tribuatur solis corporibus: & ab Ævo, quod est spirituum finitorum, principium durationis suæ habentium, atque inde successionem, sed non finem. Illa probatur testimoniis sacris; Gen. xxi, 33. Rom. xvi, 26. ubi αὐτολεξεὶ æternus appellatur. Adde Is. lvii, 15. xliv, 6. Ier. x, 10. Rom. i, 20. 1 Tim. i, 17. Apoc. i, 4, 8, 17. xxi, 6, Psal. xc, 2, 4.
units.tr: which excludes not only beginning and end but also the succession of before and after. Hence Boethius rightly describes it as the whole and perfect possession of endless life, all at once. It differs from time, strictly so called, which is attributed only to bodies; and from aevum, which belongs to finite spirits, who have a beginning of their duration and hence succession, but no end. The former is proved from sacred testimonies: Gen. 21:33; Rom. 16:26, where he is called eternal [αἰώνιος (aiōnios)]. Add Is. 57:15; 44:6; Jer. 10:10; Rom. 1:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; Rev. 1:4, 8, 17; 21:6; Ps. 90:2, 4.

units.la: Eadem patet ex Dei Primitate & Simplicitate. Quæ ut essentiæ, sic etiam existentiæ ac durationis Divinæ principium, omnemque variationem, excludunt; & actum purißimum inferunt; ipsamque adeo æternitatem.
units.tr: The same is clear from God's primacy and simplicity. These, as they are the principle of his essence, so also of his existence and duration, exclude every variation and imply pure act, and thus eternity itself.

units.la: Hanc vero Æternitatem carere successione, prefsius probamus; 1. ex Psal. xc, 4. cum 2 Petr. iii, 8. Unus dies apud Dominum, ut mille anni, & mille anni, ut unus dies. Supereminentia igitur durationis Divinæ, temporum differentias & successionem non habet.
units.tr: We prove more precisely that this eternity lacks succession: 1. from Ps. 90:4, compared with 2 Pet. 3:8: One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The supereminence of divine duration therefore does not admit differences of times or succession.

units.la: 2. Ex omnimodâ Dei Immutabilitate, de quâ th. 20. annorum enim, aliorumque temporum successio, & conversio, insignem mutationem infert.
units.tr: 2. From the all-round immutability of God, on which see thesis 20. For the succession of years and other times, and their change, implies a notable mutation.

units.la: 3. Existentia est actus essentiæ; & duratio, existentiæ permanentia, quæ se necessario habet convenienter essentiæ. Consequenter æterna Dei duratio, est ipsa ejus essentia; cujus Simplicitas partes, earumque successionem, non admittit.
units.tr: 3. Existence is the act of essence, and duration is the permanence of existence, which belongs necessarily to essence. Consequently God's eternal duration is his very essence, whose simplicity admits no parts or succession of parts.

units.la: XXVII. Obj. 1. Anni, dies, præteritum, futurum, &c. tribuuntur Deo in Sacris. Resp. Scil. ἀνθρώπο- παθῶς; sed intelligenda Θεοπρεπῶς.
units.tr: XXVII. Objection 1. Years, days, past, future, and so on, are attributed to God in the Sacred Writings. Answer: they are to be understood in human fashion [ἀνθρωπο-παθῶς], but they must be understood in a manner worthy of God [Θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus coëxistit temporum nostrorum differentiis; ergo successionem habet: aut cæteroquin nostræ temporum differentiæ sibi invicem coëxistent; quia æternitati Divinæ coëxistunt. Resp. Dei duratio manet semper eadem; sed illa coëxistentia ad nostra tempora est inadæquata: nequaquàm ergo propter æternitatis coëxistentiam, nostrum præteritum, præsens, & futurum coincidunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. God coexists with the differences of our times; therefore he has succession. Otherwise, our time-differences would coexist with one another, since they coexist with divine eternity. Answer: God's duration remains always the same, but that coexistence with our times is inadequate. Therefore our past, present, and future do not coincide because of the coexistence with eternity.

units.la: Obj. 3. Tempus mundi idem est cum æternitate Dei: nam etiam illud principio caret: mundus enim creatus est in tempore; ipsum vero tempus creatum non est, æternum ergo est. Resp. Tempus mundi non est æternum, aut increatum: Deus enim creando res successivas, eådem operâ tempus produxit: unde rectè creatum dicitur.
units.tr: Objection 3. The time of the world is the same as the eternity of God, for it too lacks a beginning: the world was created in time, but time itself was not created, so it is eternal. Answer: the time of the world is neither eternal nor uncreated. For God, in creating successive things, produced time by the same act; hence it is rightly called created.

units.la: XXVIII. Infinitas respectû Spatii, sive ubi; est Immensitas; quâ Deus absolutissimè ubique existit; nec ullos fines habet suæ præsentiæ vel quasi. Deus igitur non est in loco, vel ubi circumscriptive; quæ affectio corporum propria est: nec definitive; quæ spirituum finitorum: sed repletive totus est intrà totum mundum, ejusque partes singulas; & totus extra eum, ubi sibi ipsi præsens existit. Atque hoc contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes asserimus. Vulgò dicitur; Enter, præsenter, Deus hic, & ubique, potenter. Primò, enter: h. e. Deus in toto mundo præsens existit per essentiam suam infinitam. Deut. iv, 39. Iof. ii, 11. Iehovah est in cœlis desuper, & super terram desubter. Ierem. xxiii, 23, 24. Nunquid Deus de propinquo Ego, dixit Iehovah; & non Deus de longinquo? Psal. cxxxix, 7, -10. Quò ibo à Spiritû Tuo; & quò à faciebus Tuis fugiam? Si ascendero cœlos, ibi Tu: & stratum fecero infernum; ecce Tu: Affumfero pennas aurorae, habitavero in novissimo maris; etiam ibi manus Tua ducet me, & tenebit me dextra Tua. Adde Iei. vi, 1. lxvi, 1. Act. vii, 48, 49, 50. xvii, 24, 25, 27, 28. Secundò; præsenter; h. e. per intimam notitiam & observationem omnium eorum, quæ in illo fiunt. Psal.
units.tr: XXVIII. Infinity with respect to space, or place, is immensity, by which God exists absolutely everywhere, and has no limits to his presence, so to speak. God therefore is not in a place, or somewhere circumscriptively, which is the property of bodies; nor definitively, which is the mode of finite spirits; but he is wholly within the whole world and each of its parts by filling them, and wholly outside it, where he exists present to himself. We assert this against the Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants. It is commonly said: God is here and everywhere, present in essence, present in presence, powerful. First, in essence: that is, God exists present in the whole world through his infinite essence. Deut. iv. 39. Josh. ii. 11: "Jehovah is in heaven above, and on the earth beneath." Jer. xxiii. 23, 24: "Am I a God at hand, saith Jehovah, and not a God afar off? " Ps. cxxxix. 7-10: "Whither shall I go from thy Spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." Add Isa. vi. 1; lxvi. 1; Acts vii. 48, 49, 50; xvii. 24, 25, 27, 28. Secondly, by presence: that is, through intimate knowledge and observation of all those things that happen in it. Ps.

units.la: xxxiii,13,14,15. E coelis respexit Iehovah, & vidit omnes filios hominum: - considerans omnia opera eorum. Hebr.iv,13. „Non est creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus: omnia autem nuda & aperta sunt oculis ejus, ad quem nobis negotium. Psal. cxxxix,12,13. Jerem.xxiii,24.
units.tr: xxxiii. 13, 14, 15: "From heaven Jehovah looked down and saw all the sons of men... considering all their works." Heb. iv. 13: "There is no creature hidden from his sight; but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do." Ps. cxxxix. 12, 13; Jer. xxiii. 24.

units.la: Tertiò, potenter; h.e. per potentem operationem: Hebr.i,3. - Sustinet omnia verbo suo potente: Joh. v,17. „Pater Meus adhuc operatur, & Ego operor. 1 Cor. xii,6. Agens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Thirdly, by power: that is, through powerful operation. Heb. i. 3: "He upholds all things by the word of his power." John v. 17: "My Father is working still, and I am working." 1 Cor. xii. 6: "Working all things in all."

units.la: XXIX. Sic ergò Deus hic & ubique existit. Sed neque spatiis rerum creatarum comprehenditur: aut iis adæquatè coëxistit ipse infinitus: extra mundum in se ipso etiàm existit, qui ante mundum conditum extitit similiter. Probatur hoc specialiùs; 1. disertis testimoniis: 1 Reg. viii,27. „Cœli, & cœli cœlorum non continent Te: quantò minùs domus hæc, quam ædificavi.
units.tr: XXIX. So God exists here and everywhere. Yet he is not comprehended by the spaces of created things, nor is the infinite God coextensive with them; he also exists outside the world in himself, and likewise existed before the world was made. This is proved more specifically: 1. by explicit testimonies: 1 Kings viii. 27: "Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?"

units.la: 2 Chron. ii,6. „Quis obtinebit potestatem ad ædificandum Ei domum? nam cœli, & cœli cœlorum non comprehendent Eum; & quis ego, ut ædificem Ei domum? „Quin imò ad suffiendum ad facies Ejus. Ubi ipsam Dei essentiam designant pronomina Te, Eum, &c. non scientiam, potentiam, aut operationem ab essentiâ diversam; qualis etiàm non datur per Dei Simplicitatem, nedùm existere posset, ubi essentia Divina non existeret. Memoratur domus, non ad habitationem; sed ad suffitum faciendum. Habitationis conceptus, etiàm cœlorum incapacitas, &c. ad essentiam pertinent. Quomodò cæteroquin extra cœlos cœlorum, & sic extra mundum universum, existeret Dei scientia, vel potentia, vel operatio, &c?
units.tr: 2 Chron. ii. 6: "Who is able to build him a house, seeing the heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him? And who am I, that I should build him a house?" "Except to burn incense before him." Here the pronouns Thee, him, and so on designate the very essence of God, not knowledge, power, or operation distinct from the essence; nor is such a distinction possible given the divine simplicity, much less could it exist where the divine essence did not exist. The house is mentioned not for habitation but for burning incense. The concept of habitation, and the incapacity of even the heavens to contain him, pertain to the essence. Otherwise, how would the knowledge, power, or operation of God exist outside the heavens of heavens, and so outside the whole world?

units.la: 2. Ex infinitâ Dei perfectione: quæ requirit, ut existat in omni spatio conceptibili.
units.tr: 2. From the infinite perfection of God, which requires that he exist in every conceivable space.

units.la: 3. Ex Potentiâ: Deus extra hunc mundum potest operari, similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Ubi autem potest operari, ibi potest existere; imò existit, qui est actus purissimus.
units.tr: 3. From power: God can act outside this world, just as he could before the world was made. But where he can act, there he can exist; indeed he does exist, since he is pure act.

units.la: ꝯ. E[illegible, ~2 letters] 3. Ex Immutabilitate: ante mundum conditum existit Deus in se, modo infinito; non autem definito ad actualia spatia hujus mundi: ergo etiàm nunc similiter.
units.tr: Also, from immutability: before the world was made God existed in himself, in an infinite mode, not determined to the actual spaces of this world; therefore he exists in the same way now as well.

units.la: XXX. Observandi autem speciales quidam modi praesentiae Divinae, respectu operationum ac manife- stationum:
units.tr: XXX. Certain special modes of the Divine presence, with respect to his operations and manifestations, are also to be observed:

units.la: 1. In humana Christi natura inhabitat Deitas, per unionem hypostaticam: Col. 11, 9, Joh. 1, 14. 1 Tim, 111, 16. Rom. 1, 3, 4. ix, 5.
units.tr: 1. In the human nature of Christ the Deity dwells, by the hypostatic union: Col. 2, 9; John 1, 14; 1 Tim. 3, 16; Rom. 1, 3, 4; 9, 5.

units.la: 2. In Ecclesia universa est Deus, per Spiritum unientem, charismata distribuentem, & salutariter gubernantem, 1 Cor. XII, 11, 12, 13, Joh. XVII, 21. Matth. XXVIII, 20.
units.tr: 2. In the universal Church God is present, by the Spirit uniting, distributing gifts, and governing unto salvation: 1 Cor. 12, 11, 12, 13; John 17, 21; Matt. 28, 20.

units.la: 3. In singulis Fidelibus, per Spiritum fidei, sanctificationis, adoptionis, consolationis, & corroborationis: Joh. XIV, 23, 16, 17. 2 Cor. IV, 13. Rom. VIII, 14,-17, 26. Gal. IV, 6, 7. Psal. CXLV, 18.
units.tr: 3. In the individual faithful, by the Spirit of faith, of sanctification, of adoption, of consolation, and of strengthening: John 14, 23; 16, 17; 2 Cor. 4, 13; Rom. 8, 14–17, 26; Gal. 4, 6, 7; Ps. 145, 18.

units.la: 4. In Prophetis, Spiritû πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως sapientiam ac voluntatem suam revelante: 1 Petr. 1, 11. Hebr. 1, 1.
units.tr: 4. In the Prophets, revealing his wisdom and will by the Spirit "in many portions and in many ways" [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]: 1 Pet. 1, 11; Heb. 1, 1.

units.la: 5. In Caelo, speciali gloriae ac majestatis suae manifestatione: Isef. XLVI, 1. Matth. XVIII, 10. Hebr. XII, 22, 23. Phil. III, 20, 21. Job. XIV, 2, 3.
units.tr: 5. In Heaven, by the special manifestation of his glory and majesty: Isa. 46, 1; Matt. 18, 10; Heb. 12, 22, 23; Phil. 3, 20, 21; John 14, 2, 3.

units.la: 6. In Inferno, irae & justitiae suae vindicativae executione: Psal. CXXXIX, 8. Matth. X, 28. 2 Thess. 1, 9. Marc. IX, 44, 46.
units.tr: 6. In Hell, by the execution of his wrath and of his avenging justice: Ps. 139, 8; Matt. 10, 28; 2 Thess. 1, 9; Mark 9, 44, 46.

units.la: XXXI. Obj. 1 Deus in coelis esse dicitur; Matth. VI, 9. & habitare lucem inaccessam; 1 Tim. VI, 16. Resp. 1. in coelis est speciali modo praesentiae gloriosae; talem se ibi demonstrando, non autem existendo ibi tantum, nec alibi. 2. Sed Lux Dei inaccessa est ipsa ejus gloria & majestas, creaturis incomprehensibilis: sic ipse lux esse dicitur; 1 Joh. 1, 5. Vide ibid. verf. 7. & Psal. CIV, 1, 2. Non vero est locus aliquis, à Deo diversus.
units.tr: XXXI. Objection 1: God is said to be in heaven, Matt. 6, 9, and to dwell in unapproachable light, 1 Tim. 6, 16. Answer 1: in heaven he is present in a special mode of glorious presence, displaying himself there in such a way, and not merely existing there, nor elsewhere. 2: But the unapproachable light of God is his very glory and majesty, incomprehensible to creatures; thus he himself is said to be light, 1 John 1, 5. See the same, verse 7, and Ps. 104, 1, 2. It is not, however, some place distinct from God.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus, 1 Reg. XIX, 11, 12, negatur fuisse in vehementi vento, itemque in terræ motu, & in igni, sed in leni aurâ. Resp. Istud dicitur de extraordinario symbolo speciali cujusdam præsentiæ Divinæ, per revelatione Prophetica.
units.tr: Objection 2: God, 1 Kings 19, 11, 12, is denied to have been in the strong wind, likewise in the earthquake and in the fire, but in the gentle breeze. Answer: This is said of an extraordinary sign, a special presence of God, through prophetic revelation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Ipse negavit, se affore immorigeris; Num. xiv, 42. Ergo non est prorsus ubique. Resp. Negavi de speciali modo præsentiæ, secundum gratiam & beneficentiam.
units.tr: Objection 3: He himself denied that he would be present with the disobedient, Num. 14, 42. Therefore he is not absolutely everywhere. Answer: I deny this concerning the special mode of presence, according to grace and beneficence.

units.la: Obj. 4. Absurdè statuitur, Deum adesse in locis impuris, interesse actionibus obscœnis, esse in Diabolis, &c. Idcirco mandavit, ut excrementa in castris Israelitarum statim terrâ obtegerentur; Deut. xxiii, 12, 13, 14. Ergo. Resp. 1. Deus simplicissimus & sanctissimus rerum immundarum præsentiâ pollui minimè potest. In ipso exstant, vivunt, & moventur creaturæ qualescunque: Act. xvii, 28. etiam Diaboli, & homines pessimi. Unde cæteroquin eorum efficientiæ non certè in dependens est à Deo, ejusque Providentia. Nec Judicem suum effugere ullo modo possunt.
units.tr: Objection 4: It is absurdly maintained that God is present in impure places, takes part in obscene actions, is in devils, etc. Therefore he commanded that excrement in the camp of the Israelites be at once covered with earth, Deut. 23, 12, 13, 14. Therefore. Answer 1: God, most simple and most holy, can by no means be defiled by the presence of unclean things. In him exist, live, and move whatever creatures there are, Acts 17, 28, even devils and the worst men. Hence their efficacy, whatever it is, is certainly dependent on God and his providence. Nor can they in any way escape their Judge.

units.la: 2. In castris Israelitarum, sub istâ œconomia, voluit Deus observari munditiem cærimonialem. Confer Ezech. iv, 12, 13.
units.tr: 2. In the camp of the Israelites, under that economy, God wished ceremonial cleanness to be observed. Compare Ezek. 4, 12, 13.

units.la: Obj. 5. Absurda est existentia Dei atomica & atopica. Resp. Simplicitas Dei indivisibilitatem infert; & Infinitas localitatem physicam & circumscriptivam excludit. Deus totus, non per partes, coëxistit creaturis singulis; sed non adæquatè.
units.tr: Objection 5: The existence of God is absurdly atomic and atopic. Answer: The simplicity of God implies indivisibility, and his infinity excludes physical and circumscriptive locality. God, wholly and not by parts, coexists with each single creature; but not adequately.

units.la: Obj. 6. Mera figmenta sunt Spatia imaginaria extra mundum. Resp. At non dicimus, existere spatia realia, vel actualia, extra mundum: sed Deum existere ibi in se; similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Tertullianus: "Ante omnia Deus erat solus; ipse sibi & mundus, & locus, & omnia. Deus etiam per absolutam suam potentiam operari potest, & creaturas producere; & spatia actuare: ista igitur possibilia sunt, & sic concepibilia, atque imaginaria."
units.tr: Objection 6: Imaginary spaces outside the world are mere fictions. Answer: But we do not say that real or actual spaces exist outside the world, but that God exists there in himself, just as before the world was made. Tertullian: "Before all things God was alone; he was to himself both world, and place, and all things. God can also, by his absolute power, work and produce creatures and actualize spaces: these things, therefore, are possible, and thus conceivable, and imaginary."

units.la: XXXII. Respectû Intellectûs creati Deus est Incomprehensibilis : Psal. cxlv, 3. Magnitudinis eius non est investigatio. Job. xi, 9. Num in investigatione Deum invenies? v. 9. Rom. xi, 33, 34. 1 Tim. vi, 16. Et manifesta est ratio, ex obiecti infinitate, & subiecti finiti disproportione ad ipsum.
units.tr: XXXII. With respect to the created intellect God is incomprehensible: Ps. 145, 3; "of his greatness there is no searching," Job 11, 9; "Canst thou by searching find out God?" v. 7; Rom. 11, 33, 34; 1 Tim. 6, 16. And the reason is plain, from the infinity of the object and the disproportion of the finite subject to it.

units.la: Consequenter nulli creaturæ, in quocunque statû, convenit cognitio Dei comprehensiva, & adæquata; imò nequidem ullius attributi Divini: sed solum apprehensiva, & inadæquata.
units.tr: Consequently no creature, in any state, possesses a comprehensive and adequate knowledge of God; indeed not even of any divine attribute, but only an apprehensive and inadequate knowledge.

units.la: Obj. 1. Sic omnis nostra cognitio de Deo erit erronea: cognoscemus enim aliter, quam se habet ipsa veritas in Deo. Resp. Imò verè cognoscimus in Deo illas perfectiones, quæ verè & formaliter in ipso sunt; simulque agnoscimus, eas Deo inesse modo perfectiori, quam comprehendere possumus.
units.tr: Objection 1: Thus all our knowledge of God will be erroneous, for we shall know otherwise than the truth itself stands in God. Answer: Indeed we truly know in God those perfections which truly and formally are in him; and at the same time we acknowledge that they are in God in a more perfect mode than we can comprehend.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Joh. iii, 2. Videbimus eum, sicuti est: ergò comprehensivè. Resp. Istud intelligendum est tùm de oculari visione humanæ Christi naturæ; tùm de notitiâ essentiæ Divinæ propinquiore, ad beatitudinem nostram ordinatâ; non tamen comprehensivâ.
units.tr: Objection 2: 1 John 3, 2: "We shall see him as he is," therefore comprehensively. Answer: This must be understood both of the ocular vision of the human nature of Christ, and of the nearer knowledge of the divine essence, ordered to our blessedness; yet not comprehensively.

units.la: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Cognoscemus deum, ut ab ipso cogniti sumus: Atqui nos à Deo cogniti sumus comprehensivè: ergò, &c. Resp. Illud non est accipiendum de convenientiâ adæquatâ; sed de similitudine quâdam analogicâ. Confer Rom. viii, 29. Psal. i, 6.
units.tr: Objection 3: 1 Cor. 13, 12: "We shall know God as we also have been known by him." But we have been known by God comprehensively; therefore, etc. Answer: That is not to be taken of adequate agreement, but of a certain analogical likeness. Compare Rom. 8, 29; Ps. 1, 6.

units.la: XXXIII. Succedunt Attributa vitæ, sive secundi ge- neris; quæ etiam communicabilia appellari solent; respectû communicationis alicujus analogicæ. Vita Dei consideratur, vel ut simpliciter actuosa; vel secundùm eminentiam: priori consideratione occurrunt Intellectus, Voluntas, & Potentia; Posteriori autem, Potestas, Gloria, & Beatitudo. XXXIV. Intellectus Dei est, quo ipse omnes omni- no veritates cognoscit modo sibi convenienti: h. e. infinitè, simpliciter, & independenter. 1 Tim. i, 17.
units.tr: XXXIII. Next come the attributes of life, or of the second kind, which are also commonly called communicable, with respect to some analogical communication. The life of God is considered either as simply active or as eminent. From the first point of view come the Intellect, the Will, and the Power; from the second, the Authority, the Glory, and the Blessedness.

units.la: Soli sapienti - 1Sam. 11,3. Deus scientiarum. Psal. xciv, 9,10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: Alone wise: 1 Sam. 2:3. God of knowledge: Ps. 94:9, 10. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Dico infinite: ipse enim Intellectus Dei infinitus est; cum 1. secundum rem sit ipsa Dei essentia. 2. & modus intelligendi, convenienter naturae Divinae, absolute perfectissimus sit; adeoque infinitus, atque item 3. respectu objectorum, cognoscat omnia absolute cognoscibilia. 1 Joh. iii,20. Novit omnia. Similiter Joh. xxi,17. Item Psal. cxlvii,5. Jef. lv,9. Rom. xi,33.
units.tr: I say infinitely, for the Intellect of God is infinite, since 1. in reality it is the very essence of God; 2. its mode of understanding, agreeing with the divine nature, is absolutely most perfect and therefore infinite; and likewise 3. with respect to its objects, it knows all things that are absolutely knowable. 1 John 3:20: He knows all things. Similarly John 21:17; also Ps. 147:5; Isa. 55:9; Rom. 11:33.

units.la: Novit autem seipsum adaequate: Matth. xi,27.
units.tr: He knows himself adequately: Matt. 11:27.

units.la: 1 Cor. 11,10,11. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Et omnia alia a se perfectissime: Hebr. iv,13. Omnia sunt nuda, & intime patentia oculis ejus. Act. xv,18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) aevo omnia opera sua.
units.tr: And he knows all other things most perfectly: Heb. 4:13, All things are naked and open to his eyes. Acts 15:18, All his works are known to God from eternity.

units.la: XXXV. Scientia Dei ratione objectorum distingui- tur, in naturalem, necessariam, sive simplicis intelligentiae; & in liberam, sive visionis.
units.tr: XXXV. The knowledge of God is distinguished, according to its objects, into natural, necessary, or of simple understanding, and free, or of vision.

units.la: Scientia simplicis intelligentiae rerum quidditates simpliciter spectat, ut se habent citra respectum ad liberam Decreti Divini terminationem: sive in signo rationis antecedenter ad Decretum, quo pertinet ipsa Dei essentia, persona, sufficientia, & omnipotentia, atque hinc res possibiles.
units.tr: The knowledge of simple understanding regards the quiddities of things simply, as they are in themselves, without respect to the free determination of the divine decree; that is, in the order of reason prior to the decree, in which lie the essence, the person, the sufficiency and the omnipotence of God itself, and hence possible things.

units.la: In mente Divina igitur sunt ideae omnium possibilium. Istae autem ideae sunt perfectiones ipsius essentiae Divinae, prout imitabiles & expressibiles sunt extra Deum, & sic ab ipso cognoscuntur. A supereminenti enim & infinita potentia Dei activa, denominantur res possibiles; quatenus videlicet per illam produci, aut actuari, possunt.
units.tr: In the divine mind, therefore, are the ideas of all possible things. These ideas are the perfections of the divine essence itself, insofar as they are imitable and expressible outside God, and so they are known by him. For possible things are named from God's supereminent and infinite active power, inasmuch as they can be produced or actualized by it.

units.la: Scientia libera consideratur, ut in signo rationis consequens ad liberum Dei Decretum. Visionis autem appellatur; quia Deus per eam videt, aut praevidet determinatam rerum existentiam sub qualicunque temporis differentia.
units.tr: Free knowledge is considered as following, in the order of reason, upon God's free decree. It is called knowledge of vision because by it God sees, or foresees, the determinate existence of things under whatever difference of time.

units.la: Quaeritur, Utrum Deus res praescit, quia futurae sunt; an vero futurae sint, quia Deus eas praescit? Resp. Affirmandum potius est prius: veritas enim rei, quae est per Dei Decretum, natura praecedit veritatem cognitionis. Attamen si adeo late sumatur Praescientia, ut ipsum Dei Decretum complexu suo involvat; ut Rom. VIII, 29. XI, 2. dicendum erit posterius: & hoc sensu Praescientia Dei recte dicitur practica. Ceteroquin in ista enunciatione, Haec res futura est, quia Deus eam praescit, agnoscenda saltem est illatio Logica, a posteriori.
units.tr: It is asked whether God foreknows things because they are going to be, or whether they are going to be because God foreknows them. Answer: the former is rather to be affirmed, for the truth of a thing, which exists through God's decree, precedes in nature the truth of the knowledge. Yet if foreknowledge is taken so broadly that it includes the decree itself in its whole compass, as in Rom. 8:29 and 11:2, the latter must be said; and in this sense the foreknowledge of God is rightly called practical. Otherwise, in this proposition, This thing is going to be, because God foreknows it, there must at least be acknowledged a logical inference, from the effect to the cause.

units.la: XXXVI. Hac igitur Scientia visionis Deus omnia & singula per suum Decretum definita novit accuratissimè: utpote naturalia, & necessaria: Psal. CXLVII, 4, 8, &c. Numerans numerum stellarum: omnibus eis nomina vocabit. &c. CXXXIX, 15, 16. Non occultum fuit corpus meum a Te, quando factus fui in occulto, &c.
units.tr: Therefore by this knowledge of vision God knows most accurately all things and each thing defined by his decree, both natural and necessary: Ps. 147:4, 8, etc., Counting the number of the stars; he calls them all by their names; 139:15, 16, My body was not hidden from you, when I was made in secret, etc.

units.la: Atque item contingentia, & libera; tum bona, tum mala; etiam occultissima, & nominatim cogitationes intimas: Psal. LVI, 9. "Motionem meam numerasti: Tu "pone lachrymam meam in utre Tuo: nonne in libro Tuo? &c. CXXXIX, 2, 3. Tu cognovisti sedere meum, & resurgere meum, &c. 13. Tu possedisti renes meos. Gen. VI, 5. "Et vidit Jehovah, quod multa malitia hominis in terra, "& omnis imaginatio cogitationum cordis ejus tantum mala omni die. Adde Psal. XXXIII, 15. XL, 10. LXIX, 6. XC, 8. XCIV, 11. 1 Reg. VIII, 39. Rom. VIII, 27. Apoc. II, 20.
units.tr: And likewise contingent and free things, both good and evil, even the most hidden, and especially inmost thoughts: Ps. 56:9, "You have counted my wanderings; put my tears into your bottle; are they not in your book?" etc. 139:2, 3, You have known my sitting down and my rising up, etc.; 13, You have possessed my reins. Gen. 6:5, "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually every day." Add Ps. 33:15; 40:10; 69:6; 90:8; 94:11; 1 Kings 8:39; Rom. 8:27; Rev. 2:20.

units.la: Ac denique minima: Matth. X, 29, 30. "Unus passerculus non cadet super terram, sine Patre vestro: "Vestri autem & capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt.
units.tr: And finally the smallest things: Matt. 10:29, 30, "One sparrow shall not fall on the ground without your Father; but the very hairs of your head are all numbered."

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Deus Abrahamum tentasse, seu explorasse, dicitur; Gen. XII, 1. &c. & destendisse, ut videret, qualia essent hominum opera: Gen. XVIII,
units.tr: Objection 1. But God is said to have tested, or tried, Abraham, Gen. 22:1, etc., and to have come down to see what the works of men were like, Gen. 18:

units.la: 2. Resp. Ista accipienda sunt de pleniori, per certa specimina, manifestatione eorum, quae non Deo, sed tum ipsis illis hominibus, tum etiam aliis. in se: sed partim de symbolo aliquo extraordinario, ad gloriam & voluntatem aliquam Dei sic manifestandam; sicut etiam quodammodo fit per omnes res creatas: Rom. 1, 20. sed propius in humanâ Christi naturâ: unde Joh. xiv, 9. Qui Me vidit, vidit Patrem. Partim de visione prophetica qualicunque: partim etiam de visione illa mentali, seu notitia, quae familiarem gratiae, vel etiam gloriae fruitionem involvit; juxta Matth. xviii, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 9.
units.tr: 2. Answer: these things are to be understood of a fuller manifestation, by certain specimens, of those things which were not hidden from God, but were made known to those men themselves and to others as well. Partly they refer to some extraordinary sign, so as to manifest thus the glory and some will of God; as also in some way happens through all created things, Rom. 1:20, but more closely in the human nature of Christ, whence John 14:9, He who has seen me has seen the Father. Partly they refer to prophetic vision of whatever kind, and partly also to that mental vision, or knowledge, which involves a familiar enjoyment of grace or even of glory, according to Matt. 18:10. See above, chap. 1, th. 9.

units.la: XXIII. Ratione Tactus Deo competit Impalpabilitas, & quidem propter suam Simplicitatem: nam Tangere, vel tangi, nisi corpus, nulla potest res. Unde Christus Luc. xxiv, 39. de se resuscitato: Palpate Me; & videte: quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet; sicut me videtis habere: cum Joh. iv, 24. Deus est spiritus.
units.tr: XXIII. With respect to touch, God possesses impalpability, and indeed on account of his simplicity; for nothing can touch or be touched except a body. Hence Christ, Luke 24:39, speaking of himself after the resurrection: Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me to have; and John 4:24, God is spirit.

units.la: Obj. Act. xvii, 27. Ut quaerant Dominum, si forte palpando cum invenirent: Ergo saltem palpari potest. Resp. Istud metaphorice ad mentem pertinet.
units.tr: Objection: Acts 17:27, That they might seek the Lord, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him. Therefore he can at least be felt. Answer: that is said metaphorically, and pertains to the mind.

units.la: XXIV. Respectu artis ἐιχαστικῆς, Deus est Ineffigiabilis. Unde etiam Jes. xl, 18. Cui assimilabitis Deum; & quid similitudinis ornabitis ei? Scil. per Simplicitatem suam Deus lineamentorum, terminationum, & figurationum expers est. Item Deut. iv, 15. Non vidistis ullam imaginem in die, quâ locutus est Jehovah ad vos in Choreb, e medio ignis. Ne forte corrumpamini; & faciatis vobis sculptile, imaginem alicujus similitudinis. Confer Act. xvii, 29. Rom. 1. 22, 23.
units.tr: XXIV. With respect to the art of images (ἐικαστικῆς [eikastikēs]), God is unportrayable. Hence also Isa. 40:18, To whom will you liken God? Or what likeness will you set up for him? That is, through his simplicity God is free of lines, boundaries, and shapes. Likewise Deut. 4:15, You saw no image on the day when the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, lest perhaps you become corrupt and make for yourselves a carved image, the likeness of any form. Compare Acts 17:29; Rom. 1:22, 23.

units.la: Contra hanc veritatem, & distertum secundum Decalogi praeceptum, graviter peccant Pontificii, practice Anthropomorphitae.
units.tr: Against this truth, and against the express precept of the Decalogue, the Papists sin grievously, and in practice the Anthropomorphites.

units.la: XXV. Sequitur Infinitas; quae talem ac tantam in Deo perfectionem designat, ut nullos terminos aut fines habeat; sed eos omnes conceptibiles excedat. Haec autem consideranda est, tum respectu ipsius Essentiae; tum respectu Durationis & Spatii ubicalis; tum denique in ordine ad Intellectum. ReRespectu Essentiæ, Deus infinitus est modo persectissimo, & quam maximè positivo; ut omnes persectionum modos & gradus, qui in creaturis reperiuntur in Divina essentia sint eminenter; omnesque fines conceptibiles ipse excedat actu simplicissimo & sufficientissimo. Hinc Col. 11, 9. Omnis plenitudo Deitatis, Psal. cxlv, 3. - Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Job. xi, 7, 8, 9. Num investigatione Deum invenies? Num usque ad perfectionem Omnisufficientis (שַׁדַּי) invenies, &c.
units.tr: XXV. Infinity follows; it signifies such and so great a perfection in God that he has no limits or ends, but exceeds all that can be conceived. This must be considered in three respects: with regard to the essence itself; with regard to duration and local space; and finally in relation to the intellect. With regard to the essence, God is infinite in a most perfect and especially positive mode, so that all the modes and degrees of perfection which are found in creatures are eminently in the divine essence, and he exceeds all conceivable ends by his most simple and most sufficient act. Hence Col. 2:9, All the fullness of the Godhead; Ps. 145:3, His greatness is unsearchable; Job 11:7, 8, 9, Can you find out God by searching? Can you find out the Almighty (שַׁדַּי [Shaddai]) to perfection? etc.

units.la: Hæc Infinitas etiam facilè deducitur ex Independenti essentiæ Divinæ sufficientia superius assertâ th. 14. Qui enim tanquam causa absolute prima & Dominus supremus, reliquis entibus fines suarum perfectionum assignavit; adeò ut nec ulli fines absolute possibiles dici, aut concipi possint, nisi dependenter ab ipso: is omnem imperfectionem, non solum privativam, sed & negativam, excludit; omnemque perfectionem conceptibilem includit eminenter; & omnes limites suâ natura excedit.
units.tr: This infinity is also easily deduced from the independent sufficiency of the divine essence, asserted above in th. 14. For he who, as first cause absolutely and supreme Lord, has assigned to the other beings the ends of their perfections, so that no ends can be called or conceived as absolutely possible except dependently on him, excludes every imperfection, not only privative but also negative, and includes eminently every conceivable perfection, and exceeds all limits by his own nature.

units.la: Non intelligitur autem hoc loco Infinitas mathematica, potentialis, aut syncategorematica; sed metaphysica, actualis, & categorematica, quam sic satis explicuimus modo.
units.tr: Here, however, infinity is not understood as mathematical, potential, or syncategorematic, but as metaphysical, actual, and categorematic, which we have sufficiently explained in the manner above.

units.la: Obj. Omnia entia habent essentiam suam certam, distinctam, definitam; ac proinde etiam Deus. Essentiæ rerum consistunt in indivisibili. Resp. Deus habet essentiam certam, & ab omnibus distinctam, hoc ipso quod ea infinita sit. Atque illud indivisibile essentiæ Divinæ, intrinsecâ suâ perfectione infinitum est.
units.tr: Objection: All beings have their own certain, distinct, and definite essence; and therefore God does too. The essences of things consist in what is indivisible. Answer: God has a certain essence, distinct from all others, by the very fact that it is infinite. And that indivisible essence of the Divine being is infinite by its intrinsic perfection.

units.la: Creaturarum distantia à Divinâ perfectione, denominari solet infinita: quia nulla est earum ad hanc affinitas, aut proportio æqualitatis, vel commensurationis: finiti enim ad infinitum nulla est proportio. Interim illa à se invicem distinguuntur propriis suis perfectionibus, cumque gradibus, vel etiam speciebus.
units.tr: The distance of creatures from the Divine perfection is usually called infinite, because they have no affinity with it, nor any proportion of equality or commensurability: for there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. Meanwhile, they are distinguished from one another by their own perfections, and by their degrees, or even by their kinds.

units.la: XXVI. Infinitas Durationis est æternitas stricte dicta.
units.tr: XXVI. The infinity of duration is eternity, strictly so called.

units.la: &ta; quæ non tantum principium & finem, sed etiam successionem prioris & posterioris excludit. Unde recte à Boëthio describitur, interminabilis vitæ tota simul ac perfecta possessio. Differt autem à Tempore strictè dicto, quod hoc tribuatur solis corporibus: & ab Ævo; quod est spirituum finitorum, principium durationis suæ habentium, atque inde successionem, sed non finem. Illa probatur testimoniis sacris; Gen. xxi, 33. Rom. xvi, 26. ubi αἰωνίος æternus appellatur. Adde Isai. lvii, 15. xliv, 6. Jer. x, 10. Rom. i, 20. 1 Tim. i, 17. Apoc. i, 4, 8, 17. xxi, 6, Psal. xc, 2, 4.
units.tr: Eternity is that which excludes not only beginning and end but also any succession of before and after. Hence Boethius describes it rightly as the complete and simultaneous possession of endless life. It differs from time strictly so called, which belongs only to bodies, and from aeviternity, which belongs to finite spirits: these have a beginning of their duration and so a succession, though not an end. Eternity is proved by sacred testimonies, where it is called eternal [αἰωνίος]: Gen. 21:33; Rom. 16:26. Add Isa. 57:15; 44:6; Jer. 10:10; Rom. 1:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; Rev. 1:4, 8, 17; 21:6; Ps. 90:2, 4.

units.la: Eadem patet ex Dei Primitate & Simplicitate. Quæ ut essentiæ, sic etiam existentiæ ac durationis Divinæ principium, omnemque variationem, excludunt; & actum purissimum inferunt; ipsamque adeo æternitatem.
units.tr: The same is clear from the primacy and simplicity of God. These exclude any beginning of the divine existence and duration, as they exclude any beginning of the divine essence, and any variation; they imply a most pure act, and so eternity itself.

units.la: Hanc vero Æternitatem carere successione, prefius probamus; 1. ex Psal. xc, 4. cum 2 Petr. iii, 8. Unus dies apud Dominum, ut mille anni, & mille anni, ut unus dies. Supereminentia igitur durationis Divinæ, temporum differentias & successionem non habet.
units.tr: That this eternity lacks succession we prove first from Ps. 90:4, together with 2 Pet. 3:8: One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The supereminence of the divine duration therefore has no differences or succession of times.

units.la: 2. Ex omnimodâ Dei Immutabilitate, de quâ th. 20. annorum enim, aliorumque temporum successio, & conversio, insignem mutationem infert.
units.tr: Second, from the complete immutability of God, which I treat under thesis 20. For succession and change of years and other times implies a notable mutation.

units.la: 3. Existentia est actus essentiæ; & duratio, existentiæ permanentia, quæ se necessario habet convenienter essentiæ. Consequenter æterna Dei duratio, est ipsa ejus essentia; cujus Simplicitas partes, earumque successionem, non admittit.
units.tr: Third, existence is the act of essence, and duration is the permanence of existence, which necessarily belongs to the essence. Consequently the eternal duration of God is his very essence, and his simplicity does not admit parts or any succession of them.

units.la: XXVII. Obj. 1. Anni, dies, præteritum, futurum, &c. tribuuntur Deo in Sacris. Resp. Scil. ἀνθρωποπαθῶς; sed intelligenda Θεοπρεπῶς.
units.tr: XXVII. Objection 1. Years, days, past, future, and so on, are attributed to God in the Sacred Writings. Answer: they are said in human fashion [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς], but are to be understood in a manner worthy of God [Θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus coexistit temporum nostrorum differentiis; ergo successionem habet: aut cæteroquin nostræ temporum differentiæ sibi invicem coexistent; quia æternitati Divinæ coëxistunt. Resp. Dei duratio manet semper eadem; sed illa coëxistentia ad nostra tempora est inadæquata: nequaquàm ergo propter æternitatis coëxistentiam, nostrum præteritum, præsens, & futurum coincidunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. God coexists with our differences of time; therefore he has succession. Otherwise our differences of time would coexist with one another, because they coexist with divine eternity. Answer: the duration of God remains always the same; but that coexistence is inadequate to our times. By no means, then, do our past, present and future coincide because of the coexistence of eternity.

units.la: Obj. 3. Tempus mundi idem est cum æternitate Dei: nam etiam illud principio caret: mundus enim creatus est in tempore; ipsum vero tempus creatum non est, æternum ergo est. Resp. Tempus mundi non est æternum, aut increatum: Deus enim creando res successivas, eådem operâ tempus produxit: unde rectè concreatum dicitur.
units.tr: Objection 3. The time of the world is the same as the eternity of God, for it too lacks a beginning: the world was created in time, but time itself was not created, so it is eternal. Answer: the time of the world is neither eternal nor uncreated. For in creating successive things God produced time by the same act; hence it is rightly called created together with them [concreatum].

units.la: XXVIII. Infinitas respectu Spatii, sive ubi, est Immensitas; quâ Deus absolutissimè ubique existit; nec ullos fines habet suæ præsentiæ vel quasi. Deus igitur non est in loco, vel ubi circumscriptivè; quæ affectio corporum propria est: nec definitivè; quæ spirituum finitorum: sed repletivè totus est intrà totum mundum, ejusque partes singulas; & totus extra eum, ubi sibi ipsi præsens existit: Atque hoc contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes asserimus.
units.tr: XXVIII. Infinity with respect to space, or place, is immensity, by which God exists most absolutely everywhere, and has no limits to his presence, or anything like limits. God is therefore not in a place, or in a where, circumscriptively, which is the property of bodies; nor definitively, which is the manner of finite spirits; but repletively, he is wholly within the whole world and each of its parts, and wholly outside it, where he exists present to himself. This we assert against the Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants.

units.la: Vulgò dicitur; Enter, præsenter, Deus hic, & ubique, potenter. Primò, enter: h. e. Deus in toto mundo præsens existit per essentiam suam infinitam. Deut. IV, 39. Iof. 11, 11. Iehovah est in cœlis desuper, & super terram desubter: Ierem. XXIII, 23, 24. "Nunquid Deus de propinquo Ego, dixit Jehovah; & non Deus de longinquo? Psal. CXXXIX, 7, 10. "Quò ibo à Spiritu Tuo; & quò à faciebus Tuis fugiam? Si ascendero cœlos, ibi Tu: & stratum fecero infernum; ecce Tu: Assumsero pennas aurorae, habitavero in novissimo maris; etiàm ibi manus Tua ducet me, & tenebit me dextra Tua. Adde Isef. VI, 1. LXVI, 1. Act. VII, 48, 49, 50. XVII, 24, 25, 27, 28.
units.tr: It is commonly said: Enter, præsenter, Deus hic, & ubique, potenter. First, essentially [enter]: that is, God exists present in the whole world through his infinite essence. Deut. 4:39; Josh. 2:11: Jehovah is in heaven above and on the earth beneath. Jer. 23:23-24: "Am I a God at hand, says Jehovah, and not a God afar off?" Ps. 139:7, 10: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in the depths, behold, you are there. If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me." Add Isa. 6:1; 66:1; Acts 7:48-50; 17:24-25, 27-28.

units.la: Secundò; præsenter; h. e. per intimam notitiam & observationem omnium eorum, quæ in illo fiunt. Psal. XXXIII, 13,14,15. E cœlis respexit Iehovah, & vidit omnes filios hominum: - considerans omnia opera eorum. Hebr. IV, 13. Non est creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus: omnia autem nuda & aperta sunt oculis ejus, ad quem nobis negotium. Psal. CXXXIX, 12, 13. Jerem. XXIII, 24.
units.tr: Second, presently [præsenter]: that is, through an intimate knowledge and observation of all that happens in it. Ps. 33:13-15: Jehovah looks down from heaven and sees all the sons of men, considering all their works. Heb. 4:13: No creature is invisible in his sight; all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do. Ps. 139:12-13; Jer. 23:24.

units.la: Tertiò, potenter; h. e. per potentem operationem: Hebr. 1,3. - Sustinet omnia verbo suo potente: Joh. V, 17. Pater Meus adhuc operatur, & Ego operor. 1 Cor. XII, 6. Agens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Third, powerfully [potenter]: that is, through his mighty operation. Heb. 1:3: he upholds all things by his powerful word. John 5:17: My Father works until now, and I work. 1 Cor. 12:6: he who works all things in all.

units.la: XXIX. Sic ergò Deus hic & ubique existit. Sed neque spatiis rerum creatarum comprehenditur: aut iis adæquatè coëxistit ipse infinitus: extra mundum in se ipso etiàm existit, qui ante mundum conditum extitit similiter. Probatur hoc specialiùs; 1. disertis testimoniis: 1 Reg. VIII, 27. Cœli, & cœli cœlorum non continent Te: quantò minùs domus hæc, quam ædificavi.
units.tr: XXIX. God therefore exists here and everywhere. Yet he is not comprehended by the spaces of created things, nor does the infinite God coexist with them adequately; he also exists in himself outside the world, having likewise existed before the world was made. This is proved more particularly: first, by express testimonies: 1 Kings 8:27: Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built?

units.la: 2 Chron. II, 6. Quis obtinebit potestatem ad ædificandum Ei domum? nam cœli, & cœli cœlorum non comprehendent Eum; & quis ego, ut ædificem Ei domum? Quin imò ad suffiendum ad facies Ejus. Ubi ipsam Dei essentiam designant pronomina Te, Eum, &c. non scientiam, potentiam, aut operationem ab essentiâ diversam; qualis etiàm non datur per Dei Simplicitatem, nedùm existere posset, ubi essentia Divina non existeret. Memoratur domus, non ad habitationem, sed ad suffitum faciendum. Habitationis conceptus, etiàm cœlorum incapacitas, &c. ad essentiam pertinent. Quomodò cæteroquin extra cœlos cœlorum, & sic extra mundum universum, existeret Dei scientia vel potentia, vel operatio, &c?
units.tr: 2 Chron. 2:6: Who will have power to build him a house? For heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot comprehend him; and who am I, that I should build him a house? Indeed, except to burn incense before his face. Here the pronouns you, him, and so on, designate the very essence of God, not knowledge, power, or operation distinct from the essence. Nor is any such thing possible given the simplicity of God, much less could it exist where the divine essence did not exist. The house is mentioned not for dwelling but for burning incense. The concept of dwelling, and the incapacity even of the heavens of heavens, and so on, pertain to the essence. Otherwise, how could the knowledge, power, or operation of God exist outside the heaven of heavens, and so outside the whole universe?

units.la: 2. Ex infinitâ Dei perfectione: quæ requirit, ut existat in omni spatio conceptibili.
units.tr: Second, from the infinite perfection of God, which requires that he exist in every conceivable space.

units.la: 3. Ex Potentiâ: Deus extra hunc mundum potest operari, similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Ubi autem potest operari, ibi potest existere; imò existit, qui est actus purissimus. 3. Ex Immutabilitate: ante mundum conditum exstitit Deus in se, modo infinito; non autem definito ad actualia spatia hujus mundi: ergò etiàm nunc similiter.
units.tr: Third, from his power: God can operate outside this world, just as he did before the world was made. But where he can operate, there he can exist; indeed he does exist, being most pure act. Third, from his immutability: before the world was made God existed in himself in an infinite mode, not one defined to the actual spaces of this world; therefore he now exists in the same way.

units.la: XXX. Observandi autem speciales quidam modi praesentiae Divinae, respectu operationum ac manifestationum: 1. In humana Christi natura inhabitat Deitas, per unionem hypostaticam: Col. 11, 9. Joh. 1, 14. 1 Tim. 111, 16. Rom. 1, 3, 4. IX, 5.
units.tr: XXX. Certain special modes of the divine presence, with respect to operations and manifestations, are to be observed. First, the Deity dwells in the human nature of Christ through the hypostatic union: Col. 2:9; John 1:14; 1 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 1:3-4; 9:5.

units.la: 2. In Ecclesia universa est Deus, per Spiritum unientem, charismata distribuentem, & salutariter gubernantem, 1 Cor. XII, 11, 12, 13. Joh. XVII, 21. Matth. XXVIII, 20.
units.tr: Second, God is in the whole Church through the Spirit who unites, distributes gifts, and governs for salvation: 1 Cor. 12:11-13; John 17:21; Matt. 28:20.

units.la: 3. In singulis Fidelibus, per Spiritum fidei, sanctificationis, adoptionis, consolationis, & corroborationis: Joh. XIV, 23, 16, 17. 2 Cor. IV, 13. Rom. VIII, 14-17, 26. Gal. IV, 6, 7. Psal. CXIV, 18.
units.tr: Third, in each of the faithful, through the Spirit of faith, sanctification, adoption, consolation and strengthening: John 14:23, 16-17; 2 Cor. 4:13; Rom. 8:14-17, 26; Gal. 4:6-7; Ps. 114:18.

units.la: 4. In Prophetis, Spiritu πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως sapientiam ac voluntatem suam revelante: 1 Petr. 1, 11. Hebr. 1, 1.
units.tr: Fourth, in the prophets, by the Spirit revealing his wisdom and will, in many parts and in many ways [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]: 1 Pet. 1:11; Heb. 1:1.

units.la: 5. In Caelo, speciali gloriae ac majestatis suae manifestatione: Isai. XLVI, 1. Matth. XVIII, 10. Hebr. XII, 22, 23. Phil. III, 20, 21. Joh. XIV, 2, 3.
units.tr: Fifth, in heaven, by a special manifestation of his glory and majesty: Isa. 46:1; Matt. 18:10; Heb. 12:22-23; Phil. 3:20-21; John 14:2-3.

units.la: 6. In Inferno, irae & justitiae suae vindicativae executione: Psal. CXXXIX, 8. Matth. X, 28. 2 Thess. 1, 9. Marc. IX, 44, 46.
units.tr: Sixth, in hell, by the execution of his wrath and avenging justice: Ps. 139:8; Matt. 10:28; 2 Thess. 1:9; Mark 9:44, 46.

units.la: XXXI. Obj. 1. Deus in coelis esse dicitur; Matth. VI, 9. & habitare lucem inaccessam; 1 Tim. VI, 16. Resp. 1. in coelis est speciali modo praesentiae gloriosae; talem scilicet ibi demonstrando, non autem existendo ibi tantum, nec alibi.
units.tr: XXXI. Objection 1. God is said to be in heaven, Matt. 6:9, and to dwell in light inaccessible, 1 Tim. 6:16. Answer 1: he is in heaven in a special mode of glorious presence, namely by displaying himself there, not by existing there only and nowhere else.

units.la: 2. Sed Lux Dei inaccessa, est ipsa ejus gloria & majestas, creaturis incomprehensibilis: sic ipse lux esse dicitur; 1 Joh. 1, 5. Vide ibid. verf. 7. & Psal. CIV, 1, 2. Non vero est locus aliquis, à Deo diversus.
units.tr: 2. But the unapproachable light of God is his very glory and majesty, incomprehensible to creatures. So he is himself called light: 1 John 1:5. See the same chapter, verse 7, and Ps. 104:1, 2. Yet this light is not some place distinct from God.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus, 1 Reg. XIX, 11, 12, negatur fuisse in vehementi vento, itemque in terræ motu, & in igni; sed in leni aurâ. Resp. Istud dicitur de extraordinario symbolo speciali cujusdam præsentiæ Divinæ, pro revelatione Prophetica.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Ng 1 Kings 19:11, 12 says God was not in the strong wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in a gentle breeze. Reply: that refers to an extraordinary sign of a particular presence of God, for prophetic revelation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Ipse negavit, se affore immorigeris; Num. xiv, 42. Ergo non est prorsus ubique. Resp. Negavit de speciali modo præsentiæ, secundum gratiam & beneficentiam.
units.tr: Obj. 3. He himself said he would not be present among the disobedient: Num. 14:42. Therefore he is not altogether everywhere. Reply: he spoke of a special mode of presence, namely of grace and beneficence.

units.la: Obj. 4. Absurdè statuitur, Deum adesse in locis impuris, interesse actionibus obscœnis, esse in Diabolus, &c. Idcirco mandavit, ut excrementa in castris Israëlitarum statim terrâ obtegerentur; Deut. xxiii, 12, 13, 14. Ergo. Resp. 1. Deus simplicissimus & sanctissimus rerum immundarum præsentiâ pollui minimè potest. In ipso existunt, vivunt, & moventur creaturæ qualescunque: Act. xvii, 28. etiam Diaboli, & homines pessimi. Unde cæterôquin eorum efficientiæ non certè independens est à Deo, ejusque Providentia. Nec Julicem suum effugere ullo modo possunt.
units.tr: Obj. 4. It is absurd to hold that God is present in impure places, takes part in obscene actions, is in the devil, and so on. For this reason he commanded that the excrement in the camp of Israel be covered at once with earth: Deut. 23:12, 13, 14. Therefore... Reply: (1) God, being most simple and most holy, cannot be defiled by the presence of unclean things. In him all creatures, whatever they are, exist, live and move: Acts 17:28. This includes the devil and the most wicked men. Hence their efficiency is in no way independent of God and his providence, and they cannot in any way escape his judgment. (2) In the camp of Israel, under that economy, God willed that ceremonial cleanness be observed. Compare Ezek. 4:12, 13.

units.la: 2. In castris Israëlitarum, sub ista œconomia, voluit Deus observari munditiem cerimonialem. Confer Ezech. iv, 12, 13.
units.tr: 2. In the camp of Israel, under that economy, God willed that ceremonial cleanness be observed. Compare Ezek. 4:12, 13.

units.la: Obj. 5. Absurda est existentia Dei atomica & atopica. Resp. Simplicitas Dei indivisibilitatem infert; & Infinitas localitatem physicam & circumscriptivam excludit. Deus totus, non per partes, coexistit creaturis singulis; sed non adæquatè.
units.tr: Obj. 5. The existence of God is absurd if it is atomic and atopic. Reply: the simplicity of God implies indivisibility, and his infinity excludes physical and circumscriptive locality. God, whole and not by parts, coexists with each single creature, but not adequately.

units.la: Obj. 6. Mera figmenta sunt Spatia imaginaria extra mundum. Resp. At non dicimus, existere spatia realia, vel actualia, extra mundum: sed Deum existere ibi in se; similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Tertullianus: „Ante omnia Deus erat solus; ipse sibi & mundus, & locus, &c. omnia. Deus etiam per absolutam suam potentiam operari potest, & creaturas producere; & spatia actuare: ista igitur possibilia sunt, & sic conceptibilia, atque imaginaria.
units.tr: Obj. 6. Imaginary spaces outside the world are mere fictions. Reply: we do not say that real or actual spaces exist outside the world, but that God exists there in himself, just as he did before the world was made. Tertullian: "Before all things God was alone; he was to himself both world and place, and all things." God can also work by his absolute power, produce creatures and actualize spaces. These things are therefore possible, and so conceivable and imaginable.

units.la: Respectu
units.tr: With respect to

units.la: XXXII. Respectu Intellectus creati Deus est Incomprehensibilis: Psal. cxlv, 3. Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Job. xi, 9. Num investigatione Deum invenics? v. 9. Rom. xi, 33, 34. 1 Tim. vi, 16. Et manifesta est ratio, ex objecti infinitate, & subjecti finiti disproportione ad ipsum.
