units.tr: XXXII. With respect to the created intellect God is incomprehensible: Ps. 145:3, "His greatness is unsearchable." Job 11:7, "Canst thou by searching find out God?" Rom. 11:33, 34; 1 Tim. 6:16. The reason is plain: from the infinity of the object and the disproportion of the finite subject to it.

units.la: Consequenter nulli creaturæ, in quocunque statu, convenit cognitio Dei comprehensiva, & adæquata; imo nequidem ullius attributi Divini: sed solum apprehensiva, & inadæquata.
units.tr: Consequently no creature, in any state, has a knowledge of God that is comprehensive and adequate; indeed not even of any divine attribute, but only one that is apprehensive and inadequate.

units.la: Obj. 1. Sic omnis nostra cognitio de Deo erit erronea: cognoscemus enim aliter, quam se habet ipsa veritas in Deo. Resp. Imo verè cognoscimus in Deo illas perfectiones, quæ verè & formaliter in ipso sunt; simulque agnoscimus, eas Deo inesse modo perfectiori, quam comprehendere possumus.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Then all our knowledge of God will be erroneous, for we shall know otherwise than the truth itself is in God. Reply: rather, we truly know in God those perfections which truly and formally are in him, and at the same time we acknowledge that they are in God in a more perfect mode than we can comprehend.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Joh. iii, 2. Videbimus eum, sicuti est: ergo comprehensivè. Resp. Istud intelligendum est tum de oculari visione humanæ Christi naturæ; tum de notitia essentiæ Divinæ propinquiore, ad beatitudinem nostram ordinatâ; non tamen comprehensivâ.
units.tr: Obj. 2. 1 John 3:2, "We shall see him as he is," therefore comprehensively. Reply: this must be understood both of the bodily vision of the human nature of Christ, and of a closer knowledge of the divine essence, ordered to our blessedness, yet not comprehensive.

units.la: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Cognoscemus Deum, ut ab ipso cogniti sumus: Atqui nos à Deo cogniti sumus comprehensivè: ergo, &c. Resp. Illud non est accipiendum de convenientiâ adæquatâ; sed de similitudine quâdam analogicâ. Confer Rom. viii, 29. Psal. i, 6.
units.tr: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. 13:12, "We shall know God as we are known by him." But we are known by God comprehensively; therefore etc. Reply: that is not to be taken of an adequate agreement, but of a certain analogical likeness. Compare Rom. 8:29; Ps. 1:6.

units.la: XXXIII. Succedunt Attributa vitæ, sive secundi generis; quæ etiam communicabilia appellari solent; re- spectu communicationis alicujus analogicæ. Vita Dei consideratur, vel ut simpliciter actuosa; vel secundum e- minentiam: priori consideratione occurrunt Intellectus, Voluntas, & Potentia; Posteriori autem, Potestas, Gloria, & Beatitudo. XXXIV. Intellectus Dei est, quo ipse omnes omnino veritates cognoscit modo sibi convenienti: h. e. infinitè, simpliciter, & independenter. 1 Tim. i, 17.
units.tr: XXXIII. There follow the attributes of life, or of the second kind, which are also commonly called communicable, with respect to some analogical communication. The life of God is considered either as simply active, or according to eminence. Under the first consideration there occur intellect, will and power; under the second, authority, glory and blessedness. XXXIV. The intellect of God is that by which he knows all truths whatever in a manner suited to himself, that is, infinitely, simply and independently. 1 Tim. 1:17.

units.la: Soli sapienti - 1Sam. 11, 3. Deus scientiarum. Psal. xciv 9, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: To God alone, the wise - 1 Sam. 2:3. God of knowledge. Ps. 94:9, 10. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Dico infinitè: ipse enim Intellectus Dei infinitus est; cum 1. secundum rem sit ipsa Dei essentia. 2. & modus intelligendi, convenienter naturae Divinae, absolutè perfectissimus sit; adeoque infinitus, atque item 3. respectu objectorum, cognoscat omnia absolutè cognoscibilia. 1 Joh. 111, 20. Novit omnia. Similiter Joh. xxi, 17. Item Psal. cxlvii, 5. Jef. iv, 9. Rom. xi, 33.
units.tr: I say infinitely: for the intellect of God is infinite, since (1) in reality it is the very essence of God; (2) its mode of understanding, agreeing with the divine nature, is absolutely most perfect, and so infinite; and likewise (3) with respect to objects, it knows all things that are absolutely knowable. 1 John 3:20, "He knows all things." Likewise John 21:17; Ps. 147:5; Isa. 40:28; Rom. 11:33.

units.la: Novit autem seipsum adaequate: Matth. xi, 27.
units.tr: He knows himself adequately, Matt. 11:27.

units.la: 1 Cor. 11, 10, 11. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Et omnia alia à se perfectissimè: Hebr. iv, 13. Omnia sunt nuda, & intimè patentia oculis ejus. Act. xv, 18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua.
units.tr: And he knows all other things most perfectly: Heb. 4:13, "All things are naked and open to his eyes." Acts 15:18, "Known to God from eternity are all his works."

units.la: XXXV. Scientia Dei ratione objectorum distingui- tur, in naturalem, necessariam, sive simplicis intelligentiæ; & in liberam, sive visionis.
units.tr: XXXV. The knowledge of God is distinguished, according to its objects, into natural and necessary knowledge, or knowledge of simple intelligence, and into free knowledge, or knowledge of vision.

units.la: Scientia simplicis intelligentiæ rerum quidditates simpliciter spectat, ut se habent citra respectum ad liberam Decreti Divini terminationem: sive in signo rationis antecedenter ad Decretum, quo pertinet ipsa Dei essentia, personæ, sufficientia, & omnipotentia, atque hinc res possibiles.
units.tr: Knowledge of simple intelligence regards the natures of things in themselves, as they stand apart from any reference to the free determination of the divine decree. It belongs in the order of reason prior to the decree, and in it lie the essence of God, his persons, his sufficiency, and his omnipotence, and from these possible things.

units.la: In mente Divinâ igitur sunt ideæ omnium possibilium. Istæ autem ideæ sunt perfectiones ipsius essentiæ Divinæ, prout imitabiles & expressibiles sunt extra Deum, & sic ab ipso cognoscuntur. A supereminenti enim & infinitâ potentiâ Dei activâ, denominantur res possibiles; quatenus videlicet per illam produci, aut actuari, possunt.
units.tr: In the divine mind, therefore, are the ideas of all possibles. These ideas are the perfections of the divine essence itself, insofar as they are capable of being imitated and expressed outside God, and so are known by him. From God's supereminent and infinite active power they are called possible things, namely insofar as they can be produced or actualized by that power.

units.la: Scientia libera consideratur, ut in signo rationis consequens ad liberum Dei Decretum. Visionis autem appellatur; quia Deus per eam videt, aut praevidet determinatam rerum existentiam sub qualicunque temporis differentiâ.
units.tr: Free knowledge is considered as following, in the order of reason, God's free decree. It is called knowledge of vision because by it God sees, or foresees, the determinate existence of things under whatever distinction of time.

units.la: Quaeritur, Utrum Deus res praescīat, quia futurae sunt; an vero futurae sint, quia Deus eas praescit? Resp. Affirmandum potius est prius: veritas enim rei, quae est per Dei Decretum, natura praecedit veritatem cognitionis. Attamen si adeo late sumatur Praescientia, ut ipsum Dei Decretum complexu suo involvat; ut Rom. viii, 29. xi, 2. dicendum erit posterius: & hoc sensu Praescientia Dei recte dicitur practica. Ceteroquin in ista enunciatione, Haec res futura est, quia Deus eam praescit, agnoscenda saltem est illatio Logica, a posteriori.
units.tr: It is asked: does God foreknow things because they are future, or are they future because God foreknows them? Answer: the former must rather be affirmed, for the truth of a thing, which exists through God's decree, precedes in nature the truth of the knowledge. Yet if foreknowledge is taken so broadly that it embraces God's decree itself in its whole scope (as in Rom. 8:29; 11:2), the latter must be said, and in this sense God's foreknowledge is rightly called practical. Otherwise, in this proposition, this thing is future because God foreknows it, one must at least recognize a logical inference drawn a posteriori.

units.la: XXXVI. Hac igitur Scientia visionis Deus omnia & singula per suum Decretum definita novit accuratissime: utpote naturalia, & necessaria: Psal. cxlvii, 4, 8, &c. Numerans numerum stellarum: omnibus eis nomina vocabit. &c. cxxxix, 15, 16. Non occultum fuit corpus meum a Te, quando factus fui in occulto, &c.
units.tr: XXXVI. By this knowledge of vision, therefore, God knows all things and each thing defined by his decree most exactly, namely natural and necessary things: Ps. 147:4, 8, etc. "He counts the number of the stars; he calls them all by name." Ps. 139:15, 16: "My body was not hidden from you when I was made in secret," etc.

units.la: Atque item contingentia, & libera, tum bona, tum mala; etiam occultissima, & nominatim cogitationes intimas: Psal. lvi, 9. "Motionem meam numerasti: Tu pone lachrymam meam in utre Tuo: nonne in libro Tuo? &c. cxxxix, 2, 3. Tu cognovisti sedere meum, et resurgere meum, &c. 13. Tu possedisti renes meos. Gen. vi, 5. "Et vidit Jehovah, quod multa malitia hominis in terra, "& omnis imaginatio cogitationum cordis ejus tantum mala omni die. Adde Psal. xxxiii, 15. xl, 10. lxix, 6. xc; 8. xciv, 11. 1 Reg. viii, 39. Rom. viii, 27. Apoc. ii, 20.
units.tr: Likewise he knows contingent and free things, both good and evil, even the most hidden, and especially the inmost thoughts: Ps. 56:9 "You have numbered my wanderings; put my tears into your bottle; are they not in your book?" etc. Ps. 139:2, 3 "You have known my sitting down and my rising up," etc. v. 13 "You possessed my reins." Gen. 6:5 "And Jehovah saw that the wickedness of man on the earth was great, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil every day." Add Ps. 33:15; 40:10; 69:6; 90:8; 94:11; 1 Kings 8:39; Rom. 8:27; Rev. 2:20.

units.la: Ac denique minima: Matth. x, 29, 30. "Unus passerculus non cadet super terram, sine Patre vestro: Vestri autem & capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt.
units.tr: And finally the smallest things: Matt. 10:29, 30 "Not one sparrow falls to the ground without your Father; but even the hairs of your head are all numbered."

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Deus Abrahamum tentasse, seu explorasse, dicitur; Gen. xii, 1. &c. & descendisse, ut videret, qualia essent hominum opera: Gen. xviii,
units.tr: Objection 1. Yet God is said to have tested, or explored, Abraham, Gen. 22:1, etc., and to have come down that he might see what kind of works men did, Gen. xviii,

units.la: 2. Resp. Ista accipienda sunt de pleniori, per certa specimina, manifestatione eorum, quae non Deo, sed tum ipsis illis hominibus, tum etiam aliis minùs erant manifesta. Confer Joh. II, 24, 25.
units.tr: 2. Answer: these things are to be understood of a fuller manifestation, by certain specific signs, of things which were not manifest to God but were still less manifest either to those very men or to others. Compare John 2:24, 25.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deus non novit malos: Matth. VII, 23. XXV, 13. Resp. Scil. de notitia approbationis, aut specialis dilectionis; de quâ vide Psal. 1, 6. 2 Tim. II. 19.
units.tr: Objection 1. God does not know the wicked: Matt. 7:23; 25:13. Answer: namely of the knowledge of approval, or of special love; on which see Ps. 1:6; 2 Tim. 2:19.

units.la: XXXVII. Contingentia & libera Deus non solum scit, cùm ea sunt præsentia, & præterita, sed etiàm præ- scit futura.
units.tr: XXXVII. God not only knows contingent and free things when they are present and past, but also foreknows future things.

units.la: Atque hoc contrà Socinianos adstruimus:
units.tr: This we maintain against the Socinians:

units.la: 1. Ex eo quòd Deus omnia cognoscat; 1 Joh. III, 20, & specialiùs, ex Psal. CXXXIX, 2. 4. Intellexisti cogitationem meam à longè: Non est sermo in linguâ meâ: ecce Jehovah, Tu nosti ipsum totum.
units.tr: 1. From the fact that God knows all things: 1 John 3:20; and more specifically from Ps. 139:2, 4: "You have understood my thought from afar... there is not a word on my tongue, but behold, Jehovah, you know it all."

units.la: 2. Futura contingentia habent determinatam veritatem suæ futuritionis per Dei Decretum; consequenter Deo nota sunt per Scientiam visionis. Act. XV. 18. Vide sup. th. 34. cum Eph. I, 11. Omnia operatur secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Act. II, 23. IV, 28.
units.tr: 2. Future contingent things have a determinate truth of their futurition through God's decree, and consequently are known to God by the knowledge of vision. Acts 15:18. See above, thesis 34, together with Eph. 1:11: "He works all things according to the counsel of his will." Acts 2:23; 4:28.

units.la: 3. Ex prophetiis, earumque complemento: Unde Tertullianus adversus Marc. lib. 2. cap. 4. De præscientiâ verò quid dicam? quæ tantos habet testes, quantos fecit Prophetas. Jes. XLVI. 9, 10, 11. "Recordamini priorum à sæculo: quoniam Ego Deus &c. Annuncians ab exordio novissimam, & à quondam, quæ non facta sunt: dicens; Consilium meum stabit, &c. Vocans ab Oriente Volucrem, de terrâ longinquâ virum consilii mei: etiàm locutus sum; etiam adducam illud. Vide speciatim quæ Abrahamo prædicta: Gen. XV, 13. -16, XVIII, 18, 19. quæ Jacob nepotibus & filiis suis prænunciavit, Gen. XLVIII, 19. -XLIX, 1. -& Moses Israëlitis; Deut. XXXI, 16, 20. XXXII, 1. -Insignis est prædictio Prophetæ illius Judæi de Altari Bethelis: 1 Reg. XIII, 2, 3. quæ impleta: 2 Reg. XXIII, 16, 17, 18. Achabo & familiæ ejus accuratè prædictum fuit excidium, 1 Reg. XXI, 19. -XXII, 17. -28. complementum sequitur ibidem, verf. 30. -38. & 2 Reg. IX, 24. -X, 7. -11. Adde plurima illustria in Daniele, & reliquis Prophetis, de Regnorum translationibus, eversionibus, &c. ac potissimum tissimum de Christi nativitate, vitâ, passionibus, morte, &c.
units.tr: 3. From the prophecies and their fulfilment. Whence Tertullian, against Marcion, book 2, chapter 4: "But what shall I say of foreknowledge? It has as many witnesses as it has made prophets." Isa. 46:9-11: "Remember the former things of old, for I am God... declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand... calling a bird from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country; indeed I have spoken, and I will also bring it to pass." See especially what was foretold to Abraham, Gen. 15:13-16; 18:18, 19; what Jacob foretold to his grandsons and sons, Gen. 48:19; 49:1; and what Moses foretold to the Israelites, Deut. 31:16, 20; 32:1. Remarkable is the prediction of that Jewish prophet about the altar of Bethel, 1 Kings 13:2, 3, which was fulfilled, 2 Kings 23:16-18. The destruction of Ahab and his family was predicted precisely, 1 Kings 21:19; 22:17, 28; the fulfilment follows in the same place, v. 30-38, and in 2 Kings 9:24; 10:7-11. Add very many illustrious predictions in Daniel and the other prophets, about the transfers and overthrows of kingdoms, etc., and above all about the birth, life, sufferings, death of Christ, etc.

units.la: 4. Deinde ex Dei Immutabilitate, Æternitate, & Primitate, evidens est, ipsum non minùs obiectorum scibilium, quamdiu futura sunt, habere notitiam, quàm cum eadem sunt præsentia.
units.tr: 4. Then from God's immutability, eternity and priority it is evident that he has no less knowledge of knowable objects while they are future than when they are present.

units.la: XXXVIII. Obj. 1. Quæ certò præsciuntur, habent veritatem determinatam: futura igitur contingentia & libera non certò præsciuntur. Resp. Futurorum contingentium & liberorum veritas determinata est extrinsecè à parte Dei; non autem intrinsecè ex natura rei.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Objection 1. Things that are certainly foreknown have a determinate truth; therefore future contingent and free things are not certainly foreknown. Answer: the determinate truth of future contingent and free things is determined extrinsically, on God's side, but not intrinsically from the nature of the thing.

units.la: Obj. 2. Contingentiæ & libertati repugnat omnis necessitas. Resp. Verum est antecedens de necessitate intrinsecâ, absolutâ, consequentis; non vero de extrinsecâ, hypotheticâ, consequentiæ.
units.tr: Objection 2. All necessity is incompatible with contingency and liberty. Answer: the antecedent is true of intrinsic, absolute necessity of the consequent, but not of extrinsic, hypothetical necessity of the consequence.

units.la: XXXIX. Præscientia igitur Dei non est conditionalis, aut conditionata, sed certa & absoluta. Neque admittendum Jesuiticum Ἀδρημα, à Remonstrantibus etiam adoptatum, de Scientia in Deo Media; quâ Deus fingitur, ante omnem actum voluntatis suæ, prævidisse, quid creatura rationalis, in his vel illis rerum circumstantiis posita, pro innatâ sua libertate, effet actura; sic tamen, ut illa posset, si vellet, facere oppositum.
units.tr: XXXIX. God's foreknowledge, therefore, is not conditional or conditioned, but certain and absolute. Nor is the Jesuitical figment [Ἀδρημα] to be admitted, which the Remonstrants also adopted, concerning middle knowledge in God, by which God is imagined to have foreseen, before any act of his will, what a rational creature, placed in these or those circumstances, would do by its innate freedom, yet in such a way that it could, if it willed, do the opposite.

units.la: Verum 1. S. Scriptura causis secundis in se consideratis, circa actum voluntatis Divinæ derogat actuum liberorum determinationem. Jerem. x. 23. Novi Jehovah, quod non est hominis via ejus; nec viri ambulantis, vel præparare gressum suum. Adde Rom. xi, 35. 1 Cor. iv, 7. 2 Cor. iii, 5.
units.tr: For, first, Holy Scripture, considering secondary causes in themselves, denies that the determination of free acts belongs to them in relation to the act of the divine will. Jer. 10:23: "I know, Jehovah, that the way of man is not his own; nor is it in a man who walks to direct his own step." Add Rom. 11:35; 1 Cor. 4:7; 2 Cor. 3:5.

units.la: 2. Determinatio ista Deo, ut causæ primæ, adscribitur. Jes. xlvi. 10. Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam. Prov. xvi, 9. Cor hominis cogitabit viam suam, & Jehovah parabit gressum ejus. Prov. xxi, 1. Ut rivuli aquarum, cor Regis in manu Jehovæ: super omnia, quod voluerit, inclinabit illud. Adde Rom.
units.tr: Second, that determination is ascribed to God as first cause. Isa. 46:10: "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure." Prov. 16:9: "A man's heart devises his way, but Jehovah directs his step." Prov. 21:1: "The king's heart is in the hand of Jehovah like channels of water; he turns it wherever he wishes." Add Rom.

units.la: . ςta ; quæ non tantum principium & finem, sed etiam successionem prioris & posterioris excludit. Unde recte à Boëthio describitur, interminabilis vitæ tota simul ac perfecta possessio. Differt autem à Tempore stricte dicto, quod hoc tribuatur solis corporibus: & ab Ævo; quod est spirituum finitorum, principium durationis suæ habentium, atque inde successionem, sed non finem. Illa probatur testimoniis sacris; Gen. xxi, 33. Rom. xvi, 26. ubi αὐτολεξεὶ æternus appellatur. Adde Isa. lvii, 15. xliv, 6. Ier. x, 10. Rom. i, 20. 1 Tim. i, 17. Apoc. i, 4, 8, 17. xxi, 6, Psal. xc, 2, 4.
units.tr: ...which excludes not only beginning and end but also the succession of before and after. Whence it is rightly described by Boethius as "the complete and simultaneous possession of interminable life." It differs from time strictly so called, which is attributed only to bodies, and from aeon, which belongs to finite spirits, having a beginning of their duration and hence succession, but not an end. The former is proved by sacred testimonies: Gen. 21:33; Rom. 16:26, where God is called "eternal [αἰώνιος]". Add Isa. 57:15; 44:6; Jer. 10:10; Rom. 1:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; Rev. 1:4, 8, 17; 21:6; Ps. 90:2, 4.

units.la: Eadem patet ex Dei Primitate & Simplicitate. Quæ ut essentiæ, sic etiam existentiæ ac durationis Divinæ principium, omnemque variationem, excludunt; & actum purissimum interunt; ipsamque adeo æternitatem.
units.tr: This is also clear from God's primacy and simplicity. These, as they exclude a beginning of his essence, so also of his existence and duration, and every variation, and they establish a most pure act; and so eternity itself.

units.la: Hanc vero Æternitatem carere successione, prefius probamus; 1. ex Psal. xc, 4. cum 2 Petr. iii, 8. Unus dies apud Dominum, ut mille anni, & mille anni, ut unus dies. Supereminentia igitur durationis Divinæ, temporum differentias & successionem non habet.
units.tr: We prove first that this eternity lacks succession: 1. from Psalm 90:4 together with 2 Peter 3:8, "One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Therefore the supereminence of God's duration does not have differences of times and succession.

units.la: 2. Ex omnimodâ Dei Immutabilitate, de quâ th. 20. annorum enim, aliorumque temporum successio, & conversio, insignem mutationem infert.
units.tr: 2. From the entire immutability of God, concerning which see thesis 20. For the succession of years and other times brings in a notable change.

units.la: 3. Existentia est actus essentiæ; & duratio, existentiæ permanentia, quæ se necessario habet convenienter essentiæ. Consequenter æterna Dei duratio, est ipsa ejus essentia; cujus Simplicitas partes, earumque successionem, non admittit.
units.tr: 3. Existence is the act of essence, and duration is the permanence of existence, which necessarily belongs to essence. Consequently God's eternal duration is his very essence; and his simplicity does not admit parts, nor their succession.

units.la: XXVII. Obj. 1. Anni, dies, præteritum, futurum, &c. tribuuntur Deo in Sacris. Resp. Scil. ἀνθρωποπαθῶς; sed intelligenda Θεοπρεπῶς.
units.tr: XXVII. Objection 1. Years, days, past, future, etc., are attributed to God in the Sacred writings. Answer: they are said in a human manner [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]; but they are to be understood in a manner worthy of God [Θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus coëxistit temporum nostrorum differentiis; ergo successionem habet: aut cæteroquin nostræ temporum differentiæ sibi invicem coëxistent; quia æternitati Divinæ coëxistunt. Resp. Dei duratio manet semper eadem; sed illa coëxistentia ad nostra tempora est inadæquata: nequaquàm ergo propter æternitatis coëxistentiam, nostrum præteritum, præsens, & futurum coincidunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. God coexists with the differences of our times; therefore he has succession; or otherwise our differences of time would coexist with one another, because they coexist with the divine eternity. Answer: God's duration remains always the same; but that coexistence is inadequate to our times: by no means, therefore, do our past, present and future coincide because of the coexistence with eternity.

units.la: Tempus mundi idem est cum æternitate Dei: nam etiam illud principio caret: mundus enim creatus est in tempore; ipsum vero tempus creatum non est, æternum ergo est. Resp. Tempus mundi non est æternum, aut increatum: Deus enim creando res successivas, eâdem operâ tempus produxit: unde recte concreatum dicitur.
units.tr: The time of the world is the same as the eternity of God, for it too lacks a beginning: the world was created in time; but time itself was not created, and so it is eternal. Answer: the time of the world is neither eternal nor uncreated: for God, in creating successive things, at the same stroke produced time; whence it is rightly called concreated.

units.la: XXVIII. Infinitas respectu Spatii, sive ubi, est Immensitas; quâ Deus absolutissimè ubique existit; nec ullos fines habet suæ præsentiæ vel quasi. Deus igitur non est in loco, vel ubi circumscriptive; quæ affectio corporum propria est: nec definitive, quæ spirituum finitorum: sed repletive totus est intrà totum mundum, ejusque partes singulas; & totus extra eum, ubi sibi ipsi præsens existit. Atque hoc contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes asserimus.
units.tr: XXVIII. Infinity with respect to space, or to where, is immensity; by which God exists everywhere in the most absolute way, and has no limits to his presence, or as it were none. God therefore is not in a place, or where, circumscriptively, which is the property of bodies; nor definitively, which is that of finite spirits; but he is wholly repletively within the whole world and each of its parts, and wholly outside it, where he exists present to himself. And this we assert against the Socinians, the Anabaptists and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Vulgò dicitur; Enter, præsenter, Deus hic, & ubique, potenter. Primò, enter: h. e. Deus in toto mundo præsens existit per essentiam suam infinitam. Deut. iv, 39. Ioss. ii, 11. Iehovah est in cœlis desuper, & super terram desubter. Ierem. xxiii, 23, 24. Nunquid Deus de propinquo Ego, dixit Jehovah; & non Deus de longinquo? Psal. cxxxix, 7-10. Quò ibo à Spiritû Tuo; & quò à faciebus Tuis fugiam? Si ascendero cœlos, ibi Tu: & stratum fecero infernum; ecce Tu: Assumsero pennas aurorae, habitavero in novissimo maris; etiàm ibi manus Tua ducet me, & tenebit me dextra Tua. Adde Isa. vi, 1. lxvi, 1. Act. vii, 48, 49, 50. xvii, 24, 25, 27, 28.
units.tr: It is commonly said: Within, present, God here and everywhere, powerfully. First, within: that is, God exists present in the whole world through his infinite essence. Deut. 4:39; Joshua 2:11: Jehovah is in heaven above and on the earth beneath. Jeremiah 23:23, 24: "Am I a God at hand, says Jehovah, and not a God afar off? " Psalm 139:7-10: Whither shall I go from Your Spirit? and whither shall I flee from Your face? If I ascend into heaven, You are there; and if I make my bed in hell, behold, You are there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there Your hand shall lead me, and Your right hand shall hold me. Add Isaiah 6:1; 66:1; Acts 7:48, 49, 50; 17:24, 25, 27, 28.

units.la: Secundò, præsenter; h. e. per intimam notitiam & observationem omnium eorum, quæ in illo fiunt: Psal. xxxiii,13,14,15. E cœlis respexit Iehovah, & vidit omnes filios hominum: - considerans omnia opera eorum. Hebr. iv, 13. „Non est creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus: omnia „autem nuda & aperta sunt oculis ejus, ad quem nobis ne„gotium. Psal. cxxxix, 12, 13. Jerem. xxiii, 24.
units.tr: Secondly, present; that is, through intimate knowledge and observation of all things that happen in it: Psalm 33:13, 14, 15: Jehovah looked down from heaven and saw all the sons of men... considering all their works. Hebrews 4:13: "There is no creature invisible in his sight; but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do." Psalm 139:12, 13; Jeremiah 23:24.

units.la: Tertiò, potenter; h. e. per potentem operationem: Hebr. 1,3. - Sustinet omnia verbo suo potente: Joh. v,17. „Pater Meus adhuc operatur, & Ego operor. 1 Cor. xii, 6. Agens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Thirdly, powerfully; that is, through powerful operation: Hebrews 1:3: ...upholding all things by the word of his power; John 5:17: "My Father is still working, and I work." 1 Corinthians 12:6: working all in all.

units.la: XXIX. Sic ergò Deus hîc & ubique existit. Sed neque spatiis rerum creatarum comprehenditur: aut iis adæquatè coëxiftit ipse infinitus: extra mundum in se ipso etiàm existit, qui ante mundum conditum extitit similiter. Probatur hoc specialiùs; 1. disertis testimoniis: 1 Reg. viii, 27. „Cœli, & cœli cœlorum non continent Te: quantò minùs domus hæc, quam ædificavi.
units.tr: XXIX. Thus God exists here and everywhere. But he is not comprehended by the spaces of created things, nor does he himself, infinite, coexist adequately with them: he also exists outside the world in himself, who likewise existed before the world was made. This is proved more specifically: 1. by express testimonies: 1 Kings 8:27: "Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You; how much less this house which I have built?"

units.la: 2 Chron. ii, 6. „Quis obtinebit potestatem ad ædifi„candum Ei domum? nam cœli, & cœli cœlorum non com„prehendent Eum; & quis ego, ut ædificem Ei domum? „Quin imò ad sufficiendum ad facies Ejus. Ubi ipsam Dei essentiam designant pronomina Te, Eum, &c. non scientiam, potentiam, aut operationem ab essentiâ diversam; qualis etiàm non datur per Dei Simplicitatem, nedùm existere posset, ubi essentia Divina non exilteret. Memoratur domus, non ad habitationem; sed ad suffitum faciendum. Habitationis conceptus, etiàm cœlorum incapacitas, &c. ad essentiam pertinent. Quomodò cæteroquin extra cœlos cœlorum, & sic extra mundum universum, exiftteret Dei scientia, vel potentia, vel operatio, &c?
units.tr: 2 Chronicles 2:6: "Who shall have the power to build Him a house? For heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot comprehend Him; and who am I, that I should build Him a house? Except indeed to burn incense before His face." Here the pronouns You, Him, etc., designate the very essence of God, not knowledge, power or operation different from the essence; nor could such a thing exist through God's simplicity, much less exist where the divine essence did not exist. A house is mentioned, not for dwelling, but for burning incense. The concept of dwelling, and the incapacity even of the heavens, etc., pertain to the essence. Otherwise, how would God's knowledge, or power, or operation, etc., exist outside the heavens of heavens, and so outside the whole world?

units.la: 2. Ex infinitâ Dei perfectione: quæ requirit, ut exiftat in omni spatio conceptibili.
units.tr: 2. From the infinite perfection of God, which requires that he exist in every conceivable space.

units.la: 3. Ex Potentiâ: Deus extra hunc mundum potest operari, similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Ubi autem potest operari, ibi potest existere; imò existit, qui est actus purissimus.
units.tr: 3. From power: God can operate outside this world, just as he did before the world was made. But where he can operate, there he can exist; indeed he exists, being pure act.

units.la: ¶. Ex
units.tr: ¶. From

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 3. Ex Immutabilitate: ante mundum conditum exstitit Deus in se, modo infinito; non autem definito ad actualia spatia hujus mundi: ergo etiàm nunc similiter.
units.tr: 3. From immutability: before the world was created, God existed in himself in an infinite mode, not defined by the actual spaces of this world. Therefore he now exists in the same way.

units.la: XXX. Observandi autem speciales quidam modi praesentiae Divinae, respectu operationum ac manifestationum: 1. In humana Christi natura inhabitat Deitas, per unionem hypostaticam: Col. 11, 9, Joh. 1, 14. 1 Tim. 111, 16. Rom. 1, 3, 4. IX, 5.
units.tr: XXX. Certain special modes of the divine presence, with respect to his operations and manifestations, are to be noted. 1. In Christ's human nature the Deity dwells, through the hypostatic union: Col. 2:9; John 1:14; 1 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 1:3, 4; 9:5.

units.la: 2. In Ecclesia universa est Deus, per Spiritum unientem, charismata distribuentem, & salutariter gubernantem, 1 Cor. XII, 11, 12, 13, Joh. XVI, 21. Matth. XXVIII, 20.
units.tr: 2. God is in the universal Church, uniting it through the Spirit, distributing gifts, and governing it for salvation: 1 Cor. 12:11, 12, 13; John 16:21; Matt. 28:20.

units.la: 3. In singulis Fidelibus, per Spiritum fidei, sanctificationis, adoptionis, consolationis, & corroborationis: Joh. XIV, 23, 16, 17. 2 Cor. IV, 13. Rom. VIII, 14, 17, 26. Gal. IV, 6, 7. Psal. CXLV, 18.
units.tr: 3. In individual believers, through the Spirit of faith, of sanctification, of adoption, of consolation, and of strengthening: John 14:23, 16, 17; 2 Cor. 4:13; Rom. 8:14, 17, 26; Gal. 4:6, 7; Ps. 145:18.

units.la: 4. In Prophetis, Spiritu πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως sapientiam ac voluntatem suam revelante: 1 Petr. 1, 11. Hebr. 1, 1.
units.tr: 4. In the prophets, revealing his wisdom and will by the Spirit "in many portions and in many ways" [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]: 1 Pet. 1:11; Heb. 1:1.

units.la: 5. In Caelo, speciali gloriae ac majestatis suae manifestatione: Jef. XLVI, 1. Matth. XVIII, 10. Hebr. XII, 22, 23. Phil. III, 20, 21. Joh. XIV, 2, 3.
units.tr: 5. In heaven, by a special manifestation of his glory and majesty: Isa. 46:1; Matt. 18:10; Heb. 12:22, 23; Phil. 3:20, 21; John 14:2, 3.

units.la: 6. In Inferno, irae & justitiae suae vindicativae executione: Psal. CXXXIX, 8. Matth. X, 28. 2 Thess. 1, 9. Marc. IX, 44, 46.
units.tr: 6. In hell, by the execution of his wrath and avenging justice: Ps. 139:8; Matt. 10:28; 2 Thess. 1:9; Mark 9:44, 46.

units.la: XXXI. Obj. 1 Deus in caelis esse dicitur; Matth. VI, 9. & habitare lucem inaccessam; 1 Tim. VI, 16. Resp. 1. in caelis est speciali modo praesentiae gloriosae; talem scilicet ibi demonstrando, non autem existendo ibi tantum, nec alibi. 2. Sed Lux Dei inaccessa, est ipsa ejus gloria & majestas, creaturis incomprehensibilis: sic ipse lux esse dicitur; 1 Joh. 1, 5. Vide ibid. verf. 7. & Psal. CIV, 1, 2. Non vero est locus aliquis, à Deo diversus.
units.tr: XXXI. Objection 1. God is said to be in heaven, Matt. 6:9, and to dwell in unapproachable light, 1 Tim. 6:16. Answer 1. He is in heaven in a special mode of glorious presence, that is, by displaying there such a presence, not by existing there only and nowhere else. 2. But the unapproachable light of God is his very glory and majesty, incomprehensible to creatures. So he himself is called light: 1 John 1:5; see the same passage, verse 7, and Ps. 104:1, 2. It is not some place distinct from God.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus, 1 Reg. XIX, 11, 12, negatur fuisse in vehementi vento, itemque in terræ motu, & in igni; sed in leni aurâ. Resp. Id dicitur de extraordinario symbolo speciali cujusdam præsentiæ Divinæ, pro revelatione Prophetica.
units.tr: Objection 2. In 1 Kings 19:11, 12, God is said not to have been in the strong wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in the gentle breeze. Answer This is said of an extraordinary sign of a special presence of God, for prophetic revelation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Ipse negavit, se affore immorigeris; Num. xiv, 42. Ergo non est prorsus ubique. Resp. Negavit de speciali modo præsentiæ, secundum gratiam & beneficentiam.
units.tr: Objection 3. He declared that he would not be with the disobedient, Num. 14:42. Therefore he is not everywhere. Answer He denied it of a special mode of presence, namely that by grace and beneficence.

units.la: Obj. 4. Absurdè statuitur, Deum adesse in locis impuris, interesse actionibus obscœnis, esse in Diabolus, &c. Idcirco mandavit, ut excrementa in castris Israelitarum statim terra obtegerentur; Deut. xxiii, 12, 13, 14. Ergo. Resp. 1. Deus simplicissimus & sanctissimus rerum immundarum præsentia pollui minimè potest. In ipso exsistunt, vivunt, & moventur creaturæ qualescunque: Act. xvii, 28, etiam Diaboli, & homines pessimi. Unde cæterorum eorum efficientiæ non certè independens est à Deo, ejusque Providentia. Nec Judicem suum effugere ullo modo possunt.
units.tr: Objection 4. It is absurd to hold that God is present in impure places, takes part in obscene actions, is in the devil, and so on. Therefore he commanded that excrement in the camp of Israel be immediately covered with earth, Deut. 23:12, 13, 14. Therefore... Answer 1. God, most simple and most holy, can by no means be polluted by the presence of impure things. In him all creatures, of whatever kind, exist, live and move, Acts 17:28, even the devil and the most wicked men. Hence their operation is certainly not independent of God and his providence. Nor can they in any way escape their Judge.

units.la: 2. In castris Israelitarum, sub ista œconomia, voluit Deus observari munditiem cærimonialem. Confer Ezech. iv, 12, 13.
units.tr: 2. In the camp of Israel, under that dispensation, God willed that ceremonial cleanness be observed. Compare Ezek. 4:12, 13.

units.la: Obj. 5. Absurda est existentia Dei atomica & atopica. Resp. Simplicitas Dei indivisibilitatem infert; & Infinitas localitatem physicam & circumscriptivam excludit. Deus totus, non per partes, coexistit creaturis singulis; sed non adæquatè.
units.tr: Objection 5. The existence of God as atomic and atopic is absurd. Answer The simplicity of God implies indivisibility, and his infinity excludes physical and circumscriptive locality. God, wholly and not by parts, coexists with each single creature, but not adequately.

units.la: Obj. 6. Mera figmenta sunt Spatia imaginaria extra mundum. Resp. At non dicimus, existere spatia realia, vel actualia, extra mundum: sed Deum existere ibi in se; similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Tertullianus: „Ante omnia Deus erat solus; ipse sibi & mundus, & „locus, &c. omnia. Deus etiam per absolutam suam potentiam operari potest, & creaturas producere, & spatia actuare: ista igitur possibilia sunt, & sic concepibilia atque imaginaria.
units.tr: Objection 6. Imaginary spaces outside the world are mere fictions. Answer But we do not say that real or actual spaces exist outside the world; we say that God exists there in himself, just as he did before the world was made. Tertullian: "Before all things God was alone; he himself was to himself both world and place and all things." God also, by his absolute power, can act, produce creatures, and actualise spaces. These things are therefore possible, and so conceivable and imaginable.

units.la: Respectu
units.tr: With respect to

units.la: XXXII. Respectu Intellectus creati Deus est Incomprehensibilis: Psal. cxlv, 3. Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Job.xi,9. Nam investigatione Deum invenies? v,9. Rom. xi, 33, 34. 1 Tim. vi, 16. Et manifesta est ratio, ex objecti infinitate, & subjecti finiti disproportione ad ipsum.
units.tr: XXXII. With respect to the created intellect, God is incomprehensible: Ps. 145:3; "of his greatness there is no searching," Job 11:9; "Canst thou by searching find out God?" 5:9; Rom. 11:33, 34; 1 Tim. 6:16. The reason is evident, from the infinity of the object and the disproportion of the finite subject to it.

units.la: Consequenter nulli creaturae, in quocunque statu, convenit cognitio Dei comprehensiva, & adaequata; imo nequidem ullius attributi Divini: sed solum apprehensiva, & inadaequata.
units.tr: Consequently, no creature, in any state, has a comprehensive and adequate knowledge of God; indeed not even of any one of the divine attributes; only an apprehensive and inadequate knowledge.

units.la: Obj. 1. Sic omnis nostra cognitio de Deo erit erronea: cognoscemus enim aliter, quam se habet ipsa veritas in Deo. Resp. Imo vere cognoscimus in Deo illas perfectiones, quae vere & formaliter in ipso sunt; simulque agnoscimus, eas Deo inesse modo perfectiori, quam comprehendere possumus.
units.tr: Objection 1. Thus all our knowledge of God would be erroneous, for we would know otherwise than the truth itself is in God. Answer On the contrary, we truly know in God those perfections which truly and formally are in him; and at the same time we recognise that they belong to God in a more perfect mode than we can comprehend.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Joh. iii, 2. Videbimus eum, sicuti est: ergo comprehensive. Resp. Id intelligendum est tum de oculari visione humanae Christi naturae; tum de notitia essentiae Divinae propinquiore, ad beatitudinem nostram ordinata; non tamen comprehensiva.
units.tr: Objection 2. 1 John 3:2: We shall see him as he is; therefore comprehensively. Answer This is to be understood both of the bodily vision of Christ's human nature, and of a closer knowledge of the divine essence, ordained for our blessedness; yet not comprehensive.

units.la: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Cognoscemus Deum, ut ab ipso cogniti sumus: Atqui nos a Deo cogniti sumus comprehensive: ergo, &c. Resp. Illud non est accipiendum de convenientia adaequata; sed de similitudine quadam analogica. Confer Rom. viii, 29. Psal. i, 6.
units.tr: Objection 3. 1 Cor. 13:12: We shall know God as we are known by him. But we are known by God comprehensively; therefore, etc. Answer That is not to be taken of adequate correspondence, but of a certain analogical likeness. Compare Rom. 8:29; Ps. 1:6.

units.la: XXXIII. Succedunt Attributa vitae, sive secundi generis; quae etiam communicabilia appellari solent; respectu communicationis alicujus analogicae. Vita Dei consideratur, vel ut simpliciter actuosa; vel secundum eminentiam: priori consideratione occurrunt Intellectus, Voluntas, & Potentia; posteriori autem, Potestas, Gloria, & Beatitudo.
units.tr: XXXIII. There follow the attributes of life, or of the second kind, which are also commonly called communicable, with respect to some analogical communication. The life of God is considered either as simply active, or according to eminence. Under the former consideration occur intellect, will, and power; under the latter, authority, glory, and blessedness.

units.la: XXXIV. Intellectus Dei est, quo ipse omnes omnino veritates cognoscit modo sibi convenienti: h. e. infinite, simpliciter, & independenter. 1 Tim. i, 17. Soli sapienti - 1Sam. 11, 3. Deus scientiarum. Psal. xciv 9, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: XXXIV. The intellect of God is that by which he knows all truths whatsoever, in a manner fitting to himself, that is, infinitely, simply, and independently. 1 Tim. 1:17. To the only wise... 1 Sam. 2:3. God of knowledges, Ps. 94:9, 10. See above, chapter 1, thesis 3.

units.la: Dico infinitè: ipse enim Intellectus Dei infinitus est; cum 1. secundùm rem sit ipsa Dei essentia. 2. & modus intelligendi, convenienter naturae Divinae, absolutè perfectissimus sit; adeòque infinitus, atque item 3. respectu objectorum, cognoscat omnia absolutè cognoscibilia. 1 Joh. iii, 20. Novit omnia. Similiter Joh. xxi, 17. Item Psal. cxlvii, 5. Jes. lv, 9. Rom. xi, 33.
units.tr: I say infinitely: for the intellect of God is indeed infinite, since 1. in reality it is the very essence of God; 2. and its mode of understanding, agreeing with the divine nature, is absolutely most perfect, and therefore infinite; and likewise 3. with respect to objects, it knows all things that are absolutely knowable. 1 John 3:20: He knows all things. Similarly John 21:17. Likewise Ps. 147:5; Isa. 55:9; Rom. 11:33.

units.la: Novit autem seipsum adaequate: Matth. xi, 27.
units.tr: He knows himself adequately, however: Matt. 11:27.

units.la: 1 Cor. 11, 10, 11. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. See above, chapter 1, thesis 3.

units.la: Et omnia alia à se perfectissimè: Hebr. iv, 13. Omnia sunt nuda, & intimè patentia oculis ejus. Act. xv, 18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) aevo omnia opera sua.
units.tr: And all other things most perfectly, apart from himself: Heb. 4:13: All things are naked and laid open to his eyes. Acts 15:18: Known to God from eternity are all his works.

units.la: XXXV. Scientia Dei ratione objectorum distingui- tur, in naturalem, necessariam, sive simplicis intelligentiae; & in liberam, sive visionis.
units.tr: XXXV. The knowledge of God is distinguished by its objects into natural, necessary, or of simple understanding; and into free, or of vision.

units.la: Scientia simplicis intelligentiae rerum quidditates simpliciter spectat, ut se habent citra respectum ad liberam Decreti Divini terminationem: sive in signo rationis antecedenter ad Decretum, quo pertinet ipsa Dei essentia, personae, sufficientia, & omnipotentia, atque hinc res possibiles.
units.tr: The knowledge of simple understanding regards the essences of things simply, as they stand apart from any reference to the free determination of the divine decree. It belongs to the order of reason prior to the decree, and includes the very essence, persons, sufficiency and omnipotence of God, and hence possible things.

units.la: In mente Divinâ igitur sunt ideae omnium possibilium. Istae autem ideae sunt perfectiones ipsius essentiae Divinae, prout imitabiles & exprellibiles sunt extra Deum, & sic ab ipso cognoscuntur. A supereminenti enim & infinitâ potentiâ Dei activâ, denominantur res possibiles; quatenus videlicet per illam produci, aut actuari, possunt.
units.tr: In the divine mind, therefore, there are the ideas of all possible things. These ideas are the perfections of the divine essence itself, insofar as they can be imitated and expressed outside God, and so they are known by him. For they are called possible things from God's supereminent and infinite active power, that is, because they can be produced or brought into act by it.

units.la: Scientia libera consideratur, ut in signo rationis consequens ad liberum Dei Decretum. Visionis autem appellatur; quia Deus per eam videt, aut praevidet, determinatam rerum exsistentiam sub qualicunque temporis differentiâ.
units.tr: Free knowledge is considered as following, in the order of reason, God's free decree. It is called of vision because by it God sees, or foresees, the determinate existence of things under whatever difference of time.

units.la: Quaeritur, Utrùm Deus res praescit, quia futurae sunt; an vero futurae sint, quia Deus eas praescit? Resp. Affirmandum potius est prius: veritas enim rei, quae est per Dei Decretum, natura praecedit veritatem cognitionis. Attamen si adeo late sumatur Praescientia, ut ipsum Dei Decretum complexu suo involvat; ut Rom. viii, 29. xi, 2. dicendum erit posterius: & hoc sensu Praescientia Dei recte dicitur practica. Ceteroquin in ista enunciatione, Haec res futura est, quia Deus eam praescit, agnoscenda saltem est illatio Logica, a posteriori.
units.tr: It is asked: does God know things beforehand because they are going to be future, or are they going to be future because God foreknows them? Answer: the former is rather to be affirmed, for the truth of a thing, which exists by God's decree, precedes in nature the truth of the knowledge of it. Yet if foreknowledge is taken so broadly that it embraces the decree itself within its scope, as in Rom. 8:29 and 11:2, the latter must be said; and in this sense the foreknowledge of God is rightly called practical. Otherwise, in this statement, this thing is going to be future because God foreknows it, one must acknowledge at least a logical inference, a posteriori.

units.la: XXXVI. Hac igitur Scientia visionis Deus omnia & singula per suum Decretum definita novit accuratissime: utpote naturalia, & necessaria: Psal. cxlvii, 4, 8, &c. Numerans numerum stellarum: omnibus eis nomina vocabit. &c. cxxxix, 15, 16. Non occultum fuit corpus meum a Te, quando factus fui in occulto, &c.
units.tr: XXXVI. By this knowledge of vision, therefore, God knows all and each thing defined through his decree most accurately: both natural and necessary things, Ps. 147:4, 8, etc.: He counts the number of the stars; he calls them all by name, etc. Ps. 139:15, 16: My body was not hidden from you, when I was made in secret, etc.

units.la: Atque item contingentia, & libera; tum bona, tum mala; etiam occultissima, & nominatim cogitationes intimas: Psal. lvi, 9. Motionem meam numerasti: Tu pone lachrymam meam in utre Tuo: nonne in libro Tuo? &c. cxxxix, 2, 3. Tu cognovisti sedere meum, & resurgere meum, &c. 13. Tu possedisti renes meos. Gen. vi, 5. Et vidit Jehovah, quod multa malitia hominis in terra; & omnis imaginatio cogitationum cordis ejus tantum mala omni die. Adde Psal. xxxiii, 15. xl, 10. lxix, 6. xc, 8. xciv, 11. 1 Reg. viii, 39. Rom. viii, 27. Apoc. ii, 20.
units.tr: Likewise he knows contingent and free things, both good and evil, even the most hidden, and especially the inmost thoughts: Ps. 56:9: You have counted my wanderings; put my tears in your bottle; are they not in your book? etc. Ps. 139:2, 3: You have known my sitting down and my rising up, etc. v. 13: You possessed my reins. Gen. 6:5: And Jehovah saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil every day. Add Ps. 33:15; 40:10; 69:6; 90:8; 94:11; 1 Kings 8:39; Rom. 8:27; Rev. 2:20.

units.la: Ac denique minima: Matth. x, 29, 30. Unus passerculus non cadet super terram, sine Patre vestro: Vestri autem & capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt.
units.tr: And finally the smallest things: Matt. 10:29, 30: Not one sparrow falls to the ground without your Father; but the very hairs of your head are all numbered.

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Deus Abrahamum tentasse, seu explorasse, dicitur; Gen. xii, 1. &c. & descendisse, ut videret, qualia essent hominum opera: Gen. xviii, 2. Resp. Ista accipienda sunt de pleniori, per certa specimina, manifestatione eorum, quae non Deo, sed tum ipsis illis hominibus, tum etiam aliis. in se: sed partim de symbolo aliquo extraordinario, ad gloriam & voluntatem aliquam Dei sic manifestandam; sicut etiam quodammodo fit per omnes res creatas: Rom. 1, 20. sed propius in humanâ Christi natura: unde Joh. XIV, 9. Qui Me vidit, vidit Patrem. Partim de visione prophetica qualicunque: partim etiam de visione illa mentali, seu notitia, quae familiarem gratiae, vel etiam gloriae fruitionem involvit, juxta Matth. XVIII, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 9.
units.tr: Objection 1. Yet God is said to have tested or explored Abraham, Gen. 22:1, etc., and to have come down that he might see what kind of works men did, Gen. 18:21. Answer: these things are to be understood of a fuller manifestation, through certain specimens, of those things which were not hidden from God, but from the men themselves, and also from others. Partly they are to be understood of some extraordinary sign, so that the glory and will of God might be manifested in this way; just as in some measure it happens through all created things, Rom. 1:20; but more closely in the human nature of Christ, whence John 14:9: He who has seen me has seen the Father. Partly they are to be understood of prophetic vision of whatever kind; partly also of that mental vision, or knowledge, which involves a familiar enjoyment of grace or even of glory, according to Matt. 18:10. See above, chap. 1, th. 9.

units.la: XXIII. Ratione Tactus Deo competit Impalpabilitas, & quidem propter suam Simplicitatem: nam
units.tr: XXIII. With respect to touch, God is impalpable, and indeed on account of his simplicity; for

units.la: Tangere, vel tangi, nisi corpus, nulla potest res.
units.tr: no thing can touch or be touched except a body.

units.la: Unde Christus Luc. XXIV, 39. de se resuscitato: Palpate Me; & videte: quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere: cum Joh. IV, 24. Deus est spiritus.
units.tr: Hence Christ, Luke 24:39, speaking of himself after the resurrection: Handle me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having; and John 4:24: God is spirit.

units.la: Obj. Act. XVII, 27. "Ut quaerant Dominum, si forte palpando cum invenirent: Ergo saltem palpari potest." Resp. Istud metaphorice ad mentem pertinet.
units.tr: Objection: Acts 17:27: that they might seek the Lord, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him. Therefore he can at least be touched. Answer: that is said metaphorically, and pertains to the mind.

units.la: XXIV. Respectu artis ἐιχαστικῆς, Deus est Ineffigiabilis. Unde etiam Jef. XL, 18. Cui assimilabitis Deum; & quid similitudinis ornabitis ei? Scil. per Simplicitatem suam Deus lineamentorum, terminationum, & figurationum expers est. Item Deut. IV, 15. "Non vidistis ullam imaginem in die, quā locutus est Jehovah ad vos in Choreb, e medio ignis. Ne forte corrumpamini; & faciatis vobis sculptile, imaginem alicujus similitudinis." Confer Act. XVII, 29. Rom. 1. 22, 23.
units.tr: XXIV. With respect to the eikastic art [εἰκαστική], God is unimaginable. Hence also Isa. 40:18: To whom will you liken God? Or what likeness will you set up for him? That is, through his simplicity God is free of outlines, boundaries and shapes. Likewise Deut. 4:15: You saw no image on the day when Jehovah spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire; lest perhaps you be corrupted and make for yourselves a carved image, the likeness of some form. Compare Acts 17:29; Rom. 1:22, 23.

units.la: Contra hanc veritatem, & disertum secundum Decalogi praeceptum, gravissime peccant Pontificii, practice Anthropomorphitae.
units.tr: Against this truth, and against the plain precept of the Decalogue, the Papists sin most gravely, being in practice Anthropomorphites.

units.la: XXV. Sequitur Infinitas; quae talem ac tantam in Deo perfectionem designat, ut nullos terminos aut fines habeat; sed eos omnes conceptibiles excedat. Haec autem confidetanda est, tum respectu ipsius Essentiae; tum respectu Durationis & Spatii ubicalis; tum denique in ordine ad Intellectum.
units.tr: XXV. Next comes infinity, which designates such and so great a perfection in God that it has no limits or ends, but exceeds all that can be conceived. This must be considered with respect to the essence itself, with respect to duration and local space, and finally in relation to the intellect.

units.la: Respectu Essentiæ, Deus infinitus est modo persectissimo, & quam maximè positivo; ut omnes persectionum modos & gradus, qui in creaturis reperiuntur in Divinâ essentiâ sint eminentèr; omnesque fines conceptibiles ipse excedat actû simplicissimo & sufficientissimo. Hinc Col. 11, 9. Omnis plenitudo Deitatis, Psal. cxlv, 3. - Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Joh. xi, 7, 8, 9. Num investigatione Deum invenies? Num usque ad perfectionem Omnisufficientis (דיש) invenies, &c.
units.tr: With respect to essence, God is infinite in a most perfect and most positive mode, so that all the modes and degrees of perfection which are found in creatures are eminently in the divine essence; and by his most simple and most sufficient act he exceeds all conceivable limits. Hence Col. 2:9: all the fullness of the Godhead; Ps. 145:3: of his greatness there is no searching out. Job 11:7, 8, 9: Can you find God by searching? Can you find the Almighty [שַׁדַּי] to perfection? etc.

units.la: Hæc Infinitas etiam facilè deducitur ex Independenti essentiæ Divinæ sufficientiâ superiùs assertâ th. 14. Qui enim tanquam causa absolute prima & Dominus supremus, reliquis entibus fines suarum perfectionum assignavit; adeò ut nec ulli fines absolute possibiles dici, aut concipi possint, nisi dependenter ab ipso: is omnem imperfectionem, non solum privativam, sed & negativam, excludit; omnemque perfectionem conceptibilem includit eminenter; & omnes limites suâ naturâ excedit.
units.tr: This infinity is also easily deduced from the independent sufficiency of the divine essence asserted above, th. 14. For he who, as the absolutely first cause and supreme Lord, has assigned to the other beings the ends of their perfections, so that no ends can be called or conceived as absolutely possible except dependently on him, excludes every imperfection, not only privative but also negative; and he includes eminently every conceivable perfection, and by his nature exceeds all limits.

units.la: Non intelligitur autem hoc loco Infinitas mathematica, potentialis, aut syncategorematica; sed metaphysica, actualis, & categorematica, quam sic satis explicuimus modo.
units.tr: Yet by infinity in this place is not understood mathematical, potential, or syncategorematic infinity, but metaphysical, actual and categorematic infinity, which we have explained sufficiently in this way.

units.la: Obj. Omnia entia habent essentiam suam certam, distinctam, definitam; ac proindè etiàm Deus. Essentiæ rerum consistunt in indivisibili. Resp. Deus habet essentiam certam, & ab omnibus distinctam, hoc ipso quòd ea infinita sit. Atque illud indivisibile essentiæ Divinæ, intrinsecâ suâ perfectione infinitum est.
units.tr: Objection: all beings have their essence certain, distinct and defined; and so also God. The essences of things consist in what is indivisible. Answer: God has a certain essence, distinct from all others, by the very fact that it is infinite. And that indivisible quality of the divine essence is infinite by its intrinsic perfection.

units.la: Creaturarum distantia à Divinâ perfectione, denominari solet infinita: quia nulla est earum ad hanc affinitas, aut proportio æqualitatis, vel commensurationis: finiti enim ad infinitum nulla est proportio. Interim illa à se invicem distinguuntur propriis suis perfectionibus, càsumque gradibus, vel etiàm speciebus.
units.tr: The distance of creatures from the divine perfection is usually called infinite, because there is no affinity of theirs with it, nor any proportion of equality or commensurability: for there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. Meanwhile they are distinguished from one another by their own perfections, and by their degrees or even their species.

units.la: XXVI. Infinitas Durationis est æternitas stricte dicta
units.tr: XXVI. The infinity of duration is eternity, strictly so called

units.la: ta; quae non tantum principium & finem, sed etiam successionem prioris & posterioris excludit. Unde recte à Boëthio describitur, interminabilis vitæ totâ simul ac perfectâ possessio. Differt autem à Tempore strictè dicto, quod hoc tribuatur solis corporibus: & ab Ævo, quod est spirituum finitorum, principium durationis suæ habentium, atque indè successionem, sed non finem. Illa probatur testimoniis sacris; Gen. xxi, 33. Rom. xvi, 26. ubi αὐτολεξεὶ aeternus appellatur. Adde Isef. lvii, 15. xliv, 6. Ier. x, 10. Rom. i, 20. 1 Tim. i, 17. Apoc. i, 4, 8, 17. xxi, 6, Psal. xc, 2, 4.
units.tr: which excludes not only beginning and end but also any succession of before and after. Hence Boethius rightly describes it as "the whole and perfect possession of unending life all at once." It differs from time, strictly so called, which belongs only to bodies, and from aeviternity, which belongs to finite spirits: these have a beginning of their duration and so a succession, but no end. This is proved from the sacred testimonies: Gen. 21:33; Rom. 16:26, where God is called eternal [αἰώνιος]. Add Isa. 57:15; 44:6; Jer. 10:10; Rom. 1:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; Rev. 1:4, 8, 17; 21:6; Ps. 90:2, 4.

units.la: Eadem patet ex Dei Primitate & Simplicitate. Quæ ut essentiæ, sic etiam existentiæ ac durationis Divinæ principium, omnemque variationem, excludunt; & actum purissimum inferunt; ipsamque adeo æternitatem.
units.tr: The same is evident from God's primacy and simplicity. These exclude any beginning and any variation from the divine existence and duration, just as they do from the divine essence, and they imply a most pure act, and eternity itself.

units.la: Hanc vero Æternitatem carere successione, præsertim probamus; 1. ex Psal. xc, 4. cum 2 Petr. iii, 8. Unus dies apud Dominum, ut mille anni, & mille anni, ut unus dies. Supereminentia igitur durationis Divinæ, temporum differentias & successionem non habet.
units.tr: We prove, in particular, that this eternity lacks succession: (1) from Ps. 90:4 compared with 2 Pet. 3:8, "One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Therefore the supereminence of the divine duration has no differences of times and no succession.

units.la: 2. Ex omnimodâ Dei Immutabilitate, de quâ th. 20. annorum enim, aliorumque temporum successio, & conversio, insignem mutationem infert.
units.tr: (2) From the absolute immutability of God, which we discuss in thesis 20. For the succession of years and other times, and their change, brings a notable alteration.

units.la: 3. Existentia est actus essentiæ; & duratio, existentiæ permanentia, quæ se necessario habet convenienter essentiæ. Consequenter æterna Dei duratio, est ipsa eius essentia; cuius Simplicitas partes, earumque successionem, non admittit.
units.tr: (3) Existence is the act of essence, and duration is the permanence of existence, which necessarily belongs to essence. Consequently God's eternal duration is his very essence, and his simplicity admits no parts, nor any succession of them.

units.la: XXVII. Obj. 1. Anni, dies, præteritum, futurum, &c. tribuuntur Deo in Sacris.
units.tr: XXVII. Objection 1. Years, days, past, future, etc. are attributed to God in the Sacred Writings.

units.la: Resp. Scil. ἀνθρωποπαθῶς; sed intelligenda Θεοπρεπῶς.
units.tr: Answer: these are said anthropopathically [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς], but they must be understood as befitting God [Θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus coexistit temporum nostrorum differentiis, ergo successionem habet: aut cæteroquin nostræ temporum differentiæ sibi invicem coexistent, quia æternitati Divinæ coëxistunt. Resp. Dei duratio manet semper eadem; sed illa coëxistentia ad nostra tempora est inadæquata: nequaquàm ergo propter æternitatis coëxistentiam, nostrum præteritum, præsens, & futurum coincidunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. God coexists with the differences of our times, therefore he has succession; or otherwise our differences of time would coexist with one another, since they coexist with divine eternity. Answer: the duration of God remains always the same; but that coexistence with our times is inadequate. By no means, therefore, do our past, present and future coincide because of the coexistence with eternity.

units.la: Obj.3. Tempus mundi idem est cum æternitate Dei: nam etiam illud principio caret: mundus enim creatus est in tempore; ipsum vero tempus creatum non est, æternum ergo est. Resp. Tempus mundi non est æternum, aut increatum: Deus enim creando res successivas, eådem operâ tempus produxit: unde recte contreatum dicitur.
units.tr: Objection 3. The time of the world is the same as the eternity of God, for it too lacks a beginning: the world was created in time, but time itself was not created, so it is eternal. Answer: the time of the world is neither eternal nor uncreated. For in creating successive things God at the same stroke produced time; hence it is rightly called created.

units.la: XXVIII. Infinitas respectu Spatii, sive ubi; est Immensitas; quâ Deus absolutissimè ubique existit; nec ullos fines habet suæ præsentiæ vel quasi. Deus igitur non est in loco, vel ubi circumscriptive; quæ affectio corporum propria est: nec definitive; quæ spirituum finitorum: sed repletive totus est intra totum mundum, ejusque partes singulas; & totus extra eum, ubi sibi ipsi præsens existit. Atque hoc contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes asserimus.
units.tr: XXVIII. The infinity with respect to space, or to place, is immensity, by which God exists absolutely everywhere, and has no limits to his presence, or anything like limits. God, therefore, is not in a place, or somewhere circumscriptively, which is the property of bodies; nor definitively, which is the mode of finite spirits; but he is wholly within the whole world and each of its parts by filling them, and wholly outside it, where he exists present to himself. We assert this against the Socinians, the Anabaptists, and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Vulgò dicitur; Enter, præsenter, Deus hic, & ubique, potenter. Primò, enter: h. e. Deus in toto mundo præsens existit per essentiam suam infinitam. Deut. IV, 39. Iof. II, 11. Iehovah est in cœlis desuper, & super terram desubter. Ierem. XXIII, 23, 24. Nunquid Deus de propinquo Ego, dixit Jehovah; & non Deus de longinquo? Pfal. CXXXIX, 7, 8, 9, 10. Quò ibo à Spiritu Tuo, & quò à faciebus Tuis fugiam? Si ascendero cœlos, ibi Tu: & stratum fecero infernum, ecce Tu: Assumsero pennas aurorae, habitavero in novissimo maris, etiàm ibi manus Tua ducet me, & tenebit me dextra Tua. Adde Ies. VI, 1. LXVI, 1. Act. VII, 48, 49, 50. XVII, 24, 25, 27, 28.
units.tr: It is commonly said: "Essentially, presently, God is here and everywhere, powerfully." First, essentially: that is, God is present throughout the whole world through his infinite essence. Deut. 4:39; Josh. 2:11: Jehovah is in heaven above and on earth beneath. Jer. 23:23, 24: "Am I a God at hand, saith Jehovah, and not a God afar off?" Ps. 139:7, 8, 9, 10: "Whither shall I go from thy Spirit, or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there; if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." Add Isa. 6:1; 66:1; Acts 7:48, 49, 50; 17:24, 25, 27, 28.

units.la: Secundò; præsenter; h. é. per intimam notitiam & observationem omnium eorum, quæ in illo fiunt. Psal.
units.tr: Second, presently: that is, by intimate knowledge and observation of all that happens in it. Ps.

units.la: xxxiii,13,14,15. E cœlis respexit Iehovah, & vidit omnes filios hominum: considerans omnia opera eorum. Hebr. iv, 13. „Non est creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus: omnia „autem nuda & aperta sunt oculis ejus, ad quem nobis ne„gotium. Psal. cxxxix, 12, 13. Jerem. xxiii, 24.
units.tr: 33:13, 14, 15: Jehovah looks down from heaven and sees all the sons of men, considering all their works. Heb. 4:13: "There is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do." Ps. 139:12, 13; Jer. 23:24.

units.la: Tertiò, potenter; h. e. per potentem operationem: Hebr. 1,3. - Sustinet omnia verbo suo potente: Joh. v, 17. „Pater Meus adhuc operatur, & Ego operor. 1 Cor. xi, 6. Agens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Third, powerfully: that is, by his powerful operation. Heb. 1:3: he sustains all things by his powerful word. John 5:17: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." 1 Cor. 12:6: working all things in all.

units.la: XXIX. Sic ergo Deus hîc & ubique existit. Sed neque spatiis rerum creatarum comprehenditur: aut iis adæquatè coëxistit ipse infinitus: extra mundum in se ipso etiam existit, qui ante mundum conditum extitit similiter. Probatur hoc specialiùs; 1. disertis testimoniis: 1 Reg. viii, 27. „Cœli, & cœli cœlorum non continent Te: quanto minùs domus hæc, quam ædificavi. 2 Chron. ii, 6. „Quis obtinebit potestatem ad ædificandum Ei domum? nam cœli, & cæli cælorum non comprehendent Eum; & quis ego, ut ædificem Ei domum? „Quin imò ad suffitendum ad facies Ejus. Ubi ipsam Dei essentiam designant pronomina Te, Eum, &c. non scientiam, potentiam, aut operationem ab essentiâ diversam; qualis etiàm non datur per Dei Simplicitatem, nedùm existere posset, ubi essentia Divina non existeret. Memoratur domus, non ad habitationem; sed ad suffitum faciendum. Habitationis conceptus, etiàm cœlorum incapacitas, &c. ad essentiam pertinent. Quomodò cæteroquin extra cœlos cœlorum, & sic extra mundum universum, existeret Dei scientia, vel potentia, vel operatio, &c?
units.tr: XXIX. So God exists here and everywhere. But he is not comprehended by the spaces of created things, nor does the infinite God coexist with them adequately. He also exists in himself outside the world, just as he existed in the same way before the world was made. This is proved more particularly: (1) by express testimonies: 1 Kings 8:27: "Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?" 2 Chron. 2:6: "Who shall be able to build him a house, seeing the heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him? And who am I, that I should build him a house, except to burn sacrifice before him?" Here the pronouns "thee" and "him" designate the very essence of God, not knowledge, power, or operation distinct from the essence, which, given the divine simplicity, is not even possible, much less could it exist where the divine essence did not exist. The house is mentioned not for habitation but for burning incense. The concept of habitation, and the incapacity of even the heavens, and so on, belong to the essence. Otherwise, how would the knowledge, or power, or operation of God exist outside the heaven of heavens, and so outside the whole universe?

units.la: 2. Ex infinitâ Dei perfectione: quæ requirit, ut existat in omni spatio conceptibili.
units.tr: (2) From the infinite perfection of God, which requires that he exist in every conceivable space.

units.la: 3. Ex Potentiâ: Deus extra hunc mundum potest operari, similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Ubi autem potest operari, ibi potest existere; imò existit, qui est actus purissimus. 3. Ex Immutabilitate: ante mundum conditum existit Deus in se, modo infinito; non autem definito ad actualia spatia hujus mundi: ergo etiam nunc similiter.
units.tr: (3) From his power: God can operate outside this world, just as he could before the world was made. Where he can operate, there he can exist; indeed he exists, being most pure act. (3) From his immutability: before the world was made God existed in himself in an infinite mode, not one defined by the actual spaces of this world; therefore he exists in the same way now.

units.la: XXX. Observandi autem speciales quidam modi praesentiae Divinae, respectu operationum ac manifestationum:
units.tr: XXX. Certain special modes of the divine presence, with respect to operations and manifestations, are to be observed:

units.la: 1. In humana Christi natura inhabitat Deitas, per unionem hypostaticam: Col. 11, 9. Joh. 1, 14. 1 Tim. 111, 16. Rom. 1, 3, 4. 1X, 5.
units.tr: 1. The Deity dwells in the human nature of Christ by the hypostatic union: Col. 2, 9. John 1, 14. 1 Tim. 3, 16. Rom. 1, 3, 4; 9, 5.

units.la: 2. In Ecclesia universa est Deus, per Spiritum unientem, charismata distribuentem, & salutariter gubernantem, 1 Cor. XII, 11, 12, 13. Joh. XVII, 21. Matth. XXVIII, 20.
units.tr: 2. God is in the whole Church through the Spirit, who unites it, distributes the gifts, and governs it for salvation: 1 Cor. 12, 11, 12, 13. John 17, 21. Matt. 28, 20.

units.la: 3. In singulis Fidelibus, per Spiritum fidei, sanctificationis, adoptionis, consolationis, & corroborationis: Joh. XIV, 23, 16, 17. 2 Cor. IV, 13. Rom. VIII, 1417, 26. Gal. IV, 6, 7. Psal. CXIV, 18.
units.tr: 3. God is in individual believers through the Spirit of faith, of sanctification, of adoption, of consolation and of strengthening: John 14, 23; 16, 17. 2 Cor. 4, 13. Rom. 8, 14–17, 26. Gal. 4, 6, 7. Ps. 114, 1, 8.

units.la: 4. In Prophetis, Spiritu πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως sapientiam ac voluntatem suam revelante: 1 Petr. 1, 11. Hebr. 1, 1.
units.tr: 4. God is in the prophets, the Spirit revealing his wisdom and will "in many portions and in many ways" [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]: 1 Pet. 1, 11. Heb. 1, 1.

units.la: 5. In Caelo, speciali gloriae ac majestatis suae manifestatione: Isai. XLVI, 1. Matth. XVIII, 10. Hebr. XII, 22, 23. Phil. III, 20, 21. Joh. XIV, 2, 3.
units.tr: 5. God is in heaven, by a special manifestation of his glory and majesty: Isa. 46, 1. Matt. 18, 10. Heb. 12, 22, 23. Phil. 3, 20, 21. John 14, 2, 3.

units.la: 6. In Inferno, irae & justitiae suae vindicativae executione: Psal. CXXXIX, 8. Matth. X, 28. 2 Thess. I, 9. Marc. IX, 44, 46.
units.tr: 6. God is in hell, by the execution of his wrath and of his avenging justice: Ps. 139, 8. Matt. 10, 28. 2 Thess. 1, 9. Mark 9, 44, 46.

units.la: XXXI. Obj. 1 Deus in caelis esse dicitur; Matth. VI, 9. & habitare lucem inaccessam; 1 Tim. VI, 16. Resp. 1. in caelis est speciali modo praesentiae gloriosae; talem se ibi demonstrando, non autem existendo ibi tantum, nec alibi. 2. Sed Lux Dei inaccessa, est ipsa ejus gloria & majestas, creaturis incomprehensibilis: sic ipse lux esse dicitur; 1 Joh. 1, 5. Vide ibid. verf. 7. & Psal. CIV, 1, 2. Non vero est locus aliquis, à Deo diversus. Obj. 2. Deus, 1 Reg. XIX, 11, 12, negatur fuisse in vehementi vento, itemque in terrae motu, & in igni; sed in leni aura. Resp. Istud dicitur de extraordinario symbolo specialis cujusdam praesentiae Divinae, pro revelatione Prophetica.
units.tr: XXXI. Objection 1: God is said to be in heaven, Matt. 6, 9, and to dwell in light unapproachable, 1 Tim. 6, 16. Reply: 1. He is in heaven by a special mode of glorious presence, displaying himself there in that way, and not merely existing there, nor elsewhere. 2. But the unapproachable light of God is his very glory and majesty, incomprehensible to creatures; so he is himself called light, 1 John 1, 5; see the same chapter, verse 7, and Ps. 104, 1, 2. It is not, however, some place distinct from God. Objection 2: God, 1 Kings 19, 11, 12, is said not to have been in the strong wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in the gentle breeze. Reply: That is said of an extraordinary sign of a special divine presence, for prophetic revelation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Ipse negavit, se affore immorigeris; Num. xiv, 42. Ergo non est prorsus ubique. Resp. Negavit de speciali modo praesentiae, secundum gratiam & beneficentiam.
units.tr: Obj. 3. He himself denied that he would be present with the stubborn, Num. 14, 42. Therefore he is not altogether everywhere. Resp. He denied it of the special mode of presence, according to grace and beneficence.

units.la: Obj. 4. Absurde statuitur, Deum adesse in locis impuris, interesse actionibus obscoenis, esse in Diabolis, &c. Idcirco mandavit, ut excrementa in castris Israelitarum statim terra obtegerentur; Deut. xxiii, 12, 13, 14. Ergo. Resp. 1. Deus simplicissimus & sanctissimus rerum immundarum praesentia pollui minime potest. In ipso existunt, vivunt, & moventur creaturae qualescunque: Act. xvii, 28, etiam Diaboli, & homines pessimi. Unde caeteroquin eorum efficientia non certe in dependens est a Deo, ejusque Providentia. Nec Judicem suum effugere ullo modo possunt.
units.tr: Obj. 4. It is absurd to hold that God is present in impure places, takes part in obscene actions, is in the devils, etc. For this reason he commanded that the excrement in the camp of the Israelites be at once covered with earth, Deut. 23, 12, 13, 14. Therefore... Resp. 1. God, most simple and most holy, can by no means be defiled by the presence of unclean things. In him all creatures, whatever they are, exist, live and move, Acts 17, 28, including the devils and the most wicked men. Hence their efficiency, otherwise, is certainly not independent of God and his providence. Nor can they in any way escape their Judge. 2. Under that dispensation God willed that ceremonial cleanliness be observed in the camp of the Israelites. Compare Ezek. 4, 12, 13.

units.la: 2. In castris Israelitarum, sub ista oeconomia, voluit Deus observari munditiem cerimonialem. Confer Ezech. iv, 12, 13.
units.tr: 2. In the camp of the Israelites, under that dispensation, God willed that ceremonial cleanliness be observed. Compare Ezek. 4, 12, 13.

units.la: Obj. 5. Absurda est existentia Dei atomica & atopica. Resp. Simplicitas Dei indivisibilitatem infert; & Infinitas localitatem physicam & circumscriptivam excludit. Deus totus, non per partes, coexistit creaturis singulis; sed non adaequatè.
units.tr: Obj. 5. The existence of God is absurd if it is atomic and atopic. Resp. The simplicity of God implies indivisibility, and his infinity excludes physical and circumscriptive locality. God is wholly, not by parts, co-present with each single creature; but not adequately.

units.la: Obj. 6. Mera figmenta sunt Spatia imaginaria extra mundum. Resp. At non dicimus, existere spatia realia, vel actualia, extra mundum: sed Deum existere ibi in se; similiter ut ante mundum conditum. Tertullianus: "Ante omnia Deus erat solus; ipse sibi & mundus, & locus, & omnia. Deus etiam per absolutam suam potentiam operari potest, & creaturas producere; & spatia actuare: ista igitur possibilia sunt, & sic concepibilia, atque imaginaria."
units.tr: Obj. 6. The "imaginary spaces" outside the world are mere fictions. Resp. We do not, however, say that real or actual spaces exist outside the world; but that God exists there in himself, just as he did before the world was made. Tertullian: "Before all things God was alone; he was to himself both world, and place, and all things. God can also operate by his absolute power, and produce creatures, and actualise spaces; these things, therefore, are possible, and so conceivable, and imaginable."

units.la: XXXII. Respectu Intellectus creati Deus est Incomprehensibilis: Psal. cxlv, 3. Magnitudinis ejus non est investigatio. Job.xi,9. Num investigatione Deum invenies? v,9. Rom. xi,33, 34. 1 Tim. vi, 16. Et manifesta est ratio, ex objecti infinitate, & subjecti finiti disproportione ad ipsum.
units.tr: XXXII. With respect to the created intellect God is incomprehensible: Ps. 145, 3. "Of his greatness there is no searching," Job 11, 9. "Canst thou by searching find out God?" Job 5, 9. Rom. 11, 33, 34. 1 Tim. 6, 16. The reason is plain: from the infinity of the object and the disproportion of the finite subject to it.

units.la: Consequenter nulli creaturæ, in quocunque statu, convenit cognitio Dei comprehensiva, & adæquata; imò nequidem ullius attributi Divini: sed solùm apprehensiva, & inadæquata.
units.tr: Consequently, no creature, in any state, has a knowledge of God that is comprehensive and adequate; indeed, not even of any one divine attribute: but only one that is apprehensive and inadequate.

units.la: Obj. 1. Sic omnis nostra cognitio de Deo erit erronea: cognoscemus enim aliter, quam se habet ipsa veritas in Deo. Resp. Imò verè cognoscimus in Deo illas perfectiones, quæ verè & formaliter in ipso sunt; simulque agnoscimus, eas Deo inesse modo perfectiori, quam comprehendere possumus.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Thus all our knowledge of God would be erroneous: for we would know otherwise than the truth itself is in God. Resp. Rather, we truly know in God those perfections which truly and formally are in him; and at the same time we acknowledge that they are in God in a more perfect mode than we can comprehend.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Joh. iii, 2. Videbimus eum, sicuti est: ergò comprehensivè. Resp. Istud intelligendum est tùm de oculari visione humanæ Christi naturæ; tùm de notitiâ essentiæ Divinæ propinquiore, ad beatitudinem nostram ordinatâ; non tamen comprehensivâ.
units.tr: Obj. 2. 1 John 3, 2: "We shall see him as he is"; therefore comprehensively. Resp. That must be understood both of the bodily vision of the human nature of Christ, and of the closer knowledge of the divine essence, ordered to our blessedness; yet not comprehensive.

units.la: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. xiii, 12. Cognoscemus Deum, ut ab ipso cogniti sumus: Atqui nos à Deo cogniti sumus comprehensivè: ergò, &c. Resp. Illud non est accipiendum de convenientiâ adæquatâ; sed de similitudine quâdam analogicâ. Confer Rom. viii, 29. Psal. i, 6.
units.tr: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. 13, 12: "We shall know God, as we are known by him." But we are known by God comprehensively; therefore, etc. Resp. That is not to be taken of an adequate agreement, but of a certain analogical likeness. Compare Rom. 8, 29; Ps. 1, 6.

units.la: XXXIII. Succedunt Attributa vitæ, sive secundi ge- neris; quæ etiam communicabilia appellari solent; re- spectû communicationis alicujus analogicæ. Vita Dei consideratur, vel ut simpliciter actuosa; vel secundum e- minentiam: priori consideratione occurrunt Intellectus, Voluntas, & Potentia; Posteriori autem, Potestas, Gloria, & Beatitudo. XXXIV. Intellectus Dei est, quo ipse omnes omni- no veritates cognoscit modo sibi convenienti: h. e. infinitè, simpliciter, & independenter. 1 Tim. i, 17.
units.tr: XXXIII. Next come the attributes of life, or of the second kind, which are also commonly called communicable, because they bear some analogical communication with creatures. The life of God is considered either as simply active, or in eminence. Under the first consideration come the Intellect, the Will, and the Power; under the second, the Authority, the Glory, and the Blessedness. XXXIV. The intellect of God is that by which he knows all truths of every kind in a manner fitting to himself, that is, infinitely, simply, and independently. 1 Tim. 1:17.

units.la: Soli sapienti - 1Sam. 11, 3. Deus scientiarum. Psal. xcIV, 9, 10. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
