units.tr: To the only wise – 1 Sam. 11:3. God of knowledges. Ps. 94:9, 10. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Dico infinite: ipse enim Intellectus Dei infinitus est; cum 1. secundùm rem sit ipsa Dei essentia. 2. & modus intelligendi, convenienter naturæ Divinæ, absolutè perfectissimus sit; adeoque infinitus, atque item 3. respectù objectorum, cognoscat pmnia absolutè cognoscibilia. 1 Joh. 111, 20. Novit omnia. Similiter Joh. XXI, 17. Item Psal. cxlvii, 5. Jes. lv, 9. Rom. xi, 33.
units.tr: I say infinitely, for the intellect of God is itself infinite, since (1) its substance is the very essence of God; (2) its mode of understanding, being in agreement with the divine nature, is absolutely most perfect and therefore infinite; and likewise (3) with respect to its objects, it knows all things that are absolutely knowable. 1 John 3:20, He knows all things. Similarly John 21:17. Also Ps. 147:5; Isa. 55:9; Rom. 11:33.

units.la: Novit autem seipsum adæquatè: Matth. xi, 27.
units.tr: He knows himself adequately: Matt. 11:27.

units.la: 1 Cor. 11, 10, 11. Vide sup. cap. 1. th. 3.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. See above, chap. 1, th. 3.

units.la: Et omnia alia à se perfectissimè: Hebr. iv, 13. Omnia sunt nuda, & intimè patentia oculis ejus. Act. xv, 18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) æv o omnia opera sua.
units.tr: And he knows all other things most perfectly: Heb. 4:13, All things are naked and open to his eyes. Acts 15:18, All his works are known to God from the beginning [ἀπ' αἰῶνος].

units.la: XXXV. Scientia Dei ratione objectorum distingui- tur, in naturalem, necessariam, sive simplicis intelligentiæ, & in liberam, sive visionis.
units.tr: XXXV. The knowledge of God is distinguished by its objects into natural, necessary, or of simple intelligence, and free, or of vision.

units.la: Scientia simplicis intelligentiæ rerum quidditates simpliciter spectat, ut se habent citra respectum ad liberam Decreti Divini terminationem: sive in signo rationis antecedenter ad Decretum, quò pertinet ipsa Dei essentia, personæ, sufficientia, & omnipotentia, atque hinc res possibiles.
units.tr: The knowledge of simple intelligence regards the essences of things simply, as they stand apart from the free determination of the divine decree; that is, in the order of reason prior to the decree, to which belong the essence of God itself, his persons, his sufficiency, and his omnipotence, and from these the possible things.

units.la: In mente Divinâ igitur sunt ideæ omnium possibilium. Istæ autem ideæ sunt perfectiones ipsius essentiæ Divinæ, prout imitabiles & expressibiles sunt extra Deum, & sic ab ipso cognoscuntur. A supereminenti enim & infinitâ potentiâ Dei actiVâ, denominantur res possibiles; quatenùs videlicet per illam produci, aut actuari, possunt.
units.tr: Therefore in the divine mind there are the ideas of all possible things. These ideas are the perfections of the divine essence itself, insofar as they are capable of being imitated and expressed outside God, and so are known by him. From the supereminent and infinite active power of God they are called possible things, inasmuch as they can be produced or brought into act by that power.

units.la: Scientia libera consideratur, ut in signo rationis consequens ad liberum Dei Decretum. Visionis autem appellatur; quia Deus per eam videt, aut prævidet, determinatam rerum existentiam sub qualicunque temporis differentiâ.
units.tr: Free knowledge is considered as following, in the order of reason, upon God's free decree. It is called of vision, because by it God sees, or foresees, the determinate existence of things under whatever difference of time.

units.la: Quæritur, Utrùm Deus res præsciat, quia futuræ sunt; an vero futurae sint, quia Deus eas praescit? Resp. Affirmandum potius est prius: veritas enim rei, quae est per Dei Decretum, natura praecedit veritatem cognitionis. Attamen si adeo late sumatur Praescientia, ut ipsum Dei Decretum complexu suo involvat; ut Rom. viii, 29. xi, 2. dicendum erit posterius: & hoc sensu Praescientia Dei recte dicitur practica. Ceteroquin in ista enunciatione, Haec res futura est, quia Deus eam praescit, agnoscenda saltem est illatio Logica, a posteriori.
units.tr: The question is whether God foreknows things because they are going to be future, or whether they are going to be future because God foreknows them. Answer: the former must rather be affirmed, for the truth of a thing, which exists by the decree of God, precedes in nature the truth of the knowledge of it. Nevertheless, if foreknowledge is taken so broadly that it includes within itself the decree of God as a whole (as in Rom. 8:29; 11:2), the latter must be said; and in this sense the foreknowledge of God is rightly called practical. Otherwise, in this proposition, This thing is going to be future, because God foreknows it, at least the inference must be recognised as logical, from the effect to the cause.

units.la: XXXVI. Hac igitur Scientia visionis Deus omnia & singula per suum Decretum definita novit accuratissime: utpote naturalia, & necessaria: Psal. cxlvii, 4, 8, &c. Numerans numerum stellarum: omnibus eis nomina vocabit. &c. cxxxix, 15, 16. Non occultum fuit corpus meum a Te, quando factus fui in occulto, &c.
units.tr: XXXVI. By this knowledge of vision, therefore, God knows all things and each thing, defined by his decree, most exactly: namely natural and necessary things. Ps. 147:4, 8, etc. He counts the number of the stars; he calls them all by their names. etc. Ps. 139:15, 16, My body was not hidden from you when I was made in secret, etc.

units.la: Atque item contingentia, & libera, tum bona, tum mala; etiam occultissima, & nominatim cogitationes intimas: Psal. lvi, 9. Motionem meam numerasti: Tu pone lachrymam meam in utre Tuo: nonne in libro Tuo? &c. cxxxix, 2, 3. Tu cognovisti sedere meum, et resurgere meum, &c. 13. Tu possedisti renes meos. Gen. vi, 5. Et vidit Jehovah, quod multa malitia hominis in terra, & omnis imaginatio cogitationum cordis ejus tantum mala omni die. Adde Psal. xxxiii, 15. xl, 10. lxix, 6. xc; 8. xciv, 11. 1 Reg. viii, 39. Rom. viii, 27. Apoc. ii, 20.
units.tr: Likewise also contingent and free things, both good and evil; even the most hidden, and especially inward thoughts. Ps. 56:9, You have counted my wanderings; put my tears into your bottle; are they not in your book? etc. Ps. 139:2, 3, You have known my sitting down and my rising up, etc. (v. 13), You have possessed my reins. Gen. 6:5, And the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. Add Ps. 33:15; 40:10; 69:6; 90:8; 94:11; 1 Kings 8:39; Rom. 8:27; Rev. 2:20.

units.la: Ac denique minima: Matth. x, 29, 30. Unus passerculus non cadet super terram, sine Patre vestro: Vestri autem & capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt.
units.tr: And finally the smallest things: Matt. 10:29, 30. Not one sparrow falls to the ground without your Father; but the very hairs of your head are all numbered.

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Deus Abrahamum tentasse, seu explorasse, dicitur; Gen. xii, 1. &c. & descendisse, ut videret, qualia essent hominum opera: Gen. xviii,
units.tr: Objection 1. God is said to have tempted, or tested, Abraham, Gen. 12:1, etc., and to have gone down, that he might see what the works of men were like: Gen. 18:

units.la: 2. Resp. Ista accipienda sunt de pleniori, per certa specimina, manifestatione eorum, quae non Deo, sed tum ipsis illis hominibus, tum etiam aliis minùs erant manifesta. Confer Joh. II, 24, 25.
units.tr: 2. Answer: These things must be understood of a fuller manifestation, by certain clear proofs, of things which were not unknown to God, but were less evident to those very men and also to others. Compare John 2:24, 25.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deus non novit malos: Matth. VII, 23. XXV, 13. Resp. Scil. de notitia approbationis, aut specialis dilectionis; de quâ vide Psal. 1, 6. 2 Tim. II. 19.
units.tr: Objection 1. God does not know the wicked: Matt. 7:23; 25:13. Answer. Namely, of the knowledge of approval, or of special love; on which see Ps. 1:6; 2 Tim. 2:19.

units.la: XXXVII. Contingentia & libera Deus non solum scit, cùm ea sunt præsentia, & præterita; sed etiam præ- scit futura.
units.tr: XXXVII. God knows not only contingent and free things when they are present and past, but also foreknows them as future.

units.la: Atque hoc contra Socinianos adstruimus:
units.tr: This we maintain against the Socinians, as follows.

units.la: 1. Ex eo quòd Deus omnia cognoscat; 1 Joh. III, 20, & specialiùs, ex Psal. CXXXIX, 2. 4. Intellexisti cogitationem meam à longè: Non est sermo in linguâ meâ: ecce Jehovah, Tu nosti ipsum totum.
units.tr: 1. From the fact that God knows all things: 1 John 3:20; and more specifically from Psalm 139:2, 4: "You have understood my thought from afar. There is no speech on my tongue; behold, O Jehovah, You know it all."

units.la: 2. Futura contingentia habent determinatam veritatem suæ futuritionis per Dei Decretum; consequenter Deo nota sunt per Scientiam visionis. Act. XV, 18. Vide sup. th. 34. cum Eph. I, 11. Omnia operatur secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Act. II, 23. IV, 28.
units.tr: 2. Future contingent things have a determinate truth of their future occurrence through God's decree; consequently they are known to God by the knowledge of vision. Acts 15:18; see above, thesis 34, together with Ephesians 1:11: "He works all things according to the counsel of His will." Acts 2:23; 4:28.

units.la: 3. Ex prophetiis, earumque complemento: Unde Tertullianus adversus Marc. lib. 2. cap. 4. De præscientia verò quid dicam? quæ tantos habet testes, quantos fecit Prophetas. Jes. XLVI, 9, 10, 11. ,,Recordamini priorum à sæculo: quoniam Ego Deus &c. Annuncians ab exordio novissimam, & à quondam, quæ non facta sunt: ,,dicens; Consilium meum stabit, &c. Vocans ab Oriente Volucrem, de terrâ longinquâ virum consilii mei: etiam locutus sum; etiam adducam illud. Vide speciatim quæ Abrahamo prædicta: Gen. XV, 13. -16, XVIII, 18, 19. quæ Jacob nepotibus & filiis suis prænunciavit, Gen. XLVIII, 19, -XLIX, 1. -& Moses Israëlitis; Deut. XXXI, 16, 20. XXXII, 1. -Insignis est prædictio Prophetæ illius Judæi de Altari Bethelis: 1 Reg. XIII, 2, 3. quæ impleta: 2 Reg. XXIII, 16, 17, 18. Achabo & familiæ ejus accuratè prædictum fuit excidium, 1 Reg. XXI, 19, -XXII, 17, -28. complementum sequitur ibidem, verf. 30, -38. & 2 Reg. IX, 24. -X, 7, -11. Adde plurima illustria in Daniele, & reliquis Prophetis, de Regnorum translationibus, eversionibus, &c. ac potissimum
units.tr: 3. From prophecies and their fulfilment. Whence Tertullian, against Marcion, book 2, chapter 4: "What shall I say of foreknowledge? It has as many witnesses as it has made prophets." Isaiah 46:9, 10, 11: "Remember the former things of old, for I am God, etc. Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done; saying, My counsel shall stand, etc. Calling a bird from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country: yes, I have spoken it, and I will also bring it to pass." Consider in particular what was foretold to Abraham, Genesis 15:13–16 and 18:18, 19; what Jacob foretold to his sons and grandsons, Genesis 48:19; 49:1ff.; and what Moses foretold to the Israelites, Deuteronomy 31:16, 20; 32:1ff. Remarkable is the prediction of that Jewish prophet concerning the altar at Bethel, 1 Kings 13:2, 3, which was fulfilled in 2 Kings 23:16, 17, 18. The destruction of Ahab and his family was foretold with precision, 1 Kings 21:19; 22:17, 28; the fulfilment follows in the same place, verse 30, 38, and in 2 Kings 9:24; 10:7–11. Add the many illustrious predictions in Daniel and the other Prophets concerning the transfers and overthrows of kingdoms, etc., and especially

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: tissimum de Christi natiuitate, vitâ, passionibus, morte, &c.
units.tr: especially concerning Christ's nativity, life, sufferings, death, etc.

units.la: 4. De ique, ex Dei Immutabilitate, Æternitate, & Primitate, evidens est, ipsum non minus obiectorum scibilium, quamdiu futura sunt, habere notitiam, quàm cum eadem sunt præsentia,
units.tr: 4. Hence it is evident, from God's immutability, eternity and priority, that he has no less knowledge of knowable objects while they are still future than when they are present.

units.la: XXXVIII. Obj. 1. Quæ certò præsciuntur, habent veritatem determinatam: futura igitur contingentia & libera non certo præsciuntur. Resp. Futurorum contingentium & liberorum veritas determinata est extrinsecè à parte Dei; non autem intrinsecè ex natura rei.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Objection 1. What is foreknown with certainty has a determinate truth. Therefore future contingent and free things are not foreknown with certainty. Answer: The truth of future contingent and free things is determined extrinsically on God's side, but not intrinsically from the nature of the thing.

units.la: Obj. 2. Contingentiæ & libertati repugnat omnis necessitas. Resp. Verum est antecedens de necessitate intrinsecâ, absolutâ, consequentis; non vero de extrinsecâ, hypothetica, consequentiæ.
units.tr: Objection 2. Every necessity is incompatible with contingency and liberty. Answer: The antecedent is true of intrinsic and absolute necessity, which follows the consequent; it is not true of extrinsic, hypothetical necessity, which follows from the consequence.

units.la: XXXIX. Præscientia igitur Dei non est con estingentialis, aut conditionata, sed certa & absoluta. Neque admittendum Jesuiticum δῶρον, à Remonstrantibus etiam adoptatum, de Scientia in Deo Media; quâ Deus fingitur, ante omnem actum voluntatis suæ, præuidisse, quid creatura rationalis, in his vel illis rerum circumstantiis posita, pro innatâ sua libertate, esset actura; sic tamen, ut illa posset, si vellet, facere oppositum.
units.tr: XXXIX. Therefore God's foreknowledge is not contingential or conditional, but certain and absolute. Nor is the Jesuit "gift" [δῶρον] to be admitted, also adopted by the Remonstrants, of a so-called middle knowledge in God, by which God is imagined, before any act of his will, to have foreseen what a rational creature, placed in these or those circumstances, would do by its innate freedom, yet in such a way that it could, if it chose, do the opposite.

units.la: Verum 1. S. Scriptura causis secundis in se consideratis, circa actum voluntatis Divinæ derogat actuum liberorum determinationem. Jerem. x. 23. Novi Jehovah, quod non est hominis via ejus; nec viri ambulantis, vel præparare gressum suum. Adde Rom. xi, 35. 1 Cor. iv, 7. 2 Cor. iii, 5.
units.tr: But first, Holy Scripture, considering secondary causes in themselves, detracts from the determination of free acts in relation to the act of the divine will. Jer. 10:23. I know, O Jehovah, that the way of man is not his own; nor is it for a man who walks to direct his own steps. Add Rom. 11:35; 1 Cor. 4:7; 2 Cor. 3:5.

units.la: 2. Determinatio ista Deo, ut causæ primæ, adscribitur. Jes. xlvi. 10. "Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam. Prov. xvi, 9. "Cor hominis cogitabit viam suam, & Jehovah parabit gressum ejus. xxi, 1. "Ut rivuli aquarum, cor Regis in manu Jehovæ: super omne, quod volucrit, inclinabit illud. Adde
units.tr: Second, this determination is ascribed to God as first cause. Isa. 46:10: "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure." Prov. 16:9: "A man's heart devises his way, but Jehovah directs his steps." 21:1: "The king's heart is in the hand of Jehovah, like the watercourses; he turns it wherever he wills." Add

units.la: Rom. XI, 36. 1 Cor. IV, 7. Eph. I, 11. Phil. II. 12. Iac. IV. 14.

3. Creaturæ, ante omnem actum voluntatis Divinæ consideratæ, sunt mere possibiles; ac proindè tales etiàm earum affectiones; sed nulla earum determinatio, aut certa futuritio: affectiones enim non possunt excedere conditionem subjecti sui.
units.tr: Third, creatures considered before any act of the divine will are merely possible, and so their affections are merely possible too; but none of them has a determination or a certain futurition, for affections cannot exceed the condition of their subject.

units.la: 4. Dùm sic statuitur, ante omnem actum voluntatis Divinæ, ejusmodi rerum necessitas, ex possibili tantùm circumstantiarum concursu, & voluntate creaturæ possibilis, cui ipse Deus etiàm sit obnoxius; verè introducitur fatuissimum fatum.
units.tr: Fourth, while it is laid down that, before any act of the divine will, things of this kind have a necessity arising only from a possible concurrence of circumstances and the possible will of the creature, to which God himself would also be subject, a most foolish fate is truly introduced.

units.la: XL. Obj. 1. Istâ ratione tollitur in creaturis ratio- nalibus liberum arbitrium. Resp. Arbitrium creatum non est concipiendum, nisi perpetuò à causâ primâ dependens.
units.tr: XL. Objection 1. By this reasoning free will is removed from rational creatures. Answer: a created will is not to be conceived except as continually dependent on the first cause.

units.la: Obj. 2. Contradicentium pars altera semper vera est, altera falsa, etiam ante omnem actum voluntatis Divinæ. Ergo. Resp. Imò neutra pars potest dici verè futura, nisi per Decretum Dei.
units.tr: Objection 2. Of two contradictory propositions one is always true and the other false, even before any act of the divine will. Therefore... Answer: Indeed neither part can be said truly to be future except through the decree of God.

units.la: Obj. 3. Deus scivit, & dixit, Kehilitas tradituros Sauli Davidem, 1 Sam. XXIII, 12, non ex Decreto; aliter enim evenit, ac proinde ista non fuit Scientia visionis, Deus tamen de futuritione quâdam locutus est: ergo nec scientia Simplicis intelligentiæ fuit: consequenter media. Resp. Scivit & dixit, juxtà Decretum: decreverat autem, ut talis foret animus Kehilitarum circa Saulem & Davidem: sic ista traditio virtualiter erat futura. Interim etiam aliis mediis saluti Davidis prospectum voluit, quod ex eventu patet.
units.tr: Objection 3. God knew and said that the men of Keilah would hand Saul over to David (1 Sam. 23:12), not by decree; for it turned out otherwise, and so this was not knowledge of vision. Yet God spoke of a certain future event; therefore it was not even knowledge of simple intelligence, and consequently not middle knowledge. Answer: He knew and spoke according to his decree; he had decreed, however, what the disposition of the Keilites toward Saul and David would be, and so that betrayal was virtually going to happen. Meanwhile, by other means too he wished to provide for David's safety, as the outcome makes clear.

units.la: Obj. 4. Tyrii & Sidonii dicuntur pœnitentiam acturi fuisse, si vidissent miracula Christi; Matth. XI, 21. Istud autem pertinet ad Scientiam mediam. Resp. Animus Tyriorum & Sidoniorum minùs erat obstinatus; quin imò, juxta Decretum Dei, dispositus ad agendam pœnitentiam in sacco & cinere, si modota-
units.tr: Objection 4. The Tyrians and Sidonians are said to have repented, had they seen the miracles of Christ (Matt. 11:21). But this pertains to middle knowledge. Answer: The mind of the Tyrians and Sidonians was less obstinate; indeed, according to the decree of God, they were disposed to repent in sackcloth and ashes, if only...

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: lis causa procatarctica accessisset. Sic etiam poenitentia illa virtualiter erat futura; atque adeo pertinebat ad Scientiam visionis.
units.tr: had such a preparatory cause been added. In this way that repentance too would have come about virtually, and so it belongs to the knowledge of vision.

units.la: XLI. Intellectum Dei quoque simplicissimum dicimus: sicut Boëthius: Uno mentis cernit in ictu, Quae sint, quae fuerint, veniantque. Unde non est in Deo distinctio inter facultatem intelligendi, habitum scientiae aut sapientiae, & actum secundum.
units.tr: XLI. We also call God's understanding most simple, as Boethius does: In one glance of the mind he sees what things are, what have been, and what are to come. Hence in God there is no distinction between the faculty of understanding, the habit of knowledge or wisdom, and the second act.

units.la: Nec admittendus discursus, aut à notioribus ad ignotiora processus, neque item compositio, & divisio: nec formalis abstractio & praecisio universalium à singularibus.
units.tr: Nor is discursus to be admitted, or processus from better-known to less-known things, nor likewise composition and division, nor the formal abstraction and precision of universals from singulars.

units.la: Consequenter immutabilis quoque & infallibilis est haec Dei Scientia, etiam de creaturis contingentibus. Nam 1. Actus purissimus omnem potentiam perfectibilem excludit.
units.tr: Consequently this knowledge of God is also unchangeable and infallible, even concerning contingent creatures. For (1) a purest act excludes every perfectible potency.

units.la: 2. Perfectissima intelligendi facultas simul & semel omnia comprehendit.
units.tr: (2) The most perfect faculty of understanding comprehends all things at once and in a single moment.

units.la: 3. Dei intellectus est ipse Deus.
units.tr: (3) God's understanding is God himself.

units.la: 4. Totam suam essentiam unico actu cognoscit; in quâ etiam sunt omnia alia virtualiter & eminenter.
units.tr: (4) He knows his whole essence by one single act, in which all other things also exist virtually and eminently.

units.la: XLII. Intellectus Dei quoque independens est: quapropter Deus cognoscit per essentiam suam; non per species intelligibiles.
units.tr: XLII. God's understanding is also independent; therefore God knows through his essence, not through intelligible species.

units.la: Nam 1. Deus in agendo est prorsus independens.
units.tr: For (1) God is wholly independent in acting.

units.la: 2. Scientia Dei aeterna est; sed nihil aeternum praeter ipsum Deum.
units.tr: (2) God's knowledge is eternal; but nothing is eternal except God himself.

units.la: 3. In Deo nullum est accidens, ut substantia alia ab ipsius naturâ.
units.tr: (3) In God there is no accident, as a substance distinct from his nature.

units.la: 4. Ipsa Dei essentia est idea expressiva omnium persectionum: sed nulla est idea aliunde impressa menti Divinae.
units.tr: (4) The very essence of God is the expressive idea of all perfections; but no idea is impressed on the divine mind from elsewhere.

units.la: Ex quo fonte etiam sponte ruunt errores de fide & meritis praevisis, Scientiâ media, &c.
units.tr: From this same source errors about faith and foreseen merits, middle knowledge, and so on, readily collapse.

units.la: XLIII. Sequitur Voluntas Dei; perfectio, quâ Deus vult & amat se, ac sibi consentaneum, repugnantium vero aversatur; Jef.xlvi, re. - Omnem voluntatem meam faciam. Matth. vi, 10. Fiat voluntas tua. Rom. ix. 19. Voluntati ejus quis obstitit?
units.tr: XLIII. There follows the Will of God: a perfection by which God wills and loves himself and what is consonant with himself, and turns away from what is opposed to him. Isa. xlvi, 10: "I will do all my pleasure." Matt. vi, 10: "Thy will be done." Rom. ix, 19: "Who has resisted his will?"

units.la: Objectum Voluntatis generatim est Bonum cognitum: Divinae Voluntatis, bonum Divinum cognitum; ipse Deus, & alia in ordine ad Deum quatenus talia. Ipse bonus est independenter & infinite; atque ita solus: Matth. xix, 17. Talem ipse se cognoscit perfectissime; atque etiam amat perfectissime, qui est ipsa charitas: 1 Joh. iv, 8. Hinc Joh. iii. 35, xv, 20. Pater diligit Filium: Alia bonitatem habent a Deo communicatam & limitatam: Joh. i, 17. 1 Cor. iv. 7. Rom. xi, 35, 36. Ea autem vult in ordine ad se: Prov. xvi, 4. Omnia operatur Jehovah propter se ipsum: Rom. xi, 36. In ipsum sunt omnia. 1 Cor. x, 31. Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Contraria vero aversatur: Hab. i, 13. Puriores oculis, quam ut aspicias malum, Pfal. v, 5, 6, 7. "Non es Deus fortis, qui delectetur improbitate: non est commoraturum apud Te malum. Non consistunt insani e regione oculorum Tuorum. Odisti omnes, qui operam dant iniquitati," &c. xviii, 26, 27.
units.tr: The object of the will in general is the known good; the object of the divine will is the known divine good: God himself, and other things in relation to God as such. He is good independently and infinitely, and so alone: Matt. xix, 17. He knows himself in this way most perfectly, and he loves himself most perfectly, for he is charity itself: 1 John iv, 8. Hence John iii, 35; xv, 20: "The Father loves the Son." Other things have goodness communicated and limited by God: John i, 17; 1 Cor. iv, 7; Rom. xi, 35, 36. He wills these in relation to himself: Prov. xvi, 4: "Jehovah has made all things for himself." Rom. xi, 36: "From him, through him, and to him are all things." 1 Cor. x, 31: "Do all things to the glory of God." But he turns away from contrary things: Hab. i, 13: "You are of purer eyes than to behold evil." Ps. v, 5-7: "You are not a God who takes pleasure in wickedness; evil shall not dwell with you. The foolish shall not stand before your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity," etc. Ps. xviii, 26, 27.

units.la: Atque haec est ipsa Sanctitas Jehovae: Lev. xix, 2. "Sancti estote: quia Sanctus sum Ego, Jehovah Deus vester." Jef. vi. 2, 3. 1 Sam. ii, 2. Apoc. xv, 3, 4. Eadem Rectitudo appellatur: itemque Justitia, acceptione universali. Deut. xxxii, 4: "Rupis illius opus est perfectum; omnes enim viae illius sunt Jus: Deus fortis fidelis, & expers iniquitatis, justus & rectus est," Pfal. xi, 7. "Confer 1 Joh. i, 5. ii, 29.
units.tr: And this is the very holiness of Jehovah: Lev. xix, 2: "Be holy, for I, Jehovah your God, am holy." Isa. vi, 2, 3; 1 Sam. ii, 2; Rev. xv, 3, 4. The same is called rectitude, and likewise justice in the universal sense. Deut. xxxii, 4: "His work is perfect, for all his ways are just; a faithful God, without iniquity, just and right is he." Ps. xi, 7. Compare 1 John i, 5; ii, 29.

units.la: XLIV. Dum autem Deus in sua Sufficientia & Omnipotentia cognoscit etiam Possibilia, circa haec quoque versatur ipsius Voluntas; scil. ut objectum praejacens. Aliis ergo relictis in abysso suae Omnipotentiae, & in statu merae Possibilitatis: satis multa & varia, aeterno Voluntatis suae actu constituit ad statum Existentiae in tempore promovere, & idque ad Gloriam suam. Atque hoc appellamus Objectum terminans, vel terminatum, Voluntatis Divinæ ad extra ; prout hoc summum bonum summopere est communicativum sui ad extra, tum in genere entis, tum in genere moris: Psal. XXXIII, 5. Amat justitiam & judicium ; Benignitate Jehovæ plena est terra, CLXV, 7, 9-10, 17.
units.tr: XLIV. While God, in his sufficiency and omnipotence, also knows possibles, his will is concerned with these too, namely as a lying-before object. Leaving the rest, therefore, in the abyss of his omnipotence and in the state of mere possibility, he has by one eternal act of his will determined a sufficient and varied multitude of things to advance to the state of existence in time, and this for his own glory. We call this the terminating object, or the terminated object, of the divine will toward what is outside him, since this supreme good is greatly communicative of itself outwardly, both in the kind of being and in the kind of morals: Ps. xxxiii, 5: "He loves righteousness and judgment"; "the earth is full of the goodness of Jehovah," Ps. cxlv, 7, 9-10, 17.

units.la: In genere entis communicat Deus bonitatem suam, creaturas extra se faciendo, iisque benefaciendo realiter, per creationem & providentiam realem : atque hic præcipue occurrunt Amor, Gratia, Misericordia & Tolerantia.
units.tr: In the kind of being, God communicates his goodness by making creatures outside himself and by really doing them good through creation and real providence; and here especially love, grace, mercy and forbearance come to the fore.

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Amor Dei est Voluntas creaturis benefaciendi, & approbandi cum complacentia, quæ in iis bona sunt. Appellatur etiam Benignitas, vel Beneficentia. Spectatur autem vel intrinsecè in ipso Deo : & sic simplicissime semper idem est : vel extrinsecè, respectu efsectorum in creaturis ; & sic valde dissimilis & inæqualis est.
units.tr: The love of God is the will to do good to creatures and, with complacency, to approve what is good in them. It is also called kindness or beneficence. It is viewed either intrinsically in God himself, and so it is always most simply the same, or extrinsically, with respect to its effects in creatures, and so it is very varied and unequal.

units.la: Omnes quidem creaturas Deus quodammodo amat : Matth. v. 44, 45. Act. xiv, 16, 17. xvii, 25. speciali tamen modo hic amor se exercit erga electos & fideles in Christo : Joh. xvii, 21, 22. 1 Joh. i, 3. Estque vel Benevolentiæ, vel Complacentiæ.
units.tr: God indeed loves all creatures in a certain way: Matt. 5:44, 45; Acts 14:16, 17; 17:25. Yet this love shows itself in a special way towards the elect and the faithful in Christ: John 17:21, 22; 1 John 1:3. And it is either of benevolence or of complacency.

units.la: Amor benevolentiæ est, quo Deus electis vult benefacere, priusquam in ipsis sint ulla moraliter bona : Joh. iii, 16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium illum suum unigenitum dedit ; ut quisquis credat in eum, non perent, &c. Rom. v, 8. 1 Joh. iii, 1. Estque tum ordinativus, in decreto ; tum collativus, in executione.
units.tr: The love of benevolence is that by which God wills to do good to the elect before there is anything morally good in them: John 3:16, "God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish," etc.; Rom. 5:8; 1 John 3:1. It is both ordaining, in the decree, and conferring, in its execution.

units.la: Amor complacentiæ est, quo Deus opus suum in electis approbat. Hebr. xi, 6, 6. "Priusquam transferretur, testimonium obtinuerat, quod gratus fuerit Deo." Joh. xiv, 21. xvi, 26, 27.
units.tr: The love of complacency is that by which God approves his work in the elect. Heb. 11:5, 6: "Before he was taken up, he had the testimony that he pleased God." John 14:21; 16:26, 27.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Gratia hoc ab Amore differt, quod in objectis meritum, propriamve operum dignitatem, excludat : Rom. xi, 6. "Quod si per gratiam, non jam ex operibus;" peribus: alioquin gratia jam non est gratia. Confer Rom. iv, 5, 6; Eph. ii, 7, 8, 9. &c.
units.tr: Grace differs from love in that it excludes merit and the worth of one's own works in its objects: Rom. 11:6, "But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace." Compare Rom. 4:5, 6; Eph. 2:7, 8, 9, etc.

units.la: Gratia gratis dans, proprie in ipso Deo est. Sed ejus effecta in nobis recipiuntur varia: unde diserte, 1 Pet. iv, 10. varia Dei gratia: metonymice scil. nomen istud laxe sumtum, ad bona Naturæ etiam extendi poteft: sed usus obtinuit, ut Gratia speciali significatu contradistinguatur a Natura. Huc pertinent primò dona salutaria in Christo; ut fides, spes, charitas, &c. Qui vero ea accipiunt, ipsi Deo placent, sive grati & accepti sunt in Christo, & dona illa in ipsis; unde Gratia gratum faciens appellatur. Eph. i, 6: „Ad laudem „gloriosæ suæ gratiæ, quâ nos gratis acceptos fecit in illo Dilecto“. Sic Apostoli passim Ecclesiis gratiam precantur, eique pacem frequenter adjungunt.
units.tr: Grace that gives freely, strictly speaking, is in God himself. But its effects in us are various, whence 1 Pet. 4:10 expressly speaks of the manifold grace of God. By a metonymy, this name taken loosely can also be extended to the good gifts of nature; but usage has prevailed that grace, in a special sense, be distinguished from nature. To this belong, first, the saving gifts in Christ, such as faith, hope, love, etc. Those who receive them are pleasing to God himself, that is, they are made gracious and accepted in Christ, and those gifts are in them; hence it is called grace making one pleasing. Eph. 1:6: "To the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he made us accepted in the Beloved." So the Apostles everywhere pray for grace for the churches, and frequently add peace to it.

units.la: Verùm insuper sunt charismata quædam ad Christum & Evangelium quoque spectantia; sed cum salute æterna individuum nexum non habentia: ut gratia illuminans, & generatim persuadens, fides miraculorum, donum prophetiæ, &c. quæ quidem ex vero appellari solet gratia gratis data; sed hominum ea prædicatum per se non facit Deo gratum & acceptum in Christo. Vide 1 Cor. xii, 1, -11. 28, -31: xiii, 1, 2, 3. Huc etiam revocanda est gratia utcunque illuminans & refrænans in Gentilibus, aliisque infidelibus; ipsorum Theologia, & qualiscunque animi probitas, &c. Vide Joh. 1, 9. Gen. xx, 6.
units.tr: Moreover, there are certain charismata which also relate to Christ and the Gospel, but which have no inseparable connection with eternal salvation: such as grace that illuminates and generally persuades, the faith of miracles, the gift of prophecy, etc. These are commonly called, rightly, grace given freely; but such a thing does not in itself make a man pleasing and acceptable to God in Christ. See 1 Cor. 12:1–11, 28–31; 13:1, 2, 3. To this must also be referred the grace which in some measure illuminates and restrains the Gentiles and other unbelievers: their theology, and whatever uprightness of mind they have, etc. See John 1:9; Gen. 20:6.

units.la: XLVII. Misericordia Dei, est gratia ipsius erga objecta mísera, ut iis subveniat in malo tristi. Exod. xxxiv, 6; Jehovah misericors. Luc. vi, 36. Pater vester misericors est. Eph. ii, 4. Deus dives misericordia. Psal. lxxxvi, 15; ciii, 8. Thren. iii, 22.
units.tr: XLVII. The mercy of God is his grace towards wretched objects, so that he helps them in sad evil. Exod. 34:6, "Jehovah merciful." Luke 6:36, "Your Father is merciful." Eph. 2:4, "God, rich in mercy." Ps. 86:15; 103:8. Lam. 3:22.

units.la: Hæc generali consideratione ad omnes creaturas analogice extendi potest: 1 Tim. iv, 10. Psal. xxxvi, 7. civ. xlvii. sed speciali ac salutari modo respicit homines electos, qui propterea vasa misericordiæ appellantur. Rom. IX, 23. Hinc Tit. III, 4, 5. „Postquam benignitas & erga homines amor apparuit Servatoris nostri Dei, „non ex operibus nostris, quæ fecerimus nos, sed ex „sua miserMcordia servavit nos, &c. Psal. CIII, 13. „Ut miseretur pater filiorum, miseretur Jehovah timentium ipsum. Confer Joh. III, 16. Rom. III, 24, 25. Psal. XXXVI, 8.
units.tr: This can be extended analogically to all creatures by a general consideration: 1 Tim. 4:10; Ps. 36:7; 104; 147. But it regards the elect men in a special and saving way, who for this reason are called vessels of mercy. Rom. 9:23. Hence Titus 3:4, 5: "After the kindness and love towards men of our Saviour God appeared, not by works which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us," etc. Ps. 103:13, "As a father has pity on his children, so Jehovah has pity on those who fear him." Compare John 3:16; Rom. 3:24, 25; Ps. 36:8.

units.la: XLVIII. Patientia, seu Tolerantia, est Misericordia erga creaturas peccatrices, quatenus iis Deus adhuc multifariam benefacit, poenas differendo, vel æquiter temperando, quantum per Justitiam fieri potest.
units.tr: XLVIII. Patience, or tolerance, is mercy towards sinful creatures, insofar as God still does them good in many ways, deferring or fairly tempering punishments as far as justice allows.

units.la: Rom. II, 4, 5. An divitias-Tolerantiæ ac iræ cohibitæ contemnis? &c. Hæc etiam Longanimitas appellatur, propter diuturnam pænarum dilationem; Exod. XXXIV, 6. Psal. CIII, 8. CXLV, 8.
units.tr: Rom. 2:4, 5: "Do you despise the riches of his kindness, forbearance and long-suffering?" etc. It is also called longanimity, on account of the lasting deferral of punishments: Exod. 34:6; Ps. 103:8; 145:8.

units.la: XLIX. Succedit Bonitas Dei communicativa sui in genere moris ad creaturas intellectuales: & hic præcipuè occurrit Justitia. Deus nimirum voluit non solum veritates cognoscendas & credendas proponere, atque sic normam notitiæ & fidei constituere; verum insuper Legem præscribere, quâ præciperet agenda, prohiberet fugienda; juxta quam denique ipse se gereret in remunerando, & in puniendo.
units.tr: XLIX. Next follows the goodness of God, which communicates himself in the manner of morals to intellectual creatures; and here justice chiefly comes into view. God, to be sure, willed not only to set forth truths to be known and believed, and thus to establish a rule of knowledge and faith, but also to prescribe a law by which he commands what is to be done and forbids what is to be avoided, and according to which he himself acts in rewarding and in punishing.

units.la: Justitia hæc, est quasi habitus, aut constans voluntas, juris: & consideratur tùm in dictis, tum in factis.
units.tr: This justice is, as it were, a habit or constant will of right, and it is considered both in words and in deeds.

units.la: L. Justitia in dictis est divina virtus, exerens se in revelationum convenientiâ cum naturâ & decreto ipsius Dei, & consequenter cum hujus executione.
units.tr: L. Justice in words is a divine virtue, showing itself in the agreement of the revelations with the nature and decree of God himself, and consequently with its execution.

units.la: Huc pertinet 1. Veracitas, quæ respicit convenientiam orationis cum re. Joh. VIII, 26 „Qui me misit, verax est. Rom. III, 4. „Imò esto Deus verax. Joh. XIV, 6. Tit. I, 2. Hebr. VI, 17, 18.
units.tr: To this belongs, first, truthfulness, which regards the agreement of speech with the thing. John 8:26, "He who sent me is true." Rom. 3:4, "Indeed, let God be true." John 14:6; Titus 1:2; Heb. 6:17, 18.

units.la: 2. Fides, quæ respicit sinceritatem, ad præstandum id quod dictum est. Psal. CXVII, 2. Fides Jehovæ in sæculum. 2 Tim. II, 13. Ille fidus manet.
units.tr: Second, faithfulness, which regards sincerity in performing what has been said. Ps. 117:2, "The faithfulness of Jehovah endures forever." 2 Tim. 2:13, "He remains faithful."

units.la: 3. Constantia, quæ respicit perseverantiam propositi ti Divini, & immutabilem executionem eorum quæ ipse prædixit. Psal. xxxiii, 4. Omne opus ejus est constans. Mal. iii, 6. Jac. 1, 17. Num. xxiii, 19. 1 Sam. xv, 29.
units.tr: Third, constancy, which regards the perseverance of the divine purpose and the unchangeable execution of what he has foretold. Ps. 33:4, "All his work is steadfast." Mal. 3:6; Jas. 1:17; Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29.

units.la: LI. Infaßs, generalior est consideratio Regiminis; specialior Jurisdictionis.
units.tr: LI. Right: the general consideration is of government, the more specific of jurisdiction.

units.la: Regimine, omnes creaturas summâ æquitate & rectitudine gubernat ὁ αὐτοδίκαιος : Deut. xxxii, 4. Omnes illius viæ sunt jus. Psal. xxxiii, 4, 5.
units.tr: In government, the most just One [ὁ αὐτοδίκαιος] rules all creatures with the highest equity and rectitude: Deut. 32:4, "All his ways are right." Ps. 33:4, 5.

units.la: Jurisdictio spectat solas creaturas intellectuales, cultum rationalem Domino suo debentes. Rom. xii, 1.
units.tr: Jurisdiction concerns only intellectual creatures, who owe their Lord a rational worship: Rom. 12:1.

units.la: Estque vel Legislatoria, vel Legis executoria.
units.tr: It is either legislative or executive of the law.

units.la: Illa mandat agenda, prohibet omittenda, obedientibus promittit præmia, immorigeris vero sanctionem poenarum comminatoriam proponit. Jac. iv, 12. Unus est Legislator, qui potest servare & perdere. Adde Rom. x, 5. Deut. xxxvii, 26.
units.tr: The former commands what is to be done, forbids what is to be left undone, promises rewards to the obedient, and sets before the disobedient the threat of penal sanctions. Jas. 4:12, "There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy." Add Rom. 10:5; Deut. 27:26.

units.la: Hæc convenienter ad illam, judicia infert, & secundum opera mercedem tribuit. Jerem. xvii, 10. Scrutator cordis, -- : idque ut dem cuique secundum vias suas, secundum fructum actionum suarum. Adde Rom. ii, 6. 2 Cor. v, 10. quæ Retributio est vel remuneratoria bonorum operum, vel punitoria malorum.
units.tr: The latter, in agreement with that, brings judgments and gives a reward according to works: Jer. 17:10, "I, the searcher of the heart, … to give to each according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds." Add Rom. 2:6; 2 Cor. 5:10. This retribution is either remunerative of good works or punitive of evil ones.

units.la: LII. Renumeratio bonorum operum fit secundum promissionem gratuitam: Psal. xviii, 24, 25, 26. Rom. ii, 6, 7. 2 Thess. i, 5, 6, 7. 2 Tim. iv, 8. Deus scil. ultro promittendo se fecit nobis debitorem: Jes. xlv, 19.
units.tr: LII. The remuneration of good works takes place according to a free promise: Ps. 18:24, 25, 26; Rom. 2:6, 7; 2 Thess. 1:5, 6, 7; 2 Tim. 4:8. That is, God, by promising freely, has made himself our debtor: Isa. 45:19.

units.la: 1 Tim. iv, 8. nec se ipsum abnegare potest: 2 Tim. ii, 13. Quin & sua dona in illis coronat; non eorum merita proprie dicta: 1 Cor. iv, 7. Rom. xi, 35, 36. Luc. xvii, 10. Tenenda interim insignis differentia Fœderis Legalis, & Evangelici; quæ suo loco explicabitur.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 4:8; nor can he deny himself: 2 Tim. 2:13. Indeed he crowns his own gifts in them, not their merits properly so called: 1 Cor. 4:7; Rom. 11:35, 36; Luke 17:10. Meanwhile the notable difference between the Legal and the Evangelical covenant must be kept in view, which will be explained in its place.

units.la: LIII. Punitio peccatorum est vel castigatoria & emendatoria amicorum ac filiorum Dei lapsorum: 1 Cor. xi, 32. Dum judicamur, à Domino erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur, Hebr. xii, 5-11. Vel refrænatoria electorum nondùm vocatorum ; aut præparatoria ad eorum conversionem : Act. ix, 3, 4, 5, 9. Vel denique satisfactoria pro peccatorum demerito, quæ se exerit tùm adversùs reprobos ; tùm exeruit in Christo, vice & loco electorum, fidelium, resipiscentium.
units.tr: LIII. The punishment of sins is either castigatory and corrective for the fallen friends and sons of God: 1 Cor. xi, 32. "While we are judged, we are instructed by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world," Heb. xii, 5-11. Or it is restraining for the elect not yet called, or preparatory for their conversion: Acts ix, 3, 4, 5, 9. Or finally it is satisfactory for the desert of sins, which is exercised against the reprobate, and was exercised in Christ, in the place and stead of the elect, the faithful, and the repentant.

units.la: LIV. De Justitia vindicativa tenendùm est contra Socinianos ; primò, quòd pœnarum exactio in Sacris non solùm referatur ad severitatem, iram, indignationem, &c. sed etiam ad justitiam: aperte enim Deus justus prædicatur, & judicia ejus justa, ob pœnas infictas: 2 Chron. xii, 5, 6. Nehem. ix, 33. Psal. xi, 6, 7. cxxix, 4, 5. Threm. I, 18. Dan. ix, 14. Apoc. xvi, 5, 6, 7. xix. 2 Rom. iii, 5, 6. 2 Thess. i, 6. 2. Appellatur vindex justitiæ: Psal. ix, 5, 6. & dies justi judicii: Rom. ii, 5. Adde Act. xvii, 31. Apoc. xix. ii, 15. 3. Ad δικαίωμα Dei pertinet pœnas infligere, Rom. i. 32. 4. Justitia puniens vocatur δίκη: Act. xxviii, 4. Confer 2 Thess. i, 9. Judæ, 7. Item Hebr. ii, 2. Rom. iii, 8, xiii, 4. 1 Thess. iv, 6. Luc. xxi, 22. 2 Thess. I, 6. Hebr. x, 30. 1 Petr. ii, 14. Rom. xii, 19. Exc. Modus pœnarum refertur ad justitiam; non ipsæ pœnæ. Resp. 1. De ipsis pœnis satis patet ex allegatis plurimis. 2. Si Iustitia requirat talem modum pœnarum, non certe permittit peccata relinqui prorsus impunita: modus enim sine re modificatâ existere non potest. LV. Secundò, Justitia punitiva non est proprie effectus Voluntatis Divinæ, aut motio transiens: (quod illi volunt:) sed est aliquid perpetuò existens in Deo, ipsique essentiale. Nam 1. est ipsa Dei sanctitas, puritas, rectitudo, amor justitiæ, & odium seu aversatio peccatorum Exod. xx, 5. Deut. xxv, 16. Iof. xxiv, 19. Psal. v, 5, 6, 7. xi, 5, 6, 7. xl. 8. Prov. xi, xvii,15. Ief. i.13,14,15. Zach. viii,17. Hab. i,13. Rom. iii,5,6. 2 Thess. i,6. 1 Joh. i,5.
units.tr: LIV. Vindictive justice must be held against the Socinians. First, the exaction of penalties in the Sacred Writings is referred not only to severity, wrath, indignation, and so on, but also to justice. For God is openly proclaimed just, and his judgments just, on account of the punishments inflicted: 2 Chron. xii, 5, 6. Neh. ix, 33. Ps. xi, 6, 7. cxxix, 4, 5. Lam. i, 18. Dan. ix, 14. Rev. xvi, 5, 6, 7. xix. Rom. iii, 5, 6. 2 Thess. i, 6. 2. He is called the avenger of justice, Ps. ix, 5, 6, and the day of the just judgment, Rom. ii, 5. Add Acts xvii, 31; Rev. xix, 2; xv, 15. 3. It belongs to God's righteous decree [δικαίωμα] to inflict punishments, Rom. i, 32. 4. Justice punishing is called righteousness [δίκη], Acts xxviii, 4. Compare 2 Thess. i, 9; Jude 7. Likewise Heb. ii, 2; Rom. iii, 8; xiii, 4; 1 Thess. iv, 6; Luke xxi, 22; 2 Thess. i, 6; Heb. x, 30; 1 Pet. ii, 14; Rom. xii, 19. Exception: the manner of the punishments is referred to justice, not the punishments themselves. Answer: 1. Concerning the punishments themselves, enough is clear from the many passages cited. 2. If justice requires such a manner of punishments, it certainly does not permit sins to be left wholly unpunished, for a manner cannot exist without the thing it modifies. LV. Second, punitive justice is not properly an effect of the Divine will, or a transient motion (as they would have it), but is something perpetually existing in God and essential to him. For 1. it is the very holiness, purity, and rectitude of God, his love of justice, and his hatred or aversion toward sins: Exod. xx, 5; Deut. xxv, 16; Josh. xxiv, 19; Ps. v, 5, 6, 7; xi, 5, 6, 7; xl, 8; Prov. xi; xvii, 15; Isa. i, 13, 14, 15; Zech. viii, 17; Hab. i, 13; Rom. iii, 5, 6; 2 Thess. i, 6; 1 John i, 5.

units.la: 2. Hinc Deus dicitur ignis consumens: Deut. iv,24. Jef. xxxiii,14, Hebr. xii,29. cum Exod. xxxiv,7. Num. xiv,8. Psal. xxxiv,17. Nah. i,3.
units.tr: 2. Hence God is called a consuming fire: Deut. iv, 24; Isa. xxxiii, 14; Heb. xii, 29; compare Exod. xxxiv, 7; Num. xiv, 18; Ps. xxxiv, 17; Nah. i, 3.

units.la: 3. Consequenter ira Dei, vel excandescentia, memoratur: ἀνθρωποπαθῶς: Exod. xxxii,10,11. Num. xi,1. xvi,22. xxv,3,-11. Psal. ii,5,12. vi,2. Joh. iii,36. Rom. i,18. ii,5.8. ix,22. xi,22. Eph. v,6. Col. iii,6. Apoc. vi,16,17. unde tantus terror hominum peccatorum: Ief. xxxi,11,14. vi,5. Jud. xiii,22. Confer quæ de Simplicitate & Immutabilitate Dei diximus sup. th. 16. & 20.
units.tr: 3. Consequently the wrath of God, or his burning anger, is mentioned, spoken anthropopathically [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]: Exod. xxxii, 10, 11; Num. xi, 1; xvi, 22; xxv, 3-11; Ps. ii, 5, 12; vi, 2; John iii, 36; Rom. i, 18; ii, 5, 8; ix, 22; xi, 22; Eph. v, 6; Col. iii, 6; Rev. vi, 16, 17. Whence comes the great terror of sinful men: Isa. xxxi, 11, 14; vi, 5; Judg. xiii, 22. Compare what we have said above on the simplicity and immutability of God, th. 16 and 20.

units.la: 4. Hinc impedimentum, ne Deus peccatoribus amplius parcat, aut benefacere pergat: Gen. vi,7. Deut. xxxii,29,30. Psal. lxxxi,11,12,13. Ief. lix,2. Jer. v,25.
units.tr: 4. Hence there is an obstacle to God's sparing sinners any longer, or continuing to do them good: Gen. vi, 7; Deut. xxxii, 29, 30; Ps. lxxxi, 11, 12, 13; Isa. lix, 2; Jer. v, 25.

units.la: Obj. Atqui Deus tardus ad iram dicitur; & modo irasci, modo iram deponere, &c. Ergo. Resp. Ita quidem ἀνθρωποπαθῶς de egressu & effectu poenali. Verum inde nequaquam sequitur, quod volunt Adversarii.
units.tr: Objection. But God is said to be slow to anger, and to be now angry, now laying aside his anger, and so on. Therefore... Answer: It is indeed so, anthropopathically, with respect to the outward expression and effect of punishment. But it by no means follows from this what our opponents want.

units.la: LVI. Tertio, Egressus, sive exercitium justitiæ punitivæ, posito peccato, est necessarium; ita ut Deus peccatum impunitum relinquere non possit. Hoc probatur, 1. ex S. Scripturæ testimoniis: Exod. xxxiv,7. Qui nullo pacto non absolvit fontem; Gen. xviii,25. Nunquid Iudex universæ terræ non faciet justitiam? Ios. xxiv,19. Deus fortis zelotes est; non feret defectionem vestram, & peccata vestra. Confer alia modo allegata: & 2 Tim. ii,13. Seipsum abnegare non potest.
units.tr: LVI. Third, the outflow, or exercise, of punitive justice, once sin is posited, is necessary, so that God cannot leave sin unpunished. This is proved, 1. from the testimonies of Holy Scripture: Exod. xxxiv, 7, "who by no means acquits the guilty"; Gen. xviii, 25, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do justice?"; Josh. xxiv, 19, "God is a jealous God; he will not bear your rebellion and your sins." Compare the other passages already cited, and 2 Tim. ii, 13, "He cannot deny himself."

units.la: 2. Ex conditione Poenarum, quæ cum sint malum triste, & sic non appetibiles, procedere non possunt ab indifferenti actu voluntatis Divinæ: Ezech. xviii, 23,32. Natura igitur Dei sanctissima eas exigit, quatenus sunt bonum justitiæ.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of punishments, which, since they are a sad evil and so not desirable, cannot proceed from an indifferent act of the Divine will: Ezek. xviii, 23, 32. Therefore God's most holy nature requires them, insofar as they are a good of justice.

units.la: 3. Ex natura ipsius Peccati; quod ad poenam Meritirationem habet: adsunt enim omnes conditiones Meriti proprie dicti, quae hoc versiculo continentur.
units.tr: 3. From the nature of sin itself, which bears to punishment the relation of merit: for all the conditions of merit properly so called, which are contained in this verse, are present.

units.la: Da tua; sed quae non debes; proportio & adsit:
units.tr: Give what is yours, but what you ought not; let the proportion be there:

units.la: Non aliter Meritum dixeris esse tuum.
units.tr: In no other way may you call it your merit.

units.la: Peccata enim, ut sic, non a Deo, sed ab ipso peccante procedunt: Iac. I, 13. Ipsa prorsus debita non sunt; sed contraria obedientia debita est. Convenientissima denique proportio est, ut pro malo turpi retribuatur malum triste; & quidem pro ratione ejus qui offensus est.
units.tr: For sins, as such, proceed not from God but from the sinner himself: James i, 13. They are not in themselves things owed; but the contrary obedience is owed. Finally, the most fitting proportion is that a sad evil be rendered for a shameful evil, and indeed in proportion to the one who has been offended.

units.la: 4. Illud δικαίωμα Dei naturae nostrae impressum est: Rom. 1, 32. 11, 14, 15. Unde apud Gentiles effata illa; Ἔγγ' Θεὸς ἐκδικον ὄμμα.
units.tr: 4. That righteous decree of God [δικαίωμα] is impressed on our nature: Rom. i, 32; ii, 14, 15. Whence among the Gentiles those sayings: God's avenging eye is near [Ἔγγ' Θεὸς ἐκδικον ὄμμα].

units.la: Aspiciunt oculis Superi mortalia justis.
units.tr: The gods above look upon mortal deeds with just eyes.

units.la: Raro antecedentem scelestum Deseruit pede poena claudo.
units.tr: Rarely does punishment, with lame foot, abandon the wicked who went before.

units.la: Lento gradu ad vindictam sui Divina procedit ira; tarditatemque supplicii gravitate compensat.
units.tr: Divine wrath proceeds to avenge its own with slow step, and compensates for the tardiness of punishment by its severity.

units.la: Item Conscientia judiciorum post hanc vitam, Theologia mythologica de Nemesi, Rhadamanto, &c.
units.tr: Likewise the consciousness of judgments after this life, the mythological theology of Nemesis, Rhadamanthus, and so on.

units.la: Clarius tamen hoc jus suum Deus expressit in Lege per Mosen scripta. Deut. xxvii, 26. &c.
units.tr: Yet God expressed this right of his more clearly in the Law written through Moses: Deut. xxvii, 26, and following.

units.la: LVII. Obj. 1. De jure suo privato homines singuli remittere possunt: multo magis ergo Deus. Resp. Nego consequentiam: Rectores publici de jure publico remittere non possunt, pro libitu, & quasi jure dominii; nec Deus de jure suo naturali & judiciali.
units.tr: LVII. Objection 1. Individuals can remit their private right: much more, therefore, God. Answer: I deny the consequence. Public rulers cannot remit public right at their pleasure, and as if by a right of lordship; nor can God remit his natural and judicial right.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus ad extra operatur liberè: Ergo. Resp. Ita tamen, ut nihil naturae suae repugnans facere possit: quin ex hypothesi ad extra operatur etiam necessario.
units.tr: Objection 2. God acts freely outwardly. Therefore... Answer: Yes, but only so that he can do nothing repugnant to his own nature; indeed, on the hypothesis, he also acts outwardly of necessity.

units.la: Obj. 3. Atqui poenas differre potest. Resp. Sed quod differtur, non aufertur.
units.tr: Objection 3. But he can defer punishments. Answer: But what is deferred is not taken away.

units.la: Obj. 4. Quae peccantur adversus praecepta juris Divini positivi, prorsus non habent necessitatem ex natura Dei. Resp. Etiam illa, ex hypothesi iustius legis, repugnant obedientiae, Deo per naturam suam debitae; & sic non possunt non per justitiam ipsius naturalem puniri.
units.tr: Objection 4. Sins committed against the precepts of positive Divine law have no necessity at all from the nature of God. Answer: Even those, on the hypothesis of the justice of the law, are repugnant to the obedience owed to God by his nature; and so they cannot but be punished by his natural justice.

units.la: LVIII. Justitiae distinctio apud Philosophos usitata, in Deo locum non habet.
units.tr: LVIII. The distinction of justice used by the philosophers has no place in God.

units.la: Neque enim Distributiva praemiorum, secundum proportionem geometricam, tanquam ex debito a parte creaturarum, ipsi convenit; neque commutativa, secundum proportionem arithmeticam, quae in privatis contractibus spectatur. Quoniam nihil boni in nobis est, vel a nobis procedere potest, quod per se vim habeat Deum nobis obligandi; tum propter summam ipsius ἐξουσίαν, & potestatem in nos; tum propter omnimodam nostri ab ipso dependentiam, & obligationem ad ipsum.
units.tr: For distributive justice, which rewards according to geometric proportion as something owed on the part of creatures, does not belong to him, nor does commutative justice, which rewards according to arithmetic proportion and is found in private contracts. For there is nothing good in us, and nothing can proceed from us, that by itself has force to oblige God to us, both on account of his supreme authority [ἐξουσία] and power over us, and on account of our complete dependence on him and obligation to him.

units.la: Vidimus objectum Voluntatis Divinae, Bonum, tum in genere entis, tum in genere moris. Malum formaliter est quid privativum; adeoque per se non cognoscibile, nec appetibile. Etiam malum, triste, quatenus malum est: Ezech. xviii, 23, An ullo pacto delector morte morientis? Alia vero est ratio mali tristis, per modum poenae: sic enim est bonum justitiae; atque eatenus appetibile ex hypothesi peccati, Deut. xxviii, 63. Prov. 1, 26. xvi, 4. Isef. 1, 24.
units.tr: We have seen that the object of the divine will is the good, both in the genus of being and in the genus of morals. Evil is formally something privative, and therefore is not knowable or desirable in itself. Evil, too, is sad in so far as it is evil: Ezek. 18:23, "Do I take any pleasure in the death of one who dies?" But the nature of sad evil is different when it is considered as punishment; in this way it is the good of justice, and so far it is desirable, given the hypothesis of sin: Deut. 28:63; Prov. 1:26; 16:4; Isa. 1:24.

units.la: Malum turpe, sive peccati, in se prorsus non est appetibile Deo, per Naturam ipsius sanctissimam. Objicitur tamen Voluntati Divinae, ut permissibile & ordinabile: quod alibi explicabitur.
units.tr: The shameful evil, that is, of sin, is in itself not at all desirable to God, given his most holy nature. Yet it is presented to the divine will as permissible and ordainable, which will be explained elsewhere.

units.la: LIX. Caeterum Voluntati Divinae etiam competit Infinitas, Simplicitas, & Independentia.
units.tr: LIX. Moreover, infinity, simplicity and independence also belong to the divine will.

units.la: Infinitas 1. in se: quia secundum rem est ipsa Dei essentia. 2. Respectu objectorum, tum ipsius Dei, tum aliorum a Deo. Vide sup. th. 43, 44. & 5. ratione modi volendi; qui est absolute perfectissimus.
units.tr: Infinity belongs to it: (1) in itself, because in reality it is the very essence of God; (2) with respect to its objects, both God himself and things other than God (see above, theses 43 and 44); and (5) by reason of the manner of willing, which is absolutely most perfect.

units.la: Consequenter non est in Deo Voluntas aliqua, aut volitio, imperfecta, quae velleitas in Scholis appellatur. Psal. cxv, 3. Deus noster in ipsis cœlis est; quicquid placet, facit. Prov. xix; 21. Jes. xiv, 27. xlv, 10. Rom. ix, 19. Eph. i. 11. Repugnat nimirum tum Dei omnipotentiæ, tum ipsius sapientiæ; tum nostræ dependentiæ, tum denique nostræ impotentiæ in ordine ad Deum.
units.tr: Consequently there is in God no imperfect will or volition, which in the schools is called velleity. Psalm 115:3, "Our God is in the heavens; whatever pleases him, he does." Prov. 19:21; Isa. 14:27; 45:10; Rom. 9:19; Eph. 1:11. Such a thing clearly conflicts both with God's omnipotence, and with his wisdom; and with our dependence, and finally with our powerlessness in relation to God.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deo tribuitur expectatio uvarum, dum proferebantur labruscæ: Jes. v, 4. Ergo, &c. Resp. Expectatio ista notat, quod Deus Israelitis tempus satis longum concesserit, quo debuissent resipiscere, bona opera præstare, ipsum glorificare, &c. Sed illi meram hyprocrisin & pertinaciam produxerant.
units.tr: Obj. 1. God is said to have expected grapes when wild grapes were produced: Isa. 5:4. Therefore, etc. Resp. That expectation signifies that God granted Israel a sufficiently long time in which they ought to have repented, performed good works, glorified him, and so on. But they had produced nothing but mere hypocrisy and obstinacy.

units.la: Obj. 2. Etiam votum Deo adscribitur, Deut. v, 29. Ps. lxxxi. 14. Resp. Ita emphaticè & ἀνθρωποπαθῶς proponitur bonum hominibus salutare, per Dei promissionem; adeoque illis appetendum.
units.tr: Obj. 2. A wish is also ascribed to God: Deut. 5:29; Ps. 81:14. Resp. In this emphatic and anthropopathic way [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς] the good that is salutary for men is set forth, through God's promise, and so it is to be desired by them.

units.la: LX. Simplicitas illi etiam convenit: quia Deus unico actu vult, quicquid vult. Interim Voluntas Dei, respectu objectorum, distinguitur in realem, sive decernentem de existentia & eventu eorum, quæ fierent in genere entis: & in moralem, sive disponentem de regulis vivendi creaturarum rationalium, in genere moris.
units.tr: LX. Simplicity also belongs to it, because God wills whatever he wills by a single act. Meanwhile, the will of God, with respect to its objects, is distinguished into real, or decreeing, concerning the existence and outcome of those things which come to be in the genus of being; and into moral, or disposing, concerning the rules of living for rational creatures, in the genus of morals.

units.la: Affinis est distinctio in Voluntatem occultam, & revelatam. Juxta Deut. xxix, 29. Quæ occulta sunt penes Jehovam Deum nostrum sunto; at quæ revelata, nobis & filiis nostris usque in sæculum revelata sunt.
units.tr: Related to this is the distinction between the hidden and the revealed will, according to Deut. 29:29: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God; but the things revealed belong to us and to our children for ever."

units.la: Voluntas occulta dicitur respectu eorum, quæ Deus decrevit facere, vel permittere; sed hactenus neque per eventum, neque per prophetiam, manifestavit. Consequenter ista rationem normæ non habet; nec in eâ curiosi esse debemus. Vide Luc. xiii, 23, 24. Act. i, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: The hidden will is so called with respect to those things which God has decided to do or to permit, but which he has not yet made known either by the outcome or by prophecy. Consequently this has no character of a rule, and we ought not to be curious about it. See Luke 13:23, 24; Acts 1:6, 7, 8.

units.la: Voluntas autem revelata dicitur de iis, quæ Verbo Dei exposita nos obligant ad fidem & obedientiam.
units.tr: The revealed will, however, is said of those things which are set out in the Word of God and bind us to faith and obedience.

units.la: Similis etiam est distinctio in Voluntatem beneplaciti & signi. Illa ipsum Dei decretum notat: sive effectivum, sive permissivum & ordinativum. Psal. cxv, 3. Matth. xi, 25, 26. Luc. xii, 32, Hęc vero generatim notat indicium qualecunque, quo Deus nobis aliquid significatum vult; sive ut simpliciter credatur, quo pertinent prædictio, impletio, & rei vel facti commemoratio: sive ut actiones nostræ ad illam normam dirigantur, quo pertinent tum præceptum, promissio, exhortatio, invitatio, suasio; tam prohibitio, comminatio, dehortatio, cautio, &c. Speciatim tamen ipsum mandatum: unde Voluntas quoque mandati appellatur.
units.tr: There is also a similar distinction between the will of good pleasure and the will of sign. The former denotes God's decree itself, whether effective, permissive or ordaining. Ps. 115:3; Matt. 11:25, 26; Luke 12:32. The latter, in general, denotes whatever indication by which God wills something to be made known to us; whether that it be simply believed, to which belong prediction, fulfilment, and the recounting of a thing or deed; or that our actions be directed to that rule, to which belong precept, promise, exhortation, invitation, persuasion; as well as prohibition, threat, dissuasion, warning, etc. In particular, however, it is command itself, whence the will of command is also called the will of command.

units.la: LXI. Ex his non debet colligi ulla Voluntatis Divinæ intrinseca diversitas, nedum contrarietas ad seipsam; aut mutatio: quæ non nisi in rebus volitis locum habent. ex. gr. 1. Quod judicium extremum fit futurum, est Voluntatis revelatæ & signi; quando autem futurum fit, est Voluntatis occultæ & beneplaciti. 2. Deus omnes homines obligavit ad sanctificationem nominis sui, justitiam in dictis & factis; &c. quod est Voluntatis revelatæ, signi, & mandati; decrevit tamen permittere plurima peccata contraria; hoc autem est Voluntatis occultæ, quamdiu non innotescit ipso eventu, vel alio indicio.
units.tr: LXI. From these things it should not be inferred that there is any intrinsic diversity in the divine will, much less contrariety to itself, or change; these apply only to things willed. For example: (1) that the final judgment will take place is of the revealed and signifying will; but when it will take place is of the hidden will of good pleasure. (2) God has bound all men to the sanctification of his name and to righteousness in word and deed, etc. This belongs to the revealed will, of sign and of command; yet he has decreed to permit many contrary sins. This belongs to the hidden will, as long as it is not made known by the outcome itself or by some other indication.

units.la: 3. Deus voluit Abrahamum mandato probatorio obligare ad mactationem filii sui; quod erat Voluntatis revelatæ & mandati: decreverat tamen, ut mactatio illa non perageretur: scil. ut aries aliquis ejus loco offerretur, &c. quod prius erat Voluntatis occultæ & beneplaciti, sed postea alloquio Divino, ipsoque eventu, plene manifestatum est.
units.tr: (3) God willed to bind Abraham by a command of trial to sacrifice his son. This belonged to the revealed will and of command. Yet he had decreed that the sacrifice should not be carried out, namely that a ram should be offered in his place, etc. This was at first of the hidden will and of good pleasure, but afterwards it was fully made known by the divine address and by the outcome itself.

units.la: LXII. Independentia denique competit Voluntati Divinæ: quoniam Deus est absolute causa prima; & principium movens, immobile. Recte Thomas Aquinas; Deus vult hoc esse propter hoc, sed non propter hoc vult hoc.
units.tr: LXII. Finally, independence belongs to the divine will, since God is absolutely the first cause, and the moving principle that is itself immovable. Thomas Aquinas rightly says: God wills this to be for the sake of that, but he does not will that for the sake of this.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deus vult finem, & media ad finem: ergo. Resp. Vult finem, aut causam finalem, non sibi formaliter, sed creaturis.
units.tr: Obj. 1. God wills the end and the means to the end; therefore, etc. Resp. He wills the end, or the final cause, not for himself formally, but for creatures.

units.la: Obj. 2. Operatur omnia propter gloriam suam; quae finis est: ergo. Resp. Non tamen volitio ipsius movetur, vel causatur proprie à gloriâ suâ: sed Deus omnia alia dirigit ad gloriam suam actu independente & simplicissimo.
units.tr: Obj. 2. He works all things for his own glory, which is the end; therefore, etc. Resp. Yet his volition is not moved or caused, properly speaking, by his own glory; rather God directs all other things to his glory by an act that is wholly independent and most simple.

units.la: Obj. 3. Salus electorum est causa praedicati Euangelii. Resp. Sed non volitionis Divinae de praedicando Euangelio.
units.tr: Obj. 3. The salvation of the elect is the cause of the preaching of the Gospel. Resp. But it is not the cause of the divine volition concerning the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Obj. 4. Propter preces fidelium vult Deus misericordiam exercere: propter peccata vult improbos punire: &c. ergo. &c. Resp. Preces habent rationem medii ad effectus misericordiae; Peccata sunt causae demeritoriae poenarum; quemadmodum fides, resipiscentia, &c. media salutis; sed non volitionis Divinae.
units.tr: Obj. 4. For the prayers of the faithful God wills to exercise mercy; for sins he wills to punish the wicked; etc. Therefore, etc. Resp. Prayers have the character of a means to the effects of mercy; sins are the meritorious causes of punishments; just as faith, repentance, etc. are the means of salvation; but they are not the cause of the divine volition.

units.la: LXIII. Male igitur à Pelagianis Voluntas Dei distinguitur in absolutam & conditionatam: eo sensu, ut volitio quaedam Divina suspendatur à conditione actus humani. Itemque, in antecedentem, & consequentem: ita scil. ut Deus antecedenter ad arbitrium creaturae aliquid vellet; sed consequenter ad illud vellet ejus oppositum.
units.tr: LXIII. Therefore the Pelagians wrongly distinguish the will of God into absolute and conditional, in the sense that a certain divine volition is made dependent on the condition of a human act. Likewise they distinguish it into antecedent and consequent, namely as if God willed something antecedently in accordance with the choice of the creature, but consequently willed the opposite of it.

units.la: Observandi denique modi quidam Libertatis Divinae circa objecta: Deus enim 1. amat seipsum ex necessitate naturae suae; sed interim cum summa ratione; quae est libertas complacentiae. 2. Natura Divina absolute habet se indifferenter ad attributa Sapientiae, Potentiae, Bonitatis, extra se exerenda: attamen exerit ea necessario, ex hypothesi Decreti sui de creatione faciendâ, &c. Estque libertas contradictionis, sive exercitii. 3. Denique Deus voluit istas potius creaturarum species producere, quam alias: & haec est libertas contrarietatis, sive specificationis.
units.tr: Finally, certain modes of divine liberty concerning objects are to be observed. For God (1) loves himself from the necessity of his nature, yet nonetheless with supreme reason; this is the liberty of complacency. (2) The divine nature, considered absolutely, stands indifferently towards the attributes of wisdom, power and goodness to be exercised outside himself; yet he exercises them necessarily, given the hypothesis of his decree to make creation, etc. This is the liberty of contradiction, or of exercise. (3) Finally, God willed to produce these kinds of creatures rather than others; and this is the liberty of contrariety, or of specification.

units.la: LXIV. Succedit nunc Potentia, perfectio scil. suf-
units.tr: LXIV. Now follows Power, namely the most sufficient perfection by which God is able to bring about from himself whatever is consistent with his will.

units.la: 1 5 ficientissima, qua Deus est potens exequi ex se, quicquid Voluntati suæ est consentaneum. 1 Chron. xxix. 11, 12. ,, Tua est, o Jehovah, magnitudo & potentia: in manu Tua vis & potentia. &c. Jes. ix, 5. Jerem, xxxii, 18. Matth. vi, 13. 2 Chron. vi, 18. Hebr. 1, 3. Apoc. 1, 8. iv. 8. xv, 3. Potentia igitur Dei non est passiva, perfectibilis, receptiva formæ alicujus: ista enim non est perfectio, sed imperfectio, Divinæ naturæ nequaquam conveniens. Verùm activa: id est, talis efficientia, qua Deus hoc agit, ut creaturæ tales tali tempore ac modo existant: unde oritur, relatio rationis, à parte Dei; sed realis, à parte creaturarum.
units.tr: 1 Chron. 29:11, 12: "Yours, O Jehovah, is the greatness and the power; in your hand is strength and might," etc. Isa. 9:5; Jer. 32:18; Matt. 6:13; 2 Chron. 6:18; Heb. 1:3; Rev. 1:8; 4:8; 15:3. The power of God is therefore not passive, capable of being perfected, receptive of some form; for that is not perfection but imperfection, by no means fitting to the divine nature. It is rather active; that is, such an efficiency by which God so acts that creatures of such kinds exist at such a time and in such a manner; whence arises a relation of reason on the part of God, but a real relation on the part of creatures.

units.la: LXV. Potentia hæc Divina, verè infinita est; sive eam infespectes: Gen. xvii, 1. xxxv, 11. Ruth. I, 20, 21. sive objecta: Luc. 1, 37. sive modum operandi: Is. xl, 26. 28. Eph. I. 19. iii, 20. Phil. iii, 21.
units.tr: LXV. This divine power is truly infinite, whether you consider it in itself: Gen. 17:1; Gen. 35:11; Ruth 1:20, 21; or its objects: Luke 1:37; or its manner of working: Isa. 40:26, 28; Eph. 1:19; 3:20; Phil. 3:21.

units.la: Obj. 1. Potentia Dei contrahitur & restringitur per ipsius Voluntatem: infinita ergo non est. Resp. Non de ipsâ Dei Potentiâ proprie istud intelligi debet, sed de ejus objectis.
units.tr: Objection 1. God's power is limited and restricted by his will, and so it is not infinite. Reply: This must be understood not of God's power itself, strictly speaking, but of its objects.

units.la: Obj. 2. Intellectus Dei excedit ipsius Potentiam; nam cognoscit etiàm seipsum; sed non potest seipsum producere: Potentia igitur infinita non est. Resp. Intellectus & Potentia Dei secundum rem sunt unum idemque; atque ut ille ad omnia absolute cognoscibilia refertur; ita hæc ad omnia absolute possibilia fieri, vel producì: undè ipse Deus excluditur; quod ad perfectionem ejus pertinet.
units.tr: Objection 2. God's intellect exceeds his power, for he knows himself, yet he cannot produce himself; so his power is not infinite. Reply: God's intellect and power are one and the same in reality. Just as the intellect extends to everything that is absolutely knowable, so the power extends to everything that is absolutely possible to be made or produced. God himself is excluded from this, and that exclusion belongs to his perfection.

units.la: LXVI. Eadem in se simplicissima est: unica & immutabilis. Interim pro distincta habitudine objectorum, secundùm Voluntatem Dei, distinguì solet in absolutam & ordinatam.
units.tr: LXVI. In itself this power is most simple, one and unchangeable. Yet, according to the differing relation of its objects to the will of God, it is customarily divided into absolute and ordained.

units.la: Potentia Dei absoluta est omnium absolute possibilium; seu omnium eorum, quæ non repugnant naturæ Divinæ, nec contradictionem implicant. Matth. iii, 9. ,, Dico vobis, Deum posse etiam ex lapidibus istis excitare filios Abrahamo, xix, 26. xxvi, 35. Marc. 1, 27. xiv. 36. Luc. I, 37. xviii, 27.
units.tr: God's absolute power is that of all things absolutely possible, that is, of all those things which do not conflict with the divine nature and do not imply a contradiction. Matt. 3:9: "I tell you that God is able even from these stones to raise up children to Abraham; Matt. 19:26; 26:35; Mark 1:27; 14:36; Luke 1:37; 18:27.

units.la: Cum autem dicitur aliquid absolutè impossibile, id ab objecto Potentiae excluditur, tanquàm contradictorium naturae Divinae, vel etiàm veritati ideae Divinae: utpote alter Deus; Deum mori, aut mentiri; hominem destitui anima rationali; factum infectum reddi; &c.
units.tr: When something is said to be absolutely impossible, it is excluded from the object of power as contradicting the divine nature, or even the truth of the divine idea. Examples are: another God; God to die, or to lie; a man to be deprived of a rational soul; a thing done to be undone; etc.

units.la: De eadem tenendus hic canon; à potentia Dei absoluta ad effectum non valet consequentia.
units.tr: The following rule holds here: the consequence from God's absolute power to the effect is not valid.

units.la: Potentia Dei ordinata, alias actualis, est eorum quae Deus ut futura decrevit. De hac Rom. xi. 32. Potens est Deus rursùm eos inserere. 25. Nolim enim vos ignorare, fratres, mysterium hoc, &c. Adde Psal. cxv, 3. cxxxv, 6. Eph. I, 11.
units.tr: God's ordained power, otherwise called actual, is that of the things which God has decreed as future. To this belong Rom. 11:32: "God is able to graft them in again"; and Rom. 11:25: "For I would not have you ignorant, brethren, of this mystery," etc. Add Ps. 115:3; 135:6; Eph. 1:11.

units.la: Impossibile vero respectu hujus Potentiae est, fieri ea, de quibus Deus Decreto suo constituit ut non fierent; non fieri ea, de quibus constituit ut fierent: vel etiàm aliter fieri, quàm Deus decrevit. Sic impossibile erat, Christum non nasci tali tempore & loco, non pati talia & per tales, &c: Judicium extremum incidere in annum modo praeteritum 1666. &c.
units.tr: With respect to this power, however, it is impossible that those things should happen which God by his decree has determined should not happen, or that those things should not happen which he has determined should happen, or that anything should happen otherwise than God has decreed. Thus it was impossible that Christ should not be born at such a time and place, or not suffer such things and by such people, etc.; or that the last judgment should fall in the year just past, 1666, etc.

units.la: Obj. 1. Non extiterunt ab aeterno, imò nondum existunt objecta Potentiae ordinatae: ergo haec non est actus purus. Resp. Est actus purus & ab aeterno effectivus eorum, quae decreta sunt: sic tamen ut effecta existant in tempore, ac suo ordine; sive fuerint opera naturae, sive gratiae: Jac. I, 17. "Omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum, est supernè descendens à Patre luminum; apud quem non est transmutatio, aut conversionis obrumbatio.
units.tr: Objection 1. The objects of ordained power have not existed from eternity, indeed they do not yet exist; therefore this power is not pure act. Reply: It is pure act and from eternity effective of those things which have been decreed, yet in such a way that the effects exist in time and in their proper order, whether they are works of nature or of grace. Jas. 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change."

units.la: Obj. 2. In objectis Potentiae absolutae plurima sunt, quae nunquam existent: ergo, &c. Resp. Omnia absolutè possibilia, in Dei sufficientiâ eminenter & virtualiter insunt: ac proindè etiam ista Potentia sic est actus purus.
units.tr: Objection 2. Among the objects of absolute power there are very many which will never exist; therefore, etc. Reply: All things absolutely possible lie eminently and virtually in the sufficiency of God; and therefore this power too is thus pure act.

units.la: LXVII. Potentia Dei quae Independens est, idque
units.tr: LXVII. The power of God, which is independent, and this

units.la: facilè patet, sive eam in se, sive respectu objectorum, sive in modo operandi spectemus.
units.tr: is easily evident, whether we consider it in itself, or with respect to its objects, or in its manner of working.

units.la: Unde sequitur, res esse possibiles, quia Deus eas potest producere: non autem Deum eas posse producere, quia possibiles sunt: ita ut Potentia Dei sit causa omnis possibilitatis in creaturis. Vide Jef.xli. 4. xliv. 6. Apoc. 1, 8, Rom. xi, 36.
units.tr: Hence it follows that things are possible because God can produce them, and not that God can produce them because they are possible; so that the power of God is the cause of all possibility in creatures. See Isa. 41:4; 44:6; Rev. 1:8; Rom. 11:36.

units.la: Quin & impossibilitatis ratio ad Deum similiter referenda est: quod facilè demonstratur per æquipollentiam enunciationum, impossibile est esse, & necesse est non esse; itemque impossibile est non esse, & necesse est esse: omnis autem necessitas fundatur, vel in naturâ Dei, vel in ipsius decreto, qui seipsum abnegare non potest. 2 Tim. ii. 13.
units.tr: Indeed the reason for impossibility is likewise to be referred to God. This is easily demonstrated from the equivalence of the statements "it is impossible that something should be" and "it is necessary that it should not be," and likewise "it is impossible that it should not be" and "it is necessary that it should be." All necessity, however, is grounded either in the nature of God or in his decree, for he cannot deny himself. 2 Tim. 2:13.

units.la: LXVIII. Potestas, seu Dominium Dei sequitur, estque jus illud infinitum & independens, quo omnia alia à Deo, ipsius Dei sunt; ac proinde Deus de illis omnibus disponere potest, quicquid vult. Pfal. cxlv, 1, Regnum Tuum, Regnum est omnium sæculorum, & Dominium Tuum in unamquamque generationem. 1 Tim. vi, 15. Solus Princeps, Rex ille regum & Dominus dominorum. Vide etiam Deut. xxxii, 4. Job. xxv, 2. Pfal. lxvi. 7. cxv. 3. Prov. xvi, 4. Dan. iv, 3, 34, 35. Matth. xx, 15. Rom ix, 20, 21. xi, 36. In objectis Potestatis Divinæ prior est consideratio possibilium, altera est creaturarum actu existentium. Ad possibilia quod attinet, circa ea versatur divina Potestas, quatenus Deus ex his determinavit ad futuritionem, quæ voluit; & quidem talem, qualis eventu manifestatur: ita ut ipsa futuritio, & consequenter actualis existentia creaturarum, referenda sit ad Voluntatem Dei, ut principium imperans primò primum, ex infinitâ plenitudine Potestatis suæ Thren. iii. 37. Ecquo dicente existit aliquid, si Dominus non præceperit? Confer Act. ii. 23. iv. 28. Quod sic ad creaturas rationales, earumque statum æternum, etiam extend
units.tr: LXVIII. Power, or the dominion of God, follows, and is that infinite and independent right by which all things other than God are God's own; and therefore God can dispose of all of them as he wills. Ps. 145:13: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion endures through every generation. 1 Tim. 6:15: the only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords. See also Deut. 32:4; Job 25:2; Ps. 66:7; 115:3; Prov. 16:4; Dan. 4:3, 34, 35; Matt. 20:15; Rom. 9:20, 21; 11:36. In the objects of divine power the first consideration is of possible things, the second is of creatures actually existing.
