As for possible things, divine power is concerned with them insofar as God has determined from these to future being those which he willed, and indeed of such a kind as is made manifest by the outcome. Thus the future itself, and consequently the actual existence of creatures, is to be referred to the will of God as the first commanding principle, from the infinite fullness of his power. Lam. 3:37: "Who is there who speaks and it comes to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it?" Compare Acts 2:23; 4:28. What is thus said of rational creatures and their eternal state, one may also extend

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: extendi debet. Rom. IX, 21, 24. „An non habet potestatem figulus, &c. Quid si vero volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, pertulit multâ cum irae cohibitione vasa irae compacta ad interitum: & ut notas faceret divitias gloriae suae, erga vasa misericordiae, quae „praeparavit ad gloriam? Quos etiam voeavit, &c.
units.tr: ought to be extended. Rom. IX, 21, 24. "Has not the potter power, &c.? What if God, willing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction; and that he might make known the riches of his glory towards the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory? Whom he also called, &c."

units.la: LXIX. Quantum ad creaturas actu existentes; non minus etiam circa illas extendit sese divina Potestas, sive sint rationales, sive irrationales. 1 Chron. XXIX, 12. Dominium habet in omnia. Dan. 11, 21. Ipse mutat tempora, ac tempestates, transfert reges, & constituit reges. Psal. XXIV, 1. L. 10. 11, 12. 15. CXV, 16. Act. XVII. 24. &c. Pro ista potestate Deus universae huic naturae leges suas constituit: Gen. 1, 1. 4, 6, 9. 11, 14, VIII, 22. Job. XXXVII, 12. Psal. CIV, 5. - Prov. VI, 6, 7, 8. XXX. 24. - Jerem. VIII, 7. Sed praeter & supra eas, operatur Auctor ac Dominus naturae & ordinis naturalis, Providentiâ suâ extraordinariâ, in miraculis. Luc. I, 37. VII, 21. 22. Matth. VIII, 8, - 26.
units.tr: LXIX. As regards creatures actually existing, the divine power extends itself over them no less, whether they are rational or irrational. 1 Chron. XXIX, 12: he has dominion over all things. Dan. II, 21: he changes the times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings. Ps. XXIV, 1; Job X, 11, 12, 15; Ps. CXV, 16; Acts XVII, 24, &c. By this power God established his laws for all of nature: Gen. I, 1, 4, 6, 9, 11, 14; VIII, 22; Job XXXVIII, 12; Ps. CIV, 5; Prov. VI, 6, 7, 8; XXX, 24; Jer. VIII, 7. But beyond and above those laws, the Author and Lord of nature and of the natural order works by his extraordinary providence, in miracles: Luke I, 37; VII, 21, 22; Matt. VIII, 8, 26.

units.la: Creaturae autem rationales spectari possunt, tum in genere entis; tum in genere moris. Priori modo circa eas exercet Deus suum Dominium, eas gubernando pro suo arbitrio, etiam ignorantes, providentiâ suâ reali: quod contra Pelagianissantes ex Verbo Dei luculenter ostenditur, ex Gen. L. 20. 2 Sam. XVI, 10. Isef. X, 5, 6, 7, 15. &c. Posteriori modo, Dominium suum exerit Deus providentiâ morali, leges ferendo, faciendo, exequendo. Gen. 11, 16, 17. III, 3, 16, - 19, 22, 23, 24. VI, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, - IX, 1, &c.
units.tr: Rational creatures, however, may be considered both in the genus of being and in the genus of morals. In the former way God exercises his dominion over them, governing them at his pleasure, even when they are ignorant, by his real providence; this is clearly shown from the Word of God against the Pelagianizers: Gen. L, 20; 2 Sam. XVI, 10; Isa. X, 5, 6, 7, 15, &c. In the latter way God exercises his dominion by moral providence, by giving, making and executing laws: Gen. II, 16, 17; III, 3, 16, 19, 22, 23, 24; VI, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11; IX, 1, &c.

units.la: Ex eo quod Deus sit absolutè verax, & seipsum abnegare non possit, ac creaturae concipi nequeant, nisi cum perpetuâ dependentiâ à causâ primâ, Prov. XVI,
units.tr: From the fact that God is absolutely true and cannot deny himself, and that creatures cannot be conceived except in perpetual dependence on the first cause, Prov. XVI,

units.la: 4. Rom. XI, 36. sequitur, quod Deus non possit sese abdicare isto dominio. Haec ratio etiam postulat, ut Deus creaturis rationalibus nihil alienum à naturâ suâ proponat.
units.tr: 4; Rom. XI, 36, it follows that God cannot renounce this dominion. This reasoning also requires that God propose nothing to rational creatures that is foreign to his nature.

units.la: Pro jure Dominii sui Deus etiam potest peccata parentum imputare filiis, eaque in his punire; quin & regum, subditis. Speciatim huc pertinet imputatio peccati Adami, ad omnes ejus posteros foederaliter in ipso censitos. Rom. v, 12, -19. item nostrorum peccatorum, ad Christum. 2 Cor. v, 15, 19, 21. Gal. iii, 13.
units.tr: By right of his dominion God may also impute the sins of parents to their children, and punish them in the children; and likewise the sins of kings to their subjects. Specifically, this pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin to all his posterity, who were reckoned in him by covenant: Rom. V, 12–19; likewise of our sins to Christ: 2 Cor. V, 15, 19, 21; Gal. III, 13.

units.la: Pro jure Dominii sui Deus etiam potest peccata parentum imputare filiis, eaque in his punire; quin & regum, subditis. Speciatim huc pertinent imputatio peccati Adami, ad omnes ejus posteros foederaliter in ipso censitos. Rom. v, 12,- 19. item nostrorum peccatorum, ad Christum, 2 Cor. v, 15, 19, 21. Gal. iii. 13.
units.tr: By right of his dominion God may also impute the sins of parents to their children, and punish them in the children; and likewise the sins of kings to their subjects. Specifically, this pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin to all his posterity, who were reckoned in him by covenant: Rom. V, 12–19; likewise of our sins to Christ: 2 Cor. V, 15, 19, 21; Gal. III, 13.

units.la: Obj. Ezech. xviii. 4. Anima quae peccat, moritur; & 17. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, &c. Ergo. Resp. Istic proponitur specialis conditio, ad Israelitarum hypocrifin ac perverfitatem detegendam & convincendam: quae non debet extendi ultra propositum; nedum applicari possit ad utrumque Adamum.
units.tr: Objection: Ezek. XVIII, 4, "The soul that sins, it shall die," and 17, "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father," &c. Therefore... Answer: That is a special condition set forth there, to expose and convict the hypocrisy and perversity of the Israelites; it ought not to be extended beyond its purpose, much less applied to both Adams.

units.la: LXX. Dominium illud Dei initio diximus inde- pendens: idque propter absolutam naturae suae perse- ctionem ac eminentiam. Consequenter Deus jus suum de fe habet: Rom. xi, 35, 36.
units.tr: LXX. We said at the outset that this dominion of God is independent, and that on account of the absolute perfection and eminence of his nature. Consequently God has his right from himself: Rom. XI, 35, 36.

units.la: Male itaque Remonstrantes contendunt, omne fundamentum juris Divini in creaturam rationalem esse, 1. Beneficium creationis. 2. Maleficium creaturae peccatricis, & 3. contractum cum illa initum.
units.tr: The Remonstrants therefore wrongly contend that every foundation of divine right over the rational creature lies in (1) the benefit of creation, (2) the wrongdoing of the sinning creature, and (3) the contract entered into with it.

units.la: Verum creatio per modum beneficii, non est fundamentum juris Divini: Deus enim jam antecedenter in ipsa possibilia dominatum suum habet. Beneficium quidem ad gratitudinem obligat alterum; sed per se Dominium, aut Principatum non infert.
units.tr: But creation as a benefit is not the foundation of divine right: for God already has his dominion over possible things before them. A benefit does indeed oblige another to gratitude, but in itself it does not bring dominion or sovereignty.

units.la: Peccatum similiter non fundat potestatem Dei: Princeps enim semper habet suam potestatem, etiam puniendi, licet nemo peccet: sed peccatum solummodo est causa demeritoria poenae in tali subjecto: & conditio sine qua non, ad justum exercitium istius potestatis.
units.tr: Sin likewise does not ground God's power: for a prince always has his power, even of punishing, although no one sins; sin is only the meritorious cause of punishment in such a subject, and the condition without which there is no just exercise of that power.

units.la: Fœderatio denique, & contractus cum creaturis, hoc habet, quod Deus per συγκατάθεσιν creaturis sese quodammodo obstringat ultro, creaturas de obligatione earum ad ipsum magis convincat, & obligationem istam ad specialia quædam applicet pro re nata. Sed omnibus illis datur prius, Potestatem Dei formaliter inferens; infinita scil. Præstantia Naturæ potentissimæ, & sanctissimæ.
units.tr: Finally, federation and contract with creatures have this effect: that God by mutual [συγκατάθεσιν] consent binds himself in some way of his own accord to creatures, convinces them more firmly of their obligation to him, and applies that obligation to certain particular matters as occasion arises. But before all these, God's power is given, formally implied in them; namely the infinite excellence of a most powerful and most holy nature.

units.la: LXXI. Obj. 1.
units.tr: LXXI. Obj. 1.

units.la: Pater quilibet habet potestatem in filium, quamvis doctiorem: ergo non ratione ἐξουσίας, sed propter beneficium generationis. Resp. Imò non ob generationis beneficium; sed propter ἐξουσίαν paternitatis, ex ordinatione Divinâ.
units.tr: Any father has power over his son, even if the son is more learned. Therefore it is not by reason of authority [ἐξουσίας], but on account of the benefit of begetting. Reply: Indeed not on account of the benefit of begetting, but on account of the authority [ἐξουσίαν] of fatherhood, by divine ordinance.

units.la: Obj. 2. Unus quis in Aristocratiâ vel Democratiâ concives suos corporis & animi dotibus longè superans, non debet propterea statim Rex constitui: ergo Præstantia per se non fundat Potestatem. Resp. 1. Præstantia ista non est infinita: nec reliqui omnes ab isto uno dependent: ut quidem hîc. 2. Interim si illic de Rege eligendo consultatio ineatur, ille reliquis est præferendus, absque proprio respectu antecedentis beneficii, vel aliorum maleficii, vel contractûs mutui.
units.tr: Obj. 2. A single man in an aristocracy or democracy who far surpasses his fellow citizens in gifts of body and mind ought not for that reason to be made king at once. Therefore pre-eminence in itself does not found power. Reply 1. That pre-eminence is not infinite, nor do all the others depend on this one, as they do in the present case. 2. Meanwhile, if a deliberation about electing a king is held there, that man is to be preferred to the rest, without regard to any previous benefit, or to any wrong done by others, or to any mutual contract.

units.la: Obj. 3. Angeli hominibus multo præstantiores sunt, neque tamen potestatem in eos habent. Ergo, &c. Resp. Angelorum præstantia ab ipso Deo dependet, & sic limitata est, ut illi cum hominibus unam politiam non constituant: ac proinde mirum non est, quod eorum supra homines præstantia non inferat potestatem in eos.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Angels are far superior to men, and yet they have no power over them. Therefore, etc. Reply: The pre-eminence of angels depends on God himself and is so limited that they do not form one commonwealth with men. It is therefore no wonder that their pre-eminence above men does not carry power over them.

units.la: LXXII. Potestas Dei verè infinita, & independens, haud dubiè incommunicabilis est ad alios, eo modo quo ipsi competit. Speciatim Potestatem in statum conscientiæ internum & æternum sibi propriam ipse servavit. Ezech. XVIII, 4. Omnes animæ meæ sunt. Matth. X, 28.
units.tr: LXXII. The power of God, which is truly infinite and independent, is certainly not communicable to others in the way in which it belongs to him. In particular, he has kept for himself the power over the inner and eternal state of the conscience. Ezek. XVIII, 4. All souls are mine. Matt. X, 28.

units.la: x. 28. - Timete eum, qui potest animam & corpus conjicere in gehennam, Jac. x iv. 12. Rom. xiv, 10, 11, 12. Sed in statu externo ac temporali, Magistratui potestatem dedit, sibi quodammodo vicariam, ab ipso dependentem, & gloriae ipsius servientem: Rom. xiii, 1, -6. 1 Petr. ii, 13, 14. Deut. 1, 17. 2 Chron. xix, 17, 18.
units.tr: Matt. x. 28. Fear him who can cast both soul and body into hell; James iv. 12; Rom. xiv, 10, 11, 12. But in the external and temporal state he has given power to the magistrate, a power in some sense vicarious to himself, dependent on him and serving his glory: Rom. xiii, 1–6; 1 Pet. ii, 13, 14; Deut. i, 17; 2 Chron. xix, 17, 18.

units.la: Christus oeconomice consideratus hoc accepit, quod in humana natura evectus fit supra omnes creaturas; ac in ea reluceat suprema ista potestas; sic tamen, ut proprium ejus subjectum quo, fit natura Divina. Vide Matth. xxviii, 19. Psal. ii, 6, -9. lxxii, 1, 2, cx, 1, 2, 3. Joh. v, 22, 27. Act. xvii, 31. Rom. xiv, 9.
units.tr: Christ, considered in his economy, has received this: that, exalted in human nature, he is set above all creatures, and that this supreme power shines forth in that nature; yet in such a way that the divine nature is the proper subject by which this is so. See Matt. xxviii, 19; Ps. ii, 6–9; lxxii, 1, 2; cx, 1, 2, 3; John v, 22, 27; Acts xvii, 31; Rom. xiv, 9.

units.la: LXXIII. Succedit Gloria Dei: infinita scil. illa excellentia, qua ipse in se dignus est aestimari, ut excedens omnes omnino creaturarum perfectiones in infinitum; quapropter etiam omnes creaturae rationales suam ad Deum omnimodam subjectionem humiliter, sincere, & sanctè debent agnoscere; ipsique soli cultum religiosum praestare. De hac 1 Chron. xxix, 10. - 13. Benedictus, Jehovah, Deus Israelis patris nostri, à saeculo usque in saeculum. Tua est, ô Iehovah, gloria, &c. Psal. xix, 2. Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei fortis. Psal. viii, 2. xlvii, 2, 3. Isa. vi, 3. Rom. ix, 5. Apoc. iv, 9, 10, 11. Innotescit nobis haec Dei excellentia, tum per operationis creationis, conservationis; naturae, gratiae, misericordiae, justitiae, &c. tum per doctrinam SS. Literarum; tum denique per manifestationem in conscientiis singulorum. Psal. xix, 2. Rom. i, 19, 20, 21. Joh. ii, 11. Exprimitur autem per lucem inaccessam; 1 Tim. vi, 16. per indumentum decoris, majestatis, lucis; Psal. civ, 1, 2. item per densam tenebrositatem; Exod. xix, 16. xx, 21, xvi. 10, 1 Reg. viii, 11, 12: Heb. xii, 18. Interim media illa, per quae innotescit in nobis divina illa Excellentia, prudenter distingui debent ab ista Excellentia; quae sola est verum objectum formale cultus divini,
units.tr: LXXIII. There follows the glory of God: namely that infinite excellence by which he is in himself worthy to be esteemed, surpassing all the perfections of creatures without any exception, infinitely. Therefore all rational creatures ought humbly, sincerely and holily to acknowledge their complete subjection to God, and to render religious worship to him alone. On this see 1 Chron. xxix, 10–13: Blessed be you, O Jehovah, God of Israel our father, from age to age. Yours, O Jehovah, is the glory, etc. Ps. xix, 2: The heavens declare the glory of the strong God. Ps. viii, 2; xlvii, 2, 3; Isa. vi, 3; Rom. ix, 5; Rev. iv, 9, 10, 11. This excellence of God becomes known to us both through the works of creation and preservation, of nature, grace, mercy, justice, etc., and through the teaching of the Holy Scriptures, and finally through its manifestation in the consciences of individuals. Ps. xix, 2; Rom. i, 19, 20, 21; John ii, 11. It is expressed by the unapproachable light, 1 Tim. vi, 16; by the garment of beauty, majesty and light, Ps. civ, 1, 2; likewise by thick darkness, Exod. xix, 16; xx, 21; xvi, 10; 1 Kings viii, 11, 12; Heb. xii, 18. Yet those means through which this divine excellence becomes known in us must be carefully distinguished from that excellence itself, which alone is the true formal object of divine worship.

units.la: Excellentia qualiscunque hominum, in humanâ societate, fundat honorem; quem communiter civilem appellamus: sed iste suam latitudinem & suos gradus habet. At vero Excellentia Dei, quia infinita est, fundat honorem sibi respondentem; quem religiosum vocamus: qui propterea quoque ipsi soli proprius est.
units.tr: Whatever excellence men have in human society founds honour, which we commonly call civil; but this has its breadth and its degrees. But the excellence of God, because it is infinite, founds the honour corresponding to it, which we call religious; and for that reason it belongs to him alone.

units.la: LXXIV. Probatur hoc, 1. ex primo Decalogi præcepto: Exod.xx, 2, 3. Ego sum Iehovah Deus tuus, ne sunto tibi Dii alieni ante faciem meam. Confer, Gal. iv, 8. Rom. 1, 21, 25. Matth. iv, 10.
units.tr: LXXIV. This is proved, 1. from the first precept of the Decalogue: Exod. xx, 2, 3. I am Jehovah your God; you shall have no other gods before my face. Compare Gal. iv, 8; Rom. i, 21, 25; Matt. iv, 10.

units.la: 2. Ex Jes.xlii, 8. Ego sum Iehovah: gloriam meam alteri non dabo; nec laudem meam sculptilibus.
units.tr: 2. From Isa. xlii, 8: I am Jehovah; I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images.

units.la: 3. Ne quidem Angelis, utpote dignitate finitis, cultus ille competit. Apoc. xix, 10. xxii, 8, 9. Col. ii, 18.
units.tr: 3. Not even to angels, since they are finite in dignity, does such worship belong. Rev. xix, 10; xxii, 8, 9; Col. ii, 18.

units.la: 4. Ex fiducia in solo Deo collocandâ. Jerem.xvii,
units.tr: 4. From the trust that is to be placed in God alone. Jer. xvii,

units.la: 5. Psal.lxii, 10. cxviii, 8, 9. cxlvi, 3, 4. item 1 Chron.xvi, 12. nec non Eph.v, 5. Col. iii, 5. Job. xxxi, 24. Phil.iii, 19. & 1 Sam.xv, 23.
units.tr: 5. Psalm 62:10; 118:8, 9; 146:3, 4; likewise 1 Chronicles 16:12; also Ephesians 5:5; Colossians 3:5; Job 31:24; Philippians 3:19; and 1 Samuel 15:23.

units.la: LXXV. Consequenter orthodoxa Antiquitas contrà Arianos, Photinianos, & similes rectè hinc probavit veram Deitatem Filii & Spiritûs Sancti; quemadmodum & nos etiamnum contra Socinianos eandem veritatem afferimus.
units.tr: LXXV. Accordingly, the orthodox antiquity rightly argued from this against the Arians, the Photinians and similar heretics for the true Deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; just as we still assert the same truth against the Socinians.

units.la: Nec est quòd excipiant, Christum quâ Mediatorem adorandum esse; adeoque veram ipsius Deitatem ex adoratione colligi non posse: merito enim illud negamus, si particula quâ sumatur reduplicative; quamvis verum sit, si sumatur specificative. Hebr.i, 6. II, 9. Phil.II. 6, 11. Apoc. v, 12. cum Joh. xvii, 5. v, 23. sicut eo sensu revera illam particulam sumpserunt orthodoxi Theologi, qui Christum quâ Mediatorem adorandum esse dixerunt.
units.tr: Nor is there reason for them to object that Christ is to be adored as Mediator, and that therefore his true Deity cannot be inferred from the adoration. For we deny that rightly if the particle as [quâ] is taken reduplicatively; although it is true if it is taken specificatively. Heb. i, 6; ii, 9; Phil. ii, 6, 11; Rev. v, 12, compared with John xvii, 5; v, 23. The orthodox theologians who said that Christ is to be adored as Mediator took the particle in that sense indeed.

units.la: Sic etiam Pater, aut Deus absolutè, adoratur quatenus Deus est; non autem quâ creator, aut conservator, formaliter, sive reduplicative: licet per creationem, si-milia miliaque opera soli vero Deo propria, innotescat vera Deitas; atque ita excitemur, ad eam cultū ipsi debitā prosequendam. Psal. xix, 2, 3. Ief. xl, 26. Rom. 1, 20. Apoc. iv, 11. 1 Petr. iv, 19.
units.tr: So too the Father, or God absolutely, is adored in so far as he is God; not, however, as creator or preserver, formally or reduplicatively. Yet through creation, and through similar and countless works proper to the one true God alone, the true Deity becomes known; and so we are stirred up to pursue the worship due to him. Ps. xix, 2, 3; Isa. xl, 26; Rom. i, 20; Rev. iv, 11; 1 Pet. iv, 19.

units.la: Obj. Alia etiam religiose colenda sunt, ob sanctitatem relativam, in ordine ad Deum: Exod. iii, 5. xix, 12. Gen. xxviii, 16, 17. Eccles. v, 1. &c. Ergo. Resp. Non ipsis locis, quorum ibi fit mentio, reverentia erat præstanda: sed Deo speciali modo illic præsenti.
units.tr: Objection: Other things too are to be worshipped religiously on account of their relative holiness, in relation to God: Exod. iii, 5; xix, 12; Gen. xxviii, 16, 17; Eccles. v, 1, etc. Therefore. Reply: Reverence was not to be paid to the places themselves that are mentioned there, but to God, who was specially present there.

units.la: Idem dicendum de Tabernaculo, Arcâ Fœderis, Templo, &c.
units.tr: The same must be said of the Tabernacle, the Ark of the Covenant, the Temple, etc.

units.la: LXXVI. Restat Beatitudo; actus consummatissimus, quo Deus omnes perfectiones absolute conceptibiles, tum essentiæ, tum vitæ, ejusque eminentissimæ, in se habet independenter, simplicissime, & infinite; atque hoc ipsum plenissime cognoscit, quàm maximè vult, eo fruitur perfectissime, cum acquiescentiâ.
units.tr: LXXVI. There remains blessedness: the most perfect act by which God has in himself, independently, most simply and infinitely, all perfections that can be conceived absolutely, both of essence and of life, and those in their most eminent form; and he knows this most fully, wills it as much as possible, and enjoys it most perfectly, with complete contentment.

units.la: 1 Tim. 1, 11. Evangelium Beati Dei. vi, 15. Beatus ille.
units.tr: 1 Tim. i, 11: the gospel of the blessed God; vi, 15: the blessed one.

units.la: Huc pertinet etiam appellatio אל שדי, Gen. xvii, 1.
units.tr: To this belongs also the name אל שדי, Gen. xvii, 1.

units.la: Ac descriptio Psal. xvi, 10. xxxvi, 10. Fons vitæ.
units.tr: And the description at Ps. xvi, 10; xxxvi, 10: the fountain of life.

units.la: Nec non consideratio eorum, quæ oculus non vidit, &c. quæ paravit Deus iis, à quibus ipse diligitur; 1 Cor. ii, 9. Istud enim est verissimum principium, ac fons omnis nostræ Beatitudinis. Confer 2 Cor. xv, 28.
units.tr: Likewise the consideration of those things which eye has not seen, etc., which God has prepared for those by whom he is loved: 1 Cor. ii, 9. For this is the most true principle and the source of all our blessedness. Compare 2 Cor. xv, 28.

units.la: LXXVII. Ex dictis quædam colligimus pro praxi. 1. Quicquid entis menti nostræ occurrit præter Deum, hoc omne ad ipsum referamus, tanquam ad ens primum, & in ejus gloriam: Iesl. xl, 26. Rom. xi, 36. Act. xvii, 25-28, 1 Cor. x, 31.
units.tr: LXXVII. From what has been said we draw some conclusions for practice. 1. Whatever being presents itself to our mind apart from God, we should refer it all to him, as to the first being, and to his glory: Isa. xl, 26; Rom. xi, 36; Acts xvii, 25–28; 1 Cor. x, 31.

units.la: 2. Nomina Dei non-nisi sancte & religiose usurpemus: Exod. xx, 7. Eccl. v, 1. xii, 1. Mal. iv, 2.
units.tr: 2. Let us use the names of God only holily and religiously: Exod. xx, 7; Eccles. v, 1; xii, 1; Mal. iv, 2.

units.la: 3. Ex Dei Primitate nostram, & omnium aliorum ab ipso dependentiam, recte æstimemus: Rom. xi, 36. Act. xvii, 28.
units.tr: 3. From the primacy of God, let us rightly estimate both our own dependence and that of all other things upon him: Rom. 11:36; Acts 17:28.

units.la: 4. Simplicitati nobis mandatæ, serio demus operam: am : 1 Cor. v, 7, 8. Hebr. xii, 1. 1 Petr. II, 1, 2.
units.tr: 4. To the simplicity enjoined upon us, let us give earnest effort: 1 Cor. 5:7, 8; Heb. 12:1; 1 Pet. 2:1, 2.

units.la: 5. In Dei Immutabilitate, constanter incorruptibilitatem & gloriam quæramus: Rom. II, 7.
units.tr: 5. In the immutability of God, let us constantly seek incorruptibility and glory: Rom. 2:7.

units.la: 6. Sic Deum invisibilem requiramus puro corde, ut ipsum fide videamus, ac tandem ipso fruamur: Jef. lv, 1, 2, 3, 6. Psal. xvi, 8, 11, 10. Matth. v, 8. Hebr. xi, 17.
units.tr: 6. Let us so seek the invisible God with a pure heart that we may see him by faith and at last enjoy him: Isa. 55:1, 2, 3, 6; Ps. 16:8, 11, 10; Matt. 5:8; Heb. 11:17.

units.la: 7. Desideria nostra piè ad Infinitum illum, atque Æternum, excitemus, dirigamus; qui solus eâ æternum perfectissimè satiare potest: Psal. xlii, 2, 3, xxiii, 1, 3-xvi, 5, 8, 11. xxxvi, 8, 11. 2 Cor. iv, 16, 17, 18. v. 1.
units.tr: 7. Let us piously stir up and direct our desires toward that Infinite and Eternal One, who alone can satisfy them perfectly forever: Ps. 42:2, 3; 23:1, 3; 16:5, 8, 11; 36:8, 11; 2 Cor. 4:16, 17, 18; 5:1.

units.la: 8. Immensum, nobis semper præsentem, omnia etiam abstrusissima intime cognoscentium, ex animo veneramur. Hebr. iv, 11, 13. Psal. cxxxix, 1, 2. 2 Chron. xxiv, 22. Job. xxi, 23.
units.tr: 8. We reverently venerate from the heart the Immense One, ever present to us, who knows intimately even the most hidden things: Heb. 4:11, 13; Ps. 139:1, 2; 2 Chron. 24:22; Job 21:23.

units.la: 9. Ex tenuitatis nostræ circa Dei cognitionem conscientiâ humiliemur profundissimè: 1 Cor. xiii, 11, 12. Gal. iv, 8, 9. 2 Petr. I, 19.
units.tr: 9. From a consciousness of our slight knowledge of God, let us be most deeply humbled: 1 Cor. 13:11, 12; Gal. 4:8, 9; 2 Pet. 1:19.

units.la: 10. In Dei Sapientiâ humiliter & piè quæramus sapientiam veram: Col. iii. 10. Jac. I, 5.
units.tr: 10. In the wisdom of God, let us humbly and piously seek true wisdom: Col. 3:10; James 1:5.

units.la: 11. Sanctissimæ ipsius Voluntati nostram voluntatem subjiciamus & conformemus: Matth. vi, 10. xxvi, 42. Act. xxi, 13, 14.
units.tr: 11. Let us subject and conform our own will to his most holy will: Matt. 6:10; 26:42; Acts 21:13, 14.

units.la: 12. Ex Sanctitate, Amore, Gratiâ, Misericordiâ, Patientiâ, &c. nostram ad eas virtutes analogicam conformationem discamus: Levit. xix, 2. Matth. xxii, 37. v, 44, 45. vi, 12. Gal. vi, 1. Jac. v, 19, 20.
units.tr: 12. From his holiness, love, grace, mercy, patience, etc., let us learn an analogical conformity of ourselves to those virtues: Lev. 19:2; Matt. 22:37; 5:44, 45; 6:12; Gal. 6:1; James 5:19, 20.

units.la: 13. Omnipotenti ejus manui nos quàm humillimè submittamus; simulque impotentiam nostram agnoscentes, omnem adversus hostes nostros spirituales corroborationem in ipso quæramus: 1 Petr. v, 6. 2 Cor. xii, 9. Joh. x. 28, 29, Rom. viii, 28.
units.tr: 13. Let us submit ourselves as humbly as possible to his almighty hand; and, at the same time acknowledging our own weakness, let us seek in him all strengthening against our spiritual enemies: 1 Pet. 5:6; 2 Cor. 12:9; John 10:28, 29; Rom. 8:28.

units.la: 14. Supremæ Potestati Omnipotentis Dei conscientias nostras omnino, & quidem soli, subjiciamus. Rom. xiv, 9, Jerem. x, 7. Apoc. xv. 4.
units.tr: 14. Let us subject our consciences wholly, and to him alone, to the supreme power of Almighty God: Rom. 14:9; Jer. 10:7; Rev. 15:4.

units.la: 15. Ipsi gloriam suam deferamus sincerè ac prompte: Psal.cııı,1,2. Luc.I,46,47, 74, 75. Matth. vı, 9, 13. Rom.xı, 36. 1 Cor. x, 31.
units.tr: 15. Let us ascribe his glory to him sincerely and promptly: Ps. 103:1, 2; Luke 1:46, 47, 74, 75; Matt. 6:9, 13; Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 10:31.

units.la: 16. In Deo Beatissimo omnem nostram beatitudinem unicè quæramus: Psal.xxxııı, 12. Ixxııı,25, 26. 1 Joh. I, 3, 4.
units.tr: 16. In the most blessed God let us seek all our blessedness solely: Ps. 33:12; 73:25, 26; 1 John 1:3, 4.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Personis Divinis.
units.tr: Of the Divine Persons.

units.la: EXistentia. Perseitas. Suppositum. 1. Subsistentia, ὑπόστασις, abstractè: concretè. Persona.2. Essentia Divina quomodò prædicetur de Personis. Tres Personæ sunt in unâ Essentia. Et Persona istæ in se invicem. Personæ Divinæ descriptio. Terminus ὑπόστασις: & alii hic usitati. Numerus. 3. Probatur Personarum pluralitas. 4. Trinitas; ex V.T. collatis locis N.T. 5. Ex testimoniis N.T. 6. Probantur singulæ Personæ. Pater. Ejus Personalitas. 7. Vera Deitas. 8. Distinctio à Filio, & Sp. S. 9. An rectè dicatur, Fons & principium totius Deitatis? 10. Filius. Ejus Personalitas. 11. Deitas, probatur ex Nominibus. 12. Operibus. 14. Cultū. 15. Proprietates distinctivæ. 16. De voce Spiritus. Spiritūs Sancti Personalitas. 17. Deitas, ex Nominibus. 18. Attributis. 19. Operibus. 20. Cultū. 21. Distinctio à Patre & Filio. 22. Trium Personarum identitas essentialis. τὸ ὁμοούσιον. Paritas & Similitudo. Filius & Spir. S. etiam αὐτόθεος. ἐμχειροτονίας. 23. Rejicitur Atheismus. Arianif-
units.tr: Existence. Self-subsistence. Suppositum. 1. Subsistence [ὑπόστασις], taken abstractly and concretely. Person. 2. How the Divine Essence is predicated of the Persons. There are three Persons in one Essence, and these Persons are in one another. Description of the Divine Person. The term hypostasis and other terms commonly used here. Number. 3. The plurality of Persons is proved. 4. The Trinity, from Old Testament passages compared with New Testament passages. 5. From New Testament testimonies. 6. Each Person is proved. The Father: his personality. 7. True Deity. 8. Distinction from the Son and the Holy Spirit. 9. Whether it is rightly said that he is the fountain and principle of the whole Deity. 10. The Son: his personality. 11. His Deity, proved from the names. 12. From the works. 14. From worship. 15. Distinctive properties. 16. On the word Spirit. The personality of the Holy Spirit. 17. His Deity, from the names. 18. From the attributes. 19. From the works. 20. From worship. 21. Distinction from the Father and the Son. 22. The essential identity of the three Persons. Homoousion [τὸ ὁμοούσιον]. Equality and likeness. The Son and the Holy Spirit are also autotheos [αὐτόθεος], and self-appointed [ἐμχειροτονίας]. 23. Atheism, Arianism, Socinianism and Sabellianism are rejected.

units.la: mus, Socinianismus. Sabellianismus. 24. Discrimen inter Generationem, & Spirationem. Illa non recte explicatur per actum Intellectus; & hac per actum Voluntatis. 25. Relationes reales. Processiones. Notiones. Proprietates personales. Actus notionales. Potentia notionales. Relationes rationis. Origo Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. 26. Quomodo Persona Divina differat ab Essentia, 27. Quomodo Persona distinguantur a se invicem. 28. Objectiones solvuntur. 29. Dogma hoc fundamentale est, & ad salutem creditu necessarium. c. Remonstr. Obj. solv. 30. Usus practici. 31.
units.tr: ism, Socinianism, Sabellianism. 24. The difference between generation and spiration. The former is not rightly explained through an act of the intellect, nor the latter through an act of the will. 25. Real relations. Processions. Notions. Personal properties. Notional acts. Notional powers. Relations of reason. The origin of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. 26. How a Divine Person differs from the Essence. 27. How the Persons are distinguished from one another. 28. Objections are answered. 29. This doctrine is fundamental and necessary to be believed for salvation. Against the Remonstrants: objections answered. 30. Practical uses. 31.

units.la: I. Equitur, ut Essentiam Dei consideremus relate in suis Personis.
units.tr: I. It follows that we consider the Essence of God in relation to his Persons.

units.la: Existentia in genere est Actualitas Entis: primo quidem Substantiae; cui Perfeitas competit: sed analogice etiam Accidentis; cujus esse est inesse.
units.tr: Existence, in general, is the actuality of a being: primarily of a substance, to which perfect existence belongs, but also, by analogy, of an accident, whose being is to inhere.

units.la: Interim Substantiae secundae existunt in primis; sicut & aliae partes in suo toto. Quae autem incommunicabiliter, complete, & ultimate per se existunt, strictiore sensu subsistere dicuntur; & absolute suppositia vocantur, Graecis ὑφιστάμενα. Animam vero separatam, aliamve partem seorsum existentem, Suppositum partiale dicimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile, secondary substances exist in primary ones, just as other parts exist in their whole. Those things, however, which exist of themselves incommunicably, completely and ultimately are said to subsist in the stricter sense, and are called supposita absolutely; in Greek hyphistamena [ὑφιστάμενα]. We call a separated soul, or any other part existing on its own, a partial suppositum.

units.la: 11. Subsistentia, Graece ὑπόστασις alias rem quamlibet sub alia stantem, & eam quodammodo sustentantem, notat: sed specialius interdum abstracte usurpatur, ut designet modum entitativum, quo natura substantialis ultimo, complete, & incommunicabiliter terminatur in exiftendo: qui modus etiàm fuppofitalitas appellatur; fed fpecialiffime in intelleƈtualibus perfonalitas. Concrete autem fignificat naturam fubftantialem tali modo fubfiftendi terminatam.
units.tr: II. Subsistence, in Greek hypostasis [ὑπόστασις], elsewhere denotes any thing standing under another and in some way sustaining it; but more specifically it is sometimes used abstractly, to designate the entitative mode by which a substantial nature is ultimately, completely and incommunicably terminated in existing. This mode is also called suppositality, and in intellectual beings, most specifically, personality. Taken concretely, it signifies a substantial nature terminated in such a mode of subsisting.

units.la: Suppofitum intelleƈtuale perfona appellatur; Græce ὑπόστατον: quæ nonnullis à perfonando dicta videtur: fed verba valent usû. Interim non difplicet allufio, quafi per fe una; aut per fe fola. Defcribitur plenius, Subftantia prima, intelligens, incommunicabilis, non pars alterius, nec ab alio fuftentata.
units.tr: An intellectual suppositum is called a person, in Greek hypostaton [ὑπόστατον]. Some think it is named from personando (sounding through), but words derive their value from usage. Meanwhile, an allusion does no harm, as if it were one through itself, or alone through itself. It is described more fully thus: a first substance, intelligent, incommunicable, not a part of another, nor sustained by another.

units.la: III. Effentia Dei unica eft. Vide fup. cap. 4. th. 19. fed communis tribus Perfonis, ut & Attributa ejus.
units.tr: III. The Essence of God is one. See above, chapter 4, thesis 19. But it is common to the three Persons, as are also his Attributes.

units.la: Confequenter Effentia non prædicatur de Perfonis, ut Species de fuis Individuis: una enim eademque Effentia fingularisfima, exiftit in tribus Perfonis concrete.
units.tr: Consequently, the Essence is not predicated of the Persons as a species is of its individuals; for one and the same, most singular Essence exists concretely in the three Persons.

units.la: Rectè etiam dicimus, tres Perfonas effe in unâ iftâ Effentiâ; quatenùs in communione ejufdem numero Effentiæ conveniunt. Imò etiam, Perfonas iftas effe in fe invicem; quatenùs communis Effentia in fingulis Perfonis exiftit. Vide Joh. x, 38. xiv, 11. xvii, 21.
units.tr: We rightly also say that the three Persons are in this one Essence, insofar as they share in the same numerically one Essence. Indeed, we also say that these Persons are in one another, insofar as the common Essence exists in each of the Persons. See John 10:38; 14:11; 17:21.

units.la: Perfona Divina eft ipfa Effentia Divina peculiari modo fubfiftendi à coëffentialibus diftinƈta.
units.tr: A Divine Person is the Divine Essence itself, distinguished from its co-essential persons by a peculiar mode of subsisting.

units.la: Eftque terminus ille ὑπόστασις. Hebr. 1, 3. de Filio; Character perfonæ (τῆς ὑποστάσεως) illius; fcil. Patris. Confer 1 Joh. v, 7. Tres funt, qui teftificantur in Cœlo, Pater, Sermo & Spiritus Sanctus. Unicæ iftius Effentiæ Tres funt Perfonæ teftificantes. Unde Triada, vel Trinitatem rectè appellamus; non Triplicitatem.
units.tr: And that term is hypostasis [ὑπόστασις]: Heb. 1:3, of the Son, the character of his person (τῆς ὑποστάσεως), namely of the Father. Compare 1 John 5:7, There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. Three Persons bear witness to this one Essence. Hence we rightly call it a Triad or Trinity, not a triplicity.

units.la: Numerus autem ille eft tantum Denominatio Perfonarum plurium verè diftinƈtarum.
units.tr: Number, however, is merely a designation of several Persons truly distinct.

units.la: Aliæ voces in hoc myfterio etiam ufurpari folitæ, utpotè, τρίας, ὁμοούσιος, ἐμφανής. γένεσις, &c. secundum rem Scripturariæ sunt: quod observandum contra Antitrinitarios, & Pontificios, ad Traditiones non scriptas hic confugientes.
units.tr: Other words commonly used in this mystery, such as trias [τρίας], homoousios [ὁμοούσιος], emphanēs [ἐμφανής], genesis [γένεσις], and so on, are scriptural in substance. This must be noted against the Antitrinitarians and the Papists, who here take refuge in unwritten Traditions.

units.la: IV. In Mysterio hoc probamus primò pluralitatem personarum, per testimonia sacra V. T. Gen. 1, 1, 2. in principio creavit Deus (בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים) cœlum & terram. – & Spiritus Dei incubat superficiei aquarum. Et verf. 26, 27. Postea dixit Deus Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. 111, 22. Dixit Jehovah Deus. Ecce homo, estne sicut unus ex nobis? xi, 7. Agedum descendamus, & confundamus ibi sermonem eorum. xix, 24. Jehovah demisit, pluviam sulphuris, & ignis, à Iehova Psal. xlv: 8, Unxit Te, ô Deus, Deus Tuus, oleo gaudii præ consortibus Tuis. Confer Hebr. 1. 8, 9, Iterùm Psal. cx. 1, Dixit Jehovah Domino meo; Sede ad dexteram meam, cum Matth. xxii, 42, 43. 44. Item Prov. xxx, 4. Quod est nomen Hujus, & quod nomen Filii ipsius? Jes. xlviii, 16. Nunc enim Dominus Iehovi mittit Me, & Spiritus ejus. His adde Dan. ix, 17. cum Psal. lxxx, 15, 16. & Hos. i. 7.
units.tr: IV. In this mystery we prove, first, the plurality of Persons, through the sacred testimonies of the Old Testament. Gen. 1:1, 2: In the beginning God created (בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים) the heaven and the earth; and the Spirit of God hovered over the surface of the waters. And verses 26, 27: Afterwards God said, Let us make man in our image. 3:22: Jehovah God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us. 11:7: Come, let us go down and confound their speech there. 19:24: Jehovah rained down brimstone and fire from Jehovah. Ps. 45:8: God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. Compare Heb. 1:8, 9. Again Ps. 110:1: Jehovah said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, with Matt. 22:42, 43, 44. Likewise Prov. 30:4: What is his name, and what is his Son's name? Isa. 48:16: For now the Lord Jehovah sends me, and his Spirit. To these add Dan. 9:17 with Ps. 80:15, 16, and Hos. 1:7.

units.la: V. Secundò adstruimus nominatim Trinitatem, & quidem hâc vice ex locis quibusdam V. T. collatis potissimum cum locis N. T. utpote Psal. xxxiii, 6. Verbo Jehovæ cœli facti sunt: & Spiritu oris ejus, totus exercitus eorum, cum Joh. 1, 1: 3, 10. In principio erat Sermo ille, & Sermo ille erat apud Deum, eratque ille Sermo Deus. – Omnia per Hunc facta sunt; & absque Eo factum est nihil quod factum sit. – Et mundus per Eum factus est: sed mundus Eum non agnovit. Nec non Hebr. I, 10. Ad Filium: Et Tu in initio Dominus, terram fundasti; & opera manuum Tuarum sunt cœli. Jes vi, 1, 3, 8, 9. Tum vidi Iehovam insidentem solio celso. De Seraphim autem, Inclamans alter ad alterum dicebat; Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus est Jehovah Tzebaoth. – Deinde audivi vocem Domini, dicentis : Quem missurus sum, & quis iturus est nobis? Cui dixi ; En ego : mitte me, Tum dixit : ut dicas populo isti : Audite indesinenter, at ne intelligatis, &c. cum Ioh. xii, 36.-41. Hæc locutus est Iesus : Propterea non poterant credere, quia iterùm dixit Esaias ; Excæcavit oculos eorum, &c. Hæc dixit Esaias, quando vidit gloriam Ejus, & locutus est de Eo. Nec non Act. xxviii, 25, 26. Bene sanè Spiritus Sanctus locutus est per Esaiam Prophetam patribus nostris, dicens ; Vade ad populum istum, & dic ; Audietis, & non intelligetis; Ita scil. τριάγιον illud ad tres Personas pertinet. Confer trinam Jehovæ mentionem in solenni benedictione ; Num. vi, 24, 25, 26. Iterum Isa. lxi, 1. Spiritus Domini Jehova est super Me, ad Euangelizandum mansuetis, &c. cum Luc. iv, 17, - 22. Tunc datus est Ei (Christo) liber Esaiæ Prophetæ : cumque explicuisset librum, invenit locum, in quo scriptum erat, Spiritus Domini super Me, propterea quòd unxit me, &c. Coepit autem eis dicere; Certè hodie impleta est hæc Scriptura audientibus vobis &c. Ergo Filius Christus loquebatur de Jehovâ Patre, & Spiritu Ejus.
units.tr: V. Second, we assert the Trinity by name, and this time chiefly from certain Old Testament passages compared with New Testament passages. For example, Ps. 33:6: By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host, with John 1:1, 3, 10: In the beginning was that Word, and that Word was with God, and that Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him was nothing made that was made. And the world was made through him, but the world did not know him. Also Heb. 1:10, spoken to the Son: And thou, Lord, in the beginning hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands. Isa. 6:1, 3, 8, 9: Then I saw Jehovah sitting on a high throne. Concerning the seraphim, one cried to another, saying, Holy, holy, holy is Jehovah of hosts. Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? To which I said, Here am I; send me. And he said: Go and tell this people, Hear continually, but do not understand, etc., with John 12:36-41: Jesus spoke these things; therefore they could not believe, because again Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes, etc. Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. Also Acts 28:25, 26: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers, saying, Go to this people and say, You will hear and not understand. So, namely, that trisagion [τρισάγιον] pertains to the three Persons. Compare the threefold mention of Jehovah in the solemn blessing, Num. 6:24, 25, 26. Again Isa. 61:1: The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me, to preach good news to the meek, etc., with Luke 4:17-22: Then the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him (Christ), and when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, etc. And he began to say to them: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing, etc. Therefore the Son, Christ, was speaking of Jehovah the Father and of his Spirit.

units.la: Similiter Isa. lxiii, 7, - 11. Benignitates Jehovæ commemorabo : Nam dixit : Utique populus Meus sunt: - Angelus faciei ejus servavit eos: - Nam ipsis rebellantibus, & dolore afficientibus Spiritum sanctitatis ejus, &c. Confer etiam 2 Sam. xxiii, 2. Hag. 2, 5, 6.
units.tr: Similarly, Isa. 63:7-11: "I will commemorate the kindnesses of the LORD." For he said: "Surely they are my people." "The angel of his presence saved them." For when they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, etc. Compare also 2 Sam. 23:2 and Hag. 2:5, 6.

units.la: VI. Tertiò, clariora interim sunt testimonia N. T. utpote Matth. iii, 16, 17. Baptizatus Iesus - vidit Spiritum Dei descendentem quasi columbam ; - & ecce, vox adfuit è cælo. Hic est Filius ille Meus, &c. xxviii, 19, - Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. 2 Cor. xiii, 13. Gratia Domini Iesu Christi, charitas Dei, & communicatio Spiritus ,,Sancti sit cum omnibus vobis. 1 Joh. v,17. Tres sunt qui testificantur in cœlo; Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus Sanctus. His adde Joh. xiv, 16, 17. xv. 26. Luc. 1. 35. Rom. 1, 4. viii, 11, Gal. iv, 4, 6.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly, the testimonies of the New Testament are for the time being clearer, such as Matt. 3:16, 17: when Jesus was baptized, he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and behold, a voice came from heaven: "This is my beloved Son," etc. Matt. 28:19: "Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." 2 Cor. 13:13: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." 1 John 5:7: "There are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit." To these add John 14:16, 17; 15:26; Luke 1:35; Rom. 1:4; 8:11; Gal. 4:4, 6.

units.la: VII. Quarto denique consideranda veniunt illa SS. Literarum testimonia, quae singulas Personas Divinas Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum diserte tradunt, & distinctam earum personalitatem, ac veram Deitatem plane adstruunt.
units.tr: VII. Fourthly and finally, there come to be considered those testimonies of the holy Scriptures which expressly set forth the individual divine Persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and plainly establish their distinct personality and true deity.

units.la: Patrem hic appellamus respectu Filii aeterni, & ὁμοούσιος: Hebr. 1,5. cum Psal. II,7. & 2 Sam. vii, 14. Nam cui dixit unquam Angelorum: Filius Meus es Tu: ,,Ego hodie genui Te; Ac rursum; Ego ero Ei Pater, & Ipse erit Mihi Filius.
units.tr: Here we call him Father with respect to the eternal Son, who is ὁμοούσιος [of one substance] with him: Heb. 1:5 with Ps. 2:7 and 2 Sam. 7:14. For to which of the angels did he ever say: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you"? And again: "I will be his Father, and he will be my Son."

units.la: Quantum ad ipsius Personalitatem: expresse Hebr. 1,3. De Filio; quod fit character Personae illius: scil. Patris. Ipsi etiam competit vita, intellectus, voluntas, dominium, gloria, operationes, paternitas: Joh. v,26. Pater habet vitam in Seipso. 17. Pater Meus usque adhuc operatur. Matth. xi, 25, 26, 27. ,,Gloriam Tibi ,,tribuo Pater, Domine coeli & terrae; quod haec occultaveris a sapientibus & intelligentibus: & retexeris ea ,,infantibus. Etiam Pater, quia ita placuit Tibi. Omnia ,,Mihi tradita sunt a Patre Meo: & nemo novit Filium, ,,nisi Pater, &c. Vide etiam Joh. xvii, 1.
units.tr: As to his personality: expressly Heb. 1:3, where the Son is said to be the character of that Person, namely of the Father. To him also belong life, understanding, will, dominion, glory, operations, and paternity: John 5:26, "The Father has life in himself"; 5:17, "My Father is working until now." Matt. 11:25-27: "I give you thanks, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was pleasing to you. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father," etc. See also John 17:1.

units.la: VIII. Deitas autem ejus evincitur, 1. Nominibus Divinis: Joh. iii, 16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum miserit, &c. Adde viii, 54. xvii, 1. 3.
units.tr: VIII. His deity is proved, 1. from the divine names: John 3:16, "God so loved the world that he sent his only-begotten Son," etc. Add John 8:54; 17:1, 3.

units.la: 2. Attributis: Apoc. 1, 4. de Patre; ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν ὁ ἐρχόμενος: unde satis patet Aeternitas & Immutabilitas. Joh. v, 26. Habet vitam in Seipso. Quae est Independentia, Matth. xi, 25. Pater, Domine coeli & terrae. Quod est Dominium vere supremum.
units.tr: 2. From the attributes: Rev. 1:4 of the Father, "the one who is, who was, and who is to come" [ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν ὁ ἐρχόμενος], whence his eternity and immutability are sufficiently plain. John 5:26, "He has life in himself," which is independence. Matt. 11:25, "Father, Lord of heaven and earth," which is truly supreme dominion.

units.la: 3. Operibus Divinis: Act. iv, 24, -27. Domine, Tu es ille Deus, qui fecisti coelum & terram, mare & omnia quae in iis sunt. - Congregati sunt in hac civitate vere adversus sanctum Filium Tuum Jesum, quem unxisti, Herodes, &c. Ut facerent quaecunque manus Tua & consilium Tuum prius praedestinavit ut fierent. Nunc igitur, Domine, dispice in minas eorum; & da Servis Tuis, ut cum omni libertate loquantur sermonem Tuum, Manu Tua a Te extensa ad sanandum, signisque & prodigiis editis per nomen sancti Filii tui Jesu.
units.tr: 3. From the divine works: Acts 4:24-27: "Lord, you are that God who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them. For truly, in this city, there were gathered together against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod, etc., to do whatever your hand and your counsel had predestined to come to pass. Now therefore, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are done through the name of your holy Son Jesus."

units.la: 4. Denique ex Cultu & Honore religioso: Phil. 2, 11. - ad Gloriam Dei Patris. Matth. XVIII, 19. Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris; -. Confer Matth. XI, 25. -. Joh. XVII, 1. -. Act. IV, 24. -.
units.tr: 4. Finally, from religious worship and honour: Phil. 2:11, "to the glory of God the Father"; Matt. 18:19, "baptizing them in the name of the Father"; compare Matt. 11:25; John 17:1; Acts 4:24.

units.la: IX. Distinctio Patris a Filio & Spiritu Sancto est in Notionibus, seu Proprietatibus quibusdam characteristicis; quales sunt 1. Aseitas personalis: Pater prorsus non habet originem ab alio; sed per se subsistentiam suam & vitam habet in Se ipso: cum ipse Filio dederit vitam habere in Se ipso; Joh. V, 26. Agennetos Veteres dixerunt: Scholastici Innascibilitatem vocant; sed & Inspirabilitatem recte addidissent.
units.tr: IX. The distinction of the Father from the Son and the Holy Spirit lies in the notions, or certain characteristic properties, which are: 1. personal aseity: the Father has no origin at all from another, but has his subsistence and life of himself, in that he has given the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26). The ancients called him ἀγέννητος [unbegotten]; the Schoolmen call it innascibility, but they would have done well to add inspirability as well.

units.la: 2. Generatio activa; quae est actus peculiaris primae Personae, per quem ipsa est principium secundae. Unde illa Pater, secunda autem Filius dicitur. Atque adeo Filius vere est homoousios & autotheos; ejusdem numero Essentiae, ac verae Deitatis: Vide Hebr. 1, 3. Joh. V, 26. Psal. 2, 7. cum Hebr. 1, 5, V, 5. Act. XIII, 33.
units.tr: 2. Active generation, which is the particular act of the first Person, by which he is the principle of the second Person. Hence the first is called Father, and the second Son. And so the Son is truly homoousios [of one substance] and autotheos [God of himself], of the same numerical essence and true deity. See Heb. 1:3; John 5:26; Ps. 2:7, with Heb. 1:5; 5:5; Acts 13:33.

units.la: 3. Spiratio activa cum Filio; quae est actus notionalis; per quem Pater cum Filio est principium tertiae Personae; quae inde Spiritus Sanctus appellatur, Joh. XV, 26. Advocatus ille, quem Ego mittam vobis a Patre: Spiritus ille veritatis, qui a Patre emanat.
units.tr: 3. Active spiration with the Son, which is a notional act, by which the Father, together with the Son, is the principle of the third Person, who is therefore called the Holy Spirit (John 15:26): that Advocate whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.

units.la: 4. Primitas ordinis personalis in subsistendo: Pater enim prior est Filio, & Spiritu Sancto; cum istarum Personarum principium sit.
units.tr: 4. Priority of personal order in subsisting: the Father is indeed prior to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, since he is the principle of these Persons.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: §. Primitus ordinis personalis in operando, Pater enim operatur à se; Filius à Patre; & Spiritus Sanctus ab utroque. Vide Eph. iii, 15. Joh. iii, 16, 17. Gal. iv, 6. Joh. xv, 26. Hebr. I, 2. Psal. xxxiii, 6. 1 Cor. 2, 10.
units.tr: §. The first place in the personal order is in operating: the Father operates from himself, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. See Eph. 3:15; John 3:16, 17; Gal. 4:6; John 15:26; Heb. 1:2; Ps. 33:6; 1 Cor. 2:10.

units.la: X. Quaeritur, an Pater rectè dicatur fons & principium totius Deitatis; Resp. Plures Theologi orthodoxi sic quidem loquuntur sano sensu; attamen modus iste loquendi est ἀκυρόλογος, non accuratus: Deitas enim est natura Divina, cujus absolutè nullum est principium, nullus fons. Praeterea, si Pater esset principium totius Deitatis, suae quoque Essentiae principium foret: quod absurdum. Sed prima Persona est principium ejus, quòd Persona secunda & tertia habeant eandem quoque veram Deitatem. Atque hoc benè tenendum contra Vorstium & Episcopium.
units.tr: X. It is asked whether the Father may rightly be called the fountain and principle of the whole Deity. Answer: Several orthodox theologians speak in this way in a sound sense; yet this manner of speaking is inaccurate [ἀκυρόλογος], not precise. For the Deity is the divine nature, which absolutely has no principle and no fountain. Moreover, if the Father were the principle of the whole Deity, he would also be the principle of his own essence, which is absurd. But the first Person is the principle of the Deity in the sense that the second and third Persons have the same true Deity too. This must be firmly held against Vorstius and Episcopius.

units.la: XI. Filius Hebr. 1, 3. dicitur character personae Patris; sed & ipse persona: competit enim ipsi existentia: Joh. viii, 58. 1 Tim. iii, 16. vita; Joh. v, 26. intellectus, voluntas, & variae operationes; quae non possunt nisi personae competere: Matth. xi, 27. "Neque Patrem quisquam novit, nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius retegere.
units.tr: XI. The Son is called the character of the person of the Father (Heb. 1:3), but he is also a person himself, for existence belongs to him (John 8:58; 1 Tim. 3:16), and life (John 5:26), understanding, will, and various operations, which can belong only to a person: Matt. 11:27: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him."

units.la: Obj. Prov. viii. Sapientia appellatur: ergò. Resp: Sed ea hypostatica intelligenda est necessariò: idcircò dicitur amare amatores suos, uncta ante saeculum, edita ante abyssos, &c. verf. 17, 23, 24, 25.
units.tr: Objection: Prov. 8 calls Wisdom [the Son]; therefore... Answer: But that wisdom must necessarily be understood hypostatically; for this reason it is said to love those who love it, to have been brought forth before all ages, before the abysses, etc., vv. 17, 23, 24, 25.

units.la: XII. Probatur porrò ejus vera Deitas, primo Nominibus Divinis: tùm attributive, tùm subjectivè. Joh. 1, 1. Erat Sermo ille Deus. cum 14. Et Sermo ille factus est caro. 1 Tim. iii. 16. Deus conspicuus factus est in carne. Act. xx, 28. "Ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo ille proprio sanguine acquisivit. Phil. II, 6. "Cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam esse parem cum Deo. Imò etiàm additis illustribus epithetis, Jes. ix, 5. "Puer natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis: Vocabitur nomen ejus Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis.
units.tr: XII. Furthermore, his true Deity is proved, first, by the divine names, both attributively and subjectively. John 1:1: "The Word was God"; and verse 14: "The Word was made flesh." 1 Tim. 3:16: "God was made manifest in the flesh." Acts 20:28: "to feed the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood." Phil. 2:6: "Though he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God." Indeed, with illustrious epithets added as well, Isa. 9:5: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us; his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God."

units.la: Pater miliaque opera soli vero Deo propria, innotescat vera Deitas; atque ita excitemur, ad eam cultu ipsi debita prosequendam. Psal. xix, 2, 3. Ies. xl, 26. Rom. i, 20. Apoc. iv, 11. 1 Petr. iv, 19.
units.tr: The Father and the many works proper to the one true God make the true Deity known, and so we are stirred up to pursue it with the worship due to him. Ps. 19:2, 3; Isa. 40:26; Rom. 1:20; Rev. 4:11; 1 Pet. 4:19.

units.la: Obj. Alia etiam religiose colenda sunt, ob sanctitatem relativam, in ordine ad Deum: Exod. iii, 5. xix, 12. Gen. xxviii, 16, 17. Eccles. v, 1. &c. Ergo. Resp. Non ipsis locis, quorum ibi fit mentio, reverentia erat praestanda: sed Deo speciali modo illic praesenti.
units.tr: Objection: Other things also are to be religiously revered on account of a relative holiness, in relation to God: Exod. 3:5; 19:12; Gen. 28:16, 17; Eccl. 5:1, etc. Therefore... Answer: Reverence was not to be paid to the places themselves that are mentioned there, but to God, who was present there in a special way.

units.la: Idem dicendum de Tabernaculo, Arca Foederis, Templo, &c.
units.tr: The same must be said of the Tabernacle, the Ark of the Covenant, the Temple, etc.

units.la: LXXVI. Restat Beatitudo, actus consummatissimus, quo Deus omnes perfectiones absolute conceptibiles, tum essentiae, tum vitae, ejusque eminentissimae, in se habet independenter, simplicissime, & infinite; atque hoc ipsum plenissime cognoscit, quam maxime vult, eo fruitur perfectissime, cum acquiescentia.
units.tr: LXXVI. There remains blessedness, the most complete act, by which God has in himself, independently, most simply and infinitely, all perfections conceivable absolutely, both of essence and of life, and of the most eminent kind; and he knows this itself most fully, wills it most of all, and enjoys it most perfectly, with contentment.

units.la: 1 Tim. i, 11: Euangelium Beati Dei. vi, 15. Beatus ille.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 1:11: "the gospel of the blessed God"; 6:15: "the blessed one."

units.la: Huc pertinet etiam appellatio אל שדי, Gen. xvii, 1.
units.tr: To this belongs also the appellation El Shaddai [אל שדי], Gen. 17:1.

units.la: Ac descriptio Psal. xvi, 10. xxxvi, 10. Fons vitae.
units.tr: And the description in Ps. 16:10; 36:10: "the fountain of life."

units.la: Nec non consideratio eorum, quae oculus non vidit, &c. quae paravit Deus iis, a quibus ipse diligitur; 1 Cor. ii, 9. Istud enim est verissimum principium, ac fons omnis nostrae Beatitudinis. Confer 2 Cor. xv, 28.
units.tr: Also the consideration of "the things which eye has not seen," etc., which God has prepared for those by whom he is loved: 1 Cor. 2:9. For this is the most true principle and fountain of all our blessedness. Compare 2 Cor. 15:28.

units.la: LXXVII. Ex dictis quaedam colligimus pro praxi.
units.tr: LXXVII. From what has been said we draw some conclusions for practice.

units.la: 1. Quicquid entis menti nostrae occurrit praeter Deum, hoc omne ad ipsum referamus, tanquam ad ens primum, & in ejus gloriam: Ies. xl, 26. Rom. xi, 36. Act. xvii, 25-28, 1 Cor. x, 31.
units.tr: 1. Whatever being meets our mind apart from God, we should refer all of it to him as the first being, and to his glory: Isa. 40:26; Rom. 11:36; Acts 17:25–28; 1 Cor. 10:31.

units.la: 2. Nomina Dei non-nisi sancte & religiose usurpemus: Exod. xx, 7. Eccl. v, 1. xii, 1. Mal. iv. 2.
units.tr: 2. Let us use the names of God only holily and reverently: Exod. 20:7; Eccl. 5:1; 12:1; Mal. 4:2.

units.la: 3. Ex Dei Primitate nostram, & omnium aliorum ab ipso dependentiam, recte aestimemus: Rom. xi, 36. Act. xvii, 28.
units.tr: 3. From God's primacy let us rightly estimate our own dependence, and that of all others, on him: Rom. 11:36; Acts 17:28.

units.la: 4. Simplicitati nobis mandatae, serio demus operam : 1 Cor. v, 7, 8. Hebr. xii, 1. 1 Petr. II, 1, 2.
units.tr: 4. Let us earnestly labour toward the simplicity enjoined on us: 1 Cor. 5:7, 8; Heb. 12:1; 1 Pet. 2:1, 2.

units.la: 5. In Dei Immutabilitate, constanter incorruptibilitatem & gloriam quæramus: Rom. II, 7.
units.tr: 5. In God's immutability, let us constantly seek incorruptibility and glory: Rom. 2:7.

units.la: 6. Sic Deum invisibilem requiramus puro corde, ut ipsum fide videamus, ac tandem ipso fruamur: Jef. Iv, 1, 2, 3, 6. Pfal. xvi, 8, 11, 10. Matth. v, 8. Hebr. xi, 17.
units.tr: 6. Let us so seek the invisible God with a pure heart that we may see him by faith and at last enjoy him: Isa. 4:1, 2, 3, 6; Ps. 16:8, 11, 10; Matt. 5:8; Heb. 11:17.

units.la: 7. Desideria nostra pie ad Infinitum illum, atque Æternum, excitemus, dirigamus; qui solus eâ æternum perfectissime satiare potest: Pfal. xliii, 2, 3, xxiii, 1, - xvi, 5, 8, 11. xxxvi, 8, - 11. 2 Cor. iv, 16, 17, 18. v. 1, -
units.tr: 7. Let us piously stir up and direct our desires toward that Infinite and Eternal One, who alone can satisfy them perfectly for eternity: Ps. 43:2, 3; 23:1; 16:5, 8, 11; 36:8–11; 2 Cor. 4:16, 17, 18; 5:1.

units.la: 8. Immensum, nobis semper præsentem, omnia etiam abstrusissima intime cognoscentium, ex animo vereamur. Hebr. iv, 11, 13. Pfal. cxxxix, 1, - 2 Chron. xxiv, 22. Job. xxi, 23.
units.tr: 8. Let us fear from the heart the Immense One, ever present to us, who knows intimately even the most hidden things: Heb. 4:11, 13; Ps. 139:1, 2; 2 Chron. 24:22; Job 21:23.

units.la: 9. Ex tenuitatis nostræ circa Dei cognitionem conscientiâ humiliemur profundissime: 1 Cor. xiii, 11, 12. Gal. iv, 8, 9. 2 Petr. I, 19.
units.tr: 9. Let us be most deeply humbled by the awareness of our slightness in the knowledge of God: 1 Cor. 13:11, 12; Gal. 4:8, 9; 2 Pet. 1:19.

units.la: 10. In Dei Sapientiâ humiliter & pie quæramus sapientiam veram: Col. iii. 10. Jac. I, 5.
units.tr: 10. In God's wisdom let us humbly and piously seek true wisdom: Col. 3:10; James 1:5.

units.la: 11. Sanctissimæ ipsius Voluntati nostram voluntatem subjiciamus & conformemus: Matth. vi, 10. xxvi, 42. Act. xxi, 13, 14.
units.tr: 11. Let us subject and conform our will to his most holy will: Matt. 6:10; 26:42; Acts 21:13, 14.

units.la: 12. Ex Sanctitate, Amore, Gratiâ, Misericordiâ, Patientiâ, &c. nostram ad eas virtutes analogicam conformationem discamus: Levit. xix, 2. Matth. xxii, 37. v, 44, 45. vi, 12. Gal. vi, 1. Jac. v, 19, 20.
units.tr: 12. From his holiness, love, grace, mercy, patience, etc., let us learn to conform ourselves analogically to those virtues: Lev. 19:2; Matt. 22:37; 5:44, 45; 6:12; Gal. 6:1; James 5:19, 20.

units.la: 13. Omnipotenti ejus manui nos quàm humillime submittamus; simulque impotentiam nostram agnoscentes, omnem adversus hostes nostros spirituales corroborationem in ipso quæramus: 1 Petr. v, 6. 2 Cor. xii, 9. Joh. x. 28, 29, Rom. viii, 28.
units.tr: 13. Let us submit ourselves as humbly as possible to his almighty hand; and at the same time, acknowledging our own powerlessness, let us seek in him all strengthening against our spiritual enemies: 1 Pet. 5:6; 2 Cor. 12:9; John 10:28, 29; Rom. 8:28.

units.la: 14. Supremæ Potestati Omnipotentis DeiConscientias nostras omnino, & quidem soli, subjicianus: Rom. xiv, 9, - Jerem. x, 7. Apoc. xv. 4.
units.tr: 14. Let us subject our consciences entirely, and indeed to him alone, to the supreme power of almighty God: Rom. 14:9; Jer. 10:7; Rev. 15:4.

units.la: 15. Ipsi gloriam suam deferamus sincerè ac promptè: Psal.ciii,1,2. Luc.I,46,47, 74, 75. Matth. vi, 9, 13. Rom.xi, 36. 1 Cor. x, 31.
units.tr: 15. Let us sincerely and readily ascribe his glory to him: Ps. 103:1, 2; Luke 1:46, 47, 74, 75; Matt. 6:9, 13; Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 10:31.

units.la: 16. In Deo Beatissimo omnem nostram beatitudinem unicè quaeramus: Psal.xxxiii, 12. lxxiii,25, 26. 1 Joh. I, 3, 4.
units.tr: 16. In the most blessed God let us seek all our blessedness solely: Ps. 33:12; 73:25, 26; 1 John 1:3, 4.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: De Personis Divinis.
units.tr: On the Divine Persons.

units.la: EXistentia. Perfeitas. Suppositum. 1. Subsistentia, ὑπόστασις, abstracte: concretè. Persona.2. Essentia Divina quomodò praedicetur de Personis. Tres Personae sunt in unâ Essentiâ. Et Personae ista in se invicem. Personae Divinae descriptio. Terminus ἐνγραφῶ: & alii hic usitati. Numerus. 3. Probatur Personarum pluralitas. 4. Trinitas; ex V. T. collatis locis N. T. 5. Ex testimoniis N. T. 6. Probantur singula Personae. Pater. Ejus Personalitas. 7. Vera Deitas. 8. Distinctio à Filio, & Sp. S. 9. An recte dicatur, Fons & principium totius Deitatis? 10. Filius. Ejus Personalitas. 11. Deitas, probatur ex Nominibus. 12. Operibus. 14. Cultu. 15. Proprietates distinctivae. 16. De voce Spiritus. Spiritus Sancti Personalitas. 17. Deitas, ex Nominibus. 18. Attributis. 19. Operibus. 20. Cultu. 21. Distinctio à Patre & Filio. 22. Trium Personarum identitas essentialis. τὸ ὁμοούσιον. Paritas & Similitudo. Filius & Spir. S. etiam αὐτόθεος. ἐμἐκχώρησις. 23. Rejicitur Atheismus. Arianismus, Socinianismus. Sabellianismus. 24. Discrimen inter Generationem, & Spirationem. Illa non recte explicatur per actum Intellectus; & hac per actum Voluntatis. 25. Relationes reales. Processiones. Notiones. Proprietates personales. Actus notionales. Potentia notionales. Relationes rationis. Origo Filii, & Spiritūs Sancti. 26. Quomodo Persona Divina differat ab Essentia, 27. Quomodo Persona distinguantur à se invicem. 28. Objectiones solvuntur. 29. Dogma hoc fundamentale est, & ad salutem creditū necessarium. c. Remonstr. Obj. solv. 30. Usus practici. 31.
units.tr: Existence. Perfection. Suppositum. 1. Subsistence, hypostasis, taken abstractly and concretely. Person. 2. How the Divine Essence is predicated of the Persons. Three Persons are in one Essence, and these Persons are in one another. Description of the Divine Person. The term charactēr and other terms commonly used here. Number. 3. The plurality of Persons is proved. 4. The Trinity, from the Old Testament passages compared with the New. 5. From the testimonies of the New Testament. 6. Each of the Persons is proved. The Father; his personality. 7. True Deity. 8. His distinction from the Son and the Holy Spirit. 9. Whether it is rightly said that he is the fountain and principle of the whole Deity. 10. The Son; his personality. 11. His Deity, proved from the names. 12. From the works. 14. From worship. 15. The distinctive properties. 16. On the word Spirit. The personality of the Holy Spirit. 17. His Deity, from the names. 18. From the attributes. 19. From the works. 20. From worship. 21. His distinction from the Father and the Son. 22. The essential identity of the three Persons: homoousion. Parity and likeness. The Son and the Holy Spirit are also autotheos. Mutual indwelling. 23. Atheism is rejected; Arianism, Socinianism, Sabellianism. 24. The difference between generation and spiration. The former is not rightly explained by an act of the intellect, nor the latter by an act of the will. 25. Real relations. Processions. Notions. Personal properties. Notional acts. Notional powers. Relations of reason. The origin of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. 26. How a Divine Person differs from the Essence. 27. How the Persons are distinguished from one another. 28. Objections are answered. 29. This doctrine is fundamental, and must be believed for salvation. Against the Remonstrants; objections answered. 30. Practical uses. 31.

units.la: I. Equitur, ut Essentiam Dei consideremus relate in suis Personis.
units.tr: I. It follows that we consider the Essence of God in relation to his Persons.

units.la: Existentia in genere est Actualitas Entis: primò quidem Subsistentiæ; cui Perfectas competit: sed analogice etiam Accidentis; cujus esse est inesse.
units.tr: Existence, in general, is the actuality of a being: first indeed of subsistences, to which perfect existence belongs; but also, analogically, of an accident, whose being is to inhere.

units.la: Interim Subsistentiæ secundæ existunt in primis; sicut & aliæ partes in suo toto. Quæ autem incommunicabiliter, complete, & ultimate per se existunt, strictiore sensu subsistere dicuntur; & absolute suppositia vocantur, Græcis ὑφιστάμενα. Animam verò separatam, aliamve partem seorsùm existentem, Suppositum partiale dicimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile, secondary subsistences exist in the primary ones, just as other parts exist in their whole. Those things which exist incommunicably, completely and ultimately in themselves are said to subsist in the stricter sense, and are absolutely called supposita, in Greek hypostatha. We call a soul existing apart, or any other part existing separately, a partial suppositum.

units.la: II. Subsistentia, Græce ὑπόστασις alias rem quamlibet sub aliā stantem, & eam quodammodo sustentantem, notat: sed specialius interdum abstracte usurpatur, ut designet modum entitativum, quo natura substantialis ultimo, complete, & incommunicabiliter terminatur in existendo: qui modus etiàm suppositalitas appellatur; sed specialissime in intellectualibus personalitas. Concretè autem significat naturam substantialem tali modo subsistendi terminatam.
units.tr: II. Subsistence, in Greek hypostasis, sometimes means any thing standing under another and in some way supporting it; but more specifically it is sometimes used abstractly, to designate the entitative mode by which a substantial nature is ultimately, completely and incommunicably terminated in existing. This mode is also called suppositality, and in intellectual beings especially personality. Concretely, however, it signifies a substantial nature terminated in this mode of subsisting.

units.la: Suppositum intellectuale persona appellatur; Græce πρόσωπον: quæ nonnullis à personando dicta videtur: sed verba valent usû. Interim non displicet allusio, quasi per se una; aut per se sola. Describitur plenius, Substantia prima, intelligens, incommunicabilis, non pars alterius, nec ab alio sustentata.
units.tr: An intellectual suppositum is called a person, in Greek prosōpon. Some think the word is derived from personare, but words have their value from usage. Meanwhile an allusion is not displeasing, as if it meant one in itself, or alone in itself. It is more fully described as: a first substance, intelligent, incommunicable, not a part of another, nor sustained by another.

units.la: III. Essentia Dei unica est. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 19. sed communis tribus Personis, ut & Attributa ejus.
units.tr: III. The Essence of God is one. See above, chapter 4, thesis 19; but it is common to the three Persons, as are his attributes.

units.la: Consequenter Essentia non prædicatur de Personis, ut Species de suis Individuis: una enim eademque Essentia singularissima, existit in tribus Personis concrete.
units.tr: Consequently the Essence is not predicated of the Persons as a species is of its individuals; for one and the same most singular Essence exists concretely in the three Persons.

units.la: Rectè etiam dicimus, tres Personas esse in unâ istâ Essentiâ; quatenùs in communione ejusdem numero Essentiæ conveniunt. Imò etiam, Personas istas esse in se invicem; quatenùs communis Essentia in singulis Personis existit. Vide Joh. x, 38. xiv, 11. xvii, 21.
units.tr: We also rightly say that the three Persons are in this one Essence, inasmuch as they agree in the communion of the same numerical Essence. Indeed we also say that these Persons are in one another, inasmuch as the common Essence exists in each of the Persons. See John 10:38; 14:11; 17:21.

units.la: Persona Divina est ipsa Essentia Divina peculiari modo subsistendi à coëssentialibus distincta.
units.tr: A Divine Person is the Divine Essence itself, distinguished from its co-essential Persons by a peculiar mode of subsisting.

units.la: Estque terminus ille χαρακτὴρ. Hebr. 1, 3. de Filio; Character personæ (τῆς ὑποστάσεως) illius; scil. Patris. Confer 1 Joh. v, 7. Tres sunt, qui testificantur in Cœlo, Pater, Sermo & Spiritus Sanctus. Unicæ istius Essentiæ Tres sunt Personæ testificantes. Unde Triada, vel Trinitatem rectè appellamus; non Triplicitatem.
units.tr: And the term character is used for this. Heb. 1:3, of the Son: the character of his Person (of the substance) , that is, of the Father. Compare 1 John 5:7: There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. There are three Persons bearing witness to this one Essence. Hence we rightly call them a Triad or Trinity, not a Triplicity.

units.la: Numerus autem ille est tantum Denominatio Personarum plurium verè distinctarum.
units.tr: This number, however, is merely the designation of several Persons who are truly distinct.

units.la: Aliæ voces in hoc mysterio etiam usurpari solitæ, utpote, τρόπος ὑπάρξεως, ὁμοούσιος, ἐμπερίχωρησις. γένεσις, &c. secundum rem Scripturariæ sunt: quod observandum contra Antitrinitarios, & Pontificios, ad Traditiones non scriptas hic confugientes.
units.tr: Other terms usually employed in this mystery, such as tropos hyparxeōs, homoousios, perichōrēsis, genesis, etc., are in substance Scriptural. This must be observed against the Antitrinitarians and the Papists, who here take refuge in unwritten traditions.

units.la: iv. In Mysterio hoc probamus primò pluralitatem personarum, per testimonia sacra V. T. Gen. 1, 1, 2. „in principio creavit Deus (אלהים בראשית) cœlum & „terram. – & Spiritus Dei incubat superficiei aquarum. Et verf. 26, 27. „Postea dixit Deus Faciamus homi„nem ad imaginem nostram. iii, 22. Dixit Jehovah Deus. Ecce homo, estne sicut unus ex nobis? xi, 7. „Agedum descendamus, & confundamus ibi sermonem eorum. xix, 24. „Jehovah demisit, pluviam sulphu„ris, & ignis, à Iehova Psal. xlv: 8, „Unxit Te, o „Deus, Deus Tuus, oleo gaudii præ consortibus Tuis. Confer Hebr. 1. 8, 9, Iterum Psal. cx. 1, „Dixit Jehovah Domino meo; Sede ad dexteram meam, cum Matth. xxii, 42, 43. 44. Item Prov. xxx, 4. „Quod est nomen Hujus, & quod nomen Filii ipsius? Jes. xlviii, „16. „Nunc enim Dominus Iehovi mittit Me, & Spiritus „ejus. His adde Dan. ix, 17. cum Psal. lxxx, 15, 16. & Hos. 1. 7.
units.tr: iv. In this mystery we prove, first, the plurality of Persons by the sacred testimonies of the Old Testament. Gen. 1:1, 2: "In the beginning God created (Elohim bara'sit) the heaven and the earth. ... And the Spirit of God brooded over the surface of the waters." And verses 26, 27: "Then God said, Let us make man in our image." 3:22: "Jehovah God said, Behold, the man is become like one of us." 11:7: "Come, let us go down, and confound their speech there." 19:24: "Jehovah rained brimstone and fire from Jehovah." Psalm 45:8: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." Compare Heb. 1:8, 9. Again Psalm 110:1: "Jehovah said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand," with Matt. 22:42-44. Likewise Prov. 30:4: "What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?" Isa. 48:16: "For now the Lord Jehovah has sent me, and his Spirit." To these add Dan. 9:17 with Psalm 80:15, 16, and Hos. 1:7.

units.la: v. Secundò adstruimus nominatim Trinitatem, & quidem hac vice ex locis quibusdam V. T. collatis potissimum cum locis N. T. utpotè Psal. xxxiii, 6. „Verbo Jehovæ cœli facti sunt: & Spiritu oris ejus, to„tus exercitus eorum, cum Joh. 1, 1; 3, 10. „In princi„pio erat Sermo ille, & Sermo ille erat apud Deum, „eratque ille Sermo Deus. – Omnia per Hunc facta sunt; „& absque Eo factum est nihil quod factum sit. – Et mun„dus per Eum factus est: sed mundus Eum non agnovit. „Nec non Hebr. I, 10. Ad Filium: Et Tu in initio „Dominus, terram fundasti; & opera manuum Tuarum „sunt cœli. Ies vi, 1, 3, 8, 9. „Tum vidi Iehovam insi„dentem solio celso. De Seraphim autem, Inclamans alter ad alterum dicebat; Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus est „Jehovah Tzebaoth. – Deindè audivi vocem Domi»ni, dicentis : Quem missurus sum, & quis iturus est »nobis? Cui dixi ; En ego : mitte me, Tum dixit : »ut dicas populo isti : Audite indesinenter, at ne intel»ligatis, &c. cum Ioh. xii, 36.-41. Hæc locutus est »Iesus : - Propterea non poterant credere, quia iterum dixit Efaias ; Excæcavit oculos eorum, &c. Hæc dixit »Efaias, quando vidit gloriam Ejus, & locutus est de »Eo. Nec non Act. xxviii, 25, 26. Bene sane Spiri»tus Sanctus locutus est per Efaiam Prophetam patribus »nostris, dicens ; Vade ad populum istum, & dic ; Au»dietis, & non intelligetis, Ita scil. τριπλοῦν illud ad tres Personas pertinet. Confer trinam Jehovæ mentionem in folenni benedictione ; Num. vi, 24, 25, 26. Iterum Ief. lxi, 1. Spiritus Domini Iehova est super Me, »ad Euangelizandum mansuetis, &c. cum Luc. iv, »17, - 22. Tunc datus est Ei (Christo) liber Efaiæ »Prophetæ : cumque explicuisset librum, invenit lo»cum, in quo scriptum erat, Spiritus Domini super Me, »propterea quòd unxit me, &c. Cœpit autem eis dice»re; Certè hodiè impleta est hæc Scriptura audientibus »vobis &c. Ergo Filius Christus loquebatur de Jehovâ Patre, & Spiritu Ejus.
units.tr: v. Secondly, we establish the Trinity by name, and on this occasion chiefly from certain Old Testament passages compared with passages of the New. For example, Psalm 33:6: "By the word of Jehovah were the heavens made, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host," compared with John 1:1, 3, 10: "In the beginning was that Word, and the Word was with God, and that Word was God. ... All things were made by him, and without him was nothing made that was made. ... He was in the world, and the world was made by him, but the world did not know him." Also Heb. 1:10, spoken to the Son: "And you, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands." Isa. 6:1, 3, 8, 9: "Then I saw Jehovah sitting on a high throne." And of the seraphim, one cried to another: "Holy, Holy, Holy is Jehovah of hosts." Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" I said, "Here am I; send me." Then he said, "Go and tell this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand," etc. Compare John 12:36-41: Jesus spoke these things ... "For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, He has blinded their eyes," etc. "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him." Likewise Acts 28:25, 26: "Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying, Go to this people, and say, You will hear, and will not understand." So that threefold formula pertains to the three Persons. Compare the threefold mention of Jehovah in the solemn blessing, Num. 6:24-26. Again Isa. 61:1: "The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me, to preach good news to the meek," etc., with Luke 4:17-22. Then the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him (Christ), and when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, etc. And he began to say to them: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing, etc. Therefore Christ the Son spoke of Jehovah the Father and of his Spirit.

units.la: Similiter Jef. lxiii, 7, - 11. »Benignitates Jehovæ »commemorabo : Nam dixit : Utique populus Meus »sunt: - Angelus faciei ejus servavit eos: - Nam ipsis »rebellantibus, & dolore afficientibus Spiritum san»Ctitatis ejus, &c. Confer etiam 2 Sam. xxiii, 2. Hag. 2, 5, 6.
units.tr: Similarly, Jef. lxiii, 7–11: "I will recount the kindnesses of Jehovah. For he said: Surely they are My people. The angel of his presence saved them. For when they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit," and so on. Compare also 2 Sam. xxiii, 2; Hag. 2, 5, 6.

units.la: VI. Tertio, clariora interim sunt testimonia N. T. utpote Matth. iii, 16, 17. »Baptizatus Iesus - vidit »Spiritum Dei descendentem quasi columbam ; & ecce, vox adfuit è cœlo - Hic est Filius ille Meus, &c. xxviii, 19, - »Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. 2 Cor. xiii, 13. »Gratia Domini »Iesu Christi, charitas Dei, & communicatio Spiritus Sancti ,,Sancti sit cum omnibus vobis. 1 Joh. v,17.
