Tres sunt qui ,,testificantur in coelo; Pater, Sermo, & Spiritus Sanctus. His adde Joh. xiv, 16, 17. xv. 26. Luc. i. 35. Rom. i, 1, 4. viii, 11, Gal. iv, 4, 6.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly, the testimonies of the New Testament are for the moment clearer, such as Matth. iii, 16, 17: "When Jesus had been baptized, he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove; and behold, a voice came from heaven: This is My beloved Son," and so on. xxviii, 19: "Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." 2 Cor. xiii, 13: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." 1 Joh. v, 17: "There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit." To these add Joh. xiv, 16, 17; xv, 26; Luke i, 35; Rom. i, 1, 4; viii, 11; Gal. iv, 4, 6.

units.la: VII. Quarto denique consideranda veniunt illa S S. Literarum testimonia, quae singulas Personas Divinas, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum diserte tradunt, & distinctam earum personalitatem, ac veram Deitatem plane adstruunt.
units.tr: VII. Fourthly and finally, there come to be considered those testimonies of Holy Scripture which expressly set forth each of the divine Persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and which plainly establish their distinct personality and true Deity.

units.la: Patrem hic appellamus respectu Filii aeterni, & αυθεντια: Hebr. 1,5. cum Psal. II,7. & 2 Sam. vii, 14. Nam cui dixit unquam Angelorum; Filius Meus es Tu: ,,Ego hodie genui Te; Ac rursum; Ego ero Ei Pater, & Ipse erit Mihi Filius.
units.tr: Here we call him Father with respect to the eternal Son, and authentia [αὐθεντία]: Heb. 1, 5, with Ps. 2, 7 and 2 Sam. vii, 14. For to which of the angels did he ever say: "You are My Son; today I have begotten You"? And again: "I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to Me."

units.la: Quantum ad ipsius Personalitatem: expresse Hebr. 1,3. De Filio; quod sit character Personae illius: scil. Patris. Ipsi etiam competit vita, intellectus, voluntas, dominium, gloria, operationes, paternitas: Joh. v, 26. Pater habet vitam in Seipso. 17. Pater Meus usque adhuc operatur. Matth. xi, 25, 26, 27. ,,Gloriam Tibi tribuo Pater, Domine coeli & terrae; quod haec occultaveris a sapientibus & intelligentibus: & retexeris ea infantibus. Etiam Pater, quia ita placuit Tibi. Omnia ,,Mihi tradita sunt a Patre Meo: & nemo novit Filium, ,,nisi Pater, &c. Vide etiam Joh. xvii, 1.
units.tr: As to his personality: expressly Heb. 1, 3, concerning the Son, that he is the character of that person, namely of the Father. Life, understanding, will, dominion, glory, operations and paternity also belong to him: Joh. v, 26: The Father has life in himself. 17: My Father is working until now. Matth. xi, 25, 26, 27: "I give thanks to You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it has pleased You. All things have been delivered to Me by My Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father," and so on. See also Joh. xvii, 1.

units.la: VIII. Deitas autem ejus evincitur, 1. Nominibus Divinis: Joh. iii, 16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum miserit, &c. Adde viii, 54. xvii, 1. 3.
units.tr: VIII. His Deity is proved: 1. From the divine names: Joh. iii, 16: "So God loved the world, that he sent his only-begotten Son," and so on. Add viii, 54; xvii, 1, 3.

units.la: 2. Attributis: Apoc. 1, 4. de Patre; ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος: unde satis patet Aeternitas & Immutabilitas. Joh. v, 26. Habet vitam in Seipso. Quae est Independentia, Matth. xi, 25. Pater, Domine coeli & terrae. Quod est Dominium vere supremum.
units.tr: 2. From the attributes: Apoc. 1, 4, of the Father: ὁ ὢν, ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [who is, and who was, and who is to come]; whence eternity and immutability are sufficiently plain. Joh. v, 26: He has life in himself. This is independence. Matth. xi, 25: Father, Lord of heaven and earth. This is truly supreme dominion.

units.la: 3. Operibus Divinis: Act. iv, 24, -27. Domine, Tu es ille Deus, qui fecisti cælum & terram, mare & omnia quæ in iis sunt. - Congregati sunt in hac civitate verè adversùs sanctum Filium Tuum Jesum, quem unxisti, Herodes, &c. Ut facerent quæcunque manus Tua & consilium Tuum prius prædestinavit ut fierent. Nunc igitur, Domine, despice in minas eorum; & da Servis Tuis, ut cum omni libertate loquantur sermonem Tuum, Manu Tua à Te extensâ ad sanandum, signisque & prodigiis editis per nomen sancti Filii tui Jesû.
units.tr: 3. From the divine works: Act. iv, 24–27: "Lord, you are that God who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them." ... "For truly, in this city there have gathered against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod, and so on, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had predestined to take place. Now therefore, Lord, look upon their threats; and grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are done through the name of your holy Son Jesus."

units.la: 4. Denique ex Cultû & Honore religioso: Phil. 2, 11. - ad Gloriam Dei Patris. Matth. XVIII, 19. Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris; -. Confer Matth. XI, 25. Joh. XVII, 1. - Act. IV, 24 -.
units.tr: 4. Finally, from religious worship and honour: Phil. 2, 11: to the glory of God the Father. Matth. XVIII, 19: Baptizing them in the name of the Father. Compare Matth. XI, 25. Joh. XVII, 1. Act. IV, 24.

units.la: IX. Distinctio Patris à Filio & Spiritū Sancto est in Notionibus, seu Proprietatibus quibusdam chara- cteristicis; quales sunt
units.tr: IX. The distinction of the Father from the Son and the Holy Spirit lies in the notions, or certain characteristic properties, such as are these:

units.la: 1. Aseitas personalis: Pater prorsus non habet originem ab alio; sed per se subsistentiam suam & vitam habet in Se ipso: cùm ipse Filio dederit vitam habere in Se ipso; Joh. V, 26. Ἀγέννητον Veteres dixerunt: Scholastici Innascibilitatem vocant; sed & Inspirabilitatem recte addidisse.
units.tr: 1. Personal aseity: the Father has no origin at all from another, but has his subsistence of himself, and has life in himself, since he has given the Son to have life in himself (Joh. V, 26.). The ancients called this ἀγέννητον [agennēton, unbegotten]; the Scholastics call it innascibility, but it was rightly added that it is also inspirability.

units.la: 2. Generatio activa; quæ est actus peculiaris primæ Personæ, per quem ipsa est principium secundæ. Unde illa Pater, secunda autem Filius dicitur. Atque adeò Filius verè est ὁμοούσιος τῇ αὐτοθεος; ejusdem numero Essentiæ, ac veræ Deitatis: Vide Hebr. 1,
units.tr: 2. Active generation, which is the particular act of the first Person, by which he is the principle of the second. Hence the first is called Father and the second Son. And so the Son is truly ὁμοούσιος [homoousios] with the Father, that is, of the same numerical essence and true Deity [τῷ αὐτοθέῳ]. See Heb. 1,

units.la: 3. Joh. V, 26. Psal. 2, 7. cum Hebr. 1, 5, V, 5. Act. XIII, 33.
units.tr: 3. Joh. V, 26. Psal. 2, 7. with Hebr. 1, 5, V, 5. Act. XIII, 33.

units.la: 3. Spiratio activa cum Filio; quæ est actus notionalis, per quem Pater cum Filio est principium tertiæ Personæ; quæ inde Spiritus Sanctus appellatur. Joh. XV, 26. Advocatus ille, quem Ego mittam vobis à Patre: Spiritus ille veritatis, qui à Patre emanat.
units.tr: 3. Active spiration with the Son, which is a notional act by which the Father, together with the Son, is the principle of the third Person, who is therefore called Spiritus Sanctus. Joh. XV, 26. That Advocate whom I will send to you from the Father: that Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father.

units.la: 4. Primitas ordinis personalis in subsistendo: Pater enim prior est Filio, & Spiritū Sancto; cùm istarum Personarum principium sit.
units.tr: 4. Priority of personal order in subsisting: for the Father is prior to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, since he is the principle of those Persons.

units.la: 5. Primitas ordinis personalis in operando, Pater enim operatur à se; Filius à Patre; & Spiritus Sanctus ab utroque. Vide Eph. iii, 15. Joh. iii, 16, 17. Gal. iv, 6. Joh. xv, 26. Hebr. i, 2. Psal. xxxiii, 6. 1 Cor. 2, 10.
units.tr: 5. Priority of personal order in operating: for the Father operates from himself, the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. See Eph. iii, 15; Joh. iii, 16, 17; Gal. iv, 6; Joh. xv, 26; Hebr. i, 2; Psal. xxxiii, 6; 1 Cor. 2, 10.

units.la: X. Quaeritur, an Pater rectè dicatur fons & principium totius Deitatis; Resp. Plures Theologi orthodoxi sic quidem loquuntur sano sensu; attamen modus iste loquendi est ἀκυρόλογος, non accuratus: Deitas enim est natura Divina, cujus absolutè nullum est principium, nullus fons. Praeterea, si Pater esset principium totius Deitatis, suae quoque Essentiae principium foret: quod absurdum. Sed prima Persona est principium ejus, quòd Persona secunda & tertia habeant eandem quoque veram Deitatem. Atque hoc benè tenendum contra Vorstium & Episcopium.
units.tr: X. It is asked whether the Father may rightly be called the fountain and principle of the whole Deity. Answer: many orthodox theologians do speak thus, in a sound sense; yet this mode of speaking is ἀκυρόλογος [akyrologos], not accurate, for the Deity is the divine nature, of which there is absolutely no principle and no fountain. Moreover, if the Father were the principle of the whole Deity, he would also be the principle of his own essence, which is absurd. But the first Person is the principle of the Deity in that the second and third Persons have the same true Deity. This is to be held firmly against Vorstius and Episcopius.

units.la: XI. Filius Hebr. 1, 3. dicitur character personae Patris; sed & ipse persona: competit enim ipsi existentia: Joh. viii, 58. 1 Tim. iii, 16. vita; Joh. v, 26. intellectus, voluntas, & variae operationes; quae non possunt nisi personae competere: Matth. xi, 27. "Neque Patrem quisquam novit, nisi Filius, & cuicunque voluerit Filius revelare.
units.tr: XI. The Son (Heb. 1, 3) is called the character of the person of the Father; but he is also a person himself, for existence belongs to him (Joh. viii, 58; 1 Tim. iii, 16); life (Joh. v, 26); understanding, will and various operations, which can belong only to a person (Matth. xi, 27): "No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him."

units.la: Obj. Prov. viii. Sapientia appellatur: ergo. Resp. Sed ea hypostatica intelligenda est necessariò: idcircò dicitur amare amatores suos, unda ante saeculum, edita ante abyssos, &c. verf. 17, 23, 24, 25.
units.tr: Obj. In Prov. viii, Wisdom is named; therefore... Resp. But that must necessarily be understood hypostatically. Hence it is said to love those who love it, to be founded before the age, and brought forth before the abysses, and so on (verses 17, 23, 24, 25).

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Probatur porrò ejus vera Deitas, primo Nominibus Divinis: tùm attributive, tùm subjectivè. Joh. 1, 1. Erat Sermo ille Deus. cum 14. Et Sermo ille factus est caro. 1 Tim. iii, 16. Deus conspicuus factus est in carne. Act. xx, 28. "Ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo ille proprio sanguine acquisivit. Phil. ii, 6. "Cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam esse parem cum Deo. Imò etiàm additis illustribus epithetis, Jes. ix, 5. "Puer natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis: Vocabitur nomen ejus Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis." Pater æternitatis, Rom. ix. 5. - supra omnes Deus benedictus in sæcula. Tit. 11,13. „Expectantes adventum gloriæ magni illius Dei, ac Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi. 1 Joh. v, 20. „Et sumus in Vero illo (id est) in ejus Filio Jesu Christo. Hic est verus ille Deus, & vita illa æterna.
units.tr: Next, his true Deity is proved. First, from the divine names, both as attributes and as subjects. Joh. 1, 1. "That Word was God." Compare v. 14: "And that Word was made flesh." 1 Tim. iii, 16. "God was made manifest in the flesh." Act. xx, 28. "To feed the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood." Phil. ii, 6. "Though he was in the form of God, he did not count it robbery to be equal with God." Moreover, with illustrious epithets added: Jes. ix, 5. "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God," "Father of eternity." Rom. ix. 5: "Above all, God blessed for ever." Tit. ii, 13: "Looking for the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." 1 Joh. v, 20: "And we are in that True One, that is, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life."

units.la: Iterum Hebr. 1, 4, 8, 9, 10. ex Psal. xlv, 7. & cii, 26. „Ad Filium autem: Thronus Tuus, Deus, in sæculum sæculi: - Unxit Te, ô Deus, Deus Tuus, &c. „Et, Tu in initio, Domine, terram fundasti, &c. Psal. cx, 1. cum Matth. xxii, 43. 44. Hebr. 1, 13. „Dixit „Jehovah Domino meo. Sede ad dextram meam. 1 Cor. 2, 8. Dominus gloriæ. Apoc. xix, 16. Dominus dominantium. Joh. xx. 28. Domine, & Deus mi! Quin & ipso nomine Jehovah: Jerem. xxiii, 5, 6. „Excitabo „Davidi Germen justum: atque hoc nomen ejus - Jehovah justitia nostra. Num. xiv, 22, xxi. 5. 6. cum 1 Cor. x. 9. item Isai. vi, 1. 5. cum Joh. xii, 40, 41.
units.tr: Again, Hebr. i, 4, 8, 9, 10, from Psal. xlv, 7 and cii, 26: "But to the Son: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever... Thy God, O God, has anointed thee," etc. And: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning didst lay the foundation of the earth," etc. Psal. cx, 1 compared with Matth. xxii, 43, 44 and Hebr. i, 13: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand." 1 Cor. ii, 8: "the Lord of glory." Apoc. xix, 16: "Lord of lords." Joh. xx, 28: "My Lord and my God!" Indeed, even by the very name Jehovah: Jer. xxiii, 5, 6: "I will raise up to David a righteous branch, and this is his name: Jehovah our righteousness." Num. xiv, 22, xxi, 5, 6, compared with 1 Cor. x, 9; likewise Isa. vi, 1, 5, compared with Joh. xii, 40, 41.

units.la: XIII. Secundo, Attributis, utpote 1. Essentiali independentia:
units.tr: XIII. Secondly, from his attributes, namely: 1. essential independence:

units.la: Apoc. 1, 8. xxiii. 13. ipse Christus: Ego sum A & Ω, principium & finis, primum & ultimum. Isai. ix. 6. Pater æternitatis.
units.tr: Apoc. i, 8, xxii, 13: Christ himself says, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last." Isa. ix, 6: "Father of eternity."

units.la: 2. Infinitâ perfectione: Col. 11, 9. Omnis plenitudo Deitatis habitat in ipso corporaliter. Adde Phil. 11, 6. Joh. xvii, 5.
units.tr: 2. Infinite perfection: Col. ii, 9: "In him dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily." Add Phil. ii, 6; Joh. xvii, 5.

units.la: 3. Æternitate: Mich. v. 1. - Cujus exortus est inde à principio, à diebus sæculi. Prov. viii, 22, - 30. Jehovah possidebat me principio viæ suæ; ante opera sua, ante ullum tempus. Ante sæculum inuncta fui; ante principium, ante primordia terræ. Cum nullæ essent abyssi, edita eram: &c. Joh. 1, 1, 2, 3. „In principio erat Sermo ille. & Sermo ille erat apud Deum, &c. Conferviii, 58, & xvii, 5. Item Col. 1, 15, 17. Hebr. 1, 10, 11, 12. 1. Joh 1. 1. Apoc. 1. 8. & alibi.
units.tr: 3. Eternity: Mich. v, 1: "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting." Prov. viii, 22–30: "The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works, before any time. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth was. When there were no depths, I was brought forth," etc. Joh. i, 1, 2, 3: "In the beginning was that Word, and that Word was with God," etc. Compare viii, 58 and xvii, 5. Likewise Col. i, 15, 17; Hebr. i, 10, 11, 12; 1 Joh. i, 1; Apoc. i, 8, and elsewhere.

units.la: 4. Omnipræsentia: Matth. xviii, 20. Ubi enim sunt duo, vel tres congregati in nomine Meo, illic sum in medio illorum. xxviii, 20, Ego sum vobiscum omnibus diebus usque quae ad consummationem saeculi. Vide etiàm Joh.iii, 13.
units.tr: 4. Omnipresence: Matth. xviii, 20: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." xxviii, 20: "I am with you always, even to the end of the world." See also Joh. iii, 13.

units.la: 5. Omnipotentiâ: Apoc. 1, 8. Ille omnipotens. Ad de Phil. iii, 21. Hebr. 1, 3.
units.tr: 5. Omnipotence: Apoc. i, 8: "the Almighty." Add Phil. iii, 21; Hebr. i, 3.

units.la: 6. Omniscientiâ: Joh. xxi. 17. Domine, Tu omnia nosti. Adde 2, 24, 25. Apoc. 2. 23.
units.tr: 6. Omniscience: Joh. xxi, 17: "Lord, you know all things." Add ii, 24, 25; Apoc. ii, 23.

units.la: Obj. Tribuitur illi profectus; Luc. 2, 52. & rerum quarundam ignorantia, Marc. xiii, 32. Resp. Secundum humanam naturam, & intellectum ejus finitum.
units.tr: Obj. Growth is attributed to him, Luc. ii, 52, and ignorance of certain things, Marc. xiii, 32. Resp. According to his human nature and his finite understanding.

units.la: XIV. Tertio, Operibus Divinis: de quibus generatim; Joh. v. 17. 19, Pater Meus usque adhuc operatur; & Ego operor. - Quaecunque enim ille facit, haec etiam Filius pariter facit. Consequenter xiv, 11. propter opera credite Mihi.
units.tr: XIV. Thirdly, from the divine works, of which in general: Joh. v, 17, 19: "My Father works until now, and I work." "For whatever he does, the Son also does in the same way." Consequently xiv, 11: "Believe me for the sake of the works."

units.la: Speciatim hùc pertinet 1. Creatio: Joh. 1. 3. Omnia per Hunc (Sermonem) facta sunt, - 10. Et mundus per Eum factus est. Adde Col. 1. 16. Hebr. 1, 2, 10. Psal. xxxiii, 6.
units.tr: Specifically, the following belong here: 1. Creation: Joh. i, 3: "All things were made by him" (the Word), and v. 10: "And the world was made by him." Add Col. i, 16; Hebr. i, 2, 10; Psal. xxxiii, 6.

units.la: 2. Providentia ordinaria: Col. 1, 17. - Omnia per Eum consistunt. Heb. 1, 3. Sustinet omnia verbo illo suo potente.
units.tr: 2. Ordinary providence: Col. i, 17: "By him all things hold together." Hebr. i, 3: "He upholds all things by the word of his power."

units.la: 3. Miracula: ac nominatim Suscitatio mortuorum: Joh. v. 21. Sicut enim Pater suscitat mortuos & vivificat, ità & Filius quos vult vivificat. Illustre est exemplum suscitati Lazari: Joh. xi, 43, 44. ac potissimum, humanitatis suae propriae: Joh. 2, 19. 21, x, 17, 18. Peripsum quoque fiet Suscitatio generalis novissimo die: Joh. vi, 40. Phil. iii, 20. 21. & judicium extremum, Joh. v, 22. 27, 28, 29.
units.tr: 3. Miracles, and especially the raising of the dead: Joh. v, 21: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." An outstanding example is the raising of Lazarus, Joh. xi, 43, 44; and, above all, of his own humanity: Joh. ii, 19, 21; x, 17, 18. There will also be a general resurrection on the last day: Joh. vi, 40; Phil. iii, 20, 21; and the final judgment, Joh. v, 22, 27, 28, 29.

units.la: Unde etiàm Apostoli in ipsius nomine ac virtute Miracula fecerunt, Marc. xvi, 17; 20. Act. iii, 6.
units.tr: Hence the apostles also worked miracles in his name and by his power: Marc. xvi, 17, 20; Act. iii, 6.

units.la: 4. Singularia in Ecclesiam beneficia; utpote Prophetarum inspiratio per Spiritum suum: 1 Petr. i, 11. iii, 19.
units.tr: 4. Particular benefits to the Church; for example, the inspiration of the prophets through his Spirit: 1 Petr. i, 11; iii, 19.

units.la: Spiritûs Sancti missio: Joh. xvi, 7.
units.tr: The sending of the Holy Spirit: Joh. xvi, 7.

units.la: Sacramentorum institutio; Matth. xxxviii, 18, 19, 1 Cor. xi, 23. Spiritualis vivificatio: Eph. 11, 10. Ioh. vi, 35, 47. xv, 5.
units.tr: The institution of the sacraments: Matth. xxviii, 18, 19; 1 Cor. xi, 23. Spiritual quickening: Eph. ii, 10; Joh. vi, 35, 47; xv, 5.

units.la: Peccatorum remissio ex propria auctoritate: Matth. ix, 6.
units.tr: The remission of sins by his own authority: Matth. ix, 6.

units.la: Gratiae ac pacis donatio: Rom. 1, 7.
units.tr: The bestowal of grace and peace: Rom. i, 7.

units.la: XV. Quarto denique Cultu Divino: unde generatim, Ioh. v. 23. Ut omnes honorent Filium, prout honorant Patrem.
units.tr: XV. Fourthly and finally, from divine worship. In general: Joh. v, 23: "That all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father."

units.la: Speciatim 1. de Adoratione: Hebr. 1. 6 - Adorent Eum omnes Angeli Dei. Phil. 1 1. 10, 11. 1 Cor. 1, 2. Rom. xiv. 10. 11.
units.tr: Specifically, 1. concerning adoration: Hebr. i, 6: "Let all the angels of God worship him." Phil. ii, 10, 11; 1 Cor. i, 2; Rom. xiv, 10, 11.

units.la: 2. De Fide, Spe, & Fiducia: Ioh. xiv, 1. Creditis in Deum, etiam in Me credite. Rom. xv. 12. - Erit radix Iesse: In ipso gentes sperabunt. 1 Cor. xv. 19. Psal. 2, 12.
units.tr: 2. Concerning faith, hope and trust: Joh. xiv, 1: "You believe in God; believe also in me." Rom. xv, 12: "There shall be a root of Jesse, and in him the Gentiles shall hope." 1 Cor. xv, 19; Psal. ii, 12.

units.la: 3. De Baptismo in ipsius nomen: Matth. xxviii, 19. ac similiter de S. Coena in ipsius commemorationem: 1 Cor. xi, 24. 25. qui princeps salutis nostrae. Hebr. 2. 10. cum Act. iv. 12.
units.tr: 3. Concerning baptism in his name: Matth. xxviii, 19; and likewise concerning the Lord's Supper in his remembrance: 1 Cor. xi, 24, 25; and he is the author of our salvation, Hebr. ii, 10, compared with Act. iv, 12.

units.la: XVI. Proprietates distinctivae secundae Personae sunt, 1. Generatio passiva a Patre: Generaliori termino exortus, vel egressus; Mich. v, 1. Specialiori autem Generatio. Vide sup. th. 9. §. 2. Unde prima Persona, Πατὴρ ἰδίῳ; Ioh. v, 18. secunda autem, υἱὸς ἰδιος; Rom. v 111, 32. πρωτότοκος Hebr. 1, 6. Col. 1, 15. & μονογενὴς; Ioh. 1, 14. 18. 111, 16. 1, iv, 9. Quae Generatio non est physica; sed hyperphysica, & spiritualis: unde appellatio Λόγος, ἐν ἀρχῇ scil. ὁ ὑπόστατος; Ioh. 1, 1, 14. 1 Ioh. 1, 1, v, 7. & Sapientiae atque Intelligentiae; Prov. viii, 1. &c. Hinc Forma Dei, & Paritas cum Deo Patre; Phil. II, 5. Ioh. v, 18. Imago & Character Personae illius; 2Cor. iv, 4. Col. 1, 15. Hebr. 1. 3. quin & Unitas cum Patre; Ioh. x, 30.
units.tr: XVI. The distinctive properties of the second Person are: 1. Passive generation from the Father. In a more general sense, this is "going forth" or "issuing"; Mich. v, 1. In a more specific sense it is generation; see above, thesis 9, §2. Hence the first Person is the Father [Πατὴρ], Joh. v, 18; the second is his own Son [υἱὸς ἴδιος], Rom. viii, 32; firstborn [πρωτότοκος], Hebr. i, 6; Col. i, 15; and only-begotten [μονογενὴς], Joh. i, 14, 18; iii, 16; 1 Joh. iv, 9. This generation is not physical but hyperphysical and spiritual. Hence the appellation Word [Λόγος], "in the beginning" [ἐν ἀρχῇ], namely the hypostatic one; Joh. i, 1, 14; 1 Joh. i, 1; v, 7; and of Wisdom and Understanding, Prov. viii, 1, etc. Hence the form of God and equality with God the Father, Phil. ii, 5; Joh. v, 18; the image and character of that Person, 2 Cor. iv, 4; Col. i, 15; Hebr. i, 3; and indeed also unity with the Father, Joh. x, 30.

units.la: 2. Spiratio activa cum Patre; qua Filius cum Patre est principium tertiae Personae, Spiritus Sancti. Hinc Spiritus Filii dicitur Gal. iv, 6. Spiritus Christi; Rom. viii. 9. viii, 9. Filius enim mittit eum à Patre, Joh. xv, 26. itā ut accipiat de eo, quod est Filii: xvi, 14.
units.tr: 2. Active spiration together with the Father, by which the Son, together with the Father, is the principle of the third Person, the Holy Spirit. Hence the Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son, Gal. iv, 6, and the Spirit of Christ, Rom. viii, 9. For the Son sends him from the Father, Joh. xv, 26, so that he receives from what is the Son's, xvi, 14.

units.la: 3. Secundus modus & ordo subsistendi: Filius enim ordine personali posterior est Patre, & prior Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: 3. The second mode and order of subsisting: the Son is, in personal order, after the Father and before the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 4. Secundus modus & ordo operandi: Filius enim operatur à Patre per Spiritum Sanctum: Joh. xvi, 28. 13, 14. 15. xv, 26.
units.tr: 4. The second mode and order of operating: the Son operates from the Father through the Holy Spirit: John xvi. 28; xiii. 13, 14, 15; xv. 26.

units.la: Consequenter Filius Mediator noster factus, & sic à Patre missus, humanitatem assumtam suâ personalitate terminat in existendo: Joh. iii. 16. 2 Cor. v, 18. 19, 21. 1 Tim, ii, 5. in eâ unctus est Spiritu Sancto: Isef. lxi, 1. Psal. xlv, 8. Hebr. 1. 9. & Sacerdos per ipsum sese obtulit inculpatum Deo: Hebr. ix. 14. per eundem à mortuis suscitatus est; Rom. i, 4. 1 Pet. iii, 18. & nobis salutem impetratam applicat: Joh. xvi, 8. vi, 63. iii: 5, 6, 8. vii, 38, 39. 1 Cor. ii, 10, xii, 3. 11, 2, iii, 6, xiii, 13. Rom. viii, 1, 2, 4, 9, 11, 13, 16, 26, 27.
units.tr: Consequently the Son, made our Mediator and thus sent by the Father, terminates the assumed humanity in his own personal existence: John iii. 16; 2 Cor. v. 18, 19, 21; 1 Tim. ii. 5. He was anointed with the Holy Spirit in that humanity: Isa. lxi. 1; Ps. xlv. 8; Heb. i. 9. As priest he offered himself without blemish to God: Heb. ix. 14. Through the same Spirit he was raised from the dead: Rom. i. 4; 1 Pet. iii. 18. And he applies the salvation obtained to us: John xvi. 8; vi. 63; iii. 5, 6, 8; vii. 38, 39; 1 Cor. ii. 10; xii. 3, 11; 2 Cor. iii. 6; xiii. 13; Rom. viii. 1, 2, 4, 9, 11, 13, 16, 26, 27.

units.la: XVII. Pergimus ad tertiam personam.
units.tr: XVII. We proceed to the third person.

units.la: Voces ־ם, πνεῦμα, Spiritus, proprie flatum aut ventum significant: Exod. xv, 10. Psal. cxlvii, 18. Am. iv, 13. Metaphoricè substantiam invisibilem valdè efficacem. Sic usurpantur de materiali animâ bestiæ; Eccl. iii, 21. de immateriali hominis; Num. xvi, 22. Hebr. xii, 9. Eccl. xii, 7. Luc. xxiii, 46. Act. vii, 59. de Angelis: Hebr. i, 7. 14. Matth. viii, 16. x, 1. quin & de ipso Deo ζοῶ; Joh. iv, 24. & de tertiâ personâ ὑποστατικῶς; Matth. xxviii, 19. 1 Joh. v, 7. Metonymicè tamen de ejus effectis ac donis; Psal. li, 12. Ezech. xxxv, 26. 27. Gal. v, 17. Exod. xxxi, 3. Joh. vii, 39. Act. xix, 1.
units.tr: The words ruach [רוּחַ], pneuma [πνεῦμα] and spiritus properly signify breath or wind: Exod. xv. 10; Ps. cxlvii. 18; Amos iv. 13. Metaphorically they signify a very powerful invisible substance. So they are used of the material soul of a beast: Eccl. iii. 21; of the immaterial soul of a man: Num. xvi. 22; Heb. xii. 9; Eccl. xii. 7; Luke xxiii. 46; Acts vii. 59; of the angels: Heb. i. 7, 14; Matt. viii. 16; x. 1. Indeed they are used of God himself as living [ζῶν]: John iv. 24; and of the third person hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς]: Matt. xxviii. 19; 1 John v. 7. Metonymically, however, they are used of his effects and gifts: Ps. li. 12; Ezek. xxxvi. 26, 27; Gal. v. 17; Exod. xxxi. 3; John vii. 39; Acts xix. 1.

units.la: Ejus Personalitas patet, quòd apparuerit aliquando visibili præsentiæ suæ extraordinariæ symbolo exhibito: ut Matth. iii. 16. Act. 2, 3. 4. Quod Philippum rapuerit, & alió transtulerit; Act. viii, 39, 40. Quòd intelli„nisi Spiritus Dei. Joh. xvi. 13. Spiritus illè veritatis, dux viæ vobis erit in omnem veritatem. Omnem ergo veritatem intimè novit ille Doctor.
units.tr: His personality is shown by the fact that he has at some time appeared in a visible symbol of his extraordinary presence: as in Matt. iii. 16; Acts ii. 3, 4. That he caught away Philip and carried him to another place: Acts viii. 39, 40. That he understands [what is of God] except the Spirit of God: 1 Cor. ii. 11. John xvi. 13: "That Spirit of truth will be a guide to you into all truth." That teacher therefore knows all truth intimately.

units.la: 4. Suprema potestas, ac potentia: 1 Cor. xii, 4, 6; 11. Idem Spiritus. — Idem est Deus, agens ea omnia in omnibus. — Omnia hæc agit unus ille & idem Spiritus, distribuens privatim illa singulis, sicut vult,
units.tr: 4. Supreme power and might: 1 Cor. xii. 4, 6, 11. "The same Spirit." "It is the same God, working all things in all." "All these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each one severally as he wills."

units.la: XX. Tertio, Operibus Divinis: cujusmodi sunt, 1. Creatio, & conservatio: Gen. 1, 2. Spiritus Dei incubabat superficiei aquarum. Psal. xxxiii, 6. Spiritu oris Jehovæ totus exercitus cælorum factus est. Adde Psal. civ, 30. Job. xxvi, 13. xxxiii, 4.
units.tr: XX. Thirdly, by the divine works, such as: 1. creation and preservation: Gen. i. 2, "The Spirit of God was brooding over the surface of the waters." Ps. xxxiii. 6, "By the breath of Jehovah's mouth all the host of heaven was made." Add Ps. civ. 30; Job xxvi. 13; xxxiii. 4.

units.la: 2. Miraculorum patratio; atque ipsa Mortuorum resuscitatio. 1 Cor. xii, 9, 10. Alii vero donum sanationum datur per eundem Spiritum; alii vero operatio virtutum, alii vero genera linguarum; alii vero interpretatio linguarum. Rom. viii, 11. Sed si Spiritus ejus, qui suscitavit Iesum ex mortuis, habitat in vobis; is qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra, per inhabitantem ipsius Spiritum in vobis.
units.tr: 2. The performing of miracles, and the raising of the dead itself: 1 Cor. xii. 9, 10. "To another the gift of healing is given by the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues." Rom. viii. 11: "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you."

units.la: 3. Unctio capitis Christi; Isa. lxi, 1. ac porro Prophetarum & Apostolorum in omnem veritatem deductio; variorumque charismatum distributio: 1 Petr. i, 10, 11, 12. ii, 1, 21. 2 Sam. xxiii, 2. Joh. xvi, 13. Act. ii, 4; 1 Cor. xii, 4, -11.
units.tr: 3. The anointing of the head of Christ: Isa. lxi. 1; and further the leading of the prophets and apostles into all truth, and the distribution of various gifts: 1 Pet. i. 10, 11, 12; ii. 1, 21; 2 Sam. xxiii. 2; John xvi. 13; Acts ii. 4; 1 Cor. xii. 4–11.

units.la: 4. Regeneratio, sanctificatio, corroboratio, & obsignatio Christianorum: Joh. iii, 5, 6. „Nisi quis „fuerit genitus ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire „in regnum Dei. Quod genitum est ex Spiritu, spiri„tus est. 2 Cor. iii, 6. Spiritus vivificat. 1 Cor. vi. 11. xii, 3, 8, 9. Ezech. xxxvi, 27. Eph. iii, 16. 2 Cor. iv, 13. Rom. xv, 13.
units.tr: 4. The regeneration, sanctification, strengthening and sealing of Christians: John iii. 5, 6: "Unless someone has been born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit." 2 Cor. iii. 6: "The Spirit gives life." 1 Cor. vi. 11; xii. 3, 8, 9. Ezek. xxxvi. 27; Eph. iii. 16; 2 Cor. iv. 13; Rom. xv. 13.

units.la: 2 Tim. i, 7. Rom. xiv, 17. Eph. iv, 30.
units.tr: 2 Tim. i. 7; Rom. xiv. 17; Eph. iv. 30.

units.la: XXI. Quadripartito, Cultu religioso, qui Spiritui Sancto factis manifeste in SS. Literis attribuitur, contra quam existimant Remonstrantes: nam 1. fideles Templa Spiritus
units.tr: XXI. Fourthly, the religious worship which Holy Scripture plainly ascribes to the Holy Spirit by its deeds, contrary to what the Remonstrants think. For (1) the faithful are the temples of the

units.la: ritus Sancti sunt: 1 Cor. iii, 16, 17. vi, 19. Ergò ad religiosum ejus cultum dicati. Et Seraphicum illud τρισάγιον, Isef. vi, 3. ad Spiritum Sanctum quoque pertinet: Act. xxviii, 25.
units.tr: Holy Spirit: 1 Cor. iii. 16, 17; vi. 19. Therefore they are dedicated to his religious worship. And that Seraphic "thrice holy" [τρισάγιον], Isa. vi. 3, also pertains to the Holy Spirit: Acts xxviii. 25.

units.la: 2. In ipsius nomen Baptizamur: Matth. xxviii, 19.
units.tr: (2) We are baptized into his name: Matt. xxviii. 19.

units.la: 3. Preces & vota ad ipsum diriguntur: 2 Cor. xiii, 13. Gratia Domini Jesu Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio Sp. Sancti sit cum omnibus vobis. Quoniam scil. hic verè est communicator ac distributor bonorum spiritualium: 1 Cor. xii, 7: Item Apoc. 1, 4, 5. Gratia sit vobis - à Septem Spiritibus. Ubi Septem Spiritus dicuntur, non multiplicando subsistentias, sed respectû donorum. Undè vetus Ecclesia: Tu septiformis munere. Confer Apoc. iv, 5. v, 6. iii, 1. cum Act. ii, 3. Isef. xi, 2. & 1 Cor. xii, 4.
units.tr: (3) Prayers and vows are directed to him: 2 Cor. xiii. 13: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." Since he is truly the communicator and distributor of spiritual goods: 1 Cor. xii. 7. Likewise Rev. i. 4, 5: "Grace be to you ... from the seven Spirits." Here the "seven Spirits" are named not by multiplying persons, but with respect to the gifts. Whence the ancient Church: "Thou who art sevenfold in gift." Compare Rev. iv. 5; v. 6; iii. 1, with Acts ii. 3; Isa. xi. 2; and 1 Cor. xii. 4.

units.la: 4. Ipsi religiosè auscultandum & obtemperandum est: Psal. xcv, 7. Hodie si vocem Ejus audiveritis, &c, cum Hebr. iii, 7, 8. & Isef. lxiii, 10. Eph iv, 30. Matth. xii, 31, 32.
units.tr: (4) He is to be heard and obeyed with reverence: Ps. xcv. 7, "Today, if you hear his voice," etc., compared with Heb. iii. 7, 8; and Isa. lxiii. 10; Eph. iv. 30; Matt. xii. 31, 32.

units.la: XXII. Distinctio ejus à Patre & Filio proponitur distincta recensione in institutione Baptismi, Matth. xxviii, 19. cum Matth. iii, 16, 17. atque insuper diserta trium appellatione, 1 Joh. v, 7. Quin expressè alius dicitur, Joh. xiv, 16, 17. non tamen aliud.
units.tr: XXII. His distinction from the Father and the Son is set forth by a distinct enumeration in the institution of baptism, Matt. xxviii. 19, compared with Matt. iii. 16, 17, and moreover by the explicit naming of the three, 1 John v. 7. Indeed he is expressly called "another" [alius], John xiv. 16, 17, though not "another thing" [aliud].

units.la: Proprietatis autem characteristicæ Spiritûs Sancti sunt, 1. Spiratio passiva, vel Emanatio a Patre & Filio. Hinc Spiritus S. & Spiritus Dei passim appellatur: Imò etiam Spiritus oris Jehovæ: Psal. xxxiii, 6. & Afflatus Omnipotentis: Job. xxxiii, 4, Confer symbolum, quod Christus Discipulos suos afflaverit, &c. Joh. xx, 22. Porrò autem Pater Eum dare dicitur, & mittere in nomine Filii; Joh. xiv, 26. & per Filium; Tit. iii, 6.
units.tr: The characteristic properties of the Holy Spirit are: 1. passive spiration, or emanation, from the Father and the Son. Hence he is everywhere called the Spirit of God and the Holy Spirit; indeed also "the breath of Jehovah's mouth," Ps. xxxiii. 6, and "the breath of the Almighty," Job xxxiii. 4. Compare the sign that Christ breathed on his disciples, etc., John xx. 22. Further, the Father is said to give him and to send him in the name of the Son, John xiv. 26, and through the Son, Titus iii. 6.

units.la: Sed & Filius ipsum mittere dicitur à Patre: Joh. xv, 26. & absolutè mittere; Joh. xvi, 7. ita ut Spiritus accipiat de eo quod est Filii; verf. 15. Idcirco Spiritus Filii appellatur; Gal. iv. 6. & Spiritus Christi; Rom. viii, 9. 1 Petr. i. 11. Non ergo solùm à Patre per Filium procedit; quod Græci contra Latinos contendebant.
units.tr: But the Son is also said to send him from the Father, John xv. 26, and simply to send him, John xvi. 7, so that the Spirit receives from what is of the Son, v. 15. Therefore he is called the Spirit of the Son, Gal. iv. 6, and the Spirit of Christ, Rom. viii. 9; 1 Pet. i. 11. So he does not proceed only from the Father through the Son, as the Greeks contended against the Latins.

units.la: 2. Tertius modus & ordo subsistendi: à Patre enim & Filio procedens, subsistit.
units.tr: 2. The third mode and order of subsisting: for proceeding from the Father and the Son, he subsists.

units.la: 3. Consequenter tertius modus & ordo operandi: operatur enim à Patre & Filio; & modus operandi sequitur modum subsistendi.
units.tr: 3. Consequently, the third mode and order of operating: for he operates from the Father and the Son, and the mode of operating follows the mode of subsisting.

units.la: XXIII. Ex iis, quæ modo explicata & probata sunt, evidentissimè apparet;
units.tr: XXIII. From what has just been explained and proved, the following is most evident:

units.la: 1. Trium Personarum, quod ad Essentiam, Identitas; ita quidem ut unica & eadem numero Essentia Divina, sit trium Personarum communis: adeoque Filius, quemadmodum & Spiritus Sanctus, sit Patri ὁμοούσιος, coessentialis: propter Essentiæ identitatem: non verò tantùm ὁμοιούσιος, similis essentiæ; numero interim diversæ; quod olim volebant Ariani: Vide breviter Joh. x, 30. xvii, 11, 22. 1 Cor. xii. 4, 5. 6. 1 Joh. v, 7.
units.tr: 1. As regards the Essence, the three Persons are identical. The one and the same Divine Essence, one in number, is common to the three Persons. Hence the Son, like the Holy Spirit, is homoousios [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father, that is, coessential, because the Essence is identical. He is not merely homoiousios [ὁμοιούσιος], similar in essence but numerically different, as the Arians once held. See briefly John 10:30; 17:11, 22; 1 Cor. 12:4, 5, 6; 1 John 5:7.

units.la: 2. Æqualitas, seu paritas, & similitudo Personarum, inter se, respectu attributorum ac perfectionum essentialium. Joh. v, 18, 19, 21. 23, 26. Phil. i, 6. Quæ quidem Relationes formaliter rationis sunt: sed fundamentaliter ipsa Convenientia maximè realis est; utpote essentialiter identica. Propterea Filium & Spiritum Sanctum rectè dicimus αὐτόθεον, propter essentialem independentiam; frustrà obnitentibus quibusdam Pontificiis; & Remonstrantibus.
units.tr: 2. The Persons are equal, or on a par, and similar to one another with respect to the attributes and essential perfections. See John 5:18, 19, 21, 23, 26; Phil. 1:6. These relations are indeed formally relations of reason, but the agreement itself is fundamentally most real, since it is essentially identical. Therefore we rightly call the Son and the Holy Spirit autotheos [αὐτόθεον], God in their own right, on account of their essential independence, though some Papists and Remonstrants struggle against this in vain.

units.la: 3. Intima iflarum Personarum ἐμπεριχώρησις, mutua inexistentia, & circumcessio: Joh. i, 1. 18. xiv, 9. 10, 11. xv 11, 5. 10. 21.
units.tr: 3. These Persons intimately indwell one another, in mutual inexistence and circumcession [perichoresis, ἐμπεριχώρησις]. See John 1:1, 18; 14:9, 10, 11; 15:5, 10, 11, 21.

units.la: XXIV. Fugiendus igitur i.: Tritheismus Peratarum, Philoponi; Valentini Gentilis, &c. Tres Spiritus æter- nos, numero distinctos, asserentium.
units.tr: XXIV. Therefore the following must be avoided: 1. the Tritheism of the Peratae, of Philoponus, of Valentinus Gentilis, etc., which asserts three eternal Spirits numerically distinct.

units.la: 2. Hæreses Ariana, Samosatenianæ; Photiniana, Macedoniana; &c. Statuentes, Spiritum Sanctum esse accidentalem virtutem Dei, vel effectum aliquem in nobis, aut spiritum quem creatum; Filium vero non extitisse ante nativitatem ex Maria Virgine; & sic esse ψιλὸν ἀνθρώπων natura; qui olim erat Photinianismus, cui nunc consentit Socinianismus: vel Filium quidem extitisse ante nativitatem illam, imo ante mundum conditum: non tamen ab æterno; nec esse Patri coëssentialem; qui erat Arianismus. Sed & Valent. Gentilis Patrem Essentiatorem; Filium vero & Spiritum Sanctum Essentiatos dicebat. Valde similia habent Conr. Vorstius, Sim. Episcopius, &c.
units.tr: 2. The heresies of the Arians, Samosatenians, Photinians, Macedonians, etc., which hold that the Holy Spirit is an accidental power of God, or some effect within us, or a created spirit; and that the Son did not exist before his birth from the Virgin Mary, and so is by nature a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον]. This was once Photinianism, with which Socinianism now agrees. Or they hold that the Son indeed existed before that birth, even before the world was made, but not from eternity, and is not coessential with the Father. This was Arianism. Valentinus Gentilis also called the Father the Essentiator, and the Son and Holy Spirit the Essentiated. Conrad Vorstius, Simon Episcopius, and others hold views very similar to these.

units.la: 3. Sabellianismus, unicam statuens ut essentiam, sic quoque Personam Divinam effectibus solum, & consequenter nominibus, distinctam. Hanc haeresin etiam olim tenuisse commemorantur Praxeas, Hermogenes, Noëtiani, Patripassiani, &c.
units.tr: 3. Sabellianism, which posits a single essence and so also a Divine Person distinguished only by effects and, consequently, by names. This heresy too is recorded as having been held in former times by Praxeas, Hermogenes, the Noetians, the Patripassians, and others.

units.la: XXV. Quaeritur. 1. Quid discriminis sit inter Ge- nerationem & Spirationem? Resp. 1.
units.tr: XXV. It is asked: 1. What is the difference between Generation and Spiration? Answer 1.

units.la: Intercedit verum discrimen, & distinctarum personarum principiativum.
units.tr: A true difference exists, and it is a principle of distinct persons.

units.la: 2. Generatio activa competit soli Patri; Spiratio vero activa Patri & Filio.
units.tr: 2. Active generation belongs to the Father alone; active spiration belongs to the Father and the Son.

units.la: 3. Generatio non est postrema determinatio personalis in Divinis; Spiratio autem postrema est.
units.tr: 3. Generation is not the final personal determination in the Divine Persons; spiration is.

units.la: Scholastici dicunt, Generationem esse actum intellectus, Spirationem vero actum voluntatis. Patrem scil. intelligendo seipsum, produxisse vitalem sui imaginem Filium; ac porro Patrem & Filium amando suam Essentiam, produxisse vitalem propensionem, seu inclinationem, Spiritum Sanctum. Verum 1. Conceptus illi non sunt Scripturarii. 2. Intellectus & Voluntas, eorumque actus, sunt tribus Personis communes; non itaque principia distinctiva Personarum.
units.tr: The Scholastics say that generation is an act of the intellect, and spiration an act of the will: namely, the Father, understanding himself, produced the living image of himself, the Son; and further, the Father and the Son, loving their Essence, produced a living propensity or inclination, the Holy Spirit. But: 1. these concepts are not found in Scripture. 2. Intellect and will, and their acts, are common to the three Persons, and so are not distinctive principles of the Persons.

units.la: 3. Filius etiam cognoscit se, & Patrem; atque item Spiritus Sanctus cognoscit se, & Patrem & Filium; quin & Pater cognoscit Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. Similiter pater amat Spiritum Sanctum; atque item Spiritus Sanctus amat Patrem, & Filium, & Seipsum, &c. Sic illi conceptûs difficultatem hujus mysterii non tollunt sed augent; & plures processiones illaturi videntur: quapropter eos Auctoribus suis relinquimus.
units.tr: 3. The Son also knows himself and the Father; likewise the Holy Spirit knows himself, the Father and the Son; indeed the Father knows the Son and the Holy Spirit. Similarly the Father loves the Holy Spirit, and likewise the Holy Spirit loves the Father, the Son, and himself, and so on. Thus these concepts do not remove the difficulty of this mystery but increase it, and they seem to introduce several processions. Therefore we leave them to their authors.

units.la: XXVI. Idem afferunt, Personas Divinas constitui per Relationes, quas ideò reales vocant: duas recensent Processiones; unam per Generationem, alteram per Spirationem: & quinque Notiones, tanquàm notas, quibus cognoscitur, unam Personam distingui ab aliâ quod ad originem; Innascibilitatem, Paternitatem, Filiationem, Spirationem activam, & Processionem per Spirationem; in quibus quatuor posteriores Relationes reales dicunt. Amplius verò Innascibilitatem, Paternitatem, Filiationem, & Processionem appellant Proprietates; quia distinctè singulis Personis conveniunt; cùm Spiratio activa Patri & Filio communis fit. Sed à Proprietatibus personalibus, quæ Personas, ut ipsi loquuntur, constituunt in esse personæ, removent quoque Innascibilitatem: quod tantùm sit negatio relationis ad personam aliquam ordine priorem. Duos etiàm nuncupant Actus notionales, Generationem & Spirationem: quibus respondent totidem Potentiæ notionales, Generativa & Spirativa: tres denique Relationes rationis, Identitatem, Æqualitatem, & similitudinem: quamvis nec omnia ista apud illos extra controversiam posita sint. Sed quoniam in tantis mysteriis etiàm vera & certa dicere periculosum est; nos iis contenti sumus, quæ modò evidenter ex SS. Literis deducta sunt. Quantum verò ad originem Filii & Spiritus Sancti attinet, secundùm superiora breviter dicimus, primam Personam, eo ipso quòd talis est, à se habere subsistentiam suam: eamque ab æterno hoc egisse, ut eadem numero Essentia sua etiàm altero modo subsisteret, per Generationem; à quâ activè considerata prima Persona appellatur Pater: Secunda verò ab eâdem passivè spectatâ Filius dicitur. Ac porrò Patrem & Filium, actû iterùm æterno personali hoc egisse, ut eadem sua Essentia adhùc tertio modo subsisteret, scil. per Spirationem; unde Patrem & Filium Spirantes dicimus; tertiam verò Personam, Spiritum Sanctum. Sic pro nostro concipiendi modulo in reipsâ solidum & evidens fundamentum habemus, cui innituntur Relationes,
units.tr: XXVI. The same authors maintain that the Divine Persons are constituted by relations, which they therefore call real. They enumerate two Processions, one through generation and the other through spiration; and five Notions, as marks by which one Person is known to be distinguished from another with respect to origin: unbegottenness, paternity, filiation, active spiration, and procession through spiration. Of these, they call the last four real relations. Moreover, they call unbegottenness, paternity, filiation, and procession properties, because they belong distinctly to single Persons, since active spiration is common to the Father and the Son. But from the personal properties, which constitute the Persons (as they themselves put it) in the being of a person, they also remove unbegottenness, since this is merely the negation of a relation to a Person prior in order. They also name two notional acts, generation and spiration, to which correspond as many notional powers, the generative and the spirative. Finally they name three relations of reason: identity, equality, and similarity, although not all of these are beyond dispute among them. But since in such great mysteries it is dangerous to say even things that are true and certain, we are content with those things which have now been plainly deduced from Holy Scripture. As far as the origin of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is concerned, we say briefly, in line with what was said above: the first Person, by the very fact that he is such, has his subsistence from himself; and he has done this from eternity, so that his same numerically one Essence might also subsist in a second mode, through generation. Considered actively, the first Person is called Pater, and the second, considered passively from the same act, is called Filius. Further, the Father and the Son, by another personal act, likewise eternal, have done this, that the same Essence might subsist in a third mode, namely through spiration. Hence we call the Father and the Son Spirantes, spirating, and the third Person Spiritum Sanctum, the Holy Spirit. Thus, according to our manner of conceiving, we have a solid and evident foundation in reality on which the relations rest.

units.la: XXVII. Quæritur 2. Quomodò Persona Divina differat ab Essentiâ? Resp. 1. Distinctio illa non est solùm rationis ratiocinantis: habet enim Fundamentum in re. Essentia nimirum communis est tribus Personis; Persona verò dicit incommunicabilitatem: adeóque non reciprocantur formaliter adæquatè. Porrò, Essentia determinata est ad subsistendum per Personalitatem. Essentia denique concipitur abstractè, ut præscindat à personalitatibus: Persona verò concretè, cum certo quodam modo subsistendi.
units.tr: XXVII. It is asked 2. How does the Divine Person differ from the Essence? Answer 1. That distinction is not merely of the reasoning reason [rationis ratiocinantis], for it has a foundation in the thing. The Essence is indeed common to the three Persons, but Person denotes incommunicability. Hence the two are not formally and adequately reciprocal. Further, the Essence is determined to subsist through personality. Finally, the Essence is conceived abstractly, as set apart from the personalities, but the Person is conceived concretely, with a certain mode of subsisting.

units.la: 2. Nec tamen est realis distinctio; qualis intercedit inter rem aliam & aliam. Persona enim est ipsa Essentia cum personalitate.
units.tr: 2. Yet it is not a real distinction of the kind that exists between one thing and another, for the Person is the very Essence together with personality.

units.la: Sed 3. est distinctio rationis ratiocinatæ: illic enim spectamus rem abstractè; hic autem cum modo subsistendi.
units.tr: But 3. it is a distinction of reason reasoned [rationis ratiocinatæ], for there we regard the thing abstractly, whereas here we regard it with its mode of subsisting.

units.la: Hinc patet; non accuratè loqui eos, qui dicunt, Personas Divinas simul sumtas non distingui, ab Essentiâ; sed quidem sigillatim consideratas.
units.tr: Hence it is clear that those speak not accurately who say that the Divine Persons, taken together, are not distinguished from the Essence, but only when they are considered severally.

units.la: Item, quomodo Personæ Divinæ differant ab Attributis: Attributa enim sic cum Essentiâ identificantur, ut Personis verè communia sint: sed Personæ suis personalitatibus itâ distinguuntur, ut interim Essentiam & Attributa essentialia eadem habeant distincto modo atque ordine.
units.tr: Likewise, the Divine Persons differ from the Attributes as follows. The Attributes are so identified with the Essence that they are truly common to the Persons. The Persons, however, are distinguished by their personalities in such a way that they nonetheless have the Essence and the essential Attributes, in the same way but in a distinct mode and order.

units.la: XXVIII. Quæritur 3. Quomodò Personæ dicen- dæ sint à se invicem distingui? Resp. Distinctio hæc non solùm rationis est: nam verè Pater alius est, & Filius.
units.tr: XXVIII. Question 3. In what sense are the Persons to be said to be distinguished from one another? Answer: This distinction is not merely of reason, for the Father is truly other than the Son.

units.la: Filius alius, atque iterùm Spiritus Sanctus alius. Neque realis, eo sensû, ac si Pater esset alia res, vel aliud ens; Filius iterum aliud ens, &c. sed peculiari acceptione: quia est alia persona. Nec mirum videri debet, quod aliud exemplum simile dari non potlit: Deus enim aliud ens sibi simile non habet. Rectè autem dici potest Distinctio modalis, aut potius personalis.
units.tr: The Son is other, and again the Holy Spirit is other. The distinction is not real in the sense that the Father would be a different thing or a different being, the Son again a different being, and so on. It is distinct in a peculiar sense, because each is a different person. Nor should it seem strange that no other similar example can be given, for God has no other being like himself. It may rightly be called a modal distinction, or rather a personal one.

units.la: Sic explicatum est hoc mysterium Trinitatis ex SS. Literis: non ex principiis naturalibus: his enim positive & solide veritatem istam inferentibus destituimur. Illustratio tamen qualiscunque à posteriori petitur aliquando à Boni communicativitate; ex consideratione Solis, Animæ, Iridis, Trianguli, &c.
units.tr: This mystery of the Trinity has thus been explained from the Holy Scriptures, not from natural principles, since these fail us in establishing that truth positively and firmly. Some illustration, of whatever kind, is nevertheless sought a posteriori, sometimes from the self-communicating nature of the Good, and from the consideration of the sun, the soul, the rainbow, the triangle, and so on.

units.la: XXIX. Obj. 1. Deus unicus est: ergo non tres personæ. Resp. Unitas Essentiæ non adversatur plural- itati Personarum.
units.tr: XXIX. Objection 1. God is one; therefore there are not three persons. Answer: The unity of the essence does not stand in the way of a plurality of Persons.

units.la: Obj. 2. Non dantur plura infinita: atqui quælibet Persona Divina statuitur infinita. Resp. Quælibet Persona infinita est; sed unâ tâdemque numero infinitate: ac proinde non tria infinita dicimus; sed unum infinitum.
units.tr: Objection 2. There are not several infinites; but each Divine Person is held to be infinite. Answer: Each Person is infinite, but one and the same infinite in number; therefore we do not say that there are three infinites, but one infinite.

units.la: Obj. 3. Persona est persona per essentiam suam; consequenter tres Personæ inferunt tres Essentias. Resp. Persona non est talis per Essentiam; sed per personalitatem, sive per modum habendi istam Essentiam.
units.tr: Objection 3. A person is a person through his essence; consequently three Persons imply three essences. Answer: A Person is not such through the essence, but through personality, or through the mode of possessing that essence.

units.la: Obj. 4. Qui ante generationem non fuit, is non est verus Deus: atqui Filius, &c. Resp. Nec principium generationis, nec finem admittimus; sed generationem prorsùs æternam statuimus.
units.tr: Objection 4. He who did not exist before generation is not the true God; but the Son, etc. Answer: We admit neither a beginning nor an end of generation, but hold that the generation is utterly eternal.

units.la: Obj. 5. Si Pater Filium generavit, hoc fecit vel ex necessitate naturæ suæ; vel liberè: non prius; id enim à Deo, agente liberrimo, alienum est; non posterius; sic enim Filius potuit non generari, atque adeò non esse, & consequenter non est verus Deus. Similiter dici potest de Spiratione. Resp. Generationis actus perlo personalis necessarius est, ut non potuerit non esse; itemque Spirationis: sed & liber dici potest libertate æternæ concomitantis complacentiæ.
units.tr: Objection 5. If the Father begot the Son, he did so either from the necessity of his nature or freely. Not the former, for that is foreign to God, who acts most freely; not the latter, for then the Son could have not been begotten, and so would not exist, and consequently is not the true God. The same can be said of spiration. Answer: The act of generation is personally necessary, so that it could not not be; and likewise of spiration. Yet it can also be called free, by the freedom of an eternal and concomitant complacency.

units.la: Obj. 6. Filio non competit potentia generativa; atque adeo non omnis perfectio; quam habet Pater: cui autem deest aliqua perfectio, is non est verus Deus. Similiter de Spiritu Sancto, Resp. Potentia generativa singulis personis non est communis: cum ipsa non sit perfectio absoluta, vel attributum Essentiæ Divinæ; sed proprietas personalis primæ Personæ, &c. .
units.tr: Objection 6. The power of generating does not belong to the Son, and so he does not have every perfection which the Father has; but he who lacks some perfection is not the true God. Likewise concerning the Holy Spirit. Answer. The power of generating is not common to each Person, since it is not an absolute perfection or an attribute of the Divine Essence, but a personal property of the first Person, and so on.

units.la: Obj. 7. Christus negat se bonum; Luc. xviii, 19. ergo non est verus Deus. Resp. Non negat se bonum; sed propositâ interrogatione hoc agit, ut alterum ad rectam Bonitatis ac Deitatis suæ agnitionem adducat.
units.tr: Objection 7. Christ denies that he is good (Luke 18:19); therefore he is not the true God. Answer. He does not deny that he is good; by putting the question he does this so that the other may be led to a right recognition of his goodness and his deity.

units.la: Obj. 8. Christus disertè Patrem se majorem affirmavit. Joh. xiv. 28. Ergo. Resp. Scil. secundum humanam naturam; & œconomicè, respectû muneris Mediatorii: quæ consideratio nihil præjudicat Theologicè.
units.tr: Objection 8. Christ expressly affirmed that the Father is greater than he (John 14:28); therefore, etc. Answer. That is, according to the human nature, and economically, with respect to the office of Mediator; a consideration which does nothing to prejudice the theological doctrine.

units.la: Obj. 9. Spiritus Sanctus nondum erat; Joh. vii. 39. Ergo. Resp. Istud non debet accipi de personâ Spiritus Sancti; sed metonymicè de effusione singularium donorum post exaltationem Christi peragendâ, atque isto etiàm nomine appellari solitorum. Nam cap. 1. 32. commemoratur, Spiritum Sanctum jam descendisse in specie columbæ super Christum in baptismo ipsius, &c.
units.tr: Objection 9. The Holy Spirit was not yet (John 7:39); therefore, etc. Answer. That must not be understood of the Person of the Holy Spirit, but metonymically of the outpouring of particular gifts to be accomplished after the exaltation of Christ, which were commonly called by this name. For in chapter 1:32 it is recorded that the Spirit had already descended upon Christ at his baptism in the form of a dove, and so on.

units.la: Obj. 10. Si sint duæ personæ spirantes, etiàm erunt duæ spiratæ; & sic plures tribus. Resp. Duæ personæ spirantes propter τὸ ὁμοούσιον unius principii rationem habent, non duorum principiorum: adeoque & Spiritus una persona rectissimè statuitur.
units.tr: Objection 10. If there are two persons spirating, there will also be two persons spirated, and so more than three. Answer. Two persons spirating, on account of the homoousion [τὸ ὁμοούσιον], have the character of one principle, not of two principles; and so the one Spirit is most rightly posited as one Person.

units.la: Obj. 11. Spiritus S. mitti dicitur, donari, effundi, &c. Istud autem à vero Deo alienum est. Resp. Missio illa non de potestate superioris in inferiorem; sed ratione originis & ordinis Divinarum Personarum, in subsistendo & in operando, intelligi debet. Ut & reliqua metonymicè, & respectu manifestationum & operationum, quas ista Persona tunc exerit.
units.tr: Objection 11. The Holy Spirit is said to be sent, given, poured out, and so on. But that is foreign to the true God. Answer. That sending is not to be understood as the power of a superior over an inferior, but in terms of the origin and order of the Divine Persons, in their subsisting and in their operating. The rest is likewise metonymical, and refers to the manifestations and operations which this Person then exercises.

units.la: Obj. 12. Spiritus interpellat pro nobis, gemitibus inenarrabilis; Rom. VIII, 26. 27. inferior igitur est; non verus est Deus. Resp. Id accipiendum virtualiter eminenter; quatenus facit nos, omnesque alios fideles, genere & precari intimè, sanctè, juxta voluntatem Divinam.
units.tr: Objection 12. The Spirit intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered (Rom. 8:26, 27); therefore he is inferior and is not the true God. Answer. This is to be taken virtually and eminently, inasmuch as he makes us, and all other faithful, to groan and to pray inwardly, holily, and according to the Divine will.

units.la: Obj. 13. Solus Pater est verus Deus; Iob. XVII, 3. ergo non Filius, aut Spiritus Sanctus. Resp. Negatur antecedens: neque id exstat in loco allegato. Verùm Pater ibi dicitur ille solus verus Deus: ubi particula solus non est restrictiva subjecti, sed praedicati; ut indicetur, verum Deum esse unum solum. Atque ita excluduntur à verâ Deitate, omnia alia ab isto uno vero: non autem Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus, qui sunt unum cum Patre, in eâdem essentiâ singularissimâ.
units.tr: Objection 13. The Father alone is the true God (John 17:3); therefore not the Son or the Holy Spirit. Answer. The antecedent is denied; nor does it stand in the place cited. Rather, the Father is there called ille solus verus Deus, "that only true God," where the particle solus is restrictive not of the subject but of the predicate, so as to indicate that the true God is unum solum, one alone. Thus all things other than this one true God are excluded from true deity; but not the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are one with the Father in the same most singular essence.

units.la: Obj. 14. Essentia Divina est Pater: Filius & Spiritus Sanctus non sunt Pater: Ergo, &c. Resp. 1 Quia Essentia Divina non est incommunicabilis, sed communis tribus personaris, vitiosus est syllogismus: similiter ut hic; Aliquis homo est Petrus: Paulus, vel Jacobus non est Petrus: Ergo, &c. 2. Corrigenda igitur est major propositio hoc modo; Essentia Divina in primo modo & ordine subsistendi est Pater: & sic nihil efficietur contra nos.
units.tr: Objection 14. The Divine Essence is the Father; the Son and the Holy Spirit are not the Father; therefore, etc. Answer. 1. Because the Divine Essence is not incommunicable but common to the three Persons, the syllogism is faulty, just as this one is: some man is Peter; Paul or James is not Peter; therefore, etc. 2. The major proposition must therefore be corrected thus: the Divine Essence, in the first mode and order of subsisting, is the Father; and in this way nothing will be established against us.

units.la: XXX. Dogma hoc de S. S. Trinitate fundamentale esse, & ad salutem creditu necessarium, afferimus contra Remonstrantes: & probamus, 1. ex institutione Baptismi; Matth. XXVIII, 18, 19, 20.
units.tr: XXX. We affirm, against the Remonstrants, that this dogma of the Holy Trinity is fundamental and necessary to be believed for salvation, and we prove it, 1. from the institution of Baptism, Matt. 28:18, 19, 20.

units.la: Data est Mihi omnis potestas in coelo & in terrâ: profecti ergo docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Docentes eos servare omnia, quæ mandavi vobis; Et ecce, Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi. Amen. Notandā tanda initio Potestas, quâ Christus Sacramentum istud instituit quæ citra hoc dogma recte intelligi non poterit. Tum Præceptum docendi & baptizandi Christianos in nomen trium personarum, tanquam Domini nostri spiritualis, ex quo salus æterna pendet. Scil. ut eædem personæ distinctè apparuerunt in Baptismo ipsius Christi; sic earum confessio editur in Sacramento initiationis nostræ. Ac porrò Mandatum ista deinceps observandi, sub promissione tàm illustri; pro quâ Marc. xvi,16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur; qui verò non crediderit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age. Amen. First, the authority by which Christ instituted this sacrament must be noted, which cannot be rightly understood without this dogma. Then there is the command to teach and to baptize Christians into the name of the three Persons, as of our spiritual Lord, on whom eternal salvation depends. Just as these same Persons appeared distinctly at the baptism of Christ himself, so their confession is set forth in the sacrament of our initiation. Further, there is the mandate to observe these things thereafter, under so illustrious a promise, for which Mark 16:16: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned."

units.la: 2. Joh. xvii,3. Hæc est autem vita æterna, ut Te cognoscant, illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum At Pater, ut sic, sine Filio cognosci non potest. Hinc Joh. xiv, 1, 9, 10, 11. Creditis in Deum, etiam in Me credite. - Qui vidit Me, vidit Patrem - Non credis Me in Patre, & Patrem in Me esse? Et v, 23. Qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem Item. Joh. 11, 23. Quisquis negat Filium, nec Patrem habet: propter essentialem identitatem. Spiritus Sancti eadem est ratio. 1 Cor. xii, 3. „Propterea notum vobis facio, neminem posse dicere Jesum Dominum, nisi per Spiritum Sanctum. A verâ igitur Deitate, & consequenter à vitâ æterna aberratur, ubi Filius, aut Spiritus Sanctus, ab illâ excluditur.
units.tr: 2. John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." But the Father, as such, cannot be known without the Son. Hence John 14:1, 9, 10, 11: "You believe in God; believe also in me." "He who has seen me has seen the Father." "Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" And 5:23: "He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father." Likewise Joh. 11, 23: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father," on account of the essential identity. The same reasoning holds for the Holy Spirit: 1 Cor. 12:3: "Therefore I make known to you that no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit." Therefore they go astray from the true deity, and consequently from eternal life, where the Son or the Holy Spirit is excluded from it.

units.la: 3. A fine Euangelii: Joh. xx,31. Ut credatis Iesum esse Christum illum, Filium Dei; & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ejus, cum viii,24. Nisi credideritis, Me (eum) esse, moriemini in peccatis vestris, & 1 Joh. v, 20, 21. Scimus, Filium Dei venisse. - Hic est verus ille Deus, & vita illa æterna. Filioli, cavete vobis ab idolis. Amen. Sed absque hoc dogmate fides istius veritatis haberi nequit.
units.tr: 3. On the purpose of the Gospel: John 20:31. That you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing you may have life through his name, with John 8:24, Unless you believe that I am (he), you will die in your sins, and 1 John 5:20, 21: We know that the Son of God has come. This is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen. Without this doctrine, however, the faith of this truth cannot be had.

units.la: 4. Absque fide hujus articuli alia præcipua Christianæ Religionis dogmata recte teneri non possunt, utpote de Incarnatione Christi, ac porro de ipsius personâ sonâ, itemque de Salutis Impetratione validâ, & Applicatione efficaci.
units.tr: 4. Without faith in this article, the other principal doctrines of the Christian religion cannot be rightly held, such as the incarnation of Christ, his true and proper person, the valid obtaining of salvation, and its effective application.

units.la: Obj. 1. Plurimi hominPes pii mysterium istud captû suo non assequuntur ; nec tamen propterea æternùm damnandi: ergo, &c. Resp. Fatemur, non omnibus eundem gradum fidei explicitæ obtingere : major lux sub N. T. affulsit, quàm sub V. neque adhùc æqualem omnes mensuram accipiunt. Minimum quod sic, in salutis per Dei misericordiam consequendæ negotio, non determinamus ; sed quid revelatum ac præscriptum fit, & consequenter docendum atque discendum, observamus. De veritatis credendæ necessitate loquimur; non de cognitionis gradu ; neque de phrasi aliquâ, aut modo explicandi, probandi, vel defendendi. Per dictam vero necessitatem excluditur tùm blasphemia, impugnatio, rejectio; tùm neglectus totalis, aut ignorantia istius veritatis.
units.tr: Objection 1. Many godly people do not grasp this mystery with their understanding, yet they are not on that account to be damned eternally; therefore, etc. Answer. We grant that not all receive the same degree of explicit faith. Greater light has shone under the New Testament than under the Old, and even now not all receive an equal measure. We do not determine the minimum in the matter of obtaining salvation through God's mercy; but we observe what has been revealed and prescribed, and consequently what is to be taught and learned. We are speaking of the necessity of believing the truth, not of the degree of knowledge, nor of any phrasing, or manner of explaining, proving or defending it. By this necessity, blasphemy, attack and rejection are excluded, as well as total neglect or ignorance of this truth.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dogma illud non habet speciales usus practicos: hi enim omnes resultant ex consideratione Essentiæ Divinæ, quæ unica est; non verò ex personalitatibus, earumque distinctione. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negamus antecedens; & contrarium ostendimus.
units.tr: Objection 2. That doctrine has no special practical uses, for all of these arise from the consideration of the divine essence, which is one, and not from the persons and their distinction. Therefore, etc. Answer. We deny the antecedent, and we show the contrary.

units.la: XXXI. Usus practici potissimum occurrunt:
units.tr: XXXI. The practical uses mainly arise as follows:

units.la: 1. Pio & grato animo agnoscamus ac prædicemus admirandam Dei benignitatem, quâ sese talem etiam subsistentiis revelavit nobis familiariter: Matth. xi, 25, 26, 27. Joh. xvii, 1, 3.
units.tr: 1. With a pious and grateful mind let us acknowledge and proclaim the wonderful goodness of God, by which he has so familiarly revealed himself to us in these subsistences: Matt. 11:25, 26, 27; John 17:1, 3.

units.la: 2. Mysterium istud, à corruptâ ratione tàm alienum, sit nobis fidei, spei, charitatis, adorationis, &c. objectum: trium istarum personarum testimonio nitamur firmissime: Spiritu in nobis operante, per Filium accedamus ad Patrem, &c. Sic praxis nostra distinguitur à perfidia, idololatriâ, & superstitionibus Christianorum ac Pseudochristianorum: Joh. v, 23. xiv, 1. 1 Joh. 2, 23. v, 7, 9, 20, 21. Eph. 2, 18. iii, 12. Matth. xxviii, 19.
units.tr: 2. This mystery, so alien to corrupt reason, should be the object of our faith, hope, love, adoration, etc. Let us lean most firmly on the testimony of the three persons: with the Spirit working in us, let us come through the Son to the Father, etc. Thus our practice is distinguished from perfidy, idolatry and superstitions of Christians and Pseudo-Christians: John 5:23; 14:1; 1 John 2:23; 5:7, 9, 20, 21; Eph. 2:18; 3:12; Matt. 28:19.

units.la: 3. In operibus externis, modum & ordinem operandi internum consideremus, celebremus: Psal. xxxiii, 6. Ioh. v, 19. Hebr. I, 2, 1 Cor, 11, 10, Speciatim vero, quis sit nobis Pater cœlestis; quis frater primogenitus, Sponsor, Servator, &c. Quis Doctor ac Ductor veritatis, Sanctificator, Consolator, &c. Rom. viii, 15, 16, 17. Col. 1, 18. Apoc. I, 5. Hebr. 1, 2, 6; 8, -12, 11, 10, -13; 17. vii, 22. Matth. 1, 21. Col. 1, 19. 11, 9. Joh. xiv, 6; 16, 17; 24, 26. Rom. viii, 11. Ephef. iv, 30.
units.tr: 3. In external works let us consider and celebrate the internal mode and order of acting: Ps. 33:6; John 5:19; Heb. 1:2; 1 Cor. 11:10. Specifically, let us consider who is our heavenly Father; who is the firstborn brother, Surety, Saviour, etc.; who is the Teacher and Guide of truth, Sanctifier, Comforter, etc.: Rom. 8:15, 16, 17; Col. 1:18; Rev. 1:5; Heb. 1:2, 6; 8:12; 10:13, 17; 7:22; Matt. 1:21; Col. 1:19; 2:9; John 14:6; 16:17, 24, 26; Rom. 8:11; Eph. 4:30.

units.la: 4. Consideremus, ad quantam gloriam evecta sit caro nostra in Christo; & quanta nobis per Ipsum parata: Hebr. 2, 14, -17. Col. 1, 19, 20. II, 9, 10. Joh. I, 14. 16. xiv, 2, 3.
units.tr: 4. Let us consider to what glory our flesh has been raised in Christ, and how great the things prepared for us through him are: Heb. 2:14–17; Col. 1:19, 20; 2:9, 10; John 1:14, 16; 14:2, 3.

units.la: 5. Ex unitate trium Personarum grati æstimemus unionem & communionem nostram cum Christo, & in ipso cum SS. Trinitate: 1 Joh. v, 7. Joh. x, 29, 39, 38. xvii, 10, 11; 21, 22; 26, 27.
units.tr: 5. From the unity of the three Persons let us gratefully esteem our union and communion with Christ, and in him with the Most Holy Trinity: 1 John 5:7; John 10:29, 30, 38; 17:10, 11, 21, 22, 26, 27.

units.la: 6. Ad beatissimam illam SS. Trinitatis communionem adsciti, cum aliis fidelibus unionem & communionem alacriter & prompte colamus: 1 Joh. 1: 3. 1 Cor, xii, 11, 12, 13, &c.
units.tr: 6. Admitted to that most blessed communion of the Most Holy Trinity, let us cultivate eagerly and promptly union and communion with the other faithful: 1 John 1:3; 1 Cor. 12:11, 12, 13, etc.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De Decreto Dei.
units.tr: On the Decree of God.

units.la: Actiones Dei; immanentes; ad intra; essentiales: personales: ad extra. 1. Decretum. 2. Quid supponat; & quid notet. Quomodo Consilium appelletur. Actus vitalis Dei. 3. Summa in eo Sapientia. 4. Libertas. Æternitas. Obj. solv. 5. Quomodo seipse Deus. Obj. solv. Objectum præjacens. cens, & terminans. Ordo intentionis, & executionis. 6. Decretum Dei immutabile. 7. Generale, & speciale. 8. Decretum creationis. Providentia. 9. Objecta bona. Quid de malis. 10. Decretum de immobili vita humana termino, probatur. 11. Objectiones solvuntur. 12. Prædestinatio. Distinguitur ratione objectorum; & terminorum. Reprobatio etiam est prædestinatio, c. Pontif. & Luther. 13. Electio; & Reprobatio Angelorum. 14. Electio Hominum: certorum quorundam definitè. c. Socin. Remonstr. &c. 15. Absoluta, seu immutabiliter certa: & quidem ab æterno. Non ex prævisâ fide. c. Remonstr. & Luther. neque meritis; c. Pontif. sed ex mero Dei beneplacito. 16. Christus, quomodo ibi spectandus. Sententia Lutheranorum; atque item Remonstrantium. 17 Finis ejus. 18. Objectiones solvuntur. 19. Electionis certitudo: etiam subjectiva. 20. Objectiones solv. 21. Hominum reprobatio. Etiam certarum personarum - c. Socin. Remonstr. &c. 22. Ab æterno, & immutabiliter facta. Non ex prævisa infidelitate, &c. Sed ex Dei placito. 23. Finis ejus. 24. Objectiones solv. 25. Remonstrantium sententia. 26. Prædestinatio Angelorum, & Hominum, pariter collata. 27. Praxis. 28.
units.tr: The actions of God: immanent; ad intra; essential; personal; ad extra. 1. The decree. 2. What it presupposes and what it signifies. How it is called counsel. The vital act of God. 3. The sum of wisdom in it. 4. Liberty. Eternity. Objections answered. 5. How God is himself. Objections answered. The antecedent object. and terminating object. The order of intention and of execution. 6. The decree of God is immutable. 7. General and special. 8. The decree of creation. Providence. 9. The good objects. What of evil ones? 10. The decree concerning the fixed term of human life is proved. 11. Objections are answered. 12. Predestination. It is distinguished by reason of its objects and its termini. Reprobation is also predestination, against the Papists and Luther. 13. The election and reprobation of angels. 14. The election of men: of certain particular persons, definitely. Against the Socinians, the Remonstrants, etc. 15. Absolute, or immutably certain; and indeed from eternity. Not from foreseen faith, against the Remonstrants and Luther; nor from merits, against the Papists; but from the mere good pleasure of God. 16. How Christ is to be regarded here. The opinion of the Lutherans, and likewise of the Remonstrants. 17. Its end. 18. Objections are answered. 19. The certainty of election, including the subjective certainty. 20. Objections answered. 21. The reprobation of men, including that of certain persons. Against the Socinians, the Remonstrants, etc. 22. Made from eternity and immutably. Not from foreseen unbelief, etc., but from the pleasure of God. 23. Its end. 24. Objections answered. 25. The opinion of the Remonstrants. 26. The predestination of angels and of men, likewise compared. 27. Practice. 28.

units.la: I. SIc de Dei essentiâ & Personis. Ipso duce, ad Actiones Divinas procedimus.
units.tr: I. Thus concerning the essence and Persons of God. With him as our guide, we proceed to the Divine Actions.

units.la: Harum aliæ sunt immanentes ; aliæ transeuntes.
units.tr: Of these, some are immanent and others transient.

units.la: Immanentes sic in Deo manent, ut per se nihil extra ipsum constituant. Suntque vel ad intra, vel ad extra.
units.tr: Immanent actions remain in God in such a way that they produce nothing outside him. They are either ad intra (towards within) or ad extra (towards without).

units.la: Priores terminantur in ipsum Deum, ratione Essentiæ aut Personarum: utpote tum Essentiales, communes tribus Personis ; qualis est ex. gr. actus, quo Deus seipsum cognoscit, & amat: tum Personales, singulis Personis propriæ ; ut Generatio, & Spiratio.
units.tr: The former terminate in God himself, with respect to his essence or to the Persons. They are essential, common to the three Persons, such as the act by which God knows and loves himself; or personal, proper to each Person, such as generation and spiration.

units.la: Actus cognoscendi Patris & Filii mutuus, idem realiter est ; ut & amandi: sed modus & ordo distinctus.
units.tr: The act by which the Father and the Son know each other is mutual and is really the same; so too is the act of loving. But the mode and order are distinct.

units.la: Actiones ad extra pro termino respiciunt aliquid extra Deum ; scil. creaturas.
units.tr: Actions ad extra have as their term something outside God, namely creatures.

units.la: Voluntio assumendi Humanam naturam in Hypostasin Filii determinatè, est actio Essentialis ; servato tamen ordine & modo Personarum ; quamvis terminatio objecti, Humanæ istius naturæ, referenda sit ad hypostasin Filii distinctè.
units.tr: The will to assume human nature into the hypostasis of the Son, specifically, is an essential action; yet the order and mode of the Persons is preserved, although the term of the object, that human nature, must be referred distinctly to the hypostasis of the Son.

units.la: II. Actio Immanens ad extra est Decretum ; ipsum formaliter in Deo manens, sed objecta alia à Deo respiciens. Jes. XIV, 27. Jehovah iniit Consilium, XLVI, 10. Consilium Meum stabit. Dan. IV, 24. Decretum Altissimi hoc. Eph. I, 11. Gen. XL, 32. Act. 2, 23, IV. 28. XVII, 26, 31. Est autem actus Mentis Divinæ, ab æterno apud se liberrimè & sapientissimè constituentis, quid, & quomodo, in tempore esset futurum ad Gloriam ipsius.
units.tr: II. The immanent action ad extra is the Decree. It remains formally in God, but it regards objects other than God. Isa. 14:27. The LORD has purposed it; 46:10. My counsel shall stand. Dan. 4:24. This is the decree of the Most High. Eph. 1:11. Gen. 40:32. Acts 2:23; 4:28; 17:26, 31. It is an act of the Divine Mind, which from eternity, with perfect freedom and wisdom, determined within itself what, and how, should come to pass in time, for his glory.

units.la: III. Decretum præsupponit in Deo notitiam possibilium ; notatque ordinationem quorundam ad certam futuritionem, & quidem ad Gloriam ipsius. Prov. XVI, 4. Omnia operatur Iehovah propter Seipsum. Rom. XI. 36. xi, 36. In ipsum sunt omnia. Eph. 1, 6, Ad laudem gloriosae suae gratiae. Rom. ix, 22, 23, 24.
units.tr: III. The Decree presupposes in God knowledge of possibilities. It denotes the ordering of certain things towards a definite future, and indeed towards his own glory. Prov. 16:4. The LORD has made all things for himself. Rom. 11:36. For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things. Eph. 1:6, to the praise of the glory of his grace. Rom. 9:22, 23, 24.

units.la: Consilium aliquoties vocatur; ut patet ex praeallegatis. Verùm ab hoc conceptu removenda est omnis ignorantia, addubitatio, & succesivus mentis progressus. Nam Omnia sunt nuda & intimè patentia oculis Ejus, Heb. iv, 13. Apud quem non est transmutatio, vel conversionis obumbratio, Iac. 1, 17.
units.tr: The term counsel is sometimes used, as is clear from the passages cited above. But from this concept all ignorance, doubt and successive progress of the mind must be removed.
