For all things are naked and open to his eyes, Heb. 4:13. With whom there is no variation, nor shadow of turning, Jas. 1:17.

units.la: Concipitur ergo actus vitalis Dei, spectantis Se primariò; & in Potentiâ suâ, Possibilia; deque iis seligentis, disponentis, & ordinantis quae voluit, actû perfectissimo & simplicissimo, quamvis objecta distincta sint.
units.tr: Therefore the divine act is conceived as a vital act of God, regarding himself primarily, and, in his power, the possibles; and selecting, disposing and ordaining from among them what he willed, by a most perfect and most simple act, although the objects are distinct.

units.la: IV. Sapientia hîc summa est, omnia ad finem ultimum aptissimè ordinans: subordinatosque fines, & media, quam optimè disponens: Rom. viii, 28, 29, 30. Quos praescivit, praedestinavit; - quos praedestinavit, eos vocavit; quos vocavit, justificavit; quos justificavit, glorificavit. x, 13-17. Quomodo invocabunt, in quem non crediderint? quomodo credent, de quo non audierint? & quomodo audient, absque praedicante? quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? - Ergo Fides ex auditu est; auditus autem per Verbum Dei. Vide etiam Eph. 1, 3-6. Hos. 2, 21, 22. Rom. xi, 33, 34. Psal. xciv, 9, 10.
units.tr: IV. Here wisdom is supreme, most aptly ordering all things to the ultimate end, and most excellently arranging the subordinate ends and means. Rom. 8:28, 29, 30: Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated; whom he predestinated, them he also called; whom he called, them he also justified; whom he justified, them he also glorified. 10:13-17: How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, unless they be sent? Therefore faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God. See also Eph. 1:3-6; Hos. 2:21, 22; Rom. 11:33, 34; Ps. 94:9, 10.

units.la: V. Libertas etiàm patet tum ex Independentiâ, supremâque Potentiâ simul & Potestate; unde nulla violentia, aut coactio externa Deo accidere potest: Rom. ix, 19. Voluntati ejus quis obstitit? Tum ex summa perfectione Intellectûs & Voluntatis ipsius; quapropter omnia decernit cum summâ ratione, adeoque etiàm complacentiâ, necessitati naturali intrinsecè oppositâ: ilta celebratur, Matth. xi, 26. Pater, quia itâ Tibi placuit. Rom. xi, 34. Quis Ei fuit à consilio? Adde Psal. cxv, 3. Isai. xlvi, 10, Caecus impetus, & potentia obedientialis, Intellectui summo & perfectissimo minimè conveniunt. Sed ut Natura, sic Libertas Dei, CreaCreaturarum omnium Libertatem infinita ἐξουσία superat. Isef. xli5. Angloriabitur securis contra cædentem ipsâ? an se magnificabit serra contra agitatorem suum? Rom. ix,21. An non habet potestatem Figulus in lutum, &c.
units.tr: V. Liberty is also evident, both from his independence and from his supreme power and authority together; whence no violence or external compulsion can befall God. Rom. 9:19: Who has resisted his will? It is also evident from the highest perfection of his intellect and will. Therefore he decrees all things with the highest reason, and so also with complacency, which is intrinsically opposed to natural necessity. This is celebrated in Matt. 11:26: Father, for so it seemed good in your sight. Rom. 11:34: Who has been his counsellor? Add Ps. 115:3; Isa. 46:10. Blind impulse and obedient power do not agree with the highest and most perfect intellect. But as his nature, so his liberty surpasses the liberty of all creatures with infinite authority [ἐξουσία]. Isa. 10:15: Shall the axe boast itself against him who hews with it? Or shall the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? Rom. 9:21: Has not the potter power over the clay? etc.

units.la: V. Æternitas probatur, 1. generatim, ex Act. xv, 18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua, cum Eph.I,11, Agit omnia ex Consilio Voluntatis suæ.
units.tr: V. Eternity is proved: 1. generally, from Acts 15:18: All his works are known to God from eternity, together with Eph. 1:11: He works all things according to the counsel of his will.

units.la: 2. Specialius: 1 Cor. 2, 7. Præfinierat ante sæcula, Eph. 1, 4. Elegit nos ante jactum mundi fundamentum. 2 Tim. 1, 9. ante tempora sæculorum.
units.tr: 2. More specifically: 1 Cor. 2:7: which he had predetermined before the ages; Eph. 1:4: he chose us before the foundation of the world; 2 Tim. 1:9: before the times of the ages.

units.la: 3. Ex Immutabilitate, quæ asserta est sup.: cap. 4. th. 20. Si enim Deus extitisset aliquando sine Decreto, postea Decretum in se formasset; ea foret satis insignis mutatio.
units.tr: 3. From immutability, which was asserted above, ch. 4, th. 20: For if God had at some time existed without a decree, and afterwards had formed a decree within himself, that would be a rather remarkable change.

units.la: 4. Ex ipsius Æternitate; de quâ cap.4. th.26. Deus enim non exitit tempore infinito sine Decreto suo: cæteroquin nè nunc quidem Decretum haberet. Nec tempore finito: hoc enim æternitati non convenit.
units.tr: 4. From his eternity itself, which is treated in ch. 4, th. 26. For God did not exist for an infinite time without his decree; otherwise he would not even now have a decree. Nor for a finite time either, for this does not agree with eternity.

units.la: Obj. Omne æternum est necessarium: Decretum vero liberum est, non necessarium? Ergo. Resp. Æternitas Decreti Divini infert solummodo necessitatem ex hypothesi. Interim quatenus Deus cum summa ratione & complacentia ab æterno Decretum fecit, & sic constituit de possibilibus, cum absolutè alia & aliter constituere potuisset; agnoscendum etiam, Decretum istud esse liberrimum, & necessariò tale.
units.tr: Obj. Everything eternal is necessary; but the Decree is free, not necessary. Therefore... Resp. The eternity of the Divine Decree implies necessity only by hypothesis. Meanwhile, insofar as God, with the highest reason and complacency, made the decree from eternity, and so determined concerning the possibles, when he could have determined otherwise and differently in an absolute sense, we must acknowledge that this decree is most free, and necessarily so.

units.la: VI. Actus Decreti Divini subjectivè & principativè omnino Simplex est, & sic ipse Deus, contra Vorstium. Quamvis objectivè & terminativè spectet plurima alia à Deo.
units.tr: VI. The act of the Divine Decree, considered subjectively and as its principle, is wholly simple and so is God himself, against Vorstius. Yet objectively and as to its terminus it regards many things other than God.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deus unus est; Decreta vero multa: ergo hæc non ipse Deus. Resp. Actus ille vitalis in se etiam unicus est: sed decreta multa denominamus ab objectis.
units.tr: Obj. 1. God is one, but the decrees are many; therefore they are not God himself. Resp. That vital act is itself also single in itself, but we name the decrees as many from their objects.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus est ens necessarium; Decretum vero liberum: ergò, &c. Resp. Deus quidem est Ens maximè necessarium in existendo; sed & liberrimum in operando extra se. Similiter Decreti existentia necessaria est in Ente sapientissimo; quamvis terminatio ejus talis, respectu objectorum, liberrima.
units.tr: Obj. 2. God is a necessary being, but the decree is free; therefore, etc. Resp. God is indeed most necessary in existing, but also most free in acting outside himself. Likewise the existence of the decree is necessary in the most wise Being, although its terminating, with respect to its objects, is most free.

units.la: Distinguendum interim objectum præjacens, & terminans. Objectum præjacens sunt ipsa Possibilia, sic vel aliter determinabilia, & per summam Dei potestatem ac Sapientiam ad statuin qualemcunque determinanda. Objectum terminans, aut potius terminatum, sunt Futura, & consequenter Præsentia, vel etiam Præterita: statum enim istiusmodi habent, quia Deus ita decrevit.
units.tr: Meanwhile we must distinguish the object presupposed and the object terminating. The object presupposed is the possibles themselves, determinable in this way or that, and to be determined to whatever state by the supreme power and wisdom of God. The object terminating, or rather the terminated, are the future things, and consequently the present, or even the past: for they have this state because God so decreed.

units.la: Deus etiàm decernendo ordinem constituit in rebus decretis: qui est vel intentionis, vel executionis. Ordo intentionis ad Decretum magis proprie pertinet: prout Deus sapientissimè ad fines ordinavit sua media. Ordo executionis succedit in complemento.
units.tr: By decreeing, God also establishes an order among the things decreed, which is either of intention or of execution. The order of intention pertains more properly to the Decree, insofar as God most wisely ordained his means to ends. The order of execution follows in the completion.

units.la: Hùc pertinet Canon; Quod primum est in intentione, est postremum in executione; & contra: nam in intentione finis est causa mediorum; media sunt propter finem: sed in executione, finis est ipsum effectum, quod per media obtinetur. Confer sup. cap 4. th. 62.
units.tr: To this belongs the canon: What is first in intention is last in execution, and conversely. For in intention the end is the cause of the means, and the means are for the sake of the end; but in execution the end is the effect itself, which is obtained through the means. See above, chapter 4, thesis 62.

units.la: VII. Immutabile etiàm est Dei Decretum; & consequenter efficax, per ipsius Omnipotentiam. Sic conjunguntur Manus & Consilium Dei, Act. iv, 24. Ita Jes. xiv, 27. Consilium Jehovæ quis irritum faciat? & manum Ejus quis avertat? Prov. xix, 21. Consilium Jehovæ stabit. Vide etiàm Jes. LV, 10, 11. Consequenter, omne Decretum in se est absolutum, respectu actus Divini, independentis: nullum conditionatum; nisi sic objectivè denominetur.
units.tr: VII. God's Decree is also immutable, and consequently effective, through his Omnipotence. Thus the Hand and Counsel of God are joined, Acts 4:24. So Isaiah 14:27: Who shall annul the counsel of Jehovah? And who shall turn back his hand? Proverbs 19:21: The counsel of Jehovah shall stand. See also Isaiah 55:10, 11. Consequently, every Decree is in itself absolute, with respect to the divine act, which is independent; none is conditional, unless it is so named objectively.

units.la: VIII. Extenditse Decretum ad omnia alia à Deo: Eph. I, 11. Vide sup. th. 5. Thren. iii, 37, 38. Ecquo dicente exististit aliquid, quod Dominus non præceperit? Ex ore Excelsi, an non prodit malum quodque, & bonum? Rom. xi, 36. Estque pro nostro concipiendi modo, vel generale: ubi spectatur universa omnium objectorum amplitudo: vel speciale, quod iterum suos gradus amplitudinis habet; ut Creationis, Providentiae, de Termino vitae humanae, Praedestinationis, &c. sed postremum istud καθ' ἐξοχὴν speciale appellatur.
units.tr: VIII. The Decree extends to all things other than God: Ephesians 1:11. See above, thesis 5. Lamentations 3:37, 38: Who has spoken and it came to pass, which the Lord has not commanded? Does not good and evil come out of the mouth of the Most High? Romans 11:36. It is, according to our manner of conceiving, either general, where the whole breadth of all objects is considered, or special, which again has its degrees of breadth, as of Creation, Providence, the Term of human life, Predestination, etc. But this last is called special par excellence [καθ' ἐξοχὴν].

units.la: IX. Decretum Creationis est, quo Deus ab aeterno constituit, creaturas ex nihilo producere, in tempore; ad gloriam suam. Apoc. iv, 11. per Voluntatem Tuam sunt, & creata sunt. Act. xv, 18. Eph. i, 11.
units.tr: IX. The Decree of Creation is that by which God, from eternity, determined to produce creatures out of nothing, in time, to his glory. Revelation 4:11: through your will they are, and were created. Acts 15:18. Ephesians 1:11.

units.la: Decretum Providentiae est, quo Deus ab aeterno conftituit, Creaturas confervare, iis cooperari, easque gubernare, ad gloriam Suam. Distinguitur hoc in Essectivum quo Deus proposuit omnia bona, futura vera efficientia operari; a quo omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum descendit, Jac. i, 17. Quicquid placet facit. Pfal. cxv, 3. & in Permissivum, quo proposuit mala in causis fecundis non impedire. Act. 2, 23, 24. Definito consilio & praecognitione Dei deditum, &c. Similiter fere iv, 27, 28. Item Pfal. lxxxi, 17. Dimisi eos ambulaturos, &c. Act. xiv, 16. 17. Sivit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. cum Gen. xx, 6. Cohibui te, ne peccares in Me: idcirco non sivi te attingere eam.
units.tr: The Decree of Providence is that by which God, from eternity, determined to preserve creatures, to cooperate with them, and to govern them, to his glory. This is distinguished into the effective, by which God purposed to work all good things, which are to be effected as true, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, James 1:17. Whatever he pleases he does. Psalm 115:3. and into the permissive, by which he purposed not to hinder evils in second causes. Acts 2:23, 24: delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, etc. Similarly, nearly, Acts 4:27, 28. Likewise Psalm 81:12: I let them go on in their ways, etc. Acts 14:16, 17: he suffered all nations to walk in their own ways. Compare Genesis 20:6: I kept you from sinning against me; therefore I did not let you touch her.

units.la: X. Futura sunt proprie & per se Bona, Mala non nisi ratione subjecti boni sunt, aut fiunt; in quo tantum alterius boni privationem significant: quam supplere Deo non placet; cum etiam, si voluisset, nihil conferre potuisset. Imo vero, o Homo; tu quis es qui ex adverso respondes Deo? num dicet figmentum fictori, cur me tale fecisti? annon habet potestatem figulus, &c. Rom. ix, 20, 21.
units.tr: X. Future things are properly and in themselves good; evils are only good by reason of the subject of the good, or they come to be so; in which they signify only the privation of another good, which God does not will to supply, since even if he had willed, he could have contributed nothing. Indeed, O man, who are you who answer back against God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, Why have you made me thus? Does not the potter have power, etc.? Romans 9:20, 21.

units.la: A Decreto permissivo recte quidem procedit illatio Logica; ut a non-actione causae primae, ad nonpositionem effectus. Errant autem gravissime Adversarii, Deum hinc peccati auctorem statui calumniantes. Vere interim Deus decrevit in genere Entis bona facere, mala autem physicè permittere; consequenter etiam hæc necessario futura sunt. Matth. xviii, 7. Necesse est, ut eveniant offendicula. xxvi, 24. Filius hominis abit, sicut scriptum est de eo, &c. Luc. xxiv, 26. Nonne hæc oportuit Christum pati? &c. 2 Thess. ii, 13. Apoc. I, 1.
units.tr: From the permissive Decree a logical inference rightly proceeds, as from the non-action of the first cause to the non-positing of the effect. But the Adversaries err most gravely, slandering God as thereby made the author of sin. Truly, however, God has decreed, in the general order of being, to do good things but to permit evils physically; consequently these also are certainly to come about. Matthew 18:7: It is necessary that offenses come. 26:24: The Son of Man goes, as it is written of him, etc. Luke 24:26: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things? etc. 2 Thessalonians 2:13. Revelation 1:1.

units.la: XI. Decretum de immobili vitæ humanæ termino est, quo Deus constituit ab æterno, quamdiu quisque ho- minum determinatè victurus esset in hoc mundo.
units.tr: XI. The decree concerning the immovable term of human life is that by which God determined from eternity how long each human being was definitely going to live in this world.

units.la: Quod probatur contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes: 1. expressis S. Scripturæ testimoniis. Job. xiv, 1. 2, 5. „Homo natus muliere, brevis ætate, „- . Quandoquidem præcisi sunt dies ejus; numerus ejus penes Te est: determinationem ejus fecisti: quas non transgrediatur: Psal. xxxix, 5, 6. - Palmares dispositisti dies meos. cxxxix, 16. In libro Tuo hæc omnia scripta sunt, „(ex quibus) diebus formabantur, cum nondum ullum eorum (extaret.) Act. xvii, 25, 26. Definitis præstitutis temporibus, & positis terminis habitationis eorum. Eccl. iii, 1, 2. Cuique sua tempestas. - Tempus pariendi & tempus moriendi. Vide etiam Job. viii, 20. Jes. xxxviii, 5.
units.tr: This is proved against the Socinians, the Anabaptists, and the Remonstrants: (1) by express testimonies of Holy Scripture. Job 14:1, 2, 5: "Man, born of woman, is of few days... Since his days are cut off, his number is with Thee; Thou hast appointed his bounds, which he cannot pass." Ps. 39:5, 6: "Thou hast made my days a handbreadth." 139:16: "In Thy book all these things were written, which were being formed as days, when none of them yet existed." Acts 17:25, 26: "having appointed times, and fixed the bounds of their habitation." Eccl. 3:1, 2: "To everything there is a season... a time to be born and a time to die." See also Job 8:20 and Isa. 38:5.

units.la: 2. Ex eo, quòd Deus sit Arbiter vitæ & necis: dicens, Psal. xc, 3. Revertimini filii hominum. 1 Sam. 11, 6. Jehovah morte afficit, & in vitam restituit. cum Eph. I, 11. Act. xv, 18.
units.tr: (2) From the fact that God is the arbiter of life and death. He says, Ps. 90:3: "Return, ye sons of men." 1 Sam. 11, 6: "Jehovah kills and restores to life." Compare Eph. 1:11 and Acts 15:18.

units.la: 3. A minori: Matth. x, 29, 30, 31. Nonne duo passerculi assario veniunt: & unus ex iis non cadet in terram sine Patre vestro? Vestri vero etiam capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. Ne igitur Timete: vos multis passerculis præstatis.
units.tr: (3) From the lesser to the greater: Matt. 10:29, 30, 31: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows."

units.la: 4. Quia plurima alia, etiàm maxima ac gravissima, ab hominum vitâ dependent; quorum alioqui non esset certa futuritio. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 36, 37.
units.tr: (4) Because very many other things, even the greatest and most serious, depend on the length of human life, and without a fixed term their future occurrence would not be certain. Compare above, chap. 4, theses 36 and 37.

units.la: XII. Obj: 1. Per istiusmodi Decretum tollitur omnis creaturarum libertas & contingentia.
units.tr: XII. Objection 1: By such a decree all freedom and contingency of creatures is taken away.

units.la: Resp. Imò Deus decrevit satis multa, quae natura sua essent libera, vel contingentia; quamvis eadem necessario futura necessitate externa.
units.tr: Answer: On the contrary, God decreed many things which, by their own nature, would be free or contingent, although they are going to happen by an external necessity.

units.la: Obj. 2. Evertitur omnium mediorum necessitas & alimentorum, medicamentorum, precum, &c. Resp. Nego: Deus enim decrevit & ordinavit conditiones ac media necessaria, ad tales fines. Act. xxvii, 31. Nisi isti in navi manserint, vos servari non potestis. Hebr. xi, 6. Absque fide impossibile est Deo placere.
units.tr: Objection 2: The necessity of all means is overturned, and of food, medicines, prayers, and so on. Answer: I deny it. For God decreed and ordained the conditions and necessary means for such ends. Acts 27:31: "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved." Heb. 11:6: "Without faith it is impossible to please God."

units.la: Obj. 3. Exod. xx, 12. & alibi, piis longaevitas promittitur; contra vero Psal. lv, 24. improbi dicuntur non perventuri ad medium dierum: ergo non praestitutus est iis terminus immobilis. Aperte etiam dicuntur Ezechiae additi anni quindecim; Jef. xxxviii,
units.tr: Objection 3: Exod. 20:12, and elsewhere, long life is promised to the pious; on the contrary, Ps. 55:24 says that the wicked will not reach the middle of their days. Therefore no fixed and immovable term was appointed for them. Also, it is plainly said that fifteen years were added to Hezekiah: Isa. 38,

units.la: 5. Resp. 1. Piis promittitur beata longitudo dierum; Psal. xxiii, 6. hic quodammodo inchoanda: sed in coelesti haereditate consummanda, cujus Canaan typus fuit: non tamen in hoc saeculo producenda ultra terminum a Deo definitum. 2. Impii autem ad medium dierum non sunt perventuri; scil. quos naturaliter, habita ratione valetudinis ac roboris, supervivere potuissent. 3. Ezechiae denique post morbum istum tot anni adjecti sunt; non termino universae illius vitae prius Divinitus praefinito.
units.tr: 5. Answer: (1) A blessed length of days is promised to the pious, Ps. 23:6. This is in some way to be begun here, but to be completed in the heavenly inheritance, of which Canaan was a type; yet it is not to be extended in this age beyond the term defined by God. (2) The wicked, however, are not going to reach the middle of their days; namely, those whom, taking account of health and strength, they could naturally have outlived. (3) Finally, after that illness, so many years were added to Hezekiah; this was not because the term of his whole life had previously been predetermined by God.

units.la: XIII. Praedestinatio est Decretum Dei de Creatu- rarum rationalium statu aeterno; ad manifestandam Potentiae, Sapientiae, Gratiae, & Justitiae suae Glo- riam.
units.tr: XIII. Predestination is God's eternal decree concerning the state of rational creatures, made to manifest the glory of his power, wisdom, grace, and justice.

units.la: Ea ratione objectorum vel est Angelorum, vel Hominum.
units.tr: In respect of its objects, it is either of angels or of men.

units.la: Ratione terminorum vel est Electio, vel Reprobatio. Jef. xli, 9. Elegi te, & non reprobavi. Rom. ix, 13. Jacobum dilexi, & Esavum odio habui. 1 Thess. v, 9. Non constituit nos ad Iram, sed ad salutem obtinendam.
units.tr: In respect of its terms, it is either Election or Reprobation. Isa. xli, 9: I have chosen you, and have not rejected you. Rom. ix, 13: Jacob I have loved, and Esau I have hated. 1 Thess. v, 9: God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation.

units.la: Non recte contendunt Pontifícii & Lutherani, Damnandorum praescientiam solum esse; non Praedestinationem: cum 1. etiàm illa Decretum permissivum & ordinativum præsupponat. Et 2. Spiritus Sanctus Prædestinationem diserte in isto negotio appellet: Act.iv, 28. Ut facerent, quæcunque manus Tua & Consilium Tuum prius definierat προωρισεν) ut fierent. Atque 3. Phrases æquipollentes occurrant: utpote Judæ, 4. Præscripti ad damnationem. 1 Thess. v, 9. Et 4. Præscientia, aut Præcognitio, de Electione etiam usurpetur; Rom.viii, 29. xi. 2.
units.tr: Papists and Lutherans wrongly contend that there is only foreknowledge of the damned, and not predestination. For (1) that foreknowledge presupposes also a permissive and ordinative decree. (2) The Holy Spirit explicitly calls it predestination in this matter: Acts iv, 28: to do whatever Your hand and Your counsel had determined beforehand [προώρισεν] to come to pass. (3) Equivalent phrases occur, as in Jude 4: marked out beforehand for condemnation; and 1 Thess. v, 9. (4) Foreknowledge, or foreknowing, is also used of election: Rom. viii, 29; xi, 2.

units.la: XIV. Electio Angelorum quorundam patet, ex 1 Tim. v, 21. „Obtestor - in conspectu - Electorum Angelorum. Unde etiam aliorum Reprobatio facilè colligitur. Et Judæ, 6. Deus Angelos - judicio magni illius diei vinculis æternis sub caligine servavit. Matth.xxv, 41. In ignem æternum paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus. Addi potest argumentum à minori, ut sup. th.11, §. 3.
units.tr: XIV. The election of certain angels is evident from 1 Tim. v, 21: I charge you, in the sight of the elect angels. From this the reprobation of the others is also easily inferred. And Jude 6: God has kept the angels … in eternal chains under darkness until the judgment of the great day. Matth. xxv, 41: into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. An argument from the lesser can be added, as above, th. 11, §3.

units.la: Electio Angelorum, est Prædestinatio, quâ Deus ab æterno definitè constituit, quosdam Angelos, ubi in tempore boni & sancti essent creati, per Gratiam suam conservare & confirmare in statu isto; ad ipsorum Salutem, & Gloriam Potentiæ, Sapientiæ, & Gratiæ suæ.
units.tr: The election of angels is that predestination by which God from eternity definitely decreed that certain angels, when they were created good and holy in time, should be preserved and confirmed in that state by his grace, for their own salvation and to the glory of his power, wisdom, and grace.

units.la: Reprobatio verò est Prædestinatio, quâ similiter definitè constituit aliorum lapsum permittere, in eo ipsos relinquere & gubernare, ac propter peccata æternum condemnare; ad Gloriam Potentiæ, Sapientiæ, & Justitiæ suæ.
units.tr: Reprobation, on the other hand, is that predestination by which, in the same way, he definitely decreed to permit the fall of others, to leave them in it and govern them there, and on account of their sins to condemn them eternally, to the glory of his power, wisdom, and justice.

units.la: Interim pro suprema suâ potestate Deus talem futuritionem constituit atque ordinavit. Lapsus verò non est causa Reprobationis, volitionis istius Divinæ; quæ est independens: sed tantùm est causa demeritoria talium pœnarum,
units.tr: Meanwhile, by his supreme power, God established and ordained such a future. The fall, however, is not the cause of this divine act of reprobation, which is independent; it is only the meritorious cause of such punishments.

units.la: XV. Electio Hominum, est Prædestinatio, quâ Deus ab æterno constituit de Hominibus, ubi in tempore ad Imaginem Suam essent conditi, sed labiles; ac deinceps, Ipso permittente, in Adamo pariter lapsi §
units.tr: XV. The election of men is that predestination by which God from eternity decreed concerning men, who in time were to be created in his own image but were liable to fall; and afterwards, by his permission, fallen in Adam likewise §

units.la: quoltanda initio Potestas, quâ Christus Sacramentum istud instituit quæ citra hoc dogma rectè intelligi non potest. Tùm Præceptum docendi & baptizandi Christianos in nomen trium personarum, tanquàm Domini nostri spiritualis, ex quo salus æterna pendet. Scil. ut eædem personæ distinctè apparuerunt in Baptismo ipsius Christi; sic earum confessio editur in Sacramento initiationis nostræ. Ac porrò Mandatum ista deinceps observandi, sub promissione tàm illustri: pro quâ Marc. xvi,16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, servabitur; qui verò non crediderit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: Also at the beginning, the power by which Christ instituted this sacrament, which cannot be rightly understood apart from this doctrine. Then the command to teach and baptize Christians into the name of the three persons, as of our spiritual Lord, on which eternal salvation depends. Namely, as these same persons appeared distinctly at the baptism of Christ himself, so their confession is put forth in the sacrament of our initiation. And further, the mandate to observe these things thereafter, under so illustrious a promise, for which: Mark xvi, 16: He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned.

units.la: 2. Joh. xvii,3. Hæc est autem vita æterna, ut Te cognoscant, illum solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum At Pater, ut sic, sine Filio cognosci non potest. Hinc Joh. xiv, 1, 19, 10, 11. Creditis in Deum, etiam in Me credite. - Qui vidit Me, vidit Patrem - Non credis Me in Patre, & Patrem in Me esse? Et v, 23. Qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem Item. Joh. 11, 23. Quisquis negat Filium, nec Patrem habet: propter essentialem identitatem. Spiritus Sancti eadem est ratio. 1 Cor. xii,
units.tr: 2. John xvii, 3: This is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent. But the Father, as such, cannot be known without the Son. Hence John xiv, 1, 9, 10, 11: You believe in God; believe also in Me. He who has seen Me has seen the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in Me? And v, 23: He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father. Likewise 1 John ii, 23: Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either, on account of essential identity. The same reasoning holds for the Spirit. 1 Cor. xii,

units.la: 3. Propterea notum vobis facio, neminem posse dicere Jesum Dominum, nisi per Spiritum Sanctum. A verâ igitur Deitate, & consequenter à vitâ æterna aberratur, ubi Filius, aut Spiritus Sanctus, ab illâ excluditur.
units.tr: 3. Therefore I make known to you that no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit. Therefore one wanders from the true Deity, and consequently from eternal life, wherever the Son or the Holy Spirit is excluded from it.

units.la: 3. A fine Euangelii: Joh. xx, 31. Ut credatis Iesum esse Christum illum, Filium Dei; & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ejus, cum viii,24. Nisi credideritis, Me (eum) esse, moriemini in peccatis vestris, & 1 Joh. v, 20, 21. Scimus, Filium Dei venisse. - Hic est verus ille Deus, & vita illa æterna. Filioli, cavete vobis ab idolis. Amen. Sed absque hoc dogmate fides istius veritatis haberi nequit.
units.tr: 3. From the purpose of the Gospel: John xx, 31: That you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing you may have life through his name; with viii, 24: Unless you believe that I am (he), you will die in your sins; and 1 John v, 20, 21: We know that the Son of God has come. This is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen. But without this doctrine, faith in this truth cannot be had.

units.la: 4. Absque fide hujus articuli alia præcipua Christianæ Religionis dogmata rectè teneri non possunt, utpote de Incarnatione Christi, ac porro de ipsius per-sonâ sonâ, itemque de Salutis Impetratione validâ, & Applicatione efficaci.
units.tr: 4. Without faith in this article, the other principal doctrines of the Christian religion cannot be rightly held: for example, concerning the incarnation of Christ, and further concerning his person, likewise concerning the valid obtaining of salvation and its effective application.

units.la: Obj. 1. Plurimi homines pii mysterium istud captu suo non assequuntur; nec tamen propterea æternum damnandi: ergo, &c. Resp. Fatemur, non omnibus eundem gradum fidei explicitæ obtingere: major lux sub N. T. affulsit, quàm sub V. neque adhùc æqualem omnes mensuram accipiunt. Minimum quod sic, in salutis per Dei misericordiam consequendæ negotio, non determinamus; sed quid revelatum ac præscriptum sit, & consequenter docendum atque discendum, observamus. De veritatis credendæ necessitate loquimur; non de cognitionis gradu; neque de phrasi aliquâ, aut modo explicandi, probandi, vel defendendi. Per dictam vero necessitatem excluditur tùm blasphemia, impugnatio, rejectio; tùm neglectus totalis, aut ignorantia istius veritatis.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Very many pious men do not grasp this mystery with their understanding; yet they are not on that account to be damned eternally: therefore, etc. Resp. We grant that not all receive the same degree of explicit faith: a greater light has shone under the New Testament than under the Old, and even now not all receive an equal measure. We do not determine a minimum in this matter of obtaining salvation through God's mercy; but we observe what has been revealed and prescribed, and consequently what is to be taught and learned. We speak of the necessity of believing the truth, not of the degree of knowledge, nor of some phrase or mode of explaining, proving, or defending it. By the said necessity, both blasphemy, attack, and rejection are excluded, and also total neglect or ignorance of this truth.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dogma illud non habet speciales usus pragmaticos: hi enim omnes resultant ex consideratione Essentiæ Divinæ, quæ unica est; non verò ex personalitatibus, earumque distinctione. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negamus antecedens; & contrarium ostendimus.
units.tr: Obj. 2. That doctrine has no special practical uses: for all of these arise from consideration of the divine essence, which is one; not from the personalities and their distinction. Therefore, etc. Resp. We deny the antecedent, and we show the contrary.

units.la: XXXI. Usus practici potissimum occurrunt: 1. Pio & grato animo agnoscamus ac prædicemus admirandam Dei benignitatem, quâ sese talem etiam subsistentiis revelavit nobis familiariter: Matth. xi,25,26, 27. Joh. xvii, 1, 3.
units.tr: XXXI. The practical uses chiefly occur as follows: 1. With a pious and grateful mind let us acknowledge and proclaim the admirable kindness of God, by which he has so familiarly revealed himself to us in these subsistences: Matt. xi, 25, 26, 27; John xvii, 1, 3.

units.la: 2. Mysterium istud, à corruptâ ratione tàm alienum, sit nobis fidei, spei, charitatis, adorationis, &c. objectum: trium istarum personarum testimonio nitamur firmissime: Spiritu in nobis operante, per Filium accedamus ad Patrem, &c. Sic praxis nostra distinguatur à perfidia, idololatria, & superstitionibus Christianorum ac Pseudochristianorum: Joh. v, 23. xiv, 1. 1 Joh. 2, 23. v, 7, 9, 20, 21. Eph. 2,18. iii, 12. Matth. xxviii,19.
units.tr: 2. Let this mystery, so foreign to corrupt reason, be the object of our faith, hope, love, adoration, etc. Let us rest most firmly on the testimony of the three persons: with the Spirit working in us, let us come through the Son to the Father, etc. Thus our practice is distinguished from the perfidy, idolatry, and superstitions of Christians and Pseudo-Christians: John v, 23; xiv, 1; 1 John ii, 23; v, 7, 9, 20, 21; Eph. ii, 18; iii, 12; Matt. xxviii, 19.

units.la: 3. In operibus externis, modum & ordinem operandi internum consideremus, celebremus: Psal. xxxiii, 6. Ioh. v, 19. Hebr. I, 2, 1 Cor, 11, 10, Speciatim vero, quis sit nobis Pater cœlestis; quis frater primogenitus, Sponsor, Servator, &c, Quis Doctor ac Ductor veritatis, Sanctificator, Consolator, &c, Rom. viii, 15, 16, 17. Col. 1, 18. Apoc. I, 5. Hebr. 1, 2, 6; 8, -12, 11, 10, -13; 17. vii, 22. Matth. 1, 21. Col. 1, 19. 11, 9. Joh. xiv, 6; 16, 17; 24; 26. Rom. viii, 11. Ephef. iv, 30.
units.tr: 3. In external works let us consider and celebrate the internal mode and order of working: Ps. xxxiii, 6; John v, 19; Heb. i, 2; 1 Cor. xii, 10. Specifically, who is our heavenly Father; who is the firstborn brother, Surety, Saviour, etc.; who is the Teacher and Guide of truth, Sanctifier, Comforter, etc.: Rom. viii, 15, 16, 17; Col. i, 18; Rev. i, 5; Heb. i, 2, 6; viii, 12; xi, 10, 13, 17; vii, 22; Matt. i, 21; Col. i, 19; ii, 9; John xiv, 6, 16, 17, 24, 26; Rom. viii, 11; Eph. iv, 30.

units.la: 4. Consideremus, ad quantam gloriam evecta sit caro nostra in Christo; & quanta nobis per Ipsum parata: Hebr. 2, 14, -17. Col. 1, 19, 20. II, 9, 10. Joh. I, 14. 16. xiv, 2, 3.
units.tr: 4. Let us consider to what great glory our flesh has been raised in Christ, and how much has been prepared for us through him: Heb. ii, 14–17; Col. i, 19, 20; ii, 9, 10; John i, 14, 16; xiv, 2, 3.

units.la: 5. Ex unitate trium Personarum grati æstimemus unionem & communionem nostram cum Christo, & in ipso cum SS. Trinitate: 1 Joh. v, 7. Joh. x, 29, 39, 38. xvii, 10, 11; 21, 22; 26, 27.
units.tr: 5. From the unity of the three persons let us gratefully esteem our union and communion with Christ, and in him with the most Holy Trinity: 1 John v, 7; John x, 29, 30, 38; xvii, 10, 11, 21, 22, 26, 27.

units.la: 6. Ad beatissimam illam SS. Trinitatis communionem adsciti, cum aliis fidelibus unionem & communionem alacriter & prompte colamus: 1 Joh. 1: 3. 1 Cor. xii, 11, 12, 13, &c.
units.tr: 6. Admitted to that most blessed communion of the Holy Trinity, let us eagerly and readily cultivate union and communion with the other faithful: 1 John i, 3; 1 Cor. xii, 11, 12, 13, etc.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: Chapter VI.

units.la: De Decreto Dei.
units.tr: On the Decree of God.

units.la: Actiones Dei; immanentes; ad intra; essentiales: personales: ad extra. 1. Decretum. 2. Quid supponat; & quid notet. Quomodo Consilium appelletur. Actus vitalis Dei. 3. Summa in eo Sapientia. 4. Libertas. Æternitas. Obj. solv. 5. Quomodo seipse Deus. Obj. solv. Objectum praesaciens.
units.tr: Actions of God: immanent; directed inward; essential; personal; directed outward. 1. The decree. 2. What it presupposes and what it signifies. How it is called counsel. The vital act of God. 3. Supreme wisdom in it. 4. Liberty. Eternity. Objections answered. 5. How God is toward himself. Objections answered. The object foreseeing

units.la: I. SIc de Dei essentiâ & Personis. Ipso duce, ad Actiones Divinas procedimus.
units.tr: I. Thus concerning the essence and Persons of God. With him as our guide, we proceed to the Divine Actions.

units.la: Harum aliæ sunt immanentes ; aliæ transeuntes.
units.tr: Of these, some are immanent, and others transitive.

units.la: Immanentes sic in Deo manent, ut per se nihil extra ipsum constituant. Suntque vel ad intra, vel ad extra:
units.tr: Immanent actions remain in God in such a way that they establish nothing outside him. They are either ad intra (toward within) or ad extra (toward without).

units.la: Priores terminantur in ipsum Deum, ratione Essentiæ aut Personarum: utpote tùm Essentiales, communes tribus Personis ; qualis est ex. gr. actus, quo Deus seipsum cognoscit, & amat: tùm Personales, singulis Personis propriæ ; ut Generatio, & Spiratio.
units.tr: The former terminate in God himself, with respect to the essence or the Persons. Some are essential, common to the three Persons, such as the act by which God knows and loves himself. Others are personal, proper to each Person, such as generation and spiration.

units.la: Actus cognoscendi Patris & Filii mutuus, idem realiter est ; ut & amandi: sed modus & ordo distinctus.
units.tr: The act by which the Father and the Son know each other is mutual and is really the same, and likewise the act of loving. But the mode and order are distinct.

units.la: Actiones ad extra pro termino respiciunt aliquid extra Deum ; scil. creaturas.
units.tr: Actions ad extra have as their term something outside God, namely creatures.

units.la: Volitio assumendi Humanam naturam in Hypostasin Filii determinatè, est actio Essentialis ; servato tamen ordine & modo Personarum ; quamvis terminatio objecti, Humanæ istius naturæ, referenda sit ad hypostasin Filii distinctè.
units.tr: The will to assume the human nature into the hypostasis of the Son, in a determinate way, is an essential action. Yet the order and mode of the Persons is preserved, although the terminus of the object, that human nature, must be referred distinctly to the hypostasis of the Son.

units.la: II. Actio Immanens ad extra est Decretum ; ipsum formaliter in Deo manens, sed objecta alia à Deo respiciens. Jef. XIV, 27. Jehovah iniit Consilium, XLVI, 10. Consilium Meum stabit. Dan. IV, 24. Decretum Altissimi hoc. Eph. I, 11. Gen. XL, 32. Act. 2, 23, IV. 28. XVII, 26, 31. Est autem actus Mentis Divinæ, ab æterno apud se liberrimè & sapientissimè constituentis, quid, & quomodò, in tempore esset futurum ; ad Gloriam ipsius.
units.tr: II. The immanent action ad extra is the Decree. It remains formally in God, but it regards objects other than God. Isa. 14:27: Jehovah has taken counsel. 46:10: My counsel shall stand. Dan. 4:24: This is the decree of the Most High. Eph. 1:11. Gen. 40:32. Acts 2:23; 4:28; 17:26, 31. It is an act of the Divine Mind, by which he, from eternity, most freely and most wisely determines within himself what and how things are to come to pass in time, to his own glory.

units.la: III. Decretum præsupponit in Deo notitiam possibilium ; notatque ordinationem quorundam ad certam futuritionem, & quidem ad Gloriam ipsius. Prov. XVI, 4. Omnia operatur Iehovah propter Seipsum. Rom. XI. 36. xi,36. In ipsum sunt omnia. Eph. 1, 6. Ad laudem gloriosæ suæ gratiæ. Rom. ix,22,23,24.
units.tr: III. The decree presupposes in God the knowledge of possibles. It denotes the ordering of certain things toward a certain future event, and indeed toward his own glory. Prov. 16:4: Jehovah works all things for himself. Rom. 11:36: From him, through him, and to him are all things. Eph. 1:6: To the praise of the glory of his grace. Rom. 9:22, 23, 24.

units.la: Consilium aliquoties vocatur; ut patet ex præallegatis. Verùm ab hoc conceptu removenda est omnis ignorantia, addubitatio, & successivus mentis progressus. Nam Omnia sunt nuda & intime patentia oculis Ejus, Heb. iv, 13. Apud quem non est transmutatio, vel conversionis obumbratio. Iac. 1,17.
units.tr: The counsel is sometimes so called, as is clear from the passages already cited. But from this concept all ignorance, doubt, and successive progress of the mind must be removed. For all things are naked and open to his eyes, Heb. 4:13, and with him there is no change, nor shadow of turning, Jas. 1:17.

units.la: Concipitur ergo actus vitalis Dei, spectantis Sese primario; & in Potentia suâ, Possibilia; deque iis seligentis, disponentis, & ordinantis quæ voluit, actu perfectissimo & simplicissimo, quamvis objecta distincta sint.
units.tr: The vital act of God is therefore conceived as regarding himself primarily, and, in his power, the possibles; and, choosing, disposing, and ordering from among them what he willed, by a most perfect and most simple act, although the objects are distinct.

units.la: IV. Sapientia hic summa est, omnia ad finem ultimum aptissimè ordinans: subordinatosque fines, & media, quam optimè disponens: Rom. viii,28,29,30. Quos præscivit, prædestinavit; quos prædestinavit, eos vocavit; quos vocavit, justificavit; quos justificavit, glorificavit. x,13-17. Quomodo invocabunt, in quem non crediderint? quomodo credent, de quo non audierint? & quomodo audient, absque prædicante? quomodo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Ergo Fides ex auditu est; auditus autem per Verbum Dei. Vide etiam Eph. 1, 3-6. Hos. 2, 21, 22. Rom, xi,33,34. Psal. xciv,9,10.
units.tr: IV. Here wisdom is supreme, most aptly ordering all things to the ultimate end, and disposing the subordinate ends and means as well as possible. Rom. 8:28, 29, 30: Whom he foreknew, he also predestined; whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified. 10:13-17: How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? How shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? How shall they preach unless they are sent? So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. See also Eph. 1:3-6; Hos. 2:21, 22; Rom. 11:33, 34; Ps. 94:9, 10.

units.la: V. Libertas etiam patet tum ex Independentiâ, supremaque Potentia simul & Potestate; unde nulla violentia, aut coactio externa Deo accidere potest: Rom. ix,19. Voluntati ejus quis obstitit? Tum ex summâ perfectione Intellectûs & Voluntatis ipsius; quapropter omnia decernit cum summâ ratione, adeoque etiam complacentiâ, necessitati naturali intrinsecè oppositâ: illa celebratur, Matth. xi, 26. Pater, quia ita Tibi placuit. Rom, xi, 34. Quis Ei fuit à consilio? Adde Psal. cxv,3. Isef. xlvi,10. Cœcus impetus, & potentia obedientialis, Intellectui summo & perfectissimo minimè conveniunt. Sed ut Natura, sic Libertas Dei, CreaCreaturarum omnium Libertatem infinita ἐξουσίη superat. Isef. xli 5. An gloriabitur securis contra cædentem ipsâ? an se magnificabit serra contra agitatorem suum? Rom. ix, 21. An non habet potestatem Figulus in lutum, &c.
units.tr: V. Liberty is also evident, both from his independence and from his supreme power and authority together. Hence no violence or external compulsion can befall God. Rom. 9:19: Who has resisted his will? And from the highest perfection of his intellect and will. Therefore he decrees all things with the highest reason, and so also with complacency, which is intrinsically opposed to natural necessity. This is praised in Matt. 11:26: Father, because so it pleased you. Rom. 11:34: Who has been his counsellor? Add Ps. 115:3; Isa. 46:10. Blind impulse and obediential power are in no way fitting for the highest and most perfect intellect. But as his nature, so his liberty infinitely surpasses the liberty of all creatures, in infinite authority [ἐξουσίη]. Isa. 41:5: Shall the axe boast against him who chops with it? Or shall the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? Rom. 9:21: Has not the potter power over the clay? etc.

units.la: V. Æternitas probatur, 1. generatim, ex Act. xv, 18. Nota sunt Deo ab (omni) ævo omnia opera sua, cum Eph. I, 11, Agit omnia ex Consilio Voluntatis suæ.
units.tr: VI. Eternity is proved, 1. in general, from Acts 15:18: All his works are known to God from eternity, together with Eph. 1:11: He works all things according to the counsel of his will.

units.la: 2. Specialius: 1 Cor. 2, 7. Præfinierat ante sæcula. Eph. 1, 4. Elegit nos ante jactum mundi fundamentum. 2 Tim. 1, 9. ante tempora sæculorum.
units.tr: 2. More specifically: 1 Cor. 2:7: He had foreordained before the ages. Eph. 1:4: He chose us before the foundation of the world. 2 Tim. 1:9: before the times of the ages.

units.la: 3. Ex Immutabilitate, quæ affert a est sup. cap. 4. th. 20. Si enim Deus extiffet aliquando sine Decreto, postea Decretum in se formaret, ea foret satis insignis mutatio.
units.tr: 3. From immutability, which is treated above, chap. 4, th. 20. For if God had at some time existed without a decree, and afterwards formed a decree within himself, that would be a sufficiently notable change.

units.la: 4. Ex ipsius Æternitate, de qua cap. 4. th. 26. Deus enim non exitit tempore infinito sine Decreto suo: caeteroquin ne nunc quidem Decretum haberet. Nec tempore finito: hoc enim æternitati non convenit.
units.tr: 4. From his very eternity, which is discussed in chap. 4, th. 26. For God did not exist for an infinite time without his decree; otherwise he would not even now have a decree. Nor for a finite time, for this does not befit eternity.

units.la: Obj. Omne æternum est necessarium: Decrerum vero liberum est, non necessarium. Ergo. Resp. Æternitas Decreti Divini infert solummodo necessitatem ex hypothesi. Interim quatenus Deus cum summa ratione & complacentia ab æterno Decretum fecit, & sic constituit de possibilibus, cum absolute alia & aliter constituere potuisset; agnoscendum etiam, Decretum istud esse liberrimum, & necessario tale.
units.tr: Objection: Everything eternal is necessary; but the decree is free, not necessary. Therefore... Answer: The eternity of the Divine decree implies necessity only by hypothesis. Yet, insofar as God, with the highest reason and complacency, made the decree from eternity, and so determined concerning the possibles, although he could have determined otherwise and differently in an absolute sense, it must also be acknowledged that this decree is most free and is necessarily such.

units.la: VI. Actus Decreti Divini subjective & principative omnino Simplex est, & sic ipse Deus, contra Vorstium. Quamvis objective & terminative spectet plurima alia à Deo.
units.tr: VI. The act of the Divine decree is altogether simple subjectively and principatively, and so is God himself, against Vorstius. Although objectively and terminatively it regards many things other than God.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deus unus est; Decreta vero multa: ergo hæc non ipse Deus. Resp. Actus ille vitalis in se etiam unicus est: sed decreta multa denominamus ab objectis.
units.tr: Objection 1: God is one; but the decrees are many; therefore they are not God himself. Answer: That vital act is in itself also single; but we name the decrees many from their objects.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus est eius necessarium; Decretum vero liberum: ergò, &c. Resp. Deus quidem est Ens maximè necessarium in existendo; sed & liberrimum in operando extra se. Similiter Decreti existentia necessaria est in Ente sapientissimo; quamvis terminatio ejus talis, respectu objectorum, liberrima.
units.tr: Objection 2: God is necessary being; but the decree is free; therefore, etc. Answer: God is indeed the most necessary Being in existing, but also most free in acting outside himself. Similarly, the existence of the decree is necessary in the most wise Being, although its termination, with respect to the objects, is most free.

units.la: Distinguendum interim objectum præjacens,& terminans: Objectum præjacens sunt ipsa Possibilia, sic vel aliter determinabilia, & per summam Dei potestatem ac Sapientiam ad statum qualemcunque determinanda. Objectum terminans, aut potiùs terminatum, sunt Futura, & consequenter Præsentia, vel etiàm Præterita: statum enim istiusmodi habent, quia Deus ità decrevit.
units.tr: Meanwhile one must distinguish the preceding object and the terminating object. The preceding object is the possibles themselves, which can be determined in this or that way, and which, by the supreme power and wisdom of God, are to be determined to whatever state. The terminating object, or rather the terminated, are the future things, and consequently the present or even the past things. For they have this state because God so decreed.

units.la: Deus etiàm decernendo ordinem constituit in rebus decretis: qui est vel intentionis, vel executionis. Ordo intentionis ad Decretum magis proprië pertinet: prout Deus sapientissimè ad fines ordinavit sua media. Ordo executionis succedit in complemento.
units.tr: In decreeing, God also establishes an order among the things decreed, which is either of intention or of execution. The order of intention belongs more properly to the decree, insofar as God most wisely ordered his means to his ends. The order of execution follows in the carrying out.

units.la: Hùc pertinet Canon; Quod primum est in intentione, est postremum in executione; & contra: nam in intentione finis est causa mediorum; media sunt propter finem: sed in executione, finis est ipsum effectum, quod per media obtinetur. Confer sup. cap 4. th. 62.
units.tr: To this pertains the canon: What is first in intention is last in execution, and conversely. For in intention the end is the cause of the means, and the means are for the sake of the end; but in execution the end is the effect itself, which is obtained through the means. Compare above, chap. 4, th. 62.

units.la: VII. Immutabile etiàm est Dei Decretum; & consequenter efficax, per ipsius Omnipotentiam. Sic conjunguntur Manus & Consilium Dei, Act. iv, 24. Ita Jes. xiv, 27. Consilium Jehovæ quis irritum faciat? & manum Ejus quis avertat? Prov. xix, 21. Consilium Jehovæ stabit. Vide etiam Jes. LV, 10, 11. Consequenter, omne Decretum in se est absolutum, respectu actûs Divini indepéndentis: nullum conditionatum; nisi sic objectivè denominetur.
units.tr: VII. The Divine decree is also immutable, and consequently efficacious through his omnipotence. Thus the hand and the counsel of God are joined, Acts 4:24. So Isa. 14:27: Who can annul the counsel of Jehovah? And who can turn back his hand? Prov. 19:21: The counsel of Jehovah shall stand. See also Isa. 55:10, 11. Consequently, every decree is in itself absolute, with respect to the independent Divine act; none is conditional, unless it is so named objectively.

units.la: VIII. Extenditse Decretum ad omnia alia à Deo: Eph. I, 11. Vide sup. th. 5. Thren. iii, 37, 38. Ecquo dicente existit aliquid, quod Dominus non præceperit? Ex ore Excelsi, an non prodit malum quodque, & bonum? Rom.
units.tr: VIII. The decree extends to all things other than God: Eph. 1:11; see above, th. 5. Lam. 3:37, 38: Who is there who speaks and it comes to pass, which the Lord has not commanded? Does not evil and good proceed from the mouth of the Most High? Rom.

units.la: xr, 36 xi, 36. Estque pro nostro concipiendi modo, vel generale: ubi spectatur universa omnium obiectorum amplitudo: vel speciale, quod iterum suos gradus amplitudinis habet; ut Creationis, Providentiae, de Termino vitae humanae, Praedestinationis, &c. sed postremum istud καθ' ἐξοχὴν speciale appellatur.
units.tr: xi, 36. According to our way of conceiving it, the decree is either general, where the whole breadth of all objects is viewed, or special, which again has its own degrees of breadth, such as the decree concerning Creation, Providence, the fixed term of human life, Predestination, and so on. But this last is called special par excellence [καθ' ἐξοχὴν].

units.la: IX. Decretum Creationis est, quo Deus ab aeterno constituit, creaturas ex nihilo producere, in tempore; ad gloriam suam. Apoc. IV,11. per Voluntatem Tuam sunt, & creata sunt; Act. XV,18. Eph. I,11.
units.tr: IX. The Decree of Creation is that by which God from eternity determined to produce creatures out of nothing, in time, for his own glory. Rev. IV, 11. By your will they are, and they were created; Acts XV, 18; Eph. I, 11.

units.la: Decretum Providentiae est, quo Deus ab aeterno constituit, Creaturas conservare, iis cooperari, easque gubernare, ad gloriam Suam. Distinguitur hoc in Effectivum quo Deus proposuit omnia bona, futura vera efficientia operari; a quo omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum descendit, Jac. I,17. Quicquid placet facit. Psal. CXV, 3. & in Permissivum, quo proposuit mala in causis secundis non impedire. Act. 2, 23, 24. Definito consilio & praecognitione Dei deditum, &c. Similiter fere IV,27, 28. Item Psal. LXXXI, 17. Dimisi eos ambulaturos, &c. Act. XIV,16. 17. Sivit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. cum Gen. XX,6. Cohibui te, ne peccares in Me: idcirco non sivi te attingere eam.
units.tr: The Decree of Providence is that by which God from eternity determined to preserve creatures, to cooperate with them, and to govern them, for his own glory. This is divided into the effective, by which God purposed to bring about all future good things, from which every good gift and every perfect gift comes down, James I, 17. He does whatever pleases him, Ps. CXV, 3; and the permissive, by which he purposed not to hinder evils in secondary causes. Acts 2, 23, 24. Delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, etc. Similarly almost IV, 27, 28. Likewise Ps. LXXXI, 17. I let them go to walk, etc.; Acts XIV, 16, 17. He suffered all nations to walk in their own ways, along with Gen. XX, 6. I kept you from sinning against me; therefore I did not let you touch her.

units.la: X. Futura sunt proprie & per se Bona, Mala non nisi ratione subiecti boni sunt, aut fiunt; in quo tantum alterius boni privationem significant: quam supplere Deo non placet; cum etiam, si voluisset, nihil conferre potuisset. Imo vero, o Homo; tu quis es qui ex adverso responsas Deo? num dicet figmentum fictori; cur me tale fecisti? annon habet potestatem figulus, &c. Rom. IX, 20, 21.
units.tr: X. Future things are properly and in themselves good; evils are good only by reason of the good subject in which they are or occur, and in this they signify only the privation of another good, which God does not choose to supply, since even if he had wished, he could have contributed nothing to it. Indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, why have you made me thus? Has not the potter power over the clay, etc.? Rom. IX, 20, 21.

units.la: A Decreto permissivo recte quidem procedit illatio Logica; ut a non-actione causae primae, ad nonpositionem effectus. Errant autem gravilime Adversarii, Deum hinc peccati auctorem statui calumniantes. Vere interim Deus decrevit in genere Entis bona facere, mala autem physicè permittere ; consequenter etiam hæc necessariò futura sunt. Matth. xviii, 7. Necesse est, ut eveniant offendicula. xxvi, 24. Filius hominis abit, sicut scriptum est de eo, &c. Luc. xxiv, 26. Nonne hæc oportuit Christum pati ? &c. 2 Thess. ii, 13. Apoc. I, 1.
units.tr: From the permissive decree, a logical inference rightly proceeds, as from the non-action of the first cause to the non-positing of the effect. But our opponents err most gravely, slandering God as if he were thereby made the author of sin. Yet God truly decreed, in the general sense of being, to do good things, but to permit evils physically; consequently these also are necessarily going to be. Matt. XVIII, 7. It is necessary that offences come. XXVI, 24. The Son of Man goes, as it is written of him, etc. Luke XXIV, 26. Ought not Christ to have suffered these things? etc. 2 Thess. II, 13. Rev. I, 1.

units.la: XI. Decretum de immobili vitæ humanæ termino est, quo Deus constituit ab æterno, quamdiu quisque hominum determinatè victurus esset in hoc mundo. Quod probatur contra Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes: 1. expressis S. Scripturæ testimoniis. Job. xiv, 1. 2, 5. „Homo natus muliere, brevis ætate, „. Quandoquidem præcisi sunt dies ejus ; numerus ejus penes Te est : determinationem ejus fecisti : quas non transgrediatur: Psal. xxxix, 5, 6. - Palmares disposuisti dies meos. cxxxix, 16. In libro Tuo hæc omnia scripta sunt, „(ex quibus) diebus formabantur, cum nondum ullum eorum (extaret.) Act. xvii, 25, 26. Definitis præstitutis temporibus, & positis terminis habitationis eorum. Eccl. iii, 1, 2. Cuique sua tempestas. - Tempus pariendi & tempus moriendi. Vide etiam Job. viii, 20. Jes. xxxviii, 5.
units.tr: XI. The decree concerning the unchangeable term of human life is that by which God determined from eternity how long each of mankind would definitely live in this world. This is proved against the Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants: (1) by express testimonies of Holy Scripture. Job XIV, 1, 2, 5. Man, born of a woman, short of days, since his days are cut off; the number of them is with you; you have fixed his limit, which he will not pass. Ps. XXXIX, 5, 6. You have appointed my days as a handbreadth. CXXXIX, 16. In your book all these things were written, (out of which) days were formed, when none of them as yet existed. Acts XVII, 25, 26. Having fixed appointed times and set the limits of their habitation. Eccl. III, 1, 2. For everything there is a season, a time to be born and a time to die. See also Job VIII, 20; Isa. XXXVIII, 5.

units.la: 2. Ex eo, quòd Deus sit Arbiter vitæ & necis: dicens, Psal. xc, 3. Revertimini filii hominum. 1 Sam. 11, 6. Jehovah morte afficit, & in vitam restituit. cum Eph. I, 11. Act. xv, 18.
units.tr: (2) From the fact that God is the arbiter of life and death, saying: Ps. XC, 3. Turn back, you sons of men. 1 Sam. II, 6. The LORD kills and makes alive, compared with Eph. I, 11; Acts XV, 18.

units.la: 3. A minori: Matth. x, 29, 30, 31. Nonne duo passerculi assario veniunt: & unus ex iis non cadet in terram sine Patre vestro ? Vestri vero etiam capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. Ne igitur Timete : vos multis passerculis præstatis.
units.tr: (3) From the less to the greater: Matt. X, 29, 30, 31. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.

units.la: 4. Quia plurima alia, etiàm maxima ac gravissima, ab hominum vitâ dependent ; quorum alioqui non esset certa futuritio. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 36, 37.
units.tr: (4) Because very many other things, even the greatest and most serious, depend on the life of men, whose future occurrence would otherwise not be certain. Compare above, chap. 4, th. 36, 37.

units.la: XII. Obj. 1. Per istiusmodi Decretum tollitur omnis creaturarum libertas & contingentia. Resp. Imò Deus decrevit fatis multa, quæ natura suâ essent libera, vel contingentia; quamvis eadem necessario futura necessitate externâ.
units.tr: XII. Objection 1. By such a decree all freedom and contingency of creatures is abolished. Answer. On the contrary, God has decreed many things which by their nature would be free or contingent, although these same things are going to be by external necessity.

units.la: Obj. 2. Evertitur omnium mediorum necessitas, alimentorum, medicamentorum, precum, &c. Resp. Nego: Deus enim decrevit & ordinavit conditiones, ac media necessaria, ad tales fines. Act. xxvii, 31. Nisi isti in navi manserint, vos servari non potestis. Hebr. xi, 6. Absque fide impossibile est Deo placere.
units.tr: Objection 2. The necessity of all means is overthrown: of food, medicines, prayers, etc. Answer. I deny it. For God has decreed and ordained both the conditions and the necessary means to such ends. Acts XXVII, 31. Unless these remain in the ship, you cannot be saved. Heb. XI, 6. Without faith it is impossible to please God.

units.la: Obj. 3. Exod. xx, 12. & alibi, piis longævitas promittitur; contra vero Psal. lv, 24. improbi dicuntur non perventuri ad medium dierum: ergo non præstitutus est iis terminus immobilis. Aperte etiam dicuntur Ezechiæ additi anni quindecim; Isef. xxxviii, 5. Resp. 1. Piis promittitur beata longitudo dierum; Psal. xxiii, 6. hic quodammodo inchoanda: sed in cœlesti hæreditate consummanda, cujus Canaan typus fuit: non tamen in hoc sæculo producenda ultra terminum à Deo definitum. 2. Impii autem ad medium dierum non sunt perventuri; scil. quos naturaliter, habitâ ratione valetudinis ac roboris, supervivere potuissent. 3. Ezechiæ denique post morbum istum tot anni adjecti sunt; non termino universæ illius vitæ prius Divinitus præfinito.
units.tr: Objection 3. Ex. XX, 12, and elsewhere, long life is promised to the godly; on the contrary, Ps. LV, 24 says the wicked are said not to reach the half of their days; therefore no unchangeable term has been fixed for them. Moreover, fifteen years are said to have been added to Hezekiah; Isa. XXXVIII, 5. Answer. (1) A blessed length of days is promised to the godly, Ps. XXIII, 6, which is in a sense to be begun here, but to be completed in the heavenly inheritance, of which Canaan was a type; yet it is not to be extended in this age beyond the term set by God. (2) But the wicked are not going to reach the half of their days; namely, those whom, taking account of health and strength, they could naturally have outlived. (3) Finally, to Hezekiah, after that illness, so many years were added, not beyond the term of his whole life previously fixed by God.

units.la: XIII. Prædestinatio est Decretum Dei de Creatu- rarum rationalium statu æterno; ad manifestandam Potentiæ, Sapientiæ, Gratiæ, & Justitiæ suæ Glo- riam.
units.tr: XIII. Predestination is God's decree concerning the eternal state of rational creatures, to display the glory of his power, wisdom, grace and justice.

units.la: Ea ratione objectorum vel est Angelorum, vel Hominum.
units.tr: This decree has as its objects either angels or men.

units.la: Ratione terminorum vel est Electio, vel Reprobatio. Isef. xli, 9. Elegi te, & non reprobavi, Rom. ix, 13. Iacobum dilexi, & Esavum odio habui. 1 Thess. v, 9. Non constituit nos ad iram, sed ad salutem obtinendam.
units.tr: With respect to its terms, it is either election or reprobation. Isaiah 41:9: "I have chosen you and not rejected you." Romans 9:13: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." 1 Thessalonians 5:9: "God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation."

units.la: Non recte contendunt Pontificii & Lutherani, Damnandorum præscientiam solum esse; non Prædestinationem: cum 1. etiam illa Decretum permissivum & ordinativum praesupponat. Et 2. Spiritus Sanctus Praedestinationem diserte in isto negotio appellet: Act. iv, 28. Ut facerent, quaecunque manus Tua & Consilium Tuum prius definirat (Greek) ut fierent. Atque 3. Phrases aequipollentes occurrant: utpote Judae, 4. Praescripti ad damnationem. 1 Thess. v, 9. Et 4. Praescientia, aut Praecognitio, de Electione etiam usurpetur.; Rom. viii, 29. xi. 2.
units.tr: The Papists and the Lutherans are wrong to hold that foreknowledge of the damned alone exists, and not predestination. For (1) that foreknowledge itself presupposes a permissive and ordaining decree. (2) The Holy Spirit expressly calls this matter predestination: Acts 4:28, "to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand to come to pass [γενέσθαι]." (3) Equivalent phrases also occur: Jude 4, "marked out beforehand for condemnation"; 1 Thessalonians 5:9. (4) Foreknowledge, or prior knowing, is also used of election: Romans 8:29; 11:2.

units.la: XIV. Electio Angelorum
units.tr: XIV. The Election of Angels

units.la: quorundam patet, ex 1 Tim. v, 21. "Obtestor - in conspectu - Electorum Angelorum. Unde etiam aliorum Reprobatio facile colligitur. Et Judae, 6. Deus Angelos - judicio magni illius diei vinculis aeternis sub caligine servavit. Matth. xxv, 41. In ignem aeternum paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus. Addi potest argumentum a minori, ut sup. th. 11, §. 3.
units.tr: The election of certain angels is evident from 1 Timothy 5:21: "I charge you before God and the elect angels." From this the reprobation of the others is also easily inferred. Jude 6: God has kept the angels ... under eternal chains in darkness until the judgment of that great day. Matthew 25:41: "eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." An argument from the lesser case may be added, as above, chapter 11, §3.

units.la: Electio Angelorum, est Praedestinatio, qua Deus ab aeterno definite constituit, quosdam Angelos, ubi in tempore boni & sancti essent creati, per Gratiam suam conservare & confirmare in statu isto; ad ipsorum Salutem, & Gloriam Potentiae, Sapientiae, & Gratiae suae.
units.tr: The election of angels is that predestination by which God, from eternity, decreed definitely that certain angels, once created good and holy in time, should be preserved and confirmed in that state by his grace, to their salvation and to the glory of his power, wisdom and grace.

units.la: Reprobatio vero est Praedestinatio, qua similiter definite constituit aliorum lapsum permittere, in eo ipsos relinquere & gubernare, ac propter peccata aeternum condemnare; ad Gloriam Potentiae, Sapientiae, & Justitiae suae.
units.tr: Reprobation, by contrast, is that predestination by which God likewise decreed definitely to permit the fall of the others, to leave them and govern them in it, and to condemn them eternally on account of their sins, to the glory of his power, wisdom and justice.

units.la: Interim pro suprema sua potestate Deus talem futuritionem constituit atque ordinavit. Lapsus vero non est causa Reprobationis, voluntionis istius Divinae; quae est independens: sed tantum est causa demeritoria talium poenarum.
units.tr: Meanwhile, by his supreme power, God established and ordained such a future state of affairs. The fall, however, is not the cause of this divine reprobation, which is an independent act of will; it is only the meritorious cause of such punishments.

units.la: XV. Electio Hominum
units.tr: XV. The Election of Men

units.la: est Praedestinatio, qua Deus ab aeterno constituit de Hominibus, ubi in tempore ad Imaginem Suam essent conditi, sed labiles; ac deinceps, Ipso permittente, in Adamo pariter lapsi, quodquosdam definitè, in Christo ; per fidem ac resipiscentiam æternùm salvare ; ad gloriam Potentiæ, Sapientiæ, & Misericordiæ suæ. Actus hic Dei, ut apparet, non est segregatio ad munus aliquod, sive Politicum, sive Ecclesiasticum ; quemadmodum 1 Sam. x, 24. Videtis - ne quem elegerit Jehovah. Joh. vi, 70. Nonne Ego vos duodecim elegi: Nec populi assumtio ad externam foederis gratiosi communionem ; de quâ Deut. iv, 37. Dilexit majores tuos, elegitque semen eorum. Sed certorum hominum ordinatio, ad salutem per fidem in Christum consequendam ; Non omnium in universum; nec multitudinis vagæ. Hoc primò contra Socinianos, Remonstrantes, aliosque, probatur.
units.tr: The election of men is that predestination by which God decreed from eternity concerning men, who in time were to be created in his image but liable to fall, and who afterwards, with him permitting, fell in Adam along with the rest; that he would definitely save certain of them eternally in Christ, through faith and repentance, to the glory of his power, wisdom and mercy. This act of God, as is evident, is not a setting apart to some office, whether civil or ecclesiastical, as in 1 Samuel 10:24, "Do you see him whom Jehovah has chosen?"; John 6:70, "Did I not choose you twelve?" Nor is it the taking of a people into the external communion of the gracious covenant, of which Deuteronomy 4:37 speaks: "He loved your fathers and chose their seed after them." Rather, it is the appointment of certain men to obtain salvation through faith in Christ; not of all men universally, nor of a wandering multitude. This is proved first against the Socinians, the Remonstrants and others.

units.la: 1. Ex disertis Christi verbis: Joh. xiii, 18. Non de omnibus loquor; scio quos elegerim Luc. x, 20. Gaudete potiùs, quod Nomina vestra scripta sint in cælo. Matth. xx, 26. xxii, 14. Multi vocati, pauci Electi. xxiv, 24. xxv, 34.
units.tr: 1. From the plain words of Christ: John 13:18, "I do not speak of all; I know whom I have chosen." Luke 10:20, "Rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven." Matthew 20:16; 22:14, "Many are called, few are chosen." Matthew 24:24; 25:34.

units.la: 2. Ex dictis Apostolicis: Rom. viii, 29, 30. Quos præscivit, etiam prædestinavit conformandos imagini Filii Sui: - Quos verò prædestinavit, eos etiam vocavit, &c. ix, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Novit Dominus Suos. Similia sunt Eph. i, 3, - 6. & 1 Cor. iv, 7. Quis Te ab aliis discernit? &c.
units.tr: 2. From the apostolic sayings: Romans 8:29, 30, "Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son ... and whom he predestined, these he also called," etc.; Romans 9:12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 21, 23. 2 Timothy 2:19, "The Lord knows those who are his." Similar are Ephesians 1:3-6 and 1 Corinthians 4:7, "Who makes you differ from another?" etc.

units.la: 3. Ex Voluntatis, Decreti, ac Præscientiæ Divinæ actû purissimo.
units.tr: 3. From the purest act of God's will, decree and foreknowledge.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Secundò asserimus, Electionem esse absolutam, atque immutabiliter certam ; & talem fuisse ab æterno : Non demum fieri absolutam in momento mortis eorum, qui fideles perseveraverint. Vide sup. th. 5.
units.tr: Secondly, we assert that election is absolute and immutably certain, and that it has been so from eternity. It did not become absolute only at the moment of death of those who persevered in faith. See above, chapter 5.

units.la: Tertiò statuimus, Electionem illam factam non esse ex præviâ fide ; contra Remonstrantes, & Lutheranos: neque ex meritis prævisis ; contra Pontificios: sed ex merò placito Gratiæ Divinæ.
units.tr: Thirdly, we maintain that this election was not made on account of foreseen faith, against the Remonstrants and the Lutherans; nor on account of foreseen merits, against the Papists; but solely by the good pleasure of divine grace.

units.la: Hoc patet, 1. Ex disertis testimoniis §; Scripturæ : Rom. Rom. ix, 11, 12. Nondum enim natis pueris, &c. Non ex operibus, sed ex Vocante. 16, 18, 20, xi, 5, 6. 2 Tim. 1. 9. Non ex operibus ; sed ex Suo præstituto. Unde Christus, Matth. xi, 26, 27. Gloriam tibi tribuo Pater, quòd hæc occultaveris sapientibus & intelligentibus ; & ea detexeris infantibus. Etiam Pater, quia sic placitum est Tibi. Luc. xii, 32.
units.tr: This is evident, first, from the express testimonies of Scripture: Romans 9:11, 12, "For the children not yet born ... not of works, but of him who calls." Romans 9:16, 18, 20; 11:5, 6. 2 Timothy 1:9, "not according to works, but according to his own purpose." Hence Christ says, Matthew 11:25, 26: "I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you." Luke 12:32.

units.la: 2. Electio est ad fidem, sanctitatem, perseveran t am. Eph. I, 4. Elegit - , ut simus Sancti & inculpati. Act. xiii, 48. Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Ita Christus, Joh. xv, 16. Elegi, & constitui vos ; ut fructum adferatis. Rom. viii, 29, 30. xi, 35, 36. 1 Cor. iv, 7. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Psal. c, 3. Deut. vii, 6, 7-9. Joh. vi. 37. Sublatâ vero hâc causâ non ponitur salutaris ille effectus: Joh. viii, 47. Non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis x, 26. Non creditis, quia non estis ex Ovibus illis Meis. 1 Joh. 11, 19. Apoc. xiii, 8.
units.tr: 2. Election is to faith, holiness and perseverance. Ephesians 1:4: "He chose us that we should be holy and blameless." Acts 13:48: "As many as were appointed to eternal life believed." So Christ says, John 15:16: "I chose you and appointed you that you should bear fruit." Romans 8:29, 30; 11:35, 36; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 2 Timothy 2:19; Psalm 100:3; Deuteronomy 7:6-9; John 6:37. But when this cause is removed, that saving effect does not follow: John 8:47, "You do not hear, because you are not of God"; John 10:26, "You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep." 1 John 2:19; Revelation 13:8.

units.la: 3. Fides, vel Obedientia, non potuit prævideri sutura ; nisi consequenter ad Decretum Dei: unde cæteroquin ista futuritio? Nec Deus eam decrevit, nisi ut medium salutis consequendæ in Christo. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 39, & 42.
units.tr: 3. Faith or obedience could not have been foreseen as future unless it followed consequently upon God's decree; otherwise, how would that future be? Nor did God decree it except as the means of obtaining salvation in Christ. Compare above, chapter 4, theses 39 and 42.

units.la: XVII. Christus in Electione consideratur vel Theologicè; & sic etiàm est idem ipse Deus eligens: vel Oeconomicè; & sic ipse quoque ordinatus est, ut causa & basis omnis salutis Electorum, & caput Salvandorum:
units.tr: XVII. Christ is considered in election either theologically, and thus he is himself the same God who elects; or economically, and thus he too is ordained to be the cause and basis of all the salvation of the elect, and the head of those to be saved.

units.la: 1 Petr. I, 19, 20. Agnus - præcognitus ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Apoc. xiii, 8. Nomina scripta in libro vitæ. Agni mactati, indè à jacto mundi fundamento, &c. Eph. 1, 4. In ipso elegit, &c. Hebr. 2, 10. Principe salutis. Joh. iii, 16. Deus - Filium illum suum unigenitum dedit, ut quisquis credit in eum - habeat vitam æternam. Col. I, 19, 20. Jes. liii, 10. Joh. xvii, 6, 9, x, 29; 14, 15, 16. Rom. viii, 32. Gal. II, 16. Cant. 2 -16.
units.tr: 1 Peter 1:19, 20: "the lamb ... foreknown before the foundation of the world." Revelation 13:8: "names written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world," etc. Ephesians 1:4: "In him he chose us," etc. Hebrews 2:10: "the Prince of salvation." John 3:16: "God gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should have eternal life." Colossians 1:19, 20; Isaiah 53:10; John 17:6, 9; 10:29; 14-16; Romans 8:32; Galatians 2:16; Song of Songs 2:16.

units.la: Non autem est proprie causa meritoria ipsius Electionis; contrà Lutheranos: hoc enim independen-tiæ tiæ actûs istius Divini repugnant. Nec fundamentum pariter Electionis, si recipiatur; & reprobationis, si rejiciatur. Imo aliæ sunt causæ demeritoriæ damnationis: quamvis Christus etiàm ex accidenti objectum peccati fit. Ioh. 111, 17, 18. Misit Deus Filium, - non ut damnet mundum; sed ut servetur mundus per Eum. - Qui vero non credit, jam condemnatus est, &c. 30. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam; qui vero non obtemperat Filio, non videbit vitam; sed ira Dei manet super eum. Infideles carent medio liberationis: imò quoniam intelligentia carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum, (Rom. viii,7.) illi contra Christum & Euangelium exerunt malitiam suam, & condemnationem aggravant.
units.tr: Christ, however, is not properly the meritorious cause of election itself, against the Lutherans; for this would contradict the independence of that divine act. Nor is he the foundation of election, if it is admitted, nor of reprobation, if it is rejected. Indeed, other causes are the meritorious causes of damnation, although Christ also becomes, by accident, the object of sin. John 3:17, 18: "God sent the Son, not to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him. ... He who does not believe is already condemned," etc. 3:30: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him." Unbelievers lack the means of deliverance; indeed, since "the mind of the flesh is enmity against God" (Romans 8:7), they vent their malice against Christ and the gospel and aggravate their condemnation.

units.la: XVIII. Finis est Gloria Dei: Prov. xvi, 4. Rom. xi. 36. Eph. i, 6. Ad laudem gloriosæ suæ Gratiæ. 1 Petr. 2, 9. Vos Genus Electum; ut virtutes prædicetis Illius, &c.
units.tr: XVIII. The end is the glory of God: Prov. xvi, 4. Rom. xi, 36. Eph. i, 6. To the praise of his glorious grace. 1 Pet. ii, 9. "But you are a chosen generation, that you may show forth the virtues of him," etc.

units.la: Sapientissima vero est ordinatio Mediorum ad Finem. Deus nimirum in Hominibus, sibi quoque possibilibus, exercere volens ac manifestare Gloriam suam, per viam Gratiæ & Misericordiæ, salvâ interim etiàm Justitiâ suâ; actu simplicissimo æterni Decreti sui statuit, ut crearentur Adamus & Eva, boni, sed labiles: Fœdus operum cum iis iniretur; sed & posteritate, definite ista, in iis censita: lapsus permitteretur; & Legalis sententia promulgaretur: interim Mediator & sponsor Θεάνθρωπος constitueretur, cujus satisfactione ac merito tali, ex miseriâ istâ liberandi, & æternum salvandi essent isti definite; sic vocandi, justificandi, glorificandi.
units.tr: Now the ordering of the means to the end is most wise. God, wishing to exercise and manifest his glory in men, who are also possible for him, by the way of grace and mercy, while his justice remains intact, decreed by a most simple act of his eternal decree that Adam and Eve should be created, good but liable to fall. A covenant of works was to be made with them, and their posterity, these persons being definitely determined and reckoned in them. The fall was to be permitted, and the legal sentence was to be promulgated. Meanwhile a Mediator and Surety, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], was to be appointed, by whose satisfaction and merit these definitely determined persons were to be freed from this misery and eternally saved, and so called, justified and glorified.

units.la: XIX. Obj. 1. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri; 1 Tim. 2, 4. Ergo Electio non est certarum personarum definite. Resp. Per omnes, distributive in generâ singulorum, intelligi debet universitas electorum ex singulis nationibus, ætatibus, & conditionibus hominum: & consequenter fidelium ac respicientium. Confer Matth. iv, 24. Luc. xi, 42. Act. x, 12. Rom. xiv, 2. Obj.
units.tr: XIX. Objection 1. God wills all men to be saved (1 Tim. ii, 4). Therefore election is not of definitely certain persons. Answer: "all" must be understood distributively, of the individual kinds of men, so that it means the whole number of the elect from every nation, age and condition of men; and consequently of believers and those who look to him. Compare Matth. iv, 24. Luc. xi, 42. Act. x, 12. Rom. xiv, 2. Objection.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dilexit mundum, eique salvando Filium dedit: Joh. iii, 16. Ergo. Resp. Synecdochice intelligi debet pars electa. Confer Rom. xi, 12, 15.
units.tr: Obj. 2. He loved the world and gave his Son to save it: Joh. iii, 16. Therefore. Resp. The elect part should be understood synecdochically. Compare Rom. xi, 12, 15.
