units.la: Obj. 3. Apud Deum non est προσωπολημψία; Act. x, 34. Ergo nec certarum duntaxat personarum electio. Resp. Προσωπολημψία de Deo negatur; quod nullam qualitatem antecedenter in homine spectaverit, nedum a causa alienam, ob quam unum prae alio elegisset: Rom. ix, 20. & consequenter ad communionem Foederis salutaris adscisceret. Hoc sine discrimine nunc sub N. T. obtingit hominibus cujuscunque nationis, &c. Unde nequaquam id sequitur, quod contendunt Adversarii.
units.tr: Obj. 3. With God there is no respect of persons (Acts x, 34). Therefore election is not only of certain persons. Resp. Respect of persons [προσωπολημψία] is denied of God, since he did not look beforehand at any quality in man, much less one foreign to the cause, on account of which he would have chosen one person before another, Rom. ix, 20, and so admitted him to communion in the saving covenant. Now under the New Testament this comes to men of every nation without distinction, etc. Hence it does not at all follow what the Adversaries contend.

units.la: Obj. 4. Aliqui prius crediderunt; postea perierunt.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Some believed for a time and afterwards perished.

units.la: 1 Tim. i, 19. 20. 2 Petr. ii, 20, 21, 22. &c. Ergo Electio non est prorsus absoluta & immutabilis. Resp. Nego consequentiam. Fidem Historicam & temporariam tantum habentes perierunt; sed isti electi non fuerunt. Aliter res habet in iis, qui fide salvifica praediti sunt.
units.tr: 1 Tim. i, 19, 20. 2 Petr. ii, 20, 21, 22, etc. Therefore election is not altogether absolute and immutable. Resp. I deny the consequence. Those who had only historical and temporary faith perished, but those were not elect. It is otherwise with those who are endowed with saving faith.

units.la: Obj. 5. Absque fide impossibile est Deo placere. Hebr. xi, 6. Nemo igitur electus est, nisi ex fide praevisa; sive, ut credens. Resp. Per Fidem placemus Deo; quantum ad amorem complacentiae attinet; sed de amore benevolentiae, qui est in Electione, aliter judicandum.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Without faith it is impossible to please God. Hebr. xi, 6. Therefore no one is elect except from foreseen faith, or as believing. Resp. We please God by faith, so far as the love of complacency is concerned; but concerning the love of benevolence, which is in election, we must judge otherwise.

units.la: Obj. 6. Deus elegit pauperes mundi, divites fide, Jac. 2, 5. Ergo ex fide praevisa. Resp. Elegit, ut in tempore essent tales: non vero quasi antecedenter tales existerent, vel etiam futuri essent. Eodem versu addit Apostolus; & haeredes Regni: procul dubio, non quod antecedenter tales essent, sed ut tales fierent.
units.tr: Obj. 6. God chose the poor of the world, rich in faith. Jac. 2, 5. Therefore from foreseen faith. Resp. He chose them that they should be such in time, not as though they already were such beforehand, or were going to be. In the same verse the Apostle adds: and heirs of the kingdom; undoubtedly not because they were such beforehand, but that they should become such.

units.la: Obj. 7. Praecognitio antecedit Praedestinationem, Rom. viii, 29. ergo & Fides praevisa. Resp. Praecognitio, Rom. viii, 29. ut & xi, 2. metonymice ipsum Decretum electionis ad salutem notat; non vero praevisionem fidei: sed Praedestinatio, ut illi conformentur imagini Filii, pertinet ad mediorum ordinationem: quibus iste finis obtinendus est.
units.tr: Obj. 7. Foreknowledge precedes predestination, Rom. viii, 29. Therefore so does foreseen faith. Resp. Foreknowledge, Rom. viii, 29, as also xi, 2, metonymically denotes the decree of election to salvation itself, not the foreseeing of faith. But predestination, that they should be conformed to the image of the Son, pertains to the ordering of the means by which this end is to be attained.

units.la: Obj. 8. Electio est actus misericordiæ; Rom. IX, 23. supponit ergo objectum miserum: sed non recte dicitur, objectum electionis esse hominem possibilem. Resp. 1. Nego antecedens. Electio est actus dominii, quod Deus etiam habuit in possibilia. 2. Electi dicuntur vasa misericordiæ: quia Deus decrevit lapsum & miseriam permittere, atque inde eos per Christum liberare: hoc autem pertinet ad objectum terminans.
units.tr: Obj. 8. Election is an act of mercy, Rom. IX, 23. It therefore presupposes a wretched object; but it is not rightly said that the object of election is possible man. Resp. 1. I deny the antecedent. Election is an act of dominion, which God also had over possible beings. 2. The elect are called vessels of mercy because God decreed to permit the fall and misery, and thence to free them through Christ; but this pertains to the terminating object.

units.la: Obj. 9. Numerus possibilium infinitus est: objectum Prædestinationis non est infinitum: Ergo. Resp. Objectum præjacens est syncategorematice infinitum: sed Deus per Decretum præfinivit, quid, & quomodo futurum esset, quod ad objectum terminans pertinet.
units.tr: Obj. 9. The number of possibles is infinite; the object of predestination is not infinite; therefore. Resp. The antecedent object is syncategorematically infinite; but God, by the Decree, predefined what would be future, and how, and this pertains to the terminating object.

units.la: Obj. 10. Orthodoxi passim dicunt, Deum elegisse certos quosdam homines, ex lapsu & communi miseria erigendos, &c. Resp. Sic recte objectum terminans Decreti Divini, & quidem ex parte, proponitur: nam etiam ipse lapsus futurus erat ex Decreto Dei: nec statui debent plura Decreta in Deo realiter distincta.
units.tr: Obj. 10. The orthodox everywhere say that God chose certain men to be raised up from the fall and common misery, etc. Resp. Thus the terminating object of the divine Decree is rightly set forth, and indeed on its own side; for even the fall itself was going to happen by the decree of God. Nor should several decrees, really distinct in God, be posited.

units.la: XX. Electionis certitudo spectatur, tum objective, de qua sic satis constat ex sup. th. 7. & 16. tum subjective; prout percipitur in conscientiis fidelium. Atque ita probatur contra Socinianos, Pontificios, & Remonstrantes.
units.tr: XX. The certainty of election is considered both objectively, of which enough is established above, th. 7 and 16, and subjectively, as it is perceived in the consciences of the faithful. It is proved in this way against the Socinians, the Papists and the Remonstrants.

units.la: 1. Ex natura Fidei: Tit. 1, 1. Fides Electorum Dei eum Rom. VIII, 30. Quos prædestinavit, eos etiam vocavit. & X, 17. Fides est ex auditu; & auditus per Verbum Dei vocantis. Ac porro 1 Cor. 2, 10. Scimus, quæ Deus nobis gratificatus sit. 1 Ioh. 2, 27. Ista unctio docet vos de omnibus, &c. Ergo etiam de Electione. Confer sup. cap. 2. th. 12.
units.tr: 1. From the nature of faith: Tit. 1, 1. The faith of God's elect, and Rom. VIII, 30. "Whom he predestined, these he also called"; and X, 17, "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God who calls." Further, 1 Cor. 2, 10. "We know what God has bestowed on us"; 1 Ioh. 2, 27. "That anointing teaches you about all things," etc. Therefore also about election. Compare above, chap. 2, th. 12.

units.la: 2. Ex natura Spei; quæ non confundit expestantem : Rom. v, 5. & Fidei naturam sequitur : ista enim est Hypostasis eorum, quæ sperantur ; & demonstratio eorum, quæ non cernuntur : Hebr. xi, 1. Sic autem expectamus, & consequenter certò adipiscimur, æternam beatitudinem: Rom. viii, 23, 24, 25. quæ cum electione individuum nexum habet: Matth. xx, 23. xxv, 34.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of hope, which does not disappoint the one who expects, Rom. v, 5, and follows the nature of faith. For faith is the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen, Hebr. xi, 1. Thus we wait for, and consequently certainly obtain, eternal blessedness, Rom. viii, 23, 24, 25, which has an individual bond with election, Matth. xx, 23, xxv, 34.

units.la: 3. Quia docemur, & admonemur explorare nos ipsos, & confirmare statum nostrum spiritualem, 1 Cor. xi, 28. Exploret quisque seipsum. 2, xiii, 5. Vos ipsos tentate, an in fide sitis : vos ipsos explorate, &c. 2 Petr. i, 10, 11. Studete vocationem & electionem vestram firmam efficere. - Itâ enim ampliè subministrabitur vobis introitus in æternum Regnum, &c. Ex fructibus nimirum arbor cognoscitur: Matth. xii, 33. vii, 16, 17, 18.
units.tr: 3. Because we are taught and admonished to examine ourselves and to confirm our spiritual state: 1 Cor. xi, 28, Let each one examine himself. 2, xiii, 5, Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves, etc. 2 Petr. i, 10, 11, Be diligent to make your calling and election sure; for so an entrance will be richly supplied to you, etc. Of course, a tree is known by its fruits: Matth. xii, 33, vii, 16, 17, 18.

units.la: 4. Quia Apostoli aliorum electionem celebrârunt, & Deo pro illâ gratias egerunt. Eph. i, 3, 4, 5. Benedictus esto Deus, qui elegit: - qui prædestinavit nos in adoptionem, &c. Phil. i, 6, 7. Persuasum habens, &c. scil. extraordinariâ revelatione Divinâ. Aliàs, quisque sibi sub Deo statûs sui saltem potest esse conscius:
units.tr: 4. Because the Apostles celebrated the election of others and gave thanks to God for it: Eph. i, 3, 4, 5, Blessed be God, who chose; who predestined us to adoption, etc. Phil. i, 6, 7, Being persuaded, etc., namely by extraordinary divine revelation. Otherwise, each person can at least be conscious of his own state under God:

units.la: 1 Cor. 2, 11. quis novit ea, quæ sunt hominis ; nisi Spiritus hominis, qui in eo est?
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2, 11. Who knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?

units.la: XXI. Obj. 1. Ignoramus consilium Dei: neç nobis licet inspicere librum vitæ, &c. Ergò, Resp. Inspicimus & legimus librum vitæ à posteriori. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Abscedat ab injustitiâ, quisquis nominat nomen Christi. 1, 12. Novi cui crediderim. scil. ex libro Scripturæ, & libro conscientiæ inter se collatis.
units.tr: XXI. Obj. 1. We do not know the counsel of God, nor are we allowed to inspect the book of life, etc. Therefore. Resp. We inspect and read the book of life a posteriori. 2 Tim. 2, 19. Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity. 1, 12. I know whom I have believed. Namely, from the book of Scripture and the book of conscience compared with each other.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ista certitudo faceret homines securos & profanos : ergò non est asserenda. Resp. Finis rectè agnitus & intentus non facit hominem securum, aut profanum: quia ad illum simul media ordinata sunt, 1 Joh. iii, 3. Qui hanc spem habet, castum se conservat. servat. Phil. iii, 12, 13, 14. Persequor, an quoque apprehendam, &c.
units.tr: Obj. 2. This certainty would make men secure and profane; therefore it is not to be asserted. Resp. A goal rightly recognized and aimed at does not make a man secure or profane, because at the same time the means are ordained for it: 1 Joh. iii, 3. Whoever has this hope keeps himself pure. Phil. iii, 12, 13, 14, I press on, if I may also lay hold of it, etc.

units.la: Obj. 3. Saepius commendatur metus, & tremor. Ergo. Resp. Metû & reverentiâ filiali, qualis tunc intelligitur, certitudo illa confirmatur: Phil. ii, 12, 13, cum timore ac tremore vestram salutem consicite.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Fear and trembling are often commended; therefore. Resp. That certainty is confirmed by fear and filial reverence, such as is then understood: Phil. ii, 12, 13, work out your salvation with fear and trembling.

units.la: Obj. 4. Multi falso putant, & jactant, se electos. Ergo. Resp. Illorum falsa imaginatio non debet praejudicare verè conversis, Spiritum fidei habentibus, sic credentibus, loquentibus, & facientibus: 2 Cor. iv, 13, Jac. 2, 12.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Many falsely think and boast that they are elect; therefore. Resp. Their false imagination ought not to prejudice those who are truly converted, who have the Spirit of faith, who so believe, speak and act: 2 Cor. iv, 13, Jac. 2, 12.

units.la: XXII. Hominum Reprobatio est Praedestinatio, quâ Deus ab aeterno constituit de Hominibus, ubi boni, sed labiles essent creati, ac deinceps pariter lapsi, quosdam definitè in isto statû relinquere; juste, sapienter, & patienter gubernare, ac propter peccata aeternum condemnare; ad gloriam Potentiae, Sapientiae, & Justitiae suae.
units.tr: XXII. The reprobation of men is that predestination by which God, from eternity, decreed concerning men, who would be created good but liable to fall, and who afterwards fell likewise: to leave certain ones definitely in this state; to govern them justly, wisely and patiently; and, on account of their sins, to condemn them eternally, to the glory of his power, wisdom and justice.

units.la: Actus hic Dei etiâm primò respicit definite & nominatim personas quasdam; non generaliter infideles, aut impoenitentes, incerto eventû. Contra Socinianos, Remonstrantes, &c. Idque patet, 1. ex SS. Literis, non solùm negative: Ies. xli, 9. Non reprobavi te. 1 Thess. v, 9. Non constituit nos Deus ad iram. Apoc. xiii, 8. Nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae. Sed & positive: Judae, 4. Olim praescripti ad Damnationem. Rom. ix, 13. Esavum odio habui. 17, 18. Dicit enim Scriptura Pharaoni; Ad hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te Potentiam Meam, &c. Quem vult, indurat. 19, 22. An non habet potestatem figulus in lutum, ut ex eadem massa faciat aliud quidem vas ad decus, aliud vero ad dedecus? Quid si vero volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, pertulit multa cum irae cohibitione vasa irae compasta ad interitum. Confer Prov. xvi, 4.
units.tr: This act of God also primarily regards certain persons, definitely and by name, not unbelievers or the impenitent in general with an uncertain outcome. This is against the Socinians, the Remonstrants, etc. And this is evident: 1. from the Holy Scriptures, not only negatively: Isa. xli, 9, I have not rejected you. 1 Thess. v, 9, God has not appointed us to wrath. Apoc. xiii, 8, names not written in the book of life. But also positively: Judae, 4, long ago marked out for condemnation. Rom. ix, 13, Esau I have hated. 17, 18, For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, etc. He hardens whom he wills. 19, 22, Has not the potter power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? What if God, willing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction? Compare Prov. xvi, 4.

units.la: 2. Ex ratione Voluntatis, Decreti, Præscientiæ, atque Electionis Divinæ, de quibus suis locis.
units.tr: 2. Concerning the will, the decree, the foreknowledge, and the election of God, from the reasons for each, to be treated in their own places.

units.la: XXIII. Secundò afferimus, illam determinationem ab æterno, & immutabiliter factam esse. Rom. ix, 11. Nondum enim nati pueri, &c. Judæ 4. Jam olim præscripti. Vide sup. th. 5.
units.tr: XXIII. Secondly, we affirm that this determination was made from eternity and is immutable. Rom. ix, 11: For the children not yet born, etc. Jude 4: long ago marked out. See above, th. 5.

units.la: Tertiò, Reprobatio facta est, non ex prævisa infidelitate, impœnitentia, aut apostasia; sed ex Dei placito. Hoc probatur.
units.tr: Thirdly, reprobation was made not from foreseen unbelief, impenitence, or apostasy, but from the good pleasure of God. This is proved as follows.

units.la: 1. Ex illustri loco V. T. Prov. xvi, 4. Omnia operatur Jehovah propter Se ipsum, etiam impium ad diem mali.
units.tr: 1. From the notable passage of the Old Testament, Prov. xvi, 4: Jehovah has made all things for Himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.

units.la: 2. Ex dictis Christi; Matth. xi, 25, 26. „Quòd hæc „occultaveris sapientibus & intellegentibus,-. Etiam „Pater, quia ità placuit Tibi. Confer, xiii, 11, -15. Joh. xii, 37-40.
units.tr: 2. From the words of Christ, Matt. xi, 25, 26: "that You have hidden these things from the wise and understanding," and "Yes, Father, for so it pleased You." Compare xiii, 11-15; John xii, 37-40.

units.la: 3. Ex dictis Apostoli - Rom. ix, 11, 12, 13. Cùm nihil fecissent boni vel mali, &c. Non ex operibus; sed ex vocante. 17. de Pharaone; Ad hoc excitavi te, &c. 18. Quem vult, indurat. 19, -22. Vide sup. th. 22.
units.tr: 3. From the words of the Apostle, Rom. ix, 11, 12, 13: when they had done neither good nor evil, etc.; not of works but of him who calls. Verse 17, concerning Pharaoh: For this purpose have I raised you up, etc. Verse 18: He hardens whom He will. Verses 19-22. See above, th. 22.

units.la: 4. Ex antè probatis de Voluntate, Decreto, Scientia, & specialiùs de Electione Divina.
units.tr: 4. From what has been proved before concerning the will, the decree, and the knowledge of God, and more specifically concerning divine election.

units.la: XXIV Finis est Gloria Dei; ad quam ipse sic exserit Potentiam suam, per viam Justitiæ; ut admirandâ interim Sapientia, Bonitas, & Longanimitas simul illustretur. Rom. ix, 17. Ut ostendam in te Potentiam Meam; & annuncietur Nomen Meum in totâ terrâ. 22. Volens ostendere Iram, & notam facere Potentiam Suam. xi, 33, 34. O profundas divitias tum Sapientiæ, tum Cognitionis Dei, &c. Ex Eo, & per Eum, & in Ipsum (sunt) omnia Ipsi (sit) Gloria in sæcula! Amen.
units.tr: XXIV. The end is the glory of God, to which He puts forth His power in this way, through justice, so that meanwhile His admirable wisdom, goodness, and long-suffering are displayed together. Rom. ix, 17: That I might show My power in you, and that My name might be declared in all the earth. Verse 22: Willing to show His wrath and to make His power known. xi, 33, 34: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God, etc. For of Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things. To Him be glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: Sapientissimè igitur & sanctissimè Deus constituit de Hominibus, ut, postquàm creati essent boni, sed labiles Fœdus initum, lapsus permissus, & sententia legalis propositâ, ex ista miseria aliqui definitè non liberarentur; quin & prolapsus in peccata actualiter permitteretur; isti tales tolerarentur, gubernarentur, & & exercerentur multis modis, ac tandem juste damnarentur, ad Gloriam Ipsius sic manifestandam. Hoc autem novissimo die plenariæ executioni mandabitur, juxta sententiam; Matth. xxv, 41. Execrati, abite à Me in ignem æternum, paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus.
units.tr: Therefore God most wisely and most holily determined concerning men that, after they had been created good but mutable and a covenant had been entered into, a fall would be permitted and a legal sentence proposed; and that some would not be definitively freed from this misery. Moreover, those who fell into actual sins would be permitted to do so; these would be tolerated, governed, and exercised in many ways, and at last justly condemned, so that His glory might thus be made manifest. This will be carried into full execution on the last day, according to the sentence: Matt. xxv, 41: Depart from Me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

units.la: XXV. Obj. 1. Deus est maximè Misericors: non vult quenquam perire; 2 Pet. iii, 9. Ergò non datur absoluta quorundam hominum reprobatio. Resp. Deus non vult perire quenquam electorum: ideò additur: Patiente est in Nos animo. Et summa Dei Misericordia non est extendenda ultra ipsius Voluntatem: Rom. ix, 18. Cujus vult miseretur; &c. A Misericordiæ effectis Justa damnatio diversa quidem est; non tamen contraria.
units.tr: XXV. Objection 1: God is most merciful; He does not will that anyone should perish (2 Pet. iii, 9). Therefore an absolute reprobation of some men is not given. Answer: God does not will that any of the elect should perish; therefore it is added, He is patient toward us. The highest mercy of God is not to be extended beyond His own will: Rom. ix, 18: He has mercy on whom He wills, etc. The just damnation that follows from the effects of mercy is different, indeed, but not contrary.

units.la: Obj. 2. Absoluta illa Reprobatio aliena est à justitiâ; quæ non permittit puniri, nisi peccatores. Resp. Reprobatio est actus absoluti Dominii: damnatio verò est actus Iustitiæ: scil. peccata sunt causæ demeritoriæ damnationis, sive pœnarum; non autem Decreti, aut volitionis Divinæ.
units.tr: Objection 2: That absolute reprobation is foreign to justice, which permits punishment only of sinners. Answer: Reprobation is an act of absolute dominion; damnation, however, is an act of justice. That is, sins are the meritorious causes of damnation, or of punishments, but not of the decree or of the divine volition.

units.la: Obj. 3. Si Reprobatio foret absoluta, tàm multi homines essent necessariò damnandi; nec ullis bonis operibus exitium effugerent: hoc autem absurdum est: Ergò. Resp. Reprobi non possunt non damnari; quia non adhibent neque ex hypothesi, & in sensu composito, adhibere possunt, media salutis: in sensu diviso tamen, si ea adhiberent, salvarentur; & per mandatum Dei ad ea obligati sunt.
units.tr: Objection 3: If reprobation were absolute, so many men would necessarily be damned, and none would escape ruin by any good works; but this is absurd. Therefore... Answer: The reprobate cannot but be damned, because they do not use, and in the composite sense cannot use, the means of salvation. In the divided sense, however, if they did use them, they would be saved; and they are bound to use them by the command of God.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sic etiàm admittenda foret Reprobatio infantium: & consequenter parentes semper deberent esse soliciti de infantibus suis; an non essent reprobi; &c. Resp. 1. Infantes reprobi justè damnantur, propter reatum in Adamo; Rom. v. 16. & Deus judicans justificatur semper: Rom. iii, 4, 6. ix. 20. 21. 2. Nihil est, quod fideles soliciti sint de liberis suis in infantiâ morientibus; alia de iis facta est promissio; Gen. xvii, 7, 16. 7, 10, 13, 14. Act. 2, 39. Marc. x, 14. Adolescentes vero quàm diligentissimè instruant ad pietatem : Ephes. vi, 4.
units.tr: Objection 4: In that case the reprobation of infants would also have to be admitted, and consequently parents ought always to be anxious about their infants: are they not reprobate, etc.? Answer 1: Infants who are reprobate are justly condemned on account of guilt in Adam, Rom. v, 16; and God, when He judges, is always justified: Rom. iii, 4, 6; ix, 20, 21. Answer 2: There is nothing for believers to be anxious about concerning their children who die in infancy, since a different promise has been made concerning them: Gen. xvii, 7, 16; 7, 10, 13, 14; Acts ii, 39; Mark x, 14. But young people should be instructed in piety as diligently as possible: Eph. vi, 4.

units.la: Obj. 5. Peccatum facit hominem reprobabilem : ergo etiam propter illud futurum, ac praevisum, facta est Reprobatio. Resp. Peccatum facit hominem damnabilem, aut potius reum damnationis : sed possibilis produci, etiàm est ordinabilis ad existentiam talem, & talem statum aeternum. Subjecto possibili possibiles affectiones conveniunt. Et qui finem decernit, etiàm media ad eum ordinat, & conditiones pro re natâ.
units.tr: Objection 5: Sin makes a man reprobable; therefore reprobation was also made on account of that future and foreseen sin. Answer: Sin makes a man damnable, or rather liable to damnation; but whatever can be produced as possible is also ordainable to such existence and to such an eternal state. Possible affections belong to a possible subject. And he who decrees the end also ordains the means to it, and the conditions as the case requires.

units.la: XXVI. Male Remonstrantes quatuor Decreta subordinata statuunt: Primum, quo Deus decreverit Filium suum in Mediatorem & Salvatorem ponere. Secundum, quo resipiscentes in gratiam recipere, perseverantes per Christum salvare, impoenitentes verò damnare, constituerit. Tertium, quo decreverit media ad salutem sufficienter & efficaciter administrare, secundùm Sapientiam suam, quâ novit quid Misericordiam & Severitatem suam deceat. Quartum denique quo certas personas salvare, vel damnare decreverit.
units.tr: XXVI. The Remonstrants wrongly lay down four subordinate decrees. The first, by which God decreed to set His Son as Mediator and Saviour. The second, by which He determined to receive the penitent into grace, to save the persevering through Christ, and to condemn the impenitent. The third, by which He decreed to administer the means of salvation sufficiently and efficaciously, according to His wisdom, by which He knows what befits His mercy and His severity. The fourth and last, by which He decreed to save or to condemn certain persons.

units.la: Tribus prioribus perperam substernunt gratiam universalem; postremo, liberum hominis arbitrium. In primo spectatur jus, via, & occasio cum homine peccatore denuo agendi, & conditiones salutis praescribendi. Secundo dicitur actus fidei ignobilis & possibilis eligi, in conditionem salutis, reputandam pro persectâ Legis obedientiâ. Tertio, dicuntur quaedam saltem, eaque efficacia, media necessaria administrari; quibus homines vel statim, vel gradatim ad fidem redduntur idonei: imo etiam media illa efficaciter dicuntur administrari; quod saltem ad efficiendum sint admodùm valida. In quarto est nexus cum prioribus tantùm contingens; nam, positis illis mediis, dicunt posse
units.tr: By the first three they wrongly introduce universal grace; by the last, the free will of man. In the first, there is regard to the right, the way, and the occasion of dealing anew with the sinful man, and of prescribing the conditions of salvation. In the second, it is said that an ignoble and possible act of faith is chosen as the condition of salvation, to be reckoned as perfect obedience to the Law. In the third, it is said that certain necessary means, at least, and those efficacious, are administered, by which men are made fit for faith either at once or gradually; indeed, those means are said to be administered efficaciously in the sense that they are at least very powerful for bringing it about. In the fourth, there is only a contingent connection with the earlier decrees; for, these means having been posited, they say it can happen

units.la: * Marginal note: not legible in detail on the scan. posse fieri ut nullus salvaretur: Gratia illis resistibilis est. Breviter, talia Decreta, eoque ordine, SS. Literis non consonant: sed contra Dei Independentiam, & pro libéri Arbitrii gloria temere conficta sunt.
units.tr: * Marginal note: not legible in detail on the scan. that no one should be saved; grace is resistible for them. In short, such decrees, and in that order, do not agree with Holy Scripture, but were rashly devised against the independence of God and for the glory of free will.

units.la: XXVII. Sed paucis inter se conferamus Praedestinationem Angelorum & Hominum! In Electione utrobique finis ultimus est Gloria Bonitatis & Gratiae Divinae. Subordinatus autem, singulorum Beatitudo aeterna: Prov. xvi, 4. Hebr. xii, 22. Phil. iii, 20.
units.tr: XXVII. But let us briefly compare the predestination of angels and of men. In election, in both cases, the ultimate end is the glory of the goodness and grace of God. The subordinate end, however, is the eternal blessedness of each: Prov. xvi, 4; Heb. xii, 22; Phil. iii, 20.

units.la: Media etiam utrobique sunt creatio ad imaginem Dei, & istius recti usus, ac praxis spiritualis.
units.tr: The means in both cases are also the creation in the image of God, and the right use of that image, and spiritual practice.

units.la: Reprobationis finis est Gloria Iustitiae. Divinae in damnatis: Matth. xxv, 41. 2 Petr. ii, 4. 1 Cor. vi, 3.
units.tr: The end of reprobation is the glory of divine justice in the condemned: Matt. xxv, 41; 2 Pet. ii, 4; 1 Cor. vi, 3.

units.la: Media, bona Origo permissio defectionis, & derelictio in ista miseria: Joh. viii, 44. 2 Petr. ii, 4. Judae, 6.
units.tr: The means: a good origin, namely the permission of defection, and abandonment in this misery: John viii, 44; 2 Pet. ii, 4; Jude 6.

units.la: Differentia est in Mediis: in Angelis electis enim est Sanctitas non interrupta: Marc. viii, 38. Luc. ix, 26. cum 2 Petr. ii, 4. Judae, 6. Sed in Hominibus est Gratia per Christum Mediatorem restituta; Fides, & Resipiscentia: Matth. i, 21. Joh. iii, 16. Act. iv, 12.
units.tr: The difference lies in the means. For in the elect angels there is uninterrupted holiness: Mark viii, 38; Luke ix, 26; compare 2 Pet. ii, 4; Jude 6. But in men there is grace restored through Christ the Mediator, faith and repentance: Matt. i, 21; John iii, 16; Acts iv, 12.

units.la: 1 Tim. ii, 5, 6. &c. Unde etiam Misericordia Dei elucescit. Rom. ix, 15, 18, 23; xi, 32.
units.tr: 1 Tim. ii, 5, 6, etc. Whence also the mercy of God shines forth: Rom. ix, 15, 18, 23; xi, 32.

units.la: 2. Multis hominibus reprobis praedicatio Evangelii etiam suo modo obtingit; sed nullis Angelis: 1 Tim. iii, 16. Hebr. 2, 16.
units.tr: 2. For many reprobate men the preaching of the Gospel also comes, in its own way; but to no angels: 1 Tim. iii, 16; Heb. ii, 16.

units.la: XXVIII. Praxis esto: 1. Humiliter sublimitatem & sapientiam Decreti Divini admiremur, adoremus: Rom. xi, 32.
units.tr: XXVIII. The practice of the doctrine is as follows. 1. Let us humbly admire and adore the sublimity and wisdom of the Divine decree: Rom. 11:32.

units.la: 2. Nunquam media à fine suo separemus: Matth. iv, 6, 7. Rom. iii, 8. x, 13, -16.
units.tr: 2. Let us never separate the means from their end: Matth. 4:6, 7; Rom. 3:8; 10:13–16.

units.la: 3. Vocationem & Electionem nostram pia praxi firmam faciamus: 2 Petr. i, 10; Joh. xv, 16. 1 Petr. ii, 9. Eph. i, 4. cum Luc. xiii, 23, 24. Act. i, 7. Eum maxime reverentes ac diligentes, qui nos sic elegit: 1 Joh. iv, 9. Eph. i, 5. Josf. xxiv, 14, 15. Deut. vii, 6, 7, 8. Ps. lxiii, 9. lxxiii, 23-26.
units.tr: 3. Let us make our vocation and election firm by a pious practice: 2 Pet. 1:10; John 15:16; 1 Pet. 2:9; Eph. 1:4, compared with Luke 13:23, 24; Acts 1:7. Let us especially reverence and love Him who has thus chosen us: 1 John 4:9; Eph. 1:5; Josh. 24:14, 15; Deut. 7:6, 7, 8; Ps. 63:9; 73:23–26.

units.la: 4. Totam Salutis nostræ methodum Deo adscribimus : Phil. 2,12,13. Eph. 2,8; 9, 1 Cor. iv, 7. Ps. cxxxviii, 8.
units.tr: 4. We ascribe the whole method of our salvation to God: Phil. 2:12, 13; Eph. 2:8, 9; 1 Cor. 4:7; Ps. 138:8.

units.la: 5. Adversus omnes tentationes animum muniamus charitate Dei, & fiducia in ipso: Rom. viii, 28, - 37.
units.tr: 5. Let us fortify our minds against all temptations with the love of God and trust in Him: Rom. 8:28–37.

units.la: 1 Joh. iv, 18. cum Rom. xi, 29. 2 Tim. 2,19.
units.tr: 1 John 4:18, compared with Rom. 11:29; 2 Tim. 2:19.

units.la: 6. Creaturis peccantibus culpam omnem tribuamus : Rom. iii, 4. - ix, 19, 20, 21.
units.tr: 6. Let us attribute all guilt to the creatures who sin: Rom. 3:4; 9:19, 20, 21.

units.la: 7. Ex consideratione Severitatis Divinæ in aliis, Gratiam nobis præstitam magis admiremur, & animo grato celebremus : Rom. ix, 22,23. xi, 32, -. xii, 1.
units.tr: 7. From consideration of the severity of God toward others, let us admire more the grace shown to us and celebrate it with a grateful mind: Rom. 9:22, 23; 11:32; 12:1.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: DE CREATIONE.
units.tr: ON CREATION.

units.la: Actiones Dei transfuntes. Productio creativa. Eductiva. Creatio mundi. 1. Creatio actio Dei propria; etiam contra Pontif. 2. Objectiones solvuntur. 3. Creatura ne quidem ejus causa instrumentalis physica esse potest. Obj. solv. 4. Creatio active spectata, est ipse Deus. Obj. solv. 5. Nulla Creatura ab aterno esse potuit. 6. Objectiones solv. 7. An Mundus potuerit citius, aut serius creari. 8. Quando creatus; & quo ordine. Creatio immediata: & mediata. 9. Opera primi diei. Cœlum cœlorum. Ejus situs. 10. Angeli. Quando creati. Eorum existentia prob. c. Sadducæos, &c. 11. Nomina. Definitio. 12. Substantiæ spirituales. Eorum intellectus. Quomodo futura sciant. Eorum libertas. 13. Potentia. Affectus 14. Completa per se subsistentia. Non habent bent corpora. Neque illis convenit generatio ; aut corruptio. 15. Locus definitivus. Motus. Ævum. 16. Numerus. Ordo. Archangelus. Classes, & chori temerè à Pontif. definiuntur. 17. Boni ; & Mali. 18. Boni. Eorum officia. An cuique Homini assignatus suus Angelus custios. Obj. solv. Gabriel. Honor. 19. Mali Angeli. Spectra. Effecta alia noxia. Corporalis obsessio. Actiones circa animam. Beelzebub. 20 Æther: & Aer. 21. Terra: & Aqua. Quomodo his Spiritus incubuerit. c. Socin. & Pontif. 22. Lux Non absque subjecto ; c. Pontif. 23. Consectaria contra Philos. qu. 24. Infernus. 25. Secundo die factum expansum. Meteora. Non statim adjecta specialis approbatio. 26. Tertio die segregatæ Aquæ à Terra. More: ejus salsedo: & motus. 27. In Terra partes salsæ, sulphureæ, mercurialis: Metalla, aliaque mineralia. Ignes, & Flatus subterranei ; &c. Herbæ; frutices; arbores. Earum nutritio, & generatio. Plantanimalia: & Sponte orta. 28. Quarto die facta Luminaria: duo magna; & stellæ reliquæ: erraticæ ; fixæ. Earum usus communis. Speciales. 29. Motus. Influentia. Vanæ prædictiones Genethliacorum. Signa extraordinaria. 20. Consectarium de Solis motu, & Terræ quiete. 31. Exc. & Obj. solvuntur. 32. Animalia: atque in iis corpus ; & Anima sensitiva. Sensus, tum interni; tùm externi. Appetitus sensitivus. Facultas locomotiva. 33. Quinto die producta. Sexto. Amphibia. Homo. E-
units.tr: Actions of God that pass outward. Creative production. Eductive production. The creation of the world. 1. Creation is an action proper to God; this is also against the Papists. 2. The objections are answered. 3. A creature cannot even be the physical instrumental cause of creation. Objection answered. 4. Creation, viewed actively, is God himself. Objection answered. 5. No creature could exist from eternity. 6. Objections answered. 7. Whether the world could have been created sooner or later. 8. When it was created, and in what order. Immediate and mediate creation. 9. The works of the first day. The heaven of heavens. Its position. 10. Angels. When they were created. Their existence proved against the Sadducees, etc. 11. Names. Definition. 12. Spiritual substances. Their understanding. How they know future things. Their freedom. 13. Power. Affections. 14. Complete subsistence in themselves. They do not have bodies. Nor does generation or corruption belong to them. 15. Defined place. Motion. Aeviternity. 16. Number. Order. Archangels. Ranks and choirs rashly defined by the Papists. 17. Good and evil. 18. Good angels. Their duties. Whether each man has an angel guardian assigned to him. Objection answered. Gabriel. Honour. 19. Evil angels. Apparitions. Other harmful effects. Bodily obsession. Actions upon the soul. Beelzebub. 20. Ether and air. 21. Earth and water. How the Spirit brooded over these. Against the Socinians and the Papists. 22. Light: not without a subject; against the Papists. 23. Corollaries against the philosophers, question. 24. Hell. 25. The expanse made on the second day. Meteors. The special approval not added at once. 26. On the third day the waters were separated from the earth. Their moisture, their saltness, and their motion. 27. In the earth there are salty, sulphurous and mercurial parts: metals and other minerals, subterranean fires and winds, etc. Herbs; shrubs; trees. Their nourishment and generation. Plant-animals and spontaneous generation. 28. On the fourth day the lights were made: two great ones, and the remaining stars: wandering and fixed. Their common use and special uses. 29. Motion. Influence. The empty predictions of the astrologers. Extraordinary signs. 30. A corollary on the motion of the sun and the rest of the earth. 31. The exceptions and objections are answered. 32. Animals, and in them the body and the sensitive soul. Senses, both internal and external. Sensitive appetite. Locomotive faculty. 33. Produced on the fifth day. On the sixth: amphibians. Man.

units.la: jus partes essentiales. Adamus, & Eva. Illæ initio non bicorpor. Non Lilith. Non PræAdamita. 34. Corpus viri, unde: atque item Mulieris. Propagatio. Conformatio. 35. Anima à Deo immediatè creata. Ejus immaterialitas. Adhùc in singulis à Deo creatur immediatè. Obj. solv. Immortalitas. Intellectus. Voluntas. Iudicium. Libertas. Unio illius cum Corpore. Non modus, &c. 36. Imago Dei. Homo non factus ad Imaginem Angelorum; c. Pontif. nec ad Filium Dei incarnandum; c. Anabapt. 37. Ista Imago quid supponat. Formaliter consistit in spirituali sapientiâ, Justitia, & sanctitate; c. Socin. Obj. solv. 38. Justitia originalis. Quæstio minimè inepta & inutilis; c. Remonstr. Adam habuit potentiam credendi in Christum. 39. Rectè dicitur naturalis; c. Pontif. 40. Opinio Pontif. de morbo morali naturæ concreato: atque item Remonstr. Inclinatio ad malum verè vitiosa est. 41. Gratia primi hominis: habitualis. 42. Quæ consecutivè ad Imaginem Dei pertinuerint. Dominium. In eo Imago Dei non consistebat formaliter; c. Socin. & Remonstr. 43. Immortalitas, nisi homines peccâssent. c. Socin. 44. Illorum distinct. & obj. solvuntur. 45. Creatio singulorum momentanea: sex tamen diebus distincta. Anni tempestas. Quies septimi diei. 46. Creatura. Mundus. 47. Unus. Finitus. 48. Praxis. 49.
units.tr: His essential parts. Adam and Eve. They were not at first two-bodied. Not Lilith. Not a pre-Adamite. 34. The body of the man, whence it came, and likewise that of the woman. Propagation. Shaping. 35. The soul created immediately by God. Its immateriality. Even now in each person it is created immediately by God. Objection answered. Immortality. Understanding. Will. Judgment. Freedom. Its union with the body: not a mode, etc. 36. The image of God. Man was not made in the image of the angels, against the Papists; nor to become the incarnate Son of God, against the Anabaptists. 37. What this image presupposes. It formally consists in spiritual wisdom, justice and holiness; against the Socinians. Objection answered. 38. Original righteousness. The question is by no means foolish and useless; against the Remonstrants. Adam had the power of believing in Christ. 39. It is rightly called natural; against the Papists. 40. The opinion of the Papists on a moral disease innate to nature, and likewise of the Remonstrants. An inclination to evil is truly sinful. 41. The grace of the first man: habitual. 42. What belonged consequentially to the image of God. Dominion. In this the image of God did not formally consist; against the Socinians and Remonstrants. 43. Immortality, had men not sinned; against the Socinians. 44. Distinction of these, and the objections are answered. 45. The creation of individual things was momentary, yet distinguished into six days. The seasons of the year. The rest of the seventh day. 46. Creature. World. 47. One. Finite. 48. Practice. 49.

units.la: I. ACtiones Dei transeuntes dicuntur, per quas alia entia extra Deum constituuntur. Suntque Creatio, & Providentia.
units.tr: I. Actions are called transient [transeuntes] of God when through them other beings are established outside God. These are creation and providence.

units.la: Productio rei vel est creativa, vel eductiva. Illa est ex nihilo. Sic in principio creavit Deus Coelos & terram. Et terra erat solitudo & inanitas: Gen. 1, 1, 2. Confer Hebr. xi, 3. Quae cernimus non sunt ex apparentibus facta. Per Generationem, & Artem, multa producuntur ex materia; sed hic longe aliter factum: sc. 2 Cor, iv, 6. Deus dixit, ut e tenebris lux splendesceret, & Rom. iv, 17. Vocans quae non sunt, tanquam sint.
units.tr: The production of a thing is either creative or eductive. The former is out of nothing. So: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was waste and empty: Gen. 1:1, 2. Compare Heb. 11:3: What we see was not made out of things that appear. By generation and art many things are produced out of matter; but here it is done quite differently, namely 2 Cor. 4:6: God said, let light shine out of darkness, and Rom. 4:17: calling those things which are not as though they were.

units.la: In hac, forma materialis e potentia materiae educitur, per causam efficientem idoneam.
units.tr: In the latter, a material form is drawn out of the potency of matter, through a suitable efficient cause.

units.la: Plenius describitur Creatio, Actio Dei transiens, qua Ipse universum mundum, & quaecunque in eo sunt, principio temporis, sex diebus, produxit ex nihilo; ad gloriam Potentiae, Bonitatis, ac Sapientiae Suae demonstrandam.
units.tr: Creation is described more fully as the action of God passing outward, by which He himself, at the beginning of time, in six days, produced out of nothing the whole universe and whatever is in it, to demonstrate the glory of his power, goodness and wisdom.

units.la: II. Creatio est actio Dei propria; ita ut ex illa vera Deitas recte colligatur. Male autem statuit Avicenna, Angelum supremum creasse sibi proximum, & sic deinceps; infimum vero Angelum corpora creasse. Similiter fere Simoniani, Gnostici, aliique, creationem Angelis, Aeonibus, aliisque fictis Potestatibus tribuebant. His affines Pontificii, propter Transubstantiationem, virtutem creativam creaturis communicabilem esse disputant.
units.tr: II. Creation is an action proper to God, such that the true Deity is rightly inferred from it. But Avicenna wrongly held that the highest angel created the angel next to himself, and so on down; while the lowest angel created bodies. In much the same way the Simonians, Gnostics and others attributed creation to angels, aeons and other fictitious powers. Akin to these, the Papists, on account of transubstantiation, argue that a creative power can be communicated to creatures.

units.la: Nostra sententia probatur:
units.tr: Our view is proved:

units.la: 1. Expressis locis S. Scripturae: Psal. xix, 2, Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei, &c. Jes. xl, 26. Videte, quis creavit ista. xlv, 24. Ego Jehovah facio omnia: extendo coelos Solus: expando terram per Me ipsum. Rom. i, 20. Ex creatione intelligitur ac perspicitur aeterna Potentia ac Divinitas. Confer Gen. 1, 1. Psal. xxxiii, 6. Jes. xlv, 6, 7. †lv, 6, 7. Jerem. x, 11. Ioh. ix, 8. Hinc propterea colligitur Divina ἐξουσία: Apoc. iv, 11. Dignus es, Domine, qui accipias Gloriam, & honorem, & virtutem: quia Tu condidisti omnia: & per Voluntatem Tuam sunt, & creata sunt. Quare non mirum, Pontificios: cultum religiosum creaturis etiam communicare; & sic, quantum possunt, argumenta enervare, quibus contra Antitrinitarios, Arianos, Photinianos, &c. Deitas Filii & Spiritus S. probatur. Vide Hebr. I, 6, 8, - 12. iii, 3, 4.
units.tr: 1. By express passages of Holy Scripture: Ps. 19:2, The heavens declare the glory of God, etc. Isa. 40:26, Lift up your eyes and see who created these things. Isa. 45:12, I, Jehovah, make all things; I alone stretch out the heavens; I spread out the earth by myself. Rom. 1:20, From creation the eternal power and divinity are understood and perceived. Compare Gen. 1:1; Ps. 33:6; Isa. 45:6, 7; Isa. 55:6, 7; Jer. 10:11; John 1:3. Hence the divine authority [ἐξουσία] is also inferred: Rev. 4:11, You are worthy, O Lord, to receive glory, honour and power: for you created all things, and by your will they are and were created. Hence it is no wonder that the Papists also communicate religious worship to creatures; and so, as far as they can, they weaken the arguments by which the Deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit is proved against the Antitrinitarians, Arians, Photinians, etc. See Heb. 1:6, 8, 12; 3:3, 4.

units.la: 2. Ratione: Actio requirens infinitam potentiam, ab ente finito procedere nequit. Atqui talis est Creatio; propter infinitam terminorum distantiam: nulla enim proportio, vel affinitas est, inter nihilum, & inter ens verum, quod creatione producitur.
units.tr: 2. By reason: an action requiring infinite power cannot proceed from a finite being. But creation is such an action, on account of the infinite distance between its terms: for there is no proportion or affinity between nothing and the true being that is produced by creation.

units.la: 3. Causa creans debet esse ὑπερφυΐα; ut essentias alias, per creationem producendas, eminenter & virtualiter contineat; & citra mutationem, vel diminutionem sui, eas ex se producere pollit: hoc autem nulli creaturae convenit: sic enim infinita esset, eminenter habens τὸ esse creaturarum.
units.tr: 3. The creating cause must be supernatural [ὑπερφυΐα], so that it eminently and virtually contains the essences to be produced by creation, and can produce them from itself without change or diminution of itself. But this belongs to no creature: for then it would be infinite, eminently having the being [esse] of creatures.

units.la: 4. Substantia non recipit magis & minus: & creatae substantiae in Ente, ut genere univoco, conveniunt: consequenter una aliam, in ratione essendi absolute, causare non potest.
units.tr: 4. Substance does not admit of more and less; and created substances agree in being, as in a univocal genus; consequently one cannot cause another, absolutely in respect of being.

units.la: III. Obj. 1.
units.tr: III. Objection 1.

units.la: Inter rem creatam & nihilum non datur distantia infinita: major enim est distantia inter Deum & nihilum. Omnis res creata infinita est; & sua solum entitate distat à nihilo: distantia igitur ista finita est: & ad eam superandam non necessario requiritur Potentia activa infinita. Resp. Distantia terminorum actionis, ex habitudine unius ad alterum petenda est: non autem à perfectione, vel ab amplitudine unius termini. At vero inter substantiam creatam, & nihilum, nulla prorsus est affinitas, aut proportio; aequè ac inter Deum & nihil. Idcirco recte dicitur distantia illa infinita: nec superari potest, nisi per Potentiam activam infinitam.
units.tr: Between a created thing and nothing there is no infinite distance: for the distance between God and nothing is greater. Every created thing is infinite, and it is distant from nothing by its entity alone; therefore that distance is finite, and to overcome it an infinite active power is not necessarily required. Answer: the distance between the terms of an action is to be sought from the relation of one to the other, not from the perfection or the magnitude of one term. But between created substance and nothing there is absolutely no affinity or proportion, just as there is none between God and nothing. Hence that distance is rightly called infinite, and it can be overcome only by an infinite active power.

units.la: Obj. 2. Generatio etiam est mutatio a non esse ad esse simpliciter; & tamen creaturæ possibilis: ergo etiam Creatio. Resp. Generatio materiam præsupponit; atque hoc efficit, ut ea fiat individui in tali specie. Imo ipsa forma in potentiâ illius latuit, ex quâ educitur à causâ facultatem ita proportionatam habente. Et propter paritatem essendi, non absolutè ratione essentiæ; sed tantum ratione convenientiæ specisicæ, causa generans subjectum, potentiam ad similem formam habens, sic perficere & sibi assimilare potest.
units.tr: Objection 2. Generation too is a change from non-being to being simply, and yet it is possible for a creature: therefore creation is too. Answer: generation presupposes matter, and this brings it about that the thing made is an individual of such a species. Indeed the form itself lay hidden in the potency of that matter, from which it is drawn out by a cause having a faculty so proportioned. And because of the likeness of being, not absolutely in respect of essence but only in respect of specific agreement, a generating cause can perfect and make like to itself a subject which has a potency for a similar form.

units.la: Obj. 3. Deus omnipotens creaturas producere potuit quam maximè efficaces ad agendum; ergo etiam ad creandum. Resp. Deus secundum voluntatem suam, per omnipotentiam, dedit creaturis esse ex nihilo; & singulis sphæram activitatis ipsarum: sed hanc non-infinitam; quia id contradictorium foret.
units.tr: Objection 3. God omnipotent could have produced creatures most efficacious in acting; therefore also in creating. Answer: God, according to his will, by his omnipotence, gave to creatures existence out of nothing, and to each a sphere of their activity; but this sphere is not infinite, because that would be a contradiction.

units.la: Obj. 4. Creaturæ productæ sunt per creationem, quæ ipsa etiam creatura est: non enim est Deus. Ergo creatura per creaturam produci potest. Resp. Creatio activa non est creatura; sed est ipse Deus creans, sive hoc agens sine ullâ mutatione Sui, ut creatura existat in tempore.
units.tr: Objection 4. Created things were produced by creation, which is itself a creature, for it is not God. Therefore a creature can be produced by a creature. Answer: active creation is not a creature; it is God himself creating, that is, God acting in this way, without any change in himself, so that a creature exists in time.

units.la: Obj. 5. Omnipotentia non videtur attributum Dei incommunicabiliter proprium: quia sola Independentia talis est. Sed creatura omnipotens saltem posset aliam creaturam producere ex nihilo. Resp. Imo omnipotentia est Dei proprium attributum; infinitatem, adeoque Independentiam, involvens: & non nisi unica esse potest. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 19. §. 2. Omnipotentiam dependentem fingere, cum Pontisiciis quibusdam, est sibi contradicere.
units.tr: Objection 5. Omnipotence does not seem to be an attribute of God incommunicably proper to him, because only independence is such. But an omnipotent creature could at least produce another creature out of nothing. Answer: on the contrary, omnipotence is the proper attribute of God, involving infinity and therefore independence, and it can be only one. See above, chap. 4, th. 19, §2. To imagine a dependent omnipotence, with certain Papists, is to contradict oneself.

units.la: IV. Creatura ne quidem causa instrumentalis physica creationis esse potest: contrà quàm Ariani volebant dicentes, τὸν Λόγον creasse mundum, tanquam instrumentum Patris: nam Instrumentum physicum, à causâ principali motum, objectum attingit, eique actum aliquem imprimit, qui etiam sic virtualiter fuit in illo: sed in creatione, neque subjectum præsupponitur; neque creatura virtualiter in se habet actum absolutè essendi alterius creaturæ.
units.tr: IV. A creature cannot even be the physical instrumental cause of creation, contrary to what the Arians maintained, saying that the Word (τὸν Λόγον) created the world as an instrument of the Father. For a physical instrument, moved by the principal cause, touches the object and impresses on it some action, which was also in a manner virtually in the instrument; but in creation neither a subject is presupposed, nor does a creature virtually contain in itself the act of absolutely existing of another creature.

units.la: Obj. 1. Creatura potest esse causa instrumentalis miraculorum. Resp. 1. In miraculis supponitur objectum. 2. Et causa instrumentalis ibi datur tantùm moralis.
units.tr: Objection 1. A creature can be an instrumental cause of miracles. Answer 1: in miracles an object is presupposed. 2. And there the instrumental cause is given only as moral.

units.la: Obj. 2. Per Filium dicuntur omnia creata; Ioh. 1, 3. 10. Resp. 1. Per non semper instrumentum notare, patet ex Rom. XI, 36. 2. Filio etiam absolutè tribuitur creatio: Hebr. I, 10. Tu terram fundâsti, &c. Confer III, 3, 4. 3. Per rectè ad ordinem operandi refertur. Vide sup. cap. 5. th. 16. §. 4.
units.tr: Objection 2. All things are said to have been created through the Son, John 1:3, 10. Answer: 1. That "through" does not always denote an instrument is clear from Rom. 11:36. 2. Creation is also ascribed absolutely to the Son, Heb. 1:10: "Thou, Lord, hast laid the foundation of the earth," etc. Compare Heb. 3:3, 4. 3. The phrase is rightly referred to the order of operating. See above, chap. 5, th. 16, §4.

units.la: V. Creatio vel activè spectatur, vel passivè. Priori modo est ipse Deus creans; sive potentiam suam activam sic exerens, ut creatura existat in tempore, sine alià in Deo mutatione. Isef. XL, 28. Nonne audivisti, Deum Creatorem non defetisci, nec defatigari? &c. Psal. CII, 27, 28. Hebr. I, 10, 11, 12. Tu, Domine, Terram fundasti, &c. Tu idem es, & anni Tui non deficient, &c. Iac. 1, 17.
units.tr: V. Creation is viewed either actively or passively. In the former way it is God himself creating, that is, exerting his active power in such a way that a creature exists in time, without any other change in God. Isa. 40:28: "Hast thou not heard that God the Creator does not faint nor grow weary?" etc. Ps. 102:27, 28; Heb. 1:10, 11, 12: "Thou, Lord, hast laid the foundation of the earth," etc. "Thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail," etc. James 1:17.

units.la: Posteriori modo est ipsa creatura, quatenus actus Dei in eâ terminatur, & sic ipsa ex nihilo producitur: quia nec substantia, nec accidens, extra Deum & Creaturam datur.
units.tr: In the latter way it is the creature itself, insofar as the act of God terminates in it, and so it is produced out of nothing, because neither substance nor accident exists outside God and the creature.

units.la: Obj. 1. Si Dei actio creativa esset ipse Deus, etiam Dei actio eductiva esset ipse Deus; & consequenter eductiva esset quoque creativa: quod absurdum. Ergo, &c. Resp. Actio eductiva Dei, ut causæ primæ, activè spectata, formaliter tantum, quatenus talem terminum respicit, & tali modo, à Deo, & actione Creativâ distinguitur; non realiter.
units.tr: Objection 1. If God's creative action were God himself, then God's educing action would also be God himself; and consequently the educing action would also be creative: which is absurd. Therefore, etc. Answer: the educing action of God, as first cause, viewed actively, is distinguished from God and from the creative action only formally, insofar as it regards such a term and in such a manner, and not really.

units.la: Obj. 2. Si creatio activè spectata esset ipse Deus etiam foret æterna; & consequenter creaturæ quoque æternæ forent. Resp. Actus Dei æternus est, cujus vi in tempore creatura existit.
units.tr: Objection 2. If creation viewed actively were God himself, it would also be eternal; and consequently the creatures too would be eternal. Answer: the act of God is eternal, by whose power the creature exists in time.

units.la: Obj. 2. Electio Dei æterna est; & propterea rectè dicitur Angelus, vel Homo aliquis, ab æterno electus. Similiter etiam mundus ab æterno creatus dici deberet, si creatio activa esset æterna. Resp. Nego consequentiam. Angelus, vel Homo aliquis, rectè dicitur ab æterno electus; quia ista est actio immanens: sed aliter de actione transeunte, Creatione scil. dicendum; quæ creaturam constituit extra Deum, cum afsectionibus creaturæ convenientibus.
units.tr: Objection 2. The election of God is eternal, and therefore one rightly says that an angel or some man was elected from eternity. Similarly the world too ought to be called created from eternity, if active creation were eternal. Answer: I deny the consequence. An angel or some man is rightly said to have been elected from eternity, because that is an immanent action; but it must be said otherwise of a transient action, namely creation, which establishes the creature outside God, together with the affections suitable to the creature.

units.la: VI. Creatio in principio temporis facta est: Gen.I,1. Ante quod nihil nisi æternitas fuit. Nulla creatura ab æterno esse potuit: quare etiam ex æternitate Deitas vera solide colligitur.
units.tr: VI. Creation was made at the beginning of time: Gen. 1:1. Before which there was nothing but eternity. No creature could have existed from eternity; hence also true Deity is solidly inferred from eternity.

units.la: Rationes sunt, 1. Æternitas, ut attributum infinitum, creaturæ, tanquam subjecto finito, non convenit.
units.tr: The reasons are: 1. Eternity, as an infinite attribute, does not belong to a creature as a finite subject.

units.la: 2. Creator suam ἐξουσίαν, actûs purissimi in existendo, alteri dare nec vult, nec velle potest.
units.tr: 2. The Creator neither wills nor can will to give his own ἐξουσία, that is, his most pure act in existing, to another.

units.la: 3. Conceptus Creationis æternitatem excludit: cum enim fit productio rei ex nihilo, necesse est ante illam productionem nihil istius rei extitisse; & sic eam aliquando non fuisse.
units.tr: 3. The concept of creation excludes eternity: since the production of a thing out of nothing takes place, it is necessary that before that production nothing of that thing existed; and so at some time it was not.

units.la: 4. Ut & multiplex mundi mutatio. Præteritum enim terminatur præsenti: plures dies ab ejus initio lapsi sunt, quàm menses; & plures menses, quam anni: sed ex hypothesi, jam lapsi forent anni infiniti; infinito autem majus non datur. Durationis partes finitæ sunt; sed ex partibus finitis, infinitum constitui non potest.
units.tr: 4. So also does the manifold change of the world. For the past is bounded by the present: more days have elapsed since its beginning than months, and more months than years; but on the hypothesis, infinite years would already have elapsed, and nothing greater than infinite is given. The parts of duration are finite; but out of finite parts an infinite cannot be constituted.

units.la: VII. Obj. 1. Actiones Divinæ personales, Generatio, & Spiratio, terminum suum habuerunt ab æterno: Filius enim Patri coæternus est; atque item Spiritus Sanctus. Ergo creatio similiter ab æterno terminum suum habere potuisset. Resp. O' Λόγος genitus est, & Spiritus S. spiratus, ab æterno: sed aliter se habent actiones externæ; quæ ponunt alia entia præter Deum, entia finita, cum affectionibus finitis.
units.tr: VII. Objection 1. The personal divine actions, generation and spiration, have had their term from eternity: for the Son is coeternal with the Father, and likewise the Holy Spirit. Therefore creation could likewise have had its term from eternity. Answer: the Word was begotten, and the Holy Spirit breathed forth, from eternity; but external actions are otherwise, since they posit other beings besides God, finite beings, with finite affections.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus ab æterno omnipotens, etiam ab æterno potuit mundum creare; consequenter mundus potuit ab æterno creari. Resp. Deus certè ab æterno fuit omnipotens, atque adeo potens creare mundum: sic tamen ut mundus, & singulæ creaturæ forent finitæ, haberent affectiones finitas, etiàm durationem finitam; ac proinde initium suæ existentiæ; quod ab æternitate alienum est.
units.tr: Objection 2. God, omnipotent from eternity, could also from eternity have created the world; consequently the world could have been created from eternity. Answer: God was certainly omnipotent from eternity, and so able to create the world; yet in such a way that the world and each creature would be finite, would have finite affections, and also finite duration; and therefore a beginning of its existence, which is alien to eternity.

units.la: Obj. 3. Angeli & Homines habent æternitatem à parte posteriori: nihil ergò repugnat, quo minùs creatura aliqua eam habeat à parte priori. Resp. Creaturis illis æternitas à parte posteriori, & potentialis, sive syncategorematica, tantùm competit: unde non valet consequentia ad absolutam æternitatem, in quâ est infinitas categorematica, sive actualis; cujus subjectum finitum non est capax.
units.tr: Objection 3. Angels and men have eternity in the later direction; nothing therefore prevents some creature from having it in the earlier direction. Answer: eternity in the later direction, and potential or syncategorematic, belongs only to those creatures; whence the inference does not hold to absolute eternity, in which there is categorematic or actual infinity, whose finite subject is not capable of it.

units.la: Obj. 4. Tempus fuit æternum, ac proinde etiàm motus: hic enim mundus creatus est in tempore, sive in principio temporis: istud ergò prius extitit. Consequenter etiàm creatura similiter ab æterno existere potuit. Resp. Motus & tempus non fuerunt ab æterno: sed Deus æternus mundo principium dedit, prout voluit; & motum imprellit, qui indè continuatur; ac porrò tempus observatur, & mensuratur.
units.tr: Objection 4. Time was eternal, and therefore motion too: for this world was created in time, or at the beginning of time; therefore that existed earlier. Consequently a creature too could likewise have existed from eternity. Answer: motion and time did not exist from eternity; but God, eternal, gave the world a beginning, as he willed, and impressed motion on it, which thereafter continues; and further, time is observed and measured.

units.la: VIII. Quæritur, an mundus potuerit citiùs, aut seriùs creari, quàm creatus est? Resp. Deus ante mundum conditum exstitit solus, ipse sibi sufficientissimus; & mundo principium dedit, à quo deinceps ejus duratio continuatur & æstimatur: Quarè 1. antè principium formaliter, esse non ponitur: creando enim principium dari necesse fuit.
units.tr: VIII. It may be asked whether the world could have been created sooner or later than it was. Answer: before the world was made, God existed alone, wholly sufficient in himself. He gave the world its beginning, from which its duration continues and is measured. Therefore, (1) before the beginning there is not, formally speaking, any before, since the beginning had necessarily to be given by creating.

units.la: 2. Nec per aliquod tempus actuale, vel annos reipsâ lapsos, principium mundi anticipari potuit : nullum enim tempus tunc actû fuit, nulli anni.
units.tr: (2) Nor could the beginning of the world have been brought forward by any actual interval of time or years really elapsed, for no time then existed in act and there were no years.

units.la: 3. Neque ex hypothesi Decreti, potuit mundus citius, aut-serius creari.
units.tr: (3) Nor, on the hypothesis of the Decree, could the world have been created sooner or later.

units.la: 4. Interim in sensû divisò prius esse potuit principium mundi, vel etiam posterius : ut scil. plures, vel pauciores anni, à principio mundi, ad hunc præsentem annum, lapsi fuissent ; siquidem Deo itâ placuisset, Ægyptii, aliique, centena annorum millia modò lapsa finxerunt ; quæquidem SS. Literis plane adversantur: interim per Dei æternitatem, & absolutam potentiam, ista non erant impossibilia. Chronologi tempora sæpius distinguunt annis Periodi Julianæ, ob certiorem horum rationem. Istam vero conficiunt ex Cyclis Solis, Lunæ, & Indictionis; annorum scil. 28, 19, & 15. invicem ductorum: ut exurgat summa 7980. Secundùm quosdam mundus conditus est anno istius Periodi 763. quamvis alii aliter supputent. Sed accipiamus istam hypothesin: Deus tamen, si voluisset, potuisset mundi initium constituere in annum istius periodi 700, vel 100, vel 1. vel aliter omnino.
units.tr: (4) Meanwhile, in a divided sense, the beginning of the world could have been earlier or also later, so that more or fewer years would have passed from the beginning of the world to the present year, had God so willed. The Egyptians and others have imagined hundreds of thousands of years already past, but these plainly contradict the Holy Scriptures; yet by God's eternity and absolute power such things were not impossible. Chronologers often distinguish the times by the years of the Julian Period, for a more certain reckoning. They construct it from the cycles of the Sun, the Moon and the Indiction, namely the years 28, 19 and 15 multiplied together, so that the total is 7980. According to some, the world was created in the year 763 of this period, though others reckon differently. But let us accept this hypothesis: God, if he had willed, could still have set the beginning of the world in the year 700, or 100, or 1, or entirely otherwise.

units.la: IX. Constat ex SS. Literis, Mundum ante Diluvium extitisse annos 1656. & ante Nativitatem Christi in universum circiter 4000.
units.tr: IX. It is established from the Holy Scriptures that the world existed 1656 years before the Flood, and about 4000 years before the birth of Christ in all.

units.la: Qui verò longum ante mundi creationem otium reputant, ii Æternitatem, Sufficientiam, Actus ad intra, Decretum, & Efficientiam Dei non intelligunt.
units.tr: Those, however, who suppose a long leisure before the creation of the world do not understand the eternity, sufficiency, internal acts, decree and efficiency of God.

units.la: Ordo operis istius fuit hujusmodi : Prima dies Cœlos, Terram, Lucemque creavit. Altera distendit Spatium, discrimen Aquarum. Tertia se cernens Undas, dat Gramina campis. Quarta creat Solem, Lunam, fulgentiaque Astra. Quinta tulit Pisces; eadem genus omne Volucrum.
units.tr: The order of this work was as follows: "The first day created the heavens, the earth and light. The second stretched out the space and separated the waters. The third, seeing itself reflected in the waves, gave grasses to the fields. The fourth created the sun, the moon and the shining stars. The fifth brought forth the fishes and every kind of bird."

units.la: Sexta dedit pecudes ;post quas hominem Deus ipse,
units.tr: "The sixth gave the beasts; after these God himself"

units.la: Condidit. Hinc operis Requies, Lux septima sulsit.
units.tr: "formed man. Hence the rest of the work; the seventh light shone."

units.la: Tenenda interim distinctio Creationis in Immediatam, & Mediatam. Immediata per se creatio est ; ex nullâ omnino præjacente materiâ: Ita creati sunt Angeli; Cœlum ac Terra primo die, & Animæ hominum. Mediata facta est ex inhabili materia, quæ tamen priùs ab eodem Creatore immediatè fuerat ex nihilo producta. Itâ creatæ sunt Plantæ, Bestiæ, & Corpora Hominum. Sed Generatio Materiam habilem prærequirit.
units.tr: Meanwhile the distinction of Creation must be kept, into immediate and mediate. Immediate creation is in itself, out of no matter lying beforehand at all; so the angels were created, and the heaven and earth on the first day, and the souls of men. Mediate creation is made from unsuitable matter, which, however, had earlier been produced out of nothing immediately by the same Creator. So were created the plants, the beasts and the bodies of men. But generation requires suitable matter.

units.la: X. Opera primi diei recensentur, Gen.I, 1, -5. Ubi Cœlorum nomine intelligitur primò Cœlum Cœlorum:
units.tr: X. The works of the first day are recounted in Gen. 1:1–5, where by the name of heavens is understood, first, the highest heaven,

units.la: 1 Reg. viii, 27. h. e. supremum ; vel Tertium, alias Paradisus ; 2 Cor. xii, 2, 4. Vulgò Cœlum empyreum; & Beatorum. Singulari ratione dicitur Deus istic esse, vel habitare: Deut. xxvi, 15. Psal. cxv, 3. 16. Matth. vi, 9. & Thronus Ipsius: Ief. lxvi, 1. Domus Patris, in quâ mansiones multæ, ubi Christus suis locum parat: Joh. xiv, 2. ubi electis Regnum paratum est à jacto mundi fundamento: Matth. xxv, 34. ubi sic est nostrum πολίτευμα: Phil. iii, 20. Sicut etiam Angeli faciem Patris ibi semper vident: Matth. xviii, 10. Marc. xii, 25.
units.tr: 1 Kings 8:27, that is, the highest; or the third heaven, otherwise called Paradise, 2 Cor. 12:2, 4; commonly called the empyrean heaven, and the heaven of the blessed. God is said to be there, or to dwell there, in a singular manner: Deut. 26:15; Ps. 115:3, 16; Matt. 6:9; and that is his throne, Isa. 66:1; the house of the Father, in which are many mansions, where Christ prepares a place for his own, John 14:2; where the kingdom is prepared for the elect from the foundation of the world, Matt. 25:34; where our citizenship is, Phil. 3:20. Likewise the angels there always behold the face of the Father, Matt. 18:10; Mark 12:25.

units.la: Sitù autem existit supra omnes cœlos, nunc nobis conspicuos ; Eph. iv, 10. Estque Civitas illa habens fundamenta, cujus artifex & conditor est Deus. Hebr. xi, 10. Ex quibus satis constat, verè creaturam esse; non ipsum Deum: & esse substantiam extensam: atque adeò corpoream: sed finitam; contra Ubiquitistas.
units.tr: It exists, moreover, above all the heavens, which are now visible to us, Eph. 4:10; and it is that city which has foundations, whose architect and builder is God, Heb. 11:10. From these things it is sufficiently clear that it is truly a creature and not God himself; that it is an extended substance, and so corporeal, but finite; against the Ubiquitists.

units.la: Singula quidem istìc spectantia, nondùm plenè ac distinctè cognoscimus; dùm hìc peregrinamur, per fidem ambulantes, non per aspectum: Hebr. xi,9,13.
units.tr: Indeed, we do not yet know fully and distinctly the individual things pertaining to it, while we are pilgrims here, walking by faith and not by sight: Heb. 11:9, 13.

units.la: 2 Cor. v,7. & nondum manifestum est factum quod erimus: 1Joh.iii,2. Interim pie considerari & huc applicari potest visio Prophetica, & allegorica descriptio, Apoc. xxi,10, &c.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:7; and it is not yet manifest what we shall be: 1 John 3:2. Meanwhile the prophetic vision and the allegorical description, Rev. 21:10, etc., may be piously considered and applied here.

units.la: XI. Secundo, metonymice etiam connotari existimamus Angelos, Coeli istius habitatores, & Exercitus: Luc. 2, 13. 1 Reg. xxii, 19. Nehem. ix, 6. tanquam simul à Deo creatos: Gen. II,1. Neh. ix,6. Psal. xxxiii,6. Exod. xx,11. Unde etiam Col. 1,16. Per Eum (Filium) Condita sunt omnia, quae in Coelis sunt, & quae in terra, visibilia, & invisibilia, sive dominia, sive imperia, sive potestates, &c. Rom. xi,36. Omnia sunt e v Eo, &c. Psal. civ,4. Hebr. 1,7. Facit Angelos suos ventos, Ministros suos ignem flammantem. Ubi hic exprimitur Dei Providentia circa Angelos, ut ipsa Creatio supponatur & innuatur simul.
units.tr: XI. Secondly, we think that the angels, the inhabitants of this heaven, and the host are also connoted by metonymy, Luke 2:13; 1 Kings 22:19; Neh. 9:6, as created together with God: Gen. 2:1; Neh. 9:6; Ps. 33:6; Exod. 20:11. Hence also Col. 1:16: "By him (the Son) all things were created, which are in heaven and which are on earth, visible and invisible, whether dominions or thrones or powers," etc. Rom. 11:36: "All things are of him," etc. Ps. 104:4; Heb. 1:7: "He makes his angels winds, his ministers a flaming fire." Here the providence of God concerning the angels is expressed, so that creation itself is presupposed and hinted at at the same time.

units.la: Proprius autem de tempore primordiali colligimus, ex Job.xxxvii,4,-7. Cum fundarem terram, &c. cum canerent simul Stellae matutinae, & vociferati sunt omnes Filii Dei. Non ergo serius creati sunt: esse enim natura saltem prius est, quàm agere. Sed neque ante primum diem, & principium Mosaicum: cum hoc fuerit omnino primum; neque ante ipsum extiterit, nisi Deus in sua aeternitate; contra Arianos & Socinianos: Joh.xvii,5. Eph. 1,4. 1 Petr. 1,20. Psal. xc,2. Prov. viii,22,-.
units.tr: Moreover, we gather more precisely about the primordial time from Job 38:4–7: "When I laid the foundations of the earth," etc., "when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted." Therefore they were not created later, for being is at least by nature prior to acting. But neither were they created before the first day and the Mosaic beginning, since this was altogether the first; nor did they exist before it, except God in his eternity; against the Arians and Socinians: John 17:5; Eph. 1:4; 1 Pet. 1:20; Ps. 90:2; Prov. 8:22ff.

units.la: Obj. Atqui Moses, in describenda historia creationis, non facit specialem Angelorum mentionem. Resp. Nihil mirum; cum etiam plures creaturarum species diserte non recensuerit; ea, quae Ecclesiam militantem propriùs spectant, summatim exponere volens. Parcius de Angelis agitur passim in SS. Literis; quo magis intenti simus rebus nostris, & à superstitionibus earneamus accuratius: Col. II,18.
units.tr: Objection. But Moses, in describing the history of creation, makes no special mention of the angels. Answer: Nothing strange in that, since he did not expressly list several other kinds of creatures either, wishing to set out summarily those things which more closely concern the Church militant. The Scriptures speak sparingly of the angels throughout, so that we may be more intent on our own affairs and more carefully abstain from superstitions: Col. 2:18.

units.la: Fugiendus autem error Sadducaeorum; non esse Resurrectionem mortuorum, neque Angelum, neque Spiritum; Act. xxiii,8. quibus affines sunt Libertini; Angelos nihil aliud esse existimantes, quam cogitationes hominum, sive bonas, sive malas. In SS. Literis occurrunt testimonia satis multa: commemorantur apparitiones, & operationes, tùm in corporibus assumtis, tùm aliæ: speciatim facta circa ipsum Christum; Matth. iv,1,-11. Luc. xxii,43. indicantur præmia, & pœnæ eorum. Accedunt effecta per experientiam observata, quæ neque ad Deum, neque ad causas naturales, neque ad animas separatas referri possunt. Quin & ordo atque concinnitas universi admodùm probabiliter Angelorum existentiam suadet.
units.tr: The error of the Sadducees must be avoided, who said there is no resurrection of the dead, nor angel, nor spirit, Acts 23:8; to whom the Libertines are akin, who think the angels are nothing other than the thoughts of men, whether good or bad. In the Holy Scriptures there occur very many testimonies: appearances and operations are recorded, both in assumed bodies and otherwise, especially those done about Christ himself, Matt. 4:1–11; Luke 22:43; their rewards and punishments are indicated. Added are effects observed through experience, which can be referred neither to God, nor to natural causes, nor to separated souls. Indeed, the order and harmony of the universe very probably suggest the existence of angels.

units.la: XII. Nomina ךְלאָמ, & Ἀγγελος, ab officio defumta: unde etiàm Filius Dei œconomicè Angelus fœderis; Mal. iii,1. Jehovah; Exod. iii, 2,-3. xxiii, 20, 21. & facierum ejus dicitur: Ysf. lxiii,9. Angeli scil. annunciant, & exequuntur; quæcunque Deus mandat: Psal. cxi, 20, 21. Exercitus Cœlestes dicuntur; propter ordinem, potentiam, & promtitudinem: unde etiam Vigiles; Dan. iv,16. Ventis & igni flammanti assimilantur; ob eximium, agile, & valdè petrætrans robur. Stellæ item matutinæ nuncupantur; ob lucem sapientiæ, sanctitatis, & gloriæ; quæ bonis Angelis competit. Unde & Angelorum lucis appellatio, 2 Cor. xi, 14. Dicuntur insuper Filii Dei, quoniam à Deo creati in statu illustri, ad imaginem Ipsius. Throni, Potestates, ob gloriam, & rerum gerendarum magnitudinem, dum Deo ministrant. Profani Scriptores Græci passim Δαίμονας; Latini Genios appellant. Sunt autem Angeli, Substantiæ spirituales, per se completè subsistentes, à Deo secundùm imaginem Suam, singulari quâdam perfectione, ad ministerium Suum, conditæ. XIII. Substantias Spirituales dicimus; ut naturam in iis intellectualem, molis & extensionis corporeæ expertem, denotemus. Hebr. I, 14. Ministratorii spiritus. Matth. x,1. Impuri spiritus; viii, 16. xii, 43. Eph. vi, 12. Confer Luc. xxiv, 39. Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet. Non tamen infinita est eorum essentia; sed à Creatore limitata: nec omninò simplex; sed potentia & actus, substantia item & accidentia, in iis agnoscenda.
units.tr: XII. The names מַלְאָךְ [malʼak] and ἄγγελος [angelos] are taken from the office; whence also the Son of God, economically, is called the "Angel of the covenant," Mal. 3:1; "Jehovah," Exod. 3:2–3; 23:20–21; and is called "the angel of his face," Isa. 63:9. The angels, that is, announce and carry out whatever God commands: Ps. 103:20–21. They are called the heavenly hosts, on account of their order, power and readiness; hence also "watchers," Dan. 4:16. They are compared to winds and to a flaming fire, on account of their extraordinary, nimble and very strong power. They are also called the morning stars, on account of the light of wisdom, holiness and glory which belongs to the good angels. Hence also the title of the angels of light, 2 Cor. 11:14. They are further called sons of God, since they were created by God in an illustrious state, after his own image. Thrones and powers, on account of their glory and the greatness of the affairs they perform while ministering to God. Profane Greek writers everywhere call them δαίμονες [daimones]; the Latins call them genii. Angels are spiritual substances, wholly subsisting in themselves, created by God according to his own image, with a singular perfection, for his ministry. XIII. We call them spiritual substances in order to denote their intellectual nature, free of bulk and corporeal extension: Heb. 1:14, "ministering spirits"; Matt. 10:1, "unclean spirits"; 8:16; 12:43; Eph. 6:12. Compare Luke 24:39: "A spirit does not have flesh and bones." Yet their essence is not infinite, but limited by the Creator; nor is it altogether simple, but in them must be recognised potency and act, substance and accidents as well.

units.la: Intellectu multa cognoscunt. Matth. xvii, 10. Intuentur faciem Patris. 2 Sam. xiv, 20. Sapiens, secundum sapientiam Angeli Dei, ut cognoscat omnia quæ sunt in terra. Confer 1 Tim. iii, 16. 1 Petr. I, 12. Non tamen omnia: ut corda hominum; 1 Reg. viii, 39. diem judicii; Marc. xiii, 32. Confer Apoc. v, 3, 4, 5. Hinc etiam 1 Petr. I, 12. In quæ cupiunt Angeli introspicere. Adde Eph. iii, 10. Cognoscunt autem per species intelligibiles: etiam dianoëticè, per discursum. Confer Marc. xvi, 6. Suscitatus est; non est hic: Ecce locum, &c.
units.tr: They know many things by intellect. Matth. xvii, 10. They behold the face of the Father. 2 Sam. xiv, 20. Wise, according to the wisdom of the Angel of God, so as to know all things that are on the earth. Compare 1 Tim. iii, 16. 1 Pet. i, 12. Yet not all things: such as the hearts of men, 1 Kgs. viii, 39; the day of judgment, Mark xiii, 32. Compare Rev. v, 3, 4, 5. Hence also 1 Pet. i, 12: Into which things the Angels desire to look. Add Eph. iii, 10. They know by intelligible species, and also dianoetically, by discursive reasoning. Compare Mark xvi, 6: He is risen; he is not here. Behold the place, etc.

units.la: Signis suis indicant alii aliis sua cogitata: quæ in specie non determinamus. 1 Cor. xiii, 1. Lingua metaphoricè iis tribuitur.
units.tr: By their signs they indicate their thoughts to one another, which we do not determine in particular. 1 Cor. xiii, 1. The tongue is ascribed to them metaphorically.

units.la: Futura, non nisi ex revelatione, sciunt. Jes. xli, 22, 23. Indicate, quæ eventura sint, ut cognoscamus vos esse Deos, &c. 26. Neque ullus est qui indicet, &c.
units.tr: They know future things only from revelation. Isa. xli, 22, 23: Declare what is to come, that we may know that you are gods, etc. 26: There is none who declares, etc.

units.la: Sic & Libertas dependet à Deo, etiàm quod ad exercitium; & circumscripta est sphæra objectorum suorum.
units.tr: Thus their liberty depends on God, even as to its exercise, and the sphere of their objects is circumscribed.

units.la: XIV. Potentia eorum similiter magna quidem est: Psal. cxiii, 20, 21. Angeli valentissimi robore. 2 Thess. I, 7. Cum Angelis potentibus. Confer Col. I, 16. 2 Reg. xix, 35. Jes. xxxvii, 36. Eph. vi, 11, 12. I. 21. Hebr. I, 14. Finita tamen; ut essentia ipsorum. Hinc Mira quidem, sed non Miracula, facere possunt: Psal. lxxii, 18. Deus facit Mirabilia solus. cxxxvi, 4. Vide etiam Job. v, 20, 21. Job. x, 13, 14. Jes. xxxviii, 17.
units.tr: XIV. Their power is likewise indeed great: Ps. ciii, 20, 21: Angels mighty in strength. 2 Thess. i, 7: With the mighty Angels.
