Compare Col. i, 16; 2 Kgs. xix, 35; Isa. xxxvii, 36; Eph. vi, 11, 12; i, 21; Heb. i, 14. Yet it is finite, as their essence is. Hence they can do wonders indeed, but not miracles: Ps. lxxii, 18: God alone does wonders. cxxxvi, 4. See also Job v, 20, 21; Job x, 13, 14; Isa. xxxviii, 17.

units.la: Affectus analogicè iis tribuuntur: ut Luc. xv, 10; Apoc. xii, 12.
units.tr: Affections are ascribed to them analogically: as in Luke xv, 10; Rev. xii, 12.

units.la: XV. Completa per se subsistentia differunt ab Animabus rationalibus: atque adeò sine corporis adjun &to ἐννπος᾽άτῳ ; quâ ratione ab Hominibus distinguuntur.
units.tr: XV. Being complete substances in themselves, they differ from rational souls; and so they are without an attached body [ἐνσωμάτῳ]; by this they are distinguished from men.

units.la: Corpora igitur ne quidem tenuiora habent ; contra Iudæos, & alios: quanquàm corpora aliquando ad tempus assumserunt: ut Gen. xviii. ut & Filius Dei ibidem ; & Spiritus S. Luc. iii, 22. Cibos interim non ob necessitatem ; sed ad singularem familiaritatem præstandam, sumserunt.
units.tr: Therefore they do not have even finer bodies, against the Jews and others, although they have at times assumed bodies for a time, as in Gen. xviii; and so also the Son of God in the same place, and the Holy Spirit, Luke iii, 22. Meanwhile they took food not out of necessity, but to show a special familiarity.

units.la: Consequenter Generatio iis non convenit : Matth. xxii, 30. In resurrectione neque uxores ducunt, nec nuptum dantur ; sed sunt ut Angeli, &c. Nec corruptio ; quamvis annihilari absolute possent ; istud tamen futurum non est: Matth. xviii, 10. Hebr. xii, 22, 23. Matth. xxv, 41. Iud. 6.
units.tr: Consequently generation does not apply to them: Matt. xxii, 30: In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the Angels, etc. Nor corruption; although they could be annihilated absolutely, yet this will not happen: Matt. xviii, 10; Heb. xii, 22, 23; Matt. xxv, 41; Jude 6.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Locus, laxe dictus, definitive ; atque ita motus localis, Angelis quoque competit. Sic Luc. viii, 30. Legio erat in uno homine. Confer ii, 13. de Motu: qui etiam est successivus, ob Terminorum distantiam : velocissimus tamen ; quia nulla resistentia adest. Unde venti, & ignis flammans ; Psal. civ, 4. Seraphim alati ; Ezech. 1, 6. instar fulguris ; Luc. x, 18.
units.tr: Place, loosely speaking, belongs to them definitively; and thus local motion also pertains to Angels. So Luke viii, 30: There was a legion in one man. Compare ii, 13. Their motion is also successive, on account of the distance of the termini; yet it is most swift, because no resistance is present. Hence winds and flaming fire; Ps. civ, 4; winged Seraphim, Ezek. i, 6; like lightning, Luke x, 18.

units.la: Ævum ratione durationis iis tribuitur ; initium habens, non finem ; attamen cum successione. In ævo præteritum finitum, mensurabile, & divisibile est; suturum vero potentia & syncategorematicè infinitum.
units.tr: Aevum is ascribed to them with respect to duration; having a beginning but no end, yet with succession. In aevum the past is finite, measurable and divisible; the future, however, is infinite in potency and syncategorematically.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Numerus amplissimus ; finitus tamen est: Dan. vii, 10. Millies mille, & myrias myriadum. Apoc. v, 7. Millies centena millia, & decies centena millia. Adde Psal. lxviii, 18. Luc. 2, 13. viii, 30.
units.tr: Their number is very vast, yet finite: Dan. vii, 10: A thousand thousands, and ten thousand times ten thousand. Rev. v, 11: Thousands of thousands, and myriads of myriads. Add Ps. lxviii, 18; Luke ii, 13; viii, 30.

units.la: Quia nusquam apparet specifica Angelorum distinctio, ea temerè à Pontificiis asseritur. Numericam sufficere, ex Animabus rationalibus patet.
units.tr: Since a specific distinction of Angels nowhere appears, the Papists rashly assert it. That a numerical distinction suffices is clear from rational souls.

units.la: Bonorum ordo & concordia est sub Deo, cujus Legati sunt ; & sub Christo, qui est Caput omnis Imperii ac Potestatis; Col. 2, 10. Phil. 2, 9.
units.tr: There is an order and harmony of the good under God, whose legates they are, and under Christ, who is the Head of every Rule and Power; Col. ii, 10; Phil. ii, 9.

units.la: Archangelus alibi appellatur ; & nominatim Michael chaël. Vide Dan. x, 13. 21. xii, 1. Judæ, 9. Apoc. xii, 7. 1Thess. iv, 16. Et princeps militiæ Jehovæ; Josuæ v, 13, 14, 15, vi, 2. sed hic saltem Deus Filius intelligendus.
units.tr: The Archangel is named elsewhere, and by name Michael [Michaël]. See Dan. x, 13, 21; xii, 1; Jude 9; Rev. xii, 7; 1 Thess. iv, 16. And the prince of the host of Jehovah, Josh. v, 13, 14, 15; vi, 2; but here at least the Son of God is to be understood.

units.la: Pontificii distinctè delineant tres classes; & novem chorus; seu ordines: non adeo dissimiles Kabbalistis. Sed temerè ac superstitiosè, absque Scriptura & ratione; imò contra locum Col. 2, 18. Nequis inferat pedem in ea, quæ non vidit, temere inflatus carnis suæ sapientia.
units.tr: The Papists sketch distinctly three classes and nine choirs, or orders, not very unlike the Kabbalists. But this is done rashly and superstitiously, without Scripture and reason; indeed against the passage Col. ii, 18: Let no one enter into those things which he has not seen, rashly puffed up by the wisdom of his flesh.

units.la: Distinctio quidem aliqua datur: saltem ordinis & functionum; Col. 1, 16. Eph. 1, 21. sed quanta & qualis ea sit, nos latet.
units.tr: Some distinction is indeed given, at least of order and functions: Col. i, 16; Eph. i, 21; but how great and of what kind it is, is hidden from us.

units.la: XVIII. Interim satis evidens & necessaria est distri- butio in Bonos & Malos:
units.tr: XVIII. Meanwhile, a distribution into good and bad is sufficiently evident and necessary.

units.la: quanquam omnes Boni creati sunt: Gen. 1, 31. Confer Matth. xix, 17. Jac. 1, 13. 1 Joh. 1, 5. Perperam Judæi dicunt, Diabolos tales creatos esse secundo die; & propterea ipsi speciale approbationem non esse additam: quasi generalis non sufficeret. Sed aliquàm multi à Bonitate suâ defecerunt: Joh. viii. 44, Diabolus in veritate non perstitit. Judæ, 6. Non servârunt suam originem. 2 Petr. 2, 4. 1 Joh. iii, 8. Cum boni, sed labiles, creati essent; interim satis idonei ad perseverandum in genere causarum secundarum, sed & liberi, & sub lege constituti; antecedenter bonitate nulla privati, integritatem suam negligentes, & libertate abutentes, legi repugnantia elegerunt, & fecerunt, Deo permittente ac gubernante: Diabolus mentitur ex suo loquitur; Joh. viii, 44. Primum illius peccatum, quod ad speciem, non determinamus: infidelitatem & superbiam haud abiuisse, interim non dubitamus; potissimum ubi conferimus seductionem & lapsum hominum; Gen. iii. Adversus Malos istos nobis luctæ est: Eph. vi, 12. Joh. viii, 44. 1 Petr. v. 8. Tenenda igitur exhortatio, ibidem vers. 9. Obsistite, firmi per fidem Adde Apoc. xii, 10. Accusator fratrum, &c. Zach. 3, 1. Matth. xvi, 23.
units.tr: Although all the good angels were created (Gen. 1:31; compare Matt. 19:17; Jas. 1:13; 1 John 1:5). The Jews wrongly say that the devils were created such on the second day, and that for this reason no special approval was added to them, as if the general one were not enough. But a good many of them fell from their goodness (John 8:44: the devil did not stand in the truth; Jude 6: they did not keep their origin; 2 Pet. 2:4; 1 John 3:8). Although they were created good, yet liable to fall, and sufficiently fit to persevere in the kind of secondary causes, and also free and placed under the law, they were without any goodness beforehand; neglecting their integrity and abusing their freedom, they chose and did what was opposed to the law, God permitting and governing it. The devil "lies, speaking from his own resources" (John 8:44). We do not determine the specific nature of his first sin; we do not doubt that it was not without unbelief and pride, especially when we compare the seduction and fall of men (Gen. 3). We have a struggle against these evil beings (Eph. 6:12; John 8:44; 1 Pet. 5:8). The exhortation in the same place, verse 9, must therefore be held to: "Resist, firm in faith." Add Rev. 12:10, "the accuser of the brethren," etc.; Zech. 3:1; Matt. 16:23.

units.la: XIX. Boni per gratiam Dei confirmati sunt in æternum sancti & beati. Marc. viii, 38. cum Angelis sanctis. Matth. xviii, 10. Hebr. xii, 22, 23.
units.tr: XIX. The good angels, confirmed by the grace of God, are holy and blessed for ever (Mark 8:38, "with the holy angels"; Matt. 18:10; Heb. 12:22, 23).

units.la: Horum Officia communia ex superioribus patent: Deo scil. inservire, & quidem speciali modo circa electos; annunciare annuncianda; exequi exequenda; & Gloriam Ipsius praedicare. Apparitiones occurrunt variæ: per somnium; Gen. xxviii, 12. Matth. I, 20. Act. xxvii, 23. vel specie visibili assumtâ coram vigilantibus. Luc. I, 11, -26. - ii. 9, - xxiv, 4, 5, 6. Act. I, 10, 11. De obedientia in factis & Dei glorificatione, liquet ex Ps. cxi, 20, 21. Jef. vi, 2, 3. De ministerio salvandorum; Hebr. I, 14. Ps. xxxiv, 8. xc, 11.
units.tr: Their common offices are clear from what has been said above: namely, to serve God, and indeed in a special way with regard to the elect; to announce what is to be announced; to carry out what is to be carried out; and to proclaim his glory. Their appearances occur in various ways: in a dream (Gen. 28:12; Matt. 1:20; Acts 27:23), or in a visible form assumed before those who are awake (Luke 1:11, 26; 2:9; 24:4, 5, 6; Acts 1:10, 11). That they obey in deeds and glorify God is clear from Ps. 103:20, 21 and Isa. 6:2, 3. Concerning their ministry to those to be saved: Heb. 1:14; Ps. 34:8; 91:11.

units.la: Sed de Angelis custodibus, aut tutelaribus singulis singulorum hominum perpetuis, nihil est in S. Scriptura; nedum singulis hominibus binos Angelos esse assignatos, bonum & malum. Imo uni aliquando plurium, alias pluribus unius cura demandata legitur; Gen. xxviii, 12, xxxii, 1, 2. Ps. xxxiv, 8. Hebr. I, 14. 2 Reg. vi, 16, 17. xix, 36. Luc. xvi, 22. Matth. xviii, 10.
units.tr: But concerning guardian angels, or protectors, each one perpetually assigned to each single man, there is nothing in Holy Scripture; much less that two angels, one good and one bad, are assigned to each man. Indeed, we read that sometimes one angel is given charge over several, and at other times several over one (Gen. 28:12; 32:1, 2; Ps. 34:8; Heb. 1:14; 2 Kings 6:16, 17; 19:36; Luke 16:22; Matt. 18:10).

units.la: Postremum hunc locum temere Pontificii in oppositam sententiam trahunt. Nec eos juvat alius Act. xii, 15. cum I. illi, qui istic dicebant, Angelus ejus est; scil. Petri, non fuerint infallibiles, imo etiam actu tunc erraverint: vere enim Petrus erat; non Angelus.
units.tr: The Papists rashly draw this last passage into the opposite opinion. Nor does another passage help them, Acts 12:15, where those who were there said, "It is his angel," namely Peter's. Those people were not infallible; indeed, they were then actually mistaken, for it was truly Peter, not an angel.

units.la: 2. Nec asseruerint, esse perpetuum Petri custodem.
units.tr: 2. Nor do they prove that there is a perpetual guardian of Peter.

units.la: 3. Nec à Petro ad omnes omnino homines, vel etiam quosvis fideles, valeat consequentia.
units.tr: 3. Nor does the inference from Peter to all men, or even to any believers whatever, hold.

units.la: 4. Atque istic non custodia: sed imago; aut species Petri, fuerit spectata, quâ deceptam putabant ancillam.
units.tr: 4. And there, it was not a guardian that was seen but an image or appearance of Peter, by which they thought the maidservant had been deceived.

units.la: Observanda etiam discretio piorum ab impiis, tùm in judiciis particularibus, tum in universali, per Angelos faciendâ: Ezech. ix, 4. Apoc. vii, 3. Marc. xiii, 27. Matth. xiii, 41.
units.tr: The distinction of the pious from the impious, to be made by the angels, is also to be observed, both in particular judgments and in the universal one (Ezek. 9:4; Rev. 7:3; Mark 13:27; Matt. 13:41).

units.la: Unum Nomen, Gabrielis, quod fortitudinem Dei designat; reperitur, Dan. viii, 16. ix, 21. Luc. i, 19, 26.
units.tr: One name, Gabriel, which designates the strength of God, is found in Dan. 8:16; 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26.

units.la: Nec plura inquirenda sunt curiose: Col. 2, 18.
units.tr: Nor are more things to be inquired into curiously (Col. 2:18).

units.la: Ad Honorem potissimum pertinet, ut excellentiam & virtutes illorum, utpote sapientiam, sanctitatem; & obsequii erga Deum promtitudinem, recte æstimemus; & pro virili nostra imitemur: Matth. VI, 10. ut eos frequenter conscios & testes eorum, quæ in Ecclesia geruntur, agnoscamus; atque inde etiam magis ad officia nostra impellamur: 1 Tim. v, 21. 1 Cor. XI, 10. Si autem apparitio, vel conversatio aliqua eorum nobiscum daretur (quæ ubi fuit, extraordinaria & rara fuit,) ratione excellentiæ supra homines quidem non tamen religiose, honorandi forent: Col. 2, 18. Nemo adversum vos sibi sumat rectoris partes, in submissione animi & religioso cultu Angelorum: contra Angelicos, & Pontificios. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 74.
units.tr: It pertains chiefly to honour that we rightly esteem their excellence and virtues, such as their wisdom and holiness, and their readiness of obedience toward God; and that we imitate them to the best of our ability (Matt. 6:10); and that we acknowledge them as frequently aware of, and witnesses to, what is done in the Church; and that we are thereby impelled all the more to our duties (1 Tim. 5:21; 1 Cor. 11:10). But if some appearance or conversation of theirs with us were granted (which, where it has occurred, has been extraordinary and rare), they would indeed be honoured because of their excellence above men, but not religiously: Col. 2:18, "Let no one take upon himself the role of judge against you, in humility of mind and religious worship of angels." This is against the Angelici and the Papists. Compare above, chap. 4, th. 74.

units.la: XX. Mali Angeli, Deo permittente, possunt Homines ratione corporis & status externi, terrere, localiter movere, cruciare, obsidere, interficere. Vide 1 Sam. XXVIII, 12. Job. 1, 11, -19. II, 6, 7. Matth. VIII, 28, 31, 32: XII, 22. XVII, 15, 18.
units.tr: XX. Evil angels, God permitting, can terrify men with respect to their body and external condition, move them from place to place, torment them, besiege them, and kill them. See 1 Sam. 28:12; Job 1:11, 19; 2:6, 7; Matt. 8:28, 31, 32; 12:22; 17:15, 18.

units.la: Spectra sunt Diaboli specie externa, potissimum visibili, apparentes; ut Homines ludant, fallant, terreant. Confer Matth. XIV, 26. Luc. XXIV, 37. ubi etiam Angelos lucis mentiri possunt: 2 Cor. XI, 14. & Homines mortuos: vel absentes: 1 Sam. XVIII, 12. quomodo plurimæ fraudes sub Papatu factæ, superstitiones inductæ, &c. de Purgatorio, Missa, &c. Hominibus etiam frequenter Spectra ad imitationem Diaboli mentientibus. Negligebant enim monitum. Jef. VIII, 19. 20. Cum dixerint, Quærite a Pythonibus. - Nonne populus Deum suum requiret? pro vivis mortuos? Ad Legem & Contestationem, &c. Confer 2 Thess. 2, 9, -12. Huc etiam referenda sunt oracula, murmura Diabolica, &c. inter Gentes, &c. Cruciatus & morbos inferre possunt, partes convellendo, distorquendo, activa passivis applicando, &c.
units.tr: Apparitions are devils appearing in an external form, chiefly a visible one, in order to mock, deceive and terrify men. Compare Matt. 14:26; Luke 24:37, where they can also pretend to be angels of light (2 Cor. 11:14), and dead men or absent ones (1 Sam. 28:12). In this way very many frauds were practised under the Papacy and superstitions were introduced, concerning Purgatory, the Mass, etc. Apparitions also frequently occur to men, with the devil lying in imitation, for they neglected the warning: Isa. 8:19, 20, "When they say, Seek of the mediums and of the wizards... Should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead? To the law and to the testimony," etc. Compare 2 Thess. 2:9–12. To this also must be referred oracles, diabolical murmurings, etc., among the Gentiles. They can inflict torments and diseases by convulsing and distorting the parts, applying active things to passive ones, etc.

units.la: Corpus
units.tr: Body

units.la: Corporalis Obsessio fit, per corporis occupationem, & operationem in eo, ut à Spiritu illo impuro, tanquàm forma assistente, homo intùs miserè afficiatur, agitetur, rapiatur. Pontificii istis malis superstitiosè opponunt suos Exorcismos; quibus Diaboli non cedunt, nisi per collusionem.
units.tr: Bodily obsession happens through the occupation of the body and the operation of the unclean spirit in it, so that, as if the spirit were present as its form, the man is wretchedly afflicted, agitated and seized within. The Papists superstitiously oppose these evils with their exorcisms, to which the devils do not yield except by collusion.

units.la: Respectu Animæ actiones Diabolorum tantùm sunt objectivæ & morales, tentando, alliciendo, &c. Vide Matth. iv, 1, 3. 6, 8, 9. 1 Chron. xxi, 1. 1 Sam. xvi, 14. Item Rom. 1, 28. Eph. 2, 2. 2 Cor. iv, 4. 2 Thess. II, 11.
units.tr: With respect to the soul, the actions of the devils are only objective and moral, by tempting, enticing, etc. See Matt. 4:1, 3, 6, 8, 9; 1 Chron. 21:1; 1 Sam. 16:14; likewise Rom. 1:28; Eph. 2:2; 2 Cor. 4:4; 2 Thess. 2:11.

units.la: Unus καθ' ἐξοχὴν Diabolus, Satanas, Draco, & Beelzebub appellatur, cui Angeli sui tribuuntur; Matth. xxv, 41. Apoc. xii, 9. xx, 2. Matth. ix, 34. xii, 24, 26. 27. Confer 2 Reg. I, 2, 3, 6, 16. & 1 Cor. x, 10. Deus hujus sæculi vocatur, 2 Cor. iv, 4. Nec amplius quicquam inquirimus, nisi quomodo nobis à profundis ejus caveamus: Apoc. II, 24.
units.tr: One devil, par excellence, is called Devil, Satan, Dragon and Beelzebub, to whom his angels are attributed (Matt. 25:41; Rev. 12:9; 20:2; Matt. 9:34; 12:24, 26, 27). Compare 2 Kings 1:2, 3, 6, 16; and 1 Cor. 10:10. He is called "the god of this age" (2 Cor. 4:4). We inquire no further than how to guard ourselves against his depths (Rev. 2:24).

units.la: XXI. Tertiò etiam significari putamus substantiam corpoream tenuem, à supremo cœlo deorsum extensam. Æther enim Cœli nomine appellatur. Gen. 1, 15, 17. xv, 5. Psal. xix, 2, 5. Matth. xxiv, 29. Eph. iv, 10. Atque item Aër, Gen. vii, 11. Matth. vi, 26, xxiv, 30.
units.tr: XXI. Thirdly, we also think that a thin corporeal substance is signified, extended downward from the highest heaven. For the ether is called by the name of heaven (Gen. 1:15, 17; 15:5; Ps. 19:2, 5; Matt. 24:29; Eph. 4:10). Likewise the air (Gen. 7:11; Matt. 6:26; 24:30).

units.la: Unde totus Mundus in Cœlos & Terram passim dispescitur; nisi quod huic Mare interdum adjungatur: Gen. 2, 1, 4. xiv, 19, 22. xxiv, 3. Exod. xx, 11. xxxi, 17. Deut. iii, 24. 2 Chron. 2, 12. Esr. v, 11. Psal. lxix, 35. cxv, 15, 16. cxxi, 2. Matth. xxviii, 18. Act. iv, 24, xiv, 15, xvii, 24. 1 Cor. viii, 6. Nec ulla ratio apparet, cur plurale הַיָּם hic restringendum esset. Imò contra non videtur admittendum, fuisse tunc vacuum inter Cœlum supremum & hunc Globum terrestrem: cum etiam paulo post, lux fuerit producta, & hic globus ea colluitratus.
units.tr: Hence the whole world is everywhere divided into heavens and earth, except that the sea is sometimes added to these (Gen. 2:1, 4; 14:19, 22; 24:3; Exod. 20:11; 31:17; Deut. 3:24; 2 Chron. 2:12; Ezra 5:11; Ps. 69:35; 115:15, 16; 121:2; Matt. 28:18; Acts 4:24; 14:15; 17:24; 1 Cor. 8:6). Nor does any reason appear why the plural hayyam should be restricted here. On the contrary, it does not seem to be admitted that there was then a void between the highest heaven and this terrestrial globe, since light was also produced shortly afterwards and this globe was illuminated by it.

units.la: XXII. Succedit Terra, satis distincta à Cœlis; corpus crassum, opacum, grave; sed primum aquis circumfusa & permixta; unde Abyssi, & Aquarum
units.tr: XXII. The earth follows, quite distinct from the heavens: a thick, opaque, heavy body, but at first surrounded and mixed with water, whence the mention of the Abyss and of the Waters.

units.la: mentio: Gen.1,2. Illa vox profunditatem designat; haec naturam. Terrae, ut est Gen. I, 2. initio competebat Deformitas & inanitas. Et tenebrae erant in superficie Abyssi: & Spiritus Dei motabat super facies Aquarum: cum scil. nondum agerent causae secundae: ut Deut. xxxii,11. Aquila super Pullos suos motitabit se. Quod male à Socinianis ad Ventum, vel Angelum aliquem creatum, detorquetur: cum Creatio soli Deo competat.
units.tr: mention: Gen. 1,2. That word denotes the depth; this one denotes the nature. Of the earth, as in Gen. 1,2, deformity and emptiness belonged to it at the beginning. "And darkness was upon the face of the Abyss, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the Waters," since secondary causes did not yet act. Compare Deut. xxxii, 11: "As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young." This is wrongly twisted by the Socinians to mean the wind or some created angel, since creation belongs to God alone.

units.la: Nec cum Pontificiis indè elicienda Efficacia spiritualis aquae ad abluenda in Baptismo peccata hominum ex opere operato: quoniam Baptismus tantum sacramentalem, sive moralem vim habet sub N. T. non realem: sic enim corpus in spiritum agere non potest: nedum jam ante lapsum, ipsosque homines, istiusmodi Virtus omnibus aquis communicata censeri debeat.
units.tr: Nor, with the Papists, is the spiritual efficacy of water for washing away men's sins in Baptism to be drawn from this, ex opere operato. For Baptism under the New Testament has only a sacramental or moral force, not a real one; a body cannot thus act upon spirit. Much less, even before the Fall, should such a power be thought to have been imparted to all waters, and to men themselves.

units.la: XXIII. Aliud adhuc opus est hujus diei: scil. verf. 3. Dixit Deus; Esto Lux. Rom. iv,17. Vocans, quae non sunt, tanquam sint. 2 Cor. iv,6. Dixit, ut è Tenebris Lux splendesceret. Lux autem est Patibilis qualitas, subjectum suum sic actû perficiens, ut ipsum Radiis diffusis per se videri aptum sit, medium pellucidum illuminet, & objecta opaca reddat conspicua. Accidens illud Deus in Subjecto produxit; contra Pontificios: cum Accidentium esse sit inesse: idque in Hemisphaerio Aetheris. Sic enim divisit Deus inter Lucem ac Tenebras: & Lucem vocavit Diem: Tenebras vero Noctem. verf. 4,5.
units.tr: XXIII. Another work of this day remains, namely verse 3: "God said, Let there be light." Rom. iv, 17: "calling those things which be not as though they were." 2 Cor. iv, 6: "He said that light should shine out of darkness." Light is a passible quality, perfecting its subject in act in such a way that, by its diffused rays, it is fitted to be seen itself, illuminates the transparent medium, and makes opaque objects visible. God produced that accident in a subject, against the Papists, since it belongs to accidents to inhere; and this in the hemisphere of the aether. For thus God divided between light and darkness, and called the light Day, the darkness Night. vv. 4, 5.

units.la: XXIV. Consequenter. 1. Non fuit primo creatum Chaos, omnis formae ac distinctionis essentialis expers.
units.tr: XXIV. Consequently: (1) Chaos was not created first, devoid of all form and essential distinction.

units.la: Neque 2. ex fortuito concursu & complexu Atomorum coaluit Mundus.
units.tr: Nor (2) did the world coalesce from the chance concourse and combination of atoms.

units.la: Neque 3. Initio Materia communis facta est, quieta & solidissima; mox in particulas diversissimas divisa; unde porro extiterit triplex Materia, Subtilis, Coelestis & Terrestris.
units.tr: Nor (3) was common matter made at the beginning, quiet and most solid, and soon divided into most diverse particles, whence there then arose a threefold matter: subtle, celestial and terrestrial.

units.la: Nec 4. Terra primo Sidus fuit; & tandem Maculis obducta: qualis est quorundam inanis Philosophia.
units.tr: Nor (4) was the earth first a star, and at last covered with spots, as some empty philosophy holds.

units.la: XXV. Infernum existimamus in eodem globo tunc etiam creatum : est autem locus à supremo Cœlo remotissimus ; peccatis, ubi commissa forent, justè puniendis à Deo destinatus. Act. I, 24. De Judâ proditore : Ut abiret in locum suum. Adde Luc. xvi, 26. In hoc Carcere nunc sunt Spiritûs hominum impiorum: 1 Petr. iii, 19, 20. Confer Ps.lxiii, 10. & Mali Angeli in tartarum detrusi, & catenis caliginis traditi : 2 Pet.2. 4. Quam amplus, & ubi definitè sit non determinamus : saltem sufficit capiendis spiritibus damnatis ; atque ut post judicium extremum sufficiat capiendis hominibus damnatis cum ipsorum corporibus, Dominus sine dubio providebit. Vide 2 Petr. 3, 10, 11. Ioh. v. 29. Matth. 25, 41.
units.tr: XXV. We hold that Hell was also created at that time in the same globe. It is the place most remote from the highest heaven, appointed by God for sins, to be justly punished where they were committed. Acts I, 24, of Judas the traitor: "That he might go to his own place." Add Luke xvi, 26. In this prison the spirits of wicked men are now held: 1 Pet. iii, 19, 20. Compare Ps. lxiii, 10. And bad angels thrust down into Tartarus, and delivered into chains of darkness: 2 Pet. 2, 4. How large it is and where exactly it is we do not determine. At least it suffices to hold the condemned spirits; and that after the final judgment it will suffice to hold the condemned men with their bodies, the Lord will without doubt provide. See 2 Pet. 3, 10, 11. John v, 29. Matt. 25, 41.

units.la: XXVI. Secundo die conditum est Expansum : Gen. I, 6, 7, 8. Aër scil. in tres Regiones distinctus. Deus fecit, ut per calorem Nubes eveherentur, & constituerentur in sublimi ; in media aëris regione : Ps. civ, 3. Disponit densas nubes, &c. Jer. x, 13. Iob. 22. 8. Non supra universum Aërem ; nedùm Ætherem. Eâdem operâ Meteora facta sunt. Ps. cxlvii, 8. qui obtegit Cœlos densis Nubibus, qui comparat terræ Pluviam. 16, 17, 18. Edit Pruinam ; dejicit Gelu ; - efflat Ventum, &c. Ier. x, 13. Fulgura cum Pluvia facit, &c. Etiàm Iris ; quamvis postea ratio signi accesserit : Gen. ix, 9, - 17.
units.tr: XXVI. On the second day the expanse was made: Gen. 1, 6, 7, 8. The air, namely, was divided into three regions. God made it so that clouds might be lifted up by heat and set on high, in the middle region of the air: Ps. civ, 3, "He disposes the dense clouds," etc. Jer. x, 13. Job 22, 8. Not above the whole air, much less the aether. By the same work the meteors were made. Ps. cxlvii, 8: "who covers the heavens with dense clouds, who prepares rain for the earth." Verses 16, 17, 18: "He gives forth hoarfrost; casts down ice; sends forth the wind," etc. Jer. x, 13: "He makes lightnings with rain," etc. Also the rainbow, though the sign's meaning came later: Gen. ix, 9–17.

units.la: Huic operi non statim subjicitur specialis Approbatio; sed sequitur generalis, v. 31. Quin & eodem pertinent quæ sequuntur, v. 10. & 22. & 28. Ps. civ, 10, - 16. Vanæ autem sunt conjecturæ, Numerum Binarium esse infamem, & mali ominis; in Matrimonio scil. vel Infernum & Diabolos tunc creatos esse ; quod Kabbalistæ volunt.
units.tr: This work is not immediately followed by a specific approval, but by a general one, v. 31. Indeed, what follows also pertains to it: vv. 10, 22, 28; Ps. civ, 10–16. Vain, however, are the conjectures that the number two is infamous and of ill omen, in marriage especially, or that hell and devils were then created, as the Kabbalists maintain.

units.la: XXVII. Tertio die Aquæ reliquæ inferiores segregatæ sunt : ut emineret Terra ; ad quam Continens, Insulæ, & Peninsulæ pertinent : suis autem excavatis receptaculis continerentur Mare, Flumina & Fontes ; Gen. 1, 9, 10. Psal. xxiv, 2. Super Maria fun-
units.tr: XXVII. On the third day the remaining lower waters were separated so that Earth might rise up. To it belong the continent, islands, and peninsulas. The sea, rivers and springs were contained in their excavated receptacles: Gen. 1, 9, 10. Psal. xxiv, 2: "Upon the seas he has found-"

units.la: davis davit illam (terram), & super Flumina stabilivit illam, Civ; 5,-10. Fundavit terram super bases ejus, &c.
units.tr: ed it (the earth), "and established it upon the rivers," Ps. civ, 5–10: "He founded the earth upon its bases," etc.

units.la: Mare, admixtis ejusmodi particulis terrestribus, sal-sum est. Dulcescunt autem Aqua percolatione; ut in Fontibus: vel eductione: ut in Pluvia. Varie movetur: etiam æstu, præcipue mirabili, qui motui Lunari fere respondet.
units.tr: The sea, with such earthy particles mixed in, is salt. Waters are sweetened by percolation, as in springs, or by being drawn up, as in rain. They are variously moved, also by the tide, especially remarkable, which nearly corresponds to the motion of the moon.

units.la: XXVIII. Ex Terra adhuc humida, accedentibus etiam particulis Aëreis, & Æthereis, vel Igneis, fastas arbitramur partes Salsas, Sulphureas, & Mercurialis: ac porro Metalla, aliaque Mineralia; Itemque Ignes & Fiatus subterraneos: unde aliquando Terræ Motus: nec non Fontium & Fluviorum aquæ calidæ, acidæ, &c.
units.tr: XXVIII. From the earth still moist, with aerial, aethereal or fiery particles also coming in, we judge that saline, sulphureous, and mercurial parts were derived, and further metals and other minerals; likewise fires and subterranean blasts, whence sometimes earthquakes; and also the hot and acid waters of springs and rivers, etc.

units.la: In superficie autem produxit Deus corpora vegetabilia; Gen. I, 11, 12, 13. Herbas, Frutices, Arbores, quæ singula per Nutritionem: species autem, per Seminalem generationem conservantur. Perfectio illa dicitur Vita vegetativa. Forma substantialis in iis est Anima vegetativa. Ad opera hujus diei referenda etiam sunt Plantæ, animalia: & quæ Sponte orta nuncupantur.
units.tr: On the surface, however, God produced vegetable bodies: Gen. 1, 11, 12, 13: herbs, shrubs, trees, each preserved individually by nutrition, while the species are preserved by seminal generation. That perfection is called vegetative life. The substantial form in these is the vegetative soul. To the works of this day are also to be referred plants, animals, and what are called spontaneously arising.

units.la: XXIX. Quarto die facta sunt in expanso Ætheris Luminaria: Gen. I, 14, -19, sic dicta, quod illuminent super terram. Duo magna, Sol & Luna, ac reliquæ Stellæ: tum Erraticæ, seu Planetæ, ob motus vicissitudines sic appellatæ; tum Fixæ, sine tali ac tanta variatione: & quidem numero innumerabiles. Gen. xv, 5. Si poteris numerare stellas. Adde Jes. xl, 26. Ier. xxxi ii, 22.
units.tr: XXIX. "On the fourth day the lights were made in the expanse of the aether," Gen. 1, 14–19, so called because they shine upon the earth. The two great ones, Sun and Moon, and the remaining stars: the wandering, or planets, so called from the changes of their motion; and the fixed, without such variation; and indeed innumerable in number. Gen. xv, 5: "If thou canst number the stars." Add Isa. xl, 26; Jer. xxxiii, 22.

units.la: Usus omnium storum communis est, Illuminare; specialis Tempora distinguere: quod præcipue Solis & Lunæ officium est. Ille circumvolutione diurna Dies & Noctes efficit: Hæc vicissitudine sua Menses & Hebdomadas fere discernit. Sol iterum motu suo per Zodiacum annum, absolvit; ejusque Tempestates, secundùm Æquinoctia, & Solstitia, distinguit.
units.tr: The use of all of them is common, to give light; their special use is to distinguish times, which is chiefly the office of Sun and Moon. The former by its daily revolution makes days and nights; the latter by its changes nearly marks off months and weeks. The Sun again, by its motion through the zodiac, completes the year, and distinguishes its seasons by the equinoxes and solstices.

units.la: XXX. Motus Cœli stelliferi non fit ab Angelis; sed a Creatore initio impressus, sic deinceps continuatur: Psal. xix, 2, -7. Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, &c. Sol est tanquam Sponsus prodiens è thalamo suo : lætatur decursurus viam, &c. Job. ix, 7. Observanda interim Miracula, Jos. x, 13, 14. & Ief. xxxviii, 7. Pro vario hujus motû variæ sunt influentiæ ; speciatim ratione tempestatum anni: sic tamen, ut effecta subjaceant Arbitrio & Providentiæ Dei: Hos. 2, 21, 22. Dictum Iehovæ ; exaudiam Cœlos; & ipsi exaudient Terram; & Terra exaudiet frumentum, &c. Levit. xxvi, 19. Reddam Cœlum ut ferrum ; & terram , ut æs. Adde Gen. viii, 22. Psal. lxv, 10. Jud. v, 20.
units.tr: XXX. The motion of the starry heaven is not effected by angels, but was impressed at the beginning by the Creator and is thus continued thereafter: Ps. xix, 2–7: "The heavens declare the glory of God," etc. "The sun is as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber; he rejoices to run his course," etc. Job ix, 7. Meanwhile the miracles are to be observed, Josh. x, 13, 14, and Isa. xxxviii, 7. The influences vary with the variation of this motion, specially in respect of the seasons of the year; yet so that the effects are subject to the will and providence of God: Hos. ii, 21, 22: "The word of Jehovah: I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth; and the earth shall hear the corn," etc. Lev. xxvi, 19: "I will make your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass." Add Gen. viii, 22; Ps. lxv, 10; Judg. v, 20.

units.la: Vanæ autem sunt Astrologicæ prædictiones Gentilium: Deut. xviii, 10. Nam 1. Deo proprium est, Corda scrutari, & dirigere. 2. Immateriales operationes ad materiales causas referri non debent. 3. Non omnes effectus naturales indè certò prædici possunt, quantò minùs liberi.
units.tr: Vain, however, are the astrological predictions of the Gentiles: Deut. xviii, 10. For (1) it is proper to God alone to search and direct hearts. (2) Immaterial operations ought not to be referred to material causes. (3) Not all natural effects can thence be predicted with certainty, much less free ones.

units.la: Piè & prudenter tamen de Signis extraordinariis, Cometis, & similibus, judicandum est. Joël. 2, 29, 30. Act. 2, 19, 20. Edam ostenta in Cœlis, &c. collatâ experientiâ omnium sæculorum, & observatione prudentum.
units.tr: Yet signs that are extraordinary, such as comets and the like, ought to be judged both piously and prudently: Joel 2:29, 30; Acts 2:19, 20, "I will show wonders in the heavens," etc., with the experience of all ages and the observation of wise men taken together.

units.la: XXXI. Ex Doctrinâ Spiritûs Sancti.
units.tr: XXXI. From the Doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 1. Agnoscendum est tale Systema Mundi, ut Terra non sit, nec unquàm fuerit, Sidus ; sed cum Aquis inserioribus quàm maximè distincta sit à Cœlis & Expanso: Sol verò, & Luna, reliquæque Stellæ, dispositæ in Expanso, ad afferendum lucem super Terram, &c. Gen. I, 1, 2; 6, -9; 14, -18.
units.tr: 1. It must be acknowledged that the system of the world is such that the Earth is not, and never was, a star; but that it is most distinctly separated from the heavens and the firmament, and from the lower waters; whereas the Sun, the Moon, and the remaining stars are set in the firmament to give light upon the Earth, etc. Gen. 1:1, 2; 6–9; 14–18.

units.la: 2. Globum Terræ non moveri ; sed quiescere, & stabilem esse; atque istâ ratione distingui ab Aquis, Aëre, Sole, &c. Psal. xciii, 1. Etiam firmavit orbem, ne se moveat. 3. Elevaverunt Flumina fluctus suos. Eccl. 1, 4, 7, Generatio (una) labitur, & (altera) generatio advenit: Terra autem in sæculum stat. Oritur Sol, & occidit Sol. Subinde circumeundo pergit ventus, & ad circuitus suos revertitur ventus. Omnia Flumina pergunt ad Mare. ad locum unde pergunt Flumina, illuc revertuntur in (rursus) redeant, &c.
units.tr: 2. The globe of the earth does not move but rests and is stable, and on this ground it is distinguished from the waters, the air, the sun, etc. Ps. 93:1: He has also established the world, that it should not be moved. 3. The floods have lifted up their waves. Eccl. 1:4, 7: One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth abides for ever. The sun rises, and the sun sets. The wind goes toward the south, and turns about to the north; the wind continually whirls about, and returns again to its circuits. All the rivers run into the sea; to the place from which the rivers come, thither they return again, etc.

units.la: 3. Solem moveri; & quidem celeriter; ex naturali inclinatione, & admodum ordinatè: Eccl. I,5,6. Oritur Sol, & occidit Sol; & ad locum suum regreditur, ubi oritur. Vadit ad Meridiem, & circuit ad Aquilonem. Psal. XIX,6,7. Et ipse tanquam Sponsus egrediens de thalamo suo, gaudet ut potens, ad currendum viam. Ab extremo coelorum egressio ejus; & revolutio ejus usque ad extremo eorum.
units.tr: 3. The Sun moves, and indeed swiftly, by its natural inclination and in a very orderly way. Eccl. 1:5, 6: The sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place where it rises. It goes toward the south, and circles to the north. Ps. 19:6, 7: And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoices as a strong man to run the course. His going forth is from the end of the heavens, and his circuit unto the ends of them.

units.la: 4. Unde etiam ad Potentiam Dei extraordinariam, atque inter Miracula refertur inhibitio istius Motus, sive Statio Solis; similiter ut Lunæ & Stellarum: Jos. x, 12,13. Job. IX,7.
units.tr: 4. Hence also the restraining of this motion, that is, the standing still of the Sun, is referred to the extraordinary power of God and counted among the miracles; and likewise that of the Moon and the stars: Josh. 10:12, 13; Job 9:7.

units.la: XXXII. Exc. Phrases istæ accipiendæ sunt meta- phorice, aut metonymice: ut in illo Poëtæ; Provehi- mur portû, terræque urbesque recedunt.
units.tr: XXXII. Or, these phrases are to be taken metaphorically or metonymically, as in that line of the poet: "We are carried out of the harbour, and lands and cities recede."

units.la: Sic ut etiam Act. XXVII, 27. Nautæ dicuntur circa medium noctis suspicati, appropinquare sibi aliquam regionem. Resp. Non agitur nunc de vocula aliquâ, aut phrasi simplici; sed de enunciationibus integris, iisque variis, sic constanter à Spiritu Sancto adhibitis in enarratione & celebratione istorum operum Dei. 2. In exemplo Poëtico, priori membro motus navigantium proprie exprimitur: posteriori autem, quod vel exinde patet, remotior telluris & urbium distantia metonymice indicatur. 3. Similiter appropinquare Act. XXVII, 27. notat propinquiorem adesse; sed verum navigantium motum docet integer contextus.
units.tr: So also Acts 27:27, where the sailors are said, about midnight, to suspect that some region was drawing near to them. Answer: the question is not now about some single word or simple phrase, but about whole statements, and these various ones, which the Holy Spirit thus consistently uses in narrating and celebrating these works of God. (2) In the poetic example, the motion of the sailors is expressed properly in the first clause; in the second, the greater distance of the land and the cities, which is clear enough from this very fact, is indicated metonymically. (3) Likewise "drawing near" in Acts 27:27 signifies that a nearer land was at hand; but the true motion of the sailors is taught by the whole context.

units.la: Obj. 1. Tanta Solis & Stellarum fixarum velocitas non est conceptibilis. Resp. 1. Velocitas illa non est momentanea, sed alicujus temporis: ac proinde nequaquam repugnat omnipotentiæ Dei, vel naturæ corporum istorum cœlestium.
units.tr: Objection 1. So great a swiftness of the Sun and the fixed stars is not conceivable. Answer 1. That swiftness is not momentary but occupies some time, and therefore in no way contradicts the omnipotence of God or the nature of those heavenly bodies.

units.la: Obj. 2. Opposita sententia longe facilius explicari potest, atque omnia phænomena per eam expediri. Resp. Nostri conceptus, & facilior fortassis explicatio. tio, non est norma consilii atque operum Dei ; cujus cognitiones & vitæ non sunt ut nostræ: Ief. lv, 8.
units.tr: Objection 2. The opposite opinion can be explained far more easily, and all the phenomena can be dealt with by it. Answer: Our conceptions and perhaps easier explanation are not the rule of the counsel and works of God, whose thoughts and ways are not as ours: Isa. 55:8.

units.la: XXXIII. Sequentibus diebus Animalia facta sunt. In Irrationalium natura indagandâ præter Corpus mirabiliter conformatum & articulatum, occurrit Forma. Anima sensitiva: unde est Vita sensitiva, quæ Vegetativam supponit ; cujus tamen operationes hic nobiliores sunt.
units.tr: XXXIII. On the following days animals were made. In investigating the nature of irrational creatures, besides a body wonderfully formed and articulated, there appears a form, the sensitive soul; whence comes sensitive life, which presupposes vegetative life, though its operations here are more noble.

units.la: Sensus est facultas vitalis organica, quâ animal aptum natum est objecta corporea per idoneas species percipere & cognoscere.
units.tr: Sense is an organic vital faculty by which an animal, naturally fitted for it, is able to perceive and know corporeal objects through suitable species.

units.la: Ratione organorum Sensûs alii sunt externi ; ut Visus, Auditus, &c. alii interni ; ut Phantasia, Memoria, &c. Horum sedes est Cerebrum, officina Spirituum animalium ; qui functionibus animalibus inserviunt.
units.tr: With respect to the organs of sense, some are external, such as sight, hearing, etc.; others are internal, such as imagination, memory, etc. The seat of these is the brain, the workshop of the animal spirits, which serve the animal functions.

units.la: Sensum sequitur Appetitus sensitivus ; quo Animal in objectum sibi conveniens ; sensû perceptum & cognitum, fertur desiderando ; adversum vero fugit : ac porrò Facultas loco-motiva ; quâ Animal se totum, aut partes aliquas sui corporis, convenienter isti appetitui, de loco in locum transferre aptum natum est.
units.tr: Sense is followed by sensitive appetite, by which the animal, having perceived and known through sense an object suited to itself, is carried toward it in desire, and flees from what is adverse. Then comes the locomotive faculty, by which the animal is naturally fitted to transfer itself, or some parts of its body, from place to place in accordance with that appetite.

units.la: Ab hoc motû diversus est motus succi alimentarii ; ut & motus naturalis Cordis.
units.tr: Different from this motion is the motion of the nutritive juice, as also the natural motion of the heart.

units.la: Ità Gen.I,20. Reptificent Aquæ reptile Animæ viventis. 24. Producat Terra Animam viventem. Adde vi, 17. vii, 21, 22, 23. Lev.xvii, 14. Item Eccles. iii, 20, 21, Spiritus jumenti descendit deorsum ad terram. Prov.xii,10. Cognoscit justus Animam jumenti sui. Rationis interim expertes sunt Bestiæ: unde Judæ, 10. Ἀλόγα ζῷα. Ps. xxxii,9. Equus & Mulus expertes intelligentiæ. Job.39, 19, 20. Materialis tamen perceptio & cognitio iis concedenda est: Jef. I, 3. Agnoscit Bos possessorem, &c. Jerem. viii, 7. Ciconia novit statatempora sua: Turtur, Grus, & Hirundo observant, &c. Prov. vi, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: So Gen. 1:20, "Let the waters bring forth the moving creature that hath life"; v. 24, "Let the earth bring forth the living creature." Add Gen. 6:17; 7:21, 22, 23; Lev. 17:14. Likewise Eccl. 3:20, 21, "The spirit of the beast goeth downward to the earth"; Prov. 12:10, "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." Meanwhile, beasts are devoid of reason: hence Jude 10, "natural brute beasts" [ἄλογα ζῷα]. Ps. 32:9, "The horse and the mule have no understanding." Job 39:19, 20. Yet material perception and cognition are to be granted to them: Isa. 1:3, "The ox knoweth his owner," etc.; Jer. 8:7, "The stork knoweth her appointed times; the turtle, the crane, and the swallow observe the time of their coming," etc.; Prov. 6:6, 7, 8.

units.la: XXXIV. Quinto igitur die conditæ sunt Aves, & Pisces ; Gen. I, 20.-23. Sexto autem Terrestres Bestiae; & Homines: verf.24,25.
units.tr: XXXIV. Therefore on the fifth day the birds and the fishes were created, Gen. 1:20–23; but on the sixth day the land animals and man: vv. 24, 25.

units.la: Amphibia ex conditione praedominante aestimanda sunt.
units.tr: Amphibians are to be classed according to the predominant condition.

units.la: Homo ( Mundi hujus compendium ) est Animal rationale, ad imaginem Dei conditum. Occurrunt hic partes essentiales; Corpus sapientissimè conformatum, & Anima rationalis: atque item insignis perfectio Imaginis Divinae. Primi Homines fuerunt Adamus & Eva: Ille Pater; haec mater omnium viventium: Gen. 111,20. de una carne, & uno osse: 11, 23. Ille hujus caput: 1 Cor. XI, 3. 1 Tim. 2, 12,13. Sic fecit Deus ex uno sanguine totum genus humanum: Act. XVII, 26. Judaeorum vero fabulam de Adamo primitus bicorpore, ac Lilith priori ejus conjuge: ut & nuperum alicujus figmentum de Prae-adamitis, rejicimus.
units.tr: Man (the epitome of this world) is a rational animal, made in the image of God. Here occur the essential parts: a body most wisely formed, and a rational soul; and likewise the remarkable perfection of the divine image. The first men were Adam and Eve: he the father, she the mother of all living: Gen. 3:20; of one flesh and one bone: 2:23. He is her head: 1 Cor. 11:3; 1 Tim. 2:12, 13. Thus God made of one blood the whole human race: Acts 17:26. We reject, however, the Jewish fable that Adam was at first two-bodied, with Lilith as his earlier spouse, as also some recent figment about the Pre-Adamites.

units.la: XXXV. Quod ad Corpus; finxit Deus Hominem de Pulvere terrae: Gen. 2,7. sic אָדָם ad אֲדָמָה; Homo ad Humum referendus est.
units.tr: XXXV. Concerning the body: God formed man of the dust of the earth, Gen. 2:7. So Adam [אָדָם] is to be related to ground [אֲדָמָה]; man is to be derived from the earth.

units.la: Postea Corpus Foeminae formatum verf.21,22. de Costa Adami. Ab illis, Matrimonio Divinitus junctis, facta est deinceps universi Generis humani per generationem propagatio: secundum illud, Gen.1,28. Fructificate, augescite, & implete terram. De admirandâ Corporis conformatione vide etiam Psal. cxxxix,14,15,16. sup.cap.1. th.17. §.2. Confer graphicam plurium partium descriptionem, Eccl. xii, 3,-7.
units.tr: Afterwards the body of the woman was formed, vers. 21, 22, from the rib of Adam. From these two, joined together by God in marriage, the whole human race has since been propagated by generation, according to that saying, Gen. 1:28: "Be fruitful, increase, and fill the earth." On the wonderful structure of the body see also Ps. 139:14, 15, 16, above, chap. 1, th. 17, §2. Compare the graphic description of the several parts in Eccl. 12:3–7.

units.la: XXXVI. Anima non ex materia; sed à Deo immediate, creata est: Gen. 2, 7. Inspiravit in nares ejus spiraculum vitae; & fuit Homo in Animam viventem. Zach. xii, 1. Format spiritum hominis in eo. Hebr. xii, 9. Pater Spirituum. Eccl. xii,7. Spiritu redeunte ad Deum, qui dederat ipsum.
units.tr: XXXVI. The soul is not created from matter, but immediately by God: Gen. 2:7, "He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Zech. 12:1, "He forms the spirit of man within him." Heb. 12:9, "the Father of spirits." Eccl. 12:7, "the spirit returns to God who gave it."

units.la: Ex his sequitur, Animae immaterialitas; quam conditio & operationes ejus etiam arguunt; per reflexionem in se, & super actus suos; adeoque conscientiam, conceptus praecisivos, contemplationem immaterialium, etiam ipsius Dei: nec non judicium, & rationalem. lem complacentiam. Unde etiam diserte spiritus vocatur, Luc.xxiii, 46. Act.vii,59. Hebr.xii, 23. 1Pet.iii,19.
units.tr: From these things follows the immateriality of the soul, which its condition and operations also prove, through reflection upon itself and upon its own acts; and so through consciousness, abstract concepts, contemplation of immaterial things, even of God himself; likewise through judgment and rational complacency. Hence it is also expressly called spirit: Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59; Heb. 12:23; 1 Pet. 3:19.

units.la: 2. Illam immediatè à Deo creari in singulis. Locutio Gen.xlvi, 26. Animæ ex femore egressæ, synecdochica est; & de corpore intelligenda: nam idem nomen etiam de cadavere usurpatur. Levit.xix, 28: xxi, 1, 11. Neque propterea minus recte Homo dicitur generare Hominem: quia ad eum producendum agit, quantum per naturam potest; Corpus parando, & disponendo, ut ab Anima informetur. Sicut interficit Hominem, qui Corpus indispositum reddit ad ulteriorem informationem, & vivificationem per Animam.
units.tr: 2. That it is created immediately by God in each individual. The expression Gen. 46:26, "the souls that came out of his thigh," is synecdochical and is to be understood of the body; for the same word is also used of a corpse. Lev. 19:28; 21:1, 11. Nor for that reason is it any less correct to say that man begets man, because he acts to produce him, as far as nature allows, by preparing and disposing the body so that it may be informed by the soul. Just as one who renders a body unfit for further information and quickening by the soul is said to kill the man.

units.la: 3. Animam naturâ incorruptibilem & immortalem esse: Matth. x,28. Luc.xii, 4, 5. Animam occidere non possunt; sed Deus, Corpore occiso, Animam adhuc in gehennam conjicere potest. Eccl.xii,7. Anima redit ad Deum. 1Petr.iii, 19. Spiritus in carcere sunt. Adde Phil. 1, 21, 23. 2Cor.v,8. Luc.xxiii,46,23. xvi, 22, 23, 24.
units.tr: 3. That the soul is by nature incorruptible and immortal: Matt. 10:28; Luke 12:4, 5, "they cannot kill the soul"; but God, when the body has been killed, can still cast the soul into hell. Eccl. 12:7, "the soul returns to God." 1 Pet. 3:19, "the spirits in prison." Add Phil. 1:21, 23; 2 Cor. 5:8; Luke 23:46, 43; 16:22, 23, 24.

units.la: 4. Facultates immateriales: quæ sunt, Intellectus, per quem anima apta est objecta, quatenus vera sunt, non solum singularia & materialia, sed etiam universalia & spiritualia, percipere, dijudicare, inferre, ordinare: estque vel Noëticus, terminorum & enunciationum simplicium, citra discursum; vel Dianoëticus, per discursum, & illationem minus noti ex magis noto: atque iterum vel Theoreticus, acquiescens in ipsâ veritatis contemplatione; vel Practicus, ad praxin porrò tendens.
units.tr: 4. The immaterial faculties, which are: the intellect, through which the soul is able to perceive, judge, infer and order objects, insofar as they are true, not only singular and material but also universal and spiritual; and this is either noetic [νοητικός], concerned with simple terms and propositions without discursive reasoning, or dianoetic [διανοητικός], operating by discourse and by inferring the less known from the better known; and again, either theoretical, resting in the contemplation of truth itself, or practical, tending further toward action.

units.la: Deinde Voluntas, quæ Intellectum ordine naturæ sequitur, appetendo objecta bona, & aversando mala, quâ talia. Hùc pertinet tum simplex complacentia, vel displicentia; tùm, in ordine ad operis profecutionem, absoluta volitio, vel etiam aversatio; aut saltem velleitas.
units.tr: Then the will, which follows the intellect in the order of nature, by desiring good objects and turning away from evil ones, as such. To this belong both simple complacency or displeasure, and, in relation to carrying out a deed, absolute volition, or also aversion; or at least velleity.

units.la: Ad Intellectum Dianoëticum pertinet Judicium, quo discernitur, quæ sit rei alicujus natura, quæve ejus qualitates, aut circumstantiæ. Hoc autem recte procedit, ubi vera principia assumit, atque iis conclusiones ritè formas. formát: & firmum est, non vacillans, quoties sibi Homo probè conscius est talis sui processus.
units.tr: To the dianoetic intellect belongs judgment, by which is discerned what the nature of a thing is, and what its qualities or circumstances are. This proceeds correctly when it takes up true principles and rightly forms conclusions from them, and it is firm, not wavering, whenever the man is well aware of such a process of his own.

units.la: Voluntatis individua comes est Libertas, per quam Homo operatur ex deliberato consilio, & cum rationali complacentiâ; itâ quidem ut radicaliter ad Intellectum, executivè ad Voluntatem pertineat.
units.tr: The constant companion of the will is liberty, through which a man acts from deliberate counsel and with rational complacency; in such a way that it belongs radically to the intellect, but executively to the will.

units.la: Iudicium quidem non nisi liberè exercetur, ut neque seria veritatis contemplatio: verum indè nullo modo sequitur, Iudicium formaliter ad Voluntatem pertinere.
units.tr: Indeed judgment is exercised only freely, as also the serious contemplation of truth is; but it does not follow from this in any way that judgment belongs formally to the will.

units.la: 5. Unio arétissima; ut partes illæ essentiales unum per se constituant: sic enim homo factus est in animam viventem; Gen. 2, 7. Anima totum corpus informat. Operationes interim organicæ rationalibus inserviunt, quæ organorum conditionem intrinsecâ suâ perfectione superant: quamvis illa ad convenientem usum organorum obligata sit, donec terrestris huius domûs tabernaculum dissolvatur; 2 Cor. v, 1. Psal. xc, 3.
units.tr: 5. The union is very close, so that those essential parts constitute one thing by themselves; for thus man was made into a living soul, Gen. 2:7. The soul informs the whole body. Meanwhile the organic operations serve the rational ones, which surpass the condition of the organs by their own intrinsic perfection, although the soul is bound to the suitable use of the organs until the earthly house of this tabernacle is dissolved, 2 Cor. 5:1; Ps. 90:3.

units.la: 6. Multò minus existimandum, Animam rationalem solum esse facultatem, aut modum corporis: cum à corpore contradistincta & separabilis sit; & operationes ejus sublimiores conditione corporis impenetrabili, extensa, divisibili, irrationali.
units.tr: 6. Much less is it to be thought that the rational soul is merely a faculty or mode of the body, since it is distinct from the body and separable from it, and its higher operations are beyond the condition of the body, which is impenetrable, extended, divisible and irrational.

units.la: XXXVII. Imago Dei in Homine proponitur, Gen. 1, 26, 27. צלם; Imago, nomen concretum est; דמות; Similitudo, abstractum: & sic Imago quàm simillima denotatur. Confer Matth. iii, 11. Joh. iii, 5. Interim Imago Dei perfectissimo modo agnoscenda est in Christo. Vide sup. c. 5. th. 16. §. 1. In nobis analogicè. Hæc autem spectatur tum idealiter, Archetypa; & sic dicitur Homo secundum Deum conditus; Eph. iv, 24. tùm realiter, Estypa; sic Vir est Imago Dei, 1 Cor. xi, 7.
units.tr: XXXVII. The image of God is set forth in man, Gen. 1:26, 27. צלם [tselem], image, is a concrete noun; דמות [demuth], likeness, is abstract; and so the image is denoted as most closely resembling. Compare Matt. 3:11; John 3:5. Yet the image of God is to be recognised in the most perfect manner in Christ; see above chap. 5, th. 16, §1. In us it is analogical. This image is viewed both ideally, as archetype, and so man is said to be created according to God, Eph. 4:24; and really, as ectype; so the man is the image of God, 1 Cor. 11:7.

units.la: Imago ista notat conformitatem Hominis ad Dei perfectionem suo modo: ad Deum enim palàm referutur; non ad Angelos: Gen. 1, 26, 27. Faciamus Hominem ad Imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram. firam. Creavit itaque Deus Hominem ad Imaginem suam; ad Imaginem Dei. Adde v, 1; ix, 6. Jac. iii, 9. In Angelis quidem etiam est Imago Dei; ut patet ex sup. th. 12. sed illorum imaginem in hominibus temerè singunt Judæi & Socinani.
units.tr: This image denotes the conformity of man to the perfection of God in its own way: for it is plainly referred to God, not to the angels: Gen. 1:26, 27, "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness," "God therefore created man in his own image, in the image of God." Add 5:1; 9:6; James 3:9. In the angels indeed there is also an image of God, as is clear from above, th. 12; but the Jews and the Socinians rashly invent their image in men.

units.la: Perperam quoque Imaginem Dei ad formam corporis olim referebant Anthropomorphitæ; & nunc practicè tales Pontificii.
units.tr: The Anthropomorphites once also wrongly referred the image of God to the bodily form, and now the Papists do so in practice.

units.la: Malè item Anabaptistæ ad ideam Filii Dei, ut incarnandi; cum exemplar naturâ prius sit exemplato. Christus verò deindè post lapsum fuerit similis hominibus factus, Phil. 2, 7.
units.tr: The Anabaptists likewise err in referring it to the idea of the Son of God as about to be incarnate, since the exemplar is by nature prior to the thing copied. But Christ was made like men only afterwards, after the fall, Phil. 2:7.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ista Imago Primò Animam & facult- ates spirituales, ut subjectum præcipuum; sed formaliter dotes eximias designat, Sapientiam rerum Divina- rum, Justitiam, & Sanctitatem.
units.tr: XXXVIII. This image primarily signifies the soul and its spiritual faculties as the chief subject, but formally it signifies the outstanding endowments: wisdom in divine things, righteousness, and holiness.

units.la: Probatur hoc contra Socinianos, 1. expressis testimoniis. Col. iii, 10. In agnitionem congruentem Imagini ejus. Eph. iv, 24. Ad Justitiam & Sanctimoniam veram.
units.tr: This is proved against the Socinians: (1) by express testimonies. Col. iii, 10. Unto the knowledge after the image of him. Eph. iv, 24. In righteousness and true holiness.

units.la: 2. Ex mandatâ sæpiùs imitatione Dei: Sancti estote, quia Ego Sanctus sum, &c. Levit. xi. 44, 45. xix, 2. xx, 26. xxi, 6, 8. Estote perfecti, sicut Pater vester perfectus est; Matth. v, 48. Adde Eph. v, 1.
units.tr: (2) From the command, repeated often, to imitate God: Be holy, for I am holy, etc. Levit. xi. 44, 45; xix, 2; xx, 26; xxi, 6, 8. Be ye therefore perfect, as your Father which is in heaven is perfect, Matth. v, 48. Add Eph. v, 1.

units.la: 3. Quod omnia Dei opera fuerint valde bona; Gen. i. 31. & Homo factus sit rectus, Eccl. vii, 29. Confer Gen. 2, 23, 24; xix, 20. & 1, 26, 28. quæ quidem præclaram Sapientiam inferunt.
units.tr: (3) Because all God's works were very good, Gen. i. 31, and man was made upright, Eccl. vii, 29. Compare Gen. ii, 23, 24; xix, 20; and i, 26, 28, which indeed yield a remarkable wisdom.

units.la: Obj. 1. Protoplasti ante lapsum ignorabant, se esse nudos, ergò, &c. Resp. Non ignorabant nuditatem corporum: sed post lapsum cognoverunt se nudos esse imagine Dei; ac proindè pudore etiam suffundebantur, & molestiam ex corporis nuditate percipiebant, quibus ante lapsum locus non erat. Gen. 2, 25. iii, 7, 8.
units.tr: Objection 1. The first parents before the fall did not know that they were naked; therefore, etc. Reply. They did not fail to know the nakedness of their bodies; but after the fall they knew that they were naked in respect of the image of God, and so they were also overcome with shame and felt discomfort at the nakedness of the body, which had no place before the fall. Gen. ii, 25; iii, 7, 8.

units.la: Obj. 2. Passi sunt se decipi per Diabolum in specie Serpentis, quod ab insigni Sapientia valdè alienum est. Resp. Tunc quidem non utebantur habitu Sapientiæ, quæ naturalem ; nec proprie peccatum esse, dicunt : quo magis extollant vires liberi arbitrii.
units.tr: Objection 2. They allowed themselves to be deceived by the Devil in the form of a serpent, which is very far from remarkable wisdom. Reply. At that time, indeed, they were not using the habit of wisdom, which is natural; nor do they say that it was properly sin, so much the more do they exalt the powers of free will.

units.la: Nos fatemur Naturam physice, & in genere entis, non inferre justitiam originalem : sed neque, concupiscentiam ad peccatum inferre, concedimus.
units.tr: We grant that nature, physically and in the genus of being, does not bring with it original righteousness; but neither do we concede that it brings concupiscence to sin.

units.la: In genere moris Homo bonus & rectus factus est, exclusa illa inclinatione ad malum, Cum Lex dicat, Non concupisces, Exod. xx, 7. cum Rom. vii, 7. & concupiscentia illa repugnet perfectae dilectioni Dei. Deut. vi, 5: Matth. xxii. 37. Consequenter Jac. I, 13, - 17. „Nemo, cum tentatur, dicat ; a Deo tentor. Nam Deus tentari malis non potest ; nec quenquam tentat. Sed unusquisque tentatur, dum a propria cupiditate abstrahitur & inescatur. - Omnis donatio bona, &c. Et 1 Joh. 2, 16. Cupiditas carnis, &c. non est ex Patre : sed ex mundo. Imo natura Dei sanctissima requirit, ut creatura rationalis moraliter bona, ejusque naturalia moraliter pura, creentur : & sic facta esse, Creationis historia, aliaque sacra testimonia, confirmant.
units.tr: In the genus of morals man was made good and upright, that inclination to evil being excluded, since the Law says, Thou shalt not covet, Exod. xx, 7, and since that concupiscence is opposed to the perfect love of God. Deut. vi, 5; Matth. xxii, 37. Consequently Jac. i, 13–17: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God; for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man. But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed. … Every good gift, etc." And 1 Joh. ii, 16: The lust of the flesh, etc. is not of the Father, but is of the world. Indeed the most holy nature of God requires that a rational creature be created morally good, and its natural faculties morally pure; and that they were so made, the history of the Creation and other sacred testimonies confirm.

units.la: XLII. Gratia primi Hominis fuit gratis data: & eum Deo gratum faciebat. Donum illud gratiae non solum habituale fuit: sed etiam actualis gratia accedit; habitum illum conservans, quamdiu Deo placuit. Illud fuit auxilium sine quo non perseveratur: hoc, auxilium quo ipse tantisper itetit, ac bene operatus est. XLIII. Consecutive ad Imaginem Dei quoque pertinent Dominium & Immortalitas: Illud ad ornatum & gloriam externam; haec ad gloriam & beatitudinem internam, & quidem totius suppositi, ejusque durationem absque fine, pertinebat, sed positis ponendis.
units.tr: XLII. The grace of the first man was freely given, and it made him pleasing to God. That gift of grace was not only habituale; but actualis gratia also came in, preserving that habit for as long as it pleased God. The former was auxilium sine quo non, the help without which perseverance is not possible; the latter was auxilium quo, the help by which he continued for a time and acted well. XLIII. Consecutive to the image of God there also pertain Dominium & Immortalitas, dominion and immortality: Illud, the former, to ornament and external glory; haec, the latter, to internal glory and blessedness; and indeed it pertained to the whole person and to its duration without end, but with the conditions to be fulfilled.

units.la: De Dominio agitur, Gen. i, 26, -30. Et Dominentur, &c. In hoc solummodo, vel formaliter, imaginem Dei perperam constituunt Sociniani, & Remonstrantes. 1 Cor. xi, 7, 8, 9. Imago singulari quodam modo, & respectu prioritatis, tribuitur Viro. Confer 1 Tim. 2, 12, 13, 14. Unde etiam consecutivum istud in ipso magis locum habuit. Cæteroquin Gen. I, 26, 27. Et dominentur.Marem & Feminam creavit eos.
units.tr: Dominion is treated of at Gen. i, 26–30, and let them have dominion, etc. The Socinians and Remonstrants wrongly constitute the image of God in this alone, or formally. 1 Cor. xi, 7, 8, 9: the image is attributed to the man in a certain singular way, and with respect to priority. Compare 1 Tim. ii, 12, 13, 14. Hence that consequent attribute had more place in him. Otherwise Gen. i, 26, 27: And let them have dominion … male and female created he them.

units.la: 1. S. Scriptura diserte Imaginem Dei explicat de Sapientiâ, Justitiâ, & Sanctitate. Vide sup. th. 38.
units.tr: (1) Holy Scripture expressly explains the image of God as wisdom, righteousness, and holiness. See above, thesis 38.

units.la: 2. Hæ dotes longè præstantiores sunt Dominio seorsum consideratis.
units.tr: (2) These endowments are far more excellent than dominion considered by itself.

units.la: 3. Deus per Naturam, non per Dominium formaliter, Deus est; & nos respectu Imaginis Naturæ Divinæ consortes dicimur, 2 Petr. I, 4. Absoluta etiam principaliter spectanda, in quibus fundatur istud respectivum, & quorum consectarium est in terrestri hominum statu. Dominium enim Sapientiam, Justitiam, & Sanctitatem prærequirit, ut recte geratur; imo etiam Immortalitatem, ut perduret.
units.tr: (3) God is God formally through nature, not through dominion; and with respect to the image we are called partakers of the divine nature, 2 Pet. i, 4. The absolute attributes on which that respective attribute is founded are also to be considered first, and of these it is the corollary in the earthly state of men. For dominion requires wisdom, righteousness, and holiness in order to be exercised rightly; indeed also immortality, in order to endure.

units.la: 4. In Cœlesti beatitudine Imago Dei perfectissima erit: non tamen Dominium istiusmodi.
units.tr: (4) In heavenly blessedness the image of God will be most perfect, yet dominion of this kind will not be.

units.la: XLIV. Immortalitas
units.tr: XLIV. Immortality

units.la: totius Hominis nunc intelligitur: non tamen quasi absolutè ex naturâ, ejusque principiis, sequeretur: verùm ut Homo non fuerit moriturus; sed Deus eum vivum ac felicem conservaturus, si modò in obedientiâ perseveràsset. Mors pœnæ rationem habet; non naturæ consequens est.
units.tr: The immortality of the whole man is now understood; yet not as if it followed absolutely from nature and its principles, but in the sense that man would not be going to die; rather God would preserve him alive and happy, if only he had persevered in obedience. Death has the character of punishment; it is not a consequence of nature.

units.la: Hoc probamus contra Pelagianos, & Socinianos: 1. Ex comminatione Fœderi in principio annexâ, Gen. 2, 17. Quo die comederis, moriendo moriturus es. Ubi actum mortis corporalis excludi non debere, patet ex collatione Gen. XXVI, 11. Exod. XXI, 15, 16, 17. Iud. XIII, 22. 1 Sam. XIV, 39. 2 Sam. XII, 14. Ista autem comminatio infert immunitatem à morte, si Homo obedientiam consummâsset.
units.tr: We prove this against the Pelagians and Socinians: (1) from the threat of the covenant annexed at the beginning, Gen. ii, 17: In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die. That the act of bodily death must not be excluded is clear from a comparison with Gen. xxvi, 11; Exod. xxi, 15, 16, 17; Judg. xiii, 22; 1 Sam. xiv, 39; 2 Sam. xii, 14. But this threat implies exemption from death, had man completed his obedience.

units.la: 2. Ex locis N. T. eòdem spectantibus: Rom. V, 12. Per peccatum mors: & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccaverunt. Ac porro, 14. Mors regnavit ab Adamo usque ad Mosen, in eos etiam, qui non peccaverant ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami. Sic ex morte omnibus maximè obvia, ostenditur omnes etiam peccato obnoxios fuisse. Item 1Cor. xv, 21, 22. Per hominem (Adamum peccantem) mors. 26. ultimus hostis mors, 56. Aculeus mortis, peccatum; vis autem peccati, lex. Iterum Hebr. ix, 27, 28. Statutum est hominibus, ut semel moriantur, posteà vero judicium: ita & Christus semel oblatus, ut in seipso attolleret multorum peccata. Mors, quam sequitur judicium extremum, provenit ex Statuto, quod factum est propter peccatum; quod & mortis Christi causa fuit.
units.tr: (2) From New Testament passages bearing on the same point: Rom. v, 12: By sin death; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned. And further, v. 14: Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam. Thus from death, most obvious to all, it is shown that all were also liable to sin. Likewise 1 Cor. xv, 21, 22: By man (Adam sinning) death; v. 26: the last enemy is death; v. 56: The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. Again Heb. ix, 27, 28: It is appointed to men once to die, but after this the judgment; so Christ also, once offered, to bear the sins of many. The death which is followed by the final judgment comes from the appointment which was made because of sin, and which was also the cause of Christ's death.

units.la: 3. Ex locis generalioribus: Rom. vi, 23. Stipendia peccati mors. viii; 10, 11. Corpus mortuum propter peccatum, &c. Adde Psal. xc, 3, 12.
units.tr: (3) From more general passages: Rom. vi, 23: The wages of sin is death. Rom. viii, 10, 11: The body is dead because of sin, etc. Add Ps. xc, 3, 12.

units.la: 4. Ex consideratione Dei, & Bonitatis Ipsius: Ezech. xviii, 23. Non delectatur morte improbi: per se: Quanto minus morte justi? alia ergo mortis causa est; scil. sub ratione poenae, ut est bonum justitiae. Imò Levit. xviii, 5. servantibus mandata promittitur vita; quàm olim obsignavit Arbor vitae: Gen. iii, 22.
units.tr: (4) From consideration of God and of his goodness: Ezech. xviii, 23: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, in himself. How much less, then, in the death of the just? Death therefore has another cause, namely under the aspect of punishment, as it is a good of justice. Indeed Levit. xviii, 5 promises life to those who keep the commandments, which the Tree of Life once sealed: Gen. iii, 22.

units.la: XLV. Socinians
units.tr: XLV. The Socinians

units.la: XLV. Socinani distinguunt inter mortem aeternam, ac necessariam; & temporariam. Hanc subdividunt, in prorsus naturalem; & aliquo modo violentam. Mors aeterna ac necessaria illis est poena; ut & violenta, & vita misera generatim: aliquos enim casus excipiunt. Sed & Mors prorsus naturalis ex ipsa natura evenit, secundum illos: atque eatenus necessaria est: at vero necessariam, dixerunt esse poenalem.
units.tr: XLV. The Socinians distinguish between eternal and necessary death, and temporary death. They subdivide the latter into death that is wholly natural and death that is in some way violent. Eternal and necessary death is, for them, a punishment, as is violent death and a miserable life in general, for they make some exceptions. But death that is wholly natural, according to them, arises from nature itself, and to that extent is necessary; yet they say that what is necessary is penal.

units.la: Obj. 1. Gen. 1, 28. Crescite, & multiplicamini, &c. At vero Matrimonii usus mortem infert: Luc. xx, 35, 36. Resp. 1. Benedictio illa, & matrimonii institutio, non mortem inferunt; sed generis humani multiplicationem. 2, Luc. xx, 35, 36. Christus futurum saeculum, ab hoc, ut nunc est, distinguit. 3. Ex usu matrimonii & generatione liberorum, ut summum sequitur mortalitatis potentia remota; quam admittimus tunc etiam fuisse: sed non proxima; quam peccatum induxit; prius autem obstabat Divina conservatio, juxta prolationem. Obj. 2. Primus homo cibis etiàm utebatur ante lapsum: Gen. I, 29. Sed venter ille, & alimenta destruenda sunt: 1 Cor. VI, 13. Resp. 1. Alimenta erant media vitæ conservandæ: atque ex iis non sequitur, nisi potentia remota mortalitatis. 2 Juxta 1 Cor. VI, 13. Deus in fine sæculi etiàm καταργήσει, h. e. cessare & quiescere faciet ventrem, quatenus iste nunc cibis recipiendis & digerendis occupatur; atque item cibos, quatenus sic ventri serviunt: alia enim erit conditio Corporum glorificatorum, ubi etiàm aberit potentia ista remota.
units.tr: Objection 1. Genesis 1:28: "Increase and multiply," etc. But the use of marriage brings death: Luke 20:35–36. Reply 1. That blessing and the institution of marriage do not bring death, but the multiplication of the human race. 2. Luke 20:35–36: Christ distinguishes the future age from this present one, as it now is. 3. From the use of marriage and the begetting of children there follows only the remote power of mortality, which we admit was present even then; but not the proximate cause, which sin introduced; before the fall, the divine preservation, according to the command to increase, stood in the way of death. Objection 2. The first man also used food before the fall: Genesis 1:29. But that belly and those foods are to be destroyed: 1 Corinthians 6:13. Reply 1. Food was a means of preserving life, and from it there follows only the remote power of mortality. 2. According to 1 Corinthians 6:13, at the end of the age God will also make the belly cease and rest (καταργήσει), that is, he will make it cease to be occupied with receiving and digesting food, insofar as it now is; and likewise the foods, insofar as they thus serve the belly. For the condition of glorified bodies will be different, where that remote power will also be absent.

units.la: Obj. 3. Corpus Adami fuit animale, & terrestre: Gen. 2, 7. Ergo. Resp. Etiàm inde non sequitur, nisi potentia illa remota tantùm.
units.tr: Objection 3. Adam's body was animal and earthly: Genesis 2:7. Therefore, etc. Reply: Not even from this does it follow, except only the remote power.

units.la: Obj. 4. Tùm necessaria non fuisset Arbor vitæ. Resp. Ea vitam æternùm duraturam tantùm obsignavit.
units.tr: Objection 4. Then the tree of life would not have been necessary. Reply: It only sealed that life would last forever.

units.la: Obj. 5. Christus peccatum, ejusque vim, & pœnas, sustulit: non autem sustulit mortem temporariam. Ergo, &c. Resp. Jàm sustulit impetratione; sed nondùm plena applicatione. In regeneratione, peccati dominium tollitur: in justificatione, condemnatio; & sic pœna stricte dicta. Sed applicatio illa consummabitur in glorificatione.
units.tr: Objection 5. Christ took away sin, and its power and punishments, but he did not take away temporary death. Therefore, etc. Reply: He has indeed taken it away by impetration, but not yet by full application. In regeneration the dominion of sin is removed; in justification, condemnation, and so punishment strictly speaking. But that application will be completed in glorification.

units.la: Obj. 6. Casùs mortis violentæ citra peccatum dari potuissent varii; per aquas, ignes, feras, &c. Resp. Istiusmodi casùs temerè ab Adversariis fingùntur. Omnes aversura erat Providentia Dei: cùm ne passercùlus quidem apud ipsum in oblivione sit: Luc. XII, 6. Matth. X, 29, 30. Confer Amos. III, 6.
units.tr: Objection 6. Various cases of violent death might have occurred without sin: by waters, fires, wild beasts, etc. Reply: Such cases are rashly invented by our adversaries. Divine Providence would have averted them all, since not even a sparrow is forgotten in his sight: Luke 12:6; Matthew 10:29–30. Compare Amos 3:6.

units.la: XLVI. Itâ Creationem, respectù singulorum operum momentaneam, sex diebus distinguere, atque absolvere, Deo placuit: & quidem eo ordine, ut feré progrederetur à simplicioribus ad composita; ab imperfectioribus ad perfectiora.
units.tr: XLVI. Thus it pleased God to distinguish and complete the creation, momentary with respect to each individual work, in six days; and indeed in such an order that he proceeded from simpler to composite things, from less perfect to more perfect ones.

units.la: Hanc Autumno factam esse, probabile est.
units.tr: It is probable that this was done in autumn.

units.la: Septimo die quievit Deus à novis speciebus producendis; ùs acquievit; & diem illum sanctificavit: Gen. 2, Exod. xx, 11. Animas autem adhuc creat, quoties Homines generantur; atque omnia perpetuò conservat & gubernat: Joh. v, 17. Pater adhuc operatur.
units.tr: On the seventh day God rested from producing new kinds, and he rested; and he sanctified that day: Genesis 2; Exodus 20:11. Yet he still creates souls whenever human beings are generated, and he constantly preserves and governs all things: John 5:17: "My Father is still working."

units.la: XLVII. Singula opera, sic à Deo producta, Creaturæ vocantur; 1 Tim. iv, 4. Hebr. iv, 13. ut dependentia exprimatur; & omnis entitas referatur ad Eum, qui propter seipsum fecit omnia. Prov. xvi, 4. Rom. xi, 36. Atque ut Homines speciatim recordentur Creatoris sui: Eccl. xii, 1. Rom. I, 25. Omnes Creaturæ collectivè vocantur Mundus; Κόσμος: q. d. Ornatus: Rom. I, 20. Eph. I, 4. Specialius autem ista vox orbem terrarum; vel hominess, eorumve partem aliquam, notat: Matth. iv, 8. Joh. I, 10. 1 Joh. v, 19. Joh. I, 29. item 2 Cor. v, 19. 1 Joh. 2, 2. Rom. xi, 15.
units.tr: XLVII. The individual works thus produced by God are called creatures: 1 Timothy 4:4; Hebrews 4:13, so that dependence is expressed, and all being is referred to him who "made all things for himself": Proverbs 16:4; Romans 11:36. And so that human beings in particular may remember their Creator: Ecclesiastes 12:1; Romans 1:25. All creatures collectively are called the world (mundus; κόσμος), as if to say "ornament": Romans 1:20; Ephesians 1:4. But this word more specifically denotes the globe of the earth, or human beings, or some part of them: Matthew 4:8; John 1:10; 1 John 5:19; John 1:29; likewise 2 Corinthians 5:19; 1 John 2:2; Romans 11:15.

units.la: XLVIII. Mundus hic per aggregationem Unus est; cujus Forma substantialis, vel Anima communis, non datur: sufficit Partium talis habitudo mutua, juxta Creatoris ordinationem.
units.tr: XLVIII. This world is one by aggregation; a common substantial form or common soul of it is not given; it suffices that its parts stand in such mutual relation, according to the ordinance of the Creator.

units.la: Extra eum, similiter ut ante eum, nullam Creaturam admittimus: quemadmodum nec alium Mundum, post hunc futurum.
units.tr: Outside it, just as before it, we admit no creature; nor another world that will be after this one.

units.la: Idem nunc est Mundus; & eædem Creaturarum species, quæ per sex dies creatæ.
units.tr: The world is now the same, and the same kinds of creatures as those created in the six days.

units.la: Hujus Magnitudo finita est; & limites suos habet: quamvis nos eos definitè assignare non possumus. Jes. xl, 12. Quis mensus est pugillo suo aquas; & Cœlos spithamâ expendit; aut complexus est trientali pulverem terræ &c. Partes enim finitæ sunt; nec ullum infinitum est præter Deum: 1 Reg. viii, 27. Cœli cœlorum non capiunt te. Sic absoluta Immensitas plus dicit, quàm Ubiquitas spatiorum actualium, in quibus Creaturæ exi-stunt.
units.tr: Its magnitude is finite, and it has its limits, although we cannot assign them definitely. Isaiah 40:12: "Who has measured the waters in his hollow hand, and weighed the heavens with a span, or gathered the dust of the earth in a third part," etc. For the parts are finite, and nothing is infinite except God: 1 Kings 8:27: "The heavens of heavens cannot contain you." Thus absolute immensity says more than the ubiquity of the actual spaces in which creatures exist.

units.la: XLIX. Praxis esto: 1. Ex Creatione universa, Creatorem, ejusque Divinitatem, & æternam Potentiam, aliaque Attributa agnoscamus: Rom. 1, 19, 20. Psal. civ, 24. cxlv, 9. xix, 2.
units.tr: XLIX. Let there be practice: 1. From the whole creation let us acknowledge the Creator, his divinity, eternal power, and other attributes: Romans 1:19–20; Psalm 104:24; 145:9; 19:2.

units.la: 2. Coram tanto Creatore humiliemur: Ier.v.21, 22.
