units.tr: 2. Let us humble ourselves before so great a Creator: Jeremiah 5:21–22.

units.la: 3. In ipso speremus: Psal. cxlvi, 5, 6. lxxiii, 25. 1 Petr. iv, 19. Hebr. xiii, 5.
units.tr: 3. Let us hope in him: Psalm 146:5–6; 73:25; 1 Peter 4:19; Hebrews 13:5.

units.la: 4. Creaturis rectè & sanctè utamur: 1 Cor. xi, 31. vii, 31. 1 Tim. iv, 3, 4, 5. Ief. v, 11. Luc. xxi, 34. xvi, 2. Prov. xii, 10.
units.tr: 4. Let us use creatures rightly and holily: 1 Corinthians 11:31; 7:31; 1 Timothy 4:3, 4, 5; James 5:11; Luke 21:34; 16:2; Proverbs 12:10.

units.la: 5. Gratum animum Creatori in omnibus probemus: Psal. cxvi, 12. cxxxvi, 1, 5-9. 1 Cor. x; 31.
units.tr: 5. Let us show a grateful mind to the Creator in all things: Psalm 116:12; 136:1, 5–9; 1 Corinthians 10:31.

units.la: 6. Virtutes Bonorum Angelorum agnoscamus, & imitemur: Psal. ciii, 20, 21, 22. Matth. vi, 10. Adversus Malos vigilemus, & oremus: Eph. vi, 11, 18.
units.tr: 6. Let us acknowledge and imitate the virtues of the good angels: Psalm 103:20–22; Matthew 6:10. Let us watch and pray against the evil ones: Ephesians 6:11, 18.

units.la: 1 Petr. v, 8, 9. Matth. xxvi, 41. Iac. iv, 7.
units.tr: 1 Peter 5:8–9; Matthew 26:41; James 4:7.

units.la: 7. Observemus unde exciderimus, & restaurationi Imaginis Divinae studeamus sedulo: Apoc. ii, 5. Col. iii, 10. Eph. iv, 22, 23, 24. 2 Cor. iii, 18. v, 17.
units.tr: 7. Let us observe whence we have fallen, and diligently strive for the restoration of the divine image: Revelation 2:5; Colossians 3:10; Ephesians 4:22–24; 2 Corinthians 3:18; 5:17.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De Providentia.
units.tr: On Providence.

units.la: Providentia. Providentia; actualis. 1. Probatur, c. Atheos, & Epicur. Obj. solv. 2. Creaturarum omnium dependentia, & subjectio. 3. Providentia ordinaria. Extraordinaria. Miracula. 4. Provid. Mediata. Immediata. 5. Cur, & quomodo Deus Mediis utatur. 6. Providentia realis. Quae illi subsint. Ejus actus. 7. Conservatio Specialis. Necessaria. Quomodo res conservantur. Annihilatio. 8. Concursus. Necessarius; c. Durandum. 9. Non sufficit Concursus simultaneus; c. Pelag. Vel solum influens in effectum. Aut communis, indifferens, &c. 10. Sed agnoscendus praemovens ad agendum, & praemovens in agendo. Actiones
units.tr: Providence. Actual providence. 1. Proved against atheists and Epicureans; objections answered. 2. The dependence and subjection of all creatures. 3. Ordinary providence; extraordinary providence; miracles. 4. Mediate and immediate providence. 5. Why and how God uses means. 6. Real providence: what is subject to it, and its acts. 7. Special conservation: its necessity, how things are conserved, annihilation. 8. Concurrence: its necessity; against Durandus. 9. Simultaneous concurrence is not sufficient: against the Pelagians; or only an influence upon the effect; or a common and indifferent concurrence, etc. 10. Rather, a premotion to act and a premotion in acting must be acknowledged; actions

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII.

units.la: bona in genere entis. 11. Illa prob. c. Pontif. Anabapt. &c. 12. Objectiones solv. 13. Gubernatio. Ejus modus. 14. Objecta specialia. 15. Malorum impeditio. Quorundam permissio. 16. Hæc probatur. 17. Peccata peccatis etiam puniuntur. 18. Excæcatio, & Induratio. Negativa. Positiva. 19. Quomodo in Diabolis, & in Hominibus. Etiam electis. 20. Modus. 21. Non mera negatio; aut permissio; c. Pelag. 22. Fines istius Gubernationis. 23. Obj. solv. 24. Providentia moralis; tum late; tum stricte dicta. Hujus actus. 25. Præcepta. Cultus naturalis. Institutus. 26. Concessio, sive Permissio ethica. Regula in Adiaphoris observandæ. 27. Non malorum. 28. Revelationes, Præcepta, Prohibitiones, quomodo expressæ. 29. Concessio quomodo innotescat. 30. Variæ phrases. 31. Consilia. Contestationes. Vota. 32. Interim actus reales non excluduntur. 33. Praxis. 34.
units.tr: good in the general category of being. 11. This is proved against the Papists, Anabaptists, etc. 12. Objections answered. 13. Government. Its manner. 14. Special objects. 15. Prevention of evils. The permission of some. 16. This is proved. 17. Sins are also punished by sins. 18. Blinding and hardening. Negative. Positive. 19. How it works in devils and in men. Also in the elect. 20. Manner. 21. Not a mere negation or permission; against the Pelagians. 22. The ends of this government. 23. Objection answered. 24. Moral providence, taken both broadly and strictly. Its acts. 25. Precepts. Natural worship. Instituted. 26. Concession, or ethical permission. Rule to be observed in indifferent matters. 27. Not of evils. 28. How revelations, precepts and prohibitions are expressed. 29. How concession becomes known. 30. Various phrases. 31. Counsels. Protestations. Vows. 32. Meanwhile real acts are not excluded. 33. Practice. 34.

units.la: Præscientia Dei etiam Prævidentia appellari potest: Providentia vero sæpe è Decretum notat. Nos hoc loco executionem quandam spectamus; quæ discriminis causa Providentia actualis dicitur, & Creationem proximè sequitur. Ista est Actus Dei externus, quo ipse Creaturas jam existentes conservat & regit; atque in iis operatur eminentissimè; ad Gloriam suam. Gen. xxxi, 8. Deus providebit.
units.tr: God's foreknowledge may also be called foreseeing providence, but providence often denotes the decree itself. Here we consider a certain execution, which, to distinguish it, is called actual providence, and which closely follows creation. It is the external act of God by which he preserves and governs creatures already existing, and works in them most eminently, to his own glory. Gen. 22:14: God will provide.

units.la: 11. Ad Deum ascendendum; eique omnes Creaturas subjectas esse, contra Atheos & Epicureos probamus:
units.tr: 11. That God reaches to all things and that all creatures are subject to him, we prove against atheists and Epicureans:

units.la: 1. Ex diversis S. Scripturæ testimoniis: Act. xvii, 25, 28. Dat omnibus vitam, & halitum, & omnia. - In ipso vivimus, & movemur, & sumus. Hebr. I, 3. Sustinet omnia verbo verbo illo suo potente. Dan. 2, 20. Mutat tempora ac tempestates, transfert & constituit reges: dat sapientiam sapientibus. Psal. xcIV, 8, 9, 10. An plantator auris non audiat? aut formator oculi, an non intueatur? &c. CIV, 27, 28, 29. Act. XIV, 17. Job. V, 17. Rom. XI, 36. Eph. I, 11. Col. I, 16, 17.
units.tr: 1. From various testimonies of Holy Scripture: Acts 17:25, 28: He gives to all life, and breath, and all things. In him we live, and move, and have our being. Heb. 1:3: He upholds all things by the word of his power. Dan. 2:20: He changes the times and the seasons, removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise. Ps. 94:8–10: Shall he who planted the ear not hear? or he who formed the eye, not see? etc. Ps. 104:27–29. Acts 14:17. Job 5:17. Rom. 11:36. Eph. 1:11. Col. 1:16, 17.

units.la: 2. Ex Natura Dei absolute prima: unde omnis alia entitas & causalitas.
units.tr: 2. From the nature of God, who is absolutely first; whence every other entity and causality derives.

units.la: 3. Ex conditione Creaturarum prorsus dependente: Matth. V, 36. VI, 27. Act. XVII, 25, 28.
units.tr: 3. From the condition of creatures, which is wholly dependent: Matt. 5:36; 6:27; Acts 17:25, 28.

units.la: 4. Ex Prophetiis, Miracilis, Judiciis insolitis; itemque Operibus, quae a Creaturis ita fiunt, ut interim captum earum excedant: Nexu item & ordinatione causarum Particularium sapientissima: & dictamine conscientiae in Hominibus.
units.tr: 4. From prophecies, miracles and unusual judgments; likewise from works which creatures perform in such a way that they exceed their own capacity; also from the most wise connection and ordering of particular causes, and from the dictate of conscience in men.

units.la: Obj. In mundo sunt multa imperfecta, confusa, injusta: ergo, &c. Resp. Illa recte perpensa perfectionem, ordinem, bonitatem, & justitiam magis commendant & adstruunt: Psal. lxxiii, 16, 17. Si cogitem cognoscere hoc, laboriosum visum est in oculis meis: donec ingressus in Sanctuarium Dei, animadvertissem finem illorum.
units.tr: Objection. The world contains many imperfect, confused and unjust things; therefore, etc. Answer. When these are rightly weighed, they rather commend and establish perfection, order, goodness and justice: Ps. 73:16, 17: When I thought to know this, it seemed a toilsome task in my eyes; until I entered the sanctuary of God and perceived their end.

units.la: III. Creaturae, in quantum entia sunt, in tantum sunt dependentia a Deo sed ordinatissime. Sic omnibus competit.
units.tr: III. Creatures, insofar as they are beings, are in that measure dependent on God, yet most orderly. Thus it belongs to all of them.

units.la: 1. Potentia obedientialis, qua subjacent dispositioni Divinae actuali, pro ipsius arbitrio. Psal. CXV, 3. Deus, quicquid placet, facit. CXLVIII, 8. Ignis, & grando; nix, & exhalatio, ventus turbineus efficiens verbum Ejus.
units.tr: 1. Obediential power, by which they are subject to the actual disposition of God, according to his own will. Ps. 115:3: God does whatever pleases him. Ps. 148:8: Fire and hail, snow and vapour, stormy wind fulfilling his word.

units.la: 2. Posita est communis Lex Naturae: certus ordo omnium & singulorum: Jer. XLV, 12. Omni exercitui coelorum praecepta dedi. Jerem. XXXIII, 20. Foedus meum de die, & foedus meum de nocte. Job. XXXVIII, 10, 11, 12. de mari: Dicens, Hucusque venies, & ne procedito. - An praecepisti matutino tempori? Pf. LXXIV. 16, 17.
units.tr: 2. There is laid down a common law of nature: a fixed order of all things and of each thing. Jer. 33:25 (cf. 45:12 for the host of heaven): I have appointed the commands for all the host of heaven. Jer. 33:20: My covenant of the day and my covenant of the night. Job 38:10–12, of the sea: Saying, Thus far you shall come, and no further. Have you commanded the morning? Ps. 74:16, 17.

units.la: 3. Est quaedam Naturae inclinatio; & quasi appetitus, ipsi Legi conveniens: Pf. XIX, 6. Sol laetatur, tanquam robustus robustus decursurus viam. civ, 19. Sol- agnoscens occasum. Job. v. 7. Scintillæ prunarum in altum evolant.
units.tr: 3. There is a certain inclination of nature, and as it were an appetite, agreeing with that very Law: Ps. 19:5, 6: The sun rejoices like a strong man to run his course. Ps. 104:19: The sun knows its going down. Job 5:7: The sparks of coals fly upward.

units.la: 4. In Bestiis datur Instinctus naturalis, secundùm Facultates sensitivas: Prov. xxx, 24, -28. Quatuor ista parva sunt, humilia; tamen sunt sapientia; apprimè sapientia: Formicæ, populus infirmus; quæ comparant cibum suum: Mures montani, - : Rex non est locustis - : Aranea, &c. Confer sup. cap. 7. th. 33.
units.tr: 4. In beasts there is a natural instinct, according to their sensitive faculties: Prov. 30:24–28: These four things are little on the earth, yet they are exceedingly wise: the ants, a people not strong, which prepare their food in summer; the rock badgers; the locusts have no king, yet they go forth all of them by bands; the spider, etc. Compare above, ch. 7, th. 33.

units.la: 5. In Hominibus, & Angelis, etiàm Ratio, & Libertas: sed prorsus dependenter: Act. xvii, 25, 28. Prov. xxi, 1. Psal. cii, 20, 21.
units.tr: 5. In men and angels there is also reason and liberty, but wholly dependent: Acts 17:25, 28; Prov. 21:1; Ps. 102:20, 21.

units.la: IV. Distinguitur Providentia primò, in Ordinariam, & Extraordinariam.
units.tr: IV. Providence is first distinguished into ordinary and extraordinary.

units.la: Ordinaria secundum ordinem primitùs institutum peragitur; sive in Naturâ; ut Hos. 2, 22. Exaudiam Cœlos; & ipsi exaudient Terram, &c. Jer. xxxi, 35, 36. sive in statu Gratiæ; ut Rom. x, 17. Fides est ex auditu; auditus vero per Verbum Dei.
units.tr: Ordinary providence is carried out according to the order first instituted, whether in nature, as in Hos. 2:22: I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth, etc.; Jer. 31:35, 36; or in the state of grace, as in Rom. 10:17: Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.

units.la: Extraordinaria ab ordine isto recedit: Deus enim ostendit, se, Dominum universi; isto ordine superiorem esse. Sic Israëlitas Manna & Coturnicibus pavit; Exod. xvi, 13, 15. Sic Corvi afferebant Eliæ panem & carnem; 1 Reg. xvii, 6. Et Pauli vocatio atque conversio extraordinaria fuit: Act. ix, 3, -. Huc pertinent Miracula strictè dicta: Marc: xvi, 17, 20. 1Cor. xii, 9, 10. cum Psal. lxxxii, 18, cxxxvi, 4. Act. iii, 12, 13, 16. In quibus creaturæ duntaxat causæ instrumentales morales esse possunt: à Deo precibus ea petendo, & impetrando; eadem aliis promittendo, & futura indicando; signum denique dando circa subjectum recipiens, ad cujus præsentiam Deus effectum Miraculosum per Omnipotentiam suam, producit. Ab illis igitur longè differunt Angelorum, vel Hominum opera, quantumvis mira, seu admiranda; viribus eorum finitis facta.
units.tr: Extraordinary providence departs from that order, for God shows himself to be the Lord of the universe, superior to that order. Thus he fed the Israelites with manna and quails: Exod. 16:13–15. Thus ravens brought bread and flesh to Elijah: 1 Kings 17:6. Paul's calling and conversion was also extraordinary: Acts 9:3ff. To this belong miracles strictly so called: Mark 16:17–20; 1 Cor. 12:9, 10; compare Ps. 82:18; 136:4; Acts 3:12, 13, 16. In these, creatures can be only moral instrumental causes: by asking for and obtaining them from God by prayer; by promising them to others and indicating future events; and finally by giving a sign concerning the recipient subject, in whose presence God, through his omnipotence, produces the miraculous effect. Therefore the works of angels or men, however marvellous or admirable, which are done by their finite powers, differ greatly from these.

units.la: V. Distinguitur secundò in Mediatam, & Immediatam.
units.tr: V. Providence is distinguished secondly into mediate and immediate.

units.la: Providentia Mediata est, ubi Deus per Media operatur, Immediata, ubi absque Mediis.
units.tr: Mediate providence is where God works through means; immediate providence is where he works without means.

units.la: Medium proprie dicitur, quod inter duo extrema situm est: sed hoc loco intelligitur, quod a causa principe sic adhibetur, ut effectui producendo, & in assequendo, sua causalitate etiam serviat. Ita per Pluviam rigatur & foecundatur Terra: Frumento, aut Pane inde confecto, & Vino aluntur Homines: Psal, civ, 13, 14, 15. Ægris opus est Medico. Matth. ix, 12. Magistratus Dei Minister est, & vindex ad iram ei, qui quod malum est fecerit: Rom. xiii, 4. Elisæus per Eliam vocatus est: 1 Reg. xix, 19, Vide ibid. verf. 5: Isef. 38, 21. 1 Tim. v, 8, Hebr. I, 14. Psal. xci, 11, xxxiv, 8. Gen. iii, 24. xix, 13. 2 Sam. xxiv, 16. 2 Reg. xix, 35. Apoc. xvi, 1, &c.
units.tr: A medium properly means what lies between two extremes, but here it is understood as what the primary cause employs in such a way that it also serves the producing and attaining of the effect by its own causality. Thus the earth is watered and made fruitful by rain; men are nourished by grain, or the bread made from it, and by wine: Ps. 104:13, 14, 15. "The sick have need of a physician," Matt. 9:12. The magistrate is God's minister and an avenger for wrath against him who does evil: Rom. 13:4. Elisha was called through Elijah: 1 Kings 19:19; see ibid. v. 5; Isa. 38:21; 1 Tim. 5:8; Heb. 1:14; Ps. 91:11, 34:8; Gen. 3:24; 19:13; 2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Kings 19:35; Rev. 16:1, etc.

units.la: Sed Immediatè Deus Mosen vocavit: Exod. iii, 6, allocutus est: Num. xii, 8. sustentavit: Deut. ix, 9, 18. Similiter Paulus immediate vocatus est: Gal. I, 1.
units.tr: But God called Moses immediately (Exod. 3:6), spoke with him (Num. 12:8), and sustained him (Deut. 9:9, 18). Likewise Paul was called immediately: Gal. 1:1.

units.la: vi. Deus Mediis utitur, non ex indigentia; sed ex abundantia Bonitatis Suæ; unde creaturis causalitatem aliquam communicare etiam placuit. Sed ad omnipotentiam Dei nullum est Mediorum discrimen: 1Sam. xiv, 6. Non est Jehovæ impedimentum, quin servet multis, aut paucis.
units.tr: 6. God uses means not from need, but from the abundance of his goodness; hence it has pleased him also to impart some causality to creatures. But for the omnipotence of God there is no difference between means: 1 Sam. 14:6, "There is no hindrance to the LORD to save by many or by few."

units.la: Hinc 1. Mediis vilissimis quandoque utitur. 1 Cor. I, 27, 28. Quæ stulta, infirma, ignobilia, in mundo, & pro nihilo habita, elegit Deus, &c. Confer 2 Chr. 24. 24.
units.tr: Hence: 1. He sometimes uses the most base means: 1 Cor. 1:27, 28, "God has chosen the foolish, the weak, the base and despised things of the world," etc. Compare 2 Chr. 24:24.

units.la: 2. Media aptissima reddit aliquando inefficacia: Hos. iv, 10. Comedentes non saturabuntur, - Psal. xxxiii, 16, 17. - Mendax est Equus ad salutem, &c.
units.tr: 2. He sometimes makes the most apt means ineffective: Hos. 4:10, "They shall eat and not be satisfied." Ps. 33:16, 17, "The horse is a false hope for safety," etc.

units.la: 3. Contra illorum naturam operatur: Dan. iii, 17. Deus, - potens est eripere nos a fornace ignis accensa. Confer verf. 22, 24. Ita respectu finis operis multa per accidens fiunt; non item respectu finis operantis. Ex. gr. Evangelium per se ad salutem spectat; per accidens est odor mortis ad mortem. 2 Cor. 2, 14, 16. Conf. Rom. I, 16. & VII, 12, 13. X, 4, 5. 4. Ubi Mediis utitur Deus, virtus illorum ab ipso immediatè pendet : Psal. cxxvii, 1, 2. Nisi Jehovah ædificet, frustra laborant ædificatores : nisi Jehovah custodiat civitatem: frustra sedulus sit custos, &c. Confer Ies. xxviii, 26. Iterùm Deut. viii, 3. Matth. 4, 4. Non solo pane vivit homo ; sed omni eo, quod prodit ex ore Iehovæ. Confer Levit. xxvi, 26. Ezech. iv, 16. Mich. vi, 14. Hag. i, 6. & Levit. xxvi, 5. - Deut. xxviii, 3. - Hag. 2, 20. 1 Cor. iii, 5, 6, 7. Quis est Paulus, &c.? Neque is qui plantat, est aliquid ; neque is qui rigat, sed Deus, qui dat crescendi vim. Adde Ies. x, 5, 6, 7, 15.
units.tr: 3. He works against their nature: Dan. 3:17, "God is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace." Compare vv. 22, 24. Thus with respect to the end of the work, many things happen per accidens; not so with respect to the end of the agent. For example, the Gospel by its nature looks to salvation; per accidens it is "the savour of death unto death," 2 Cor. 2:14, 16. Compare Rom. 1:16; 7:12, 13; 10:4, 5. 4. Where God uses means, their power depends immediately on him: Ps. 127:1, 2, "Unless the LORD build the house, they labour in vain who build it; unless the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain." Compare Isa. 28:26. Again, Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4, "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of Jehovah." Compare Lev. 26:26; Ezek. 4:16; Mic. 6:14; Hag. 1:6; and Lev. 26:5; Deut. 28:3; Hag. 2:20; 1 Cor. 3:5, 6, 7, "Who is Paul? ... Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the growth." Add Isa. 10:5, 6, 7, 15.

units.la: 5. Causæ secundæ sæpè sine suo excidunt ; sed Deus nunquàm : Prov. xix, 21. Consilium Jehovæ stabit. Gen. l, 20. Vos cogitaveratis contra me malum. Sed Deus cogitavit illud in bonum convertere, ut est die hoc, &c. Rom. viii, 28.
units.tr: 5. Second causes often fail without their own fault, but God never does: Prov. 19:21, "The counsel of the LORD shall stand." Gen. 50:20, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, as it is this day," etc. Rom. 8:28.

units.la: VII. Tertio distinguitur Providentia in Realem, & Moralem.
units.tr: VII. Providence is distinguished thirdly into real and moral.

units.la: Illa circa qualescunque creaturas versatur, quatenùs sunt entia prorsùs dependentia; circa entitatem talem : Hæc circa creaturas Rationales, ut sic. Sed ad utramque revocandi sunt etiàm actùs negativi ; permissionis scil. tùm physicæ, tum ethicæ.
units.tr: The former is concerned with creatures of whatever kind, insofar as they are entirely dependent beings, with respect to such entity; the latter concerns rational creatures as such. But negative acts must also be referred to both, namely acts of permission, both physical and ethical.

units.la: Providentiæ reali subsunt omnes in universum Creaturæ : Col. i, 17. Hebr. I, 3. Eph. i, 11. Vide supra th. 2. Specialiùs, I. de Cœlo : Ies. xl, 26. Attollite in sublime oculos vestros, & videte quis creaverit ista ; producens numero suo exercitum ipsorum : &c. Matth. v, 45. Facit ut Sol suus oriatur, &c. Job. ix, 7. Psal. civ, 19.
units.tr: All creatures in general are subject to real providence: Col. 1:17; Heb. 1:3; Eph. 1:11. See above, thesis 2. More specifically: 1. Of the heavens: Isa. 40:26, "Lift up your eyes on high and see who created these things, bringing out their host by number..." Matt. 5:45, "He makes his sun rise..." Job 9:7; Ps. 104:19.

units.la: 2. De Hominibus : 1 Sam. 2, 6, -10. Jehovah morte afficit, & in vitam restituit - : deprimit & tollit, &c. Psal. xxxvi, 7. xc, 3. Act. xvii, 25. Matth. x, 30, vi, 30, 34. 1 Cor. ix, 9, 10. 1 Tim. iv, 10. Jac. iv, 15.
units.tr: 2. Of men: 1 Sam. 2:6, 10, "The LORD kills and makes alive; he brings down and lifts up," etc. Ps. 36:7; 90:3; Acts 17:25; Matt. 10:30; 6:30, 34; 1 Cor. 9:9, 10; 1 Tim. 4:10; Jas. 4:15.

units.la: 3. De Bestiis : Ps. xxxvi, 7. cxlvii, 9. Dat Jumentis cibum suum : Pullis corvorum, qui crocitant. civ, 10, 11, 12; 18, 20, 21. Matth. vi, 26. Intuemini in Volucres cœli: Sed Pater ille vester cœlestis alit eas, x, 29. Job. xxxix, x, 16-19.
units.tr: 3. Of beasts: Ps. 36:7; 147:9, "He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry." Ps. 104:10, 11, 12, 18, 20, 21. Matt. 6:26, "Look at the birds of the air; yet your heavenly Father feeds them," and 10:29. Job 39:16-19.

units.la: 4. De Plantis: Psal. civ, 14,-17. Faciens ut germinet Fœnum ad jumentum; & Herba ad hominis usum, &c. Satiantur Arbores Jehovæ; Cedri, &c. Matth vi,28, 29, 30. Discite, quomodo Lilia agrorum augescant, &c. Quodsi Herbam agri--Deus ita circumvestit, &c.
units.tr: 4. Of plants: Ps. 104:14-17, "He causes the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man," etc. "The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon..." Matt. 6:28, 29, 30, "Consider how the lilies of the field grow," etc. "If God so clothes the grass of the field..."

units.la: 6. De Liberis actionibus: Prov. xvi, 9. Animus Hominis excogitat viam suam; sed Iehovah statuit gressum ejus. xxi, 1. Ut rivi aquarum, sic Animus Regis est in manu Jehovæ; quocunque vult, inclinat eum. Jerem. x. 23. Novi, Jehovah, non esse penes Hominem viam ejus; non esse penes virum ambulantem, vel dirigere gressum suum.
units.tr: 6. Of free actions: Prov. 16:9, "A man's heart plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps." 21:1, "Like channels of water, the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will." Jer. 10:23, "I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself; it is not in man who walks to direct his steps."

units.la: Sic omnia huic Providentiæ subsunt; sed inæqualiter, ratione effectuum: Matth. vi, 26. Nonne vos multo præstatis iis. 30. Quodsi Herbam agri-Deus ita circumvestit; nonne vos multo magis-? 1 Tim. iv,10. Conservator omnium Hominum; maximè verò Fidelium. 1 Cor. ix, 9. Num Boves Deo curæ sunt? Comparatè scil. ad Homines, & Ministros Dei.
units.tr: Thus all things are subject to this providence, but unequally, with respect to their effects: Matt. 6:26, "Are you not of much more value than they?" v. 30, "If God so clothes the grass of the field... will he not much more clothe you?" 1 Tim. 4:10, "the preserver of all men, especially of believers." 1 Cor. 9:9, "Does God care for oxen?" That is, in comparison with men and God's ministers.

units.la: Ad Providentiam Realem pertinent Conservatio, Concursus, & Gubernatio.
units.tr: To real providence belong conservation, concurrence and government.

units.la: VIII. Conservatio est actus Providentiæ, quo Deus essentiam & facultates creaturarum continuat, juxta placitum suum. Est ergo suppositi, & virtutum. Neque generalis tantum; sed & specialis. Nehem. ix, 6. Tu fecisti Cœlos, -- & Terram; -&c. Et tu Conservas hæc omnia. Psal. xxxvi,7. Homines & Jumenta conservas. Vide etiam Apoc. iv, 11. Act. xvii, 25, 28, Col. I,17, Hebr. I, 3. Psal. civ, 29, 30.
units.tr: VIII. Conservation is the act of providence by which God continues the essence and faculties of creatures according to his good pleasure. It therefore concerns both the supposit and its powers. It is not only general but also special: Neh. 9:6, "You made the heavens... and the earth... and you preserve all these things." Ps. 36:7, "You preserve man and beast." See also Rev. 4:11; Acts 17:25, 28; Col. 1:17; Heb. 1:3; Ps. 104:29, 30.

units.la: Estque necessaria; propter omnimodam Creaturarum dependentiam, ut in fieri, sic etiam in esse; continuata enim existentia, ejusdem est conditionis cum efsentia primum producta. Imo Conservatio nihil aliud est, quam continuata Creatio; ac proinde non nisi à Deo procedit: Rom. I, 20.
units.tr: It is necessary, on account of the complete dependence of creatures, both in becoming and in being: for continued existence is of the same condition as the essence first produced. Indeed, conservation is nothing other than continued creation, and therefore proceeds from God alone: Rom. 1:20.

units.la: Sicut alia Creatione immediata producta sunt; alia mediata: sic etiam se habet Conservatio; quæ Creationem sequitur, sed Concursum & Gubernationem antecedit; prius enim est ipsum esse, quam agere, aut in agendo dirigi.
units.tr: Just as some things are produced by immediate creation and others by mediate, so conservation also stands: it follows creation, but precedes concurrence and government; for being itself comes before acting, or being directed in acting.

units.la: Conservantur autem alia eadem numero, quæ creata fuerunt; ut Angeli, Animæ rationales, Sol, Luna, &c. alia eadem specie; ut Plantæ, Bestiæ, &c. Nonnulla secundum aliquam sui partem mutationi obnoxia sunt; cæterum in statu suo perstiftunt; ut Elementa.
units.tr: Some things are preserved in the same number as they were created, such as angels, rational souls, the sun and the moon. Others are preserved in the same kind, such as plants and beasts. Some are subject to change in some part of themselves, but otherwise remain in their state, such as the elements.

units.la: Ex superioribus satis patet, Conservationem omnino esse actum positivum: ei opponitur Annihilatio; mera negatio actus conservativi; cum huius terminus ad quem sit nihilum. Perit ergo, quod non conservatur, & quousque non conservatur amplius: Psal. civ, 29. Aufers spiritum eorum; deficiunt, & in pulverem suum revertuntur.
units.tr: From what has been said above, it is quite plain that Conservation is altogether a positive act. Annihilation is opposed to it, being the mere negation of the conserving act, since its terminus is nothing. Whatever is not conserved therefore perishes, and it stays perished for as long as it is not conserved: Psalm 104:29. You take away their breath; they die, and return to their dust.

units.la: IX. Concursus est actus Providentiæ, quo Causæ secundæ à Primâ ad agendum excitantur, applicantur, ac promoventur efficaciter: Phil. II, 13. Deus est, qui efficit in vobis ipsum velle, & ipsum agere. 1 Cor. IV, 7. Quid habes, quod non acceperis? Prov. XXI, 1. Act. XVII, 25, 28. Rom. XI, 35, 36. Psal. XXXIII, 15. Isef. X, 5, 6, 7, 15. Jerem. X, 23.
units.tr: IX. Concurrence is an act of Providence by which secondary causes are stirred up by the First Cause to act, are applied to acting, and are efficaciously advanced: Phil. 2:13. It is God who works in you both to will and to do. 1 Cor. 4:7. What do you have that you did not receive? Prov. 21:1. Acts 17:25, 28. Rom. 11:35, 36. Psalm 33:15. Isa. 10:5, 6, 7, 15. Jer. 10:23.

units.la: Non sufficit ergò cum Durando statuere generalem solùm conservationem causarum secundarum in suo esse: perfectio enim præsentis actionis positivæ non potest esse independens.
units.tr: It is therefore not enough, with Durandus, to hold only a general conservation of secondary causes in their being, for the perfection of a present positive action cannot be independent.

units.la: X. Nec sufficit Pelagianorum Concursus simultaneus tempore & naturâ: quia sic Causa secunda independenter agere inciperet: hoc enim, unde alterum dependet, eatenus prius est: atque ità Deus non foret causa prima. Contra Rom. XI, 35, 36. Quis prior dedit ei? - Nam omnia sunt ex eo. 1 Cor. IV, 7. Et cur non etiam etiàm creatura sine Deo posset actionem continuare; cum Inchoatio alicujus rei majus quid sit, quam ejusdem inchoatæ similis Continuatio?
units.tr: X. Nor is the concurrence of the Pelagians enough, a concurrence simultaneous in time and in nature, because on that view a secondary cause would begin to act independently. For that on which another depends is by that very fact prior, and so God would not be the first cause. Against this: Rom. 11:35, 36. Who has first given to him? For all things are from him. 1 Cor. 4:7. And why should not the creature also be able to continue its action without God, since the beginning of something is greater than the continuation of the same thing once begun?

units.la: Nec satis est statuere Concursum influentem in essectum; non vero in causam secundam: sic enim Causa secunda revera esset independens, atque adeo prima; quamvis effectus esset dependens.
units.tr: Nor is it sufficient to hold that concurrence flows into the effect, but not into the secondary cause. For then the secondary cause would really be independent, and therefore prior, even though the effect were dependent.

units.la: Neque item sufficit Concursus communis, indifferens, indeterminatus; & determinabilis per actionem creaturæ: quoniam ex ista hypothesi Creatura, ut determinans, esset prior concursu sic determinato.
units.tr: Likewise, a common, indifferent, indeterminate concurrence, which is determined by the action of the creature, is not sufficient either, since on this hypothesis the creature, as the determining factor, would be prior to the concurrence so determined.

units.la: XI. Statuendum ergo, quòd Deus sit Causa prima, activè præmovens Causam secundam ad agendum, ac deinceps promovens in agendo: Creatura verò hoc respectu se habeat passivè; quamvis respectû effectûs se habeat activè. Imo eadem actio est Dei & Creaturæ; sed diverso modo atque ordine. Interim Creatura talis actionis suæ est causa formaliter efficiens: Deus verò est causa eminenter efficiens, & virtualiter transitiva: Jac. 1, 17.
units.tr: XI. It must therefore be held that God is the first cause, actively pre-moving the secondary cause to act and afterwards advancing it in acting; but the creature stands in this respect passively, although in respect of the effect it stands actively. Indeed, the same action belongs to God and to the creature, but in a different mode and order. Meanwhile the creature is the formally efficient cause of its own action, whereas God is the eminently efficient cause and virtually transitive: James 1:17.

units.la: Actiones ut sic, in genere Entis, omnes bonæ sunt. In Peccatis verò distinguendum est inter Actum substratum, qui similiter metaphysice bonus est; & inter ἀνομίαν, privationem bonitatis moralis debitæ esse: cujus non est causa efficiens; ac proinde neque concursus ad eam formaliter.
units.tr: Actions as such, in the genus of being, are all good. In sins, however, one must distinguish between the substrate act, which is likewise metaphysically good, and [ἀνομία] lawlessness, which is the privation of the moral goodness that is due. The latter has no efficient cause, and consequently concurrence does not contribute to it formally.

units.la: XII. Concursum hunc contra Pelagianizantes Pontificios, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes, plenius probamus:
units.tr: XII. We prove this concurrence more fully against the Pelagianizing Papists, the Anabaptists and the Remonstrants:

units.la: 1. Locis generalibus S. Scripturæ, præallegatis th. 9. Adde Jerem. XVIII, 6. Ut argilla in manu figuli, ita vos &c. Jac. IV, 15, 16. Dicere debuistis: Si Dominus voluerit, &c. Vide etiam sup. th. 2. & 7.
units.tr: 1. By the general passages of Holy Scripture cited above, thesis 9. Add Jer. 18:6. Like clay in the potter's hand, so are you, etc. James 4:15, 16. You ought to say, If the Lord wills, etc. See also above, theses 2 and 7.

units.la: 2. Testimoniis magis specialibus, de operibus moraliter bonis. Vide 1 Cor. IV, 7. Phil. II, 13. sup. th. 9. Item Jerem. XXXI, 18. Converte me, ut convertar 33. Indam Legem meam menti eorum, -. Ezech, XXXVI, 26, 27,28. Et dabo vobis cor novum, & spiritum novum ponam in medio vestri, &c. Iohan. VI, 44. Nemo potest venire ad me nisi Pater traxerit eum. XV, 5. 1 Cor. XII, 3, 6. Phil. 1, 29. 2 Tim II, 24, 25. Hebr. XIII, 20. Jac, I, 17, 18.
units.tr: 2. By more specific testimonies concerning morally good works. See 1 Cor. 4:7; Phil. 2:13, cited above, thesis 9. Likewise Jer. 31:18, Turn me, and I shall be turned; 31:33, I will put my law in their inward parts. Ezek. 36:26, 27, 28, And I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit in the midst of you, etc. John 6:44, No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. John 15:5. 1 Cor. 12:3, 6. Phil. 1:29. 2 Tim. 2:24, 25. Heb. 13:20. James 1:17, 18.

units.la: 3. Ex quibusdam locis, ubi speciatim agitur de actibus moraliter malis: Gen. XLV, 7, 8. Non vos misistis me huc: sed Deus ipse, &c. Exod. VII, 3. Ego obdurabo cor Pharaonis. 2 Thess. II, 11. Mittet eis Deus efficaciam erroris. 2 Sam. XII, 11. 12. XVI, 10, 11. Rom. I, 24, 25.
units.tr: 3. From certain passages where the subject is specifically morally evil acts: Gen. 45:7, 8, It was not you who sent me here, but God himself, etc. Exod. 7:3, I will harden Pharaoh's heart. 2 Thess. 2:11, God will send them a strong delusion. 2 Sam. 12:11, 12; 16:10, 11. Rom. 1:24, 25.

units.la: 4. Rationibus ex Dependentia Creaturarum, & Dei Independentia ac prima causalitate: nam
units.tr: 4. From arguments based on the dependence of creatures and the independence of God and his primary causality, for:

units.la: α. Omnis Motionis analysis debet fieri in primum Motorem immobilem.
units.tr: α. Every analysis of motion must be traced back to the first unmoved Mover.

units.la: β. Omnis Effectus, & Actus, ad Causam primam reduci debet.
units.tr: β. Every effect and every act must be referred back to the first cause.

units.la: γ. Deus praescit omnia secundum Consilium suum determinatum: Concursus igitur indeterminatus esse non potest.
units.tr: γ. God foreknows all things according to his determinate counsel; therefore concurrence cannot be indeterminate.

units.la: δ. Efficientia Dei active est ipse Deus; terminative vero est simul tempore cum actione Creaturarum; prior tamen natura; quia Deus est causa prima.
units.tr: δ. The efficiency of God is, actively, God himself; terminatively, however, it is simultaneous in time with the action of the creatures, yet prior in nature, because God is the first cause.

units.la: XIII. Obj. 1. Ezech. XVIII. 23. 32. XXXIII, 11. Deus non delectatur morte peccatoris; sed ut convertatur, & vivat: neque tamen sequitur omnino conversio: Ergo Concursus Dei non est determinans. Resp. Non delectatur morte in se; vult conversionem & vitam; Voluntate illam mandante, hanc promittente. Sed iste non est Concursus Providentiae realis, de quo nunc agimus.
units.tr: XIII. Objection 1. Ezek. 18:23, 32; 33:11: God takes no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live; yet conversion does not always follow. Therefore God's concurrence is not determining. Reply: He takes no pleasure in death in itself; he wills conversion and life, the one by his commanding will, the other by his promise. But this is not the real concurrence of Providence, which is what we are now discussing.

units.la: Obj. 2. Prov. XVI, 1. Homo praeparat cor. Zach. 1, 3. convertit se: ergo, &c. Resp. Sed non sine Dei operatione, per quam Ipse facit nos operari.
units.tr: Objection 2. Prov. 16:1, The man prepares his heart; Zech. 1:3, Turn yourselves: therefore, etc. Reply: Yes, but not without God's operation, by which he himself makes us act.

units.la: Obj. 3. Matth. XXIII, 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos; - sed tu noluisti: Ergo, &c. Resp. 1. Christus exprobrat Hierosolymitanis, quod ipse quide mvolumii. 5. 36. 37. cvii, 23,-30.
units.tr: Objection 3. Matt. 23:37, How often I would have gathered your children, but you would not: therefore, etc. Reply 1. Christ rebukes the Jerusalemites because he himself was willing, but they were not; cf. John 5:36, 37; Psalm 107:23–30.

units.la: Sic 1. singula ad certa Objecta determinantur. Vide th. 7. Item 1 Reg. xxii, 34. Quidam jaculans arcu simplici animo, percussit Regem Israelis, &c. Ezech. xxi, 21, 22, 23. Jon. 1. 7 Actor. 1, 26.
units.tr: So, first, single acts are determined to particular objects; see thesis 7. Likewise 1 Kings 22:34, A certain man drew his bow at a venture and struck the king of Israel, etc. Ezek. 21:21, 22, 23. Jonah 1:7. Acts 1:26.

units.la: 2. Actiones Creaturarum suis Limitibus circumscribuntur. Job. 1, 12. Deus Diabolo: Tantummodo in ipsum ne mittito manum tuam. II, 6. Verumtamen vitam ejus serva. Adde xxxviii, 10, 11.
units.tr: 2. The actions of creatures are circumscribed within their limits. Job 1:12, God to the Devil: Only do not put forth your hand against him. 2:6, But spare his life. Add 38:10, 11.

units.la: 3. In Fines suos accuratissime diriguntur: Jef. lv, 10, 11. Cum descendit pluvia, non revertitur illuc; sed inebriat terram, facitque ut pariat &c. Sic erit Verbum meum, &c. Prov. xix, 21. Multae Cogitationes insunt animo cujusque: sed Consilium Jehovae ipsum stabit. Jef. x, 5, &c. Luc. II, 1, &c. Matth. II, 5, 6. cum Mich. v, 1. & Genef. xlix, 10.
units.tr: 3. They are directed most exactly to their ends: Isa. 55:10, 11, As the rain comes down, it does not return there, but waters the earth and makes it bring forth, etc. So shall my word be, etc. Prov. 19:21, Many plans are in a person's heart, but the counsel of the LORD will stand. Isa. 10:5, etc. Luke 2:1, etc. Matt. 2:5, 6, with Mic. 5:1 and Gen. 49:10.

units.la: 4. Mala etiam in Bonum convertuntur: Rom. viii, 28. Novimus, iis qui diligunt Deum, omnia simul adjumento esse ad bonum. Gen. L, 20. Sed Deus cogitavit illud in bonum convertere. Confer Luc. xxiv, 26. Act. iv, 10, 11, 12; 27, 28.
units.tr: 4. Evils also are turned into good: Rom. 8:28, We know that for those who love God all things work together for good. Gen. 50:20, But God meant it for good. Compare Luke 24:26; Acts 4:10, 11, 12, 27, 28.

units.la: XV. Singula Deus convenienter naturae suae gubernat; sive ea necessaria fuerint, sive contingentia, sive libera.
units.tr: XV. God governs each thing in a manner fitting to his nature, whether those things are necessary, contingent, or free.

units.la: Sic gubernantur 1. Res Humanae: Prov. xxi, 2. Dives & pauper inter se occurrunt, efficiente hos omnes Jehova. x, 24. Quod formidat Improbus, id evenit ei; quod desiderant Justi, dabit Deus. 22. Benedictio Jehovae ditat, &c. Adde Ps. cxxvii, 1, 2, 1 Sam. II, 6, 7, 8. Actor. xvii, 25, 26.
units.tr: Thus are governed: (1) human affairs. Prov. xxi, 2. The rich and the poor meet together, Jehovah making them all. x, 24. What the wicked fear comes upon them; what the righteous desire, God will give. 22. The blessing of Jehovah makes rich, etc. Add Ps. cxxvii, 1, 2; 1 Sam. ii, 6, 7, 8; Acts xvii, 25, 26.

units.la: 2. Speciatim Matrimonia: Matth. xix, 6. Quod Deus conjunxit, &c. Act. xvii, 28, 29. ipsius Progenies sumus. Illustre est exemplum Isaaci; Genef. xxiv, 14, 18, 27, &c.
units.tr: (2) Especially marriages. Matt. xix, 6. What God has joined together, etc. Acts xvii, 28, 29. We are also his offspring. The example of Isaac is famous: Gen. xxiv, 14, 18, 27, etc.

units.la: 3. Vita ad Terminum usque praestitutum. Vide sup. cap. 6. th. 11.
units.tr: (3) Life, up to the appointed end. See above, ch. 6, th. 11.

units.la: 4. Bellorum exitus: Psal. xliv, 2, 7. O Deus, auxi-libus nostris audivimus, - Te manu Tua gentes expulisse: Per Te Hostes cornu feriemus. &c. xlvi, 9, 10, 11. Agite, videte opera Jehovæ! ut disponat desolationes in terra, faciens, ut cessent Bella-, arcum perfringat, & truncet hastam, &c. Prov. xxi, 31. Equus aptatur ad diem prælii, sed Jehovæ est ipsa salus. Confer Exod. xv, 3, &c. ac porro historiam Bellorum Domini, & promissiones de hostibus in manus Israelitarum tradendis, &c.
units.tr: (4) The outcomes of wars. Ps. xliv, 2, 7. O God, we have heard with our ears... that you drove out the nations with your hand; through you we shall push down our enemies with horns, etc. xlvi, 9, 10, 11. Come, see the works of Jehovah, who makes desolations in the earth, causing wars to cease, breaking the bow and cutting the spear in two, etc. Prov. xxi, 31. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but safety belongs to Jehovah. Compare Exod. xv, 3, etc., and further the history of the Lord's wars, and the promises that enemies would be delivered into the hands of the Israelites, etc.

units.la: 5. Periodi Imperiorum, Regnorum, & Rerum publicarum: Dan. II, 22, Transfert Reges, & constituit Reges. v, 21, &c.
units.tr: (5) The cycles of empires, kingdoms and commonwealths: Dan. ii, 22, He removes kings and sets up kings. v, 21, etc.

units.la: 6. Minima: ut Locustæ, Pediculi, &c. Exod. viii, 17. x, 12. Deut. xxviii, 38. Joël. i, 4. Act. xii, 23. Capilli: Matth. x, 30. Herbæ; vi, 30.
units.tr: (6) The smallest things, such as locusts, lice, etc.: Exod. viii, 17; x, 12; Deut. xxviii, 38; Joel i, 4; Acts xii, 23. Hairs: Matt. x, 30. Grass: vi, 30.

units.la: 7. Etiam Mala tristia: Am. iii, 6. An erit malum in civitate, quod Jehovah non efficiat. Threnor. iii, 37, 38, 39. Ex ore Excelsi an non prodit malum quodque, & bonum? &c. Hebr. xii, 6, 7. 1 Cor. xi, 32. 2 Thess. 1, 6, 8, 9.
units.tr: (7) Even grievous evils: Amos iii, 6. Is there evil in a city which Jehovah does not bring about? Lam. iii, 37, 38, 39. Does not good and evil alike come out of the mouth of the Most High? etc. Heb. xii, 6, 7; 1 Cor. xi, 32; 2 Thess. i, 6, 8, 9.

units.la: XVI. Major difficultas est in Gubernatione Malorum turpium.
units.tr: XVI. The greater difficulty lies in the governance of foul evils.

units.la: Hæc Deus interdum impedit: Genes. xx, 6. Cohibui te, ne peccares in Me. 31, 7. Non permisit ei Deus, ut damno afficeret me. 1 Cor. x, 13. Act. xviii, 9, 10. Sæpe physice permittit: Psal. lxxxi, 13. Dimisi eos ambulare, ex sententia animi sui; dicens, Abeant cum pravis consiliis suis! Act. xiv, 16. Sivit omnes Gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. Confer Matth. 8. 31, 32. Et quidem consulto, ac volens: Rom. ix, 18. Quem vult, indurat.
units.tr: Sometimes God hinders these. Gen. xx, 6. I kept you from sinning against me. xxxi, 7. God did not permit him to do me harm. 1 Cor. x, 13; Acts xviii, 9, 10. Often he permits them physically. Ps. lxxxi, 13. I let them go according to the desire of their hearts, saying, Let them go with their wicked counsels! Acts xiv, 16. He allowed all nations to walk in their own ways. Compare Matt. viii, 31, 32. And indeed deliberately and willingly. Rom. ix, 18. Whom he wills, he hardens.

units.la: XVII. Defectum moralem Deus relinquit in actu illo subistrato: complexum vero peccaminosum sanctissimè & sapientissimè limitat, ac dirigit in finem bonum. Hinc efficax Permissio dicitur.
units.tr: XVII. God leaves the moral defect in that act which lies beneath, but he limits and directs the sinful complex most holily and wisely to a good end. Hence it is called efficacious permission.

units.la: Probatur autem 1. de Objectorum, aliarumque circumstantiarum determinatione, ex allegatis th. 14. §. 1. Adde 2 Sam. xvi, 10, 11. Jehovah edixit, Maledic Davidi. 1 Reg. 22. 20, 23. Dixit Jehovah, quis pelliciet, &c.? Tum dixit; Pellicies; & prævalebis: exi, & fac ita. &c. Exod. 4. 21. 9. 12. Psal. cv, 25. Isa. 19. 14.
units.tr: It is proved first from the determination of the objects and other circumstances, from the passages cited in th. 14, §1. Add 2 Sam. xvi, 10, 11. Jehovah has commanded, Curse David. 1 Kings xxii, 20, 23. Jehovah said, Who will entice...? Then he said, You shall entice and prevail; go out and do so, etc. Exod. iv, 21; ix, 12. Ps. cv, 25. Isa. xix, 14.

units.la: 2. De Gradibus, vide th. 14. §. 2. Adde 1 Cor. X,13. Deus non sinet vos tentari supra id quod potestis. Actor. II, 27. ex Psal. XVI, 10.
units.tr: (2) On degrees, see th. 14, §2. Add 1 Cor. x, 13. God will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear. Acts ii, 27, from Ps. xvi, 10.

units.la: 3. De Finium ordinatione: Josh. XI, 20. A Jehova fuit, quod obstirmabant cor suum, ut interneccioni devoverct illas. 1 Cor. X,13. Una cum tentatione praestabit exitum, ut possitis sufferre. Jac. V,11. Beatos praedicamus eos, qui sustinent. Tolerantiam Job audistis, & finem Domini vidistis. Genes. XLV,8. Exod. XIV,17. 1 Reg. XII,15. Actor. III,18.
units.tr: (3) On the ordering of ends. Josh. xi, 20. It was from Jehovah that they hardened their hearts, so that he might devote them to destruction. 1 Cor. x, 13. Together with the temptation he will provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it. Jas. v, 11. We call those blessed who endure. You have heard of the patience of Job and seen the end the Lord brought about. Gen. xlv, 8; Exod. xiv, 17; 1 Kings xii, 15; Acts iii, 18.

units.la: XVIII. Specialiùs peccata peccatis punit Deus:
units.tr: XVIII. More particularly, God punishes sins by sins.

units.la: quandoque in aliis: 2 Sam. XII, 11, 12 Eo quod sprevistime,Suscitaturus sum contra te malum e domo tua, &c. Jud. IX, 23, 24. Immisit Deus affectum malum inter Abimelechum & Sichemitas: - ut rediret injuria, &c.
units.tr: Sometimes in others. 2 Sam. xii, 11, 12. Because you have despised..., I will raise up evil against you from your own house, etc. Judg. ix, 23, 24. God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the Shechemites, so that the wrong might return, etc.

units.la: 1 Reg. XI, 26 Quandoque in ipsis: 2 Theff. II, 10, 11, 12. Propterea quod amorem veritatis non receperunt,-ideo mittet eis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio, &c. Rom. I, 24,-27.
units.tr: 1 Kings xi, 26. Sometimes in the sinners themselves. 2 Thess. ii, 10, 11, 12. Because they did not receive the love of the truth... therefore God will send them the working of error, so that they believe a lie, etc. Rom. i, 24-27.

units.la: XIX. Occurrunt interim Excaecatio & Induratio.
units.tr: XIX. Meanwhile blindness and hardening occur.

units.la: Illa dicit privationem sapientiae spiritualis, adeo ut creatura coeco impetu deinceps ruat in peccatum & exitium. Haec vero dicit privationem flexionis & conformationis ad normam Legis Divinae. Jes. VI, 9, 10. I, ut dicas populo isti: audite indesinenter; at ne intelligatis: & videte indesinenter, neque cognoscatis. Fac, ut pinguescat cor populi istius, &c. Rom. I, 21, 22, 28. Vanifacti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est cor, &c. Utraque considerari potest vel ut actus Dei, vel ut creaturae. Deo autem tribuitur aliquando solum negative; atque ita simpliciter negatur collatio sapientiae, & flexionis ad normam: aliquando positive, prout Deus gubernatione judiciali propter antecedens demeritum creaturam rationalem punit spirituali caecitate aut duritiâ majore & graviore, quam prius in eâ extitit. Sed quemadmodum a Deo procedit, poenalis, est: quatenus autem in Creaturis subjectivè inest, est culpabilis. Rom. ix, 17, 18. Dicit Scriptura Pharaoni, Ad hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te potentiam meam, &c.
units.tr: The former signifies the privation of spiritual wisdom, so that the creature then rushes on into sin and destruction with blind impetus. The latter signifies the privation of bending and conforming to the norm of the Divine Law. Isa. vi, 9, 10. Go, say to this people: Hear continually, but do not understand; see continually, but do not know. Make the heart of this people fat, etc. Rom. i, 21, 22, 28. They became futile in their reasonings, and their heart was darkened, etc. Both may be considered either as an act of God or as an act of the creature. To God, however, it is sometimes attributed only negatively, and thus the bestowal of wisdom and of conformity to the norm is simply denied; sometimes positively, insofar as God, by judicial government, on account of antecedent demerit, punishes the rational creature with spiritual blindness or hardness greater and more grievous than that which previously existed in it. But insofar as it proceeds from God, it is penal; insofar as it inheres subjectively in creatures, it is culpable. Rom. ix, 17, 18. Scripture says to Pharaoh, For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, etc.

units.la: XX. In Hominibus protoplastis, ut & in Diabolis primùm peccantibus, Deus isto tempore negative, actualem usum sapientiæ & sanctimoniæ non excitavit. In posteris autem cæcitas & duritia tùm habitualiter, vel nativa, vel acquisita spectatur; tum actualiter. Nativa pertinet ad Peccatum originale. Acquisita dicit nativæ corruptionis incrementum ratione graduum, per crebros actùs & consuetudinem peccandi. Actualis denique in actibus secundis cernitur.
units.tr: XX. In the first parents, as also in the devils who first sinned, God at that time negatively did not stir up the actual use of wisdom and holiness. In their posterity, however, blindness and hardness are regarded both habitually, either native or acquired, and actually. The native kind belongs to original sin. The acquired kind denotes an increase of native corruption by degrees, through frequent acts and the habit of sinning. The actual kind is finally seen in subsequent acts.

units.la: Utraque in Electos nondum conversos etiàm cadit. Eph. II, 3. Eramus natura filii irae, ut & reliqui. In Regenitis, totalis, & ad finem regnans, aut prævalens, non habet locum: sunt enim Lux in Domino: Eph. v, 8. & habent cor carneum: Ezech. xxxvi, 26. Partialis tamen, eaque sensibilis, in iis etiàm agnoscenda est: Jac. iii, 2. In multis impingimus omnes; 1 Cor. xii, 9. Ex parte cognoscimus. Hùc pertinet querela, Jef. lxiii, 17. Quare sineres aberrare nos, Iehovah, à viis Tuis? torrefaciens obdurares animum nostrum à reverentià Tui?
units.tr: Both also fall upon the elect not yet converted. Eph. ii, 3. We were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also were. In the regenerate, the total kind, reigning to the end or prevailing, has no place, for they are light in the Lord, Eph. v, 8, and they have a heart of flesh, Ezek. xxxvi, 26. A partial kind, however, and one that is perceptible, is to be acknowledged in them too. James iii, 2. In many things we all stumble. 1 Cor. xii, 9. We know in part. To this pertains the complaint of Isa. lxiii, 17. Why, Jehovah, do you let us wander from your ways, and harden our heart so that we do not fear you?

units.la: XXI. Modus Excœcationis & Indurationis, licet occultus, semper tamen justus est.
units.tr: XXI. The manner of blinding and hardening, although hidden, is nevertheless always just.

units.la: Hùc pertinet 1. Non-collatio, imò propter antecedens peccatum justa ablatio, boni habitualis: Rom. i, 21, 24. Tradidit eos Deus cupiditatibus cordium ipsorum ad immunditiam. 26, 27. Fœdis affectibus. 28. In mentem omnis judicii expertem, &c.
units.tr: To this pertains, first, the non-bestowal, or rather the just withdrawal on account of antecedent sin, of habitual good. Rom. i, 21, 24. God gave them up to the lusts of their hearts, to uncleanness. 26, 27. To shameful passions. 28. To a mind void of all judgment, etc.

units.la: 2. Non-impeditio, imò directio hostium spiritualium, ad talia objecta: ut de Pseudo-prophetis; 1 Reg. xxii, 22, 23. & de Antichristo; 2 Thess. II, 9, 10, 11. Cujus adventus est ex vi illâ efficaci Satanæ, cum omni potentiâ, & signis ac prodigiis mendacibus. - Idcò igitur mittet eis Deus efficaciam erroris, &c.
units.tr: Second, the non-hindrance, or rather the direction, of spiritual enemies toward such objects: as with false prophets, 1 Kings xxii, 22, 23, and with Antichrist, 2 Thess. ii, 9, 10, 11, whose coming is by the powerful working of Satan, with all power and lying signs and wonders. Therefore God will send them the working of error, etc.

units.la: Oblatio bonorum, quibus homines suo vitio abuuntur : ut Occasionum internarum ; Exod. 1, 9, 12. Externarum ; Genes. xxxvii, 5. Exod. v, 2 Jes. 2, 9. 2 Cor. 11, 16. Item Beneficiorum, erga alios, quibus invident ; & erga ipsos, quibus abuuntur homines corruptissimi: Tit. 1, 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum. Rom. 11, 4, 5. Et Poenarum, quibus indurantur: Jerem. v, 3. o Iehovah, percutis eos ; sed non dolent : consumis eos ; renuunt accipere eruditionem ; reddunt faciem suam obfirmatiorem petrâ ; renuunt converti.
units.tr: The offering of goods, which men abuse by their own fault: such as internal occasions, Exod. i, 9, 12; external ones, Gen. xxxvii, 5; Exod. v, 2; Isa. ii, 9; 2 Cor. xi, 16. Likewise benefits toward others, which they envy, and toward themselves, which the most corrupt men abuse. Titus i, 15. To the polluted and unbelieving nothing is clean. Rom. xi, 4, 5. And punishments, by which they are hardened. Jer. v, 3. O Jehovah, you strike them, but they do not grieve; you consume them, but they refuse to receive instruction; they make their faces harder than rock; they refuse to return.

units.la: XXII. Ex superioribus patet, non sufficere, si cum Jesuitis, aliisque Pelagianizantibus, in hoc negotio statuatur mera negatio, vel nuda permissio: nam 1. Requiritur saltem positiva providentia ad actum substratum, & in ordine ad finem.
units.tr: XXII. From what has been said above it is clear that it is not enough, as the Jesuits and other Pelagianizers hold in this matter, to posit a mere negation or bare permission. For (1) a positive providence is required at least for the substratum of the act, and in relation to the end.

units.la: 2. Actus judicialis non nisi positivè procedit; ob tale demeritum, tali modo.
units.tr: (2) A judicial act proceeds only positively, on account of such a demerit and in such a manner.

units.la: 3. Precamur non induci in tentationem: Matth. vi, 13. atque alibi passim occurrunt phrases positivum actum inferentes.
units.tr: (3) We pray that we not be led into temptation (Matth. 6:13); and elsewhere there occur everywhere phrases implying a positive act.

units.la: XXIII. Fines, ad quos actus peccaminosi diriguntur, sunt, 1. Manifestatio Tolerantiae Divinae: Rom. II, 4. & Justitiae, tùm in reprobis: ix, 22. Quod si volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, &c. Prov. xvi, 4. tùm in ipso Christo: Rom. iii, 25, 26. Ad demonstrationem justitiae suae, &c.
units.tr: XXIII. The ends to which sinful acts are directed are: (1) the manifestation of the divine forbearance (Rom. 2:4) and of justice, both in the reprobate (Rom. 9:22: "What if God, willing to show wrath and to make known his power, etc."; Prov. 16:4) and in Christ himself (Rom. 3:25, 26: "for the demonstration of his justice, etc.").

units.la: 2. Manifestatio Sapientiae ac Misericordiae Divinae in Electis salvandis: Rom. xi, 31, 32. Conclusit Deus omnes illos in inobedientiam, ut omnium illorum misereretur. O profundas divitias tùm Sapientiae, tum Cognitionis Dei! &c. v, 20. Ubi amplificatum est peccatum, ibi superabundavit gratia.
units.tr: (2) The manifestation of the wisdom and mercy of God in the elect who are to be saved (Rom. 11:31, 32: "God has shut up all of them in disobedience, that he might have mercy upon all of them. O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! etc."; 5:20: "Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound").

units.la: 3. Profunda fidelium humiliatio: Matth. ix, 13. Non veni vocatum justos ; sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Thren. v, 15. Væ nobis, quod peccaverimus! iii, 40, 41. Jerem. II, 19.
units.tr: (3) The deep humbling of the faithful (Matth. 9:13: "I came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance"; Lam. 5:15: "Woe unto us, that we have sinned!"; 3:40, 41; Jer. 2:19).

units.la: 4. Multiplex fidelium probatio, victoria, & gloria: Luc. XXII, 31. Satanas appetiit vos, quos ventilare sicut triticum: &c. Psal. XXVI1, 24. Cum cadit justus, non dejicitur, &c. 2 Cor. XII, 9. Potentia Mea, per infirmitatem consummatur. Phil. IV. 13. Omnia valeo per Eum, qui me corroborat, nempe Christum, &c. 1 Joh. V, 4. Hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, nempe fides nostra.
units.tr: (4) The manifold trial, victory and glory of the faithful (Luke 22:31: "Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat," etc.; Psalm 37:24: "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down," etc.; 2 Cor. 12:9: "My power is made perfect in weakness"; Phil. 4:13: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me," namely Christ, etc.; 1 John 5:4: "This is the victory that overcomes the world," namely our faith).

units.la: XXIV. Obj. Ex Gubernatione istâ sequi videtur, quod Deus fit causa peccati: ergo ea non est admittenda. Resp. Istud nego. Qui equum vitio proprio claudicantem regit, is nequaquàm est causa claudicationis.
units.tr: XXIV. Objection: from this government it seems to follow that God is the cause of sin; therefore it is not to be admitted. Reply: I deny this. One who guides a horse that limps through its own fault is by no means the cause of the limping.

units.la: Inft. 1. Atqui Deus statuitur actûs peccaminosos dirigere ad sua objecta, & in suos fines: ergo, &c. Resp. Iterum nego consequentiam. Tota Dei directio sancta est: neque quicquam agit; vel intendit, nisi bonum, & bene; & finem suum sic semper assequitur, licet creaturæ peccantes aliud & aliter sibi propositum habeant.
units.tr: Objection 1: But God is said to direct sinful acts to their objects and to their ends; therefore, etc. Reply: I again deny the consequence. The whole direction of God is holy; nor does he do or intend anything except what is good, and well; and so he always attains his end, although sinning creatures have something else and otherwise proposed to themselves.

units.la: Inft. 2. Multæ phrases asperæ circa hoc negotium occurrunt in scriptis Theologorum. Resp. 1. Communis Ecclesiarum nostrarum confessio ex publicis earum formulis petenda est; non ex privatis scriptis quorundam Theologorum. 2. Nec facile ex scriptis nostrorum Theologorum in hoc negotio producentur phrases, aut sententiæ; quarum similes, vel æquipollentes, non reperiantur in SS. Literis; aut etiam similes, vel duriores, in scriptis ipsorum Adversariorum.
units.tr: Objection 2: Many harsh phrases about this matter occur in the writings of theologians. Reply: (1) The common confession of our churches is to be sought from their public formularies, not from the private writings of certain theologians. (2) Nor will phrases or opinions be readily produced from the writings of our theologians on this matter for which similar or equivalent ones are not found in the Holy Scriptures, or even similar or harsher ones in the writings of the adversaries themselves.

units.la: XXV. Providentia moralis vel late vel stricte sumi- tur.
units.tr: XXV. Moral providence is taken either broadly or strictly.

units.la: Priori modo ad eam pertinet omnis motio objectiva, & tropica, sive metaphorica, per externa signa, aliaque objecta; & sic ad Bestias se etiam extendit. Posteriori modo versatur circa Creaturas tantùm rationales; & quidem sic, ut istæ, earumque actiones, ab illâ dependeant in genere moris.
units.tr: In the former sense there belongs to it every objective and tropical motion, that is, metaphorical, through external signs and other objects; and in this way it extends even to the beasts. In the latter sense it is concerned only with rational creatures, and indeed in such a way that these, and their actions, depend upon it in the genus of morals.

units.la: Actûs hujus Providentiæ vel spectant veritates agnoscendas & credendas, vel officia à nobis præstanda. Veritates illas respicit Divina revelatio explicatoria &c. & assertoria; de quâ sup. cap. 1. th. 26; 32. & cap. 2. th.2. 4; 8, 9.
units.tr: The acts of this providence either regard truths to be known and believed, or duties to be performed by us. The divine revelation, explanatory, etc., and assertory, respects those truths; concerning which see above, chapter 1, theses 26, 32, and chapter 2, theses 2, 4, 8, 9.

units.la: Ad Officia præstanda pertinent primario Præcepta, Promissiones, & Præmia; secundario etiàm Concessiones: ad vitia fugienda Prohibitiones, Comminationes, & Pœnæ.
units.tr: To the performing of duties belong primarily the precepts, promises and rewards, and secondarily also the concessions; to the avoiding of vices belong the prohibitions, threatenings and punishments.

units.la: XXVI. Præcepit Deus cultum sibi convenientem, tùm absolutè & immutabiliter, per naturam suam; unde cultus naturalis vocatur: tùm ex hyphotesi, & quodammodò mutabiliter, per liberam voluntatis suæ determinationem; qui cultus institutus nuncupatur. Similiter etiàm Deus prohibuit quædam necessariò, & immutabiliter; alia liberè, & mutabiliter.
units.tr: XXVI. God commands the worship fitting to himself, both absolutely and immutably, through his nature; whence it is called natural worship; and also by hypothesis, and in some measure mutably, through the free determination of his will; this worship is called instituted. Likewise God has also prohibited certain things necessarily and immutably, and others freely and mutably.

units.la: XXVII. Concessio, sive permissio ethica, est rerum mediarum. Concessio de Rebus, permissio de Actionibus magis accommodatè dicitur. Circa omnes tales actùs tenendæ sunt hæ Regulæ: ut fiant 1. Ex fide, & cum certâ persuasione, quod talis actus sit licitus, ac nos in eo etiàm Deo grati & accepti per Christum.
units.tr: XXVII. Concession, or ethical permission, is said of indifferent things; concession is more fittingly said of things, permission of actions. Concerning all such acts the following rules are to be observed, that they be done: (1) from faith, and with the certain persuasion that such an act is lawful, and that we are also thereby pleasing and acceptable to God through Christ.

units.la: 2. Ex charitate, & citra aliorum scandalum, vel incommodum. 3. Sanctè, in gloriam Dei. Rom. xiv, 23. Quod ex fide non est, peccatum est. 15. Si propter escam tuam frater tuus tristitiâ afficitur, non jam secundùm charitatem ambulas. Tit. 1, 15. Omnia munda mundis: pollutis autem & incredulis nihil est mundum. 1 Cor. viii, 13. Si esca offendiculo est fratri meo, non edam carnes in æternum, ne sim offendiculo fratri meo. x, 31. Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Col. iii, 17. Adeo ut nullus actus in individuo sit indifferens. Omnium & singulorum reddenda erit ratio: 2 Cor. v, 10. usque ad verbum otiosum: Matth. xii, 36.
units.tr: (2) From charity, and without scandal or inconvenience to others. (3) Holily, to the glory of God. Rom. 14:23: "Whatever is not of faith is sin." 14:15: "If because of your food your brother is grieved, you no longer walk according to charity." Tit. 1:15: "To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure." 1 Cor. 8:13: "If food is a stumbling block to my brother, I will eat no flesh forever, lest I be a stumbling block to my brother." 10:31: "Do all to the glory of God." Col. 3:17. So that no single act is indifferent in itself. An account of all and of each will have to be rendered: 2 Cor. 5:10, even to the idle word: Matth. 12:36.

units.la: XXVIII. Nullum per se malum præcipere, vel ethicè permittere, potest Deus: sed ubi physicè permissum, & à creaturâ commissum est, punit necessario. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 56. Nec ullo modo ejus auctor esse potest: Jac. 1, 13. Deus tentari malis non potest, nec quemquam tentat.
units.tr: XXVIII. God can command nothing evil in itself, nor permit it ethically; but where it has been physically permitted and committed by a creature, he necessarily punishes it. See above, chapter 4, thesis 56. Nor can he in any way be its author: James 1:13: "God cannot be tempted with evil, nor does he tempt anyone."

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: XXIX. Revelationes credendorum, Praecepta agendorum, & Prohibitiones fugiendorum, Deus plenissime Verbo suo expressit, sive διαθήκην sive χρηματισμὸν: Matth. xv, 9. Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, quae sunt mandata hominum. Luc. x, 25, 26. In Lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis: &c. Interim Exempla cum laude proposita, Praeceptis accensenda sunt; cum vituperio autem, vel redargutione commemorata, Prohibitionibus sunt annumeranda. Quin & Praemia prudenter observanda, cumque Praeceptis & Promissionibus conferenda sunt: Poenae autem similiter ad Prohibitiones & Comminationes referendae. Rom. xv, 4. Nam quae ante scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam ante scripta sunt. i, 18. Patet ira Dei e coelo adversus omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum. ii, 4. Benignitatem Dei ad resipiscentiam te deducere. Vide etiam 1 Cor. x, 11. xi, 1. Jac. v, 10, 11. iv, 3, 4, 5. Hag. i, 5, 6, ii, 19, 20.
units.tr: XXIX. God has most fully expressed in his Word the revelations of things to be believed, the precepts of things to be done, and the prohibitions of things to be avoided, whether under the name of covenant (διαθήκη) or of oracular communication (χρηματισμός): Matt. 15:9, "In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." Luke 10:25-26, "What is written in the Law? How do you read it?" etc. Meanwhile, examples set forth with praise are to be reckoned among the precepts, and those recorded with blame or rebuke are to be counted among the prohibitions. Indeed, rewards are also to be carefully noted and compared with the precepts and promises; punishments, likewise, are to be referred to the prohibitions and threatenings. Rom. 15:4, "For whatever things were written before were written for our instruction." 1:18, "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men." 2:4, "The goodness of God leads you to repentance." See also 1 Cor. 10:11; 11:1; James 5:10-11; 4:3-5; Hag. 1:5-6; 2:19-20.

units.la: XXX. Concessio, licet omnis negativa censeri possit, quia istic neque Praeceptio neque Prohibitio eatenus facta est; distribuitur tamen in expressam, & tacitam.
units.tr: XXX. A permission, although every permission may be regarded as negative, since in it neither a precept nor a prohibition has been given, is nevertheless divided into express and tacit.

units.la: Expressa occurrit Gen. ii, 16. De fructu omnis arboris hujus horti libere comedes, &c. Levit. xi, 2, 3. Haec sunt animalia, quae vos comedetis, &c. 9, 10. Act. x, 15. Quae Deus purificavit, tu ne polluito. Rom. xiv, 14. Col. ii, 14, 16, 17; 20, 21. Tit. i, 15. Gal. iv, 1-7; 9, 10. Deut. xxiii, 20.
units.tr: An express permission occurs at Gen. 2:16, "Of every tree of this garden you may freely eat," etc. Lev. 11:2-3, "These are the animals which you shall eat," etc.; 9-10. Acts 10:15, "What God has cleansed, do not you call common." Rom. 14:14. Col. 2:14, 16-17, 20-21. Titus 1:15. Gal. 4:1-7, 9-10. Deut. 23:20.

units.la: Tacita per S. Scripturae perfectionem colligitur, ubi nec praeceptio nec prohibitio facta est.
units.tr: A tacit permission is gathered from the perfection of Holy Scripture, where neither a precept nor a prohibition has been given.

units.la: XXXI. Interim in Concessionibus quibusdam singulares circumstantiae inferunt obligationem agendi id quod concessum est: ut de Matrimonio, Gen. i, 28. Foetificate, & augescite, & implete terram: si conferatur cum 1 Cor. vii, 7. Unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, &c. & ibid. verf. 37. Nonnullae etiam ad forum Soli tantum pertinent: ut de libello Repudii; Deut. xxiv, 1, cum Matth. xix, 7, 8. Ex superioribus patet, Permissiones ethicas quandoque exprimi eodem modo ac Præcepta; à quibus tamen per circumstantias, & aliorum locorum collationem, distingui debent. Quin & Permissiones solùm physicæ simili modo interdùm exprimuntur; ut Num. xxi, 20, cum 32. Surge, abi cum iis. 1 Reg. 22,22. Exi, & fac ita. Joh. xiii, 27. Quod facis, mox facito.
units.tr: XXXI. Yet in some permissions particular circumstances imply an obligation to do what has been permitted: as concerning marriage, Gen. 1:28, "Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth"; if this is compared with 1 Cor. 7:7, "Each has his own gift from God," etc., and ibid. verse 37. Some also pertain only to the civil court: as concerning the bill of divorce, Deut. 24:1, compared with Matt. 19:7-8. From what has been said above it is clear that ethical permissions are sometimes expressed in the same way as precepts, from which, however, they must be distinguished by circumstances and by comparison with other passages. Indeed, merely physical permissions are sometimes expressed in a similar way, as at Num. 21:20 compared with 32, "Rise up, go with them." 1 Kings 22:22, "Go out and do so." John 13:27, "What you are doing, do quickly."

units.la: XXXIL. Pro φιλανθρωπία suâ Deus in Præceptis etiàm aliquando eorum honestatem, æquitatem, justitiam, & utilitatem proponit: undè Consilia appellantur; ut Apoc. iii, 18. Consilium do tibi, ut emas à me aurum igni exploratum, &c. Psal. xvi, 7. Benedicam Iehovæ, qui dedit consilium mihi, &c. Hæc absurdè Pontificii accipiunt de Officiis non mandatis communiter; sed quibusdam particulariter solum propositis, ad persectionem Euangelicam: quæ autem putant sic fieri, ea opera supererogationis vocant. Nos non nisi speciali modo exprimendi à Præceptis differre dicimus.
units.tr: XXXII. In his philanthropy God sometimes also sets forth in his precepts their honesty, equity, justice, and usefulness; whence they are called counsels: as at Rev. 3:18, "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire," etc.; Ps. 16:7, "I will bless the LORD, who has given me counsel," etc. The Papists absurdly take these things to be duties not commanded generally, but proposed only particularly to some, for Evangelical perfection; and those things which they think are done in this way they call works of supererogation. We say only that they differ from precepts in the special mode of expression.

units.la: Similiter Obtestationes, sive Contestationes, adhibentur; ejusmodi expressiones Præceptorum & Prohibitionum, in quibus Deus ad pleniorem justitiæ & æquitatis suæ demonstrationem, ipsas Creaturas rationales, & earum conscientiam, aliasque analogicè & suo modo, testes advocat. Deuter. iv, 26. Contestor contra vos hodie cœlum & terram, &c. xxx, 18,19. Psal. lxxxi, 9. Audi populus mi, & Contestabor te. Jes. 1,4. v, 3, 4.
units.tr: Similarly, adjurations, or solemn attestations, are employed; these are expressions of precepts and prohibitions in which God, to a fuller demonstration of his justice and equity, calls to witness the rational creatures themselves, and their conscience, and others analogically and in their own way. Deut. 4:26, "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today," etc.; 30:18-19. Ps. 81:9, "Hear, my people, and I will testify against you." Isa. 1:4; 5:3-4.

units.la: Occurrunt etiam alicubi Vota, sive Optationes; quibus Deus ἀνθρωποπαθῶς indicat, quàm bona sit, Hominibusque appetenda, & quantoperè ipsi Deo probetur, mandata obedientia; adhæc quomodo illi præstandæ occasiones, adminicula, & incitamenta plurima suppeditet; nec non quàm serio velit nexum obedientiæ istius cum præmio promisso. Psal. lxxxi, 14, 15. O si populus meus auscultâsset mihi, &c. Vide etiàm Deut. v, 29. Itâ Christus, Luc. xix, 41,42. cùm appropinquaret Hierosolymis, Visâ urbe, flevit super eâ, dicens; Si vel tu nôffes hoc saltem tuo die, quæ ad pacem tuam pertinent! Confer 2 Cor. v, 20.
units.tr: Wishes, or desires, also occur somewhere; by these God, in an anthropopathic manner, indicates how good obedience to the commandments is, and how much it is to be sought by men, and how greatly it is approved by God himself; further, how he supplies many opportunities, aids, and incitements for rendering it; and also how earnestly he wishes the connection of this obedience with the promised reward. Ps. 81:14-15, "O that my people had listened to me," etc. See also Deut. 5:29. So Christ, Luke 19:41-42, when he drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, wept over it, saying, "If only you had known on this your day the things that belong to your peace!" Compare 2 Cor. 5:20.

units.la: XXXIII. Actûs morales à realibus accuratè distinguendi sunt: hi per illos non excluduntur; sed ut præstetur obedientia, accedere debent. Alias tantùm obligatio ad officium infertur, & voluntas mandati innotescit; cui dùm scientes & volentes refragantur homines, fiunt inexcusabiles: Ezech, II, 4, 5. Ut sciant Prophetam fuisse in medio sui. 2 Cor. II, 14. 15, 16. - His quidem odor mortis ad mortem.
units.tr: XXXIII. Moral acts must be carefully distinguished from real ones: the latter are not excluded by the former; but in order that obedience may be rendered, they ought to accompany them. Otherwise only obligation to duty is brought in, and the will of the command becomes known; when men, knowing and willing, resist it, they become inexcusable: Ezek. 2:4-5, "that they may know that a prophet has been among them." 2 Cor. 2:14-16, "To the one indeed the odor of death to death."

units.la: XXXIV. Ad Praxin, 1. Providentiam Dei piè in omnibus contemplemur, & alios similiter excitemus: Psal. xciv, 8, 9, 10. Jef. xl, 26. Matth. vi, 26, 30. Act. xiv, 17. xvii, 24, 28.
units.tr: XXXIV. For practice: (1) let us piously contemplate the providence of God in all things, and similarly stir up others: Ps. 94:8-10; Isa. 40:26; Matt. 6:26-30; Acts 14:17; 17:24, 28.

units.la: 2. Sub manû Omnipotentis humiliemur: Jac. iv, 7, 10. 1 Petr. v, 6.
units.tr: (2) Let us humble ourselves under the hand of the Almighty: James 4:7, 10; 1 Pet. 5:6.

units.la: 3. Justissimum Dei Imperium in omnia agnoscamus, prædicemus: Job. 1, 21. Psal. cxv, 3. Dan. iv, 35.
units.tr: (3) Let us acknowledge and proclaim the most just dominion of God over all things: Job 1:21; Ps. 115:3; Dan. 4:35.

units.la: 4. Eum toto animo revereamur, qui intimè omnibus præ est, & in omnibus operatur: Act. xvi, 25, 28. Psal. xxxiii, 15. In Prosperis gratitudinem præstemus: Psal. cvii, 8. cxvi, 12. cxlv, 10, 15, 16. Jac. i, 17. 1 Tim. vi, 17: Amemus: Psal. cxvi, 1. lv, 33. In Adversis coram Ipso patientes simus: Hebr. xii, 5, &c. Job. 1, 21. 2 Sam. xv, 10, 11.
units.tr: (4) Let us revere with our whole soul him who is inwardly over all and works in all: Acts 17:25, 28; Ps. 33:15. In prosperity let us render gratitude: Ps. 107:8; 116:12; 145:10, 15-16; James 1:17; 1 Tim. 6:17. Let us love: Ps. 116:1; 55:23. In adversities let us be patient before him: Heb. 12:5, etc.; Job 1:21; 2 Sam. 15:10-11.

units.la: 5. Mediis ne nimiùm tribuamus: Psal. cxxvii, 1, 2. 2 Chron. xv, 12. Matth. iv, 4. Neque tamen temerè negligamus: Actor. xxvii. 31. Matth. iv, 7. 2 Reg. v, 13.
units.tr: (5) Let us not attribute too much to means: Ps. 127:1-2; 2 Chron. 15:12; Matt. 4:4. Yet let us not carelessly neglect them: Acts 27:31; Matt. 4:7; 2 Kings 5:13.

units.la: 6. Omnem folicitudinem in Deum devolvamus: Psal. lv, 23. 1 Petr. v, 7. Hebr. xiii, 5, 6, Psal. xxiii, 1. 4, 6. 1 Sam. xvii, 37. 2 Tim. iv, 17, 18. Eph. iii, 19, 20. Rom. viii, 28. Gen. L, 20, xxii, 8.
7. Providentiam moralem, vitæ nostræ regulam, respiciamus, & observemus perpetuò: Psal. cxix, 4, 5, 17, 18, 19, 33-37.
units.tr: (7) Let us regard and constantly observe moral providence, the rule of our life: Ps. 119:4-5, 17-19, 33-37.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De Fœdere Legali.
units.tr: Of the Legal Covenant.

units.la: Jus. Injuria. Quis illud postulet. Quæ eorum capacia.
units.tr: Right. Injury. Who may claim it? What things are capable of it?

units.la: 1. Jus Dei: tùm naturale; tùm positivum. Jus naturale respectû nostri. Institutum. Quid JCtis Jus naturæ. Gentium. Civile. 2. Jus creaturarum rationalium. Magistratuum. Subditorum. 3. Lex. Divina. Æterna. Humana. 4. Jus & Lex non contraria. Societatis civilis initium non à mutuo metû. Norma juris non defensio vitæ & membrorum. Voluntas non absolutè subjicienda Hominibus. Non omnis Pœna propter peccantium correctionem. c. Hobb. 5. Lex Divina. Cerimonialis. Politica. 6. Moralis. Decalogus. Lex charitatis. Actus religiosi circa proximum. 7. Argumenta singulorum Præceptorum. 8. Integra Lex Moralis non est Juris ipsi Deo naturalis. 9. Attamen Juris nobis naturalis. Obj. solv. 10. Eadem fuit ante Mosen. 11. Probatur ampliùs inductione, de Præceptis tab. post. 12. Similiter de Præceptis tab. pr. 13. Objectiones de Sabbatho solv. 14. Jus naturale primævum. Secundarium. 15. Eadem Lex Moralis adhùc obtinet sub N. T. 16. Etiam quartum Præceptum. Obj. solv. 17. Sententiæ Pontif. Socin. Anabapt. &c. 18. Idolatria Pontif. in Angelis, refutatur. 19. Non rogandi, ut pro nobis intercedant. Obj. solv. 20. In Christo, secundùm hum. nat. B. Virgine Maria. Sanctis demortuis: Patronis: Canonizatis 21. Refutatur. 22. Non rogandi, ut pro nobis intercedant. Obj. solv. 23. In Pontifice Rom. 24. In Pane eucharistico. 25. In Cruce. 26. In Reliquiis. 27. In Imaginibus. 28. Refut. & Obj. solv. 29. In Rebus consecratis. Agnis Dei· 30. In Divis chimaericis, &c. Sanctis non-sanctis. 31. Magia datur, c. Neo-Sadduc. Obj. solv. 32. Papatui vere impingitur. 33. Non omnis ignorantia est inculpata. 34. Species ejus vitiosæ. Obj. solv. 35. An sola Haeresis posset Hominem subjicere aeternæ damnationi. 36. An Haeretici, ut sic, extremo supplicio afficiendi, 37. Odium adversus Deum. Obj. solv. 38. Falsa gratiarum actio. Salutatio Angelica, Pontif. 39. Non orandum pro mortuis: c. eosd. Obj. solv. 40. Orationem Dominicam posse usurpari pro formula precandi; c. Brown. 41. Rectè appellamus Patrem nostrum. Et rogamus, ut Veniat Regnum Ipsius. c. Muhamm. 42. Quis ὁ ἀγτῶ ὁ ἐπιῶσι. Obj. solv. 43. Aliæ explicationes. 44. Remissio nostra in petitione quintâ, qualis; & quem respectum habeat ad Remissionem Dei. 45. Doxologia verè canonica: c. Pontif. 45. Jejunium. Non consistit in discrimine ciborum: c. eosd. 46. Objectiones solvuntur. 47. Non est per se cultus religiosus. Obj. solv. 48. Non opus poenale, & satisfactorium justitiæ Divinæ. Nec debent esse ordinaria absoluta & perpetua. c. eosd. Obj. solv. 49. Inanis eorundem verborum repetitio. 50. Votum. Soli Deo vovendum. 51. Ejus materia. Vota Papistica. Monastica 52. Male Socinian contendunt, Christum primo Præcepto addidisse mandatum generale de Precibus Deo faciendis. 53. Formulam Orationis Dominicæ. 54. & Mandatum de Ipso adorando. 55. Imagines in secundo Decalogi præcepto. Pontificiorum refutantur. 56. Objectiones solv. 57. Non usurpanda, nec asservanda in talem usum. 58. Imagines creaturarum. 59. Usus illicitus. 60. Non habendæ pro libris Laicorum. 61. Εθελοθρησκεία. Pontificiorum. 62. Secundum Præceptum à Christo non auctum: c. Socin. 63. Secundum vere distinctum à primo: c. Pontif. 64. Perperàm statuunt Socin. Tertio præcepto additum esse à Christo, Ne temerè juremus, &c. 65. Non omne Juramentum (sub N. T. illicitum: c. Anabapt. Obj. solv. 66. Male item Socin. Additum illi Juramentum per Christum. 67. Non jurandum per Sanctos, aliaisve creaturas; c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 68. Festa proprie dicta non sunt sub N. T. observanda; nedum in honorem Sanctorum: c. eosd. Obj. solv. 69.
