Qui Pater & Mater in quinto Præcepto. 70. Liberis non licet vovere vitam Monasticam, invitis Parentibus: c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 71. Nec Matrimonium sic contrahere. 72. Christianus Magistratui Politico parere potest; quin & eum gerere, bonâ conscientiâ: c. Anabapt. 73. Objectiones solvuntur. 74. Aliquando etiam in judicio agere licet adversus fratrem, apud Magistratum fidelem. Obj. solv. 75. Magistratus honore ac dignitate supra bus nostris audivimus, - Te manu Tua gentes expulisse: Per Te Hostes cornu feriemus. &c. xlvi, 9, 10, 11. Agite, videte opera Jehovae! ut disponat desolationes in terra, faciens, ut cessent Bella-, arcum perfringat, & truncet hastam, &c. Prov. xxi, 31. Equus aptatur ad diem praelii, sed Jehovae est ipsa salus. Confer Exod. xv, 3, &c. ac porro historiam Bellorum Domini, & promissiones de hostibus in manus Israelitarum tradendis, &c.
units.tr: 1. The right of God: both natural and positive. Natural right with respect to us. Instituted. What the jurists call natural law, law of nations, civil law. 2. The right of rational creatures: of magistrates, of subjects. 3. Law: divine, eternal, human. 4. Right and law are not opposed. The beginning of civil society is not from mutual fear. The norm of right is not the defence of life and limbs. The will is not to be absolutely subjected to men. Not every punishment is for the correction of sinners. Against Hobbes. 5. Divine law: ceremonial, political. 6. Moral law: the Decalogue, the law of charity, religious acts towards our neighbour. 7. Arguments for the individual precepts. 8. The whole moral law is not natural right belonging to God himself. 9. Yet it is natural right for us. Objection answered. 10. The same law was in force before Moses. 11. This is further proved by induction, concerning the precepts of the second table. 12. Similarly concerning the precepts of the first table. 13. Objections about the Sabbath answered. 14. Natural right: primeval and secondary. 15. The same moral law still holds under the New Testament. 16. Also the fourth precept. Objection answered. 17. Opinions of the Papists, Socinians, Anabaptists, etc. 18. Papist idolatry concerning angels is refuted. 19. We should not ask them to intercede for us. Objection answered. 20. In Christ according to his human nature; the Blessed Virgin Mary; dead saints; patrons; the canonized. 21. Refuted. 22. We should not ask them to intercede for us. Objection answered. 23. In the Roman Pontiff. 24. In the eucharistic bread. 25. In the Cross. 26. In relics. 27. In images. 28. Refutation and answer to objections. 29. In consecrated things; the Lambs of God. 30. In chimerical divinities, etc.; in saints and non-saints. 31. Magic is given (against the Neo-Sadducees). Objection answered. 32. This truly strikes at Papacy. 33. Not all ignorance is blameless. 34. Its faulty kinds. Objection answered. 35. Whether heresy alone could subject a man to eternal damnation. 36. Whether heretics, as such, are to be punished with the extreme penalty. 37. Hatred against God. Objection answered. 38. False thanksgiving. The Angelic Salutation, Papist. 39. We should not pray for the dead; the same people. Objection answered. 40. The Lord's Prayer may be used as a formula of prayer (against Browne). 41. We rightly call him our Father, and we ask that his Kingdom may come (against Muhammad). 42. What is the ἐπιούσιος bread [τὸν ἄρτον τὸν ἐπιούσιον]? Objection answered. 43. Other explanations. 44. Our forgiveness in the fifth petition, of what kind, and what regard it has to God's forgiveness. 45. The doxology is truly canonical (against the Papists). 45. Fasting. It does not consist in the distinction of foods (against the same). 46. Objections are answered. 47. It is not in itself religious worship. Objection answered. 48. It is not a penal work or a satisfaction to divine justice, nor ought it to be an absolute and perpetual ordinance (against the same). Objection answered. 49. The empty repetition of the same words. 50. A vow: to be made to God alone. 51. Its matter: Papist vows, monastic vows. 52. The Socinians wrongly contend that Christ added to the first precept a general command about making prayers to God. 53. The form of the Lord's Prayer. 54. And the command to worship him. 55. Images in the second precept of the Decalogue: the Papists' views are refuted. 56. Objections answered. 57. They are not to be used, nor kept for such a use. 58. Images of creatures. 59. Unlawful use. 60. They are not to be regarded as books for the laity. 61. Will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] of the Papists. 62. The second precept was not enlarged by Christ (against the Socinians). 63. The second is truly distinct from the first (against the Papists). 64. The Socinians wrongly hold that a third precept was added by Christ, "Thou shalt not swear rashly," etc. 65. Not every oath is unlawful under the New Testament (against the Anabaptists). Objection answered. 66. Likewise the Socinians are wrong that the oath "by Christ" was added to it. 67. One must not swear by saints or other creatures (against the Papists). Objection answered. 68. Festivals properly so called are not to be observed under the New Testament, much less in honour of saints (against the same). Objection answered. 69. Who are father and mother in the fifth precept. 70. Children may not vow the monastic life against the wishes of their parents (against the Papists). Objection answered. 71. Nor may they contract marriage in that way. 72. A Christian may obey the civil magistrate, and indeed may hold office with a good conscience (against the Anabaptists). 73. The objections are answered. 74. Sometimes it is also lawful to bring a suit against a brother before a faithful magistrate. Objection answered. 75. The magistrate is set above us in honour and dignity. [Scripture passages:] "We have heard with our ears... Through Thee we shall push back our enemies; through Thee we shall gore our foes with the horn," etc. Ps. 46:9–11: "Come, behold the works of Jehovah, who makes desolations in the earth, causing wars to cease, who breaks the bow and cuts the spear in two," etc. Prov. 21:31: "The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but salvation is Jehovah's." Compare Exod. 15:3, etc., and further the history of the wars of the Lord, and the promises that enemies would be delivered into the hands of Israel, etc.

units.la: 5. Periodi Imperiorum, Regnorum, & Rerum publicarum: Dan. II, 22, Transfert Reges, & constituit Reges. v, 21, &c.
units.tr: 5. The cycles of empires, kingdoms, and commonwealths. Dan. 2:22: "He removes kings and sets up kings." Dan. 5:21, etc.

units.la: 6. Minima: ut Locustae, Pediculi, &c. Exod. viii, 17. x, 12. Deut. xxviii, 38. Joel. 1, 4. Act. xii, 23. Capilli: Matth. x, 30. Herbae; vi, 30.
units.tr: 6. The smallest creatures, such as locusts, lice, etc. Exod. 8:17; 10:12. Deut. 28:38. Joel 1:4. Acts 12:23. Hairs: Matt. 10:30. Grass: Matt. 6:30.

units.la: 7. Etiam Mala tristia: Am. iii, 6. An erit malum in civitate, quod Jehovah non efficiat. Threnor. iii, 37, 38, 39. Ex ore Excelsi an non prodit malum quodque, & bonum? &c. Hebr. xii, 6, 7. 1 Cor. xi, 32. 2 Thess. 1, 6, 8, 9.
units.tr: 7. Even grievous evils: Amos 3:6, "Shall there be evil in a city which the LORD hath not done?" Lam. 3:37–39, "Who is it that speaketh, and it cometh to pass, when the Lord commandeth it not? Out of the mouth of the Most High proceedeth not evil and good?" etc. Heb. 12:6–7; 1 Cor. 11:32; 2 Thess. 1:6, 8–9.

units.la: XVI. Major difficultas est in Gubernatione Malorum impium.
units.tr: XVI. The greatest difficulty lies in God's governing of the wicked deeds of the impious.

units.la: Haec Deus interdum impedit: Genes. xx, 6. Cohibui te, ne peccares in Me. 31, 7. Non permisit ei Deus, ut damno afficeret me. 1 Cor. x, 13. Act. xviii, 9, 10. Saepe physice permittit: Psal. lxxxi, 13. Dimisi eos ambulare ex sententia animi sui, dicens, Abeant cum pravis consiliis suis! Actor. xiv, 16. Sivit omnes Gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. Confer Matth. 8, 31, 32. Et quidem consulto, ac volens: Rom. ix, 18. Quem vult, indurat.
units.tr: God sometimes hinders these deeds: Genes. 20:6, I restrained you, so that you would not sin against Me. 31:7, God did not allow him to harm me. 1 Cor. 10:13. Act. 18:9, 10. He often permits them physically: Psal. 81:13, I let them walk according to the desires of their own heart, saying, Let them go with their wicked counsels! Actor. 14:16, He allowed all nations to walk in their own ways. Compare Matth. 8:31, 32. And indeed he does this deliberately and willingly: Rom. 9:18, Whom he wills, he hardens.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Defectum moralem Deus relinquit in actu illo subistrato: complexum vero peccaminosum sanctissimé & sapientissimé limitat, ac dirigit in finem bonum. Hinc efficax Permissio dicitur.
units.tr: God leaves the moral defect in that act, which has been undertaken, but he most holily and wisely limits the sinful whole and directs it to a good end. Hence it is called efficacious permission.

units.la: Probatur autem 1. de Objectorum, aliarumque circumstantiarum determinatione, ex allegatis th. 14. §. 1. Adde 2 Sam. xvi, 10, 11. Jehovah edixit, Maledic Davidi. 1 Reg. 22. 20, 23. Dixit Jehovah, quis pellicet, &c.? Tum dixit; Pellicies; & praevalebis: exi, & fac ita. &c. Exod. 4. 21. 9. 12. Psal. cv, 25. Jes. 19, 14. 2.
units.tr: This is proved, first, from the determination of the objects and of the other circumstances, from what was alleged in thesis 14, §1. Add 2 Sam. 16:10, 11, Jehovah has commanded, Let him curse David. 1 Kings 22:20, 23, Jehovah said, Who will entice, etc.? Then he said, You will entice, and you will prevail: go out and do so, etc. Exod. 4:21; 9:12. Psal. 105:25. Isa. 19:14; 2.

units.la: 2. De Gradibus, vide th, 14. §.2. Adde 1 Cor. x,13. Deus non sinet vos tentari supra id quod potestis. Actor. II, 27. ex Psal. xvi, 10.
units.tr: Second, concerning the degrees, see thesis 14, §2. Add 1 Cor. 10:13, God will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear. Acts 2:27, from Psal. 16:10.

units.la: 3. De Finium ordinatione: Jos. xi, 20. A Jehova fuit, quod obstirmabant cor suum; ut interneccioni devoveret illas. 1 Cor. x,13. Una cum tentatione præstabit exitum, ut possitis sufferre. Jac. v,11. Beatos prædicamus eos, qui sustinent. Tolerantiam Job audistis, & finem Domini vidistis. Genef. xlv, 8. Exod. xiv,17. 1 Reg. xii,15. Actor. iii,18.
units.tr: Third, concerning the ordering of ends: Josh. 11:20, It was from Jehovah that they hardened their hearts, so that he might devote them to destruction. 1 Cor. 10:13, Together with the temptation he will provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it. Jas. 5:11, We count those blessed who endure. You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end intended by the Lord. Gen. 45:8. Exod. 14:17. 1 Kings 12:15. Acts 3:18.

units.la: XVIII. Specialius peccata peccatis punit Deus:
units.tr: XVIII. God punishes sins by means of sins, more particularly:

units.la: quandoque in aliis: 2 Sam. xii, 11, 12 Eo quod sprevisti me, - Suscitaturus sum contra te malum e domo tua; &c. Jud. ix,23,24. Immisit Deus affectum malum inter Abimelechum & Sichemitas: - ut rediret injuria, &c. 1 Reg. xi, 26. Quandoque in ipsis: 2 Thess. II, 10, 11, 12. Propterea quod amorem veritatis non receperunt,-ideo mittet eis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio, &c. Rom. 1, 24,-27.
units.tr: sometimes in others: 2 Sam. 12:11, 12, Because you have despised me, … I will raise up evil against you from your own house, etc. Judg. 9:23, 24, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the Shechemites … so that the wrong would be avenged, etc. 1 Kings 11:26. Sometimes in the sinners themselves: 2 Thess. 2:10, 11, 12, Because they did not receive the love of the truth … therefore God will send them the working of error, so that they believe the lie, etc. Rom. 1:24–27.

units.la: XIX. Occurrunt interim Excæcatio & Induratio.
units.tr: XIX. Blindness and hardening are met with here.

units.la: Illa dicit privationem sapientiæ spiritualis, adeo ut creatura cæco impetu deinceps ruat in peccatum & exitium. Hæc vero dicit privationem flexionis & conformationis ad normam Legis Divinæ. Jef. vi, 9, 10. I, ut dicas populo isti: audite indesinenter; at ne intelligatis: & videte indesinenter, neque cognoscatis. Fac, ut pinguescat cor populi istius, &c. Rom. 1, 21, 22, 28. Vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est cor, &c.
units.tr: The former denotes the privation of spiritual wisdom, so that the creature thereafter rushes headlong into sin and ruin with blind impetus. The latter, however, denotes the privation of bending and conforming to the rule of the divine Law. Isa. 6:9, 10, Go, and say to this people: Listen continually, but do not understand; and look continually, but do not perceive. Make the heart of this people fat, etc. Rom. 1:21, 22, 28, They became vain in their reasonings, and their heart was darkened, etc.

units.la: Utraque consiederari potest vel ut actus Dei, vel ut creaturæ. Deo autem tribuitur aliquando solum negative; atque ità simpliciter negatur collatio sapientiæ, & flexionis ad normam: aliquando positive, prout Deus gubernatione judiciali propter antecedens demeritum creaturam rationalem punit spirituali cæcitate aut duritiâ majore & graviore, quam prius in eâ extitit.
units.tr: Both can be considered either as acts of God or as acts of the creature. To God, however, they are ascribed sometimes only negatively, and thus simply the withholding of wisdom and of bending to the rule is denied; sometimes positively, insofar as God, by judicial governance, on account of prior demerit, punishes the rational creature with a greater and more grievous spiritual blindness or hardness than it had before.

units.la: Sed quemadmodum à Deo procedit, pœnalis, est: quatenus tenùs autem in Creaturis subjectivè inest, est culpabilis. Rom. ix, 17, 18. Dicit Scriptura Pharaoni, Ad hoc ipsum excitavi te, ut ostendam in te potentiam meam, &c.
units.tr: But insofar as it proceeds from God, it is penal; insofar as it is subjectively present in creatures, it is culpable. Rom. 9:17, 18. Scripture says to Pharaoh, For this very purpose I have raised you up, so that I may show my power in you, etc.

units.la: XX. In Hominibus protoplastis, ut & in Diabolis primùm peccantibus, Deus isto tempore negative, actualem usum sapientiæ & sanctimoniæ non excitavit. In posteris autem cœcitas & duritia tùm habitualiter, vel nativa, vel acquisita spectatur; tum actualiter. Nativa pertinet ad Peccatum originale. Acquisita dicit nativæ corruptionis incrementum ratione graduum, per crebros actùs & consuetudinem peccandi. Actualis denique in actibus secundis cernitur.
units.tr: XX. In the first human beings, and also in the devils who sinned first, God at that time did not, negatively, stir up the actual use of wisdom and holiness. In their posterity, however, blindness and hardness are considered both habitually, either innate or acquired, and actually. The innate pertains to original sin. The acquired denotes the increase of the innate corruption by degrees, through frequent acts and the habit of sinning. The actual, finally, is seen in subsequent acts.

units.la: Utraque in Electos nondum conversos etiàm cadit. Eph. II, 3. Eramus naturâ filii iræ, ut & reliqui. In Regenitis, totalis, & ad finem regnans, aut prævalens, non habet locum: sunt enim Lux in Domino: Eph. v, 8. & habent cor carneum: Ezech. xxxvi, 26. Partialis tamen, eaque sensibilis, in iis etiàm agnoscenda est: Jac. iii, 2. In multis impingimus omnes, 1 Cor. xiii, 9. Ex parte cognoscimus. Hùc pertinet querela, Jef. lxiii, 17. Quare sineres aberrare nos, Iehovah, à viis Tuis? torrefaciens obdurares animum nostrum à reverentiâ Tui?
units.tr: Both also fall upon the elect who are not yet converted. Eph. 2:3, We were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also were. In the regenerate, the total and dominant or prevailing kind has no place: for they are light in the Lord, Eph. 5:8, and they have a heart of flesh, Ezek. 36:26. Yet a partial kind, and that sensible, must be acknowledged in them too: Jas. 3:2, In many things we all stumble. 1 Cor. 13:9, We know in part. To this pertains the complaint of Isa. 63:17, Why, Jehovah, do you let us wander from your ways, and harden our heart so that we do not fear you?

units.la: XXI. Modus Excæcationis & Indurationis, licet occultus, semper tamen justus est.
units.tr: XXI. The mode of blinding and hardening, though hidden, is always nonetheless just.

units.la: Hùc pertinet 1. Non-collatio, imò propter antecedens peccatum justa ablatio, boni habitualis: Rom. i, 21, 24. Tradidit eos Deus cupiditatibus cordium ipsorum ad impuritatem, 26, 27. Fœdis affectibus. 28. In mentem omnis judicii expertem, &c.
units.tr: To this belongs: 1. Non-bestowal, or rather just withdrawal, on account of a prior sin, of habitual good: Rom. i, 21, 24. God gave them up to the lusts of their hearts unto uncleanness; 26, 27. to vile affections; 28. to a mind devoid of all judgment, etc.

units.la: 2. Non-impeditio, imò directio hostium spiritualium, ad talia objecta: ut de Pseudo-prophetis; 1 Reg. xxii, 22, 23, & de Antichristo; 2 Thess. II, 9, 10, 11. Cujus adventus est ex vi illâ efficaci Satanæ, cum omni potentiâ, & signis ac prodigiis mendacibus. - Ideò igitur mittet eis Deus efficacium erroris, &c.
units.tr: 2. Non-hindrance, or rather direction, of spiritual enemies toward such objects: as with false prophets, 1 Kings xxii, 22, 23, and with Antichrist, 2 Thess. ii, 9, 10, 11. Whose coming is by the efficacious power of Satan, with all power, and with lying signs and wonders. - Therefore God will send them a strong delusion, etc.

units.la: 3. Oblatio bonorum, quibus homines suo vitio abuabuntur: ut Occasionum internarum; Exod. 1, 9, 12. Externarum; Genes. xxxvii, 5. Exod. v, 2 Jef. 2, 9. 2 Cor. 11, 16. Item Beneficiorum, erga alios, quibus invident; & erga ipsos, quibus abuntur homines corruptissimi: Tit. 1, 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum. Rom. 11, 4, 5. Et Poenarum, quibus induruntur: Jerem. v, 3. o Iehovah, percutis eos; sed non dolent: consumis eos; renuunt accipere eruditionem; reddunt faciem suam obfirmatiorem petra; renuunt converti.
units.tr: 3. The offering of goods, which men by their own fault abuse: such as internal occasions (Exod. i, 9, 12), external ones (Gen. xxxvii, 5; Exod. v, 2; Isa. ii, 9; 2 Cor. xi, 16). Likewise benefits toward others, which they envy, and toward themselves, which the most corrupt men abuse: Tit. i, 15. To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean. Rom. xi, 4, 5. And punishments, by which they are hardened: Jer. v, 3. O Jehovah, you strike them, but they do not grieve; you consume them; they refuse to receive instruction; they make their faces harder than rock; they refuse to turn.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Ex superioribus patet, non sufficere, si cum Jesuitis, aliisque Pelagianizantibus, in hoc negotio statuatur mera negatio, vel nuda permissio: nam 1. Requiritur saltem positiva providentia ad actum subfratum, & in ordine ad finem.
units.tr: From what has gone before it is plain that it is not enough, as the Jesuits and other Pelagianizers hold in this matter, to posit mere negation or bare permission. For 1. at least a positive providence is required for the act to take place, and with respect to an end.

units.la: 2. Actus judicialis non nisi positive procedit; ob tale demeritum, tali modo.
units.tr: 2. A judicial act proceeds only positively: on account of such a demerit, in such a way.

units.la: 3. Precamur non induci in tentationem: Matth. vi, 13. atque alibi passim occurrunt phrases positivum actum inferentes.
units.tr: 3. We pray not to be led into temptation: Matt. vi, 13. And elsewhere phrases implying a positive act occur everywhere.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Fines, ad quos actus peccaminosi dirigunttur, sunt, 1, Manifestatio Tolerantiae Divinae: Rom. II. 4. & Justitiae, tum in reprobis: ix, 22. Quod si volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, &c. Prov. xvi, 4. tum in ipso Christo: Rom. iii, 25, 26. Ad demonstrationem justitiae suae, &c.
units.tr: The ends toward which sinful acts are directed are: 1. the manifestation of divine forbearance, Rom. ii, 4, and of justice, both in the reprobate (ix, 22: But what if God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, etc. Prov. xvi, 4), and in Christ himself (Rom. iii, 25, 26: To demonstrate his justice, etc.).

units.la: 2. Manifestatio Sapientiae ac Misericordiae Divinae in Electis salvandis: Rom. xi, 31, 32. Conclusit Deus omnes illos in inobedientiam, ut omnium illorum misereatur. O profundas divitias tum Sapientiae, tum Cognitionis Dei! &c. v, 20. Ubi amplificatum est peccatum, ibi superabundavit gratia.
units.tr: 2. The manifestation of divine wisdom and mercy in the elect who are to be saved: Rom. xi, 31, 32. God has shut up all of them in disobedience, that he may have mercy on all of them. O the deep riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! etc. v, 20: where sin was multiplied, there grace did abound all the more.

units.la: 3. Profunda fidelium humiliatio: Matth. ix, 13. Non veni vocatum justos: sed peccatores ad resipiscentiam. Thren. v, 16. Vae nobis, quod peccavimus! iii, 40, 41. Jerem. II, 19.
units.tr: 3. The profound humbling of the faithful: Matt. ix, 13. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Lam. v, 16. Woe to us, that we have sinned! iii, 40, 41. Jer. ii, 19.

units.la: 4. Multiplex fidelium probatio, victoria, & gloria: Luc. xxii, 31. Satanas appetiit vos, quos ventilare sicut triticum: &c. Psal. xxvii, 24. Cùm cadit justus, non dejicitur, &c. 2 Cor. xii, 9. Potentia Mea, per infirmitatem consummatur. Phil. iv. 13. Omnia valeo per Eum, qui me corroborat, nempè Christum, &c. 1 Joh. v, 4. Hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, nempè fides nostra.
units.tr: 4. The manifold trial, victory, and glory of the faithful: Luke xxii, 31. Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you like wheat, etc. Ps. xxvii, 24. When the righteous falls, he is not cast down, etc. 2 Cor. xii, 9. My power is made perfect in weakness. Phil. iv, 13. I can do all things through him who strengthens me, namely Christ, etc. 1 John v, 4. This is the victory that overcomes the world, namely our faith.

units.la: XXIV. Obj. Ex Gubernatione istâ sequi videtur, quod Deus sit causa peccati: ergò ea non est admittenda. Resp. Istud nego. Qui equum vitio proprio claudicantem regit, is nequaquàm est causa claudicationis.
units.tr: XXIV. Objection: from this government it seems to follow that God is the cause of sin; therefore it is not to be admitted. Answer: I deny this. One who guides a horse that limps through its own fault is by no means the cause of the limping.

units.la: Inst. 1. Atqui Deus statuitur actûs peccaminosos dirigere ad sua objecta, & in suos fines: ergò, &c. Resp. Iterùm nego consequentiam. Tota Dei directio sancta est: neque quicquam agit; vel intendit, nisi bonum, & benè; & finem suum sic semper assequitur, licet creaturæ peccantes aliud & aliter sibi propositum habeant.
units.tr: Objection 1: But God is said to direct sinful acts to their objects and to their ends; therefore, etc. Answer: again I deny the consequence. All of God's direction is holy; he does nothing and intends nothing except what is good, and does it well; and so he always attains his end, although sinning creatures have something else, and in another way, proposed to themselves.

units.la: Inst. 2. Multæ phrases asperæ circa hoc negotium occurrunt in scriptis Theologorum. Resp. 1. Communis Ecclesiarum nostrarum confessio ex publicis earum formulis petenda est; non ex privatis scriptis quorundam Theologorum. 2. Nec facilè ex scriptis nostrorum Theologorum in hoc negotio producentur phrases, aut sententiæ, quarum similes, vel æquipollentes, non reperiantur in SS. Literis; aut etiàm similes, vel duriores, in scriptis ipsorum Adversariorum.
units.tr: Objection 2: Many harsh phrases about this matter occur in the writings of theologians. Answer 1: The common confession of our churches is to be sought in their public formularies, not in the private writings of certain theologians. 2: Nor will phrases or statements easily be produced from the writings of our theologians on this matter for which like or equivalent ones cannot be found in Holy Scripture, or even similar or harsher ones in the writings of the adversaries themselves.

units.la: XXV. Providentia moralis vel latè vel strictè sumitur. Priori modo ad eam pertinet omnis motio objectiva, & tropica, sive metaphorica, per externa signa, aliaque objecta; & sic ad Bestias se etiàm extendit. Posteriori modo versatur circa Creaturas tantùm rationales; & quidem sic, ut istæ, earumque actiones, ab illâ dependeant in genere moris.
units.tr: XXV. Moral providence is taken either broadly or narrowly. In the former sense, to it belongs every objective and tropical motion, that is, metaphorical, through external signs and other objects; and in this sense it also extends to beasts. In the latter sense it is concerned only with rational creatures, and indeed in such a way that these, and their actions, depend upon it in the genus of morals.

units.la: Actûs hujus Providentiæ vel spectant veritates agnoscendas & credendas, vel officia à nobis præstanda. Veritates illas respicit Divina revelatio explicatoria &c. & assertoria ; de quâ fup. cap. 1. th. 26; 32. & cap. 2. th.2, 4; 8,9.
units.tr: The acts of this providence concern either truths to be recognized and believed, or duties to be performed by us. Divine revelation, explanatory, etc., and assertory, concerns those truths; on which see above, ch. i, th. 26, 32, and ch. ii, th. 2, 4, 8, 9.

units.la: Ad Officia præstanda pertinent primario Præcepta, Promissiones, & Præmia ; secundario etiàm Concessiones : ad vitia fugienda Prohibitiones, Comminationes, & Pœnæ.
units.tr: To the performing of duties belong primarily Precepts, Promises, and Rewards, and secondarily also Concessions; to the shunning of vices belong Prohibitions, Threats, and Punishments.

units.la: XXVI. Præcepit Deus cultum sibi convenientem, tùm absolutè & immutabiliter, per naturam suam ; unde cultus naturalis vocatur : tùm ex hyphotesi, & quodammodò mutabiliter, per liberam voluntatis suæ determinationem ; qui cultus institutus nuncupatur. Similiter etiam Deus prohibuit quædam necessariò, & immutabiliter ; alia liberè, & mutabiliter.
units.tr: XXVI. God commands the worship fitting to himself, both absolutely and immutably, through his nature (whence it is called natural worship), and both by hypothesis and in some measure mutably, through the free determination of his will (which is called instituted worship). Likewise God has forbidden certain things necessarily and immutably, and others freely and mutably.

units.la: XXVII. Concessio, sive permissio ethica, est rerum mediarum. Concessio de Rebus, permissio de Actionibus magis accommodatè dicitur. Circa omnes tales actùs tenendæ sunt hæ Regulæ: ut fiant 1. Ex fide, & cum certâ perfuasione, quod talis actus sit licitus, ac nos in eo etiàm Deo grati & accepti per Christum.
units.tr: XXVII. Concession, or ethical permission, concerns indifferent things. "Concession" is more properly used of things, "permission" of actions. Concerning all such acts the following rules are to be observed, that they be done: 1. from faith, and with a firm persuasion that such an act is lawful, and that in it we are also pleasing and acceptable to God through Christ.

units.la: 2. Ex charitate, & citra aliorum scandalum, vel incommodum. 3. Sanctè, in gloriam Dei. Rom. xiv, 23. Quod ex fide non est, peccatum est. 15. Si propter escam tuam frater tuus tristitiâ afficitur, non jam secundum charitatem ambulas. Tit. 1, 15. Omnia munda mundis : pollutis autem & incredulis nihil est mundum. 1 Cor. viii, 13. Si esca offendiculo est fratri meo, non edam carnes in æternum, ne sim offendiculo fratri meo. x, 31. Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Col, iii, 17. Adeo ut nullus actus in individuo sit indifferens. Omnium & singulorum reddenda erit ratio : 2 Cor. v, 10. usque ad verbum otiosum: Matth. xii, 36.
units.tr: 2. From charity, and without scandal or harm to others. 3. Holily, to the glory of God. Rom. xiv, 23. Whatever is not of faith is sin. 15. If because of food your brother is grieved, you are no longer walking in love. Tit. i, 15. To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure. 1 Cor. viii, 13. If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, lest I cause my brother to stumble. x, 31. Do all to the glory of God. Col. iii, 17. So that no single act in its individual instance is indifferent. An account of all and of each will have to be given: 2 Cor. v, 10; down to the idle word: Matt. xii, 36.

units.la: XXVIII. Nullum per se malum præcipere, vel ethicè permittere, potest Deus : sed ubi physicè permissum, & à creaturâ commissum est, punit necessario. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 56. Nec ullo modo ejus auctor esse potest : Jac. 1, 13. Deus tentari malis non potest, nec quenquam tentat. XXIX. Revelationes credendorum, Præcepta agendorum, & Prohibitiones fugiendorum, Deus plenissimè Verbo suo expressit, sive διαθήκην sive νόμον: Matth. xv, 9. Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas, quæ sunt mandata hominum. Luc. x, 25, 26. In Lege quid scriptum est? quomodo legis: &c. Interim Exempla cum laude propositæ, Præceptis accensenda sunt; cum vituperio autem, vel redargutione commemorata, Prohibitionibus iunt annumeranda. Quin & Præmia prudenter observanda, cumque Præceptis & Promissionibus conferenda sunt: Pœnæ autem similiter ad Prohibitiones & Comminationes referendæ. Rom. xv, 4. Nam quæ ante scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam ante scripta sunt. i, 18. Patet ira Dei è cœlo adversus omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum. II, 4. Benignitatem Dei ad resipiscentiam te deducere. Vide etiam 1 Cor. x, 11. xi, 1. Jac. v, 10, 11. iv, 3, 4, 5. Hag. i, 5, 6, II, 19, 20.
units.tr: XXVIII. God can command nothing evil in itself, nor permit it ethically; but where it is permitted physically and committed by a creature, he necessarily punishes it. See above, ch. iv, th. 56. Nor can he in any way be its author: Jas. i, 13. God cannot be tempted with evil, nor does he tempt anyone. XXIX. God has most fully expressed in his Word the revelations of things to be believed, the precepts of things to be done, and the prohibitions of things to be shunned, whether called covenant or law: Matt. xv, 9. In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. Luke x, 25, 26. What is written in the law? How do you read it? etc. Meanwhile, examples set forth with praise are to be reckoned among the precepts, but those recalled with blame or rebuke are to be counted among the prohibitions. Indeed, rewards too are to be observed prudently and compared with the precepts and promises; punishments likewise are to be referred to the prohibitions and threats. Rom. xv, 4. For whatever was written before was written for our instruction. i, 18. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. ii, 4. The goodness of God leads you to repentance. See also 1 Cor. x, 11; xi, 1; Jas. v, 10, 11; iv, 3, 4, 5; Hag. i, 5, 6; ii, 19, 20.

units.la: XXX. Concessio, licet omnis negativa censeri possit, quia icтic neque Præceptio neque Prohibitio eatenus facta est; distribuitur tamen in expressam, & tacitam.
units.tr: XXX. Concession, although every concession may be regarded as negative, since here neither a precept nor a prohibition has been made in that respect; it is nevertheless divided into express and tacit.

units.la: Expressa occurrit Gen. II, 16. De fructu omnis arboris hujus horti libere comedes, &c. Levit. xi, 2, 3. Hæc sunt animalia, quæ vos comedetis, &c. 9, 10. Act. x, 15. Quæ Deus purificavit, tu ne polluito. Rom. xiv, 14. Col. II, 14, 16, 17; 20, 21. Tit. i, 15. Gal. iv, 1-7; 9, 10. Deut. xxiii, 20.
units.tr: Express concessions occur at Gen. 2:16: "Of every tree of this garden you may freely eat," etc. Lev. 11:2, 3: "These are the animals which you may eat," etc.; 9, 10. Acts 10:15: "What God has cleansed, do not you call unclean." Rom. 14:14. Col. 2:14, 16, 17, 20, 21. Titus 1:15. Gal. 4:1-7, 9, 10. Deut. 23:20.

units.la: Tacita per S. Scripturæ perfectionem colligitur, ubi nec præceptio nec prohibitio facta est.
units.tr: Tacit concessions are gathered from the perfection of Holy Scripture, where neither precept nor prohibition has been made.

units.la: XXXI. Interim in Concessionibus quibusdam singulares circumstantiæ inferunt obligationem agendi id quod concessum est: ut de Matrimonio, Gen. i, 28. Fœtificate, & augescite, & implete terram: si conferatur cum 1 Cor. vii, 7. Unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, &c. & ibid. verf. 37. Nonnullæ etiam ad forum Solitantum pertinent: ut de libello Repudii; Deut. xxiv, 1, cum Matth. xix, 7, 8. Ex superioribus patet, Permissiones ethicas quandoque exprimi eodem modo ac Præcepta; à quibus tamen per circumstantias, & aliorum locorum collationem, distingui debent. Quin & Permissiones solum physicæ simili modo interdum exprimuntur; ut Num. xxi, 20, cum 32. Surge, abi cum iis. 1 Reg. 22, 22. Exi, & fac itā. Joh. xiii, 27. Quod facis, mox facito.
units.tr: XXXI. Yet in certain concessions particular circumstances imply an obligation to do what has been conceded: as with marriage, Gen. 1:28: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth"; if this is compared with 1 Cor. 7:7: "Each has his own gift from God," etc., and in the same chapter v. 37. Some also pertain to the forum of the Sollicitudo... [i.e., the forum of conscience]: as with the bill of divorce, Deut. 24:1, compared with Matt. 19:7, 8. From the above it is clear that ethical permissions are sometimes expressed in the same way as precepts, from which, however, they must be distinguished by the circumstances and by comparison with other passages. Indeed physical permissions too are sometimes expressed in a similar way: as at Num. 22:20 compared with 32: "Rise, go with them." 1 Kings 22:22: "Go out and do so." John 13:27: "What you do, do quickly."

units.la: XXXI. Pro φιλανθρωπία sua Deus in Præceptis etiam aliquando eorum honestatem, æquitatem, justitiam, & utilitatem proponit: unde Consilia appellantur; ut Apoc. iii, 18. Consilium do tibi, ut emas à me aurum igni exploratum, &c. Psal. xvi, 7. Benedicam Iehovæ, qui dedit consilium mihi, &c. Hæc absurdè Pontificii accipiunt de Officiis non mandatis communiter; sed quibusdam particulariter solum propositis, ad persectionem Euangelicam: quæ autem putant sic fieri, ea opera supererogationis vocant. Nos non nisi speciali modo exprimendi à Præceptis differre dicimus. Similiter Obtestationes, sive Contestationes, adhibentur; ejusmodi expressiones Præceptorum & Prohibitionum, in quibus Deus ad pleniorem justitiæ & æquitatis suæ demonstrationem, ipsas Creaturas rationales, & earum conscientiam, aliasque analogicè & suo modo, testes advocat. Deuter. iv, 26. Contestor contra vos hodiè cœlum & terram, &c. xxx, 18, 19. Psal. lxxxi, 9. Audi populme mi, & Contestabor te. Jes. 1, 4. v. 3, 4. Occurrunt etiam alicubi Vota, sive Optationes, quibus Deus ἀνθρωποπαθῶς indicat, quàm bona sit, Hominibusque appetenda, & quantoperè ipsi Deo probetur, mandata obedientia; adhæc quomodo illi præstandæ occasiones, adminicula, & incitamenta plurima suppeditet; nec non quàm serio velit nexum obedientiæ illius cum præmio promisso. Psal. lxxxi, 14, 15. O si populus meus auscultâsset mihi, &c. Vide etiam Deut. v, 29. Itâ Christus, Luc. xix, 41, 42, cum appropinquaret Hierosolymis, Visâ urbe, flevit super ea, dicens ; Si vel tu nôffes hoc saltem tuo die, quae ad pacem tuam pertinent ! Confer 2 Cor. v, 20.
units.tr: XXXI. For his philanthropy God in precepts also sometimes sets forth their honesty, equity, justice and usefulness; whence they are called counsels: as at Rev. 3:18: "I counsel you to buy of me gold refined by fire," etc. Ps. 16:7: "I will bless the LORD, who has given me counsel," etc. The Papists absurdly understand these as duties not commonly commanded, but only proposed particularly to some, for evangelical perfection; and those things which they think are done in this way they call works of supererogation. We say only that they differ from precepts in the special mode of expression. Similarly, obtestations or contestations are employed: expressions of precepts and prohibitions of this kind, in which God, for a fuller demonstration of his justice and equity, calls to witness the rational creatures themselves, and their conscience, and others analogically and in their own way. Deut. 4:26: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today," etc.; 30:18, 19. Ps. 81:9: "Hear, O my people, and I will testify against you." Isa. 1:4; 5:3, 4. There also occur somewhere vows, or wishes, by which God, in human fashion, indicates how good obedience to the commandments is and how greatly it is pleasing to God himself, and how many occasions, aids and incentives he supplies for rendering it; and how seriously he wishes the bond of that obedience with the promised reward. Ps. 81:14, 15: "O that my people had listened to me," etc. See also Deut. 5:29. So Christ, Luke 19:41, 42, when he drew near to Jerusalem: "Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: If you had known, even you, at least in this your day, the things which belong to your peace!" Compare 2 Cor. 5:20.

units.la: XXXIII. Actûs morales à realibus accuratè distinguendi sunt: hi per illos non excluduntur ; sed ut praestetur obedientia, accedere debent. Alias tantùm obligatio ad officium infertur, & voluntas mandati innotescit ; cui dùm scientes & volentes refragantur homines, fiunt inexcusabiles : Ezech, II, 4, 5. Ut sciant Prophetam fuisse in medio sui. 2 Cor. II, 14. 15, 16. - His quidem odor mortis ad mortem.
units.tr: XXXIII. Moral acts must be carefully distinguished from real ones: the former are not excluded by the latter, but must accompany them if obedience is to be rendered. Otherwise only an obligation to duty is introduced and the will of the command becomes known; and when men knowingly and willingly resist it, they become inexcusable: Ezek. 2:4, 5: "That they may know that a prophet has been among them." 2 Cor. 2:14, 15, 16: "To the one indeed a savour of death unto death."

units.la: XXXIV. Ad Praxin, 1. Providentiam Dei piè in omnibus contemplemur, & alios similiter excitemus: Psal. xciv, 8, 9, 10. Jef. xl, 26. Matth. vi, 26, 30. Act. xiv, 17. xvii, 24, 28.
units.tr: XXXIV. As to practice: (1) Let us piously contemplate the providence of God in all things, and similarly stir up others: Ps. 94:8, 9, 10; Isa. 40:26; Matt. 6:26, 30; Acts 14:17; 17:24, 28.

units.la: 2. Sub manû Omnipotentis humiliemur: Jac. iv, 7, 10. 1 Petr. v, 6.
units.tr: (2) Let us humble ourselves under the hand of the Almighty: James 4:7, 10; 1 Pet. 5:6.

units.la: 3. Justissimum Dei Imperium in omnia agnoscamus, praedicemus: Job. 1, 21. Psal. cxv, 3. Dan. iv, 35.
units.tr: (3) Let us acknowledge and proclaim the most just dominion of God over all things: Job 1:21; Ps. 115:3; Dan. 4:35.

units.la: 4. Eum toto animo revereamur, qui intimè omnibus praesit, & in omnibus operatur: Act. xvii, 25, 28. Psal. xxxiii, 15. In Prosperis gratitudinem praestemus: Psal. cvii, 8. cxvi, 12. cxlv, 10, 15, 16. Jac. 1, 17. 1 Tim. vi, 17: Amemus: Psal. cxvi, 1. iv, 33. In Adversis coram Ipso patientes simus: Hebr. xii, 5, &c. Job. 1, 21. 2 Sam. xv, 10, 11.
units.tr: (4) Let us revere with our whole soul him who inwardly presides over all and works in all: Acts 17:25, 28; Ps. 33:15. In prosperity let us show gratitude: Ps. 107:8; 116:12; 145:10, 15, 16; James 1:17; 1 Tim. 6:17; let us love: Ps. 116:1; 4:33. In adversity let us be patient before him: Heb. 12:5, etc.; Job 1:21; 2 Sam. 15:10, 11.

units.la: 5. Mediis ne nimium tribuamus: Psal. cxxvii, 1, 2. 2 Chron. xv, 12. Matth. iv, 4. Neque tamen temerè negligamus: Actor. xxvii. 31. Matth. iv, 7.
units.tr: (5) Let us not attribute too much to means: Ps. 127:1, 2; 2 Chron. 15:12; Matt. 4:4. Yet let us not rashly neglect them: Acts 27:31; Matt. 4:7.
2 Kings 5:13.

units.la: 6. Omnem solicitudinem in Deum devolvamus: Psal. lv, 23. 1 Petr. v, 7. Hebr. xiii, 5, 6, Psal. xxiii, 1. 4, 6. 1 Sam. xvii, 37. 2 Tim. iv, 17, 18. Eph. iii, 19, 20. Rom. viii, 28. Gen. L, 20, xxii, 8.
7. Providentiam moralem, vitae nostrae regulam, respiciamus, & observemus perpetuò: Psal. cxix, 4, 5, 17, 18, 19; 33-37.
units.tr: (7) Let us regard the moral providence, the rule of our life, and observe it constantly: Ps. 119:4, 5, 17, 18, 19, 33-37.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De Fœdere Legali.
units.tr: On the Legal Covenant

units.la: Jus. Injuria. Quis illud postulet. Quæ eorum capacia. 1. Jus Dei: tùm naturale; tùm positivum. Jus naturale respectû nostri. Institutum. Quid JCtis Jus naturæ. Gentium. Civile. 2. Jus creaturarum rationalium. Magistratuum. Subditorum. 3. Lex. Divina. Æterna. Humana. 4. Jus & Lex non contraria. Societatis civilis initium non à mutuo metû. Norma juris non defensio vitæ & membrorum. Voluntas non absolutè subjicienda Hominibus. Non omnis Pœna propter peccantium correctionem. c. Hebb. 5. Lex Divina. Cerimonialis. Politica. 6. Moralis. Decalogus. Lex charitatis. Actus religiosi circa proximum. 7. Argumenta singulorum Præceptorum. 8. Integra Lex Moralis non est Juris ipsi Deo naturalis. 9. Attamen Juris nobis naturalis. Obj. solv. 10. Eadem fuit ante Mosen. 11. Probatur amplius inductione, de Præceptis tab. post. 12. Similiter de Præceptis tab.pr. 13. Objectiones de Sabbatho solv. 14. Jus naturale primavum. Secundarium. 15. Eadem Lex Moralis adhuc obtinet sub N. T. 16. Etiam quartum Præceptum. Obj. solv. 17. Sententiæ Pontif. Socin. Anabapt. &c. 18. Idololatria Pontif. in Angelis, refutatur. 19. Non rogandi, ut pro nobis intercedant. Obj. solv. 20. In Christo, secundum hum. nat. B. Virgine MaMaria. Sanctis defunctis: Patronis: Canonizatis. 21. Refutatur. 22. Non rogandi, ut pro nobis intercedant. Obj. solv. 23. In Pontifice Rom. 24. In Pane eucharistico. 25. In Cruce. 26. In Reliquiis. 27. In Imaginibus. 28. Refut. & Obj. solv. 29. In Rebus consecratis. Agnis Dei. 30. In Divis chimaericis, &c. Sanctis non-sanctis. 31. Magia datur, c. Neo-Sadduc. Obj. solv. 32. Papatui vere impingitur. 33. Non omnis ignorantia est inculpata. 34. Species ejus vitiosæ. Obj. solv. 35. An sola Hæresis posset Hominem subjicere æterna damnationi. 36. An Hæretici, ut sic, extremo supplicio afficiendi, 37. Odium adversus Deum. Obj. solv. 38. Falsa gratiarum actio. Salutatio Angelica, Pontif. 39. Non orandum pro mortuis: c. eofd. Obj. solv. 40. Orationem Dominicam posse usurpari pro formula precandi; c. Brown. 41. Recte appellamus Patrem nostrum. Et rogamus, ut Veniat Regnum Ipsius. c. Muhamm. 42. Quis ὁ ἀγτῶ ὁ ἐπιέσι. Obj. solv. 43. Aliæ explicationes. 44. Remissio nostra in petitione quintâ, qualis; & quem respectum habeat ad Remissionem Dei. 45. Doxologia vere canonica: c. Pontif. 45. Jejunium. Non consistit in discrimine ciborum: c. eofd. 46. Objectiones solvuntur. 47. Non est per se cultus religiosus. Obj. solv. 48. Non opus pœnale, & satisfactorium justitiæ Divinæ. Nec debent esse ordinaria absoluta & perpetua. c. eofd. Obj. solv. 49. Inanis eorundem verborum repetitio. 50. Votum. Soli Deo povendum. 51. Ejus materia. Vota Papistica. Monastica 52. Male Sociniani contendunt, Christum primo Præcepto addidisse mandatum generale de Precibus Deo faciendis. 53. Formulam Orationis Dominicæ. 54. & Mandatum de Ipso adorando. 55. Imagines in secundo Decalogi præcepto. Pontificiorum refutantur. 56. Objectiones solv. 57. Non usurpanda, nec asservanda in talem usum. 58. Imagines creaturarum. 59. Usus illicitus. 60. Non habendæ pro libris Laicorum. 61. Ἐθελοθρησκεία. Pontificiorum. 62. Secundum Præceptum a Christo non auctum: c. Socin. 63. Secundum vere distinctum a primo: c. Pontif. 64. Perperam statuunt Socin. Tertio præcepto additum esse a Christo, Ne temere juremus, &c. 65. Non omne Juramentum (sub N. T. illicitum: c. Anabapt. Obj. solv. 66. Male item Socin. Additum illi Juramentum per Christum. 67. Non jurandum per Sanctos, aliave creaturas; c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 68. Festa proprie dicta non sunt sub N. T. observanda; nedum in honorem Sanctorum: c. eosd. Obj. solv. 69. Qui Pater & Mater in quinto Præcepto. 70. Liberis non licet vovere vitam Monasticam, invitis Parentibus: c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 71. Nec Matrimonium sic contrahere. 72. Christianus Magistratui Politico parere potest; quin & eum gerere, bona conscientia: c. Anabapt. 73. Objectiones solvuntur. 74. Aliquando etiam in judicio agere licet adversus fratrem, apud Magistratum fidelem. Obj. solv. 75. Magistratus honore ac dignitate supes superior est personis Ecclesiasticis : c. Pontif. 76. Christus non auxit v. Præceptum : c. Socin. 77. Supplicium capitale non illicitum: c. Anabapt. 78. Nec omne Bellum. Obj. solv. 79. Nec inculpata Tutela. 80. Nemini Corpus suum flagellare, aut incidere licet, ex devotione, &c. c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 81. Christus non auxit sextum Prac. c. Socin. 82. Gradus circa Matrimonium prohibiti, Lev. xviii. sunt morales : c. Pontif. 83. Conftitutio Juris Canonici. 84. Magistratus Politicus recte etiam judicat de causis Matrimon. c. eofd. 85. Publica Matrimonii confirmatio. 86. Cœlibatus non absolute præferendus Matrimonio: c. Pontif. 87. Objectiones solv. 88. Non illicitum Ministris Ecclesiasticis, & Religiosis: c. eofd. 89. Objectiones solv. 90. Male distinguunt iidem inter nuptias primas, & fecundas, &c. Obj. solv. 91. Adulterium legitima causa Divortii. Matrimonium quoque dirimitur per malitiosam Desertionem. Obj. solv. 92. Divortium vitæ Monastica causa illicitum: c. Pontif. 93. Atque item propter Excommunicationem: c. Anabapt. Obj. solv. 94. Repudium sub V. T. etiam in conscientia illicitum. 95. Itemque Polygamia 96. Objeƈt. solv. 97. Christus non auxit Præceptum vii. c. Socin. 98. Distinctio dominiorum est juris Divini : c. Cœnobitas, & Anapt. qu. Obj. solv. 99. Fœnus iniquum tribus modis. 100. Objectiones solv. 101. Christus non auxit Præceptum viii. 102. Mendacium omne illicitum. 103. Etiam Officiosum.
units.tr: Right. Injury. Who may claim it? Which beings are capable of it? 1. The right of God: both natural and positive. Natural right with respect to us. Instituted. What the jurists mean by natural right, the right of nations, civil right. 2. The right of rational creatures. Of magistrates. Of subjects. 3. Law. Divine. Eternal. Human. 4. Right and law are not contrary. The beginning of civil society does not come from mutual fear. The norm of right is not the defence of life and limbs. The will is not to be absolutely subjected to men. Not every penalty is for the correction of sinners. Against Hobbes. 5. Divine law: ceremonial, political. 6. Moral law: the Decalogue. The law of charity. Religious acts towards one's neighbour. 7. Arguments for the individual precepts. 8. The whole moral law is not natural to God's own right. 9. Nevertheless it is natural to us as right. Objection answered. 10. The same law was in force before Moses. 11. This is proved further by induction concerning the precepts of the second table. 12. Similarly concerning the precepts of the first table. 13. Objections concerning the Sabbath answered. 14. Natural right: primary. Secondary. 15. The same moral law still holds under the New Testament. 16. Also the fourth precept. Objection answered. 17. The opinions of the Papists, Socinians, Anabaptists, etc. 18. The idolatry of the Papists in angels is refuted. 19. We must not ask the saints to intercede for us. Objection answered. 20. In Christ according to his human nature; in the Blessed Virgin Mary; in the departed saints; patrons; canonized saints. 21. Refuted. 22. We must not ask them to intercede for us. Objection answered. 23. In the Roman Pontiff. 24. In the eucharistic bread. 25. In the Cross. 26. In relics. 27. In images. 28. Refutation, and objections answered. 29. In consecrated things. The Lambs of God. 30. In chimerical deities, etc.; in saints and non-saints. 31. The existence of magic, against the neo-Sadducees. Objection answered. 32. It truly strikes at the Papacy. 33. Not every ignorance is blameless. 34. Its vicious kinds. Objection answered. 35. Whether heresy alone could subject a man to eternal damnation. 36. Whether heretics, as such, are to be visited with the extreme penalty. 37. Hatred against God. Objection answered. 38. False thanksgiving. The Angelic Salutation of the Papists. 39. We must not pray for the dead; against the same. Objection answered. 40. The Lord's Prayer may be used as a formula for prayer; against the Brownists. 41. We rightly call God our Father, and we ask that his Kingdom may come; against the Muhammadans. 42. What is epiousios [ἐπιούσιος]? Objection answered. 43. Other explanations. 44. Our forgiveness in the fifth petition: what kind it is, and what relation it bears to God's forgiveness. 45. A doxology truly canonical; against the Papists. 45. Fasting does not consist in the choice of foods; against the same. 46. Objections are answered. 47. Fasting is not in itself religious worship. Objection answered. 48. It is not a penal and satisfactory work for divine justice, nor ought such works to be absolute and perpetual. Against the same. Objection answered. 49. The empty repetition of the same words. 50. A vow: to be made to God alone. 51. Its matter. Papistical vows. Monastic vows. 52. The Socinians wrongly contend that Christ added to the first precept a general command concerning prayers to be made to God. 53. The form of the Lord's Prayer. 54. And the command to worship him. 55. Images in the second precept of the Decalogue. The views of the Papists are refuted. 56. Objections answered. 57. Images are not to be used, nor kept for such use. 58. Images of creatures. 59. Illicit use. 60. Images are not to be regarded as books for the laity. 61. Self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] of the Papists. 62. The second precept was not enlarged by Christ; against the Socinians. 63. The second precept is truly distinct from the first; against the Papists. 64. The Socinians wrongly hold that Christ added to the third precept, "Do not swear rashly," etc. 65. Not every oath is unlawful under the New Testament; against the Anabaptists. Objection answered. 66. Likewise the Socinians wrongly hold that the oath "by Christ" was added. 67. We must not swear by saints or other creatures; against the Papists. Objection answered. 68. Feasts properly so called are not to be observed under the New Testament, much less in honour of saints; against the same. Objection answered. 69. Who are father and mother in the fifth precept. 70. Children may not vow monastic life against their parents' wishes; against the Papists. Objection answered. 71. Nor may they contract marriage in that way. 72. A Christian may obey the political magistrate, and indeed may hold office with a good conscience; against the Anabaptists. 73. Objections are answered. 74. Sometimes it is even lawful to bring a suit against a brother before a faithful magistrate. Objection answered. 75. The magistrate is superior in honour and dignity to ecclesiastical persons; against the Papists. 76. Christ did not enlarge the fifth precept; against the Socinians. 77. Capital punishment is not unlawful; against the Anabaptists. 78. Nor is every war unlawful. Objection answered. 79. Nor is blameless self-defence unlawful. 80. No one may lawfully scourge or cut his own body out of devotion, etc.; against the Papists. Objection answered. 81. Christ did not enlarge the sixth precept; against the Socinians. 82. The degrees of kinship prohibited in marriage (Lev. 18) are moral; against the Papists. 83. The constitution of canon law. 84. The political magistrate also rightly judges matrimonial causes; against the same. 85. The public confirmation of marriage. 86. Celibacy is not absolutely to be preferred to marriage; against the Papists. 87. Objections answered. 88. It is not unlawful for ecclesiastical ministers and religious persons; against the same. 89. Objections answered. 90. The same writers wrongly distinguish between first and second marriages, etc. Objection answered. 91. Adultery is a lawful cause of divorce. Marriage is also dissolved by malicious desertion. Objection answered. 92. Divorce for the sake of monastic life is unlawful; against the Papists. 93. Likewise on account of excommunication; against the Anabaptists. Objection answered. 94. Repudiation under the Old Testament was unlawful even in conscience. 95. Likewise polygamy. 96. Objection answered. 97. Christ did not enlarge the seventh precept; against the Socinians. 98. The distinction of property is of divine right; against the cenobites and Anabaptists. Objection answered. 99. Usury is unjust in three ways. 100. Objections answered. 101. Christ did not enlarge the eighth precept. 102. Every lie is unlawful. 103. Even the officious lie.

units.la: Obj. solv. 104. Itémque Æquivocationes, & Mentales reservationes. 105. Objectiones solv. 106. Perfidia: etiàm circa infideles, & hæreticos: c. Pontif. 107. Christus non auxit Præceptum IX. c. Socin. 108. De Concupiscentia unicum Præceptum: c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 109. Motus primò primi ex concupiscentiâ originali, verè peccata: c. Pontif. Remonstr. &c. Obj. solv. 110. Christus non auxit Præceptum x. 111. Nec universa Legi Morali addidit mandata quædam. 112. Lex ista simpliciter est norma obedientiæ nostræ, &c. 113. Pactum, Fœdus, in SS. Literis. Fœdera Politicis qualia. 114. Fœdus primum, Legale. 115. Conditio per illud præstanda. 116. Posteri in Adamo censiti. 117. Sanctio pœnalis. 118. Liberalis promissio. 119. Arbor scientiæ boni ac mali. Obj. solv. 120. Arbor vitæ. 121. Paradisus. Commentum Pontificiorum. 122. Sabbathum. 123. Duratio istius Fœderis. Obj. solv. 124. Praxis. 125.
units.tr: Objection answered. 104. Likewise equivocations and mental reservations. 105. Objections answered. 106. Perfidy, even towards unbelievers and heretics; against the Papists. 107. Christ did not enlarge the ninth precept; against the Socinians. 108. Concerning concupiscence there is a single precept; against the Papists. Objection answered. 109. The first motions arising from original concupiscence are truly sins; against the Papists, the Remonstrants, etc. Objection answered. 110. Christ did not enlarge the tenth precept. 111. Nor did he add certain particular commands to the whole moral law. 112. This law is simply the norm of our obedience, etc. 113. Pact and covenant in Holy Scripture. What kinds of political covenants there are. 114. The first covenant, the legal covenant. 115. The condition to be fulfilled through it. 116. Posterity reckoned in Adam. 117. The penal sanction. 118. The gracious promise. 119. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Objection answered. 120. The tree of life. 121. Paradise: the invention of the Papists. 122. The Sabbath. 123. The duration of this covenant. Objection answered. 124. Practice. 125.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Quod alicui debetur moraliter, Jus vocari solet: cui contraria est Injuria. Spectatur interdùm ratio, propter quam illud sic debetur; ità dicimus, aliquid Jure meum, vel tuum esse: aliàs intelligitur id ipsum, quod sic debetur; ità dicimus, alteri Jus suum tribuere. Verum etiàm ulterius Lex, aut Legum collectio, aut Ars boni & æqui, Jus appellatur.
units.tr: What is owed to someone in moral terms is commonly called Right (jus), and its contrary is Injury. Sometimes the ground on which it is owed is considered, and so we say that something is mine or yours by right. At other times what is owed in this way is itself understood, and so we say that one gives another his right. Further still, law, or a collection of laws, or the art of the good and the fair, is also called Right.

units.la: Illud postulat Rector, aut Princeps, auctoritate publicâ: sed & privatus, modo sibi conveniente; Jus suum ipse æstimans, & alterum de eo monens, vel etiàm Rectoris potestatem coactivam implorans. Unde dè ; quæ Ratione destituuntur , Juris capacia non sunt ; ut nec Injuriæ.
units.tr: A ruler or prince demands this by public authority, but so does a private person, in a manner suited to himself, judging his own right and warning another about it, or even invoking the coercive power of the ruler. Hence things destitute of reason are not capable of right, any more than of injury.

units.la: A Jure dicuntur Justitia, Juste agere, & Justus; quibus contraria sunt Injustitia, Injuste agere, & Injustus.
units.tr: From Right come justice, to act justly and just; their contraries are injustice, to act unjustly and unjust.

units.la: II. Dei ἐξουσία independens est; atque adeo etiam Jus in Creaturas. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 68. & 70. Ubi autem existunt creaturæ rationales, hæ ipsi necessario debent cultum & obedientiam rationalem. Huc pertinet primò Jus Dei naturale, quod necessario fluit ex Sanctitate Naturæ illius eminentissimæ; quanquam concomitante Libertate complacentiæ; deinde etiam Jus positivum, quod oritur ex determinatione Arbitrii Divini, per Libertatem contradictionis, vel etiam contrarietatis.
units.tr: II. God's authority (ἐξουσία) is independent, and so also is His right over creatures. See above, chapter 4, theses 68 and 70. Where rational creatures exist, they necessarily owe Him worship and rational obedience. To this belongs first the natural right of God, which necessarily flows from the sanctity of his most eminent nature, though accompanied by the liberty of good pleasure; and then also the positive right, which arises from the determination of the divine will through liberty of contradiction, or even of contrariety.

units.la: Verum respectu nostri Jus naturæ dicitur, quod Deus Imaginem sanctitatis & justitiæ suæ exprimens, naturæ nostræ in primâ ejus constitutione imprellit, ad honestorum à turpibus discriminationem; unde post lapsum supersunt quædam reliquiæ. Ab illo contradistinguitur Jus institutum; tum ab ipso Deo, per supernaturalem duntaxat revelationem & constitutionem; tùm per Gentium, vel Reipublicæ, vel Communitatis alicujus consensum & placitum, secundum Deum.
units.tr: With respect to us, however, natural right is that which God, expressing the image of his own holiness and justice, impressed on our nature in its first constitution, for the discrimination of the honourable from the base; whence certain remnants survive after the fall. From this is distinguished instituted right: on the one hand, that which comes from God himself through supernatural revelation and constitution alone; on the other, that which comes through the consent and decision of the nations, or of a commonwealth, or of some community, in accordance with God.

units.la: A Jurisconsultis vero Jus Naturæ describitur strictius, quod Natura omnia animantia docuit; scil. materialiter. Jus Gentium vero, quod naturali ratione inter homines constitutum, apud omnes peræque custoditur. Civile denique, quod unaquæque civitas constituit. Jus Romanum interim κατ' ἐξοχὴν appellari solet Civile.
units.tr: The jurists, however, describe natural right more strictly, as that which Nature taught all living things, namely materially. The law of nations is that which is established among men by natural reason and observed alike by all. Civil law, finally, is that which each state establishes. Meanwhile Roman law is commonly called civil by preeminence (κατ' ἐξοχὴν), civil law.

units.la: III. Creaturis rationalibus omne jus suum duntaxat convenit dependenter à Deo, & ipsius Jure. Tenendum hoc de Hominibus Magistratum gerentibus, respectu Subditorum: Rom. XIII, 1, 2, 4, 5. "Non enim est Potestas, nisi à Deo; & quæ sunt Potestates, „sunt à Deo ordinatæ. Itaque quisquis obsistit Potesta„ti, Dei ordinationi obsistit. – Dei minister est; vin„dex ad iram ei, qui quod malum est fecerit. Qua„ propter necesse est subjici, non solùm propter iram, sed „etiam propter conscientiam. Propterea Judicium, quod per eos fertur, Dei esse dicitur; Deut. 1, 17. & pro Deo; 2 Chron. XIX, 6.
units.tr: III. Every right belongs to rational creatures only dependently on God and on his right. This is to be held of men who bear magistracy, with respect to their subjects: Rom. 13:1, 2, 4, 5. "For there is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained of God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God. ... He is God's minister, an avenger to execute wrath on him who does evil. Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath but also for conscience's sake." Therefore the judgment that is passed by them is said to be God's: Deut. 1:17; and to be given for God: 2 Chron. 19:6.

units.la: Ac porro de Subditis, eorumque jure inter se: Levit. XIX, 13–. Ne fraudem facito proximo tuo, -: sed timebis à Deo tuo, &c. Ephef. VI, 1. Liberi, auscultate in Domino parentibus vestris: id enim est justum. Et de servis, verf. 6, 7. Non ad oculum servientes; - facientes ex animo quæ vult Deus, &c. Adde Jac. 1, 27. IV, 11, 12.
units.tr: Further, concerning subjects and their right among themselves: Lev. 19:13. "You shall not defraud your neighbour ... but you shall fear your God," etc. Eph. 6:1: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right." And concerning servants, vers. 6, 7: "not serving with eye-service ... doing from the heart what God wills," etc. Add Jas. 1:27; 4:11, 12.

units.la: IV. Lex à legendo dicitur: quia publice legi, & sic promulgari solet. Hebraice תורה, à ירה, unde etiam הורה docuit, monuit. Græce Νόμος, à Νέμω, tribuo; quia exponit jus suum cuique tribuendum. Est autem Constitutio ejus qui jus imperii habet, publicè declarans, quænam prosequenda sint, tanquàm honesta ac justa; & quæ fugienda, tanquàm turpia ac injusta; atque itâ subditos moraliter obligant; expressaferè sanctione pœnarum comminatoria adversùs transgressores; ad ordinem honestè bonum in communitate servandum.
units.tr: IV. Lex (law) is said to come from legendo (reading), because it is publicly read and so promulgated. In Hebrew, torah [תורה], from yarah [ירה], whence also horah [הורה], taught, admonished. In Greek, nomos [νόμος], from nemo, I assign, because it sets out that each one's right is to be assigned to him. It is the constitution of one who holds the right of rule, publicly declaring what is to be pursued as honourable and just, and what is to be shunned as base and unjust; and so it binds subjects morally, with penalties for transgressors generally expressed in threat, in order to keep an honourable and good order in the community.

units.la: Nobis de Lege Divinâ agendum. Hujus archetypum vocatur Lex æterna: quæ est Legis rationalibus creaturis ferendæ idea in mente Divinâ: vel ipsa sanctitas naturæ Divinæ, utpotè imitabilis in vitâ creaturarum rationalium, & ex morali debito imitanda casu quo creaturæ rationales exisferent. Scholastici eam latiùs accipiunt; ut etiam complèctatur ordinem gubernationis bestiarum, cœlorum, & totius naturæ. Sed Lex proprie dicta ad creaturas irrationales non pertinet; ut neque Jus.
units.tr: We must now speak of Divine Law. Its archetype is called the eternal law: this is the idea, in the divine mind, of the law to be given to rational creatures, or the very sanctity of the divine nature, as imitable in the life of rational creatures and to be imitated by them from moral obligation, in the event that rational creatures should exist. The Scholastics take it more broadly, so that it also embraces the order by which beasts, heavens and all of nature are governed. But law properly so called does not pertain to irrational creatures, any more than right does.

units.la: Istius ἐκτύπου in tempore creaturis rationalibus proponitur, easque moraliter obligat; sive proponatur interna inspiratione, vel impressione in mentem; sive voce externa; sive etiam scripto.
units.tr: This copy is set before rational creatures in time, and binds them morally, whether it is proposed by internal inspiration or impression on the mind, or by an external voice, or also in writing.

units.la: Omnis autem Lex humana, propter dependentiam, ex Divina deduci debet commodè, & ad eam reduci: atque hac solùm ratione conscientias obligat: Rom. XIII, 1-6.
units.tr: Every human law, however, on account of its dependence, ought to be conveniently deduced from the divine law and brought back to it; and only on this ground does it bind consciences: Rom. 13:1–6.

units.la: V. Itâ Lex ordinata est ad communem Iuris in Republicâ notitiam & observantiam. Perperam verò Neoterici quidam statuunt, 1. Quod Ius nihil aliud fit, quam Libertas naturalis; à Legibus non constituta, sed relicta: quodque hanc primo restringat Lex naturalis & Divina; residuam restringant Leges Civiles, ac tandem Constitutiones particularium Urbium & Societatum. Quod consequenter Ius & Lex sint contraria; tanquam Libertas & Vinculum. Male. Sic enim illa demum Juris Divini forent, de quibus ordinatione Divinâ nihil esset constitutum positive; sed quæ præterita negative: & Juris Civilis, quæ per Leges Civiles præterendo essent relicta; non sublata, aut restricta. Imo Jurisprudentiæ obiectum proprium ac directum forent Legum præterita; non ipsæ Leges & Constitutiones.
units.tr: V. Thus law is ordained for the common knowledge and observance of right in the commonwealth. But some modern writers wrongly hold: 1. That right is nothing other than natural liberty, not constituted by laws but left free; that natural and divine law first restricts this liberty, civil laws restrict what remains, and finally the constitutions of particular cities and societies restrict the rest. Consequently right and law are contraries, as liberty and bond. This is wrong. For in that case the things of divine right would be those about which nothing had been positively determined by divine ordinance, but which are passed over negatively; and the things of civil right would be those which, being passed over by the civil laws, were left and neither removed nor restricted. Indeed the proper and direct object of jurisprudence would be the things passed over, not the laws and constitutions themselves.

units.la: 2. Quod Societatis civilis initium fit à mutuo metû: quia Status naturæ fit status belli; in quo unicuique facere liceat, quæcunque, & in quoscunque libet. Quod Norma juris & juste sacti fit defensio vitæ & membrorum: Lex autem naturalis nihil aliud fit, quam Dictamen rectæ rationis, circa ea quæ agenda vel omittenda sunt, ad vitæ membrorumque conservationem, quantum fieri potest diuturnam. Quod prima & fundamentalis Lex naturæ fit, Quærendam esse pacem, ubi haberi potest; ubi non potest, defensionem & belli auxilia. Consequenter Jus in omnia non esse retinendum: ad Contractus & Pacta veniendum; atque iis standum esse, ad pacem scil. conciliandam. Quod Injuria, ei soli fieri possit; polfit, quicum contrahimus, &c. Quòd Jus illud primæ-vum, ad statum belli pertinens, reviviscat in moderamine legitimæ defensionis ; & propterea ii, qui supplicio afficiendi sunt, vinculis constringantur, &c. Malè. Natura enim nostra non aliter concipienda est, quàm ut dependens à Deo, Summo, & Sanctissimo, tùm realiter, tùm moraliter. Neque primum principium practicum est bonum nostrum ; conservatio nostri: sed à Deo, per ipsius Legem, obligati sumus ad Juris observantiam, Injuriæ fugam, etiàm ante nostros contractus & pacta.
units.tr: 2. That the beginning of civil society is mutual fear, because the state of nature becomes a state of war, in which each may do whatever he pleases to whomever he pleases. That the norm of right and of what is justly done is the defence of life and limbs, and that natural law is nothing other than the dictate of right reason concerning what is to be done or omitted for the preservation of life and limbs for as long as possible. That the first and fundamental law of nature is that peace is to be sought where it can be had, and where it cannot, defence and the means of war. Consequently right is not to be retained over all things; one must come to contracts and pacts and abide by them, namely in order to secure peace. That injury can be done only to one with whom we contract, and so on. That the primitive right, belonging to the state of war, revives in the moderation of lawful defence, and therefore those who are to be punished are bound in chains, and so on. This is wrong. For our nature is not to be conceived otherwise than as dependent on God, the Highest and Most Holy, both really and morally. Nor is our own good, the preservation of ourselves, the first practical principle; rather, we are bound through God's law to observe right and to flee injury, even before our contracts and pacts.

units.la: 3. Quòd unusquisque Voluntatem suam, alterius unius Hominis, vel Concilii, Voluntati rectè ità subjiciat ; ut pro Voluntate omnium & singulorum habendum sit, quicquid de rebus ad communem Pacem necessariis unus ille voluerit. Quòd illi, qui summum in Civitate Imperium adepti sunt, nullam Civibus possint facere injuriam: nec Domini Servis, aut Parentes Liberis. Quod Mater originaliter Liberorum Domina sit; Pater vero, vel alius quispiam, jure ab illa derivato. Quod Subditi non peccent, quoties mandata Principum suorum, quæ sibi injusta esse videntur, exequuntur. Quòd Subditus non debeat sibi arrogare cognitionem justi & injusti. Quod erronea sit vox, Regibus non esse obtemperandum ; nisi justa præceperint; cum ante imperia justum & injustum non existant: Reges autem legitimi, quæ imperant, justa faciant imperando ; quæ vetant, vetando injusta: Privati vero homines, dum cognitionem boni & mali ad se trahunt, cupiant esse sicut Reges: atque huc spectet, omnium Dei Præceptorum antiquissimum illud, Gen. 2, 17. De Ligno scientiæ boni & mali ne comedas: & antiquissima Tentationum Diabolicarum, cap. III, 5. Eritis sicut Dii, scientes bonum & malum: & prima Dei cum Homine expostulatio, vers. 11. Quis indicavit tibi, quod nudus esses; nisi quod ex Ligno, de quo præceperam tibi, ne comederes, comedisti. Male. Deus enim per naturam suam independenter sanctus est, & Jus suum habet: nos vero per naturam nostram dependentem ißo obligamur necessario: atque ex Dei ordinatione, tum Magistratûs, ipsius ministri; tum Parentes; tum alii qualescunque, originaliter jus aliquod suum habent; quod quidem nulli creaturæ violare licet. Hinc nullis Hominibus obediendum est, nisi secundum Deum: & quicquid à nobis fiet, cum cognitione justi ac honesti, & certâ hujus conscientiâ plenâque persuasione, faciendum est coram Deo; quem in omnibus spectare & revereri debemus: Act. v, 29. Rom. xiv, 5, 12, 23.
units.tr: 3. That each person should rightly subject his will to the will of one other man or of a council, so that whatever that one wills concerning matters necessary for common peace is to be held as the will of all and of each. That those who have attained the supreme power in the state (imperium) can do no injury to the citizens, nor masters to their slaves, nor parents to their children. That the mother is originally mistress of the children, but the father, or anyone else, has right derived from her. That subjects do not sin whenever they carry out the commands of their princes that seem unjust to them. That a subject ought not to arrogate to himself knowledge of the just and unjust. That it is an erroneous saying that kings are not to be obeyed unless they command what is just, since before rule there is no just and unjust; legitimate kings, rather, make just by commanding whatever they command, and unjust by forbidding whatever they forbid; private men, however, while they draw to themselves knowledge of good and evil, desire to be like kings. To this relates that most ancient of all God's precepts, Gen. 2:17, "Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat"; and the most ancient of the devilish temptations, ch. 3:5, "You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil"; and God's first expostulation with man, vers. 11, "Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" This is wrong. For God is independently holy through his nature and has his own right; but we, through our dependent nature, are necessarily bound by this very fact. And by God's ordination, magistrates, who are his ministers, and parents, and others of whatever kind, originally have some right of their own, which no creature may lawfully violate. Hence men are to be obeyed by no one except according to God; and whatever is done by us with knowledge of what is just and honourable, and with certain conscience and full persuasion of it, must be done before God, whom we ought to regard and revere in all things: Acts 5:29; Rom. 14:5, 12, 23.
1 Cor. x. 31. Jac. iv. 12.

units.la: 4. Quod in Ultione, sive Pœnis, spectandum sit, non malum præteritum, sed bonum futurum: hoc est, quod Pœnas infligere nullo alio fine licitum sit, nisi ut ipse qui peccavit corrigatur, vel alii supplicio ejus moniti fiant meliores: quia Ultio, quatenus solum præteritum consideratur, nihil aliud sit præter triumphum, & gloriam animi, quæ ad nullum finem dirigitur; cum finis futura res sit; & quod ad nullum finem dirigitur, vanum sit. Male. Justitia Dei vindicativa nequaquam vane exigit pœnas æternas ob peccata præterita, in suam ipsius gloriam; non autem ad correctionem damnatorum, aliorumve in judicio extremo præmonitionem. Prov. xvi, 4. Et Satisfactio Christi non ad hos tantum fines referenda est; sed potissimum ad demonstrationem Justitiæ Divinæ, ut sit ipse justus, & justificans eum qui est ex fide Jesu: Rom. iii, 25, 26.
units.tr: 4. As for what must be considered in vengeance, or punishments, the point is not the past evil but the future good. That is, it is lawful to inflict punishments for no other end than that the one who sinned may be corrected, or that others may be warned by his punishment and become better. For vengeance, insofar as it looks only to the past, is nothing but triumph and the pride of spirit, directed to no end; since the end must be a future thing, and whatever is directed to no end is empty. False. The vindictive justice of God by no means demands eternal punishments for past sins in vain, for his own glory alone and not for the correction of the damned or for warning others at the last judgment (Prov. xvi, 4). Nor is Christ's satisfaction to be referred only to these ends, but chiefly to the demonstration of the justice of God, so that he may be just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus (Rom. iii, 25, 26).

units.la: VI. Lex igitur Divina Creaturis rationalibus, & speciatim Hominibus, officia sua præscribit. Mich. vi, 8. „Indicavit tibi, ô homo, quid sit bonum: ecquid Jehovah requisivit abs te, nisi ut exerceas jus, & ames benignitatem, & modeste ambules cum Deo tuo.
units.tr: VI. The divine law therefore prescribes its duties to rational creatures, and especially to men. Mic. vi, 8: "He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you, but that you do justice, and love mercy, and walk humbly with your God?"

units.la: Illa dispescitur in Moralem, Cerimonialem, & Politicam Mosaicam.
units.tr: This law is divided into the Moral, Ceremonial, and Mosaic Political law.

units.la: Cerimonialis completitur constitutiones de cerimoniis typicis & cultu œconomico V. T. quæ Chriftum ejusque officia ac beneficia tunc præfigurârunt, & Euangelium promissionis confirmârunt; quanquam interim statum Ecclesiæ adolescentis duriuscule exercuerunt. Gal. iv,1,-4. Col. 2, 16,17. Hebr. ix,9,10. x,1. Dan. ix, 27. Instituta ista formaliter, sub ratione talium signorum & typorum, ad Euangelium pertinent: verum actus istic materialiter mandati, & sic hominum conscientias obligantes, tanquam additamenta vel ampliationes ad secundum & quartum Decalogi præceptum pro isto tempore referri debuerunt:
units.tr: The Ceremonial law comprises the regulations concerning the typical ceremonies and the economic worship of the Old Testament, which then prefigured Christ and his offices and benefits, and confirmed the gospel of promise, although meanwhile they burdened the condition of the young Church rather harshly (Gal. iv, 1–4; Col. ii, 16, 17; Heb. ix, 9, 10; x, 1; Dan. ix, 27). These institutions, formally, under the aspect of such signs and types, belong to the gospel; but the acts commanded in them materially, and so binding the consciences of men, ought to be referred, for that time, as additions or extensions to the second and fourth precepts of the Decalogue.

units.la: Cum Deus etiam singulari ratione vellet esse Princeps Israëlitarum; Jud. viii, 23. 1. Sam. viii,7. cum Exod. xix, 5, 6. Deut. vii, 6. ipse in istâ ⊖ εσκεχτ singulares Leges Politicas tulit; constitutiones ad statum istius Reip. & ad judicia forensia spectantes, generalibus & communibus Præceptis Moralibus adjectas, & subsumtas in peculiari istâ Politiâ, atque in terra ei Divinitus datâ. Vide Exod. xxi,1, &c. Gen. xlix,10. Eph. ii, 12,-16.
units.tr: Since God wished, by a singular right, to be the Prince of the Israelites (Judg. viii, 23; 1 Sam. viii, 7; compare Exod. xix, 5, 6; Deut. vii, 6), he himself enacted in that people singular political laws: regulations pertaining to the state of that commonwealth and to the judicial courts, added to the general and common moral precepts and subsumed under them in that peculiar polity and in the land divinely given to it. See Exod. xxi, 1 ff.; Gen. xlix, 10; Eph. ii, 12–16.

units.la: VII. Lex Moralis appellatur καθ' ἐξοχὴν, quæ mandata de moribus vivendi, omnibus hominibus communiter, ex sanctissimâ Dei voluntate præscripta, completitur: sicut Euangelium credenda de Christo continet. Decalogus vulgò dicitur; quia Deus ipse decem præceptis distinxit, & sic duabus tabulis lapideis exaravit: Deut. iv, 13. x, 4. Vocatur etiam Lex charitatis; quia finis & complementum ejus est charitas; vinculum perfectionis: 1 Tim. 1, 5. Rom. xiii, 8. Col. iii, 14. Universa enim ejus observantia duplici dilectionis officio, Dei scil. & proximi, absolvitur: Matth. xxii, 37,-40. Verùm istic secundum magnum mandatum simile dicitur primo; quia ab eodem Legilegislatore, & sic eâdem auctoritate, ad utramque dilectionem simili pietatis affectû præstandam, obligati sumus; atque adeò proximum nostrum propter Deum, & in ordine ad Deum diligere debemus. Sic utraque ista dilectio indissolubili vinculo nunc altera alteri cohæret: qui enim proximum non diligit, is non præstat Deo hunc debitum actum obedientiæ; neque in proximo agnoscit & æstimat imaginem Dei, quemadmodum per Legem tenetur; quod dilectioni Divinæ adversatur: 1 Johan. iv, 19, 20. Qui verò Deum non diligit, fieri non potest ut is proximum verè diligat propter Deum, & in ordine ad ipsum. Conscientia enim debet se Deo immediate subjicere, & absolutè; ac propter mandatum Dei, atque in ipsius gloriam, proximo etiam officia Divinitus præscripta præstare. Actus isti, ad proximum relati, civiles tantum sunt: sed quatenus interim devotâ mente mandato Dei attendimus, huic nos sincerè subjicimus, sic Deo parere satagimus, & gloriæ ipsius operam damus, iidem cultûs religiosi rationem habent: Jac. 1, 27. Religiosus enim cultus - hic est, invisere orphanos & viduas in afflictione ipsarum, &c
units.tr: VII. The Moral Law is called, par excellence [καθ' ἐξοχήν], that which comprises the commands about how to live, prescribed to all men in common from the most holy will of God, just as the gospel contains what is to be believed about Christ. It is commonly called the Decalogue, because God himself distinguished it by ten precepts and so inscribed it on two tables of stone (Deut. iv, 13; x, 4).
