It is also called the Law of love, because its aim and fulfilment is love, the bond of perfectness (1 Tim. i, 5; Rom. xiii, 8; Col. iii, 14). For its whole observance is summed up in the twofold duty of love, namely of God and of neighbour (Matt. xxii, 37–40). But there the second commandment, like the great one, is said to come first, because we are bound by the same Lawgiver, and so by the same authority, to render each love with a like affection of piety; and therefore we ought to love our neighbour for God's sake and in relation to God. Thus these two loves cohere with each other by an indissoluble bond: for whoever does not love his neighbour does not render to God this due act of obedience, nor recognises and esteems in the neighbour the image of God, as the Law requires; which is contrary to divine love (1 John iv, 19, 20). And whoever does not love God cannot truly love his neighbour for God's sake and in relation to him. For the conscience ought to submit itself to God immediately and absolutely, and to perform for the neighbour also the duties divinely prescribed, for the command of God and to his glory. These acts, referred to the neighbour, are merely civil; but insofar as meanwhile we attend to the command of God with a devout mind, submit ourselves sincerely to it, strive thus to obey God and labour for his glory, the same acts have the character of religious worship (Jas. i, 27: "Religious worship... is this, to visit orphans and widows in their affliction," etc.).

units.la: VIII. Prior tabula completitur actûs dilectionis & obedientiæ ipsi Deo immediatè deferendos.
units.tr: VIII. The first table comprises the acts of love and obedience to be paid immediately to God himself.

units.la: Sic primo præcepto cavetur, ut ipse יהוה אלהים omnino, & quidem solus, habeatur & colatur pro uno vero Deo; sive ut ipsi soli tribuatur cultus Religionis, tanquàm objecto suo proprio & adæquato. Secundo præcepto docetur, quibus mediis institutis ipsi cultus Religionis fit deferendus: non per simulachra, aut qualemcunque ἐθελοθρησκείαν; sed quemadmodum ipse Deus ordinavit; per Ministerium Verbi & Sacramentorum, &c. Præcepto tertio, quali sermone de Deo & rebus Divinis, vel ad Deum, loquendum fit: non temerè, aut irreverenter; sed adhibitâ semper piâ & religiosá attentione ac reverentiâ. Quarto præcepto, quo appropriato tempore potissimùm: itâ scil. ut sex dies operarios perpetuò excipiat unus Sabbathicus, exercitiis religionis ac pietatis, quâ publicè, quâ privatim, omninò impendendus ; omissò interim omni opere servili & ordinariæ vocationis nostræ in negotiis hujus sæculi ; nisi quæ occurrant præsentis inevitabilis necessitatis, aut necessariæ charitatis: Matth. xii, 7, 10, 11, 12. Luc. xiii, 15, 16.
units.tr: Thus by the first precept it is provided that the LORD God [יהוה אלהים] be wholly, and indeed alone, held and worshipped as the one true God; that is, that the worship of religion be given to him alone as its proper and adequate object. The second precept teaches by what instituted means the worship of religion is to be paid to him: not through images or any self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία], but as God himself has ordained, through the ministry of the Word and the sacraments, etc. The third precept says in what manner one ought to speak of God and divine things, or to God: not rashly or irreverently, but always with pious and religious attention and reverence. The fourth precept says at what time, above all: namely, that one day in seven, the Sabbath, is always to be set apart after six working days, to be wholly devoted to the exercises of religion and piety, both public and private, with every servile work and the ordinary business of our calling in the affairs of this age set aside, except those that arise from present unavoidable necessity or necessary charity (Matt. xii, 7, 10–12; Luke xiii, 15, 16).

units.la: Posterior tabula præscribit officia proximo præstanda ; sed propter Deum, &c. scil. cum respectû alicujus superioritatis ; quid Parentibus, Magistratibus, &c. debeatur ; quinto præcepto: tum citra istiusmodi respectum ; ubi vel ipsi vitæ prospicitur, ejusque securitati ; in sexto præcepto: vel castitati ; in septimo: vel bonis externis ; in octavo: vel vitæ homileticæ ; in nono: vel denique de primis etiam mentis & affectuum motibus bene dirigendis, instruimur ; quod fit decimo præcepto.
units.tr: The second table prescribes the duties to be performed toward the neighbour, but for God's sake, etc.; namely, with regard to some superiority: what is owed to parents, magistrates, etc. is taught in the fifth precept; then, without such regard, where provision is made for life itself and its security, in the sixth precept; or for chastity, in the seventh; or for external goods, in the eighth; or for the good name of one's neighbour, in the ninth; and finally we are instructed in rightly directing even the first movements of mind and affections, which is done by the tenth precept.

units.la: IX. De Virtutibus per singula præcepta speciatim mandatis, vitiisque prohibitis, agemus σὺν Θεῷ in Compendio practico: nunc generales quasdam de Lege morali quæstiones, & controversias quæ cum Adversariis circa ejus præcepta intercedunt, expediemus. Quæritur autem primò; An integra Lex moralis sit Juris Divini naturalis ; atque adeò absolutè immutabilis & indispensabilis? Resp. Jus Divinum naturale nunc intelligitur, quod ex naturâ Dei necessariò fluit: & sic contradistinguitur à Iure Divino positivo. Talis est cultus Dei naturalis ; qui primo præcepto potissimùm exigitur: sed cultus institutus, ad quem secundo præcepto potissimùm obligati sumus, & tempus definitum, quo iste solenniter præstandus, aliaque istiusmodi, ad Ius Divinum positivum pertinent ; utpotè in posteriori tabulâ, de quorundam hominum superioritate. rioritate, dominiorum distinctione, gradibus in matrimonio observandis, &c. Negamus igitur, omnia & singula Decalogi præcepta, quæque iis comprehensa sunt, esse Iuris ipsi Deo naturalis, & sic absolutè immutabilis atque indispensabilis ipsi Deo.
units.tr: IX. We shall deal with the virtues commanded and the vices forbidden under each precept individually in the practical compendium, with God's help [σὺν Θεῷ]. Now we shall settle certain general questions about the moral Law, and the controversies which arise with our adversaries concerning its precepts. First, then, the question is: Is the whole moral Law of natural divine right, and so absolutely immutable and indispensable? Answer. By natural divine right is meant that which flows necessarily from the nature of God, and so is distinguished from positive divine right. Such is the natural worship of God, which is required chiefly by the first precept; but the instituted worship, to which we are bound chiefly by the second precept, and the fixed time at which it is to be solemnly performed, and other things of this kind, belong to positive divine right; as in the second table, concerning the superiority of certain men, the distinction of dominions, the degrees to be observed in marriage, etc. We therefore deny that all and each of the precepts of the Decalogue, and whatever is comprehended in them, are of right natural to God himself, and so absolutely immutable and indispensable to God himself.

units.la: X. quæritur secundò; An tota Lex moralis sit Juris nobis naturalis? Resp. Affirm. Itascil. ut saltem implicitè & virtualiter tota contineatur in communibus illis notionibus practicis, quæ hominibus initio concreatæ fuerunt, &cum naturâ pariter propagandæ; consequenter si integra mansisset imago Dei in hominibus, illa etiam tota indè deduci, vel eò reduci, potuisset; nunc verò post lapsum ac tantam naturæ corruptionem elici saltem potest, quantum sufficit ad ἀναπολογησίαν Gentilium Lege scriptâ destitutorum: Rom. 1, 20. qui propterea jus Dei agnoscere dicuntur; verf. 32. & sibi ipsis Lex; ut qui offendant opus Legis scriptum in cordibus suis, unà testimonium reddente ipsorum conscientiâ; cap. 2, 14, 15. Atque amplius, iii, 19, 20. "Scimus, quæcunque Lex dicit, iis qui in Lege sunt dicere; ut omne os obstruatur, & obnoxius fiat totus mundus condemnationi Dei. Propterea ex operibus Legis nulla caro justificabitur in conspectu ejus: &c.
units.tr: X. The second question: Is the whole moral Law of natural right for us? Answer. Affirmative. That is, it is contained in such a way, at least implicitly and virtually, in those common practical notions which were implanted in men at the beginning, and are propagated together with nature; consequently, if the image of God had remained whole in men, the whole of it could also have been deduced or reduced thence; but now, after the fall and so great a corruption of nature, it can be drawn out at least so far as suffices for the defence [ἀπολογία] of the Gentiles destitute of the written Law (Rom. i, 20), who for this reason are said to know the right of God (v. 32), and to be a law to themselves, as those who show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness together with them (ch. ii, 14, 15). And further, iii, 19, 20: "We know that whatever the Law says, it says to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may become liable to the condemnation of God. Therefore by the works of the Law no flesh will be justified in his sight," etc.

units.la: Obj. Atqui actualis & distincta singulorum officiorum notitia per naturam non inest singulis hominibus; neque ex ratione naturali elici potest: etiam in iis quæ ad cultum Dei naturalem pertinent, & ad benè ordinatam hominum societatem necessaria sunt, plurimi defectus passim in Gentibus deprehenduntur. Resp. A statu per lapsum corrupto, non valet consequentia ad statum primævum; & ad naturam, qualis initio condita fuit. Quin imò de Gentilibus, aliisque infidelibus, id minùs mirandum est; cum etiam inter eos, qui Christianam Religionem utcunque profitentur, varii errores contra Jus Divinum reperiantur; &c. XI. Quaeritur tertiò ; An igitur eadem Lex moralis fuerit etiam ante Mosen? Resp. Lex scripto expressa ab ipso Deo, duabus tabulis & decem per eas praeceptis distincta, variisque commentariis, explicationibus & applicationibus Θεοπνεύστως aucta, & sic Israelitis tradita fuit primum per Mosen. Psal. ciii, 7. Notas fecit vias suas Mosi; posteris Israelis actiones suas. Johan. 1,17. Lex illa per Mosen data est. Galat. iii, 19. Quid igitur Lex? transgressionum (plenius aperiendarum, hominumque de iis convincendorum) gratia adjecta est, &c. Atque ita metonymice & synecdochice Lex in SS. Literis frequentissime usurpatur. Utpote Rom. v, 13. Usque ad Legem peccatum erat in mundo, &c. non quasi Lex antea prorsus non extitisset: Peccatum enim est Legis transgressio; ἀνομία: 1 Joh. iii. 4. & consequenter, ubi non est Lex, ibi nec transgressio est: Rom. iii, 15. sed quia prius non extitit eo modo. Cum vero ipsi Gentiles, Lege scriptâ destituti, sibi sint Lex, & opus Legis in cordibus suis scriptum gerant, &c. multo magis, imo perfecte, in ipsis protoplastis adhuc integris, Iuris istius Divini ac Legis moralis cognitio extitisse censenda est.
units.tr: Objection: Yet the actual and distinct knowledge of each separate duty is not present in every man by nature, nor can it be drawn from natural reason. Even in matters that pertain to the natural worship of God and are necessary for a well-ordered human society, many defects are found everywhere among the Gentiles. Answer: The consequence does not hold from the state corrupted by the Fall to the original state, or to nature as it was first created. Indeed, this is less surprising in the case of the Gentiles and other unbelievers, since even among those who in some way profess the Christian religion, various errors against Divine Law are found, etc. XI. The third question is: Was this same moral law also in force before Moses? Answer: The law, set down in writing by God himself, distinguished into two tables and ten precepts, and increased by various commentaries, explanations and applications [Θεοπνεύστως, divinely inspired], was first delivered to the Israelites through Moses. Psal. ciii, 7. He made known his ways to Moses, and his doings to the children of Israel. John 1:17. That law was given through Moses. Gal. iii, 19. What then is the law? It was added because of transgressions (to be disclosed more fully, and to convict men of them), etc. And so, by metonymy and synecdoche, the Law is very often used in the Holy Scriptures. Thus Rom. v, 13. Until the law, sin was in the world, etc., not as if the law had not existed at all before; for sin is the transgression of the law, lawlessness [ἀνομία]: 1 John iii. 4. And consequently, where there is no law, there is also no transgression: Rom. iii, 15. But the law had not existed in that way before. Since the Gentiles themselves, destitute of the written law, are a law to themselves and bear the work of the law written in their hearts, etc., much more, indeed perfectly, the knowledge of that Divine right and moral law must be judged to have existed in the first parents themselves while they were still unimpaired.

units.la: XII. Thesin nostram inductione amplius probamus; similiter ut Apostolus Iacobus, II, 10, 11, concatenationem officiorum Lege praescriptorum asserturus, eam ostendit in istis praeceptis, Ne moechris, & Ne occidas: caeterorum enim est par ratio. Et Paulus, Rom. xiii, 9. omnia posteriores Tabulae praecepta ad unam summam revocat similiter: Siquidem illud, Non moechaberis, Non occides, Non furaberis, Non falsum testimonium dices, Non concupisces, & siquod aliud est praeceptum, in hoc sermone summatim comprehenditur, Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum.
units.tr: XII. We prove our thesis further by induction, just as the Apostle James, wishing to assert the interconnection of the duties prescribed by the law, shows it in these precepts, Do not commit adultery and Do not kill (James 2:10, 11); for the same reasoning applies to the rest. Paul likewise reduces all the precepts of the second table to one summary, Rom. xiii, 9. For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

units.la: Istud autem α. Non Moechaberis, & quae eò pertinent, protoplastis etiam praescripta & cognita fuisse liquido constat ex verbis Adami de Eva, Genes. 2, 23,24, Hæc demùm vice adest os ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea. --- Relinquet est vir patrem suum & matrem suam ⁊ & adhærebit uxori suæ, erruntque in carnem unam. Et cap. 1, 27, 28. Marem & fœminam creavit eos. Deinde benedixit eis Deus, &c. Hinc ipse Servator deducit, Conjugium esse unius viri cum unâ muliere individuam vitæ societatem, contra Iudæorum repudia, quanquam propter duritiem cordis eorum politice permissa; Matth. xix, 3-9. Eodem modo facile colligitur, polygamiam, adulterium, scortationem, &c. esse illicita.
units.tr: α. Thou shalt not commit adultery, and what pertains to it, is clearly shown to have been prescribed and known to the first parents as well, from the words of Adam about Eve, Gen. 2:23, 24: This at last is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. ... Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh. And Gen. 1:27, 28: Male and female created he them. And God blessed them, etc. From this the Saviour himself deduces that marriage is the lifelong union of one man with one woman, against the divorces of the Jews, although these were politically permitted because of the hardness of their hearts; Matt. 19:3-9. In the same way it is easily gathered that polygamy, adultery, fornication, etc., are unlawful.

units.la: β. Exinde etiam Paulus officia maritorum erga uxores deducit, Eph.v,28,29,30. & viri dignitatem præ muliere, 1 Tim.II, 13. ex eo, quod Adamus prior formatus sit; deinde Eva: scil. in auxilium ipsi commodum: Gen. II,18,20. Similiter 1 Cor. xi,7,8,9. Vir non debet operire caput: (quod esset signum subjectionis:) cùm is imago sit & gloria Dei; at mulier gloria viri est. &c. Adde ibidem, 14, 15. Anne natura quidem ipsa hoc vos docet, quòd viro quidem comatum esse dedecori sit: &c. Ex eodem illo fundamento façillimè deduci potest utriusque parentis ἐξουσίᾳ præ liberis. Imò ex istis verbis Gen. II, 24. Relinquet est vir, &c. clarissimè liquet liberorum primùm in vitâ cœlibe obligatio ad parentes, ac porro etiam in conjugio pro re natâ & ratâ.
units.tr: β. From this, Paul also derives the duties of husbands towards their wives, Eph. 5:28, 29, 30, and the dignity of the man above the woman, 1 Tim. 2:13, from the fact that Adam was formed first and then Eve, namely as a suitable help for him: Gen. 2:18, 20. Similarly, 1 Cor. 11:7, 8, 9: A man ought not to cover his head (because that would be a sign of subjection), since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man, etc. Add in the same place, 14, 15: Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to have long hair is a dishonour, etc. From the same foundation the authority of each parent over the children can very easily be deduced. Indeed, from these words of Gen. 2:24, Therefore shall a man leave, etc., it is quite clear that the obligation of children to their parents lies first in the unmarried state, and afterwards also in marriage, as the circumstances and the ratified arrangement require.

units.la: γ. Ex imagine Dei in singulis hominibus spectandâ, colligitur eorum æstimatio & dilectio mutua: atque adeo præceptum illud, Non occides: Gen. 1x, 5. Nam & proximi execratio propterea fugienda est: Jac. 1 11,9. Unde non solum Caini homicidium arguitur; Gen. iv, 10,11,12. sed etiam vultus iracundus; vers. 5,6,7. atque ipse se dignum judicavit, qui vicinum ab obvio quolibet interficeretur; 13,14.
units.tr: γ. From the image of God to be regarded in each man, their mutual esteem and love are inferred, and so that precept, Thou shalt not kill: Gen. 9:5. For even the cursing of a neighbour must therefore be avoided: James 3:9. Hence not only the murder of Cain is condemned, Gen. 4:10, 11, 12, but also the angry countenance, vers. 5, 6, 7; and he himself judged himself worthy to be killed by whomever might meet him, 13, 14.

units.la: δ.
units.tr: δ.

units.la: §. Illud autem Non furaberis, colligitur ex dictis, Genes. 1, 28, 29. Implete terram, eamque subjicite: & dominamini, &c. collato dilectionis officio. Nam multiplicatis hominibus, multiplicari, aut potius dividi, necessario debuit jus in terram & creaturas terrestres: singuli suas habere debuerunt habitationes, & sua dominia rerum subjectarum, seu occupatarum; nec unus alteri eas debuit eripere. Unde etiam Actor. XVII, 25, 26. Ipse dat omnibus vitam, & halitum, & omnia. Fecitque ex uno sanguine totam gentem hominum, ut habitaret super universa superficie terræ, definitis præstitutis temporibus, & positis terminis habitationis eorum.
units.tr: §. That Thou shalt not steal is inferred from what is said in Gen. 1:28, 29, Fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion, etc., when compared with the duty of love. For when men were multiplied, the right over the land and the earthly creatures necessarily had to be multiplied, or rather divided: each was to have his own habitations and his own dominions over the things subject to him, or occupied by him, and one was not to snatch them from another. Hence also Acts 17:25, 26: He giveth to all life, and breath, and all things. And hath made of one blood all nations of men, for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.

units.la: ¶. Similiter ex imagine Dei, qui est Deus veritatis; Psal. XXXI, 6. elicitur illud, Non dices falsum testimonium. Ad illam enim pertinet justitia & sanctimonia veritatis: Eph. IV, 24. Unde Diaboli ab illa defectio sic exprimitur. Joh. VIII, 44. In veritate non perstitit. atque item Hominum, Rom III, 4. Omnis autem homo mendax.
units.tr: ¶. Similarly, from the image of God, who is the God of truth (Ps. 31:6), is derived Thou shalt not bear false witness. For to that image belong righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:24). Hence the Devil's falling away from it is expressed thus: He abode not in the truth (John 8:44); and likewise that of men: But every man is a liar (Rom. 3:4).

units.la: §. Ex eadem justitia & sanctitate vera, etiam colligi potest illud, Non concupisces: omnes scil. motiones voluntatis & affectuum, etiam primas, juste ac sancte regendas & habendas esse.
units.tr: §. From the same true righteousness and holiness, it can also be gathered that Thou shalt not covet: namely, that all movements of the will and the affections, even the first ones, must be justly and holily governed and held in check.

units.la: XIII. Prioris tabulæ similis est ratio.
units.tr: XIII. The reasoning for the first table is similar.

units.la: α. Agnoscendum enim & religiose colendum esse unum verum Deum, ad cujus imaginem conditi erant protoplasti, quique omnia fecit propter seipsum; alienos autem Deos nequaquam habendos, sic facile cognoverunt: Col. III, 10. Eph. IV, 24.
units.tr: α. We must acknowledge and worship with reverence the one true God, after whose image the first parents were created, and who made all things for himself; that other gods must by no means be had, they readily understood. Col. 3:10; Eph. 4:24.

units.la: β. Quin & sanctum illum ac zeloten, præter cultum ipsius naturalem, non alio quam à se instituto, colendum esse. Spiritum illum infinitum nulla imagine corporea exprimendum, nec in ea, aut per eam, suum ipsi cultum deferendum.
units.tr: β. Moreover, that holy and jealous God is to be worshipped by the worship that is natural to him, and not by any other than that instituted by himself. That infinite Spirit is not to be expressed by any bodily image, nor is his worship to be offered in or through such an image.

units.la: γ. Itemque sanctissimum sermonis, ut & omnium quae in ipsis ac penes ipsos erant, auctorem, sermone irreverenti aut temerario non esse dehonestandum; sed omnino pie celebrandum.
units.tr: γ. Likewise, the most holy author of speech, and of all the things that are in and around them, is not to be dishonoured by irreverent or rash speech, but is to be celebrated altogether piously.

units.la: §. Nec de Sabbathi observantia dubitandum: juxta Gen. II,2,3. Cum autem perfecisset Deus die septimo opus suum, quod fecerat; quievit ipso die septimo ab omni opere suo quod fecerat: Et benedixit Deus diei septimo, & sanctificavit ipsum; cum in eo quievisset ab omni opere suo, quod creaverat Deus, faciendo. Isto scil. tempore, atque ea occasione, cum Deus sex diebus opera creationis absolvisset, iisque finem imposuisset die septimo; ipse diei septimo benedixit singulari quodam modo, & benedicendo sacrum esse voluit, atque exercitiis Religionis sancte transfigendum. Per sex dies operarios protoplasti hortum Edenis non solum custodire, sed & colere debuerunt; imo & terram subjicere: Gen. II,15. I,28. Verum ab isto opere quiescendum fuit quoque die septimo; cultui Divino quiete vacandum; eoque magis ad aeternam & caelestem quietem adspirandum.
units.tr: §. Nor is there any doubt about the observance of the Sabbath, according to Gen. 2:2, 3: And on the seventh day God finished his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had rested from all his work which God had created by making. That is, at that time, and on that occasion, when God had completed the works of creation in six days and had brought them to an end on the seventh day, he blessed the seventh day in a singular way, and by blessing it willed it to be holy and to be spent in the exercises of religion. For six working days the first parents were to keep and also to cultivate the garden of Eden, indeed to subdue the earth (Gen. 2:15; 1:28). But they were also to rest from that labour on the seventh day, to devote the rest to the worship of God, and so much the more to aspire to the eternal and heavenly rest.

units.la: 2. In quarto Decalogi praecepto, Exod. xx,8,11. eadem primaevae institutionis ratio adjungitur: Nam sex diebus perfecit Jehovah caelum ipsum, & terram, & mare, & quicquid est in eis; quievit vero die illo septimo: idcirco benedixit Jehovah diei Sabbathi, & sanctificavit illum.
units.tr: 2. In the fourth precept of the Decalogue (Exod. 20:8, 11) the same reason of the original institution is added: For in six days Jehovah made heaven itself, and earth, and sea, and whatever is in them; but he rested on that seventh day; therefore Jehovah blessed the day of the Sabbath and sanctified it.

units.la: 3. Ejusdem institutionis pristinae repetitio, vel restitutio quasi postliminio, occurrit etiam in historia mannae singulis diebus in deserto colligendae; nisi quod sexto quoque die dupla portio esset colligenda, una pro ipso sexto, altera pro sequente septimo die, quo sancta quies agi debuit: Exod. XVI,4,5;22,23,25,26.
units.tr: 3. A repetition, or as it were a restoration by right of return, of the same original institution also occurs in the story of the manna, which was to be gathered every day in the wilderness; except that on the sixth day a double portion was to be gathered, one for the sixth day itself and the other for the following seventh day, on which holy rest was to be observed (Exod. 16:4, 5, 22, 23, 25, 26).

units.la: 4. Addimus Hebr. iv,3,4. "Introimus enim in requiem nos, qui credidimus; sicut dixit; Itaque ,,juravi in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam: ,, quamvis operibus à jacto mundi fundamento factis. Ita ,,enim dixit quodam in loco de septimo die; Et requie-,,vit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis. Istic Sabbathum hebdomadale, secundum superiora, etiam diserte refertur ad quietem ipsius Dei, operibus à jacto mundi fundamento factis, tanquam ad suum principium: & ab eo distinguitur Sabbatismus terræ Canaan, ex molesta peregrinatione per desertum; typus beatæ quietis in cœlesti patria fidelibus obtinen-dæ.
units.tr: 4. We add Heb. 4:3, 4: "For we who have believed enter into rest, as he said: 'So I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter into my rest,' although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has said somewhere of the seventh day, 'And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.'" There, according to what has been said above, the weekly Sabbath is also expressly referred to the rest of God himself, with works finished from the foundation of the world, as to its beginning; and from this is distinguished the Sabbath-rest of the land of Canaan, after the tiresome wandering through the wilderness, as a type of the blessed rest to be obtained by believers in the heavenly fatherland.

units.la: XIV. Obj. 1.
units.tr: XIV. First objection.

units.la: Omne morale pertinet ad imaginem Dei in homine; & consequenter necessario fluit ex natura ipsius Dei: Sed præceptum de Sabbatho hebdomadali non fluit ex ea necessariò: Ergò quarti præcepti alia est ratio. Resp. Nego, quicquid morale est, & sic ad imaginem Dei in homine pertinet, necessario fluere ex natura Dei. Deus etiam quædam libere ab ipso determinata, potuit naturæ humanæ initio præscribere ac inscribere, & ad imaginem suam referre; atque hoc fecit. Confer sup. th. 9.
units.tr: Every moral precept pertains to the image of God in man, and consequently flows necessarily from the nature of God himself. But the precept concerning the weekly Sabbath does not flow necessarily from that nature. Therefore the fourth precept has another reason. Answer: I deny that whatever is moral, and so pertains to the image of God in man, must flow necessarily from the nature of God. God could, at the beginning, prescribe and inscribe on human nature certain things that he had freely determined, and refer them to his image; and this he did. See above, section 9.

units.la: Obj. 2, Sabbathum est simpliciter cerimoniale, & signum typicum sanctificationis sub V. T. atque ita ordinatum ad Christum venturum, &c. Ergo non est morale; nec fuit ab initio. Exod. xxxi, 13. Sabbatha mea servatote: nam signum est inter me & vos, per generationes vestras: ad cognoscendum, me Jehovam esse, qui sanctifico vos. Ezech. xx, 10, 11, 12. ,,Eduxi ipsos e terra ,,Ægypti, & abduxi ipsos in desertum: ubi dedi ipsis ,,statuta mea, & jura mea nota feci ipsis; quæ qui faceret ,,homo, viveret per ea. Ac etiam Sabbatha mea dedi ipsis, ut essent signo inter me & ipsos, ut sciretur me Jehovam sanctificare ipsos. &c. Resp. 1. Cum numero multitudinis Sabbatha appellantur, collectivè intelligenda sunt omnia, quibus istud nomen ex usu SS. Scripturæ convenit: utpotè Levit. xvi. 31. xxiii, 32. 39. xxv, 2. 4. non præcise, nec etiam absolute hebdomadarium. 2. Isto hebdomadali die sacro fideles Deum sanctificabant suo modo; ipsique simul à Deo sanctificabantur; h. e. in verâ sanctimoniâ confirmabantur & promovebantur, per gratiam Divinam in Messiâ: hoc ipsum tunc in præsenti experiebantur; simulque, juxta promissionem Divinam, de futuro per religiosam observationem Sabbathi colligebant. Sed non omne signum statim est mera cerimonia ac typus V. T. Messiam venturum præfigurans. Certè etiam nunc fideles ac pii experiuntur, & colligunt, se per piam sui Sabbathi, sive diei Dominici observationem, confirmari ac promoveri in sanctificatione per gratiam Christi, &c. 3. Faciles etiàm admittimus, observationem Sabbathi hebdomadalis sub V. Test. ex speciali quâdam ordinatione Divinâ accepisse quoque respectum & usum cerimoniale typicum præfigurativum Christi ac beneficiorum ejus. Verùm indè non magis sequitur, Sabbathum ab initio fuisse talem typum, vel etiàm sub V. T. non habuisse in se aliquid morale; quàm ex Gen. ix, 12, -. sequitur, iridem ab initio fuisse tale signum mundi non amplius interituri per diluvium; vel etiam post istam ordinationem, non fuisse meteorum aliquod naturale. 4. Nec magis ex loco Ezechielis colligi potest, Sabbathum ante deductionem Israëlitarum in desertum prorsùs non obtinuisse, quam alia præcepta, quæ, fatentibus iis qui hîc à nobis dissentiunt, verè sunt moralia. 5. Sed deinceps verf. 13. atque iterum, 24. exprobrat Deus Israëlitis, quod jura sua non fecissent, statuta sua sprevissent, ac Sabbatha profanâssent: & consequenter, 25. dedisset tpsis statuta non bona, & jura per quæ non vivērent. Quoniam scil. propter peccata, non pertinebant ad ipsos bona cæteroquin promissa; sed pœnæ in sanctione comminatoria expressæ. Confer Rom. vii, 10, 12, 13. 12, 13. itemque Psal. lxxxi, 12, 13. Interim, quoniam nonnulli statuta non bona, & jura per quæ non viverent; exponunt de institutis merè cerimonialibus; observa quoque, Sabbatha ab illis clarissimè distingui.
units.tr: Second objection: The Sabbath is simply ceremonial, and a typical sign of sanctification under the Old Testament, and so ordained to point to the coming Christ, etc. Therefore it is not moral, nor was it from the beginning. Exod. 31:13: Keep my Sabbaths; for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am Jehovah who sanctifies you. Ezek. 20:10, 11, 12: I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness; there I gave them my statutes and made known to them my judgments, which if a man does, he shall live by them. And also my Sabbaths I gave them, to be a sign between me and them, that it might be known that I am Jehovah who sanctifies them, etc. Answer 1. Since the Sabbaths are called by a plural number, all the things to which that name properly belongs in the usage of Holy Scripture are to be understood collectively: for example Lev. 16:31; 23:32, 39; 25:2, 4, not precisely or even absolutely the weekly Sabbath. 2. On that weekly holy day the faithful sanctified God in their own way, and at the same time were themselves sanctified by God; that is, they were confirmed and advanced in true holiness through the divine grace in the Messiah. This they then experienced in the present, and at the same time, according to the divine promise, gathered from the religious observance of the Sabbath for the future. But not every sign is at once a mere ceremony and a type of the Old Testament prefiguring the coming Messiah. Certainly even now the faithful and the pious experience, and gather, that they are confirmed and advanced in sanctification through the grace of Christ by the pious observance of their own Sabbath, that is, the Lord's Day, etc. 3. We readily admit that the observance of the weekly Sabbath under the Old Testament, by a special divine ordinance, also received a ceremonial, typical and prefigurative respect and use relating to Christ and his benefits. But it does not follow from this that the Sabbath was such a type from the beginning, or that even under the Old Testament it did not have in itself something moral; any more than it follows from Gen. 9:12 that the rainbow was such a sign from the beginning of a world not to perish again by flood, or that, even after that ordinance, it was not some natural meteor. 4. Nor can it be gathered from the passage in Ezekiel that the Sabbath had altogether not been in force before the leading of the Israelites into the wilderness, any more than the other precepts which, as those who dissent from us here admit, are truly moral. 5. But afterwards, in verse 13, and again in verse 24, God reproaches the Israelites that they had not done his judgments, had despised his statutes, and had profaned his Sabbaths; and consequently, in verse 25, that he had given them statutes that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live. Since, that is, on account of their sins, the other good things promised to them did not belong to them, but only the punishments expressed in the threatening sanction. Compare Rom. 7:10, 12, 13, and likewise Ps. 81:12, 13. Meanwhile, since some expound statutes that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live as referring to institutions that are purely ceremonial, observe also that the Sabbaths are there most clearly distinguished from them.

units.la: XV. Sed neque omittenda videtur distinctio Juris hominibus naturalis, in primævum, & secundarium. Primævum spectat naturam à Deo primum institutam, & sic integram. Atque hoc, juxta integritatem imaginis Divinæ, procul dubio integrum extitit in protoplastis; & per ordinationem Dei etiam sic propagandum fuisset ad posteros, nisi lapsus intervenisset: adeò quidem, ut hi eadem præcepta moralia deducturi fuissent ex congenitis κοιναῖς ἐννοίαις; simulque ex piâ animi inclinatione faciles admissuri parentum suorum, aliorumve, instructiones istiusmodi explicatorias & applicatorias; quemadmodum etiam alia præcepta particularia cultûs instituti, utpote de Arbore vitæ, & Scientiæ boni ac mali, &c. atque adeo etiam de die determinato, quo Sabbathum hebdomadale fuisset observandum.
units.tr: XV. But the distinction of natural law for men into primeval and secondary also seems not to be omitted. The primeval pertains to nature as first instituted by God, and so in its integrity. This, according to the integrity of the divine image, undoubtedly existed whole in the first parents; and by the ordinance of God it would also have been propagated in this way to posterity, had the fall not intervened: so much so that they would have derived these same moral precepts from innate common notions [κοιναῖς ἐννοίαις]; and at the same time, from a pious disposition of mind, would have readily admitted such explanatory and applicatory instructions from their parents or others; just as also other particular precepts of instituted worship, such as concerning the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, etc., and indeed also concerning the fixed day on which the weekly Sabbath was to be observed.

units.la: Ius naturale secundarium respicit naturam humanam per lapsum ista integritate destitutam, gravissimaque corruptione ac plurimis miseriis vitiatam. In hoc statû amissa est perfectio illa habitualis sapientiæ, etiam agendorum, tum quod ad ipsa principia, tum quod ad facilitatem conclusiones inde deducendi & agnoscendi: quæ amissio ad mortem spiritualem pertinet: quamvis superstites manserint quædam reliquiæ. Imo ratione circumstantiarum multæ applicationes aliter fieri debuerunt in hoc jure secundario, quam faciendæ fuissent in primævo: ut in judiciis politicis, de sontibus scil. puniendis, etiam capitali supplicio; de Bello, Servitute, Misericordiâ, &c. Quod autem in Iure isto secundario, in statû mere naturali, sic decerat; cum virtualiter vel eminenter etiam comprehensum fuisset primævo illo, posteà suppletum est per Divinam revelationem, Legis moralis repetitoriam, & quasi restauratoriam; speciatim vero prout ea ministerio Mosis facta est, & Israëlitis tradita, ac postmodum saepius repositá & inculcata.
units.tr: Secondary natural law concerns human nature as it is after the fall, deprived of that integrity and corrupted by grave depravity and many miseries. In this state the habitual wisdom of doing, that perfection, has been lost, both as regards the principles themselves and as regards the ease of deducing and recognising conclusions from them. This loss belongs to spiritual death, although some remnants have survived. Indeed, because of circumstances, many applications in this secondary law have had to be made differently from how they would have been made in the original law, as in political judgments, namely concerning the punishment of offenders, even by capital punishment; and concerning war, slavery, mercy, and so on. What was lacking in this secondary law in the purely natural state, although it was virtually or eminently contained in that original law, was afterwards supplied by divine revelation, as a repetition and, as it were, a restoration of the moral law. This was done especially in the form in which it was delivered to the Israelites through the ministry of Moses, and afterwards often repeated and inculcated.

units.la: XVI. Quaeritur quarto, An eadem Lex moralis adhuc obtineat sub N. T. ? Resp. Affirm. 1. Quia Lex moralis omnes homines & semper obligat, quod ad mores vivendi.
units.tr: XVI. Fourthly, it is asked: whether the same moral law still holds under the New Testament? Answer: Yes. First, because the moral law binds all men and always, as far as the manner of living is concerned.

units.la: 2. Hinc Christus, Matth. v, 17, 18, 19. Ne existimate me venisse, ut dissolvam Legem aut Prophetas: non veni, ut eam dissolvam; sed ut eam impleam: umbris typicis veritatem substituendo; praedictiones de Messiâ consummando; requisitam ab ipso obedientiam praestando; & alios eorum officia verè ac plene docendo. Amen quippè dico vobis; usquedum praeterierit caelum & terra, iῶτα unum aut unus apex nequaquam praeterierit ex Lege, usquedum omnia facta fuerint. Moralia praecepta minime erant abroganda, aut iis quicquam derogandum, usque in consummationem saeculi. Quisquis igitur solverit unum ex mandatis hisce minimis, & ita docuerit homines, minimus vocabitur in regno coelorum: quisquis autem fecerit & docuerit, ille vocabitur magnus in regno coelorum. Sic Legem istam communem ac perpetuam Servator proponit, cujus omnia & singula praecepta, etiam ad minimum, sub N. T. forent observanda ac docenda: quemadmodum ipse deinceps asserit & vindicat contra Pharisaeos.
units.tr: Second, hence Christ, Matt. 5:17-19: Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to destroy them, but to fulfil them: by substituting the truth for the typical shadows; by completing the predictions about the Messiah; by rendering the obedience required of him; and by truly and fully teaching their duties. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will by any means pass from the Law, until all things have been done. The moral precepts were by no means to be abrogated, nor was anything to be taken away from them, until the consummation of the age. Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments, and so teaches men, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them, he will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Thus the Saviour sets forth this common and perpetual Law, all whose precepts, each and every one, even the least, were to be observed and taught under the New Testament, as he himself afterwards asserts and defends against the Pharisees.

units.la: 3. Consequenter eadem Lex moralis ab Apostolis etiam propósita est & inculcata sub N. T. Iac. 2. 8, -11, Quodsi Legem regiam praestatis, secundum Scripturam, Diliges proximum tuum ut te ipsum, bene facitis: Sin vero personam respicitis, peccatum committitis; & redarguimini à Lege veluti transgressores. quisquis enim totam Legem servaverit, impegerit autem in uno, damnas factus est omnium. Nam qui dixit, Ne moechiaris, dixit etiam, Ne occidas: quodsi non fueris moechatus
units.tr: Third, consequently the same moral law was also proposed and inculcated by the Apostles under the New Testament. James 2:8-11: If you fulfil the royal law, according to the Scripture, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, you do well. But if you respect persons, you commit sin, and are convicted by the Law as transgressors. For whoever keeps the whole Law, but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all. For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder; now if you do not commit adultery but do commit murder, you have become a transgressor of the Law.

units.la: Nota: the printed text ends with the catchword. mœchatus; occideris autem, factus es transgressor Legis. Ita loquimini, et ita facite, ut per Legem libertatis judicandi. Tota igitur Lex, cujus præcepta quædam Apostolus istic recensuit, viget etiam sub N. T. & est Christianis Lex libertatis ipsorum; unde omnis bonitas & malitia moralis æstimanda ac judicanda. Similiter Rom. XIII, 7,8,9 Reddite igitur omnibus quod debetis. -- Nemini quicquam debete, nisi hoc, ut alii alios diligatis: Nam qui diligit alterum Legem implevit. Siquidem illud, Non mœchaberis, &c. Reliqua vide sup. th. 12. Item Ephes. VI, 1,2,3. Liberi, auscultate in Domino parentibus vestris: id enim est justum. Honora patrem tuum & matrem: quod est præceptum primum cum promissione, ut bene tibi fit, & fis longævus super terra. Sic ad Legem, cujus sunt ista præcepta, tanquam ad normam justi & decori, sub N.T. etiam remittimur.
units.tr: So speak, and so act, as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. The whole Law, of which the Apostle there recounted some precepts, is in force also under the New Testament, and is the law of liberty for Christians; by it all moral goodness and wickedness is to be measured and judged. Similarly, Rom. 13:7-9: Render therefore to all what you owe. Owe nothing to anyone, except that you love one another; for he who loves another has fulfilled the Law. For the command, You shall not commit adultery, etc. For the rest see above, thesis 12. Likewise Eph. 6:1-3: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honour your father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise, that it may go well with you and that you may live long on the earth. Thus under the New Testament we are also referred back to the Law, of which these precepts are part, as to the rule of what is just and proper.

units.la: 4. Per inductionem. Præcepta posterioris tabulæ omnia & singula repetuntur in locis N. Test. proximè allegatis. Ad priorem vero tabulam quod attinet: de primo præcepto patet, ex I Cor. VIII, 4,5,6. Scimus idolum nihil esse in mundo; & nullum esse Deum alium, nisi unum, &c. cum Matth. XXII, 37. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Joh. IV, 24. Deus est spiritus: & qui adorant eum, oportet ut spiritu ac veritate adorent. I Joh. V, 21. Filioli, cavete vobis ab idolis.
units.tr: Fourth, by induction. All and each of the precepts of the second table are repeated in the New Testament passages cited just above. As for the first table: concerning the first precept it is clear from 1 Cor. 8:4-6: We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one, etc.; and from Matt. 22:37: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc.; John 4:24: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth; 1 John 5:21: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

units.la: De secundo item, ex Rom. I, 23. Mutarunt enim gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in effigiem imaginem corruptibilis hominis, & volucrium, & quadrupedum, & reptilium, &c. 25. Ut qui veritatem transmutarint in falsitatem. Cum Act. XVII, 24,25. Cum sit cæli & terræ Dominus, in manu factis templis non habitat: nec manibus hominum colitur.
units.tr: Concerning the second likewise, from Rom. 1:23: They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the form of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of reptiles, etc.; 25: who exchanged the truth of God for a lie. Compare Acts 17:24-25: Since he is Lord of heaven and earth, he does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands.

units.la: De tertio similiter, ex Matth. V, 34,35. Ne jurate omnino: neque per cœlum; quia thronus Dei est: neque per terram; quia scabellum est pedum ejus. XII, 36. Dico vobis; Quodcunque verbum otiosum locuti fuerint homines, de eò reddituros rationem in die judicii. 1 Petr. iii,15. Dominum Deum sanctificate in cordibus vestris. Estote autem semper parati ad reddendum cuilibet petenti rationem ejus spei quæ in vobis est, cum mansuetudine & timore, conscientiam bonam habentes.
units.tr: Concerning the third likewise, from Matt. 5:34-35: Do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool. 12:36: I tell you, that men will give account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken. 1 Pet. 3:15: Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. And always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience.

units.la: XVII. Nec minus de quarto, ex Matth. xxiv,20. Orate, ne fiat fuga vestra hyeme, neque Sabbatho. Ergo sub N. T. tempore excidii Hierosolymitani, & fugæ ex ista occasione, atque adeo deinceps ad consummationem sæculi, observari adhuc debuit Sabbathum eâ conscientia, ut fideles necesse habuerint, ex mandato Christi, deprecari ne fuga in ipsum incideret. Adeo molestum iis esse debet, si turbentur exercitia Religionis isto die solenniter & quiete peragenda. Attamen una cum iis, quæ ad œconomiam V. T. proprie pertinuerant, mutata quoque diei circumstantia; & pro septimo die ex ordine creationis, substituto primo. Hinc, sicut Judaica Sabbathorum observatio, pariter ac Festorum & Novilunionorum, nec non ciborum ac potuum, redarguitur Col. 2, 16, 17. & alibi; quod mox patebit: Apostoli suo exemplo primum diem septimanæ fidelibus commendarunt. Sic Act. xx,7. „Primo autem die hebdomadis, congregatis discipulis, ad frangendum panem, Paulus differebat cum eis, abiturus postridie: produxitque sermonem usque in mediam noctem. Confer Matth. xxviii,1. Marc. xvi,2. Luc. xxiv,1. Joh. xx,1,19.“ unde evidentissimum, quis appellari soleat dies primus, aut per Hebraïsmum μία σαββάτων. Adde Gen. 1,5. Expressa etiam est ordinatio, 1 Cor. xvi, 1, 2. „Porro de collecta in sanctos, quemadmodum ordinavi Ecclesiis Galatiæ, ita & vos facite. Primo quoque die hebdomadis unusquisque vestrum apud se seponat, recondens ut thesaurum, quod pro Dei benignitate licuerit. Nec dubitandum, quin alii actus solennes, ad cultum Dei & communionem sanctorum spectantes, ad eundem quoquoque diem pariter pertinuerint: unde etiam iste dies Dominicus appellatur; Apoc. 1, 10. analogice ut cœna Dominica, 1 Cor. xi, 20. Consequenter observatio Dominici in Ecclesia primitiva erat quasi tessera Christianismi. Athanasius, Hom. de Semente: Olim certè prisci illis hominibus in summo pretio Sabbatum fuit; quam quidem solennitatem Dominus in diem Dominicam transtulit. Vide etiam Catechesin Belgicam: quæst. 103: Post-Acta Synodi Nationalis Dordracenæ, Sess. 164. atque ipsa Acta, Sess. 14.
units.tr: XVII. Nor less concerning the fourth, from Matt. 24:20: Pray that your flight may not be in winter, nor on the Sabbath. Therefore under the New Testament, at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem and the flight occasioned by it, and indeed thereafter until the consummation of the age, the Sabbath was still to be observed, with such conscience that the faithful, by Christ's command, had to pray that flight might not fall upon it. It ought to be a hardship for them if the religious exercises to be performed solemnly and quietly on that day are disturbed. Yet, together with those things which properly belonged to the economy of the Old Testament, the circumstance of the day has also been changed, and the first day has been substituted for the seventh day of the order of creation. Hence, just as the Jewish observance of Sabbaths, as well as of feasts and new moons, and also of foods and drinks, is rebuked in Col. 2:16-17 and elsewhere, as will soon be shown, so the Apostles by their example commended the first day of the week to the faithful. Thus Acts 20:7: "On the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to leave the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight." Compare Matt. 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1, 19. Whence it is most evident what is usually called the first day, or by Hebraism one of the Sabbaths. Add Gen. 1:5. The ordinance is also expressly stated, 1 Cor. 16:1-2: "Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of the week let each of you put aside and store up whatever he has been prospered with, so that no collections need be made when I come." Nor is there any doubt that other solemn acts, pertaining to the worship of God and the communion of the saints, likewise belonged to that same day; hence it is also called the Lord's Day, Rev. 1:10, by analogy with the Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 11:20. Consequently the observance of the Lord's Day in the primitive Church was, as it were, the token of Christianity. Athanasius, Homily on the Semente: Certainly in former times the Sabbath was held in the highest honour by those men; but the Lord transferred that solemnity to the Lord's Day. See also the Belgic Confession, question 103; the Acts of the National Synod of Dort, session 164; and the Acts themselves, session 14.

units.la: Obj. 1. Præceptum de Sabbatho non est morale. Coloss. ii, 16, 17. Nequis igitur vos damnet ob cibum, vel potum, aut respectu festi aut novilunii, aut Sabbatorum: Quæ sunt umbra rerum futurarum; at corpus, est Christi. Sabbata pariter cum festis, novilunis, &c. dicuntur umbra rerum futurarum, &c ergo fuerunt tantum cerimonialia typica: non moralia. Resp. Cum Apostolus istic Sabbata appellat, loquitur de Sabbathis, quæ & quatenus typica fuerunt, & sic œconomiæ V. T. propria: id suo modo etiam pertinet ad Sabbathum hebdomadale, respectu peculiaris usus & [illegible, ~4 letters] sub V. T. Sed non absolute; quasi nihil in eo esset morale, cerimoniis typicis antiquius, atque etiam posterius, & alterius conditionis. Certe Apostolus ibidem cibum & potum appellat; nec tamen absolute omnem eorum usum intelligit; sed distinctionem cerimonialem typicam, quæ ad œconomiam V. T. pertinuit, & per libertatem N. T. abrogata est. Interim verus & necessarius eorum usus, imo etiam distinctio quædam, respectu sanitatis conservandæ aut curandæ, nequaquam istic prohibetur; cum per Legem moralem ad ea obligati simus quemadmodum etiam ad observationem alicujus Sabbathi hebdomadalis.
units.tr: Objection 1. The precept concerning the Sabbath is not moral. Col. 2:16, 17: Let no one therefore judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths; which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's. The Sabbaths, like the feasts, new moons, etc., are said to be a shadow of things to come, and therefore they were only typical ceremonial observances, not moral. Answer: When the Apostle speaks here of Sabbaths, he means the Sabbaths insofar as they were typical, and so proper to the economy of the Old Testament. In its own way this also applies to the weekly Sabbath, with respect to its particular use and [illegible, ~4 letters] under the Old Testament. But it does not apply absolutely, as if there were nothing moral in it, older or later than the typical ceremonies and of another kind. Certainly the Apostle in the same place calls food and drink such things too, yet he does not mean absolutely every use of them, but the ceremonial and typical distinction that belonged to the economy of the Old Testament and has been abrogated by the freedom of the New. Meanwhile, the true and necessary use of these things, and even a certain distinction of them with respect to preserving or restoring health, is in no way forbidden here, since by the moral law we are bound to them just as we are bound to the observance of some weekly Sabbath.

units.la: Obj. 2. Galat. iv, 9, 10, 11. Quomodo convertitis vos retrorsum ad infirma & egena elementa, quibus ad superiora regressi servire vultis. Dies observatis, & menses, & tempora. ra, & annos. Metuo de vobis, ne frustra fatigatus sim apud vos. Ergò, &c. Resp. Etiam istic solùm reprehenditur dierum, &c. observatio, quatenùs pertinuit ad infirma & egena elementa mundi, ad typos & pædagogiam V. T. Sed non quælibet dierum ac temporum prudens observatio ad res opportunè agendas. Vide Eccl. iii, 1,-. Prov. x, 5. xx, 4. Eph. v, 16. Quin & 1 Cor. xvi, 1, 2. de primo die hebdomadis, ipsis Galatis nominatim per Apostolum ordinato. Hujus ergo alia est ratio.
units.tr: Objection 2. Gal. 4:9, 10, 11: How do you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you desire to be in bondage once more? You observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid for you, lest I have laboured among you in vain. Therefore, etc. Answer: Here too only the observance of days, etc., is rebuked, insofar as it pertained to the weak and beggarly elements of the world, to the types and the pedagogy of the Old Testament. But not every prudent observance of days and times, for doing things at the proper moment, is condemned. See Eccl. 3:1ff.; Prov. 10:5; 20:4; Eph. 5:16. Indeed, see also 1 Cor. 16:1, 2, concerning the first day of the week, which the Apostle expressly ordained for the Galatians themselves. Therefore the reason for this is different.

units.la: Obj. 3. Rom. xiv, 5, 6. Alius quidem æstimat diem præ die, alius autem peræquè æstimat quemvis diem. Unusquisque in animo suo plenè certioratus esto. Qui curat diem, Domino curat: & qui non curat diem, Domino non curat. Qui edit, Domino edit, &c. Istic dierum discretio & observatio iterum conjungitur cum discretione ciborum. Ergo præcepto morali non sumus obligati ad diem aliquem Sabbathicum. Resp. Nego consequentiam; similiter ut in superioribus. Infirmi fide, & necdum satis instructi de veritate & libertate Christianâ, æstimabant & observabant aliquos dies, ut & ciborum discrimina, ex Lege cerimoniali Judaïca, vel etiam fortasse ex superstitione Gentili. Sed probe instructi & firmi fide, aliter statuebant & faciebant. Inde autem non magis colligi debet, nullum nunc agnoscendum esse Sabbathum hebdomadale, aut diem Dominicum; quàm cibos non esse discernendos ratione diætæ.
units.tr: Objection 3. Rom. 14:5, 6: One man esteems one day above another; another esteems every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He who regards the day, regards it to the Lord; and he who does not regard the day, to the Lord he does not regard it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, etc. Here the distinction and observance of days is again joined with the distinction of foods. Therefore we are not bound by a moral precept to any particular Sabbath day. Answer: I deny the consequence, just as in the foregoing cases. The weak in faith, and not yet sufficiently instructed in the truth and the Christian liberty, esteemed and observed certain days, as also distinctions of foods, from the Jewish ceremonial law, or perhaps even from Gentile superstition. But those who were well instructed and firm in faith judged and acted otherwise. Yet from this it ought not to be concluded that no weekly Sabbath or Lord's day is now to be acknowledged, any more than that foods are not to be distinguished on grounds of diet.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sabbathum per Legem quondam mandatum, erat septimus dies à creatione: atqui dies Dominicus alius est: ergo Lex ista nos non obligat ad diem Dominicum. Resp. Sabbathum est dies Deo cum quiete sacer. Initio quidem iste dies incidebat in septimum à creatione: id enim tunc manifestè indicabat circumstantia temporis. Eundem quoque indicavit ratio, quæ quarto Decalogi præcepto subjecta jecta est. Generaliori tamen modo comprehensa sunt ipsa verba præcepti : Recordare diei Sabbathi, ut sanctifices illum. Sex diebus operaberis, & facies omne opus tuum. At die septimo Sabbathum erit Jehovæ Deo tuo: non facies ullum opus, &c. quibus verbis omnino satisfit, ubi post sex dies operarios sequitur unus sacra quiete transfigendus; is enim sic quoque septimus est: videlicet nunc sub N. T. postquam scriptis Θεοπνεύστοις dies Dominicus indicatus & ordinatus est; qui non minus post sex alios identidem recurrit. Et ad hujus observantiam in his circumstantiis non minus obligamur per quartum præceptum; quam per præceptum, Diliges proximum tuum ut te ipsum, obligamur ad diligendum eos homines, qui nunc exstant: aut per præceptum, Honora patrem tuum, &c. nunc obligatur ad honorandum vitricum, cui iste obtigit, &c.
units.tr: Objection 4. The Sabbath, commanded of old by the Law, was the seventh day from creation; but the Lord's day is another day; therefore that Law does not bind us to the Lord's day. Answer: The Sabbath is a day set apart to God with rest. At the beginning, indeed, this day fell on the seventh from creation, for the circumstance of time then clearly indicated this. The reason subjoined to the fourth precept of the Decalogue also indicated the same. Yet the words of the precept itself are comprehended in a more general way: Remember the day of the Sabbath, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of Jehovah thy God; thou shalt not do any work, etc. These words are altogether satisfied where, after six working days, there follows one to be spent in holy rest; for this one is also the seventh in this way. Namely, now under the New Testament, since the Lord's day has been indicated and ordained in the God-breathed [θεοπνεύστοις] Scriptures, it recurs again and again after six others no less than before. And we are bound to observe it in these circumstances no less by the fourth precept than we are bound by the precept, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, to love the men who now exist, or by the precept, Honour your father, etc., we are now bound to honour a stepfather, whom we have happened to receive, etc.

units.la: XVIII. Pontificii volunt, Christum non tantum esse Redemtorem, sed etiam Legislatorem; adeoque Legem novam dedisse, quæ quidem continet triplicia præcepta, Moralia, Sacramentalia, & Fidei. Vide etiam sup. cap. 3. th. 34. Obj. 3.
units.tr: XVIII. The Papists want Christ to be not only the Redeemer but also the Lawgiver; and so they hold that he gave a new law, which indeed contains three kinds of precepts: moral, sacramental, and of faith. See also above, chap. 3, th. 34, Obj. 3.

units.la: Sociniani quoque, & Anabaptistæ, cum sequacibus Remonstrantibus, contendunt, Legem moralem à Christo esse correctam, & perfectiorem redditam, additis de novo Præceptis variis; ut post quædam indicabitur. Urgent autem imprimis illud Matth. v. aliquoties repetitum, ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις ... ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, &c. Resp. 1. Pharisæi & Scribæ passim jactabant Traditiones Seniorum suorum, quibus irrita faciebant, & transgrediebantur mandata Dei: Matth. xv, 2, 3, 6, 9. cum revera essent inania hominum commenta, & detorsiones Legis Divinæ in sensum prorsus alienum, imo etiam decisiones contrariæ: Matth. v, 31, 38, 43. Illud autem ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις accipi potest, tanquam dictum est ab antiquis; mamajoribus scil. ac prædecessoribus Pharisæorum & Scribarum, glossematum atque errorum istorum auctoribus, vel traditoribus. 2. Si omninò accipiendum est, dictum est antiquis, sive ad antiquos; id tamen intelligi deberet, ut antiquis ejusdem sectæ hominibus istud traditum esset à suis præceptoribus: non à Deo, aut à Mose ac Prophetis, fidelibus & infallibilibus Dei ministris; sed ab hominibus seductoribus, veritatem interim & auctoritatem Divinam mentientibus.
units.tr: The Socinians also, and the Anabaptists, together with their followers the Remonstrants, contend that the moral law was corrected by Christ and made more perfect, with various new precepts added, as will be shown below in some cases. They urge especially that passage of Matt. 5, repeated several times: You have heard that it was said to the ancients [ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις] ... but I say to you [ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν], etc. Answer: 1. The Pharisees and scribes constantly boasted of the traditions of their elders, by which they made void and transgressed the commandments of God (Matt. 15:2, 3, 6, 9), when in truth they were empty inventions of men and distortions of the Divine Law into a quite alien sense, and even contrary decisions (Matt. 5:31, 38, 43). But the phrase it was said to the ancients [ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις] may be taken as it was said by the ancients, that is, by the forefathers and predecessors of the Pharisees and scribes, the authors or transmitters of those glosses and errors. 2. If it must be taken absolutely as it was said to the ancients or to the men of old, it would still have to be understood that this was handed down to the men of old of the same sect by their own teachers, not by God, nor by Moses and the Prophets, the faithful and infallible ministers of God, but by seducing men who meanwhile falsely claimed the truth and Divine authority.

units.la: XIX. Nunc paucis perstringemus controversias circa singula Decalogi præcepta occurrentes. Circa primum excutienda venit initio multiplex Idololatria Papatus: ut 1. in cultu Angelorum. 2. In cultu hominum. 3. In cultu rerum inanimatarum. Et 4. in cultu entium fictorum. Pontificii Angelos etiam religiosè colendos docent, & praxi sua confirmant; maximè verò Archangelum Michaelem (quem creatum statuunt), & reliquos Angelos coram Deo assistentes, Principes aulæ cœlestis, Ecclesiarum omnium præsides, hominum mediatores ac præpositos, ut appellant: quorum septem nomina assignant; qui per se, aut per alios à se missos, defendant nos à septem vitiis capitalibus, ad contrarias virtutes hortentur, tentationibus obsistant, occasiones peccandi removeant, &c. atque item Angelos tutelares singulorum. Vide sup. cap. 7. th. 19.
units.tr: XIX. Now we shall briefly touch on the controversies arising over the individual precepts of the Decalogue. Concerning the first, the manifold idolatry of the Papacy must first be examined: (1) in the worship of Angels; (2) in the worship of men; (3) in the worship of inanimate things; and (4) in the worship of fictitious beings. The Papists teach that Angels also are to be worshipped religiously, and confirm this by their practice; above all the Archangel Michael (whom they hold to be created), and the rest of the Angels standing before God, princes of the heavenly court, presidents of all churches, mediators and overseers of men, as they call them. Of these they assign seven names, who by themselves, or through others sent by them, defend us from the seven capital vices, exhort us to the contrary virtues, resist temptations, remove occasions of sinning, etc.; and likewise the guardian Angels of individuals. See above, chap. 7, th. 19.

units.la: Opponimus autem isti Idololatriæ, 1. generalia mandata, quibus cultus religiosus soli Deo reservatur; Jes. xlii,8. Matth. iv,10. ex Deuter. vi,13. x,20.
units.tr: We oppose this idolatry, first, with general commands by which religious worship is reserved for God alone: Isa. 42:8; Matt. 4:10, from Deut. 6:13; 10:20.

units.la: 2. Specialem prohibitionem, ne Angelis iste cultus deferatur, propositam per Apostolum; Coloss. ii,18.
units.tr: Second, with a special prohibition, that this worship not be offered to Angels, set forth by the Apostle: Col. 2:18.

units.la: 3. Aliam iterum prolatam per Angelum, Apoc. xix,10. atque iteratam, xxii,8,9.
units.tr: Third, with another prohibition, spoken through an Angel, Rev. 19:10, and repeated, Rev. 22:8, 9.

units.la: 4. Accedit ratio: Angelis non competit illa ἐξουσία, quæ fundat cultum religiosum: cùm sint entia creata & finita; quorum perfectiones finitæ & dependentes sunt. Neque iis competit omnipræsentia; ut semper nobis adessent, atque adeò eos compellare possemus, quoties liberet: neque omniscientia; ut nos, & necessitates nostras, & preces nostras, semper cognoscerent. 1 Reg. viii, 39. Tu enim nosti solus cor omnium filiorum hominum. Matth. xviii, 10. Dico vobis; Angelos eorum (parvulorum) in cœlis per omne tempus videre faciem Patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Ubi spiritus sacram functionem obeuntes, ministerii causâ emittuntur quidem, propter hæredes salutis futuros; Hebr. i, 14. sed opere perafto, revertuntur in cœlum: Luc. 2, 15.
units.tr: Fourth, there is a reason: the power that grounds religious worship does not belong to Angels, since they are created and finite beings whose perfections are finite and dependent. Nor is omnipresence proper to them, so that they could always be present to us and we could address them whenever we like; nor omniscience, so that they would always know us, our needs, and our prayers. 1 Kings 8:39: For you alone know the heart of all the children of men. Matt. 18:10: I tell you that their Angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. Where spirits perform their sacred function, they are indeed sent out for the sake of ministry, on account of those who will be heirs of salvation (Heb. 1:14), but when the work is done they return to heaven (Luke 2:15).

units.la: XX. Imò ne quidem rogandi sunt, ut pro nobis intercedant apud Deum; aut preces nostras Deo offerant & gratas faciant: nam
units.tr: XX. Indeed, they should not even be asked to intercede for us with God, or to offer our prayers to God and make them acceptable, for the following reasons:

units.la: 1. Nullum mandatum, neque exemplum istiusmodi, occurrit in SS. Literis.
units.tr: 1. No command or example of this kind occurs in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: 2. In hâc vitâ, & hoc rerum statû, non habemus talem familiaritatem & conversationem cum Angelis.
units.tr: 2. In this life and in this state of things we do not have such familiarity and fellowship with the angels.

units.la: 3. Preces nostras Deo per Angelos offerri, quasi aliàs Deus eas ignoraret, aut negligeret; vel etiàm gratas & acceptas reddi per Angelos, quasi isti aliquid conferrent ad gratiam Dei nobis conciliandam, à SS. Literis alienissimum est.
units.tr: 3. That our prayers should be offered to God through the angels, as if God otherwise did not know them or ignored them, or that they should be made pleasing and acceptable through the angels, as if the angels contributed something toward reconciling God's grace to us, is utterly foreign to the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: 4. Intercessio Mediatoria soli Christo Θεανθρώπῳ, Mediatori Dei & hominum, propria est; ut suo loco demonstrabitur.
units.tr: 4. Mediatorial intercession belongs to Christ alone, the God-man [Θεανθρώπῳ], the Mediator between God and men, as will be shown in its place.

units.la: Obj. 1. Gaudium est apud Angelos Dei super uno peccatore resipiscente: Luc. xv, 10. ergò res & actiones nostras minimè ignorant: quin imò utiliter à nobis invocantur. Resp. Gaudium & congratulationem super peccatore resipiscente agnoscimus; qui est actus charitatis Angelicæ erga nos: sic Deum celebrant super tali gratiâ in nos collatâ, ubi ea ipsis innotescit. Hinc tamen prorsus non sequitur, eos preces nostras Deo offerre & gratas facere; neque nos eorum intercessionem precibus nostris, & quidem religiosis, expetere debere.
units.tr: Obj. 1. There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents: Luke 15:10. Therefore they are by no means ignorant of our affairs and actions; rather, they are usefully invoked by us. Reply. We acknowledge the joy and rejoicing over a repentant sinner, which is an act of angelic love toward us; so they praise God for such grace bestowed upon us, when it becomes known to them. From this, however, it by no means follows that they offer our prayers to God and make them acceptable, nor that we ought to seek their intercession by our prayers, and indeed religious prayers.

units.la: Obj.2. Jacob Ephraïmo & Menassæ precatur benedictionem Angeli : Gen. xlviii, 15. Ergo. Resp. Sed Angeli increati. Vide sup. cap. 4 th. 10.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Jacob prays for a blessing on Ephraim and Manasseh from the angel: Gen. 48:15. Therefore. Reply. But the angel was uncreated. See above, chapter 4, thesis 10.

units.la: Obj. 3. Angeli tamen pro hominibus intercedunt : Zach. 1, 12. Apoc. viii, 3. Resp. 1. Zach. 1, 12. Angelis Jehovæ proponitur in visione prophetica, ut intercedens pro Hierosolymis & civitatibus Judæ. 2. Apoc. viii, 3. Angelus dicitur adstitisse altari, thuribulum aureum tenuisse, & preces omnium sanctorum obtulisse super altari aureo. Sed ista ad ipsum Christum, ejusque functionem Sacerdotalem in cœlo, quoque pertinent ; non ad Angelum aliquem creatum.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Yet angels intercede for men: Zech. 1:12; Rev. 8:3. Reply. 1. Zech. 1:12: the angel of Jehovah is presented in a prophetic vision as interceding for Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. 2. Rev. 8:3: the angel is said to have stood at the altar, held a golden censer, and offered the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar. But these things pertain to Christ himself and his priestly function in heaven, and not to any created angel.

units.la: Obj. 4. Tob. xii, 15. Raphael dicitur unus ex septem illis Angelis, qui preces sanctorum deferunt. Ergo. Resp. Cum iste locus apocryphus sit, hoc ipsum quod habet, non probat : Confer Tob. v, 15. Angelos autem vel invocandos, vel religiosè colendos esse, non habet.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Tob. 12:15: Raphael is said to be one of the seven angels who bring the prayers of the saints. Therefore. Reply. Since this passage is apocryphal, what it says does not prove the point. Compare Tob. 5:15. Nor does it teach that angels are to be invoked or religiously worshipped.

units.la: Obj. 5. David Psal. cxiii, 20. Angelos invocat hoc modo ; Benedicite Jehovæ Angeli ejus, fortes robore, facientes verbum ejus, ad obtemperandum voci verbi ejus. Ergo. Resp. Ibi David per prosopopœiam exprimit, Angelos omnino servire gloriæ Divinæ : sed non magis docet religiosam invocationem Angelorum, quàm omnium creaturarum, cum subjung t, v. 22. Benedicite Jehovæ omnia opera ejus, in omnibus locis dominationis ejus.
units.tr: Obj. 5. David, Psalm 113:20, invokes the angels in this way: Bless Jehovah, his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, obeying the voice of his word. Therefore. Reply. There David, by prosopopoeia, expresses that the angels wholly serve the divine glory; but he no more teaches the religious invocation of angels than of all creatures, since he adds at verse 22: Bless Jehovah, all his works, in all places of his dominion.

units.la: XXI. Secundò committunt iidem Idololatriam in hominibus
units.tr: XXI. Secondly, the same men commit idolatry in regard to men,

units.la: : scil. in Christo secundum humanam naturam, in Virgine Mariâ, in Sanctis demortuis, atque etiam in Pontifice Romano.
units.tr: namely in Christ according to his human nature, in the Virgin Mary, in the saints who have died, and even in the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Christum omnino adorandum & religiosè colendum, ex animo credimus, & confitemur, secundùm SS. Literas : itàscil ut adorabilitas fundetur formaliter in Divinâ ipsius ὑπόστασις. Humana verò natura, si præcisè consideretur, per mentem abstractá à Deitate, utut ipsâ minimè separar, agnosci quidem debet Ἀόγος adjunctum substantiale ἐνυπόστατον, & organon conjunctissimum; adorabilis tamen propterea non est.
units.tr: We firmly believe and confess, according to the Holy Scriptures, that Christ is wholly to be adored and religiously worshipped; namely, that his adorability is grounded formally in his divine hypostasis. But the human nature, if considered precisely, by the mind abstracted from the Deity, although by no means separated from it, must indeed be acknowledged as the substantial Word [Λόγος] joined to it, hypostatically united [ἐνυπόστατον] and most closely conjoined instrument [ὄργανον]; yet on that account it is not to be adored.

units.la: In B. Virgine Maria Idololatriam committunt multis modis: cujus non solùm intercessionem petunt apud Deum; sed ipsi potestatem supremam, imò & jus imperii in Christum tribuunt, Deum eam faciunt, sic adorant & celebrant. Huc pertinent Biblia, & Psalterium Mariæ, Horruli, Rosaria, Sabbathum, Officium, &c.
units.tr: In the Blessed Virgin Mary they commit idolatry in many ways. They not only seek her intercession with God, but also attribute to her supreme power, indeed even a right of rule over Christ; they make her God, and so adore and celebrate her. To this belong the Bibles and Psalter of Mary, the Little Hours, the Rosaries, the Sabbath, the Office, and so on.

units.la: Alios quoque Sanctos demortuos, colunt iidem religiosè, sive adorant; & voce vel mente supplicantes, ad eorum orationes opcmque confugiunt; memorias eorum frequentant per suos dies festos, octavas, vigilias, encænia; Missas etiam celebrant in eorum honorem, & ad obtinendam ipsorum intercessionem, adduntlectiones, hymnos, officia, litanias, processiones; Templa iis dedicant, & altaria; imagines erigunt, cereos accendunt, &c.
units.tr: Other dead saints they likewise worship religiously, or adore; praying aloud or in mind, they flee to their prayers and aid. They frequent their memorials through their feast days, octaves, vigils and dedications; they also celebrate Masses in their honour and to obtain their intercession, adding readings, hymns, offices, litanies and processions. They dedicate temples and altars to them, erect images, light candles, and so on.

units.la: Numerus eorum, qui tales habentur, & sic colunturferè infinitus est: invocantur autem vel omnes simul; vel singuli seorsùm. Potissimum vero Patroni, Præfecti, aut Divi tutelares; quibus specialis potestas & cura personarum, rerum, locorum, vel temporum, Divinitùs creditur demandata; & Ecclesiasticè aut Papaliter sic declarata.
units.tr: The number of those who are held to be such and so worshipped is almost infinite. They are invoked either all together or one by one. Especially the patrons, prefects, or tutelary saints, to whom a special power and care of persons, things, places, or times is believed to have been committed by God, and so declared by the Church or by the Pope.

units.la: Eidem idololatriæ subservit Canonizatio; quæ est canonica & regularis institutio ipsius Papæ, ut quis pro Sancto honoretur, ac pro eo fiat solenne officium. Apotheosin Divorum suorum alibi appellant. Proximus ad eam gradus est Beatificatio, quâ quis à Papâ solenniter declaratur beatus.
units.tr: To the same idolatry serves canonization, which is the canonical and regular institution by the Pope himself, by which someone is honoured as a saint and a solemn office is held for him. They elsewhere call this the apotheosis of their divine ones. The next step to it is beatification, by which someone is solemnly declared blessed by the Pope.

units.la: XXII. Idololatriæ hactenus in hominibus descriptæ, opponimus 1. generale argumentum, contra religiosum cultum Angelorum quoque productum th. 19. quod Deus illum sibi soli vindicaverit.
units.tr: XXII. Against the idolatry thus far described in men, we set forth, first, the general argument, also brought forward against the religious worship of angels in thesis 19: that God has claimed this for himself alone.

units.la: 2. Ex conditione objectorum: Eos colere religiosè, qui non sunt natura Dii, est illorum qui verum Deum non agnoscunt: qui vero hunc agnoscunt, eundem solum sic colunt; Gal. iv, 8. Ipse Deus Psal. L, 15. Invoca me in die angustiae: eruam te; & honorificabis me. Similiter etiam Christus à Discipulis rogatus, ut ipsos precari doceret, praescripsit modum precandi, Pater noster, &c. Luc. xi, 1, 2. &c. Nullum vero extat indicium de Maria, aliisve Sanctis, religiosè colendis. Ἐξοχὴ quae istum cultum fundat, iis non competit; cum entia creata & finita sint: nec omniscienția, aut cognitio eorum quae hic geruntur, & nobis eveniunt. Hinc respectu eorum, quae apud viventes in hac terra aguntur, Eccl. ix, 5. Mortui nesciunt quicquam. Ita Josuae dicebatur, 2 Reg. xxii, 20. Ecce ego recolligam te ad patres tuos, & recolligeris in sepulchra tua in pace; & non videbunt oculi tui universum malum, quod ego induco in locum istum. Et Ecclesia ad Deum, Jes. lxiii, 16. Tu enim Pater noster es; etiamsi Abraham nesciat nos, & Israel non agnoscat nos: tu tamen Jehovah Pater noster, redemtor noster, a saeculo est nomen tuum.
units.tr: 2. From the condition of the objects: to worship religiously those who are not God by nature belongs to those who do not acknowledge the true God; but those who acknowledge him worship him alone in this way: Gal. 4:8. God himself, Psalm 50:15: Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall honour me. Likewise, when Christ was asked by his disciples to teach them how to pray, he prescribed the manner of praying, Our Father, etc., Luke 11:1, 2, etc. But there is no indication whatever concerning Mary or other saints being worshipped religiously. The excellence [ἐξοχή] which founds this worship does not belong to them, since they are created and finite beings; nor do they have omniscience, or knowledge of what is done here and happens to us. Hence, with respect to what is done among the living on this earth, Eccl. 9:5: The dead know nothing. So it was said to Josiah, 2 Kings 22:20: Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered into your grave in peace; and your eyes shall not see all the evil that I bring upon this place. And the Church says to God, Isa. 63:16: For you are our Father; though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us, yet you, Jehovah, are our Father, our Redeemer; your name is from everlasting.

units.la: 3. A pari: Nemo coli debet religiosè nisi in quem etiam credimus fide Divinâ: ut enim veritas absolutè summa & infallibilis se habet ad fidem Divinam: sic etiam infinita & independens ἐξοχὴ se habet ad cultum religiosum. Hinc Rom. x, 13, 14. Quisquis enim invocaverit nomen Domini, salvabitur. Quomodo igitur invocabunt eum, in quem non crediderint? Cum fides sit ἐλεγχος πραγμάτων; Hebr. xi, 1. Consequenter etiam ex fide petimus à Deo, quae credimus ipsum nobis dare velle; id enim necessarium est, ut secundum voluntatem ipsius oremus; 1 Joh. v, 14. atque ita postulemus cum fide, nihil ambigentes; Jac. 1, 6. neque adoremus, quod nescimus; Joh. iv, 22.
units.tr: 3. From parity: no one ought to be worshipped religiously except the one in whom we also believe with divine faith.
