For as absolute and infallible truth stands in relation to divine faith, so also infinite and independent excellence stands in relation to religious worship. Hence Rom. 10:13, 14: For whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Since faith is the evidence of things not seen [ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων], Heb. 11:1. Consequently, we also ask God, by faith, for what we believe he is willing to give us; for it is necessary that we pray according to his will, 1 John 5:14, and so we ask with faith, doubting nothing, James 1:6, nor do we worship what we do not know, John 4:22.

units.la: 4. A judicio & voluntate ipsorum Sanctorum: Qui verò Sancti sunt, nolunt sibi cultum religiosum deferri. Cùm Actor. x, 25. Cornelius occurrens Petro, & accidens ad ejus pedes, adoraret ipsum; Petrus erexit illum, dicens; Surge: & ego ipse homo sum. Similiter xiv. 11,–15. cùm Lystrenses visa miraculo, quod per Paulum & Barnabam erat factum, tauros vittatos adducerent, atque illis sacrificare vellent; illi, diruptis pallis suis, infilicrunt in turbam, clamantes ac dicentes; Viri, cur ista facitis? Nos quoque sumus homines, eisdem quibus vos affectionibus obnoxii; annunciantes ut a vanis istis rebus conversatis vos ad Deum illum vivum, qui fecit cœlum, & terram, & mare, & omnia quæ in eis sunt. Eodem modo, ut Angelus, Apoc. xix, 10. & xxii, 8, 9.
units.tr: 4. From the judgment and will of the saints themselves: those who are truly saints do not wish religious worship to be paid to them. When Cornelius, meeting Peter, fell at his feet and worshipped him, Acts 10:25, Peter raised him up, saying: Stand up; I myself am also a man. Similarly, Acts 14:11–15, when the Lystrans, having seen the miracle which had been done through Paul and Barnabas, brought oxen decked with garlands and wished to sacrifice to them, they, tearing their garments, leapt into the crowd, crying out and saying: Men, why do you do these things? We too are men, subject to the same passions as you, announcing to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven, and earth, and sea, and all that is in them. In the same way, the angel, Rev. 19:10 and 22:8, 9.

units.la: Ex antiquis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus multa in eandem sententiam facilè produci possunt; nominatim ex Hilario, Augustino, Epiphanio, &c.
units.tr: Many arguments to the same effect can easily be drawn from the ancient teachers of the Church, namely from Hilary, Augustine, Epiphanius, and others.

units.la: XXIII. Sed neque precibus sollicitandi sunt Beati, ut suis orationibus pro nobis intercedant apud Deum, aut Christum. Obstant rationes in negotio Angelorum productæ, th. 20.
units.tr: XXIII. But the blessed should not be solicited with prayers to intercede for us with God or Christ. The reasons adduced in the matter of the angels (th. 20) stand in the way.

units.la: Obj. 1. At sancti cœlites intercedunt pro nobis; 2 Maccab. xv, 11, 12. Ergo. Resp. Istic describitur insomnium Judæ Maccabæi, quod vidisset Oniam Pontificem defunctum intercedentem pro populo Judaico; atque ex eo audivisset, idem quoque facere Prophetam Jeremiam: sed præterquam quod locus sit apocryphus, & somnium narret; non dicit, eos pro singulis Judæis, & singulorum necessitatibus esse precatos; multò minùs, fideles id ipsum ab illis petiisse suis precibus. Et quidsi Maccabæus somniâsset, Jeremiam & Oniam adhuc vixisse, vel iterum vixisse, (quod somniantibus de mortuis non est insolens,) atque ita eos precatos fuisse pro populo, quemadmodum soliti fuerant viventes, & tunc faciebant etiam omnes pii?
units.tr: Obj. 1. But the holy heavenly inhabitants intercede for us; 2 Maccabees 15:11, 12. Therefore. Resp. That passage describes a dream of Judas Maccabeus, in which he had seen the high priest Onias, now dead, interceding for the Jewish people, and had heard from him that Jeremiah the prophet did the same. But apart from the fact that the book is apocryphal and merely recounts a dream, it does not say that these men prayed for individual Jews and their individual needs, much less that the faithful asked this of them in their prayers. And what if Maccabeus had dreamed that Jeremiah and Onias were still alive, or had come back to life (which is not unusual in dreams about the dead), and that they prayed for the people as they used to do when alive, as all the godly then did as well?

units.la: Obj. 2. Apocal. v, 8. quatuor animalia & viginti quatuor seniores prociderunt coram. Agno, cum citharis & phialis aureis, quæ erant preces sanctorum. Ergo. Resp. 1. Visio illa intelligi potest de Ecclesiâ catholicâ, quæ sic preces suas coram Christo fundit, ac per ipsum offert Patri. 2. Si omninò intelligenda esset Ecclesiæ pars triumphans, istorum sanctorum orationes non tamen evincerentur fuisse intercessiones, nedùm peculiares, & quidem aliorum precibus expetitæ.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Revelation 5:8. The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, holding harps and golden bowls, which were the prayers of the saints. Therefore. Resp. 1. That vision can be understood of the catholic Church, which pours out its prayers before Christ in this way and offers them through him to the Father. 2. Even if it had to be understood of the triumphant part of the Church, it would still not be proved that these saints' prayers were intercessions, let alone special ones, and sought by the prayers of others.

units.la: Obj. 3. Genes. xlviii, 16. prædixit Jacob nomen suum vocandum super filios Josephi: hi ergo post mortem erant illum invocaturi. Resp. Committitur ψιλολογία. Melius Cajetanus ad locum: „est „ea phrasis Hebræis peculiaris; ut dicant, vocari no„men alicujus super aliquem, pro vocari aliquem alicujus „nomine: ut constat Isai. iv. & Dan. ix.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Genesis 48:16. Jacob foretold that his name would be called over the sons of Joseph; therefore these men were to invoke him after death. Resp. This is a case of mere wordplay. Cajetan explains the place better: "This phrase is peculiar to the Hebrews, who say the name of someone is called upon someone for someone is called by someone's name, as is clear from Isaiah 4 and Daniel 9."

units.la: Obj 4. Job. v, 1. Convertere ad aliquem sanctorum. Mandatur ergo eorum invocatio. Resp. In Hebræo est, Ad quem sanctorum vertes te? ubi nec de mortuis agitur, nec de religiosa invocatione; sed docetur, nullum à sanctis auxilium obtineri posse adversus Deum. Confer Ezech. xiv, 14.20.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Job 5:1. Turn to one of the saints. Therefore their invocation is commanded. Resp. In the Hebrew it reads, To which of the saints will you turn? Here there is no talk of the dead, nor of religious invocation, but it is taught that no help can be obtained from the saints against God. Compare Ezekiel 14:14, 20.

units.la: Obj. 5. Luc. xvi, 27.28. damnatus epulo legitur intercedisse pro fratribus suis; multò magis id faciunt beati cœlites. Ergo. Resp. Ex isto textu non magis colligi debet, Abrahamum à divite illo mortuo reipsa invocatum fuisse pro fratribus adhuc viventibus; quam divitem illum mortuum sublatis oculis vidisse Abrahamum, & Lazarum in hujus sinu cubuisse; vel Lazarum potuisse digitum immittere in aquam, & sic refrigerare linguam illius: quæ quidem à naturâ animarum separatarum alienissima sunt. Neque item sequitur; si anima divitis nuper mortui, retinuit memoriam fratrum suorum, quos in hac vita reliquerat; Sanctos igitur habere notitiam omnium, quæ post mortem ipsorum apud viventes geruntur. Tenendus parabolæ scopus, quod divites propter opum suarum abusum damnati, nullo deinde levamine potiri tiri possint; atque hoc argumento homines ab isto abusu debeant absterreri, & observare media ordinaria ad promovendam refipiscentiam instituta atque concessa.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Luke 16:27, 28. The condemned rich man is read to have interceded for his brothers; much more do the blessed heavenly inhabitants do so. Therefore. Resp. From this text it cannot be inferred any more than that Abraham was really invoked by that dead rich man on behalf of his brothers still living; or that the rich man, lifting up his eyes, saw Abraham, and Lazarus lying in his bosom; or that Lazarus could dip his finger in water and so cool his tongue. These things are altogether foreign to the nature of separated souls. Nor does it follow that, if the soul of the rich man who had recently died retained a memory of his brothers whom he had left in this life, the saints therefore have knowledge of everything that is done among the living after their death. The point of the parable must be kept: the rich men, condemned for abusing their wealth, can then obtain no relief; and by this argument men ought to be deterred from such abuse, and to observe the ordinary means instituted and granted for promoting repentance.

units.la: Obj. 6. Angelus salutavit beatam virginem ; Luc. 1,28, & sanêta Elisabetha ; verf. 42. Resp. Ista salutatio & gratulatio, continent tum apprecationem alicujus boni à Deo ad ipsam, convenienter isti rerum statui ; tum denunciationem & prædicationem bonorum, quæ ei à gratiâ Divinâ obtigerant, ac porrò eventura erant. Quo etiam nomine ipsa se beatam prædicandam humilis agnoscit;verf. 48. Sed minimè sequitur, eam propterea religiosè invocandam esse ; nedum tali formulâ.
units.tr: Obj. 6. The angel greeted the blessed Virgin, Luke 1:28, and the holy Elisabeth greeted her, verse 42. Resp. That greeting and congratulation contains both a prayer for some good from God on her behalf, suited to her condition, and a declaration and proclamation of the good things which had come to her from divine grace and were yet to come. In this same sense the humble woman herself acknowledges that she will be called blessed, verse 48. But it by no means follows that she is therefore to be invoked religiously, much less in such a formula.

units.la: Obj. 7. Luc. xix, 17, 19. Famuli fideles à Rege suo dicuntur præficiendi aliquot civitatibus ; ergò sancti cœlites sciunt & curant ea quæ hic aguntur ; & consequenter recte invocantur. Resp. In ista parabola sic denotatur gloria iis tribuenda, qui donis à Christo acceptis recte fuerint usi ; quemadmodum alibi cœlestis beatitudo proponitur sub allegoriâ nuptiarum, aut convivii, &c. Matth. xxii, 2, &c. viii, 11. Sed Regnum ipsius Christi non est de hoc mundo, Johan. xviii, 36. consequenter neque ministris suis pro mercede distribuit regna, provincias, urbes, &c. hujus mundi.
units.tr: Obj. 7. Luke 19:17, 19. Faithful servants are said by their king to be set over several cities; therefore the holy heavenly inhabitants know and care for what is done here, and consequently may rightly be invoked. Resp. In this parable the glory due to those who have rightly used the gifts received from Christ is portrayed in this way, just as elsewhere heavenly blessedness is set forth under the allegory of a wedding feast or banquet, etc. Matthew 22:2 etc., 8:11. But the kingdom of Christ himself is not of this world, John 18:36; consequently he does not distribute kingdoms, provinces, cities, etc. of this world to his ministers as wages.

units.la: XXIV. Quantum ad Pontificem Romanum, in ea idololatriam quoque satis crassam & apertam committunt, cùm eum non tantùm Vice-Deum salutant, sed etiam in terris Deum ; atque insuper ei tribuunt Divinam majestatem, omnipotentiam, potestatem dispensandi de jure, & supra jus, contra Apostolum, contra Vetus Testamentum, &c. Quid mirum ergò Papam, ubi electus est, super altari constitui ; Imperatores & Reges ejus pedes deosculari ; utrumque gladium ei assignari, &c. Quæ quidem indicâsse, est refutâsse, juxta 2 Thef. 11, 4.
units.tr: XXIV. As for the Roman Pontiff, they commit a quite gross and open idolatry in this too, since they greet him not merely as Vice-God but as God on earth; moreover they ascribe to him divine majesty, omnipotence, the power to dispense from law and above law, against the Apostle, against the Old Testament, etc. What wonder, then, that when the Pope is elected he is set up upon the altar; that emperors and kings kiss his feet; that both swords are assigned to him, etc.? To point out these things is in fact to refute them, according to 2 Thessalonians 2:4.

units.la: XXV. Succedit idololatria in Rebus inanimatis: hæ autem sunt Panis eucharistiae, Crux, Reliquiae, Imagines, & Res aliae consecratae.
units.tr: XXV. Idolatry extends to inanimate things, and these are the bread of the Eucharist, the Cross, relics, images, and other consecrated things.

units.la: In Pane eucharistiae est ἀρτολατρεία : scil. ex falsa hypothesi Transsubstantiationis; dum vere & proprie ipsum Christum reputant id, quod ostentat Sacerdos, panem adorant, & cultum latriae (ut loquuntur) ei exhibent.
units.tr: In the bread of the Eucharist there is artolatria [ἀρτολατρεία], namely from the false hypothesis of transubstantiation; since they truly and properly regard Christ himself as that which the priest displays, they adore the bread and render to it what they call latria worship.

units.la: Verum 1. Christus sacramentum Coenae instituens, ejus adorationem nullo modo praecepit.
units.tr: But, first, Christ, instituting the sacrament of the Supper, nowhere commanded its adoration.

units.la: 2 Apostoli neque doctrinâ, neque praxi suâ, talem adorationem probârunt.
units.tr: Second, the Apostles, neither by their teaching nor by their practice, approved any such adoration.

units.la: 3. Quod externè in illo sacramento conspicitur, & percipitur, non est verè ac proprie ipse Christus; sed panis & vinum usurpantur in ipsius recordationem, & ad obsignandam communionem corporis ac sanguinis ejus: sic ibi adoratur, quod falso Deus putatur.
units.tr: Third, what is outwardly seen and received in that sacrament is not truly and properly Christ himself; rather bread and wine are used in his remembrance and to seal communion with his body and blood. Thus there is adored what is falsely thought to be God.

units.la: 4. Ipsi etiam Adversarii Transsubstantiationem suspendunt ex Sacerdotis conficientis intentione: spectatores vero nunquam certi esse possunt de ejus intentione: consequenter ne propria quidem fide Papistica certi esse possunt, illum esse Christum verè ac proprie; atque ita adorant quod nesciunt: Joh. iv, 22.
units.tr: Fourth, the Adversaries themselves make transubstantiation depend on the intention of the priest who consecrates; but the onlookers can never be certain of his intention. Consequently, even by their own Papist faith, they cannot be certain that it is truly and properly Christ; and so they adore what they do not know: John 4:22.

units.la: XXVI. In Cruce est σαυρολατρεία.
units.tr: XXVI. In the Cross there is staurolatry [σταυρολατρεία].

units.la: Illo autem nomine nunc non solùm intelligitur ipsum illud singulare lignum, in quo Christus pependit; sed etiam Crux ex qualicunque materiâ ad illius similitudinem facta, aut quomodocunque repraesentata. Thomas parte 3. qu. 25. art. 4, „Illi exhibemus latriae cultum, „in quo ponimus spem salutis: sed in Cruce Christi po„nimus spem salutis: cantat enim Ecclesia; O Crux ave, „spes unica, Hoc passionis tempore; Auge piis justitiam, „Reisque dona veniam. Ergo Crux Christi est adoranda „adoratione latriae. - Si vero loquamur de effigie Crucis „Christi in quacunque alia materia, puta lapidis, vel li„gni, argenti, & auri; sic veneramur Crucem tantùm ut „Imaginem Christi, quam veneramur adoratione latriae. Sic etiam varia effecta supernaturalia ei tribuunt; ut quod mirificè augeat devotionem; excitet spem & fiduciam obtinendæ remissionis peccatorum, itemque charitatem ergà Deum, & recordationem omnis virtutis, &c.
units.tr: By that name is now meant not only that single piece of wood on which Christ hung, but also any cross made of whatever material in its likeness, or represented in any way. Thomas, part 3, q. 25, art. 4: "We offer the worship of latria to that in which we place our hope of salvation. But we place our hope of salvation in the Cross of Christ; for the Church sings: O Cross, hail, our only hope, in this time of the Passion; increase justice in the pious, and grant pardon to the guilty. Therefore the Cross of Christ is to be adored with the adoration of latria. But if we speak of the image of the Cross of Christ in any other material, such as stone, wood, silver or gold, then we venerate the Cross only as the image of Christ, which we venerate with the adoration of latria." They also attribute various supernatural effects to it, such as that it wonderfully increases devotion, arouses hope and confidence of obtaining the forgiveness of sins, and likewise love of God, and remembrance of every virtue, and so on.

units.la: Opponimus. 1. Crassissimam esse idololatriam; cùm cultus religiosus deferatur rei inanimatæ, ne quidem civilis honoris capaci.
units.tr: We object: 1. It is gross idolatry, since religious worship is paid to an inanimate thing, which is not even capable of civil honour.

units.la: 2. Nullum planè præceptum, aut exemplum, talis cultus occurrere in SS. Literis.
units.tr: 2. No precept or example of such worship occurs at all in the Sacred Scriptures.

units.la: 3. Culpandi alias forent Apostoli, quòd non statim ipsam Crucem, in quâ pependerat Christus, asservaverint, fidelibus istud σταυρὸς commendaverint, &c.
units.tr: 3. The Apostles would otherwise be open to blame, because they did not at once preserve the very Cross on which Christ hung, and did not commend to the faithful that "cross" (σταυρός), and so on.

units.la: 4. Per respectum ad Christum Crux potiùs in detestatione haberi deberet; cum ipsi Christo fuerit instrumentum & symbolum execrationis: Gal. iii, 13.
units.tr: 4. With respect to Christ, the Cross ought rather to be held in detestation, since it was to Christ himself an instrument and symbol of execration: Gal. 3:13.

units.la: Et Crux in passione Christi ne quidem fuit instrumentum activum, sed tantùm passivum: cum active quodammodo se habuerint clavi, lancea, flagella, &c. magis autem milites crucifigentes, aut manûs eorum: potiùs ergo pictæ & fictæ manûs omnium militum adorari deberent; magis autem vivæ, imo omnium hominum, & omnes homines.
units.tr: Nor in the passion of Christ was the Cross even an active instrument, but only a passive one; whereas the nails, the spear, the scourges and so on were active in some way, and still more the soldiers who crucified him, or their hands. Therefore the painted and feigned hands of all the soldiers ought rather to be adored; still more the living hands, indeed the hands of all men, and all men themselves.

units.la: Obj. 1. Crux Christi in SS. Literis tantoperè celebratur: de eâ gloriabantur Apostoli; sed ejus hostes erant hæretici & seductores: 1 Cor. 2, 2. Phil. iii, 18. Resp. Crux ibi metonymicè mortem Christi maledictam significat, quam ipse pro nobis subiit, nos ab execratione liberaturus: ut 1 Cor. 2, 2. Phil. iii, 18. Alibi etiam crux nobis ferenda, metaphorice significat passiones, quæ nobis immittuntur, & quibus nos utcunque materialiter conformamur Christo in suis passionibus: ut Matth. xvi, 24. Rom. viii, 17.
units.tr: Objection 1. The Cross of Christ is so greatly celebrated in the Sacred Scriptures; the Apostles gloried in it; but its enemies were heretics and seducers: 1 Cor. 2:2; Phil. 3:18. Reply: there the Cross, by metonymy, signifies the accursed death of Christ, which he himself underwent for us, to free us from the curse. So 1 Cor. 2:2; Phil. 3:18. Elsewhere too the cross to be borne by us metaphorically signifies the sufferings that are laid upon us, and by which we are in some measure conformed materially to Christ in his sufferings: as Matt. 16:24; Rom. 8:17.

units.la: Obj. 2. Similitudo, repræsentatio, & respectus ad crucem, in quâ Christus pependit, & commemoratio passionum ipsius, efficit ut signum Crucis fit religiose colencolendum. Resp. Ista non possunt fundare cultum religiosum aliorum entium ab uno vero Deo; & magis inveniuntur in aliis, quæ tamen ne quidem Pontificii sic colunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. The likeness, representation and reference to the cross on which Christ hung, and the commemoration of his sufferings, make the sign of the Cross to be worshipped religiously. Reply: these cannot found religious worship of any beings other than the one true God; and they are found even more in other things, which not even the Papists worship in this way.

units.la: Obj. 3. Crux præfigurata fuit sub V. T. Exod. xii, 22. Ezech. ix, 4. Gen. xlviii, 14. Ergo, &c. Resp. Sanguis agni Paschalis illitus postibus domuum Israelitarum, Exod. xii, 22. & adhibita signatura (Thau) Ezech. ix, 4. cum Ap. vii, 4. xiv, 1, nequidem fuerunt signa crucis. Quod vero Jacob manibus decussatis benedixerit filiis Josephi, Gen. xlviii, 14. factum est speciali de causa, quæ ex textu patet; sine tali mysterio.
units.tr: Objection 3. The Cross was foreshadowed under the Old Testament: Exod. 12:22; Ezek. 9:4; Gen. 48:14. Therefore, etc. Reply: the blood of the Paschal lamb smeared on the doorposts of the houses of Israel, Exod. 12:22, and the mark (Thau) applied in Ezek. 9:4, compared with Apoc. 7:4 and 14:1, were not even signs of the cross. But that Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph with crossed hands, Gen. 48:14, happened for a special reason, which is clear from the text, and without any such mystery.

units.la: Obj. 4. Multa miracula per signum Crucis facta sunt. Ergo. Resp. Miracula, quæ jactantur ad stabiliendam istam idololatriam, accenseri debent signis ac prodigiis mendacibus, de quibus, 2 Thess. 2, 9.
units.tr: Objection 4. Many miracles have been done by the sign of the Cross. Therefore... Reply: the miracles that are boasted of in order to establish this idolatry must be reckoned among the lying signs and wonders spoken of in 2 Thess. 2:9.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Gentiles olim jactarunt & ostentarunt Reliquias quasdam; Jovis; Dianæ, &c. Sic etiam commemorantur alibi Reliquiæ Sanctorum V. Test. Sed Reliquiæ N. T. jactantur & ostentantur ferè infinitæ; utpote ipsius Christi; respectu infantiæ, vitæ adultæ, passionis, & exaltationis. Itemque Reliquiæ Mariæ, Apostolorum, Martyrum, aliorumque Sanctorum. Scil. quemadmodum olim Scribæ & Pharisæi sepulchra Prophetarum ædificabant, & monumenta justorum ornabant; dum puritatem doctrinæ deseruerant, atque omnia confspurcabant hypocrisi & legis transgressione; Matth. xxiii, 28, 29. similiter Pontificii, dum salutarem veritatem corruperunt, & in SS. Literas, præstantissimas Prophetarum atque Apostolorum Reliquias, multis modis injurii sunt, indicatas modo Reliquias adorant, & religiose colunt, per habitudinem scil. ad eos, quorum Reliquiæ sunt; sive latriâ, sive dulia.
units.tr: The Gentiles of old boasted of and displayed certain relics: of Jupiter, of Diana, and so on. Likewise relics of the saints are mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. But relics of the New Testament are boasted of and displayed almost without number: namely those of Christ himself, with respect to his infancy, his adult life, his passion and his exaltation; likewise relics of Mary, of the Apostles, of the martyrs and of other saints. Just as of old the scribes and Pharisees built the sepulchres of the prophets and adorned the monuments of the righteous, while they had deserted the purity of doctrine and polluted everything with hypocrisy and transgression of the law (Matt. 23:28, 29), so the Papists, having corrupted the saving truth and done many kinds of wrong to the Sacred Scriptures, the most excellent relics of the prophets and apostles, now worship and religiously honour the relics that are pointed out, namely through their relation to those whose relics they are, whether with latria or with dulia.

units.la: Nos breviter opponimus hæc Argumenta:
units.tr: We briefly oppose the following arguments:

units.la: i. Nullum in SS. literis extat præceptum, vel
units.tr: 1. There exists in the Sacred Scriptures no precept or

units.la: exemplum, talis cultûs: atque adeo est ἐιδωλολατρεία; Col.2, 23.
units.tr: example of such worship; and it is therefore idolatry [εἰδωλολατρεία]: Col. 2:23.

units.la: 2. Reliquiæ non sunt Deus; imo ne quidem res animatæ: nequaquam ergo religiose colendæ; sed valde absurda est ista idololatria.
units.tr: 2. Relics are not God; indeed they are not even living things. They are by no means to be worshipped religiously; and this idolatry is utterly absurd.

units.la: 3. Reliquiarum illarum nulla est certitudo Divina; & plurimarum ne quidem humana: ergo ex fide Divinâ cultus ille prorsus non procedit: Rom. x, 14, xiv, 23. Joh. iv, 22.
units.tr: 3. There is no divine certainty about those relics, and for most of them not even human certainty. Therefore that worship does not proceed from divine faith at all: Rom. 10:14; 14:23; John 4:22.

units.la: 4. Deus ipse corpus Mosis abscondidit; ne Israëlitæ eo ad idololatriam abuterentur: Deut. xxxiv, 6. Et Paulus diserte, 2 Cor. v, 16. Nos posthac neminem novimus secundum carnem: quodsi etiam novimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius novimus. Ea igitur, quæ ad Corpus Christi pertinuissent, vel etiam ad Sanctos qualescunque, nequaquam religiose asservari & coli debent.
units.tr: 4. God himself hid the body of Moses, lest the Israelites should abuse it to idolatry: Deut. 34:6. And Paul expressly says: 2 Cor. 5:16: "Henceforth we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer." Therefore those things which would have pertained to the body of Christ, or even to any saints whatever, ought by no means to be religiously preserved and worshipped.

units.la: Obj. 1. Moses ossa Josephi ex Ægypto transtulit. Ergo. Resp. Sepelienda scil. in terrâ promissionis: Exod. xiii, 19. quod ad rationem typicam istius terræ, & ad excitandam aliorum fidem, pertinuit; non ad religiosum cultum istorum ossium.
units.tr: Objection 1. Moses carried the bones of Joseph out of Egypt. Therefore... Reply: they were to be buried in the land of promise: Exod. 13:19. This pertained to the typical meaning of that land and to the stirring up of the faith of others, not to religious worship of those bones.

units.la: Obj. 2. Tactis ossibus Elisæi, mortuus quidam revocatus est in vitam; 2 Reg. xiii, 21. Resp. Non tamen propterea religiose illa coluerunt Israelitæ; neque sic colere debuerunt.
units.tr: Objection 2. A dead man was restored to life by touching the bones of Elisha: 2 Kings 13:21. Reply: nevertheless the Israelites did not therefore worship those bones religiously, nor ought they to have done so.

units.la: Obj. 3. Josias reverenter habuit ossa Prophetæ; 2 Reg. xxiii, 16, 17, 18. Resp. Ossa veri Prophetæ noluit cum ignominiâ & maledictione comburi, ut fiebat ossibus idololatrarum. Sed nihil de eorum cultu religioso.
units.tr: Objection 3. Josiah treated the bones of the prophet with reverence: 2 Kings 23:16, 17, 18. Reply: he refused to have the bones of the true prophet burned with disgrace and curse, as was done to the bones of idolaters. But nothing is said of their religious worship.

units.la: Obj. 4. Mulier sanguinis profluvio laborans, tactâ Christi fimbriâ fuit sanata, &c. Ergo. Resp. Virtus illa ab ipso Christo processit: Luc. viii, 44, 46. Similiter sudaria & semicinctia Pauli deferebantur ad ægros, tunc ista methodo miraculosè sanandos: Act. XIX,12. Quemadmodum eodem fine ægri ad umbram Petri delati sunt: v,15. Verum inde non magis colligi debet religiosus cultus illius fimbriæ, istorum sudariorum ac semicinctiorum, quam hujus umbræ.
units.tr: Objection 4. A woman suffering from a flow of blood was healed by touching the hem of Christ's garment, etc. Therefore... Reply: that power came from Christ himself: Luke 8:44, 46. Likewise handkerchiefs and aprons of Paul were carried to the sick, to be miraculously healed in that way: Acts 19:12. In the same way the sick were carried to the shadow of Peter: Acts 5:15. Yet from this no more should be inferred a religious worship of that hem, or of those handkerchiefs and aprons, than of that shadow.

units.la: Obj. 5. Cadavera Sanctorum contumeliis affici neutiquam debent; sed honeste haberi. Resp. Verum etiam hinc cultus eorum religiosus minime sequitur.
units.tr: Objection 5. The corpses of the saints ought by no means be treated with contempt, but kept with honour. Reply: Granted; but from this their religious worship by no means follows.

units.la: XXVIII. Imagines religiosas Pontificii habent, & faciunt, quam plurimas; Dei, etiam S.S. Trinitatis, Christi, nominatim Crucifixi, Mariæ, aliorum Sanctorum, itemque Angelorum: imo religiose etiam colunt. Sic enim Thomas Aquinas Summæ parte 3. qu. 25. art. 3. „ Dicendum est, quod Imagini Christi, in „ quantum est res quædam, puta lignum sculptum, vel „ pictum, nulla reverentia exhibetur: quia reverentia non nisi rationali naturæ debetur. Relinquitur „ergo, quod exhibeatur ei reverentia solum in quantum est Imago: & sic sequitur, quod eadem reverentia exhibeatur Imagini Christi, & ipsi Christo, cum ergo „Christus adoretur adoratione latriæ; consequens „est, quod ejus imago fit adoratione latriæ adoranda. — „Nos autem adoramus adoratione latriæ Imaginem Christi, qui est verus Deus: non propter ipsam Imaginem, „sed propter rem, cujus imago est.
units.tr: XXVIII. The Papists have very many religious images, and make them: of God, even of the Holy Trinity, of Christ, especially of the Crucified, of Mary, of other saints, and likewise of angels; indeed they even worship them religiously. For so Thomas Aquinas, Summa part 3, q. 25, art. 3: "It must be said that no reverence is shown to the image of Christ as it is a certain thing, for instance carved or painted wood, since reverence is owed only to a rational nature. It remains, therefore, that reverence is shown to it only insofar as it is an image; and thus it follows that the same reverence is shown to the image of Christ and to Christ himself. Since therefore Christ is adored with the adoration of latria, it follows that his image is to be adored with the adoration of latria." — "But we adore with the adoration of latria the image of Christ, who is true God, not on account of the image itself, but on account of the thing of which it is the image."

units.la: Bellarminus paulo aliter, lib. 2. de imaginibus cap. 21. „Sit igitur hæc prima sententia, sive propositio: Imagines Christi & Sanctorum venerandæ sunt, non solum per „accidens & improprie; sed etiam per se & proprie; ita ut „ipsæ terminent venerationem, ut in se considerantur, & „non solum ut vicem gerunt exemplaris. Probatur primo, „quia Concilium VII. act. 7. definivit, Imagines Christi „esse venerandas; sed non latriâ: vult igitur esse venerandas per se, & proprie, aliquo cultu. — Concilium ibidem „definit, Imagines venerandas eo modo quo venerantur Evangelia & sacra vasa; atqui ista honorantur per se & proprie. — Quarto, In ipsa Imagine vere inest aliquid »quid sacrum, nimirùm similitudo ad rem sacram, & »ipsa dedicatio sive consecratio Divino cultui : ergo »ipsæ in se, non solum ut prototypi vicem gerunt, honore »dignæ sunt. Deinde cap. 23. »Quòd imago possit coli »improprie eo cultu, quo ipsum exemplar, probatur: nam »aliquando Imago accipitur pro ipso exemplari; & »ea, quæ fierent circa ipsum exemplar, si adesset præ»sens, fiunt circa imaginem ; mente tamen defixâ in »exemplari. - Quòd autem possit Imago adorari adora»tione ipsius exemplaris, proprie quidem, sed per accidens, »probatur: &c. Atque iterum cap. 25. »Cultus qui »per se, & proprie debetur Imaginibus, est cultus quidam »imperfectus, qui analogicè & reductive pertinet ad speciem »ejus cultus, qui debetur exemplari. - Probatur: sicut se »habet Imago ad suum exemplar, itâ se habet cultus »Imaginis ad cultum exemplaris: &c. .
units.tr: Bellarmine, somewhat differently, in book 2 on images, chapter 21: "Let this then be the first thesis, or proposition: Images of Christ and of the Saints are to be venerated not only accidentally and improperly, but also per se and properly; so that they themselves terminate the veneration, as they are considered in themselves, and not only as standing in for the exemplar. It is proved, first, because the Seventh Council, in its seventh session, defined that images of Christ are to be venerated, but not with latria: it wills therefore that they be venerated per se and properly, with some kind of worship. The council in the same place defines that images are to be venerated in the way in which the Gospels and the sacred vessels are venerated; but these are honoured per se and properly. Fourth, there truly exists in the image itself something sacred, namely the likeness to a sacred thing, and the dedication or consecration to divine worship: therefore the images themselves, in themselves and not only as standing in for the prototype, are worthy of honour." Then in chapter 23: "That an image can be worshipped improperly with the same worship as the exemplar itself is proved: for sometimes the image is taken for the exemplar itself; and the things that would be done to the exemplar, if it were present, are done to the image, with the mind nevertheless fixed on the exemplar. — That an image can indeed be adored with the adoration of the exemplar itself, properly but accidentally, is proved: etc." And again in chapter 25: "The worship which is due per se and properly to images is a certain imperfect worship, which pertains analogically and reductively to the species of that worship which is due to the exemplar. — It is proved: just as the image stands to its exemplar, so the worship of the image stands to the worship of the exemplar: etc."

units.la: XXIX. Opponimus isti cultui duo priora Argumenta
units.tr: XXIX. We set against this worship the two earlier arguments

units.la: th. 37. adversus Λειψανολατρείαν producta.
units.tr: Thes. 37, brought forward against relic-worship [Λειψανολατρείαν].

units.la: Addimus 3. Angeli & Homines, quamvis à Deo ad imaginem ipsius conditi, non sunt tamen religiosè colendi; multò minùs imagines qualescunque ab hominibus factæ.
units.tr: We add a third point: angels and men, although made by God in his image, are nevertheless not to be worshipped religiously; much less images of any kind made by men.

units.la: 4. Imo severè passim prohibetur & perstringitur omnis omninò cultus simulachrorum, tum in V. tum in N. Test. Levit. XXVI, 1. Non facietis vobis idola & sculptile, & statuam non erigetis vobis, neque lapidem pictum ponetis in terra vestra, ut incurvetis vos ei: ego enim Jehovah Deus vester. Deut. IV. 16, 26, 27, 28 V, 8, 9. Item Rom. I, 23, 25. Mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in simulachrum imaginis corruptibilis hominis;--- Ut qui veritatem transmutarint in falsitatem; & venerati sint & coluerint res conditas παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα, præter Creatorem. Absolutè igitur illicita est simulachrorum veneratio: neque causam istam juvant distinctiones & extinctiones, per accidens, improprie, analogice, reductive, nisi forte, ut Pontifícii dicantur saltem idololatræ per accidens,
units.tr: Fourth, all worship of images whatever is sternly forbidden and condemned throughout, in both the Old and the New Testament. Leviticus 26:1: "You shall not make for yourselves idols or graven images, nor set up a statue for yourselves, nor place a painted stone in your land, to bow down before it; for I am the LORD your God." Deuteronomy 4:16, 26, 27, 28; 5:8, 9. Likewise Romans 1:23, 25: "They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man ... who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than [παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα] the Creator." The worship of images is therefore absolutely unlawful; nor do the distinctions and qualifications help this cause, of accidentally, improperly, analogically, reductively, unless perhaps the Papists are to be called idolaters only accidentally,

units.la: T. dens, impropriè, analogicè, & reductive.
units.tr: improperly, analogically, and reductively.

units.la: Obj. 1. Arca fœderis sub V. T. adorabatur; & imagines Cherubim: Ergo. Resp. Arca non debuit adorari; sed Deus tantum, cujus singularem quandam præsentiam illa symbolice significabat. Similiter nec imagines Cherubim adorari debuerunt.
units.tr: Objection 1. The ark of the covenant was adored under the Old Testament, and the images of the cherubim: therefore. Answer. The ark ought not to have been adored, but God alone, whose particular presence the ark symbolically signified. Likewise the images of the cherubim ought not to have been adored.

units.la: Obj. 2. Item Serpens æneus; tanquam insignis typus Christi: Ergo. Resp. Iste etiàm non debuit adorari: imò cum ad religiosum ejus cultum prolaberentur Israelitæ, rectè eum confregit & è medio sustulit Ezechias; 2 Reg. XVIII, 4.
units.tr: Objection 2. Likewise the bronze serpent, as a notable type of Christ: therefore. Answer. That too ought not to have been adored; indeed, when the Israelites fell into religious worship of it, Hezekiah rightly broke it in pieces and removed it; 2 Kings 18:4.

units.la: Obj. 3. Rex adoratur civiliter; & purpura, aliaque insignia, propter Regem: Ergo. Resp. Qui Regem adorat civiliter, non adorat propterea quæcunque Regis sunt; utpote equum, vestem, umbram: sed & imagines ab hominibus factæ, quâ tales, nullam veram relationem ad Deum habent.
units.tr: Objection 3. A king is adored civilly, and the purple and other insignia for the sake of the king: therefore. Answer. One who adores a king civilly does not on that account adore whatever belongs to the king, such as his horse, his garment, his shadow; but images made by men, as such, have no true relation to God.

units.la: Obj. 4. Psal. XCIX, 5. præcipitur veneratio scabelli pedum Dei. Resp. Non scabelli; sed ipsius Dei: sic autem monentur homines, se incurvare quasi ad scabelluni pedum ipsius. Male Vulgatus: Adorate scabellum pedum ejus.
units.tr: Objection 4. Psalm 99:5 commands the veneration of God's footstool. Answer. Not of the footstool, but of God himself; and men are admonished in this way to bow down as if toward his footstool. The Vulgate translator wrongly renders: "Adore his footstool."

units.la: Obj. 5. Ex reverentiâ majestatis Divinæ, cujus thronus est cœlum, nec falsò, nec temerè jurandum est per cœlum: ergo cultus relativus debetur cœlo. Resp. Nego consequentiam. Nequaquam inde sequitur, cœlum, vel ullam aliam creaturam, religiosè colendam esse.
units.tr: Objection 5. Out of reverence for the divine majesty, whose throne is heaven, one ought neither falsely nor rashly to swear by heaven: therefore a relative worship is due to heaven. Answer. I deny the consequence. It by no means follows from this that heaven, or any other creature, is to be worshipped religiously.

units.la: XXX. Pergo ad Res Consecratas. Consecrare, est rem aliquam destinare & applicare ad peculiarem usum sacrum. Sic ergo mutatur status rei: accidit ei sanctitas relativa; & specialis quidam respectus ad Deum, ejusque cultum. Pontificii Benedictionem consecratoriam peragunt certis quibusdam formulis & ritibus, ex potestate scil. atque auctoritate Ecclesiæ. Eius terminum etiam vocant Sacramentale. Hoc vero, secundum ipsos, disponit ad Sacramenta, & ad gratiam. tiam; non autem ex opere operato eam confert. Porro tribuunt illi virtutem spiritualem, ad remittenda peccata venialia, ad avertendas insidias & insultus Diaboli, ad homines in virtute confirmandos, ad morbos sanandos, ac tandem, ut rerum spiritualium fit signum mysticum.
units.tr: XXX. I proceed to consecrated things. To consecrate is to set apart some thing and apply it to a particular sacred use. In this way the state of the thing is changed: a relative holiness and a certain special relation to God and his worship attach to it. The Papists perform the consecratory blessing with certain formulas and rites, by the power and authority, namely, of the Church. They also call its term the Sacramental. This, according to them, disposes toward the sacraments and toward grace, but does not confer grace ex opere operato. Furthermore they attribute to it a spiritual power: for remitting venial sins, for averting the snares and assaults of the Devil, for strengthening men in virtue, for healing diseases, and finally, as a mystical sign of spiritual things.

units.la: Initio genere excellunt Agni Dei, Christus allegorice Agnus, & Agnus Dei, appellatur: ut Joh. I, 29; 36. 1 Petr. I, 19. Apoc. v, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, vi, 1, 16, &c. tum propter qualemcunque similitudinem; tum propter veritatem sub V. T. praefiguratam Agno Paschali, Agni jugis sacrificii, &c. Hinc gliscente superstitione pingi & fingi coeperunt imagines Agnorum, tanquam signa commemorativa Christi. Postea vero perventum est ad Agnes cereos; qui pro amuletis etiam usurpati: acceperunt deinde eorum confectio & consecratio per Papam Romanum.
units.tr: At the beginning, the Lambs of God excel in kind: Christ is called allegorically the Lamb, and the Lamb of God, as in John 1:29, 36; 1 Peter 1:19; Revelation 5:6, 8, 9, 12, 13; 6:1, 16, etc.; partly on account of some kind of likeness, partly on account of the truth prefigured under the Old Testament by the Paschal Lamb, the lamb of the continual sacrifice, etc. Hence, as superstition grew, images of lambs began to be painted and fashioned, as commemorative signs of Christ. Later, however, they came to wax lambs, which were also used as amulets; then their making and consecration came to be taken over by the Roman Pope.

units.la: Argumenta contra idololatriam in rebus consecratis, ex superioribus nullo negotio desumi possunt à quolibet.
units.tr: Arguments against idolatry in consecrated things can be drawn without any trouble by anyone from what has been said above.

units.la: Adversarii vero, duabus potissimum hypothesibus nituntur: 1. Quod sanctitas relativa, & virtus aliqua spiritualis, fundet cultum religiosum. 2. quod consecratio ab hominibus excogitata, citrà Dei Verbum, etiam inferat sanctitatem relativam & virtutem spiritualem. Sed falsae sunt istae hypotheses. Ad Antiquitatem frustra provocant; cujus consensum hic non habent. Effecta quidem admiranda Rerum quarundam consecratarum jactant & deprædicant; sed non probant: neque enim admittendum, sic facta esse: nec ea, quae forte facta sunt, facta esse à Deo, tanquam approbante & confirmante ista Sacramentalia; & non potius fraude Diabolicâ, aut à Deo homines probante, vel justo judicio, in illiusmodi errores tradente; sive in iis indurante. Vide Matth. XXIV, 24. VII, 22, 23. Deut. XIII, 1, 2, 3. 2 Thess. 2, 9, 10, 11.
units.tr: The adversaries, however, rest mainly on two hypotheses: 1. that a relative holiness and some spiritual power founds religious worship; 2. that a consecration devised by men, apart from the Word of God, also brings in a relative holiness and a spiritual power. But these hypotheses are false. They appeal in vain to antiquity, whose consensus they do not have here. They indeed boast of and proclaim the marvellous effects of certain consecrated things, but do not prove them: for it is not to be admitted that they were so done; nor that those things which perhaps were done were done by God, as approving and confirming these sacramentals; rather they were done by diabolical deceit, or by God, who permits men to be led into such errors on account of a just judgment, or hardens them in them. See Matthew 24:24; 7:22, 23; Deuteronomy 13:1, 2, 3; 2 Thessalonians 2:9, 10, 11.

units.la: XXXI. Superest quartum caput Idololatriæ Papi-fticæ in cultû Entium fictorum: Divorum scil. chimæricorum ; qui nunquàm fuerunt in rerum naturâ ; aut quos fuisse nullâ saltem fide historicâ, ne quidem vulgari humanâ constat: vel etiàm nullo modo constat, eos fuisse sanctos ; sed potius fuisse inimicos & persecucores salutaris veritatis ac veræ sanctitatis, aut hæreti-cos, aut phantasticè superstitiosos.
units.tr: XXXI. There remains the fourth head of Papist idolatry, in the worship of fictitious beings: namely of chimerical saints, who never existed in nature, or whose existence is not established by any historical faith, not even by ordinary human faith; or indeed it is in no way established that they were saints at all, but rather that they were enemies and persecutors of saving truth and true holiness, either heretics or fantastically superstitious.

units.la: In primis occurrit fabula Ursulæ cum suo femineo comitatu undecies mille Virginum; cujus res gestæ conjiciuntur in annum Christi ccxxxviii. Sed isti mythologiæ rectè opponitur; 1. Quod Scriptores & Historici istius temporis, imo & sequentium aliquot sæculorum, qualescunque, nihil tale commemorent.
units.tr: First occurs the story of Ursula with her female company of eleven thousand virgins; whose deeds are assigned to the year of Christ 238. But this mythology is rightly opposed: 1. because the writers and historians of that time, and indeed of some of the following centuries, whatever they were, record nothing of the kind.

units.la: 2. Insufficientia Testium: sunt enim aliqui notoriè mendaces; neque ab ipsis Adversariis admittuntur. Ita Legendam auream ipsorum nonnulli ferream appellant; ejusque Auctorem, plumbei cordis & ferrei oris, &c. Qui primi indefinitè talis cujusdam rei gestæ meminerunt, valde remoti fuerunt ab illo tempore ; longius autem qui mythologiam descripserunt ; neque inter se consentiunt, nec sibi ipsis fidunt.
units.tr: 2. The insufficiency of the witnesses: for some of them are notoriously liars, and are not admitted even by the adversaries themselves. Thus some of them call their Golden Legend an iron one, and its author of a leaden heart and an iron mouth, etc. Those who first mentioned such a deed in an indefinite way were very remote from that time; and those who described the mythology at greater length do not agree among themselves, nor do they trust themselves.

units.la: 3. Testimonia, judicia, & argumenta contraria, quorundam Adversariorum.
units.tr: 3. The testimonies, judgments and arguments of certain adversaries.

units.la: 4. Quod historia nullo modo cum tempore conciliari possit ; neque cum circumstantiis locorum, regionum, &c. unde etiam alii aliam deinde chronologiam & topographiam commenti sunt ; neque cum descriptione rerum, personarum, factorum, &c.
units.tr: 4. History cannot in any way be reconciled with time, nor with the circumstances of places, regions, and so on. This is why others afterwards devised different chronologies and topographies. Nor can it be reconciled with the description of things, persons, deeds, and so on.

units.la: Ejusdem farinæ est fabula Trium Regum, eorumque cultus in Papatu ; atque item Catharinæ, Christophori, Georgii, Longini, Martialis, Petronellæ, Veronicæ, Margaretæ, Hippolyti, Septem dormientium, &c.
units.tr: Of the same kind is the fable of the Three Kings and their cult among the Papists, and likewise the legends of Catherine, Christopher, George, Longinus, Martial, Petronilla, Veronica, Margaret, Hippolytus, the Seven Sleepers, and so on.

units.la: Affinis existit invocatio Rerum quarundam inanimatarum ; ac fi ratione, sanctitate, beatitudine, & facultate hominibus succurrendi, gaudérent; utpote Ave sanctum Chrisma: Sancte Iudaei, ora pro nobis: Sanctissima Dei mappa, ora pro nobis, &c.
units.tr: Related to this is the invocation of inanimate things, as though they possessed reason, holiness, blessedness and the power to help men. Examples are "Hail, holy chrism," "Holy Jews, pray for us," "Most holy cloth of God, pray for us," and so on.

units.la: Adde Sanctos non-sanctos; sed haereticos; aut idololatras, aut improbos, aut fatuos, &c. itemque Exsanctos, ex Sanctorum catalogo, in quo prius comparuerunt, & honorati fuerunt, postea expunctos.
units.tr: Add the "non-saints," who were saints but were heretics, idolaters, wicked men or fools, and so on. Add also the "ex-saints" (Exsancti), who were once listed in the catalogue of saints, where they appeared and were honoured, but were afterwards struck off.

units.la: Multis igitur modis Pontificii serviunt iis, qui non sunt natura Dii; Gal. iv, 8. colunt res conditas, praeter Creatorem, qui est benedictus in saecula; Rom. I, 25. & idola, quae nihil sunt in mundo; 1 Cor. viii, 4. Neque quicquam eos juvat distinctio inter λατρείαν, & δουλείαν; quasi illa soli Deo esset propria; haec creaturis foret communis: quibus aliquando addunt ὑπερδουλείαν, B. Virgini Mariae tribuendam, vel etiam humanae naturae Christi, &c. Ista enim distinctio neque ex SS. Literis, neque ex probatis auctoribus, confirmari potest: sed ad palliandam multiplicem ipsorum idololatriam temere excogitata & assumta est. Alium usum verbi λατρεύω vide in Versione Graeca, Deut. xxviii, 48. & Levit. xxiii, 7. nec non verbi δουλεύω, Gal. iv, 8. &c.
units.tr: In many ways, therefore, the Papists serve those who are not by nature gods; Gal. iv, 8. they worship created things besides the Creator, who is blessed for ever; Rom. i, 25. and idols, which are nothing in the world; 1 Cor. viii, 4. Nor does the distinction between worship [λατρείαν] and service [δουλείαν] help them at all, as if the former belonged to God alone and the latter were common to creatures. They sometimes add a third, hyper-service [ὑπερδουλείαν], to be given to the Blessed Virgin Mary or even to the human nature of Christ, and so on. This distinction cannot be confirmed either from Holy Scripture or from approved authors. It was rashly devised and adopted to cloak their manifold idolatry. For the other use of the verb "to worship" [λατρεύω], see the Greek version of Deut. xxviii, 48. and Lev. xxiii, 7. and also of the verb "to serve" [δουλεύω], Gal. iv, 8. and so on.

units.la: XXXII. Quoniam Neo-Saddutcei, Libertini aut Semi-Libertini quidam, omnem Magiam aliquando negare audent: omniaque ejus effecta, vel ad causas naturales, vel ad agendi celeritatem, vel ad deliria melancholica, &c. referre conantur; haec argumenta illis opponimus:
units.tr: XXXII. Since certain Neo-Sadducees, Libertines or semi-Libertines sometimes dare to deny all magic, and try to refer all its effects either to natural causes, or to the speed of action, or to melancholic delusions, and so on, we oppose these arguments to them:

units.la: 1. S. Scriptura peccatis gravissimis accenset Magiam; severe eam prohibet, ac puniendam decernit: Exod. xxii, 18. Levit. xix, 31. xx, 27. Deut. xviii, 10, 11, 12, 1. Sam xv, 23. xxviii, 9. 2 Reg. xxiii, 24.
units.tr: 1. Holy Scripture counts magic among the gravest sins. It forbids it severely and decrees that it be punished. Exod. xxii, 18. Lev. xix, 31. xx, 27. Deut. xviii, 10, 11, 12. 1 Sam. xv, 23. xxviii, 9. 2 Kings xxiii, 24.

units.la: 2 Chron. xxxiii, 6. Jes. viii, 19. xlvii, 9, 12, 13. Jerem. xxvii, 9. Mich. v, 11. Act. xiii, 6, 10. Gal. v, 19, 20. Apoc. xxi, 8. quod certe non faceret, si nulla talis in rerum natura daretur.
units.tr: 2 Chron. xxxiii, 6. Isa. viii, 19. xlvii, 9, 12, 13. Jer. xxvii, 9. Mic. v, 11. Acts xiii, 6, 10. Gal. v, 19, 20. Rev. xxi, 8. Certainly it would not do this if no such art existed in the nature of things.

units.la: 2. Commemorat exempla Magorum; Exod. vii, 11, &c. viii, 7, 18. Num. xxii, 5, &c. xxiii, 23.
units.tr: 2. It recounts examples of magicians. Exod. vii, 11, etc.; viii, 7, 18. Num. xxii, 5, etc.; xxiii, 23.

units.la: 1 Sam. XXVIII, 7, &c. 1 Chron. X, 13,14. Dan. II, 2. Act. VIII, 9. &c. XIII, 6, &c. XVI, 16. XIX, 13.
units.tr: 1 Sam. xxviii, 7, etc.; 1 Chron. x, 13, 14; Dan. ii, 2; Acts viii, 9, etc.; xiii, 6, etc.; xvi, 16; xix, 13.

units.la: 3. Consequenter etiam utitur variis modis loquendi, & sententiis, quibus ista veritas submternitur: Psal. LVIII, 5. Eccl. X, 11, Jer. VIII, 17. Gal. I, 1.
units.tr: 3. Consequently it also uses various modes of speaking and sayings by which this truth is laid down: Ps. lviii, 5; Eccl. x, 11; Jer. viii, 17; Gal. i, 1.

units.la: 4. Accedit multiplex experientia, quae neque ad causas naturales, neque ad ipsum Deum, aut ad Angelos bonos, referri potest: unde relinquitur, eam ad artem hanc nefariam ac Diabolicam referri debere. Huc pertinet consensus multorum Conciliorum, Patrum, Theologorum, Jureconsultorum, Medicorum, Philosophorum, Historicorum, &c.
units.tr: 4. There is also manifold experience, which can be referred neither to natural causes, nor to God himself, nor to good angels. Whence it follows that it must be referred to this wicked and diabolical art. To this belongs the agreement of many Councils, Fathers, theologians, jurists, physicians, philosophers, historians, and so on.

units.la: Obj. 1. Multa dicta & conficta sunt de Magis, quae tamen probata nunquam fuerunt, neque probari potuerunt; multa ad causas naturales revocari possunt, vel ad delíria melancholica, aut delusiones Satanæ, &c. Resp. Id nullo modo probat, nullam unquam in rerum natura extitisse, vel etiamnum existere, veram Magiam.
units.tr: Objection 1. Many things have been said and invented about magicians which were never proved and could not be proved. Many things can be referred to natural causes, or to melancholic delusions, or to the deceptions of Satan, and so on. Answer: This in no way proves that true magic has never existed in the nature of things, or that it does not still exist.

units.la: Obj. 2. Impossibile videtur pactum aliquod Magicum iniri cum Diabolo. Resp. Neg. satis enim patet, Diabolum liberaliter multa posse promittere; (vide Matth. IV, 9. Gen. III, 5.) atque etiam nonnulla praestare, Deo permittente: consequenter neque abfurdum est, ut hominibus assensum illi praebentibus pactum ejusmodi contrahatur.
units.tr: Objection 2. It seems impossible that some magical pact should be entered into with the devil. Answer: I deny it. For it is quite plain that the devil can lavishly promise many things (see Matt. iv, 9; Gen. iii, 5), and also perform some things, with God permitting. Consequently it is not absurd that such a pact should be contracted with men who give assent to him.

units.la: XXXIII. Quaeritur, An Papatui vere impingi possit Magia? Resp. Aff. Nam 1. publica auctoritate & lege istic exercetur ac traditur saltem Magia indirecta: quod apparet ex arte exorcistica, variisque verborum formulis, cerimoniis, ac sacramentalibus; dum iis efficacia tribuitur, quam tamen nec per naturam habent, neque per supernaturalem Dei promissionem aut constitutionem.
units.tr: XXXIII. It is asked whether magic can truly be charged against the Papacy. Answer: Yes. For, first, by public authority and law, at least indirect magic is practised and handed down there. This appears from the art of exorcism, and from the various verbal formulas, ceremonies and sacramentals, to which efficacy is attributed that they have neither by nature nor by God's supernatural promise or ordinance.

units.la: 2. Multa istic acta & scripta sunt Magica, sine publica censura & coercitione.
units.tr: Second, many magical acts and writings have occurred there without public censure or restraint.

units.la: XXXIV. Quæritur etiam, an omnis ignorantia sit inculpata? Neg. non solùm de ignorantia pravæ dispositionis, sed & privativâ eorum, quæ Deus ad bene beatéque vivendum revelavit: atque hoc contra Pontificios probamus :
units.tr: XXXIV. It is asked also whether every ignorance is blameless. Denied. This holds not only of ignorance arising from a bad disposition, but also of the privative ignorance of those things which God has revealed for living well and blessedly. We prove this against the Papists:

units.la: 1. A Sapientiæ & scientiæ encomiis & commendatione, ignorantiæ autem vituperio ac reprehensione, passim obviis. Deut. XXXII, 28, 29. Gens periens consiliis sunt; - Si sapientes essent, intelligerent novissimum suum. 1 Reg. IX, 29, - 34. Dedit autem Deus sapientiam Salomoni, & intelligentiam multam valdè, &c. Prov. 8, 1, 11. Nonne Sapientia clamat, - Intelligite simplices astutiam; & stolidi, intelligite corde, &c. Col. III. 16. Sermo Christi inhabitet in vobis copiosè cum omni sapientiâ: Eph. V, 15, 16, 17. Videte igitur, quomodo accuratè ambuletis, non ut insipientes, sed ut sapientes: &c.
units.tr: 1. Wisdom and knowledge are everywhere praised and commended, and ignorance censured and reproved. Deut. xxxii, 28, 29: "A nation void of counsel... if they were wise, they would understand their latter end." 1 Kings ix, 29-34: "God gave Solomon wisdom and very great understanding, etc." Prov. viii, 1, 11: "Does not wisdom cry out? ... Understand, you simple ones, cunning; and you fools, understand with the heart," etc. Col. iii, 16: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly with all wisdom." Eph. v, 15, 16, 17: "See then that you walk carefully, not as unwise but as wise," etc.

units.la: 2. A præstantiâ cognitionis rerum Divinarum, ubi objecta sunt nobilissima, omnique studio & contemplatione dignissima; ipse Deus Opt. Max. & ea quæ ad Deum, ad ipsius gloriam, nostramque æternam beatitudinem pertinent.
units.tr: 2. The excellence of the knowledge of divine things proves it, since its objects are most noble and most worthy of all study and contemplation: God himself, the Best and Greatest, and everything that pertains to God, to his glory and to our eternal blessedness.

units.la: 3. A necessitate; cum nec fides; nec pietas, neque salus, absque eâ possint consistere: quin & ipsa Divina revelatio hominem statim obliget ad agnitionem & contemplationem istarum veritatum, quas eo fine Deus revelavit. Rom. X, 13, 14. Quisquis igitur invocaverit nomen Domini, servabitur. Quomodo igitur invocabunt eum, in quem non crediderint? quomodo autem credent ei, de quo non audierint - 1 Joh. V, 10. Qui non credit Deo, mendacem eum fecit; quia non credidit testimonio, quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo.
units.tr: 3. It proves it from necessity, since neither faith, nor piety, nor salvation can exist without it. Indeed divine revelation itself binds a man at once to the knowledge and contemplation of those truths which God revealed for this end. Rom. x, 13, 14: "Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe him of whom they have not heard?" 1 John v, 10: "He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony God gave concerning his Son."

units.la: 4. A conditione subjectorum: omnes enim homines natura scire desiderant: qui certè appetitus à primâ hominis ad imaginem Dei creatione reliquus est; Imò per animam rationalem homines sumus: ratiocinari ergò, atque ita cognitionem variarum rerum, in-priprimis ad salutem Divinitus revelatarum, quærere, hominis naturæ maximè consentaneum; hanc verò negligere, ei adversum est, & maximè damnosum. Act. XVII, 27, 28. Ut quærerent Dominum, si forte palpando eum invenirent: &c. 1 Cor. 1, 21. -placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis servare credentes.
units.tr: 4. It proves it from the condition of the subjects. For all men by nature desire to know, and this desire certainly remains from the first creation of man in the image of God. Indeed we are men through the rational soul; therefore to reason, and so to seek the knowledge of various things, especially those divinely revealed for salvation, is most consonant with human nature, while to neglect it is contrary to human nature and most harmful. Acts xvii, 27, 28: "that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him," etc. 1 Cor. i, 21: "it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe."

units.la: XXXV. Speciatim verò malum turpe, sive peccatum, censeri debet ignorantia veritatum à Deo revelatarum, & ad salutem consequendam necessariarum: in iis scil. qui eas audiverunt: 1 Joh. v, 10. ac porro omnis ignorantia, tum juris, tum facti, in iis, quæ omnes homines communiter ad honestè ac piè vivendum, & peculiariter singuli pro ratione status sui Oeconomici, Politici, Ecclesiastici, Scholastici, &c. scire tenentur. Psal. LXXXII, 5. Nihil norunt, nec intelligunt, in tenebris ambulant: nutant omnia fundamenta terræ. Et manifesta est ratio à necessitate medii ad finem. Maxime autem peccaminosa est istiusmodi ignorantia contraria, tum etiam affectata, ex malitia, vel ex supina negligentia. Joh. III. 19. Hæc autem est condemnatio, quod lux venit in mundum: sed dilexerunt homines potius tenebras, quam lucem: quia sunt eorum mala opera. Imo neque prorsus excusari potest talium veritatum ignorantia invincibilis, quæ partem facit peccati originalis inhærentis: quoniam ea vincibilis tamen, & voluntaria, est in causa. Quæ vincibilis est causæ proximæ, nec tamen affectata, excusat quidem in tantum (ut loquuntur), non vero in totum. Hinc 1. 1 Tim. 1, 13. Prius eram blasphemus, & persecutor, & injuriis alios afficiens; sed misericordia sum donatus. Nam ignorans id faciebam, fidei expers. Vere igitur in iis etiam peccavit. Et Christus aperte, Luc. XII, 47, 48. Qui non novit, & fecit digna plagis, cædetur plagis paucis. Porrò cuicunque multum datum fuerit, multum repetetur ab eo: &c.
units.tr: XXXV. Specifically, ignorance of the truths revealed by God and necessary for obtaining salvation must be counted an evil and shameful thing, or a sin, in those who have heard them: 1 John v, 10. Further, every ignorance, whether of law or of fact, is sinful regarding those things which all men are commonly bound to know for living honestly and piously, and which each person is bound to know in particular according to his economic, political, ecclesiastical or scholastic station, and so on. Ps. lxxxii, 5: "They know nothing, nor do they understand; they walk in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken." The reason is plain from the necessity of the means to the end. Ignorance of this kind is most sinful when it is contrary to the truth, and also when it is affected, arising from malice or from slothful negligence. John iii, 19: "And this is the condemnation, that the light has come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil." Indeed the invincible ignorance of such truths, which forms part of the inherent original sin, cannot be wholly excused, since in its cause it is nonetheless vincible and voluntary. Ignorance that is vincible in its proximate cause, yet not affected, excuses indeed to this extent (as they say), but not entirely. Hence 1 Tim. i, 13: "I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent man; but I received mercy, for I did it ignorantly, in unbelief." Truly, then, he sinned in these things too. And Christ plainly says, Luke xii, 47, 48: "He who did not know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few stripes. But to whomever much has been given, of him much will be required," etc.

units.la: 2. Specialius de ignorantia Gentilium, qui Luce evangelii... Luce evangelii ... Euangelicâ, imo & instructione Verbi, erant destituti; Act.xiv,15,16. Ut à vanis istis rebus convertatis vos ad Deum illum vivum; qui fecit cælum, &c. Quique præteritis ætatibus sivit omnes Gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere. Rom. 1,21,-25. Vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus suis, & obtenebratum est desipiens cor eorum. Quamobrem etiam tradidit eos Deus cupiditatibus cordium ipsorum,&c. Eph.iv,17,18,19. Ne vos amplius ambuletis, sicut reliquæ Gentes ambulant, in vanitate mentis suæ: Tenebris obscuratam mentem habentes,&c. 1Thes.iv,5. Non in morbo cupiditatis: sicut Gentes, quæ non noverunt Deum.
units.tr: 2. More specifically concerning the ignorance of the Gentiles, who were deprived of the light of the gospel, indeed of evangelical instruction and of the preaching of the Word: Acts 14:15-16: That you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven, etc. who in past ages suffered all nations to walk in their own ways. Rom. 1:21-25: They became vain in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened. Therefore God also gave them up to the lusts of their own hearts, etc. Eph. 4:17-19: That you walk no longer as the other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, etc. 1 Thess. 4:5: Not in the passion of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God.

units.la: 3. Similiter de seductis: Matth. xv,14. Quodsi cæcus cæco dux viæ fuerit, ambo in foveam cadent. 2Thess.2,10, 11,12. Propterea quod amorem veritatis non receperunt, ut salvi fierent. Ideo igitur mittet illis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut ipsi credant mendacio; ut dammentur omnes, qui non crediderint veritati. Adde 2Petr 2,1, 2. Judæ, 10, 13.
units.tr: 3. Similarly concerning those who are led astray: Matt. 15:14: If the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch. 2 Thess. 2:10-12: Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved. Therefore God will send them a strong delusion, that they should believe a lie, so that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth. Add 2 Pet. 2:1-2; Jude 10, 13.

units.la: 4. Propterea cognitionis studium tam serio in SS. Literis urgeri solet, Phil. I, 9,10. Hoc oro; ut charitas vestra adhuc magis ac magis exundet in cognitione & omni sensu: Ut exploretis quæ differunt,&c. 2Petr.I,5.6,9. Ad hoc ipsum vero vos omni prætereà collato studio, adjicite fidei vestræ virtutem, virtuti vero notitiam; &c.
units.tr: 4. For this reason the pursuit of knowledge is customarily urged so earnestly in the Holy Scriptures: Phil. 1:9-10: This I pray, that your love may abound still more and more in knowledge and in all discernment, so that you may approve the things that differ, etc. 2 Pet. 1:5-6, 9: For this very reason, applying all diligence, add to your faith virtue, and to virtue knowledge, etc.

units.la: Obj. 1. Joh.ix,41. Si cæci essetis, non haberetis peccatum: ergo ignorantia excusat à peccato. Resp. Dictum istud Christi non debet absolutè intelligi, quasi nullum prorsùs habituri fuissent peccatum: sed comparatè de tali ac tanto peccato. Similiter accipiendum est illud, Joh. xv,24. Si opera non fecissem inter eos, quæ nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent.
units.tr: Objection 1. John 9:41: If you were blind, you would have no sin. Therefore ignorance excuses from sin. Reply: That saying of Christ ought not to be understood absolutely, as if they would have had no sin at all, but comparatively, concerning such and so great a sin. Likewise that passage must be taken: John 15:24: If I had not done among them works which no one else did, they would not have had sin.

units.la: Obj. 2. Cognitio, eique opposita ignorantia, pertinet ad intellectum: ac proinde non habet rationem bonitatis, vel malitiæ moralis; quia omne peccatum debet esse liberum; libertas vero est voluntatis, &c. Resp. Libertas quidem formaliter est voluntatis; sed & intellectus non exsistit sine voluntate; imo, qui cognitionem gnitioni studet, libere ei studet; qui eam stulte contemnit, aut negligit supine, libere eam contemnit, vel negligit. Ita ignorantiae etiam competit malitia moralis.
units.tr: Objection 2. Knowledge, and the ignorance opposed to it, belongs to the intellect; therefore it has no character of moral goodness or wickedness, because every sin must be voluntary, and freedom belongs to the will, etc. Reply: Freedom is indeed formally of the will; but the intellect also does not exist apart from the will. Indeed, one who eagerly pursues knowledge pursues it freely, and one who foolishly despises it, or carelessly neglects it, despises or neglects it freely. Thus moral wickedness also belongs to ignorance.

units.la: XXXVI. Quær. An sola hæresis, absque aliis pec- catis contra charitatem Dei & proximi, possit homi- nem subjicere æternæ damnationi?
units.tr: XXXVI. Question: Can heresy alone, apart from other sins against the love of God and of neighbour, subject a man to eternal damnation?

units.la: Resp. Cum nemo fidelis in hac vita prorsus immunis esse possit ab omnibus peccatis contra charitatem Dei & proximi; multo minus putandum est, hæreticum aliquem perfecte sanctum esse, exceptâ solâ hæresi mentali. Interim ipsa hæresis per se etiam vere peccatum est; atque adeo commune peccati stipendium quoque demeretur: quod contra Remonstrantes, observandum.
units.tr: Answer: Since no believer in this life can be wholly free from all sins against the love of God and neighbour, it is much less to be thought that any heretic is perfectly holy, excepting only mental heresy. Meanwhile heresy itself, in itself, is truly a sin; and therefore it also merits the common wages of sin. This is to be observed against the Remonstrants.

units.la: Hinc 1. inter opera carnis, quæ hominem ab hæreditate Regni Dei excludunt, enumerantur hæreses; Gal. v, 19, 20, 21.
units.tr: Hence, first, heresies are listed among the works of the flesh, which exclude a man from the inheritance of the Kingdom of God: Gal. 5:19-21.

units.la: 2. Diserte hæreses exitiales appellantur, 2 Petr. II, 1. & exitia tribuuntur hæreticis; non solum seducentibus, sed etiam seductis, v. 2. Minimè vere prior Petri sententia accipienda est discretive, quasi hæreses exitiales ab aliis hæresibus salutaribus distingueret; non magis quam 1 Petr. IV, 3. nefarii simulachrorum cultus ab aliis licitis simulachrorum cultibus discernuntur.
units.tr: Second, heresies are expressly called destructive heresies (2 Pet. 2:1), and destruction is ascribed to heretics, not only to those who seduce but also to those who are seduced (v. 2). The former saying of Peter is by no means to be taken as distinctive, as if it distinguished destructive heresies from other, wholesome heresies; no more than in 1 Pet. 4:3 the wicked worship of images is distinguished from other lawful worship of images.

units.la: 3. Aperte damnatio illis denunciatur, 1 Tim. I, 19, 20. 2 Tim. II, 17, 18, 20. Rom. III, 8.
units.tr: Third, damnation is plainly declared against them: 1 Tim. 1:19-20; 2 Tim. 2:17-18, 20; Rom. 3:8.

units.la: 4. Cum ignorantia veri Dei hominem justæ damnationi Divinæ subjiciat; 2 Thess. I, 8. & cœcus cœcum dücem sequens, pariter cadat in foveam; Matth. XV, 14. quomodo hæresis censebitur innoxia; quæ ipsi fidei, sapientiæ salutari, cultui Divino, & novæ creaturæ tam directe adversatur?
units.tr: Fourth, since ignorance of the true God subjects a man to just divine damnation (2 Thess. 1:8), and the blind man who follows a blind leader likewise falls into the ditch (Matt. 15:14), how will heresy be judged harmless, when it is so directly opposed to faith itself, to saving wisdom, to divine worship, and to the new creature?

units.la: XXXVII. Quær. An hæretici, ut sic, extremo supplicio per Magistratum afficiendi sint? Resp. Neg. Quia non subest in simplici hæresi causa sufficiens in ordine ad Politiam, cur talis ac tanta pœna illis infligenda genda esset : non magis quam in animi profanitate, superbia, odio, avaritia, &c. Atque hoc, ut contra Pontificios, eorumque inquisitionem, & sanguinaria edicta, vivicomburia, &c. afferimus: sic eadem opera Remonstrantes, Libertinos, & similes refellimus; qui nostrae Theologiae haereticidium impingunt. Fatemur interim, si ad haeresin accedant blasphemiae contra Deum, seductiones aliorum ad idololatriam vel errores exitiales, tranquillitatis publicae turbatio insignis, nec per mitiora coërceri potuerint, Magistratum Politicum tandem etiam ad capitale supplicium progredi posse: tanquam gloriae Divinae vindicem, & utriusque tabulae Legis custodem: Deut. xvii, 19. xiii, 5. Rom. xiii, 4. 1 Tim. ii, 2.
units.tr: XXXVII. Question: Are heretics, as such, to be punished with the extreme penalty by the magistrate? Answer: No. Because in simple heresy there is no sufficient cause, in relation to the civil polity, why so great and severe a punishment should be inflicted on them, no more than for profanity of mind, pride, hatred, avarice, etc. And this we assert against the Papists and their inquisition, and their bloody edicts, burning alive, etc.; in the same work we also refute the Remonstrants, the Libertines, and similar groups, who charge our theology with advocating the killing of heretics. We do concede, however, that if blasphemies against God, the seduction of others to idolatry or destructive errors, or a notable disturbance of public tranquillity, are added to heresy, and cannot be restrained by milder means, the civil magistrate may at last proceed even to capital punishment, as the avenger of divine glory and guardian of both tables of the Law: Deut. 17:19; 13:5; Rom. 13:4; 1 Tim. 2:2.

units.la: Obj. Matth. xiii, 29, 30. Ne colligendo zizania, eradicetis simul cum eis triticum. Sinite utraque simul crescere usque ad messem; &c. Resp. Fatemur ante diem extremi judicii non posse omnia omnino scandala ex Ecclesia instituta tolli per separationem & ejectionem: hoc tamen non obstat, quo minus Ecclesiastica disciplina in scandalis satis manifestis exerceatur, sine periculo eradicandi tritici. Similiter etiam Magistratus Politicus, ut alios facinorosos certe punire potest; sic tales quoque pro re nata: neque magis quam illis, patrocinatur sententia illa parabolica haereticis, blasphemis, seductoribus, & turbatoribus.
units.tr: Objection: Matt. 13:29-30: Lest while gathering the tares you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest, etc. Reply: We concede that before the day of the last judgment not all scandals can wholly be removed from the Church by separation and expulsion; yet this does not prevent ecclesiastical discipline from being exercised against sufficiently manifest scandals, without danger of uprooting the wheat. Likewise the civil magistrate can certainly punish other criminals, and so also such persons as occasion requires; nor does that parabolic saying favour heretics, blasphemers, seducers, and disturbers any more than it favours those others.

units.la: XXXVIII. Odium adversus Deum saepe memoratur in SS. Literis: utpote Exod. xx, 5, in tertiam & quartam generationem eorum qui oderunt me. Num. xxxv. Dispergantur inimici tui; & fugiant odio habentes te, a facie tua! Joh. xv, 18, 24, 25. Rom. i, 30. Dei osores, cum viii, 7. Quoniam quod sapit caro, inimicitia est adversus Deum: Legi enim Dei non subjicitur: nam ne potest quidem. Et juxta postremum illum textum, aliosque parallelos recte Catechesis nostra, qu. 5. Natura propensus sum ad odium Dei & proximi Idque observandum contra Libertinos & Remonstrantes.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Hatred against God is often mentioned in the Holy Scriptures: as in Exod. 20:5, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me. Num. 35: Let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee from your face! John 15:18, 24-25; Rom. 1:30, haters of God; Rom. 8:7: Because the mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. And according to this last text and other parallel passages, our Catechism rightly says in Question 5: By nature I am inclined to hate God and my neighbour. This is to be observed against the Libertines and the Remonstrants.

units.la: Obj. Deus non potest odio haberi ab homine; cum sit, ipsum summum bonum. Resp. Isto argumento probatur quidem, Deum non debere odio haberi; sed debere amari: non vero Deum non posse odio haberi. Impii certe Deum non considerant, ut summum bonum, vel saltem non ut ipsis summum bonum: sed ut adversarium istarum voluptatum, aliorumque peccatorum, quibus ipsi unice delectantur; & ut justum judicem, ipsis malum, dum pro malis turpibus iis retribuit mala tristia: de quo Pfal. xviii, 27. Cum mundo mundus eris, & cum perverso perverse agis. Adde v, 5, 6, 7. Dum vero sic Deus obversatur menti & conscientiae ipsorum: nihil mirum est illos Deo adversari, eum odisse, horrescere, blasphemare.
units.tr: Objection: God cannot be hated by a man, since he is the supreme good itself. Reply: This argument proves indeed that God ought not to be hated, but ought to be loved; it does not prove that God cannot be hated. The impious certainly do not consider God as the supreme good, or at least not as their own supreme good, but as the adversary of those pleasures and other sins in which they alone delight, and as the just judge who, for their base wickedness, repays them with sad evils. Concerning this, Ps. 18:26: With the pure you show yourself pure, and with the perverse you deal perversely. Add Ps. 5:5-7. But when God thus confronts their mind and conscience, it is no wonder that they oppose God, hate him, shudder at him, and blaspheme.

units.la: XXXIX. Falsa gratiarum actio est, quae pro gratiarum actione habetur, vel obtruditur: neque est tamen: utpote apud Pontificios Salutatio Angelica, de qua Job. Chapeaville in Elucidatione Catechismi Romani, part. 4. qu. 6. concl. 3. "Inter omnes gratiarum actiones facile primum locum tenet Angelica salutatio, Luc. 1. Ave Maria gratia plena, Dominus tecum, benedicte tu in mulieribus. Illis enim verbis, secundum communem Patrum expositionem, Deum summis & habendis laudibus, & gratiis agendis celebramus, quod Sanctissimam Virginem omni coelestium donorum munere cumulavit; ipsique Virgini singularem illam gratulamur felicitatem. &c. Sed 1. cum ipsi salutationem recte appellent, sicut etiam diserte appellatur Luc. 1, 29. & quidem fit salutatio Angeli ad Mariam; falso & absurde habetur pro gratiarum actione erga Deum. Salutatio enim est exoptatio salutis ad hominem; atque adeo species quaedam precationis, qua salutem & prosperitatem a Deo precamur homini, quem salutamus.
units.tr: XXXIX. That is a false thanksgiving which is regarded, or foisted upon us, as thanksgiving, and yet is not one; such as among the Papists the Angelic Salutation, concerning which Job. Chapeaville, in his Elucidation of the Roman Catechism, part 4, question 6, conclusion 3, says: "Among all acts of thanksgiving the Angelic Salutation easily holds the first place, Luke 1: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you, blessed are you among women. For by these words, according to the common exposition of the Fathers, we celebrate God with the highest praises and thanks, because he has heaped upon the Most Holy Virgin every gift of heavenly bounty; and to the Virgin herself we congratulate that singular happiness, etc." But first, since they rightly call it a salutation, as it is also expressly called in Luke 1:29, and indeed it is the salutation of the angel to Mary, it is falsely and absurdly regarded as a thanksgiving to God. For a salutation is a wish for salvation directed to a man; and so it is a kind of prayer, by which we ask from God salvation and prosperity for the man whom we greet.

units.la: 2. In eâ non dirigitur sermo ad Deum, quod fieri deberet in gratiarum actione erga Deum: sed ad ipsam Mariam.
units.tr: 2. In that salutation the speech is not addressed to God, as it ought to be in an act of thanksgiving to God, but to Mary herself.

units.la: 3. Maria in cœlis modo triumphans, tali prosperitatis apprecatione prorsus non eget, imo ea in ipsam injuria est.
units.tr: 3. Mary, now triumphant in heaven, has no need at all of such an appeal for prosperity; indeed, such an appeal is an injury to her.

units.la: 4. Qualiscunque illa Mariæ invocatio est idololatrica. Vide sup. th. 21, 22.
units.tr: 4. Any such invocation of Mary is idolatrous. See above, thesis 21 and 22.

units.la: XL. Non orandum pro mortuis: pie enim defuncti, beati cœlites, intercessione nostra non egent: neque in tali statu sunt, ut sic vel mala ab ipsis averti, vel bona iis per nos impetrari possint, aut debeant: unde nec exemplum ullum talis intercessionis comparet in SS. Literis: contra Pontificios.
units.tr: XL. One must not pray for the dead. The pious departed, the blessed inhabitants of heaven, have no need of our intercession, nor are they in such a state that evils can be turned away from them, or goods obtained for them through us, or that either can or ought to happen.
