Hence no example of such intercession appears in the Holy Scriptures. Against the Papists.

units.la: Obj. 2 Maccab. XII, 44-46. Nisi enim eos, qui ceciderant, resurrecturos Iudas speraret, superfluum videretur et vanum orare pro mortuis. Sancta ergo et salubris est cogitatio pro defunctis orare, ut a peccatis solvantur. Resp. 1. Apocryphus est iste locus, ac prorsus invalidus probare aliquid ad fidem morésque vivendi pertinens. 2. Conceptæ fuerunt preces, & oblata sacrificia, secundum istam œconomiam; ne ira Dei ulterius exardesceret, plurEsve anathematis causa consumeret. Confer Deut. XXI, 7, 8. cum VII, 25, 26. & Ios. VII, 11, 12. Neque enim pro mortuis ulla fuerunt instituta sacrificia. 3. Auctor istius libri ad defunctos retulit, errore judicii; dum scripsit non ut oportuit, sed ut potuit, rerum sacrarum non satis peritus, vinumque affuso liquore noxio vitiãns. Vide 2 Maccab. XV, 39, 40.
units.tr: Objection: 2 Maccabees 12:44-46. For unless Judas had hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would seem superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. Therefore it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the departed, that they may be released from their sins. Reply: 1. That passage is apocryphal and wholly unable to prove anything that pertains to faith or to the conduct of life. 2. The prayers were offered and the sacrifices made according to that economy, lest the wrath of God should blaze up further or consume them on account of the anathema. Compare Deut. 21:7,8 with 7:25,26, and Josh. 7:11,12. For no sacrifices were ever instituted for the dead. 3. The author of that book referred these things to the dead through an error of judgement, since he wrote not as he ought but as he could, not being sufficiently skilled in sacred matters, and by pouring in a noxious liquid he spoils the wine. See 2 Maccabees 15:39,40.

units.la: XLI. Errant Brownistæ, dum contendunt: orationem Dominicam regulam solum esse, à Christo nobis eo fine traditam, ut indicet, quæ, & quo ordine, petenda à Deo sint; non ut pro precatione ipsa usurpetur, vel precationis sit formula. Sed minimè ista pugnant, regulam esse & exemplar ad quod precationes nostræ faciendæ sint; ut oremus quemadmodum oportet; atque interim esse etiam precationem. Errant nihilominus & Pontificii, in alterum extremum abeuntes, atque omnibus fere occasionibus adhibentes eandem illam formulam: aut aliquoties eam per sphærulas suas precatorias; cum salutatione Angelica, super-stitiose annumerantes. Quemadmodum neque putandum est, non cohæstare aliam precationem sine illa: vel omnibus precationibus illam necessario adjungendam. Aliam esse mentem Servatoris, ex ipsius, ut & Apostolorum, aliorumque sanctorum praxi, quoties eorum precationes commemorantur, manifestissimum est.
units.tr: XLI. The Brownists err when they contend that the Lord's Prayer is only a rule, given to us by Christ for this end: to show what, and in what order, things are to be asked of God; not that it should be used as a prayer itself or serve as a form of prayer. But these things by no means conflict: that it is both a rule and a pattern to which our prayers are to be conformed, so that we pray as we ought, and that at the same time it is also a prayer. The Papists also err, going to the opposite extreme and using that same formula on almost every occasion, or superstitiously counting it among their prayers by means of their little spheres, together with the Angelic Salutation. Nor should one think that another prayer cannot stand without it, or that it must necessarily be added to all prayers. That the mind of the Saviour was otherwise is most plain from his own practice, and that of the Apostles and other saints, whenever their prayers are recorded.

units.la: XLII. In exordio Precationis Dominicæ Patrem appellantes; & quidem nostrum, Deum sic invocamus, ut paternam ejus bonitatem simul confiteamur.
units.tr: XLII. In the opening of the Lord's Prayer we address God as Father, and indeed as our Father, so that in invoking him we at the same time confess his fatherly goodness.

units.la: Mahommedani istam Dei appellationem nimis superbam, & blasphemiæ affinem, reputant perperam: at vero sic 1. precatio nostra plurimum distat à precibus qualicumque infidelium, qui verum illum Deum vel prorsus ignorant, vel saltem ut Patrem suum in Filio & Spiritu S. invocare non possunt: Gal. iv, 7, 8, 9.
units.tr: The Mohammedans think this appellation of God too proud and akin to blasphemy, but wrongly. Indeed, in this way 1. our prayer differs greatly from the prayers of any unbelievers, who either do not know that true God at all, or at least cannot invoke him as their Father in the Son and the Holy Spirit: Gal. 4:7,8,9.

units.la: 2. Filialis amor ac reverentia in animis nostris excitatur: Mal. i. 6. 1 Pet. i, 17.
units.tr: 2. Filial love and reverence are stirred up in our souls: Mal. 1:6. 1 Pet. 1:17.

units.la: 3. Fiducia accenditur, etiam de precatione exaudienda: Rom. viii, 15, 16, 17, 26, 27. Matth. vii, 11.
units.tr: 3. Confidence is kindled, even concerning the hearing of our prayer: Rom. 8:15,16,17,26,27. Matt. 7:11.

units.la: Male iidem culpant petitionem secundam; Veniat Regnum tuum! quia Deus ubique sit, suaque providentia nunc & semper omnia gubernet: istud enim hic præsuppono imus: sed pro salutari ædificatione nostri, & Ecclesiæ universæ, atque in cœlestem & consummatam beatitudinem ac gloriam translatione, supplicamus.
units.tr: The same men wrongly find fault with the second petition, "Thy kingdom come!", on the ground that God is everywhere and now and always governs all things by his providence. For I presuppose that here; but we pray for the salutary building up of ourselves and of the whole Church, and for our translation into heavenly and consummated blessedness and glory.

units.la: XLIII. Quarta petitione pro hac temporali vitâ, ejusque incolumitate & conservatione, ac rebus ei necessariis, precamur quoque: nam & ipsi huic vitæ summ constat pretium, Eccl. ix, 4. Cuicunque consociato cum omnibus viventibus, est spes: nam canis vivus est melior leone mortuo. Propterea sedulo debet observari: Eph. 5,16. Redimentes opportunitatem, quoniam dies mali sunt. Hoc tempus in futuram æternitatem influit; & prout benè malève transactum fuerit, talis erit hominis in æternitate conditio. Hic vita vel acquiritur, vel amittitur. Eccl.xi,3. 2 Cor.v,10. Rom. 2,4, 5, 6. Gal.vi,10.
units.tr: XLIII. In the fourth petition we also pray for this temporal life, for its safety and preservation, and for the things necessary to it. For this life itself is clearly of the highest price: Eccl. 9:4. "To him who is joined with all the living there is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion." Therefore it must be carefully observed: Eph. 5:16. "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. This time flows into future eternity, and according as it has been spent well or ill, such will be the condition of the man in eternity." Here life is either gained or lost. Eccl. 11:3. 2 Cor. 5:10. Rom. 2:4,5,6. Gal. 6:10.

units.la: 1 Pet.1,17. Nunc tempus est, quo Deum animo simul & corpore, cum Ecclesiâ militante, & ad hujus ædificationem, sic glorificare debemus & possumus, quemadmodum nobis incumbit. In morte ista eo fine ac modo fieri non possunt. Psf. vi,6. Quoniam non est in morte memoria Tui: in sepulchro quis confitebitur Tibi? Confer xxx,10. lxxxviii,12. cxv,17. Isef.xxxviii,18. Unde etiam Psf.cxviii,17. Non moriar; sed vivam: & narrabo opera Jah. Paulus quidem statum spirituum consummatorum spectans, mortem sibi pro lucro reputavit, & cum Christo esse desideravit, quod hoc sibi foret melius; Phil. 1,21,23. verum considerans, quid in hac vita, apud Ecclesiam militantem agere posset; subjecit verf. 24,25. Sed permanere in carne, magis necessarium est propter vos: Et hoc confisus, novi me mansurum esse, & permansurum cum vobis omnibus, ad vestrum profectum & gaudium fidei. Ideo Deus quoque promissiones hujus vitæ piis fecit: 1 Tim.iv,8. Eph.vi,2,3. Rom.iv,13. Exod.xx,12. Levit. xxvi,4, - 11. Deut. xxviii,1,-14. Et similis est precatio Aguris. Prov, 30, 8. Paupertatem & divitias ne dederis mihi: ale me cibo qui convenit mihi. Itemque votum Jacobi, Gen. xxviii, 20, 21. Si fuerit Deus mecum; - dederitque mihi panem ad vescendum, & vestimentum ad induendum; Revertus quoque fuero in pace ad domum patris mei; erit Iehovah mihi in Deum.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1:17. Now is the time in which we ought and are able to glorify God, with soul and body alike, together with the militant Church and for its edification, just as is incumbent upon us. In death these things cannot be done in this way or to this end. Ps. 6:6. "For in death there is no remembrance of thee; in the grave who will confess to thee?" Compare Ps. 30:10, 88:12, 115:17, Isa. 38:18. Whence also Ps. 118:17: "I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of Jah." Paul, indeed, looking to the state of the perfected spirits, counted death gain for himself and desired to be with Christ, since that would be better for him: Phil. 1:21,23. But considering what he could do in this life, among the militant Church, he added in verses 24 and 25: "But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. And trusting in this, I know that I shall remain and remain with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith." Therefore God also made promises of this life to the pious: 1 Tim. 4:8. Eph. 6:2,3. Rom. 4:13. Exod. 20:12. Lev. 26:4-11. Deut. 28:1-14. Similar is the prayer of Agur, Prov. 30:8: "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is convenient for me." Likewise the vow of Jacob, Gen. 28:20,21: "If God will be with me, and give me bread to eat and clothing to put on, and I return in peace to my father's house, then Jehovah shall be my God."

units.la: Obj.1. Neccssaria ad hanc vitam & ejus vires petere, est βαλτολογία & πολυλογία illa Gentilium, quam Christus damnavit; Matth.vi,7. Resp: Neg. Istud enim peccatum non est in re, quæ petitur, sed in modo orandi: dum precationis valor constituitur in prolixitate, & frequenti atque inani ejusdem sermonis repetitione. Confer 1 Reg. xv11, 82. Jef. 1, 15.
units.tr: Objection 1. To ask for the things necessary for this life and its strength is that "vain repetition and much speaking" of the Gentiles which Christ condemned: Matt. 6:7. Reply: Denied. For that sin lies not in the thing asked for, but in the manner of praying, when the worth of prayer is made to consist in length and in the frequent and empty repetition of the same words. Compare 1 Reg. 17, 82 and Isa. 1, 15.

units.la: Obj. 2. Christus eodem capite verf. 25.-prohibuit, ne foliciti fimus animæ, id est vitæ nostræ, quid manducemus; & corpori nostro, quid induamus; tum etiam de crastino, verf. 34. Ergo. Resp. Non tamen omnem vitæ curam prohibuit; quæ alibi diserte præcipitur; ut Eph iv, 28. v, 29. 2 Theff. iii, 8, -12. 1 Tim. v, 8. sed folicitudinem nimis anxiam, cum desidentia erga Deum, & dispendio rerum spiritualium, conjunctam.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ in the same chapter, verse 25, forbade us to be anxious about our life, that is, what we shall eat; and about our body, what we shall put on; and also about tomorrow, verse 34. Therefore... Reply: He did not, however, forbid all care for life, which is expressly commanded elsewhere: Eph. 4:28, 5:29; 2 Thess. 3:8-12; 1 Tim. 5:8. What he forbade was an overly anxious solicitude, joined with indifference toward God and the loss of spiritual things.

units.la: Obj. 3. Promisit item verf. 33. quærentibus primo regnum Dei & justitiam ejus, ista omnia esse adjicienda: Ergo. Resp. Non tamen promisit adjicienda, fine omni nostro labore, cura, oratione: nedum prohibuerit quærere & precari temporalem necessitatem, post ea quæ spectant ad regnum Dei & justitiam ejus.
units.tr: Objection 3. He also promised, in verse 33, that all these things would be added to those who seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Therefore... Reply: He did not, however, promise that they would be added without any labour, care or prayer on our part; much less did he forbid us to seek and pray for temporal need, after those things which pertain to the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

units.la: Obj. 4. Precibus nostris ea petimus, quæ in nostra potestate non sunt: Ergo non recte alimenta. Resp. Ubi nos laboramus nostro modo, benedictione Divina prorsus indigemus, ut rem faciamus; atque istam benedictionem recte precamur: Pfal. cxxvii, 1, 2. Si Jehovah non ædificet domum, frustra laborant ædificantes eam: Si Ichovah non custodiat civitatem, frustra vigilat custos. Frustra vobis est maturantibus surgere, tardantibus sedere, edentibus panem dolorum, &c. Nihil igitur ex arte nobis dabimus, nisi Deus artem, & victum ad artem dederit: imo & ex victu virium conservationem ac restaurationem à Deo dari necesse est. Pro omnibus istis acceptis Deo agendæ sunt gratæ. Deut. viii, 10. Rom. xiv, 6. 1 Tim. iv, 3, 4. atque adeo pro accipiendis preces quoque dicendæ.
units.tr: Objection 4. By our prayers we ask for things that are not in our power; therefore it is wrong to ask for food. Reply: Where we labour in our own way, we altogether need the divine blessing if the thing is to succeed, and we rightly pray for that blessing: Ps. 127:1,2. "Unless Jehovah build the house, they labour in vain who build it; unless Jehovah keep the city, the watchman watches in vain. It is vain for you to rise early and sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows, etc." Therefore we shall gain nothing from our craft unless God gives both the craft and the sustenance for the craft. Indeed, it is necessary that the preservation and restoration of our strength by food also be given by God. For all these things received, thanks are to be rendered to God: Deut. 8:10. Rom. 14:6. 1 Tim. 4:3,4. And so prayers are to be said for receiving them as well.

units.la: XLIV. Eorum, qui aliter interpretantur; alii de pane Eucharistico exponunt; alii panem Verbi Divi- ni, vel ipsum Christum, intelligunt. Sed Eucharistia tunc
units.tr: XLIV. Of those who interpret otherwise: some explain it of the Eucharistic bread; others understand the bread of the Word of God, or Christ himself. But the Eucharist

units.la: tunc nondum nota, aut instituta fuit; panem vero prorsus ignotum petere, Christus nequaquam docuit. Obscurius quoque fuisset, si panem Verbi Divini, vel scipsum intellectum voluisset Christus τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον appellando; nec ulla voce addita, unde ista metaphora potuisset intelligi: imo & restrictio σήμερον, Matth. vi, 11. cri adversatur. Rectius Discipuli, cum de pane spirituali, ipso Christo, ageretur, Joh. vi, 34. Domine, da nobis semper panem istum!
units.tr: The Eucharist was then not yet known or instituted, and Christ never taught people to ask for bread of which they knew nothing at all. It would also have been more obscure if Christ had meant the bread of the Word of God, or himself, by calling it "our bread, the bread for the coming day" [τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον], with no added word by which such a metaphor could be understood. Indeed the qualifier "today" [σήμερον] in Matt. 6:11 contradicts it. The disciples were more correct when, speaking of the spiritual bread, that is Christ himself, they said in John 6:34: "Lord, give us this bread always!"

units.la: Non nemo τὸν ἐπιούσιον venturum interpretatur, ac si esset τὸν ἐπιόντα, qui scil. ultimo tempore venturus est, in die judicii: ut intelligatur ipse Christus, panis noster, qui tunc venturus est, ut cum eo & in eo resurgamus, virtute corporis ipsius, quod hic in Eucharistia sumimus: sed illa tunc fuerunt obscuriora, quam ut sic Discipulis proponi debuerint, neque pro tam brevi formula satis distincta à petitione, Veniat regnum tuum! Et quid tum sibi vult restrictio σήμερον, vel καθ' ἡμέραν?
units.tr: Some take ἐπιούσιον to mean "the coming one" [τὸν ἐπιόντα], that is, the one who will come at the last time, on the day of judgment, so that Christ himself is understood as our bread, who will come then, so that we may rise with and in him by the power of his body, which we here receive in the Eucharist. But those things were then too obscure to be set before the disciples in this way, and in so brief a formula they are not distinct enough from the petition "Thy kingdom come." And what then does the qualifier "today" [σήμερον], or "daily" [καθ' ἡμέραν], mean?

units.la: Neque istam expositionem probat, quod dicitur Euangelium à Matthæo scriptum Hebraicè, non Græcè; ejus authenticum exemplar servatum fuisse apud Nazaræos & Ebionitas; atque in eo Hieronymum legisse, לחם יחד: istæ enim hypothesis à vero alienæ sunt; nec evincunt id quod intenditur.
units.tr: Nor does this explanation gain support from the claim that Matthew's Gospel was written in Hebrew, not Greek; that its authentic copy was preserved among the Nazarenes and Ebionites; and that in it Jerome read "lechem yachad" [לחם יחד]. For these hypotheses are foreign to the truth, and do not prove what they are meant to prove.

units.la: XLV. Remissio, quæ nobis tribuitur petitione quintâ, iracundiæ & vindictæ privatæ adversatur; non autem justitiæ punitivæ publicæ.
units.tr: XLV. The forgiveness which is granted to us in the fifth petition is opposed to anger and private vengeance, not to public punitive justice.

units.la: Respectus vero, quem nostra remissio habet ad Divinam, non dicit utriusque paritatem; sed qualemcunque similitudinem analogicam: omnis enim actio Divina infinite persectior est actione nostra: & remissio Dei est remissio proprie dicta, & quidem Rectoris absolutè supremi, quæ non fit nisi intercedente satisfactione; nostra vero est improprie dicta, privatorum utcunque læsorum, quæ satisfactionem minimè requirit.
units.tr: The relation which our forgiveness has to the divine forgiveness does not imply that the two are equal, but only some sort of analogical likeness. For every divine action is infinitely more perfect than our action. God's forgiveness is forgiveness properly so called, and indeed that of the absolutely supreme Ruler, which does not occur except through an intervening satisfaction. Ours, however, is forgiveness improperly so called, that of private persons who have been wronged in some way, which does not at all require satisfaction.

units.la: 2. Remissio nostra non est causa antecedens procatarctica remissionis Divinæ ; sed effectus ex ea consequens: fides enim salvifica statim in nobis ponit justificationem ; atque in eâ Divinam remissionem erga nos terminatam; deinde charitatem erga Deum & proximum imperat ; ex hâc resultat nostra remissio erga proximum nostrum. Luc. vii, 47, 48, 50. Dico tibi, remissa esse multa illa peccata ipsius ; nam dilexit multum: cui autem paulum remittitur, paululum diligit. Dixit autem ei, Remissa sunt tibi peccata.-Fides tua te servavit. Col. iii, 13. Sufferentes alii alios, & condonantes vobis mutuo, si quis adversus aliquem habuerit querelam: sicut & Christus condonavit vobis, ita & vos. Sic nostra remissio erga proximum, sequitur remissionem Christi erga nos; & conformatur utcunque ad istud exemplar gratiæ ac misericordiæ nobis factæ. Non est igitur, quod Muhammedani istam petitionem carpant, tanquam injuriam Divinæ Majestati; cui nos regulam aliquam ex facto nostro vellemus præscribere.
units.tr: 2. Our forgiveness is not the antecedent, procatarctic cause of divine forgiveness, but an effect following from it. For saving faith at once places justification in us, and in it the divine forgiveness toward us is terminated; then it commands love toward God and neighbour, and from this love our forgiveness toward our neighbour results. Luke 7:47, 48, 50: I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much; but to whom little is forgiven, he loves little. And he said to her, Your sins are forgiven. Your faith has saved you. Col. 3:13: Bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if anyone has a complaint against someone; just as Christ forgave you, so also must you. Thus our forgiveness toward our neighbour follows Christ's forgiveness toward us, and is shaped, in some measure, after that pattern of grace and mercy shown to us. There is therefore no reason for the Muhammadans to find fault with this petition, as if it were an insult to the divine Majesty, to which we would be prescribing some rule based on our own deed.

units.la: 3. Justificatio, & sic remissio peccatorum nostrorum, simul & semel peragitur, cum primum credere incipimus fide salvificâ; sed ejus applicatio perceptibilis & consolatoria super peccatis identidem commissis, atque adeò ejus sensus in conscientia nostra, quoties præxin fidei ac resipiscentiæ super peccatis illis iteramus, atque ita Deum precamur, iteratur sæpissimè; simulque fit executio quædam istius sententiæ, quatenus actû etiam liberamur ab afflictionibus, quæ istorum peccatorum causâ nobis vel immitti cœperunt, vel immittendæ alioqui fuissent. Ista sententiæ judicialis modò latæ applicatio ad sensum conscientiæ nostræ, ejusdemque executio liberatoria à quibusdam afflictionibus, sequitur quidem actum charitatis & remissionis nostræ erga proximum: sed actus ille noster nullo modo est antecedens causa procatarctica justificationis, aut remissionis Divinæ erga nos: cujus non est alia istiusmodi causa; nisi justitia Christi pro nobis præstita, quæ satisfactionem & meritum ipsius complectitur; fides vero instrumenti rationem habet ad accipiendam unionem & communionem cum Christo, qui nobis factus est justitia à Deo. Imo nec ulla alia opera nostra verè bona, quocunque modo præcedunt justificationem ac remissionem Divinam ergà nos; cum fide posteriora sint, & successivè fiant; justificatio verò, utpotè actus judicialis, relativam duntaxat mutationem nostri inferens, in momento peragatur. Malè igitur, post Pontificios & Socinianos, etiam Remonstrantes, ex hac petitione, aliisque similibus locis, colligunt, bona opera ad justificationem consequendam necessaria esse, necessitate si non efficientiæ, saltem præsentiæ: imo istiusmodi locutiones, Nisi remiseritis hominibus offensas ipsorum, Pater etiam vester non remittet vobis offensas vestras, volunt, mafeciam conditionem in se continere, quæ conditio, ut causa sine quâ non, efficientiam aliquam necessario in conceptu suo involvat. Fatemur quidem, juxta Matth. vi, 15, xviii, 35. alicujus non-remittere, tanquam peccatum omissionis, causam esse cur ipse punitur sine remissione; sed non contra sequitur, nostrum remittere esse antecedentem causam justificationis nostræ coram Deo.
units.tr: 3. Justification, and so the remission of our sins, is accomplished at once and in a single act, when we first begin to believe with saving faith. But its application, which is perceptible and consoling, to the sins committed again and again, and thus its sense in our conscience, is repeated very often, as often as we renew the exercise of faith and repentance concerning those sins and so pray to God. At the same time there is a certain execution of that sentence, insofar as we are also actually freed from the afflictions which had begun to be sent upon us on account of those sins, or which would otherwise have been sent. This application of the judicial sentence, now pronounced, to the sense of our conscience, and its liberating execution from certain afflictions, indeed follows upon an act of our charity and forgiveness toward our neighbour. But that act of ours is in no way the antecedent procatarctic cause of justification or of divine remission toward us. There is no other cause of this kind except the righteousness of Christ performed for us, which embraces his satisfaction and merit. Faith, however, has the character of an instrument for receiving union and communion with Christ, who was made righteousness to us by God. Indeed, no other works of ours that are truly good precede God's justification and remission toward us in any way, since they come after faith and are done successively; but justification, as a judicial act bringing about only a relative change in us, is accomplished in a moment. Therefore they wrongly infer, following the Papists, the Socinians, and also the Remonstrants, from this petition and other similar passages, that good works are necessary for obtaining justification, with a necessity if not of efficiency, at least of presence. Indeed, such expressions as "If you do not forgive men their offences, your Father also will not forgive you your offences" want to contain a condition in themselves, and that condition, as a cause without which the thing does not happen, must necessarily involve some efficiency in its very concept. We grant indeed that, according to Matt. 6:15 and 18:35, not forgiving someone, as a sin of omission, is the cause why the unforgiving person himself is punished without forgiveness. But it does not follow in reverse that our forgiving is the antecedent cause of our justification before God.

units.la: XLV. Doxologia, Quia tuum est regnum, & potentia & gloria in sæcula, exstat Matth. vi, 13. in exemplaribus Græcis vetustissimis & probatissimis; atque in Versionibus Syriacâ, Persicâ, Æthiopicâ: & consentanea est similibus doxologiis, Apoc. iv, 11, v, 12, 13. 14. Nec rejicienda est, aut omittenda, 1. quod eam non habeat Vulgata vers. Latina: quæ nihil derogat editioni authenticæ.
units.tr: XLV. The doxology, "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever," is found in Matt. 6:13 in the most ancient and most approved Greek manuscripts, and in the Syriac, Persian and Ethiopic versions. It agrees with similar doxologies, Rev. 4:11; 5:12, 13, 14. Nor is it to be rejected or omitted, 1. because the Vulgate Latin version does not have it; for this detracts nothing from the authentic edition.

units.la: Neque 2. quod Lucas eam non expresserit: sæpius enim accidit, ut quod in uno Scriptore sacro prætermissum, vel admodum breviter propositum est, id ex alio debeat supplerí, Neque ȷ. auctoritas Ecclesiae Romanae urgeri debet adversus editionem authenticam; & Ecclesiam Graecam quae istam sequitur.
units.tr: Nor 2. because Luke has not expressed it. For it often happens that what is omitted, or only very briefly stated, in one sacred writer must be supplied from another. Nor 3. should the authority of the Roman Church be urged against the authentic edition, nor that of the Greek Church, which follows it.

units.la: XLVI. Precibus aliquando adjungitur Jejunium; spontanea ac pia abstinentia à cibo & potū, ad tempus suscepta, ut ista ratione indignitatem nostram humiles coram Deo declaremus, lascivientem carnem magis subigamus, &.ad preces aliaque religionis exercitia melius comparemur, Vide 1 Sam. VII, 6: 2, III, 35. XII,16. Joel. 2, 15. Jon,III,7. Matth. VI,16,17,18. Luc. 2,37. Act. XIII,3. XIV,23. 1 Cor. VII, 5. IX,25. 26,27. Sed perperam à Pontificiis constituitur in discrimine ciborum; quod vere superstitiosum est, & SS. Literis contrarium. 1 Cor. X,25,26. Quicquid in macello venditur, edite: nihil discriminantes propter conscientiam. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo ejus. Col.2,16,17. Nequis igitur vos damnet ob cibum, vel potum, &c. 20.-23. Quid, ut viventes in mundo, placitis adstringimini: Ne ejus taxis, neq; tetigeris? Quae omnia sunt comparata ipso usu ad corruptionem,-. 1 Tim. IV,3,4,5. apostatis, ac deceptoribus, qui doctrinas Daemoniorum sectantur, tribuitur, quod jubeant abstinere à cibis, quos Deus condidit, ad participandum cum gratiarum actione, fidelibus, & iis qui noverunt veritatem. Nam quicquid condidit Deus, bonum est; nec quicquam rejiciendum est, si cū gratiarum actione sumatur. Sanctificatur enim per verbum Dei, & preces. Vide etiam Rom. XIV. 3,4,6,14,17,20. Tit, 1,15. Matth. XV, 11.
units.tr: XLVI. Fasting is sometimes joined to prayers: a voluntary and pious abstinence from food and drink, undertaken for a time, so that by this means we may humbly declare our unworthiness before God, subdue the wanton flesh more, and become better prepared for prayer and other exercises of religion. See 1 Sam. 7:6; 2 Sam. 3:35; 12:16; Joel 2:15; Jonah 3:7; Matt. 6:16, 17, 18; Luke 2:37; Acts 13:3; 14:23; 1 Cor. 7:5; 9:25, 26, 27. But the Papists wrongly set it up as a distinction of foods, which is truly superstitious and contrary to the Holy Scriptures. 1 Cor. 10:25, 26: Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat, making no distinction for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness. Col. 2:16, 17: Let no one therefore judge you in respect of food or drink, etc. (20-23) Why, as if living in the world, are you subject to decrees: Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch? All these things are meant to perish in the using. 1 Tim. 4:3, 4, 5: this is attributed to apostates and deceivers who follow the doctrines of demons, that they command abstaining from foods which God created, to be partaken of with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For whatever God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. See also Rom. 14:3, 4, 6, 14, 17, 20; Tit. 1:15; Matt. 15:11.

units.la: Ex quibus colligi possunt ista argumenta: 1. Discrimen ciborum, quod sub V.T. obtinuit per ipsius Dei Legem cerimonialem, jam sub N.T. est abrogatum; atque adeo libertati Christianae contrarium. Multo minus arbitratu humano nunc aliud discrimen ei surrogandum est.
units.tr: From these the following arguments may be drawn: 1. The distinction of foods that held under the Old Testament by God's own ceremonial Law has now, under the New Testament, been abrogated, and so is contrary to Christian liberty. Much less may some other distinction now be substituted for it by human judgment.

units.la: 2. Deus omnium ciborum, quos condidit, fidelibus suis jam sub N.T. liberum usum ordinavit; sed cum sanctificatione & gratiarum actione conjunctum. Cen-tratis traria igitur prohibitio huic Divinæ ordinationi, & sanctificationi, adversatur.
units.tr: 2. Under the New Testament God has ordained for his faithful people the free use of all the foods he created, but joined with sanctification and thanksgiving. A contrary prohibition is therefore opposed to this divine ordinance and sanctification.

units.la: 3. Quæ idolis erant immolata, si in macello vendėrentur, liberâ conscientiâ potuerunt comedi, propter illam ordinationem Dei, qui est omnium Dominus. Multo minùs circa quaslibet carnes conscientiæ debent gravari, aut ligari.
units.tr: Things that had been offered to idols could be eaten with a clear conscience if they were sold in the meat market, on account of that ordinance of God, who is the Lord of all. Much less should consciences be burdened or bound concerning any kind of meat whatever.

units.la: 4. Contraria sententia nititur tantum placitis hominum, gratiam Novi Testamenti ignorantium, vel ei adversantium; ipso usû comparata est ad corruptionem, inanem duntaxat speciem sapientiæ & humilitatis habet; est apostatarum, ac deceptorum, qui doctrinas dæmoniorum sectantur, & hypocritarum falsiloquorum, quorum conscientia cauterio resecta est: ac proindè ea non debet tolerari in Ecclesiâ Christianâ.
units.tr: 4. The contrary opinion rests only on the opinions of men, who are ignorant of the grace of the New Testament or opposed to it. By practice it is turned to corruption; it has only the empty appearance of wisdom and humility. It belongs to apostates and deceivers who follow the doctrines of demons, and to hypocrites who speak lies, whose conscience has been seared as with a hot iron. Therefore it ought not to be tolerated in the Christian Church.

units.la: XLVII. Obj. In V. T. piè observata fuit distinctio ciborum, & sic jejunatum, à Daniele & sociis ejus, Eli- sæo & filiis Prophetarum, itemque à Rechabitis. Er- gò.
units.tr: XLVII. Objection. In the Old Testament the distinction of foods was observed piously, and so Daniel and his companions fasted, and Elisha and the sons of the prophets, and likewise the Rechabites. Therefore.

units.la: Resp. 1. Daniel & socii ejus, cap. 1, 8, 12. &c. non distinxerunt cibos ex humano placito, multò minùs in ista distinctione jejunium constituerunt: sed piè decreverunt non pollui cibis de mensa regis Ethnici allatis, secundùm Legem cerimonialem, quæ tunc obtinuit.
units.tr: Answer 1. Daniel and his companions (ch. 1:8, 12, etc.) did not make a distinction of foods from human decree, much less did they establish a fast by that distinction. Rather, out of piety they resolved not to defile themselves with the food brought from the table of the heathen king, in accordance with the ceremonial law which was then in force.

units.la: 2. Idem Daniel, ubi visionibus Propheticis esset intentus, & speciatim visionis cujusdam de rebus gravibus, & ad Ecclesiam Dei quoque spectantibus, intelligentiam quæreret, de se testatur, x, 2, 3. Lugebam tribus hebdomadibus dierum. Panem desideriorum non comedi; nec caro, nec vinum, introierunt in os meum: nec unguento unctus sum, donec complerentur tres hebdomades dierum. Sic quia humiliatio illa diuturnior fuit, quam ut persecto jejunio transigi potuisset naturaliter, insigni frugalitate & sobrietate fuit traducta; abstinentia à pane desiderabili, carne, vino, & unguento: longè aliter, quam apud Pontificios agi solet; ubi panis præstantissimus, pisces sces delicatissimi, cum oleo quantivis pretii, aliisque bellariis, & ferculis opiparis, comeduntur tempore jejunii, quod vocant; in refectionem scilicet: neque ifcud per liquidum, etiam vinum generosissimum, solvi putatur. Daniel certè non minus à pane desiderabili, & à vino, abstinuit; quam à carne: neque inter aquatilium carnes, & carnes volatilium atque terrestrium animalium, discrevisse putandus est; quasi illarum eius minus obstaret jejunio, quam harum. Vide Levit. xi, 8, 11. 1 Cor. xv, 39.
units.tr: 2. The same Daniel, when he was intent on prophetic visions, and in particular was seeking understanding of a certain vision concerning weighty matters that also bear on the Church of God, testifies about himself (x. 2, 3): "I was mourning for three weeks of days. I ate no desirable bread; neither flesh nor wine entered my mouth; nor was I anointed with ointment, until three weeks of days were complete." Because this humiliation lasted longer than a complete fast could naturally have carried through, it was spent with remarkable frugality and sobriety: abstinence from desirable bread, meat, wine and ointment. This is quite unlike what is usually done among the Papists, where the finest bread, the most delicate fish with oil of any price, and other dainties and lavish dishes are eaten at the time of the so-called fast, namely for refreshment; nor is it thought that the fast is broken by liquids, even the most noble wine. Daniel certainly abstained no less from desirable bread and wine than from meat; nor should he be thought to have distinguished between the flesh of aquatic creatures and the flesh of birds and land animals, as if the former hindered the fast less than the latter. See Lev. xi. 8, 11; 1 Cor. xv. 39.

units.la: 3. Elisæus, 2 Reg. iv, 38, 39. filios prophetarum ramis sylvestribus & amaris pavit; non jejunii aut religionis, sed penuriæ causâ.
units.tr: 3. Elisha (2 Kings iv. 38, 39) fed the sons of the prophets with wild boughs and bitter herbs, not for the sake of fasting or religion, but from want.

units.la: 4. Rechabitæ ab usu vini perpetuo abstinuerunt, imo nec vites plantârunt, neque tementem fecerunt, neque domos ædificârunt, Jerem. xxxv, 6, - 10. non religionis gratiâ; sed ut præcepto patris sui parerent, qui singularem frugalitatem ils mandavit. Sic ergo ab usu vini abstinuerunt; sed nihil de eorum abstinentia à carnibus, aut opinione jejunii in tali distinctione ciborum.
units.tr: 4. The Rechabites abstained from the use of wine perpetually; indeed they did not plant vines, nor sow seed, nor build houses (Jer. xxxv. 6–10). This was not for the sake of religion, but so that they might obey the command of their father, who had enjoined singular frugality on them. So they abstained from wine; but there is nothing about abstinence from meat, or the notion of fasting, in such a distinction of foods.

units.la: Obj. 2. Simile est exemplum Johannis Baptistæ; Matth. 3, 4. Et Paulus abstinentiam à quibusdam cibis docuit, Rom. 14, 21. 1 Cor. 8, 12, 13. itemque Synodus Hierosolymitana; Act. 15, 2, 20, 21, 28, 29. Resp. 1. Joh. Baptista locutis & melle agrestì victitavit; Matth. 3, 4. quod in extraordinario illo præcone pœnitentiæ, altero Eliâ & Messiæ prodromo, singularis quidem frugalitatis fuit; sed nihil inde confici potest pro lege Ecclesiastica cum carnium prohibente, pisces interim præstantissimos, aliaque bellaria delicata & pretiosa permittente, & quidem opinione jejunii.
units.tr: Objection 2. The example of John the Baptist is similar (Matt. 3:4). And Paul taught abstinence from certain foods (Rom. 14:21; 1 Cor. 8:12, 13), and likewise the Synod of Jerusalem (Acts 15:2, 20, 21, 28, 29). Answer 1. John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey (Matt. 3:4). In that extraordinary herald of repentance, a second Elijah and forerunner of the Messiah, this was indeed a sign of singular frugality. But nothing can be drawn from it for an ecclesiastical law forbidding meat, while it meanwhile permits the finest fish and other delicate and costly dainties, and indeed under the notion of fasting.

units.la: 2. Paulus, Rom. xiv, 21. ratione charitatis perindè abstinendum docet ab omnibus, quibus proximus esset offendendus; ac similiter 1 Cor. viii, 12, 13. quod prorsus ad jejunium non pertinet.
units.tr: 2. Paul (Rom. 14:21) teaches that, for the sake of charity, one must abstain from all things by which a neighbour would be offended; and similarly (1 Cor. 8:12, 13). This does not pertain to fasting at all.

units.la: 3. In Synodo Apostolorum & Seniorum Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae, decretum, ut ex Gentilismo conversi abstinerent etiam à suffocato & sanguine; quod eorum esus recens ex Judaismo conversos valde offenderet; Act.xv, 2, 20, 21, 28, 29. ac proinde istud decretum fuit temporarium, usquedum libertas Christiana satis esset promulgata & confirmata. Sed nec inde colligi potest quicquam pro distinctione ciborum, quae sub Papatu obtinet, etiam sine ulla ratione scandali, & in qua jejunium istic constitui solet.
units.tr: 3. In the Synod of the Apostles and elders of the Church of Jerusalem it was decreed that those converted from Gentilism should also abstain from what is strangled and from blood, because eating them would greatly offend those recently converted from Judaism (Acts 15:2, 20, 21, 28, 29). That decree was therefore temporary, until Christian liberty had been sufficiently published and confirmed. But nothing can be drawn from it in favour of the distinction of foods that prevails under the Papacy, even without any reason of scandal, and in which fasting is usually established.

units.la: XLVIII. Interim jejunium humiliationis signum est, & quoddam adminiculum. Joel. II, 12. Converti- mini ad me, toto corde vestro, & in jejunio, & fletu, & planctu.
units.tr: XLVIII. Meanwhile, fasting is a sign of humiliation and a certain aid. Joel 2:12: "Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning."

units.la: Sed pro cultu Divino, aut ejus parte per se, absurdè habetur à Pontificiis; cum ejus revera eadem sit ratio, quae fletus ac planctus. Id confirmatur his rationibus: 1. Est exercitatio corporalis; atque adeo per se adiaphora, seu mediae conditionis: diserte enim Apostolus, 1 Tim. iv, 8. Exercitatio corporalis ad pauca utilis est: quia videl. ad cultum spiritualem ordinari, atque ita per accidens prodesse poterit suo modo; cum ipsa pietas ad omnia fit utilis, ut quae promissionem habeat vitae praesentis ac futurae. Atque iterum de istiusmodi rebus, Col II, 23. Quae rationem quidem habent sapientiae, in eo quod corpori non parcant: nec tamen ullius sunt pretii: cum ad ea spectent, quibus farcitur caro: ad cibum scil. & ad potum. Nec non 1 Cor. viii, 8. Esca nos non commendat Deo: &c. Confer vi, 13. Escae ventri destinatae sunt, & venter escis: Deus autem & hunc & has adolebit.
units.tr: But the Papists absurdly regard fasting as worship of God, or as a part of it in itself, although its real reason is the same as that of weeping and mourning. This is confirmed by these arguments: (1) It is a bodily exercise, and so in itself a thing indifferent, or of intermediate status. For the Apostle says plainly, 1 Tim. 4:8: "Bodily exercise profiteth little," because, that is, it is ordained for spiritual worship, and so may benefit in some way by accident; whereas "godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come." And again, of such things, Col. 2:23: "Which things indeed have a show of wisdom, in will-worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh;" and 1 Cor. 8:8: "Meat commendeth us not to God," etc. Compare 1 Cor. 6:13: "Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them."

units.la: 2. Alia omnino est conditio status nostri spiritualis, ac proinde & cultus: Rom. xiv, 17, 18. Non enim est regnum Dei esca & potus; sed justitia, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum Sanctum. His autem subservire debent instrumenta nostra corporalia: xii, 1, 2. Adhortor igitur vos, ut sistatis corpora vestra hostiam vivam, sanctam, placentem centem Deo rationalem illum cultum vestrum. - Transformate vos per renovationem mentis vestræ, ad hoc ut probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei, bona illa, placens, ac perfecta. Quod ergo per se rationale non est, & sic voluntati Divinæ conformatum; ac sanctum, id per se cultus Divinus esse non potest. Hoc exigit natura Dei: Ioh. iv, 24. Deus est spiritus: & qui adorant eum, oportet ut spiritu ac veritate adorent. Quemadmodum etiam imago Dei proprie consistit in dotibus spiritualibus: Col. iii, 10, Eph. iv, 24.
units.tr: (2) The condition of our spiritual state is entirely different, and so too is worship. Rom. 14:17, 18: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." Our bodily instruments ought, however, to serve these ends. Rom. 12:1, 2: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God." What is not in itself rational, and so not conformed to the Divine will, but holy, therefore cannot in itself be Divine worship. The nature of God requires this: John 4:24: "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Just as the image of God properly consists in spiritual gifts: Col. 3:10; Eph. 4:24.

units.la: 3. Ipsi Hypocritæ frequenter jejunant: atque eorum jejunia serió perstringuntur: quod autem hypocritis commune est, & in iis reprehenditur, id per se non est cultus Divinus. Sic Jes. lviii, 4, 5. Ecce ad litem & contentionem jejunatis, & ut percutiatis pugno impie. Ne jeiunetis posthàc, sicut hodie; &c. Zach, 7. 5. Cum jejunastis & planxistis in quinto mense & septimo, idque jam septuaginta annis, nunquid jejunium jejunastis propter Me? Ipse hypocrita ille Pharisæus, Luc. 18, 12. jejuno bis hebdomade. Et Salvator, id genus homines spectans; Matth. vi, 16. Cum autem jejunatis, ne siote ut hypocritæ, tetrico vultu, &c.
units.tr: (3) Hypocrites themselves often fast, and their fasts are seriously rebuked. So Isa. 58:4, 5: "Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high... Is it such a fast that I have chosen?" Zech. 7:5: "When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?" That hypocritical Pharisee, Luke 18:12, fasted twice a week. And the Saviour, looking at men of this kind, Matt. 6:16: "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance," etc.

units.la: 4. Propterea etiam Salvator discipulos suos jejunia omittentes, cum litem iis moverent discipuli Johannis, defendit; & rebus lætis ista non convenire, docuit; Matth. 9, 15, 16, 17. Num possunt filii thalami lugere, quamdiu cum eis est sponsus? Aderunt autem dies, cum tolletur ab eis sponsus, & tunc jejunabunt. Nullus autem indit panniculum novum in vestimentum vetus, &c.
units.tr: (4) For this reason the Saviour also defended his disciples when they did not fast, and the disciples of John raised a dispute with them; and he taught that such fasting does not suit joyful occasions. Matt. 9:15, 16, 17: "Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast. No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment," etc.

units.la: Non igitur omni tempori, sed tempori luctus tantum, convenit jejunium: alias omitti recte potest. Unde manifestum est, non esse per se cultum Dei; sed effectum & signum luctus, qui etiam ipse per se cultus Dei non est.
units.tr: Fasting therefore suits not every time, but only a time of mourning; otherwise it may rightly be omitted. Hence it is plain that it is not in itself worship of God, but an effect and sign of mourning, which is itself not in itself worship of God either.

units.la: Obj. Joël. II, 15. Sanctificate jejunium. Ergo. Resp. Nego consequentiam: Similiter enim præcipitur vestimentum. fibus proximè sequentibus, congregatio populi egressùs sponsi de cubili suo & sponlæ de thalamo suo, ploratus sacerdotum, &c. quæ tamen per se cultum Dei non constituunt ; sed ejus adjuncta & adminicula sunt ; atque hoc nomine præcipitantur.
units.tr: Objection: Joel 2:15: "Sanctify a fast." Therefore... Answer: I deny the consequence. For in the same way the verses that immediately follow command the gathering of the people, the bridegroom to go out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet, the weeping of the priests, etc., which nevertheless do not constitute worship of God in themselves, but are its accessories and aids; and it is under this description that they are commanded.

units.la: XLIX. Verùm absurditatem istam superat alia eorundem Pontificiorum absurditas, quâ statuunt, jejunia, & alia quædam istiusmodi, esse opera pœnalia satisfactoria pro peccatis, in ordine ad justitiam Dei punitivam ; atque insuper meritoria apud Deum. Sed de hâc alibi.
units.tr: XLIX. But a further absurdity of the same Papists surpasses this absurdity, by which they maintain that fasts, and certain other such things, are penal and satisfactory works for sins, with regard to the punitive justice of God; and moreover meritorious before God. But of this elsewhere.

units.la: Nec libertati Christianæ, & rationi jejuniorum ab ipso Christo expositæ Matth. ix, 15, 16, 17. conveniunt jejunia ordinaria absoluta & perpetua ; ac potissimum si ea sint valdè frequentia. Male igitur in Papismo, & quidem Papistice observanda, urgentur jejunia feriæ sextæ, vel etiam quartæ ; nec non quatuor temporum, in primâ scil. hebdomada Quadragesimæ, in hebdomadâ Pentecostes, in tertiâ hebdomadâ Septembris, atque iterum in tertiâ hebdomadâ Decembris ; itemque jejunium Quadragesimale, prætensa etiam institutione Apostolicâ, sed falso, præter & contra SS. Literas, ac veram antiquitatem Ecclesiasticam.
units.tr: Ordinary fasts, absolute and perpetual, do not agree with Christian liberty, nor with the reason for fasting set out by Christ himself, Matt. 9:15, 16, 17, especially if they are very frequent. Therefore fasts on Friday, or even on Wednesday, are wrongly urged in Popery, and indeed observed in the Papist manner; likewise the fasts of the Ember days, namely in the first week of Lent, in the week of Pentecost, in the third week of September, and again in the third week of December; and likewise the Lenten fast, which is falsely claimed to have apostolic institution, but is against and beyond the Holy Scriptures and true ecclesiastical antiquity.

units.la: Objiciunt 1. Exempla Mosis, Eliæ, & ipsius Christi, pro jejunio suo Quadragesimali. Resp. Sed ista omnino dissimilia sunt, cum ille bis, hi semel tot dies jejunaverint, speciali de causâ, & quidem miraculose, absque ullo cibo : Pontificii vero suum Quadragesimale quotannis iterent, & ciborum discriminatione celebrent.
units.tr: They object, first, the examples of Moses, Elijah, and Christ himself, for their Lenten fast. Answer: But those cases are wholly dissimilar, since those men fasted for so many days, the first two times and the last once, for a special reason, and indeed miraculously, without any food; whereas the Papists repeat their Lent every year and celebrate it with a distinction of foods.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dies purim, de quibus Esth. ix, 17. & seqq. fuerunt istius conditionis. Ergo. Resp. Illi dies non fuerunt jejunii, sed festivitatis, in memoriam tantæ liberationis per supplicationem & jejunium Divinitus acceptæ : & quidem instituti sub V. T. à reginâ Esthera, & Mordechæo, ad illustrem quoque dignitatem evecto; ex auctoritate politica, juxta officium gratitudinis erga Deum, & commemorationis beneficiorum ejus: si non Spiritu prophetico; atque ita ab universo populo libenter recepti. Consequenter ex illis non possunt colligi jejunia ordinaria & perpetua, sub N. T. lege Ecclesiastica, aut à Papâ Romano, omnibus gentibus obtrudenda, vel obtrusa.
units.tr: Objection 2: The days of Purim, concerning which Esth. 9:17 ff., were of this kind. Therefore... Answer: Those days were not days of fasting, but of festivity, in memory of so great a deliverance, received from God through supplication and fasting; and indeed they were instituted under the Old Testament by Queen Esther and Mordecai, who had been raised to a distinguished position, by civil authority, in accordance with the duty of gratitude towards God and the remembrance of his benefits, if not by prophetic Spirit; and so they were gladly received by the whole people. Consequently, from those days no ordinary and perpetual fasts can be inferred under the ecclesiastical law of the New Testament, nor fasts imposed, or already imposed, on all nations by the Roman Pope.

units.la: Obj. 3. Jejunia quædam à Judæis celebrata fuerunt sub captivitate Babylonicâ. Ergò. Resp. sed illi dies deinde, sublata ista causâ, fuerunt conversi in festivos, edicente ipso Deo, Zach. viii: 19. Unde nullo pacto colligi possunt stata jejunia in perpetuum observanda, & quidem sub N. T.
units.tr: Objection 3. Certain fasts were observed by the Jews during the Babylonian captivity. Therefore... Answer: But those days afterwards, when that cause was removed, were turned into festive days, God himself commanding it, Zech. 8:19. Hence by no means can it be inferred that fixed fasts are to be observed in perpetuity, and indeed under the New Testament.

units.la: Obj. 4. Christus prædixit, & docuit habenda ejusmodi jejunia; Matth. ix. 15. Ergo. Resp. Istic prædicitur quidem fore, ut Christiani urgente necessitate jejunent: sed nihil inde sequitur pro ordinariis & perpetuis jejuniis, & quidem Papistice servandis.
units.tr: Objection 4. Christ foretold and taught that such fasts should be held: Matt. 9:15. Therefore... Answer: There it is indeed foretold that Christians will fast under pressing necessity; but nothing follows from this in favour of ordinary and perpetual fasts, and indeed fasts to be kept in the Papist manner.

units.la: I. Vitiatur etiam precatio per inanem eorundem verborum repetitionem; quasi ea, propter iterationem istiusmodi ac prolixitatem, futura esset efficacior, Deoque grata, & exaudienda. Per istam βαττολογίαν ἢ πολυλογίαν non posse gratiam impetrari, 1. satis declaravit Deus sub V. T. Jef. 1, 15.
units.tr: I. Prayer is also spoiled by the empty repetition of the same words, as if it would be more effective, pleasing to God, and worthy of being heard, because of such repetition and length. That God has sufficiently declared under the Old Testament, Isa. 1:15, that grace cannot be obtained through this battology or polylogy [βαττολογίαν ἢ πολυλογίαν].

units.la: 2. Et Christus in N. T. Matth. vi, 7.
units.tr: 2. And Christ in the New Testament, Matt. 6:7.

units.la: 3. Tales homines faciunt se similes Gentilibus, verâ Dei cognitione ac fide destitutis: Matth. vi, 7, 8.
units.tr: 3. Such men make themselves like the Gentiles, who are destitute of the true knowledge and faith of God: Matt. 6:7, 8.

units.la: 4. Accedit ratio: frustra scil. adhibentur frequentes illæ repetitiones, & diuturni clamores sine mente; quia Deus satis novit quibus egeamus, & paratus est necessaria dare omnibus serio petentibus secundum voluntatem ipsius; Matth. vi, 8. Joh. xvi: 26, 27. 1 Joh. v, 14, 15.
units.tr: 4. There is also this reason: those frequent repetitions and long clamours without understanding are used in vain, because God knows well what we need, and is ready to give what is necessary to all who seriously ask according to his will: Matt. 6:8; John 16:26, 27; 1 John 5:14, 15.

units.la: Rejicienda igitur Pontificiorum Rosaria, aut Sphaerulæ precatoriæ, per quas ad numerum recitantur orationes, atque inde major earum præsumitur efficacia. cia. Itemque boatū Monachorum in templis; cum quibus conferendi clamores Baalitarum, 1 Reg. xviii, 26, 27, 28.
units.tr: Therefore the Papists' rosaries, or prayer-beads, by which prayers are recited by count, and from which greater efficacy is presumed, must be rejected. So too must the bellowing of the monks in the churches, which may be compared with the shouting of the Baalites, 1 Kings 18:26, 27, 28.

units.la: LI. Sequitur Votum, Religiosa pollicitatio rei alicujus Deo gratæ, in ejus gloriam præstandæ; vel etiam rei ingratæ, similiter omittendæ.
units.tr: LI. Next comes the vow: a religious promise to perform something pleasing to God for his glory, or similarly to omit something displeasing to him.

units.la: Hunc actum religionis soli Deo deferendum, satis evidenter docent SS. Literæ: Pf. lxxvi, 12. Vovete, & reddite Jehovæ Deo vestro. Vide etiam Num. xxx, 2, 3, Deut. xxiii; 21, 23. Psal. l, 14, cxvi, 14. Isef. xix; 21.
units.tr: That this act of religion is owed to God alone the Holy Scriptures teach quite clearly: Psalm 76:12, "Make vows and pay them to Jehovah your God." See also Numbers 30:2, 3; Deuteronomy 23:21, 23; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 116:14; Isaiah 19:21.

units.la: 2. Accedunt exempla Sanctorum; utpotè Jacobi, Gen. xxviii, 20, 21, 22.
units.tr: 2. Examples of the saints also agree, such as that of Jacob, Genesis 28:20, 21, 22.

units.la: 3. Quia in voto inest religiosa invocatio, quæ soli Deo debetur.
units.tr: 3. Because a vow contains religious invocation, which is owed to God alone.

units.la: 4. Quia vovendum est ei soli, à quo omnia bona nos oportet expectare, cui pro beneficiis acceptis debemus gratias agere, cui intimè animum nostrum cognoscit, de-ue omnibus nostris judicare potest; ut cuique ad rem ipsam attendenti satis manifestum est; hæc autem omnia soli Deo conveniunt.
units.tr: 4. Because one must vow to him alone, from whom we ought to expect all good things, to whom we owe thanks for benefits received, who knows our heart intimately and can judge all our works. This is plain enough to anyone who attends to the matter itself, and all these things belong to God alone.

units.la: LII. Vota fieri debent de faciendis iis, quæ Deo placent; aut omittendis, quæ displicent. Deo autem placere intelliguntur, tum quæ ipse præcepit in specie; tum etiam talis usus rerum alias indifferentium, qualis ratione circumstantium ad gloriam Dei, nostramque & aliorum ædificationem valentem conducit. Vide Gen. xxviii, 2, 22. Quia sub V. T. deberet esse votum Naziræatus; ipse Deus e presliis Num. vi, 1, -21. De aliis itern votis, quid, & quomodo sibi placeret, exposuit Levit. xxvii, 2, -14. atque alibi: imo & speciālia nonnulla, quæ displicerent, indicavit, Levit. xxii, 23 Deut. xxiii, 18. Quemadmodum vero in universo cultu Divino improbanda erit ἐθελοθρησκεία, sic etiam in Votis. Vide Deut. xii, 8. Isef. xxix, 13. Matth. xv, 9. Col. 2, 23.
units.tr: LII. Vows ought to be made about doing what pleases God, or omitting what displeases him. God is understood to be pleased both by what he has commanded in particular, and also by such use of things otherwise indifferent as, in view of the circumstances, tends to the glory of God and to our and others' edification. See Genesis 28:2, 22. Under the Old Testament there was to be a vow of the Nazirite, which God himself laid down in detail, Numbers 6:1–21. Concerning other vows, he set out what and how they should please him, Leviticus 27:2–14, and elsewhere; indeed he also indicated some particular things that displease him, Leviticus 22:23; Deuteronomy 23:18. But just as will-worship is to be condemned in the whole worship of God, so it is also to be condemned in vows. See Deuteronomy 12:8; Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:9; Colossians 2:23.

units.la: Hujusmodi sunt Vota Papistica de suscipiendâ peregrinâgrinatione religionis ergò, de processione sacrâ, &c. & speciatim Monastica, & perpetuo cœlibatû, spontanea paupertate, & cœcâ obedientiâ ergâ superiores suos ac regulas Monasticas. Sed 1. S. Scriptura vitam illam Monasticam nec mandat, nec docet.
units.tr: Of this kind are the Papistic vows of undertaking pilgrimage for the sake of religion, of sacred processions, and so on; and especially the monastic vows of perpetual celibacy, voluntary poverty, and blind obedience towards their superiors and the monastic rules. But, first, Holy Scripture neither commands nor teaches that monastic life.

units.la: 2. Opinionem de Satisfactionibus ac Meritis propriis, & Perfectione etiam supererogatoriâ, qui Monachorum Papalium scopus est, Euangelium refellit validissime; dum in solo Christo justitiam quærendam, ac fide apprehendendam, proponit.
units.tr: 2. The opinion about satisfactions and one's own merits, and even about supererogatory perfection, which is the aim of the Papal monks, the Gospel refutes most powerfully, since it sets forth that righteousness is to be sought in Christ alone and apprehended by faith.

units.la: 3. Neque Consilia Divina à Præceptis differunt realiter. Vide sup. cap. 8. th. 32.
units.tr: 3. Nor do the divine counsels really differ from the precepts. See above, chapter 8, thesis 32.

units.la: 4. In specie: a. Paupertatem nusquam ut bonum morale, pluribus vero locis malum triste, proponit S. Pagina: Prov. VI, 11. XXX. 8, 9. Act. XX, 35. 2 Cor. VIII, 9. Hoc autem nemo sibi ultrò debet arcessere, sed Divinitus immissum patienter ac sapienter ferre:
units.tr: 4. In particular: a. Holy Scripture nowhere presents poverty as a moral good, but in many places as a sad evil. Proverbs 6:11; 30:8, 9; Acts 20:35; 2 Corinthians 8:9. Yet no one ought to seek it for himself of his own accord, but to bear patiently and wisely what is sent by God,

units.la: 2 Cor. XI, 26, 27. Phil. IV. 11, 12. Confer Math. XIX, 20, &c.
units.tr: 2 Corinthians 11:26, 27; Philippians 4:11, 12. Compare Matthew 19:20, etc.

units.la: β. Cœlibatum non nisi donum continentiæ habentibus, ac pro ratione temporum, & respectû necessitatis, commendat: 1 Cor. VII, 7, 9, 26, 28, 32, 37. Luc. 23, 28, 29. Hebr. 13, 4. 1 Tim. 4, 1, 2, 3, III, 2, 4, 5.
units.tr: β. It commends celibacy only to those who have the gift of continence, and according to the circumstances of the times and the need of the case: 1 Corinthians 7:7, 9, 26, 28, 32, 37; Luke 23:28, 29; Hebrews 13:4; 1 Timothy 4:1, 2, 3; 3:2, 4, 5.

units.la: γ. Et probationem eorum, quæ per homines præcipiuntur, ac de iis judicium decretionis, requirit, Deoque semper magis obediendum, quàm hominibus, inculcat: 1 Thess. V, 21. 1 Joh. IV, 1. 1 Cor. X, 15. Act. IV, 19, V. 29.
units.tr: γ. It requires the testing of what is commanded by men, and a judgment of discernment about it, and it constantly inculcates that God is to be obeyed rather than men: 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1; 1 Corinthians 10:15; Acts 4:19; 5:29.

units.la: LIII. Socinian exististimant, Christum in N. T. auxisse decem illa præcepta, ac perfectiora reddidisse: speciatim autem primo adjecisse, 1. præceptum generale, de precibus Deo faciendis: 2. formulam orationis Dominicæ; & 3. præceptum de adorando etiam Christo.
units.tr: LIII. The Socinians think that Christ in the New Testament increased the ten commandments and made them more perfect. Specifically, they hold that he added, first, a general precept concerning making prayers to God; second, the form of the Lord's Prayer; and third, the precept of adoring Christ also.

units.la: Verum primo sub V. T. fuit eadem obligatio ad preces Deo faciendas super omni necessitate, juxta volunvoluntatem ipsius tunc quoque revelatam : sic enim
units.tr: But first, under the Old Testament there was the same obligation to make prayers to God in every need, according to the will of God which was then also revealed. For thus:

units.la: 1. Ipse Deus, Psal. L, 15. Invocante in die angustiæ: eruam te; & honorificabis me. XCI, 15. Invocabit me; & exaudiam eum, &c. Adde, XCV, 6. Jes. LV, 6. Imò etiam, Deut. VI, 13. Jehovam Deum tuum timebis, & ipsum coles; quam sententiam Servator expressit hoc modo, Matth. IV, 10. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illum solum coles.
units.tr: 1. God himself says, Psalm 50:15, "Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver you, and you shall honour me." Psalm 91:15, "He shall call upon me, and I will answer him," etc. Add Psalm 95:6; Isaiah 55:6. Indeed Deuteronomy 6:13, "You shall fear Jehovah your God, and serve him," which the Saviour expressed in this way, Matthew 4:10: "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone."

units.la: 2. Universa doctrina de sacrificiis Deo offerendis, hanc veritatem innuit etiàm satis aperte: quis enim dubitat, preces sacrificiis adjungi debuisse, atque istas suffitû sacro propterea fuisse adumbratas? Vide Iob XLII, 8, 9, 10. Psal. CXLI, 2. Confer Luc. I, 10. Act. III, 1.
units.tr: 2. The whole doctrine of offering sacrifices to God also hints at this truth quite plainly. For who doubts that prayers ought to have been joined to the sacrifices, and that for this reason they were foreshadowed by the sacred incense? See Job 42:8, 9, 10; Psalm 141:2. Compare Luke 1:10; Acts 3:1.

units.la: 3. Accedit praxis fidelium; utpotè Danielis, etiam contra gravissimam Regis prohibitionem; VI, 11, 12. Adeo ut istius exercitii omissio habita fuerit pro notâ summæ impietatis; Psal. XIV, 4.
units.tr: 3. Add the practice of the faithful, such as Daniel's, even against the most grave prohibition of the king, Daniel 6:11, 12. So much so that the omission of this exercise was regarded as a mark of the greatest impiety, Psalm 14:4.

units.la: 4. Imo etiam Gentiles hoc officium agnoverunt utcunque, & alii idololatræ, ac superstitiosi; qui preces quoque usurpârunt, secundùm conscientiam voluntatis Divinæ: quanto autem magis hoc de populo Dei, & fœderatis fidelibus, agnoscendum est?
units.tr: 4. Indeed even the Gentiles acknowledged this duty in some measure, and other idolaters and superstitious people, who also used prayers, according to their awareness of the divine will. How much more must this be acknowledged of the people of God and the faithful in covenant!

units.la: LIV. Secundo, Formula orationis Dominicæ non constituit novum aliquod præceptum; sed est medium à Christo propositum, quo nos in praxi precum (quam à nobis postulat primum Decalogi præceptum) juvaremur ac dirigeremur.
units.tr: LIV. Second, the form of the Lord's Prayer does not establish any new precept. It is rather a means proposed by Christ, by which we might be helped and directed in the practice of prayer, which the first commandment of the Decalogue requires of us.

units.la: 2. Singulæ etiam particulæ istius orationis satis aperte fuerunt comprehensæ ac propositæ scriptis V. T. Exordium quidem in locis, Ies. LXIII, 16. Tu enim Pater noster es, &c. Mal. I. 6. Quod si Pater ego sum, ubi est honor meus? Ies. LXVI, 1. Sic dixit Iehovah, Cœlum est solium meum, &c.
units.tr: 2. Each single part of that prayer was also quite plainly contained and set forth in the writings of the Old Testament. The opening, indeed, in such passages as Isaiah 63:16, "For you are our Father, etc."; Malachi 1:6, "If I am a Father, where is my honour?"; Isaiah 66:1, "Thus says Jehovah: Heaven is my throne, etc."

units.la: Petitio prima similiter, Psal. VIII, 2. Iehovah Domine noster, quam grande est nomen tuum in universa terrâ: qui posuisti gloriam tuam super cœlos! Adde, CXV, 1.
units.tr: The first petition likewise: Psalm 8:2, "Jehovah, our Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth, who have set your glory above the heavens!" Add Psalm 115:1.

units.la: Secunda ; Psal. II, 6. Ego constitui Regem meum super Tʒionem montem sanctum meum. Adde, lxxxiʒ 1. 7. 11, 20. lxxiv, 2.
units.tr: The second: Psalm 2:6, "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." Add Psalm 83:1, 7, 11, 20; Psalm 74:2.

units.la: Tertia ; Psal. cxliii, 10. Doce me facere voluntatem Tuam ; quia Tu es Deus meus : Spiritus Tuus bonus deducat me in terrâ rectâ. xxv, 4, 5.
units.tr: The third: Psalm 143:10, "Teach me to do your will, for you are my God; let your good Spirit lead me into the land of uprightness." Psalm 25:4, 5.

units.la: Quarta ; Prov. xxx, 8. Aleme cibo qui convenit mihi, Gen. xxviii, 20, 21.
units.tr: The fourth: Proverbs 30:8, "Feed me with the food that is convenient for me." Genesis 28:20, 21.

units.la: Quinta ; Psal. xxv, 11. Propter nomen tuum Iehovah, parce iniquitati meæ : quoniam multa est. 11, 3, 4.
units.tr: The fifth: Psalm 25:11, "For your name's sake, Jehovah, pardon my iniquity, for it is great." Psalm 11:3, 4.

units.la: Sexta item; Ps. xix, 14. Etiàm à superbis prohibe servum Tuum, ne dominentur mihi: tunc perfectus ero, & mundus ero à prævaricatione magna. cxix, 36, 37.
units.tr: The sixth likewise: Psalm 19:13, "Keep your servant also from presumptuous sins, that they not have dominion over me; then shall I be perfect, and I shall be clear of great transgression." Psalm 119:36, 37.

units.la: Ac tandem Conclusio ; 1 Chron. xxix, 11. Tibi, ô Iehovah, est magnificentia, & potentia, & gloria, & decor : cuncta enim, quæ in cælo sunt & in terrâ ; tua sunt. Tuum est, ô Jehovah regnum, & exaltatio super omnes qui sunt in caput. Psal. xli, 14. Benedictus Jehovah Deus Israelis sæculo, & usque in sæculum. Amen & Amen.
units.tr: And finally the conclusion: 1 Chronicles 29:11, "Yours, O Jehovah, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the majesty; for all that is in heaven and in earth is yours. Yours, O Jehovah, is the kingdom, and you are exalted above all as head." Psalm 41:14, "Blessed be Jehovah, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen."

units.la: LV. Neque tertio illud de adorando Christo censeri debet per ipsum primo Decalogi præcepto adjectum sub N.T. cum 1. ipse sit idem æternus & verus Deus cum Patre ac Spiritu Sancto, eàdemque religione semper colendus.
units.tr: LV. Nor should the third point, concerning the adoration of Christ, be considered to have been added by Christ himself under the New Testament to the first commandment of the Decalogue. For, first, he is the same eternal and true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and is always to be worshipped with the same worship.

units.la: 2. Propterea etiam scriptum est, Psal. 2, 12. Osculamini Filium, ne forte irascatur. - Beati omnes qui sperant in eo. Et xcvii, 7. Incurvate vos Ei, omnes Dii, cum Heb. 1, 6. Partim autem, cum inducit Primogenitum in orbem terrarum, dicit; Et adorent Eum omnes Angeli Dei. Sic adorationem Filii ex illo V.T. loco allegavit Apostolus. Adde Gen. xlvi ii, 16.
units.tr: 2. For this reason it is also written, Ps. 2:12: "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry. Blessed are all who put their trust in him." And Ps. 97:7: "Bow down before him, all you gods." Likewise Heb. 1:6, where, when he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: "And let all the angels of God worship him." Thus the Apostle cited the worship of the Son from that Old Testament passage. Add Gen. 48:16.

units.la: 3. In N.T. perstringitur idololatria Gentilium tali argumento. Rom. 1, 25. quod venerati sint & coluerint res conditas, præterito Creatore, qui est benedictus in sæcula. Ac similiter, Gal. iv, 8. Imo tum quidem ignorantes Deum, serviebatis iis, qui natura non sunt Dii. At si tunc obtinuisset sententia Socinistica, quam proclive fuisset Gentilibus regerere; Quid in eo absurdi; cum etiam vos Christiani veneremini & colatis Christum, ex novo quodam ipsius præcepto, qui tamen res condita est, non Deus natura, nec olim adoratus, aut adorari jussus?
units.tr: 3. In the New Testament the idolatry of the Gentiles is condemned by this argument: Rom. 1:25, that they venerated and worshipped created things, passing over the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Similarly Gal. 4:8: "Indeed at that time, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods." But if the Socinian opinion had prevailed then, how easy it would have been for the Gentiles to retort: what is absurd about it, since you Christians also venerate and worship Christ by some new command of his own, although he is a created thing, not God by nature, and was never worshipped before or commanded to be worshipped?

units.la: LVI. Imagines in secundo Decalogi præcepto spectantur ut media, quibus homines sibi Deum externè conan- tur repræsentare, & mentem in ipsum dirigere.
units.tr: LVI. Images are regarded under the second precept of the Decalogue as means by which people try to represent God to themselves outwardly, and to direct the mind towards him.

units.la: Quæritur autem, An liceat in talem usum conficere imagines ipsius Dei; & porrò confectas ejusmodi imagines sic retinere & usurpare? Nos negativam tenemus adversus Pontificios, quorum contraria est sententia ac praxis; dum variis modis Deum, & S. Trinitatem pingunt, & fingunt; potissimùm verò Deum Patrem in formâ hominis senis, triplici coronâ, ac deinceps reliquo Papali amictû vestiti; Filium in forma viri juvenis, aut agni vexilliferi; Spiritum Sanctum verò in formâ columbæ.
units.tr: The question is whether it is lawful to make images of God himself for such a use, and further, having been made, to keep and employ such images in this way. We hold the negative against the Papists, whose opinion and practice are the contrary; for they paint and fashion God and the Holy Trinity in various ways, above all depicting God the Father in the form of an old man with a triple crown and then clothed in the rest of the papal vestments; the Son in the form of a young man, or of a lamb bearing a banner; and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.

units.la: Opponimus hæc Argumenta; 1. Ista imaginum & simulachrorum ipsius Dei ac personarum Divinarum formatio prorsùs adversatur naturæ Divinæ spirituali, simplicissimæ, & infinitæ; in quâ non est visibilitas, nec lineamenta, eorumve ductus ac terminatio, aut extensio ulla, nec ulli limites; adeò ut prorsùs sit ineffigiabilis. Consequenter per istiusmodi imagines non verè repræsentatur verus Deus; sed falsum & fallax Deitatis signum absurdè exhibetur. Hinc Jerem. x, 14, 15. Mendacium est conflatile ejus; Vanitas sunt, &c. Hab. 2, 18. Conflatile, & quod docet mendacium
units.tr: We set against these practices the following arguments: (1) The formation of images and likenesses of God himself and of the divine persons is utterly opposed to the divine nature, which is spiritual, most simple and infinite; in it there is no visibility, no outline, no contour or boundary, no extension at all, and no limits; so that it is wholly incapable of being portrayed. Consequently such images do not truly represent the true God; rather, they absurdly exhibit a false and deceptive sign of the Deity. Hence Jer. 10:14, 15: "Its molten image is a lie; there is no breath in them," etc. Hab. 2:18: "A molten image, and a teacher of lies."

units.la: 2. Reprehenditur istiusmodi simulachrorum effectio, tanquam absurda, & in Deum injuria: Jes. xl, 18. Cui igitur assimilabitis Deum? Et quam similitudinem disponetis ei? Et de ipsis Gentilibus; Rom. I, 22, 23, 25. Cum se dicerent sapientes, stulti facti sunt. Mutarunt enim gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in simulachrum imaginis corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum & quadrupedum &c.
units.tr: (2) The making of such likenesses is condemned as absurd and an injury to God: Isa. 40:18: "To whom then will you liken God? Or what likeness will you set up for him?" And concerning the Gentiles themselves, Rom. 1:22, 23, 25: "Claiming to be wise, they became fools. For they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the form of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts," etc.

units.la: 3. Prohibetur severissimè, ipsis verbis secundi præcepti, Exod. xx,4,5. Deut. v,8,9. Non facies tibi sculptile, neque ullam similitudinem eorum quæ sunt in cœlo sursum, &c. Itemque Deut. iv,15,16. Cavete ergo diligenter animabus vestris: Ne forte corrumpatis vias vestras, & facietis vobis sculptile, aut imaginem ullius simulachri, &c. 23. 24. Cavete vobis, ne forte oblivisceamini pacti Jehovæ Dei vestri, & faciatis vobis sculptile, aut imaginem cujuscunque rei: Nam Jehovah Deus tuus ignis consumens est, Deus zelotes.
units.tr: (3) It is most strictly forbidden, in the very words of the second precept: Exod. 20:4, 5; Deut. 5:8, 9: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of what is in heaven above," etc. Likewise Deut. 4:15, 16: "Take good heed therefore to your souls, lest you act corruptly and make for yourselves a carved image or the likeness of any figure," etc. 23, 24: "Take heed to yourselves, lest you forget the covenant of Jehovah your God, and make for yourselves a carved image or the likeness of anything; for Jehovah your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God."

units.la: LVII. Obj. 1.
units.tr: LVII. Objection 1.

units.la: Homo à Deo conditus est ad ipsius imaginem: ergo recte conficitur imago Dei ad similitudinem hominis. Resp. Nego consequentiam: nam 1. imago ista proprie constitit in dotibus ac perfectionibus spiritualibus; quæ imagine corporeâ exprimi non possunt. 2. Retorqueo argumentum: cum enim tot homines exstant in mundo, ac tot hominum imagines, jam frustra impenduntur tanti labores & sumptus conficiendis peculiaribus imaginibus Dei.
units.tr: Man was created by God in his image; therefore it is right to make an image of God in the likeness of man. Answer. I deny the consequence. For (1) that image properly consists in spiritual gifts and perfections, which cannot be expressed by a bodily image. (2) I turn the argument back: since there are so many men in the world, and so many images of men, it is already in vain that such great labour and expense are spent on making special images of God.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus aliquoties visibili aliquo signo se conspiciendum præbuit: ergo. Resp. Deus quidem interdum aliquo symbolo præsentiam suam extraordinariam, respectu extraordinariæ alicujus operationis ac revelationis, demonstravit: utpote in rubo ardente, specie columbæ, &c. non vero essentiam suam tali imagine repræsentavit, aut repræsentandam docuit: sed contrarium ipse docuit, Deut. iv,15,16 & alibi.
units.tr: Objection 2. God has on several occasions allowed himself to be seen under some visible sign; therefore, etc. Answer. God indeed at times showed his extraordinary presence by some symbol, in connection with some extraordinary operation or revelation, as in the burning bush, in the form of a dove, and so on. But he did not represent his essence by such an image, nor did he teach that it should be so represented; on the contrary, he himself taught the opposite, Deut. 4:15, 16, and elsewhere.

units.la: Obj.3. Virtutes & vitia, aliaque istiusmodi, quin & Angeli, imagine exhiberi possunt: ergo. Resp. Imo eorum operationes solum signo hieroglyphico utcunque repræsentantur; verum ipsæ essentiæ sic non exprimuntur. Quicquid autem in Deo est, per ipsius simplicitatem est ipse Deus: atque id, quo Deus est, & à creaturis distinctus, tale est, ut nullo simulachro possit exprimi.
units.tr: Objection 3. Virtues and vices, and other things of this kind, and even angels, can be presented by an image; therefore, etc. Answer. Indeed their operations are represented in some way only by a hieroglyphic sign; but their essences are not so expressed. Whatever is in God is, through his simplicity, God himself; and that by which God is God, and distinct from creatures, is of such a kind that it cannot be expressed by any likeness.

units.la: Obj.4. In meditationibus de Deo, & orationibus ad ipsum, Deum nobis repræsentamus imagine mentali: ergo. Resp. Non est necessum, imo nec licitum, Deum concipi ut corporeum, vel aliter finitum, atq; ita simulachrum aliquod Dei in mente nostrâ confici: is enim non foret verus conceptus veri Dei; sed conceptus alicujus creaturæ, loco veri Dei; atque adeò conceptus idololatricus. Neque tamen omnino nihil concipimus, qui foret conceptus atheisticus. Sed formamus de Deo conceptus plures inadæquatos; quemadmodum apprehensivè, non comprehensivè, ipsum cognoscimus. Sic ergò concipimus veram substantiam spiritualem, suâ perfectione omnes creaturas prorsus & infinitè transcendentem.
units.tr: Objection 4. In meditations on God, and in prayers to him, we represent God to ourselves by a mental image; therefore, etc. Answer. It is neither necessary nor even lawful to conceive God as corporeal or otherwise finite, and so to form some likeness of God in our mind; for that would not be a true conception of the true God, but the conception of some creature in place of the true God, and therefore an idolatrous conception. Yet we do not conceive of him in no way at all, which would be an atheistic conception. Rather, we form of God several inadequate conceptions, just as we know him apprehensively, not comprehensively. Thus we conceive of him as a true spiritual substance, which by its perfection transcends all creatures utterly and infinitely.

units.la: LVIII. Sed neque confectæ ejusmodi imagines sic usurpari debent, nec asservari in talem usum: ita enim continuatur atque augetur peccatum in prima ea- rum confectione inchoatum.
units.tr: LVIII. But images once made must not be used in this way, nor kept for such a purpose. For in this way the sin that began with their first making is continued and increased.

units.la: 2. Ista usurpatione peccatur formaliter adversus ἰμφατικώταλα hujus Præcepti verba; Non incurvabis te eis, neque coles ea; Exod.xx,5.
units.tr: 2. By this use the very words of this commandment are violated formally, the most emphatic [ἐμφατικώτατα] words: You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them; Exod. 20:5.

units.la: 3. In detestationem idololatriæ, Deus instrumenta ejus propria destrui mandavit aliquoties: inter alia Deut. vii,25,26.
units.tr: 3. To express detestation of idolatry, God commanded that its instruments be destroyed on several occasions, among them Deut. 7:25, 26.

units.la: Atque ita 4. cum laude referetur de Rege Hizkijahu, 2 Reg. xviii,4. Ipse sustulit excelsa, & contrivit statuas, & succidit lucum: confregitque serpentem æreum, quem fecerat Moses; quia usque ad dies illos filii Israëlis suffiebant ei: & vocavit eum Nehustan.
units.tr: And so, 4. with praise, King Hezekiah is recorded as having done so, 2 Kings 18:4: He himself removed the high places, broke the statues, and cut down the grove; he also broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the children of Israel burned incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan.

units.la: LIX.
