T. etiam per ipsius nomen jurare liceat; cum non ostendant id ipsum in N. T. sic formaliter expressum.
units.tr: 4. We add an argument ad hominem: since our adversaries often demand that things be expressly stated by us, they can less rightly, and in keeping with their own method, say that this third precept was increased by Christ, so that under the New Testament it is lawful to swear even by his name; since they do not show that this very thing is so formally expressed in the New Testament.

units.la: LXVIII. Sed Pontificii existimant, licitè etiam jurari posse per Sanctos, aliasque creaturas: prorsus idololatricè: cum & hanc cultus religiosi speciem sibi soli reservatam voluerit verus Deus; Deut. vi, 13, 14. Jehovam Deum tuum timebis, & ipsum colės, ac per nomen ejus jurabis. Similiter x, 20. Quæ Christus allegat hoc modo, Matth. iv, 10. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illum solum coles. Ipsi ergo soli proprius est ille cultus, cujus species est juramentum. Vide iterum Ies. xlv, 23. Propterea tam ægre fert Deus, si per alios juretur: Jerem. v, 7. Am. viii, 14. Zephan. i, 5.
units.tr: LXVIII. But the Papists think it is lawful to swear also by the saints and other creatures, which is wholly idolatrous, since the true God has wished this species of religious worship to be reserved to himself alone. Deut. vi, 13, 14. Thou shalt fear Jehovah thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name. Similarly x, 20, which Christ cites in this way, Matt. iv, 10: Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve. That worship, of which swearing is a species, is therefore proper to him alone. See again Isa. xlv, 23. Hence God takes it so ill when one is sworn by others: Jer. v, 7. Amos viii, 14. Zeph. i, 5.

units.la: 2. Hoc indicant ipsæ formulæ, Vivit Jehovah; Invoco Deum testem in animam meam, &c. Jerem. iv, 2.
units.tr: 2. The very formulas indicate this: As Jehovah lives; I call God to witness upon my soul, etc. Jer. iv, 2.

units.la: 3. Solus Deus est omnisciius, ac proinde solus idoneus qui invocetur super animam & conscientiam nostram: 1 Reg. viii, 39. Tu enim nosti solus cor omnium filiorum hominum. Jerem. xvii, 9, 10. Fraudulentum est cor prae omnibus rebus, & perversum, quis cognoscet illud? Ego Iehovah scrutans cor, probans renes, &c.
units.tr: 3. God alone is omniscient, and therefore alone fit to be invoked over our soul and conscience: 1 Kings viii, 39. For thou alone knowest the heart of all the sons of men. Jer. xvii, 9, 10. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know it? I, Jehovah, search the heart and try the reins, etc.

units.la: 4. Soli etiam Deo convenit suprema potestas judiciaria, ut posset poenas spirituales & aeternas infligere: consequenter in juramentis ad ipsum solum est provocandum. Deut. xxxii, 35. Mea est ultio, & retributio. Matth. x, 28. Metuite potius eum, qui potest & animam & corpus perdere in gehennâ.
units.tr: 4. Supreme judicial power also belongs to God alone, so that he alone can inflict spiritual and eternal punishments; consequently in oaths one must appeal to him alone. Deut. xxxii, 35. Vengeance is mine, and recompense. Matt. x, 28. Fear rather him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

units.la: Obj. 1. Per creaturas recte juratum est, Cant. II, 7. III. 5. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalemi, per capreas, vel cervas agri: Alibi, per vitam Pharaonis, per animam alicujus hominis, &c. Ergo. Resp. 1. Verba illa in Cantico possunt etiam hoc modo transferri: Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalemi, quae estis apud capreas, vel cervas agri. Vel possunt sic accipi; Filiae Jerusalemi, per Deum vos adjuro, ut estis affectae erga capreas, vel cervas agri, ita hujus amoris habete rationem. 2. Alicubi potest intelligi comparatio aliqua, vel illustratio rei per aliquod simile: ut si quis diceret; quam vere nunc dies est, aut nos vivimus, &c, atque ita accipi possunt ista, Gen. xlii, 5 1. Vivit Parho. 1 Sam. 1, 26. Vivit anima tua, Domine mi. 3. In dictis & factis Josephi, Hannae, & similium, agnoscenda quidem est necessario authentia historiae; sed non item normae. 4, Possunt etiam inter jurandum assignari quaedam, in quibus puniri velimus, si pejeremus, aut nobis bene fieri cupiamus, si vere juremus; atque ita recte commemorari potest anima nostra; ut 2 Cor. I, 23. Sed nequaquam licet jurare per animam, hoc est jurando animam invocare.
units.tr: Obj. 1. It has been rightly sworn by creatures: Cant. II, 7; III, 5. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes or the hinds of the field. Elsewhere, by the life of Pharaoh, by the soul of some man, etc. Therefore. Reply 1. Those words in the Song can also be rendered thus: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, who are among the roes or the hinds of the field. Or they may be taken thus: Daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by God, as you are affected towards the roes or hinds of the field, so keep regard for this love. 2. Somewhere some comparison or illustration of a thing by some likeness may be understood, as if someone said, how truly it is day now, or as we live, etc.; and in this way those passages can be understood: Gen. xlii, 15, As Pharaoh lives; 1 Sam. i, 26, As your soul lives, my lord. 3. In the sayings and deeds of Joseph, Hannah and the like, the authenticity of the history must indeed be acknowledged, but not its status as a rule. 4. In swearing, certain things may also be named, by which we wish to be punished if we forswear, or wish well to ourselves if we swear truly; and so our soul may rightly be mentioned, as in 2 Cor. I, 23. But it is by no means lawful to swear by the soul, that is, to invoke the soul in an oath.

units.la: Obj. 2. Qui jurat per cœlum, per terram, per Hierosolymam, &c. obligatur ad faciendum quod juravit: sic validum est illud juramentum; & consequenter licitum. Resp. Nego consequentiam: quamvis enim homo sic pejerare minimè debeat, & coram Deo reus constituatur, propter respectum istarum creaturarum, atque ipsius juramenti qualiscunque ad Deum: inde nullo modo sequitur, tales jurandi modos esse licitos, aut legitimos. Vide Matth. xxiii, 20, 21, 22.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Whoever swears by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, and so on, is bound to do what he has sworn; so such an oath is valid, and consequently lawful. Resp. I deny the consequence. Although a man ought by no means to forswear himself in this way, and stands guilty before God, on account of his regard for these creatures and for the oath itself, in whatever sense it is made to God, it by no means follows that such modes of swearing are lawful or legitimate. See Matt. 23:20, 21, 22.

units.la: LXIX. Quartum præceptum esse morale & perpetuum; non cerimoniale duntaxat, & per Christum sub N. T. abrogatum, ut volunt Sociniani, patet ex dictis th. 13. §. d. & th. 17. Sed in N. T. non esse Festa proprie dicta; sive dies anniversarios, ratione mysterii, ex religiosâ devotione, ob conscientiam propriam, necessario observandos, nedum in honorem Angelorum, vel hominum Sanctorum, probamus contra Pontificios, 1. quia ista observatio prorsus caret institutione Divinâ; quâ tamen omnis religio niti debet; Col. II, 23. & Matth. xv, 9. ex Jes. xxix, 13.
units.tr: LXIX. That the fourth commandment is moral and perpetual, and not merely ceremonial and abrogated by Christ under the New Testament, as the Socinians hold, is clear from what was said in thesis 13, section d, and thesis 17. But that there are no feasts properly so called in the New Testament, that is, annual days to be necessarily observed for the sake of a mystery, out of religious devotion and for one's own conscience, still less in honour of angels or holy men, we prove against the Papists: (1) because this observance altogether lacks divine institution, on which all religion ought to rest (Col. 2:23; Matt. 15:9, from Isa. 29:13).

units.la: 2. Caret exemplo Apostolorum, Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ, & antiquitatis primævæ, ut patet ex SS. Literis, ac porro ex historiis, aliisque scriptis Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: (2) It lacks the example of the Apostles, of the apostolic Church, and of the earliest antiquity, as is clear from the Holy Scriptures and further from histories and other ecclesiastical writings.

units.la: 3. Repugnat Verbo Dei; ac nominatim locis, Rom. xiv, 5, 6. Gal. iv, 10, 11. Col. 2, 16. 17. Nec citra Verbum Dei oportet nos quicquam excipere, nisi judicari velimus decipere.
units.tr: (3) It conflicts with the Word of God, and especially with the passages Rom. 14:5, 6; Gal. 4:10, 11; Col. 2:16, 17. Nor, apart from the Word of God, ought we to make any exception, unless we wish to be judged deceivers.

units.la: 4. Magna est ista symbolizatio cum superstitionibus Gentilium, & cum typicis observationibns Israelitarum: quæ per N. T. abrogatæ sunt, atque hujus libertati omnino adversantur. Gal. v, 1. In libertate igitur, quâ Christus nos liberavit, perstate; & ne regredientes implicamini servitutis jugo.
units.tr: (4) This kind of symbolising is closely akin to the superstitions of the Gentiles and to the typical observances of the Israelites, which have been abrogated under the New Testament and are wholly opposed to its liberty: "Stand fast, therefore, in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of bondage" (Gal. 5:1).

units.la: Illis vero speciatim, quæ honori Angelorum, vel hohominum Sanctorum, dicata sunt, applicari possunt argumenta ista idololatriæ superius opposita. Quemadmodum etiam Sabbathum Mariæ, & Jubilæa eadem methodo refutari facilè possunt; nisi quod hæc insuper involvant Indulgentiarum Papalium absurditates absurdissimas. Martinalia, Regalia; aliaque Festa pinguia, comessationibus, compotationibus, jocis, & voluptatibus carnalibus celebrari solita, sua similiter speciala mala habent.
units.tr: Those arguments against idolatry that were raised above can be applied especially to those observances that are dedicated to the honour of angels or holy men. In the same way, the Sabbath of Mary and the Jubilees can easily be refuted by the same method, except that these additionally involve the most absurd absurdities of the papal indulgences. The Martinmas feasts, the Regalia, and other fat feasts, usually celebrated with carousing, drinking bouts, jests and carnal pleasures, likewise have their own particular evils.

units.la: Obj. 1. Diem Dominicum hebdomatim observant omnes Christiani ex traditione vel constitutione Ecclesiasticâ. Ergo. Resp. Nego antecedens; quantum enim attinet ad tempus hebdomadarium, sic quartum Decalogi præceptum nos obligat; specialius autem istum diem, talemque ejus appellationem, ex Scripturâ N. T. deducimus; non verò ex aliâ traditione, vel institutione solum Ecclesiasticâ.
units.tr: Obj. 1. All Christians observe the Lord's Day every week by tradition or ecclesiastical constitution. Therefore... Resp. I deny the antecedent. For as far as the weekly period is concerned, the fourth commandment binds us in this way; but we derive this day more specifically, and its name, from the Scripture of the New Testament, not from some other tradition or merely ecclesiastical institution.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dies supplicationis: atque item Eucharistici habentur etiam per suas occasiones. Ergo. Resp. Ista praxis in genere Verbo Dei nititur, applicatio verò ad certos dies, ex prudenti causarum & circumstantiarum observatione instituitur pro re natâ; & quidem ex Dei præscripto.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Days of supplication, and likewise Eucharistic days, are also held on their own occasions. Therefore... Resp. This practice rests in general on the Word of God; but its application to certain days is established, as circumstances require, from a prudent observation of causes and circumstances; and indeed it is done by God's prescription.

units.la: Obj. 3. Quotannis etiam in Ecclesiis Reformatis observari solent Dies nativitatis, & resurrectionis Christi, ac missionis Spiritus Sancti, cum sequentibus proximis, vel etiam Dies circumcisionis, & ascensionis. Resp. At non ratione mysterii; neque ob conscientiam propriam: sed ratione ordinis, & scandali turbarumque evitandarum gratia; quamvis istæ historiæ, tum in doctrinâ catechetica, tum aliis occasionibus variis, tractari etiam possint & soleant.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Every year the days of the birth and resurrection of Christ and of the sending of the Holy Spirit, with the following days nearest to them, or even the day of the circumcision and of the ascension, are customarily observed in the Reformed Churches. Resp. But not for the sake of a mystery, nor for one's own conscience; rather for the sake of order, and for the sake of avoiding scandal and disturbances. Although these histories may also be, and usually are, treated both in catechetical teaching and on various other occasions.

units.la: LXX. In quinto præcepto Patris & Matris nomine primò quidem intelligendi sunt parentes proprie dicti: Prov. XXIII, 22. Sed porro quotquot, ex ordinatione Divinâ in quocunque statu, Oeconomico PolitiPolitico, Ecclesiastico, aliis præfecti sunt: Parentum enim in liberos prima est insignis præfectura, maximéque naturalis. Hinc Patrum appellatio, aliæque similes, talibus quoque communicantur; Rom. ix, 5. Joh. viii, 39. Exod. iii, 15. Num. ii, 34. Item Ruth. iii, 1. Esth. ii, 7. Gen. iii, 10. Imo & 2 Reg. v, 1. Ista ad statum Oeconomicum pertinent: similia occurrunt in Politico; 1 Sam. xxiv, 12. Jud. v, 7. Et in Ecclesiastico; 2 Reg. ii, 12. 1 Cor. iv, 15. Philem. 10. Tam late igitur hic ista appellatio accipi debet; ut officia inferiorum omnium erga suos superiores, & vicissim superiorum erga suos inferiores, huc proprie pertineant.
units.tr: LXX. In the fifth commandment, the name of Father and Mother must first of all be understood of parents properly so called (Prov. 23:22). But further, it applies to all who, by divine ordinance, are set over others in any state, whether domestic, political or ecclesiastical; for the first and most distinguished, and most natural, authority is that of parents over children. Hence the title of Father, and other similar titles, are also applied to such persons (Rom. 9:5; John 8:39; Exod. 3:15; Num. 2:34). Likewise Ruth 3:1; Esth. 2:7; Gen. 3:10; indeed also 2 Kings 5:1. These belong to the domestic state; similar instances occur in the political: 1 Sam. 24:12; Judg. 5:7; and in the ecclesiastical: 2 Kings 2:12; 1 Cor. 4:15; Philem. 10. So widely, therefore, must this title be taken here, that the duties of all inferiors towards their superiors, and conversely of superiors towards their inferiors, properly belong here.

units.la: LXXI. Quæritur 1: An liceat Liberis vitam Mona- sticam vovere, aut suscipere, invitis Parentibus?
units.tr: LXXI. Question 1: Is it lawful for children to vow or to take up the monastic life against the will of their parents?

units.la: Resp. Neg: contra Pontificios, qui hoc licitum putant, modo Parentes Liberorum auxilio carere possint; & Liberi ad annos pubertatis pervenerint; utpote mares ad annum ætatis decimum quartum, feminæ vero ad duodecimum: Sed 1. istud adversatur reverentiæ, obedientiæ, & fidei Parentibus, per hoc præceptum debitæ. Confer Eph. vi, 1, 2. Col. iii, 20. Imo, quamvis nunc forte videantur Parentes indigere posse Liberorum auxilio: evenire potest facile, ut brevi eo maximè egeant.
units.tr: Resp. No: against the Papists, who think this lawful provided that the parents can do without the help of their children and the children have reached the years of puberty, namely boys at the age of fourteen and girls at twelve. But (1) this conflicts with the reverence, obedience and faithfulness owed to parents by this commandment. Compare Eph. 6:1, 2; Col. 3:20. Indeed, although parents may perhaps now seem able to do without the help of their children, it can easily happen that in a short time they will be in greatest need of it.

units.la: 2. Si Liberi sub V. T. vota Deo caeteroquin grata & accepta, concepissent, Parentes ea vel rata habere, vel irrita facere potuerunt: at sine Parentum consensu non fuerunt valida. Num. xxx, 5, 6.
units.tr: (2) If under the Old Testament children had made vows to God that were otherwise pleasing and acceptable, parents could either ratify them or make them void; but without the consent of the parents they were not valid. Num. 30:5, 6.

units.la: 3. Christus diserte reprehendit morem istum Pharisæis usitatum, quo Liberi se aut sua Deo sacra faciebant, atque ita Parentum auxilio subtrahebant; Matth. xv, 5, 6. Marc. vii, 11, 12, 13.
units.tr: (3) Christ expressly rebuked that custom, common among the Pharisees, by which children dedicated themselves or their possessions to God and thus withdrew them from their parents' support: Matt. 15:5, 6; Mark 7:11, 12, 13.

units.la: 4. Accedit ratio: nemo potest absolute Deo vovere, quod suum non est: ac Liberi non sunt sui ipsorum; sed Parentum possessio; Psal. cxxvii, 3. Confer sup. th. 52.
units.tr: (4) There is also this reason: no one can absolutely vow to God what is not his own; and children are not their own, but the possession of their parents (Ps. 127:3). Compare above, thesis 52.

units.la: Obj. 1. Deut. XXXIII, 9. Qui dicit patri suo & matri suæ, Non vidi eum; & fratres suos non cognovit: nam custodierunt eloquium Tuum, & pactum Tuum servaverunt. Istos Levitas imitantur, qui sic vitam Monasticam ingrediuntur: Ergo. Resp. Levitæ singulari præcepto Dei obligati erant ad occidendum, sine discrimine, aut respectu personarum, quosvis sibi obvios, qui sese polluissent impuro Moabiticarum commercio; Num. XXV, 5, 7, 8. Sed de vitâ Monasticâ nullum extat præceptum Dei.
units.tr: Obj. 1. "He who says to his father and mother, I have not seen him, and does not acknowledge his brothers, for they have kept your word and observed your covenant" (Deut. 33:9). The Levites are imitated by those who thus enter the monastic life; therefore... Resp. The Levites were bound by a special command of God to kill, without distinction or regard for persons, whoever they met who had polluted themselves by impure intercourse with the Moabite women (Num. 25:5, 7, 8). But there is no command of God concerning the monastic life.

units.la: Obj. 2. Matth. X, 37. oportet nos Christum diligere supra parentes. & Act. IV, 19. V, 29. Deo magis obedire, quam ullis hominibus. Ergo. Resp. Sed cum Deus Verbo suo vitam Monasticam omnino non instituerit, aut commendaverit; illis votis non ostenditur dilectio Christi, neque obedientia Dei: imo potius ista dilectio & obedientia postulat, ut Parentibus præstetur suus honor; atque adeo vota illa omittantur, rejiciantur, & redarguantur.
units.tr: Obj. 2. We ought to love Christ above parents (Matt. 10:37), and to obey God rather than any men (Acts 4:19; 5:29). Therefore... Resp. But since God has not at all instituted or commended the monastic life in his Word, the love of Christ and the obedience of God are not shown by those vows; indeed, rather, that love and obedience demand that due honour be paid to parents, and therefore those vows be set aside, rejected and refuted.

units.la: LXXII. Quæritur 2. An liceat Liberis contrahere matrimonium Parentibus insciis, aut invitis? Resp. Neg. similiter; & sententiam probamus primo iisdem argumentis proxime adductis: nam 1. honor & obedientia Parentibus, per ordinationem & legem Dei debita, omnino requirit, ut ne tantam rem aggrediantur Liberi, ipsis insciis, vel invitis.
units.tr: LXXII. Question 2: Is it lawful for children to contract marriage without the knowledge or against the will of their parents? Resp. No, likewise; and we approve this opinion, first by the same arguments just adduced: for (1) the honour and obedience due to parents by the ordinance and law of God altogether require that children should not undertake so great a matter without the knowledge or against the will of their parents.

units.la: 2. Si Parentes vota Liberorum, Deo factas, potuerunt irrita reddere, multo magis contractus cum homine ineundus ad illorum arbitrium referri debet.
units.tr: (2) If parents could make void the vows of their children made to God, much more must a contract to be entered into with a man be referred to their judgement.

units.la: 3. Si Liberi non debuerunt se, aut sua, Parentibus subducere, ut Deo sacra facerent: multo minus ut conjugi adhæreant, Parentibus insciis, aut invitis.
units.tr: (3) If children ought not to withdraw themselves or their possessions from their parents in order to dedicate them to God, much less should they cling to a spouse without their parents' knowledge or against their will.

units.la: 4. Quia sunt Parentum possessio, non licet iis sese Parentibus, citra ipsorum consensum, subducere; itaque familia relicta, ad aliam transfire, aut novam erierigere, quod fit in matrimonio : Gen. II, 24.
units.tr: (4) Because children are the possession of their parents, it is not lawful for them to withdraw themselves from their parents without the parents' consent; and so, leaving the family, to pass over to another, or to set up a new one, which happens in marriage: Gen. 2:24.

units.la: Accedunt aliæ rationes, utpote 1. quod passim SS. Literæ parentibus tribuant dare filias suas nuptum, & accipere filiis suis uxores. Exod. xxxiv, 16. Deut. vii, 3, 1 Cor. vii, 37, 38. Imo etiamsi forte virgo a quo juvene esset seducta & vitiata, atque ita res non integra; liberum tamen fuit patri illius in politia Israelitica eam illi non dare uxorem: Exod. 22, 16, 17.
units.tr: There are further reasons: (1) Holy Scripture everywhere assigns to parents the giving of their daughters in marriage and the taking of wives for their sons (Exod. 34:16; Deut. 7:3; 1 Cor. 7:37, 38). Indeed, even if a virgin had perhaps been seduced and violated by some young man, so that the matter was no longer intact, it was still open to her father, under the Israelite polity, not to give her to him as a wife (Exod. 22:16, 17).

units.la: 2. Consentiunt exempla, non solum Hagarae, circa filium Ismaelem, Gen. xxi, 21. sed & Abrahami, circa Isaacum; xxiv, 3, - & Bethuelis circa filiam Rebeccam, verf. 50, 51. Judae circa filium suum primogenitum; xxxviii, 6. Calebi, circa filiam; Iud. I, 12. Simsonis, qui parentum suorum consensum requisivit; xiv, 1, 2.
units.tr: (2) Examples agree: not only that of Hagar concerning her son Ishmael (Gen. 21:21), but also that of Abraham concerning Isaac (Gen. 24:3), and of Bethuel concerning his daughter Rebekah (vv. 50, 51), of Judah concerning his firstborn son (Gen. 38:6), of Caleb concerning his daughter (Judg. 1:12), and of Samson, who sought the consent of his parents (Judg. 14:1, 2).

units.la: 3. Per matrimonium filii, parentes ejus acquirunt nurum, quae fit quasi filia ipsorum; parentes vero filiae, acquirunt generum, qui fit quasi filius ipsorum: sed ista acquisitio consensum ipsorum omnino requirit.
units.tr: (3) Through the marriage of a son, his parents acquire a daughter-in-law, who becomes as it were their own daughter; and the parents of a daughter acquire a son-in-law, who becomes as it were their own son. But such an acquisition absolutely requires their consent.

units.la: Obj. 1. Matrimonium est Sacramentum; ac proinde consensus parentum non est de ejus necessitate. Resp. Nos istam hypothesin secundum SS. Literas rejicimus.
units.tr: Objection 1. Marriage is a sacrament, and therefore the consent of parents is not necessary to it. Reply: We reject that hypothesis in accordance with Holy Scripture.

units.la: Obj. 2. Consonat exemplum Esavi; Gen. xxvi, 34, 35. Resp. Inde factum quidem apparet, cui convenit αὐθεντικα historiae, non vero jus, & αὐθεντικα normae.
units.tr: Objection 2. The example of Esau agrees with this: Gen. xxvi, 34, 35. Answer: The fact indeed appears from that account, and it belongs to the authority [αὐθεντικά] of history; but it does not establish a right, nor does it have the authority [αὐθεντικά] of a norm.

units.la: LXXIII. Tenendum vero contra Anabaptistas,
units.tr: 73. But on the other hand, we must hold against the Anabaptists

units.la: quod non solum Christianus Magistratui Politico subesse ac parere; sed etiam eum gerere, posse bona conscientia. Nam 1 Rom. xiii, 1, -7. Apostolus supereminentem potestatem, non Dei permissionem vocat; sed ordinationem, & ministros Dei in bonum, & ad laudem eorum qui recte agunt. Neque loquitur de Magistratibus infidelibus tantum, aut quatenus tales erant: sed communiter de isto munere, & officiis eò pertinentibus. Confer Deut. I, 17. 2 Chron. 19, 6. Sic etiàm juxta 1 Tim. II, 1, 2, 3. Deum rogare debent fideles pro Regibus & Magistratibus, non solum ut convertantur qui infideles sunt, neque ut potestatem illam suam deponant; sed ut sub eorum regimine tranquillam & quietam vitam degant subditi, cum omni pietate ac honestate. Quod autem tali modo, ac tali fine, Deum precamur, id bonæ conscientiæ non adversatur. Juxta Tit. 3, 1. imperia & potestates pertinent ad defensionem ac promotionem omnium bonorum operum: talis est ista Dei constitutio. Et juxta 1 Petr. II, 13,-16. parendum est illi ordinationi propter Dominum, qui eam constituit. Apostolus interim humanam ordinationem vocat, tum quod specialis forma regiminis, & applicatio ad singulares personas, per homines ordinetur ac perficiatur; tum quod occupentur proprie iis, quæ ad vitam & conversationem hominum in hoc mundo pertinent.
units.tr: that a Christian may not only be subject to and obey the political magistrate, but may also hold that office with a good conscience. For in Rom. xiii, 1-7, the Apostle calls the supreme power not a permission of God but an ordinance, and the magistrates ministers of God for good and for the praise of those who do right. Nor does he speak only of unbelieving magistrates, or of them merely as such, but in general of that office and the duties belonging to it. Compare Deut. I, 17; 2 Chron. 19, 6. Likewise, according to 1 Tim. II, 1, 2, 3, the faithful ought to pray to God for kings and magistrates, not only that unbelievers among them may be converted, nor that they may lay down their power, but that under their rule the subjects may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all godliness and honesty. Now that we pray to God in such a manner and to such an end is not opposed to a good conscience. According to Tit. 3, 1, rulers and powers serve the defence and promotion of all good works; such is this constitution of God. And according to 1 Pet. II, 13-16, we must submit to that ordinance for the Lord's sake, who established it. The Apostle, meanwhile, calls it a human ordinance both because the particular form of government, and its application to individual persons, is ordered and carried out by men, and because it is concerned properly with those things which pertain to the life and conduct of men in this world.

units.la: 2. In V. T. non solum occurrunt multa exempla Regum, Principum, Judicum, piorum & laudatorum; sed etiam prædictiones de talibus sub N. T. suturis: ut Isef. 44, 23. lx, 3, 10. cum Apoc. 21, 24. In conversione igitur ad Christum, non debent deponere suam potestatem & gloriam; sed in bonum & ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ eam conferre.
units.tr: (2) In the Old Testament there occur not only many examples of kings, princes and judges who were pious and commended, but also predictions that such men will be found under the New Testament: as in Isa. 44:23; 60:3, 10, compared with Rev. 21:24. In their conversion to Christ, therefore, they ought not to lay down their power and glory, but to bring it to the good and building up of the Church.

units.la: 3. In ipso N. T. occurrunt exempla fidelium ac piorum Magistratuum, qui non depositerunt istam suam potestatem; sed sancte ea usi sunt. Sic Luc. 23, 50, 51. commemoratur quidam nomine Joseph, Senator, vir bonus ac justus. Joh. 4, 46,-53. regius quidam, qui credidit ipse, ac domus ejus tota. Act. 10, 1, 2. Cornelius, centurio, pius ac timens Deum, cum tota domo sua; &c. XIII, 12. Sergius Paulus Proprætor ad fidem conversus. Sed nihil omnino in omnibus illis,
units.tr: (3) In the New Testament itself there occur examples of faithful and pious magistrates who did not lay down their power but used it holily. Thus in Luke 23:50, 51 there is mentioned a certain man named Joseph, a councillor, a good and just man. In John 4:46–53 a certain royal official who believed himself, and his whole household. In Acts 10:1, 2 Cornelius, a centurion, pious and fearing God, with his whole household; etc. In Acts 13:12 Sergius Paulus the proconsul was converted to the faith. But in none of those cases

units.la: Y quod vel dignitatem ac potestatem suam Politicam depositerint, vel deponere debuerint.
units.tr: did anyone either lay down his political dignity and power, or ought he to have laid it down.

units.la: LXXIV. Obj. 1. Christus solus Ecclesiæ suæ Caput & Rex est: Ergo. Resp. Sed Caput & Rex spiritualis: Joh. 18, 36. Hoc autem Regnum Christi nequaquam tollit potestatem & regimen Politicum; quod exercent Reges, Principes, & Magistratus, in hominem exteriorem, & quidem in iis quæ ad tranquillitatem Reip. pertinent.
units.tr: LXXIV. Objection 1. Christ alone is the Head and King of his Church; therefore... Reply: He is the spiritual Head and King (John 18:36). But this kingdom of Christ by no means abolishes the political power and government which kings, princes and magistrates exercise over the outward man, and indeed in those matters which pertain to the tranquillity of the commonwealth.

units.la: Obj. 2. Matth. 20, 25, 26. Scitis, Principes gentium in eos dominari; & Magnates authoritate uti in eos: Verum non ita erit inter vos, &c. Resp. Discipulis Christi merum ministerium, & quidem plane alterius ordinis, erat demandatum; idcirco alienissimos eos esse oportebat à cogitationibus illis, & affectatione dominii ac gloriæ mundanæ. Confer 1 Petr. 5, 3. Neque ut Dominantes cleris; sed ut qui sitis exemplaria gregis. Verum à ministris Ecclesiasticis, sive extraordinariis, sive ordinariis, non valet consequentia ad Magistratus Politicos. Hi etiam vocantur Ministri Dei, Rom. 13, 4. qui est Rex Regum & Dominus Dominorum; 1 Tim. 6, 15. sed ita ut potestas superemineus, & jus gladii, iisdem tribuatur, tum ad ultionem facinorosorum, tum ad laudem bene agentium; Rom. 13, 1, 3, 4. 1 Petr. 2, 13, 14. qua potestate etiam uti possunt, ac debent, Ecclesiæ bono; Jef. 49, 23.
units.tr: Objection 2. Matt. 20:25, 26. You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great men exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you, etc. Reply: To the disciples of Christ a mere ministry, and indeed one of a plainly different order, was committed; therefore they had to be very far from those thoughts and from the pursuit of lordship and worldly glory. Compare 1 Pet. 5:3: Not as lording it over the clergy, but as being examples to the flock. But the inference from the ecclesiastical ministers, whether extraordinary or ordinary, to the political magistrates does not hold. These too are called ministers of God (Rom. 13:4), who is King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. 6:15); but in such a way that the supreme power and the right of the sword are given to them, both for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of those who do well (Rom. 13:1, 3, 4; 1 Pet. 2:13, 14), a power which they too can and ought to use for the good of the Church (Isa. 49:23).

units.la: Obj. 3. In Ecclesia, juxta Christi institutionem obtinet quoque potestatem & usus Clavium, seu disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ; Matth. 16, 19. XVIII, 17, 18. 1 Cor. 5, 2, 5, 7, 9; 11, 12, 13. Ergo. Resp. Potestas illa ministerialis est, ad ordinem Ecclesiasticum pertinens; totaque ad statum hominis spiritualem & æternum ordinata: ac proinde nequaquam tollit potestatem & usum Gladii, qui ad ordinem Politicum, & statum hominis externum ac temporalem proprie pertinet.
units.tr: Objection 3. In the Church, according to Christ's institution, the power and use of the keys, or of ecclesiastical discipline, also holds good (Matt. 16:19; 18:17, 18; 1 Cor. 5:2, 5, 7, 9; 11:12, 13). Therefore... Reply: That power is ministerial, belongs to the ecclesiastical order, and is wholly ordered to the spiritual and eternal state of man; and therefore it by no means abolishes the power and use of the sword, which properly belongs to the political order and to the outward and temporal state of man.

units.la: LXXV. Nec prorsus illicitum censeri debet, si quis fratrem suum in jus vocet apud Magistratum, &
units.tr: LXXV. Nor should it be judged altogether unlawful if someone summons his brother before the magistrate and

units.la: judicio adversùs eum experiatur; ubi scil. causa satis gravis est, neque aliter ea expediri potest, & ratio scandali abest. Hunc enim in finem ab ipso Deo ordinata est potestas Politica, ut tranquillam & quietam vitam degamus, cum omni pietate & honestate; 1 Tim. 2, 2. ad defensionem ac laudem bene agentium; Rom. 13, 3, 4. 1 Petr. 2, 14. & ut judicetur inter virum ac fratrem ejus; Deut. 1, 16.
units.tr: brings a lawsuit against him, namely where the cause is weighty enough, cannot otherwise be settled, and there is no ground of scandal. For to this end political power has been ordained by God himself, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life with all godliness and honesty (1 Tim. 2:2), for the defence and praise of those who do well (Rom. 13:3, 4; 1 Pet. 2:14), and that a case may be judged between a man and his brother (Deut. 1:16).

units.la: Obj. 1. Matth. 5, 40. Ei qui vult tecum contendere, ac tunicam tuam capere, dimitte etiam pallium. Ergò. Resp. Id proprie pertinet ad homines litium amantes, & contentionum sectatores; ex iracundiâ, aut vindictæ studio; ut aliis damnum inferant: docetque, potius perferendam esse injuriam novam, quam ut malum malo rependamus.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matt. 5:40. To the one who wants to go to law with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. Therefore... Reply: That properly pertains to people who love lawsuits and pursue quarrels, out of anger or a desire for revenge, so that they may inflict harm on others; and it teaches that one should rather endure a fresh injury than repay evil with evil.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Cor. 6, 1. Sustinet aliquis vestrûm, negotium habens adversùs alterum, judicio experiri sub injustis, ac non sub sanctis? Resp. Apostolus istic non absolutè omnem juris processum interdicit; sed adversùs fratres, & quidem apud judices infideles & injustos: quod in istis Ecclesiæ Christianæ primordiis valde scandalosum erat. Idcirco vult, ut lites suas potius committant Arbitris, etiam minimis, aut vilissimis, in Ecclesiâ: vers. 4, 5.
units.tr: Objection 2. 1 Cor. 6:1. Does any of you, having a dispute with another, dare to go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Reply: The Apostle there does not absolutely forbid every legal process, but only against brothers, and indeed before unbelieving and unjust judges; which in those first beginnings of the Christian Church was very scandalous. Therefore he wishes them rather to entrust their disputes to arbiters, even the least or lowliest in the Church (vv. 4, 5).

units.la: LXXVI. Contra Pontificios etiam tenendum; Ma- gistratum Politicum honore & dignitate non esse infe- riorem, sed superiorem, personis Ecclesiasticis: quo- niam
units.tr: LXXVI. Against the Papists it must also be held that the civil magistrate is not inferior but superior to ecclesiastical persons in honour and dignity, for the following reasons:

units.la: 1. Magistratui Politico competit potestas supereminens, & quidem talis à Deo ordinata; Rom. 13, 1. unde quoque Imperia & Potestates appellantur, quibus obtemperandum; etiam propter conscientiam: Tit. 3, 1. Rom. 13, 5.
units.tr: 1. The civil magistrate holds a supreme power, and one so ordained by God (Rom. 13:1). Hence the magistracies and powers are also called authorities, to which we must submit, even for conscience's sake (Tit. 3:1; Rom. 13:5).

units.la: 2. Eorum est Dominari, & Auctoritate uti in subditos: Matth. 20, 25.
units.tr: 2. It belongs to them to rule and to exercise authority over their subjects (Matt. 20:25).

units.la: 3. Tribuitur iis jus Gladii, & Potestas coactiva, ad ultionem facinorosorum, quibus propterea terrori sunt; & ad laudem bene agentium; Rom. 13, 3, 4. 1 Petr. 2, 14.
units.tr: 3. They are given the right of the sword and coercive power, to punish evildoers, who for that reason are a terror to them, and to praise those who do well (Rom. 13:3, 4; 1 Pet. 2:14).

units.la: 4. Contra vero personis Ecclesiasticis merum ministerium, & ministerialis dispensatio mysteriorum Dei ac Christi, tribuitur: 1 Cor. 3, 5, 9. IV, 1. 2, III, 6, 8, 9. IV, 1, 5, V, 19, 20; Iisque dominatio diserte prohibita est; Matth. 20, 26. 1 Petr. 5, 3.
units.tr: 4. On the other hand, ecclesiastical persons are assigned pure ministry and the ministerial stewardship of the mysteries of God and Christ (1 Cor. 3:5, 9; 4:1; 2 Cor. 3:6, 8, 9; 4:1, 5; 5:19, 20). Lordship over others is expressly forbidden to them (Matt. 20:26; 1 Pet. 5:3).

units.la: Obj. Atqui personis Ecclesiasticis demandatae sunt Claves Regni coelorum; & peccatorum remissio: sic versantur circa nobilius objectum; Matt. 16, 19. XVIII, 18. Job. 20, 23. 2 Cor. 4, 1. iisque tribuuntur arma militiae, Divinitus valida, &c. 2 Cor. 10, 4, 5, 6. Resp. 1. Ista omnia iis non architectonice, sed solum ministerialiter conveniunt; Claves Regni coelorum ipsi Christo competunt principaliter; Apoc. 1, 18, III, 7. 2. Fatemur quidem, bona spiritualia, coelestia, aeterna, nobiliora esse corporalibus, terrenis, & temporalibus: inde tamen non sequitur, quod volunt Adversarii. Aequa enim institui debet comparatio; ut Dominus spiritualis, coelestis, aeternus, ipse Christus, comparetur cum Dominis corporalibus, terrenis, & temporalibus, Magistratibus Politicis, iisque praeferatur. Sed non sequitur, Ministros Ecclesiasticos, idcirco honore ac dignitate superiores esse Magistratu Politico. Mathesis quidem ratione objecti dignior est Mercatura: verum non quivis puer Mathesi utcunque dans operam, aut famulus Mathematico fortasis inserviens, ejusque instrumenta portans, idcirco dignior est quovis Mercatore.
units.tr: Objection. But the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the remission of sins have been committed to ecclesiastical persons; thus they are concerned with a nobler object (Matt. 16:19; 18:18; John 20:23). Also the weapons of warfare, mighty through God, are given to them (2 Cor. 10:4, 5, 6). Answer. (1) All these things belong to them not architectonically, but only ministerially. The keys of the kingdom of heaven belong principally to Christ himself (Rev. 1:18; 3:7). (2) We grant indeed that spiritual, heavenly and eternal goods are nobler than bodily, earthly and temporal ones; yet it does not follow what the adversaries want. The comparison ought to be made on equal terms: just as the spiritual, heavenly and eternal Lord, Christ himself, is compared with bodily, earthly and temporal lords, the civil magistrates, and is preferred to them, so it does not follow that ecclesiastical ministers are superior to the civil magistrate in honour and dignity. Mathematics is indeed by reason of its object more worthy than trade; yet not every boy who is somehow devoted to mathematics, or a servant who perhaps serves a mathematician and carries his instruments, is for that reason worthier than any merchant.

units.la: LXXVII. Rejiciendus nunc etiam error Socinianorum; qui exis\-timant, Christum hoc quintum Decalogi praeceptum, pro N. T. perfectius redditurum, addidisse ei officia Magistratuum & Subditorum, Virorum & Uxorum, Dominorum & Servorum. Ista enim officia non solum locis Novi, sed etiam V. T. passim comprobantur. Atque in V. T. Patrum appellatio aliis etiam Superioribus tribuitur satis diserte; ut oftentum th. 70. Specialius vero Superiores debere se suis Inferioribus aequos probare, ad instar Patrum, patet ex Deut. 17, 15, 20. E medio fratrum tuorum constitues super te Regem: - Ne elevetur cor ejus supra fratres ipsius. Job. 29, 16. Pater eram pauperibus; & causam, quam non noveram, investigabam. Ita Joseph, Gen. xlv, 8. Deus posuit me in patrem ipsi Pharaoni, & in dominum universæ familiæ ejus. Addi possunt generalia præcepta de dilectione proximi, in V. T. satis obvia. Ex quibus inter se, & cum hoc præcepto collatis satis liquet, etiam sub V. T. officia illa præscripta fuisse.
units.tr: LXXVII. The error of the Socinians must now also be rejected. They think that Christ, who would make this fifth precept of the Decalogue more perfect for the New Testament, added to it the duties of magistrates and subjects, of husbands and wives, of masters and servants. For these duties are confirmed not only in the places of the New Testament but also everywhere in the Old. And in the Old Testament the title of father is quite clearly given also to other superiors, as was shown at thesis 70. More specifically, that superiors ought to show themselves equitable to their inferiors, after the manner of fathers, is plain from Deut. 17:15, 20: "You shall set over you a king from among your brothers... that his heart be not lifted up above his brothers." Job 29:16: "I was a father to the poor, and I searched out the cause which I did not know." So Joseph (Gen. 45:8): "God has made me a father to Pharaoh himself, and lord of his whole household." General precepts about love of neighbour, which are common enough in the Old Testament, may also be added. From these, compared with one another and with this precept, it is quite clear that those duties were prescribed even under the Old Testament.

units.la: LXXVIII, Sexto præcepto non adversatur supplicium capitale, quod per justam legitimi Magistratus sententiam, homicidis, aliisve facinorosis irrogatur: ista enim nequaquam est vis injusta: sed actus justitiæ, constitutioni Divinæ consentaneus, quod contra Anabaptistas defendimus. Deus enim 1. sanctionem ejusmodi pœnalem statim à diluvio disertè legitur expressisse; Gen. 9, 6. atque iterum in lege Mosaica, Levit. 24, 17. Num. 35, 16, -. 30, -. Deut. 19, 12, 13. De aliis item facinoribus similia multa occurrunt in V. T. Sed & in N. T. illa repetuntur & comprobantur; Matt. 26, 52. Quicunque acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt. Apoc. 13, 10. Si quis gladio occiderit, oportet eum gladio occidi. Ita hactenus stabilitur lex ista talionis.
units.tr: LXXVIII. The sixth precept does not oppose capital punishment, which is inflicted on murderers and other criminals by the just sentence of a lawful magistrate. For this is by no means unjust violence, but an act of justice in agreement with the divine ordinance, which we defend against the Anabaptists. For, first, God is read to have expressly laid down such a penal sanction immediately after the flood (Gen. 9:6), and again in the Mosaic law (Lev. 24:17; Num. 35:16, 30; Deut. 19:12, 13). Many similar provisions for other crimes also occur in the Old Testament. But these are also repeated and confirmed in the New Testament: "All who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matt. 26:52); "If anyone kills with the sword, he must be killed with the sword" (Rev. 13:10). In this way the law of retaliation is thus far established.

units.la: 2. Deus Magistratum etiam sub N. T. ministrum suum esse voluit, gladio armatum, ad ultionem facinoroforum, & ad laudem ac defensionem recte agentium, Rom. 13. 4. 1 Petr. 2, 14.
units.tr: 2. Under the New Testament too, God willed the magistrate to be his minister, armed with the sword, to punish evildoers and to praise and defend those who do right (Rom. 13:4; 1 Pet. 2:14).

units.la: 3. Neque aliter subditi tranquillam & quietam vitam degere possent, cum omni pietate & honestate; in quem tamen finem Magistratus à Deo ordinati sunt; 1 Tim. 2, 2.
units.tr: 3. Otherwise subjects could not lead a tranquil and quiet life, with all godliness and honesty; yet magistrates have been ordained by God for this very end (1 Tim. 2:2).

units.la: LXXIX. Imo & bellum aliquod licitum statuimus, contra eosdem; si videl. justa & satis gravi de causa suscipiatur; & quidem à Magistratu legitimo, aut superiori potestate; atque insuper juste geratur, parcendo quoad ejus fieri potest innoxiis. Probatur hoc 1. ex locis sæpius allegatis. Rom. 13, 4, 6. 1 Petr. 2, 14, 1 Tim. 2, 1, 2. In bello enim Magistratus gladio utitur adversus societatem facinorosorum, qui non aliter puniri possunt; neque aliter adversus eorum violentiam publica tranquillitas defendi & conservari potest.
units.tr: LXXIX. Indeed we also maintain that some war against these same persons is lawful, provided it is undertaken for a just and sufficiently grave cause, and certainly by a lawful magistrate or superior power, and moreover is waged justly, sparing the innocent as far as possible. This is proved, first, from the passages often cited (Rom. 13:4, 6; 1 Pet. 2:14; 1 Tim. 2:1, 2). For in war the magistrate uses the sword against the society of evildoers, who cannot otherwise be punished; nor can public tranquillity be otherwise defended and preserved against their violence.

units.la: 2. Clarius etiam Apoc. 13, 10. Siquis in captivitatem agit, in captivitatem abit. quæ potissimum bellica talio est.
units.tr: 2. Even more clearly, Rev. 13:10: "If anyone leads into captivity, he will go into captivity," which is above all a retaliation in war.

units.la: 3. Johannes Baptista à militibus interrogatus, Luc. 3, 14. Et nos quid faciemus? respondit; Neminem concutite, neque dolo opprimite; & contenti esse stipendiis vestris. sed ipsam militiam minimè prohibuit.
units.tr: 3. John the Baptist, when asked by soldiers, "What shall we do?" (Luke 3:14), answered: "Do violence to no one, nor oppress anyone by fraud, and be content with your wages." Yet he did not at all forbid soldiering itself.

units.la: 4. Accedunt exempla piorum militum, ac militiæ ducum: centurionis alicujus; Matth. 8, 5, 8, 10. atque item alterius, Cornelii nomine, Act. 10, 1, 2. qui tamen in sui conversione istud vitæ genus non deseruerunt, nec deserere jussi sunt. Et Paulus Apostolus comitatu ac defensione militum usus est, Act. 23, 13. Quemadmodum etiam fides bellicorum heroum celebratur, & ad imitationem proponitur; Hebr. xi, 32, 33, 34.
units.tr: 4. To this are added the examples of pious soldiers and of military commanders: of a certain centurion (Matt. 8:5, 8, 10), and likewise of another, named Cornelius (Acts 10:1, 2), who nevertheless did not abandon that way of life at their conversion, nor were they ordered to abandon it. And the Apostle Paul made use of the escort and protection of soldiers (Acts 23:13). Just as also the faith of warlike heroes is celebrated and set forth for imitation (Heb. 11:32, 33, 34).

units.la: Obj. 1. Davidi, bellicoso Principi, qui multum sanguinis fuderat, non fuit sub V. T. permissa Templi ædificatio; 1 Chron. 28, 3. Ergo. Resp. Templum istud pertinuit ad cultum cerimonialem, quo Christus, ejusque officia ac beneficia præfigurabantur; ac specialiter pax spiritualis cum Deo per Christum procuranda: idcirco Deus non à Principe illo bellicoso, sed à filio ejus Salomone, Principe pacifico, ac singulari typo Christi, istud Templum voluit ædificari; quo plura typica consPIRarent melius.
units.tr: Objection 1. David, a warlike prince who had shed much blood, was not permitted under the Old Testament to build the Temple (1 Chr. 28:3). Therefore... Answer. That Temple belonged to the ceremonial worship, by which Christ and his offices and benefits were prefigured, and by which spiritual peace with God through Christ was specially to be procured. Therefore God willed that this Temple be built not by that warlike prince but by his son Solomon, a prince of peace and a singular type of Christ, so that the many typical features might better agree together.

units.la: Obj. 2. De pace N. T. illustres exstant prophetiæ; Isa. 2, 4. xi, 6. Resp. Istæ proprie spectant ad pacem spiritualem cum Deo & in conscientiis fidelium; Rom. 5, 1. Eph. 2, 14, 17. Phil. 4, 7. Col. 1, 20. Quantum vero ad externam pacem attinet, Christus satis dicerte, Matt. 10, 34. Neexistimate, me venisse immittere pacem cem in terram: non veni immittere pacem, sed gladium. Dùm ergò infideles hostiliter sese opponunt Euangelio & fidelibus, vel aliter injusti justitiæ & justis, Magistratus Christiani durâ illâ necessitate adacti licitè possunt, imò etiàm debent, suos subditos, veritatem, & justitiam, defendere eâ potestate ac potentiâ, quam in illum finem iis dedit Deus.
units.tr: Objection 2. There are famous prophecies concerning the peace of the New Testament (Isa. 2:4; 11:6). Answer. These properly look to spiritual peace with God and in the consciences of the faithful (Rom. 5:1; Eph. 2:14, 17; Phil. 4:7; Col. 1:20). As far as external peace is concerned, Christ says quite plainly: "Do not think that I have come to bring peace on earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword" (Matt. 10:34). Therefore, while unbelievers set themselves in hostility against the Gospel and the faithful, or unjust men against justice and the just, Christian magistrates, driven by that hard necessity, may lawfully, and indeed ought, to defend their subjects, the truth and justice, with that power and might which God has given them for that end.

units.la: LXXX. Similiter quoque afferimus inculpatam tutelam; si quis adversùs latronem, aliumve aggressorem violentum & infestum, urgenti necessitati pareat, ac vitam suam tueatur; etiamsi forte contingeret latronem vel aggressorem illum pertinacem interim vulnerari, vel etiàm occidi. Quisque enim lege naturali obligatus est ad vitæ suæ conservationem ac defensionem adversus qualemcunque vim privatam & injustam.
units.tr: LXXX. Similarly we also affirm that blameless self-defence is lawful: if anyone, when a robber or another violent and hostile aggressor attacks him, yields to urgent necessity and protects his life, even if it should happen that the robber or persistent aggressor is meanwhile wounded or even killed. For everyone is bound by the natural law to preserve and defend his life against any private and unjust violence whatever.

units.la: 1. Eph. 5, 29. Nullus unquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit: imo enutrit ac fovet eam; sicut & Dominus Ecclesiam. Nemini licet suam vitam odisse, aut suâ se vitâ privare, aut consentire volenti privare; sed quisque tenetur impedire injustam cædem sui, ne incidat in crimen αὐτοφονίας participatæ,
units.tr: 1. Eph. 5, 29. "No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as the Lord does the Church." It is not lawful for anyone to hate his own life, to deprive himself of it, or to consent to another who wishes to deprive him of it. Rather, each person is bound to prevent the unjust killing of himself, lest he fall into the crime of self-murder [αὐτοφονίας].

units.la: 2. Matth. 22, 39. Diliges proximum tuum, ut te ipsum. Quemadmodum verò non licet nobis permittere cædem proximi, si impedire possimus; ita neque nostram ipsorum.
units.tr: 2. Matt. 22, 39. "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." Just as we may not permit the killing of a neighbour when we are able to prevent it, so neither may we permit the killing of ourselves.

units.la: Adde 3. casum hujusmodi expressum de fure nocturno, Exod. 22, 2. Si in effossione inventus fuerit fur, & percussus fuerit, mortuusque fuerit: non erit percussor mortis obnoxius. Quia nimirum per noctem non potest satis discerni, quid agat, quidque intendat effossor, nec facile aliunde auxilium peti. Si autem interdiu in loco solitario, vel aliter incommodo, idem vel gravius periculum aliquem urgeat, talis defensio sui nequaquam illicita est censenda.
units.tr: Add a third, express case, concerning the nocturnal thief: Exod. 22, 2. "If a thief is found breaking in, and is struck so that he dies, the one who struck him is not guilty of bloodshed." Clearly, by night one cannot sufficiently discern what the burglar is doing or intends, nor is help easily sought from elsewhere. But if by day, in a lonely place or in some other unsafe situation, a similar or greater danger presses upon someone, such self-defence is by no means to be judged unlawful.

units.la: Obj. Matt. 5, 39. Ne obsistite improbo: sed qui te cædet in dexteram tuam maxillam, obverte ei & alteram, & Rom. 12, 17. Ne17. Nemini malum pro malo vicissim reddentes. 19. Non ipsi vosmet ipsos ulciscentes. Ergo. Resp. Istis sententiis quidem prohibetur privata vindicta, & particularis retributio mali pro malo: non tamen 1. processus judicii à Magistratu legitimo institutus; quem Deus tali potestate & auctoritate armavit; imo & mandato obligavit, ad defensionem bonorum, & ultionem facinoroso‐ rum.Neque 2. necessaria sui defensio, adversus infestum aggressorem: si vero contingat eum interim vulnerari, veletiam ex vulneribus mori, hoc ipse suæ violentiæ ac pertinaciæ imputet; non inculpatæ tutelæ, quam oppressus, urgente necessitate & jure naturali, adhibet.
units.tr: Objection: Matt. 5, 39. "Do not resist an evil person; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also." And Rom. 12, 17, 19: "Repay no one evil for evil." "Do not avenge yourselves." Therefore... Answer: These sayings forbid private vengeance and the particular repayment of evil for evil; they do not forbid (1) the process of judgment instituted by a lawful magistrate, whom God has armed with such power and authority, and indeed bound by command, for the defence of good people and the punishment of criminals; nor (2) the necessary self-defence against an aggressor who attacks us. If it happens that he is wounded in the meantime, or even dies from his wounds, let him impute this to his own violence and obstinacy, not to the blameless defence which the one attacked employs under pressing necessity and by natural right.

units.la: LXXXI. Sed neque licet homini corpus suum, sive ex superstitione, sive qualicunque animi ægritudine, incidere, vulnerare, flagellare, &c. Nam 1. ista adversantur dilectioni, quam quisque per legem naturæ debet suæ propriæ carni: Eph. 5,29.
units.tr: LXXXI. But neither is it lawful for a man to cut, wound, scourge, etc. his body, whether from superstition or from any kind of disturbance of mind. For (1) such things are contrary to the love which each person owes by the law of nature to his own flesh: Eph. 5, 29.

units.la: 2. Satis expressus est locus, atque isti legi confentaneus, Levit. 21, 5. In carne sua non incident ullam incifuram.
units.tr: (2) The passage is clear enough, and agrees with this law: Lev. 21, 5. "They shall not make any cutting in their flesh."

units.la: 3. Est quædam symbolizatio cum idololatris & superstitiosis: sic enim extat de Sacerdotibus Baaliticis, 1 Reg. 18,28. Incidebant se juxta morem suum, cultris & lanceolis, donec perfunderent se sanguine. Similes quoque sunt mores Gentilium in quibusdam partibus Indiæ.
units.tr: (3) There is a certain association with idolaters and superstitious people. For so it stands written of the priests of Baal, 1 Kings 18, 28: "They cut themselves, according to their custom, with knives and lancets, until the blood poured out on them." Similar customs are also found among the Gentiles in certain parts of India.

units.la: 4. Superstitiosam istiusmodi sævitiem Paulus etiam perstringit. Col. II, 23. Quæ rationem quidem habent sapientiæ in cultu voluntario, & submissione animi, & in eo quod corporis non parcant; nec tamen ullius sunt pretii.
units.tr: (4) Paul also condemns this kind of superstitious cruelty. Col. 2, 23: "Which indeed have a show of wisdom in self-chosen worship, and humility of mind, and in that they spare not the body; but are of no value."

units.la: Hoc igitur nomine rejiciendæ sunt Pontificiorum flagellationes spontaneæ, à Monachis, aliisque pœnitentibus, adhiberi solitæ; ac multum commendatæ, tanquam insigniter satisfactoriæ: sed contra rationes modo indicatas, sine ullâ ratione verè Theologicâ, sine ullo exemplo in S S. Literis laudato, vel approbato. Obj. 1. Christus flagellatus est; Matth. xxvii, 26. Atque item Apostoli; Actor. 5, 40. Paulus cum Silâ: xvi, 23. Vide etiàm 2 Cor. xi, 24, 25. Resp. Ab hostibus id passi sunt; sed nemo eorum sibi ipsi tales cruciatus intulit.
units.tr: On this ground, therefore, the spontaneous flagellations which the Papists commonly employ, practised by monks and other penitents, and highly commended as especially satisfactory, must be rejected. They are contrary to the reasons just indicated, without any truly theological basis, and without any example in the Holy Scriptures to commend or approve them. Objection 1: Christ was scourged, Matt. 27, 26; likewise the Apostles, Acts 5, 40; Paul with Silas, Acts 16, 23. See also 2 Cor. 11, 24, 25. Answer: They suffered these things at the hands of enemies; but none of them inflicted such torments upon himself.

units.la: Obj. 2. Carnis crucifixio commendatur; Gal. 5, 24. Resp. Sed per carnem tunc intelligi debet vetus homo seu corruptio naturæ; quæ virtute crucifixionis ac mortis Christi pro nobis, subigi & mortificari debet quotidiè à quolibet regenito & sanctificato, ut novus homo capiat incrementum.
units.tr: Objection 2: The crucifixion of the flesh is commended, Gal. 5, 24. Answer: But by "flesh" must then be understood the old man, or the corruption of nature, which by the power of the crucifixion and death of Christ for us must be subdued and mortified daily by every regenerate and sanctified person, so that the new man may grow.

units.la: Obj. 3. 1 Cor. 9, 27. Contundo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo. Resp. Corpus scil. peccati; ne illud pergeret adeò adversari spiritui, eumque impedire: quò quidem pertinuit abstinentia ab ejusmodi alimentis, deliciis, aliisque commoditatibus, quibus temperamentum posset inclinari ad quædam peccata; nec non jejunia, orationes, exercitia virtutum contrariarum; ut hæc redderentur magis familiares & faciles: non verò sævitia in propriam substantiam.
units.tr: Objection 3: 1 Cor. 9, 27: "I beat my body and bring it into subjection." Answer: That is, the body of sin, lest it should continue to oppose the spirit so strongly and hinder it. To this belong abstinence from such foods, delicacies and other comforts by which the temperament might be inclined to certain sins; also fasts, prayers, and exercises of contrary virtues, so that these might become more familiar and easy. But it does not mean cruelty against one's own substance.

units.la: Obj. 4. Medici aliquandò membrum aliquod extirpandum censent, vel urendum, ad conservationem reliqui corporis: Ergò. Resp. Recte sic censent, urgente necessitate satis gravi: sed spontanea sui flagellatio, nec ad corporis, nec ad animæ conservationem utilis est, nedùm necessaria: imò contrà propriæ satisfactionis opinio gratiæ Euangelicæ quam maximè adversatur; & sic summoperè noxia est.
units.tr: Objection 4: Physicians sometimes judge that some limb must be cut off or cauterised for the preservation of the rest of the body. Therefore... Answer: They judge rightly so, when the necessity is sufficiently grave. But spontaneous self-flagellation is useful neither for the preservation of the body nor of the soul, let alone necessary. Indeed, the opinion of one's own satisfaction is most strongly opposed to the grace of the Gospel, and so it is most harmful.

units.la: LXXXII. Errant Socinians, dùm contendunt, sextum præceptum sub N. T. auctum esse mandato charitatis ergà inimicos; & prohibitione iræ, atque convitiorum in proximum, necnon vindictæ. Quod enim ad dilectionem inimicorum attinet, ea sub V. T. quoque mandata fuit; Prov. 25, 21, 22. Exod. 23, 4, 5. Quin & Paulus Rom. 12, 20. allegato priori illo testimonio, eam probavit.
units.tr: LXXXII. The Socinians are wrong when they contend that under the New Testament the sixth commandment has been enlarged by the command of love towards enemies, and by the prohibition of anger, of reproaches against a neighbour, and also of vengeance. For as far as the love of enemies is concerned, this was commanded under the Old Testament also: Prov. 25, 21, 22; Exod. 23, 4, 5. Indeed Paul, too, proved it by citing the former testimony, Rom. 12, 20.

units.la: Y s.
units.tr: Y s.

units.la: Quantum vero ad iram, (temerariam scil. vel immoderatam,) convitium, (similiter malignum,) & vindictam (privatam,) ea charitati proximo debitae, & sub V.T. mandatae, adversantur satis aperte: & diserte prohibentur, Lev. 19, 17, 18. Ne odio habeas fratrem tuum in corde tuo: neque impinges illi crimen. Non ulcisceris te, neque reservabis odium contra filios populi tui; sed diliges proximum tuum, sicut te ipsum. De ira etiam, Eccl. 7, 9. Ne festines in spiritu tuo ad irascendum: quia ira in sinu stultorum requiescit. Adde Prov. 14, 29.
units.tr: As far as anger is concerned (namely rash or immoderate anger), reproach (likewise malicious), and vengeance (private), these are quite plainly contrary to the love owed to a neighbour and commanded under the Old Testament; and they are expressly forbidden: Lev. 19, 17, 18. "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall not bring a charge against him. You shall not take vengeance, nor keep a grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Concerning anger also, Eccl. 7, 9: "Do not be quick in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools." Add Prov. 14, 29.

units.la: LXXXIII. Circa septimum praeceptum non est cum Pontificiis putandum, gradus in matrimonio prohibi- tos, Lev. 18, 6, - 18, 24, 25. XX, II, 12, 14, 17, 19-23.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Regarding the seventh commandment, the Papists must not be followed in thinking that the degrees of prohibition in marriage, Lev. 18:6–24, 25; 20:2, 11, 12, 14, 17, 19–23, pertain only to the Mosaic civil or ceremonial laws, so that the power of the Roman Pope to make and dispense with them might be enlarged and made more profitable.

units.la: pertinuisse solum ad leges forenses Mosaicas, vel ad caeremoniales; quo liberior & fructuosior Papae Romano afferatur potestas de illis constituendi ac dispensandi. Nam Gentiles iisdem quoque fuerunt obligati; & ob earum transgressionem terra dicitur evomuisse suos incolas; Levit. 18, 24, - XX, 22. Unde Paulus ad Gentium consensum provocat in iustiusmodi casu, 1 Cor. 5, 1.
units.tr: For the Gentiles were bound by the same laws, and because of their transgression the land is said to have vomited out its inhabitants (Lev. 18:24; 20:22). Hence Paul appeals to the consensus of the Gentiles in a case of this kind (1 Cor. 5:1).

units.la: Obj. 1. Filii τῶν πεπορνευκότων germanas sorores suas duxerunt. Ergò. Resp. 1. Id procul dubio factum est ex speciali dispensatione Divina, quae istas personas à Legis obligatione exemit, Lege interim manente, & posteros omninò obligante: sive ex speciali constitutione, ut Legis obligatio & vigor in eorum posteris demum sumeret initium.
units.tr: Objection 1: The sons of those who had committed fornication (τῶν πεπορνευκότων) took their own sisters as wives. Therefore... Answer 1: This undoubtedly happened by a special dispensation of God, which exempted these persons from the obligation of the Law, while the Law itself remained in force and bound their posterity absolutely; or else by a special ordinance, so that the obligation and force of the Law should only begin with their posterity.

units.la: Obj. 2. Abraham de Sara, Gen. 20, 12. Vere soror mea est, filia patris mei; veruntamen non est filia matris meae, & fuit mihi in uxorem. Resp. Inde tamen non omnino constat, eam Terachi Patris Abrahami filiam naturalem fuisse: cum sic etiam appellari potuerit illius ex fratre neptis, vel aliter consanguinea, filiae loco habita; & minime certum fit, eandem fuisse Saram, quae Jisca, Gen. XI, 29. Si tamen filia illius naturalis fuisset, concedimus, Abrahamum, citra dispensationem Divinam, eam neque uxorem ducere, neque deinceps in Matrimonio retinere potuisse licitè.
units.tr: Objection 2: Abraham said of Sarah, "She is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife" (Gen. 20:12). Answer: It does not altogether follow from this that she was a natural daughter of Terah, Abraham's father, since she could also be called that as a granddaughter of his brother, or as a relative otherwise, and was regarded as a daughter. Nor is it at all certain that she was the same as Sarah, who is Iscah (Gen. 11:29). Yet if she had been his natural daughter, we concede that Abraham could not lawfully have taken her as wife, or afterwards kept her in marriage, apart from a divine dispensation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Onan à patre Judà jussus est uxorem ducere Thamaram viduam fratris fui prædefuncti, Gen. 38, 8. Cui facto convenit Lex, Deut. 25, 6. Vide etiam Matth. 22, 24, 25, 26. Resp. Verùm illa in affinitate exceptio ab ipso Legislatore, Generis humani & Legis illius Domino, fieri potuit, & facta est, per absolutissimam ipsius potestatem; Exceptione Regulam non tollente, sed in reliquis confirmante.
units.tr: Objection 3: Judah told Onan to take as wife Tamar, the widow of his deceased brother (Gen. 38:8). The Law agrees with this deed (Deut. 25:5, 6). See also Matt. 22:24–26. Answer: That exception in the case of affinity could indeed be made, and was made, by the Lawgiver himself, the Lord of the human race and of that Law, by his most absolute power; the exception does not abolish the rule but confirms it in other cases.

units.la: LXXXIV. Sed jure Canonico veteri Nuptiæ in lineâ transversali fuerunt prohibitæ usque ad gradum septi- mum; novo autem ad quartum inclusivè.
units.tr: LXXXIV. But by the older Canon Law, marriages in the collateral line were forbidden up to the seventh degree; by the newer law, up to and including the fourth.

units.la: Neque solùm illo Jure approbata & confirmatâ est Consanguinitas civilis, sed introducta quoque Cognatio spiritualis, ex Baptismo & Confirmatione. Atque ita jure Decretalium ista Cognatio contrahitur, 1. inter baptizatum & susceptorem de baptismo. 2. Inter eundem baptizatum, & suscipientis filios; ejusque uxorem, quam ante istam susceptionem cognovit carnaliter. Atque item 3. Inter suscipientem, & baptizati patrem ac matrem. Imò etiàm 4. quæ de suscipiente dicta sunt, eadem ad baptizantem quoque transferuntur. Ac similiter in Confirmatione. Atque illa Cognatio non solùm dicitur impedire Matrimonium contrahendum, sed etiàm contractum dirimere. Verùm postea Concilium Tridentinum Cognationem istam quodammodò restrinxit; statuitque, ut unus tantùm vir, aut una mulier, vel ad summum unus & una, baptizatum suscipiant; inter quos ad baptizatum ipsum, & utrumque ejus parentem, nec non inter baptizantem & baptizatum & hujus utrumque parentem, tantùm ea contrahatur: atque item, ne confirmantem & confirmatum, ejus patrem & matrem, ac tenentem, egrediatur. Sed peram ἀπερ Γεγφῆς. Quin imò omnes verè fideles in
units.tr: Not only was civil kinship approved and confirmed by that law, but also spiritual kinship was introduced, arising from baptism and confirmation. Thus by the law of the Decretals this kinship is contracted: (1) between the baptized person and the sponsor at baptism; (2) between the same baptized person and the sponsor's children, and the sponsor's wife, whom he had known carnally before that sponsorship; likewise (3) between the sponsor and the parents of the baptized person; indeed (4) whatever is said of the sponsor is also transferred to the one who baptizes. The same holds for confirmation. And this kinship is said not only to hinder a marriage about to be contracted but also to dissolve one already contracted. But afterwards the Council of Trent restricted this kinship to some extent: it decreed that only one man or one woman, or at most one man and one woman, should stand as sponsors for the baptized person; and that it is contracted only between them and the baptized person and his parents, and likewise between the one who baptizes and the baptized person and his parents; and similarly that it should not extend to the one confirming and the one confirmed, his father and mother, and his sponsor. But enough of this [ἀπερ Γεγφῆς]. Indeed, all truly faithful people are mystically united in Christ, as members of the same body, as brothers and sisters, and so on; yet marriage is not hindered by this but sanctified (1 Cor. 7:39).

units.la: ἀπερ Γεγφῆς: Greek, as printed. in Christo mystice uniti sunt, ut membra ejusdem corporis, ut fratres & sorores, &c. unde tamen Matrimonium non impeditur, sed sanctificatur : 1 Cor. 7, 39.
units.tr: [ἀπερ Γεγφῆς] ...in Christ mystically united, as members of one body, as brothers and sisters, etc.; yet by this marriage is not hindered but sanctified: 1 Cor. 7:39.

units.la: LXXXV. Pontificii plurimum tribuunt juri suo Canonico: verum in nostra Ecclesia, imo & Republica, nullum illud, quatenus tale est, auctoritatem habet. Sed ex Verbo Dei & Jure Divino quæstiones Matrimoniales decidendæ sunt in ordine ad interiorem statum conscientiæ, forum poli, ipsamque communionem Ecclesiasticam : ubi Antecessoribus Ecclesiasticis sua potestas antecessoria ministerialis vere competit. Interim Magistratus Politicus ex jure Civili & Municipali, & secundum Verbum Dei, judicare etiam potest ac debet, non solum de Matrimonii accidentalibus, dote puta arrhis, & similibus; verum insuper de ipsis substantialibus, in ordine ad statum Politicum, qui externus est & temporalis : Politia enim constituitur ex Familiis, quæ sine Matrimonio non consistunt. Perperam vero dicti Adversarii omnem de Matrimonio & causis Matrimonialibus cognitionem soli foro Ecclesiastico competere statuunt; ex falsa hypothesi, quod Matrimonium sit Sacramentum : contrarium nos σὺν Θεῷ probabimus suo loco.
units.tr: LXXXV. The Papists attribute very great weight to their Canon law; but in our Church, and indeed in the commonwealth, that law has no authority as such. Matrimonial questions must be decided from the Word of God and divine law, with respect to the inner state of conscience, the forum of heaven, and ecclesiastical communion itself; in these matters the ecclesiastical ministers truly hold their own ministerial authority. Meanwhile the political magistrate, by civil and municipal law, and according to the Word of God, can and must also judge not only of the accidental features of marriage, such as dowry, earnest money and the like, but also of its essentials, with respect to the political state, which is external and temporal; for the commonwealth is made up of families, which cannot exist without marriage. The said adversaries wrongly maintain that all knowledge of marriage and of matrimonial cases belongs solely to the ecclesiastical court, on the false hypothesis that marriage is a sacrament; we shall prove the contrary, with God's help, in its proper place.

units.la: LXXXVI. Publica quidem Matrimonii confirmatio Politica est, & Lege positiva humana recte introducta : tum quia Reip. interest, ut legitime contrahantur Matrimonia; atque ut publice constet, quis cujus maritus sit, & quæ cujus uxor, ad evitanda adulteria, aliaque istiusmodi peccata : tum quia ad Magistratum Politicum pertinet ea curare, quæ ad statum externum & Politicum proprie spectant. Sed Ecclesiæ quoque interest, ut circa rem tantam observentur quæ Deus in Verbo suo præscripsit; ut cognoscat, per quos & quomodo propagetur Ecclesia, quantum attinet ad eos qui in communione fœderis gratiæ nascuntur; atque ut pro illis preces publice concipiantur, & benedictio iis juxta voluntatem Dei impertiatur. Ita hæc recte fieri defendimus contra Brownistas: interim distinctio facienda est inter ejusmodi Ecclesiæ membra; quorum fides ac pietas satis est explorata; & inter alios homines, de quorum fide & pietate non constat.
units.tr: LXXXVI. The public confirmation of marriage is indeed a political matter, rightly introduced by human positive law; both because it is in the interest of the commonwealth that marriages be lawfully contracted, and that it be publicly known who is whose husband and who whose wife, in order to avoid adultery and other sins of this kind; and because it belongs to the political magistrate to take care of those things that properly concern the external and political state. But it is also in the interest of the Church that in so great a matter those things which God has prescribed in his Word be observed, so that it may know through whom and how the Church is propagated, as far as concerns those who are born into the communion of the covenant of grace; and so that prayers may be offered publicly for them, and blessing bestowed upon them according to the will of God. Thus we maintain that these things are rightly done, against the Brownists; yet a distinction must be made between such members of the Church whose faith and piety are sufficiently proven, and other people, whose faith and piety are not established.

units.la: LXXXVII. Pontificii Virginitatem ac Vitam cœlibem extollunt mirum in modum, & Matrimonio longè præferunt. Nos in utroque statu sua tum commoda, tùm etiam incommoda, agnoscimus; & pro conditione personarum ac temporum, vel hunc, vel illum, potius amplectendum dicimus: non vero absolutè Virginitati ac Cœlibatui primas esse tribuendas. Nam 1. Deus in primâ rerum creatione, hominumque integritate, non modò marem & feminam fecit eos, conjugio junxit, iftiq; statui vitæ benedixit; Gen. 1,27,28. II,21,24. sed diserte etiam in Adami Cœlibatû imperfectio quædam notatur; II,20. At homini non invenit adjutorium, quod esset coram eo. & minor bonitas, quàm foret in Conjugio: 18. Dixerat Jehovah Deus; Non bonum est, hominem esse solum; propterea faciam ei adjutorium, quod sit coram eo. Post lapsum non minor, sed potius major, est necessitas istius adjutorii: Eccl. 4,9,-12. Melius sunt duo quam unicus; quia est eis merces melior ex labore suo. Quia si ceciderint, unus eriget socium suum: væ ergo illi uni, &c.
units.tr: LXXXVII. The Papists extol virginity and the celibate life wonderfully, and set them far above marriage. We acknowledge in each state its advantages and also its disadvantages; and according to the condition of persons and times we say that one or the other is rather to be embraced; but virginity and celibacy must not be absolutely given the first place. For first, God, in the first creation of things and the integrity of human beings, not only made them male and female, joined them in marriage, and blessed that state of life (Gen. 1:27, 28; 2:21, 24); but also clearly marks a certain imperfection in Adam's celibacy: "But for man no helper was found who would be suitable for him" (2:20), and a lesser goodness than there would be in marriage: "The LORD God had said, It is not good for man to be alone; therefore I will make him a helper suitable for him" (2:18). After the fall the need for that helper is not less but rather greater: "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, one will lift up his companion; woe then to the one who is alone, etc." (Eccl. 4:9–12).

units.la: 2. Christus secundum carnem ex Virgine natus est; sed Viro desponsata, imò in ejus domum jam assumta; ne contemnerentur Nuptiæ: Matth. 1,18,21,25. Luc. 1,27. II,5. Nuptiis in Cana Galilææ celebratis ipse cum matre ac discipulis suis quoque interfuit, easque primo suo miraculo condecoravit; Joh. 2,1,2,11.
units.tr: Second, Christ was born according to the flesh of a virgin, but was betrothed to a man, indeed already taken into his house, so that marriage should not be despised (Matt. 1:18, 21, 25; Luke 1:27; 2:5). At the wedding in Cana of Galilee he was present himself with his mother and his disciples, and honoured that marriage by his first miracle (John 2:1, 2, 11).

units.la: 3. Est medium à Deo ordinatum, non modò ad Generis humani, & Rerum publ. verum etiam ad ipsius Ecclesiæ propagationem, conservationem, & incrementum. Hinc Eva, Adamo nupta, utpote vera mater omnium viventium, nomen accepit; Gen. 3,20. Atque itā Mal. I, 15. Quid fecit unicus ille? Quaesivit semen Dei. Et ipse Deus ad Abrahamum, Gen. 12, 2. Faciam te in gentem magnam, & benedicam tibi, ac magnificabo nomen tuum; & eris benedictio. Adde 15, 4, 5. XVII, 4–12.
units.tr: Third, marriage is a means ordained by God not only for the propagation, preservation and increase of the human race and of the commonwealth, but also of the Church itself. Hence Eve, wife of Adam, received her name as the true mother of all the living (Gen. 3:20). And so Mal. 1:15: "What did that one do? He sought a godly offspring." And God himself said to Abraham: "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great; and you shall be a blessing" (Gen. 12:2). Add Gen. 15:4, 5; 17:4–12.

units.la: 4. Accedit speciālis utilitas, imò necessitas, ex praescripto Divino, in illis qui donum continentiæ non habent: neque enim omnibus istud obtingit; nec de eo precibus & jejuniis impetrando omnibus promissio est facta; non certè illis, quibus aliter datum est à Deo, & per quorum Nuptias ipsi Genus humanum, vel etiam Ecclesiam, propagare placitum: 1 Cor. 7, 7. Unde etiam Apostolus, de Viduis agens, 1 Tim. 5, 14. Velim igitur juniores nubere, liberos gignere, domum administrare, nullam occasionem dare adversario ad convitiandum.
units.tr: 4. There is also a special benefit, indeed a necessity, arising from the divine ordinance for those who do not have the gift of continence. For this gift is not given to everyone, and no promise has been made that everyone will obtain it by prayers and fasting. It is certainly not promised to those whom God has otherwise appointed, and through whose marriages it has pleased him to propagate the human race and even the Church: 1 Cor. 7:7. Hence the Apostle also, speaking of widows, says: 1 Tim. 5:14. I would therefore have the younger women marry, bear children, and manage their households, giving the adversary no occasion to speak evil.

units.la: Neque adeò mirandum, si rejecto illo incontinentiæ remedio, impurum Coelibatum amplexa, omnia passim foedis libidinibus confpurcârit meretrix Babylonica, concubinatū, fornicationibus, adulteriis, non contenta. Certè quod olim ad Romanos scripsit Apostolus, idem in vitiosiorem eorum progeniem applicatur merito, I, 26, 27. Propterea tradidit eos Deus fœdis affectibus: masculi, relicto naturali usu feminæ, exarserunt in libidine alius in alium, &c.
units.tr: Nor is it any wonder that the Babylonian harlot, having rejected that remedy for incontinence and embraced an impure celibacy, has everywhere defiled everything with foul lusts, not content with concubinage, fornications and adulteries. What the Apostle once wrote to the Romans is rightly applied to their more wicked offspring, Rom. 1:26, 27. For this reason God gave them up to shameful passions: their men, abandoning the natural use of women, burned with lust for one another, and so on.

units.la: LXXXVIII. Obj. 1. Sub V. T. immunditiescon- trahebatur etiam ex maritali & legitimo concubitu; Levit. xv, 16, 18.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Obj. 1. Under the Old Testament, uncleanness was also contracted from lawful marital intercourse; Lev. 15:16, 18.

units.la: Hinc Deus Legem suam promulgaturus coram universis Israelitis, mandavit, ne ad uxores suas accederent; Exod. xix, 15. Similiter etiam Sacerdos Achimelech, panem sacrum daturus Davidi & viris qui unà cum eo aderant, inquisivit, num à mulieribus sibi cavissent; 1 Sam. xxi, 4. Resp. Cerimonialis tantùm fuit ista immunditia: verùm ex eâ minimè sequitur, statum Conjugii, ejusque usum, per se moraliter impurum esse, vel illicitum; non magis quàm ex animalibus sub V. T. immundis colligi debet, quòd corum eorum esus aut contrectatio etiam sub N.T. sit illicita & moraliter impura.
units.tr: Hence God, about to promulgate his law before all the Israelites, commanded them not to approach their wives: Exod. 19:15.
