Likewise the priest Ahimelech, when he was about to give the holy bread to David and the men who were with him, asked whether they had kept themselves from women: 1 Sam. 21:4. Answer: that uncleanness was merely ceremonial. Nor does it follow from it that the married state and its use are in themselves morally impure or unlawful, any more than it should be inferred from the animals that were unclean under the Old Testament that eating or handling them is also unlawful and morally impure under the New Testament.

units.la: Obj. 2 Isef. LVI, 3, 4, 5. Insignis promissio facta est Eunuchis: ergo. Resp. Ibi tum alienigenis, tum Eunuchis, qui sub V. T. per Legem cerimonialem arcebantur a sacris, promittitur fore, ut per fidem sub N. T. admittantur ad eandem communionem, & privilegia eadem cum reliquis: sic amplitudo hujus gratiæ exprimitur synecdochicè.
units.tr: Obj. 2 Isa. 56:3, 4, 5. A remarkable promise was made to eunuchs: therefore... Answer. There it is promised, both to foreigners and to eunuchs, who under the Old Testament were excluded from the sacred things by the ceremonial law, that through faith under the New Testament they will be admitted to the same fellowship and to the same privileges as the rest. Thus the breadth of this grace is expressed by synecdoche.

units.la: Obj. 3. Rom. 8, 8. Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt: tales autem sunt conjugati: ergo. Resp. Imo in carne esse dicuntur, qui Spiritum regenerantem & sanctificantem non habentes, corruptæ suæ naturæ obsequuntur. Hoc patet ex contextu, & locis parallelis. Sed pessimè illud transfertur & applicatur ad Conjugium; quod Apostolus diserte asseruit honorabile inter quosvis, & cubile impolutum; Hebr. 13, 4.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Rom. 8:8. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But such are the married: therefore... Answer. Rather, those are said to be in the flesh who, not having the regenerating and sanctifying Spirit, follow the corruption of their nature. This is clear from the context and from parallel passages. But that text is very badly translated and applied to marriage, which the Apostle plainly affirmed to be honourable among all, and the bed undefiled: Heb. 13:4.

units.la: Obj. 4. Virginitatem & Cœlibatum commendat idem Apostolus, ut quantum fieri posset ita viverent Corinthii; VII, 1, 7, 8, 26, 38, 40. Ergo. Resp. Non tamen absolutè, omnes, & semper; sed qui ita donum haberent: verf. 2, 7, 17, 37. & quidem propter instantem necessitatem; verf. 26. & afflictionem in carne, cujus eos immunes esse optabat; verf. 28. Pauciora quidem Cœlibes circa cultum Dei impedimenta habere, Conjugatos majorem solicitudinem de rebus hujus vitæ, indicat, verf. 32, 33, 34. id tamen accipi debet non prorsus absolutè & universaliter; sed positis ponendis, remotis removendis, atque in isto rerum statu ut plurimum: laqueum propterea non injecit; verf. 35.
units.tr: Obj. 4. The same Apostle commends virginity and celibacy, and wishes the Corinthians to live thus as far as possible: 1 Cor. 7:1, 7, 8, 26, 38, 40. Therefore... Answer. Not absolutely, for all and always, but for those who have the gift in this way: vv. 2, 7, 17, 37. And indeed this is because of the present necessity, v. 26, and the affliction in the flesh, from which he wished them to be free, v. 28. That the unmarried have fewer hindrances to the worship of God, and the married more anxiety about the affairs of this life, he indicates in vv. 32, 33, 34. Yet this must be understood not as wholly absolute and universal, but with things to be posited being posited and things to be removed being removed, and that for the most part in the present state of affairs. Therefore he did not cast a snare: v. 35.

units.la: Obj. 5. Apoc. 14, 4. celebrantur aliquàm multa millia eorum, qui cum mulieribus non sunt inquinati, quod sint virgines. Ergo Resp. Ita scil. meretrici Babylonicæ prorsùs dissimiles sunt, qui sedulo sibi cavent ab idololatriâ & omni aliâ impuritate spirituali, atque adeò sive extra Conjugium, sive in eo, castitati & puritati etiam etiàm dant operam : fi autem contigerit, eos aliquandò pollui vitiis contrariis, abluunt fe sanguine Agni pér fidem & refipifcentiam sinceram.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Rev. 14:4. There are celebrated some many thousands of those who were not defiled with women, because they are virgins. Therefore... Answer. Thus, indeed, those are wholly unlike the Babylonian harlot who diligently guard themselves against idolatry and every other spiritual impurity, and therefore, whether outside marriage or within it, also devote themselves to chastity and purity. But if it happens that they are sometimes stained by contrary vices, they wash themselves in the blood of the Lamb through faith and sincere repentance.

units.la: LXXXIX. Sed neque putandum est, cum iisdem Adversariis, Matrimonium saltem Ministris Ecclesiafticis & Religiosis esse illicitum; aut ab iis exigendum votum Coelibatûs. Nam 1. ad ipsos etiàm pertinent generales rationes, de honestate, utilitate, imò & neceffitate Conjugii pro ratione circumstantiarum. Gen. II, 18. Non est bonum, hominem esse solum, &c. Eccl. 4, 9. Meliores sunt duo, quam unicus, &c. Hebr. 13.4. Honorabile est inter quosvis Conjugium, & cubile impollutum. Qui Ecclesiasticos & Religiosos excipiunt, dùm exceptionem suam non probant, nec probare possunt, censendi sunt decipere.
units.tr: LXXXIX. Nor should it be thought, with the same Adversaries, that marriage is at least unlawful for ecclesiastical and religious ministers, or that a vow of celibacy is to be required of them. For, first, the general reasons concerning the honesty, usefulness, and indeed necessity of marriage, according to the circumstances, apply to them too: Gen. 2:18, It is not good that man should be alone, etc.; Eccl. 4:9, Two are better than one, etc.; Heb. 13:4, Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled. Those who except ecclesiastical and religious persons, while they do not prove their exception and cannot prove it, are to be judged deceivers.

units.la: 2. Consonant exempla Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, & Prophetiffarum; nec non Nafiræorum, Levitarum, Sacerdotum; ipsiusque adeò Sacerdotis summi, sub V.T. ubi de Conjugii prohibitione nehilum; sed leges & præcepta varia pro eo. Ac porro in N.T. Matth. 8, 14. Christus dicitur socrum Petri febricitantem miraculosè fanaffe. Uxorem igitur habuit Petrus. Insignis etiàm est locus 1 Cor. 9, 5. Annon licet nobis sororem uxorem circumducere, ut & reliquis Apostolis, & fratribus Domini, & Cephæ? Reliqui igitur Apoftoli, & fratres Domini, & nominatim Cephas five Petrus, uxorem quique suam circumduxerunt; eoque magis oneri fuerunt Ecclesiis; quod Paulus & Barnabas non item fecerunt, ut Ecclesiis parcerent.
units.tr: Second, the examples of the Patriarchs, the Prophets and prophetesses agree, as do those of the Nazirites, the Levites and the priests, and indeed of the high priest himself under the Old Testament. There is no prohibition of marriage in these, but various laws and precepts about it. Furthermore, under the New Testament, Matt. 8:14 says that Christ miraculously healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever. Peter therefore had a wife. The passage 1 Cor. 9:5 is also remarkable: Have we not the right to lead about a sister as a wife, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Therefore the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and especially Cephas or Peter, did lead about their wives; and they were all the more a burden to the churches, which Paul and Barnabas did not do, in order to spare the churches.

units.la: 3. Diserte etiam de Ministris N.T. Tit. 1, 5, 6. Conftituas oppidatim Presbyteros, sicut ego tibi ordinavi. Siquis est inculpabilis, unius uxoris vir, liberos habens fideles, qui non sint obnoxii criminis luxus, aut subjici nescii. Similiter 1 Tim. III, 2, 4, 5. Oportet igitur Episcopum irreprehensibilem esse, unius uxoris virum, -- Qui suæ domui bene præsit, qui liberos habeat subditos, cum omni honestate. Nam fiquis propria proprie domui praeesse nescit, quomodo Ecclesiam Dei curabit? Qui unius uxoris vir est, domui suae bene praeest, & liberos habet subditos, ac porro virtutibus & donis ibi commemoratis est instructus, is idoneus est qui eligatur in Episcopum.
units.tr: Third, the ministers of the New Testament are spoken of explicitly. Titus 1:5, 6: Appoint elders in every town, as I directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not open to accusation of debauchery or disobedience. Similarly 1 Tim. 3:2, 4, 5: Therefore a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife... who rules his own house well, who has his children in subjection, with all dignity. For if anyone does not know how to rule his own house, how will he care for the Church of God? He who is the husband of one wife, rules his own house well, has his children in subjection, and is further furnished with the virtues and gifts mentioned there, is fit to be chosen as bishop.

units.la: 4. Apostolus 1 Tim. 4, 1, 2, 3. diserte praedixit fore, ut posterioribus temporibus defecisserent quidam à fide, attenti spiritibus deceptoribus ac doctrinis Daemoniorum; Prohibentium contrahere Matrimonium, &c. Unde liquet, prohibitionem Matrimonii & Esculentorum sub N. T. non esse doctrinam Dei, Apostolorum, fidorumque Doctorum; sed deceptorum, hypocritarum, imo & Daemoniorum. Quod accipiendum de prohibitione tum Matrimonii; tum etiam Alimentorum, quae & quatenus Deus concessit ad usum rectum & pium; unde nullo saltem modo excipi debet Matrimonium Ministrorum Ecclesiasticorum, cujus concessionem & usum ipse Apostolus, eodem Spiritu, quo hanc defectionem praedixit, etiam docuit praecedenti cap. III.
units.tr: Fourth, the Apostle 1 Tim. 4:1, 2, 3 clearly foretold that in later times some would fall away from the faith, attending to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons; forbidding marriage, etc. From this it is clear that the prohibition of marriage and of foods under the New Testament is not the doctrine of God, of the Apostles, or of faithful teachers, but of deceivers, hypocrites, and indeed of demons. This is to be understood of the prohibition both of marriage and of foods, which God has granted for right and pious use. Hence the marriage of ecclesiastical ministers should in no way be excepted, since its permission and use the Apostle himself taught, by the same Spirit by whom he foretold this apostasy, in the preceding chapter 3.

units.la: XC. Obj. 1. Salvator noster ex Virgine natus est: atque ipse coelebs vixit. Ergo Resp. Natus est ex Virgine; sed Viro desponsata, & in familiam ejus assumta: nec ipse contraxit Matrimonium secundum carnem; quia non venerat Genus humanum carnali generatione propagaturus; sed per sui ipsius oblationem sibi semen spirituale acquisiturus: Isf. LIII, 10.
units.tr: XC. Obj. 1. Our Saviour was born of a virgin, and he himself lived unmarried. Therefore... Answer. He was born of a virgin, but betrothed to a man and received into his family. Nor did he himself enter into marriage according to the flesh, because he had not come to propagate the human race by carnal generation, but to acquire for himself a spiritual seed by offering himself: Isa. 53:10.

units.la: Obj. 2. Paulus quoque coelebs vixit; 1 Cor. 7, 7, 8. Resp. Esto. Verum & ipse scripsit, 7. Sed unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem ita, alius autem ita. Qui igitur donum ex Deo habent non ad Coelibatum, sed ad Conjugium iis Conjugio nequaquam est interdicendum, Et 9. Quod si se non continent, Matrimonium contrahant: nam melius est matrimonium contrahere, quam uri. Qui igitur in conscientia turbantur eâ causâ, & in exercitiis suis piis impediuntur, remedium à Deo
units.tr: Obj. 2. Paul also lived unmarried: 1 Cor. 7:7, 8. Answer. Granted. But he also wrote, v. 7: But each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that. Therefore those who have a gift from God not for celibacy but for marriage must by no means be forbidden marriage. And v. 9: But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore those who are troubled in conscience on this account, and are hindered in their pious exercises, must certainly be permitted to use the remedy ordained and shown by God

units.la: Cap. IX. De Fœdere Legali. 553 à Deo ordinatum & monstratum adhibere omnino permittendi sunt. Vide ibid. 26, 35, 37.
units.tr: Chap. IX. Of the Legal Covenant. 553. ordained and shown by God, ought in every way to be permitted. See ibid. 26, 35, 37.

units.la: Obj. 3. Idem Apostolus monuit verf. 5. Ne fraudate alter alterum, nisi fiquid ex consensu ad tempus quoddam, ut vacetis jejunio & precibus. At Sacerdotes quotidie debent rei sacræ operam dare. Ergo. Resp. Apostolus non de qualicunque re sacra loquitur; sed de extraordinariis exercitiis supplicationis ejusmodi, ubi precibus & jejunio vacatur pariter. Interim ista de causa non semper, necnimis diu, ab usu Matrimonii abstinendum esse, docet verbis proxime sequentibus; Et rursum simul convenite, ne tentet vos Satanas, propter incontinentiam vestram. Imo ipse Conjugii usus Verbo & precibus etiam sanctificatur: 1 Tim. 4, 3, 5. Tit. 1, 15. Hebr. 13, 4. nedum cum omnibus exercitiis pietatis, qua publicis, qua privatis, fit ἁγιάζεται.
units.tr: Objection 3. The same Apostle warned in verse 5: "Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by consent for a certain time, that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer." But priests ought every day to labour at sacred work. Therefore... Answer: The Apostle is not speaking of any sacred work whatever, but of extraordinary exercises of supplication of this kind, where people give themselves equally to prayer and fasting. Meanwhile, for this reason, he teaches in the words immediately following that abstinence from the use of marriage is not to be practised always, nor for too long: "And come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." Indeed the very use of marriage is sanctified by the Word and prayer: 1 Tim. 4:3, 5; Titus 1:15; Heb. 13:4; and much more is it sanctified [ἁγιάζεται] by all the exercises of piety, both public and private.

units.la: Obj. 4. Tit. 1, 7, 8. Oportet Episcopum inculpabilem esse, temperantem, justum, pium, continentem & 1 Tim. 5, 22. Teipsum purum conserva. Ergo. Resp. Apostolus illo contextu ad Titum Matrimonium nequaquam prohibuit, vel exclusit; imo inclusit, tanquam legitimum medium continentiæ: ideo enim proxime præmisit, verf. 6. Si quis est inculpabilis, unius uxoris vir, liberos habens fideles, &c. Similiter altero ad Timotheum, voluit ut ipse ne quidem peccatis alienis communicaret, quemadmodum præcesserit proxime: non autem ut exisitimare deberet Matrimonium puritati adversum esse, saltem in Episcopo, qui ejusdem epistolæ cap. III, 2. ab eodem Apostolo edoctus erat; Oportet igitur Episcopum irreprehensibilem esse, unius uxoris virum, &c.
units.tr: Objection 4. Titus 1:7, 8: "A bishop must be blameless, temperate, just, holy, continent"; and 1 Tim. 5:22: "Keep yourself pure." Therefore... Answer: In that passage to Titus the Apostle by no means forbade or excluded marriage; rather he included it as a lawful means of continence. For this reason he had just before said, verse 6: "If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children," etc. Similarly in the other letter, to Timothy, he wished that he himself should not even share in the sins of others, as he had said just before; but he did not intend that marriage should be thought hostile to purity, at least in a bishop, who had been taught by the same Apostle in the same letter, chapter 3:2: "A bishop therefore must be blameless, the husband of one wife," etc.

units.la: Obj. 5. Aliqui Patres valde laudarunt & commendarunt Virginitatem & Cœlibatum; maxime in Ministris Ecclesiasticis: Hieronymus adversus Jovinianum, &c. Resp. Sed negamus ab initio fuisse sic. Clemens Alexandrinus Stromatum lib III. ferio talibus obsistit: atque idem egerunt alii. Memorabilis est sententia Ænèæ Sylvii, seu Papæ Pii II. quam commemorat Platina in ejus vita; Sacerdotibus magna ratione sublatas Nuptias, majori restituendas videri.
units.tr: Objection 5. Some Fathers greatly praised and commended virginity and celibacy, especially in ecclesiastical ministers: Jerome against Jovinian, etc. Answer: We deny that it was so from the beginning. Clement of Alexandria, in the third book of the Stromata, firmly opposes such views, and others have done the same. The saying of Aeneas Sylvius, or Pope Pius II, which Platina records in his life, is memorable: that marriage, taken away from priests for weighty reasons, seems rather to be restored for greater ones.

units.la: XCI. Perperàm quoque distinguunt iidem Adversarii inter primas Nuptias, & inter secundas post obitum priotis conjugis; quasi hæ minus essent bonæ; & personam omnino redderent inhabilem ad ordinem Ecclesiasticum. Hic autem à Romanensibus non adeo discrepant Græci; qui mortuâ priore conjuge, non permittunt Ministrum Ecclesiasticum transire ad secundas Nuptias; aut si quis extra S. Ministerium constitutus secundas Nuptias contraxerit, eum, tanquam διγαμον, à Ministerio arcent. Malè. Nam 1. quæ rationes suadent Nuptias primas, mortuâ conjuge suadere etiam possunt secundas, vel tertias; utpote, Non bonum est, hominem esse solum, &c. Item, Propter fornications suam quisque uxorem habeto, & proprium quæque virum habeto; &c.
units.tr: XCI. The same adversaries likewise wrongly distinguish between first marriages and second marriages after the death of the first spouse, as if the latter were less good and rendered the person wholly unfit for the ecclesiastical order. Here the Greeks do not differ greatly from the Romanists: when a former spouse has died, they do not permit an ecclesiastical minister to pass to a second marriage; or if anyone who has not been placed in the holy ministry has contracted a second marriage, they exclude him from the ministry as a digamous man [διγαμον]. This is wrong. For, first, the reasons that recommend first marriage, when a spouse has died, can also recommend second or third marriages; for example, "It is not good for man to be alone," etc. Likewise, "Let each man have his own wife because of fornication, and let each woman have her own husband," etc.

units.la: 2. Paulus diserte non minùs de viduis, quam de cœlibus, 1 Cor.7,8,9. Quod si se non continent: Matrimonium contrahant. Atque iterum. 39. Uxor alligata est legi quamdiu vivit vir ipsius: quod si obdormiverit vir ipsius, libera est ad cui velit nubendum; tantum in Domino. Et de mulieribus viduis, 1 Tim. V, 14. Velim igitur juniores nubere, &c.
units.tr: Second, Paul expressly speaks no less of widows than of the unmarried, 1 Cor. 7:8, 9: "But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry." And again, verse 39: "A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has fallen asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord." And concerning widowed women, 1 Tim. 5:14: "I desire therefore that the younger women marry," etc.

units.la: 3. Christus casum sibi propositum de muliere septem maritis ex ordine nuptâ, Matth. 22, 25,26. minimè improbavit; quasi posteriores nuptiæ fuissent illicitæ, vel minus bonæ.
units.tr: Third, Christ did not in the least disapprove of the case put to him of a woman who was married in succession to seven husbands, Matt. 22:25, 26, as though the later marriages had been unlawful or less good.

units.la: 4. Manifesta est ratio; quia persona mortua non amplius habet partem in hac vitâ; neque consequenter impedire potest, quò minùs qui fuit ejus maritus, aut quæ uxor, transeat ad altera vota.
units.tr: Fourth, the reason is plain: a dead person no longer has a share in this life, and consequently cannot hinder the surviving husband or wife from passing to other vows.

units.la: Obj. In Episcopo, vel etiam Diacono eligendo, requiritur Tit.1,6. 1 Tim. 3,2,12. ut sit unius uxoris vir: ergò. Resp. Scil. non διγαμος, aut πολύγαμος simultaneus ; qui pariter haberet consuetudinem cum uxoribus pluribus; vel unâ, aut pluribus male repudiatis aliam duxisset, ex vitioso more tum Judæorum tum etiam Gentilium ; à quo non statim omnes, Ecclesiæ Christianæ nomen dantes, erant immunes;quique tolerari potuit aliquantisper, per prima illa initia,in Christianis novitiis : at quo minus istud malum permaneret, & defenderetur in Ecclesiâ, saltem tales à S Ministerio debuerunt arceri. Aliter res habet in digamiâ successiva : cujus enim prior conjux diem suum obiit, is desiit illi obstrictus esse conjugali vinculo, alteram vero ducens uxorem, non duarum uxorum , sed unius vir iterum evadit. Similiter de vidua ad Ecclesiæ ministerium allegenda, cautum est 1 Tim. 5, 9. ut fuerit unius viri uxor.
units.tr: Objection. In choosing a bishop, or even a deacon, it is required (Titus 1:6; 1 Tim. 3:2, 12) that he be "the husband of one wife"; therefore... Answer: Namely, not a man who is digamous or polygamous [πολύγαμος] at the same time, who would at once keep company with several wives, or who, having one or several wives badly put away, had taken another, following the wicked custom both of the Jews and of the Gentiles; from which not all who gave their names to the Christian Church were at once free. Such a custom could be tolerated for a while in the first beginnings, among novice Christians; but so that this evil should not remain and be defended in the Church, such men at least ought to have been excluded from the holy ministry. The matter is otherwise with successive digamy. For when a man's first wife has died, he has ceased to be bound to her by the marriage bond, and in taking another wife he becomes again the husband of one wife, not of two. Similarly, concerning a widow to be enrolled for the ministry of the Church, it is provided in 1 Tim. 5:9 that she should have been "the wife of one husband."

units.la: XCII. Sed nulli homini solvere Matrimonii vinculum licet; Matth. 19, 6. Solutum tamen, vel non fuisse contractum, ex Verbo Dei declarare licet, quibus facultatem illam tum in Politiâ, tum in Ecclesiâ ipse dedit, qui non est incompositi status auctor, sed pacis, atque omnia decenter & ordine fieri vult ; 1 Cor. 14, 33. 40. Talem igitur casum unum expressit Christus, Matth. 5, 32. Quisquis dimiserit uxorem suam, extra rationem fornicationis, facit ut ea moechetur. Et 19, 9. Quicunque dimiserit uxorem suam, nisi ob fornicationem, & aliam duxerit, moechatur : & qui dimissam duxerit, moechatur. Ubi exceptio causæ fornicationis, sive adulterii, ostendit, virum, qui dimittit uxorem adulteram, & aliam ducit, non peccare. Totalis dimissio intelligitur ; non partialis, quoad thorum tantum : de illa enim erat sermo, & diserte exprimitur, de alia in prioris locum ducenda. Nisi ista fiant adulterii causâ, moechatur vir sic dimittens & ducens ; quia prius vinculum non est solutum: quin & mulier conditionem repudii facile accipiens, atque alteri nubens, similiter adulterium committit; nec non alter ille qui sic dimissam ducit.
units.tr: XCII. Yet it is lawful for no man to dissolve the bond of marriage (Matt. 19:6). Nevertheless, it is lawful to declare from the Word of God that a marriage has been dissolved, or that it was never contracted, since he who is the author not of disorder but of peace, and who wills that all things be done decently and in order, gave this power both in the state and in the Church (1 Cor. 14:33, 40). Christ therefore expressed one such case: Matt. 5:32, "Whoever puts away his wife, apart from the reason of fornication, makes her commit adultery." And 19:9: "Whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her who has been put away commits adultery." Here the exception of the cause of fornication, or adultery, shows that the husband who puts away an adulterous wife and marries another does not sin. What is meant is total dismissal, not partial, as regards the bed only; for it was of that that he spoke, and it is expressly stated that another is to be taken in the place of the first. Unless these things are done for the cause of adultery, the husband who so puts away and marries commits adultery, because the first bond has not been dissolved; and the wife too, who readily accepts the condition of divorce and marries another, likewise commits adultery; and so does that other man who takes her who has been put away in this way.

units.la: Alterum casum Matrimonii dirimendi expressit Apostolus, 1 Cor. 7, 12, 13, 15. Si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem, quæ libens consentiat ad habitandum cum eo, ne eam dimittito: Et uxor, quæ habet virum infidelem, qui libens consentiat ad habitandum cum eâ, ne eum dimittito.At si infidelis discedit, discedatur: non est servituti subjectus frater, aut soror, in hujusmodi rebus. Scilicet in malitiosa illa desertione pars deserens, similiter ut adulterium committens, reipsâ rumpit vinculum mutuum, ac definit esse una caro cum alterâ: ac proinde hæc definit etiam obligari. Confer 1 Tim. 5, 9. Quodsi quis suis, & maxime domesticis, non providet, fidem abnegavit, & est infideli deterior. Consequenter ubi constat de adulterio, aut de malitiosa desertione, Magistratus Politicus Politicè potest declarare, partem innocentem jam esse ab illo vinculo liberatam, ac proinde habilem ad contrahendum alterum Matrimonium. Quemadmodum Theologi ex Verbo Dei etiam declarare possunt, istam à priore vinculo libertatem, ac de novo contrahendi facultatem, in conscientiâ coram Deo esse licitam & validam.
units.tr: The Apostle expressed another case in which marriage may be dissolved, 1 Cor. 7:12, 13, 15: "If any brother has an unbelieving wife, who is willing to dwell with him, let him not put her away; and a woman who has an unbelieving husband, who is willing to dwell with her, let her not put him away. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; a brother or a sister is not under bondage in such matters." Clearly, in that malicious desertion the party who deserts, just as one committing adultery, in fact breaks the mutual bond and ceases to be one flesh with the other; and consequently that party is no longer bound either. Compare 1 Tim. 5:8: "But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." Consequently, where adultery or malicious desertion is established, the civil magistrate may declare politically that the innocent party has now been freed from that bond, and so is able to contract another marriage. In the same way theologians may also declare from the Word of God that this freedom from the former bond, and the power of marrying anew, are lawful and valid in conscience before God.

units.la: Obj. Matth. 19, 6. Quod Deus conjunxit, homo ne separato: Ergò. Resp. Inde solum sequitur, peccasse eos, qui adulterio, aut malitiosâ desertione, separationem fecerunt; non vero, peccare eos, qui illam factam esse deinceps pronunciant.
units.tr: Objection. Matt. 19:6: "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder." Therefore... Answer: From this it follows only that those who separated by adultery or malicious desertion have sinned; it does not follow that those who afterwards declare that the separation has been made are sinning.

units.la: XCIII. Sed nequaquam admittimus alias Matri- monii prorsùs dirimendi causas.
units.tr: XCIII. But we by no means admit any other causes for completely dissolving a marriage.

units.la: Imò verò negamus, contra Pontificios, Divortium Religionis gratia, h. e, vitæ Monasticæ ergo, faciendum esse; tum in Matrimonio consummato, quamvis forte communis consensus isto tempore adsit; tum etiam in Matrimonio rato, quamvis non consummato. Et quidem 1. ob generalem Christi sententiam, Matth. 19, 6. Non amplius sunt duo, sed una caro: quod ergo Deus conjunxit, homo ne separato.
units.tr: Indeed, against the Papists we deny that divorce is to be made for the sake of religion, that is, for the sake of monastic life: both in a consummated marriage, even if by common consent at that time, and in a ratified marriage that is not consummated. And first, because of the general saying of Christ, Matt. 19:6. So they are no longer two, but one flesh: what therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.

units.la: 2. Specialius cavit Apostolus, 1 Cor. 7, 5. Nefraudate alter alterum; nisi si quid ex consensu ad tempus quoddam, ut vacetis jejunio & precibus; & rursum simul convenite, ne tentet vos Satanas propter incontinentiam vestram. Unde satis manifestum est, quod non liceat Matrimonium ratum prorsus abrumpere Religionis causa: nunc enim, eo ipso quod Matrimonium ratum est, uxor proprium corpus non amplius habet in potestate; sed vir: similiter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate; sed uxor: 1 Cor. 7, 4. Atque item, quod personae, quarum Matrimonium est consummatum, ne quidem consensu mutuo id prorsus debeant abrumpere; cum ob rationem adjectam, usum solummodo intermittere iis liceat ad quoddam tempus.
units.tr: 2. The Apostle gave a more specific warning, 1 Cor. 7:5. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a certain time, that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer; and then come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence. From this it is sufficiently clear that it is not lawful to break off a ratified marriage altogether on account of religion. For now, by the very fact that the marriage is ratified, the wife no longer has power over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife, 1 Cor. 7:4. And likewise, persons whose marriage is consummated ought not to dissolve it entirely even by mutual consent; for, for the reason added, they may be permitted to abstain from its use only for a certain time.

units.la: 3. Non licet Liberis, arbitratu proprio, se, aut sua, Parentibus suis subtrahere, Religionis etiam Divinitus institutae causa, ad quam illi speciale iliusmodi mandatum non habent: Matth. 15, 5, 6. Multo minus id licet alteri Conjugum, ubi Matrimonium modo ratum est, quamvis non consummatum.
units.tr: 3. Children may not, at their own discretion, withdraw themselves or their goods from their parents, even on the ground of religion divinely instituted, for which they have no such special command: Matt. 15:5, 6. Much less is this permitted to one of the spouses, where the marriage is only ratified and not consummated.

units.la: 4. Vita Monastica prorsus superstitiosa est, & ab hominibus male introducta, sub Religionis praetextu. Eo magis igitur hic quadrat illud Christi, Matth. 15, 6. Irritum fecistis praeceptum Dei per traditionem vestram.
units.tr: 4. Monastic life is utterly superstitious, and was badly introduced by men under the pretext of religion. All the more, therefore, does that saying of Christ fit here, Matt. 15:6. You have made void the commandment of God through your tradition.

units.la: XCIV. Similiter contra Anabaptistas quosdam afferimus, non alias legitimi Divortii causas esse admittendas; & specialius Divortium propter Excommunicationem alterius partis non esse licitum: nam 1. tale Divortium in SS. Literis nusquam docetur, aut approbatur.
units.tr: XCIV. Similarly, against certain Anabaptists we maintain that no other causes of lawful divorce are to be admitted; and more specifically, that divorce on account of the excommunication of one party is not lawful. For, first, such a divorce is nowhere taught or approved in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: 2. Matrimonium ad statum naturae pertinet, atque ex eo ad statum gratiae & in Ecclesiam traductum est: Excommunicatio vero pertinet ad Ecclesiam institutam. Gratia autem naturam perficit quidem, sed minime destruit: ac proinde non destruit statum, qui jam ante lapsum obtinuit; sed sanctificat eum quoad fieri potest: 1 Cor. 7, 14.
units.tr: 2. Marriage belongs to the state of nature, and from there has been brought over into the state of grace and into the Church. Excommunication, however, belongs to the Church as instituted. Now grace indeed perfects nature, but by no means destroys it; and therefore it does not destroy the state that already obtained before the fall, but sanctifies it as far as possible: 1 Cor. 7:14.

units.la: 3. Excommunicatus haberi quidem debet ut Ethnicus & Publicanus; Matth. 18, 17. sed non deteriore loco : at vero cum Ethnico, vel publicano, quia talis est, non licet Divortium facere: 1 Cor. 7, 12, 13.
units.tr: 3. The excommunicated person is indeed to be held as a heathen and a tax collector, Matt. 18:17, but not in a worse position than that. Yet with a heathen or a tax collector, precisely because he is such, it is not lawful to make a divorce: 1 Cor. 7:12, 13.

units.la: Obj. Apostolus prohibet, ne fideles cum excommunicatis habeant commercium, ne commisceantur, nec unà edant quidem; 1 Cor. 5, 9. 11. 2 Thess. III, 15. Ergò. Resp. Omnis non necessaria familiaritas prohibetur, in ordine ad Ecclesiasticam societatem, & ad communicationem in peccatis, ob quæ illi sunt excommunicati, & de quibus ista ratione ad pudorem debent adduci. Confer Tit. III, 10, 11. 2 Joh. 10, 11. Verùm sic non laxantur vincula Politica, aut OEconomica, quibus alii aliis obstricti sunt.
units.tr: Objection. The Apostle forbids the faithful to have dealings with the excommunicated, to mix with them, or even to eat with them: 1 Cor. 5:9, 11; 2 Thess. 3:15. Therefore... Answer. Every unnecessary familiarity is forbidden, with regard to ecclesiastical fellowship and to communion in the sins for which they have been excommunicated, and by which they ought to be brought to shame. Compare Titus 3:10, 11; 2 John 10, 11. But in this way the political or domestic bonds by which some are bound to others are not loosened.

units.la: XCV. Ex loco Deut. 24, 1,-4. patet, inter Israelitas usitatum fuisse Repudium, & Politicè permissum, aut toleratum, ad evitanda graviora mala in Politia; atque adeo non punitum, nec prohibitum statuto Politico: non fuit tamen Ethicè permissum, aut in conscientia coram Deo licitum. Probatur hoc 1. ex assertione Christi, Matth. 5, 13, 32. Dictum est autem; Quisquis dimiserit uxorem suam, det ei libellum abscessionis. Ego vero dico vobis, Quisquis dimiserit uxorem suam, extra rationem fornicationis, facit ut ea mæchetur. &c. Eadem sententia repetitur, 19, 9. Atqui Christus non fuit novus Legis-lator; sed eadem Lex moralis indè ab initio fuit communis norma morum vivendi; quam Christus propterea à corruptelis Pharisæorum, aliorumque similium, repurgavit, sùeque integritati restituit.
units.tr: XCV. From Deut. 24:1-4 it is clear that divorce (repudium) was customary among the Israelites and was permitted or tolerated by the state, to avoid greater evils in the commonwealth. Thus it was neither punished nor forbidden by political statute; yet it was not permitted ethically, nor was it lawful in conscience before God. This is proved, first, from the assertion of Christ, Matt. 5:31, 32. It has been said, Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, apart from the reason of fornication, makes her commit adultery, etc. The same saying is repeated at 19:9. But Christ was not a new lawgiver; rather, the same moral law has been the common rule of living from the beginning. Christ therefore cleansed it from the corruptions of the Pharisees and others like them, and restored it to its integrity.

units.la: 2. Ex probatione Christi, per argumenta à prima institutione Matrimonii desumta, cum ipsi quæstio à Pharisæis esset propósita, 19, 3,- 6. Licene hominem dimittere uxorem suam quavis ex causa? Ille respondens dixit eis; Non legistis, (Gen. I, 27,) Opificem ab initio fecisse masculum & feminam? Et dixisse; (II, 24.) Propterea relinquet homo patrem & matrem, & agglutinabitur uxori suæ, & qui duo fuerant, erunt una caro. Itaque non amplius sunt duo, sed una caro. Quod ergo Deus conjunxit, homo ne separato.
units.tr: 2. From Christ's proof, by arguments drawn from the first institution of marriage, when the Pharisees put the question to him, Matt. 19:3-6. Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause? He answered them: Have you not read that the Creator made them male and female from the beginning, and said (Gen. 2:24), For this cause a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh? So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.

units.la: 3. Ex defensione istius sententiæ, tum adversus Pharisæorum objectionem; tum etiam adversus difficultatem ab ipsis Discipulis motam; Matth. 19,7,8. Dicunt ei (Pharisæi); Cur ergo Moses præcepit dare libellum dimissionis, & eam dimittere? Dicit eis; Quoniam Moses pro duritia cordis vestri permisit vobis dimittere uxores vestras: cæterum à principio non fuit itâ. Porro autem 10, 11. Dicunt ei Discipuli ejus; Si tale est negotium hominis cum uxore, non expedit uxorem ducere. Ipse vero dixit eis; Non omnes sunt capaces hujus sermonis, sed ii quibus datum est. Scilicet; ab hac nubendi necessitate non possunt esse omnes liberi, nisi quibus datum est Divinitus. Confer 1 Cor. 7, 7.
units.tr: 3. From the defence of this saying, both against the objection of the Pharisees and against the difficulty raised by the Disciples themselves, Matt. 19:7, 8. They say to him (the Pharisees): Why then did Moses command to give a bill of divorce and to put her away? He says to them: Because Moses, for the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to put away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. Further, at 10, 11: His disciples say to him: If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry. But he said to them: Not all are capable of this saying, but only those to whom it is given. That is, not all can be free from this necessity of marrying, but only those to whom it has been given by God. Compare 1 Cor. 7:7.

units.la: 4. In eandem sententiam optime etiam accipitur locus Mal. II, 14, 15, 16. Quoniam Jehova testis est inter te, & inter uxorem adolescentiæ tuæ, in quam tu prævaricaris; cum ipsa sit socia tua, & uxor fœderis tui. Et an non unum fecit; (Adamum scil. ex cujus costa formavit Evam; eamque sic illi conjunxit, ut isti duo essent in carnem unam.) dum reliduum spiritus erat ei? (Ita ut plures feminas ab initio creare potuisset, & Adamo conjungere; nisi duorum tantum individua societas in Matrimonio ipsi placuisset) Et quid unus iste? Quæsivit semen Dei. (Prolem legitimam, secundum ipsius Dei ordinationem & benedictionem.) Idcirco cavete in spiritu vestro, & ne prævaricemini. Sic Deus populum ab isto peccato dehortatur.
units.tr: 4. The passage Mal. 2:14-16 is also very well taken in the same sense: Because the LORD is witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. And did he not make one (namely Adam, from whose rib he formed Eve and joined her to him, so that the two should be one flesh), while the spirit remained in him? (So that he could have created many women from the beginning and joined them to Adam, had not the society of only two individuals in marriage pleased him.) And what did that one seek? The seed of God. (Legitimate offspring, according to God's own ordinance and blessing.) Therefore take heed to your spirit, and do not deal treacherously. Thus God dissuades the people from this sin.

units.la: XCVI. Polygamia hic intelligitur, cum quis maritus plures uxores habet simul. Ea 1. adversatur primæ institutioni Matrimonii; Gen. II, 23, 24. ubi Eva ex costa Adami formata, ei Connubio juncta est; atque edictum, ut etiam deinceps maritus & uxor essent in carnem unam. Istòc Christus provocat, Matth. 19, 5. Qui duo fuerant, erunt una caro. Atque item Paulus, Eph. 5, 31. non solùm repetivit eadem: sed & similitudinem transtulit ad Ecclesiæ unionem cum Christo; & cuique marito officia sua circa uxorem suam indè deduxit, verf. 33, 34,
units.tr: XCVI. Polygamy is understood here, when a husband has several wives at the same time. This is, first, contrary to the first institution of marriage, Gen. 2:23, 24, where Eve, formed from Adam's rib, was joined to him in wedlock, and the command was given that husband and wife should also thereafter be one flesh. Christ appeals to this, Matt. 19:5: The two shall be one flesh. Likewise Paul, Eph. 5:31, not only repeats the same words but also transfers the likeness to the union of the Church with Christ, and from it derives each husband's duties toward his own wife, vv. 33, 34.

units.la: 2. Idem Paulus etiàm diserte, 1 Cor. 7, 2. Propter fornications, suam quisque uxorem habeto, & proprium quemque virum habeto. Et verf. 4. Uxor proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed vir: similiter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed uxor.
units.tr: 2. The same Paul also says expressly, 1 Cor. 7:2. Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. And v. 4: The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife.

units.la: 3. In Episcopo etiàm, vel Presbytero eligendo, prærequiritur conditio, ut sit irreprehensibilis, sive inculpabilis, unius uxoris vir; 1 Tim. 3, 2. Tit. 1, 6. Atque item, ut Diaconi sint unius uxoris mariti; 1 Tim. III, 12. Quin, & de viduâ in Ecclesiæ ministerium allegendâ, cautum est, 1 Tim. V, 9. ut fuerit unius viri uxor. Unde omninò sequitur, polygamum simultaneum non esse irreprehensibilem, aut inculpabilem.
units.tr: 3. Also in choosing a bishop or elder, it is a prerequisite that he be blameless, or irreproachable, the husband of one wife: 1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6. Likewise, deacons are to be husbands of one wife: 1 Tim. 3:12. Moreover, concerning a widow to be enrolled for the ministry of the Church, it is provided, 1 Tim. 5:9, that she has been the wife of one husband. Whence it altogether follows that a man who is simultaneously polygamous is not blameless or irreproachable.

units.la: 4. Imò & vestigium aliquod istius Juris naturalis comparet in quibusdam Bestiis; utpote in Avibus illis, quarum solarum usum admisit Deus olim in Sacrificiis; Columbis & Turturibus: similiter etiàm in Oloribus, &c.
units.tr: 4. Indeed, some trace of this natural right also appears in certain beasts, namely in those birds alone whose use God once permitted in sacrifices: doves and turtledoves. Likewise also in swans, etc.

units.la: XCVII. Polygamia adhùc obtinet, & licita puta- tur, apud Muhammedanos, & Gentiles: eadem fuit sententiæ quorundam fanaticorum; utpote Bernardini Ochini, Davidis Georgii, &c.
units.tr: XCVII. Polygamy still prevails, and is thought lawful, among the Muhammadans and the Gentiles. The same opinion was held by certain fanatics, such as Bernardino Ochino and David George, etc.

units.la: Obj. 1. Viro jure Divino concessa est potestas præ uxore. Ergò. Resp. Sic tamen ut hæc sit ejus socia: Mal. II, 14. Ubi quis autem plures uxores ducit, tùm hæ deprimuntur nimium: tùm ille multis se difficultatibus implicat, quibus ejus potestas vel prorsùs infringitur, vel in tyrannidem degenerat.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Authority over the wife has been granted to the husband by divine right. Therefore... Resp. Yet in such a way that she is his companion: Mal. 2, 14. But where someone marries several wives, then these are too much oppressed, and he entangles himself in many difficulties, by which his authority is either utterly broken or degenerates into tyranny.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ad majorem Generis humani propagationem videtur illa conducere. Ergò. Resp. Verùm non est quærenda qualiscunque propagatio; sed secundum ipsius Dei duntaxat ordinationem; τὰ δὲ γένη ὡρισμένα, Act. 17,28.
units.tr: Obj. 2. That seems to conduce to a greater propagation of the human race. Therefore... Resp. But propagation of whatever kind is not to be sought; it must be according to God's own ordinance alone: τὰ δὲ γένη ὡρισμένα [the times and the boundaries of their habitation were determined], Acts 17:28.

units.la: Obj. 3. Polygamia suam vetustatem habet: & nititur exemplis plurimorum Patriarcharum. Ergo. Resp. Sed ab initio non fuit ita; Matth. 19,8. & alia quædam peccata, utpote Mendacium atque Homicidium, antiquiora sunt; Job. 8,44. neque tamen propterea desierunt esse peccata. Lamech, Adami per Kaïnum trinepos, primus legitur duas uxores duxisse, Genef. 4, 19, 23. Jacobum, Davidem, Salomonem, aliosque Polygamiâ peccasse dicimus; quia contra primævam & sanctam Matrimonii institutionem, & ordinem quærendi feminis Dei, egerunt; neque quicquam constat de dispensatione circa illam Legem in illis à Deo factâ.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Polygamy has its antiquity and rests on the examples of many patriarchs. Therefore... Resp. But it was not so from the beginning, Matt. 19:8; and other sins, such as lying and murder, are older, John 8:44, and yet they have not on that account ceased to be sins. Lamech, the great-great-grandson of Adam through Cain, is the first read of as having taken two wives, Gen. 4:19, 23. We say that Jacob, David, Solomon and others sinned by polygamy, because they acted against the primeval and holy institution of marriage and the order God had set for seeking offspring; nor is anything established about a dispensation from God in their case regarding that law.

units.la: Instr. Non subjicitur illis narrationibus reprehensio, vel improbatio, aut pœnitentia. Resp. Improbatio satis colligitur ex primævâ Matrimonii institutione, & aliorum praxi meliori. Neque mirandum, si speciali ejusmodi pœnitentia non commemoretur, cùm & plurima alia facta silentio involvantur. Loti ebrietas, & incestus cum utraque suâ filia, commemoratur similiter, non expressâ ibidem reprehensione, vel improbatione, aut speciali illius pœnitentiâ de istis peccatis, Gen. 19, 30, ~.
units.tr: Instr. No rebuke, disapproval or repentance is attached to those narratives. Resp. Disapproval is sufficiently gathered from the primeval institution of marriage and from the better practice of others. Nor is it strange if no special repentance of this kind is recorded, since many other deeds are also passed over in silence. The drunkenness of Lot and his incest with each of his daughters is likewise recorded, without any express rebuke or disapproval there, or any special repentance for those sins, Gen. 19:30 ff.

units.la: Obj. 4. 2 Sam. 12, 7, 8, 9. Sic ait Jehovah Deus Israëlis, Ego unxi te, ut esses Rex super Israëlem: - Dedique tibi domum domini tui, & uxores domini tui in sinum tuum: &c. Ergo. Resp. Sic beneficia in ipsum collata, eaque varia, recensset Deus: quibus ille ad majorem gratitudinem, atque obedientiam Deo præstandam, permoveri debuisset: etiam bonum aliquod jucundum, quod ille per providentiam Dei realem, accedente permissione quâdam physicâ, & tolerantiâ quasi politicâ acceperat, in uxoribus quoque Saulis: scil. cùm haberet uxores adeò multas, tantò magis abstinere debuit ab uxore, quæ Urijæ erat unica, ab adulterio sic qualificato, quin & cœde ei addità. Sed ipsius πολυγαμίας permissio ethica indè colligi non debet: non magis quàm adulterii & incestûs ex illis, quæ sequuntur verf. 12. Tu fecisti abscondite; ego faciam hoc coram toto Israële, & coram Sole.
units.tr: Obj. 4. 2 Sam. 12:7, 8, 9. Thus says Jehovah, God of Israel: I anointed you to be king over Israel... and I gave you your master's house, and your master's wives into your bosom, etc. Therefore... Resp. God recounts in this way the benefits conferred upon him, various as they were, so that he ought to have been moved to greater gratitude and obedience toward God; he also received some pleasant good through God's real providence, with a certain physical permission and a quasi-political toleration, namely in the wives of Saul too. Since he had so many wives, he ought all the more to have refrained from the wife of Uriah, who was his only one, from adultery so qualified, and indeed with murder added. But a permission of polygamy itself should not be inferred from this on ethical grounds, any more than of adultery and incest from those things which follow in verse 12: You did it secretly; I will do this before all Israel, and before the sun.

units.la: XCVIII. Socinianî perperam existimant, Christum & Apostolos, huic præcepto addidisse pro N. T. 1, quòd Concupiscentia alienæ uxoris etiam sit adulterium: 2. quòd Polygamia, ac Divortium extra casum adulterii, sint illicita; & 3. quòd omnis Scortatio, impuritas, turpiloquium, gestûs & contrectationes libidinosæ, sint prohibita.
units.tr: XCVIII. The Socinians wrongly suppose that Christ and the Apostles added to this precept, for the New Testament: 1. that the desire for another's wife is also adultery; 2. that polygamy, and divorce outside the case of adultery, are unlawful; and 3. that all fornication, impurity, obscene speech, and lustful gestures and touches are forbidden.

units.la: Ad primum enim quod attinet; Concupiscentia alienæ uxoris adulterio accensenda est: quoniam 1. Præcepto huic spirituali, qualis est tota Lex, etiam adversatur; tanquam adulterium cordis.
units.tr: For as to the first point: the desire for another's wife is to be counted as adultery, because 1. it is also contrary to this spiritual precept, which the whole Law is; as adultery of the heart.

units.la: 2. Propterea Salomon id serio prohibuit; Prov. 6, 25. Jeremias reprehendit; v, 8. & Job tam sedulò vitavit; xxxi, 1.
units.tr: 2. For this reason Solomon seriously forbade it, Prov. 6:25; Jeremiah rebukes it, 5:8; and Job avoided it so diligently, 31:1.

units.la: 3. Accensetur malis fructibus ebrietatis: Prov. 23, 33.
units.tr: 3. It is counted among the evil fruits of drunkenness: Prov. 23:33.

units.la: 4. Decimo Decalogi præcepto diserte prohibetur concupiscentia uxoris alienæ, quæ deliberationem præcedit: quæ verò suscipitur deliberato consilio, & sic intentionem talis objecti magis formatam & specialem completitur; magis etiam censeri debet peccatum, & ad hoc præceptum referri.
units.tr: 4. The tenth precept of the Decalogue expressly forbids the desire for another's wife, which comes before deliberation. But when it is taken up by deliberate counsel, and so completes a more formed and specific intention toward such an object, it ought all the more to be judged a sin and referred to this precept.

units.la: Quantum ad secundum: Polygamiam simultaneam, & Divortium extra casum adulterii, adversari primæ institutioni Matrimonii, atque adeò peccatis hoc præcepto prohibitis accenseri debere; non autem haberi pro nova quadam Christi prohibitione; patet ex sup. th. 95. & 96.
units.tr: As to the second point: that simultaneous polygamy and divorce outside the case of adultery are opposed to the first institution of marriage, and so ought to be counted among the sins forbidden by this precept, and not to be held as some new prohibition by Christ, is evident from the above, theses 95 and 96.

units.la: Quod ad tertium, peccata tùm oris, tùm operis, quæ tanquam adminicula subserviunt peccatis aliis, huic præcepto magis directè & aperte adversantibus, tàm in V. quàm in N. T. solent redargui. Vide Prov. 6,23,24. VII, 5,-27. Eccl. 7,5,6,7. Job. 31,1. Psal. 119,37. Prov. 5, 20. VII, 10,11, 12. Jef. 3, 16.Ezech. 16, 49. Prov. 23, 29,-35. Jef. 5, 11,-14. Hof. 4, 11. Am. 4, 4,-7. Quid quòd etiàm sub V, T. impudicitia cordis fuerit prohibita; quanto magis igitur ista oris, & operis?
units.tr: As to the third point: sins of the mouth and of the deed, which serve as aids to other sins that more directly and openly oppose this precept, are usually rebuked both in the Old and in the New Testament. See Prov. 6:23, 24; 7:5, 27; Eccl. 7:5, 6, 7; Job 31:1; Ps. 119:37; Prov. 5:20; 7:10, 11, 12; Jer. 3:16; Ezek. 16:49; Prov. 23:29–35; Isa. 5:11–14; Hos. 4:11; Amos 4:4–7. What of the fact that even under the Old Testament the impurity of the heart was forbidden? How much more, then, that of the mouth and of the deed?

units.la: XCIX. In Octavo præcepto supponitur distinctio dominiorum, de quâ vide sup. th. 12. §. 3. Adde, naturæ consentaneum esse, ut liberi Matrimonium ineuntes, distinctas familias constituant; atque adeò distincta etiàm habeant, vel acquirant media, quæ ad familiæ sustentationem necessaria sunt. Gen. II, 24.
units.tr: XCIX. The Eighth Precept presupposes the distinction of ownership, concerning which see above, thesis 12, §3. Add that it is in accordance with nature that children who enter marriage should set up separate households, and so should also have or acquire the means necessary for sustaining the family. Gen. 2:24.

units.la: Absurdè igitur fures aliqui disputare interdum præsumunt, omnia debere esse communia. Nec melius Monachi cœnobitæ; atque itèm Anabaptistæ quidam.
units.tr: Therefore some thieves absurdly presume at times to argue that all things ought to be held in common. No better are the cenobite monks, and likewise certain Anabaptists.

units.la: Nam 1. ostensum est, distincta rerum dominia in jure naturæ fundata esse.
units.tr: For 1. it has been shown that distinct ownership of things is founded in the law of nature.

units.la: 2. Nisi distincta forent: rerum dominia, nullus esset locus furtis, nullus justitiæ commutativæ.
units.tr: 2. Unless there were distinct ownerships of things, there would be no place for theft, and no place for commutative justice.

units.la: 3. Non posset liberalitas exerceri; nec specialius eleemosynæ erogari de nostro.
units.tr: 3. Liberality could not be exercised, nor could alms be given more particularly from what is ours.

units.la: 4. Periret etiàm istud officium, quòd Parentes debeant filiis thesauros congerere; 2 Cor. XII, 14.
units.tr: 4. That duty too would perish, by which parents ought to lay up treasures for their children; 2 Cor. 12:14.

units.la: Objicitur 1. exemplum Ecclesiæ primitivæ; Act. II. 44. IV, 32. Resp. 1. ex facto particulari fidelium istius temporis & loci, non sequitur jus universale, quod omnes semper debeant servare. 2. Neque illo ipso tempore omnes tenebantur privata rerum suarum dominia absolutè deponere: sed potuissent ea sibi servare: Actor. 5, 4. Verùm liberè ac liberaliter fideles tunc plurima contulerunt ad sustentationem pauperum, & in alios usûs Ecclesiasticos, prout persuadebat necessitas. 3. Imò etiàm mox ex illis, quæ
units.tr: It is objected 1. the example of the primitive Church; Acts 2:44; 4:32. Resp. 1. From a particular fact of the faithful of that time and place it does not follow that there is a universal right which all must always observe. 2. Nor at that very time were all bound absolutely to give up the private ownership of their goods; they could have kept them for themselves: Acts 5:4. But the faithful then freely and generously contributed very much for the support of the poor, and for other ecclesiastical uses, as necessity urged. 3. Indeed, soon afterwards distributions for the uses of the poor were made from those things which had been laid at the feet of the Apostles; and thus these portions became distinct possessions. Acts 4:34, 35: There was no one needy among them... but distribution was made to each as anyone had need. 4. Furthermore, from the common practice of other churches, from the use of collections and alms, from the prohibition of theft, etc., it is evident that there was not a community of all goods there, but distinct ownership of things.

units.la: ad pedes Apostolorum fuerunt deposita, facta sunt distributiones in usus pauperum; atque ita distincta possessiones istarum portionum. cap. IV, 34, 35. Nullus erat egenus inter eos:- distribuebatur autem singulis prout cuique opus erat. 4. Deinceps vero ex communi praxi aliarum Ecclesiarum, ex usu collestarum & eleemosynarum, ex furtorum prohibitione, &c. patet, non fuisse illic omnium bonorum communionem; sed distincta rerum dominia.
units.tr: were laid at the feet of the Apostles, and distributions were made for the use of the poor; and thus the possessions of those portions were distinct. Act. 4, 34, 35. There was no one needy among them... but distribution was made to each according as each had need. 4. Furthermore, from the common practice of the other churches, from the use of collections and alms, from the prohibition of theft, etc., it is plain that there was not a communion of all goods there, but distinct ownership of things.

units.la: Objicitur 2. Communio sanctorum. Resp. Ea potissimum consistit in pari fidelium unione mystica cum Christo, tanquam membrorum in unum corpus, sub isto capite; unde fluunt qualiacunque charitatis officia pro re natâ ergâ seinvicem exercenda; non autem absoluta illa communio bonorum temporalium.
units.tr: It is objected 2. The communion of saints. Resp. It consists chiefly in the equal mystical union of the faithful with Christ, as members in one body under this head; from which flow whatever offices of charity are to be exercised toward one another as occasion requires; not, however, an absolute communion of temporal goods.

units.la: C. Prohibetur interim etiàm Fœnus; iniquum scil. lucrum ex pecuniâ mutuo datâ. Non quidem omnem usuram rejicimus; h. e. quicquid ultra sortem recipitur; sed immoderatam. Aliquam enim usuram Deus permisit populo suo: Deut. 23, 20. Extranco fœnerabis. Hoc nimirum æquum est, ut dum alter meâ pecuniâ quæstum facit, ego partem aliquam istius quæstus recipiam: similiter ut si alteri agrum meum conserendum cedam, æquum est ut pro agro partem aliquam segetis, aut aliud quid æquivalens, recipiam. Confer 2 Cor. 8, 13, 14. & Matth. 7, 12.
units.tr: C. Meanwhile usury is also forbidden, that is, unfair gain from money lent. We do not, indeed, reject all interest, that is, whatever is received beyond the principal, but immoderate interest. For God permitted his people some interest: Deut. 23:20: To a foreigner you shall lend at interest. Clearly it is fair that while another makes a profit with my money, I should receive some part of that profit; likewise, if I give my field to another to sow, it is fair that for the field I should receive some part of the crop, or something else of equal value. Compare 2 Cor. 8:13, 14, and Matt. 7:12.

units.la: Iniquum vero fœnus censetur trisariâm:
units.tr: Usury, however, is judged to be unjust in three respects:

units.la: 1. Respectû objectorum; non debet accipi à depauperatis, vel attenuatis; qui non ad quæstum faciendum, sed necessitatis sublevandæ gratiâ, pecuniâm sibi mutuo dari petunt. Hic charitas postulat, ut gratis detur mutuo. Exod. 22, 25. Levit. 25, 35, 36, 37. Deut. 15, 11. XXIII, 19, 20. Similiter Luc. 6, 35, 36. Vide etiam Nehem. 5, 3, - 13.
units.tr: 1. With respect to the objects: it ought not to be taken from the impoverished or the straitened, who ask to be lent money not for the sake of making a profit but to relieve their need. Here charity requires that the loan be given free of charge. Exod. 22, 25. Levit. 25, 35, 36, 37. Deut. 15, 11. 23, 19, 20. Similarly Luke 6, 35, 36. See also Nehem. 5, 3–13.

units.la: 2. Respectû quantitatis; usura quæ accipietur licitè, non debet modum excedere; sed aptam pro-portioportionem fervare cum lucro, quod ex pecunia, accedente alterius industria, percipi solet. Ubi spectandus communis mutuantium consensus, experientia, & consuetudo. Si ergo communi usu receptum fit, ut ex centum mutuo sumtis solvantur quatuor, aut tria & semis, pro usura annua; nimirum accipere censendus est, qui duodecim, quindecim, viginti, vel amplius accipit; ubi scil. de sorte & usura pariter, non magis periclitatur quàm alii. Hoc palam adversatur æquabilitati, 2 Cor. 8, 13, 14. & legi charitatis, Levit. 19, 18. Matth. 22, 39. Rom. 13, 9. Matth. 7, 12. Luc. 6, 31. 1 Cor. 13, 5. Phil. 4, 5. Vide etiam, Psal. 15, 5, Prov. 28, 8. Ierem. 15, 10. Ezech. 22, 12. Luc. 19, 8.
units.tr: 2. With respect to the quantity: the interest that may lawfully be taken must not exceed a measure; it must keep a fitting proportion to the gain that is usually drawn from money when another's industry is added to it. Here the common consent of lenders, experience and custom are to be considered. If, therefore, it is the accepted common practice that from a hundred lent four or three and a half are paid as annual interest, then he is to be judged to take too much who takes twelve, fifteen, twenty or more; for in that case the lender is not exposed to any greater risk to his principal and interest together than others are. This plainly runs counter to equity, 2 Cor. 8, 13, 14, and to the law of charity, Levit. 19, 18; Matt. 22, 39; Rom. 13, 9; Matt. 7, 12; Luke 6, 31; 1 Cor. 13, 5; Phil. 4, 5. See also Psal. 15, 5; Prov. 28, 8; Jer. 15, 10; Ezek. 22, 12; Luke 19, 8.

units.la: Similiter etiam 3. respectu pignorum; omninò postulat charitas & æquitas, ne in securitatem sortis, vel etiam usuræ, accipiantur & retineantur vestimenta, vel instrumenta, necessaria, ut quis opera vocationis suæ obeat, Ecclesiam adeat, alibi honestè sese exhibeat, exercitia pietatis observet, adversus incommoda noćturna se tueatur, &c. Exod. xxii, 26, 27. Deut. xxiv, 6, 12, 13, 17. Ezech. xviii, 7, 12. xxxii, 15.
units.tr: Likewise, 3. with respect to pledges: charity and equity absolutely require that clothing or tools necessary for a man to carry out the work of his calling, to attend the Church, to present himself decently elsewhere, to observe the exercises of piety, or to protect himself against the discomforts of the night, etc., not be taken and kept as security for the principal or even for the interest. Exod. 22, 26, 27; Deut. 24, 6, 12, 13, 17; Ezek. 18, 7, 12; 33, 15.

units.la: CI. Hæ conditiones observari debent; & secun- dum eas judicium instituendum est de Judæis fœnerator- ibus, aliisque trapezitis.
units.tr: CI. These conditions ought to be observed, and according to them judgment is to be made concerning Jewish moneylenders and other bankers.

units.la: Objicitur 1. Diuturna tolerantia, permissio, vel etiam approbatio superioris Potestatis. Resp. Ea neminem liberat in foro conscientiæ & poli. Quibus vis hominibus superior est Deus, qui secundum suam ipsius Legem judicat.
units.tr: Objection 1: long toleration, permission, or even approval by the higher power. Answer: this frees no one in the forum of conscience and before God. Above every human power is God, who judges according to his own Law.

units.la: Obj. 2. Mercatores, majus lucrum percipiunt: nec tamen culpantur. Ergò. Resp. 1. Illud perpetuum non est. 2. Nec similem de mercibus accipiendis aut de pretio sibi solvendo, securitatem semper habent mercatores; sed plurima pericula eos experiri necesse est.
units.tr: Objection 2: merchants gain a greater profit, and yet they are not blamed. Therefore... Answer 1: that gain is not constant. 2: merchants do not always have the same certainty in receiving goods or in being paid the price; they must instead undergo many dangers.

units.la: 3. Quia
units.tr: 3. Because

units.la: 3. Quin & ipsis ratio habenda est, ne lucrum excedat æquitatem; neque in venditione peccent adversùs charitatem & misericordiam pauperibus debitam.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, account must also be taken of them, so that their gain does not exceed equity, and that they do not sin in selling against the charity and mercy owed to the poor.

units.la: Obj. 3. Necessitas postulat. Ergò. Resp. 1. Non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniat bonum. 2. Quomodò aliter subveniri possit hominibus cujuscunque conditionis mutuum petentibus, varia alibi exhibita sunt confilia.
units.tr: Objection 3: necessity demands it. Therefore... Answer 1: evil must not be done that good may come. 2: various other counsels for how people of any condition who ask for a loan may otherwise be helped have been set out elsewhere.

units.la: CII. Sed & contra Socinianos hîc notamus, Prohibitionem avaritiæ, atque itém luxus in alimentis & vestitû, non esse à Christo primùm profectam sub N. T. atque ità Legem eâ auctam ac perfectiorem redditam.
units.tr: CII. But also against the Socinians we note here that the prohibition of covetousness, and likewise of luxury in food and clothing, was not first introduced by Christ under the New Testament, and that the Law was not thereby increased and made more perfect.

units.la: Ad avaritiam enim quòd attinet, 1. David eàm deprecatur, tanquàm malam, & Legi Divinæ adversam; Psal. 119, 36, 37.
units.tr: For as far as covetousness is concerned: 1. David deprecates it as evil and contrary to the Divine Law; Psal. 119, 36, 37.

units.la: 2. Idem alios ab eâ dehortatur; Psal. 62, 11. Salomon comminatione etiàm absterret; Prov. 15, 27. & Deus reprehendit per Ezechielem; xxxiii, 31.
units.tr: 2. The same David dissuades others from it; Psal. 62, 11. Solomon also deters with a threat; Prov. 15, 27. And God rebukes it through Ezekiel; 33, 31.

units.la: 3. Iob protestatur, quòd ab eâ sibi caverit; xxxi, 16, -20, 24, 25.
units.tr: 3. Job declares that he guarded himself against it; 31, 16–20, 24, 25.

units.la: 4. Quin imò Exod. XX, 17. decimo Decalogi præcepto prohibita est concupiscentia omnium eorum, quæ sunt proximi nostri, etiàm in motibus primò primis: quantò magis igitur illicita, ac prohibita fuisse, censenda est avaritia?
units.tr: 4. Indeed, in Exod. 20, 17, the tenth precept of the Decalogue forbids the desire for all those things which belong to our neighbour, even in its first movements. How much more, then, must covetousness be judged unlawful and forbidden?

units.la: Similiter de luxû in alimentis patet, ex pœnâ lapidationis, quæ decreta fuit in filios prodigos & contumaces; Deut. 21, 20, 21. Et xxix, 19. grandis statuitur iniquitas ejus, qui adderet ebriam sitienti. Graves etiàm dehortationes, & comminationes adversùs istum luxum extant, Prov. 23, 20, 21, 29, -. Is. 5, 11, 12, 22. Ezech. 16, 49. Am. 6, 4, 5, 6.
units.tr: Likewise, concerning luxury in food, it is clear from the penalty of stoning decreed against prodigal and rebellious sons; Deut. 21, 20, 21; and 29, 19 sets down great iniquity for the one who would add drunkenness to thirst. There are also grave dissuasions and threats against this luxury; Prov. 23, 20, 21, 29; Isa. 5, 11, 12, 22; Ezek. 16, 49; Amos 6, 4, 5, 6.

units.la: Atque item in vestibus; Is. 3, 16, -. Zephan. 1, 8.
units.tr: And likewise in clothing: Isa. 3, 16; Zeph. 1, 8.

units.la: CIII. Quantum ad nonnum Præceptum: adversùs
units.tr: CIII. As regards the ninth Precept: against

units.la: mendacia tenendae 1. difertae eorum prohibitiones, & præcepta veracitatis: Levit. 19, 11. Zach. 8, 16. Eph. 4, 25. Jac. 5, 12.
units.tr: lying: 1. their prohibitions and the precepts of truthfulness are set forth: Levit. 19, 11; Zech. 8, 16; Eph. 4, 25; Jas. 5, 12.

units.la: 2. Mendacium est proprium opus Diaboli, ac filiorum ejus: Johan. VIII, 44. Isa. XXVIII, 15. Tit. 1, 12.
units.tr: 2. Lying is the proper work of the Devil and of his children: John 8, 44; Isa. 28, 15; Titus 1, 12.

units.la: 3. Sicut Deus, est Deus veritatis, & verax: Psal. XXXI, 6. Rom. III, 4. mentiri nescius; Tit. 1, 2. nec dolus fuit in ore Christi; Isa. 53, 9. 1 Petr. 2, 22. ita Deus veritatem vult in renibus; Psal. 51, 8. & suos regenerat in veritatem: Ephes. 4, 20, -25. Col. 3, 9. 10. Psal. XXXII, 1, 2. Isa. LXIII, 8.
units.tr: 3. As God is the God of truth, and true, Psal. 31, 6; Rom. 3, 4, he knows not how to lie, Titus 1, 2; nor was there guile in the mouth of Christ, Isa. 53, 9; 1 Pet. 2, 22; so God desires truth in the inward parts, Psal. 51, 8, and regenerates his own into truth; Eph. 4, 20–25; Col. 3, 9, 10; Psal. 32, 1, 2; Isa. 63, 8.

units.la: 4. Accedit odium Dei; quod adversus hoc peccatum nominatim aliquoties denunciatur: Psal. 5, 7. Prov. 6, 16, 19. XII, 22. XIX, 9. Apoc. XXI, 8. XXII, 15.
units.tr: 4. To this is added the hatred of God, which is expressly declared against this sin several times: Psal. 5, 7; Prov. 6, 16, 19; 12, 22; 19, 9; Rev. 21, 8; 22, 15.

units.la: CIV. Nequaquam vero excipimus mendacia officio- sa, quibus quis sibi ipsi, vel etiam aliis prospicit, ad ignominiam vel damnum evitandum, aut bonum utile vel jucundum consequendum.
units.tr: CIV. We do not, however, exempt officious lies, by which someone looks out for himself or for others, to avoid disgrace or loss, or to obtain some advantage or pleasure.

units.la: Nam 1. argumenta modo producta, generalia sunt; & hæc etiam redarguunt.
units.tr: For, (1) the arguments just produced are general, and these also refute such lies.

units.la: 2. Non sunt facienda mala ut eveniat bonum: Rom. III, 8. atque ab omni specie mali abstinendum est:
units.tr: (2) Evil is not to be done so that good may come of it: Rom. III, 8. and one must abstain from every appearance of evil:

units.la: 3. Nullum mendacium est ex veritate: 1 Johan. II, 21.
units.tr: (3) No lie comes from the truth: 1 Johan. II, 21.

units.la: 4. Causam Dei mendaciis agere non licet; ergo nec hominum: Job. XIII, 7.
units.tr: (4) It is not lawful to serve God's cause with lies, and therefore not men's either: Job. XIII, 7.

units.la: Obj. 1. Remedium istud aliquando necessarium est, ut quis hostium manus effugiat, violentiam hominis furiosi avertat, &c. Ergo. Resp. Imo quibusvis aliis modis, veritati & juri consentaneis, id prudenter tentandum est: sin minus, quidvis patiatur homo potius, quam mendacio suo Dei inclementiam adversum se concitet, & apud alios hoc sibi conciliet, ut deinceps ne quidem vera dicenti fides habeatur.
units.tr: Objection 1. This remedy is sometimes necessary, so that someone may escape the hands of enemies, or turn aside the violence of a madman, and so on. Therefore (it is lawful). Reply: On the contrary, one must prudently attempt by any other means that agree with truth and right; and if these fail, a person should rather suffer anything than by his lie stir up God's displeasure against himself, and win for himself such a reputation among others that afterwards no one would give credence even when he tells the truth.

units.la: Obj. 2. Exempla quædam in SS. Literis occurrunt, Gen. XVIII, 15. XXVII, 19. Ios. II, 5, 6. Matth. XXVI, 72. Resp. Ista non probant jus; sed ἀνθεντιαν historiæ solum habent: adeoque ipsa mendacia approbata censeri non debent.
units.tr: Objection 2. Certain examples occur in the Holy Scriptures: Gen. XVIII, 15; XXVII, 19; Josh. II, 5, 6; Matt. XXVI, 72. Reply: These examples do not prove a right; they belong only to the narrative of the history [ἀνθεντιαν], and so the lies themselves ought not to be regarded as approved.

units.la: Obj. 3. Speciatim de obstetricibus mulierum Hebræarum, Exod. I, 19, 20. Resp. 1. Si mentitæ fuerint, peccârunt eatenùs: neque ista fuit causa benedictionis Divinæ, quam perceperunt; sed beneficentia in Israëlitas. 2. Interim certum non videtur, eas esse mentitas: quod enim dixerunt, fœminas Hebræas fortiores fuisse Ægyptiis, satis est verofimile; tùm ex Divina in ipsas benedictione; tùm ex laboribus ac molestiis, quibus erant assuetæ. Itemque, quod dixerunt, peperisse Hebræas ante obstetricum adventum, non videtur; in plærisque saltem, a vero alienum; maximè si obstetrices eas de mandato Regis fecerint priùs certiores, atque istiusmodi consilium dederint.
units.tr: Objection 3. Specifically, concerning the midwives of the Hebrew women, Exod. I, 19, 20. Reply: (1) If they lied, they sinned to that extent; nor was that the reason for the divine blessing they received, but rather the kindness shown to the Israelites. (2) Meanwhile it does not seem certain that they lied. For what they said, that Hebrew women were stronger than Egyptian women, is quite probable, both from the divine blessing upon them and from the labours and hardships to which they were accustomed. Likewise, what they said, that the Hebrew women had given birth before the midwives arrived, does not seem, at least in most cases, to be far from the truth, especially if the midwives had first informed them of the king's command and had given them such advice.

units.la: CV. Eadem est ratio æquivocationum & mentalium reservationum, quod potissimùm contra Iesuitas tenendum.
units.tr: CV. The same reasoning applies to equivocations and mental reservations, which is to be held chiefly against the Jesuits.

units.la: Æquivocationes dicuntur locutiones ambiguæ, quibus, dùm alio prorsùs sensu usurpantur, quam alter existimar, dolus committitur, atque itâ peccatur contrà sinceritatem & charitatem; ad imitationem scil. patris mendaciorum ac fraudum.
units.tr: Equivocations are called ambiguous expressions by which deceit is committed while they are used in a sense quite different from what the other person supposes; and thus one sins against sincerity and charity, namely in imitation of the father of lies and of deceits.

units.la: Mentales verò reservationes intelliguntur, ubi orationis pars tantùm aliqua foràs profertur, altera verò in mente reservatur, quæ ad illius integritatem & veritatem omninò requiritur: ut si quis quod hodiè vel heri fecit, dicat se non fecisse; atque in mente reservet, abhinc annum, aut sæculum; vel, eo sine ut alteri hoc narret &c.
units.tr: Mental reservations, however, are understood to be cases where only some part of a statement is spoken aloud, while another part is kept back in the mind, which is wholly required for the statement's integrity and truth: for example, if someone who did a thing today or yesterday says that he did not do it, and keeps in his mind a year or a century ago; or so that he may not tell this to another, and so on.

units.la: Sed etiam in his 1. ipsa enunciatio falsa est, & animo dicentis minimè consentanea: quod autem in mente reservatur, non est λόγῳ προφορικός; atque adeò nec pars enunciationis, per quam suppleri posset defectus veritatis ethicæ.
units.tr: But even in these cases, (1) the statement itself is false and quite inconsistent with the mind of the speaker; and what is kept back in the mind is not a spoken word (λόγῳ προφορικός), and so it is not a part of the statement through which the lack of ethical truth could be supplied.

units.la: 2. Reprehenduntur ac prohibentur occultæ istiusmodi fraudes; & pii eas à se removent: Psal. xii,
units.tr: (2) Such hidden frauds are condemned and forbidden, and the godly keep them far from themselves: Psalm xii,

units.la: 3. Jerem. ix, 8. 1 Petr. ii, 1. 2 Cor. iv, 2.
units.tr: (3) Jer. ix, 8; 1 Pet. ii, 1; 2 Cor. iv, 2.

units.la: 3. Commendatur sinceritas, a quâ istæ artes prorsus alienæ sunt: Iac. v, 12. Iob. 1, 48.
units.tr: (3) Sincerity is commended, and these arts are wholly foreign to it: James v, 12; John i, 48.

units.la: 4. Istæ artes adversantur charitati: nemo enim secum itâ agi velit, in rebus ad ipsum pertinentibus.
units.tr: (4) These arts are opposed to charity, for no one would wish to be dealt with in this way in matters that concern himself.

units.la: CVI. Obj. 1. Non omnis veritas omnibus, & semper, & planè dicenda est: ergò. Resp. Concedimus antecedens: videndum enim quid necessitas, vel utilitas respectû gloriæ Divinæ aut respectû proximi nostri, poscat, vel etiàm prohibeat. Sed verum saltem esse oportet illud, quod dicitur: hoc autem istic non fit.
units.tr: CVI. Objection 1. Not every truth is to be told to everyone, always, and completely; therefore (the objection). Reply: We grant the antecedent, for one must consider what necessity or usefulness, with respect to the glory of God or with respect to our neighbour, requires or even forbids. But it is enough that what is said be true; and this is not what happens here.

units.la: Obj. 2. Abraham, Gen. xxii, 2. dixit de Sarâ uxore suâ; Soror mea est. Ergo. Resp. Verba ista in se vera fuerunt, quemadmodum ipse explicuit, verf. 12. Fraudem interim commisit Abraham; dum veritatem necessariam celavit; verf. 11. Debuisset enim uxorem potius profiteri, quam ejus pudicitiam in periculum tàm evidens adducere.
units.tr: Objection 2. Abraham, Gen. xxii, 2, said of Sarah his wife: "She is my sister." Therefore (it was lawful). Reply: These words were in themselves true, as he himself explained, verse 12. Yet Abraham committed a fraud, in that he concealed a necessary truth, verse 11. For he ought rather to have declared his wife, than to expose her chastity to such an evident danger.

units.la: Simile est exemplum Isaaci, Gen: xxvi. 7.
units.tr: The example of Isaac, Gen. xxvi, 7, is similar.

units.la: Obj. 3. Iohxi, 11. Christus Lazari mortem somnum appellavit. Ergo. Resp. Metaphoricè: ac potissimum eam mortem, unde ille tam brevi esset excitandus. Dum vero discipuli istam veritatem non capiebant, expositit eam apertè, verf. 14. 15.
units.tr: Objection 3. John xi, 11: Christ called Lazarus's death a sleep. Therefore (it was lawful). Reply: Metaphorically, and especially with respect to that death from which Lazarus was to be raised so soon. But when the disciples did not grasp this truth, he explained it plainly, verses 14, 15.

units.la: Aliud exemplum fere simile est Matth. ix, 24, 25.
units.tr: Another example, nearly similar, is Matt. ix, 24, 25.

units.la: Obj. 4. Christus Marc. xiii, 32. dixit, se ignorare diem judicii. Resp. Id planè accipiendum est de ipso secundum humanam naturâ, & intellectum humanum.
units.tr: Objection 4. Christ, Mark xiii, 32, said that he did not know the day of judgment. Reply: This must be understood plainly of him according to his human nature and human understanding.

units.la: Obj. 5. Paulus Act. xxiii, 5. dixit, se nescivisse istum esse Pontificem maximum. Resp. Id ab ipso vere ac sincere dictum exi-stimamus; dum in illo Judæorum consessu omnia admodum confuse agebantur.
units.tr: Objection 5. Paul, Acts xxiii, 5, said that he did not know that this man was the high priest. Reply: We judge that he said this truly and sincerely, since in that assembly of the Jews everything was being conducted in great confusion.

units.la: Obj.6. Idem, verf.5, clamavit in consessu; Viri fratres, ego Pharisæus sum, filius Pharisæi: de spe & resurrectione mortuorum ego in judicium vocor. Resp. Vere erat Pharisæi filius, atque ipse deinceps in Pharisaismo educatus & institutus; imo etiam adhuc in iis quæ inter Pharisæos & Sadducæos solebant controverti, Pharisæorum sententiam tenebat; ac nominatim de resurrectione mortuorum, insigni illo capite Religionis. Interim minime negavit, se Christianum esse, vel Apostolum quanquam isto tempore id non dixit: sed & perrecturus, atque istud confessurus fuisse videtur; nisi per seditionem fuisset impeditus, verf. 7. Confer xxiv, 14-15. 16. xxvi, 4, -- 23 & 1 Cor. xv, 3, 4, 12,-
units.tr: Objection 6. The same, verse 5, cried out in the assembly: "Brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee; I am being called into judgment concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead." Reply: He truly was the son of a Pharisee, and he himself had afterwards been brought up and instructed in Pharisaism; indeed, even still he held the Pharisees' opinion on those matters which used to be disputed between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and specifically on the resurrection of the dead, that notable article of religion. Yet he by no means denied that he was a Christian or an apostle, although at that time he did not say so; but it seems he was going to proceed and would have confessed it, had he not been hindered by the sedition, verse 7. Compare xxiv, 14, 15, 16; xxvi, 4, 23; and 1 Cor. xv, 3, 4, 12.

units.la: CVII. Perfidia
units.tr: CVII. Perfidy

units.la: huc etiam referenda est; fraus, qua quis dictis aut promissis non stat. Psal. xv, 4. beatus prædicatur, qui cum juravit in malum, h. e. in detrimentum suum, non mutat. Nec admittenda est exceptio in fide data infidelibus, vel hæreticis; propter argumenta generalia superius producta.
units.tr: This also belongs here: fraud, by which someone does not keep to his words or promises.
