Psalm 15:4 pronounces blessed the one who, having sworn to his hurt, that is, to his own detriment, does not change. Nor is any exception admitted for a promise given to unbelievers or heretics, on account of the general arguments set out above.

units.la: Addi possunt specialia; 1. A reprehensione perfidiæ filiorum Jacobi in Sichemitas: Gen. xxxiv. 25, 30. xlix, 5. 6, 7.
units.tr: Specific arguments can also be added. (1) From the rebuke of the perfidy of the sons of Jacob against the Shechemites: Genesis 34:25, 30; 49:5, 6, 7.

units.la: 2. Ab exemplo, cum quadam commendatione memorato, fœderis a Josua & primoribus Israelitarum imprudenter pacti cum Gibeonitis, attamen religiose servati. Ios. ix, 15,-21. x 10,-14.
units.tr: (2) From the example, with some commendation, of the covenant made rashly by Joshua and the leaders of the Israelites with the Gibeonites, yet kept faithfully: Joshua 9:15-21; 10:10-14.

units.la: 3. A pœnis Sauli & populo ejus immissis, quod fœdus istud violasset: 2 Sam. xxi, 1, 2.
units.tr: (3) From the punishments inflicted on Saul and his people because he had violated that covenant: 2 Samuel 21:1, 2.

units.la: 4. Ab improbatione perfidiæ Zedekijæ in Nebucadnezarem; 2 Chron. xxxvi, 13.
units.tr: (4) From the disapproval of the perfidy of Zedekiah towards Nebuchadnezzar: 2 Chronicles 36:13.

units.la: Contraria erat sententia & praxis Concilii Constantiensis; quod Imperatores & Principes possent ac deberent rescindere salvum conductum hæreticis, aut de hæresi suspectis, datum; ubi ita visum esset Judici Ecclesiastico. Quod ipsum satis aperte agnovit Concilium Tridentinum, Seff. 2.
units.tr: The view and practice of the Council of Constance were contrary: that the emperors and princes could and should revoke a safe-conduct given to heretics, or to those suspected of heresy, when the ecclesiastical judge had so decided. The Council of Trent also acknowledged this quite plainly, Session 2.

units.la: Quod autem dicitur in negotio Iohannis Huffii, & Hieronymi Pragensis, salvum conductum ab Imperatore Sigismundo datum quidem fuisse Politicè; sed Concilium, tanquàm Judicem competentem & superiorem, aliter censuisse; id Antichristo, & filio perditionis dignum quidem est; sed minimè consentaneum SS. Literis.
units.tr: As for what is said about the affair of John Hus and Jerome of Prague, that a safe-conduct was indeed given by the Emperor Sigismund on political grounds, but that the Council, as the competent and superior judge, judged otherwise: that is indeed worthy of Antichrist and the son of perdition, but by no means agrees with the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: CVIII. Tenendum & hic contra Socinianos, Christum & Apostolos non primùm sub N.T. prohibuisse Mendacium temerarium, Simulationes ac Dissimulationes, itémque Detractiones, & Condemnationes temerarias.
units.tr: CVIII. Here too we must hold, against the Socinians, that Christ and the Apostles did not first forbid under the New Testament rash lying, simulations and dissimulations, and likewise rash detractions and condemnations.

units.la: Nam 1. omne mendacium in universum, atque adeò etiàm temerarium, non verò hoc solum, probavimus illicitum esse, & semper fuisse, productis quoque testimoniis ex V.T. & rationibus ad ipsum etiàm pertinentibus.
units.tr: For (1) we have proved that every lie in general, and therefore also a rash one, and not this alone, is unlawful and has always been so, the testimonies from the Old Testament and the reasons bearing on this matter also having been produced.

units.la: 2. De simulationibus, ac dissimulationibus, quatenùs in iis falsitas aliqua asseritur, aut veritas necessaria celatur, idem manifestum est: nec non de detractionibus, & condemnationibus temerariis. Admodùm diserta sunt inter alia, quæ extant Levit. xix. 15. 16. Psal. xv. 1. 2. 3. ci. 2. 4. -7.
units.tr: (2) Concerning simulations and dissimulations, insofar as some falsehood is asserted in them or necessary truth is concealed, the same is clear; and likewise concerning rash detractions and condemnations. Among other passages, those in Leviticus 19:15, 16 and Psalm 15:1, 2, 3; 101:2, 4-7 are quite explicit.

units.la: CIX. Succedit tandem decimum Decalogi præceptum. Exod. xx. 17. Deut. v. 21. Confer Rom. vii. 7. & xiii. 9. Ex quibus inter se collatis statim colligimus, hoc revera unicum præceptum esse, non duo distincta; contrà quàm velint Pontificii, quos hic temerè sequuntur Lutherani; ut suppleant numerum denarium, postquàm in gratiam imaginum suarum secundum præceptum negârunt esse distinctum à primo.
units.tr: CIX. At last comes the tenth precept of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21. Compare Romans 7:7 and 13:9. From these passages compared with one another we immediately conclude that this is really a single precept and not two distinct ones, contrary to what the Papists wish, whom the Lutherans rashly follow here, so that they may make up the number ten, after denying that the second precept is distinct from the first, for the sake of their images.

units.la: Nam 1. Paulus manifestè indicat, distincto quodam præcepto prohiberi qualemcunque inordinatam concupiscentiam; dum breviter dixit, Non concupisces.
units.tr: For (1) Paul plainly indicates that some distinct precept forbids every kind of disordered concupiscence, when he briefly says, "You shall not covet."

units.la: 2. Prohibetur generatim concupiscentia omnium eorum, quæ sunt proximi nostri, ut pariter in Exodo & in Deuteronomio apparet; ubi species quædam recensentur, sentur, & reliquæ omnes istius generis palàm indicantur porro: ac proinde non debent hic ita spectari specialia objecta, ut pro eorum distinctione præcepta quoque distinguerentur; sic enim non duo tantum, sed multo plura, forent statuenda.
units.tr: (2) Coveting of all those things that belong to our neighbour is forbidden in general, as appears equally in Exodus and in Deuteronomy, where certain kinds are listed and all the rest of that sort are plainly indicated besides. Therefore the specific objects should not be regarded here in such a way that the precepts would be distinguished by their distinction; for in that case not two but many more would have to be posited.

units.la: 3. In Exodo prius recensetur domus proximi, deinde ejus uxor, &c. in Deuteronomio contrà prius uxor proximi, deinde ejus domus, & reliqua quæ sunt ipsius. Utrum igitur dicendum potius nonum; utrum decimum præceptum? Adversarii hic ordinem in Deuteronomio expressum sequi malunt: verum sic in Exodo, ubi ipsius Dei oraculum describitur, post octo priora præcepta, proposita fuisset pars aliqua decimi præcepti, deinde nonum præceptum, ac deinceps reliqua ad supplementum decimi præcepti necessaria; quod a Legislatore sapientissimo, qui idem est Deus ordinis, alienum censeri debet. Sed minus mirandum, si Mosis in sua repetitione, quæ extat Deut. v. accurate servato ordine ac distinctione singulorum præceptorum, in hoc vel isto speciali præcepto ordinem verborum nonnihil immutaverit, vel etiam objecta specialia aliquanto plenius expresserit; rei magis intentus, quam verbis: sicut etiam factum in quarto præcepto, &c.
units.tr: (3) In Exodus the house of the neighbour is listed first, then his wife, etc.; in Deuteronomy, on the contrary, the neighbour's wife comes first and then his house and the rest of his belongings. Which should we therefore call the ninth and which the tenth precept? Our opponents prefer to follow the order expressed in Deuteronomy. But if that were so in Exodus, where the very oracle of God is described, then after the eight preceding precepts some part of the tenth precept would be set forth, then a ninth precept, and afterwards the rest needed to complete the tenth precept; this must be thought alien to the most wise Lawgiver, who is also the God of order. But it is less surprising if Moses, in his repetition which is found in Deuteronomy 5, while carefully keeping the order and distinction of the individual precepts, somewhat altered the order of words in this or that particular precept, or even expressed the specific objects a little more fully, being more concerned with the matter than with the words; as was also done in the fourth precept, and so on.

units.la: 4. Omnia ista ad concupiscentiam spectantia unico tantum versu comprehenduntur; etiam in Bibliis interlinearibus Antverpiæ editis, &c. cum tamen alia præcepta, quantumvis brevia, utpote sextum, septimum, & octavum, singula distinctis versibus sint comprehensa.
units.tr: (4) All these things that pertain to concupiscence are comprehended in only one verse, as also in the interlinear Bibles printed at Antwerp, etc., whereas other precepts, however brief, such as the sixth, seventh and eighth, are each comprehended in separate verses.

units.la: Obj. 1. Distincta est concupiscentia uxoris proximi, sub ratione boni jucundi; a concupiscentia servi, bovis, &c. sub ratione boni utilis: Ergo. Resp. Nego consequentiam: quia 1. si conditio objectorum, modufque specialis in ea tendendi, spectetur, jam peccata ista præceptis superioribus prohibita sunt. 2. Et quidsi quis uxorem alterius concupisceret sub ratione boni utilis; vel ancillam, aut agrum, &c. sub ratione boni jucundi ?
units.tr: Objection 1. Coveting a neighbour's wife is distinct, under the aspect of a pleasant good, from coveting a servant, an ox, etc., under the aspect of a useful good. Therefore... Answer: I deny the consequence; for (1) if the condition of the objects and the special manner of tending towards them is considered, then these sins are already forbidden by the preceding precepts. (2) And what if someone coveted another's wife under the aspect of a useful good, or a maidservant, or a field, etc., under the aspect of a pleasant good?

units.la: Obj. 2. Ante prohibitionem sculptilium non præcedit nota D; quæ in Deuteronomio statim sequitur post verba, ne concupiscas uxorem proximitui. Resp. Ista nota D, aut ᗡ, non est authentica: sed a descriptoribus curiose, & sæpe sine judicio addita, ad indicandum, quomodo ista periodus, aut istud colon, in priori exemplo, unde facta erat descriptio, cohæserit cum antecedentibus; eademne linea, an distincta.
units.tr: Objection 2. Before the prohibition of graven images there does not stand the mark D, which in Deuteronomy immediately follows the words "you shall not covet your neighbour's wife." Answer: that mark D (or its variant) is not authentic. Copyists added it carefully, but often without judgment, to show how that period or colon in the earlier copy, from which the transcription was made, joined with what comes before, whether on the same line or as a separate clause.

units.la: CX. Motus primo primi, ex habituali peccato inhabitante proficiscentes, hoc præcepto proprie prohibentur: quos consequenter vere peccata esse asserimus, contra Pontificios, Remonstrantes, aliosque Persectistas.
units.tr: CX. Motions of the first movement, arising from the habitual sin dwelling within, are properly forbidden by this precept; and we assert that they are consequently truly sins, against the Papists, the Remonstrants, and other Perfectionists.

units.la: Hoc distincte probamus, 1 ex diserto Apostoli testimonio, Rom. vii. 7. Talis autem cupiditas, sive concupiscentia, istic prohibetur, qualem pro peccato non reputant quotquot Legem illam sanctam & spiritualem non recte didicerunt; atque adeo etiam ipse Paulus non reputavit, ante actualem conversionem suam. At vero deliberatum consilium de peccato patrando, & durantem complacentiam in peccato mente concepto, vere peccata esse, non possunt ignorare quotquot vel Legem naturæ utcunque meditantur: unde necessum est, priorem & subtiliorem quandam concupiscentiam istic intelligi.
units.tr: We prove this distinctly: (1) from the plain testimony of the Apostle, Romans 7:7. Now that kind of desire, or concupiscence, is forbidden there, which all those do not count as sin who have not rightly learned that holy and spiritual Law; and so the Apostle Paul himself did not count it as sin before his actual conversion. But that deliberate purpose of committing sin, and a lasting delight in sin conceived in the mind, are truly sins, which all those cannot be ignorant of who meditate on the law of nature in any way at all. Hence it is necessary that a former and more subtle kind of concupiscence be understood here.

units.la: 2. Ex definitione peccati, 1 Iohan. iii, 4. ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία. Sed prima illa concupiscentia actualis discrepat a Lege, & fit contra eam. Lex enim spiritualis est; Rom. vii, 14. & obedientiam postulat ex toto corde, integris viribus, omni cogitatione; Matth. xxii, 37. Luc. x, 27.
units.tr: (2) From the definition of sin, 1 John 3:4: hamartia estin hē anomia [ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία]. But that first actual concupiscence differs from the Law and is done against it. For the Law is spiritual, Romans 7:14, and demands obedience from the whole heart, with all strength and every thought; Matthew 22:37; Luke 10:27.

units.la: 3. Procedit ex malo principio: Matth. xv, 19. Gal. v, 17. 1 Iob. ii, 16. Atqui non potest arbor mala fructus ētus bonos edere: Matth. vii, 18.
units.tr: (3) It proceeds from an evil principle: Matthew 15:19; Galatians 5:17; 1 John 2:16. But a bad tree cannot bear good fruit: Matthew 7:18.

units.la: 4. Ab effectis: ipsa enim hominem seducit, & peccatum ulterius producit: Jac. I, 14, 15.
units.tr: (4) From its effects: for it itself seduces a man and brings forth sin further, James 1:14, 15.

units.la: Sed etiam hic statuendum, primæ istius concupiscentiæ actualis principium prohiberi eadem opera; ipsum scil. peccatum originale inhærens, & qualemcunque vitiositatem habitualem: eorumque reliquias in ipsis regenitis.
units.tr: But here too we must hold that the principle of this first actual concupiscence is forbidden at the same time, namely the original sin dwelling within, and any habitual viciousness whatever, together with the remnants of these in the regenerate themselves.

units.la: Obj. 1. In his non præcedit deliberatum consilium; atque adeo non sunt voluntaria. Ergo. Resp. Nego consequentiam: quia peccatum originale inhærens, est moralis quædam vitiositas, Legi Divinæ adversa, voluntaria in causa; imo etiam in nobis, voluntate quadam consequente. Vitiositates autem aliæ habituales acquisitæ, insuper voluntariæ sunt voluntate antecedente & concomitante. Actualis denique concupiscentia inordinata, etiam voluntaria est voluntate quadam concomitante.
units.tr: Objection 1. In these there does not precede deliberate purpose, and so they are not voluntary. Therefore... Answer: I deny the consequence; for the original sin dwelling within is a certain moral viciousness, adverse to the Divine Law, voluntary in its cause, and even in us by a certain consequent will. Other acquired habitual vicious dispositions, moreover, are voluntary by antecedent and concomitant will. Finally, actual disordered concupiscence is also voluntary by a certain concomitant will.

units.la: Obj. 2. Regeniti concupiscentiæ resistunt frequenter, & actum ejus reprimunt. Ergo. Resp. Hoc faciunt per gratiam Spiritus: iidem tamen, dum imperfecta est vita spiritualis, in se habent istum actum; eumque suum esse, & quidem ἀνομον, non possunt non agnoscere.
units.tr: Objection 2. The regenerate often resist concupiscence and check its act. Therefore... Answer: They do this through the grace of the Spirit; yet while their spiritual life is imperfect, they still have this act in themselves, and they cannot but acknowledge it as their own, and indeed as lawless [ἀνομον, anomon].

units.la: Obj. 3. Sunt tantum veteris hominis. Ergo. Resp. In regenitis recte distinguitur novus homo a reliquiis veteris hominis: attamen istæ reliquiæ sunt ejusdem personæ: Rom. vii, 17, 20, 23, 25. Jac. I, 14.
units.tr: Obj. 3. They belong only to the old man. Therefore... Resp. In the regenerate, the new man is rightly distinguished from the remnants of the old man; yet these remnants belong to the same person: Rom. 7:17, 20, 23, 25; Jas. 1:14.

units.la: CXI. Circa hoc præceptum errant quoque Socinian: statuentes, quod Christus ei sub N. T. adjecerit, Animum non esse oblectandum concupiscentia rei alienæ, neque fovendam ejus cogitationem. Ista enim, & plura, jam sub V. T. hoc ipso decimo præcepto fuisse prohibita, patet ex superioribus. Et Paulus ex eo colligit diserte, Rom. vii, 7. Confer Psal. CXXXI, 2.
units.tr: CXI. The Socinians also err about this precept. They hold that Christ, under the New Testament, added this command: the mind is not to be delighted by the desire for another's property, nor is the thought of it to be cherished. That these things, and more besides, were already forbidden under the Old Testament by this very tenth commandment is clear from what was said above. Paul also expressly draws this conclusion from it, Rom. 7:7. Compare Ps. 131:2.

units.la: CXII. Æquè absurdè statuunt iidem, Christum præter universam istam Legem, tulisse insuper alia quædam præcepta moralia; nimirum de sui Abnegatione, de Tolerantia crucis, & Imitatione ipsius Christi.
units.tr: CXII. The same people argue just as absurdly that Christ, beyond the whole of that Law, also gave certain further moral precepts: namely, on self-denial, on bearing the cross patiently, and on imitating Christ himself.

units.la: Quod enim primò attinet ad Abnegationem sui, præceptum satis antiquum esse patet, 1. si respiciamus Abrahamum, Gen. XII. 1.
units.tr: As for first self-denial, that the precept is quite ancient is clear: (1) if we look at Abraham, Gen. 12:1.

units.la: 2. Eandem exigit ipsa Lex, Deut. VI, 5. Sic enim abneganda fuit omnis cupiditas, cogitatio, inclinatio, dilectioni & obedientiæ Dei adversa.
units.tr: (2) The Law itself demands the same, Deut. 6:5. For every desire, thought and inclination that is opposed to the love and obedience of God had to be denied in this way.

units.la: 3. Ex Prophetis etiam facile est colligere illud officium: utpote Jerem.III, 17. IV, 3, 4. VII, 23, 24.
units.tr: (3) From the Prophets too it is easy to gather this duty, for example Jer. 3:17; 4:3, 4; 7:23, 24.

units.la: 4. Illustria exempla quoque occurrunt, Psal. CXXXI, 1, 2. Job. XXXI, 1.
units.tr: (4) Striking examples also occur: Ps. 131:1, 2; Job 31:1.

units.la: Secundo, de Tolerantia crucis, sive afflictionum, castigationum, & probationum Dei, demonstratur facile; 1. ex Prov. III. 11, 12. Huc respicit Apostolus, Hebr. XII, 1, 5, 6.
units.tr: Second, that we must bear the cross patiently, that is, God's afflictions, chastisements and trials, is easily shown: (1) from Prov. 3:11, 12. The Apostle has this in view at Heb. 12:1, 5, 6.

units.la: 2. Præclara etiam sunt, 1 Sam. III, 18. Itemque Job. I, 21. II, 10. Thren. III. 27, 39. Mich. VII, 8, 9. Psal. CXXIX, 1, 2.
units.tr: (2) There are also excellent passages: 1 Sam. 3:18; likewise Job 1:21; 2:10; Lam. 3:27, 39; Mic. 7:8, 9; Ps. 129:1, 2.

units.la: 3. Consimilia indicantur in N. T. ubi hæc praxis confirmatur exemplis ex V. T. depromtis: Hebr. XI, 25, 26. 35-38. XII, 1. Jac. 5, 10, 11.
units.tr: (3) Similar things are set out in the New Testament, where this practice is confirmed by examples taken from the Old: Heb. 11:25, 26, 35–38; 12:1; Jas. 5:10, 11.

units.la: Tertio, de Imitatione Christi satis etiam patet ex mandatis, ubi Deus sanctitatem suam sub V. T. imitandam præcepit: utpote Levit. XIX, 2. si nimirum conferantur ea, quæ de Christi Θεανθρωπίας obedientia, humilitate, cæterisque virtutibus, jam olim fuerunt prædicta; Dan. IX, 24. Psal. XL, 7, 8, 9. Jes. LIII, 6, 7. Zach. IX, 9. In iis enim sita est Imitatio Christi: Matth. XI, 29. Phil. II, 5-8. 1 Petr. II. 20, 21.
units.tr: Third, that we must imitate Christ is also plain enough from the commands in which God under the Old Testament ordered his own holiness to be imitated, for example Lev. 19:2, provided that we compare these with what was foretold long ago about the obedience, humility and other virtues of Christ, the God-man: Dan. 9:24; Ps. 40:7–9; Isa. 53:6, 7; Zech. 9:9. For the imitation of Christ consists in these: Matt. 11:29; Phil. 2:5–8; 1 Pet. 2:20, 21.

units.la: Quin & virtutes singulæ, quas nos in Christo observare atque imitari oportet, in V. T. fuerunt etiam propositæ ac mandatæ.
units.tr: Indeed, each single virtue that we ought to observe and imitate in Christ was also set forth and commanded in the Old Testament.

units.la: CXIII. Cæterum Lex illa vel simpliciter secundum le spectatur: vel prout est instrumentum primi Fœderis. Priore modo saltem est norma obedientiæ: specifice præscribens debitum dependentiæ nostræ moralis ad Divinam ὑπεξουσίαν, & jus absoluti illius Dominii: unde fluit obligatio nostri ad præstanda ossicia mandata, & fugienda vitia contraria. Sed hactenus Deus nullo modo obligatus est Homini, ad gratitudinem ei referendam, vel remunerationem faciendam pro obsequio & cultu sibi præstito. Job. xxxv, 7. Si justus es, quid das Ei? aut quid de manu tua accepit? Psal. xvi, 2. Bonum meum non pervenit ad Te. Rom. xi, 35. Quis prior dedit Ei, & reddetur ipsi? Luc. xvii, 9, 10. Num gratiam habet servo illi, quia fecit quæ ipsi edita fuerant? Non puto. Ita & vos, cum feceritis omnia, quæ edita sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus: nam quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Naturaliter tamen actus humanus, si qua morali malitia laboret, eo ipso convenientem pœnam demeretur; per justitiam Dei vindicativam. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 56.
units.tr: CXIII. Moreover, that Law is considered either simply in itself, or as the instrument of the first Covenant. In the former way it is at least a rule of obedience, specifically prescribing the due dependence of our moral nature upon the divine hypexousia [ὑπεξουσία, subjection], and the right of that absolute Dominion; whence arises our obligation to perform the duties commanded and to flee the contrary vices. But God is in no way bound to man so far as to owe him thanks or to make him a reward for the service and worship rendered to him. Job 35:7: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand? Ps. 16:2: My goodness does not reach to you. Rom. 11:35: Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? Luke 17:9, 10: Does he have thanks for that servant, because he did what had been commanded to him? I think not. So also you, when you have done all the things commanded to you, say: We are unprofitable servants; for we have done what we ought to have done. Yet by nature a human act, if it is marked by any moral wickedness, thereby deserves a fitting punishment, through the vindictive justice of God. See above, chap. 4, th. 56.

units.la: CXIV. Vox Hebræa בְּרִית pactum, conventionem, & fœdus notat: Græci διαθήκην appellant; q. d. dispositionem. Laxiore significatu quodlibet firmum statutum, etiam de rebus inanimatis, sic nuncupatur. Jerem. xxxiii, 20, 25. Fœdus meum de die, & fœdus meum de nocte. Occurrit etiam generale fœdus, quod Deus non solum cum hominibus pepigit, sed ad bestias quoque extendit, & iride obsignavit; de mundo non perdendo per diluvium; Gen. ix, 9, - 16.
units.tr: CXIV. The Hebrew word בְּרִית [berith] means pact, agreement, and covenant; the Greeks call it διαθήκη [diathēkē], as if to say a disposition. In a looser sense any firm ordinance is so named, even concerning inanimate things: Jer. 33:20, 25: My covenant of the day, and my covenant of the night. There also occurs a general covenant, which God made not only with humans but extended also to the beasts, and sealed with the rainbow, that the world would not be destroyed by a flood: Gen. 9:9–16.

units.la: Fœdera autem Politicis sunt Conventiones publicæ, quæ fiunt jussu summæ potestatis, & in quibus populus iræ Divinæ obstringi solet, si minus fletur dictis. Per ea interdum idem constituitur, quod est Juris naturæ: utpote inter hostes a bello discedentes; vel etiam inter eos, qui nihil ante contraxerunt; ne scil. alii alios lædant, &c. Interdum Juri naturæ aliquid adjicitur. Sunt-
units.tr: Covenants, however, in political usage are public agreements, made by command of the supreme power, and by which a people is usually bound to the wrath of God if it does not keep what was agreed. By them sometimes the same thing is established that belongs to the law of nature, for example between enemies who withdraw from war, or also between those who have contracted nothing before, so that they do not harm one another, and so on. Sometimes something is added to the law of nature.

units.la: Suntque vel Fœdera æqualia, συνθῆκαι; quæ utrimque se habent eodem modo. Vel inæqualia, ὑπονόμαι; ut si pars potentior auxilia promittat, nec restipuletur; sive majora promittat: aut respectu partis minus dignæ ac potentis (προσάγματα, ἐπιλάγματα) ubi aliquando fit imperii translatio, vel saltem imminutio, vel onera quædam imponuntur.
units.tr: Covenants are either equal, synthēkai [συνθῆκαι], in which both sides stand in the same way; or unequal, hyponomai [ὑπονόμαι], as when the more powerful party promises help and does not require anything in return, or promises more; or with respect to the less worthy and weaker party (prosagmata, epilagmata [προσάγματα, ἐπιλάγματα]), where sometimes a transfer of rule takes place, or at least a diminution, or certain burdens are imposed.

units.la: Fœdera item sunt vel amicitiæ, vel reconciliationis: in his supponitur offensa; in illis non item.
units.tr: Covenants are also either of friendship or of reconciliation: in the latter an offence is presupposed; in the former it is not.

units.la: CXV. Fœdus primum, de quo nunc agendum, alias Legale appellatur, vel Optrum; interdum etiam Naturæ: estque inæquale, & amicitiæ inæqualis. Describitur autem plenius; Quod Deus cum Adamo, ac pariter cum universo Genere humano, quod in eo tanquam capite censitum fuit, ita pepigit; ut ipsum Jus naturæ, Lege comprehensum, firmaverit, tum sanctione poenali adversus transgressores, tum liberali promissione erga eos qui perfectam obedientiam forent consummaturi; ad demonstrandam per omnia secula gloriam potestatis, gratiæ, & justitiæ suæ. Confiderabimus autem deinceps 1. specialem ejus Modum, 2. Confirmationem, 3. Signa, & 4 Durationem. Ad Modum illum pertinet, tum Conditio præstanda, quam Deus stipulatus est; tum Ordo generis humani, quem Deus pro suo jure constituit.
units.tr: CXV. The first covenant, of which we are now to speak, is otherwise called Legal, or Of Works; sometimes also of Nature. It is unequal, like a friendship between unequals. It is described more fully thus: that God so covenanted with Adam, and likewise with the whole human race, which was reckoned in him as its head, that he confirmed the very law of nature, comprised in the Law, both by a penal sanction against transgressors and by a generous promise towards those who were to bring perfect obedience to completion, in order to display through all ages the glory of his power, grace and justice. We shall consider next, (1) its particular Mode, (2) its Confirmation, (3) its Signs, and (4) its Duration. To that Mode belong both the Condition to be performed, which God stipulated, and the Order of the human race, which God established by his own right.

units.la: CXVI. Conditio præstanda, erat perfecta totius Legis observantia; omnium scil. & singulorum præceptorum, quovis loco ac tempore, singulis actibus humanis, ad extremum virium. Deut. vi. 5. Matth. XXII, 37,38: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Deut. XXVII, 26. Gal. III, 10. Execrabilis est, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, ut faciat ea. Jac. II, 10. Quisquis enim totam Legem servaverit, impegerit autem in uno, damnas factus est omnium. Scil. propter omnimodam Hominum à Deo dependentiam; Act. XVII, 25,-28. Rom. xi, 36. & Legis Divinæ spiritualitatem ac sanctitatem; Rom. vii, 12, 14.
units.tr: CXVI. The condition to be performed was the perfect observance of the whole Law; that is, of all and each of the precepts, in every place and at every time, in every human act, with the utmost of one's strength. Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37, 38: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc. Deut. 27:26; Gal. 3:10: Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them. Jas. 2:10: For whoever has kept the whole Law, but has stumbled in one point, has become guilty of all. That is, on account of the complete dependence of humans upon God, Acts 17:25–28; Rom. 11:36; and on account of the spirituality and holiness of the divine Law, Rom. 7:12, 14.

units.la: Ista autem conditio, juxta verborum formulam in rigore suo acceptam, præstari debuit a quovis Homine in propria persona. Levit. xviii, 5. Ezech. xx, 11. Rom. x, 5. Gal. iii, 12. Qui præstiterit ea, vivet per illa sine ulla mentione Sponsoris, aut Servatoris.
units.tr: This condition, moreover, taken in the strict sense of the words, had to be performed by any human in his own person: Lev. 18:5; Ezek. 20:11; Rom. 10:5; Gal. 3:12: He who does these things shall live by them, without any mention of a Surety or a Saviour.

units.la: CXVII. Quantum attinet ad Ordinem Generis humani: Adamus primus & universalis pater fuit omnium Hominum: sicut Eva eorum mater: Gen. III, 20. Confer Act. xvii, 26. Sed & ipse Adamus principium quoque Mulieris, & caput ejus: Gen. II, 21, 22, 23. Eph. v, 23. Sic omnes Posteri virtualiter fuerunt in Adamo, tanquam causa prima istius Generis: quæ est Consideratio physica. Verum ad istam accessit alia Constitutio politica & fœderalis, ut omnes Posteri in Adamo censerentur: atque adeo Adamus vel eorum bono esset perseveraturus in statu integritatis, cursumque obedientiæ consummaturus, ad justitiam & gloriam æternam; vel etiam eorum malo esset lapsurus, eidemque secum calamitati & exitio eos simul involuturus.
units.tr: CXVII. As far as the Order of the human race is concerned: Adam was the first and universal father of all humans, just as Eve was their mother: Gen. 3:20; compare Acts 17:26. But Adam was also the beginning and head of the woman: Gen. 2:21–23; Eph. 5:23. Thus all posterity was virtually in Adam, as the first cause of this race; this is the physical consideration. But to this there was added another political and federal constitution, by which all posterity was reckoned in Adam; and so Adam was either to persevere, for their good, in the state of integrity and to complete the course of obedience to justice and eternal glory, or else, for their harm, he was to fall, and along with himself was to draw them into the same calamity and ruin.

units.la: Similiter Hebr. vii, 9, 10. Levi in lumbis Abrahami proavi sui existens virtualiter, in eodem quoque decimas censebatur dedisse Melchizedeko. Certe prohibitio Arboris scientiæ boni & mali, Adamo facta, Gen. II, 17. ad Evam extenditur, III, 3. Et ad Posteros quoque pertinuit eadem obligatio realis (non personalis): hinc Protoplasti, ubi peccassent, Paradiso exclusi, & ab aditu atque usu Arboris vitæ remoti fuerunt una cum Posteris suis; terra item maledictioni subjecta fuit, multæque calamitates immissæ, Posterorum quoque incommodo: statutum similiter omnibus semel mori; atque in universum omne figmentum cogitationum cordis humani evasit malum inde à pueritia, &c. Gen. III, 22, 23, 24. 16, -19. Hebr. ix, 27. Gen. vi, 5. viii, 21. Clarissimè etiam Apostolus, 1 Cor. xv, 22. In Adamo omnes moriuntur. Per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors: & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccarunt. --qui (Adamus) est typus illius (Christi) qui erat futurus. --- Per unam offensam (reatus venit) in omnes homines ad condemnationem, &c. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 69.
units.tr: Similarly Heb. 7:9, 10: Levi, being virtually in the loins of his forefather Abraham, was also counted as having given tithes to Melchizedek in him. Certainly the prohibition of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, made to Adam (Gen. 2:17), extends to Eve (3:3). And the same real (not personal) obligation pertained also to posterity: hence the first parents, when they sinned, were excluded from Paradise and removed from access to and use of the tree of life, together with their posterity; the earth likewise was made subject to the curse, and many calamities were sent, to the disadvantage of their posterity as well; it was similarly appointed that all should die once; and in general every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart became evil from childhood, etc. (Gen. 3:22, 23, 24; 3:16–19; Heb. 9:27; Gen. 6:5; 8:21). The Apostle also most clearly says (1 Cor. 15:22): In Adam all die. Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so death passed upon all men, in whom all sinned. Adam is the type of him (Christ) who was to come. Through one offence (guilt came) upon all men to condemnation, etc. Compare above, chapter 4, thesis 69.

units.la: CXVIII. Ad Confirmationem pertinet primo San- ctio poenalis, sive Comminatio poenarum adversus pec- cata, si ea committerentur.
units.tr: CXVIII. Belonging to the confirmation of this covenant is first the penal sanction, or the threatening of punishments against sins, should they be committed.

units.la: Ubi non solum Deus clarè expressit, quid Justitia sua vindicativa postularet: sed ipsi quoque Homines hanc Foederis conditionem amplectentes, & cum libertate complacentiæ subeuntes, ex sua etiam parte se obstrinxerunt Deo per istum contractum, ad quem sic Deus per συγκατάθεσιν processit. Unde magis justificantur Dei judicia adversus peccatores, quando iis facit secundum verba fœderis, Jerem. xi, 18.
units.tr: Here God not only clearly expressed what his avenging justice required, but men themselves, embracing this condition of the covenant and undertaking it with a willing pleasure, bound themselves to God by their own part in this contract, to which God thus came by mutual consent. Whence God's judgments against sinners are the more justified, when he deals with them according to the words of the covenant (Jer. 11:8).

units.la: Sanctio illa breviter expressa est Gen. II, 17. "De fructu Arboris scientiæ boni & mali ne comedas: nam quo die comederis de eo, moriendo morieris. Confer Rom. vi, 23. "Stipendia peccati mors: donum autem Dei est vita æterna in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Et v, 14, 18. "Regnavit mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosen, - in omnes homines ad condemnationem. Item Eph. 2. 1, 3. Mortui in offensis & peccatis: -- natura filii irae. Ex quibus patet, intelligendam esse omnem mortem miseram, non solum corporalem & temporalem, sed quoque spiritualem & æternam.
units.tr: That sanction was briefly expressed in Gen. 2:17: "Of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for in the day you eat of it, dying you shall die." Compare Rom. 6:23: "The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." And 5:14, 18: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses ... upon all men to condemnation." Likewise Eph. 2:1, 3: Dead in trespasses and sins ... by nature children of wrath. From these it is evident that every misery of death is to be understood, not only bodily and temporal, but also spiritual and eternal.

units.la: Paulo aliter repetita est eadem Comminatio Deut. 27. 26. Gal. 3. 10. Execrabilis est, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, &c. Confer Gen. 3. 18, 19. "Maledicta esto terra propter te: cum dolore comedito proventum ejus omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ: eaque spinam ,,& carduum proferto tibi.--Infudore vultus tui vescitor cibo, donec revertaris in humum, &c. Itemque Levit. 26. 14.-. Deut. 28. 15.-. ex quibus constat de Maledictione hujus sæculi, initiis dolorum deinceps consummandorum. Adde Matth. 25. 41. Execrati, abite à Me in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus, quod est æternum istius Execrationis complementum.
units.tr: The same threatening is repeated somewhat differently in Deut. 27:26 and Gal. 3:10: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things, etc. Compare Gen. 3:17–19: "Cursed is the ground for your sake; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles to you. ... In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground," etc. Likewise Lev. 26:14ff.; Deut. 28:15ff. From these it is clear concerning the curse of this age, the beginnings of sorrows to be afterwards brought to completion. Add Matt. 25:41: "Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels," which is the eternal completion of that curse.

units.la: GXIX. Deinde ad Confirmationem istius Fœderis
units.tr: CXIX. Next, belonging to the confirmation of this covenant

units.la: quoque pertinet Liberalis promissio. Deus enim, ex superabundanti sua bonitate ac φιλανθρωπία, gratis ac fine remuneratione quæri & coli non voluit: Jef. 45. 19. Hebr. xi. 6. Atque ita se ultro Hominibus obligavit: & quodammodo iis debitorem fecit, ubi consummatus esset cursus obedientiæ. Sic autem Vitam illis promisit: ut non solum immunes essent suturi ab omni morte; verum etiam deinceps transferendi in gloriosam beatitudinem cœlestem, & proximiorem communionem ipsius Dei. Vide Psal. 16. 12. Ita enim Moses describit justitiam quæ est ex Lege, quod qui præstiterit ea, vivet per illa: Rom. 10. 5. Gal. 3. 12. Levit. 18. 5. Ezech. 20. 11. Ubi quidem reipsa eadem Vita intelligenda est, quam postmodum nobis Christus acquisivit. Vide Rom. 10. 4. viij. 4. Unde etiam ipse Juveni interroganti, Quid faciam, ut Vitam æternam possideam? mandata Legis propositit primum, Matth. 19. 16, 17. ac statim Cælum, Regnum cœlorum, vel Regnum Dei, appellavit, Vitam illam æternam explicans; verf. 21. 23. Luc. 18. 24.
units.tr: is also the gracious promise. For God, out of his overflowing goodness and philanthropy, did not wish to be sought and worshipped freely and without reward (Isa. 45:19; Heb. 11:6). And so he bound himself to men of his own accord, and in some way made himself their debtor, once the course of obedience had been completed. He promised them life in such a way that they would not only be free from all death, but would also be afterwards translated into glorious heavenly blessedness and a closer communion with God himself. See Ps. 16:11 (12). For thus Moses describes the righteousness which is of the law, that the man who does those things shall live by them (Rom. 10:5; Gal. 3:12; Lev. 18:5; Ezek. 20:11). Here indeed the same life is to be understood which Christ afterwards obtained for us. See Rom. 10:4; 8:4. Whence also to the young man asking, What shall I do that I may possess eternal life? he first proposed the commandments of the Law (Matt. 19:16, 17), and immediately called that eternal life the heaven, the kingdom of heaven, or the kingdom of God, explaining it (vv. 21, 23; Luke 18:24).

units.la: Hactenus pietas Promissionem habet præsentis ac suturæ Vitæ: 1 Tim. 4. 18. omnis generis beneficiorum in hoc sæculo: Exod. 20. 12. Levit. 26. 3,-13. Deut. 28. 1,-14. & beatitudinis ac gloriæ æternæ in altero sæculo: Rom. xi. 7. Observandum interim, in gratiosa ejusmodi repetitione post lapsum, bona fere proponi convenienter præsenti Hominis conditioni; atque ita ut jus illud, respectu omnium salvandorum, nunc funditur in Christo.
units.tr: Thus godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1 Tim. 4:8): of every kind of benefit in this age (Exod. 20:12; Lev. 26:3–13; Deut. 28:1–14), and of blessedness and eternal glory in the other age (Rom. 11:7). It is to be observed meanwhile that in such a gracious repetition after the fall, the goods proposed are mostly those suited to man's present condition; and so that right, with respect to all who are to be saved, is now poured out in Christ.

units.la: CXX. Sequuntur Signa Fœderis illius. Hic autem initio se offert Arbor scientiæ boni ac mali: Gen. 11. 9. cujus esu Deus Homini interdixerat; verf. 17. ut scil. isto symbolo Hominis obedientia probaretur; eademque opera confirmaretur, si is obedientiam præstaret & consummaret, certa bonorum affluentia, & malorum immunitas; sin secus, bonorum amissio, & malorum indubitata successio. Sic enim signative accipienda est ista Arboris illius appellatio.
units.tr: CXX. There follow the signs of that covenant. Here at the beginning there presents itself the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:9), whose eating God had forbidden to man (v. 17), so that by this symbol man's obedience might be tested; and it would be confirmed by the same means: if he rendered and completed obedience, there would be a sure abundance of goods and immunity from evils; but otherwise, loss of goods and the undoubted succession of evils. For in this way that name of the tree is to be understood as signifying.

units.la: Obj. 1. Ista Arbor videtur habuisse naturalem facultatem acuendi ingenium, & faciendi sensus magis promtos atque expeditos ad suas operationes: ac proinde ejus usu vere acquiri potuisset sapientia, aut scientia perfectior. Resp. Tale quidem erat seductoris & homicidæ Diaboli mendacium; Gen. 3. 5. cui male fidem adhibuit Mulier peccare incipiens; verf. 6. Sed nulla causa materialis per se producere potest essectum immaterialem. Spiritibus autem animalibus perpetuo & satis apte restaurandis suppeditabant procul dubio alia satis multa; quibus tamen ista appellatio non tribuitur.
units.tr: Objection 1. That tree seems to have had a natural power of sharpening the wit and making the senses more ready and nimble for their operations; and therefore by its use wisdom or a more perfect knowledge could truly have been acquired. Reply. Such indeed was the lie of the seducer and murderer, the devil (Gen. 3:5), to which the woman foolishly gave credence when she began to sin (v. 6). But no material cause can of itself produce an immaterial effect. Moreover, for the constant and fairly apt restoration of the animal spirits there were doubtless many other sufficient things; yet this name is not assigned to them.

units.la: Obj. 2. Si signum fuit ista Arbor, signum fuit mortis & miseriæ. Resp. Imo non minus erat Arbor Scientiæ boni, quam mali; prout obedientia præstanda esset, vel non esset: quemadmodum jam explicatum est, & conditioni Hominis sub isto Fœdere conveniebat.
units.tr: Objection 2. If that tree was a sign, it was a sign of death and misery. Reply. On the contrary, it was no less the tree of the knowledge of good than of evil, according as obedience was to be rendered or not, as has already been explained, and as was fitting to man's condition under this covenant.

units.la: Obj. 3. Sacramenta percipi debent ab Hominibus Fœderatis: at ista Arbor percipi non debuit. Resp. Fructus ejus edi quidem non debuit: attamen Arbor conspici, ejusque ordinatio symbolica agnosci potuit & debuit; non minus quam in Iride, Gen. 9. 12, 13, 14. Ac porro in aliis Sacramentis, non ejusdem modi est perceptio: 1 Cor. 10. 1, 2, 3.
units.tr: Objection 3. Sacraments ought to be received by men in covenant, but that tree ought not to have been received. Reply. Indeed its fruit ought not to have been eaten; yet the tree could be seen, and its symbolic appointment acknowledged, and ought to have been, no less than in the rainbow (Gen. 9:12–14). Moreover, in other sacraments the reception is not of the same kind (1 Cor. 10:1, 2, 3).

units.la: CXXI. Deindè illustris erat Arbor vitæ, in medio Paradisi, Gen. 2. 9. præclarum vitæ ac gloriæ æternæ sacramentum; sed juxta promissionem & conditionem istius Fœderis. Hinc porro cap. 3. 22. Homo ex ea comedens, dicitur victurus in sæculum: quoniam ejus esus ex ordinatione Divina, obsignabat, & sic certo inferebat, vitam æternam; verum Homines per lapsum re signatâ destituti, usu signi necessario prohiberi debuerunt.
units.tr: CXXI. Next, the tree of life was conspicuous in the middle of Paradise (Gen. 2:9), an excellent sacrament of life and eternal glory, but according to the promise and condition of this covenant. Hence also in chapter 3:22 man, eating from it, is said to be going to live for ever; since its eating, by divine appointment, sealed and so surely conveyed eternal life. But men, through the fall, the thing signified having been lost, had necessarily to be debarred from the use of the sign.

units.la: Obj. Vocatur potius Arbor vitæ, quod haberet virtutem physicam vitæ in æternum producendæ; atque adeo esset remedium contra omnes morbos, omnem corruptionem, & ipsam senectutem, &c. Resp. 1. Morbi & corruptiones maximam habent diversitatem: omnis autem medicatio fieri debet per contraria: consequenter ea per unam arborem, aut ejus fructus, fieri non potuit naturaliter. 2. Et quid tum de ruina ædium, incendio, viaquarum, &c. quæ pericula alibi producunt Adversarii? 3. Neque istiusmodi remedium erat necessarium: cum omnia alimenta essent satis salubria; ipsiqueHomines ea sapientia præditi, ut singulis fuissent recte usuri; nec etiam alia incommoda mortifera eventura, Deo omnia benigne & potenter disponente, juxta promissionem suam, ad Hominum immortalitatem & gloriam æternam; si modo in primæva integritate, suoque officio, perstitissent.
units.tr: Objection. It is rather called the tree of life because it had a physical power of producing life for ever; and so it would be a remedy against all diseases, all corruption, and old age itself, etc. Reply. 1. Diseases and corruptions have the greatest diversity; but every cure ought to be effected by contraries; consequently these could not be naturally effected by one tree or its fruit. 2. And what then of the collapse of buildings, fire, water-floods, etc., which the adversaries say produce dangers elsewhere? 3. Nor was such a remedy necessary, since all foods were sufficiently wholesome, and men themselves were endowed with such wisdom that they would have used each rightly; nor would other deadly inconveniences have befallen them, God disposing all things kindly and powerfully, according to his promise, towards human immortality and eternal glory, provided only that they had persisted in original integrity and in their duty.

units.la: Inst. Apoc. 22, 2. „In medio foro ejus (Hierosoly„mæ) & ex utraque parte fluminis erat Arbor Vitæ se„rens fructus duodecim, per menses singulos edens fru„ ctum suum; & folia sua ad sanitatem Gentium. Ergo etiam in Paradiso terrestri Arbor vitæ erat ad sanitatem. Resp. Sic per visionem & figurationem Propheticam delineatur perpetua virtus vivifica & beatifica Servatoris nostri; qui nunc sub Fœdere Euangelico vere nobis impetravit, atque etiam applicat realiter, id ipsum quod sub Fœdere Legali olim significabat Arbor illa vitæ.
units.tr: Inst. Apoc. 22, 2. "In the midst of its street (of Jerusalem), and on either side of the river, was the Tree of Life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month; and its leaves for the healing of the nations." Therefore the Tree of Life was also in the earthly Paradise for healing. Answer: In this way, through a prophetic vision and figure, is depicted the perpetual life-giving and blessing power of our Saviour, who now under the Gospel covenant has truly obtained for us, and also actually applies, the very thing that tree of life once signified under the legal covenant.

units.la: CXXII.
units.tr: CXXII.

units.la: Affinis est consideratio ipsius Paradisi, Horti amoenissimi cum quatuor suis fluviis, in orientali parte Hedenis; quae est in Babylonia, parte Mesopotamiae, &c. Gen. II, 8, -. Iste enim singulari sua amoenitate, ac potissimum contenta Arbore vitae, ipsum Coelum tertium, sive beatorum, & gaudium aeternum, quoque significavit. Unde Coelum istud Paradisi nomine diserte appellatur, 2 Cor. XII, 2, 4. Luc. XXIII, 43. Apoc. II. 7.
units.tr: Related to this is the consideration of Paradise itself, the most pleasant garden with its four rivers, in the eastern part of Eden, which is in Babylonia, in the part of Mesopotamia, etc. Gen. 2:8. For that place, by its singular pleasantness and especially by the Tree of Life it contained, also signified the third heaven, the abode of the blessed and eternal joy. Hence that heaven is expressly called Paradise, 2 Cor. 12:2, 4; Luke 23:43; Rev. 2:7.

units.la: Sed post peccatum Deus Homines Paradiso expulit, reddituque prohibuit, appositis Cherubinis, cum flamma gladii sese vibrantis: Gen. III, 23, 24. Hodie autem ille superstes non est; & maxime vero simile, quod per Diluvium fit corruptus.
units.tr: But after the sin, God drove men out of Paradise and forbade their return, placing Cherubim there with a flaming sword flashing about: Gen. 3:23, 24. Today, however, it no longer survives; and it is most likely that it was destroyed by the Flood.

units.la: Vanissimum vero est Pontificiorum commentum, ex detorsione loci Apoc. XI, 3, &c. de Paradiso adhuc superstite, & Enocho atque Elia in eum translatis, ibique permansuris usque ad congressum suum cum Antichristo; a quo sint occidendi, postea tamen virtute Divina resuscitandi, & in Coelum assumendi.
units.tr: Utterly vain is the Papists' invention, drawn from a distortion of Rev. 11:3, etc., concerning Paradise still existing, and Enoch and Elijah having been translated into it, and remaining there until their encounter with Antichrist; by whom they are to be slain, and afterwards by divine power raised again and taken up into heaven.

units.la: CXXIII.
units.tr: CXXIII.

units.la: Sed neque omittenda videtur observatio Sabbathi; de cujus primaeva institutione diximus sup. th. 13. ut illa beatam requiem a cursu obedientiae fideliter consummato in Coelis agenda, sabbatismum perpetuum ac gloriosissimum, utcunque etiam adumbraverit, & studium ejus promoverit. Heb. 4, 3, 4. Introimus enim in requiem nos qui credimus, sicut dixit, Psa. 95, 11. Itaque juravi in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam: licet operibus a jacto mundi fundamento factis. Ita enim dixit quodam in loco de septimo die, Gen. 2, 2. Et quievit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis, &c. 9, 10. Itaque reliquus est aliquis sabbatismus populo Dei. Nam qui ingressus est in requiem ipsius, requievit & ipse ab operibus suis; quemadmodum a suis Deus. Ita signo illo primaevo illustratur beata requies & gloria, quam Deus isto Foedere Protoplastis promisserat.
units.tr: Nor does the observance of the Sabbath seem to be omitted; of whose primitive institution we spoke above, in chapter 13, so that it might, in whatever way, have foreshadowed and promoted the longing for that blessed rest to be enjoyed in heaven after the course of obedience has been faithfully completed, a perpetual and most glorious Sabbath-rest. Heb. 4:3, 4. For we who believe enter into rest, as he said, Ps. 95:11: "So I swore in my anger, They shall not enter into my rest," although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he spoke in a certain place of the seventh day thus, Gen. 2:2: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works," etc. 9, 10: "Therefore there remains a Sabbath-rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his." Thus by that primeval sign is illustrated the blessed rest and glory which God had promised to the first-formed man by this covenant.

units.la: CXXIV. Superest ejus Duratio. Hæc autem mundo, & hominibus in eo viventibus, coæva est: quin & Judicium, quod ejus executio, erit æternum: Hebr. vi, 2. Marc. iii, 29. Aliter tamen se habet in Hominibus, qui sibi prorsus relinquuntur, extra salutarem Christi communionem; aliter in vere Christianis. Priores omnino manent sub isto Fœdere, ac per ipsum condemnantur: sic ira Dei manet ἐπὶ τὰς ἀπειθοῦντας, Joh. iii, 36. & eos occupat ad finem usque: 1 Thess. ii, 16. Hactenus ergo Fœdus legale non est abrogatum; neque quicquam ei derogatum.
units.tr: CXXIV. There remains its duration. This, indeed, is coeval with the world and with the men living in it; nay, the judgment, of which it is the execution, will be eternal: Heb. 6:2; Mark 3:29. Yet it stands otherwise with men who are left wholly to themselves, outside the saving communion of Christ; otherwise with those who are truly Christian. The former remain entirely under this covenant and are condemned through it: thus the wrath of God remains upon the disobedient, John 3:36, and seizes them to the end: 1 Thess. 2:16. Hitherto, therefore, the legal covenant has not been abrogated, nor anything taken away from it.

units.la: In posterioribus non fit stricta istius Fœderis executio, juxta verborum formulam: sic enim illi, propter peccata sua, servari non possent: at vero per Christi satisfactionem a reatu redemti sunt; & ab execratione liberati; ejusdemque obedientia universum jus Legis pro iis impletum. Rom. vi ii, 1, -4. Gal. iii, 13. Scil. Fœdus istud explicatum est a Deo clementissimo κατ' ἐπιείκειαν: & consequenter loco nostro admissa solutio ἀντὶ λύτρου, a Redemtore dignißimo nobisque conjunctissimo; ac porro ab eodem impleta omnis justitia, qua nos justi constitueremur, per gratiosam Dei imputationem; 2 Cor. v. 15, 17, 18, 19, 21. Matth. 3. 15. Rom. 5. 19. iv. 5. 6. cum 19. 18. Philem. Ita quidem, ut fit Ipse Justus, & Justificans eum qui est ex Fide Jesu. Siquidem Deus unus est, qui justificabit Circumcisionem ex Fide, & Præputium per Fidem. Legem igitur inutilem reddimus per Fidem? Absit. Imo Legem stabilimus: Rom. 3. 26, 30, 31.
units.tr: In the latter, the strict execution of this covenant, according to the wording of its formula, does not take place: for in that way they could not be preserved on account of their sins; but through Christ's satisfaction they have been redeemed from guilt and freed from the curse; and by his obedience the whole right of the Law has been fulfilled on their behalf. Rom. 8:1-4; Gal. 3:13. That is, this covenant has been explained by a most merciful God according to equity [κατ' ἐπιείκειαν]; and consequently the solution admitted in our place is a ransom [ἀντὶ λύτρου], given by a most worthy Redeemer, most closely united to us; and further, by the same Redeemer all righteousness has been fulfilled, by which we are constituted righteous through God's gracious imputation: 2 Cor. 5:15, 17, 18, 19, 21; Matt. 3:15; Rom. 5:19; 4:5, 6, compared with 19, 18; Philem. Thus indeed it comes about that he is himself just and justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus. For God is one, who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith. Do we then make void the Law through faith? By no means. Rather we establish the Law: Rom. 3:26, 30, 31.

units.la: Obj. 1. Matth. 11, 13. Omnes Prophetæ, & ipsa Lex, usque ad Johannem prophetarunt. Ergo Lex & Fœdus Legale non durant post Johannem Baptistam. Resp. Non agitur istic propriè de Lege morali, aut Fœdere Legali; sed de œconomia Prophetica, & Ceremoniali typica, V. T. Christum venturum prænunciante atque adumbrante; cui finem imposuit Johannes nes Baptista, Christum præsentem demonstrans: Joh. 1, 19, 36.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matt. 11:13: "All the Prophets and the Law itself prophesied until John." Therefore the Law and the legal covenant do not last after John the Baptist. Answer: Strictly speaking, the passage is not about the moral Law or the legal covenant, but about the prophetic economy and the typical ceremonial, foretelling and foreshadowing the coming of Christ in the Old Testament; this John the Baptist brought to an end, when he pointed to Christ as present: John 1:19, 36.

units.la: Obj. 2. Rom. 6, 14. Non estis sub Lege: sed sub Gratia. Resp. Fideles sunt sub Fœdere gratiæ; ac per ipsum liberati: non a Legis usu normali; sed ab ejus condemnatione, & rigore Fœderali.
units.tr: Objection 2. Rom. 6:14: "You are not under the Law, but under grace." Answer: The faithful are under the covenant of grace and are freed through it: not from the normal use of the Law, but from its condemnation and its federal rigour.

units.la: Obj. 3. Hebr. 8, 10, -. ex Jerem. 31, 31, -. Quamobrem hoc est pactum, -. Dum novum dicit, antiquavit prius, &c. Resp. Proponuntur istic bona Euangelica, quæ quidem clariora & uberiora sunt sub N. T. Per hanc autem œconomiam antiquata est prior V. T. sub qua durior erat pædagogia, & rigidior inculcatio Fœderis Legalis. Unde tamen non sequitur, Fœdus Legale abrogatum esse absolute.
units.tr: Objection 3. Heb. 8:10 ff., from Jer. 31:31 ff.: "Therefore this is the covenant..." "In saying new, he has made the first old," etc. Answer: The good things of the Gospel are set forth there, which are indeed clearer and more abundant under the New Testament. Through this economy, however, the former dispensation under the Old Testament, under which the pedagogy was harsher and the inculcation of the legal covenant more rigid, has been made obsolete. Yet it does not follow from this that the legal covenant has been abrogated absolutely.

units.la: Obj. 4. 1 Tim. 1, 9, 10. Legem justo non esse positam; sed sceleratis, -. Resp. Iterum in ratione Fœderis, sanctio poenalis spectatur synecdochice: ea autem non premit justos; etiam in Christo Euangelice. Attamen quia Christus pro iis jus Legis complevit, non debet colligi absoluta abrogatio.
units.tr: Objection 4. 1 Tim. 1:9, 10: "The Law is not laid down for the just, but for the wicked..." Answer: Again, in respect of the covenant, the penal sanction is regarded synecdochically; yet this does not oppress the just, even in Christ under the Gospel. Nevertheless, because Christ has fulfilled the right of the Law on their behalf, an absolute abrogation should not be inferred.

units.la: CXXV. Pro Praxi; 1. Ex consideratione Legis, ac Fœderis Legalis, ad fontem & archetypum ascen- damus: Sanctitatem Jehovæ meditemur, admire- mur, imitemur: Levit. 19. 2. 3.
units.tr: CXXV. For practice: 1. Let us ascend from the consideration of the Law and of the legal covenant to the source and archetype: let us meditate upon the holiness of Jehovah, marvel at it, and imitate it: Lev. 19. 2, 3.

units.la: 2. Normam illam rectissimam sequamur tota vita, omnibus actionibus; nihil excipientes, nihil divellentes: Psal. 19. 9. - 13. 119, 2, 4, &c. Matth. v, 17, 20, 48. Jac. 2. 4, 8, 10, 12. Gal. 6. 16.
units.tr: 2. Let us follow that most upright rule all our life and in all our actions, excepting nothing and detaching nothing from it: Ps. 19. 9–13; 119. 2, 4, etc.; Matt. 5. 17, 20, 48; Jas. 2. 4, 8, 10, 12; Gal. 6. 16.

units.la: 3. Sic justam Legis Sanctionem contemplemur, ut Liberationem nostri per vicariam Christi Satisfactionem, juxta Euangelium, pie admiremur: 2. Cor. v, 14, 15.
units.tr: 3. Let us so contemplate the just sanction of the Law that we devoutly marvel, according to the Gospel, at our deliverance through Christ's vicarious satisfaction: 2 Cor. 5. 14, 15.

units.la: 4. Scientes terrorem illum Domini, alios doceamus fugere a futura ira, eosque ad fidem adducamus, juxta vocationem nostram: 2 Cor. 5, 11. Matth. 3. 7.
units.tr: 4. Knowing the terror of the Lord, let us teach others to flee from the coming wrath, and bring them to faith, according to our calling: 2 Cor. 5. 11; Matt. 3. 7.

units.la: 5. Dum jus Legis pro nobis a Christo impletum est; Rom. 8. 4, atque hæc nobis facta est Lex libertatis, Iac. 1. 25. 2, 12. excitet nos amplissima ac saluberrima promissio, ad novam obedientiam & alacrem gratitudinem; Hebr. 11, 6. 12. 18, -24.
units.tr: 5. Since the right of the Law has been fulfilled for us by Christ, Rom. 8. 4, and this law has been made for us a law of liberty, Jas. 1. 25; 2. 12, let the most ample and most wholesome promise stir us up to a new obedience and a ready gratitude: Heb. 11. 6; 12. 18–24.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De Peccato.
units.tr: On Sin.

units.la: Cognitio nostri. Malum. Peccatum. 1. Contra Legem Divinam proprie. 2. Non positivum, aut substantiale; nec mere negativum : sed privativum. Subjectum quod, & quo. 3. Ejus non causa efficiens; sed deficiens. Non omne peccatum est voluntarium, antecedente judicio ac deliberatione. 4. Non habet finem per se ac proprie dictum. 5. Macula. 6. Reatus, tum potentialis, tum actualis. 7. Pontificii male distinguunt Reatum culpæ, & pœnæ. Obj. solv. 8. Conscientia condemnans, & spiritus servitutis. 9. Utilitas distinctionis inter Maculam, & Reatum. 10. Pœna. Quomodo ad Bestias etiam referatur. 11. Castigatio. Probatio. Martyrium. 12. Pœna damni, & sensus. 13. Peccatum vel omissionis, vel commissionis. 14. Habituale, vel Actuale. 15. Angelorum, vel Hominum. 16. In Hominibus peccatum primum. Ejus causæ principales deficientes. Libere. 17. Causa procatarctica. Serpens. Methodus 18. Consummatum. Inchoatum. 19. Deus illius non causa efficiens; nec privative deficiens. Permisit tamen; &
units.tr: Knowledge of ourselves. Evil. Sin. 1. Properly, a transgression against the Divine Law. 2. Not positive or substantial, nor merely negative, but privative. Its subject, both what and in which. 3. Its cause is not efficient but deficient. Not every sin is voluntary, with prior judgment and deliberation. 4. It has no end in the strict and proper sense. 5. Stain. 6. Guilt, both potential and actual. 7. The Papists wrongly distinguish the guilt of fault from the guilt of punishment. Objection answered. 8. A condemning conscience and the spirit of bondage. 9. The usefulness of the distinction between stain and guilt. 10. Punishment. How it also applies to beasts. 11. Chastisement. Trial. Martyrdom. 12. Punishment of loss and of sense. 13. Sin either of omission or of commission. 14. Habitual or actual. 15. Of angels or of men. 16. In men, the first sin. Its principal deficient causes. Freely. 17. The provocative cause. The serpent. Method. 18. Completed. Begun. 19. God is not the efficient cause of that sin, nor its privative deficient cause. He permitted it, however, and

units.la: CXII. Æque absurdè statuunt iidem, Christum præter universam istam Legem, tulisse insuper alia quædam præcepta moralia; nimirùm de sui Abnegatione, de Tolerantia crucis, & Imitatione ipsius Christi.
units.tr: CXII. Equally absurdly the same writers maintain that Christ, besides this whole Law, gave some further moral precepts: namely, concerning self-denial, the endurance of the cross, and the imitation of Christ himself.

units.la: Quod enim primò attinet ad Abnegationem sui, præceptum satis antiquum esse patet, 1. si respiciamus Abrahamum, Gen. xii. 1.
units.tr: For as to the first, self-denial, it is plain that the precept is quite ancient: 1. if we look to Abraham, Gen. 12:1.

units.la: 2. Eandem exigit ipsa Lex, Deut. vi, 5. Sic enim abneganda fuit omnis cupiditas, cogitatio, inclinatio, dilectioni & obedientiæ Dei adversa.
units.tr: 2. The Law itself demands the same, Deut. 6:5. For every desire, thought and inclination opposed to the love and obedience of God had to be denied in this way.

units.la: 3. Ex Prophetis etiam facilè est colligere illud officium: utpote Jerem.III, 17. iv, 3, 4. vii, 23, 24.
units.tr: 3. From the Prophets too it is easy to gather this duty, as in Jer. 3:17; 4:3, 4; 7:23, 24.

units.la: 4. Illustria exempla quoque occurrunt, Psal. cxxxi, 1, 2. Job. xxxi, 1.
units.tr: 4. Illustrious examples also occur, Ps. 131:1, 2; Job 31:1.

units.la: Secundo, de Tolerantia crucis, sive afflictionum, castigationum, & probationum Dei, demonstratur facilè; 1. ex Prov. III. 11, 12. Huc respicit Apostolus, Hebr. xii, 1, 5, 6.
units.tr: Secondly, concerning the endurance of the cross, or of afflictions, chastisements and trials sent by God, it is easily shown: 1. from Prov. 3:11, 12. The Apostle has this in view, Heb. 12:1, 5, 6.

units.la: 2. Præclara etiam sunt, 1 Sam. III, 18. Itemque Job. I, 21. II, 10. Thren. III. 27, 39. Mich. vii, 8, 9. Psal. cxxix, 1, 2.
units.tr: 2. Notable also are 1 Sam. 3:18; likewise Job 1:21; 2:10; Lam. 3:27, 39; Mic. 7:8, 9; Ps. 129:1, 2.

units.la: 3. Consimilia indicantur in N. T. ubi hæc praxis confirmatur exemplis ex V. T. depromtis: Hebr, xi, 25, 26. 35, -38. xii, 1. Jac. 5, 10, 11.
units.tr: 3. Similar passages are pointed out in the New Testament, where this practice is confirmed by examples taken from the Old: Heb. 11:25, 26, 35–38; 12:1; James 5:10, 11.

units.la: Tertiò, de Imitatione Christi satis etiam patet ex mandatis, ubi Deus sanctitatem suam sub V. T. imitandam præcepit: utpote Levit. xix, 2. si nimirum conferantur ea, quæ de Christi Θεανθρώπου obedientia, humilitate, cæterisque virtutibus, jam olim fuerunt prædicta; Dan. ix, 24. Psal. xl, 7, 8, 9. Jesaj. liii, 6, 7. Zach. ix, 9. In istis enim sita est Imitatio Christi: Matth. xi, 29. Phil. II, 5, -8. 1 Petr. II. 20, 21.
units.tr: Thirdly, concerning the imitation of Christ, it is also sufficiently clear from the commands in which God under the Old Testament ordered his own holiness to be imitated, as in Lev. 19:2, if one compares these with what was foretold long ago of the obedience, humility and other virtues of Christ, the God-man; Dan. 9:24; Ps. 40:7, 8, 9; Isa. 53:6, 7; Zech. 9:9. For the imitation of Christ consists in these things: Matt. 11:29; Phil. 2:5–8; 1 Pet. 2:20, 21.

units.la: Quin & virtutes singulæ, quas nos in Christo observare atque imitari oportet, in V. T. fuerunt etiam propositæ ac mandatæ.
units.tr: Indeed each single virtue which we ought to observe and imitate in Christ was also set forth and commanded in the Old Testament.

units.la: CXIII. Cæterum Lex illa vel simpliciter secundum se spectatur: vel prout est instrumentum primi Fœderis. Priore modo saltem est norma obedientiæ: specifice præscribens debitum dependentiæ nostræ moralis ad Divinam ὑπεροχὴν, & jus absoluti illius Domini: unde fluit obligatio nostri ad præstanda ossicia mandata, & fugienda vitia contraria. Sed hactenus Deus nullo modo obligatus est Homini, ad gratitudinem ei referendam, vel remunerationem faciendam pro obsequio & cultu sibi præstito. Job. xxxv, 7. Si justus es, quid das Ei; aut quid de manu tua accepit? Psal. xvi, 2. Bonum meum non pervenit ad Te. Rom. xi, 35. Quis prior dedit Ei, & reddetur ipsi? Luc. xvii, 9, 10. Num gratiam habet servo illi, quia fecit quæ ipsi edicta fuerant? Non puto. Ita & vos, cum feceritis omnia, quæ edicta sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus: nam quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Naturaliter tamen actus humanus, si qua morali malitia laboret, eo ipso convenientem pœnam demeretur; per justitiam Dei vindicativam. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 56.
units.tr: CXIII. Moreover that Law is considered either simply in itself, or as the instrument of the first covenant. In the former way it is at least the rule of obedience, specifically prescribing the due dependence of our moral nature upon the Divine eminence and the right of that absolute Lord; whence arises our obligation to perform the duties commanded and to flee the contrary vices. But so far God is in no way bound to man to return gratitude or to make recompense for the obedience and worship rendered to him. Job 35:7: If you are righteous, what do you give him, or what does he receive from your hand? Ps. 16:2: My good does not reach to you. Rom. 11:35: Who first gave to him, that it should be repaid to him? Luke 17:9, 10: Does he have thanks for that servant, because he did what had been commanded him? I think not. So you also, when you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; for we have done what we ought to have done. Yet naturally a human act, if it suffers from some moral malice, thereby deserves a fitting punishment, through the avenging justice of God. See above, chapter 4, thesis 56.

units.la: CXIV. Vox Hebræa בְּרִית pactum, conventionem, & fœdus notat: Græci διαθήκην appellant; q. d. dispositionem. Laxiore significatu quodlibet firmum statutum, etiam de rebus inanimatis, sic nuncupatur. Jerem. xxxiii, 20, 25. Fœdus meum de die, & fœdus meum de nocte. Occurrit etiam generale fœdus, quod Deus non solum cum hominibus pepigit, sed ad bestias quoque extendit, & iride obsignavit; de mundo non perdendo per diluvium; Gen. ix, 9, -16.
units.tr: CXIV. The Hebrew word בְּרִית signifies a pact, an agreement, and a covenant; the Greeks call it διαθήκη, as if to say a disposition. In a looser sense any firm ordinance, even concerning inanimate things, is so named. Jer. 33:20, 25: My covenant of the day, and my covenant of the night. There also occurs a general covenant, which God made not only with men but extended to the beasts too, and sealed with the rainbow, concerning the world not to be destroyed by the flood; Gen. 9:9–16.

units.la: Fœdera autem Politicis sunt Conventiones publicæ, quæ fiunt jussu summæ potestatis, & in quibus populus iræ Divinæ obstringi solet, si minus fletur dictis. Per ea interdum idem constituitur, quod est Juris naturæ: utpote inter hostes a bello discedentes; vel etiam inter eos, qui nihil ante contraxerunt; ne scil. alii alios lædant, &c. Interdum Juri naturæ aliquid adjicitur. Suntque vel Fœdera æqualia, συνθῆκαι: quæ utrimque se habent eodem modo. Vel inæqualia, ἄνισοι; ut si pars potentior auxilia promittat, nec restipuletur; sive majora promittat: aut respectu partis minus dignæ ac potentis (προσαγμαῖα, ὑπαγμαῖα) ubi aliquando fit imperii translatio, vel saltem imminutio, vel onera quædam imponuntur.
units.tr: Covenants among politics are public agreements, made by command of the supreme power, and by which a people is usually bound to the wrath of God if they do not keep what has been said. By them sometimes the same thing is established as belongs to the law of nature: for example, between enemies withdrawing from war; or even between those who have contracted nothing before, namely that they should not harm one another, etc. Sometimes something is added to the law of nature. And they are either equal covenants, συνθῆκαι, which bind both sides in the same way; or unequal, ἄνισοι, as when the stronger party promises aid and does not require a return, or promises greater things; or with respect to the less worthy and weaker party (προσαγμαῖα, ὑπαγμαῖα), where sometimes a transfer of rule takes place, or at least a diminution, or certain burdens are imposed.

units.la: Fœdera item sunt vel amicitiæ, vel reconciliationis: in his supponitur offensa; in illis non item.
units.tr: Covenants likewise are either of friendship or of reconciliation: the latter presuppose an offence; the former do not.

units.la: CXV. Fœdus primum, de quo nunc agendum, alias Legale appellatur, vel Operum; interdum etiam Naturæ: estque inæquale, & amicitiæ inæqualis. Describitur autem plenius; Quod Deus cum Adamo, ac pariter cum universo Genere humano, quod in eo tanquam capite censitum fuit, ita pepigit; ut ipsum Jus naturæ, Lege comprehensum, firmaverit, tum sanctione poenali adversus transgressores, tum liberali promissione erga eos qui perfectam obedientiam forent consummaturi; ad demonstrandam per omnia secula gloriam potestatis, gratiæ, & justitiæ suæ. Considerabimus autem deinceps 1. specialem ejus Modum.
units.tr: CXV. The first covenant, of which we now have to speak, is otherwise called Legal, or of works, and sometimes also of nature; and it is unequal, like a friendship between unequals. It is described more fully thus: that God so covenanted with Adam, and likewise with the whole human race, which was reckoned in him as its head, that he confirmed the natural law itself, comprised in the Law, both by a penal sanction against transgressors and by a generous promise to those who would bring perfect obedience to completion; to demonstrate through all ages the glory of his power, grace and justice. We shall consider next 1. its particular mode.

units.la: 2. Confirmationem, 3. Signa, & 4 Durationem. Ad Modum illum pertinet, tum Conditio præstanda, quam Deus stipulatus est; tum Ordo generis humani, quem Deus pro suo jure constituit.
units.tr: 2. its confirmation, 3. its signs, and 4. its duration. To that mode belong both the condition to be performed, which God stipulated, and the order of the human race, which God established by his own right.

units.la: CXVI. Conditio præstanda, erat perfecta totius Legis observantia; omnium scil. & singulorum præ- ceptorum, quovis loco ac tempore, singulis actibus humanis, ad extremum virium.
units.tr: CXVI. The condition to be fulfilled was perfect observance of the whole Law: of all and each of its precepts, in every place and at every time, in every human act, to the utmost of one's strength.

units.la: Deut. vi. 5. Matth. xxii, 37,38: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Deut. xxvii, 26. Gal. III, 10. Execrabilis est, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, ut faciat ea. Jac. II, 10. Quisquis enim totam Legem servaverit, impegerit autem in uno, damnas factus est omnium. Scil. propter omnimodam Hominum à Deo dependentiam; Act. xvii, 25,-28. Rom. xi, 36. & Legis Divinæ spiritualitatem ac sanctitatem; Rom. vii, 12, 14.
units.tr: Deut. vi. 5. Matth. xxii. 37, 38: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," etc. Deut. xxvii. 26. Gal. iii. 10: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them." Jac. ii. 10: "For whoever keeps the whole Law, but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all." This is because of man's complete dependence on God: Acts xvii. 25-28. Rom. xi. 36. And because of the spirituality and holiness of the divine Law: Rom. vii. 12, 14.

units.la: Ista autem conditio, juxta verborum formulam in rigore suo acceptam, præstari debuit a quovis Homine in propria persona. Levit. xviii, 5. Ezech. xx, 11. Rom. x, 5. Gal. iii, 12. Qui præstiterit ea, vivet per illa sine ulla mentione Sponsoris, aut Servatoris.
units.tr: But this condition, taken strictly according to the form of words, had to be fulfilled by every man in his own person: Lev. xviii. 5. Ezek. xx. 11. Rom. x. 5. Gal. iii. 12: "He who does these things shall live by them," with no mention of a Surety or Saviour.

units.la: CXVII. Quantum attinet ad Ordinem Generis humani: Adamus primus & universalis pater fuit omnium Hominum: sicut Eva eorum mater: Gen. III, 20. Confer Act. xvii, 26. Sed & ipse Adamus principium quoque Mulieris, & caput ejus: Gen. II, 21, 22, 23. Eph. v, 23. Sic omnes Posteri virtualiter fuerunt in Adamo, tanquam causa prima istius Generis: quæ est Consideratio physica. Verum ad istam accessit alia Constitutio politica & fœderalis, ut omnes Posteri in Adamo censerentur: atque adeo Adamus vel eorum bono esset perseveraturus in statu integritatis, cursumque obedientiæ consummaturus, ad justitiam & gloriam æternam; vel etiam eorum malo esset lapsurus, eidemque secum calamitati & exitio eos simul involuturus.
units.tr: CXVII. As regards the order of the human race: Adam was the first and universal father of all men, just as Eve was their mother: Gen. iii. 20. Compare Acts xvii. 26. But Adam himself was also the source and head of the woman: Gen. ii. 21-23. Eph. v. 23. Thus all posterity were virtually in Adam, as the first cause of this race. This is the physical consideration. To it, however, another was added, a political and federal constitution, by which all posterity were reckoned in Adam. So Adam would either, for their good, persevere in the state of integrity and complete the course of obedience to justice and eternal glory; or, to their harm, would fall, and would drag them down with himself into the same calamity and ruin.

units.la: Similiter Hebr. vii, 9, 10. Levi in lumbis Abrahami proavi fui existens virtualiter, in eodem quoque decimas censebatur dedisse Melchizedeko. Certe prohibitio Arboris scientiæ boni & mali, Adamo facta, Gen. II, 17. ad Evam extenditur, III, 3. Et ad Posteros quoque pertinuit eadem obligatio realis (non personalis): hinc Protoplasti, ubi peccassent, Paradiso exclusi, & ab aditu atque usu Arboris vitæ remoti fuerunt una cum Posteris suis; terra item maledictioni subjecta fuit, multæque calamitates immissæ, Posterorum quoque incommodo: statutum similiter omnibus semel mori; atque in universum omne figmentum cogitationum cordis humani evasit malum inde à pueritia, &c. Gen. III, 22, 23, 24. 16, 19. Hebr. ix, 27. Gen. vi, 5. viii, 21. Clarissimè etiam Apostolus, 1 Cor. xv, 22. In Adamo omnes moriuntur. Rom. v, 12, 14, -19. Per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors: & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccarunt. --qui (Adamus) est typus illius (Christi) qui erat futurus. --- Per unam offensam (reatus venit) in omnes homines ad condemnationem, &c. Confer sup. cap. 4. th. 69.
units.tr: Similarly Heb. vii. 9, 10: Levi, being virtually in the loins of his forefather Abraham, was reckoned to have paid tithes to Melchizedek in him. Certainly the prohibition concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, given to Adam (Gen. ii. 17), extends to Eve (iii. 3). The same real (not personal) obligation also pertained to posterity. Hence the first parents, when they had sinned, were excluded from Paradise and removed from access to and use of the tree of life, together with their posterity. The earth likewise was made subject to the curse, and many calamities were sent, to the disadvantage of posterity too. It was similarly decreed that all should die once; and in general every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart became evil from childhood, etc. Gen. iii. 22, 23, 24; 16, 19. Heb. ix. 27. Gen. vi. 5; viii. 21. The Apostle states it most clearly: 1 Cor. xv. 22: "In Adam all die." Rom. v. 12, 14-19: "Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin; and so death spread to all men, in whom all sinned." ... "Adam, who is the type of him who was to come." ... "Through one offence [guilt came] upon all men to condemnation," etc. Compare above, chapter 4, thesis 69.

units.la: CXVIII. Ad Confirmationem pertinet primo San- ctio poenalis, sive Comminatio poenarum adversus pec- cata, si ea committerentur.
units.tr: CXVIII. To the confirmation belongs, first, the penal sanction, or the threat of punishments against sins, should they be committed.

units.la: Ubi non solum Deus clarè expressit, quid Justitia sua vindicativa postularet: sed ipsi quoque Homines hanc Foederis conditionem amplectentes, & cum libertate complacentiae subeuntes, ex sua etiam parte se obstrinxerunt Deo per istum contractum, ad quem sic Deus per συνθήκην προσφέρει. Unde magis justificantur Dei judicia adversus peccatores, quando iis facit secundum verba foederis, Jerem. xi, 18.
units.tr: Here God not only clearly expressed what his avenging justice required, but men themselves, embracing this condition of the covenant and undertaking it with willing pleasure, bound themselves to God on their own part by this contract, to which God thus makes his offer by way of a covenant [συνθήκην προσφέρει]. Hence God's judgments against sinners are more justified when he deals with them according to the words of the covenant: Jer. xi. 18.

units.la: Sanctio illa breviter expressa est Gen. II, 17. De fructu Arboris scientiae boni & mali ne comedas: nam quo die comederis de eo, moriendo morieris. Confer Rom. vi, 23. Stipendia peccati mors: donum autem Dei est vita aeterna in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Et v, 14, 18. Regnavit mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosen, - in omnes homines ad condemnationem. Item Eph. 2. 1, 3. Mortui inoffensis & peccatis: -- natura filii irae. Ex quibus patet, intelligendam esse omnem mortem miseram, non solum corporalem & temporalem, sed quoque spiritualem & aeternam.
units.tr: That sanction is briefly expressed in Gen. ii. 17: "Of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on the day you eat of it, dying you shall die." Compare Rom. vi. 23: "The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." And v. 14, 18: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses ... upon all men to condemnation." Likewise Eph. ii. 1, 3: "Dead in offences and sins ... by nature children of wrath." From these passages it is plain that every misery is to be understood as death, not only bodily and temporal but also spiritual and eternal.
