units.la: Paulo aliter repetita est eadem Comminatio Deut. 27. 26. Gal. 3. 10. Execrabilis est, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, &c. Confer Gen. 3. 18, 19. Maledicta esto terra propter te: cum dolore comedito provenitum ejus omnibus diebus vitae tuae: eaque spinam ,,& carduum proferto tibi.--Infudore vultus tui vescitor cibo, donec revertaris in humum, &c. Itemque Levit. 26. 14.-. Deut. 28. 15.-. ex quibus constat de Maledictione hujus sæculi, initiis dolorum deinceps consummandorum. Adde Matth. 25. 41. Execrati, abite à Me in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus, quod est æternum istius Execrationis complementum.
units.tr: The same threat is repeated, in somewhat different words, at Deut. xxvii. 26 and Gal. iii. 10: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," etc. Compare Gen. iii. 18, 19: "Cursed is the ground for your sake; in toil you shall eat of its produce all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you ... by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground," etc. Likewise Lev. xxvi. 14 ff. and Deut. xxviii. 15 ff. From these it is established that the curse of this age has begun, with the beginnings of sorrows to be afterwards completed. Add Matth. xxv. 41: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." This is the eternal completion of that curse.

units.la: CXIX. Deinde ad Confirmationem istius Fœderis quoque pertinet Liberalis promissio. Deus enim, ex superabundanti sua bonitate ac φιλανθρωπία, gratis ac fine remuneratione quæri & coli non voluit: Jef. 45. 19. Hebr. xi. 6. Atque ita se ultro Hominibus obligavit: & quodammodo iis debitorem fecit, ubi consummatus esset cursus obedientiæ. Sic autem Vitam illis promisit: ut non solum immunes essent suturi ab omni morte; verum etiam deinceps transferendi in gloriosam beatitudinem cœlestem, & proximiorem communionem ipsius Dei. Vide Psal. 16. 12. Ita enim Moses describit justitiam quæ est ex Lege, quod qui præstiterit ea, vivet per illa: Rom. 10. 5. Gal. 3. 12. Levit. 18. 5. Ezech. 20. 11. Ubi quidem reipsa eadem Vita intelligenda est, quam postmodum nobis Christus acquisivit. Vide Rom. 10. 4. viij. 4. Unde etiam ipse Juveni interroganti, Quid faciam, ut Vitam æternam possideam? mandata Legis propositit primum, Matth. 19. 16, 17. ac statim Cælum, Regnum cælorum, vel Regnum Dei, appellavit, Vitam illam æternam explicans; verf. 21. 23. Luc. 18. 24.
units.tr: CXIX. Next, the confirmation of this covenant also includes the gracious promise. For God, out of his overflowing goodness and philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία], did not wish to be sought and worshipped freely and without reward: Isa. xlv. 19. Heb. xi. 6. So he bound himself to men of his own accord, and in a way made himself their debtor, once the course of obedience had been completed. He promised them life in such a way that they would be not only exempt from all death, but also afterwards to be transferred to glorious heavenly blessedness and closer fellowship with God himself. See Ps. xvi. 12. For this is how Moses describes the righteousness which is of the Law: that the man who does these things shall live by them: Rom. x. 5. Gal. iii. 12. Lev. xviii. 5. Ezek. xx. 11. Here indeed the same life is to be understood which Christ afterwards won for us: see Rom. x. 4 and viii. 4. Hence also, when a young man asked him, "What shall I do that I may possess eternal life?", he first set before him the commandments of the Law, Matth. xix. 16, 17, and at once called that eternal life "heaven," "the kingdom of heaven," or "the kingdom of God," explaining it thus: verses 21, 23. Luke xviii. 24.

units.la: Haftenus pietas Promissionem habet præsentis ac suturæ Vitæ: 1 Tim. 4. 18. omnis generis beneficiorum in hoc sæculo: Exod. 20. 12. Levit. 26. 3,-13. Deut. 28. 1,-14. & beatitudinis ac gloriæ æternæ in altero sæculo: Rom. xi. 7. Observandum interim, in gratiosa ejusmodi repetitione post lapsum, bona fere proponi convenienter præsenti Hominis conditioni: atque ita ut jus illud, respectu omnium salvandorum, nunc fundetur in Christo.
units.tr: Thus godliness has the promise of the present life and of the life to come: 1 Tim. iv. 8; of every kind of blessing in this age: Exod. xx. 12. Lev. xxvi. 3-13. Deut. xxviii. 1-14; and of blessedness and eternal glory in the other age: Rom. xi. 7. Meanwhile it is to be observed that in such a gracious repetition after the fall, the goods promised are generally set forth as suited to man's present condition, and that this right, with respect to all who are to be saved, is now founded in Christ.

units.la: CXX. Sequuntur Signa Fœderis illius. Hic autem initio se offert Arbor scientiæ boni ac mali: Gen. 11. 9. cujus esu Deus Homini interdixerat; verf. 17. ut scil. isto symbolo Hominis obedientia probaretur; eademque opera confirmaretur, si is obedientiam præstaret & consummaret, certa bonorum affluentia, & malorum immunitas; sin secus, bonorum amissio, & malorum indubitata successio. Sic enim signative accipienda est ista Arboris illius appellatio.
units.tr: CXX. The signs of that covenant follow. Here, at the outset, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil presents itself: Gen. ii. 9, whose eating God had forbidden man (verse 17). The purpose was that by this symbol man's obedience might be tested, and confirmed by the same act: if he rendered and completed obedience, there would be a sure abundance of good things and immunity from evils; but if otherwise, the loss of good things and the undoubted succession of evils. For in this sense that name of the tree is to be taken as a sign.

units.la: Obj. 1. Ista Arbor videtur habuisse naturalem facultatem acuendi ingenium, & faciendi sensus magis promtos atque expeditos ad suas operationes: ac proinde ejus usu vere acquiri potuisset sapientia, aut scientia perfectior. Resp. Tale quidem erat seductoris & homicidæ Diaboli mendacium; Gen. 3. 5. cui male fidem adhibuit Mulier peccare incipiens; verf. 6. Sed nulla causa materialis per se producere potest effectum immaterialem. Spiritibus autem animalibus perpetuo & satis apte restaurandis suppeditebant procul dubio alia satis multa; quibus tamen ista appellatio non tribuitur.
units.tr: Objection 1. That tree seems to have had a natural power of sharpening the wits and making the senses more ready and agile for their operations; so by its use wisdom or a more perfect knowledge could truly have been acquired. Answer: Such indeed was the lie of the seducer and murderer, the devil (Gen. iii. 5), to which the woman, beginning to sin, gave too ready belief (verse 6). But no material cause can of itself produce an immaterial effect. The animal spirits, which could be perpetually and quite aptly restored, were no doubt supplied by many other things; yet this name is not assigned to those.

units.la: Obj. 2. Si signum fuit ista Arbor, signum fuit mortis & miseriæ. Resp. Imo non minus erat Arbor Scientiæ boni, quam mali; prout obedientia præstanda esset, vel non esset: quemadmodum jam explicatum est, & conditioni Hominis sub isto Fœdere conveniebat.
units.tr: Objection 2. If that tree was a sign, it was a sign of death and misery. Reply: On the contrary, it was no less the Tree of the Knowledge of Good than of Evil, depending on whether obedience was to be rendered or not, as has already been explained, and as suited the condition of man under that covenant.

units.la: Obj. 3. Sacramenta percipi debent ab Hominibus Fœderatis: at ista Arbor percipi non debuit. Resp. Fructus ejus edi quidem non debuit: attamen Arbor conspici, ejusque ordinatio symbolica agnosci potuit & debuit; non minus quam in Iride, Gen. 9. 12, 13, 14. Ac porro in aliis Sacramentis, non ejusdem modi est perceptio: 1 Cor. 10. 1, 2, 3. CXXI. Deinde illustris erat Arbor vitæ, in medio Paradisi, Gen. 2. 9. præclarum vitæ ac gloriæ æternæ sacramentum; sed juxta promissionem & conditionem istius Fœderis. Hinc porro cap. 3. 22. Homo ex ea comedens, dicitur victurus in sæculum: quoniam ejus esus ex ordinatione Divina, obsignabat, & sic certo inferebat, vitam æternam; verum Homines per lapsum re signata destituti, usu signi necessario prohiberi debuerunt.
units.tr: Objection 3. Sacraments ought to be received by men in covenant, but that tree ought not to have been received. Reply: Its fruit indeed ought not to have been eaten. Yet the tree could be seen, and its symbolic ordination could and should have been recognized, no less than in the rainbow, Gen. 9:12-14. Moreover, the manner of receiving is not of the same kind in the other sacraments: 1 Cor. 10:1-3. CXXI. Next, the Tree of Life was conspicuous in the middle of Paradise, Gen. 2:9, an excellent sacrament of life and eternal glory, but according to the promise and condition of this covenant. Hence also Gen. 3:22: the man who eats of it is said to be going to live forever, since its eating, by divine ordinance, sealed and so certainly conveyed eternal life. But men, deprived of the thing signified through the fall, had necessarily to be kept from the use of the sign.

units.la: Obj. Vocatur potius Arbor vitæ, quod haberet virtutem physicam vitæ in æternum producendæ; atque adeo esset remedium contra omnes morbos, omnem corruptionem, & ipsam senectutem, &c. Resp.1. Morbi & corruptiones maximam habent diversitatem: omnis autem medicatio fieri debet per contraria: consequenter ea per unam arborem, aut ejus fructus, fieri non potuit naturaliter. 2. Et quid tum de ruina ædium, incendio, via aquarum, &c. quæ pericula alibi producunt Adversarii? 3. Neque istiusmodi remedium erat necessarium: cum omnia alimenta essent satis salubria; ipsique Homines ea sapientia præditi, ut singulis fuissent recte uti; nec etiam alia incommoda mortifera eventura, Deo omnia benigne & potenter disponente, juxta promissionem suam, ad Hominum immortalitatem & gloriam æternam; si modo in primæva integritate, suoque officio, perstitissent.
units.tr: Objection: It is rather called the Tree of Life because it had a physical power of producing life forever, and so would have been a remedy against all diseases, all corruption, and old age itself, etc. Reply: (1) Diseases and corruptions are very diverse, but every cure must be by contraries; consequently they could not naturally be cured by one tree or its fruit. (2) And what then of the collapse of buildings, fire, the flow of waters, etc., which the adversaries bring forward as dangers elsewhere? (3) Nor was such a remedy necessary, since all foods were sufficiently wholesome, and men themselves were endowed with such wisdom that they could use each rightly; nor would other deadly inconveniences have arisen, since God was disposing all things kindly and powerfully, according to his promise, toward human immortality and eternal glory, provided only that they had persisted in original integrity and in their duty.

units.la: Inst. Apoc. 22, 2. „In medio foro ejus (Hierosolymæ) & ex utraque parte fluminis erat Arbor Vitæ ferens fructus duodecim, per menses singulos edens fructum suum; & folia sua ad sanitatem Gentium. Ergo etiam in Paradiso terrestri Arbor vitæ erat ad sanitatem. Resp. Sic per visionem & figurationem Propheticam delineatur perpetua virtus vivifica & beatifica Servatoris nostri; qui nunc sub Fœdere Euangelico vere nobis impetravit, atque etiam applicat realiter, id ipsum quod sub Fœdere Legali olim significabat Arbor illa vitæ.
units.tr: Objection from Rev. 22:2: "In the middle of the street of the city (of Jerusalem), and on either side of the river, was the Tree of Life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month, and its leaves for the healing of the nations." Therefore the Tree of Life was also for healing in the earthly Paradise. Reply: Thus through prophetic vision and figurative representation is depicted the perpetual life-giving and blessed power of our Saviour, who now under the Gospel covenant has truly obtained for us, and also actually applies, that very thing which under the Legal covenant that tree of life formerly signified.

units.la: CXXII. Affinis est consideratio ipsius Paradisi, Horti amoenissimi cum quatuor suis fluviis, in orientali parte Hedenis; quae est in Babylonia, parte Mesopotamiae, &c. Gen. 11,8,-. Iste enim singulari sua amoenitate, ac potissimum contenta Arbore vitae, ipsum Coelum tertium, sive beatorum, & gaudium aeternum, quoque significavit. Unde Coelum istud Paradisi nomine diserte appellatur, 2 Cor. xii, 2, 4. Luc. xxiii, 43. Apoc. ii, 7.
units.tr: CXXII. Related to this is the consideration of Paradise itself, the most pleasant garden with its four rivers, in the eastern part of Eden, which is in Babylonia, part of Mesopotamia, etc., Gen. 2:8. For that garden, by its singular pleasantness and especially by the Tree of Life it contained, also signified the third heaven, the abode of the blessed and eternal joy. Whence that heaven is expressly called by the name of Paradise: 2 Cor. 12:2, 4; Luke 23:43; Rev. 2:7.

units.la: Sed post peccatum Deus Homines Paradiso expulit, reddituque prohibuit, appositis Cherubinis, cum flamma gladii sese vibrantis: Gen. iii, 23, 24. Hodie autem ille superstes non est; & maxime vero simile, quod per Diluvium sit corruptus.
units.tr: But after sin God drove men out of Paradise and forbade their return, placing cherubim with a flaming sword flashing: Gen. 3:23, 24. Today, however, it does not survive, and it is most likely that it was destroyed by the Flood.

units.la: Vanissimum vero est Pontificiorum commentum, ex detorsione loci Apoc. xi, 3, &c. de Paradiso adhuc superstite, & Enocho atque Elia in eum translatis, ibique permansuris usque ad congressum suum cum Antichristo; a quo sint occidendi, postea tamen virtute Divina resuscitandi, & in Coelum assumendi.
units.tr: Far more empty is the fiction of the Papists, drawn from a distortion of the passage Rev. 11:3, etc., concerning a Paradise still surviving, into which Enoch and Elijah were translated and where they will remain until their encounter with Antichrist. By him they are to be killed, but afterwards by divine power they are to be raised again and taken up into heaven.

units.la: CXXIII. Sed neque omittenda videtur observatio Sabbathi; de cujus primaeva institutione diximus sup. th. 13. ut illa beatam requiem a cursu obedientiae fideliter consummato in Coelis agendâ, sabbatismum perpetuum ac gloriosissimum, utcunque etiam adumbraverit, & studium ejus promoverit. Heb. 4,3,4., Introimus enim in requiem nos qui credimus, sicut dixit, Psa. 95, 11. Itaque juravi in ira mea, si ingressuri sint in requiem meam: licet operibus a jacto mundi fundamento factis. Ita enim dixit quodam in loco de septimo die, Gen. 2,2. Et quievit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis, &c. 9,10., Itaque reliquus est aliquis sabbatismus populo Dei. Nam qui ingressus est in requiem ipsius, requievit & ipse ab operibus suis; quemadmodum a suis Deus. Ita signo illo primaevo illustratur beata requies & gloria, quam Deus isto Foedere Protoplastis promisserat.
units.tr: CXXIII. Nor does the observance of the Sabbath seem to be passed over. We spoke of its primeval institution above, th. 13, and it so foreshadowed, in some measure, the blessed rest to be enjoyed in heaven after the course of obedience has been faithfully completed, a perpetual and most glorious sabbath, and promoted the pursuit of it. Heb. 4:3, 4: "For we who believe enter into rest, as he has said, Ps. 95:11, 'So I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter into my rest,' although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has said somewhere of the seventh day, Gen. 2:2, 'And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,' etc." 9, 10: "So there remains a sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his." Thus by that primeval sign the blessed rest and glory, which God had promised to the first parents under this covenant, is illustrated.

units.la: CXXIV. Superest ejus Duratio.
units.tr: CXXIV. Its duration remains.

units.la: Hæc autem mundo, & hominibus in eo viventibus, coæva est: quin & Judicium, quod ejus executio, erit æternum: Hebr. vi, 2. Marc. iii, 29. Aliter tamen se habet in Hominibus, qui sibi prorsus relinquuntur, extra salutarem Christi communionem; aliter in vere Christianis. Priores omnino manent sub isto Fœdere, ac per ipsum condemnantur: sic ira Dei manet ἐπὶ τὰς ἀπειθῆντας, Joh. iii, 36. & eos occupat ad finem usque: 1 Thess. ii, 16. Hactenus ergo Fœdus legale non est abrogatum; neque quicquam ei derogatum.
units.tr: This covenant is coeval with the world and with the people living in it; indeed the judgment, of which it is the execution, will be eternal: Heb. 6:2; Mark 3:29. Yet it stands differently for men left entirely to themselves, outside the saving communion of Christ, and differently for true Christians. The former remain wholly under this covenant and are condemned by it; thus the wrath of God remains upon the disobedient (ἐπὶ τὰς ἀπειθοῦντας) (John 3:36) and seizes them to the end (1 Thess. 2:16). Hitherto, therefore, the legal covenant has not been abrogated, and nothing has been taken away from it.

units.la: In posterioribus non fit stricta istius Fœderis executio, juxta verborum formulam: sic enim illi, propter peccata sua, servari non possent: at vero per Christi satisfactionem a reatu redemti sunt; & ab execratione liberati; ejusdemque obedientia universum jus Legis pro iis implerum. Rom. vi ii, 1, -4. Gal. iii, 13. Scil. Fœdus istud explicatum est a Deo clementissimo κατ' ἐπιείχειαν: & consequenter loco nostro admissa solutio ἀντὶ λύτρου, a Redemtore dignissimo nobisque conjunctissimo; ac porro ab eodem impleta omnis justitia, qua nos justi constitueremur, per gratisam Dei imputationem; 2 Cor. v. 15, 17, 18, 19, 21. Matth. 3. 15. Rom. 5. 19. iv. 5. 6. cum 19. 18. Philem. Ita quidem, ut sit Ipse Justus, & Justificans eum qui est ex Fide Jesu. Siquidem Deus unus est, qui justificabit Circumcisionem ex Fide, & Præputium per Fidem. Legem igitur inutilem reddimus per Fidem? Absit. Imo Legem stabilimus: Rom. 3. 26, 30, 31.
units.tr: In the latter case the strict execution of this covenant, according to the wording of the formula, does not take place, for they could not have been preserved on account of their sins. But through Christ's satisfaction they have been redeemed from guilt and freed from the curse, and by his obedience the whole right of the Law has been fulfilled on their behalf (Rom. 8:1, 4; Gal. 3:13). That is to say, this covenant has been set forth by most merciful God κατ' ἐπιείκειαν [kat' epieikeian, with forbearance]; and consequently the solution admitted in our passage, ἀντὶ λύτρου [anti lytrou, as a ransom], is given by a most worthy Redeemer, most closely joined to us; and further, by the same Redeemer all righteousness has been fulfilled, by which we are made righteous through God's gracious imputation (2 Cor. 5:15, 17–19, 21; Matt. 3:15; Rom. 5:19; 4:5–6, with 19, 18; Philem.). So indeed that he is himself just, and justifying him who is of the faith of Jesus (Rom. 3:26). For God is one, who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith. The law, then, do we make void through faith? God forbid. Rather we establish the law (Rom. 3:26, 30, 31).

units.la: Obj. 1. Matth. 11, 13. Omnes Prophetæ, & ipsa Lex, usque ad Johannem prophetarunt. Ergo Lex & Fœdus Legale non durant post Johannem Baptistam. Resp. Non agitur istic proprie de Lege morali, aut Fœdere Legali; sed de œconomia Prophetica, & Ceremoniali typica, V. T. Christum venturum prænunciante atque adumbrante; cui finem imposuit Johannes
units.tr: Obj. 1. Matth. 11:13. All the Prophets and the Law itself prophesied until John. Therefore the Law and the legal covenant do not endure after John the Baptist. Answer. The passage does not speak properly of the moral Law or the legal covenant, but of the prophetic economy and the typical ceremonial law, which announced and foreshadowed the coming of Christ in the Old Testament; John put an end to this.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: 5. Dum jus Legis pro nobis a Christo implerum est ; Rom. 8. 4, atque hæc nobis facta est Lex libertatis, Iac. 1. 25. 2, 12. excitet nos amplissima ac saluberrima promissio, ad novam obedientiam & alacrem gratitudinem ; Hebr. 11, 6. 12. 18, -24.
units.tr: 5. Since the right of the Law has been fulfilled for us by Christ (Rom. 8. 4), and this Law has been made for us a law of liberty (Jas. 1. 25; 2. 12), let the most ample and most wholesome promise stir us up to new obedience and eager gratitude (Heb. 11. 6; 12. 18–24).

units.la: De Peccato.
units.tr: Of Sin.

units.la: Cognitio nostri. Malum. Peccatum. 1. Contrà Legem Divinam proprie. 2. Non positivum, aut substantiale; nec mere negativum: sed privativum. Subjectum quod, & quo. 3. Ejus non causa efficiens; sed deficiens. Non omne peccatum est voluntarium, antecedente judicio ac deliberatione. 4. Non habet finem per se ac proprie dictum. 5. Macula. 6. Reatus, tum potentialis, tum actualis. 7. Pontificii male distinguunt Reatum culpa, & pœna. Obj. solv. 8. Conscientia condemnans, & spiritus servitutis. 9. Utilitas distinctionis inter Maculam, & Reatum. 10. Pœna. Quomodo ad Bestias etiam referatur. 11. Castigatio. Probatio. Martyrium. 12. Pœna damni, & sensus. 13. Peccatum vel omissionis, vel commissionis. 14. Habituale, vel Actuale. 15. Angelorum, vel Hominum. 16. In Hominibus peccatum primum. Ejus causa principales deficientes. Libere. 17. Causa procatarctica. Serpens. Methodus 18. Consummatum. Inchoatum. 19. Deus illius non causa efficiens; nec privative deficiens. Permisit tamen; ordinavit in finem bonum. Quaestiones solv. 20. Libere peccarunt Protoplasti; & tamen aliquo respectu necessario. 21. Tentationes interim variae 22. Gravitas istius peccati. 23. Effecta. 24. Peccatum originale. 25. Imputatum: c. Pelag. Socin. &c. 26. Posteri. Excipitur Christus. 27. Effectus. Obj. solv. 28. Peccatum originale inharens. 29. Probatur, c. Socin. Anabapt. &c. 30. Non excipienda Virgo Maria.Obj. solv. 31. Modus propagationis 32. Effecta. Obj. solv. 33. De Libertate: & de Servo arbitrio; c. Pontif. Socin. &c. 34. Objectiones solv. 35. Quod de ista corruptione relinquitur in regenitis, &c. vere peccati rationem habet. 36. Paulus Rom. 7. 15, --. loquitur de se regenito. 37. Peccata actualia. Eorum causa. 38. Peccatum per se. Per accidens. Circa Deum directe. Circa proximum. 39. Peccata interna. Externa. Spiritualia. Carnalia. Extra proprium corpus. In proprium corpus. 40. Ex ignorantia. Infirmitate. Malitia. 41. Conscientiam vastantia. Clamantia. 42. Male Pontificii dividunt in Mortalia, & Venialia./Obj. solv. 43. Remissibilia. Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum. 44. Quae istud constituant. Judicium de eo difficillimum. Pontificii male statuunt plures ejus species. 45. Peccata manifesta. Occulta. 46. Aliis graviora unde. 47. Iteratio. Recidiva. 48. Consuetudo peccandi. Peccatum regnans. An cadat in regenitos. Peccatum tentans. In deliciis. Odio habitum 49. Fructus. Mors spiritualis; in genere damni. In genere sensus. Moderatio interna. Externa. 50. Mortis corporalis inchoatio interna; in genere damni. Sensus. Externa; &c. Moderatio. 51. Mortis corporalis Consummatio. De Corpore. De Anima 52. Mortis spiritualis consummatio. 53. Praxis. 54.
units.tr: Knowledge of ourselves. Evil. Sin. 1. Properly, against the Divine Law. 2. Not positive or substantial, nor merely negative, but privative. Subject which and subject in which. 3. Its efficient cause is not; rather its deficient cause. Not every sin is voluntary, with prior judgment and deliberation. 4. It has no end properly so called in itself. 5. Stain. 6. Guilt, both potential and actual. 7. The Papists wrongly distinguish guilt of fault and guilt of punishment. Objection solved. 8. Condemning conscience and spirit of bondage. 9. Usefulness of the distinction between stain and guilt. 10. Punishment. How it is also referred to beasts. 11. Chastisement. Trial. Martyrdom. 12. Punishment of loss and of sense. 13. Sin either of omission or of commission. 14. Habitual or actual. 15. Of angels or of men. 16. In men, the first sin. Its principal causes are deficient. Freely. 17. Procatarctic cause. The serpent. Method. 18. Consummated. Begun. 19. God is not its efficient cause, nor privatively deficient. He permitted it, however, and ordained it to a good end. Questions solved. 20. The protoplasts sinned freely, and yet in some respect necessarily. 21. Meanwhile, various temptations. 22. The gravity of this sin. 23. Effects. 24. Original sin. 25. Imputed: against the Pelagians, Socinians, etc. 26. Posterity. Christ is excepted. 27. Effect. Objection solved. 28. Original sin inherent. 29. Proved, against the Socinians, Anabaptists, etc. 30. The Virgin Mary is not to be excepted. Objection solved. 31. The mode of propagation. 32. Effects. Objection solved. 33. On liberty and on the bondage of the will; against the Papists, Socinians, etc. 34. Objections solved. 35. What remains of this corruption in the regenerate, etc., truly has the nature of sin. 36. Paul, Rom. 7. 15 ff., speaks of himself as regenerate. 37. Actual sins. Their cause. 38. Sin in itself. By accident. Directly against God. Against one's neighbour. 39. Sins internal. External. Spiritual. Carnal. Outside one's own body. Against one's own body. 40. From ignorance. From weakness. From malice. 41. Laying waste the conscience. Crying out. 42. The Papists wrongly divide sins into mortal and venial. Objection solved. 43. Remissible. The sin against the Holy Spirit. 44. What constitutes it. Judgment on it is very difficult. The Papists wrongly set out many species of it. 45. Manifest sins. Hidden sins. 46. Whence some are graver than others. 47. Repetition. Relapse. 48. Custom of sinning. Reigning sin. Whether it falls on the regenerate. Tempting sin. Sin in delights. Held in hatred. 49. Fruit. Spiritual death; in general, of loss. In general, of sense. Internal moderation. External. 50. The beginning of bodily death, internal; in general, of loss. Sense. External, etc. Moderation. 51. The consummation of bodily death. On the body. On the soul. 52. The consummation of spiritual death. 53. Practice. 54.

units.la: I. Tilissima & valde necessaria est Cognitio nostri ipsorum: 1 Cor. 11, 28. 2, xiij. 5. Triplex autem Status cognoscendus est pro hoc sæculo; Naturæ Institutæ, Destitutæ, & Restitutæ; sive Integritatis, Lapsus, & Gratiæ: atque item pro futuro, Status, vel Gloriæ, vel Cruciatuum æternorum. De Natura instituta, ejusque Integritate, diximus sup. cap. 7. th. 34, 45. nunc tractationem de Fœdere Legali commodissime excipit dissertatio de Peccato, seu Lapsu, & Natura destituta,
units.tr: I. Very fine and very necessary is the knowledge of ourselves (1 Cor. 11. 28; 2 Cor. 13. 5). Three states are to be known for this age: of nature as instituted, deprived, and restored; that is, of integrity, of the fall, and of grace. Likewise for the future, the state is either of glory or of eternal torments. About nature as instituted and its integrity we spoke above (ch. 7, th. 34, 45). Now the treatment of the covenant of law is most fittingly followed by the dissertation on sin, or the fall, and nature deprived.

units.la: Malum generatim est privatio boni. Peccatum vero est malum morale: aut plenius, Aberratio, vel Exorbitatio Creaturæ rationalis a Lege sibi lata. Hebraice חטאה h. e. aberratio: ut Iud. 20. 16. Funda mittens lapidem ad capillum, & non peccare faciebat; sive non sinebat aberrare. Confer Deut. 5. 32, 33. Phil. 3. 12, 14. Gal. 6, 16. Græce ἁμαρτία: describitur autem, quod sit ἀνομία, 1 Ioh. 3. 4. Alias παράβασις, παράπτωμα, & παράκοη appellatur: Rom. 5. 14, 19.
units.tr: Evil in general is the privation of good. Sin, however, is moral evil; or, more fully, an aberration or exorbitation of a rational creature from the law laid down for it. In Hebrew it is חטאה [chatah], that is, aberration, as in Judg. 20. 16: "a slinger who could cast a stone at a hair, and not miss" (that is, "who did not let them go astray"). Compare Deut. 5. 32, 33; Phil. 3. 12, 14; Gal. 6. 16. In Greek it is ἁμαρτία [hamartia]; it is described as ἀνομία [anomia, lawlessness], 1 John 3. 4. Elsewhere it is called παράβασις [parabasis], παράπτωμα [paraptōma], and παράκοη [parakoē], Rom. 5. 14, 19.

units.la: 2. Legem hic omnino spectari, manifestum est. Rom. 4. 15. Ubi non est Lex ibi nec est Transgressio. 5, 13. Peccatum non reputatur, non existente Lege. 3. 20. Per Legem est cognitio Peccati. adde 7. 7.
units.tr: That the law is wholly in view here is manifest. Rom. 4. 15: "Where there is no law, there is no transgression." 5. 13: "Sin is not imputed when there is no law." 3. 20: "By the law is the knowledge of sin." Add 7. 7.

units.la: Unus autem in Theologia proprie occurrit Legislator, qui potest servare & perdere: Iac. 4. 12. atque ipsius Lex: Psal. 51. 6. Tibi Tibi soli peccaveram. Cum vero Pontifex Romanus sibi arrogat jus sanciendi aliquid sub peccato mortali, ac faciendi de non peccato peccatum, & contra manifeste præscfert, se esse Deum atque adeo fe Antichristum demonstrat : 2 Thess. 2. 4.
units.tr: In theology, however, only one Lawgiver properly comes into view, "who is able to save and to destroy" (Jas. 4. 12), and his law: "Against you, you only, have I sinned" (Ps. 51. 6). But when the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself the right to enact something under pain of mortal sin, and to make a non-sin into a sin, and against all this openly sets himself forth as God, he thereby shows himself to be the Antichrist (2 Thess. 2. 4).

units.la: Hominibus quidem fit injuria : verum tunc peccatur proprie circa ipsos, & contra Deum ac Legem ipsius. Interim qui supereminentem Potestatem habent, Leges etiam ferre & Statuta condere possunt; quibus obtemperandum propter conscientiam, & propter Dominum : Rom. 8. 1-5. Petr. 2. 32, 17. Istorum transgressio, peccatum quoque est, & reatum inducit, per se ac directe in foro soli: indirecte etiam ac mediate, per Divinam ordinationem, in foro poli.
units.tr: Injury is indeed done to men; but then sin is properly committed against themselves and against God and his law. Meanwhile, those who have supreme authority can also enact laws and make statutes, which must be obeyed for the sake of conscience and for the Lord's sake (Rom. 8. 1–5; 1 Pet. 2. 13, 17). The transgression of these is also sin, and it induces guilt: directly and immediately, in the forum of the earth only; indirectly and mediately, through divine ordinance, in the forum of heaven.

units.la: Quæ autem ab Ecclesia, per Antecessores, ordinis & communis ædificationis gratia constituuntur, prudenti deductione ex Verbo Dei, & applicatione ad præsentes circumstantias, sic serio observari debent: Hebr. 8. 17. 1 Cor. 14. 32, 40. Matth. 18. 17. Attamen Dominatio iis non competit: 1 Petr. 5. 3. Matth. 20. 25, 26. cum 23. 8, 9, 10. sed Ministerium: 1 Cor. 4. 1, 2, 5, 18, 19, 30. Consequenter non habent potestatem Leges ferendi; neque contra ipsos proprie peccatur: sed circa ipsos, eorumque defectiones & applicationes recte factas, contra Deum: Luc. 10. 16. Excessus igitur cavendus, contra Pontificios; atque item defectus, contra Libertinos & homines ἀτάκτως.
units.tr: Those things which are established by the Church, through its predecessors, for the sake of order and common edification, by prudent deduction from the Word of God and application to present circumstances, ought to be seriously observed in this way (Heb. 13. 17; 1 Cor. 14. 32, 40; Matt. 18. 17). Yet dominion does not belong to them (1 Pet. 5. 3; Matt. 20. 25, 26, compared with 23. 8–10); rather ministry (1 Cor. 4. 1, 2, 5, 18, 19, 30). Consequently they have no power of enacting laws; nor is sin properly committed against them, but concerning them and their defections and rightly made applications, it is committed against God (Luke 10. 16). Excess, therefore, is to be guarded against, in the case of the Papists; and likewise defect, in the case of the Libertines and men who are disorderly [ἀτάκτως].

units.la: 3. Sic patet, Peccatum formaliter non esse quid positivum; nedum substantiale; alteri Principio, Deo alicui malo, adscribendum: quemadmodum olim delirabant Manichæi. Nec mere negativum: sic enim nihil foret; & qui minime operarentur, imo minime existerent, maxime peccarent. Sed esse aliquid privativum; ut in subjecto capaci absit bonitas moralis debita inesse, seu necessaria conformitas cum Lege.
units.tr: 3. Thus it is clear that sin, formally, is not something positive, much less substantial, to be ascribed to another principle, some evil god, as the Manichaeans once raved. Nor is it merely negative; for then it would be nothing, and those who did least would sin most, indeed would least exist. Rather, it is something privative: that is, in a capable subject there is lacking the moral goodness that ought to be present in it, or the necessary conformity with the law.

units.la: Subjectum quod sunt Creaturæ quædam rationales; tum Angeli, tum Homines. Subjectum quo sunt eorum Facultates naturales; itemque Habitus, Affectus, & Actiones; quatenus singula suo modo recedunt a norma sibi praescripta.
units.tr: The subject which is certain rational creatures, both angels and men. The subject in which are their natural faculties, likewise their habits, affections, and actions, insofar as each of these in its own way departs from the norm prescribed for it.

units.la: IV. Peccati formaliter nulla est Causa efficiens directa & proprie dicta: nedum Deo sanctissimo talis efficientia tribuenda sit. Iac. 1. 13. Nemo, cum tentatur, dicat, A Deo tentor: nam Deus tentari malis non potest; nec quenquam tentat. Sed creatura rationalis peccans, est ejus Causa deficiens; quatenus aberrat à norma & perfectione sibi praescripta.
units.tr: IV. Formally, sin has no efficient cause that is direct and properly so called; much less is such efficiency to be attributed to most holy God: "Let no one, when he is tempted, say, 'I am tempted by God'; for God cannot be tempted with evils, and he tempts no one" (Jas. 1. 13). But a rational creature that sins is its deficient cause, insofar as it wanders from the norm and perfection prescribed for it.

units.la: Neque tamen cum Pontificiis, & Socinianis, eorumque sequacibus, afferendum. Nullum dari peccatum proprie dictum, quod non sit voluntarium, antecedente judicio ac deliberatione, & formali actu voluntatis: aliter enim res habet, 1. in peccato originali; de quo inferius. Itemque 2. in lapsibus per subitam occupationem & inadvertentiam: Gal. 6, 1. Nec non 3. in ipsa addubitatione ac deliberatione de peccato aliquo committendo; & in ordinatis motibus primo primis voluntatis atque affectuum, contra Legem Dei, cum acquiescentia & complacentia qualicunque, saltem interpretativa aut virtuali, & concomitante.
units.tr: Yet we must not say, with the Papists and the Socinians and their followers, that there is no sin properly so called which is not voluntary, with prior judgment and deliberation and a formal act of the will. For the matter stands otherwise: (1) in original sin, of which below; likewise (2) in lapses through sudden occupation and inadvertence (Gal. 6. 1); and also (3) in the very hesitation and deliberation about committing some sin, and in the disordered first motions of the will and the affections against the law of God, with some kind of acquiescence and complacency, at least interpretative or virtual, and accompanying them.

units.la: V. Cum sit exorbitatio a recta norma, & vero scopo, Finem per se ac proprie dictum etiam non habet: sicut enim omnis Finis intenditur sub ratione boni; ita Medium appetitur & assumitur propter Finem, ut conducibile ad ipsum: quod Peccato formaliter, tanquam privativo, non convenit. Peccantes quidem sibi Finem aliquem proponunt; bonum apparens jucundum, vel utile; sed miserè decipiuntur. Rom. 3. 8. Non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniat bonum. Qui Apostolos interim rebant, putantes secultum praestare Deo, Iob. 16. 2. intentione sua excedebant. Prov. 10. 28. Expectatio improborum perit. Deus tamen peccata creaturarum sic gubernat, ita ut abutitur, ut per accidens serviant Gloriæ suæ, & Electorum saluti.
units.tr: V. Since sin is a deviation from the right rule and the true end, it does not have an end properly so called. For just as every end is aimed at under the aspect of good, so a means is sought and taken up for the sake of the end, as leading to it; and this does not formally belong to sin, which is privative. Sinners indeed propose to themselves some end, an apparent good that is pleasant or useful; but they are miserably deceived. Rom. 3:8: "We must not do evil that good may come." Those who in the meantime slandered the Apostles, thinking they render service to God, went beyond their intention. Prov. 10:28: "The expectation of the wicked perishes." God nevertheless so governs the sins of creatures, and so uses what they abuse, that they serve by accident his glory and the salvation of the elect.

units.la: VI. Ad Effecta & Adjuncta quod attinet; occurrunt primo Macula, & Reatus; ac porro Pœnæ.
units.tr: VI. As to the effects and adjuncts of sin, there occur first the stain (macula) and the guilt (reatus); and next the punishments.

units.la: Macula est spiritualis deformitas ac turpitudo in peccatore qua tali, pulchritudini Imaginis Divinæ contraria. Matth. 15. 19, 20. Ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malæ, &c. Hæc sunt quæ polluunt hominem. Tit I. 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum; sed polluta est eorum & mens, & conscientia. Apoc. xxii, 11. Qui sordidus est, sordescat adhuc Psal xiv, 3. Simul putidi facti sunt Isef. vi, 5. Vir pollutus labiis sum, &c. lxiv, 6. Sumus ut immundus nos omnes, &c. Adde Iob. xv, 14. Prov. xx, 9. & confer Psal. xlv, 12, 14. 1 Petr. III, 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: The stain is a spiritual deformity and foulness in the sinner as such, contrary to the beauty of the Image of God. Matt. 15:19, 20: "Out of the heart come evil thoughts, etc. These are the things that defile a man." Titus 1:15: "To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and conscience are defiled." Rev. 22:11: "He who is filthy, let him be filthy still." Ps. 14:3: "They have together become putrid." Isa. 6:5: "I am a man of unclean lips, etc." Isa. 64:6: "We are all become like an unclean thing, etc." Add Job 15:14, Prov. 20:9, and compare Ps. 45:12, 14; 1 Pet. 3:3, 4, 5.

units.la: Hinc peccans honore privatur, & in contemtum adducitur coram Deo, omnibusque sanctis. 1 Sam. II. 30. Contemtores mei leves fient. Isef. lxiv, 6. Sicut panniculus abjectissimus, &c. Rom. III, 23. Peccaverunt, ac deficiuntur gloria Dei. Hos. 4, 7. Gloriam eorum ignominia commutabo. Adde Pro. III, 35. Ierem. iii, 25. Dan. xii, 2.
units.tr: Hence the sinner is deprived of honour and brought into contempt before God and all the saints. 1 Sam. 2:30: "Those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed." Isa. 64:6: "Like a most abject rag, etc." Rom. 3:23: "They have sinned and come short of the glory of God." Hos. 4:7: "I will change their glory into shame." Add Prov. 3:35, Jer. 3:25, Dan. 12:2.

units.la: Accedit aversatio & abominatio ipsius Dei, maxime in peccatis gravioribus. Prov. III, 32. Abominationi est Jehovæ præfractus. vi, 16, 17. Sex ista odit Jehovah; immo septem abominationi sunt animæ ejus: oculi elati, &c. Confer Isef. I, 15. Hab. I, 13. Psal. v, 5, 6.
units.tr: There is added the aversion and abomination of God himself, especially in the graver sins. Prov. 3:32: "The perverse man is an abomination to Jehovah." Prov. 6:16, 17: "Jehovah hates these six things; indeed seven are an abomination to his soul: haughty eyes, etc." Compare Isa. 1:15, Hab. 1:13, Ps. 5:5, 6.

units.la: Item pudor intus; h. e. metus ex propriæ turpitudinis conscientia: Ierem. 3, 24, 25. Pudendum istud confumsit laborem patrum nostrorum, Iacemus in pudore nostro, &c. Dan. 9. 7. Nobis pudor facici. Rom. 6. 21. De quibus nunc erubescitis. Et fuga quandoque foris; conatus quanquam irritus, effugiendi præsentiam Dei, qui istam turpitudinem tantopere aversatur. Exemplum est in Protoplastis, Gen. 3. 7. Adde Proverb. 28.
units.tr: Likewise there is inward shame, that is, fear arising from the consciousness of one's own foulness: Jer. 3:24, 25: "That shameful thing has devoured the labour of our fathers; let us lie down in our shame, etc." Dan. 9:7: "To us belongs confusion of face." Rom. 6:21: "The things of which you are now ashamed." And sometimes outward flight, an attempt, though vain, to escape the presence of God, who so greatly abhors this foulness. The example is in our first parents, Gen. 3:7. Add Prov. 28:1.

units.la: 1. Fugiunt improbi, nemine persequente. Confer Isef. 2. 14. xxxiij. 14. Hos. 10. 8. Luca 23. 30. Apocal. 6, 16. ix. 6.
units.tr: 1. "The wicked flee when no one pursues." Compare Isa. 2:14, 33:14; Hos. 10:8; Luke 23:30; Rev. 6:16, 9:6.

units.la: VII. Reatus est obligatio peccatoris ad pœnam luendam, juxta Legis sanctionem. Rom. 5. 16. Reatus est ex una offensa ad condemnationem. 3, 19. Ut-obnoxius fiat totus mundus condemnationi Dei. Levit. 5.2,- 6. Immundus est, & reus. -- Et adducet reatum suum Iehovæ. ubi metonymice hostia intelligitur. A reatu peccata etiam appellantur debita; Matth. 6.12. cum Luc.11. 4. & peccatores dicuntur esse sub peccato; Rom. 3. 9. vel in peccatis suis; 1 Cor. 15, 17.
units.tr: VII. Guilt is the obligation of the sinner to bear punishment, according to the sanction of the Law. Rom. 5:16: "Guilt arises from one offence to condemnation." Rom. 3:19: "That the whole world may become liable to the condemnation of God." Lev. 5:2–6: "He is unclean and guilty... and he shall bring his guilt before Jehovah," where by metonymy the sacrifice is meant. From guilt sins are also called debts: Matt. 6:12, with Luke 11:4; and sinners are said to be under sin, Rom. 3:9, or in their sins, 1 Cor. 15:17.

units.la: Speċtatur autem reatus, tum in actu primo, sive potentialis; tum in actu secundo, sive actualis. Priori modo in se & absolute consideratur peccati demeritum ex justitia Divina; ut sit dignum puniri. Sic Rom. 1. 32. appellatur Ius Dei, ut Legis transgressores digni sint morte. Posteriore modo consideratur actualis obligatio ad pœnam, propter demeritum illud re ipsa infligendam; ut peccatum sit actu puniendum. Ira Rom. 1, 18. Patet ira Dei e cœlo adversus omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum, ut qui veritatem injuste detinent. 2, 1,
units.tr: Guilt is considered both in the first act, that is, potentially, and in the second act, that is, actually. In the first way the demerit of sin is considered in itself and absolutely, from the justice of God, so that it is worthy of punishment. Thus Rom. 1:32 calls it the right of God, that transgressors of the Law are worthy of death. In the second way the actual obligation to punishment is considered, on account of that demerit to be really inflicted, so that the sin is actually to be punished. Thus Rom. 1:18: "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness." Rom. 2:1, 2.

units.la: 2. Inexcusabilis es, o homo, quisquis alium damnas. Scimus, judicium Dei esse secundum veritatem adversus eos qui talia agunt.
units.tr: 2. "You are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judge another. We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things."

units.la: Reatus in actu primo inseparabilis est a peccato, propter hujus repugnantiam adversus Sanctitatem & Justitiam Dei. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 54, 55, 56. sed in actu secundo separari potest respectu ipsius peccatoris, per interveniens remedium satis validum: sicut fidelibus propter Satisfactionem Christi peccata ipsorum remittuntur; neque ulla est iis condemnatio, nec justa amplius eorum criminatio. Eph. 1, 7. Col. 1, 14. 2 Cor. 5, 19, 21. Rom 8, 1, 33. 34.
units.tr: Guilt in the first act is inseparable from sin, on account of its opposition to the holiness and justice of God; see above, ch. 4, theses 54, 55, 56. But in the second act it can be separated, as far as the sinner himself is concerned, by an intervening remedy sufficiently powerful: as, for believers, sins are remitted on account of the satisfaction of Christ; and for them there is no condemnation, nor any just accusation of their crimes. Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14; 2 Cor. 5:19, 21; Rom. 8:1, 33, 34.

units.la: VIII. Absurde Pontificii distinguunt inter reatum culpæ, & pœnæ: ita quidem ut contendant, remissa culpa retineri frequenter pœnam: atque ista ratione locum facere conentur suis satisfactionibus in ordine ad Justitiam Divinam, pro pœnis temporalibus, tum in hac vita, tum post eam in Purgatorio. Sed Reatus est vinculum, inter culpam & poenam intercedens, sive obligatio ex culpa ad poenam. Per Remissionem vero tollitur ista obligatio: ubi autem ea sublata est respectu culpæ, ex quo principio processerat; non potest remanere respectu poenæ, tanquam termini. Relata sunt simul natura: uno eorum sublato, etiam necessario tollitur alterum, quatenus tale est. Ubi sublatum est vinculum conjugale respectu mariti, non potest manere respectu uxoris, &c. Rom. 7. 1, 2, 3.
units.tr: VIII. The Papists absurdly distinguish between the guilt of fault and the guilt of punishment, so that they contend that, though the fault is forgiven, the punishment often remains; and on this ground they try to make room for their satisfactions, in relation to divine justice, for temporal punishments, both in this life and after it in Purgatory. But guilt is the bond lying between fault and punishment, or the obligation arising from fault to punishment. By remission indeed this obligation is removed; but where it has been taken away with respect to the fault from which the principle proceeded, it cannot remain with respect to the punishment, as its term. Correlatives are destroyed together in nature: when one of them is removed, the other is also necessarily removed, so far as it is such. When the marriage bond has been dissolved with respect to the husband, it cannot remain with respect to the wife, etc. Rom. 7:1, 2, 3.

units.la: Obj. 2 Sam. 7. 13, 14. Davidi remissum fuit peccatum suum, & sic sublatus reatus culpæ: filiolus ipsius tamen erat morte multandus, quod ille inimicos Dei blasphemare fecisset; retentus igitur fuit reatus poenæ istius temporalis. Resp. Ista Davidi fuit castigatio paterna; eo magis necessaria, ut tolleretur offendiculum, neque fideles putarentur talia peccata prorsus impune committere: sed non fuit poena stricte dicta, & ad justitiam Dei vindicativam satisfactoria: ac proinde nec retentus fuit reatus poenæ.
units.tr: Objection: 2 Sam. 7:13, 14. David's sin was forgiven, and so the guilt of fault was removed; yet his little son had to be put to death, because David had caused the enemies of God to blaspheme; therefore the guilt of this temporal punishment remained. Answer: That chastisement of David was a fatherly correction, the more necessary so that the stumbling-block might be removed, and so that the faithful might not think that such sins are committed altogether with impunity. But it was not a punishment strictly so called, nor satisfactory to the avenging justice of God; and therefore the guilt of punishment did not remain.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Reatum frequenter sequitur Conscientia condemnans, & horrorem atque cruciatum inducens: Rom. 2. 15. Cogitationibus ipsæ mutuo accusantibus. Ief. 47, 20, 21. Improbi, ut mare propulsum. — Ita nulla est pax, inquit Deus meus, improbis. Huc pertinet spiritus servitutis; Rom. 8. 15. unde peccatores metu mortis per omnem vitam damnati sunt servitutis; Hebr. 2. 15 & Diaboli horrescunt; Iac. 2, 19. Confer Iob. 3. 20. Ier. 2. 19.
units.tr: Guilt is often followed by a condemning conscience, which brings on horror and torment. Rom. 2:15: their thoughts accusing one another. Isa. 47:20, 21: The wicked are like the sea that is driven out. There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked. To this belongs the spirit of bondage, Rom. 8:15, by which sinners through fear of death are all their lifetime held in bondage, Heb. 2:15, and the devils tremble, Jas. 2:19. Compare Job 3:20 and Jer. 2:19.

units.la: X. Utilissima est ista Maculæ & Reatus distinctio; 1. ut recte intelligantur variæ phrases S. Scripturæ: priori enim respectu sordes, vulnera, sanguis, &c. aliquoties commemorantur; posteriori, debita, offensa, crimina, &c.
units.tr: X. This distinction between stain and guilt is very useful: (1) so that the various phrases of Holy Scripture may be rightly understood; for with respect to the former, filth, wounds, blood, and the like are sometimes mentioned, and with respect to the latter, debts, offences, crimes, and the like.

units.la: 2. Ut recte distinguatur Iustificatio a Sanctificatione: illa enim Reatum proprie spectat: hæc Maculam: atque item Iustitia imputata, ab inhærente; quarum illa ad materiam Justificationis pertinet; hæc Sanctificationis effectus est: contra Pontificios, Socinianos, &c.
units.tr: (2) So that justification may be rightly distinguished from sanctification. The former concerns guilt properly, the latter stain. Likewise imputed righteousness is distinguished from inherent righteousness; the former belongs to the matter of justification, the latter is an effect of sanctification. Against the Papists, the Socinians, and others.

units.la: 3. Quo melius percipiatur, sublato Reatu actuali per Justificationem, remanere tamen utcunque Maculam in hac vita, etiam in baptizatis.
units.tr: (3) So that it may be better perceived that, although actual guilt is removed by justification, stain nevertheless remains in some measure in this life, even in the baptized.

units.la: XI. Reatus ex Peccato fluit directe & immediate; Pœna, dispositive, & mediante Reatu. Est autem Pœna, Malum triste a Rectore inflictum propter demeritum peccati. 2 Theff. 1,6,-. Iustum est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem: infligent ultionem iis, qui Deum nesciunt; - qui pœnam pendant ignis æterni. Judæ, 7. Ignis æterni pœnam sustinebis.
units.tr: XI. Guilt arises from sin directly and immediately; punishment arises dispositively and through the medium of guilt. Punishment is a sad evil inflicted by the Ruler on account of the demerit of sin. 2 Thess. 1:6, 7: It is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you; and to you who are troubled rest with us, when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed, and Jude 7: suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

units.la: Materiale pœnæ est Afflictio, seu Mali tristis perpessio in Creatura rationali: Formale autem est Respectus ad culpam; sive Ordinatio ad luendum pro demeriro peccati, secundum dictamen Justitiæ. Hæc enim est Pœna proprie & stricte dicta. Sic Diaboli, & Homines reprobi, punientur in æternum; ac similiter Christus punitus est, ut Sponsor, loco & vice electorum suorum.
units.tr: The material element of punishment is affliction, or the suffering of a sad evil in a rational creature; the formal element is its relation to guilt, that is, its ordering towards making satisfaction for the demerit of sin according to the dictate of justice. This is punishment properly and strictly speaking. So the devils and reprobate men will be punished for ever, and likewise Christ was punished as Surety, in the place and stead of his elect.

units.la: Bestiæ, aliæque creaturæ irrationales, ut juris, ita peccati, & pœnæ, per se capaces non sunt. Pœnæ tamen utcunque subiiciuntur; 1. cum homines propter sua peccata, ubi illis frequenter abutuntur, in istis suis possessionibus, & rebus ad ipsorum utilitatem, commoditatem, vel oblectationem ordinatis, puniuntur: Gen. 3. 17, 18. Rom. 8. 20, 21. 2. Si bestiæ etiam materialiter faciant, quod in hominibus enorme crimen foret, Deus in detestationem talis facti, bestias quoque simili malo tristi aliquando voluit affici; Gen. 9. 5. Exod. 21. 28, 29. Levit. 20. 15. 16.
units.tr: Beasts and other irrational creatures are not capable, as of right, so of sin and punishment, in themselves. Yet they are in some way made subject to punishments: (1) when men are punished for their sins, which they frequently abuse, in those possessions of theirs and things ordered to their use, convenience or pleasure, Gen. 3:17, 18; Rom. 8:20, 21. (2) If beasts also do materially what would be an enormous crime in men, God, in detestation of such a deed, has sometimes willed that beasts too be afflicted with a similar sad evil, Gen. 9:5; Exod. 21:28, 29; Lev. 20:15, 16.

units.la: XII. Laxe & improprie pœna quoque appellatur, malum triste, quod quidem peccati causa perfertur: non tamen in compendium culpæ; sed ad emendationem & salutem eorum, qui sic exercentur. Talis est 1. Castigatio, stigatio, παιδεία; Paterna correctio: qua a peccatis retrahimur, & ad Deum atque officia nostra salutariter compellimur. 1 Cor. 11. 32. Dum judicamur, a Domino erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Hebr. 12. 5.-11. Obliti estis adhortationis, quæ vobis tanquam filiis loquitur, Fili mi, ne parvi facito Castigationem Domini; neque animo frangitor, cum ab Eo argueris: Quem enim diligit Dominus, castigat, &c. ad commodum nostrum, ut participes simus sanctimoniæ ipsius. - Postea fructum tranquillum justitiæ reddit iis, qui per eam fuerint exercitati.
units.tr: XII. Loosely and improperly, the term punishment is also applied to a sad evil which is indeed inflicted on account of sin, but not as a payment of guilt; rather for the amendment and salvation of those who are so exercised. Such are (1) chastisement (castigatio), discipline [παιδεία], a fatherly correction, by which we are drawn back from sins and salutarily compelled towards God and our duties. 1 Cor. 11:32: When we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world. Heb. 12:5-11: You have forgotten the exhortation which speaks to you as to sons, My son, do not despise the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him; for whom the Lord loves he chastens, and so on, for our profit, that we may share his holiness. Afterwards it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

units.la: 2. Affinis est Probatio, δοκιμασία; qua exploratur & manifestatur, quid sit de statu hominis spiritualis, ejusque virtutibus; quid de fide, charitate, obedientia, constantia, &c. quo majus incrementum capiant filii Dei, & ad gloriam promoveantur. Sic explorati, magis innotescunt sibi ipsis, aliisque fidelibus, imo etiam Angelis: 1 Cor, 4. 9. Deus autem explorare dicitur, quatenus media ordinat & dirigit in istum finem. Gen. 22. 1 Deus tentavit Abraham. 12. Nunc cognovi, quod timens Dei es; quod non peperceris filio tuo, unico tuo, propter Me. Rom. 5. 3, 4, 5. Etiam gloriamur de afflictionibus, scientes quod afflictio tolerantiam efficiat; tolerantia vero experientiam; Experientia autem spem: porro spes non pudefacit. - Iac. 1, 2, 3, 4. Summo gaudio ducite, fratres mei, quoties in tentationes varias incideritis: illud scientes, exploratonem fidei vestræ efficere tolerantiam; &c. Vide etiam 5. 10, 11. Similiter 1 Petr. 1: 6, 7. Ut exploratio fidei vestræ multo pretiosior explorationè auri, quod perit, & tamen per ignem exploratur, invenietur vobis esse laudi, & honori, & gloriæ, cum revelabitur Jesus Christus.
units.tr: (2) Akin to this is probation [δοκιμασία], by which it is tested and shown what is the state of a man's spiritual life and his virtues, and what his faith, love, obedience, steadfastness, and so on are, so that the sons of God may grow the more and be advanced to glory. Thus those who are tried are more fully made known to themselves, to other believers, and even to the angels, 1 Cor. 4:9. God is said to test, insofar as he ordains and directs means to this end. Gen. 22:1: God tempted Abraham. Verse 12: Now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me. Rom. 5:3-5: We also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope; and hope does not disappoint. Jas. 1:2-4: Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience, and so on. See also 5:10, 11. Similarly 1 Pet. 1:6, 7: that the proof of your faith, being much more precious than gold which perishes though it is tested by fire, may be found to your praise, honour and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

units.la: 3. Accedit Martyrium, (Testimonium): quod est doctrinæ Euangelicæ confirmatio, per fortem & constantem afflictionum, cruciatuum, ipsiusque mortis violentæ, pro ea tolerantiam. Ipse Christus fidus ille Testis appellatur, Apoc. I. 5. Qui etiam Apostolis suis dixit, Act. I, 8, Eritis mihi Testes, -: Et Math. 5. 10, 11, 12. Beati, quos persequuntur homines justitiae causa: -. Apoc. 2, 13. Antipas Martyr ille meus fidelis occisus est, -. Vide etiam 11. 3, -. Col. I, 24, 25. Phil. I, 12, 13, 14, Sed speciali usu Ecclesiastico Martyres appellantur, qui pro confirmatione Evangelii mortem oppetunt; reliqui vero, qui damna, carceres, cruciatus, exilia pro eadem veritate sustinent, Confessores dicuntur.
units.tr: (3) There is also martyrdom (testimony): this is the confirmation of the evangelical doctrine through a steadfast and constant endurance of afflictions, torments, and even a violent death for it. Christ himself is called the faithful witness, Rev. 1:5, who also said to his apostles, Acts 1:8, You shall be my witnesses; and Matt. 5:10-12: Blessed are those whom men persecute for righteousness' sake. Rev. 2:13: Antipas, my faithful martyr, was slain. See also 11:3. Col. 1:24, 25; Phil. 1:12-14. But in special ecclesiastical usage those are called martyrs who meet death for the confirmation of the Gospel; the rest, who suffer losses, prisons, torments, and exile for the same truth, are called confessors.

units.la: Fieri autem potest, ut Castigatio simul sit Probatoria: vel etiam aliquando Martyrii rationem habeat: quamvis alio respectu. Vide Hebr. 12.2,-11. 1 Petr. 4. 12.
units.tr: It can happen, however, that chastisement is at the same time probationary, or even sometimes has the character of martyrdom, though in another respect. See Heb. 12:2-11; 1 Pet. 4:12.

units.la: XIII. Poena proprie dicta est tum damni, tum sensus.
units.tr: XIII. Punishment, properly so called, is of two kinds: of loss and of sense.

units.la: Poena damni est privatio salutaris & gloriosae communionis cum Deo, juxta ipsius sententiam. Gen. 4, 14. En, expellis me hodie -- ut a facie Tua abscondam me Matth. 7. 23. Discedite a Me, -, 25. 41. Execrati, abite a Me. 2 Thess. I, 9. expulsi a facie Domini, et gloria virium Ipsius.
units.tr: Punishment of loss is the privation of salutary and glorious communion with God, according to his own sentence. Gen. 4:14, "Behold, you drive me out this day… and from your face I shall be hidden." Matt. 7:23, "Depart from me." Matt. 25:41, "Depart from me, you cursed." 2 Thess. 1:9, "banished from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power."

units.la: Poena sensus notat cruciatus positivos, quales impiis non solum immittuntur in hac vita, sed & post eam durabunt absque fine. Matth. 25. 41. Abite a Me, in ignem aeternum. Marc. 9. 46. Ubi vermis eorum non moritur, et ignis non extinguitur. Apoc. 14. 11. Fumus tormenti ipsorum ascendet in saecula saeculorum: nec habebunt requiem die, nec nocte.
units.tr: Punishment of sense denotes positive torments, which are inflicted on the wicked not only in this life but will also endure after it, without end. Matt. 25:41, "Depart from me into the eternal fire." Mark 9:46, "where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched." Rev. 14:11, "The smoke of their torment will rise for ever and ever, and they will have no rest day or night."

units.la: XIV. Peccatum dividitur multifariam: primo enim vel est commissionis, vel omissionis.
units.tr: XIV. Sin is divided in many ways. First, it is either of commission or of omission.

units.la: Peccatum commissionis adversatur praecepto negativo, dum agitur, quod prohibitum est. Hic actus subistratus metaphysice bonus est in genere entis: sed per repugnantiam adversus Legem Dei, caret bonitate morali.
units.tr: Sin of commission runs counter to a negative precept, when what has been forbidden is done. This act, considered as a thing, is metaphysically good in the order of being; but because it is contrary to the law of God, it lacks moral goodness.

units.la: Peccatum omissionis adversatur praecepto affirmativo, dum non agitur quod mandatum est. Hic facultas, aut habitus, cessat ab exercitio, quo occupari deberet juxta præscriptum: adeoque vel nihil agitur, h.e. nullum opus notabile; vel aliud agitur, quod istis circumstantiis non convenit.
units.tr: Sin of omission runs counter to an affirmative precept, when what has been commanded is not done. Here a faculty or habit ceases from the exercise by which it ought to have been occupied according to the rule; and so either nothing is done, that is, no notable work; or something else is done which does not fit these circumstances.

units.la: Omissio autem vel est totalis, sive totius officii mandati ; vel partialis, sive modi alicujus, aliusve adjuncti necessarii.
units.tr: Omission, moreover, is either total, that is, of the whole duty commanded, or partial, that is, of some manner or some necessary accompanying circumstance.

units.la: XV. Secundo peccatum est vel habituale, vel actuale.
units.tr: XV. Second, sin is either habitual or actual.

units.la: Habituale notat difformitatem moralem, in subjecto suo, analogice per modum actus primi: unde ipsum subjectum vitiatur ac deturpatur, & quæcunque ab eo procedunt Rom.8,7,1. Quod sapit caro, inimicitia est adversus Deum Legi enim Dei non subjicitur: nam nec potest quidem. Ergo qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Tit.1,15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum; sed polluta est eorum & mens, & conscientia. Matth. 7,18. Non potest arbor mala fructus bonos ferre.
units.tr: Habitual sin denotes a moral deformity in its subject, analogically, by way of a first act; whereby the subject itself is corrupted and disfigured, and everything that proceeds from it. Rom. 8:7, "The mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Therefore those who are in the flesh cannot please God." Titus 1:15, "To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and conscience are defiled." Matt. 7:18, "A bad tree cannot bear good fruit."

units.la: Actuale vero est actus secundus, sive actio, difformitate tali laborans: sive cogitatum, dictum, aut factum contra Legem Dei. Matth. 15,19,20. „Ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malæ, cædes, adulteria, scortationes, furta, falsa testimonia, maledicta.
units.tr: Actual sin, on the other hand, is a second act, or action, labouring under such deformity: whether a thought, word or deed against the law of God. Matt. 15:19-20, "Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders."

units.la: XVI. Tertio peccatum est vel Angelorum, vel Hominum.
units.tr: XVI. Third, sin is either that of angels or that of men.

units.la: De malis Angelis, eorumque lapsu diximus sup.cap. 7. th.18. Sed post primam illam apostasiam, secuta sunt, & perpetuo sequuntur, plura peccata: exinde enim omnes eorum actiones, vel universali ἀνομία laborant; vel saltem in principio, fine, & modo agendi deficiunt. Confer Matth.7,18. Tit.1.15. Omnes certe & singuli illi 1. libere defecerunt totaliter. 2. Nec Mediatorem habent, per quem restituantur. Vide Hebr.11,14,16,17. 3. Consequenter etiam libere in apostasia sua ipsi perseverant absque fine, & sine ulla resipiscentia. 4. Et justo Dei judicio relinquuntur ac servantur æternæ condemnationi. 2 Petr. 11,4. Deus Angelis, qui peccaverunt, non pepercit, sed in tartarum detrusos catenis caliginis tradidit, damnationi servatos. Similia sunt Judæ. 6 Et Matth. 25. 41. in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus.
units.tr: We have spoken of the evil angels and their fall above, in chapter 7, thesis 18. But after that first apostasy several sins followed, and continually follow; for from that time all their actions labour either under a universal lawlessness [ἀνομία], or at least are defective in their beginning, end and manner of acting. Compare Matt. 7:18; Titus 1:15. Indeed all and each of those angels, 1, freely and wholly fell away. 2, They have no Mediator through whom they may be restored. See Heb. 11:14, 16, 17. 3, Consequently, freely, in their apostasy, they persevere themselves without end and without any repentance. 4, And by the just judgment of God they are left and kept for eternal condemnation. 2 Pet. 2:4, "God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into hell and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be kept for judgment." Similar things are said of Jude 6, and Matt. 25:41, "into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels."

units.la: XVII. De peccatis Hominum agendum uberius.
units.tr: XVII. The sins of men must be treated more fully.

units.la: Occurrit ibi Peccatum primum, & alia a primo orta.
units.tr: There occur here the first sin and the others arising from the first.

units.la: Primum est ipsa primorum Hominum a primæva integritate defectio, per transgressionem præcepti Divini de non gustando fructu Arboris scientiæ boni & mali. Gen. 3, 1, -7.
units.tr: The first is the very defection of the first men from their primeval integrity, through the transgression of the divine precept not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Gen. 3:1-7.

units.la: Causæ principales efficientes, vel potius deficientes, fuerunt ipsi Homines protoplasti: sed Eva prior, quæ etiam Adam mum seduxit: Gen. 3. 6. 2 Cor. 11, 3. Hinc 1 Tim. 11, 14. Adamus non fuit seductus (scil. prior, & tali modo per serpentem;) sed Mulier seducta, causa transgressionis fuit. Alibi tamen Adamus in hoc negotio potissimum commemoratur, tanquam Caput posteritatis politice ac fœderaliter in ipso comprehensæ & confirmæ: Rom. 5,12,14,15,16,18,19. 1 Cor. 15,21,22.
units.tr: The principal efficient causes, or rather deficient causes, were the first-formed humans themselves; but Eve went first and also seduced Adam. Gen. 3:6; 2 Cor. 11:3. Hence 1 Tim. 2:14, "Adam was not deceived (namely, first, and in this manner, through the serpent); but the woman, being deceived, was the cause of the transgression." Elsewhere, however, Adam is especially mentioned in this business, as the head of posterity, in which he was politically and federally included and represented: Rom. 5:12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22.

units.la: Libere autem sic defecerunt Protoplasti; seque inclinarunt ad illud, quod Deus prohibuerat. Eccl. 7, 29. Solummodo vide! hoc inveni, Deum ipsum fecisse hominem rectum; ipsos autem quærere rationcinia plurima.
units.tr: Freely indeed did the first parents thus fall away, and they inclined themselves to that which God had forbidden. Eccl. 7, 29. "Behold, this only have I found: that God made man upright, but they have sought out many devices."

units.la: XVIII. Causa Procatarctica ad peccandum pellicens fuit Diabolus; Tentator ille; Matth. 4, 3. Pater mendacii, & Homicida a principio; Joh. 8. 44. Idem rufus Draco, & antiquus Serpens appellatur metaphorice & metonymice. Apoc. 12. 3, 4, 9. 20. 2. tum propter similitudinem versutiæ, quæ Serpenti naturalis est; tum κατὰ μνήμην, quod ille Serpentem ingressus, sub tali specie ac forma deceperit Evam; tum denique ob convenientiam inimicitiæ, quæ ex illo tempore fuit inter Serpentes & Homines: Gen. 3. 1. 4. 5. 15. Dolum ergo texit Diabolus, animali callido & versuto ad eum abusus; Non quidem ignorarunt Protoplasti, Serpentem esse ἄλογον ζῷον: verum Diabolus rei novitate, ac doli methodo callidissima, illos detinuit, cepit, decepit.
units.tr: XVIII. The procatarctic cause that enticed them to sin was the Devil, that Tempter; Matt. 4, 3. the father of lies and a murderer from the beginning; John 8, 44. The same one is also called, metaphorically and by metonymy, the dragon and the ancient serpent. Rev. 12, 3, 4, 9; 20, 2. This is so partly because of the likeness to the cunning that is natural to the serpent, partly by association [κατὰ μνήμην], because he entered the serpent and under that appearance and form deceived Eve, and finally on account of the enmity that has existed between serpents and men from that time: Gen. 3, 1, 4, 5, 15. The Devil therefore wove his trick, abusing for this purpose an animal that is crafty and sly. Indeed the first parents did not fail to know that the serpent is an irrational animal [ἄλογον ζῷον]; but the Devil, by the novelty of the thing and by the most cunning method of his deceit, held them, caught them, and deceived them.

units.la: Tentator primum Dubitationem injicere conatus est, de sensu prohibitionis Divinae; ambigue quaerens, Gen. 3. 1. Etiamne edixisse Deum, ne comedatis ex omni fructu arborum hujus horti? Cum vero Mulier distincte reposuisset Divinam concessionem, prohibitionem, & sanctionem; verf. 2, 3. ille in sanctionem aperte incurrit; Non utique moriemini; verf. 4. & ad falsam prohibitionis causam confugit: Novit enim Deus, quo die comederitis ex eo, aperturos se oculos vestros; & vos fore sicut Deos, scientes boni ac mali: verf. 5. Sic ille malum triste, Praecepti transgressoribus certo eventurum, negavit; & bonum insigne, quod Deus invideat, promisit impudentissime. Hac κυβεία τῆς παντοργίας, χαὶ μεθοδεία τῆς ἀπλάνης, vera primum in dubium trahendo; ac deinceps ea tanquam falsa rejiciendo & contraria substituendo, seduxit initio Evam; ac per eam deinceps Adamum: illa enim, ubi accepisset de fructu isto, & comedisset, etiam comedendum dedit Viro suo secum, qui comedit; verf. 6. Mulierem vero a verbis processisse ad verbera, & sic Maritum compulisse ad peccati societatem, inane Iudaeorum commentum est.
units.tr: The Tempter first tried to cast doubt on the meaning of the divine prohibition, asking ambiguously: Gen. 3, 1. "Has God indeed said that you shall not eat of every tree of this garden?" But when the woman had clearly answered by setting out the divine permission, prohibition, and sanction, vv. 2, 3. he openly ran counter to the sanction: "You shall not surely die," v. 4. and he took refuge in a false account of the reason for the prohibition: "For God knows that on the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil," v. 5. Thus he denied that the grievous evil, certain to befall the transgressors of the precept, would come, and most shamelessly promised a notable good which God begrudged. By this trickery of all craft and method of deceit [κυβεία τῆς παντοργίας, καὶ μεθοδεία τῆς ἀπλάνης], first calling the true things into doubt, and then rejecting them as false and substituting contrary things, he at the outset seduced Eve, and through her afterwards Adam. For she, when she had taken of that fruit and eaten, also gave it to her husband with her, who ate; v. 6. But that the woman proceeded from words to blows, and so compelled her husband to join in the sin, is an empty fiction of the Jews.

units.la: XIX. Ita peccatum istud consummatum quidem fuit actuali comestione illius fructus; sed prius inchoatum fuit intus. Ubi Protoplasti audivissent quae a Tentatore proponebantur, statim ea exigere debuissent ad Verbum ipsius Dei, cui fides habenda est sine ulla dubitatione; atque sic illa, tanquam falsa & fallacia, rejicere debuissent cum indignatione. Confer Matth. 4 3. - 10. Nunc initium peccati fuisse videtur nonobservatio veracitatis Divinae in istis circumstantiis, atque adeo dubitatio; deinde perversum judicium de isto fructu, sapientia, beatitudine, atque ipso Deo; & inordinatus appetitus majoris excellentiae & conformitatis cum Deo; ac porro propositum exequendi; quod excepit ipsa consummatio.
units.tr: XIX. So this sin was indeed completed by the actual eating of that fruit, but it was begun earlier, within. When the first parents heard what the Tempter put forward, they ought at once to have tested it by the Word of God Himself, to which faith is to be given without any doubt; and so they ought to have rejected those things as false and deceitful, with indignation. Compare Matt. 4, 3–10. Now the beginning of sin seems to have been the failure to observe the truthfulness of God in these circumstances, and thus doubt; then a perverse judgment about that fruit, about wisdom, blessedness, and God Himself; and an inordinate desire for greater excellence and likeness to God; and further the purpose of carrying it out, which was followed by the completion itself.

units.la: Justitia originalis in Protoplastis habitualiter fuit integra, quin & actualiter, ratione circumstantiarum, usquedum peccatum illud inchoaretur: sed in primo peccandi momento privative abfuit illius exercitium, sive actus secundus tunc necessarius. Sic Homo non usus est habitu suo, quo uti potuisset ac debuisset; ipse causa formaliter efficiens libera actionum suarum, & libere deficiens respectu istius ἀνομίας: Verum culpabilis ista omissio statim induxit deformitatem spiritualem; sic extincta & amissa est habitualis illa bonitas.
units.tr: Original righteousness in the first parents was indeed whole as to its habit, and even as to its exercise, in view of the circumstances, until that sin was begun; but at the first moment of sinning its exercise, or the second act then required, was lacking by privation. Thus man did not use his habit, which he could and ought to have used; he himself was the formal efficient cause, free in his actions, and freely failing with respect to that lawlessness. But this blameworthy omission at once brought in spiritual deformity; thus that habitual goodness was extinguished and lost.

units.la: XX. Deus nequaquam fuit lapsus illius causa efficiens: tum quia ipse sanctissimus: Jac. 1. 13. tum quia peccati, tanquam formaliter privativi, nulla est causa efficiens proprie dicta. Nec fuit privative deficiens: quia non tenetur operari omne bonum, ubique & semper, ad extremum virium suarum; est enim agens liberrimum. Sufficit, ipsum quaecunque operatur operari sancte, & convenienter ad gloriam suam, juxta decretum voluntatis suae.
units.tr: XX. God was in no way the efficient cause of that fall: both because he is most holy (Jas. 1. 13), and because for sin, which is formally privative, there is no efficient cause properly so called. Nor was he privatively deficient, since he is not bound to work every good, everywhere and always, to the utmost of his powers; for he is a most free agent. It is enough that whatever he does, he does holily and fittingly to his own glory, according to the decree of his will.

units.la: Permisit tamen peccatum formaliter; quatenus non impedivit, quo minus homo in ista operatione deficeret moraliter. Sic autem non-egit, atque adeo fuit non-auctor. Interim in actu substrato cooperatus est Deus, ut Causa prima, eminentissime & sanctissime; cujus cogitationis & viae a nostris plurimum discrepant: Isai. 55. 8, 9. Ordinavit denique complexum illud in finem bonum, juxta consilium suum sanctissimum & sapientissimum; qui omnia facit propter seipsum, etiam improbum in diem mali: Prov. 16. 4. atque omnes concludit in inobedientiam, ut omnium misereretur: Rom. xi. 32. Confer sup. cap. 8. th. 16, 17: 23, 24.
units.tr: Yet he permitted sin formally, insofar as he did not prevent man from failing morally in that action. But he did not act thus, and so he was not the author. Meanwhile, in the underlying act God cooperated as first cause, most eminently and most holily; whose thoughts and ways differ greatly from ours (Isa. 55. 8, 9). Finally, he ordered that whole complex to a good end, according to his most holy and wise counsel; he who makes all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil (Prov. 16. 4), and shut up all under disobedience, that he might have mercy on all (Rom. 11. 32). See above, ch. 8, th. 16, 17, 23, 24.

units.la: Qu. 1. Num Deus antecedenter Homini subtraxerit gratiam habitualem? Neg. Nusquam id patet: neque neque consentaneum est bonitati Divinæ. Sed Homo jam peccans non utebatur gratia sua habituali: atque adeo Deus, qui dederat Homini posse quod vellet, sive auxilium sine quo non potuisset perseverare, non dedit illi actu velle quod posset, sive auxilium quo reipsa perseveraret; seu non excitavit actum secundum eo modo & gradu, ut Homo superaret istam tentationem. Neque tamen Homini concreata fuit aliqua inclinatio ad malum. Vide sup. cap. 7, th. 41.
units.tr: Q. 1. Did God antecedently withdraw habitual grace from man? No. This nowhere appears, nor is it consistent with divine goodness. But man, already sinning, was not using his habitual grace; and so God, who had given man the power to will what he wished, that is, the help without which he could not have persevered, did not give him the actual willing of what he could do, that is, the help by which he would in fact have persevered; or he did not stir up the secondary act in such a way and to such a degree that man would overcome that temptation. Yet no inclination to evil was innate in man. See above, ch. 7, th. 41.

units.la: Qu. 2. An fieri potuerit, ut Homo gratia habituali uteretur, eam in actum secundum deduceret, & sic de facto recte operaretur, sine prævio & excitante concursu Dei? Neg. Id enim tum primitati Divinæ, tum dependentiæ humanæ, prorsus adversatur. Vide sup. cap. 8, th. 11, 12. Unde tamen non sequitur, Hominem obligatum fuisse ad impossibile: habitualiter enim præditus fuit potentia obediendi Deo, & perseverandi in sua integritate; quanquam dependenter a Causa prima, ut convenit Causæ secundæ. Interim non data actuali illa excitatione ad obedientiam & perseverantiam, hactenus saltem Homo potuit & debuit non tendere vitiose in oppositum. Imo posita etiam prædeterminatione & excitatione Dei ad actum illum substratum, ista Dei efficientia infert quidem efficientiam Creaturæ; & negatio aliqua ex parte Dei, infert quoque in Creatura absentiam ejus quod negatum, sive non datum est: verum ea non est vitiosa, seu peccaminosa; nisi quatenus ipsa Creatura rationalis formaliter deficit in genere moris, a norma sibi præscripta, & quidem libere.
units.tr: Q. 2. Could it have happened that man made use of habitual grace, brought it into the secondary act, and so in fact acted rightly, without a prior and exciting concurrence of God? No. For this is wholly contrary both to divine primacy and to human dependence. See above, ch. 8, th. 11, 12. Yet it does not follow from this that man was obliged to the impossible: for he was endowed habitually with the power to obey God and to persevere in his integrity, though dependently on the first cause, as belongs to a secondary cause. Meanwhile, if that actual stirring up to obedience and perseverance was not given, at least so far man could and ought not to tend viciously toward the opposite. Indeed, even if God's predetermination and excitation to that underlying act is posited, that divine efficiency does imply the efficiency of the creature; and some withholding on God's part implies also the absence in the creature of what was withheld, or not given. Yet this is not vicious or sinful, except insofar as the rational creature itself formally falls short, in the sphere of morals, of the norm prescribed to it, and does so freely.

units.la: XXI. Libere igitur peccarunt Protoplasti; nimirum intrinseca libertate causæ, spontaneitatis, & complacentiæ, etiam cum jam laberentur: quin imo libertate contradictionis, & contrarietatis, si respectus habeatur ad conditionem ipsorum antecedentem, & in sensu divisio.
