Si vero lapsus ille referatur ad
units.tr: XXI. The first parents therefore sinned freely, namely with the intrinsic freedom of cause, of spontaneity, and of complacency, even as they were already falling; indeed with freedom of contradiction and contrariety, if regard is had to their antecedent condition, and in the divided sense. But if that fall is referred

units.la: Decretum Dei, Scientiam visionis, & Providentiam actualem, rectè dicitur evenisse necessario; necessitate scil. extrinseca, consequentiæ, ex hypothesi, immutabilitatis, infallibilitatis, & in sensu composito; non autem intrinseca necessitate causæ, consequentis, absoluta, &c. ut unumquodque, dum est, eo ipso quod est, necessario est; quod jam fit, quantumvis libere, eo ipso quod fit, necessario fit. Quod observandum contra Jesuitas, Socinianos, Anabaptistas, Remonstrantes, & Lutheranos.
units.tr: to God's decree, to the knowledge of vision, and to actual providence, it is rightly said to have happened necessarily: namely by extrinsic necessity of consequence, on the hypothesis of immutability and infallibility, and in the composite sense; but not by intrinsic necessity of cause, of consequent, absolute, and so on. For each thing, while it is, is necessarily so by the very fact that it is; and what now happens, however freely, necessarily happens by the very fact that it happens. This is to be observed against the Jesuits, Socinians, Anabaptists, Remonstrants, and Lutherans.

units.la: XXII. Distinguendæ interim Tentationes respectu Evæ: 1. Diaboli ad ipsam; seductoria, & vitiosa. 2. Dei ad Evam; probatoria, & sancta. 3. Evæ ad Deum; exploratoria veracitatis & constantiæ Divinæ, mala, 4. Evæ ad seipsam; excitatoria & seductoria sui ad peccatum porro committendum.
units.tr: XXII. Meanwhile temptations with respect to Eve must be distinguished: 1. Of the devil to her: seductive and vicious. 2. Of God to Eve: probative and holy. 3. Of Eve to God: testing the truthfulness and constancy of God, and evil. 4. Of Eve to herself: stirring and seducing herself to commit sin further.

units.la: Itemque respectu Adami: 1. Evæ ad ipsum; seductoria. 2. Dei ad ipsum; probatoria. 3. Adami ad Deum; exploratoria. 4. Adami ad seipsum; seductoria.
units.tr: Likewise with respect to Adam: 1. Of Eve to him: seductive. 2. Of God to him: probative. 3. Of Adam to God: testing. 4. Of Adam to himself: seductive.

units.la: Simili fere ratione in singulis Hominum peccatis tentationes istiusmodi conjungi solent.
units.tr: In much the same way, temptations of this kind are usually joined to each of men's sins.

units.la: XXIII. gravitas hujus peccati non ex pretio fructus prohibiti æstimanda est; neque solum intemperantia, aut qualiscunque superbia, putanda. Sed respicienda 1. Majestas Dei infinita; cujus Lex transgrediendo violata est. Hinc Rom. 5. 14,-19. transgressio, offensa, & contumacia appellatur.
units.tr: XXIII. The gravity of this sin is not to be judged by the worth of the forbidden fruit, nor is it to be thought to lie only in intemperance or in any kind of pride. Rather one must consider: 1. The infinite majesty of God, whose law was violated by transgression. Hence in Rom. 5. 14-19 it is called transgression, offence, and rebellion.

units.la: 2. Facilitas abstinendi ab illo fructu, cum alii supeterent abunde: Gen. 2. 16, 17. III. 2, 3.
units.tr: 2. The ease of abstaining from that fruit, since others were abundantly available (Gen. 2. 16, 17; 3. 2, 3).

units.la: 3. Ratio symbolica istius arboris; in qua Deus speciatim Hominum obedientiam probare voluit.
units.tr: 3. The symbolic meaning of that tree, in which God specifically wished to test men's obedience.

units.la: 4. Insignis Hominum conditio, in ista sua integritate.
units.tr: 4. Man's distinguished condition in that integrity of his.

units.la: 5. Ratio Fœderis, respectu Posterorum.
units.tr: 5. The nature of the covenant with respect to posterity.

units.la: 6. Præceptorum Dei, atque adeo obedientia, & peccatum peccatorum plurimorum concatenatio: nam in lapsu isto fuit congeries in credulitatis, ingratitudinis, contumaciae erga Deum, curiositatis, ambitionis, contrectationis rei alienae, assensus falso testimonio praebiti, defectionis ad hostem Dei, crudelitatis erga ipsos, & immanis ἀσορ-γίας erga posteros suos.
units.tr: 6. The concatenation of God's precepts, and thus of obedience and of the many sins: for in this fall there was a heap of sins: unbelief, ingratitude, contumacy toward God, curiosity, ambition, the handling of another's property, assent given to a false testimony, defection to the enemy of God, cruelty toward themselves, and monstrous profligacy [ἀσωτία] toward their posterity.

units.la: Hinc non male peccatum istud dicitur gravissimum tum intensive, spectando gradum malitiae in ejus consummatione; tum extensive, spectando singula quae in eo involvuntur, etiam effecta turpia ac tristia.
units.tr: Hence this sin is not wrongly called most grave, both intensively, looking at the degree of malice in its consummation, and extensively, looking at each of the things involved in it, including its shameful and sad effects.

units.la: Quin imo licet Eva peccaverit prior, peccatum Adami tamen insignem gravitatem habet: tum per ejus eminentiam prae Muliere; tum quod Caput universi Generis humani constitutus esset.
units.tr: Indeed, although Eve sinned first, Adam's sin nonetheless has a remarkable gravity: both because of his eminence above the woman, and because he had been constituted head of the whole human race.

units.la: XXIV. Effecta occurrunt primo in ipsis Protoplastis: & quidem communiter; 1. Amissio justitiae originalis; eique contraria Deformitas: peccando enim ista fuit abjecta; haec vero contracta; efficienter, respectu ipsorum Protoplastorum; & meritorie, respectu Justitiae Divinae, unde Mors ista spiritualis immissa.
units.tr: XXIV. The effects appear first in the first parents themselves, and indeed in common: 1. The loss of original righteousness, and the deformity contrary to it. For by sinning that righteousness was cast off, and this deformity was contracted: efficiently with respect to the first parents themselves, and meritoriously with respect to divine justice; whence this spiritual death was sent in.

units.la: Obj. Uno actu non excutitur habitus. Resp. Neg. cum etiam uno actu tota sanitas, ipsaque vita naturalis auferri possit; nec primum peccatum fuerit actus simplex, sed ex plurimis compositus.
units.tr: Objection: a habit is not expelled by one act. Reply: denied, since by one act the whole health, and natural life itself, can be taken away; nor was the first sin a simple act, but composed of many.

units.la: Huc pertinet ineptitudo ad omne bonum spirituale salutare; & inclinatio ad mala opposita; Gen 6. 5. VIII. 21. Joh. 8. 34. Rom. 8. 7.
units.tr: To this belong the inability to every saving spiritual good and the inclination to the opposite evils (Gen. 6. 5; 8. 21; John 8. 34; Rom. 8. 7).

units.la: 2. Reatus coram Deo: Rom. 3. 19: v. 12, 16.
units.tr: 2. Guilt before God (Rom. 3. 19; v. 12, 16).

units.la: 3. Terror conscientiae; molestus sensus nuditatis cum pudore; & talis vestium necessitas: Gen 3. 7, 8, 21.
units.tr: 3. Terror of conscience; the troubling sense of nakedness, with shame, and the consequent need of such clothing (Gen. 3. 7, 8, 21).

units.la: 4. Ejectio ex Paradiso: Gen. 3. 22, 23, 24.
units.tr: 4. Expulsion from Paradise (Gen. 3. 22, 23, 24).

units.la: 5. Omnis generis aerumnae & calamitates in hac vita: Job. 7. 1.
units.tr: 5. Every kind of hardship and calamity in this life (Job 7. 1).

units.la: 6. Inimicitia Serpentis, ipsiusque Diaboli: Gen. 3. 15. Eph. 6. 11, 12. 7. Mors temporalis, atque æterna; nisi intervenïret redemtio Christi: Gen. 2.17. iij.19. Deut. 27. 26. Gen. 3.15.
units.tr: 6. The enmity of the Serpent, and of the devil himself (Gen. 3. 15; Eph. 6. 11, 12). 7. Temporal death and eternal death, unless the redemption of Christ intervened (Gen. 2. 17; 3. 19; Deut. 27. 26; Gen. 3. 15).

units.la: Adamo speciália fuerunt, singularis molestia & difficultas in rebus suis agendis; in labore manuum lassitudo, &c. cardui & spinæ in agris colendis; &c. Gen. 3.17, 18, 19.
units.tr: Peculiar to Adam were a singular trouble and difficulty in carrying out his affairs; weariness in the labour of his hands, and so on; thistles and thorns in cultivating the fields, and so on (Gen. 3. 17, 18, 19).

units.la: Evæ, dura & molesta ad Virum subjectio; & multiplex in prolis gestatione, partu, atque educatione difficultas: Gen. 3.16.
units.tr: To Eve: a harsh and grievous subjection to her husband, and manifold difficulty in bearing, bringing forth, and rearing offspring (Gen. 3. 16).

units.la: Serpenti etiam suo modo imposita est quædam pœna, in detestationem facti; ut scil. per ventrem serperet, ac terram lamberet, vel ederet, cum molestia & contemtu, atque ut Hominum inimicitiam experiretur: Gen. 3.14, 15.
units.tr: To the Serpent also, in its own way, a certain punishment was imposed, as a mark of detestation of the deed: namely that it should creep on its belly and lick, or eat, the dust, with discomfort and contempt, and that it should experience the enmity of men (Gen. 3. 14, 15).

units.la: Quin & universa Creatura Mundi aspectabilis, subjecta est vanitati, maledictioni, & servituti corruptionis: Gen. 3. 14, 17, 18. Eccl. 1. 2. Rom. 8. 20, 21, 22.
units.tr: Nay, the whole creation of the visible world is also subjected to vanity, to curse, and to the bondage of corruption: Gen. 3. 14, 17, 18. Eccl. 1. 2. Rom. 8. 20, 21, 22.

units.la: Quæ autem de Protoplastis recensuimus, eadem ad posteros quoque justo Dei judicio extensa & propagata sunt: Rom. 8. 7. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Eph. 2. 3, 5. Rom. 3. 19. ij. 14, 15. Job. 7. 1. XIV. 1, 2. 1 Petr. 5.
units.tr: What we have recounted about the first parents applies also to their posterity by the just judgment of God: Rom. 8. 7. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Eph. 2. 3, 5. Rom. 3. 19. ii. 14, 15. Job 7. 1. xiv. 1, 2. 1 Pet. 5.

units.la: XXV. Succedunt Peccata a primo orta, tum Originale, tum Actualia.
units.tr: XXV. Sins arising from the first sin follow, both original and actual.

units.la: Originale est Culpa ex primo illo lapsu universam Generis humani naturam, prout ea in Adamo fuit censita, ream faciens, atque inficiens miserrime. Rom. 5. 12. Per unum Hominem Peccatum in Mundum introiit, ac per Peccatum Mors: & ita in omnes Homines Mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccarunt. Eph. 2, 3. Eramus natura filii iræ, ut etiam reliqui. Istud autem spectatur tum Imputatum; tum Inhærens.
units.tr: Original sin is the guilt arising from that first fall, which makes the whole nature of the human race, as it was reckoned in Adam, liable to punishment and miserably corrupts it. Rom. 5. 12. Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so death passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned. Eph. 2. 3. We were by nature children of wrath, as the rest also. This is considered both as imputed and as inherent.

units.la: XXVI. Imputatum est Fructus ille primi peccati, quo ipsum, juxta constitutionem Fœderis Legalis, æstima-
units.tr: XXVI. Imputed sin is that fruit of the first sin by which, according to the constitution of the legal covenant, it is reckoned

units.la: æstimatur naturale; ita quidem ut universam illam naturam eidem cum Protoplastis reatui involvat. Probatur hoc contra Pelagianos, Socinianos, aliosque eorum sequaces, 1. expressis quibusdam restimoniis: Eph. 2, 3. Ubi filii irae intelligendi passive; h.e. obnoxii irae Divinae. Tales autem omnes homines sunt natura; scil. nunc vitiatâ; & quidem per eum qui universam naturam repraesentavit. 1 Cor. 15.21, 22. Per Hominem mors. In Adamo omnes moriuntur. Rom. 5. 12. Per unum Hominem &c. Uno illo peccante omnes peccarunt; atque ita mors in omnes pervasit. 14. Regnavit autem Mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosen, ineos etiam qui non peccaverunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adami, qui est typus illius qui erat futurus. Eidem reatui implicantur, qui non peccarunt similiter ut Adamus in persona propria; sed tantum peccarunt in Capite illo: quemadmodum fideles justificantur in Christo, cujus ille typus factus est 15.-19. Illius unius offensa multi mortui sunt. Reatus quidem ex una offensa ad condemnationem.-Per unam offensam Mors regnavit per unum. Per contumaciam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi. Ex una igitur offensa, & contumacia unius hominis, est reatus multorum ad condemnationem, &c.
units.tr: as natural; so that it involves that whole nature in the same guilt as the first parents. This is proved against the Pelagians, Socinians, and their other followers: (1) by certain express testimonies. Eph. 2. 3. Here children of wrath must be understood passively, that is, liable to the divine wrath. All men are such by nature, that is, now corrupted, and this through him who represented the whole nature. 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22. By man came death. In Adam all die. Rom. 5. 12. Through one man, etc. By that one man's sin all sinned, and so death passed upon all. Rom. 5. 14. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression, who is a type of him who was to come. Those who did not sin personally as Adam did are bound to the same guilt; they sinned only in that head, just as believers are justified in Christ, of whom Adam was made a type. Rom. 5. 15–19. By the offence of one many died. The judgment was by one offence unto condemnation. By one man's offence death reigned by one. By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners. Therefore by one offence and the disobedience of one man, the guilt of many comes to condemnation, etc.

units.la: 2. Ab effectu; Morte parvulorum, ante ulla ipsorum peccata actualia. Mors enim hominis omnino poenae rationem habet. Vide sup. cap. 7. th. 44. Ergo in infantibus, sine peccato suo actuali morientibus, agnosci debet aliud; scil. originale imputatum.
units.tr: (2) From the effect: the death of infants before any actual sins of their own. For death of a man has altogether the character of punishment. See above, chap. 7, th. 44. Therefore in infants who die without any actual sin of their own, something else must be recognised, namely imputed original sin.

units.la: 3. A consequente remotiori; necessitate redemtionis per Christum. Matth. 18. 11. Venit enim Filius hominis ut servet quod perierat. ix. 12. Iis qui valent non est opus Medico; sed iis qui male se habent. Act. 4. 12. Nec est in alio quoquam salus, &c. Vide etiam Job. 14. 6. Marc. 16. 16. Joh. 3. 36. 2 Cor. 5. 15, 19, 21. Ubi Infantes salvandi quoque includuntur. Marc. 10. 14, 16. Sinite Pueruios venire ad Me, & ne prohibete eos: talium enim est Regnum Dei. - Et cum accepisset eos in ulnas, impositis in eos manibus, benedixit eis. Act. xi, 38, 39. Baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomen Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum: - Vobis enim facta est promissio, & liberis vestris, &c. Confer Gen. 17, 7, 10, 12. Ergo etiam Infantes per naturam ex lapsu corruptam perierant.
units.tr: (3) From a more remote consequence: the necessity of redemption through Christ. Matt. 18. 11. For the Son of man came to save that which was lost. ix. 12. They that are whole have no need of a physician, but they that are sick. Acts 4. 12. Neither is there salvation in any other, etc. See also John 14. 6. Mark 16. 16. John 3. 36. 2 Cor. 5. 15, 19, 21. Where infants who must be saved are also included. Mark 10. 14, 16. Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of God. And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them. Acts 2. 38, 39. Let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins. For the promise is unto you, and to your children, etc. Compare Gen. 17. 7, 10, 12. Therefore infants too had perished by nature corrupted by the fall.

units.la: 4. A consequente propinquiori; vitiositate omnibus nunc per naturam inhærente: quoniam enim Deus justo suo judicio omnes conclusit in inobedientiam; Rom. xi. 32. (quod mox plenius explicabitur & confirmabitur,) inde etiam manifestum evadit peccatum illud Posteris imputari, atque in iis sic puniri.
units.tr: (4) From a nearer consequence: the vitiated condition now inherent in all by nature. For since God by his just judgment has concluded all under disobedience (Rom. 11. 32, which will be explained and confirmed more fully soon), it also becomes plain that that sin is imputed to posterity and punished in them accordingly.

units.la: XXVII. Intelligendi autem omnes Posteri, qui ab Adamo geniti sunt, ac porro descenderunt, juxta ordinem sub isto Fœdere institutum, cum benedictione illa, Fœtificate, & augescite; & implete terram; Gen. 1. 28. quique sic in ipso censiti fuerunt.
units.tr: XXVII. All the posterity are to be understood as included, those who were born from Adam and afterwards descended, according to the order instituted under that covenant with the blessing, Be fruitful and multiply, and replenish the earth, Gen. 1. 28, and who were thus reckoned in him.

units.la: Solus igitur Christus excipitur; Mediator & Sponsor Novi Fœderis: adeoque non censitus in Adamo fœderaliter: a quo contradistinguitur, ut quadantenus typo; Rom. 5. 14. 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22, 45, 47, 48, 49. Quanquam respectu humanæ naturæ utcunque virtualiter physice in illo fuit; juxta genealogiam, Luc. 3. 2338. Sed qui venit servare quod perierat; Matth. 18. 11. non erat venturus, si Adamus in sua integritate perstitisset; neque juxta ordinem tunc constitutum. Unde postmodum non naturali illo modo, ex Viro & Muliere; sed supernaturali Spiritus Sancti operatione conceptus est in Virgine, &c. Vide Gen. 3. 15. Isef. 7. 14. Matth. 1. 18, 20. Luc. 1. 34, 35.
units.tr: Christ alone is therefore excepted, the Mediator and Surety of the New Covenant, and so he was not reckoned in Adam as a covenant head, from whom he is distinguished as being in some measure a type. Rom. 5. 14. 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22, 45, 47, 48, 49. Yet with respect to human nature he was in some way virtually and physically in him, according to the genealogy, Luke 3. 23–38. But he who came to save what was lost, Matt. 18. 11, would not have been coming had Adam persevered in his integrity, nor according to the order then established. Hence afterwards he was conceived in the Virgin not by the natural way, from man and woman, but by the supernatural operation of the Holy Spirit, etc. See Gen. 3. 15. Isa. 7. 14. Matt. 1. 18, 20. Luke 1. 34, 35.

units.la: XXVIII. Effectus proximus peccati istius imputati, est Reatus omnium Adamitarum, h. e. in ipso fœderaliter censitorum. Rom. 5. 16. Unde consequuntur effectus remotiores: omnis generis calamitates, cruciatus, & miseriæ; sive simpliciter tristes, sive etiam turpes: tum in hac vita, tum post eam in æternum. Ista enim pariter Mortis nomine comprehenduntur; Gen. 2, 17. Confer Rom. 5. 12, 14. Quare etiam Condemnatio diserte appellatur, Rom. 5. 16, 18.
units.tr: XXVIII. The immediate effect of this imputed sin is the guilt of all the Adamites, that is, of those reckoned in him under the covenant. Rom. 5. 16. From this follow more remote effects: every kind of calamity, torment and misery, whether simply sad or even shameful, both in this life and after it for eternity. For these are likewise comprehended under the name of death. Gen. 2. 17. Compare Rom. 5. 12, 14. Therefore it is also expressly called condemnation, Rom. 5. 16, 18.

units.la: Obj. 1. Servator parvulis tribuit Regnum Cœlorum; Marc. 10. 14. Idem Sancti dicuntur; 1 Cor. 7. 14. Ergo. Resp. Non ratione naturæ; sed gratiæ, in Christo.
units.tr: Obj. 1. The Saviour attributes the Kingdom of Heaven to little children, Mark 10. 14. The same are called holy, 1 Cor. 7. 14. Therefore. Resp. Not by reason of nature, but of grace, in Christ.

units.la: Obj. 2. Christus Job. 9.2,3.negat, parentes illius cæci peccatis suis hoc esse in specie demeritos ut iste cæcus nasceretur. Ergo. Resp. Inde nequaquam sequitur, peccatum Adami non imputari Posteris in ipso censitis.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Christ (John 9. 2, 3) denies that the parents of that blind man had so sinned as to cause him to be born blind. Therefore. Resp. It by no means follows from this that the sin of Adam is not imputed to posterity reckoned in him.

units.la: Obj. 3. Jac. 4. 11. Deus pepercit illis parvulorum millibus. Ergo. Resp. Non tamen absolute adversatur Divinæ justitiæ, vel etiam misericordiæ, peccata Parentum Liberis imputare; atque hos idcirco simul punire: ut factum in Diluvio, & alibi.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Jonah 4. 11. God spared those thousands of little children. Therefore. Resp. Yet it is not absolutely contrary to divine justice, or even to mercy, to impute the sins of parents to their children and so to punish them together with them, as happened in the Flood and elsewhere.

units.la: Obj. 4. Adamo peccante, nos non extitimus; ergo nec una peccavimus, aut in peccatum illud consensimus. &c. Resp. Extitimus virtualiter in Adamo, & fœderaliter in ipso comprehensi atque censiti sumus: unde illud peccatum non est a nobis alienum.
units.tr: Obj. 4. When Adam sinned we did not yet exist; therefore we did not sin in him or consent to that sin, etc. Resp. We existed virtually in Adam, and were comprehended and reckoned in him under the covenant; hence that sin is not alien to us.

units.la: XXIX. Peccatum originale inhærens, est habitualis congenita vitiositas, ex primo illo peccato orta, per quam natura nostra prorsus inepta est ad omne bonum spirituale salutare, & proclivis ad mala opposita.
units.tr: XXIX. Inherent original sin is a habitual, innate vitiation, arising from that first sin, by which our nature is wholly unfit for any spiritual and saving good, and inclined to the opposite evils.

units.la: Non autem est ipsa Hominis substantia; qui Flacci Illyrici erat error: nam 1. Substantia Deum auctorem habet.
units.tr: It is not, however, the very substance of man, which was the error of Flacius Illyricus. For first, substance has God as its author.

units.la: Atque adeo 2. bonitatem suam in genere entis.
units.tr: And so, secondly, it has its goodness in the category of being.

units.la: 3. Filius Dei ejusdem speciei substantiam assumsit hypostatice; sed absque omni peccato.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Son of God assumed the substance of the same species hypostatically, but without any sin.

units.la: 4. In regeneratione, sanctificatione, & glorificatione, non mutantur homines substantialiter; sed qualitatibus solum: interim ab ista vitiositate liberantur.
units.tr: Fourthly, in regeneration, sanctification and glorification, men are not changed in substance but only in qualities, and meanwhile they are freed from this vitiation.

units.la: Obj. Sæpius in SS. Literis appellatur Caro, Corpus peccati, Membra terrena, Homo vetus, &c. Ergo. Resp. Ista per metonymiam subjecti pro adjuncto dicuntur: & moralem universæ naturæ nostræ corruptionem indicant.
units.tr: Obj. Scripture often calls it flesh, body of sin, earthly members, old man, etc. Therefore. Resp. These are said by metonymy of the subject for the adjunct, and they indicate the moral corruption of our whole nature.

units.la: Neque tamen putanda est mera negatio, seu carentia justitiæ originalis, quæ etiam bruto, aut lapidi, tribui potest: sed est vera ejus privatio, & quidem in subjecto activo rationali. Hinc ergo facultates, habitus, & affectus, quoties in actum deducuntur, vel feruntur in objecta mala, & sic male; vel in objecta bona, sed male. Unde Peccatum peccans, Lex membrorum & peccati, &c. appellatur, Rom. 7. 13, 17, 20, 23, 26. Jac. 1. 14.
units.tr: Yet it must not be thought a mere negation, or the mere lack of original righteousness, which could be ascribed even to a beast or a stone. It is a true privation of it, and indeed in a rational active subject. Hence the faculties, habits and affections, whenever they are brought into act, either tend toward evil objects and so act badly, or tend toward good objects but act badly. Whence they are called sin that sins, the law of the members and of sin, and so on: Rom. 7. 13, 17, 20, 23, 26; Jas. 1. 14.

units.la: XXX. Probatur nunc ista vitiositas, adversus Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes; 1. Locis quibusdam diserte & communiter universam illam corruptionem nativam docentibus:
units.tr: XXX. This vitiosity is now proved against the Socinians, Anabaptists and Remonstrants: 1. by certain passages that plainly and commonly teach this universal native corruption:

units.la: Job. 14. 4. Quis edat mundum ex immundo? ne unus quidem. Job. 3. 6. Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est. Ita quidem ut dum talis manet, a Regno Dei excludatur. Gen. 6. 5. Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis hominum tantummodo malum est omni tempore. 8. 24. Figmentum cordis hominis est malum a pueritia ipsius. Omnis igitur, etiam prima, operatio mentis humanæ, in statu hoc naturali, mala est moraliter. Psal. 51, 7. En, in iniquitate formatus sum; & in peccato fovit me mater mea. Adde Gen. 5. 3. Jes. 48. 8. Lviii. 4. Ezech. 16. 3, 6. Jerem. 17. 9.
units.tr: Job 14. 4: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one." Job 3. 6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh," so that, while it remains such, it is shut out from the Kingdom of God. Gen. 6. 5: "Every imagination of the thoughts of the heart of man is only evil continually." Gen. 8. 24: "The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." Therefore every operation of the human mind, even the first, in this natural state, is morally evil. Psalm 51. 7: "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me." Add Gen. 5. 3; Isa. 48. 8; Isa. 58. 4; Ezek. 16. 3, 6; Jer. 17. 9.

units.la: 2. Prefius explicatur ista corruptio, respectu facultatum, habituum, affectuum, & actionum. Rom. 8. 7. Quod sapit carnem, inimicitia est adversus Deum. Legi enim Dei non subjicitur: nam ne potest quidem. Sic autem caro est, quicquid ex carne natum. 1 Cor. 2, 14. Animalis homo non est capax eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; sunt enim ei stultitia, nec potest ea cognoscere: quia spiritualiter dijudicantur. Animalis autem est, qui supernaturali gratia Spiritus Sancti destituitur. Confer verf. 15. & Judæ, 19. Iterum Eph. 2. 1, 2,3. Cum effetis mortui in lapsibus & peccatis, in quibus olim ambulastis, ut est vita mundi hujus. Eramusque natura, ut etiam reliqui. 1v.17,18. Sicut reliquæ Gentes ambulant, in vanitate mentis suæ: Tenebris obscuratam mentem habentes, & alienati a vita Dei, propter ignorantiam quæ est in ipsis, per obdurationem cordis ipsorum.
units.tr: 2. This corruption is explained more precisely with respect to the faculties, habits, affections and actions. Rom. 8. 7: "The carnal mind is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be." For what is born of the flesh is flesh. 1 Cor. 2. 14: "The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." The natural man is one who lacks the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit. Compare v. 15 and Jude 19. Again Eph. 2. 1, 2, 3: "You hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins, wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world," and "were by nature the children of wrath, even as others." Eph. 4. 17, 18: "The Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart."
Add Eph. 5. 8; Titus 3. 3; 1. 15; Rom. 6. 19.

units.la: 3. Ex necessitate regenerationis & sanctificationis. Joh. 3. 5. Nisi quis genitus sit iterum, non potest videre Regnum Dei. Nisi quis fuerit genitus ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in Regnum Dei. Per naturam igitur caremus vita spirituali. Eph. 4. 22, 23, 24. Edocti deponere, quod ad pristinam conversationem attinet, veterem illum hominem, qui de sedufricibus cupiditatibus sese corrumpit: Renovari verospiritu mentis; Et induere novum illum hominem, qui secundum Deum conditus est ad justitiam & sanctimoniam veram. Vetus homo propter corruptionem exuendus est; novus, ad imaginem conditoris Dei, induendus necessario. II. 5. Etiam nos, cum in offensis mortui essemus, una vivificavit. Per naturam ergo spiritualiter mortui sumus: propterea vivificatione opus est. Adde 2 Cor. 5. 17, 18. Ezech 36. 26.
units.tr: 3. From the necessity of regeneration and sanctification. John 3. 5: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the Kingdom of God," and "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of God." By nature, therefore, we lack spiritual life. Eph. 4. 22, 23, 24: taught "to put off, concerning the former conversation, the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." The old man must be put off because of his corruption; the new man must necessarily be put on, created after the image of God. Eph. 2. 5: "Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together." Therefore by nature we are spiritually dead, and so vivification is needed. Add 2 Cor. 5. 17, 18; Ezek. 36. 26.

units.la: Huc olim pertinebat Circumcisionis necessitas, quæ Cordis circumcisionem signabat: Gen. 17. 10,-14. cum Deut. 10. 16. xxx. 6. Jerem. 4. 4. & nunc Baptismi, spiritualem immunditiem necessario expurgandam indicantis: Col. 2. 11, 12. Act. 2. 38, 39. xxij. 16.
units.tr: To this formerly pertained the necessity of circumcision, which signified circumcision of the heart (Gen. 17. 10–14, with Deut. 10. 16; 30. 6; Jer. 4. 4); and now the necessity of baptism, which indicates that spiritual uncleanness must necessarily be purged (Col. 2. 11, 12; Acts 2. 38, 39; 22. 16).

units.la: 4. Ex Reliquiis istius corruptionis in regenitis & sanctificatis. Phil. 3. 12. Non quod jam metam apprehenderim, aut jam jam consummatus. Jac. 3. 2. In multis enim impingimus omnes. 1 Joh. 1. 8, 9, 10. Si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. &c. Gal. 5. 17. Nam Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum: Spiritus autem adversus Carnem: hæc vero inter se oppositæ sunt, ut non quæcunque que volueritis, eadem faciatis. Differta est in hanc rem quereka Apostoli, Rom. 7. 14.-. Ego carnalis sum, venditus ut subjicerer peccato. (Ratione istarum reliquiarum) Quod enim perpetro, (peccans,) non agnosco, (non approbo, qua modo regenitus). Non enim quod volo, (voluntate regenita.) hoc ago; sed quod odi; hoc facio. 17. Nunc itaque non amplius ego id perpetro (ille ego, qui nunc sum; novus homo;) sed peccatum, quod in me habitat, id perpetrat, &c. Unde facile patet, qualis, & quanta, sit corruptio in homine naturali.
units.tr: 4. From the remnants of this corruption in the regenerate and sanctified. Phil. 3. 12: "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect." Jas. 3. 2: "For in many things we offend all." 1 John 1. 8, 9, 10: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us," and so on. Gal. 5. 17: "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." The Apostle's complaint on this matter is set out at Rom. 7. 14: "I am carnal, sold under sin." (With respect to these remnants:) "For that which I do" (sinning) "I allow not" (I do not approve, as one now regenerate). "For what I would, that do I not" (with a regenerate will); "but what I hate, that do I." 17: "Now then it is no more I that do it" (that I who now am the new man), "but sin that dwelleth in me" performs it, and so on. Whence it is easily clear what, and how great, is the corruption in natural man.

units.la: XXXI. Quomodo ad omnes Adami posteros extendatur ista corruptio, atque interim Christi alia sit ratio, satis innotescit ex dictis th. 27.
units.tr: XXXI. How this corruption extends to all the posterity of Adam, while the case of Christ is otherwise, is sufficiently clear from what was said in thesis 27.

units.la: Mariam Virginem non item excipimus, neque immaculatam conceptionem ei tribuimus, cum Pontificii. Quemadmodum ea neque peccatorum actualium fuit expers; juxta generalia effata, 1 Reg. 8. 46. Prov. 20. 9. Eccles. 7. 20. Jac. 3. 2. 1 Joh. 1. 8, 10. communem precationem; Matth. 6. 12. & Christi reprehensionem ad eam; Luc. 2. 49. Joh. 2. 4. Unde etiam ipsa Servatore indiguit; Luc. 1. 47. Joh. 14. 6. Actor. 4. 12.
units.tr: We do not likewise except the Virgin Mary, nor do we ascribe to her an immaculate conception, as the Papists do. For she was not free of actual sins either, according to the general sayings: 1 Kings 8. 46; Prov. 20. 9; Eccl. 7. 20; Jas. 3. 2; 1 John 1. 8, 10; and according to the common prayer, Matt. 6. 12, and Christ's rebuke of her, Luke 2. 49; John 2. 4. Whence she too stood in need of the Saviour: Luke 1. 47; John 14. 6; Acts 4. 12.

units.la: Obj. 1. Christus ex Maria non potuit nasci sine labe hæreditaria, nisi & ipsa ejus fuerit immunis. Resp. Neg.
units.tr: Objection 1. Christ could not have been born of Mary without hereditary stain, unless she too had been free of it. Reply: Denied.

units.la: 1. Alia enim Christi est ratio; qui in Adamo labente non fuit censitus. 2. Eadem consequentia ab ista labe eximi possent parentes Virginis Mariæ, ac porro illorum parentes, & majores, usque ad ipsum Adamum.
units.tr: 1. For Christ's case is different, since he was not reckoned as fallen in Adam. 2. By the same consequence, the parents of the Virgin Mary could be exempted from this stain, and likewise their parents and ancestors, up to Adam himself.

units.la: Obj. 2. Psal. 19. 5. In Sole posuit tabernaculum suum: ergo B. Virgo est prorsus immaculata. Resp. Vulgatus Interpres vitiose sic reddidit illum textum; ubi non agitur de B. Virgine, neque Christi in ea conceptione: sed celebratur, quomodo Deus Soli in regione cœlesti assignaverit suum spatium, quasi ad lineas decurrendum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Psalm 19. 5: "In the sun hath he set his tabernacle," therefore the Blessed Virgin is altogether immaculate. Reply: The Vulgate translator rendered that text wrongly. It is not about the Blessed Virgin, nor about Christ's conception in her; it celebrates how God assigned to the sun its own space in the heavenly region, as if to run along fixed lines.

units.la: Obj. 3. Cant. 1. 15. Ecce, tu pulchra es, amica mea! Ergo, &c. Resp. Istud de Ecclesia mystica dicitur, & respectu gratiæ; non de Maria, & respectu naturæ.
units.tr: Objection 3. Song 1. 15: "Behold, thou art fair, my love!" Therefore, etc. Reply: That is said of the mystical Church, and with respect to grace; not of Mary, and with respect to nature.

units.la: XXXII. Spiritualis iste morbus hæreditarius propagatur media generatione naturali: analogice ut fit in corporalibus morbis hæreditariis. A Patribus carnis nostræ, (Hebr. 12. 9.) cum quibus Matres, ut causas socias, una comprehendimus, (Psal. 51. 7.) procedit tale corpus organicum, multiplici intemperie laborans: hinc proficiscuntur affectus inordinati; & mores animi inclinantur. Animæ quidem à Deo creantur, sed nunc absque justitia originali. Producitur substantia spiritualis, cum suis facultatibus naturalibus, & quibusdam habitibus, exiguis Imaginis Divinæ reliquiis: sed non cum habituali ista integritate, quæ initio fuit in Protoplastis. Hactenus Deus se habet negative: sed subjectum ita productum habet se privative. Verum insuper actus positivus judicialis ex parte Dei agnoscendus est, quo ipse icтam privationem in subjecto operativo ordinat in pœnam primi peccati; quod Posteris imputari, imo Posteros in Adamo etiam commisisse, probatum est superius. Hinc jam Facultates infirmæ, & ad spiritualia salutaria naturaliter ineptæ: Habitus imperfecti, & vitiati: Intellectus spirituali stultitia laborat; Voluntas, prosanitate, & rebellione adversus Deum, ac Legem Ipsius: Affectus, omnino inordinati: Corporis membra sunt organa injustitiæ ad serviendum peccato: Actiones omnes peccaminosæ, &c. Job. 15. 5. Rom. 5. 6. viij. 3, 7. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Eph. 4. 18. ij. 1, 2, 3. Tit. 3. 3. Rom. 6. 13, 16, 17. Matth. 7. 17, 18. Job. 3. 6. Job. 14. 4. Tit. 1. 15. Qui enim rationaliter operari aptus natus & proclivis est, nec potest bene, necessario operatur male moraliter.
units.tr: XXXII. This spiritual hereditary disease is propagated by natural generation, analogously as hereditary bodily diseases are. From the fathers of our flesh (Heb. 12. 9), together with whom we include the mothers as joint causes (Psalm 51. 7), there proceeds such an organic body, labouring under manifold intemperance; hence inordinate affections arise and the dispositions of the mind are inclined. Souls indeed are created by God, but now without original righteousness. A spiritual substance is produced with its natural faculties and certain habits, slight remnants of the Divine Image, but not with that habitual integrity which was at the beginning in our first parents. Thus far God stands in a negative relation; but the subject so produced stands in a privative one. Moreover, a positive judicial act on God's part must be acknowledged, by which he ordains that privation in the operative subject as the punishment of the first sin; that this is imputed to posterity, and indeed that posterity also committed it in Adam, has been proved above. Hence now the faculties are weak and naturally unfit for saving spiritual things; the habits are imperfect and corrupted; the intellect labours under spiritual folly; the will is perverse and rebellious against God and his Law; the affections are wholly disordered; the members of the body are instruments of unrighteousness for serving sin; all actions are sinful, and so on: Job 15. 5; Rom. 5. 6; 8. 3, 7; 1 Cor. 2. 14; Eph. 4. 18; 2. 1, 2, 3; Titus 3. 3; Rom. 6. 13, 16, 17; Matt. 7. 17, 18; Job 3. 6; Job 14. 4; Titus 1. 15. For whoever is by nature apt and inclined to act rationally, and cannot act well, necessarily acts badly in the moral sense.

units.la: XXXIII. Ista ratione 1. universum Genus humanum in se vilissimum est coram Deo, prorsus contemnendum & abominandum: Eccl. 1. 2. Psal. 62. 9. Cxliv. 3, 4. Tit. 3. 3. Eph. 2. 3. 2. Miser-
units.tr: XXXIII. By this reasoning, first, the whole human race is in itself most vile before God, utterly to be despised and abhorred: Eccl. 1. 2; Ps. 62. 9; Ps. 144. 3, 4; Tit. 3. 3; Eph. 2. 3.

units.la: 2. Miserrimæ servituti mancipatum : Job. 8. 34. Rom. 6. 16, 17, 20, 21. vij. 14, 23, 26.
units.tr: 2. Enslaved to a most wretched servitude: John 8. 34; Rom. 6. 16, 17, 20, 21; 7. 14, 23, 26.

units.la: 3. Inde omnis generis peccata actualia : Matth. 7. 17, 18. Jac. 1. 14, 15.
units.tr: 3. Hence arise sins of every kind, actual: Matt. 7. 17, 18; Jas. 1. 14, 15.

units.la: 4. Ac pro rata crescit reatus : Rom. 3. 4, 5, 19. v. 20, 21, 23.
units.tr: 4. And the guilt grows in proportion: Rom. 3. 4, 5, 19; 5. 20, 21, 23.

units.la: 5. Conscientia prorsus mala est : Tit. 1. 15. Jes. 57. 21.
units.tr: 5. The conscience is utterly defiled: Tit. 1. 15; Isa. 57. 21.

units.la: Obj. 1. Sanguis infantium dicitur innoxius : Psal. 106. 38. Nulla igitur vitiositas iis inhæret. Resp. Istud dicitur; quia nullum adhuc peccatum actuale commiserunt; nedum quo meriti essent, ab hominibus violenta istiusmodi morte multari.
units.tr: Objection 1. The blood of infants is called innocent: Ps. 106. 38. Therefore no vitiation cleaves to them. Answer: That is said because they have not yet committed any actual sin, much less that they would have deserved to be put to death by such a violent death at the hands of men.

units.la: Obj. 2. Destituuntur usu rationis: consequenter non sunt subjecta capacia alicujus peccati. Resp. Non quidem peccati actualis; sed tamen originalis, ut imputati, ita quoque inhærentis.
units.tr: Objection 2. They lack the use of reason; consequently they are not capable subjects of any sin. Answer: Not indeed of actual sin, but nevertheless of original sin, both as imputed and as inherent.

units.la: Obj. 3. Aliqui fuerunt sanctificati, vel etiam Spiritu Sancto repleti, inde ab utero materno; ut Jeremias, Johannes Baptista, &c. Ergo. Resp. Quæ a gratia supernaturali procedunt, a natura distingui debent: neque illa negant, aut statim tollunt, omnem naturæ corruptionem.
units.tr: Objection 3. Some were sanctified, or even filled with the Holy Spirit, from the womb, as Jeremiah, John the Baptist, and others. Therefore... Answer: What proceeds from supernatural grace must be distinguished from nature; nor do those gifts deny, or at once remove, all corruption of nature.

units.la: Obj. 4. Multi parentes sunt fideles & sancti: per eos ergo saltem non propagatur peccatum originale. Resp. 1. Generatio destinata est ad propagandam per se naturam; non gratiam. 2. Ad propagationem illam intervenium quidem parentes proximè; sed potissimum spectandus est Adamus, in quo corrupta est universa natura.
units.tr: Objection 4. Many parents are faithful and holy; therefore at least through them original sin is not propagated. Answer: 1. Generation is destined to propagate nature as such, not grace. 2. Parents indeed intervene as the immediate agents of that propagation, but chiefly Adam must be regarded, in whom the whole nature was corrupted.

units.la: XXXIV. Homini subjectivè inest sua Libertas; sed subordinata Libertati Divinæ, & dependens à summa Providentia; ut ostensum est suis locis. Nunc ex superioribus etiam deducimus contra Pontifícios, Socinianos, Anabaptistas, & Remonstrantes, facultatem illam in homine irregenito, per nativam corruptionem sem, impeditam esse, quo minus se possit exerere ad bona spiritualia salutaria: atque adeo hominis naturalis arbitrium, in ordine ad ista objecta appetenda & prosequenda, non esse liberum; ut quidem est ad objecta naturalia, aut civilia, & moraliter mala; sed esse servum corruptioni & malitiae.
units.tr: XXXIV. Liberty is inherent in man subjectively, but it is subordinate to the Divine Liberty and dependent on the supreme Providence, as has been shown in their places. Now from what has gone before we also deduce, against the Papists, Socinians, Anabaptists, and Remonstrants, that this faculty in the unregenerate man is hindered by native corruption from being able to exert itself toward saving spiritual goods; and thus the natural human will, in relation to desiring and pursuing those objects, is not free, as it is with respect to natural or civil objects and morally evil things, but is a slave to corruption and malice.

units.la: Demonstratur hoc 1. disertis testimoniis: Joh. 8. 34, 36. Quisquis operam dat peccato, servus est peccati. Itaque si vos Filius in libertatem vindicarit, vere liberi eritis. Tantisper homo naturalis est servus peccati. Rom. 6. 6, 7, 16, 17, 19. Veterem illum nostrum hominem cum Eo crucifixum esse, ne nos amplius serviamus peccato. - An nescitis, quod cui sistitis vos servos ad obediendum, ejus servi estis, cui auscultatis? - Fuistis quidem servi peccati. - Exhibuistis membra vestra serva impuritati & iniquitati, ad patrandam iniquitatem. 2 Petr. 2. 19. Cum ipsi servi sint corruptelae: siquidem a quo quis superatus est, huic etiam in servitutem est addictus. Confer 2 Tim. 2. 25, 26.
units.tr: This is demonstrated, first, by plain testimonies: John 8. 34, 36: "Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin. So if the Son shall set you free, you will be truly free." For so long a natural man is a slave of sin. Rom. 6. 6, 7, 16, 17, 19: "that our old man was crucified with Him, so that we should no longer serve sin." "Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of him whom you obey? ... You were indeed slaves of sin. ... You presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity, for committing iniquity." 2 Pet. 2. 19: "For they themselves are slaves of corruption; for by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also bound as a slave." Compare 2 Tim. 2. 25, 26.

units.la: 2. Ex Morte spirituali; & necessitate vivificationis, &c. Naturaliter mortuus nullas actiones vitales potest producere: nec spiritualiter mortuus, actiones spirituales salutares. Eph. 2. 1, 2. Cum essetis mortui in lapsibus & peccatis: In quibus olim ambulastis; ut est vita hujus mundi. 5. Etiam nos, cum in offensis mortui essemus, una vivificavit cum Christo. IV. 18. Tenebris obscuratam mentem habentes, & alienati a vita Dei, &c. Matth. 8. 22. Mortui (spiritualiter) sepeliant mortuos suos (corporaliter). Hinc opera eorum mortua dicuntur: Hebr. 6. 1. ix. 14. Sed in Christo est vita: Joh. 1. 5. xiv. 6.
units.tr: 2. From spiritual death, and the necessity of quickening, etc. A man naturally dead cannot produce any vital actions, and a man spiritually dead cannot produce spiritual actions that are saving. Eph. 2. 1, 2: "When you were dead in trespasses and sins, in which you once walked, according to the course of this world." 2. 5: "Even when we were dead in offenses, He made us alive together with Christ." 4. 18: "Having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God," etc. Matt. 8. 22: "The dead (spiritually) bury their dead (bodily)." Hence their works are called dead: Heb. 6. 1; 9. 14. But in Christ is life: John 1. 4; 14. 6.

units.la: 3. Expresse inculcatur omnimoda nostra impotentia, respectu bonorum spiritualium salutarium. Joh. 15. 5. Seorsim a me nihil potestis facere. 1 Cor. 3. 5. Non quod idonei sumus per nos ipsos ad cogitandum quicquam, velut ex nobis ipsis: &c. Matth. 7. 18. Non potest teft arbor mala fructus bonos ferre. Rom. 5. 6. Cum nullis adhuc viribus effemus. &c. Adde cap. 8. 3,7. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Deut. 29. 4.
units.tr: 3. Our complete impotence with respect to saving spiritual goods is expressly insisted upon. John 15. 5: "Apart from me you can do nothing." 1 Cor. 3. 5: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves," etc. Matt. 7. 18: "A bad tree cannot bear good fruit." Rom. 5. 6: "When we were still without strength," etc. Add chap. 8. 3, 7; 1 Cor. 2. 14; Deut. 29. 4.

units.la: 4. Et manifesta est contraria dispositio, inclinatio, & occupatio: Tit. 1. 15. Pollutis & incredulis nihil est mundum: sed polluta est eorum & mens, & conscientia.
units.tr: 4. And the contrary disposition, inclination, and occupation is manifest. Tit. 1. 15: "To the polluted and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and conscience are polluted."

units.la: 1 Cor. 2. 14. Animalis homo, &c. sunt enim ei stultitia. Quia scil. subjectivè in ipsius mente inest spiritualis stultitia. Rom. 8. 7. Quod sapit caro, inimicitia est adversus Deum. xiv. 23. Quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum est. Eph. 4. 22. Vetus ille homo de seductricibus cupiditatibus se corrumpit. Adde Gen. 6. 5. viij. 21. Ierem. 13. 23.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2. 14: "The natural man ... for they are foolishness to him." This is because spiritual folly inheres subjectively in his mind. Rom. 8. 7: "The mind of the flesh is enmity against God." 14. 23: "Whatever is not of faith is sin." Eph. 4. 22: "The old man is corrupted by deceitful lusts." Add Gen. 6. 5; 8. 21; Jer. 13. 23.

units.la: XXXV. Obj. 1.
units.tr: XXXV. Objection 1.

units.la: Philosophi, aliique inter Gentiles sapientia & virtute conspicui, plurima praeclare secerunt; Socrates, Aristides, Cato Major, Seneca, &c. Ergo. Resp. 1. Sed iidem ambitionis, aliorumque viciorum, mancipia fuerunt. 2. Quae absolutè, secundum specificationem operum, censeri possent bona; subjectivè tamen fuerunt spiritualiter mala, ratione principii, finis, & modi agendi; atque adeo splendida peccata.
units.tr: The philosophers and others among the Gentiles who were distinguished by wisdom and virtue did many excellent things: Socrates, Aristides, Cato the Elder, Seneca, and so on. Therefore... Answer 1. But these same men were slaves of ambition and of other vices. 2. Their works, considered absolutely, according to the kind of deed, could be counted good; yet subjectively they were spiritually evil, by reason of their principle, their end, and their manner of acting; and so they were splendid sins.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Cor. 7. 37. Nec adigitur necessitate, sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem, &c. Ergo. Resp. A Libertate in actionibus ad naturam, & ad vitam civilem spectantibus, utpote de matrimonio contrahendo, aut secus, &c. non valet consequentia ad Libertatem in spiritualibus salutaribus.
units.tr: Objection 2. 1 Cor. 7:37: "He is under no necessity, but has power over his own will," etc. Therefore... Answer: The inference from liberty in actions that pertain to nature and civil life, such as contracting marriage or not, etc., does not hold for liberty in spiritual matters that bring salvation.

units.la: Obj. 3. Matth. 23. 37. Quoties volui aggregare liberos tuos.--& noluistis. Qui autem possunt nolle, iidem quoque possunt velle. Resp. Homines corruptissimi stultè possunt contemnere & repudiare bona spiritualia: quae est eorum amentia, & inimicitia adversus Deum: sed propterea non possunt in isto suo statu eadem bona spiritualia rectè aestimare, eligere, & prosequi. Obj. 4. Deut. 30. 19. Vitam & mortem proposui, benedictionem & maledictionem : deligat ergo vitam, &c. Æque igitur possunt eligere vitam & benedictionem. Resp. 1. Ex Præceptis, Promissionibus, Comminationibus, &c. recte colligitur obligatio ad officium; non autem facultas ad præstandum istud officium in statu naturali corrupto. 2. In universa Israelitarum multitudine aliqui saltem fuerunt regeniti & sanctificati, qui per istam gratiam potuerunt etiam deinceps eligere vitam. Fieri quoque potuit, ut nonnulli audita illa exhortatione & obtestatione, quæ erat instrumentum morale, accedente intus hyperphysica operatione Spiritus Sancti, reipsa converterentur; & sic spirituali facultate eligendi vitam ac benedictionem instruerentur: dum reliqui sic magis ad officium obligabantur: & de peccatis suis convincebantur.
units.tr: Objection 3. Matt. 23:37: "How often would I have gathered your children... and you would not." But those who can refuse can also will. Answer: Most corrupt men can foolishly despise and reject spiritual goods; this is their madness and their enmity against God. But for that very reason, in their present state, they cannot rightly esteem, choose, and pursue those same spiritual goods. Objection 4. Deut. 30:19: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life," etc. Therefore they can equally choose life and blessing. Answer 1. From precepts, promises, threats, etc., an obligation to duty is rightly inferred; but not the ability to perform that duty in the corrupt natural state. 2. In the whole multitude of Israelites there were at least some who were regenerate and sanctified, and who through this grace could thereafter choose life. It could also happen that some, having heard that exhortation and entreaty, which was a moral instrument, were actually converted, the inward hyperphysical operation of the Holy Spirit accompanying it; and so they were furnished with the spiritual ability to choose life and blessing, while the rest were thereby more bound to duty and convicted of their sins.

units.la: XXXVI. Sicut in Iustificatione fideles absolvuntur & liberantur à reatu, omnique poena stricte dicta; quanquam in hac vita adhuc remanent castigationes, explorationes, &c. ita quoque in Regeneratione & Sanctificatione extinguitur vetus homo; non quidem ut statim prorsus esse desinat; sed ut saltem non dominetur, atque indies magis subigatur, & destruatur, donec cum fine huius vitæ omnino aboleatur. Vide Rom. 6. 6. Col. 3. 5,6,7. 2 Cor. 4. 16. Hebr. 4. 9, 10.
units.tr: XXXVI. Just as in justification the faithful are absolved and freed from guilt and from every punishment strictly so called, although in this life chastisements, trials, etc. still remain, so too in regeneration and sanctification the old man is put to death; not indeed so that he ceases altogether at once, but so that at least he does not rule, and is daily more subdued and destroyed, until he is wholly abolished together with the end of this life. See Rom. 6:6; Col. 3:5-7; 2 Cor. 4:16; Heb. 4:9-10.

units.la: Quod autem de naturali corruptione reliquum est in regenitis, justificatis, baptizatis, &c. vere etiam peccati rationem habet. Hoc contra Pontificios, aliosque afferimus, 1. expressis quibusdam testimoniis: Rom. 713. Peccatum admodum peccans. 17. 20. Peccatum, quod in me habitat: 21. Mihi malum adjacet. 23. Lex peccati, quæ est in membris meis. Hebr. 12. 1. Peccatum, ad nos circumcingendos proclive. Scil. peccatum illud habituale est causa peccatorum actualium.
units.tr: But what remains of natural corruption in the regenerate, the justified, the baptized, and so on, truly also has the character of sin. We assert this against the Papists and others: 1. by certain express testimonies: Rom. 7:13, "sin working exceedingly sinful"; 7:17, 20, "sin that dwells in me"; 7:21, "evil lies close at hand to me"; 7:23, "the law of sin which is in my members"; Heb. 12:1, "sin which easily entangles us." That is, that habitual sin is the cause of actual sins.

units.la: 2. Plane adversatur integritati Imaginis Divinæ, perfectioni nostræ morali: Eph. 4. 22, 23, 24. Col. 3. 7, 8, 10, 12.
units.tr: 2. It plainly opposes the integrity of the Divine Image and our moral perfection: Eph. 4:22-24; Col. 3:7-8, 10, 12.

units.la: 3. Manifesta est diffo-mitas à Lege Dei: Gal. 5. 16, 17. Quod concupiscit Caro, ne perficite. Nam Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum. Jac. 1. 14, 15. Unusquisque tentatur, dum à propria cupiditate abstrahitur & inescatur, &c.
units.tr: 3. There is a manifest discord with the Law of God: Gal. 5:16-17, "Do not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit"; Jas. 1:14-15, "Each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire," etc.

units.la: 4. De ea dolent & conqueruntur fideles: Rom. 7. 24. Ærumnosus ego homo! quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? cum 8. 10: Corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum. Vide etiam sup. cap. 9. th. 110.
units.tr: 4. The faithful grieve over it and complain of it: Rom. 7:24, "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" Compare 8:10: "The body indeed is dead because of sin." See also above, chap. 9, th. 110.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Nec dubitandum, quin Paulus Rom. 7. 14.. loquatur de se ipso, ut jam tum vere regenito: nam 1. diserte loquitur de se ipso, & quidem in praesenti tempore; verf. 14, 15, 16. &c.
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt that Paul in Rom. 7:14 speaks of himself as one already truly regenerate: for 1. he speaks of himself expressly, and indeed in the present tense; vv. 14, 15, 16, etc.

units.la: 2. Praedicat Legem mentis suae, & Hominem interiorem, secundum quem delectabatur Lege Dei; verf. 15, 16, 22, 23, 26.
units.tr: 2. He professes the law of his mind and the inner man, according to which he delighted in the Law of God; vv. 15, 16, 22, 23, 26.

units.la: 3. Serio & anxie conqueritur de peccato, quod in ipso erat reliquum; & oderat illud; verf. 14, 15, 17, 21, 23, 24.
units.tr: 3. He seriously and anxiously complains of the sin that remained in him, and hated it; vv. 14, 15, 17, 21, 23, 24.

units.la: 4. Certus erat de redemptione per Christum: atque isto nomine gratias agebat Deo; verf. 25.
units.tr: 4. He was certain of redemption through Christ, and on this account gave thanks to God; v. 25.

units.la: Exc. Irregenitus etiam meliora videre & probare potest. Resp. Potest naturali conscientia cognoscere & approbare ea, quae civiliter bona sunt; non autem spiritualiter: neque iis delectatur.
units.tr: Objection. The unregenerate too can see and approve better things. Answer. He can by natural conscience know and approve those things which are good in a civil sense, but not spiritually; nor does he delight in them.

units.la: Obj. Loquitur de homine carnali, vendito ut subjiceretur peccato: atqui talis non est regenitus. Resp. Sic appellat non absolute; sed a reliquiis carnis. Confer 1 Cor. 3. 1, 3. cum I, 2. Idem interim secundum hominem interiorem, novus ille Paulus, vere serviebat non peccato, sed Legi Divinae; eaque delectabatur: sic peccatum non faciebat, nec volebat; sed odio habebat.
units.tr: Objection. He speaks of the carnal man, sold so as to be subject to sin; but such a man is not regenerate. Answer. He does not call him that absolutely, but on account of the remnants of the flesh. Compare 1 Cor. 3:1, 3 with 1, 2. Meanwhile, according to the inner man, that new Paul truly served not sin but the Divine Law, and delighted in it; thus he did not commit sin nor will it, but hated it.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Ex originali illa vitiositate oriuntur deinceps peccata actualia; ut actiones ex habitu; & fructus mali ex arbore mala: Matth. 7. 17, 18. Jac. 1. 15. Unde peccatum peccans appellatur; Rom. 7. 13.
units.tr: From that original corruption there then arise actual sins, as actions arise from a habit, and bad fruit from a bad tree: Matth. 7. 17, 18. Jac. 1. 15. Hence sin is called sinning sin; Rom. 7. 13.

units.la: Accedunt horum aliæ etiam passim causæ internæ: utpote, 1. pravi habitus acquisiti; si homines sint edocti male facere, &c. Jerem. 13. 23.
units.tr: There are also, here and there, other internal causes added to these, namely: (1) acquired bad habits, when men have been taught to do evil, etc. Jerem. 13. 23.

units.la: 2. Ignorantia facti, vel etiam juris: 1 Tim 1. 13. 1 Cor. 2. 8. Act. 3. 17. Psal. 147. 20. cum Act. 14. 16.
units.tr: (2) Ignorance of fact, or also of law: 1 Tim. 1. 13; 1 Cor. 2. 8; Acts 3. 17; Ps. 147. 20, with Acts 14. 16.

units.la: 3. Infidelitas: Rom. 14. 23. Tit. 1, 15.
units.tr: (3) Unbelief: Rom. 14. 23; Tit. 1. 15.

units.la: 4. Vacuitas reverentiæ Dei; Gen. 20. 11. Psal. IV, 20. 21.
units.tr: (4) Lack of reverence for God: Gen. 20. 11; Ps. IV, 20, 21.

units.la: 5. Mentis cæcitas, & cordis duritiæ: Eph. IV, 17, 18.
units.tr: (5) Blindness of mind and hardness of heart: Eph. IV, 17, 18.

units.la: 6. Carnis infirmitas: Matth. 26, 41.
units.tr: (6) Weakness of the flesh: Matt. 26. 41.

units.la: 7. Inordinata concupiscentia: Jac. 1, 15.
units.tr: (7) Disordered concupiscence: Jas. 1. 15.

units.la: 8. Subjectio ad serviendum peccato: Rom. 6. 16. 1 Reg. 21, 25.
units.tr: (8) Subjection, so as to serve sin: Rom. 6. 16; 1 Kings 21. 25.

units.la: 9. Alia peccata, propter cognationem, affinitatem, vel dispositionem: 1 Tim. 6. 10. 1 Joh. 2. 16. Ezech. 16. 49.
units.tr: (9) Other sins, on account of kinship, affinity, or disposition: 1 Tim. 6. 10; 1 John 2. 16; Ezek. 16. 49.

units.la: Atque item externæ: 1. Diabolus, tenator & seductor: Joh. 8. 44. Matt. 4. 3. 2 Cor. 2. 11. XI, 3. 1 Petr. 5. 8. Eph. 6. 11, 12. Apoc. 2. 24.
units.tr: And likewise external causes: (1) the devil, the tempter and seducer: John 8. 44; Matt. 4. 3; 2 Cor. 2. 11; XI, 3; 1 Pet. 5. 8; Eph. 6. 11, 12; Rev. 2. 24.

units.la: 2. Mundus corruptus: 1 Job. 5. 19. Quò pertinent hominum mundanorum consilia prava, doctrinæ falsæ ac fallaces, invitationes, & persuasiones malæ, tentationes tum ad dextram, tum ad sinistram: Prov. 1. 10, 15. Matth. 7. 15, 16. Apoc. 2. 14. 1 Cor. 15. 33. Dan. 3. 6. Act. 26. 11.
units.tr: (2) The corrupt world: 1 John 5. 19. To this belong the wicked counsels of worldly men, false and deceptive doctrines, evil invitations and persuasions, and temptations both to the right and to the left: Prov. 1. 10, 15; Matt. 7. 15, 16; Rev. 2. 14; 1 Cor. 15. 33; Dan. 3. 6; Acts 26. 11.

units.la: 3. Res prosperæ, quibus plurimi per abusum luxuriant: Ezech. 16, 49. Psal. 62. 11. Rom. 2. 4. Prov. 30. 8, 9.
units.tr: (3) Prosperous circumstances, by the abuse of which very many grow wanton: Ezek. 16. 49; Ps. 62. 11; Rom. 2. 4; Prov. 30. 8, 9.

units.la: 4. Ex accidenti etiam ipsa Lex Divina: Rom. 7. 9, 10, 11.
units.tr: (4) Incidentally, the Divine Law itself: Rom. 7. 9, 10, 11.

units.la: XXXIX. Peccata isto dispescuntur multifariam.
units.tr: XXXIX. Sins are divided in many ways.

units.la: Ratione materiæ, aliud est peccatum per se; aliud per accidens. Peccatum per se dicitur, ubi ipsa talis actio objective prohibita est Lege Divina: ut idololatria, furtum, mendacium, &c. Per accidens, ubi ipsa actio mandata est, vel saltem ethice permissa; sed vitiatur ex conditione efficientis, finis, modi, aliarumve circumstantiarum: ut actus liberalitatis, justitiae, temperantiae, fortitudinis, &c. in Socrate, Aristide, Scipione, Alexandro M. &c. Tit. 1. 15. Rom. 14. 23; 18, 19, 20. Matth. 6. 1. Vitiositatem illam vere Deus improbat; attamen opus, utcunque bonum, ab homine infideli factum, pro admirabili sua tolerantia, & gratia, temporalibus adhuc beneficiis quandoque compensat. Ezech. 29. 19, 20. 1 Reg. 21. 27, 28, 29.
units.tr: With regard to matter, one sin is sin in itself, another is sin incidentally. A sin is said to be sin in itself where the action as such is objectively forbidden by the Divine Law: such as idolatry, theft, lying, etc. It is sin incidentally where the action itself is commanded, or at least ethically permitted, but is vitiated by the condition of the agent, the end, the manner, or other circumstances: such as acts of generosity, justice, temperance, and courage, etc., in Socrates, Aristides, Scipio, Alexander the Great, etc. Tit. 1. 15. Rom. 14. 23; 18, 19, 20. Matth. 6. 1. God truly disapproves of that viciousness; yet by his wonderful forbearance and grace he sometimes rewards, with temporal benefits, a work, however good, done by an unbelieving man. Ezech. 29. 19, 20. 1 Reg. 21. 27, 28, 29.

units.la: Ratione objectorum, vel peccatur circa ipsum Deum directe; vel circa proximum. 1 Sam 2. 25. Si peccaverit ullus in alterum, judicabit eum Magistratus: sed si in Jehovam ullus peccat, quis eret Illum? Luc. 15. 18, 21. Peccavi in caelum, & in tuo conspectu. Tenenda hic distributio Decalogi in duas Tabulas: unde porro subdivisiones institui possunt, secundum singula Praecepta.
units.tr: With regard to objects, sin is committed either directly against God himself, or against the neighbour. 1 Sam 2. 25. If a man sin against another, the magistrate shall judge him; but if any man sin against Jehovah, who shall intercede for him? Luke 15. 18, 21. I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. The division of the Decalogue into two Tables must be kept here, and from it further subdivisions can be made according to the individual Precepts.

units.la: XL. Ratione subjectorum, peccata alia sunt interna cordis, vel animi; quae ipso intellectu, voluntate, aut affectibus intus patrantur. Psal. 14. 1. Stultus dicit in corde suo; Non est Deus. Matth. 15. 19. Ex corde egrediuntur cogitationes malae. v. 28. Quicunque irascitur fratri suo temere, -. Huc autem potissimum pertinent primo addubitatio, & prima quaeque inclinatio ad approbanda, appetenda, amplectenda, patranda, quae Lege prohibita sunt: tum morosa in objectis illis apprehensis delectatio: ac porro deliberatum consilium de iis patrandis.
units.tr: XL. With regard to subjects, some sins are internal, of the heart or mind, which are committed inwardly, in the intellect, the will, or the affections. Psal. 14. 1. The fool says in his heart, There is no God. Matth. 15. 19. Out of the heart come evil thoughts. v. 28. Whoever is angry with his brother without cause. To this belong chiefly: first, doubting, and every first inclination to approve, desire, embrace, or carry out what the Law forbids; then, a lingering delight in those objects once grasped; and finally, deliberate counsel to carry them out.

units.la: Alia vero sunt externa; & foras exeruntur, tum ore, tum opere. Rom. 3. 13, 14. Linguis suis ad dolum abusi sunt, &c. Matth. v. 22. Quicunque dixerit fratri suo, Raca; -. Quisquis autem dixerit, Fatue, &c. Adde 12. 36. Item Rom. 6. 19. Exhibuistis membra vestra serva impuritati & iniquitati, ad patrandam iniquitatem. Adde III, 15, 16. Iterum alia dicuntur spiritualia; quæ sic ipsâ mente committuntur, ut eam proprie & proximè contaminent, & Diaboli imaginem ei per se imprimant: ut blasphemia, hæresis, superbia, invidia, mendacium, &c.
units.tr: Others, however, are external, and break out either by word or by deed. Rom. 3. 13, 14. They have abused their tongues for deceit, etc. Matth. v. 22. Whoever says to his brother, Raca; ... But whoever says, You fool, etc. Add 12. 36. Also Rom. 6. 19. Present your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity, to commit iniquity. Add III, 15, 16. Again, others are called spiritual; these are committed in the mind itself in such a way that they properly and immediately defile it, and imprint the image of the Devil upon it, such as blasphemy, heresy, pride, envy, lying, etc.

units.la: Alia carnalia; quæ voluptates corporeas, ac porro exteriorem corporis conditionem & habitum proximè spectant; atque ita corpus etiam polluunt, & hominem belluis quodammodo assimilant: ut ebrietas, fornicatio, homicidium, rapina, &c. Vide Rom. 1, 21, 24. ubi ostenditur, quomodo Deus peccata spiritualia carnalibus puniverit.
units.tr: Others are carnal, which relate chiefly to bodily pleasures and further to the external condition and habit of the body; and so they also pollute the body and to some extent make men like beasts: such as drunkenness, fornication, murder, robbery, etc. See Rom. 1. 21, 24, where it is shown how God has punished spiritual sins by carnal ones.

units.la: Affinis est distributio, secundùm quam plurima peccata committuntur extra proprium corpus, ratione objecti terminantis: ut falsum testimonium, furtum, &c. alia proprium corpus; polluendo, vel etiam debilitando illud insigniter: ut scortatio, ebrietas, &c. 1 Cor. 6, 18. Fugite scortationem: omne peccatum (ut plurimum) quod fecerit homo, extra corpus est: sed qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat.
units.tr: A related division is that by which very many sins are committed outside the body, by reason of the object on which they terminate, such as false witness, theft, etc.; while others are committed against one's own body, polluting or even seriously weakening it, such as fornication, drunkenness, etc. 1 Cor. 6. 18: Flee fornication. Every sin that a man commits (for the most part) is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body.

units.la: XLI. Ratione principiorum; alia ex ignorantia procedunt: homo scil. ignorat se isto opere peccare; omissurus potius, si hoc scivisset. Ista autem est Ignorantia practica, Juris particularis, & Puræ negationis; aut facti. Act. 3, 17. Fratres, scio vos per ignorantiam ista fecisse. 1 Cor. 2, 8. Si cognovissent, neque quam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. 1 Tim. 1, 13. Misericordia sum donatus. Nam ignorans (id) faciebam.
units.tr: XLI. With regard to principles, some sins proceed from ignorance: that is, a man does not know that he sins by this deed, and would rather have refrained had he known. This is practical ignorance, of particular law, or of pure negation, or of fact. Acts 3. 17. Brethren, I know that you did these things through ignorance. 1 Cor. 2. 8. Had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. 1 Tim. 1. 13. I was shown mercy, for I did it in ignorance.

units.la: Alia ex infirmitate; ubi peccator succumbit tentationi vires suas superanti, quanquam sciens habitualiter, & absolutè: scil. priusquam judicio comparato statuerit, quid sibi in istis circumstantiis juxta voluntatem Dei agendum sit, subitariâ tentatione occupatur & labitur; vel etiam diuturnâ graviore, dum judicium practicum interim falsis rationibus, vel affectibus obnubilatur. Gal. 6, 1. Fratres, etiam si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliqua offensa; considerans (unusquisque) temet ipsum, ne & tu tenteris. Hebr. 5.2. de Pontifice. Quod & ipse, circumdatus sit infirmitate. Vide etiam 12.1. Num. 15. 27, 28.
units.tr: Others arise from weakness, where the sinner gives way to a temptation that overpowers his strength, although he knows the law habitually and absolutely; that is, before he has formed a judgment about what he ought to do in these circumstances according to the will of God, he is seized by a sudden temptation and falls; or even by a lasting and more grievous one, while in the meantime his practical judgment is clouded by false reasonings or affections. Gal. 6. 1. Brethren, even if a man is overtaken in some offence, each one considering himself, lest you too be tempted. Heb. Heb. 5. 2, of the High Priest: since he himself is beset with infirmity. See also 12. 1. Num. 15. 27, 28.

units.la: Alia denique ex malitia; ubi peccans, animo perverso eligit, & audacter prosequitur malum morale, quamvis sic cognitum; dum hic & nunc ipsum apprehendit ut bonum jucundum, vel utile, vel gloriosum. Ita in his inest deliberatum consilium & audax rebellio contra sanctissimam Dei Legem; atque adeo actualis ignorantia Juris, etiam universalis, & Ignorantia affectata, ac pravae disposit ionis. Num. 15. 30, 31. Anima, quae fecerit manu excelsa, (vel elata,) Iehovam probris afficit: atque excidetur anima illa e medio populi sui. Quia verbum Iehovae sprevit, & praeceptum ejus irritum fecit, &c.
units.tr: Lastly, others arise from malice, where the sinner with a perverse mind chooses and boldly pursues a moral evil, although he knows it as such, while here and now he grasps it as pleasant, useful, or glorious. In these there is therefore deliberate counsel and bold rebellion against the most holy Law of God, and so actual ignorance of the law, even of the universal law, and affected ignorance and a depraved disposition. Num. 15. 30, 31. The soul that does anything with a high hand (or defiantly) reproaches Jehovah, and that soul shall be cut off from the midst of its people, because it has despised the word of Jehovah and made void his commandment, etc.

units.la: Priora duo genera in regenitos & sanctificatos cadunt non item tertium; nisi secundum similitudinem aliquam, ubi gratia actuali aliquamdiu destituuntur, & caro in iis tantisper praevalet: sed irregenitis hoc proprium est.
units.tr: The first two kinds fall upon the regenerate and sanctified, but the third does not, except in a certain likeness, where they are for a while deprived of actual grace and the flesh prevails in them for a time; but this is proper to the unregenerate.

units.la: XLII. Ratione effectorum, quaedam peccata prae aliis dicuntur vastare conscientiam; h. e. insigni sua enormitate ac malitia illam deturbare ob officio indicandi, dirigendi, retrahendi, accusandi condemnandi, juxta judicium ipsius Dei. Sic 1 Tim. 1. 19. aliqui dicuntur, bona conscientia repulsa, naufragium fidei fecisse. Et 4, 2. quorundam conscientia cauterio resecta, ut sensum amiserit. Hos. 4.11. Scortatio, vinumque, & mustum, intercipit mentem. Rom. 1,21,24,26,28. Vani facti sunt in ratiociniationibus suis; & obtenebratum est cor eorum intelligentia carens. Tradidit eos Deus in mentem omnis judicii expertem.
units.tr: XLII. With regard to effects, some sins are said to lay waste the conscience; that is, by their notable enormity and malice they overthrow it in its office of indicating, directing, restraining, accusing, and condemning, according to the judgment of God himself. Thus in 1 Tim. 1. 19 some are said to have rejected a good conscience and made shipwreck of faith; and in 4. 2 the conscience of some is said to be seared with a hot iron, so that they have lost their feeling. Hos. 4. 11. Whoredom, wine, and new wine take away the understanding. Rom. 1. 21, 24, 26, 28. They became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened... God gave them up to a reprobate mind, which is without judgment.

units.la: Item quaedam prae aliis appellantur clamantia; quod graviorem poenam, eamque exemplarem, & praesentem postulent. Gen. 4,10, 11. Ecce vocem sanguinum fratris tui, me ab ipsa humo inclamantiu. Nunc itaque tu maledictus esto, &c. 18,20,21. Clamor Sodomae & Gomorræ cum multus sit, & peccatum ipsorum cum grave sit valde: Descendam nunc. &c. Confer xv,16. Iterum Exod. 22.22,23, 24. Nullam viduam, aut orphanum, affligitote. Si qua afflictione afflixeris eam; (Nam si tantillum clamet ad me, utiq; exauditurus sum clamorem ejus) Tum accensa ira mea occidam vos gladio, &c. Jac.5.4. Ecce merces operariorum, qui messuerunt regiones vestras, per vos interversa, clamat: & vociferationes eorum qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt. Confer Rom.2.4.
units.tr: Likewise, some sins are called crying sins above others, because they demand a heavier punishment, one that is exemplary and immediate. Gen. 4:10, 11. Behold the blood of your brother cries out to me from the ground. Now therefore you are cursed, etc. 18:20, 21. Because the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is exceedingly grave: I will go down now, etc. Compare 15:16. Again Exod. 22:22-24. You shall afflict no widow or orphan. If you afflict them in any way (for if they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry), then my anger will be kindled and I will kill you with the sword, etc. James 5:4. Behold, the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back, cry out; and the outcry of those who mowed has entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. Compare Rom. 2:4.

units.la: XLIII. Pontificii male distinguunt inter peccata mor- talia, & venialia.
units.tr: XLIII. The Papists wrongly distinguish between mortal and venial sins.

units.la: Mortalia dicunt fieri contra Legem Dei; & mortem seu condemnationem æternam demereri. Venialia vero dicunt fieri præter Legem, & per se ac sua natura non mortem, sed veniam mereri; interveniente scil. expiatione, aut satisfactione hominum, sive in hac vita, sive in Purgatorio.
units.tr: They say mortal sins are committed against the Law of God and deserve death, that is, eternal condemnation. Venial sins, they say, are committed apart from the Law, and by their own nature merit not death but pardon, through the intervention of expiation or satisfaction made by men, whether in this life or in Purgatory.

units.la: Nos sic venialia nulla agnoscimus: 1.quia S.Scriptura nusquam docet istam distinctionem; neque ullam remissionem, nisi quæ fit fidelibus, per gratiam, in Christo. Eph. 1.7, In quo habemus redemptionem, per sanguinem Ipsius; remissionem offensarum, prout est dives Ipsius gratia 1 Joh.1.7. Sanguis Iesu Christi Filii ejus purificat nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: We, however, acknowledge no venial sins in this way: (1) because Holy Scripture nowhere teaches this distinction, nor any remission except that which is granted to believers, through grace, in Christ. Eph. 1:7, In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, according to the riches of his grace. 1 John 1:7, The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.

units.la: 2. S. Scriptura prorsus aliter loquitur de peccatis; & quidem in universum: Rom. 6.23. Matth. 5.19. Gal. 3.10. Iac. 2.10.
units.tr: (2) Holy Scripture speaks quite differently of sins, and indeed generally: Rom. 6:23; Matt. 5:19; Gal. 3:10; James 2:10.

units.la: 3. Omne peccatum adversatur Legi Divinæ; quæ est unica vitæ nostræ & morum regula: 1 Joh. 3.4. cum Psal. 19.8. Matth. 22,37,38,39. & Deut.27,26.
units.tr: (3) Every sin is opposed to the Divine Law, which is the sole rule of our life and conduct: 1 John 3:4, compared with Ps. 19:8; Matt. 22:37, 38, 39; and Deut. 27:26.

units.la: 4. Omne peccatum, qua tale, adversatur infinitæ & sanctissimæ Majestati Divinæ, eamque offendit: consequenter inducit reatum isti offensæ convenientem, poenarum æternarum.
units.tr: (4) Every sin, as such, is opposed to the infinite and most holy Majesty of God and offends it; consequently it brings on the guilt of eternal punishments befitting such an offence.

units.la: Obj. 1. Iac.1,15. Peccatum, ubi consummatum est, gignit mortem: ergo non omne est mortale. Resp. I-
units.tr: Objection 1. James 1:15: sin, when it is accomplished, brings forth death; therefore not every sin is mortal. Answer: [The passage indicates the common method and progress]...

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] (catchword continues on next page: flic loci indicatur communis methodus,! & progressus à concupiscentia originali, ad actualem volaticam, ad delectationem morosam,ad consilium deliberatum, ad media destinata, ad consummationem, ad mortem. Verum sic nequaquam omnia, quæ consummationem antecedunt, liberantur a reatu mortis. Neque ipsi Pontificii id ausint afferere.
units.tr: [illegible, about three letters] (catchword continues on the next page: this passage indicates the common course and progress from original concupiscence to actual consent, to delight that lingers, to deliberate intention, to chosen means, to completion, to death). But in this way, by no means are all the things that precede completion freed from the guilt of death. Nor would the Papists themselves dare to assert this.

units.la: Obj. 2. Matth. 5, 22. Quædam peccata dicuntur inducere reatum gehennæ; alia solum reatum judicii, aut confessus. Ergo. Resp. Istic allegorice, similitudine defumta a variis Judæorum judiciis & suppliciis, docetur inæqualitas peccatorum, atque ipsius reatus, ratione graduum: sic tamen ut omnis reatus in foro poli æternus sit, & maneat, nisi interveniat gratia Euangelica.
units.tr: Objection 2. Matt. 5:22: some sins are said to bring the guilt of Gehenna, others only the guilt of judgement or council. Therefore... Answer: There, by allegory, taken from the various Jewish judgements and punishments, the inequality of sins and of their guilt is taught according to degrees; yet in such a way that all guilt is eternal in the court of heaven and remains, unless evangelical grace intervenes.

units.la: Obj. 3. Diserte appellatur peccatum ad mortem; 1 Joh. 5. 16, 17. Ergo. Resp. Sed illud est prorsus irremissibile: unde nec aliis permittitur orare pro iis, qui istud commiserunt; ut mox explicabitur. Sed Pontificii aliter loquuntur de suo mortali.
units.tr: Objection 3. It is expressly called a sin unto death: 1 John 5:16, 17. Therefore... Answer: But that sin is absolutely unpardonable; hence it is not permitted to others to pray for those who have committed it, as will soon be explained. The Papists, however, speak otherwise of their mortal sin.

units.la: XLIV. Remissibilia tamen sunt, & de facto remittuntur, quælibet peccata omnium eorum, qui sincere resipiscunt, & Christum Servatorem vera fide amplectuntur. Act. 10, 43. Huic omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accepturum per nomen Ejus quemvis, qui crediderit in Eum. Rom. 8. 1. Nulla igitur nunc est condemnatio iis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu &c. Una vero peccati species ab aliis discernitur, tanquam irremissibilis: Matth. 12. 31, 32. „Quod„vis peccatum & blasphemia remittetur hominibus: „blasphemia vero in Spiritum Sanctum non remittetur „hominibus. Et quisquis locutus fuerit adversus Filium „hominis, remittetur ei: quisquis autem fuerit locutus „adversus Spiritum Sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque „in hoc sæculo, neque in futuro. pro quo Marc. 3. 29. Non habet remissionem in æternum; sed tenetur æterno judicio.
units.tr: XLIV. Nevertheless, all sins whatsoever of all those who sincerely repent and embrace Christ as Saviour with true faith are pardonable, and in fact are pardoned. Acts 10:43: To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins through his name. Rom. 8:1: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, etc. One kind of sin, however, is distinguished from the others as unpardonable: Matt. 12:31, 32. "Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men; but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven men.
