For first, under the Old Testament the legal covenant was rigidly inculcated again and again, and only tempered by evangelical consolations, so clearly and sweetly; and accordingly the people was held in a certain kind of servitude. But under the New Testament the Gospel itself is preached more clearly; the grace of both sanctification and adoption is greater, and so is the liberty: Heb. 8. 8-10, etc.; Jer. 31. 31, etc.; Gal. 3. 24, 26. Then under the Old Testament that yoke of the ceremonial law held sway, burdensome and heavy. But all this has been utterly abolished in the New Testament, whence Paul says, Gal. 5. 1, 2, 3: "Stand firm, therefore, in the liberty by which Christ has set us free, and do not again be caught in a yoke of servitude," etc. See also Acts 15. 10.

units.la: XLII. Ratione quantitatis, primo intensive sub N. T. dona gratiæ sunt infigniora; & efficacior ordinarie per Spiritum est applicatio, quam sub V. Unde illa oppofitio Litera, & Spiritus, ministerii condemnationis ac mortis, & justitiæ ac vitæ, quatenus tunc Spiritus fe parcius exerebat ad justitiam & vitam: 2 Cor. 3. 6,-9; 18.
units.tr: XLII. With respect to quantity: first, intensively, the gifts of grace are more distinguished under the New Testament, and the application through the Spirit is ordinarily more effective than under the Old. Whence comes that opposition of letter and Spirit, of the ministry of condemnation and death and the ministry of righteousness and life, inasmuch as then the Spirit showed himself more sparingly in righteousness and life: 2 Cor. 3. 6-9, 18.

units.la: Deinde extensive, respectu locorum & gentium, de qua restrictione sub V. T. Pfal. 147. 19,20. Indicat verba sua Iacobo, statuta & jura sua Israeli. Non fecit ita ulligenti, &c. Confer Eph. 2. 13. Vos qui olim eratis longinqui, propinquifactieftis. Adde Gal. 3. 28. Iob. 4. 21,23. Nec non respectu temporis; quatenus oeconomia V. T. juxta prophetiam Dan. 9. 24,27. abolenda, & novum pactum veteri erat successurum: ita ut vetus pactum per novum istud prorsus fit antiquatum: Hebr. 8. 7. & seqq. oeconomia vero N. T. ad consummationem sæculi duratura: Matth. 28. 19, 20. Quapropter & hæc postrema tempora dicuntur: Act. 2. 17.
units.tr: Then, extensively, with respect to places and nations; of this restriction under the Old Testament: Ps. 147. 19, 20. "He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not dealt thus with any nation," etc. Compare Eph. 2. 13: "You who once were far off have been brought near." Add Gal. 3. 28; John 4. 21, 23. Likewise with respect to time, insofar as the economy of the Old Testament, according to the prophecy of Dan. 9. 24, 27, was to be abolished, and the new covenant was to succeed the old, so that the old covenant is utterly made obsolete by that new one: Heb. 8. 7 ff. But the economy of the New Testament is to last until the consummation of the age: Matt. 28. 19, 20. Wherefore these are also called the last times: Acts 2. 17; 1 Tim. 4. 1; 1 John 2. 18, since no other doctrine and no other economy is to be expected after this.

units.la: 1 Tim. 4.1. 1 Iob. 2. 18. cum post hac non alia doctrina, non alia oeconomia, expectari debeat.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 4. 1; 1 John 2. 18, since no other doctrine and no other economy is to be expected after this.

units.la: XLIII. Atque ita afferimus contra Judæos; 1. Meffiam dudum venisse; & quæ in terris erant peragenda omnia confummasse. 2. Gentiles ad salutarem ejus communionem etiam vocatos. & 3. Oeconomiam V. T. carnalem & umbraticam, hac œconomia N.T. magis spirituali & gloriosa esse permutatam.
units.tr: XLIII. And so we maintain against the Jews: 1. that the Messiah has long since come and has completed all that was to be done on earth; 2. that the Gentiles too have been called to his saving communion; and 3. that the carnal and shadowy economy of the Old Testament has been exchanged for this more spiritual and glorious economy of the New.

units.la: Primo Aduentum Messiæ jamdudum præteriisse, probamus; 1. Ex statu Judæorum politico: Sic Gen.49.10. Non recedet Sceptrum à Iuda, nec Legislator de medio pedum ejus usquedum venerit Schiloh; & ipsi obedientia populorum. Vaticinium illud de Messia exponendum, ex ipso verborum contextu cuilibet obvium est; atque adeo cum Tempus adventui Messiæ destinatu præcise assignetur, omnisque potestas, tum Regum, tum Ducalis, & Legislatoria penes tribum Judæ mansura dicatur, donec veniret Messias, Rex ille spiritualis, cui omnes populi in fide essent paituri; jam autem omnis potestas a gente Judaica dudum fit sublata; ipsum Messiam dudum venisse, necessum est. Adde Prophetias, 2 Sam.7.15,16. Psal.89.4, 5,30 36, 37. Jer.33. 17,20,21,22. 2 Reg. 8.19. Isef. 9.5, 6.
units.tr: First, we prove that the advent of the Messiah has long since passed: 1. from the political state of the Jews. Thus Gen. 49. 10: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples." That prophecy about the Messiah is obvious to anyone from the very context of the words. And so, since the time appointed for the Messiah's coming is precisely assigned, and all power, royal, ducal and legislative, is said to remain with the tribe of Judah until the Messiah, that spiritual King, should come, to whom all peoples would submit in faith, but now all power has long since been taken from the Jewish nation, it is necessary that the Messiah has long since come. Add the prophecies: 2 Sam. 7. 15, 16; Ps. 89. 4, 5, 30, 36, 37; Jer. 33. 17, 20, 21, 22; 2 Kings 8. 19; Isa. 9. 5, 6.

units.la: 2 Ex statu Judæorum Ecclesiastico: Hag. 2.7, 10.-Adhuc pusillum illud est; & commoturus sum cœlos, & omnes gentes, ut veniant ad desiderium omnium gentium: implebo hanc domum gloria.-Meum est argentum, & meum est aurum.-Major futura est gloria domus hujus posterioris quam illius prioris:-nam in loco hoc dabo pacem, &c. Agitur ibi de Templo posteriore, cui præ priore, & quidem brevi major gloria promittitur; non quæ consisteret in auro, argento, &c. sed in pace; eaque non corporali, quæ durante Templo secundo non fuit valde insignis; sed spirituali: quo sensu ipse Messias appellatur, Princeps pacis; Isef. 9 6. qui proinde venturus debuit intelligi stante adhuc Templo secundo. Cum autem Templum illud secundum fit eversum, consequens est & ipsum Messiam dudum venisse.
units.tr: 2. From the ecclesiastical state of the Jews: Hag. 2. 7, 10: "Yet a little while, and I will shake the heavens and all nations, so that they come to the desire of all nations; I will fill this house with glory. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former; for in this place I will give peace," etc. There it is a question of the later Temple, to which, compared with the former, and indeed shortly, greater glory is promised; not such as would consist in gold, silver and the like, but in peace; and that not bodily peace, which while the second Temple stood was not very conspicuous, but spiritual peace, in which sense the Messiah himself is called the Prince of Peace, Isa. 9. 6, who therefore ought to be understood as coming while the second Temple still stood. But since that second Temple has been overthrown, it follows that the Messiah has long since come.

units.la: Similiter Mal.3.1. Ecce, Ego mittirus sum Angelum meum, qui expediat viam ante me: & repente veniet in Templum suum Dominus, quem vos quæritis; & Angelus fœderis, quo vos delectamini. Ecce venturus est! atque iterum iv. 5. Ecce Ego missurus sum vobis Eliam Prophetam, antequam veniat dies Iehovæ maximus & reverendus. Scil. mittendus erat Messias, Dominus cujus erat Templum, Angelus ille fœderis, cujus præcursor Elias; atque ille confestim expectabatur, brevi mittendus ad Templum. Sic illum quasi advenientem demonstravit postremus Propheta; cujus finem, Euangelii sui principium fecit Marcus, i. 1, 2.
units.tr: Similarly, Mal. 3. 1: "Behold, I will send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before me; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his Temple, and the angel of the covenant in whom you delight. Behold, he is coming!" and again iv. 5: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet before the great and dreadful day of the LORD comes." That is, the Messiah, the Lord whose Temple it was, the angel of that covenant, whose forerunner was Elijah, was to be sent; and he was expected at once, soon to be sent to the Temple. So the last Prophet pointed to him as one who was as it were already coming; and Mark made the end of this prophecy the beginning of his Gospel, Mark 1. 1, 2.

units.la: 3. Ex illustri vaticinio, Dan. 9. 24,- 27, ubi utraque status, & utriusque excisio, diserte proponitur; ac simul definitum tempus exprimitur, quo venire debuit Messias. Sic autem habet textus; Septimanæ septuaginta decisæ sunt super populum tuum, & super civitatem sanctam tuam, ad cohibendum defectionem, & ad obsignandum peccata, & ad expiandum iniquitatem & ad adducendum justitiam perpetuam, & ad obsignandum visionem ac prophetam, & ad ungendum Sanctum sanctorum. Igitur cognoscito, & intelligito, ab enunciatione verbi de reducendo populo, & de ædificandis Hierosolymis, usque ad Messiam antecessorem, fore septimanas septem; deinde septimanas sexaginta duas.- Post septimanas autem illas sexaginta duas excidetur Messias; sed non propter se.- Corroborabit vero multis Fœdus septimana una: dimidio autem septimanæ abolebit sacrificium, & munus, &c. De Messia agi, palàm est ex aperta ejus designatione, verf. 24. & 26. quin imo talia de eo commemorantur, verf. 24. quæ non possunt nisi Messiæ competere. Et quidem illa omnia evenire debuerunt intra 70. hebdomadas à restauratione populi & urbis tunc facienda, ad ultimam utriusque excisionem. Hebdomadas autem annorum hoc loco intelligendas esse, (de quibus etiam Levit. 25. 8.) plus quam manifestum est: unde consequenter summa conficitur annorum 490. Cum vero tempus illud, & multa insuper sæcula dudum præterierint, rursum colligimus, Messiam quoque dudum venisse.
units.tr: 3. From the famous prophecy in Daniel 9:24-27, where both the state of the people and the destruction of each city are clearly set out, and at the same time the fixed time when the Messiah was due to come is stated. The text reads: Seventy weeks are decreed upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophet, and to anoint the most Holy. Know therefore and understand that from the going forth of the word to restore and to build Jerusalem, until the Messiah the prince, there shall be seven weeks; and sixty-two weeks. After those sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be cut off, but not for himself. And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week; and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and oblation to cease, etc. That the Messiah is meant is plain from his explicit designation in verses 24 and 26, and indeed such things are recorded of him in verse 24 as can apply to none but the Messiah. All these things were bound to happen within seventy weeks, from the restoration of the people and the city, which was then to be carried out, down to the final destruction of both. That the weeks here are to be understood as weeks of years (as also in Lev. 25:8) is more than clear; from this the sum of 490 years follows. Since that time, and many centuries besides, have long since passed, we conclude again that the Messiah has also long since come.

units.la: Addimus propter affinitatem : Dan. 2. 44, 45. In diebus Regum istorum, suscitabit Deus cœli Regnum, quod in sæcula non destruetur; & Regnum ipsum populo alieno non relinquetur: comminuet, & consummabit omnia illa regna; ipsum autem persistet in sæcula. Quandoquidem vidisti è monte excscindi Lapidem, qui non est in ullis manibus, &c. Messiæ regnum hic necessario intelligenduum est : nullum enim aliud tam perpetuum & constans datur; nec alii, illud de Lapide, sine manibus exciso, potest applicari. Confer Ief. 28. 16. Psal. 118. 21, 22. Illud autem suscitandum dicitur in diebus Regum istorum, Ægypti sc. & Asiæ minoris; Seleucidarum & Lagidarum. Confer Dan. xj. 4. ij. 41, 42, 43. viij. 21. 22, 23. Cum vero priora illa regna non solum a Romanis devicta & occupata sint, sed & ipsum illud Romanum imperium dudum occiderit; consequens est, & ipsum Messiam dudum venille.
units.tr: We add, because of their kinship, Daniel 2:44, 45: In the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to another people; it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, but it shall stand for ever. Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, etc. The kingdom of the Messiah must necessarily be understood here, for no other is given so enduring and constant; nor can that prophecy about the stone cut out without hands be applied to anyone else. Compare Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:21, 22. Moreover, the kingdom is said to be raised up in the days of those kings, namely of Egypt and of Asia Minor, the Seleucids and the Lagids. Compare Daniel 11:4; 2:41, 42, 43; 8:21, 22, 23. But since those earlier kingdoms were not only conquered and occupied by the Romans, but that very Roman empire has long since fallen, it follows that the Messiah too has long since come.

units.la: 4. Ex quibusdam circumstantiis, ut quod nasci debuerit Bethlehemæ, in oppido Iudæ : Mich. 5. 1, 2. ex semine Abrahami, Isaaci, & Iacobi; Gen. 22. 18. tribu autem Iudæ; 49. 8, 10. & quidem ex familia Davidis; Ief. xi. 1. &c. 2 Sam. 7. 22. Psal. 132, 10, 11. cujus nomine Messias frequenter insignitur; Ierem. 30. 9. Hos. 3. 5. & alibi. Sed cum oppidum illud jampridem fuerit desolatum ac dirutum; & tota gentis Iudaicæ politia prorsus eversa, personis omnino dispersis, & distinctionibus tribuum ac familiarum penitus sublatis, evidens est Messiam jam venille; & frustra venturum à Iudæis expectari.
units.tr: 4. From certain circumstances: that he was to be born at Bethlehem, a town of Judah (Micah 5:1, 2); of the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Gen. 22:18); of the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49:8, 10), and indeed of the family of David (Isaiah 11:1; 2 Sam. 7:12; Psalm 132:10, 11), by whose name the Messiah is often designated (Jer. 30:9; Hos. 3:5, and elsewhere). But since that town has long been desolate and razed, and the whole polity of the Jewish nation utterly overthrown, its people scattered everywhere and the distinctions of tribes and families entirely abolished, it is evident that the Messiah has already come, and that the Jews wait for one who is to come in vain.

units.la: His addi possunt nonnulla ad hominem ex propriis Iudæorum sententiis, & opinionibus de Adventu Messiæ.
units.tr: Some further points may be added, argued against the Jews themselves, from their own opinions and views about the coming of the Messiah.

units.la: XLIV. Obj. 1. Elias nondum venit, qui Messiæ viam parare debuit : Mal. 4. 5. Resp. Elias dudum venit : non quidem Thisbites ille; sed alter, ejus spiritū & virtute; Johannes Baptista; Luc. 1. 17. cum Matth. xi. 14. xvij. 12.
units.tr: XLIV. Objection 1. Elijah has not yet come, who was to prepare the way for the Messiah (Mal. 4:5). Answer: Elijah has long since come; not indeed that Tishbite, but another, in his spirit and power: John the Baptist (Luke 1:17; compare Matt. 11:14 and 17:12).

units.la: Obj. 2. Hactenus mons Tzionis non est exaltatus; nec obtigit illa pax, de qua Jef. 2. 2,3,4. Resp. Locus ille allegorice de illustri Ecclesiæ statu sub N. T. accipiendus est; cujus gloria potissimum consisteret in vocatione Gentium, pace spirituali, & mystica sanctorum communione
units.tr: Objection 2. Until now the mountain of Zion has not been exalted, nor has that peace come about of which Isaiah 2:2, 3, 4 speaks. Answer: That place is to be understood allegorically, of the illustrious state of the Church under the New Testament, whose glory consists chiefly in the calling of the Gentiles, in spiritual peace and in the mystical communion of the saints.

units.la: Obj. 3. Zach. 6. 12, 15. Templum à Messiâ exstruendum dicitur; quod non factum. Ergo. Resp. Imo Templum spirituale, ex Judæis & Gentibus collectum est, & porro colligitur: 1 Petr. 2. 4. 5.
units.tr: Objection 3. Zechariah 6:12, 15 says that the Temple is to be built by the Messiah, which has not been done. Therefore, etc. Answer: On the contrary, a spiritual Temple, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, has been built and is still being built: 1 Peter 2:4, 5.

units.la: XLV. Vocationem Gentium prædixit Moses: Gen. 49. 10. istic enim adventui Schilonis adjungitur obedientia populorum. Et jam ante, ix. 27. Alliciet Deus Iapherum, ut habitet in tentoriis Schemi. Iterum Deut. 32.21. Ad zelotypiam commoveboeos, per eum qui non est populus; per gentem stultam provocaboeos. 43. Cantate Gentes, & Populus ejus! Confer Rom. 10. 19. XV. 10.
units.tr: XLV. Moses foretold the calling of the Gentiles: Genesis 49:10, for there the coming of Shiloh is joined with the obedience of the peoples. And earlier, in chapter 9:27: God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem. Again, Deuteronomy 32:21: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities; and I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation. And Psalm 117 (Vulg. 116): Praise the Lord, all ye nations. Compare Romans 10:19 and 15:10.

units.la: 2. Probatur ea ex Psalmis; ij. 8,-Donabo gentes in possessionem tuam, & fines terræ jus possessionis tuæ. lxxij. 8,-11. Dominabitur à mari uno ad alterum, & à flumine quaqua sunt fines terræ. Coram eo honorem exhibentes incurvabunt se barbari.-Omnes gentes servient ei. Adde xxij. 28. lxvij. 3,-6. &c.
units.tr: 2. This is proved from the Psalms: Psalm 2:8: I shall give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession. Psalm 72:8-11: He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. All kings shall fall down before him; all nations shall serve him. Add Psalm 22:28, Psalm 67:3-6, and so on.

units.la: 3. Ex Prophetis; Isef. 2, 2, 3,4. Erit ergo ultimis temporibus, ubi constitutus fuerit mons domus Iehovæ in vertice aliorum montium; - ut confluant ad eum omnes gentes,-dicentes; Venite, ut ascendamus in montem Iehovæ; ut doceat nos de viis suis, &c.xj. 10: Erit etiam tempore illo, ut ad eum qui è radice Isaï stabit in signum populorum, gentes consulturæ veniant, &c. Vide insuper Jerem. 7. 19,-21. Dan. 7. 13,14. Hos. 1, 10,-12. Joel. 2. 28. Confer Rom. 4. 11, 12.21. Complementum illustre habemus in orbe Christiano, si consideretur, qui olim obtinuit; Gentilismus. Hinc de Ministris Euangelii, Rom. 10. 18. in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum & ad ultima ma orbis terrarum verba eorum: juxta mandatum Servatoris, Matth. 28. 19. Ite, & docete omnes gentes, &c. Confer Col. 1:28. Rom. 4. 9,-12,16, & seqq.
units.tr: 3. From the Prophets: Isaiah 2:2, 3, 4: It shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established in the top of the mountains, and all nations shall flow unto it, saying, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, that he may teach us of his ways, etc. Isaiah 11:10: In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek, etc. See also Jeremiah 16:19-21; Daniel 7:13, 14; Hosea 1:10-12; Joel 2:28. Compare Romans 4:11, 12, 21. We have a glorious fulfilment in the Christian world, if one considers what Gentilism once held. Hence, concerning the ministers of the Gospel, Romans 10:18: Their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world, in accordance with the command of the Saviour, Matthew 28:19: Go and teach all nations, etc. Compare Colossians 1:28 and Romans 4:9-12, 16 and following.

units.la: Obj. Nondum omnes Gentiles conversi sunt; & multi à Christo defecerunt ad Muhammedismum, aliasque hæresies, errores, & schismata. Resp: Sufficit, si multi ex iis olim fuerint conversi, aut hodie etiamnum convertantur; atque ita illi adducantur, & conserventur efficaciter, qui ex Dei proposito ad istam gratiæ communionem vere pertinent.
units.tr: Objection. Not all the Gentiles have yet been converted; and many have fallen from Christ to Muhammadanism, and to other heresies, errors and schisms. Answer. It is enough if many of them have been converted in the past, or are still being converted today, and thus those are brought in and effectually preserved who, by God's purpose, truly belong to this communion of grace.

units.la: XLVI. Tertio, Permutationem œconomiæ V. T. in Oeconomiam N. magis spiritualem & gloriosam, sive abrogationem cultus cerimonialis typici V. T. & exhibitionem ipsius corporis in N. quod utique eminentiorem œconomiæ nostræ statum haud obscure indigitat, asserimus; 1. Ex diserta prophetia, Dan. 9. 24,-27. ubi cum morte Messiæ conjungitur consequens urbis Hierosolymitanæ excidium; atque adeo actualis abrogatio sacrificiorum legalium, reliquique cultus cerimonialis; cujus illa erat metropolis.
units.tr: XLVI. Thirdly, we assert that the change of the Old Testament economy into the more spiritual and glorious economy of the New, or the abrogation of the typical ceremonial worship of the Old Testament and the presentation of its body in the New, which surely points clearly to the more eminent state of our economy, is proved: 1. From the explicit prophecy in Daniel 9:24-27, where the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, as a consequence, is joined with the death of the Messiah; and thus the actual abrogation of the legal sacrifices and of the rest of the ceremonial worship, of which that city was the metropolis.

units.la: 2. Ex imperfecta ratione typica. Typis enim non potest competere ipsa virtus & efficacia rerum signatarum: ac proinde in iis non est subsistendum. Hinc ipse Christus ad Patrem suum, Psal. 40. 7,-9. Sacrificio & munere non es deleatus;-holocaustum & oblationem pro peccato non expetivisti. Tum dixi; Ecce, venio, facere voluntatem tuam, Deus mi! Sic per sacrificia, & cultum cerimonialem, qui obtinuit sub V. T. salutis nostræ negotium confici non potuit; sed veritas in Christo debuit compleri; & exhibito corpore sub N. T. umbram oportuit cessare. Confer Exod. 25. 40. cum Hebr. 8. 5.
units.tr: 2. From the imperfect nature of types. For the power and efficacy of the things signified cannot belong to the types themselves, and therefore one must not rest in them. Hence Christ himself said to his Father, Psalm 40:7-9: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. Then said I, Lo, I come, to do thy will, O my God. Thus the business of our salvation could not be accomplished through sacrifices and the ceremonial worship that held under the Old Testament; rather the truth had to be fulfilled in Christ, and with the body presented under the New Testament the shadow had to cease. Compare Exodus 25:40 with Hebrews 8:5.

units.la: 3. Ex restrictione Legis cerimonialis; ad unum populum, certam terram, & definitam metropolim: ita Circumcisio restringitur ad Abrahamum; ejusque posteros, per ætates, vel generationes suas; & quidem addita ᵃ a promissione de inhabitanda terra Canaan: Gen 17.7, 8.9. Idem quoque de Sacerdotio dicitur, Levit.7. 36. Confer xxiv. 3. Deut. 4.5,14.vj. 1.xj.31, 32. & alia. Cum igitur populus iste non posset amplius constituere distinctam politiam, & gentes etiam remotissimæ ad eandem religionis & gratiæ salutaris societatem esset adducendæ: quod sub N. T. factum; omnes certe in unam urbem, ad unum Templum, aliquoties convenire quotannis non potuerunt: atque adeo necessum est, ut cultus isti tantum populo, loco, & tempori peculiaris, cessarit.
units.tr: 3. From the restriction of the ceremonial Law to one people, one land, and one defined metropolis: so circumcision was restricted to Abraham and his posterity through their ages or generations, and indeed with the addition of the promise about inhabiting the land of Canaan: Gen. 17:7, 8, 9. The same is said of the priesthood, Lev. 7:36. Compare Lev. 24:3; Deut. 4:5, 14; 6:1; 11:31, 32, and others. Since that people could no longer maintain a distinct polity, and since even the most remote nations were to be brought into the same fellowship of religion and saving grace, which was done under the New Testament, they certainly could not all gather in one city, at one Temple, several times a year. It is therefore necessary that those rites, peculiar to one people, one place and one time, should cease.

units.la: 4. Ex conditione Novi Fœderis; Jer. 31. 31. &c. cum Hebr. 8.7, &c. ubi vero Novum promittitur, idque magis spirituale, antiquatio & abrogatio prioris indicatur. Sceptrum & Legislator istius œconomiæ tolli debuerunt: Gen. 49,10. Messias, maximus Propheta, audiri debuit: Deut. 18. 15. Psal. 2. 7, 10. Idem Sacerdos esse debuit, ordinis diversi ab Aharonico: Psal.110. 4. Per eundem assumendi Sacerdotes & Levitæ ex quacunque gente, ad Sacrificia alia spiritualia; Isef. 66. 20, 21. Confer Zach. 14. 20, 21. Mal. 1. 11. Isef. 19. 18, 19. Jerem. 3. 19. xvj. 14. Atque ita factum re ipsa: Abrogatum est sacerdotium Leviticum, & simul tota Lex cerimonialis: Hebr. 7. 12, 18, 19, 24. viij. 7, &c. ix, 9. x, 1, 9, 10, 18. Act. 15. 1,5, 10. Gal. 2.18. iv. 5. v. r.-5. Col. 2.14. Nominatim loca & tempora cerimonialiter sacra; Joh. 4. 21, 23. Rom. 14. 5, 6. Gal. 4. 10, 11. Col. 2.16, 17. Discrimen nationum, & ciborum; Act. 10, 13, 15, Rom. 14,2, 14. 17. Atque item Circumcisio; Gal. 2. 3, 4. v. 3, 4.
units.tr: 4. From the condition of the New Covenant: Jer. 31:31, etc., with Heb. 8:7, etc. Where a New Covenant is promised, and one that is more spiritual, the antiquating and abrogation of the former is thereby indicated. The sceptre and the lawgiver of that economy had to be removed: Gen. 49:10. The Messiah, the greatest Prophet, had to be heard: Deut. 18:15; Ps. 2:7, 10. He had to be a priest of an order different from Aaron's: Ps. 110:4. Through him priests and Levites were to be taken from any nation for other, spiritual sacrifices: Isa. 66:20, 21. Compare Zech. 14:20, 21; Mal. 1:11; Isa. 19:18, 19; Jer. 3:19; 16:14. And so it was done in fact: the Levitical priesthood was abrogated, and at the same time the whole ceremonial Law: Heb. 7:12, 18, 19, 24; 8:7, etc.; 9:9; 10:1, 9, 10, 18. Acts 15:1, 5, 10. Gal. 2:18; 4:5; 5:1-5. Col. 2:14. Specifically, places and times sacred in a ceremonial way: John 4:21, 23; Rom. 14:5, 6; Gal. 4:10, 11; Col. 2:16, 17. The distinction of nations and of foods: Acts 10:13, 15; Rom. 14:2, 14, 17. Likewise circumcision: Gal. 2:3, 4; 5:3, 4.

units.la: Idem dicendum de Lege Forensi Mosaica, quatenus ea isti populo in illa terra fuit præscripta, imo ipsius Legis cerimonialis quodammodo pars fuit & vinculum. Sic ergo Sceptrum, & Legislator, & Politia post adventum Messiæ tolli, alia vero conditio persectior & spiritualior succedere, debuit.
units.tr: The same must be said of the Mosaic forensic Law, insofar as it was prescribed to that people in that land; indeed, in a sense it was itself part and bond of the ceremonial Law. Thus the sceptre, the lawgiver and the polity had to be removed after the coming of the Messiah, and another, more perfect and more spiritual condition had to succeed them.

units.la: XLVII. Obj. 1. Lex Dei perfecta : Psal. 19. 8. cui nihil addendum, vel demendum : Deut. 4. 2. xij. 32. Ergò nec Cerimonialis, aut Politica, debuit abrogari. Resp. Toti S. Scripturæ perfectio sua competit integraliter, & singulis ejus partibus analogice partialiter : sed indè non sequitur, quod singula contenta omnes & singulos, ubique & semper, obligent ad observantiam. Lex enim cerimonialis & forensis, obligarunt solum ad terminum sui complementi; Moralis in perpetuum.
units.tr: XLVII. Objection 1. The Law of God is perfect: Ps. 19:8, and nothing is to be added to it or taken from it: Deut. 4:2; 12:32. Therefore neither the ceremonial nor the political law ought to have been abrogated. Reply: Perfection belongs to the whole of Scripture integrally, and to its individual parts analogically and in part. But it does not follow from this that the individual contents oblige all and each, everywhere and always, to observance. For the ceremonial and forensic laws obliged only up to the term of their fulfilment; the moral law obliges in perpetuity.

units.la: Obj. 2. Lex cerimonialis aliquoties dicitur observari debuisse יהוה, Resp. Vox illa non semper absolutam æternitatem notat; sed aliquando durationem tantum ad terminum quem communem in isto rerum genere : Exod. 21. 6. 1 Sam. 1. 22. Psal. 61. 5. Ies. 32. 14. Jerem. 5. 22. Mal. 3. 4. Unde frequenter adjungi solet limitatio. Ad generationes istius populi.
units.tr: Objection 2. The ceremonial law is said several times to have to be observed for ever [עולם]. Reply: That word does not always denote absolute eternity, but sometimes only a duration up to the term common in that kind of thing: Exod. 21:6; 1 Sam. 1:22; Ps. 61:5; Isa. 32:14; Jer. 5:22; Mal. 3:4. Hence a limitation is often added: "for the generations of this people."

units.la: Obj. 3. Ipse Jesus professus est, se non venisse ut Legem solveret, sed ut eam impleret; Matth. 5. 17. Resp. Recte : implevit Legem, tum Cerimonialem, cujus veritas & complementum in ipso fuit; tum Moralem, universam ejus obedientiam consummando, à corruptelis humanis eam vindicando, & ut perpetuam vitæ normam puritati suæ restituendo.
units.tr: Objection 3. Jesus himself professed that he had come not to dissolve the Law but to fulfil it: Matt. 5:17. Reply: Rightly so. He fulfilled the Law, both the ceremonial, whose truth and completion were in him, and the moral, by consummating its whole obedience, by vindicating it from human corruptions, and by restoring it to its purity as the perpetual rule of life.

units.la: XLVIII. Pro Praxi; 1. Summam ipsius Dei & Mediatoris nostri φιλανθρωπίαν, in hoc Fœdere gratiæ demonstratam pie agnoscamus : 1 Joh. 4. 9, 10.
units.tr: XLVIII. For practice: 1. Let us piously acknowledge the supreme philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] of God and of our Mediator, displayed in this covenant of grace: 1 John 4:9, 10.

units.la: 2. Internæ hujus Fœderis communioni serio studeamus: 1 Joh. 1. 3.
units.tr: 2. Let us earnestly strive for the inner communion of this covenant: 1 John 1:3.

units.la: 3. Euangelium, quo Fœdus istud annunciatur, maximi semper faciamus: Rom. 1. 16. x, 8, 17. 1 Cor. 2, 2.
units.tr: 3. Let us always hold the Gospel, by which this covenant is announced, in the highest esteem: Rom. 1:16; 10:8, 17; 1 Cor. 2:2.

units.la: 4. Felicitatem hujus Oeconomiæ, tum claritate, tum libertate, tum etiam amplitudine sua, præ veteri apprime commendabilem, prudenter æstimemus:
units.tr: 4. Let us wisely value the felicity of this economy, which is especially commendable compared with the old, both for its clarity, its liberty, and also its breadth.

units.la: 2 Cor. 3. 18. Gal. 5. 1, 13. 5. 5. In hac majori gratiæ intensione, quæ nunc obtinetur, ejusdemque ampliori extensione, non tantum de propria nostra salute, sed & aliorum conversione, sedulo laboremus: 2 Petr. 1. 5,-8. Phil. 2. 12. 1 Thess. 5. 11. Hebr. x. 24.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 3:18; Gal. 5:1, 13. 5. In this greater intensity of grace which now obtains, and in its wider extension, let us diligently labour not only for our own salvation but also for the conversion of others: 2 Pet. 1:5-8; Phil. 2:12; 1 Thess. 5:11; Heb. 10:24.

units.la: CAP. XII. De Christo Mediatore.
units.tr: CHAP. XII. Concerning Christ the Mediator.

units.la: משיח Χριστός. Unctio ista. Christiani. 1. Jesus. Minoritarum Jesus typicus. Iesuita. Istud nomen non prosequendum cultu adorationis. Object. solv. Neque ipsum chartæ inscriptum, haberi debet pro remedio adversus pestem, &c. Nazarenus. 2. Descriptio Jesu Christi Mediatoris. 3. Debuit esse Deus & Homo. 4. Duæ naturæ sæpius conjunctim proponuntur in SS. Literis. Natura Divina. 5. Natura humana veritas. 6. Ortus causa efficiens prima. 7. Principium ex quo; c. Anabapt. 8. Objectiones solv. 9. Sententia Socini. Corporis conformatio. 10. Maria Virgo; solv. Non vovit perpetuam virginitatem; c. Pontif. 11. Duarum naturarum unio hypostatica. 12. Unitas personæ. 13. Sententiæ Nestorianorum. Eutychianorum. Monothelectarum. 14 Objectiones solv. 15. Nulla mutatio Deitatis. Patripassiani. Non mutatio personæ τῶ Λόγῳ. In Humanitate Gratia unionis personalis. Charismata. 16. Sanctitas & impeccabilitas. Obj. solv. 17. Sapientia. Potentia. 18. In persona, Gratia muneris Mediatorii. Communicatio idiomatum in esse reali, in modo prædicandi. 19. Sententia Lutheranorum. Obj. solv. 20. Omnipræsentia non competit humanæ naturæ. Obj. solv. 21. Nec Omniscientia, aut Virtus vivificandi. Potestas remittendi peccata. Majestas, & Gloria Divina. 22. Communio apotelesmatum. 23. Officium Christi. Mediator. Etiam apud Deum pro hominibus; reconciliationem vere peragens. 24. Objectiones solv. 25. Mediator secundum utramque naturam; c. Pontif. Socin. &c. 26. Non Angelorum. Obj. solv. 27. Factus statim post lapsum. 28. Unus; c. Pontif. 29. Sponsor noster. Obj. solv. 30. Redemtor. 31. Exc. & Obj. solv. 32. Salvator, verus; perfectus; unicus. Obj. solv. 33. Unctus, Propheta. Sacerdos. Rex. Plenissime opitulatur necessitatibus nostris. Ordo istorum munerum. 34. Munus Propheticum. 35. Ejus perfectio. Fidelitas. Efficacia. Modi. 36. Munus Sacerdotale verum ac proprie dictum; c. Socin. Obj. solv. 37. Ejus typi. 38. Summus Sacerdos V. T. Melchizedek. 39. Oblatio Christi. 40. Unica; in cruce: c. Socin. Obj. solv. 41. Sententia Pontif. Crux non altare proprie. 42. Oblationis effectus. Non obtulit etiam pro seipso; c. Socin. 43. Intercessio. Hæc Christo propria. 44. Munus Regium, spirituale. Pluribus modis universale; sed cum discrimine 45. Ejus actus. 46. Istud Regnum Christo proprium. 47. Status Christi incarnandi. Incarnati. Humiliationis. 48. Nativitas. Non facto clauso utero c. Pontif. & Luther. Obj. solv. 49. Vita privata. Paupertas. Humilitas. Subjectio ad Legem Dei. Circumcisio. Præsentatio coram Domino. 50. Vita publica. Ejus initiatio. Non raptus in cœlum: c. Socin. Obj. solv. 51. Peractio. Paupertas. Non Mendicitas: c. Pontif. Conclufio. 52. Mors. Actus. 53. Inchoatio mortis spiritualis. Moderatio. Inchoatio mortis corporalis. Mitigatio. 54. Consummatio mortis spiritualis. Descensus ad inferos. Christus vere passus in anima rationali: c. Pontif. 55. Consummatio mortis corporalis. Sepultura. 56. Non descendit proprie ad limbum infernalem; c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 57. Fines humiliationis istius. 58. Status Exaltationis. 59. Resurrectio. Ejus actus duplex. Praedicta. Facta virtute Divina: etiam ipsius Christi. Fines ejus. Quomodo comprobata. 60. Ascensio in Caelum. Subjectum. Termini. Modus. Tempus. Praedicta. Causa efficiens. Fines. 61. Ratio ordinis. Testes. 62. Non omnipraesentia Christi secundum humanam naturam; c. Luther. nec multipraesentia; c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 63. Sessio ad dextram Dei. 64. Causa ejus efficiens. Fines. 65. Male Lutherani inde colligunt ubiquitatem Christi secundum humanam naturam. Et Socin. Christum per eam factum esse Filium Dei, &c. 66. Jesus Christus est verus Messias: c. Jud. Obj. solv. 67. Praxis. 68.
units.tr: Messiah [משיח], Christ [Χριστός]. That anointing. Christians. 1. Jesus. The Minorites' typical Jesus. Jesuit. This name is not to be given the worship of adoration. Objection, answered. Nor should the name, written on paper, be regarded as a remedy against plague, etc. Nazarene. 2. Description of Jesus Christ the Mediator. 3. He had to be God and Man. 4. The two natures are often set forth together in the Holy Scriptures. The divine nature. 5. The true human nature. 6. Origin: the efficient cause, first. 7. The principle from which; against the Anabaptists. 8. Objections, answered. 9. The opinion of Socinus. The bodily formation. 10. The Virgin Mary; answered. He did not vow perpetual virginity; against the Papists. 11. The hypostatic union of the two natures. 12. The unity of the person. 13. The opinions of the Nestorians, Eutychians and Monothelites. 14. Objections, answered. 15. No change in the Deity. The Patripassians. No change of person in the Word. In the humanity, the grace of the personal union. Gifts. 16. Holiness and impeccability. Objection, answered. 17. Wisdom. Power. 18. In the person, the grace of the mediatorial office. Communication of attributes in real being, in the mode of predication. 19. The opinion of the Lutherans. Objection, answered. 20. Omnipresence does not belong to the human nature. Objection, answered. 21. Nor omniscience, or the power of giving life. The power of forgiving sins. The majesty and divine glory. 22. The communion of the saving acts. 23. The office of Christ. Mediator. Also before God on behalf of men; truly effecting reconciliation. 24. Objections, answered. 25. Mediator according to both natures; against the Papists, Socinians, etc. 26. Not of angels. Objection, answered. 27. Made immediately after the fall. 28. One; against the Papists. 29. Our surety. Objection, answered. 30. Redeemer. 31. Exceptions and objection, answered. 32. Saviour: true, perfect, unique. Objection, answered. 33. Anointed, Prophet, Priest, King. He most fully helps our needs. The order of these offices. 34. The prophetic office. 35. Its perfection. Faithfulness. Efficacy. Manner. 36. The priestly office, true and properly so called; against the Socinians. Objection, answered. 37. Its types. 38. The high priest of the Old Testament: Melchizedek. 39. The offering of Christ. 40. Unique; on the cross; against the Socinians. Objection, answered. 41. The opinion of the Papists. The cross is not properly an altar. 42. The effect of the offering. He did not offer also for himself; against the Socinians. 43. Intercession. This belongs to Christ alone. 44. The kingly office, spiritual. Universal in several ways, but with a distinction. 45. Its acts. 46. This kingdom belongs properly to Christ. 47. The state of Christ's incarnation. Incarnate. Of humiliation. 48. Nativity. Not with the womb closed; against the Papists and Luther. Objection, answered. 49. Private life. Poverty. Humility. Subjection to the law of God. Circumcision. Presentation before the Lord. 50. Public life. Its beginning. Not a rapture into heaven; against the Socinians. Objection, answered. 51. Its completion. Poverty. Not begging; against the Papists. Conclusion. 52. Death. Its acts. 53. The beginning of spiritual death. Moderation. The beginning of bodily death. Mitigation. 54. The completion of spiritual death. The descent into hell. Christ truly suffered in the rational soul; against the Papists. 55. The completion of bodily death. Burial. 56. He did not properly descend to the infernal limbo; against the Papists. Objection, answered. 57. The ends of this humiliation. 58. The state of exaltation. 59. Resurrection. Its acts are twofold. Foretold. Accomplished by divine power, even by Christ himself. Its ends. How it is attested. 60. Ascension into heaven. Subject. Termini. Manner. Time. Foretold. Efficient cause. Ends. 61. The reason of the order. Witnesses. 62. Christ is not omnipresent according to the human nature; against the Lutherans; nor multipresent; against the Papists. Objection, answered. 63. Sitting at the right hand of God. 64. Its efficient cause. Ends. 65. The Lutherans wrongly infer from this the ubiquity of Christ according to the human nature. And Socinus, that Christ became the Son of God through it, etc. 66. Jesus Christ is the true Messiah; against the Jews. Objection, answered. 67. Practice. 68.

units.la: I. MEDIATOR Foederis Evangelici Hebraice frequenter מָשִׁיחַ appellatur; h. e. Unctus: à rad. מָשַׁח, utpote peculiari quadam ratione præ consortibus suis unctus; Psal. 45. 8. & à Patre suo, ad negotium salutis nobis impetrandæ & applicandæ unicè designatus. Act. 4. 12. Cæteroquin nomen illud laxiore significatu aliis etiam commune est: ut 1 Sam. 24. 7. 2, 1, 21. Psal. 105. 15. In N. T. Μεσσίας dicitur; quod Græcè redditur nomine idem significante, Χριστὸς, à verbo χρίω, Ungo; Joh. 1. 41. 4, IV, 25.
units.tr: I. The Mediator of the Gospel covenant is frequently called in Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ [Messiah], that is, Anointed, from the root מָשַׁח, since he was anointed in a peculiar way above his companions; Psal. 45. 8. He was uniquely appointed by his Father for the work of obtaining and applying our salvation. Acts 4. 12. Otherwise that name in a looser sense is also common to others, as 1 Sam. 24. 7; 2. 1, 21; Psal. 105. 15. In the New Testament he is called Μεσσίας [Messias], which is rendered in Greek by the name with the same meaning, Χριστὸς [Christ], from the verb χρίω, I anoint; John 1. 41; 4. 25.

units.la: De Unctione illa vide specialius Jes. 61. 1. Psal. 2. 6. Act. 4. 27. quæ cum in omnia & singula ejusdem Corporis mystici membra à Capite quodammodo dimanet, juxta locum 1 Joh. 2. 27 Unctio, quam vos accepistis ab Eo, manet in vobis, &c. nihil mirum ab ista unione, & spirituali christianatis communione cum Christo, fideles denominari Christianos; qui titulus Antiochiæ primum usurpatus: Act. xi. 26. & deinceps alibi quoque frequentatus; xxvj, 28. 1 Petr. 4. 15, 16. ad nos tandem pari ratione traductus est.
units.tr: On that anointing see more fully Isa. 61. 1; Psal. 2. 6; Acts 4. 27. Since it flows in some way from the Head into each and every member of the same mystical body, according to the passage 1 John 2. 27, "The anointing which you have received from him abides in you," etc., it is no wonder that the faithful are called Christians from this union and spiritual fellowship with Christ. This title was first used at Antioch, Acts 11. 26, and afterwards was used elsewhere too, Acts 26. 28; 1 Pet. 4. 15, 16. It was at last handed down to us by the same reasoning.

units.la: II. Nomen proprium, ab ipso Deo per Angelum ei impositum, est Ἰησοῦς, Jesus, à rad. יְשַׁע quod in Hiph. הוֹשִׁיעַ, Salvum fecit, Liberavit. Atque hinc Matth. 1. 21. Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum: Ipse enim liberabit populum suum ex peccatis ipsius. Sic Jesus idem valet, quod Servator.
units.tr: II. The proper name, given to him by God himself through the angel, is Ἰησοῦς [Jesus], from the root יְשַׁע, which in the Hiphil is הוֹשִׁיעַ [hoshia], "he saved, he delivered." Hence Matt. 1. 21: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Thus Jesus means the same as Saviour.

units.la: Ac proinde non nisi blasphemè inter Pontificios, Minoritæ, Franciscum suum Jesum typicum appellant; quemadmodum & Loyolitæ sectam suam vocant Societatem Jesu, & Jesuitas: plures enim Servatores, aut Servatoris socios, Scriptura prorsus ignorat; quin imo Servator de se, Jes. 63. 3. Torcular calcavi solus; nam ex populis nullus vir mecum. & verf. 5. Quum intuerer, nullum esse adjutorem, &c.
units.tr: Therefore it is only blasphemously that the Minorites among the Papists call their Francis a typical Jesus; just as the Loyolites call their sect the Society of Jesus, and themselves Jesuits. For Scripture altogether knows of no several saviours or companions of the Saviour; rather the Saviour says of himself, Isa. 63. 3: "I have trodden the winepress alone; of the peoples there was no man with me," and verse 5: "I looked, and there was no helper," etc.

units.la: Perperam eidem Nomini tribuitur singularis quædam sanctitas; cujus gratia ipsum auditû perceptum, identidem cultu adorationis esset prosequendum: cultus ille non nisi personæ debetur. Nomen autem signis accensendum est. Neque itud nomen dicendum magis sanctum, quam יהוה, aliave similia.
units.tr: A certain singular holiness is wrongly ascribed to this name, on account of which, whenever it is heard, it should be given the worship of adoration. That worship is due to the person alone. The name, moreover, is to be counted among signs. Nor is that name to be called more holy than יהוה [Jehovah], or other similar names.

units.la: Obj. Phil. 2. 10. Ut in nomine Jesu omne genu se flectat, &c. Resp. Id metonymicè de personâ intelligendum; ut Act. 4. 12.
units.tr: Objection: Phil. 2. 10: "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow," etc. Answer: this is to be understood metonymically of the person, as in Acts 4. 12.

units.la: Nec minus absurde nomen Jesu chartæ inscriptum, vel insuper additis nominibus Mariæ & Annæ, ex collo suspenditur, aut valvis affigitur, &c. tanquam pro-
units.tr: Equally absurdly, the name of Jesus is written on paper, or, with the names of Mary and Anne added besides, is hung from the neck or fixed to doors, etc., as if it were

units.la: 110-0 / 0-0110-0 prophylacticon adversus pestem, aliave mala, &c.
units.tr: 110-0 / 0-0110-0 a prophylactic against plague or other evils, etc.

units.la: Nomini Iesu frequenter additur agnomen Nazareni: Marc. x. 47. Luc. 18. 37. & alibi: de cujus origine vide Matth. 2. 21,-23. cum Isf. xi,. 1.
units.tr: The name Jesus is frequently joined with the surname Nazarene: Mark 10. 47; Luke 18. 37, and elsewhere. For its origin see Matt. 2. 21–23 together with Isa. 11. 1.

units.la: III. Iesus Christus Mediator est secunda Essentiae Divinae Persona, quae Naturam vere humanam ex substantia Virginis Mariae, quantum ad Corpus attinet, in plenitudine temporis assumsit, eamque sibi univit hypostatice; ad opus redemtionis & salutis nostrae peragendum. Joh. 1. 14. Sermo ille factus est caro. 1 Tim. iij. 16 Deus conspicuus factus est in carne. Gal. 4. 4, 5. Postquam venit plenum tempus, emisit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum Legi subjectum; ut eos, qui Legi subjecti erant, redimeret.
units.tr: III. Jesus Christ the Mediator is the second Person of the Divine Essence, who, in the fullness of time, assumed a truly human nature, as regards the body, from the substance of the Virgin Mary, and united it to himself hypostatically, to accomplish the work of our redemption and salvation. John 1. 14: The Word was made flesh. 1 Tim. 3. 16: God was manifested in the flesh. Gal. 4. 4, 5. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law.

units.la: IV. Mediator noster omnino Θεάνθρωπος esse debuit, h. e. Deus & Homo in una Persona; ut esset verus ille Immanuel, Isf. 7. 14. & utriusque naturae, tum Divinae, tum humanae particeps, quae apud Deum & Homines erant peragenda, vere expediret. Hebr. 5. 1. 1 Tim. 2. 5,6.
units.tr: IV. Our Mediator had altogether to be God-man, that is, God and Man in one Person, so that he might be that true Immanuel, Isa. 7. 14, and so that, being a partaker of both natures, divine and human, he might truly fit the things which were to be done before God and before men. Heb. 5. 1; 1 Tim. 2. 5, 6.

units.la: Homo ut esset, requirebat ipsa Dei Justitia; quae peccatum punire noluit, nisi in ea natura quae peccasset: Gen. 2. 17. Redemtor igitur, & Vindex noster suturus, nobis conjunctissimus, & quidem per omnia similis, fieri debuit: Hebr. 2. 14. 17. excepto tamen peccato: iv, 15. Nam cum ipse peccator ne quidem pro se posset satisfacere; Psal. 130. 3. nedum pro aliis; xlix, 8. consequens est, ut Vas, & Sponsor noster factus; & ipsemet Legi subjectus, sanctus esset ac justus: Hebr. 7. 26, 27. ut nos ab execratione Legis redimeret: Gal. 3. 13. atque omnem obedientiam Legi debitam, ad jota & apicem unum, praestaret: Matth. 5. 17. iij. 15. Sic ille pro peccatis pati debuit, justus pro injustis, &c. 1 Petr. 3. 18. Rom. 5. 19. viij. 3, 4. 2 Cor. 5. 21. Hinc Filius Dei non Angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahae: Hebr. 2. 16. ut & Is qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sint omnes: verf. 11. Deus ut esset, requirebat, tum salutis Impetratio, tum ejusdem Applicatio. Impetratio quidem: Nam infiniti valoris satisfactio pro reatu praestanda. Sacerdotem, Sacrificium, & Intercessionem immensae dignitatis ac meriti postulabat: neque enim aliter infinitae Majestatis offensa poterat expiari, quam ejus sanguine, qui esset infinitus: Act. 20. 28. non aliter ira Patris placari, quàm ejus reconciliatione, qui esset Filius dilectissimus: Rom. 5. 10. non aliter potestas Satanae & mortis aboleri, quàm ab eo, qui omnibus Diabolis potentior, mortis potestatem & imperium vere haberet: Hebr. 2. 15. cum Apoc. 1, 18.
units.tr: Man, so that he might be, was required by God's own justice, which was unwilling to punish sin except in the nature that had sinned: Gen. 2. 17. Our Redeemer and Avenger, therefore, who was to come, had to be most closely joined to us and indeed made like us in all things: Heb. 2. 14, 17, except sin: Heb. 4. 15. For since the sinner himself could not make satisfaction even for himself, Ps. 130. 3, much less for others, Ps. 49. 8, it follows that he who became our surety and sponsor, and himself subject to the Law, had to be holy and just: Heb. 7. 26, 27, so that he might redeem us from the curse of the Law: Gal. 3. 13, and render to the Law every obedience due to it, down to the last jot and tittle: Matt. 5. 17; 3. 15. Thus he had to suffer for sins, the just for the unjust, etc.: 1 Pet. 3. 18; Rom. 5. 19; 8. 3, 4; 2 Cor. 5. 21. Hence the Son of God took up not angels but the seed of Abraham: Heb. 2. 16, so that both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one: ver. 11. God, so that he might be, was required both for the obtaining of salvation and for its application. For obtaining it indeed: for a satisfaction of infinite value had to be rendered for the guilt. It demanded a priest, a sacrifice and an intercession of immense dignity and merit; for the offence against infinite Majesty could not be expiated in any other way than by the blood of one who was infinite: Acts 20. 28. The wrath of the Father could not be appeased in any other way than by the reconciliation of one who was his most beloved Son: Rom. 5. 10. The power of Satan and of death could not be abolished in any other way than by him who, being more powerful than all the devils, truly had the power and rule of death: Heb. 2. 15; with Rev. 1. 18.

units.la: Atque item Applicatio: Nam & illa potentiam requirebat infinitam; cum non alius nos efficaciter ad imaginem Dei potuerit restaurare, nisi qui esset imago Dei invisibilis: Col. 1. 15. non alius nos Dei filios facere, nisi qui esset Filius Dei naturalis: Hebr. 1. 3. non alius justitiam nobis donare, nisi qui esset Jehovah justitia nostra: Jerem. 23. 6. non alius Spiritum conferre, nisi is à quo Ille procedit: Joh. 15. 26. nec alius vitam aeternam nobis dare, nisi qui esset ipsa vita: Joh. 14. 6.
units.tr: So too for application: for that also required infinite power, since no one else could effectively restore us to the image of God, except one who was the invisible image of God: Col. 1. 15; no one else could make us sons of God, except one who was the natural Son of God: Heb. 1. 3; no one else could give us righteousness, except one who was Jehovah our righteousness: Jer. 23. 6; no one else could confer the Spirit, except him from whom the Spirit proceeds: John 15. 26; and no one else could give us eternal life, except one who was life itself: John 14. 6.

units.la: V. Hinc etiam duae istae Naturae toties conjunctim proponuntur: ut Jes. 9. 5. - Puer natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis; - cujus nomen - Deus fortis robustissimus, Pater aeternitatis, &c. Mich. 5. 1. Tu, Bethlehem Ephratae, - ex te Mihi prodibit, futurus dominator in Israele; cujus exortus inde à principio, à diebus saeculi sunt. Joh. 1. 14. Sermo ille factus est Caro; et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam ut Unigeniti à Patre. Rom. 1. 3, 4. De Filio suo facto ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, declarato Filio Dei potenter, - ix. 5. - Ex quibus est Christus, quod ad carnem attinet; qui est supra omnes Deus benedictus in saecula. Adde Act. 20. 28. 1 Tim. 3. 16. Tit. 2. 13, 14. Hebr. 1, 3. ix. 14.
units.tr: V. Hence also these two natures are so often set forth together: as in Isa. 9. 5, "A child is born to us, a son is given to us," and "whose name is the mighty God, the everlasting Father," etc.; Mic. 5. 1, "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from ancient days"; John 1. 14, "The Word became flesh, and we beheld his glory, the glory of the only begotten from the Father"; Rom. 1. 3, 4, "concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and was declared to be the Son of God in power"; 9. 5, "Of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever." Add Acts 20. 28; 1 Tim. 3. 16; Titus 2. 13, 14; Heb. 1. 3; 9. 14.

units.la: Sed distinctè considerandæ veniunt Duæ illæ naturæ, & earum Unio hypostatica. Prior natura est Divina, re ipsa quidem communis tribus Personis; at hic spectanda prout subsistit secundâ personalitate, τῷ Λόγῳ. De ea autem egimus, quantum satis est; cap. 5. th. 11,16. Altera est Natura humana; cujus tum veritatem, tum ortum exponemus.
units.tr: But the two natures, and their hypostatic union, must be considered distinctly. The first nature is the divine, which in reality is common to the three Persons; but here it is to be viewed as it subsists in the second personality, the Word. We have treated of it sufficiently in chapter 5, theses 11 and 16. The other is the human nature; we shall set out both its truth and its origin.

units.la: VI. Veritatem Scriptura docet; Hominem appellando; Joh. 8. 40. Rom. 5. 15. 1 Tim. 2. 5. Item Virum; Act. 17. 31. Jes. 53. 3. & Filium hominis; Matth. 8. 20. 9. 6. & passim. Unde etiam alter Adamus dicitur; 1 Cor. 15. 45. Quin imo partes Hominis essentiales, Animam & Corpus, cum suis Affectionibus, ei tribuendo.
units.tr: VI. Scripture teaches the truth of it, by calling him man: John 8. 40; Rom. 5. 15; 1 Tim. 2. 5. Likewise a man: Acts 17. 31; Isa. 53. 3; and the Son of man: Matt. 8. 20; 9. 6, and often elsewhere. Whence he is also called the second Adam: 1 Cor. 15. 45. Indeed, the essential parts of man, soul and body, together with their affections, are ascribed to him.

units.la: Anima ipsi tribuitur, Jes. 53. 10, 11. Matth. 26; 38. ejusque facultates, Intellectus; Luc. 2. 51. Marc. 13, 32. & voluntas; Matth. 26, 39. Ac porro Affectus, ut Gaudium; Luc. x, 21. Tristitia; Matth. 26, 38. Luc. 19, 41. Metus; Hebr. 5, 7. Ira; Marc. 3. 5. & cæteræ infirmitates istiusmodi miserabiles (non culpabiles), quas ipsemet in vita humili subinde expertus est; Hebr. 4. 14. Consequenter Anima humana de Christo non est neganda; nec ipsa Deitas cum Apollinaristis loco animæ substituenda.
units.tr: A soul is attributed to him: Isa. 53. 10, 11; Matt. 26. 38; and its faculties, the understanding: Luke 2. 51; Mark 13. 32, and the will: Matt. 26. 39. Further, the affections, such as joy: Luke 10. 21; sorrow: Matt. 26. 38; Luke 19. 41; fear: Heb. 5. 7; anger: Mark 3. 5; and the other such miserable (though not blameworthy) infirmities, which he himself from time to time experienced in his humble life: Heb. 4. 14. Consequently a human soul is not to be denied of Christ, nor is the Deity itself to be substituted in place of the soul, as the Apollinarians did.

units.la: Corpus ei quoque adscribitur; Hebr. x, 5, 10. 1 Petr. 2. 24. & in institutione Cœnæ; Luc. 22, 19. & Caro; Joh. 6. 51. Atque etiam proprietates Corporis: ut sunt Localitas, Visibilitas, Finitudo; Luc. 2, 7. Marc. 16,6. Palpabilitas: Luc. 24, 39. & similes aliæ. Nec non infirmitates Corporis: Videl. Somnus; Matth. 8. 24. Fames; 4, 2. Fatigatio & Sitis; Iob. 4. 6, 7. Rejiciendus igitur Marcionitarum & Manichæorum error, qui veritatem Corporis Christi negarunt; & ejus carnem, passionis omnis experrem, dixerunt.
units.tr: A body is also ascribed to him: Heb. 10. 5, 10; 1 Pet. 2. 24; and in the institution of the Lord's Supper: Luke 22. 19; and flesh: John 6. 51. Likewise the properties of a body: such as location, visibility, finitude: Luke 2. 7; Mark 16. 6; palpability: Luke 24. 39; and other similar things. Nor the infirmities of the body: namely sleep: Matt. 8. 24; hunger: Matt. 4. 2; weariness and thirst: John 4. 6, 7. Therefore the error of the Marcionites and Manichaeans, who denied the truth of Christ's body and said that his flesh was free of every experience of suffering, is to be rejected.

units.la: VII. Ad Ortum humanæ istius naturæ quod attinet;
units.tr: VII. As far as the origin of this human nature is concerned;

units.la: net; ejus Causa efficiens prima est Deus triunus: Act. 13. 32. -Deus excitavit Israeli Servatorem Iesum. Confer Gal. 4. 4. Hebr. x, 5. Item Phil. 2. 7. Ipse se inanivit forma servi accepta, &c. Et Luc. 1, 35.-Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te.--Matth. 1. 20. Salvo interim cuique Personae suo ordine operandi, & Filio terminatione istius humanitatis per suam hypostasin. Proxime tamen efficientia ista tribuenda est Sp. Sancto; qui portionem aliquam ex substantia Virginis, ad generationem apta, seperavit; & eminentissimâ suâ virtute supplens defectum Viri, Corpusculum humanum inde formavit, animam rationalem ei increavit, eodemque hoc momento totum illud humanae naturae efficienter univit cum Persona Λόγος, & à prima sua origine sanctificavit.
units.tr: its efficient cause, first of all, is the triune God: Acts 13:32, "God raised up for Israel a Saviour, Jesus." Compare Gal. 4:4; Heb. 10:5; likewise Phil. 2:7, "He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," etc. And Luke 1:35, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you." Matt. 1:20. Meanwhile each Person keeps his own order of working, and the Son terminates this humanity in his own hypostasis. Nevertheless, this efficiency is to be attributed most immediately to the Holy Spirit, who separated some portion of the substance of the Virgin, fit for generation, and, supplying by his most eminent power the lack of a man, formed from it a small human body, created a rational soul for it, and at that very moment efficiently united that whole human nature with the Person of the Word, and sanctified it from its first origin.

units.la: VIII. Principium ex quo unicum, & simul Causa ef- ficiens secunda sui ordinis, fuit foecunda substantia Vir- ginis Mariae.
units.tr: VIII. The principle from which, as the sole and at the same time secondary efficient cause in its order, came the fruitful substance of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: Haec erat ex tribu Judae, Hebr. 7. 14. Matth. 1. 1, 2, -15. Luc. 3. 23, -38. Istud autem contra Valentinianos, Apollinaristas, eorumque sequaces Anabaptistas, probe observandum: qui contendunt, Servatorem non ex ipsa substantia Virginis Mariae carnem assumsisse; sed eam coelitus adduxisse ex substantia ipsius Dei, vel Sp. S. modo aliquo inexplicabili factam, aut originis incertae; sic in uterum Virginis immissam & suo tempore in lucem editam. Nos catholicam veritatem asserimus:
units.tr: She was of the tribe of Judah, Heb. 7:14; Matt. 1:1, 2, 15; Luc. 3:23, 38. This, however, is to be carefully observed against the Valentinians, the Apollinarians, and their followers the Anabaptists, who contend that the Saviour did not assume flesh from the very substance of the Virgin Mary, but brought it down from heaven, from the substance of God himself or of the Holy Spirit, made in some inexplicable manner or of uncertain origin, and so sent into the womb of the Virgin and in due time brought forth into the light. We assert the Catholic truth:

units.la: 1. Quia diserte appellatur Semen mulieris; Gen. 3, 15. cum Hebr. 2. 14. Semen Abrahami: 22, 18. cum Gal. 3. 16. ex Semine Davidis: Rom. 1. 3. Act. 13. 33. Nec est quod Adversarii excipiant, foeminas semen non habere; cum & Scriptura, Hebr. xi, 11. Levit. 12. 2. & natura, contrarium doceant.
units.tr: 1. Because he is expressly called the Seed of the woman, Gen. 3:15; compare Heb. 2:14; the Seed of Abraham, Gen. 22:18; compare Gal. 3:16; of the Seed of David, Rom. 1:3; Acts 13:33. Nor is it an objection that the adversaries raise, that women have no seed, since both Scripture, Heb. 11:11, and Leviticus 12:2, and nature teach the contrary.

units.la: 2. Ex phrasibus aequipollentibus; ut quod dicatur Fructus ventris Mariae; Luc. 1. 42. Fructus lumborum Davidis; Act. 2, 30. juxta promissionem 2 Sam. 7. 12. 1 Chron. 17. 11. Atque huc spectant termini Generationis, Conceptionis, Impregnationis, Partus, & similes; Matth. 1, 16, 18, 20, 23. & alibi
units.tr: 2. From equivalent phrases: such as that he is called the Fruit of Mary's womb, Luke 1:42; the Fruit of David's loins, Acts 2:30, according to the promise of 2 Sam. 7:12 and 1 Chron. 17:11. To this point also belong the terms generation, conception, impregnation, birth, and similar ones: Matt. 1:16, 18, 20, 23, and elsewhere.

units.la: 3. Ex appellatione Filii: sic κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocatur Filius hominis sup. th. 6. specialius autem Filius Mariae. Marc. 6. 3. & Maria vicissim, Mater Jesu; Matth. 1. 18. Luc. 1. 43. Joh. 19, 25.
units.tr: 3. From the appellation of Son: thus he is called, pre-eminently, the Son of Man, see above, thesis 6; more specifically, the Son of Mary, Mark 6:3; and Mary in turn, the Mother of Jesus, Matt. 1:18; Luke 1:43; John 19:25.

units.la: 4. Ex Genealogiis, Matth. 1. 1,-15. Luc. 3, 23,quarum verus finis est, ortum humanae naturae Christi demonstrare.
units.tr: 4. From the genealogies, Matt. 1:1–15; Luke 3:23–38, whose true purpose is to demonstrate the origin of Christ's human nature.

units.la: IX. Obj. 1. Servator noster dicitur Conceptus ex Spir. S. Ergo. Resp. Praepositio Ex non semper notat causam materialem; sed quandoque efficientem: Rom. xi. 36. 1 Cor. 1, 30. ut & hoc loco.
units.tr: IX. Objection 1. Our Saviour is said to be conceived of the Holy Spirit. Therefore... Reply: the preposition "of" (ex) does not always denote the material cause; sometimes it denotes the efficient cause: Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 1:30; and so also in this place.

units.la: Obj. 2. Joh. 6. 33; 51. Panis ille Dei is est, qui de caelo descendit, & dat vitam mundo, --. Ego sum panis ille verus, qui de caelo descendi. Panis autem, quem ego dabo, caro mea est: Ergo caro localiter e caelo descendit. Similia sunt Eph. 4. 9, 10. Joh. 3, 13. Resp. Ista. Joh. 6. 33, 51. dicuntur quod persona λόγος e caelo descenderit Θεοπρεπῶς, & in carne manifestata sit; ad vitam spiritualem electis suis impetrandam, eamque instar mannae caelestis efficienter confervandam.
units.tr: Objection 2. John 6:33, 51: "That is the bread of God, which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world," ... "I am that living bread which came down from heaven. And the bread that I will give is my flesh." Therefore his flesh came down locally from heaven. Similar are Eph. 4:9, 10 and John 3:13. Reply: these passages from John 6:33, 51 are said because the Person of the Word came down from heaven θεοπρεπῶς [in a manner befitting God], and was manifested in the flesh, to obtain spiritual life for his elect, and to sustain it efficiently, in the manner of the heavenly manna.

units.la: 2. Sic etiam de Persona Θεοπρεπῶς intelligi debet Descensus ille in infimas partes terrae, unde postmodum ascendit longe supra omnes caelos, Eph. 4. 9, 10. Atque item 3. locus Joh. 3, 13. nisi quod Ascensus istic metaphorice ad mentem, seu ad intellectum, referendus sit; quo Filius non terrena solum, sed & caelestia intime novit.
units.tr: 2. In the same way the descent into the lower parts of the earth, from which he afterwards ascended far above all the heavens, Eph. 4:9, 10, must also be understood of the Person θεοπρεπῶς. And likewise the third passage, John 3:13, except that the ascent there is to be referred metaphorically to the mind, or to the understanding, by which the Son knows intimately not only earthly but also heavenly things.

units.la: Obj. 1. 1 Cor. 15, 47. Primus homo e terra pulvereus: secundus homo, ipse Dominus e caelo, &c. Resp. Et ibi de Persona agitur, beatae resurrectionis principio; eiusque gloriosa virtus & potestas caelestis denotatur secundum communicationem idiomatum.
units.tr: Objection 1. 1 Cor. 15:47: "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven," etc. Reply: here too the Person is in view, as the origin of the blessed resurrection; and his glorious virtue and heavenly power are denoted according to the communication of idioms.

units.la: Obj. 4. Joh. 3. 6. Quod genitum est ex carne, caro est, scil.
units.tr: Objection 4. John 3:6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh," namely...

units.la: Cap. XII.
units.tr: Chapter XII.

units.la: peccaminosa. Consequenter Christus, si ex substantia Mariæ carnem suam accepisset, eidem corruptioni foret obnoxius. Sed hoc absurdum est. Ergo. Resp. Participatio illa corruptionis ad Christum extendi non debet. Vide sup. cap. 10. th. 27.
units.tr: sinful. Consequently, if Christ had received his flesh from the substance of Mary, he would be subject to the same corruption. But this is absurd. Therefore... Reply: That sharing in corruption must not be extended to Christ. See above, chapter 10, thesis 27.

units.la: X. Affinis est sententia Socini, admittentis quidem Christum hominem ex ipsa Dei substantia non esse genitum; imo ex substantia Matris non minus accepisse, quàm alii ex suis matribus accipiant: sed insuper comminiscentis, virtutem Dei in uterum Virginis substantiam aliquam creatam immisisse, aut ibi creasse; ex qua Christus, juncto eo quod ex Virginis substantia accepit, verus Homo generatus sit. Adeo quidem ut Christus qua Homo, non Matrem tantum habuerit, nempe Virginem Mariam, sed Patrem quoque, videl. Deum. At vero cum conceptus iste non sit Scripturarius, sed absurde confictus operosa refutatione non indiget: neque enim Deum patrem Christi, qua hominis, proprie dicendum, vel ex eo planum est, quod pater ita dici soleat à generatione activa, per quam alia persona ejusdem naturæ generatur. Sed humanitas Christi, natura a Deo diversissima est.
units.tr: X. The opinion of Socinus is related to this. He admits that Christ as man was not begotten from the very substance of God; indeed he received from his mother's substance no less than others receive from their mothers. But he further invents that the power of God introduced into the Virgin's womb some created substance, or created it there, from which Christ, joined with what he received from the Virgin's substance, was generated as a true man. So that Christ, as man, had not only a mother, namely the Virgin Mary, but also a father, namely God. But since this conception is not scriptural, but absurdly fabricated, it does not need a laborious refutation. For it is plain that God cannot properly be called the Father of Christ as man, since "father" is usually said of active generation, by which one person of the same nature is begotten by another. But the humanity of Christ is of a nature most diverse from God.

units.la: De Corpore Christi multi contendunt, illud prorsus unico momento paratum & conformatum fuisse, quamvis postea successive perductum ad perfectam quantitatem. 1. Quia virtus agentis fuerit infinita. 2. nec Filius Dei assumserit aliquod imperfectum & inanimatum. 3. & Corpus Christi fuerit assumtum mediante anima.
units.tr: Many contend about the body of Christ that it was prepared and formed in a single moment, although afterwards it was brought gradually to full size. (1) Because the power of the agent was infinite. (2) Nor did the Son of God assume something imperfect and inanimate. (3) And because the body of Christ was assumed through the mediation of a soul.

units.la: Verum rationes istæ non evincunt, nullas præparationes ac dispositiones in substantia illa præcessisse: nam 1. ex infinita virtute agentis, recte quidem colligitur, quid potuerit; non quid voluerit, Deus. 2. Ipsa generatio formaliter facta est in momento: ex materia satis præparata formatum est corpusculum humanum, eodemque momento anima rationalis creata, & ei indita; simulque humana ista natura sustentata ac terminata hypostasi ℨ Λόγῳ; atque adeo Filius Dei non assumsit aliquid imperfectum, aut inanimatum, sed animatum eodem illo momento, ac perfectum essentialiter & integraliter in genere & pro conditione humanæ naturæ jam nunc genitæ.
units.tr: But these reasons do not prove that no preparations and dispositions preceded in that substance. For (1) from the infinite power of the agent one rightly infers what God could do, not what God willed to do. (2) The generation itself was formally accomplished in a moment: from matter sufficiently prepared the little human body was formed, and in the same moment a rational soul was created and infused into it; and at the same time this human nature was sustained and terminated by the hypostasis of the Word. And so the Son of God did not assume something imperfect or inanimate, but something animated in that very moment, and perfect in essence and integrity, according to the condition of human nature already begotten. (3) Just as the due time of gestation followed the formation, so I do not see why it should be denied that a due time also preceded, in which the generative matter was nourished and prepared for the due formation of the foetus.

units.la: 3. Quemadmodum ergo justum Gestationis tempus post Conformationem subsecutum est, ita non video, cur negandum sit, justum etiam tempus præcessisse, quo materia genitalis foveretur, ac præpararetur, ad justam fœtus conformationem.
units.tr: XI. The Virgin conceived and afterwards bore a son, according to the prophecy of Isaiah 7:14, whose fulfilment is indicated in Matthew 1:18 and Luke 1:27, 31, 34, 35. Thus she was a virgin before the birth, and also in the birth; nor is it likely that the vessel, once impregnated by the Holy Spirit, was afterwards known carnally by a man.

units.la: XI. Virgo autem concepit, ac deinceps peperit; juxta prophetiam, Jes. 7. 14. cujus complementum indicatur Matth. 1. 18,-. Luc. 1. 27, 31, 34, 35. Sic illa ante partum, atque etiam in partu, Virgo fuit: nec verisimile est, vas illud a Sp. Sancto semel impraegnatum, ab homine postea fuisse cognitum carnaliter.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matthew 1:18: "Before they came together," etc. Reply: The word "come together" can conveniently be understood not of the use of marriage, but of living together, or of the bringing of the Virgin into the house. See verses 20, 24.

units.la: Obj. 1. Matth. 1. 18. Priusquam ipsi convenissent, &c. Resp. Illud Convenire, non de usu matrimonii; sed de cohabitatione, aut Virginis in domum deductione, commodè potest intelligi. Vide verf. 20. 24.
units.tr: Objection 2. Verse 25: "Joseph did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son." Therefore he knew her afterwards. Reply: The particles "until" and similar ones, when they deny that something happened before a certain limit, do not necessarily imply that the thing happened or will happen immediately after that limit. Compare 2 Samuel 6:23; Matthew 28:20.

units.la: Obj. 2. verf: 25. Neque cognovit eam Josephus, quousque peperisset Filium illum suum primogenitum: Ergo postea cognovit eam. Resp. Particulæ non quousque, & similes, dum quid negant factum ante certum terminum, non necessario statim inferunt post illum terminum id factum, vel futurum. Confer 2 Sam. 6. 23. Matth. 28, 20.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ is called "the firstborn son of Mary." Therefore... Reply: He is so called because his mother bore no one before him, not as if she had borne several after him. See the law concerning the redemption of firstborn sons, Numbers 18:15, 16; that is, "firstborn" is the same as "opening the womb," Exodus 13:2; Numbers 8:16; Luke 2:23.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus appellatur Primogenitus Filius Mariæ. Ergo. Resp. Sic appellatur, quia Mater neminem peperit ante ipsum; non quasi plures post ipsum peperisset. Vide Legem de redimendis primogenitis; Num. 18. 15, 16. Scil. primogenitus idem est, qui adaperiens matricem; Exod. 13. 2. Num. 8. 16. Luc. 2, 23.
units.tr: Objection 4. The brethren and sisters of the Lord Jesus are mentioned: Matthew 13:55, 56. Therefore... Reply: These words sometimes denote kinsfolk and relatives, as in Genesis 13:8 and elsewhere. Unless perhaps Joseph was a widower, and these were his children from an earlier marriage; and so the brethren of the Lord Jesus were so by affinity.

units.la: Obj. 4. Fratres & Sorores Domini Jesu appellantur. tur. Matth. 13, 55, 56. Ergò. Resp. Voces istæ Cognatos & Agnatos subinde notant: ut Gen. 13. 8. & alibi. Nisi forte Josephus fuerit viduus, & isti ejus liberi ex priore conjugio; atque adeo fratres Domini Iesu affinitate.
units.tr: Objection 4. The brothers and sisters of the Lord Jesus are so called (Matt. 13:55, 56). Therefore... Answer: These words also denote kinsmen and relatives in general, as in Gen. 13:8 and elsewhere. Unless perhaps Joseph was a widower, and these were his children by a former marriage; and so the brothers of the Lord Jesus would be such by affinity.

units.la: Pontificii in gratiam sui Monachatus contendunt, B. Virginem ante istam annunciationem fecisse votum perpetuæ virginitatis; eo quod dixerit, Luc. 1, 34. Virum non cognovi. Resp. Absurde: eadem enim non potuit virginitatem Deo, & nuptias simul Josepho promittere: cum nupta non habeat proprium corpus in potestate; 1 Cor. 7. 4.
units.tr: The Papists, in support of their monastic life, contend that the Blessed Virgin made a vow of perpetual virginity before the annunciation, because she said (Luke 1:34), "I do not know a man." Answer: This is absurd. For she could not at the same time promise her virginity to God and promise marriage to Joseph, since a married woman does not have her own body in her power (1 Cor. 7:4).

units.la: XII. Succedit duarum Naturarum Unio hypostatica:
units.tr: XII. The hypostatic union of the two natures follows.

units.la: ubi primo spectanda Actio uniendi, sive ipsa unitio, quæ est actio Dei, per quam effectum est, ut ista humana natura, cum natura Divina (prout hæc in secunda Persona subsistit) eadem illa hypostasi sustentaretur, ac ultimate terminaretur in existendo. Ea efficienter quidem SS. Trinitati communis est; terminative vero soli Personæ secundæ adscribenda.
units.tr: Here we must consider first the act of uniting, that is, the uniting itself, which is the action of God by which this human nature was brought about so that, together with the divine nature (as the divine nature subsists in the second Person), it is sustained by that same hypostasis and ultimately terminated in existence. This act is common to the Most Holy Trinity as to its efficient cause, but is to be ascribed to the second Person alone as its terminus.

units.la: Porro autem actionis istius effectus formalis est Unio, sive Status unitatis hypostaticæ, in quo deinceps permanserunt duæ istæ Naturæ. Atque ista Unio vere est personalis. Hinc Ioh. 1. 14. Sermo ille factus est caro. Scil. per talem unionem: similiter fere ut Gen. 2. 7. Finxit Iehovah Deus hominem de pulvere terræ, sufflavitque in nares ejus spiraculum vitæ: sic factus est homo in animam viventem. Et Col. 2. 9. Inhabitat in eo omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter; sic in ista humanitate, & in isto corpore, tanquam adjuncto substantali ἐνυπόστατῳ, existit, & sese exserit perfectissima Deitatis sufficientia. Confer 1 Tim. 3. 16.
units.tr: Further, the formal effect of this action is the union, or state of hypostatic unity, in which these two natures have since remained. And this union is truly personal. Hence John 1:14: The Word was made flesh, namely through such a union, much as Gen. 2:7: The LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul. And Col. 2:9: In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily; so in this humanity and in this body, as in a substantial adjunct enhypostatic [ἐνυπόστατῳ], the most perfect sufficiency of the Godhead exists and shows itself. Compare 1 Tim. 3:16.

units.la: XIII. Exprimitur etiam istud mysterium per Corporis adaptationem; Hebr. x. 5. & cum peculiari respectu ad Filium, per Assumtionem, vel Acceptionem: Phil. 2, 6, 7, 8. Hebr. 2. 16. qui tamen non Hominem assumfit, aut Personam humanam; sed Naturam humanam tantum, propria personalitate destitutam: verum ὁ Λόγος sua hypostasi terminat eam ultimate in existendo, ut una solum Persona fit.
units.tr: XIII. This mystery is also expressed by the adaptation of a body, Heb. 10:5; and, with particular reference to the Son, by assumption or acceptance: Phil. 2:6, 7, 8; Heb. 2:16. Yet he did not assume a man or a human person, but only a human nature, destitute of its own personality; but the Word [ὁ Λόγος] terminates it ultimately in existence by his own hypostasis, so that there is only one Person.

units.la: Atq; hinc 1. diserte unus Mediator dicitur, 1 Tim. 2. 5. non duo: & 1 Cor. 1, 13. Christus divisus esse negatur.
units.tr: And hence, first, he is expressly called one Mediator, 1 Tim. 2:5, not two; and in 1 Cor. 1:13 it is denied that Christ is divided.

units.la: 2 Illi Personae ab isto assumtionis momento, duae distinctae Naturae in SS. Literis passim assignantur; Divina & humana.
units.tr: Second, from the moment of this assumption, two distinct natures, divine and human, are ascribed to that Person throughout the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Iremque 3. Attributa, tum Divina, tum humana.
units.tr: Third, there are attributes, both divine and human.

units.la: Nec non 4. Opera duum generum; adeoque duo principia ἐνεργητικά: imo etiam passiones humanae, & principium tale παθητικόν; à Natura Divina manifestissime distinctum.
units.tr: Fourth, there are works of two kinds, and therefore two active principles; indeed even human passions, and a passive principle of that kind, clearly distinct from the divine nature.

units.la: XIV. Nestoriani olim, ut duas in Christo Naturas, sic duas quoque Personas, statuebant; Unionem vero
units.tr: XIV. The Nestorians of old, while they posited two natures in Christ, also posited two Persons; but they acknowledged no union except a relative one [σχετικὴν].

units.la: nullam agnoscebant, nisi σχετικὴν, relativam. Sed contra hos orthodoxa Antiquitas veritatem solide asseruit; Unionem scil. inter duas distinctas Christi Naturas, esse vere ὑποστατικήν, substantialem. Atque ita factam esse unam eandemque substantiam primam intelligentem, &c. Et quidem Ἀδιαιρέτως, indivise, ut Persona non dividatur, nec in ea alius & alius agnoscatur: atque item Ἀχωρίστως, inseparabiliter: ut humana ista Natura separari ab hypostasi τῷ Λόγῳ non potuerit a primo Unionis hypostaticae momento, nec separata unquam extiterit, ne quidem in triduo mortis.
units.tr: But against them the orthodox antiquity solidly asserted the truth: that the union between the two distinct natures of Christ is truly hypostatic [ὑποστατικήν], substantial, and that thus one and the same first intelligent substance was made. And indeed it is indivisibly [Ἀδιαιρέτως], so that the Person is not divided, nor is one and another recognised in him; and likewise inseparably [Ἀχωρίστως], so that this human nature could not be separated from the hypostasis of the Word from the first moment of the hypostatic union, and never existed separated, not even during the three days of death.

units.la: Eutychiani, in alterum extremum ruentes, putarunt, post incarnationem, unam solum in Christo fuisse Naturam: sive per conversionem humanitatis in Divinitatem; sive duabus Naturis in unam Naturam per confusionem, aut commixtionem, coeuntibus.
