Sed contra istos eadem orthodoxa Antiquitas asseruit, in una Christi Persona esse vere aliud & aliud: & quidem Ἀτρέπτως, sine conversione; ut enim in Deitatem nulla cadit conversio, sic ea ex conversione alterius naturae fieri minime potest. Et Ἀσυγχύτως, sine confusione, tum Naturarum, tum proprietatum utriusque Naturae; cum nec Deitas ullo modo mutabilis sit, nec humanitas Attributorum Divinorum capax, ut subjectum quo; neque Deitas proprietatum humanarum: nec Attributa Divina realiter differant a Natura Divina. Unde veteres admodum concinne: Nequaquam distinctione Naturarum sublata propter Unionem: sed potius servata cujusque Naturae proprietate; & in unam Personam, atque unam subsistentiam, concurrente. Huc etiam pertinet Distichon:
units.tr: The Eutychians, rushing to the opposite extreme, thought that after the incarnation there was only one nature in Christ, either through the conversion of the humanity into the divinity, or through the two natures coalescing into one by confusion or mixture. But against these the same orthodox antiquity asserted that in the one Person of Christ there truly are one thing and another: indeed unchangeably [Ἀτρέπτως], without conversion; for just as no conversion falls upon the Deity, so it can by no means be made from the conversion of another nature. And unconfusedly [Ἀσυγχύτως], without confusion, both of the natures and of the properties of each nature; since neither is the Deity in any way changeable, nor is the humanity capable of the divine attributes as the subject in which, nor the Deity of human properties; nor do the divine attributes really differ from the divine nature. Whence the ancients very neatly said: The distinction of the natures is by no means abolished on account of the union; rather the property of each nature is preserved, and they concur into one Person and one subsistence. To this also pertains the couplet:

units.la: Sum quod eram; nec eram quod sum: nunc dicor utrumque:
units.tr: I am what I was; nor was I what I am: now I am called both,

units.la: Ignoras, nisi me stirpe ab utraque tenes.
units.tr: You would not know me, unless you hold me from both lineages.

units.la: Eutychianis affines erant Monothelitae, qui unicam duntaxat in Christo voluntatem agnoscebant. Hoc autem absurdum esse, vel ex eo liquet, quod duae distinctae Naturae intellectuales, duas quoque distinctas voluntates inferant.
units.tr: Akin to the Eutychians were the Monothelites, who acknowledged only one will in Christ. That this is absurd is clear even from the fact that two distinct intellectual natures imply two distinct wills as well.

units.la: xv. Obj. 1. Ubi existit utraque pars essentialis ad Hominem constituendum necessaria, ibi etiam existit Persona humana: atqui hic praeter Personam & Λόγος existit utraque illa pars essentialis: ergo. Resp. Partes essentiales in homine non faciunt formaliter Personam; sed Modus existendi completè, incommunicabiliter, & sic ultimatè: at vero Humanitas Christi ultimatam terminationem per se non habet, sed in Persona τῷ Λόγῳ.
units.tr: XV. Objection 1. Where both parts essential for constituting a man exist, there a human person also exists; but here, besides the Person and the Word, both those essential parts exist; therefore. Answer: the essential parts in a man do not formally make a Person; rather the mode of existing, complete, incommunicable, and thus ultimate. But the humanity of Christ does not of itself have ultimate termination, but has it in the Person of the Word.

units.la: Obj. 2. Illud imperfectionem argueret in Humanitate Christi. Ergo. Resp. Neg. Cum ea habeat quaecunque ad perfectionem humanae naturae requiruntur; & modus perfectior satis compensat absentiam imperfectioris.
units.tr: Objection 2. That would argue imperfection in the humanity of Christ; therefore. Answer: I deny it. For it has whatever is required for the perfection of human nature; and a more perfect mode sufficiently makes up for the absence of the less perfect.

units.la: Obj. 3. Talis duarum substantiarum unio, sine earum confusione, fieri non potest. Ergo. Resp. Neg. Quemadmodum enim in Homine, in eadem natura singulari, Anima & Corpus distincte suam essentiam, & proprietates habent: sic in Christo utraque Natura suam habet essentiam, & sua attributa; non obstante unione personali. Et Deitatis personalitas sustentat, atque ultimate terminat in existendo, Naturam istam humanam suis proprietatibus praeditam.
units.tr: Objection 3. Such a union of two substances cannot happen without their confusion; therefore. Answer. I deny it. For just as in a man, in the one singular nature, soul and body have their essence and properties distinctly, so in Christ each nature has its own essence and its own attributes, notwithstanding the personal union. And the personality of the Deity sustains and ultimately terminates in existence this human nature endowed with its own properties.

units.la: Obj. 4. Christus Nicodemo dicebat, Filium hominis esse in cælo: Joh. 3. 13. & Paulus Act. 20; 28. Deum acquisivisse Ecclesiam proprio suo sanguine: ita quae sunt unius naturae, tribuuntur alteri. &c. Resp. Negamus sequelam. Consideratio personae in concreto, non debet confundi, cum alterutrius naturae consideratione in abstracto.
units.tr: Objection 4. Christ said to Nicodemus that the Son of man is in heaven, John 3:13; and Paul, Acts 20:28, says that God acquired the Church with his own blood; thus what belongs to one nature is attributed to the other, etc. Answer. We deny the consequence. The consideration of the Person in the concrete ought not to be confused with the consideration of either nature in the abstract.

units.la: XVI. Deitati nulla hinc accidit mutatio; sed re- latio rationis accessit solum ab illa efficientia ad extra.
units.tr: XVI. No change comes to the Deity from this; a relation of reason was added only from that efficiency directed outward.

units.la: Nec putandum cum Patripassianis, quod Pater, aut Sp. S. eadem opera sit incarnatus, passus, mortuus, &c. in sua humanitate; cum humanitas in hypostasin Filii tantum sit assumta. Quin imo nec ipsi Personae & Λόγῳ mutatio accidit, etiamsi per hanc hypostasin formaliter in existendo terminata sit Humana Christi natura.
units.tr: Nor is it to be thought, with the Patripassians, that the Father or the Holy Spirit was incarnate, suffered, died, and so on in his humanity by the same act, since the humanity was assumed only into the hypostasis of the Son. Indeed, no change comes even to the Person himself or to the Word [Λόγῳ], although the human nature of Christ is formally terminated in existing through this hypostasis.

units.la: Humanitati vero accidit, primo, Modus ille existendi in ista hypostasi, quem vulgo Gratiam unionis personalis vocant; ac deinde singularia quaedam Charismata, seu Gratiae habituales; quibus humana Christi natura prae caeteris creaturis insigniter fuit locupletata: Joh. III, 34. Non enim Huic admetitur Deus Spiritum. scil. simili mensura, quali reliquis hominibus admeritur. Adde Psal. 45. 8. Jes. xi. 1. xlij. 1. Joh. 1, 14. Act. 10. Act.10.38. Col.1.19.1J.3,9. Inprimis igitur hic spectanda eius Sanctitas, Sapientia, & Potentia.
units.tr: To the humanity, however, there happens first that mode of existing in this hypostasis which they commonly call the grace of personal union; and then certain singular charismata, or habitual graces, by which the human nature of Christ was remarkably enriched above the other creatures: John 3:34, "For God does not give the Spirit to him by measure," that is, in the same measure in which he is given to the rest of men. Add Ps. 45:8; Isa. 11:1; 42:1; John 1:14; Acts 10; Acts 10:38; Col. 1:19; 1 John 3:9. Chiefly, therefore, his holiness, wisdom, and power are to be considered here.

units.la: XVII. Quod ad Sanctitatem attinet; hanc ipsa unctio Sp. S. a primo conformationis momento humanae Christi naturae praestitit: & quidem ita, ut ipsa non tantum immunis fuerit a peccato originali, sed plane impeccabilis, adeo ut ne quidem actu peccare potuerit. Proptererea 1. ex illa Spiritus Sancti operatione Sanctum illud vocatur; Luc.1.35.
units.tr: XVII. As far as holiness is concerned, the anointing of the Holy Spirit itself bestowed this on the human nature of Christ from the first moment of its formation, and indeed so that it was not only free from original sin but altogether impeccable, so that it could not even actually sin. Therefore, (1) from that operation of the Holy Spirit he is called "holy": Luke 1:35.

units.la: 2. Spiritus S. electos salvandos regenerat & sanctificat, ut observent praecepta Dei; Ezech.36.26. atque efficit in iis ipsum velle, & ipsum agere, pro gratuita sua benevolentia; Phil.2.13. Multo magis igitur idem Spiritus debuit esse efficax in Natura ςυντοσάτῳ illi Personae, cujus est iste Spiritus.
units.tr: (2) The Holy Spirit regenerates and sanctifies the elect to be saved, so that they observe the precepts of God, Ezek. 36:26, and he works in them both to will and to do, by his free goodwill, Phil. 2:13. Much more, therefore, the same Spirit ought to have been effective in the nature co-subsistent [συνυποστάτῳ] with that Person, whose Spirit he is.

units.la: 3. Talis omnino nos decebat Pontifex, sanctus, ab omni malo remotus, sine labe, &c. Hebr.7.26,27. Id postulabat, tum justitia Divina: nam Jus Dei pro nobis impleri non poterat a peccatore: tum veritas Divina, juxta aeternum Decretum, & Praedictiones ac Typos V.T.
units.tr: (3) Such a high priest in every way became us: holy, separated from evil, without stain, and so on, Heb. 7:26, 27. This was demanded both by the divine justice, for the right of God could not be fulfilled for us by a sinner, and by the divine truth, according to the eternal decree and the predictions and types of the Old Testament.

units.la: Obj. 1. Formalis effectus personalitatis est, naturam ultimate tantum terminare in existendo; non vero eam impeccabile praestare. Resp. Hoc loco non est spectanda qualiscunque personalitas; sed personalitas Personae essentialiter sanctissimae. Nunc autem in Natura tam arcte τῷ Λόγῳ unita, necesse fuit τὸν Λόγον per Spiritum sanctificationis, simul operari convenienter suae sanctitati.
units.tr: Objection 1. The formal effect of personality is only to terminate the nature ultimately in existing; it does not furnish it with impeccability. Answer: Here we are not to consider any personality whatever, but the personality of a Person who is essentially most holy. Now, since the nature is so closely united to the Word, it was necessary that the Word, through the Spirit of sanctification, should at the same time act in a manner befitting his holiness.

units.la: Obj. 2. Vita Personae istius Divinae non statim fecit Humanitatem illam immortalem: ergo nec ejus Sanctitas fecit impeccabilem. Resp. Negamus consequentiam: Deus enim non aversatur, vel odit, mortem peccatoris, aut Sponsoris pro peccatoribus, quatenus ea est bonum justitiae; sed eam postulat, & approbat: Prov.J.26. Deut.28.63. Ies.53.10. Hebr.10.7,9,10. Peccatum vero nequaquàm postulat vel approbat; sed aversatur & odit: Psal. 45. 8. v. 5,6,7.
units.tr: Objection 2. The life of that divine Person did not at once make that humanity immortal; therefore neither did his holiness make it impeccable. Answer: We deny the consequence. For God does not turn away from or hate the death of a sinner, or of a surety for sinners, insofar as it is a good of justice; rather he requires and approves it: Prov. 1.26; Deut. 28:63; Isa. 53:10; Heb. 10:7, 9, 10. But sin he by no means requires or approves; rather he turns away from it and hates it: Ps. 45:8, vv. 5, 6, 7.

units.la: Obj. 3. Per istam impeccabilitatem tolleretur libertas arbitrii in humana Christi Natura. Resp. Neg. Imo stabilitur: cum peccabilitas meram imperfectionem dicat; & majoris longe sit perfectionis, bonum morale sanctitati Divinæ prorsus conforme, constanter velle quam posse illud repudiare.
units.tr: Objection 3. Through that impeccability, liberty of will would be removed from the human nature of Christ. Answer: No. On the contrary, it is established, since peccability denotes mere imperfection; and it is of far greater perfection to will constantly what is morally good and wholly conformed to the divine holiness than to be able to reject it.

units.la: XVIII. Quantum ad Sapientiam Christi, secundum humanam ipsius Naturam; illa apprimè insignis est; non tamen infinita: cùm subjectum ejus quo, sit finitum; adeoque progressu temporis incrementum ceperit; Luc. 2.52. quin imo quædam ignoraverit; Marc. xi.13. xiij. 32. ignorantiâ videl. puræ negationis.
units.tr: XVIII. As to the wisdom of Christ according to his human nature, it is indeed remarkably distinguished, yet not infinite, since the subject by which it operates is finite; and so it has grown with the passage of time, Luke 2:52. Indeed, he was ignorant of some things, Mark 11:13; 13:32, namely with the ignorance of pure negation.

units.la: Exc. Christus tunc ignorabat diem extremi judicii, ut Doctor; quia nondum debuit, aut voluit, eum Discipulis indicare. Resp. Simili modo etiam Pater dicendus fuisset eum ignorare.
units.tr: Objection. Christ, as Teacher, was then ignorant of the day of the last judgement, because he did not yet have to, or wish to, indicate it to the disciples. Answer: In the same way the Father too would have to be said to be ignorant of it.

units.la: Obj. Omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ in eo absconditi dicuntur, Col. 2. 3. Resp. Illud de Personâ in concrero est accipiendum; non de Natura humanâ in abstracto.
units.tr: Objection. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are said to be hidden in him, Col. 2:3. Answer: That is to be understood of the Person in the concrete, not of the human nature in the abstract.

units.la: Potentia Christo quà Homini etiàm insignis competit, sed finita. Ac proindè Virtus physica principalis ad patrandaMiracula ei secundum humanamNaturam non est adscribenda; Ipse enim in eorum patratione preces adhibuit; Ioh. xi. 41, 42. Humanitas igitur istic se habuit, ut instrumentum morale.
units.tr: Power also belongs to Christ as man, remarkably, but finite. Therefore the principal physical virtue for performing miracles is not to be ascribed to him according to his human nature; for in performing them he used prayers, John 11:41, 42. The humanity there therefore acted as a moral instrument.

units.la: XIX. Succedit in Personâ Gratia muneris Mediatorii quod scil. Christus secundum utramque Naturam sit Mediator; & sic etiam ut Homo, gratus & acceptus Deo: Ies. 42. 1. Matth. 3. 17; ac talis ab hominibus agnoscendus, & sic recipiendus: xvij. 5. Act. 3. 22. ex Deut. 18.15.
units.tr: XIX. There follows in the Person the grace of the mediatorial office, namely that Christ, according to both natures, is Mediator, and thus also as man is pleasing and acceptable to God, Isa. 42:1; Matt. 3:17; and so is to be acknowledged by men and received accordingly, Matt. 17:5; Acts 3:22, from Deut. 18:15.

units.la: Spectanda porro Communicatio idiomatum, tum in esse reali, tum in modo prædicandi. Communicatio idio-mamatum in esse reali, nihil aliud est, quam concursus, aut conjunctio Attributorum & Proprietatum utriusque Naturæ, in eadem Persona; quæ necessario sequitur hypostaticam Unionem duarum istarum Naturarum. Communicatio vero idiomatum in modo prædicandi, sequitur modum essendi.
units.tr: Further, the communication of idioms is to be considered, both in real being and in the mode of predication. The communication of idioms in real being is nothing other than the concurrence or conjunction of the attributes and properties of each nature in the same Person, which necessarily follows from the hypostatic union of these two natures. The communication of idioms in the mode of predication follows the mode of being.

units.la: De Persona igitur non solum rectè prædicantur quæ ei secundum utramque Naturam communiter conveniunt: Ex. gr. Jesus Christus est Mediator, &c.
units.tr: Therefore, not only are those things rightly predicated of the Person which belong to him in common according to both natures (e.g. Jesus Christ is Mediator, etc.).

units.la: Verum insuper Attributa & Proprietates alterutrius Naturæ: Ex. gr. Christus est æternus, immortalis, &c. itemque, Christus in tempore natus est, mortuus est, &c.
units.tr: But moreover the attributes and properties of either nature are predicated of him (e.g. Christ is eternal, immortal, etc.; likewise, Christ was born in time, died, etc.).

units.la: Quin imo de Persona ab alterutra Natura, sed in concreto, denominatâ, rectè prædicantur enunciata, & proprietates alteri naturæ convenientes: Ex. gr. Deus, (Filio λόγῳ intellecto,) aut Filius Dei, natus est ex Maria Virgine, &c. Vide Act. 20. 28. Iste homo, aut Filius hominis, cum apud Nicodemum esset in terra, simul erat in cœlo, &c. Joh. 3. 13. Hæc omnia vere dicuntur. Alibi tamen Spiritus S. plenius & distinctius loquitur; ut Rom. 1.3,4. IX. 5. Act. 2. 30.
units.tr: Indeed, of the Person, named from either nature but in the concrete, statements are rightly made and properties belonging to the other nature are rightly predicated: e.g. God (the Word [λόγῳ] being understood), or the Son of God, was born of the Virgin Mary, etc. See Acts 20:28; "This man," or "the Son of man," while he was on earth with Nicodemus, was at the same time in heaven, etc., John 3:13. All these things are truly said. Elsewhere, however, the Holy Spirit speaks more fully and distinctly, as in Rom. 1:3, 4; 9:5; Acts 2:30.

units.la: XX. Perperam ergo Lutherani Nestorianismum nobis impingunt; quasi non realem, sed solummodo verbalem, Communicationem idiomatum statueremus: ipsi vero, dum quorundam Attributorum realem communicationem requirunt, aut transfusionem de Natura Divina in humanam, nominatim Omnipræsentiæ, Omniscientiæ, Omnipotentiæ, Virtutis vivificandi, Peccata remittendi, atque adeo Majestatis Divinæ, ab indirecto saltem Eutychyanismo excusari non possunt, & in Dei Simplicitatem injurii sunt; per quam Attributa Divina nec à se invicem, nec ab essentiâ Divina, realiter differunt; adeo ut cui unum Attributum convenit, nit, ei omnia conveniant, atque ipsa Essentia.
units.tr: XX. Therefore the Lutherans wrongly fasten Nestorianism upon us, as if we posited a merely verbal, and not a real, communication of idioms. They themselves, while they require a real communication of certain attributes, or a transfusion from the divine nature into the human, namely of omnipresence, omniscience, omnipotence, the power of quickening and of forgiving sins, and so of divine majesty, cannot be excused from at least an indirect Eutychianism, and they do injury to the simplicity of God, through which the divine attributes do not differ really from one another or from the divine essence; so that to whom one attribute belongs, to him all belong, and the essence itself.

units.la: Obj. 1. In Homine vita Animæ communicatur Corpori: ergo Attributa Divina possunt etiam communicari humanæ Naturæ in Christo. Resp. Animæ vita spiritualis Corpori non communicatur: Corpus enim non intelligit, aut vult; sed Anima, aut Homo secundum animam. Interim Corpus vivum denominatur, quatenus Anima informatum est, sic ab ea movetur, eique in operationibus suis servit quantum potest.
units.tr: Objection 1. In man the life of the soul is communicated to the body; therefore divine attributes can also be communicated to the human nature in Christ. Answer: The spiritual life of the soul is not communicated to the body, for the body does not understand or will; the soul, or the man according to the soul, does. Meanwhile the body is called living insofar as it is informed by the soul, is moved by it, and serves it in its operations as far as it can.

units.la: Obj. 2. Ferro candenti communicatur intensus ille calor, & lux; quæ cæteroquin Ignis proprietates sunt. Resp. Ista est συνδύαξις: nam particulæ Igneæ insinuarunt se pori s Ferri; sic Ferrum permeant; atque ipsæ in Ferro calent & lucent; non vero ipsum Ferrum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Intense heat and light are communicated to red-hot iron, which are otherwise properties of fire. Answer: This is a mere juxtaposition [συνδύαξις]. For the particles of fire have insinuated themselves into the pores of the iron and so permeate it; they themselves glow and shine in the iron, but the iron itself does not.

units.la: Obj. 3. Col. 2. 9. Plenitudo Deitatis habitat in Christo corporaliter: ergo in corpore Christi insunt attributa Divina. Resp. 1. Corporaliter synecdochicè idem est quod personaliter. 2. In humana Christi natura, & in corpore ejus, existit etiam natura Divina, & consequenter attributa Divina; sed non adæquate; neque sic, ut humana natura, vel corpus ejus, esset subjectum quo attributorum Divinorum.
units.tr: Objection 3. Col. 2:9: "The fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ bodily"; therefore divine attributes inhere in the body of Christ. Answer: (1) "Bodily," taken synecdochically, is the same as "personally." (2) In the human nature of Christ, and in his body, the divine nature also exists, and consequently the divine attributes; but not adequately, nor in such a way that the human nature, or his body, would be the subject by which the divine attributes operate.

units.la: XXI. Omnipræsentia humanæ Christi naturæ non competit, ex Unione hypostatica:
units.tr: XXI. The omnipresence of Christ's human nature does not follow from the hypostatic union.

units.la: 1. Quia Unio hypostatica jam cum ipsa fœtus conformatione in utero Virginis facta est; ac proinde, si ea Omnipræsentiam humanæ naturæ inferret, hæc utero Virginis non fuisset conclusa, ex utero non vere prodiisset, fasciis involvi, in præsepi deponi, circumcidi, &c. non potuisset: contra Luc. 2. 5,-7. 12, 16, 21.
units.tr: 1. Because the hypostatic union was already effected at the very formation of the foetus in the Virgin's womb. Therefore, if that union carried omnipresence to the human nature, that nature would not have been enclosed in the Virgin's womb, could not truly have come forth from the womb, been wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger, circumcised, and so on. This is contrary to Luc. 2. 5-7, 12, 16, 21.

units.la: 2. Christus secundum humanitatem suam uno loco tantum, non pluribus simul, fuit præsens, durante statu humiliationis: Joh. xi. 15. Gaudeo, Me illic non fuisse; sed eamus ad eum ! Lazarum scil. defunctum. Et verf. 32. Maria soror Lazari; Domine, si fuisses hic, non esset mortuus frater meus. Adde Luc. 2. 22. Matth. 2. 14, 20, 22, 23. Luc. 2. 42. Marc. 6. 45. Joh. 6. 17. &c.
units.tr: 2. According to his humanity, Christ, while in the state of humiliation, was present in only one place at a time, not in several at once: Joh. 11. 15: I am glad that I was not there, but let us go to him, namely to Lazarus, who had died. And v. 32: Mary, the sister of Lazarus: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Add Luke 2. 22; Matth. 2. 14, 20, 22, 23; Luke 2. 42; Mark 6. 45; John 6. 17, etc.

units.la: 3. Similiter à Resurrectione ex mortuis. Diserte Angelus, Marc. 16. 6. Non est hic: Ecce locus, ubi posuerant Eum. Adde Luc. 24. 39, 40. Act. 1. 3.
units.tr: 3. Likewise after the resurrection from the dead. The angel says plainly, Mark 16. 6: He is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. Add Luke 24. 39, 40; Acts 1. 3.

units.la: 4. Neque aliter factum per Ascensionem in coelum: de qua ipse, Joh. 16. 5. Nunc abeo ad Eum, qui misit Me. 7. Confert vobis, ut Ego abeam, &c. atque iterum verf. 28. Prodii a Patre, & veni in mundum: iterum relinquo mundum, & proficiscor ad Patrem. Et 17. 11 Non sum amplius in mundo. & sic porro. Confer Luc. 24. 51. Act. 1. 9, 11. iij, 21. 1 Cor. xi. 26. Atque huc pertinet valida Pauli consequentia ad instructionem fidei; Hebr. 8. 4. Nam si esset in terra, ne Sacerdos quidem esset. Adde Matth. 24. 26. Et ad exhortationem: Col. 3. 1,2. Si resurrexistis cum Christo, superna quaerite, ubi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens. Superna sapite, non terrestria. Adde 2 Cor. 5. 6, 8. Phil. 1. 23.
units.tr: 4. Nor was it otherwise with the ascension into heaven, of which he himself says, John 16. 5: Now I go to him who sent me. 7: It is expedient for you that I go away, etc. And again v. 28: I came forth from the Father, and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father. And 17. 11: I am no longer in the world. And so on. Compare Luke 24. 51; Acts 1. 9, 11; 3. 21; 1 Cor. 11. 26. To this belongs also Paul's strong argument, for the instruction of faith, Heb. 8. 4: For if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest. Add Matth. 24. 26. And for exhortation, Col. 3. 1, 2: If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth. Add 2 Cor. 5. 6, 8; Phil. 1. 23.

units.la: Obj. 1. Eph. 4. 10. & 1, 23. Christus dicitur omnia in omnibus adimplere. Ergo est ubique praesens, & quidem secundum humanam naturam. Resp. Implet omnia; non quidem omnia spatia, corporali sua praesentia; sed totam Ecclesiam, donis & benedictionibus: quatenus videl, in omnibus & singulis electis perficit, quaecunque ad vitam & pietatem pertinent. Implet etiam omnia, quae de Ipso per Prophetas praedicta sunt.
units.tr: Objection 1. Eph. 4. 10 and 1. 23 say that Christ fills all things in all. Therefore he is present everywhere, and indeed according to his human nature. Answer: He fills all things, not indeed all spaces by his bodily presence, but the whole Church with gifts and blessings, namely in that he brings to completion, in all and each of the elect, whatever pertains to life and godliness. He also fills all things that were foretold of him by the prophets.

units.la: Obj. 2. Matth. 18. 20. & xxviij, 20. Christus fidelibus promisit suam praesentiam. Ergo. Resp. Istica gitur de speciali modo praesentiae, secundum Deitatem; & singulari manifestatione gloriosae pariter ac gratiosae suae Majestatis, per charismata, & benedictiones spirituales: non autem de præsentia corporali.
units.tr: Objection 2. Matth. 18. 20 and 28. 20: Christ promised his faithful his presence. Therefore... Answer: These passages speak of a special mode of presence, according to the Deity, and of a singular manifestation of his glorious and gracious majesty, through the charismata and spiritual blessings, not of bodily presence.

units.la: Obj. 3. Si natura humana Christi non esset adæquatè præsens Divinæ, inde sequeretur naturarum à se invicem divulsio. Resp. Neg. cum humanitas personalitate ἀλόγου ultimate terminetur, ubi existit: Divinitatis vero ut alia natura, sic alia quoque sit existentia & præsentia.
units.tr: Objection 3. If the human nature of Christ were not present in the fullest sense to the divine, it would follow that the natures are torn apart from one another. Answer: Denied. For the humanity is terminated ultimately in the impersonal [ἀλόγου] personality where it exists; but the Divinity, being another nature, has also another existence and presence.

units.la: XXII. Omniscientiam quoque humanæ Christi naturæ non esse communicatam, ut hæc esset sub- jectum ejus quo, ex iis apertum est, quæ diximus th. 18.
units.tr: XXII. The omniscience of Christ's human nature was likewise not communicated to it so as to be the subject by which it knows, as is clear from what we said in thesis 18.

units.la: Idem de omnipotentiâ dicendum 1. quia subjectum finitum est.
units.tr: The same is to be said of omnipotence, first because the subject is finite.

units.la: 2. Quia in humanitate Christi manifesta satis fuit potentia obedientialis passiva.
units.tr: Second, because in the humanity of Christ a passive obediential power was sufficiently manifest.

units.la: 3. Quia isto respectu Christo tribuuntur deprecationes & supplicationes, cum clamore valido & lachrymis, apud Eum qui poterat ipsum servare, &c. Hebr. 5 7.
units.tr: Third, because in this respect supplications and entreaties are attributed to Christ, with strong crying and tears, before him who was able to save him, etc. Heb. 5. 7.

units.la: Obj. Attamen Christo homini tribuitur potentia summa, infinita: Phil. 3. 21. Hebr. 2. 8. 1 Cor. 15. 27. Act. 10. 38. Resp. Ista de Persona dicuntur in concreto.
units.tr: Objection: Nevertheless, supreme and infinite power is attributed to Christ as man: Phil. 3. 21; Heb. 2. 8; 1 Cor. 15. 27; Acts 10. 38. Answer: Those things are said of the Person in the concrete.

units.la: De cæteris, utpote Virtute vivificandi; de qua 1 Cor. 15. 21. atque item de extremo Judicio: quod Filio hominis œconomice demandatum est; Matth. 16. 27. Joh. 5. 27. Act. 17. 31. idem judicium erit: quemadmodum & de Potestate remittendi peccata, quæ absolute summa Christo tantum competit, quatenus Deus est: Luc. 5. 20, 24. & supremus omnium Dominus ac Rector: Jac. 4. 12.
units.tr: As for the others, such as the power of quickening, of which 1 Cor. 15. 21 speaks, and likewise the final judgment, which has been committed economically to the Son of man (Matth. 16. 27; John 5. 27; Acts 17. 31), the same is true of the judgment; and likewise of the power of forgiving sins, which belongs absolutely and supremely to Christ only, insofar as he is God (Luke 5. 20, 24), and of his being the supreme Lord and Ruler of all (Jas. 4. 12).

units.la: De Majestate & Gloriâ, vide sup. cap. 4. th. 75.
units.tr: For his majesty and glory, see above, chapter 4, thesis 75.

units.la: XXIII. Succedit Communio Apotelesmatum. Apo- telesma hoc loco est opus aliquod Christi Mediatoris, ad officii sui functionem pertinens. Communio autem ea
units.tr: XXIII. There follows the communion of the apotelesmata. An apotelesma in this place is some work of Christ the Mediator pertaining to the performance of his office. The communion is this: that these works proceed from the person of the God-man according to each nature, the divine nature contributing in them what is its own and the human nature what is its own; whence these works are called theandric.

units.la: ea est, ut opera ista procedant à persona Θεανθρώπω, secundum utramque naturam; Divina in illis conserente quod suum est, & humana quod suum est: unde ista opera Θεανδρικά appellantur. O' ἐνεργῶν igitur unus est Christus Mediator, producens tale ἀποτέλεσμα. Τὸ ἐνεργητικὸν, sive principium activum quo, geminum est; Natura Divina & humana. Η' ἐνέργεια, operatio, similiter gemina est; ut principium quo Τὸ ἐνέργημα denique, seu ἀποτέλεσμα unumquodque, Personae tribuendum est: hujusmodi sunt, Redemtio, Vivificatio, Miraculorum patratio, Ecclesiae gubernatio, Judicii administratio, &c. In his agit utraque natura quod suum est, cum alterius communione; Verbo scil. operante quod Verbi est, & Carne exequente quod carnis est.
units.tr: Therefore he who works is one Christ the Mediator, producing such an effect [ἀποτέλεσμα]. The active principle, or that by which he acts [Τὸ ἐνεργητικὸν], is twofold: the divine nature and the human. The operation [Η' ἐνέργεια] is likewise twofold, as is the principle by which it is done. Finally, the work or effect [Τὸ ἐνέργημα] of each, that is, the apotelesma, is to be ascribed to the Person; such are redemption, quickening, the working of miracles, the government of the Church, the administration of judgment, etc. In these each nature does what is its own, in communion with the other: the Word working what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh.

units.la: XXIV. Hactenus de Persona Christi. Spectandum nunc ejus Officium, quo Ipse defungitur œconomice ad salutem hominum electorum, & in Dei gloriam. Hoc autem exprimitur potissimum istis titulis; Mediator, Sponsor, Redemtor, Salvator, Unctus.
units.tr: XXIV. So far concerning the Person of Christ. We must now consider his Office, by which he economically discharges the task of saving the elect and of the glory of God. This is expressed chiefly by these titles: Mediator, Surety, Redeemer, Saviour, Anointed.

units.la: Christus est Mediator Dei & Hominum: 1 Tim. 2. 5. qui ut Persona, sic officio, medius intercedit: non tantum ut Interpres Dei, quo Deus ad foedera cum hominibus pangenda utatur; & per quem populus, de voluntate Divina sufficienter instructus, ad Deum accedat: quod est Socini commentum. Sed alterius plane, & sublimioris conditionis; apud Deum pro Hominibus, & apud Homines nomine Dei, vere peragens omnia ad pacem & salutem illis valide impetrandam, atque efficaciter applicandam, necessaria. Hinc 1. Apostolus μεσίτευμα istud explicans, 1 Tim. 2. 6. dicit; Se ipsum dedit redemtionis pretium (ἀντίλυτρον) pro omnibus.
units.tr: Christ is the Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2. 5), who intervenes as mediator both in person and in office: not merely as an interpreter of God, through whom God uses to make covenants with men and through whom the people, sufficiently instructed about the divine will, approach God. That is the invention of Socinus. Rather he performs, in a far higher and plainly different condition, before God on behalf of men, and before men in the name of God, all the things truly necessary to obtain peace and salvation for them effectively and to apply them. Hence (1) the Apostle, explaining this office of mediation [μεσίτευμα], says at 1 Tim. 2. 6 that he gave himself as the ransom price of redemption [ἀντίλυτρον] for all.

units.la: 2. Hebr. 9. 15. Ob id novi testi Mediator est, ut morte ad redemtionem transgressionum intercedente, qui vocati erant, promissam æternam hæreditatem acciperent.
units.tr: (2) Heb. 9. 15: Therefore he is the Mediator of a new testament, so that, death intervening for the redemption of transgressions, those who were called might receive the promised eternal inheritance.

units.la: 3. Similiter, xij. 24. Novi pacti Mediatori Jesu tribuitur sanguis aspersionis, meliora loquens quam loquatur Abel.
units.tr: (3) Likewise, 12. 24: The sprinkled blood is ascribed to Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant, speaking better things than Abel.

units.la: Et 4. viij, 16. Tanto præstantior functio Sacerdotalis, quanto præstantioris pacti Mediator est, &c. Ergo Christi Mediatio functionem Sacerdotalem involvit peccatorum expiatoriam, nostrique cum Deo reconciliatoriam per mortem Ipsius, & sanguinis effusionem. Vide amplius Rom. 5. 10. 2 Cor. 5. 19, 21. Col. 1. 19, -22. Eph. 2. 11, -17.
units.tr: And (4) 8. 6: The priestly function is as much more excellent as the Mediator of the more excellent covenant is, etc. Therefore the mediation of Christ includes a priestly function, expiating sins and reconciling us to God through his death and the shedding of his blood. See further Rom. 5. 10; 2 Cor. 5. 19, 21; Col. 1. 19-22; Eph. 2. 11-17.

units.la: XXV. Obj. 1. Principes internuncios suos ad foedera cum rebellibus pangenda non mittunt, nisi jam vere sint placati. Ergo etiam Deus per Mediatorem non erat placandus. Resp. 1. Negamus, Christum duntaxat esse Internuncium. 2. Etiam Principes placari volentes, conditiones foederis & pacis rebellibus solent præscribere; quemadmodum in hoc negotio Deus Mediatorem constituit; cujus Sacrificio Ipse placari, & cujus intercessione nos in Ipsius gratiam reduci voluit: Rom. 3. 25, 26. Confer Job. 42. 7, 8, 9.
units.tr: XXV. Objection 1. Princes do not send their go-betweens to make covenants with rebels unless they are already truly appeased. Therefore God also was not to be appeased through a Mediator. Answer: (1) We deny that Christ is merely a go-between. (2) Even princes who wish to be appeased are accustomed to prescribe the terms of covenant and peace to rebels; just as in this matter God appointed a Mediator, by whose sacrifice he himself wished to be appeased and through whose intercession he wished to bring us back into his favour: Rom. 3. 25, 26. Compare Job 42. 7, 8, 9.

units.la: Obj. 2. Moses dicitur Mediator, cum internuncius solum esset; Gal. 3. 19. cum Deut. 5. 5. & Act. 7. 57, 58. Resp. 1. In veritate plus esse, quam in typo, nihil mirum. 2. Moses non tantum nomine Dei internuncium egit apud populum; sed pro populo apud Deum intercessit quoque: Exod. 32. 30. &c. Deut. 9. 18, 19. & oblatis sacrificiis altare conspersit eorum sanguine, ac porro etiam populum: Exod. 24. 5, -7.
units.tr: Objection 2. Moses is called a mediator, though he was only a go-between: Gal. 3. 19, compared with Deut. 5. 5 and Acts 7. 57, 58. Answer: (1) It is no surprise that the reality exceeds the type. (2) Moses did not merely act as a go-between for God before the people; he also interceded for the people before God: Exod. 32. 30 and following; Deut. 9. 18, 19. And after the sacrifices were offered, he sprinkled the altar with their blood, and then the people also: Exod. 24. 5, 6, 7.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus aliquoties dicitur nos Deo reconciliasse, non vero Deum nobis. Ergo. Resp. Cum omnis reconciliatio fit reciproca, utrumque recte dicitur, & alterum ex altero sequitur. Vide Matth. 5, 24. Interim ei reconciliatio activa potiori jure competit, qui hoc maxime egit, ut amicitia restauraretur.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ is sometimes said to have reconciled us to God, but never God to us. Therefore... Answer: Since all reconciliation is mutual, both expressions are rightly used, and one follows from the other. See Matt. 5. 24. Yet the active reconciliation belongs with better right to him who chiefly worked to restore the friendship.

units.la: XXVI. Mediator autem est Christus secundum utramque naturam; non secundum Divinam tantum: quod contendebat Osiander: nec secundum humanam duntaxat; quod volebat Stancarus; & communiter Pontif. atque item Socinianí: isti, ut propriis suis satisfactionibus & meritis velificentur; hi, quia non nisi humanam in Christo naturam agnoscunt. Sed 1. proponitur nobis Mediator, ut Θεάνθρωπος, & ...: Matth. 1. 21, 23. ex Isef. 7. 14. Quae appellatio utramque naturam conjunctim respicit. Confer Hof. 1. 7. Jer. 23. 6. & Heb. x. 5. ex Pf. 40. 7. 8. Neutra igitur temere excludenda est.
units.tr: XXVI. The Mediator is Christ according to both natures, not according to the divine nature alone, as Osiander contended, nor according to the human nature alone, as Stancarus wished, and as the Papists commonly do, and likewise the Socinians: the former so that he may be credited with his own satisfactions and merits, the latter because they acknowledge only a human nature in Christ. But first, the Mediator is set before us as the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], and so on: Matt. 1. 21, 23, from Isa. 7. 14. This title looks to both natures together. Compare Hos. 1. 7, Jer. 23. 6, and Heb. 10. 5, from Ps. 40. 7, 8. Neither nature, therefore, is to be rashly excluded.

units.la: 2. In morte propter peccata nostra; & in resurrectione ad justificationem nostram. Rom. 4. 24. exeruit se utraque natura. Joh. x. 17, 18. Ego depono animam meam, ut eam rursus assumam. Nemo tollit eam a me; sed Ego depono eam per Me ipsum: Auctoritatem habeo deponendi eam, & auctoritatem habeo rursus eam assumendi. Hoc praeceptum accepi a Patre meo. Cum Christus sibi praeceptum a Patre datum commemorat, manifeste loquitur, ut Mediator & Sponsor: ubi Auctoritatem animae deponendae, ejusque rursum assumendae, dicit, Deitatem indicat; sic tamen ut effectus formalis fuerit in Humanitate. Similiter 1 Petr. 3. 18. Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit, justus pro injustis, ut nos ad Deum adduceret: morte quidem affectus carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu. Confer Rom. 1. 1, 4.
units.tr: Second, in his death "for our sins" and in his resurrection "for our justification" (Rom. 4. 24), both natures show themselves. John 10. 17, 18: I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment I have received from my Father. When Christ recalls the command given him by the Father, he speaks plainly as Mediator and Surety. When he speaks of the power to lay down his soul and to take it up again, he indicates the Deity, yet in such a way that the formal effect is in the humanity. Similarly 1 Pet. 3. 18: Christ once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God; put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit. Compare Rom. 1. 1, 4.

units.la: 3. Virtus oblationis ac redemtionis Christi & animarum nostrarum purificatio, ad operationem Divinam cum humana conjunctam refertur, Hebr. 9. 13, 14. Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, &c. quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum aeternum se ipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam vestram a mortuis operibus, ad colendum Deum vivum? 1 Joh. 1. 7. Act. 20, 28.
units.tr: Third, the power of Christ's offering and redemption, and the purification of our souls, is referred to a divine operation joined with a human one: Heb. 9. 13, 14. For if the blood of bulls and goats, etc., how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God? Also 1 John 1. 7 and Acts 20. 28.

units.la: 4. Atque ita requirunt reliqua ἀποτελέσματα, quæ sunt opera Θεανδρικά; unio nostri cum Deo, Vita spiritualis, &c. Joh. 17. 21,-23. Ut omnes unum sint, sicut Tu Pater in Me, & Ego in Te; ut & ipsi in Nobis unum sint, Et Ego gloriam, quam dedisti Mihi, dedi eis; ut sint unum, sicut & nos unum sumus. Ego in eis, & Tu in Me; ut sint consummati in unum. Gal. 2. 20. Vivit in me Christus, &c. Adde 1 Cor. 1. 30. 2. v, 17. Eph. 3. 17,-18. Hebr. 2. 11. 1 Joh. 4. 9.
units.tr: Fourth, the remaining effects [ἀποτελέσματα], which are theandric [Θεανδρικά] works, require the same: our union with God, spiritual life, and so on. John 17. 21-23: That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you; that they also may be one in us... And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one. I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one. Gal. 2. 20: Christ lives in me, etc. Add 1 Cor. 1. 30, 2 Cor. 5. 17, Eph. 3. 17, 18, Heb. 2. 11, 1 John 4. 9.

units.la: Obj. 1 Tim. 2. 5. Mediator dicitur, Homo Jesus Christus: Ergo secundum humanam naturam. Resp. Sed non solum. Similiter ut Act. xx. 28. Deus dicitur Ecclesiam acquisivisse suo proprio sanguine: sed non exclusa, imo inclusa, humana natura.
units.tr: Objection: 1 Tim. 2. 5 calls the Mediator "the man Christ Jesus"; therefore he is so according to the human nature. Answer: But not only so. Similarly, in Acts 20. 28 God is said to have acquired the Church by his own blood; yet the human nature is not excluded there but included.

units.la: XXVII. Christus Mediator est Hominum electo- rum; non Angelorum.
units.tr: XXVII. Christ is the Mediator of elect men, not of angels.

units.la: 1. Quia Christi μεσιτευμα est redemtorium & reconciliatorium; quod in Angelos non quadrat: cum lapsorum non fit restitutio; & reliquorum conservatio tantum & confirmatio in suo statu.
units.tr: (1) Because Christ's mediatorial office [μεσιτευμα] is redemptive and reconciling, which does not fit the angels, since there is no restoration of the fallen, and the rest are only kept and confirmed in their state.

units.la: 2. Christus est Mediator Novi fœderis; quod melioribus promissis sancitum est: Hebr. 12. 34. viij. 16. neque ad Angelos pertinet.
units.tr: (2) Christ is the Mediator of the New Covenant, which was established on better promises (Heb. 8. 6; 12. 24), and this does not pertain to the angels.

units.la: 3. Ut Mediator esset, persona medius esse debuit inter partes, & utriusque naturæ particeps: at vero Christus Angelos non assumsit: Hebr. 2. 16.
units.tr: (3) For someone to be a mediator, the person must stand between the parties and share in both natures. But Christ did not take on the angels: Heb. 2. 16.

units.la: 4. Munus Mediatorium diserte restringitur ad Homines: 1 Tim. 2. 5. Mundum: 2 Cor. 5. 19. Populum suum: Matth. 1. 21. atque hinc ipse Angelus tam emphatice ad Pastores; Luc. 2. 10. 11. Evangelizo vobis gaudium magnum:--nempe natum esse Vobis hodie Servatorem, &c.
units.tr: (4) The mediatorial office is expressly restricted to men: 1 Tim. 2. 5; to the world: 2 Cor. 5. 19; to his people: Matt. 1. 21. Hence the angel also speaks so emphatically to the shepherds: Luke 2. 10, 11: "I bring you good news of great joy... for there is born to you today a Saviour," etc.

units.la: Obj. 1. Col. 1. 20. Ut per Eum reconciliaret omnia Sibi,-tum quæ in terra: tum quæ in cœlis: Ergo & Angeli per Christum reconciliati sunt, &c. Resp. Per ea quæ in cœlis, intelligi possunt fideles jam tum defuncti; funđi ; quorum Animæ erant in cœlis. Aut si qui ipsos Angelos malit intelligere, sensus esse poterit, homines electos Deo per Christum reconciliatos, eadem opera cum Angelis Dei amicis quodammodo reconciliari : quemadmodum Hebr. 12. 22, 23.
units.tr: Objection 1. Col. 1. 20: that through him he might reconcile all things to himself, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Therefore the angels also have been reconciled through Christ. Answer: By "things in heaven" may be understood the faithful who had already died, whose souls were in heaven. Or if anyone prefers to understand the angels themselves, the sense can be that the elect men, reconciled to God through Christ, are at the same time in some way reconciled with the friendly angels of God, as in Heb. 12. 22, 23.

units.la: Obj. 2. Col. 2. 10. Christus dicitur Caput omnis imperii & potestatis. Ergo etiam Angelorum. Consequenter eorum quoque Mediator est. Resp. Christus gloria & potestate supra omnes creaturas longè evectus est ; quæ proinde alacriter & promte ipsi debent inservire ; etiam Angeli. Verum inde non sequitur, Ipsum esse Mediatorem Angelorum.
units.tr: Objection 2. Col. 2. 10: Christ is called the head of every rule and authority. Therefore also of the angels, and consequently he is their Mediator too. Answer: Christ is exalted far above all creatures in glory and power, so they ought to serve him readily and promptly, the angels too. But it does not follow from this that he is the Mediator of the angels.

units.la: XXVIII. Mediator ille ab æterno quidem præordinatus fuit decreto Dei, ad munus Mediatorium : unde præcognitus dicitur ante jacta mundi fundamenta; 1 Petr. 1. 20. & nos in Ipso electi ante jactum mundi fundamentum ; Eph. 1. 4. Attamen actu demum cœpit esse Mediator statim post lapsum Adamis ubi Ipse etiam talis declaratus est in prima Euangelii promulgatione ; Gen. 3. 15. Et tunc demum existebant partes, inter quas Mediatorem intervenire necesse erat ; Homines miseri, & Deus per eorum inobedientiam offensus, sed per Mediatorem illum electis reconciliari volens.
units.tr: XXVIII. That Mediator was indeed foreordained from eternity by the decree of God for the mediatorial office, whence he is said to be "foreknown before the foundation of the world" (1 Pet. 1. 20), and we are "chosen in him before the foundation of the world" (Eph. 1. 4). Yet he actually began to be Mediator immediately after the fall of Adam, when he was also declared to be such in the first proclamation of the gospel: Gen. 3. 15. And only then did there exist the parties between whom a mediator had to intervene: miserable men, and God offended by their disobedience, yet willing to be reconciled to the elect through that Mediator.

units.la: Consequenter 1. ὁ Λόγος peccata electorum jam tum fuscepera expiauda Sacrificio sui corporis, suo tempore adaptandi. Vide factum illud. Jef. 53. 10. Si posuerit pro reatu, &c. Et de Sacerdotio ; Psal. 110. 4. xl. 7, 8, 9. cum Hebr. x. 5, 7, 10. Item Zach. 1. 8. 10, 11, 12. Et Dan. ix. 17; Psal. 80. 15, 16, 18.
units.tr: Consequently: (1) the Word [ὁ Λόγος] had already undertaken the sins of the elect, to be atoned for by the sacrifice of his body, to be applied at its appointed time. See that deed: Isa. 53. 10, "If he shall make his soul an offering for sin," etc. And concerning the priesthood: Ps. 110. 4; 40. 7, 8, 9, compared with Heb. 10. 5, 7, 10. Likewise Zech. 1. 8, 10, 11, 12; Dan. 9. 17; Ps. 80. 15, 16, 18.

units.la: 2 Variis modis revelavit ea, quæ ad salutem consequendam requirebantur : 1 Petr. 1. 11. iij. 19. Gen. 18. 1, 2, 9, 10, 13, 14, 17, 21, 33. xxij. 1, 2, 11, 12. 15, 18. cum Joh. 8. 56, 58. &c.
units.tr: (2) He revealed in various ways those things which were required for obtaining salvation: 1 Pet. 1. 11; 3. 19; Gen. 18. 1, 2, 9, 10, 13, 14, 17, 21, 33; 22. 1, 2, 11, 12, 15, 18, compared with John 8. 56, 58, etc.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiam collegit, gubernavit, servavit : Gen. 48. 16. Exod. 23. 20, 23. Jef. 63. 9. cum 1 Cor. x. 4. 9. Psal.
units.tr: (3) He gathered, governed and preserved the Church: Gen. 48. 16; Exod. 23. 20, 23; Isa. 63. 9; compared with 1 Cor. 10. 4, 9; Ps.

units.la: 4. Fideles cum ipso spiritualem unionem & communionem habuerunt : 1 Cor. x. 4, 9. Sic justificati & salvati sunt: Gen. 15. 6. xxij, 17, 18. xlix, 10, 18. Act. x, 43. xv, 11. &c.
units.tr: (4) The faithful had a spiritual union and communion with him: 1 Cor. 10. 4, 9. Thus they were justified and saved: Gen. 15. 6; 22. 17, 18; 49. 10, 18; Acts 10. 43; 15. 11, etc.

units.la: Obj. Christus est Mediator secundum utramque naturam; ac proinde non fuit Mediator ante incarnationem. Resp. Hoc solum sequitur, quod incarnatio suo tempore necessario fieri debuerit; cum sine ea non potuerint peragi omnes actus muneris Mediatorii.
units.tr: Objection: Christ is Mediator according to both natures; therefore he was not Mediator before the incarnation. Answer: This only follows, that the incarnation had necessarily to take place at its appointed time, since without it none of the acts of the Mediatorial office could have been performed.

units.la: XXIX. Unus autem agnoscendus est Mediator; non plures: ut 1. diserte exponitur, 1 Tim. 2. 5. Similiter, Act. 4. 12. Neque aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est, per quod nos oportcat salvari. & 1 Cor. 3. 11. Nemo aliud fundamentum ponere potest, &c.
units.tr: XXIX. One Mediator, however, is to be acknowledged, not several; as is expressly set out in 1 Tim. 2:5. Similarly Acts 4:12, "Neither is there salvation in any other; for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved," and 1 Cor. 3:11, "For other foundation can no man lay," etc.

units.la: 2. Nulla talis persona datur præter Christum, qualis ad μεσίτευμα requiritur.
units.tr: 2. No such person is given besides Christ as the office of mediator (μεσίτευμα) requires.

units.la: 3. Nec alii competunt actiones, ad reconciliationem nostri cum Deo necessariæ.
units.tr: 3. Nor do the actions necessary for the reconciliation of us with God belong to anyone else.

units.la: 4. Fides in Ipsum solum, est unicum medium salutis percipiendæ: Joh. 3. 16, 18, 36. Marc. 16. 15, 16.
units.tr: 4. Faith in him alone is the only means of obtaining salvation: John 3:16, 18, 36; Mark 16:15, 16.

units.la: Pontificii perperam plures saltem Mediatores intercessionis statuunt: quod speciatim alibi refutabitur.
units.tr: The Papists wrongly set up several mediators of intercession at least; this will be refuted specifically elsewhere.

units.la: XXX. Titulo Sponsoris Dominus Jesus indicatur, se ipsum pro nobis obligasse, ad peragenda & sustinenda omnia, quæ ad nostri liberationem, & salutem pertinebant. Ita 1. ἐγγυῶς Hebr. 7. 22. Tanto melioris pacti Sponsor factus est Jesus. &c. Pacti nimirum, quo ipse spopondit, se pro nobis impleturum conditiones impetrandæ remissionis peccatorum, & vitæ æternæ. Prius Sacerdotem dixerat Apostolus; iste autem constituitur pro Hominibus in iis, quæ apud Deum agenda: Hebr. v. 1. Confer Sponsionem Pauli pro Onesimo; Philem. 18, 19. Iremq; loca Heb. x. 7, 10. Ps. xl. 8. 9. lxix. 5.
units.tr: XXX. By the title of Surety (Sponsor) the Lord Jesus is shown to have bound himself for us, to perform and undergo all things that pertained to our deliverance and salvation. So in the first place (ἐγγυῶς), Heb. 7:22, "By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament." That is, of the covenant by which he himself undertook to fulfil for us the conditions of obtaining the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. The Apostle had earlier called him a priest; but this one is appointed for men in those things that are to be done before God, Heb. 5:1. Compare Paul's surety for Onesimus, Philem. 18, 19; and the passages Heb. 10:7, 10; Ps. 40:8, 9; 69:5.

units.la: 2. Clare etiam indicatur Christi substitutio in locum nostrum, tanquam Sponsoris: sic enim dicitur Pro nobis passus & mortuus, ipse innocens & justus. Hebr. 2. 9. Ut Pro omnibus mortem gustaret. Joh. xi. 50. Moreretur pro populo. 2 Cor. 5. 15. Unus pro omnibus, ac si illi omnes essent mortui. Adde Luc. 22. 19. 20. 1 Cor. 11. 24, 25. Rom. 5. 7. 8. 1 Tim. 2. 6. Tit 2. 14. 1 Petr. 2. 21. iij. 18. iv, 1. Neque solum in hoc negotio usurpatur praepositio ὑπὲρ; sed etiam ἀντὶ, quae surrogationem aperte notat: ut Matth. 20. 28. Marc. x. 45. Ut det animam suam redemtionis pretium pro multis; ἀντὶ πολλῶν. Similiter quoque traditus dicitur propter peccata nostra. Rom. 4. 25. tanquam causam demeritoriam istarum perpessionum, ex hypothesi sponsionis.
units.tr: 2. Christ's substitution in our place, as Surety, is also clearly indicated: for he is said to have suffered and died for us, himself innocent and just. Heb. 2:9, "that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man"; John 11:50, "that he should die for the people"; 2 Cor. 5:15, "one died for all, then were all dead." Add Luke 22:19, 20; 1 Cor. 11:24, 25; Rom. 5:7, 8; 1 Tim. 2:6; Tit. 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:21; 3:18; 4:1. Nor is the preposition ὑπέρ alone used in this business, but also ἀντί, which plainly denotes substitution: as in Matt. 20:28 and Mark 10:45, "to give his life a ransom for many" (ἀντὶ πολλῶν). Likewise he is also said to have been "delivered for our sins," Rom. 4:25, as the meritorious cause of those sufferings, given the hypothesis of the suretyship.

units.la: 3. Eodem respectu dicitur peccata nostra tulisse in corpore suo. 1 Petr. 2. 24. & ipse justus multos justificare quorum iniquitates bajulaverit; Jef. 53. 11. Quin etiam incurrisse in eum poena omnium nostrum; ibid. verf. 6.
units.tr: 3. In the same respect it is said that he "bare our sins in his own body," 1 Pet. 2:24; and that he, the just one, "shall justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities," Isa. 53:11; and moreover that the punishment of us all fell upon him, ibid., verse 6.

units.la: 4. Apostolus emphatice, Gal. 3. 13. Christus nos redemit ab execratione Legis, dum pro nobis factus est execratio. Et 2 Cor. 5. 21. Fecit Deus ut qui peccatum non novit, pro nobis Peccatum esset, (h. e. ut poenas peccatis nostris debitas ferret;) ut nos efficeremur Justitia Dei in eo. Confer Rom. 4. 3, 5. 9, -11 22, -25. & v, 19.
units.tr: 4. The Apostle says emphatically, Gal. 3:13, "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us." And 2 Cor. 5:21, "God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us" (that is, that he might bear the punishments owed to our sins), "that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Compare Rom. 3:24, 25; 5:9–11, 22–25; and 5:19.

units.la: Obj. In debitis pecuniariis Sponsores admittuntur; cum brevis manus fictione, pecunia unius censeri possit fieri alterius: sed in poenis corporalibus, utpote propria persona perferendis, hoc locum non habet. Resp. Personae quidem peccatrices juxta rem Foederis Legalis erant in obligatione: sed facta ejus interpretatione κατ' ἐπιείκειαν, substitutio Sponsoris admissa est; qui poenas essentialiter easdem tulit, quas nos eramus promeriti, & durationis aeternitatem infinita dignitate sua compensavit.
units.tr: Objection: In pecuniary debts sureties are admitted, since by a fiction of a short hand the money of one can be reckoned as made the money of another; but in bodily punishments, which must be borne in one's own person, this has no place. Answer: The sinning persons were indeed bound under the legal covenant as to its substance; but, the law being interpreted by equity (κατ' ἐπιείκειαν), the substitution of a surety was admitted; who bore essentially the same punishments that we had deserved, and by his infinite dignity made up for the eternity of their duration.

units.la: XXXI. Redemtor, alias Vindex; Hebraice גֹּאֵל, Græce ἀπολυτρωτὴς, & ὁ ἐνομένος, dicitur. Sub V. T. specialiter גֹּאֵל appellari consueverat, qui jus redimendæ hæreditatis, & feminis suscitandi propinquo suo fine liberis defuncto habebat; juxta Levit. 25. 25, 26. Exemplum infigne occurrit Ruth. 2. 20. iij, 9, 12. iv, 1, 3, 6, 8, 14. Sic Christus, propinquus & frater noster, causam nostram, cum annexo ejus onere, in fe recepit; & persoluto liberationis pretio, quod per justitiam Dei debebatur, è captivitate & miseria spirituali nos redemit, atque in libertatem vindicavit. De hoc in V. T. Job. xix. 25. Ego novi Redemtorem meum vivere. Jef. 59. 20. Veniet ad Tzion Redemtor.
units.tr: XXXI. The Redeemer, otherwise called the Avenger; in Hebrew גֹּאֵל, in Greek ἀπολυτρωτής and ὁ ἐνομένος. Under the Old Testament the one who had the right to redeem an inheritance and to raise up seed for a deceased kinsman who had died childless was specially called the go'el, according to Lev. 25:25, 26. A notable example occurs in Ruth 2:20; 3:9, 12; 4:1, 3, 6, 8, 14. So Christ, our kinsman and brother, took up our cause together with its burden; and, having paid the price of deliverance which was owed by the justice of God, redeemed us from captivity and spiritual misery, and vindicated us into liberty. Of this in the Old Testament: Job 19:25, "I know that my Redeemer liveth." Isa. 59:20, "The Redeemer shall come to Zion."

units.la: 2. Clarius in N T. Rom. 3. 24 Justificantur gratis, ejus gratiâ, per Redemtionem factam in Christo Jesu. Eph. 1. 7 In quo habemus Redemtionem, per sanguinem ipsius, quod repetitur Col. 1. 14. Adde Tit. 2. 14. Hebr. 9. 12, 1 Petr. 1. 18, 19. In tribus locis prioribus est vox ἀπολύτρωσις, quam Socinus definit, Liberationem captivi e manu detinentis pretio detinenti dato. Sed per se patet, captivitatem spiritualem hic spectandam: (vide Jef. 52. 2. Eph. 4. 8. 2 Tim. 2. 26.) & talis pretii datonem qualis in poenis obtinet. Unde in locis allegatis expresse adjicitur sanguis Christi; itemque 1 Petr. 1. 18, 19. appellatio Agni, & quidem opposite ad aurum, argentum, &c. quibus alias inter homines Redemtio nonnunquam peragitur. His adde emphaticam ἀντίλυτρον expressionem. 1 Tim. 2. 5, 6. Confer Matth. 20. 28. Marc. x. 45: cum Pfal. 49. 8, 9.
units.tr: 2. More clearly in the New Testament: Rom. 3:24, "Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus"; Eph. 1:7, "In whom we have redemption through his blood," which is repeated at Col. 1:14. Add Tit. 2:14; Heb. 9:12; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19. In the first three passages the word is ἀπολύτρωσις, which Socinus defines as the liberation of a captive from the hand of the holder by a price paid to the holder. But it is plain in itself that spiritual captivity is to be considered here (see Isa. 52:2; Eph. 4:8; 2 Tim. 2:26), and a giving of a price such as obtains in punishments. Hence in the passages cited the blood of Christ is expressly added; likewise in 1 Pet. 1:18, 19 the designation of the Lamb, and indeed set in contrast to gold, silver, etc., by which among men redemption is at other times effected. To these add the emphatic expression ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. 2:5, 6. Compare Matt. 20:28; Mark 10:45 with Ps. 49:8, 9.

units.la: 3. Alia constructione Hebr. 9. 15. dicitur Mors Christi intercessisse ad Redemtionem transgressionum. Ita scil. notatur compensatio criminum, sive satisfactio pro iis.
units.tr: 3. In another construction, Heb. 9:15, the death of Christ is said to have intervened for the redemption of transgressions. Thus, namely, the compensation of crimes, or satisfaction for them, is noted.

units.la: 4. Huc etiam pertinent phrases æquipollentes; 1 Cor. 6. 20. vij, 23. Emtiesfis pretio. Act. 20. 28. Deus Ecclesiam proprio suo sanguine acquisivit. Adde Gal. 4. 4. 5. iij, 13. Joh. 6. 51.
units.tr: 4. To this also belong equivalent phrases: 1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23, "You are bought with a price." Acts 20:28, God "purchased the Church with his own blood." Add Gal. 4:4, 5; 3:13; John 6:51.

units.la: XXXII. Exc. Verbum Redimendi frequentissimè sumitur pro qualicunque liberatione. Resp. Impropria istius vocis significatio non adeo frequens est, quam quidem opinantur Adversarii: nam multis in locis, ut Exod. 15. 13. Deut. 7. 8. aliisque, ubi de liberatione Israelitarum ex Ægypto per Mosen agitur, (quæ redemptionis nostræ per Christum typus erat) adhibitum fuit, atque adeo recte consideratur λύτρον, redemptioni isti typicæ conveniens; Agnorum scil. Paschalium: Cum cæteroquin cædendi etiam fuissent ipsorum primogeniti; quibus deinde surrogati sunt Levitæ, & reliqui siclis æstimati ac redemti: Exod. 12. 12, 13; 22, 23, 27. xiij, 2. xxx, 12, 13. Num. 3. 47. viij, 14, 19. Atque hinc Moses redemptionis istius typicæ minister, typice etiam Αυτρωτής appellatur; Act. 7. 35. In aliis locis quam plurimis ipsius Christi Redemtio innuitur.
units.tr: XXXII. Objection: The word "to redeem" is most frequently taken for any kind of deliverance. Answer: The improper meaning of this word is not so frequent as the Adversaries suppose; for in many places, such as Exod. 15:13; Deut. 7:8, and others, where the deliverance of the Israelites out of Egypt through Moses is treated (which was a type of our redemption through Christ), it is used, and rightly so considered as a ransom (λύτρον) suited to that typical redemption, namely of the Paschal lambs; although otherwise their firstborn too would have been slain, for whom the Levites were then substituted, and the rest were valued at shekels and redeemed: Exod. 12:12, 13; 22:22, 23, 27; 13:2; 30:12, 13; Num. 3:47; 8:14, 19. And hence Moses, the minister of this typical redemption, is typically also called the redeemer (λυτρωτής): Acts 7:35. In very many other places the redemption of Christ himself is indicated.

units.la: Obj. 1. Dicimur à Diabolo captivi facti; 2 Tim. 2. 26. & metu mortis damnates servitutis, cujus ille habebat imperium; Hebr. 2. 14, 15. consequenter λύτρον non Deo, sed Diabolo fuisset persolvendum. Resp. Homo peccando obligatus erat, & Deo, & Diabolo: nam quantum ad culpam, Deum offenderat, & Diabolo se subdiderat, ei consentiens: quantum vero ad pœnam, Deo principaliter obligatus erat, ut Iudici; Diabolo tantum ut tortori: quapropter per respectum ad Deum justitia postulabat, ut Homo sic redimeretur; non autem per respectum ad Diabolum.
units.tr: Objection 1: We are said to have been made captives by the Devil, 2 Tim. 2:26, and to have been held in servitude through fear of death, over which he had dominion, Heb. 2:14, 15; consequently the ransom ought to have been paid not to God but to the Devil. Answer: Man by sinning was bound both to God and to the Devil: for as to guilt, he had offended God and had subjected himself to the Devil, consenting to him; but as to punishment, he was bound principally to God as Judge, and to the Devil only as torturer. Therefore justice, with respect to God, required that man be redeemed in this way; but not with respect to the Devil.

units.la: Obj. 2. Christus totus Dei fuit, aut (ex vestra sententia) ipse Deus summus: nihil igitur potuit Deo summo tradere & persolvere. &c. Resp. In debito pœnali non requiritur realis traditio & acceptio: sufficit pœnas ferri, & æstimari, in ordine ad justitiam punitivam; sicut etiam fit in damnatis. Obj. 3. Apoc. 5. 9. xiv. 4. & alibi, dicimur Deo emt per sanguinem Christi. At vero pretium non debetur nec persolvitur ei, cui res emta acquiritur. Ergo. Resp. Ante hanc ἀπολύτρωσιν Dominio ac Iudicio Dei procul dubio eramus subjecti: sed liberati sumus ab ipsius ira & justitia vindicativa, per Christi ἀντίλυτρον, in ordine ad istam justitiam. Summus autem finis est, ut ex illa miseria redemti, Deo serviamus liberali sanctitate ac justitia in gloriam Ipsius: Luc. 1. 74, 75. Rom. 6, 13, 16, 19, 22, 23. Hebr. 9. 14.
units.tr: Objection 2: Christ belonged wholly to God, or (by your view) is himself the supreme God; therefore he could hand over and pay nothing to the supreme God, etc. Reply: In a penal debt, a real handing over and acceptance are not required. It is enough that penalties are borne and reckoned in relation to punitive justice, as also happens with the damned. Objection 3: Rev. 5:9 and 14:4, and elsewhere, say that we are bought to God by the blood of Christ. But a price is not owed or paid to the one to whom the purchased thing is acquired. Therefore, etc. Reply: Before this redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] we were without doubt subject to the dominion and judgment of God, but we have been freed from his wrath and vindictive justice through Christ's counter-price [ἀντίλυτρον], in relation to that justice. The chief end, however, is that, redeemed from that misery, we should serve God in free holiness and righteousness, to his glory: Luke 1:74, 75; Rom. 6:13, 16, 19, 22, 23; Heb. 9:14.

units.la: XXXIII. Salvatorem sonat nomen proprium Iesu: de quo sup. th. 2.
units.tr: XXXIII. The proper name Jesus means Savior: on which see above, thesis 2.

units.la: Hic autem est Salvator verus, persectus, & unicus. Verum dicimus, opposite ad typos V. T. quorum veritas per ipsum praestita est: Ioh. 1. 17. & nominatim ad Iesum illum alias Iosuam, filium Nun, qui Israelitas salvos introduxit in terram Canaan; Hebr. 4. 8. cum Deut. 31. 23. Ios. 1. 2, 6. Itemque ad alterum, filium Iozedek, Sacerdotem maximum, quo in sacris Antec essore facta est restitutio ex captivitate Babylonica; Esr. 3. 1, 2. Zach. 3. 1, 4, 5.
units.tr: Here, then, is the true, perfect, and only Savior. We say true, as opposed to the types of the Old Testament, whose truth has been brought about by him: John 1:17, and especially in reference to that Jesus, otherwise called Joshua, son of Nun, who brought the Israelites safe into the land of Canaan (Heb. 4:8, with Deut. 31:23; Josh. 1:2, 6), and likewise to the other, the son of Jozadak, the high priest, under whom, in the sacred assembly, the restoration from the Babylonian captivity took place (Ezra 3:1, 2; Zech. 3:1, 4, 5).

units.la: Perfectum; ratione termini a quo, omnis miseriae spiritualis; & termini ad quem, omnimodae salutis, tum impetratae, tum applicatae: Hebr. 7. 25. Servare perfecte potest eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum. Col. 2. 9, 10. In eo inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter: Et estis in eo completi. 2 Petr. 1. 3. Prout Divina vis ipsius omnia nobis donavit, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent. Adde Hebr. x. 24. Rom. 8.
units.tr: Perfect: with respect to the starting point, from all spiritual misery; and with respect to the goal, to all salvation, both obtained and applied: Heb. 7:25, He is able to save perfectly those who come to God through him. Col. 2:9, 10, In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and you are complete in him. 2 Pet. 1:3, since his divine power has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness. Add Heb. 10:24; Rom. 8.
John 1:16; 1 John 1:7.

units.la: Unicum, ob rationes allegatas sup. th. 29. Perpetuam ergo Pontificii salutem suam, tum in propriis, tum in aliorum hominum satisfactionibus ac meritis quaerunt; quasi non foret in nostro Iesu omnis plenitudo. Gal. 5. 4. Inanes facti estis, separati a Christo, quicunque per legem justificamini; & a gratia excidistis. Adde Isef. 55. 2. Ierem. 2. 13. Obj. 1 Tim. 4. 16. Intentus esto tibi ipsi, & doctrinæ & permane in istis: id enim si feceris, & te ipsum servabis, & eos qui te audierint. Ergo etiam alii servant, &c. Ref. Non salutem impetrando, nec principaliter applicando: sed per gratiam Dei in Christo, viam ingrediendo, & aliis monstrando, quâ itur ad possessionem ac fruitionem salutis: Eph. 2. 8, 9. 2 Cor. 5. 19, 20. 1, iij. 5.
units.tr: Only, for the reasons alleged above, th. 29. Therefore the Papists seek their salvation, both in their own satisfactions and merits and in those of other men, as if there were not in our Jesus all fullness. Gal. 5:4, You are emptied of Christ, all who are justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace. Add Isa. 55:2; Jer. 2:13. Objection: 1 Tim. 4:16, Take heed to yourself and to the teaching, and continue in these things; for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. Therefore others also save, etc. Answer: Not by obtaining salvation, nor by applying it as a principal cause, but by entering the way through the grace of God in Christ, and by showing to others the way by which one goes to the possession and enjoyment of salvation: Eph. 2:8, 9; 2 Cor. 5:19, 20; 1 Tim. 4:5.

units.la: XXXIV. Superest titulus Unctionis; unde agnomē Christi: sup. th 1. Unctio cerimonialis sub V.T. ad triplex officium legitur adhibita; Propheticum Reg. 19. 16. Sacerdotale; Exod 30. 30. Lev. 8. 12. & Regium; 1 Sam. 10, 1. xvj. 13. 1 Reg. 19. 15. 16. Sic Divina illorum ordinatio ad ista officia, & simul speciali pro re nata donorum collatio, quasi peculiari sacramento fuit obsignata.
units.tr: XXXIV. There remains the title Anointed, from which comes the name Christ: see above, th. 1. In the Old Testament, anointing in the ceremonial sense is found used for three offices: the prophetic (1 Kings 19:16); the priestly (Exod. 30:30; Lev. 8:12); and the royal (1 Sam. 10:1; 16:13; 1 Kings 19:15, 16). So God's appointment of those men to these offices, and at the same time the special bestowal of gifts as occasion required, was, as it were, sealed with a peculiar sacrament.

units.la: Christus autem conjunctim est Propheta: Deut. 18. 15. Prophetam e medio tui, e fratribus tuis, sicut ego sum, suscitabit tibi Iehovah Deus tuus: ei auscultate. quod Christo applicatur, Act. 3. 22. Item Ies. 61. 1, 2. Spiritus Domini Iehovi est super me, eo quod Unxit Iehovah me, ad evangelizandum mansuetis, ad proclamandum captivis libertatem, &c. Confer Luc. 4. 16, 21.
units.tr: Now Christ is at once Prophet: Deut. 18:15, The LORD your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your midst, from your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen. This is applied to Christ in Acts 3:22. Likewise Isa. 61:1, 2, The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to preach good news to the meek, to proclaim liberty to the captives, etc. Compare Luke 4:16, 21.

units.la: Sacerdos; Psal. 110. 4. Iuravit Iehovah; Tu es Sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchizedek, cum Hebr. 7. 15, 17; 24, 26. Similiter Zach. 6. 12. 13. Sic ait Iehovah: Ecce virum, cujus nomen est GERMEN: Eritque Sacerdos in solio suo, &c.
units.tr: Priest: Ps. 110:4, The LORD has sworn, You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, with Heb. 7:15, 17, 24, 26. Similarly Zech. 6:12, 13, Thus says the LORD: Behold the man whose name is THE BRANCH; and he shall be priest on his throne, etc.

units.la: Rex: Psal. 2. 6. Ego inungens Regem meum, præfeci Tzioni. Zach. 9. 9. Exulta, Filia Tzionis! ecce Rex tuus adveniet tibi, justus, & salute præditus. Apoc. 17. 14. Agnus vincet eos, quoniam Rex Regum est.
units.tr: King: Ps. 2:6, I have anointed my King and set him over Zion. Zech. 9:9, Rejoice, daughter of Zion! Behold, your King comes to you, just and endowed with salvation. Rev. 17:14, The Lamb will conquer them, because he is King of kings.

units.la: Sic ergo Christus necessitati nostræ opitulatur plenissime: Ignorantiæ, docendo, ut Propheta; Reatui, expiando, & justitiam impetrando, ut Sacerdos; reliquis malis tristibus, ab iis nos eripiendo, & salutem conferendo, ut Rex: 1 Cor. 1. 30. Ordine naturæ primum est Munus Sacerdotale, quo salus nobis impetratur: tur: succedit Propheticum, quo haec impetrata annunciatur, & moraliter revelatur: sequitur Regium, quo eadem applicatur reali efficacia. De Prophetico tamen tractari solet primo loco, quia ipsum ante alia nobis percipitur, & nos in reliquorum notitiam ducit.
units.tr: Thus Christ meets our need most fully: in ignorance, by teaching, as Prophet; in guilt, by atoning and obtaining righteousness, as Priest; and in the other sad evils, by rescuing us from them and conferring salvation, as King (1 Cor. 1:30). In the order of nature the priestly office comes first, by which salvation is obtained for us; the prophetic follows, by which these obtained benefits are announced and morally revealed; and then the royal, by which the same benefits are applied with real efficacy. Yet the prophetic office is usually treated first, because it is perceived by us before the others and leads us to the knowledge of them.

units.la: XXXV. Munus ergo Christi Propheticum est, quo ipse sapientia rerum Divinarum instructissimus, eandem fideliter & efficaciter docet, praecipue populum suum, ad ejus salutem, & Dei gloriam. Hinc κατ' ἐξοχὴν Doctor appellatur; Matth. 23. 8, 10. & Apostolus professionis nostrae; Hebr. 3. 1. Nec mirum, cum ipse sit ὁ Λόγος; Joh. 1. 1, 14. & Sapientia hypostatica; Prov. 8. 1. & seqq. Consequenter Prophetia aliter omnino competit Christo, quam ullis aliis Prophetis: scil. non tantum per modum actus secundi transeuntis; sed per modum habitus semper in ipso manentis: non ex principio externo, sed interno Sp. S. qui ipse est Spiritus Filii; Gal. 4. 6. Unde arcana Dei ad instructionem populi docere potuit, quoties & quantum ipse voluit. Joh. 3. 12, 13. Si terrena dixero vobis, & non creditis, quomodo si dixero vobis coelestia, credetis? Nullus enim ascendit in coelum, nisi qui descendit a coelo; nempe Filius hominis qui est in coelo. 34. Is demum quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur; non enim huic admetitur Deus Spiritum. Sic ille Summus fuit Propheta: reliqui tantum subordinati; & ab ipso, ac ipsius Spiritu, acceperunt revelationes, quando & quantum ipsi placuit: Jerem. 42. 7, -. 1 Petr. 1. 10, 11, 12.
units.tr: XXXV. The office of Christ, then, is prophetic, by which he himself, most fully instructed in the wisdom of divine things, teaches the same faithfully and effectively, especially to his own people, for their salvation and the glory of God. Hence he is called the Teacher par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] (Matt. 23:8, 10), and the Apostle of our profession (Heb. 3:1). Nor is this surprising, since he is the Word [Λόγος] (John 1:1, 14) and hypostatic Wisdom (Prov. 8:1 ff.). Consequently prophecy belongs to Christ in a way entirely different from any other prophets: namely, not merely by way of a transient second act, but by way of a habit that always remains in him; not from an external principle, but from the internal Holy Spirit, who is himself the Spirit of the Son (Gal. 4:6). Hence he could teach the hidden things of God for the instruction of the people, as often and as much as he himself willed. John 3:12, 13, If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? For no one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, namely the Son of Man who is in heaven. 34: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God does not give him the Spirit by measure. So that Highest One was the Prophet; the rest were only subordinate, and from him and by his Spirit they received revelations, when and as much as it pleased him (Jer. 42:7; 1 Pet. 1:10, 11, 12).

units.la: XXXVI. Docuit autem omnia ad salutem necessaria, sive fidem spectes, sive mores vivendi: Evangelium ut ipse implevit, sic impletum primus praedicavit. Hebr. 2. 3. Quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem; quae cum primum enarrari coepit per ipsum Dominum, &c. speciatim vero prophetias ac typos V. T. in seipso compleri clare demonstravit: & Legê morale a corruptelis Pharisaeorum probe vindicata, unice observandam docuit.
units.tr: XXXVI. He taught, moreover, all things necessary for salvation, whether you look to faith or to the conduct of life. As he himself fulfilled the Gospel, so he was the first to preach what had been fulfilled. Heb. 2:3, How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which, when it was first spoken through the Lord himself, etc. In particular he clearly demonstrated that the prophecies and types of the Old Testament were fulfilled in himself; and he taught that the moral law, properly freed from the corruptions of the Pharisees, was to be observed alone.

units.la: Ipse in hoc munere summam praestitit fidelitatem. Fidelis dicitur, Hebr. 3. 2. Viam Dei in veritate docuit, fatentibus adversariis; Matth. 22. 16. Hinc tam pathetice. xxiij. 37. Quoties volui congregare liberos tuos, ut gallina congregat pullos suos! Adjunxit quoque efficaciam tum moralem, docendo solide, prudenter, familiariter, cum gratia & auctoritate: Matth. 7. 29. Ioh. 7. 45, 46. Iremque doctrinam suam multis miraculis confirmando; Matth. 4. 23, 24. xj. 4,5. Joh. 5. 19, 20, 21, 36. x, 37, 38. tum insuper realem intellectum subjective illuminando ad veritatem agnoscendam; & voluntatem flectendo, ad obsequium: potissimum per veram regenerationem & sanctificationem, ad fidem salvificam & sanctimoniam minime simulatam; Act. 5. 31. xvj. 14. Luc. 17. 5. Eph: 1, 17, 18.
units.tr: In this office he showed the highest faithfulness. He is called faithful (Heb. 3:2). He taught the way of God in truth, as even his adversaries confessed (Matt. 22:16). Hence so movingly (Matt. 23:37): How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks! He also added efficacy, both moral, by teaching soundly, prudently, familiarly, with grace and authority (Matt. 7:29; John 7:45, 46); and by confirming his teaching with many miracles (Matt. 4:23, 24; 11:4, 5; John 5:19, 20, 21, 36; 10:37, 38); and moreover real, by subjectively illuminating the intellect to recognise the truth, and by bending the will to obedience, chiefly through true regeneration and sanctification, to saving faith and holiness that is not feigned (Acts 5:31; 16:14; Luke 17:5; Eph. 1:17, 18).

units.la: Caeterum doctrinam suam tum immediate propositit; non intercedete creaturae alicujus opera: quemadmodum sub V. T. Patriarchis & Prophetis ipse nonnunquam apparuit, & mysteria salutis revelavit; Gen. 18, 22. cum Joh. 8. 56. atque iterum in diebus carnis suae Discipulos suos, aliosque familiariter docuit: Matth. 4. 17, 18; 23. v, 1, -, Luc. 4. 15, -22. tum mediate, per Ministros, sive extraordinarios, sive ordinarios: Eph. 4, 11, 12. rarius per Angelos: Apoc. 1. 1. Luc. 2. 8, -14 Hebr. 22. 2. Interna autem realiter efficax operatio fidei & resipiscentiae ab ipso Christo per Spiritum suum, procedit semper immediate; quanquam ad externam & moralem operationem, causae illae instrumentales mediae accedunt:
units.tr: Moreover, he set forth his teaching both immediately, without the intervention of any creature's work, just as under the patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament he sometimes appeared in person and revealed the mysteries of salvation (Gen. 18:22 with John 8:56), and again in the days of his flesh he taught his disciples and others familiarly (Matt. 4:17, 18; 23:1; Luke 4:15, 22); and mediately, through ministers, whether extraordinary or ordinary (Eph. 4:11, 12), and more rarely through angels (Rev. 1:1; Luke 2:8, 14; Heb. 2:2). But the inward, really effective operation of faith and repentance always proceeds immediately from Christ himself through his Spirit, although those intermediate instrumental causes come in for the outward and moral operation.

units.la: XXXVII. Munus Christi Sacerdotale, ordinatum est ad peccata nostra expianda; & favorem compla- centiae Divinae nobis conciliandum.
units.tr: XXXVII. The priestly office of Christ is ordained to expiate our sins and to win for us the favour of the divine good pleasure.

units.la: Huc pertinet generalis Descriptio, Hebr. 5, 1. Omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumtus pro hominibus constituitur in iis quae apud Deum agenda sunt, ut offerat dona & victimas pro peccatis.
