Confer sup. th. 34. ubi modo probavimus, Christum Sacerdotem esse. Sed nunc contra Socinianos afferimus amplius, Christum esse verum sacerdotem: atque hoc ipsius officium vere distinctum, ut à Prophetico, sic à Regio. Nam
units.tr: To this belongs the general description in Heb. 5:1: "Every high priest, taken from among men, is appointed for men in those things which pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins." See above, thesis 34, where we have just proved that Christ is a priest. But now against the Socinians we assert further that Christ is a true priest, and that this office of his is truly distinct, as from the prophetic, so from the kingly. For

units.la: 1. In Christo est veritas omnium eorum, quæ Lege Cerimoniali præfigurabantur: Iob. 1, 17. Col. 2. 17. Hebr. 10. 1. Ergo verum Sacerdotium, & veri actus Sacerdotalis in ipso agnosci debent, ex Sacerdotio, & actibus Sacerdotalibus typicis V. T.
units.tr: 1. In Christ is the truth of all those things which were foreshadowed by the ceremonial law (John 1:17; Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1). Therefore the true priesthood and the true priestly acts must be recognised in him, from the priesthood and the typical priestly acts of the Old Testament.

units.la: 2. Hebr. 5. 1 describitur verus ac proprie dictus Pontifex: atque ista descriptio mox Christo applicatur, verf. 5 -9. Similiter fere, viij. 3. Omnis Pontifex ad offerenda dona & victimas constituitur: Unde necesse fuit, Hunc quoque habere quod offerret.
units.tr: 2. In Heb. 5:1 a true and properly so-called high priest is described, and this description is soon applied to Christ, vv. 5–9. Similarly, almost, in 8:3: "Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices." Hence it was necessary that "this one also have something to offer."

units.la: 3. Christus est Sacerdos secundum ordinem, non Aharonis, sed Melchizedeki, & quidem talis cum juramento constitutus: Hebr. 7. 21. Ergo verus & proprie dictus. Fideles enim sub N. T. qui metaphorice Sacerdotes appellantur, nulli ordini accensentur. Et siquidem non ipsa veritas, sed similitudo solum spectaretur, certe Christus similitudinem satis insignem habet cum Sacerdotibus Aharonicis.
units.tr: 3. Christ is a priest according to the order not of Aaron but of Melchizedek, and indeed one constituted with an oath (Heb. 7:21). Therefore he is a true and properly so-called priest. For believers under the New Testament, who are called priests metaphorically, are not enrolled in any order. And if it were not the truth itself but only the likeness that was in view, Christ certainly has a very striking likeness to the Aaronic priests.

units.la: 4. Apostolus Hebr. 7. & seqq. ex instituto probat, Christum in ratione Sacerdotii longe præstantiorem esse Sacerdotibus Legalibus. Sed metaphoricus Sacerdos non potest esse perfectior vero Sacerdote in ratione ipsius Sacerdotii; cum ista veritate destituatur.
units.tr: 4. The Apostle in Heb. 7 and following sets out to prove that Christ, in the matter of priesthood, is far superior to the legal priests. But a metaphorical priest cannot be more perfect than a true priest in the very nature of the priesthood, since he is destitute of that truth.

units.la: Obj. 1. Hebr. 3. 1. duo solum officia Christi commemorantur; Propheticum & Sacerdotale: Ergo Sacerdotale non est reipsa distinctum à Regio. Resp. Nego consequentiam: nam & Regium ei tribuitur, tum alibi, tum Hebr. 1. 2, 8, 13. & actus muneris Regii plane differunt ab actibus muneris Sacerdotalis.
units.tr: Objection 1. Heb. 3:1 mentions only two offices of Christ, the prophetic and the priestly. Therefore the priestly is not really distinct from the kingly. Answer: I deny the consequence. For the kingly office is also ascribed to him, both elsewhere and in Heb. 1:2, 8, 13; and the acts of the kingly office plainly differ from the acts of the priestly office.

units.la: Obj. 2. Sacerdotio substernitur, quod Christus sit Filius Dei; idem alibi Regno substernitur: Ergo. Resp. Iterum nulla est consequentia: eadem illa excellentia præprærequirebatur in utroque ilto officio; imo etiam in Prophetico ejus munere, ad salutarem effectum.
units.tr: Objection 2. The priesthood is grounded in the fact that Christ is the Son of God; the same is grounded elsewhere in the kingship. Therefore... Answer: Again there is no consequence. The same excellence was required in each of those offices, and indeed in his prophetic office too, for its saving effect.

units.la: XXXVIII. Typi autem respectu istius officii suerunt, non solum Summus Sacerdos V. T. ex ordine Levitico; & specialiter extra eum ordinem Melchizedek: sed etiam Sacerdotes reliqui. Confer sup. cap. 2. th.24,25,26. Hos enim non esse hic omittendos, quemadmodum & reliqua sacra expiatoria præter anniversaria & stata illa, quæ pro toto populo fiebant, contra Socinianos etiam probamus:
units.tr: XXXVIII. The types with respect to this office were not only the high priest of the Old Testament from the Levitical order, and specially, outside that order, Melchizedek, but also the other priests. See above, chapter 2, theses 24, 25, 26. For we also prove against the Socinians that these are not to be omitted here, as neither are the other expiatory sacred rites apart from those annual and fixed ones which were performed for the whole people:

units.la: 1. Quia Hebr. 9. 13. omnis omnino carnalis per victimas purificatio, quæ in conscientia non poterat consummare cultorem cum spirituali purgatione Christi conferatur; cujus sanguis nos purgat ab omni peccato. Neque enim Apostolus in specie tantum agit de sanguine victimarum in anniversario expiationis sacrificio; quem sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum appellat, verf. 12. sed in genere de omnibus victimis & purgationibus V. T. recensendo sanguinem taurorum, & hircorum, & cinerem juvencæ, verf. 13. Vide quæ sequuntur verf. 21. &c.
units.tr: 1. Because in Heb. 9:13 all carnal purification by victims, which could not perfect the worshipper in conscience, is compared with the spiritual cleansing of Christ, whose blood cleanses us from every sin. For the Apostole does not speak only in particular of the blood of the victims in the annual sacrifice of atonement, which he calls the blood of "bulls and goats" (v. 12), but in general, enumerating all the victims and purifications of the Old Testament, the blood of "bulls and goats" and "the ashes of a heifer" (v. 13). See what follows, v. 21, etc.

units.la: 2. Quia Hebr. 10.1. Lex cerimonialis in universum dicitur obtinuisse umbram futurorum bonorum. & verf. 5,6,8. nominantur, Sacrificium, Oblatio, Holocautomata, & Hostia pro peccato; quæ certe latius patent anniversariis iltis & statis sacris: quod autem de iis negatur, id unicæ oblationi corporis Christi tribuitur verf. 10. Ac deinceps verf 11. Apostolus de omni Sacerdote universim loquitur, qui quotidie (N. B) adstat, sacram functionem obiens, & eadem offerens hostias quæ nunquam possint auferre peccata: Christum vero asserit, una pro peccatis in perpetuum oblata victima, consedisse ad dextram Dei, verf. 12.
units.tr: 2. Because in Heb. 10:1 the ceremonial law is said generally to have "a shadow of good things to come"; and in vv. 5, 6, 8 are named "sacrifice, offering, burnt offerings, and sin offering," which certainly extend more widely than those annual and fixed sacred rites. What is denied of them, however, is ascribed to "the one offering of the body of Christ" (v. 10). And thereafter in v. 11 the Apostle speaks of every priest in general, who "daily" (note this) "stands ministering and offering often the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins"; but he asserts that Christ, having offered one victim for sins for ever, "sat down at the right hand of God" (v. 12).

units.la: 3. Quia similiter Col. 2, 17. omnia & singula Legis cerimonialis instituta, dicuntur umbra rerum futurarum; corpus autem Christi: Itemque Job. 1, 17. Lex per Mosen data; gratia autem & veritas per Iesum Christum facta. Consequenter in omnibus istis ratio typi agnoscenda est; nec sola sacrificia summi Sacerdotis stata & anniversaria pro typis admittenda.
units.tr: 3. Because likewise in Col. 2:17 all and each of the institutions of the ceremonial law are called "a shadow of things to come," whereas the body is Christ's; and likewise in John 1:17, "the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Consequently in all these the nature of a type is to be recognised; and not only the stated and annual sacrifices of the high priest are to be admitted as types.

units.la: 4. Agni Paschales, potissimum in prima institutione, vim aliquam typice expiatoriam habuerunt; Exod. 12, 13, 22, 23, 27. cujus memoria quotannis recolebatur: atque interim Christus præfigurabatur; 1 Cor. 5. 7. Ioh. 19. 36. Ergo non subsistendum in solis illis sacrificiis anniversariis summi Sacerdotis, & statis illis quæ reputant Sociniani.
units.tr: 4. The Paschal lambs, especially in their first institution, had a certain typical expiatory force (Exod. 12:13, 22, 23, 27), and their memory was renewed every year; and meanwhile Christ was foreshadowed (1 Cor. 5:7; John 19:36). Therefore one must not rest in those annual sacrifices of the high priest alone, and those fixed rites which the Socinians reckon up.

units.la: XXXIX. Interim haud gravate concedimus, illustrioris typi rationem fuisse in Summo Sacerdote: maxime autem in Melchisedeko. 1. Quia ipsum hujus nomen notat Regem justitiæ: Christus vero justus, nos sua justitia constituit justos: Ies. 53. 11. Ierem. 13, 6. 1 Cor. 1. 30. 2. v. 21.
units.tr: XXXIX. Meanwhile we readily concede that the more illustrious type was in the high priest, but most of all in Melchizedek. 1. Because his very name signifies "King of righteousness"; and Christ, being righteous, makes us righteous by his righteousness (Isa. 53:11; Jer. 23:6; 1 Cor. 1:30; 2 Cor. 5:21).

units.la: 2. Quia ipse erat Rex Salem, h. e. Pacis. At Christus vere est Princeps pacis; Ies. 9. 5. & pax nostra Eph. 2. 14.
units.tr: 2. Because he himself was "King of Salem," that is, of peace. But Christ is truly the "Prince of Peace" (Isa. 9:5), and "our peace" (Eph. 2:14).

units.la: 3. Quia simul erat Rex hominum, & Dei Sacerdos. Idem de Christo dicendum, juxta th. 34.
units.tr: 3. Because he was at the same time king of men and priest of God. The same is to be said of Christ, according to thesis 34.

units.la: 4. Quia Abrahamo benedixit, & decimas ab eo accepit, atque adeo ab ipso Levi in lumbis ejus. Hoc enim quoque pertinuit ad eminentiam Christi præfigurandam: Hebr. 7. 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10.
units.tr: 4. Because he blessed Abraham and received tithes from him, and so Levi himself in the loins of Abraham. For this also pertained to foreshadowing the eminence of Christ (Heb. 7:4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10).

units.la: 5. Quia nec ejus genealogia, nec ætas, usquam commemoratur: nam & Christi generatio, præsertim Divina est ineffabilis; atque item æterna duratio.
units.tr: 5. Because neither his genealogy nor his age is recorded anywhere; for both the generation of Christ, especially the divine, is ineffable, and likewise his eternal duration.

units.la: 6. Quia denique nullos, vel Antecessores, vel Successores, in Sacerdotio habuit: sic enim & Christus unicus est Sacerdos, peccata nostra vere expians, & conscientias mundans, quoad statum internum & æternum; quod nulli vel ante, vel post eum competit; Hebr. 13. 8. cum 10, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12. vij. 23, 24.
units.tr: 6. Because finally he had no predecessors or successors in the priesthood. So too Christ is the sole priest, truly expiating our sins and cleansing consciences, as to his internal and eternal state; which belongs to no one either before or after him (Heb. 13:8, with 10:2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12; 7:23, 24).

units.la: XL. Actus Sacerdotales potissimum sunt Oblatio &
units.tr: XL. The priestly acts are chiefly oblation and

units.la: Intercessio. Oblatio est Actus Christi Sacerdotalis, quo se ipsum sanctissimum, nobisque conjunctissimum, suscepto in se omni nostro reatu, semel in cruce per Sp. Sanctum Deo obtulit; ad faciendam peccatorum nostrorum expiationem, & impetrandam remissionem iniquitatum æternam. Hinc Eph.5.2. Christus tradidit semet ipsum pro nobis oblationem ac victimam Deo, in odorem bonæ fragantiæ. Hebr. 9.14. Quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum se ipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus ad colendum Deum vivum?
units.tr: intercession. Oblation is the priestly act of Christ by which, once on the cross, he offered himself, most holy and most closely joined to us, having taken upon himself all our guilt, to God through the Holy Spirit, to make expiation for our sins and to obtain the eternal remission of iniquities. Hence: Eph. 5.2. Christ gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God, as a fragrant odour of sweet smell. Heb. 9.14. How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

units.la: Christus autem idem Sacerdos fuit secundum utramque naturam conjunctim: Hebr.5.6,7. cum Psal.110.4. Sacrificium; secundum humanam tantum: unde speciatim Corpus exprimitur, Hebr. x. 5. 10. 1 Petr.2.24. Col. 1.21,22. Sanguis, Col. 1.20. Hebr. 9.12. xiij, 12. & Anima Isef. 53.10. Matth. xx.28. Ac denique Altare, secundum Divinam naturam proprie; cum ab eâ processerit sanctificatio & valor Sacrificii; Hebr. 9.14. xiij,10,12,15. cum Matth.23.19. & Joh. 17,19.
units.tr: Christ was the same Priest according to both natures together: Heb. 5.6, 7, with Ps. 110.4; Sacrifice. According to the human nature alone, the body is specifically named: Heb. 10.5, 10; 1 Pet. 2.24; Col. 1.21, 22; the blood: Col. 1.20; Heb. 9.12; 13.12; and the soul: Isa. 53.10; Matt. 20.28. Finally, the Altar belongs properly to the divine nature, since from it came the sanctification and value of the sacrifice: Heb. 9.14; 13.10, 12, 15, with Matt. 23.19 and John 17.19.

units.la: XLI. Unica duntaxat est oblatio Christi, quam ipse peregit in Cruce: unde 1. Hebr. 9.11,12. Christus per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium æternam redemtionem nactus. Vide porro verf. 15,-18; 22,23.
units.tr: XLI. The oblation of Christ is unique, the one he accomplished on the Cross. Hence, (1) Heb. 9.11, 12: Christ entered once for all into the holy place through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. See further vv. 15–18, 22, 23.

units.la: 2. Iterum verf. 25,-28. Neque ut sæpe offerat semet ipsum: -sed nunc semel, - ad peccatum per immolationem sui ipsius in medio tollendum, factus est manifestus. Christus semel oblatus, &c.
units.tr: (2) Again, vv. 25–28: Nor that he should offer himself often, but now once, at the end of the ages, he has appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Christ, offered once, etc.

units.la: 3. Similiter x. 10. -Sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factam.
units.tr: (3) Similarly, x. 10: We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

units.la: Deinde 4. verf. 12. Una pro peccatis oblata in perpetuum victima, consedit ad dextram Dei, & verf. 14. Unica enim oblatione consummavit in perpetuum eos quisanctificantur.
units.tr: Then (4), vv. 12, 14: He offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, and sat down at the right hand of God; for by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified.

units.la: Sociniani contra negant, Christum in terris vere Sacerdotem fuisse, ibique Sacrificium obtulisse: sed passiones & mortem ejus putant fuisse conditionem tantum præcedaneam, ad functionem Sacerdotalem in Cœlis demum peragendam.
units.tr: The Socinians deny on the contrary that Christ was truly a Priest on earth and offered sacrifice there; they hold that his sufferings and death were only a preceding condition, the priestly function being completed later in heaven.

units.la: Obj. 1. Hebr. 7. 26. Pontifex noster sublimior cœlis evadere debuit: cum alioquin, Si esset in terra, ne Sacerdos quidem esset; viij. 4. Ergo, &c. Resp. Nihil inde colligitur; nisi quod Christus, ut functiones suas Sacerdotales plene obiret, cœleste sacrarium, ad peragendam Intercessionem, debuerit ingredi. Nam si post oblatum sacrificium semper in terris mansisset, ibique omnem functionem sacerdotalem absolvisset; Sacerdotium ipsius, nec Levitico præstantius fuisset, nec efficacius.
units.tr: Objection 1. Heb. 7.26. Our High Priest had to become higher than the heavens, since otherwise, if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest; 8.4. Therefore, etc. Answer. Nothing follows from this except that Christ, in order to discharge his priestly functions fully, had to enter the heavenly sanctuary to carry out intercession. For if after offering the sacrifice he had always remained on earth and there completed every priestly function, his priesthood would be neither more excellent nor more effective than the Levitical.

units.la: Obj. 2. Hebr. 7. 16. Pontifex dicitur factus secundum vim indissolubilis vitæ. Ergo Pontifex non fuit, quamdiu mortalis. Resp. Apostolus minime negat Christum fuisse Pontificem, priusquam actu haberet humanam vitam indissolubilem; sed docet solum eam ad absolvendas functiones aliquando fuisse necessariam, verf. 25. Interim Christus vim indissolubilis vitæ habuit secundum Deitatem, etiam cum mortalis esset, & moreretur, secundum humanitatem; qua virtute postmodum humana ipsius natura facta est immortalis: Joh. 2, 19. x, 18. Hebr. 9. 14. 1 Petr. 3. 18. Rom. 1, 4.
units.tr: Objection 2. Heb. 7.16. The High Priest is said to have been made according to the power of an indissoluble life. Therefore he was not a High Priest as long as he was mortal. Answer. The Apostle by no means denies that Christ was a High Priest before he actually possessed an indissoluble human life; he teaches only that this was necessary at some point for completing his functions, v. 25. Meanwhile Christ had the power of an indissoluble life according to his Deity, even when, according to his humanity, he was mortal and died; by that power his human nature afterwards became immortal: John 2.19; 10.18; Heb. 9.14; 1 Pet. 3.18; Rom. 1.4.

units.la: Obj. 3. Hebr. 5. 9. 10. Cum perfectus esset redditus, dicitur, factus obedientibus sibi omnibus causa salutis æternæ: appellatus à Deo Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchizedeki. Ergo ante illam consummationem non fuit Sacerdos. Resp. Illud dicitur respectu applicationis gloriosæ, quam in Cœlis peragit modo gloriosò; licet etiam prius salutem promiserit & contulerit plurimis: Matth. 9. 2, 6. Joh. 6. 33. Luc. 23. 43. Hoc respectu Intercessionis perpetuæ: Hebr. 7. 25. Quemadmodum ergo prius etiam fuit Mediator; Redemtor, Salvator; sic quoque Sacerdos.
units.tr: Objection 3. Heb. 5.9, 10. When he was made perfect, it is said that he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, and was addressed by God as a Priest after the order of Melchizedek. Therefore he was not a Priest before that completion. Answer. That is said with respect to the glorious application which he now carries out in heaven in a glorious manner; although he had also earlier promised and conferred salvation on many: Matt. 9.2, 6; John 6.33; Luke 23.43. It is said with respect to his perpetual intercession: Heb. 7.25. Just as therefore he was already Mediator, Redeemer and Saviour, so also was he Priest.

units.la: XLII. Sed & Pontificii oblationem Christi adhuc quotidianam statuunt in Missa, per Sacerdotes suos, pro peccatis, ut loquuntur; tum viventium, tum mortuorum in commentitio suo Purgatorio laborantium. Verum de abominando illo & Antichristiano sacro alibi ex professo.
units.tr: XLII. But the Papists also hold that the oblation of Christ is still daily repeated in the Mass by their priests, for sins, as they put it, both of the living and of the dead who suffer in their imaginary Purgatory. But of that abominable and Antichristian sacrifice I shall speak elsewhere, expressly.

units.la: Crux in oblatione Christi non fuit propriè Altare: cum istud victimam sanctificet: Matth. 23. 19. Sed merum duntaxat maledictionis symbolum fuit: scriptum est enim: Execrabilis est quisquis pendet in ligno: Gal. 3. 13. Deut. 21. 23.
units.tr: The Cross in the oblation of Christ was not properly an altar, since the altar sanctifies the victim: Matt. 23.19. It was merely a symbol of curse, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree: Gal. 3.13; Deut. 21.23.

units.la: XLIII. Proprius oblationis Christi effectus est, vera peccatorum expiatio, & remissionis impetratio: Eph. 1: 7. Col. 1. 14. Rom. 3. 24, 25. quam ipse pro omnibus & singulis electis impetravit sufficienter, & applicat efficaciter: Hebr. x, 14. Rom. 8. 34.
units.tr: XLIII. The proper effect of the oblation of Christ is the true expiation of sins and the obtaining of remission: Eph. 1.7; Col. 1.14; Rom. 3.24, 25. This he obtained sufficiently for all and each of the elect, and applies effectively: Heb. 10.14; Rom. 8.34.

units.la: Nec audiendus hâc in parte Socinus, contendens ex locis Hebr. v, 3. & vij. 26, 27. Christum non minus, quam legalem Pontificem, quemadmodum pro populo, ita etiam pro semet ipso, pro peccatis obtulisse: nam posterius istud membrum Christo non est applicandum; qui cum esset sanctissimus, necesse non habuit pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre. Hebr. 7. 26. Nec est quod Adversarius ad infirmitatem carnis confugiat; hoc est, ad mortalitatem & patibilitatem in Christo: illa enim à peccatis diversissima est: iv, 15. Et quæ, sodes super propria mortalitate & patibilitate in cœlis fieri potuit oblatio; cum Christus, ex Socini sententia, post resurrectionem demum, in cœlis Sacerdos factus, immortalis jam tum & impatibilis fuerit?
units.tr: Socinus must not be heard on this point, contending from Heb. 5.3 and 7.26, 27 that Christ offered, no less than the legal high priest, as for the people, so also for himself, for sins. For that latter clause does not apply to Christ, who, being most holy, had no need to offer victims for his own sins: Heb. 7.26. Nor is there reason for the adversary to take refuge in the infirmity of the flesh, that is, in mortality and passibility in Christ; for that is most unlike sin: 4.15. And how, pray, could an oblation be made in heaven concerning his own mortality and passibility, since Christ, according to Socinus's opinion, was made Priest in heaven only after the resurrection, when he was already immortal and impassible?

units.la: XLIV. Sequitur Intercessio, Actus Christi Sacerdotalis, quo æternam oblationis suæ virtutem, suamque de promovenda salute nostra voluntatem, convenienter nunc statui suo glorioso, in cœlis repræsentat coram Patre. Hinc Hebr. 9. 12. ingressus dicitur coeleste sacrarium, per proprium sanguinem, aeternam redemtionem nactus: atque ita verj. 24. comparere coram facie Dei pro nobis. Sic Advocatum habemus apud Patrem; 1 Joh. 2. 2. qui pro nobis interpellat; Rom. 8. 34. & quidem ita, ut Pater eum exaudiat; Joh. xi. 42. nos ipse diligat; xvj, 27. & nondum clamantibus respondeat; Isf. 65. 24. Imo etiam Christus per Spiritum suum in cordibus fidelium interpellat gemitibus inenarrabilibus. Rom. 8. 26. Precesque nostras, & gratiarum actiones, quae in ipsius nomine fiunt, Deo acceptas facit: Apoc. 8. 3. 4. Joh. 14. 13, 14. xvj, 23. Confer Eph. 3, 12. Hebr. 4, 16.
units.tr: XLIV. There follows intercession, the priestly act of Christ by which, now fittingly in his glorious state, he presents in heaven before the Father the eternal efficacy of his oblation and his will to advance our salvation. Hence Heb. 9.12: he is said to have entered the heavenly sanctuary through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption; and so, v. 24, to appear before the face of God for us. Thus we have an Advocate with the Father, 1 John 2.2, who intercedes for us, Rom. 8.34; and indeed in such a way that the Father hears him, John 11.42, loves us himself, 16.27, and answers before we call, Isa. 65.24. Indeed Christ also, through his Spirit in the hearts of believers, intercedes with unspeakable groanings, Rom. 8.26. And he makes our prayers and thanksgivings, which are offered in his name, acceptable to God: Rev. 8.3, 4; John 14.13, 14; 16.23. Compare Eph. 3.12; Heb. 4.16.

units.la: Intercessio ista Mediatoria, soli Christo propria est; non Angelis, aut Sanctis demortuis communis: Nam 1. solus Christus est Pontifex noster, habetque hoc officium ἀρχιερεύς: Hebr. v. 5, 6. vij. 4, 6, 7, 11, 16, 17, 21, 22, 24. &c.
units.tr: This mediatorial intercession belongs to Christ alone; it is not common to Angels or to the departed Saints. For (1) Christ alone is our High Priest, and holds this office as high priest [ἀρχιερεύς]: Heb. 5.5, 6; 7.4, 6, 7, 11, 16, 17, 21, 22, 24, etc.

units.la: 2. Cujus est ipse oblatio, ejus quoque est oblationis repraesentatio, Hebr. 9. 12, 24. Rom. 8, 34. 1 Joh. 2. 1. 2.
units.tr: (2) He whose own is the oblation, to him also belongs the representation of the oblation: Heb. 9.12, 24; Rom. 8.34; 1 John 2.1, 2.

units.la: 3. Nec ullus est, qui immediate pro nobis ad Deum accedat, praeter eum qui est מדבר Joh. 14. 6. Eph. 3. 12.
units.tr: (3) Nor is there anyone who immediately approaches God for us, except him who is the Mediator [מליץ]: John 14.6; Eph. 3.12.

units.la: 4. Reliqui omnes, quos Pontificii Intercessores volunt, singulares nostras necessitates ignorant: Isf. 63. 16. Joh. 14. 21. 2 Reg. 22. 20. Confer sup. cap. 9. th. 23
units.tr: (4) All the rest whom the Papists want as intercessors do not know our particular needs: Isa. 63.16; John 14.21; 2 Kings 22.20. Compare above, chapter 9, thesis 23.

units.la: XLV. Munus Christi Regium est, quo ipse omnia cum auctoritate gubernat ac dispensat, ad salutem ele- ctorum.
units.tr: XLV. The kingly office of Christ is that by which he himself governs and dispenses all things with authority, for the salvation of the elect.

units.la: Sic ipse Rex appellatur, Psal. 2. 6. Pastor; Joh. x. 11, 14: Magnus pastor; Hebr. 13. 20. Princeps Pastorum; 1 Petr. 5. 4. & Caput Ecclesiae; Eph. 1. 22 V. 23. Col. 1. 18. Prout autem duplex est ipsius Christi consideratio, ita potestas Regia ei competit, tum Theologice, qua Deo praecise; tum Oeconomice, qua Mediatori. Sed posterior consideratio hujus loci est propria. Regnum hoc Christi terrenum non est; sed spirituale: neque enim venit Filius hominis, ut sibi ministretur, sed ut ministret; Matth.20. 28. quapropter ipse tam emphatice; Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo: Joh. 18. 36. Confer Joh. 6. 15. Luc. 17. 20, 21. Item Zach. 9. 9. Jes. 53. 2, 3.
units.tr: Thus the King himself is called: Shepherd, Ps. 2:6; the Great Shepherd, John 10:11, 14; the Chief Shepherd, Heb. 13:20; the Prince of Shepherds, 1 Pet. 5:4; and the Head of the Church, Eph. 1:22, 23; Col. 1:18. Now, since Christ may be considered in two ways, so kingly power belongs to him both theologically, as God strictly considered, and economically, as Mediator. But the latter consideration is the one proper to this place. This kingdom of Christ is not earthly but spiritual: "for the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve," Matt. 20:28. Therefore he says so emphatically, "My kingdom is not of this world," John 18:36. Compare John 6:15; Luke 17:20, 21; likewise Zech. 9:9; Isa. 53:2, 3.

units.la: Estque universale, tum respectu omnium saeculorum: unde aeternum dicitur, & stabit in saecula: Dan. 2. 44. cujus non erit finis: Luc. 1. 33. tum etiam respectu subjectorum: Psal. 2. 8. Dona bogentes in possessionem tuam, & fines terrae jus possessionis tuae. Dan. 7. 14. Huic datus est dominatus, gloriaque & regnum; ut omnes populi, nationes; & linguae ei serviant. Attamen sub aliquo discrimine; alii enim Christo subjiciuntur fideliter, & ex animo; de quibus Psal. 110. 3. Populi tui oblationes voluntariae, &c. Hos autem Ipse quadam participatione facit Reges, qui regnabunt in terra inchoate, quod vocatur Regnum gratiae; & in caelis perfecte, quod est Regnum gloriae: Apoc. 5. 10. iij. 21. Alii non nisi inviti, & tanquam rebelles, contrario animo prorsus affecti, Regem istum, ut Judicem severum, extimescunt; qui interim eorum ministerio, ad electos suos varie exercendos, subinde solet uti; sed tandem, ut hostes subjugatos, juste puniet. De quibus vide Matth. 7. 21, 22, 23. viij. 12. 2 Petr. 2.
units.tr: It is also universal, both with respect to all ages, whence it is called eternal and "shall stand for ever," Dan. 2:44, "of which there shall be no end," Luke 1:33; and also with respect to its subjects: "Ask of me, and I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession," Ps. 2:8; "To him was given dominion, glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him," Dan. 7:14. Yet this is with some distinction: for some submit to Christ faithfully and from the heart, of whom Ps. 110:3 speaks: "Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power," etc. These he himself, by a certain participation, makes kings, who shall reign on earth in a beginning form, which is called the kingdom of grace, and in heaven in perfection, which is the kingdom of glory: Rev. 5:10; 3:21. Others submit only unwillingly and as rebels, utterly disposed in an opposite mind, and they dread that King as a severe Judge; yet in the meantime he is wont to use their service for variously exercising his elect, but at last he will justly punish them as subdued enemies. On these see Matt. 7:21, 22, 23; 8:12; 2 Pet. 2.

units.la: 1. Atque istud Regnum Potentiae dicitur.
units.tr: 1. This is called the kingdom of power.

units.la: XLVI. Actus ejus sunt potissimum, 1. Ecclesiae collectio: sic Christus oves ipse adducit: Joh. x. 16.
units.tr: XLVI. His acts are chiefly these: 1. The gathering of the Church: thus Christ himself "brings" his sheep, John 10:16.

units.la: 2. Collectae conservatio: Virtutis Dei praesidio custodiuntur; 1 Pet. 1. 5.
units.tr: 2. The preservation of those gathered: they "are kept by the power of God," 1 Pet. 1:5.

units.la: 3. Gubernatio per Verbum & Spiritum: Docet suos facere placita ipsius, & Spiritu suo bono deducit; Psal. 143. 10.
units.tr: 3. Governance through the Word and the Spirit: "He teaches his people to do his will, and leads them by his good Spirit," Ps. 143:10.

units.la: 4. Defensio: Non peribunt in aeternum, neque rapiet eos quisquam e manu ipsius; Joh. 10. 28.
units.tr: 4. Defence: "They shall never perish, neither shall any pluck them out of my hand," John 10:28.

units.la: 5. Glorificatio: Repositia est ipsis justitiae corona quam reddet ipsis Dominus in illo die; 2 Tim. 4. 8.
units.tr: 5. Glorification: "There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord shall give me in that day," 2 Tim. 4:8.

units.la: 6. Hostium gloriosa subjectio: Nam oportet eum regnare, usque quo omnes inimicos subjecerit pedibus ejus; 1 Cor. 15. 25.
units.tr: 6. The glorious subjection of enemies: "For he must reign, till he has put all enemies under his feet," 1 Cor. 15:25.

units.la: Eorumque 7 justa punitio: Siquidem justum est apud Deum, vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem in revelatione Domini Jesu de coelo, &c. 2 Thess. 1. 6. 7.
units.tr: And 7. their just punishment: "Since it is a righteous thing with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give rest to you who are afflicted, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven," etc., 2 Thess. 1:6, 7.

units.la: XLVII. Consequenter foli Christo proprium est hoc Regnum: Nam 1. Ipsi, ut Mediatori, ista ἐξουσία passim attribuitur: ut ostensum.
units.tr: XLVII. Consequently this kingdom belongs to Christ alone. For: 1. This authority [ἐξουσία] is attributed to him, as Mediator, throughout Scripture, as has been shown.

units.la: 2. Substernitur ei Divina Filiatio: Pfal. 2. 6, 7-8. Hebr. 1. 1, 5-9.
units.tr: 2. The Divine Sonship is the foundation of it: Ps. 2:6, 7, 8; Heb. 1:1, 5–9.

units.la: 3. Actus ejus tales sunt, ut a mera creatura prosicisci non possint.
units.tr: 3. His actions are such that they cannot proceed from a mere creature.

units.la: 4. Ipse dicitur Caput: Eph. 1. 22. v. 23 Fundamentum unicum: 1 Cor. 3. 11. & Sponsus Ecclesiae; Joh. 3. 29. quae ut Casta Virgo uni tantum sistenda Viro, scil. Christo; 2 Cor. xi, 2. Sic omnia unitatem spirant.
units.tr: 4. He himself is called the Head (Eph. 1. 22; v. 23), the only Foundation (1 Cor. 3. 11), and the Bridegroom of the Church (John 3. 29), which, as a chaste virgin, is to be presented to one husband only, namely Christ (2 Cor. 11. 2). Thus everything breathes unity.

units.la: Unum igitur in hoc Regno spirituali Monarcham, & unum Dominum pie confitemur, juxta Eph. 4. 5. cujus Principatui subordinatum est in Ecclesiis Ministerium: Eph. 4. 11. 1 Cor. 4. 1, 2. Sed Dominus diserte, Luc. 22. 25, 26. Reges gentium dominantur eis; -. Vos autem non ita estote. Confer Matth. 23. 8, 9-12. Sic ruit jam sua sponte, Antichristianum istud Pontificiorum commentum, quo Petrum fingunt fuisse Principem Apostolorum, & Vicarium Christi: nam praeterquam quod inepta sit a Petro ad Pontificem consequentia; ad ipsam Petri confessionem, & sincerum de muneris sui functione testimonium, eos ablegamus; qui 1 Petr. v, 1, 2, 3. Presbyteros, qui inter vos sunt, precor ego, una Presbyter, -- Pascite Dei gregem -- non ut dominantes Cleris, sed ut qui sitis exemplaria gregis. Confer Gal. 2. 6-9; 11, -. 2 Cor. xi. 5. &c.
units.tr: We therefore confess one Monarch in this spiritual kingdom, and one Lord, according to Eph. 4. 5, and the ministry in the churches is subordinate to his rule (Eph. 4. 11; 1 Cor. 4. 1, 2). But the Lord says plainly, Luke 22. 25, 26: "The kings of the nations lord it over them; ... but you shall not be so." Compare Matt. 23. 8, 9–12. So that Antichristian fiction of the Papists collapses of its own accord, the notion that Peter was the prince of the Apostles and the Vicar of Christ. Apart from the fact that the inference from Peter to the Pope is absurd, we send them back to Peter's own confession and his sincere testimony about the discharge of his office, who says (1 Pet. 5. 1, 2, 3): "The elders who are among you I exhort, I who am a fellow elder ... feed the flock of God ... not as lording it over the clergy, but as examples to the flock." Compare Gal. 2. 6–9, 11; 2 Cor. 11. 5, etc.

units.la: XLVIII. Hactenus de Officiis Christi. Nunc de ra-
units.tr: XLVIII. So far concerning the offices of Christ. Now his state must be examined.

units.la: rio ejus Statu dispiciendum: alius enim fuit status ipfius Incarnandi; de quo fup. alius Incarnati Atque hic iterum vel Humiliationis est, vel Exaltationis. Status humiliationis est, in quo Mediator noster Θεάνθρωπῳ realiter Legi fuit subjectus,ad peragenda & fustinenda in humanitate sua omnia,quæ per justitiam Dei ad nostri redemtionem & salutem æterna pertinebant. De hoc, Phil. 2. 7, 8 ipse fe inanivit forma fervi accepta, & habitu inventus ut homo, ipse fe submisit, factus obediens usque ad mortem,&c. Atque iterum, Gal. 4. 4,
units.tr: The manner of his state is to be considered, for there was one state of his incarnation, treated above, and another of Christ incarnate. This second state is either of humiliation or of exaltation. The state of humiliation is that in which our Mediator, as God-man [θεάνθρωπος], was truly made subject to the Law, in order to perform and endure in his humanity everything that pertained, by the justice of God, to our redemption and salvation. Of this, Phil. 2:7, 8: He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in human likeness, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, etc. And again, Gal. 4:4,

units.la: 5. Emisit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum Legi subjectum; ut eos, qui Legi subjecti erant, redimeret. Interim spectandæ veniunt in hoc statu ejus Vita & Mors, ac rursus, Vitæ Initium & Progressus. Ad Initium pertinent Conceptio, & Conformatio; de quibus fup. th. 7.-13. & Nativitas.
units.tr: 5. God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law. Meanwhile, in this state, his life and death are to be considered, and again his beginning and progress in life. The beginning includes his conception and formation, treated above in theses 7 to 13, and his nativity.

units.la: XLIX. Nativitas Christi est, Ipsius fecundum humanam naturam,ex utero Virginis Mariæ justo tempore in lucem facta editio. Luc. 2. 6, 7. Circa modum hujus, non assentimur Pontificiis, & Ubiquitariis, qui contendunt, Mariam peperisse clauso utero, & fine dolore: Nam 1. & ipsa dies purgationis suæ habuit, quibus impletis infans Hierosolymam adductus est, Domino sistendus juxta Legem, Exod. 13. 2. Luc. 2. 22, 23. Omnis masculus primogenitus (Græce, aperiens uterum,) sanctus Domino erit, &c. Sic apertio uteri plane asseritur, fine qua verus partus existere non potuisset; cum dimensionum penetratio contradictoria fit: nec miraculofum ex utero exitum Scriptura doceat. Istam vero solutionem post lapsum dolor comitatur; juxta Gen. 3. 16. Nec de Maria secus est statuendum; quæ & ipsa peccatrix fuit, & aliis quoque doloribus obnoxia: Luc. 2. 35. Obj. 1. Cant. 4, 12. Hortus clausus, fons obsignatus, &c. Ergo. Resp. Locus ille non de Virgine Maria, sed allegorice de Ecclesia intelligendus est; quæ optima fide se castam confervat Christo, & fructus suos ac proventus integros.
units.tr: XLIX. The nativity of Christ is the bringing forth into the light, at the due time, of him according to his human nature, from the womb of the Virgin Mary. Luke 2:6, 7. As to the manner of this, we do not agree with the Papists and the Ubiquitarians, who contend that Mary gave birth with her womb closed and without pain. For, first, she too had her days of purification, after which the infant was brought to Jerusalem to be presented to the Lord according to the Law, Exod. 13:2; Luke 2:22, 23: Every male that opens the womb (in Greek, opening the womb [διανοῖγον μήτραν]) shall be holy to the Lord, etc. Thus the opening of the womb is plainly asserted, and without it a true birth could not have taken place, since penetration of dimensions is contradictory; nor does Scripture teach any miraculous exit from the womb. But after the Fall that opening is accompanied by pain, according to Gen. 3:16. Nor is it to be held otherwise of Mary, who was herself a sinner and subject to other sorrows: Luke 2:35. Objection 1. Song 4:12. A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, etc. Therefore. Reply. That passage is to be understood not of the Virgin Mary but allegorically of the Church, which in sincere faith keeps herself chaste for Christ, and her fruits and produce whole.

units.la: Obj. 2. Isef. 66. 7,8. Cum nondum parturiet pepererit: eum nondum invadet dolor eam, jam posuerit marem. Ergo. Resp. Istud quoque de mirifice gignendis in Vocatione Gentium Ecclesiæ liberis accipiendum est. Ideo sequitur: An efficeretur, ut pariat terra die uno? an gignetur gens vice una? quod parturit, simulque parit Tzion filios suos.
units.tr: Objection 2. Isaiah 66:7, 8: Before she travailed she brought forth; before pain came upon her she bore a male child. Therefore. Reply. This too must be understood of the children of the Church being wondrously brought forth in the calling of the Gentiles. Hence it follows: Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day? Shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her sons.

units.la: Obj. 3. Sic Maria non mansisset virgo in partu: Ergo. Resp. Ista uteri apertio non magis, quam expurgatio menstrua, adversatur virginitati: hæc enim proprie consistit in negatione commercii virilis.
units.tr: Objection 3. So Mary would not have remained a virgin in childbirth. Therefore. Reply. That opening of the womb is no more opposed to virginity than the menstrual purgation is, for virginity properly consists in the denial of intercourse with a man.

units.la: I. In progressu spectanda primum Vita privata; ubi statim apparuit insignis Paupertas, & Humilitas: unde 2 Cor. 8. 9. Notis beneficentiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Eum propter vos pauperem esse factum &c. Ita mox a nativitate fasciis involutus, & in præsepi reclinatus est, eo quod non esset ipsis locus in diversorio: Luc. 2.7. & ingrediens mundum, dixit: Ecce adsum - ut faciam, Deus, voluntatem tuam: Hebr. x. 5, 7. Sic inchoavit statim humilem subjectionem suam ad Legem Dei; eamque tum Moralem, tum Cerimonialem & Politicam Mosaicam; cum non solum esset creatura rationalis, & civis mundi; sed Filius Abrahami, Israelita, & minister circumcisionis factus. Sic ergo speciatim Parentibus & Magistratibus, adeoque & Legibus Politicis humanis, ac nominatim Imperatoriis, in tali tunc Politia, fuit subjectus. Vide Luc. 2. 51. Matth. 17. 24. -27. Interim eximendi sunt casus, ubi Ipse operationibus Divinis, aut formaliter Mediatoriis occupabatur: Job. 2. 4, 5. xix, 26. Luc. 2. 48, 49. Sed & peculiariter obligavit eum Divina constitutio, & propria Ipsius sponsio, ad ea præstanda ac perferenda, quæ satisfactionis ac meriti nomine pro electis debebantur: Jes. 53. 10. 11, 12. Matth. 20. 28. Job. x. 18. Phil. 2. 6. 7, 8. Gal. 4. 4. 5. Rom. 5. 18. 19. viij. 3, 4. x, 4. In ipsa infantia respectu Legis cerimonialis valde conspicua est Circumcisio; Luc. 2. 21. cum Gen. 17. 7, 10,-14. Levit. 12. 3. Ubi materialiter, Ipsum etiam oportuit subire actum illum obedientiae. Vide Matth. 3. 15. 2. Formaliter, obsignatio promissionis foederalis optime conveniebat Sponsori & Capiti electorum suorum: ut ipse, qua homo, eam quoque crederet certissime. 3. Quin imo peccatorum remissio (scil. populi sui) per satisfactionem ipsius impetranda, & vita aeterna ipsius merito acquirenda, rectissime sic ipsi obsignata fuit: sicut aequum est Sponsorem dum pro debitore numerare incipit, apocham accipere. 4. Idem dicimus de gratia sanctificationis, quatenus ea à capite ad membra redundat. Similiter tenendum, de aliis Sacramentis, quibus Ipse insuper usus est.
units.tr: I. In the progress of his life, the first thing to be considered is his private life, in which his great poverty and humility at once appeared, whence 2 Cor. 8:9: You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, etc. So, soon after his birth, he was wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn, Luke 2:7; and coming into the world, he said: Lo, I come, O God, to do your will, Heb. 10:5, 7. Thus he at once began his humble subjection to the Law of God, both moral, ceremonial, and the Mosaic political law, since he was not only a rational creature and citizen of the world, but also a son of Abraham, an Israelite, and made a minister of circumcision. So, in particular, he was subject to parents and magistrates, and so also to human political laws, and especially to the imperial laws, in that polity of his time. See Luke 2:51; Matt. 17:24–27. Meanwhile, cases are to be excepted where he was occupied with divine works or formally with his mediatorial office: John 2:4, 5; 19:26; Luke 2:48, 49. But also the divine appointment and his own promise specially bound him to perform and endure those things which were owed for the sake of satisfaction and merit on behalf of the elect: Isa. 53:10, 11, 12; Matt. 20:28; John 10:18; Phil. 2:6, 7, 8; Gal. 4:4, 5; Rom. 5:18, 19; 8:3, 4; 10:4. In infancy itself, with respect to the ceremonial law, circumcision is very conspicuous: Luke 2:21, compared with Gen. 17:7, 10–14; Lev. 12:3. Here, materially, he too had to undergo that act of obedience: see Matt. 3:15. Formally, the sealing of the covenant promise was most fitting for the Surety and Head of his elect, so that he himself, as man, might most certainly believe it as well. (3) Indeed, the remission of sins (namely of his people) to be obtained through his satisfaction, and eternal life to be acquired by his merit, were most rightly sealed to him in this way, just as it is fitting that a surety, when he begins to pay on behalf of the debtor, should receive a receipt. (4) We say the same of the grace of sanctification, insofar as it flows from the head to the members. Similarly, what is held of the other sacraments, which he himself also used.

units.la: Vide etiam de Praesentatione coram Domino; Luc. 2. 22,23,24. juxta Legem, Levit. 12. 2,4, 6, 8. Exod. 13. 2. Num. 8. 16.
units.tr: See also concerning the presentation before the Lord: Luke 2:22, 23, 24, according to the Law, Lev. 12:2, 4, 6, 8; Exod. 13:2; Num. 8:16.

units.la: LI. Vita porro publica fuit, qua ipse palam se Messiam esse manifestavit. Hujus Initiatio facta est aliquanto post, quam Johannes Baptista, Ipsius prodromus. (Mal. 3. 1. iv, 5, 6. Luc. 1. 5, 80.) ministerium suum publice inchoaret: à quo Christus annos circiter 30 natus, in Jordane baptizatus est. Spiciatim illic notandum ipsius Johannis de Christo testimonium; imo & Coeli, Christo orante, apertio; itemque vox Patris coelitus missa, ac de Filio testificans; & Spir. Sancti super eum descensus in specie columbae: Joh. 1. 26,36. Luc. 3. 21,-23. Matth. 3. 11,-17. Marc. 1. 7,-11. atque adeo solennis eius introductio ad munus suum publice obeundum. Subsecuta est ejus per Spiritum deductio in desertum. jejunium 40. dierum, & multiplex Diaboli tentatio: Matth. 4. Luc. 4. & Marc. 1.
units.tr: LI. Moreover, his life was public, in which he openly showed himself to be the Messiah. Its beginning was made a little after John the Baptist, his forerunner (Mal. 3:1; 4:5, 6; Luke 1:5, 80), had publicly begun his ministry; at about thirty years of age Christ was baptized by him in the Jordan. Especially to be noted there is John's own testimony concerning Christ; indeed also the opening of heaven while Christ prayed; likewise the voice of the Father sent from heaven, bearing witness concerning the Son; and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him in the form of a dove: John 1:26, 36; Luke 3:21–23; Matt. 3:11–17; Mark 1:7–11; and so his solemn introduction to the public discharge of his office. There followed his leading into the wilderness by the Spirit, a fast of forty days, and the manifold temptation by the Devil: Matt. 4; Luke 4; Mark 1.

units.la: Rejicimus autem commentum Socinianorum, qui Christum per hoc tempus in Coelum raptum, & à Patre suo voluntatem ipsius, & omnia quae ad muneris sui functionem pertinebant, edoctum volunt: neque enim Sp. Sanctus nos tale quid docet; & nostrum non est sapere, supra id quod scriptum est: 1 Cor. 4. 6.
units.tr: We reject, however, the fiction of the Socinians, who want Christ during this time to have been caught up into heaven and taught by his Father his will and everything that pertained to the performance of his office. For the Holy Spirit does not teach us any such thing, and it is not ours to be wise beyond what is written: 1 Cor. 4:6.

units.la: Obj. 1. Joh. 3. 13. Resp. Vide sup. th. 9.
units.tr: Objection 1. John 3:13. Reply. See above, thesis 9.

units.la: Obj. 2. Atqui Paulus in Coelum raptus fuit: 2 Cor. 12. 2, 3, 4. quanto magis ergo de Christo id statuendum? Resp. De Paulo quidem incertum est, utrum in corpore, an extra corpus, fuerit raptus. Sed ab ipso ad Christum non valet consequentia: hic enim necesse non habuit doceri a principio Personae suo extrinseco.
units.tr: Objection 2. But Paul was caught up into heaven: 2 Cor. 12:2, 3, 4. How much more, then, must this be affirmed of Christ? Reply. Concerning Paul it is indeed uncertain whether he was caught up in the body or outside the body. But the inference from him to Christ does not hold, for Christ had no need to be taught from the beginning by anything extrinsic to his Person.

units.la: Obj. 3. Moses per 40. dies ac noctes fuit in monte Horeb cum Deo: Deut. 9. 9, 11. Ergo. Resp. Esto. At non fuit in Coelum raptus: & alia est ratio Moisis, ut famuli; alia Christi, ut Filii Dei: Hebr. 3. 5, 6. Joh. 1. 18.
units.tr: Objection 3. Moses was with God on Mount Horeb for forty days and nights: Deut. 9:9, 11. Therefore. Reply. Granted. But he was not caught up into heaven, and the position of Moses as a servant is one thing, that of Christ as the Son of God another: Heb. 3:5, 6; John 1:18.

units.la: LII. Peraftio vitae publicae complectitur potissimum Euangelii praedicationem, & Miraculorum patratio- nem; quae in Historiis Euangelicis copiose recen- sentur.
units.tr: LII. The public life consisted chiefly of the preaching of the Gospel and the working of miracles, which are recounted at length in the Gospel histories.

units.la: Adjuncta quoque fuit Paupertas: Matth. 8. 20. sed absque mendicitate, & voto singulari; aut tali ratione exempli, cujus imitatio in nobis esset satisfactoria, & meritoria: quod tenendum contra mendicantes Pontificiorum ordines, eorumque vota spontaneae paupertatis.
units.tr: Poverty also accompanied it: Matt. 8. 20. But it was without begging and without any special vow, or else for such a reason of example that imitating it would be satisfactory and meritorious in us. This must be maintained against the mendicant orders of the Papists and their vows of voluntary poverty.

units.la: Obj. Luc. 8. 2, 3. Ergo. Resp. Verum ista proprie non fuit eleemosyna sed retributio qualiscunque pro institutione spirituali, aliisque beneficiis ab ipso acceptis. Vide Matth. x. 10. 1 Cor. 9. 4, - 14. Gal. 6. 6.
units.tr: Objection: Luke 8. 2, 3. Therefore (Christ begged). Answer: Those things were properly not alms, but a kind of return for the spiritual instruction and other benefits he had received from them. See Matt. 10. 10; 1 Cor. 9. 4-14; Gal. 6. 6.

units.la: Conclusio vitae Christi fuit ejus praeparatio ad Mortem; quae consistebat partim in hujus mediatione: Joh. 13. 31, & seqq. partim in Discipulorum de ea instructione & consolatione; xiv, xv, xvj. partim in singulari quadam precatione: xvij.
units.tr: The conclusion of Christ's life was his preparation for death. This consisted partly in his mediation: John 13. 31ff.; partly in instructing and comforting the disciples about it: chs. 14, 15, 16; and partly in a singular prayer: ch. 17.

units.la: LIII. Sequitur Mors s Extremus humiliationis actus, quo Christus pro peccatis electorum subiit poenas quàm maxime horribiles, ad satisfaciendum justitiae Divinae, & gloriam ejus declarandam. Actum dicimus; non meram passionem: propterea quod Ipse, tanquàm Sponsor noster, volens & ex consilio eam subiit. Unde ipse de se, Joh. x. 11. Bonus pastor animam suam deponit pro ovibus. & 18. Nemo tollit eam à me, sed ego depono eam per me ipsum. Talis autem & tanta fuit ista poena, ut gravitate sua in isto subjecto patiente, universam illam miseriam aequarit, quam omnia & singula electorum peccata demerebantur: ac proinde eadem genera, membra, & gradus in eâ possunt observari, quae in poenis aliorum.
units.tr: LIII. Death follows, the final act of humiliation, in which Christ underwent, for the sins of the elect, punishments as horrible as possible, to satisfy divine justice and to declare its glory. We call it an act, not mere passion, because he himself, as our Surety, undertook it willingly and by counsel. Hence he says of himself, John 10. 11: The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; and v. 18: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. Such and so great was this punishment that, by its weight in this suffering subject, it equalled the whole misery which all and each of the sins of the elect deserved. Therefore the same kinds, members and degrees can be observed in it as in the punishments of others.

units.la: LIV. Inchoatio igitur Mortis spiritualis in genere damni, fuit, Amissio istius gaudii spiritualis in humanâ Christi natura, quod alias ex fruitione Dei & summae gratiae perceperat, atque etiamnum percipere potuisset. In genere sensus, fuit irae Divinae degustatio, & subjectio quaedam temporaria ad potestatem tenebrarum: unde orta deprecatio seria; sed tamen cum insigni submissione ad voluntatem Patris: Luc. 22. 42, quam excepit Sudor sanguineus: verf. 44. adhibita interim moderatione, tum interna, per aliqualem remissionem praesurae in animâ; tum externâ, per corroborationem alloquii Angelici: verf. 43.
units.tr: LIV. The beginning, therefore, of spiritual death, in the genus of loss, was the loss of that spiritual joy in Christ's human nature which he had otherwise received from the enjoyment of God and of supreme grace, and could still have received. In the genus of sense, it was a tasting of divine wrath and a certain temporary subjection to the power of darkness. Hence arose a earnest prayer, yet with remarkable submission to the Father's will: Luke 22. 42. This was followed by a bloody sweat: v. 44. Meanwhile moderation was applied: internal, by a certain slight relief of the anguish in his soul; and external, by strengthening through the angelic address: v. 43.

units.la: Inchoatio mortis corporalis interna, fuit Debilitatio, quae suppositâ corporis mortalitate per vim externam inferebatur.
units.tr: The internal beginning of bodily death was weakness, which, given the mortality of the body, was inflicted by external force.

units.la: Externa, & quidem in genere damni, quod ex Discipulis suis à Juda fuerit proditus: Matth. 26. 47, 50. à Petro ter abnegatus. 69-74. a reliquis desertus: verf. 56. a populo reprobatus & pessimo sicario posthabitus; xxvij. 20,-25. vestibus suis denudatus, 28, 35. ac tandem necessario potû destitutus: Psalm. 19. 28, 29.
units.tr: External things, indeed in the genus of loss: he was betrayed by Judas, one of his own disciples: Matt. 26. 47, 50; denied three times by Peter: vv. 69-74; deserted by the rest: v. 56; rejected by the people and set behind a most wicked assassin: 27. 20-25; stripped of his clothes: vv. 28, 35; and finally deprived of the necessary drink: Psalm 19. 28, 29.

units.la: In genere sensus, fuit Apprehensio probrosa, tanquam latronis: Marc. 14.46,-48. Judicia iniquissima, tum Ecclesiastica; Joh. 18. 13, 14, 19,-24. tum Politica; Matth. 27. 11,-26. multiplex irrisio, contumelia, percussio; 26, 31. Luc. 22. 63, 65. Atque ipsa tandem Crucifixio & quidem nudato corpore, inter duos latrones: ad quam accessit potatio aceti felle & myrrha mixti, blasphemiae frequentes, & sarcastica tituli inscriptio: Luc. 23. 33. Matth. 27. 31, 33,-49.
units.tr: In the genus of sense, there was a shameful arrest, as of a robber: Mark 14. 46-48; most iniquitous judgments, both ecclesiastical, John 18. 13, 14, 19-24, and civil, Matt. 27. 11-26; manifold mockery, insult and striking: vv. 26, 31; Luke 22. 63, 65. And finally the crucifixion itself, with the body naked, between two robbers. To this were added a drink of vinegar mixed with gall and myrrh, frequent blasphemies, and the sarcastic inscription of the title: Luke 23. 33; Matt. 27. 31, 33-49.

units.la: Verum & hic mitigatio quaedam fuit; utpote Majestatis Divinae manifestatio in militibus voce sua prostratis: Joh. 18. 6. Innocentiae testificatio ab ipso Pilato aliquoties facta; xix. 4, 6. nec non a Juda proditore; Matth. 27. 3,-5. denique & auxilium Simonis Cyrenaei in cruce ferendâ, & frequentis turbae compassio: Luc. 23. 26, 27.
units.tr: But even here there was some mitigation: a manifestation of his divine majesty, when soldiers were thrown prostrate by his voice: John 18. 6. A testimony to his innocence was made several times by Pilate himself: John 19. 4, 6; and also by Judas the traitor: Matt. 27. 3-5. Finally there was the help of Simon of Cyrene in carrying the cross, and the compassion of a large crowd: Luke 23. 26, 27.

units.la: LV. Consummatio mortis spiritualis in genere damni, fuit, Derelictio illa Patris, & omnis consolationis ac laetitiae spiritualis ad tempus destitutio; unde suprema illa, & pathetica moribundi exclamatio. Deus mi! Deus mi! Quare dereliquisti me! Matth. 27. 46.
units.tr: LV. The consummation of spiritual death, in the genus of loss, was that desertion by the Father, and the temporary withdrawal of all spiritual consolation and joy. Hence that final and pathetic cry of the dying man: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Matt. 27. 46.

units.la: In genere sensus fuit, Maledictio, & extrema judicii Divini perpessio, adversus electorum peccata. Hinc pro nobis dicitur factus execratio, cujus symbolum fuit suspensio in cruce; ut nos ab execratione redimeret; Gal. 3. 13. & pro nobis peccatum factus, ut nos efficeremur justitia Dei in eo; 2 Cor. 5. 21. Atque ita circumderunt eum dolores mortis, & angores inferni obvenerunt ei: Psal. 18. 16. qui est Descensus ejus ad inferos; prout Catechesis nostra in Symbolo Apostol. recte explicat μεταφορικῶς. Verum interim est, quod istud Symbolum nec ab ipsis Apostolis ita sit compositum: nec illa verba, Descendit ad inferos, ab initio ei fuerint inserta. Sed insuper satis commode ea accipiuntur de passionibus Christi in anima, ante mortem; quamvis morti & sepulturæ sint subjecta: videtur enim rerum potius, quàm temporum, ordo servatus; adeò ut externa, & ad oculum magis conspicua, præmittantur; interna vero & spiritualia postmodum subsequantur.
units.tr: In the genus of sense there was the curse, and the extreme suffering of divine judgment against the sins of the elect. Hence he is said to have been made a curse for us, whose symbol was suspension on the cross, that he might redeem us from the curse: Gal. 3. 13; and made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him: 2 Cor. 5. 21. And thus the pains of death surrounded him, and the sorrows of hell came upon him: Psalm 18. 16. This is his descent to the dead, as our Catechism rightly explains it, metaphorically [μεταφορικῶς], in the Apostles' Creed. It is true, however, that this Creed was not composed in this form by the Apostles themselves, nor were the words He descended into hell inserted in it from the beginning. But they are fairly suitably taken of the sufferings of Christ in the soul before death, although they are joined to his death and burial. For the order seems to be one of things rather than of times: the external and more conspicuous events are placed first, and the internal and spiritual ones follow afterwards.

units.la: Sic igitur Christus vere pro nobis in anima passus est: neque solum in sensualitate, aut parte, vel facultate illius inferiore; ut Pontificii loquuntur; sed etiam in ipsa rationalitate, seu facultate superiore. Addimus nunc specialius Jes. 53. 10, 11. Propter laborem animæ suæ, &c. & Matth. 26. 38. Undiquaque tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. Imo quemadmodum Deo cultum rationalem debemus, in spiritu & veritate præstandum tota anima; Rom. 12, 1. Joh. 4. 24, Matth. 22. 37. sic ejus omissio, & praxis contraria, pœnas demeretur proportionatas, in spiritu & facultate rationali etiam perferendas. Eas autem Sponsor in se receperat. Idque tenendum inprimis contra Pontif. qui animæ Christi quoad rationalitatem attribuunt visionem beatificam ab ipsa statim conformatione: sed perperam: unio quidem hypostatica hoc præstitit, ut humana Christi natura, principium & habitum charismatum semper in se retineret; sed actus tamen secundus, & sensus gaudii spiritualis, pro tempore suspensus est: scil. Radios subtraxit Divinitas, ut pateretur humanitas.
units.tr: Thus Christ truly suffered for us in soul: not only in sensuality, or in its lower part or faculty, as the Papists speak, but also in rationality itself, that is, the higher faculty. We add now more specifically Isa. 53. 10, 11: On account of the labour of his soul, etc., and Matt. 26. 38: My soul is sorrowful unto death on every side. Indeed, just as we owe God a rational worship, to be rendered in spirit and in truth with the whole soul (Rom. 12. 1; John 4. 24; Matt. 22. 37), so its omission and the contrary practice deserve proportionate punishments, to be borne also in spirit and in the rational faculty. The Surety had received these upon himself. This must be held especially against the Papists, who attribute to the soul of Christ, as to its rationality, the beatific vision from the very moment of its union. This is wrong. The hypostatic union indeed brought it about that the human nature of Christ always retained in itself the principle and habit of the gifts; but the second act, and the sense of spiritual joy, was suspended for the time: The Godhead withdrew its rays, so that the manhood might suffer.

units.la: LVI. Consummatio mortis corporalis, fuit, Ipsa separatio Animæ à Corpore, salva interim utriusque unione cum Persona τ Λόγῳ. Joh. 19. 30. Cum accepisset Iesus acetum, dixit; Consummatum est; & inclinato capite tradidit spiritum.
units.tr: LVI. The consummation of bodily death was the very separation of the soul from the body, while the union of each with the Person of the Word [τῷ Λόγῳ] was preserved. John 19. 30: When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished; and bowing his head he gave up the spirit.

units.la: Vera autem fuit ista Mors; non simulata, vel ficta: & quidem ipsius Christi; non alterius cujuspiam Christo subfituti.
units.tr: This death was indeed true; not simulated or feigned. And it was the death of Christ himself, not of some substitute put in his place.

units.la: Mortem respectu Corporis excepit Sepultura, a Joseph o Arimathæo, spectabili ac divite Senatore Hierosolymitano, procurata; adjuvante etiam Nicodemo. mo: secundum prophetiam Isef. 53. 9. Et dedit cum impiis sepulturam ejus & cum divite in mortibus ejus. Sed explorata prius a Pilato Mortis veritate; & adhibita per milites non ossium fractione, (uti in latronibus factum. Vide Exod. 12. 46. Num. 9. 12.) sed lateris perfossione; secundum Zach. 12. 10. Confequenter juxta typum Ionae, per tria vuχθήμεςα, quae tamen synecdochice accipienda, extitit in corde terrae: Matth. 12. 10. Jon. 1. 17. Horae fuerunt in universum circiter 40. unde nata primum videtur Quadragesima, ejusque Iejunium; tempus scil. quo Sponsus fuit ablatus; Matth. 9. 15.
units.tr: Burial followed the death, with respect to the body. It was procured by Joseph of Arimathea, a distinguished and wealthy senator of Jerusalem, with Nicodemus also helping, according to the prophecy of Isa. 53. 9: And they gave him his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his deaths. But the truth of his death had first been ascertained by Pilate, and it was carried out by the soldiers not by breaking his bones (as was done to the robbers; see Exod. 12. 46; Num. 9. 12) but by piercing his side, according to Zech. 12. 10. Consequently, according to the type of Jonah, he was in the heart of the earth for three days and nights (which are to be taken synecdochically): Matt. 12. 10; Jonah 1. 17. The hours came to about forty in all, whence the Quadragesima and its fast seem first to have arisen: the time, namely, when the Bridegroom was taken away; Matt. 9. 15.

units.la: LVII. Interim fingendus non est cum Pontificiis localis Christi descensus ad limbum infernalem; ut animas fidelium V. T. in eo tantisper detentas, liberaret; ac secum in coelum adduceret. Neque etiam statuendus, cum Lutheranis, similis fere ad inferos descensus, ad triumphandum istic de Diabolo, Morte, &c. Sed quemadmodum communiter in morte hominis, pulvere revertente in terram, spiritus revertitur ad Deum; Eccles. 12. 7. sic etiam spiritus Christi, quem ipse per modum depositi in manus Patris sui jam ante commendarat. Luc. 23. 46. ipso crucifixionis suae die in coelum receptus est. Unde ipse morti vicinus ad latronem resipiscentem; Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso; Luc. 23. 43. quod conferendum cum 2 Cor. 12. 2, 4.
units.tr: LVII. Meanwhile we should not imagine, with the Papists, a local descent of Christ into the limbo of hell, to free from there the souls of the faithful of the Old Testament who were held in it, and to bring them with him into heaven. Nor should we hold, with the Lutherans, a roughly similar descent into hell to triumph there over the Devil, Death, and so on. Rather, just as in the death of a man the dust returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to God, Eccles. 12. 7, so also the spirit of Christ, which he had already commended into the hands of his Father by way of a deposit, Luke 23. 46, was received into heaven on the very day of his crucifixion. Hence, being near death, he said to the penitent thief, Today you will be with me in Paradise, Luke 23. 43, which is to be compared with 2 Cor. 12. 2, 4.

units.la: Obj. 1. Matth. 12. 40. memoratur existentia Christi in Corde terrae: quod Infernum damnatorum, aut ejus Limbum, notat. Resp. Imo sic denotatur Sepultura; non localis descensus ad Infernum damnatorum, vel Limbum aliquem infernalem. Cor metaphorice interiora notat, & medium quodammodo; non autem praecise centrum, aut id quod centro proximum est. Vide Exod. 15. 8. Deut. 4. 11. 2 Sam. 18. 14. Et Animae separatae nulla istic mentio.
units.tr: Objection 1. Matt. 12. 40 mentions Christ's being in the heart of the earth, which denotes the hell of the damned, or its limbo. Reply: On the contrary, burial is thereby denoted, not a local descent into the hell of the damned or some infernal limbo. Heart metaphorically denotes the inner parts, and in a certain way the middle, but not precisely the centre, or what is nearest the centre. See Exod. 15. 8, Deut. 4. 11, 2 Sam. 18. 14. Moreover, there is no mention there of the separated soul.

units.la: Obj. 2. Act. 2. 27. ad Christum applicatur illud Psal. 16. 10. Non derelinques animam meam apud inferos. Resp. ꝥ fynecdochice Personam notat & porro interdum Corpus vitæ expers: ut Levit. 19. 28. xxj. 1. ינּ vero non definite locum damnatorum: sed statum & conditionem mortuorum, quâ talium, in loco qualicunque; & frequenter Sepulchrum; juxta Gen. 37. 35. Num. 16. 30. 33. &c.
units.tr: Objection 2. Acts 2. 27 applies to Christ that saying of Psal. 16. 10, You will not leave my soul in hell. Reply: Here the word denotes by synecdoche the person, and at times further the body deprived of life, as in Lev. 19. 28, 21. 1. The Hebrew word, however, does not define the place of the damned, but the state and condition of the dead, as such, in any place whatever; and it frequently means the grave, according to Gen. 37. 35, Num. 16. 30, 33, etc.

units.la: Obj. 3. Rom. x. 7. ex Deut. 30. 12, 13. Quis descendet in abyssum? hoc est, Christum ex mortuis reducere? Ergo Christus fuit localiter in abysso, sive inferno, Resp. Imo, juxta Apostolum, doctrina Evangelica copiose satis inter Christianos erat exhibita; ut necesse non fuerit, ad eam penitius investigandam, vel cœlum quasi conscendere, vel in abyssum descendere, acsi Christus vel ex summis, vel ex imis eum in finem foret revocandus. Sed nihil de inferno damnatorum, aut Christi ad eum descensu locali.
units.tr: Objection 3. Rom. 10. 7, from Deut. 30. 12, 13: Who will descend into the abyss? that is, to bring Christ back from the dead? Therefore Christ was locally in the abyss, or hell. Reply: On the contrary, according to the Apostle, the Evangelical doctrine had been presented among Christians copiously enough, so that there was no need, in order to investigate it more deeply, either to ascend to heaven as it were, or to descend into the abyss, as if Christ were to be recalled for this purpose either from the heights or from the depths. But there is nothing here about the hell of the damned, or about Christ's local descent into it.

units.la: Obj. 4. 1 Petr. 3. 18, 19. Christus per Spiritum profectus, dicitur prædicasse spiritibus qui sunt in carcere. Resp. Ibi non agitur de anima Christi separata; sed de Spiritu ipsius qui in Prophetis fuit; 1 Petr. 1. 11. Neque de spiritibus fidelium V. T.; nedum tanquam in limbo existentibus: sed de iis, qui in diebus Noachi fuerunt immorigeri, quantumvis ejus præconio ad resipiscentiam vocati.
units.tr: Objection 4. 1 Petr. 3. 18, 19: Christ, put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit, is said to have preached to the spirits who are in prison. Reply: That passage is not about the separated soul of Christ, but about his Spirit, which was in the prophets, 1 Pet. 1. 11. Nor is it about the spirits of the faithful of the Old Testament, much less as existing in limbo; it is about those who were disobedient in the days of Noah, however much they were called to repentance by his preaching.

units.la: LVIII. Sic de Statu Humiliationis; cujus Fines fuerunt.
units.tr: LVIII. Thus concerning the State of Humiliation, and what its ends were.

units.la: 1. Ut Christus humiliter consummando omnem justitiam, nos justos constitueret, & vita æterna dignos: Rom. 5. 19. Apoc. 3. 4.
units.tr: 1. That Christ, by humbly fulfilling all righteousness, might make us righteous and worthy of eternal life: Rom. 5. 19, Rev. 3. 4.

units.la: 2. Ut mortem maledictam subeundo, nos à morte & maledictione liberaret: 2 Cor. 5. 15. Gal. 3. 13.
units.tr: 2. That by undergoing a cursed death, he might free us from death and from the curse: 2 Cor. 5. 15, Gal. 3. 13.

units.la: 3. Ut in ipsius tentationibus, deserrionibus, &c. adversus istiusmodi mala remedium haberemus validissimum, & victoriam certissimam: Hebr. 2. 17. 18. Joh. 16. 33. 4. Ut virtute crucifixionis, mortis, & sepulturæ Christi, vetus noster homo magis ac magis crucifigeretur, mortificaretur, & sepeliretur: Rom. 6. 2,-8. Col. 3. 3, 5. Gal. 5. 24.
units.tr: 3. That in his temptations, desertions, and so on, we might have a most powerful remedy against such evils, and a most certain victory: Heb. 2. 17, 18, John 16. 33. 4. That by the power of the crucifixion, death, and burial of Christ, our old man might be more and more crucified, mortified, and buried: Rom. 6. 2-8, Col. 3. 3, 5, Gal. 5. 24.

units.la: LIX. Succedit Status Exaltationis, in quo Christus secundum humanam naturam, singularem præ cæteris creaturis potestatem & gloriam accepit, ita quidem ut gloria Deitatis in illa simul declaretur, modo illustrissimo.
units.tr: LIX. There follows the State of Exaltation, in which Christ, according to his human nature, received a power and glory singular above other creatures, so that the glory of the Deity is at the same time declared in it, in a most illustrious manner.

units.la: De hoc Phil. 2. 8. - Deus ipsum infummam extulit sublimitatem; ac donavit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen, &c. & Hebr. 2. 9. Iesum illum cernimus honore & gloria coronatum. Addè 12. 2. Apoc. 1. 18. Tres autem sunt gradus Exaltationis, extremæ Humiliationi in Morte, Sepultura, & Descensu ad inferos, respondentes; Resurrectio ex mortuis, Ascensio in cælum, & Sessio ad dextram Patris.
units.tr: Concerning this, Phil. 2. 8: God exalted him to the highest height, and gave him the name which is above every name, etc.; and Heb. 2. 9: We see Jesus crowned with honour and glory. Add Heb. 12. 2, Rev. 1. 18. There are three degrees of Exaltation, corresponding to the lowest point of Humiliation in death, burial, and descent into the underworld: the resurrection from the dead, the ascension into heaven, and the sitting at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: LX. Resurrectio est primus gradus Exaltationis, quo Christus e statu & loco mortuorum ad vitam gloriosam evectus est. Vide Marc. 16. 9. Cum autem resurrexisset Iesus mane, &c. Rom. 4. 24, 25. 1 Cor. 15. 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: LX. The Resurrection is the first degree of Exaltation, by which Christ was raised from the state and place of the dead to a glorious life. See Mark 16. 9, Now when Jesus had risen early, etc.; Rom. 4. 24, 25; 1 Cor. 15. 3, 4, 5.

units.la: Atque huc pertinet primo actus internus; ipsa scil. gloriosa Christi revivificatio, secundum humanam naturam, quæ involvit, 1. Animæ reductionem ad Corpus. 2. Corporis transmutationem ad incorruptibilitatem & gloriam. 3. Utriusque unionem redintegratam & inseparabilem. Rom. 6. 4, 9, 10. 1 Cor. 15. 20; 42, 43; 53. Secundo etiam actus externus; videl. Exitus è sepulchro, ad manifestationem vitæ illius restitutæ. Marc. 16. 6.
units.tr: To this belongs, first, the internal act, namely the glorious revivification of Christ according to his human nature, which involves: 1. the reunion of the soul with the body; 2. the transformation of the body to incorruptibility and glory; 3. the restored and inseparable union of both. Rom. 6. 4, 9, 10; 1 Cor. 15. 20, 42, 43, 53. Secondly, there is also the external act, namely the coming forth from the tomb, for the manifestation of that restored life. Mark 16. 6.

units.la: Hæc prædicta fuit, Psal. 16. 10. cx. 7. Isef. 53. 10. & Hos. 6. 2. Accessit typus Ionæ Prophetæ; Ion. 17. 11, 10. cum Matth. 12. 40.
units.tr: This was foretold in Psal. 16. 10, 110. 7, Isa. 53. 10, and Hos. 6. 2. The type of the prophet Jonah was added: Jonah 1. 17, 2. 10, compared with Matt. 12. 40.

units.la: Facta autem est virtute Divina, quæ Christo cum Patre & Spir. S. pariter competit: quapropter hæc actio & Patri adscribitur, Eph.1.19. 20. & ipse Filio, Iob.2.19, 21. x, 17, 18. & Spir. Sancto, 1 Petr. 3.18. Rom. 1. 4.
units.tr: It was effected by divine power, which belongs equally to Christ together with the Father and the Holy Spirit; for this action is ascribed to the Father, Eph. 1. 19, 20, and to the Son himself, John 2. 19, 21, 10. 17, 18, and to the Holy Spirit, 1 Pet. 3. 18, Rom. 1. 4.

units.la: Fines ejus erant,1. Ut se Filium Dei justificatum, 1 Tim. 3. 16. & alios justificantem, declararet: Rom. 4. 25. 1 Cor. 15. 17.
units.tr: Its ends were: 1. that he might declare himself to be the Son of God, justified, 1 Tim. 3. 16, and justifying others, Rom. 4. 25, 1 Cor. 15. 17.

units.la: 2. Ut victoriam plenissimam de morte partam obsignaret: 1 Cor 15. 57.
units.tr: 2. That he might confirm the most complete victory over death that had been won: 1 Cor. 15. 57.

units.la: 3. Ut reliquas officii sui partes in vita gloriosa adimpleret: Rom. 8. 34. Hebr. 7. 16, 17. Apoc. 1, 17. 18.
units.tr: 3. That he might fulfil the remaining parts of his office in glorious life: Rom. 8. 34, Heb. 7. 16, 17, Rev. 1. 17, 18.

units.la: 4. Ut resurrectionis nostrae, tum spiritualis, tum corporalis, hypostasis, exemplar, & initiatio foret: Rom. 6.4, 5. Eph. 2. 5, 6. 1 Cor. 15. 20, 21, 22, 23; 49. Phil. 3. 20. 21.
units.tr: 4. That he might be the pattern, the exemplar, and the beginning of our resurrection, both spiritual and bodily: Rom. 6. 4, 5, Eph. 2. 5, 6, 1 Cor. 15. 20, 21, 22, 23, 49, Phil. 3. 20, 21.

units.la: Hanc factam comprobarunt Angeli; Matth. 28. 2,3. & seqq. Ipse Christus per 40. dies, tum apparitionibus & signis variis; Act. 1. 3. tum etiam probationibus Scripturariis; Luc. 24. 25,-27 & Homines; potissimum 500. illi fratres; 1 Cor. 15. 6. Mulieres; Matth. 28. 8, 10, 11. Petrus; Luc. 24. 34. Discipuli Emauntici; 35. Atque ipsi denique Apostoli, qui juxta munus sibi demandatum, per totum terrarum orbem huic veritati testimonium praebuerunt: Marc. 16. 20. Act. 1. 8, 11; 32.
units.tr: This resurrection was attested by angels, Matt. 28. 2, 3, and following. Christ himself, over forty days, by various appearances and signs, Acts 1. 3, and also by proofs from Scripture, Luke 24. 25-27; and by men: above all the five hundred brothers, 1 Cor. 15. 6; women, Matt. 28. 8, 10, 11; Peter, Luke 24. 34; the disciples going to Emmaus, Luke 24. 35. And finally the Apostles themselves, who, according to the office committed to them, bore witness to this truth throughout the whole world: Mark 16. 20, Acts 1. 8, 11, 32.

units.la: LXI. Ascensio in Caelum est secundus gradus exaltationis, quo Christus secundum humanam naturam, de terra in Caelum supremum evectus est localiter & visibiliter, ubi existit Ecclesiae bono, donec revertatur ad extremum & universale judicium. Marc. 16. 19. Dominus, postquam locutus esset eis, sursum receptus est in Caelum.
units.tr: LXI. The Ascension into Heaven is the second degree of exaltation, by which Christ, according to his human nature, was carried locally and visibly from earth into the highest heaven, where he exists for the good of the Church until he returns to the last and universal judgement. Mark 16. 19: The Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven.

units.la: Subjectum mobile fuit ipse Christus secundum humanam naturam: eadem igitur Anima, & idem Corpus, in resurrectione unita, hic specifari debent. Nec statuendum cum Socin. Christum hoc depositisse, & aliud essentiâ spirituale assumsisse: nam neque Scriptura id docet; neque citra evidentem contradictionem Corpus essentiâ spirituale, fingi potest.
units.tr: The subject that was moved was Christ himself according to his human nature; therefore the same soul and the same body, united in the resurrection, must be specified here. Nor should we hold, with the Socinians, that Christ laid aside this body and assumed another, spiritual in essence; for Scripture does not teach this, and a body spiritual in essence cannot be imagined without evident contradiction.

units.la: Terminus a quo fuit Mons Oliveti, prope Bethaniam: Luc.24.50,51. Terminus ad quem, Coelum supremum, five Coelum beatorum: Eph.4.10. Hebr.7,26.
units.tr: The starting point was the Mount of Olives, near Bethany: Luke 24:50, 51. The end point was the highest heaven, or the heaven of the blessed: Eph. 4:10; Heb. 7:26.

units.la: Quod ad Modum attinet, Ascensio illa facta est localiter, terram deserendo, & per media sursum tendendo; ac simul visibiliter, Discipulis motum istum visu suo aliquamdiu observantibus: Act.1. 9,-11.
units.tr: As to the manner, the ascension took place locally, by leaving the earth and rising upward through the intervening space; and at the same time visibly, the disciples watching that movement with their eyes for some time: Acts 1:9-11.

units.la: Quantum ad Tempus, facta est postquam Christus 40. dies Resurrectionis suæ veritatem sufficienter asseruisset, & Discipulos suos de variis adhuc instruxisset.
units.tr: As to the time, it took place forty days after Christ, having sufficiently established the truth of his resurrection and having instructed his disciples further on various matters.

units.la: Prædicta ea fuit Psal. 68.19. cum Eph.4. 8,-11. & præfigurata, Summo Sacerdote, quotannis Sanctum Sanctorum ingrediente, quod Coeli erat exemplar. Levit. 16.12,-17. cum Hebr. 9. 7,24.
units.tr: It was foretold in Ps. 68:19, cited with Eph. 4:8-11, and prefigured when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies every year, which was a copy of heaven: Lev. 16:12-17, compared with Heb. 9:7, 24.

units.la: Causa efficiens eadem fuit, quæ Resurrectionis; Virtus scil. Divina: atque hinc respectu Patris Assumtio dicitur; sed respectu filii, Ascensio: Act.1.11. Accedente suo modo Corporis glorificati conditione; 1 Cor.15.44,46,49.
units.tr: The efficient cause was the same as in the resurrection, namely divine power; and for this reason, with respect to the Father it is called an assumption, but with respect to the Son an ascension: Acts 1:11, the condition of the glorified body being added in its own way: 1 Cor. 15:44, 46, 49.

units.la: Fines fuerunt, 1. Ut humanam suam naturam jam vere glorificatam in vero gloriæ domicilio collocaret; se Dominum coelestem demonstraret: deque hostibus suis triumpharet gloriosissime: Eph.1. 20,21. 1 Cor.15.47,-49. Eph.4. 8.
units.tr: The ends were: (1) that he might place his human nature, now truly glorified, in the true dwelling of glory, and show himself to be the heavenly Lord, and triumph most gloriously over his enemies: Eph. 1:20, 21; 1 Cor. 15:47-49; Eph. 4:8.

units.la: 2. Ut ea quæ in coelis ad salutem electorum erant peragenda, Intercessione sua expediret; & Spiritum interim, cum variis donorum distributionibus, ad suos mitteret: Hebr. 9. 24. Joh.14.2,3. xvj,7.
units.tr: (2) that he might, by his intercession, bring about those things in heaven which were to be done for the salvation of the elect; and in the meantime send the Spirit to his own with various distributions of gifts: Heb. 9:24; John 14:2, 3; 16:7.
