units.la: 3. Ut suorum nomine possessionem Regni coelestis adiret; atque adeo & nos Ascensionis nostræ in Coelum, argumentum haberemus certissimum: Eph. 2.6. 1 Cor.15.49. Joh.17.24. Apoc.3.21.
units.tr: (3) that he might enter into possession of the heavenly kingdom in the name of his own; and so that we might have a most certain pledge of our own ascension into heaven: Eph. 2:6; 1 Cor. 15:49; John 17:24; Rev. 3:21.

units.la: 4. Ut in Coelestium meditatione essemus perpetui, & ad superna semper attenti : Col. 3. 1. Phil. 3. 20.
units.tr: (4) that we might be constantly engaged in meditation on heavenly things and always attentive to what is above: Col. 3:1; Phil. 3:20.

units.la: LXII. Ordinis ratione Christus recte dicitur primus in Coelum ascendisse : Hebr. 9. 8. Hoc declarante Sp. Sancto nondum factam fuisse manifestam ad Sacrarium viam, priore Tabernaculo adhuc consistente. Quamdiu igitur duravit prius Tabernaculum, via ad Sacrarium, quod Coelum adumbrabat, non fuit manifesta : obstabat enim Velum intermedium. Hoc autem ruptum fuit in morte Christi : Matth. 27. 51. Et sic ipse moriens aperitionem Coeli impetravit ipso actu. Animae quidem fidelium V. T. prius tempore ascenderant : Col. 1. 20. cum Hebr. 12. 23. imo etiam Enoch & Elias anima & corpore conjunctis : Gen. 5. 24. Hebr. XI. 5. 2 Reg. 2. 11. sed id factum praevia virtute impetrationis Christi.
units.tr: LXII. In the order of things, Christ is rightly said to have ascended first into heaven: Heb. 9:8. The Holy Spirit declares by this that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made manifest while the former tabernacle still stood. As long, therefore, as the former tabernacle lasted, the way into the sanctuary, which foreshadowed heaven, was not manifest, for the intervening veil stood in the way. But this was torn at the death of Christ: Matt. 27:51. And so he, dying, obtained the opening of heaven by that very act. Indeed the souls of the faithful of the Old Testament had ascended earlier in time: Col. 1:20, compared with Heb. 12:23; even Enoch and Elijah, with soul and body joined together: Gen. 5:24; Heb. 11:5; 2 Kings 2:11. But this came about through the prior power of Christ's intercession obtained for them.

units.la: Testes hujus Ascensionis fuere Apostoli : Act. 1. 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10. atque item duo Angeli, qui eam confirmarunt : 10. 11.
units.tr: The witnesses of this ascension were the apostles: Acts 1:2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10; and likewise the two angels who confirmed it: Acts 1:10, 11.

units.la: LXIII. Ex superioribus sequitur, Christum secundum humanam naturam nunc tantum in Coelo esse, non ubique; ut existimant Lutherani : nec in Coelo, atque insuper in multis distinctis terrae locis simul; ut volunt Pontificii. Sed plenius orthodoxam sententiam adstruimus;
units.tr: LXIII. It follows from what has been said that Christ, according to his human nature, is now in heaven only, and not everywhere, as the Lutherans think; nor in heaven and at the same time in many distinct places of the earth, as the Papists maintain. But we establish the orthodox view more fully:

units.la: 1. Ex iis S. Scripturae locis, quae ipsum terram prorsus deseruisse confirmant : sic ipse de se, Joh. 16. 28. Relinquo mundum; & proficiscor ad Patrem. xvij, 11. Non sum amplius in mundo, &c. Matth. 26. 11. Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum; Me vero non semper habebitis.
units.tr: (1) from those passages of Holy Scripture which confirm that he has altogether left the earth. So he says of himself: John 16:28, "I leave the world and go to the Father"; John 17:11, "I am no longer in the world," etc.; Matt. 26:11, "The poor you will always have with you, but me you will not always have."

units.la: 2. Ex iis, quae Coelum supremum, oppositae ad Terram, pro loco continente ipsi attribuunt : ut Mar. 16. 19. -Sursum receptus est in Coelum. Act. 3. 21. Quem oportet quidem Coeli capiant, ad tempora restitutionis omnium. Item Act. 1. 11. Luc. 24. 51.
units.tr: (2) from those passages which ascribe to him the highest heaven, set over against the earth, as the containing place: such as Mark 16:19, "He was received up into heaven"; Acts 3:21, "whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things." Likewise Acts 1:11; Luke 24:51.

units.la: 3. Ex iis, quae reditum ipsius e Coelo in nubes, ad extremum judicium, localiter, & visibiliter futurum, docent: sic Act. 1. 11. Ita veniet, quemadmodum spectastis eum proficiscentem in Cœlum. Matth. 24. 30. Videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus cœli, &c. xxv, 31, 32. Cum autem venerit Filius Hominis; tunc sedebit in throno gloriæ suæ, & cogentur coram eo omnes gentes, &c.
units.tr: (3) from those passages which teach that his return from heaven in the clouds, to the final judgment, will take place locally and visibly: thus Acts 1:11, "He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven"; Matt. 24:30, "They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven," etc.; Matt. 25:31, 32, "When the Son of Man comes, then he will sit on the throne of his glory, and all nations will be gathered before him," etc.

units.la: 4. Ex ipsius Christi & Apostolorum instructionibus adversus hæreses & superstitiones; atque item hortationibus, ad studium sanctimoniæ, & praxin fidei ac spei. Hinc Matth. 24. 26. Si dixerint vobis, Ecce in deserto est, ne egredimini: Ecce in conclavibus, ne credite. Hebr. 8. 4. Si esset in terra, nec Sacerdos quidem esset. Col. 3. 1. Si resurrexistis cum Christo, superna quærite, ubi Christus est ad dextram Dei sedens. 2 Cor. 5. 6, 8. Phil. 1. 23.
units.tr: (4) from the teachings of Christ himself and of the apostles against heresies and superstitions, and likewise from exhortations to the pursuit of holiness and to the practice of faith and hope. Hence Matt. 24:26, "If they say to you, Behold, he is in the desert, do not go out; behold, he is in the inner rooms, do not believe it"; Heb. 8:4, "If he were on earth, he would not even be a priest"; Col. 3:1, "If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God"; 2 Cor. 5:6, 8; Phil. 1:23.

units.la: 5. Adde veritatem & unitatem humanæ naturæ in Christo; atque adeo Corporis impenetrabilitatem, extensionem, localitatem, & similes ejus affectiones; quas ut non destruxit Unio hypostatica, sic neque Glorificatio. Vide sup. th. 21.
units.tr: (5) add the reality and unity of the human nature in Christ; and so the impenetrability, extension, locality and similar affections of the body, which the hypostatic union did not destroy, and neither has glorification destroyed them. See above, chapter 21.

units.la: Obj. Stephanus post Ascensionem vidit Christum; Act. 7. 55, 56. & Paulus, ix. 3, 4, 5; 17. xvij, 9. xxiij. 11. & Johannes: Apoc. 1. 10, 12, 13. Ergo. Resp. Visiones illæ ecstaticæ, aut aliter extraordinariæ, ne quidem pro illo tempore localem Christi secundum humanam naturam in terris præsentiam inferunt; nedum perpetuam, sed invisibilem: cum Christus duntaxat in eorum phantasia & intellectu, intentionaliter; aut aliter symbolicè, fuerit repræsentatus.
units.tr: Objection: Stephen saw Christ after the ascension, Acts 7:55, 56; and Paul, Acts 9:3, 4, 5; 17; 23:11; and John, Rev. 1:10, 12, 13. Therefore... Answer: those visions, being ecstatic or otherwise extraordinary, do not imply even for that time a local presence of Christ according to his human nature on earth, much less a perpetual one; but an invisible one, since Christ was represented only in their imagination and understanding, intentionally, or otherwise symbolically.

units.la: LXIV. Sessio ad Dextram Dei est tertius & summus gradus Exaltationis; quo Christus Mediator à Deo evectus est ad supremam in Cœlo potestatem & gloriam, supra omnes Creaturas. Marc. 14. 62. Videbitis Filium hominis sedentem ad dextram potentiæ Dei. Rom. 8. 35. Eph. 1. 20, 23. Hebr. 8. 1. xij, 2. juxta propheticas phetiam Psal. 110. 1, 2. Est autem modus loquendi improprius, à Regibus, aliisque personis illustribus, defumtus; qui aliquos interdum honoris causa ad dextram suam collocant, & sic reliquis præferunt. Vide Psal. 45. 10. 1 Reg. 2. 19. Matth. 20. 21. Sic denotatur summum & inaccessum gloriæ fastigium, ad quod Resurrectio, & Ascensio, viæ instar fuerunt: quapropter & nos Resurrectionis quidem atque Ascensionis reddimur participes; sed non proprie Sessionis ad Dextram Patris. Hebr. 1. 13. Cui Angelorum dixit unquam; Sede ad dextram meam, &c.
units.tr: LXIV. The session at the right hand of God is the third and highest degree of exaltation, by which Christ the Mediator was raised by God to supreme power and glory in heaven, above all creatures: Mark 14:62, "You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God"; Rom. 8:34; Eph. 1:20, 23; Heb. 8:1; 12:2; according to the prophetic words of Ps. 110:1, 2. The manner of speaking, however, is improper, taken from kings and other illustrious persons, who sometimes place certain persons at their right hand for the sake of honour, and so prefer them to the rest: see Ps. 45:10; 1 Kings 2:19; Matt. 20:21. Thus is denoted the highest and inaccessible summit of glory, to which the resurrection and ascension were as the way. For this reason we too are made partakers of the resurrection and of the ascension, but not properly of the session at the right hand of the Father: Heb. 1:13, "To which of the angels did he ever say, Sit at my right hand, etc.?"

units.la: LXV. Causa hujus efficiens eadem est, quæ in gradibus Exaltationis prioribus.
units.tr: LXV. The efficient cause of this is the same as in the earlier degrees of exaltation.

units.la: Fines autem; 1. Ut caput nostrum tam gloriose exaltatum, nos etiam ad sui unionem & communionem adduceret; suumque Spiritum membris suis gloriosé communicaret. Act. 2. 33. Itaque dextrâ Dei sursum sublatus, & promissum Sp. Sanctum adeptus à Patre, effudit quod vos nunc cernitis & auditis. Confer Matth. 28. 18, 19. Rom. 12. 5, 6. Eph. 2. 22, 23.
units.tr: The ends, however, are: (1) that our head, so gloriously exalted, might also bring us into union and communion with himself, and gloriously impart his Spirit to his members: Acts 2:33, "Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit, he has poured out what you now see and hear." Compare Matt. 28:18, 19; Rom. 12:5, 6; Eph. 2:22, 23.

units.la: 2. Ut suos gloriose conservaret, ac defenderet, & cœlestis tandem gloriæ secum participes facerer: Matth. 28. 20. Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi. Apoc. 3. 21. Qui vicerit, tribuam ei, ut sedeat mecum in throno meo: ut & ego vici, & sedeo cum Patre meo, in throno ejus.
units.tr: (2) that he might gloriously preserve and defend his own, and at last make them partakers with himself of heavenly glory: Matt. 28:20, "I am with you always, to the end of the age." Rev. 3:21, "To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne."

units.la: Sic ergo Mediator noster Θεάνθρωπος, tanquam Rex Ecclesiæ, Regiam suam potestatem illustri modo nunc exerit: 1 Cor. 15. 25. atque hinc præsens ejus functio Sacerdotalis omnino Regia est; Intercessio videl. gloriosissima & efficacissima ad salutem electorum, & vindictam hostium: Apoc. 8. 3, 5. Imo & Prophetia ejus Regia est, per potentem Sp. Sancti cum prædicatione Ministrorum cooperationem: 1 Thess. 1. 5. Marc. 16. 20.
units.tr: Thus our Mediator, God-man, as King of the Church, now exercises his royal power in a glorious manner: 1 Cor. 15:25. Hence his present priestly function is wholly royal: namely, a most glorious and efficacious intercession for the salvation of the elect and the punishment of enemies: Rev. 8:3, 5. Indeed his prophetic office is also royal, through the powerful cooperation of the Holy Spirit with the preaching of the ministers: 1 Thess. 1:5; Mark 16:20.

units.la: LXVI. Frustra interim Lutherani ex hac Sessione Christi ad Dextram Dei, ubiquitatem ejus secundum humanam ipsius naturam colligunt: nam distinguendum est inter Dextram Dei, & Sessionem ad Dextram Dei. Atque adeo ob specialem hujus phrasios significationem nequaquam sequitur, Christum secundum humanam naturam præsentem adesse, ubicunque illud est, quod improprie nonnunquam Dextra Dei appellatur: non magis quam urbs aliqua ad mare, aut flumen, sita, dicenda est adæquate existere, ubi illud mare, aut flumen, existit.
units.tr: LXVI. Meanwhile the Lutherans vainly infer from this sitting of Christ at the right hand of God that he is everywhere present according to his human nature. For a distinction must be drawn between the right hand of God and the sitting at the right hand of God. Hence, on account of the special meaning of this phrase, it by no means follows that Christ according to his human nature is present wherever that is which is improperly sometimes called the right hand of God; just as a city situated by the sea or by a river is not to be said to exist adequately wherever that sea or river exists.

units.la: Tenendum etiam contra Socinianos, eorumque se-quaces Remonstrantes, hanc Sessionem ad Dextram Dei, non esse veram ac propriam causam, cur Christus appelletur Filius Dei; quemadmodum neque Nativitatem ex Virgine, Patrațonem miraculorum, vel Resurrectionem ex mortuis: sed solam æternam ineffabilem generationem, qua est Filius Dei proprius, unigenitus. &c. quæ per actus jam proxime recensitos multifariam quidem fuit declarata, & sic præsupposita; sed non fundata, vel formaliter posita.
units.tr: We must also hold, against the Socinians and their followers the Remonstrants, that this sitting at the right hand of God is not the true and proper cause why Christ is called the Son of God; nor are his nativity from the Virgin, his working of miracles, or his resurrection from the dead. Rather, it is his eternal and ineffable generation alone, by which he is the proper and only-begotten Son of God, etc. These things, through the acts just now recounted, were indeed declared in many ways and so presupposed, but they were not founded, nor formally established, by them.

units.la: Concedimus interim Christo secundum humanam naturam eminentiori quadam ratione ea competere; vel similia iis, ob quæ fideles appellantur filii Dei: verum in subjecto, ubi significatio propria locum habet, ea omnino agnoscenda est; nec ad rationes metaphoricæ significationis, quales in subjectis metaphoricè sic dictis attendi solent, confugiendum.
units.tr: Meanwhile we concede that these things belong to Christ according to his human nature in a more eminent manner, or things similar to those on account of which the faithful are called sons of God. Yet where the proper meaning has its place, these things must wholly be acknowledged as such, and one must not take refuge in the grounds of metaphorical meaning, such as are usually considered in subjects said metaphorically in this way.

units.la: LXVII. Superest ut contra Judæos concludamus, Jesum Christum, in quem Christiani credimus, esse verum Messiam, olim sub V. T. promissum & expectatum: supposito enim Messiam jam pridem venille, quod probatum dedimus, cap.11.th.43. inquirendum omnino, quis ille sit; & pro Messia agnoscendus haud dubie, cui omnia ista χρῑτήρια conveniunt. Tale igitur formamus Argumentum: Cui competunt omnia de Messia olim praedicta & praefigurata,& quidem soli, is pro vero Messia agnosci & recipi debet: Sed Jesu Christo, in quem Christiani credimus, ista omnia competunt, & quidem soli. Ergo. Major manifestissimae veritatis est, postquam ante asseruimus, Messiam dudum venisse. Minor etiam in superioribus probata est per partes: tum quoad Personam, ejusque ortum secundum humanam naturam, vitam, ejusque adjuncta, & mortem, atque exaltationem; tum quoad officia & beneficia: nisi quod de Salutis impetratione & applicatione pluribus etiam agendum sit deinceps.
units.tr: LXVII. It remains that against the Jews we conclude that Jesus Christ, in whom we Christians believe, is the true Messiah, promised and expected of old under the Old Testament. For, supposing that the Messiah has already come, which we proved in chapter 11, thesis 43, it must necessarily be inquired who he is; and he is undoubtedly to be acknowledged as the Messiah to whom all these marks (criteria) apply. We therefore frame the argument thus: He to whom all the things foretold and foreshadowed concerning the Messiah apply, and to him alone, is to be acknowledged and received as the true Messiah. But all these things apply to Jesus Christ, in whom we Christians believe, and to him alone. Therefore... The major premise is of the clearest truth, since we asserted earlier that the Messiah has long since come. The minor premise was also proved in the preceding part by parts: both as to the Person and his birth according to human nature, his life and its circumstances, and his death and exaltation; and as to his offices and benefits, except that the obtaining and application of salvation must also be treated at more length hereafter.

units.la: Obj. 1. Nomen Messiae appellandum fuit יהושע; non Iesus: Isf. 7. 14. Resp. Scil. quemadmodum Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, &c. 9. 5. itemque Iehovah Iustitia nostra; Jerem. 23. 6. Sic igitur elogia & tituli exprimuntur: non ipsum nomen proprium; quod ei in Circumcisione fuisset imponendum, & inter Homines communiter usurpandum.
units.tr: Objection 1. The name of the Messiah ought to be called Jeshua (יהושע), not Jesus: Isaiah 7:14. Answer: Just as Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, etc. (Isa. 9:5), and likewise Jehovah our righteousness (Jer. 23:6), so the titles and appellations are expressed in this way; not the proper name itself, which was to be imposed on him at circumcision and commonly used among men.

units.la: Obj. 2. Nec Iesu Christo conveniunt ista. Isf. 7. 15,16. de Esu butyri & lactis, deque Terra interim liberanda. Ergo. Resp. Prius facit duntaxat ad denotandam humanam Christi naturam, & communem educationis puerilis fortem; tantillo autem temporis spatio, quantulum inter infantis nativitatem, ac primam discretionis notitiam, intercedere solet, liberatio terrae futura Achazo promittitur. Vide similia de filio Prophetae, cap. viij, 3,4.
units.tr: Objection 2. Nor do these things apply to Jesus Christ: Isaiah 7:15, 16, concerning the eating of butter and milk, and concerning the land being meanwhile delivered. Therefore... Answer: The former serves only to denote the human nature of Christ and the common lot of childhood upkeep; and the deliverance of the land, which is promised to Ahaz, is to come about within the brief span of time that usually lies between the birth of an infant and its first knowledge of discernment. Compare similar things concerning the prophet's son, chapter 8:3, 4.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus dixit se Filium Dei, Regnum mundanum non erexit, humilis vixit, a primoribus populi rejectus fuit, mortem maledictam sustinuit, &c. Ergo. Resp. Ista nequaquam urgenda sunt contra hoc fidei & salutis nostrae mysterium: sed agnoscenda potius, tanquam vera & necessaria Messiae requisita; ut ex praemissis jam satis manifestum est. LXVIII. Pro Praxi; 1. Hunc unicum Mediatorem Θεάνθρωπον vera fide agnoscamus: Joh. 3. 16. xvij,3. In sanguine ipsius reconciliationem & pacem quæramus: Rom. 5. 10, 11. Eph. 2. 13, 14, &c. In illo Sponsore nostro ἀντιψύχῳ confidamus: Hebr.7.22. 2 Cor. 5.21. In illo Redemtore liberationem credamus: Job. 19. 25. Eph. 1. 7. In illo Salvatore perfecto unice acquiescamus: Hebr. 7. 24, 25. Act. 4. 12.
units.tr: Objection 3. Christ said that he was the Son of God, did not set up an earthly kingdom, lived in humility, was rejected by the leaders of the people, endured a cursed death, etc. Therefore... Answer: These things are by no means to be urged against this mystery of our faith and salvation; rather they are to be acknowledged as true and necessary requisites of the Messiah, as is now sufficiently clear from what has been said. LXVIII. For practice: 1. Let us acknowledge with true faith this one Mediator, God-man: John 3:16; 17:3. In his blood let us seek reconciliation and peace: Rom. 5:10, 11; Eph. 2:13, 14, etc. In that Surety of ours (antipsychos) let us trust: Heb. 7:22; 2 Cor. 5:21. In that Redeemer let us believe in deliverance: Job 19:25; Eph. 1:7. In that perfect Savior let us rest alone: Heb. 7:24, 25; Acts 4:12.

units.la: 2. Tantum illum Prophetam audiamus: Deuteron. 18. 18, 19. cum Act. 3. 22. In ipsius Sacerdotali oblatione, nostri à peccatis purificationem constituamus: Hebr. 9. 13, 14. 1 Joh. 1. 7. & in ejusdem jugi Intercessione, de favore complacentiæ Divinæ plenè persuasi, precibus nostris frequenter in ejus nomine ad Deum accedamus: 1 Joh. 2. 1. 2. Hebr. 4. 16. Regi nostro spirituali libentes nos subjiciamus: Psal. 2. 6, 10,-12, cx,3. & viventes in Regno Gratiæ, ad Regnum Gloriæ contendamus: Apoc. 3. 21. 2 Tim. 4. 6,-8.
units.tr: 2. Let us hear only that Prophet: Deut. 18:18, 19, with Acts 3:22. In his priestly offering let us place our purification from sins: Heb. 9:13, 14; 1 John 1:7. And in his continual intercession, being fully persuaded of the favor of divine good pleasure, let us frequently draw near to God with our prayers in his name: 1 John 2:1, 2; Heb. 4:16. Let us gladly submit ourselves to our spiritual King: Psalm 2:6, 10–12; 110:3. And living in the kingdom of grace, let us strive toward the kingdom of glory: Rev. 3:21; 2 Tim. 4:6–8.

units.la: 3. Vitam ejus sanctissimam sedulo imitemur:
units.tr: 3. Let us diligently imitate his most holy life:

units.la: 1 Joh. 3. 3. Eph. 4. 26, 21, 24. Quoad Intellectum, Voluntatem, & Affectus, ei quam proxime conformemur: Col. 2. 3. Matth. 26. 39. Psal. 40. 9. In perpessionibus hujus mundi, toleramus; Hebr. 12. 1, 2. In tentationibus Diaboli, vigilantiam; 1 Petr. 5. 8, 9. & in omnibus adversis, constantiam adhibeamus: 1 Petr. 2. 19,-24. donec ex hac miseriarum valle liberati, in cœlestis Gloriæ domicilium elevemur: Rom. 8. 17,-19.
units.tr: 1 John 3:3; Eph. 4:20, 21, 24. As to understanding, will, and affections, let us be conformed to him as closely as possible: Col. 2:3; Matt. 26:39; Psalm 40:9. In the sufferings of this world let us endure: Heb. 12:1, 2. Against the temptations of the devil let us apply watchfulness: 1 Pet. 5:8, 9; and in all adversities let us show constancy: 1 Pet. 2:19–24, until, delivered from this valley of miseries, we are raised to the dwelling of heavenly glory: Rom. 8:17–19.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: De Salutis Impetratione.
units.tr: On the Procuring of Salvation.

units.la: Salus. Ejus impetratio. 1. Satisfacere. Obligatio. Solutio. Remissio.Novatio.Delegatio.Accep-tilatio. Dispensatio. 2. In hoc negotio non acceptilatio.Nec solutio rei per expressam Legis formulam debita, &c. Sed remissio propter antecedentem Satisfactionem. 3. Causa efficiens prima. quasi proëgumena. procatartica. 4. Deus hic non proprie spectandus, ut pars offensa: neque ut Dominus absolutus. Sed ut Rector. 5. Est actus Jurisdictionis. 6. Non Legis abrogatio: nec derogatio. Sed interpretatio καὶ ἐξήγησιν. 7. Causa efficiens altera. Proëgumena. Materia. Forma. Fines. 8. Sententia Socin. & Remonstr. qu. Orthodoxa probatur. 9. Objectiones solv. 10. Meritum. Causa efficiens prima. Altera formaliter exequens. Materia. Forma. Finis. Probatur. 11. Sententia Socin. Obj. solv. 12. Christus nobis etiam meritus est fidem & regenerationem: c. Remonstr. 13. Intercessio Christi. Finis cui, non Angeli: nec omnes & singuli homines, c. Pontif. Remonstr. &c. 14. Objectiones solv. 15. Sententia Adversariorum. 16. Christus etiam sibi gloriam cœlestem meritus est. 17. Sententia Scholast. Obj. solv. 18. Et pro se quoque precatus. 19. Rejiciuntur Satisfactiones & merita alia. Thesaurus Ecclesiæ, &c. c. Pontif. 20. Refutantur. 21. Objectiones solv. 22. Praxis. 23.
units.tr: Salvation. Its procuring. 1. To satisfy. Obligation. Payment. Remission. Novation. Delegation. Acceptilation. Dispensation. 2. In this matter there is no acceptilation, nor payment of the debt by the express formula of the Law, etc., but remission on account of the prior Satisfaction. 3. The first efficient cause, as it were prolegomena, procatartica. 4. God is not to be regarded here properly as the injured party, nor as absolute Lord, but as Ruler. 5. It is an act of Jurisdiction. 6. It is not an abrogation of the Law, nor a derogation, but an interpretation [καὶ ἐξήγησιν]. 7. The second efficient cause: prolegomena, matter, form, ends. 8. The view of the Socinians and Remonstrants is refuted, and the orthodox view is proved. 9. Objections answered. 10. Merit: first efficient cause; second, formally executing; matter; form; end. Proved. 11. The view of the Socinians. Objection answered. 12. Christ has also merited for us faith and regeneration, against the Remonstrants. 13. The intercession of Christ: the end to which it is directed is not the angels, nor all and each man, against the Papists, Remonstrants, etc. 14. Objections answered. 15. The view of the adversaries. 16. Christ has also merited heavenly glory for himself. 17. The view of the Scholastics. Objection answered. 18. And he also prayed for himself. 19. The other satisfactions and merits are rejected: the treasury of the Church, etc., against the Papists. 20. Refuted. 21. Objections answered. 22. Practice. 23.

units.la: I. [A]Gendum nunc ex ordine instituto de Beneficiis ChristiMediatoris distinête, Salutis Impetratione, & ejusdem impetratæ Applicatione.Salus ista completitur Immunitatem à malis culpæ ac pœnæ,& Fruitionem bonorum justitiæ ac gloriæ. Salutis impetratio est, ejus acquisitio, Iustitiæ & Constitutioni ipsius Dei consentanea. In qua spectanda primum Satisfactio & Meritum; ac deinde Intercessio.
units.tr: I. We must now treat, in the order laid down, of the benefits of Christ the Mediator, distinguishing the procuring of salvation and the application of the same procured salvation. This salvation is completed in immunity from the evils of guilt and punishment, and in the enjoyment of the goods of righteousness and glory. The procuring of salvation is its acquisition, consistent with the justice and the very constitution of God. In considering this, first comes satisfaction and merit, and then intercession.

units.la: II. Satisfacere, cui respondet τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιεῖν, Marc. 15. 15. sonat Præstare quod satis est, & desiderium alicujus implere: ut si in compensationem culpæ fiat, quod jus Dei postulat, adhibita interim insigni ἔντευξις. Ex Culpa nimirum oritur Obligatio ad Pœnam; quemadmodum ex Credito, ad Solutionem convenientem. Talis autem obligatio vel antecedente solutione tollitur, vel citra solutionem. Solutio alia ipso facto liberat debitorem; ut si solvatur id ipsum, quod erat in obligatione: alia non item; ut si solvatur aliud, quam id quod erat in obligatione: quo casu necessum est, ut intercedat aliqua Remissio; & talis solutio, si admittatur, speciali nomine Satisfactio dicitur. Hujusmodi liberatio ali quando fit substitutione novæ obligationis; atque ea est Novatio: vel novi debitoris; quæ est Delegatio: aliquando etiam omnimodâ obligationis peremtione; quæ circa debitum solennibus quibusdam verbis peracta, Acceptilatio, solutio imaginaria; circa pœnam, communi nomine Gratia, Venia, Indulgentia, Abolitio appellatur. Cum solutio recusabilis admittitur in materia pœnæ, fit quædam Legis Relaxatio. Cum Legislator mentem suam in Lege, vel ejus Sanctione, minus plenè expressam, declarat; & τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον, quod alias urgendum videbatur, explicando mitigat; obtinet Interpretatio καθ' ἔντευξιν. Cum vero Legis manentis obligatio circa quasdam personas aut res tollitur, ea est DifDispensatio, sed respectu Debitoris est Remissio.
units.tr: II. To satisfy, to which corresponds τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιεῖν [to hikanon poiein] (Mark 15:15), means to do what is enough and to fulfil someone's desire: as when, in compensation for a fault, what the right of God demands is rendered, with some notable entreaty added. From guilt there arises an obligation to punishment, just as from a debt there arises an obligation to a suitable payment. Such an obligation is removed either by a prior payment or without payment. One kind of payment frees the debtor by the very fact, when the very thing which was owed in the obligation is paid; another kind does not, when something other than what was owed is paid. In that case some remission must intervene, and such a payment, if it is accepted, is called by the special name satisfaction. Liberation of this kind sometimes takes place by the substitution of a new obligation, and this is novation; or of a new debtor, and this is delegation; and sometimes by the complete cancellation of the obligation, which, when done in respect of a debt with certain solemn words, is acceptilation, an imaginary payment; in respect of punishment it is called by the common name grace, pardon, indulgence, release. When a payment that may be refused is admitted in a matter of punishment, there is a certain relaxation of the Law. When the Legislator declares his mind, not fully expressed in the Law or its sanction, and softens what otherwise seemed to be enforced with strict justice by explaining it, there is an interpretation by entreaty [καθ' ἔντευξιν]. But when the obligation of a law that remains in force is removed with respect to certain persons or things, this is a dispensation, but with respect to the debtor it is a remission.

units.la: III. In hoc nostro negotio non est Acceptilatio, i. quia solum acceptilatur ea res, quae caeteroquin accipi posset: at Poenam non accipit Rector. 2. Christus non praestitit solutionem imaginariam; sed verum & aequivalens λύτρον persolvit.
units.tr: III. In our present business there is no acceptilation, first, because only such a thing is accepted as might otherwise be received, but a ruler does not accept a punishment; second, Christ did not render an imaginary payment, but paid a true and equivalent ransom [λύτρον].

units.la: Neque etiam Solutio ipsius rei per expressam Legis formulam debitae: nec Novatio, aut Delegatio: sed est Remissio propter antecedentem Satisfactionem Christi, tanquam causam liberationis nostrae impetratoriam: Sic enim differte, Eph. 1. 7. In quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem lapsuum, ex divite ipsius gratia. Rom. 3. 24,25. Ut qui justificentur gratis, ejus gratia, per redemtionem factam in Jesu Christo; quem praestituit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad demonstrationem justitiae suae, &c.
units.tr: Nor is it a payment of the very thing owed by the express formula of the Law, nor a novation or delegation; it is a remission on account of the prior satisfaction of Christ, as the cause that procures our liberation. For Scripture speaks thus: Ephesians 1:7, "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, according to the riches of his grace." Romans 3:24-25, "Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, etc."

units.la: IV. Hujus nostrae liberationis Causa efficiens prima est ipse Deus: Jes. 53. 10. Joh. 3. 16. 2 Cor. 5. 18. 19,21. Ubi occurrit Causa quasi prolegumena, Ipsius tum Misericordia, tum Justitia: Psal. 85. 11. Misericordiae, quasi Procatarctica obversatur nostra Miseria; unde nos Deus misericors liberatos voluit convenienti quodam modo: Rom. 9. 32. Justitiae, nostra Peccata; quatenus haec reatum inducunt: propterea illa Satisfactionem postulavit, priusquam nos liberaremur. Atque adeo hic omnino agnoscenda est causa quaedam antecedens legitima, sive juridica, praeter Dei & Christi voluntatem: unde Christus traditus dicitur propter peccata nostra. Rom. 4. 25. minime autem mortuus δωρεάν; Gal. 2. 21.
units.tr: IV. The first efficient cause of this our liberation is God himself: Isaiah 53:10; John 3:16; 2 Corinthians 5:18, 19, 21. Here there appear the causes, as it were prolegomena, of his mercy and of his justice: Psalm 85:11. Over against his mercy, as a procatartic, stands our misery; wherefore God, being merciful, willed to free us in a suitable manner: Romans 9:32. Over against his justice stand our sins, insofar as they bring about guilt; therefore justice demanded satisfaction before we were freed. And so here must certainly be acknowledged some antecedent cause, lawful or juridical, besides the will of God and of Christ; hence Christ is said to have been delivered up for our sins, Romans 4:25, but by no means to have died gratuitously [δωρεάν], Galatians 2:21.

units.la: V. Deus interim hic considerandus est, non simpliciter ut Pars offensa; quia parti offensae per se non competit jus puniendi: cum punire sit actus ϝ ὑπεροχῆς. Neque etiam simpliciter, ut Dominus absolutus: hic enim, qua talis, de suo facere potest quod vult; Deus autem peccata prorsus impunita dimittere non potest. Sed
units.tr: V. Meanwhile God is to be considered here not simply as the injured party, since the injured party does not of itself have the right to punish, for to punish is an act of superior power. Nor again simply as absolute Lord, for he as such may do what he wills with his own; but God cannot dismiss sins altogether unpunished. But

units.la: Vide sup. Cap. 4. th. 56.
units.tr: See above, chap. 4, th. 56.

units.la: Sed considerandus proprie ut Rector ; qui Juris custos & vindex est, & quasi τὸ δίκαιον ἔμψυχον : cujus est poenas infligere ; vel etiam à poenis liberare, quem punire posset pro rigore. Poena enim in coactione ultimum est; coactio autem non competit, nisi Superiori. Unde vindicta privata tam ferio prohibetur;Matth. 5. 39. Rom. 12. 19. xiij. 4.
units.tr: He is to be considered properly as Ruler, who is the guardian and avenger of the Law, and as it were the living embodiment of what is right, whose office it is to inflict punishments, or also to release from punishments one whom he could punish with full severity. For punishment is the last resort in coercion, and coercion belongs only to a superior. Hence private vengeance is so strictly forbidden: Matthew 5:39; Romans 12:19; 13:4.

units.la: VI. Consequenter actus Dei in hoc negotio est Actus Jurisdictionis ; ad quam pertinet juris normam praescribendi, sanciendi, atque item causas ad eam cognoscendi, judicandi, & exequendi potestas. Si actus ipse consideretur citra speciale respectum ad sanctionem, recte dicitur Punitio unius ad impunitatem aliis procurandam: aut si ipsa quoque sanctio spectetur, est via ad temperamentum aliquod ejusdem Legis ; ita quidem, ut Lege manente, & vigorem suum obtinente, nos tamen a condemnatione immunes evadamus: Rom. 8. 1. quod posito peccato, fieri non potuisset in strikta Legis executione.
units.tr: VI. Consequently the act of God in this matter is an act of jurisdiction, to which belongs the power of prescribing and sanctioning the norm of law, and likewise of hearing, judging and executing cases before it. If the act itself is considered without special regard to the sanction, it is rightly called the punishment of one to procure impunity for others; or if the sanction itself is also taken into view, it is a way to some moderation of the same Law, in such a way that, while the Law remains and keeps its force, we nevertheless escape condemnation: Romans 8:1, which, once sin was posited, could not have happened under strict execution of the Law.

units.la: VII. Neque tamen facta est Legis abrogatio ; cum infideles ejus sanctioni etiamnum maneant obnoxii: Joh. 3. 36. 1 Thess. 2. 16. Nec Legi quicquam derogatum est: nam usquedum praeterierit coelum & terra iota unum, aut unus apex, nequaquam praeterierit ex Lege; Matth. 5. 18. Nec facta est Dispensatio; cum obligatio nostra ad poenam non fuerit impliciter sublata ; sed in Sponsorem translata. Verum facta est Interpretatio καὶ ἐγγύησιν, qua Sponsor dignissimus, nobisque conjunctissimus, admissus est loco nostro ; ejusque satisfactio aequivalens, pro poenis nostris.
units.tr: VII. Yet no abrogation of the Law has taken place, since unbelievers still remain liable to its sanction: John 3:36; 1 Thessalonians 2:16. Nor has anything been derogated from the Law, for until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall in no way pass from the Law: Matthew 5:18. Nor has a dispensation taken place, since our obligation to punishment was not simply removed but transferred to a surety. Rather, an interpretation [καὶ ἐγγύησιν] has taken place, by which a most worthy surety, most closely united to us, was admitted in our place, and his satisfaction, equivalent to our punishments, was accepted.

units.la: VIII. Causa efficiens altera est Christus Mediator, qua talis ; & quidem volens: Jes. 53. 7, 10, 12. Psal. 40. 7, 8. cum Hebr. x. 5,-10. Protegumena ei respondens est, tum summa Christi aptitudo ad peragendam sic nostri liberationem. Vide sup. cap. 12. th. 5. 6. tum summa ipsius φιλανθρωπία: Joh. 15. 13. Gal. 2. 20.
units.tr: VIII. The second efficient cause is Christ the Mediator, as such, and indeed willing: Isaiah 53:7, 10, 12; Psalm 40:7-8, compared with Hebrews 10:5-10. Corresponding to this as prolegomena is, on the one hand, the supreme fitness of Christ to accomplish our liberation in this way (see above, chap. 12, th. 5, 6), and on the other hand his supreme philanthropy: John 15:13; Galatians 2:20.

units.la: Quasi materiam constituunt voluntarias perpessiones malorum tristium, quæ Christus Θεάνθρωπω per universam suam vitam humilem animâ & corpore pro nobis sustinuit.
units.tr: The voluntary endurance of grievous evils, which Christ, the God-man, bore for us through his whole humble life, in soul and body, constitutes the matter.

units.la: Forma vicem præstat ratio pœnæ pro nobis vicariæ, ex respectu perpessionum illarum ad nostrum demeritum; & quidem validæ, ad λύτρον pro nobis præstandum, ex dignitate Persone Θεάνθρωπος, & tali ipsius Dei constitutione.
units.tr: The form is supplied by the nature of punishment borne vicariously on our behalf, with respect of those sufferings to our demerit; and indeed of sufficient validity to render the ransom on our behalf, from the dignity of the Person, the God-man, and from such a constitution of God himself.

units.la: Finis propinquus est, nostra immunitas à miseria; h. e. tum a reatû: Rom. 5. 9. 1 Thess. 1. 10. tum etiàm a turpitudine & servitute ipsius peccati: Rom. 6. 4, 6. 11, 18. Tit. 2. 14.
units.tr: The immediate end is our freedom from misery, that is, both from guilt (reatus) and from the defilement and slavery of sin itself: Rom. 5. 9; 1 Thess. 1. 10; Rom. 6. 4, 6, 11, 18; Tit. 2. 14.

units.la: Finis summus est demonstratio gloriosæ Misericordiæ: Eph. 1. 6,-8. & Justitiæ Divinæ; Rom. 3. 25,26.
units.tr: The ultimate end is the display of God's glorious mercy (Eph. 1. 6-8) and of his divine justice (Rom. 3. 25, 26).

units.la: IX. Socinani veram Christi Satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris prorsus negant: Ipse Socinus de Christo Servatore part. 1. cap. 1. dicit - „Iesum Christum „ideoServatorem esse, quia salutis æternæ viam nobis „annunciaverit, confirmaverit; & in suâ ipsius persona, cum vitæ exemplo, tum ex mortuis resurgendo, manifestè ostenderit; vitamque æternam nobis „ei fidem habentibus ipse daturus sit. Divinæ autem „Justitiæ per quam peccatores damnari mereremur, „pro peccatis nostris, neque illum satisfecisse; neque ut „satisfaceret, opus fuisse. Similiter idem alibi, ac passim Socinianî; sed nec multo aliter Steph. Curcellæus in Dissertatione de Vocibus Trinitatis, &c. §. 30. aliique sequaces.
units.tr: The Socinians utterly deny that Christ made a true satisfaction for our sins. Socinus himself, in On Christ the Saviour, part 1, chapter 1, says: "Jesus Christ is called Saviour because he announced and confirmed to us the way of eternal salvation, and showed it plainly in his own person, both by the example of his life and by rising from the dead; and he himself will give eternal life to those of us who believe in him. But as for the justice of God, by which we deserved to be condemned as sinners, he did not satisfy it for our sins, nor was there any need for him to make satisfaction." He says the same thing elsewhere, and the Socinians say it everywhere. Stephen Curcellaeus, in his Dissertation on the Words of the Trinity, §30, and other followers, differ little, if at all, from this.

units.la: Nos orthodoxam veritatem breviter confirmamus; Christum videl. Mediatorem & Sponsorem Θεάνθρωπον, poenas pro nobis vicarias sustinendo, demeritum peccatorum nostrorum, in ordine ad Iustitiam Dei, sufficienter compensasse: atque ita nobis immunitatem a miseria vere impetrasse. Illud autem probamus quatuor potissimum Argumentorum classibus defumtis a totidem titulis; videl. Sponsor, Redemtor, Sacerdos, Mediator.
units.tr: We briefly confirm the orthodox truth: that Christ, the Mediator and Surety who is God-man, by enduring vicarious punishments for us, sufficiently compensated for the guilt of our sins in relation to the justice of God, and so truly obtained for us freedom from misery. We prove this chiefly by four classes of arguments, drawn from four titles: Surety, Redeemer, Priest, and Mediator.

units.la: 1. Ex titulo Sponsoris in hunc modum argumentamur: Qui ipse innocens & justus, tanquam Sponsor, obligatus pro nobis in iis, quæ apud Deum agenda erant; pro nobis & loco nostro, pro peccatis nostris & propter ea, sic execrationi ex Lege Divina pro nobis subjectus; mortem violentam, ignominiosam, & maledictam, atque adeo pœnas peccatorum nostrorum, tulit; & quidem æquivalentes, per dignitatem Personæ, iis pœnis, quas ipsi alias ferre debuissemus; Is vere pro nobis satisfecit: Sed Christus, &c. Major certissima est; cum nihil amplius ad veram Satisfactionem requiri posset. Minor autem patet ex cap. 12. th. 30.
units.tr: 1. From the title of Surety we argue as follows. He who, though innocent and just himself, as Surety was bound on our behalf in the matters to be transacted before God, and who for us and in our place, for our sins and because of them, was thus made subject to the curse of the Divine Law, and bore a violent, shameful, and accursed death, and so the punishments of our sins, and indeed punishments equivalent (by the dignity of his Person) to those we ourselves ought otherwise to have borne, he truly satisfied for us. But Christ, etc. The major premise is most certain, since nothing more could be required for true satisfaction. The minor is clear from chapter 12, thesis 30.

units.la: 2. Ex titulo Redemtoris: Qui ipse insons & sanctus tanquam Redemtor noster, soluto pro nobis Redemtionis pretio, & ad culpam nostram redimendam; sic pretioso sanguine suo pro nobis fuso; nos ab Execratione Legis Divinæ redemit; atque in populum sibi peculiarem nos acquisivit & liberavit; Is vere pro nobis Satisfecit: Sed Christus, &c. Major similiter certissima est, per sufficientem enumerationem eorum, quæ ad satisfactionem requiruntur. Minor vero probata est dicto cap. 12. th. 31.
units.tr: 2. From the title of Redeemer: He who, himself blameless and holy, as our Redeemer, paid the price of redemption on our behalf in order to buy back our guilt, and so, by shedding his precious blood for us, redeemed us from the curse of the Divine Law, and acquired and freed us as his own special people, he truly satisfied for us. But Christ, etc. The major premise is likewise most certain, through a sufficient enumeration of what is required for satisfaction. The minor has been proved in the said chapter 12, thesis 31.

units.la: 3. Ex Oblatione Sacerdotali: Qui omnino sanctus, tanquam verus Sacerdos, ipse corpus suum cruenta oblatione, accedente Divina ipsius virtute, pro nobis obtulit in cruce; sic remissionem nobis impetravit; ac purificationem, in ordine ad conscientiam & cœlestia, pro nobis peregit; peccata nostra expiavit; nos in conscientia, quoad impetrationem, consummavit; Deum suo sanguine nobis placavit; & Gratiam Ipsius ista ratione nobis conciliavit; Is vere pro nobis satisfecit; Sed Christus &c. Major itidem evidentissimæ veritatis est: Minor autem jam asserta, ibid. th. 37,-.
units.tr: 3. From the priestly offering: He who was altogether holy, as the true Priest, offered his body for us on the cross as a bloody sacrifice, by the added power of his divine nature; and so obtained for us remission, and accomplished for us purification, with respect to the conscience and heavenly things; expiated our sins; perfected us in conscience, as regards the obtaining of grace; reconciled God to us by his blood; and in this way won over his grace for us. He truly satisfied for us. But Christ, etc. The major premise is of the most evident truth. The minor has already been asserted, ibid., thesis 37.

units.la: 4. Ex titulo Mediatoris denique: Qui cum esset sanctissi-
units.tr: 4. Finally, from the title of Mediator: He who, since he was most holy

units.la: CAP. XIII. De Salutis Impetratione.
units.tr: CHAP. XIII. On the Obtaining of Salvation.

units.la: stissimus, dignissimus, & nobis conjunctissimus, tanquam Mediator ⌐ןשׁוּעַ, seipso pro nobis in ἀντίλυτρον dato, ita ut morte sua redemtionem transgressionum nostrarum perageret; sui sanguinis fusione & aspersione pacifica inimicitiam peremit; ac Deo nos reconciliavit; Is vere pro nobis satisfecit: Sed Christus, &c. Major item certissima est. Minor autem probata ibid th. 24.
units.tr: Most holy, most worthy, and most closely joined to us, as Mediator [יְשׁוּעָה, Yeshua], having given himself for us as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], so that by his death he might accomplish the redemption of our transgressions; by the shedding and sprinkling of his blood he destroyed enmity, made peace, and reconciled us to God. He truly satisfied for us. But Christ, etc. The major premise is likewise most certain. The minor is proved in the same place, th. 24.

units.la: X. Obj.1. Satisfactio Christi pro peccatis nostris injustissima foret: sic enim fontibus sponte dimissis, Deus insontem punivisset eorum loco. Ergo. Resp. Imo ea neque ex parte materiæ, neque ex parte formæ, injusta censeri debet. Non ex parte materiæ: Christus enim afflictiones malorum tristium omnino pertulit, Deo sic disponente, & Christo consentiente: ubi nulla prosus injuria; fatentibus id ipsum Adversariis. Non ex parte formæ, sive ratione pœnalitatis ex reatu peccatorum nostrorum; quem Sponsor volens in se recepit; & supremus Dominus volenti imputavit; atque adeo idem Rector ab eo exegit: nam puniri aliquem ob peccata aliena, ipsis nocentibus dimissis, non est simpliciter injustum; nec absolute contra naturam pœnæ. Vide Thren. 5.7. 2 Sam. 24.17.
units.tr: X. Obj. 1. The satisfaction of Christ for our sins would have been most unjust, for in that case God would have punished an innocent man in place of the guilty, though they had freely let their debts go. Therefore. Resp. On the contrary, it ought not to be judged unjust either on the side of the matter or on the side of the form. Not on the side of the matter: for Christ endured the afflictions of grievous evils entirely, God so disposing and Christ consenting, where there is no injury at all, as the Opponents themselves admit. Not on the side of the form, or with respect to the penal character arising from the guilt of our sins, which the Surety willingly took upon himself, and which the supreme Lord imputed to the one willing; and so the same Ruler exacted it from him. For for someone to be punished for the sins of others, while the guilty themselves are let off, is not simply unjust, nor absolutely contrary to the nature of punishment. See Lam. 5:7; 2 Sam. 24:17.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus voluit, & potuit, peccata nobis condonare sine vera pro iis satisfactione; sic enim pœnas, intercedente solum pœnitentia, aliquoties remisit. Resp. Neg. antecedens. Ad probationem ejus quod attinet, Deus quidem interveniente aliqua pœnitentia pœnas nonnunquam distulit, aut mitigavit; sed non prorsus abstulit nisi fidelibus & resipiscentibus, propter satisfactionem Christi.
units.tr: Obj. 2. God was willing and able to forgive us our sins without a true satisfaction made for them, for he has sometimes remitted punishments on the intercession of repentance alone. Resp. I deny the antecedent. As for the proof, God indeed sometimes deferred or lessened punishments when some repentance intervened; but he did not entirely remove them, except for believers and those who repent, and that on account of Christ's satisfaction.

units.la: Obj. 3. Verbum ἀφιέναι excludit omnem satisfactionem. Ergo. Resp. Neg. sed contrarium est χαρατὴν: hinc Rei insontis in judicio facta absolutio, ἄφεσις etiam appellari potest; quanto magis nocentium ob satisfactionem Sponsoris, ab ipso Rectore dati. Obj.
units.tr: Obj. 3. The word ἀφιέναι [to forgive] excludes every satisfaction. Therefore. Resp. I deny this. The contrary is in fact the case: the absolution granted to an innocent defendant in a court can also be called ἄφεσις [remission], and how much more so the absolution of the guilty, granted by the Ruler himself on account of the Surety's satisfaction. Obj.

units.la: ᵗᵒ Obj. 4. Parabola Matth. 18. omnem satisfactionem excludit. Ergo. Resp. Ista parabola ultra scopum suum non est extendenda; utpote quae similitudine, a debito pecuniario sumta, benignitatem commendat, & omnem in proximum saevitiem & privatam vindictae cupiditatem prohibet: non autem excluditur omnis exactio poenae, caeteroquin nec ipsi sontes a Judice forent plectendi. Ac proinde ut diversa est ratio debiti pecuniarii respectu Juris privati, a debito poenali respectu juris publici; sic etiam aliter se habet remissio. Deus igitur remittit convenienter naturae suae sanctissimae & justitiae rectorali; nos vero convenienter conditioni nostrae privatae.
units.tr: 4. Obj. 4. The parable in Matt. 18 excludes every satisfaction. Therefore. Resp. That parable is not to be stretched beyond its purpose, since by a likeness drawn from a monetary debt it commends kindness and forbids all cruelty toward a neighbour and every desire for private vengeance. It does not, however, exclude every exaction of punishment, otherwise the guilty themselves would not be punished by the judge. Accordingly, just as the reckoning of a monetary debt under private law differs from a penal debt under public law, so too the remission differs. God therefore remits in a manner consistent with his most holy nature and his rectoral justice; we, however, in a manner consistent with our private condition.

units.la: Obj. 5. Saltem vox χαρίζεσθαι in hoc negotio usurpata, Col. 2.13. iij. 13. omnem satisfactionem excludit. Resp. Ea solum notat beneficium indebitum: tale autem est remissio respectu nostri; Tit. 3. 3. quamvis non item ratione Christi; cujus sanguine emti & redemti dicimur. 1 Petr. 1, 19. unde Deus nobis dicitur χαρίζεσθαι ἐν Χριστῷ, Eph. 4. 32.
units.tr: Obj. 5. At least the word χαρίζεσθαι [to forgive freely], used in this matter in Col. 2:13 and 3:13, excludes every satisfaction. Resp. That word denotes only an undeserved benefit, and remission with respect to us is of this kind (Tit. 3:3), although not in the same way with respect to Christ, by whose blood we are said to have been bought and redeemed (1 Pet. 1:19). Hence God is said to forgive us χαρίζεσθαι ἐν Χριστῷ [in Christ] (Eph. 4:32).

units.la: Obj. 6. Christus patiendo exemplum nobis reliquit:
units.tr: Obj. 6. Christ, by suffering, left us an example:

units.la: 1 Petr. 2. 24. Phil. 2, 5-8. Ergo pro nobis non satisfecit: satisfactionem talem enim imitari nec possumus, nec debemus. Resp. Reliquit exemplum imitandum materialiter, sed non formaliter.
units.tr: (1 Pet. 2:24; Phil. 2:5-8.) Therefore he did not satisfy for us, for we can neither imitate such a satisfaction nor ought to. Resp. He left an example to be imitated materially, but not formally.

units.la: XI. Succedit Meritum; Actus Christi Mediatoris, quo ipse consummata universa Legis obedientia, & sic praestita conditione, quam ea requirebat, jus vitae aeternae, atque omnia bona salutaria, electis suis digne acquisivit.
units.tr: XI. There follows Merit: the act of Christ the Mediator by which, having fully completed the whole obedience of the Law, and so having fulfilled the condition which it required, he acquired for his elect, worthily, the right to eternal life and all saving goods.

units.la: Causa ejus efficiens prima fuit ipse Deus.
units.tr: Its first efficient cause was God himself.

units.la: Altera formaliter exequens fuit Christus.
units.tr: The second, formally acting cause was Christ.

units.la: Materia fuit universa Christi justitia, sanctitas, & obedientia.
units.tr: The matter was the whole righteousness, holiness and obedience of Christ.

units.la: Formae vicem praestitit dignitas istius obedientiae, ad acquirendum, secundum Legis promissionem & pactum; stum, jus vitæ æternæ, cum omnibus bonis salutaribus.
units.tr: The worth of that obedience took the place of the form, for acquiring, according to the promise and covenant of the Law, the right to eternal life together with all saving goods.

units.la: Finis vero, ut ne Lex fieret irrita; & nos ea salva jus illud salutare adipisceremur.
units.tr: The end, however, was that the Law should not be made void, and that we, with the Law preserved, might obtain that saving right.

units.la: Hæc autem sequentibus Argumentorum classibus illustrantur & confirmantur; quibus instruendis servient tituli, Lex, Alter Adamus, & Justitia.
units.tr: These things are illustrated and confirmed by the following classes of arguments, for the arrangement of which the headings Law, Second Adam, and Righteousness will serve.

units.la: Primo igitur argumentamur ex consideratione ipsius Legis; quæ promissionem habuit annexam, Quisecerit ea, vivet in iis: Levit. 18. 5. Rom. 10: 5. Christus autem ea pro nobis fecit: Rom. 3. 30, 31. viij. 2, 3, 4. x, 3, 8. Matth. 5. 17. Ergo & vitam nobis per ea acquisivit.
units.tr: First, then, we argue from consideration of the Law itself, which had attached to it the promise: "The one who does them shall live by them" (Lev. 18:5; Rom. 10:5). Christ, however, fulfilled them for us (Rom. 3:30-31; 8:2-4; 10:3, 8; Matt. 5:17). Therefore he also acquired life for us through them.

units.la: 2. Ex consideratione Adami: quemadmodum enim primo Adamo, tanquam capiti fœderali, competit demeritum reatus ad condemnationem & mortem suorum; sic etiam secundo Adamo, tanquam iterum capiti fœderali electorum salvandorum, competit meritum justitiæ ad justificationem & vitam suorum. Luculenter utrumque vide, Rom. 5. 14, 18, 19. 21. 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22; 45.
units.tr: 2. From consideration of Adam: just as to the first Adam, as federal head, belonged the demerit of guilt, bringing condemnation and death on his descendants, so also to the second Adam, as again the federal head of the elect who are to be saved, belongs the merit of righteousness, bringing justification and life to his own. See both clearly in Rom. 5:14, 18, 19, 21; 1 Cor. 15:21-22, 45.

units.la: 3: Ex ipsa Justitia, & Justificatione nostri in Christo; quæ, ut bonum positivum, ipsum jus vitæ æternæ, involvit; ita meritum omnino infert: Matth. 3. 15. cum Gal. 4. 4. Phil. 2. 8. Hebr. 10. 9, 10. Hinc ipse appellatur Jehovah justitia nostra; Jerem. 23. 6. & cognitione sui multos dicitur justificaturus ipse justus; Jes. 53. 11. atque item factus nobis à Deo justitia; 1 Cor. 1. 30. Adde 2 Cor 5. 21. Phil. 3. 8, 9.
units.tr: 3. From Righteousness itself, and our justification in Christ, which, as a positive good, involves the right to eternal life itself, and so necessarily implies merit: Matt. 3:15, with Gal. 4:4; Phil. 2:8; Heb. 10:9-10. Hence he himself is called "Jehovah our righteousness" (Jer. 23:6), and it is said that by his knowledge the Just One himself will justify many (Isa. 53:11); likewise he is "made by God righteousness for us" (1 Cor. 1:30). Add 2 Cor. 5:21; Phil. 3:8-9.

units.la: XII. Contraria est Socini sententia, qui lib. 3. c. 5. de Christo Servatore contendit Christum nobis nihil „omnino vel meruisse, vel mereri potuisse: nam inquit „ille, si velitis, eum ut Hominem id præstitisse, falsum „ id esse ex eo deprehenditur, quod homo ne sibi quidem ipsi quicquam mereri possit, nedum ut aliis meretur: si ut Deum, illud plane ridiculum est, cum „Deus
units.tr: XII. Contrary to this is the opinion of Socinus, who in book 3, chapter 5, about Christ the Saviour, contends that Christ merited nothing at all for us, or could merit nothing: for, he says, "if you wish to say that he did this as Man, that is shown to be false by the fact that a man cannot merit anything even for himself, much less for others; if as God, that is plainly ridiculous, since God..."

units.la: Cap. XIII.
units.tr: Cap. XIII.

units.la: „Deus mereri prorsus nequeat; sed donet ac largia„tur, & meritis, si quæ sunt, digna præmia repen„dat, &c.
units.tr: "God cannot merit anything at all, but he gives and bestows, and repays worthy rewards to merits, if there are any, etc."

units.la: Obj. 1. Christus, tanquam creatura rationalis, omnem obedientiam pro seipso præstare debuit: nihil ergo per eam pro aliis mereri potuit. Resp. Christus Θεάνθρωπος non solum pro se, ut Homine; sed etiam pro suis, obedientiam præstitit: quemadmodum quis negotium aliquod pro se expedire potest; & simul, tanquam procurator, aliorum nomine. Et cum poena inobedientiæ Adami ad posteros quoque pertingat; quid mirum, si merces ex dignitate operum Θεανθρωπικῶν ad ipsos etiam electos pari ratione derivetur?
units.tr: Obj. 1. Christ, as a rational creature, owed all obedience on his own behalf, so he could merit nothing for others through it. Resp. Christ, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], rendered obedience not only for himself as man but also for his own people, just as someone may carry out some business for himself and at the same time, as a procurator, on behalf of others. And since the penalty of Adam's disobedience reaches also to his posterity, what is strange if the reward, from the worth of the God-man's works [Θεανθρωπικῶν], is likewise passed on to the elect themselves?

units.la: Obj. 2. Opus unius non potest fieri alterius. Ergo nec Christus quicquam nobis potuit mereri. Resp. Opus unius formaliter non potest fieri alterius; sed quidem virtualiter: sic enim potest quis sibi, & propinquis suis, etiam post se venturis, præmium mereri.
units.tr: Obj. 2. One person's work cannot be done by another. Therefore Christ could not merit anything for us either. Resp. One person's work cannot be done by another formally, but it can virtually: for in this way someone can merit a reward both for himself and for his kin, even those who will come after him.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus, ex vestra sententia, perpessionibus suis satisfecit pro omnibus suorum peccatis, non solum commissionis, sed etiam omissionis: ergo vi istius satisfactionis censentur etiam fideles nihil boni omisisse, atque adeo omne bonum præstitisse: consequenter isto Merito nihil erat opus. Resp. Propter satisfactionem quidem censentur nihil boni omisisse, quatenus ista omissio inferebat reatum; pro quo sic satisfactum est. Sed propterea non statim censentur omne bonum præstitisse positive. Huc pertinebat absolutissima illa omnis justitiæ consummatio pro nobis etiam præstita.
units.tr: Obj. 3. According to your view, Christ by his sufferings satisfied for all the sins of his people, not only sins of commission but also of omission. Therefore, by virtue of that satisfaction, the faithful are also considered to have omitted no good and so to have performed every good, and consequently there was no need for merit. Resp. Indeed, they are considered to have omitted no good, in so far as that omission brought guilt, for which satisfaction has been made. But it does not follow at once that they are considered to have performed every good positively. To this belongs that most complete fulfilment of all righteousness, which was also rendered on our behalf.

units.la: XIII. Remonstrantes in Apol. sua negant, Christum nobis meritum esse fidem & regenerationem. Nos oppositum probamus:
units.tr: XIII. The Remonstrants, in their Apology, deny that Christ merited for us faith and regeneration. We prove the opposite:

units.la: 1. Christus se dedit, & sanctificavit, pro suis; ut & ipsi sanctificarentur in veritate: Joh. 17. 19. Eph. 5. 25, 26. 2. Deus nobis per Spir. S. in Christo, & propter Christum, dat regenerationem & fidem: Act. 5. 31. xj. 18. cum Eph. 1. 3, 4. Phil. 1. 29. 1 Petr. 1, 2, 3: 2, 1. 1, 3, 4.
units.tr: 1. Christ gave himself and sanctified himself for his own, that they too might be sanctified in truth: John 17:19; Eph. 5:25, 26. 2. God gives us regeneration and faith through the Holy Spirit, in Christ and on account of Christ: Acts 5:31; 11:18, compared with Eph. 1:3, 4; Phil. 1:29; 1 Pet. 1:2, 3; 2:1; 1:3, 4.

units.la: 3. Regeneratio & fides nobis conferuntur juxta promissionem Novi Fœderis: Jerem. 31, 33, 34, Ezech. 36. 25, -27. cum Hebr. 8. 8, -12. x, 16, &c. Jàm vero sanguis Christi fusus, est sanguis Novi Fœderis, in quo istud ratum & confirmatum est: Matth. 26. 28. Hebr. 9. 15. - 18. Qui nos purgat ab omni peccato; 1 Joh. 1. 7.
units.tr: 3. Regeneration and faith are conferred on us according to the promise of the New Covenant: Jer. 31:33, 34; Ezek. 36:25–27, compared with Heb. 8:8–12; 10:16, etc. Now the blood of Christ poured out is the blood of the New Covenant, in which this has been ratified and confirmed: Matt. 26:28; Heb. 9:15–18; and it cleanses us from all sin: 1 John 1:7.

units.la: 4. Gratia ista nobis obsignatur Sacramentis, tanquam sigillis istius Fœderis; Baptismus enim est Sacramentum insitionis nostræ in Christum, ad communionem mortis ac resurrectionis ipsius; atque adeo ablutionis peccatorum, regenerationis, & resipiscentiæ: Rom. 6. 3. 6. 1. Cor. 12. 13. Act. 22. 16. Marc. 1. 4; Tit. 3. 5. S. Cœna vero est Sacramentum nutritionis spiritualis, incrementi, & corroborationis, in ista communione & gratia ex morte Christi: 1 Cor. 10. 4, 16. xj, 20, 23, -25. 12. 13.
units.tr: 4. This grace is sealed to us by the sacraments, as seals of this covenant. For Baptism is the sacrament of our engrafting into Christ, to communion in his death and resurrection, and so of the washing away of sins, of regeneration, and of repentance: Rom. 6:3, 6; 1 Cor. 12:13; Acts 22:16; Mark 1:4; Titus 3:5. And the Lord's Supper is the sacrament of spiritual nourishment, growth and strengthening, in that communion and grace which flow from the death of Christ: 1 Cor. 10:4, 16; 11:20, 23–25; 12:13.

units.la: Obj. Fidem & Resipiscentiam Deus à nobis postulat; & quidem sub comminatione mortis æternæ: ergo ista non sunt beneficia nobis per meritum Christi acquisita. Resp. Officia quidem nobis præscribuntur moraliter; sed per naturæ nostræ corruptionem & indignitatem, necesse est etiam realiter conferri beneficia, gratiam habitualem & actualem, quibus præstemus officia; & quidem ex merito Christi.
units.tr: Obj. God requires faith and repentance from us, and that under threat of eternal death. Therefore these are not benefits acquired for us by the merit of Christ. Resp. Indeed, these duties are prescribed to us morally; but because of the corruption and unworthiness of our nature, the benefits must necessarily also be conferred really, habitual and actual grace, by which we perform these duties; and indeed these come from the merit of Christ.

units.la: XIV. De Intercessione Christi pro nobis, jam dixi- mus cap. 12. th. 44.
units.tr: XIV. On the intercession of Christ for us, we have already spoken in chapter 12, thesis 44.

units.la: Sed hujus solum loci est, quod Christus æternum Satisfactionis ac Meriti sui valorem, simulque propensam Voluntatem suam, ut salus isto pacto nobis parta, actu applicetur, coram Patre jugiter repræsentet; & sic applicationem promoveat.
units.tr: But it belongs to this place only that Christ continually presents before the Father the eternal value of his satisfaction and merit, together with his favourable will, so that the salvation obtained by this covenant may actually be applied to us; and thus he promotes the application.

units.la: Satis de Salutis impetratione secundum partes: Videndum nunc de fine cui. Impetrationem istam ad Angelos non esse extendendam; neque Christum eorum Mediatorem dicendum, probavimus fup. cap.12. th. 27. Addimus nunc contra Pontif. Anabapt. Remonstrantes, & alios quoscunque gratiæ universalis patronos, non omnibus & singulis Hominibus salutem impetratam; sed certis duntaxat personis: idque confirmamus,
units.tr: Enough on the obtaining of salvation with respect to its parts. Now we must consider the end for which it was obtained. We have shown above, in chapter 12, thesis 27, that this obtaining is not to be extended to the angels, nor is Christ to be called their Mediator. We now add, against the Papists, the Anabaptists, the Remonstrants and all other patrons of universal grace, that salvation was not obtained for all and each of men, but only for certain persons. And we confirm this:

units.la: Primo à Restrictionibus in hoc negotio passim usurpari solitis. Istæ autem in SS. Literis fiunt, 1. ad Multos : Matth. 26. 28. Rom. 5. 19. Isef. 53. 11, 12. Matth. 20. 28. Hebr. 9. 28.
units.tr: First, from the restrictions commonly used in this matter. These occur in Holy Scripture: 1. "for many": Matt. 26:28; Rom. 5:19; Isa. 53:11, 12; Matt. 20:28; Heb. 9:28.

units.la: 2. Ad Vocatos : Hebr. 9. 15. Ad Fideles: Joh. 3. 16. Act. 10. 43. Rom 3. 22, 25, 26. x. 4. cum 2 Theff. 3. 2. Tit. 1, 1. Ad Sanctificatos: Hebr. 10. 14. Joh. 17. 19, 20, 21.
units.tr: 2. "for the called": Heb. 9:15; "for the faithful": John 3:16; Acts 10:43; Rom. 3:22, 25, 26; 10:4, compared with 2 Thess. 3:2; Titus 1:1; "for the sanctified": Heb. 10:14; John 17:19, 20, 21.

units.la: 3. Ad Ecclesiam: Act. 20. 28. Eph. 5. 25,-27. ad Filios Dei: Joh. xj. 51. 52. ad Oves Christi: Joh. 10. 14,-16, 26,-28. ad Populum suum: Matth. 1, 21.
units.tr: 3. "for the Church": Acts 20:28; Eph. 5:25–27; "for the children of God": John 11:51, 52; "for the sheep of Christ": John 10:14–16, 26–28; "for his people": Matt. 1:21.

units.la: 4. Ad eos,qui Christo à Patre fuerunt dati : Ioh. 17. 2,4. 6,-9; 11, 15,-17; 24. Et ad eos, quos Deus & Christus dilexit summopere: Ioh. 15. 13. 1 Ioh. 3. 16. Rom. 5. 8, 9.
units.tr: 4. "for those who were given to Christ by the Father": John 17:2, 4, 6–9; 11, 15–17, 24; and "for those whom God and Christ have loved above all": John 15:13; 1 John 3:16; Rom. 5:8, 9.

units.la: 5. Excluso etiam mundo reliquo: Ioh. 17. 9. Ac proinde Salutis impetratio ad omnes in universum non extenditur.
units.tr: 5. The rest of the world being excluded also: John 17:9. Therefore the obtaining of salvation does not extend to all in general.

units.la: Secundo a Consequentibus, quæ individuo nexu sequuntur Salutis impetrationem. Talis est 1. Non Damnatio; sive Immunitas a damnatione: Rom. 8. 34. Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est:-qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Ideo nemo electos Dei potest condemnare, quia Christus pro iis mortuus est, atque etiam pro iis interpellat: quia vero omnes infideles damnantur, omnino sequitur, Christum pro ipsis nec mortuum esse, nec interpellare. Imo si condemnarentur aliqui, pro quibus Christus esset mortuus, sequeretur Deum eadem peccata bis punire; quod a justitia Dei alienissimum est. Adde, quod per istam sententiam Christus pro iis etiam statuatur mortuus, qui cum ipse moreretur, jam erant damnati; quod certe absurdissimum est.
units.tr: Secondly, from the consequences which follow the obtaining of salvation by an inseparable bond. Such is 1. Non-condemnation, or immunity from condemnation: Rom. 8:34, Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. Therefore no one can condemn the elect of God, because Christ died for them and also intercedes for them. But because all unbelievers are condemned, it follows altogether that Christ neither died for them nor intercedes for them. Indeed, if some were condemned for whom Christ had died, it would follow that God punished the same sins twice, which is most alien to the justice of God. Add that by this opinion Christ is also held to have died for those who, when he died, were already condemned, which is certainly most absurd.

units.la: 2. Salvatio: Rom. 5. 10. Nam si, cum inimici essemus, Deo reconciliati fuimus, per mortem Filii ejus multo magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius. Sic omnes, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, & quos ipse Deo reconciliavit, certissime etiam servantur, per ipsius vitam: At vero non omnes & singuli, non infideles servantur per vitam Christi: ergo pro omnibus & singulis, etiam infidelibus, Christus non est mortuus; nec eos Deo reconciliavit. Confer Joh. 3. 36.
units.tr: 2. Salvation: Rom. 5:10, For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. So all those for whom Christ died, and whom he reconciled to God, are most certainly also saved by his life. But not all and each, not unbelievers, are saved by the life of Christ. Therefore Christ did not die for all and each, including unbelievers, nor did he reconcile them to God. Compare John 3:36.

units.la: 3. Vocatio similiter non omnibus & singulis, nullo excepto, semper obtingit; teste experientia; atque etiam S.Script. tum sub V.T. Psal. 147. 19, 20. Act. 14. 16. tum sub N.T. xvj. 6, 7. Qui autem non vult sermonem reconciliationis omnibus & singulis annunciari, is etiam in morte sua omnium & singulorum salutem non intendit. Ratio consequentiae est, Quia fides est ex auditu, & auditus per Verbum Dei; Rom. x. 8, 14, 17. tanquam ordinarium medium applicandae reconciliationis. Qui autem non vult medium, ad finem omnino & manifeste necessarium, is neq; finem vult, sive intendit.
units.tr: 3. Calling likewise does not always come to all and each, without exception; experience bears witness to this, and Holy Scripture too, under the Old Testament, Ps. 147:19, 20; Acts 14:16, and under the New Testament, Acts 16:6, 7. Whoever does not wish the word of reconciliation to be announced to all and each, does not intend the salvation of all and each in his death. The reason for the inference is, because faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God, Rom. 10:8, 14, 17, as the ordinary means of applying the reconciliation. Whoever does not will the means, which is altogether and manifestly necessary for the end, neither wills nor intends the end.

units.la: 4. De Liberatione a servitute peccati, de Regeneratione, & similibus, idem dicendum: nam & ista certo obtingunt omnibus, quibus impetrata sunt; minime vero obtingunt omnibus & singulis hominibus, nullo excepto: non igitur omnibus & singulis ea Christus impetravit; neque consequenter remissionem peccatorum, & vitam aeternam; ob indissolubilem nexum beneficiorum salutarium inter se.
units.tr: 4. The same must be said of deliverance from the slavery of sin, of regeneration, and similar benefits. These certainly come to all for whom they have been obtained, but they by no means come to all and each of mankind without exception. Christ therefore did not obtain them for all and each, and consequently not the forgiveness of sins and eternal life either, because of the indissoluble bond between the saving benefits.

units.la: Tertio, Similiter ex Electione colligimus, non omnibus & singulis salutem impetratam esse; idque ex iis S. Scripturae locis, quae certos quosdam homines, non vero omnes & singulos, ad vitam aeternam, & media ischuc spectantia, aeterno Dei consilio destinatos dorent. Vide sup. cap. 6. th. 15. Unde omnino sequitur, Dei intentionem, cum Christum in mortem traderet, non fuisse, omnes & singulos per eam sibi reconciliare, & sic eos aeternum salvare: sed illos solum, quos ad salutem, & media salutis, elegit; ac Christum consequenter eos solos accepisse salvandos; iisque solis, non aliis, salutem impetrasse.
units.tr: Thirdly, we likewise gather from election that salvation was not obtained for all and each. This follows from those passages of Holy Scripture which appoint certain men, and not all and each, to eternal life and to the means that lead to it, by the eternal counsel of God. See above, chap. 6, thesis 15. From this it clearly follows that God's intention, when he delivered Christ to death, was not that all and each should be reconciled to him through it and so be saved eternally, but only those whom he chose for salvation and the means of salvation. Accordingly, Christ received those alone to be saved, and he obtained salvation for those alone and for no others.

units.la: Quarto, Idem denique deducimus ex consideratione Novi Foederis: nam cum ad ejus internam & mysticam communionem non omnes & singuli pertineant; sed soli electi, vocati, fideles: Vide sup. cap. 11. th. 6. Et cum Deus illos solos vere ac salutariter in communionem istius Foederis adscisçat, & ipse etiam Christus Mediator ac Sponsor hujus Foederis non alium scopum sibi propositum habeat: evidens est, hanc tantum fuisse Dei & Christi in Salutis impetratione intentionem; nequaquam vero ad omnes & singulos aequaliter eam extendendam.
units.tr: Fourthly, we deduce the same thing from the consideration of the New Covenant. For since not all and each belong to its inward and mystical communion, but only the elect, the called, and the faithful (see above, chap. 11, thesis 6), and since God truly and savingly admits only those into the communion of this covenant, and Christ himself as Mediator and Surety of this covenant has no other aim set before him, it is evident that this alone was the intention of God and Christ in obtaining salvation, and that it is by no means to be extended equally to all and each.

units.la: XV. Obj. 1.
units.tr: XV. Obj. 1.

units.la: Deus Mundum ita dilexisse dicitur, ut dederit Filium suum unigenitum, &c. Et ipse Christus, tollere peccata Mundi, &c. Joh. 3. 16. j. 29. 1, 11, 1, 2. Resp. In appellatione Mundi hoc notandum, quod ea frequenter accipiatur synecdochice: & quidem sic, ut nonnunquam spectetur excellentia dignitatis; atque adeo sola universitas fidelium & electorum denotetur: uti fit in locis allegatis, atque insuper Rom. xi, 12.
units.tr: It is said that God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, etc., and that Christ himself takes away the sin of the world, etc. (John 3:16; 1:29; 1 John 2:2). Answer: In the word world it must be noted that it is often taken synecdochically, sometimes so that excellence of dignity is in view, and so the whole body of believers and elect alone is meant, as in the passages cited and, besides, in Rom. 11:12.

units.la: 2. Cor. 5. 19. nonnunquam vero excellentia multitudinis, seu numeri; ut sola universitas infidelium & reproborum designetur: quemadmodum 2 Petr. 2. 5. Joh. 17. 9.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:19. Sometimes, however, it signifies excellence of multitude or number, so that the whole body of unbelievers and reprobate alone is designated, as in 2 Pet. 2:5 and John 17:9.

units.la: Obj. 2. Similiter omnium aliquando fit mentio: 1 Tim. 2. 6. Hebr. 2. 9. Rom. 5. 18. &c. Ergo. Resp. Distributive scil. in genera singulorum; non in singula generum. Confer Mat. 4. 23. xij. 32. Rom. 14. 2. & Apoc. 5. 9.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Likewise, mention is sometimes made of all (1 Tim. 2:6; Heb. 2:9; Rom. 5:18, etc.). Therefore... Answer: It is meant distributively, that is, of the kinds of each, not of each of the kinds. Compare Matt. 4:23; 12:32; Rom. 14:2; and Rev. 5:9.

units.la: Obj. 3. 2 Petr. 2. 1. Futuri dicuntur falsi Doctores, qui subintroducerent haereses exitiales; etiam Dominum, qui illos mercatus est, abnegantes. Ergo Christus etiam redemit eos, qui damnantur. Resp. Intelligenda est illorum acquisitio, & obligatio ad ministerium Christi, per dona quaedam ac beneficia in ipsos collata; attamen non salutaria: sed nihil de ipsorum acquisitione per sanguinem Christi ad salutem.
units.tr: Obj. 3. 2 Pet. 2:1: There will be false teachers who will bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them. Therefore Christ also redeemed those who are condemned. Answer: Their acquisition and their binding to the ministry of Christ must be understood, through certain gifts and benefits conferred on them, yet not saving ones; but nothing is said of their acquisition by the blood of Christ unto salvation.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sic etiam de peccantibus in Spiritum S. dicitur, quod rursum crucifigant sibi Filium Dei, & ignominiae exponant: Hebr. vi 6. Resp. Christus semel pro electis suis crucifixus est, & ignominiae expositus: tales vero, quantum in ipsis est, Christum denuo sibi crucifigunt, & hostibus veritatis ludibrio exponunt; idque suo ipsorum exitio: nequaquam vero ad salutem suam, quam Christus nunquam intendit.
units.tr: Obj. 4. Likewise of those who sin against the Holy Spirit it is said that they crucify again the Son of God for themselves, and expose him to shame (Heb. 6:6). Answer: Christ was crucified once for his elect and exposed to shame; but such men, so far as lies in them, crucify Christ again for themselves and expose him to the mockery of the enemies of the truth, and this to their own destruction, but by no means to their salvation, which Christ never intended.

units.la: Obj. 5. Iterum, x. 28. agitur de eo, qui Filium Dei conculcarit, & sanguinem foederis, per quem fuerat sanctificatus, profanum duxerit; & Spiritum gratiae contumelia affecerit. Resp. Ille scil. Filium Dei, quantum in se est, conculcat; & profanum ducit sanguinem illum foederis, per quem ipse Christus fuerat sanctificatus: Joh. 17. 19; vel ipsum Foedus sanctificatum, h. e. sancte confirmatum: vel etiam ille, de quo isthic sermo est, sanctificatus fuit, verum nonsalutariter, sed externe tantum, quatenus ad externam Ecclesiae communionem vocatus, suo modo accessit quoque; scil. tanquam sus lota, ad volutabrum caeni deinde revertens. Sic etiam contumelia afficit Spiritum gratiae, auctorem illum gratiae salutaris in aliis; sed & donorum quorundam gratiae, non tamen salutarium, in ipso.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Again, Heb. 10:28 speaks of one who has trampled under foot the Son of God, and counted the blood of the covenant, by which he had been sanctified, a common thing; and has insulted the Spirit of grace. Answer: That man, so far as he is concerned, tramples under foot the Son of God and counts profane that blood of the covenant by which Christ himself had been sanctified (John 17:19); or the covenant itself is called sanctified, that is, solemnly confirmed; or else he of whom the text speaks was sanctified, but not savingly, only outwardly, insofar as, called to the outward communion of the Church, he too came in his own way, namely, like a sow washed, who afterwards returns to the wallowing of the mire. So too he insults the Spirit of grace, the author of saving grace in others, but also of certain gifts of grace, not however saving ones, in himself.

units.la: Obj. 6. Etiam asserit Catechesis, quaest. 37. Christum iram Dei adversus peccatum universi generis humani sustinuisse. Ergo. Resp. Sed non dicit, Christum sustinuisse iram Dei pro universo genere humano; ea intentione, ut omnes & singulos, nullo excepto, redimeret: aliter omnino intentionem eam & finem Christi exprimit in sequentibus; & ad Nos, h. e. ad Fideles, restringit. XVI. Adversarii in varias se vertunt formas: fuerunt enim qui universalem redemtionem urgerent; quasi restitutionem omnium & singulorum in eum statum unde in Adamo fuerant prolapsi; adeoque homines propter impoenitentiam & infidelitatem suam deinceps tantum damnandos, tanquam propter relapsum.
