Alii contendunt, Deum & Christum à suâ parte salutem omnium & singulorum hominum intendisse & procurasse sufficienter; quamvis non efficaciter: cum applicatio solis fidelibus & resipiscentibus obtingat; reliqui vero reddantur inexcusabiles. Remonstrantes alicubi urgent, Christum pro omnibus & singulis mortuum esse, & sic remissionem impetrasse, ea tamen lege, ut nemo, nisi fidelis, ista remissione peccatorum actu fruatur. Alibi, Christum id impetrasse, ut Deus posset & vellet nobis bene facere, eâ conditione, qua ipsi consultum videretur; eamque impetrationem quamvis nemini applicatam, vel intercedente omnium incredulitate irritam, firmam tamen, & ex naturâ suâ certam, esse posse. Veletiam, Christum satisfactione suâ Patri acquisivisse jus Novum Foedus ineundi cum hominibus, sub quacunque conditione, tam operum, quam fidei; Patrem vero praetulisse conditionem fidei, sic tamen ut ejus impletio pendeat a libero hominis arbitrio. Sed quam absurde haec omnia conficta sint, ex iis quae jam diximus, plus quam manifestum est.
units.tr: Obj. 6. The Catechism also affirms, question 37, that Christ bore the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Therefore... Answer: But it does not say that Christ bore the wrath of God on behalf of the whole human race with the intention of redeeming all and each, without exception. Otherwise it expresses that intention and purpose of Christ quite differently in what follows, and restricts it to us, that is, to the faithful. XVI. The opponents turn themselves into various forms. For some urged a universal redemption, as though all and each were restored to the state from which they had fallen in Adam, so that men, on account of their impenitence and unbelief, are henceforth to be condemned only as relapsed. Others contend that God and Christ, on their part, intended and sufficiently procured the salvation of all and each, though not effectually, since application comes only to the faithful and the repentant, while the rest are rendered inexcusable. The Remonstrants at some points urge that Christ died for all and each and so obtained forgiveness, yet on this condition, that no one but a believer enjoys that forgiveness of sins in fact. Elsewhere they hold that Christ obtained this, that God might and would do us good on whatever terms seemed good to him; and that this obtaining, though applied to no one, or made void by the unbelief of all, could nevertheless be firm and, by its very nature, certain. Or again, that Christ by his satisfaction acquired for the Father the right to enter a New Covenant with men under whatever condition, either of works or of faith; and that the Father preferred the condition of faith, yet so that its fulfilment depends on man's free will. But how absurdly all these things are invented is more than plain from what we have already said.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Quaeritur, an ipse Christus sibi etiam salutem impetrarit? Resp. Quantum ad oblationem Christi pro se, illam sup. cap. 12. th. 43. contra Socinum negavimus. De Merito tamen, & Precibus, aliter dicendum. Nam,
units.tr: It is asked whether Christ himself also obtained salvation for himself. Reply: As to Christ's offering for himself, we denied it against Socinus above, chap. 12, thesis 43. But concerning his merit and his prayers, something different must be said. For:

units.la: 1. Christus ex speciali pacto Legi se subjecit, & conditiones ad vitam & gloriam aeternam requisitas omnino implevit. Hinc Phil. 2. 8, 9. Habitu inventus ut homo, ipse se submisit, factus obediens usque ad mortem , mortem autem crucis ; quapropter (διο) etiam Deus ipsum in summam extulit sublimitatem ; ac largitus est ei nomen, quod est supra omne nomen. Et Hebr. 12. 2, Intuentes in fidei Ducem & consummatorem Jesum, qui pro (ἀντὶ) sibi proposito gaudio toleravit crucem, ignominia contemta. Particulae illae διο & ἀντὶ commutationem praemii gloriosi pro obedientia notant ; nec deest ulla conditio ad Meritum requisita.
units.tr: 1. Christ, by a special covenant, submitted himself to the Law and fully fulfilled the conditions required for eternal life and glory. Hence Phil. 2:8, 9: "Being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore [διὸ] God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name." And Heb. 12:2: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him [ἀντὶ] endured the cross, despising the shame." Those particles διὸ and ἀντὶ denote the exchange of a glorious reward for obedience, and no condition required for merit is lacking.

units.la: 2. Ipse Christus etiam justificatus est Spiritu : 1 Tim. 3. 16. cum implevisset omnem justitiam : Matth. 3. 15. & jus legis: Rom. 8. 4. ne ipsa fieret irrita : iij, 31. Sibi ergo meritus est justificari, & vitam ac gloriam aeternam sibi adjudicari.
units.tr: 2. Christ himself was also justified in the Spirit: 1 Tim. 3:16, since he had fulfilled all righteousness: Matt. 3:15, and the right of the law: Rom. 8:4, so that the law itself would not be made void: Rom. 3:31. Therefore he merited to be justified for himself, and eternal life and glory were adjudged to him.

units.la: 3. Lex dicebat ; Qui fecerit ista, vivet per ea: Levit. 18. 5. Hanc Christus non venit solvere, sed implere: Matth. 5. 17. Consequenter etiam vivit per eam. Ubi Meritum secundum Legem conspicuum est.
units.tr: 3. The Law said: "The man that doeth those things shall live in them": Lev. 18:5. Christ did not come to destroy this Law, but to fulfil it: Matt. 5:17. Consequently he also lives by it. Here the merit according to the Law is plainly visible.

units.la: 4. Christus ex plenitudine & perfectione justitiae suae nobis quoque factus est justitia: Joh. 1. 16. 1 Cor. 1. 30. Ipse igitur antecedenter, juxta ordinem naturae, habuit illam justitiam; & ex Capite communicatur ea membris ipsius.
units.tr: 4. Christ, of his fullness and the perfection of his righteousness, has also been made righteousness to us: John 1:16; 1 Cor. 1:30. Therefore he antecedently, according to the order of nature, possessed that righteousness, and from the Head it is communicated to his members.

units.la: XVIII. Cum Scholasticis tamen non dicimus, Christum etiam incarnandum fuisse, & sibi vitam ac gloriam aeternam meriturum, etiamsi Adamus non fuisset lapsus: nam Christus nobis natus est; Isef. 9. 5. & nobis Salvator datus: Matth. 1. 21. & factus sub Legem, ut eos, qui Legi subjecti erant, redimeret: Gal. 4. 4, 5. Eo ipso autem quod factus est homo, & legi subjectus, quae irrita fieri non debuit, ipse etiam ut homo obedientiam praestare debuit, quam Lex requirebat, & sub cujus conditione ea vitam promittebat.
units.tr: XVIII. With the Scholastics, however, we do not say that Christ would have been incarnate and would have merited eternal life and glory for himself even if Adam had not fallen. For Christ was born for us: Isa. 9:5; was given to us as Saviour: Matt. 1:21; and was made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law: Gal. 4:4, 5. Yet by the very fact that he was made man and subject to the law, which ought not to be made void, he himself as man was also bound to render the obedience which the Law required, and under whose condition it promised life.

units.la: Obj. 1. Christus pro nobis omnem obedientiam praestare debuit; atque adeo praestitit: Ergo non pro se; neque sic sibi aliquid est meritus. Resp. Per infinitam Personæ dignitatem sufficiebat ipsius justitia sibi, & nobis conjunctim, acquirendæ vitæ æternæ.
units.tr: Objection 1. Christ was bound to render all obedience on our behalf, and so he rendered it; therefore not on his own behalf, nor did he thus merit anything for himself. Reply: Through the infinite dignity of the Person, his righteousness was sufficient to acquire eternal life for himself and for us together.

units.la: Obj. 2. Unio hypostatica necessario ponebat statim beatitudinem & gloriam completam in humana Christi natura. Resp. Hoc negamus: sed potuit aptitudinem tantum ejus impetraudæ; sicut postea sibi & suis vere impetravit.
units.tr: Objection 2. The hypostatic union necessarily implied that blessedness and complete glory were present at once in the human nature of Christ. Reply: We deny this. He was able only to obtain the aptitude for it, just as afterwards he truly obtained it for himself and for his own.

units.la: XIX. De Precibus Christi in vita humili quibus sui corroborationem petiit, & liberationem, secundum humanam naturam, constat ex Hebr. 5, 7. In diebus carnis suæ, deprecationibus & supplicationibus oblatis, cum clamore valido & lachrymis, apud eum, qui poterat ipsum servare a morte, & exauditis precibus liberatus est ex metu. Adde Joh. 17. 1, 2, 4, 5. xij. 27. Marc. 14, 35, 36, 39.
units.tr: XIX. That Christ, in his humble life, offered prayers by which he sought strengthening and deliverance for his human nature, is evident from Heb. 5:7: "Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared" [liberatus est ex metu]. Add John 17:1, 2, 4, 5; 12:27; Mark 14:35, 36, 39.

units.la: XX. Satisfactioni & Merito Christi quam maxime contrariantur Satisfactiones & Merita, quæ finguntur, aliorum hominum: Christus enim ut vere ac plene, sic etiam solus, salutem suis impetravit; quod tenendum contra Infideles, imo & contra Pontifices, qui Satisfactiones pro poenis temporalibus statuunt, tum Proprias, tum Alienas. Proprias intelligunt poenas, a Deo immissas, sive post hanc vitam in Purgatorio, sive in hac vita: itemque opera poenalia, vel per Sacerdotem in confessione impositta, quæ est Satisfactio sacramentalis; vel sponte suscepta, ut sunt Preces, jejunia, eleemosynæ, &c. Alienæ Satisfactiones iis sunt, cum alii pro aliis satisfaciunt, per opera poenalia sponte ab iis suscepta, vel ita saltem ut ad alios redundet utilitas, ab iis, qui plus quam satis esset, præstiterunt. Atque huc pertinet Thesaurus Ecclesiæ, ex supere rogationibus Christi & Sanctorum, cujus dispensatorem agit Papa in suis Indulgentiis: Accedunt Missæ pro vivis & mortuis; itemque Suffragia pro defunctis. IStæ satisfactiones, secundum ipsos, spectant justitiam & judicium ipsius Dei: alia vero est ratio satisfactionis Canonicæ, qua satisfic tisfit Ecclesiae in foro foli. Iidem similiter statuunt Merita hominum, tum propria, ad Vitam aeternam, per bona opera secundum Legem Dei facta: vel etiam ad Aureolam, sive Coronulam in vita aeterna, per opera plus quam perfecta, Lege Dei non praescripta, sed facta juxta Consilia Euangelica. Vide sup. cap. 8. th. 32. tum etiam Aliena, aliorum videl. hominum pro aliis, nominatim per opera supererogationis.
units.tr: XX. The satisfactions and merits which are feigned as belonging to other men are most strongly opposed to the satisfaction and merit of Christ. For Christ, as he truly and fully obtained salvation for his own, so also obtained it alone; and this must be held against unbelievers, and even against the Papists, who posit satisfactions for temporal punishments, both proper and alien. By proper satisfactions they mean punishments imposed by God, whether after this life in Purgatory or in this life; likewise penal works imposed by the priest in confession, which is sacramental satisfaction; or works undertaken voluntarily, such as prayers, fastings, almsgivings, etc. Alien satisfactions are those when some make satisfaction for others, through penal works voluntarily undertaken by them, or at least in such a way that the benefit flows to others, from those who have done more than was necessary. To this belongs the treasury of the Church, made up of the superabundant merits of Christ and the Saints, of which the Pope acts as dispenser in his Indulgences. To these are added the Masses for the living and the dead, and likewise the suffrages for the departed. These satisfactions, according to them, regard the justice and judgment of God himself. But the canonical satisfaction, by which satisfaction is made to the Church in the outward court alone, has a different character. The same men likewise posit the merits of men: both proper, toward eternal life, through good works done according to the Law of God; or even toward an aureole, or little crown, in eternal life, through works more than perfect, not prescribed by the Law of God but done according to the evangelical counsels. See above, chap. 8, thesis 32. And also alien merits, namely of some men for others, specifically through works of supererogation.

units.la: XXI. Sed nos errores istos refutamus.
units.tr: XXI. But we refute these errors:

units.la: 1. Ex consideratione ipsius Christi, cujus Satisfactio & Meritum sunt perfectissima; atque ipse unicus populi sui Salvator. Vide sup. cap. 12. th. 23.
units.tr: 1. From the consideration of Christ himself, whose satisfaction and merit are most perfect, and who is the only Saviour of his people. See above, chap. 12, thesis 23.

units.la: 2. Ex consideratione aliorum hominum; quorum talis ac tantus est reatus, ut ne quidem pro se ipsis satisfacere possint; nedum vitam & beatitudinem mereri, aut, pro aliis ista praestare: nam nemo est qui non peccet; 1 Reg. 8. 46. qui sit justus in terra, & faciat bonum; Eccles. 7. 20. & omnes quotidie necesse habemus remissionem debitorum nostrorum precari; Matth. 6. 12. Adde Job. 14. 4. Prov. 20. 9. Jes. 54. 6. Jac. 3. 2. Rom. 3. 19,20,28.
units.tr: 2. From the consideration of other men, whose guilt is so great and so serious that they cannot even make satisfaction for themselves, much less merit life and blessedness, or provide these things for others. For there is no man who does not sin: 1 Kings 8:46; there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good: Eccl. 7:20; and we all daily have need to pray for the forgiveness of our debts: Matt. 6:12. Add Job 14:4; Prov. 20:9; Isa. 54:6; James 3:2; Rom. 3:19, 20, 28.

units.la: 3. Ex consideratione rei: poenas enim per Legem debebamus non temporales solum, sed aeternas; & ad acquirendum jus vitae aeternae, justitia omnibus numeris absoluta opus erat. At vero Foedus Euangelicum non commutat reatum aeternum temporali; nec justitiam imperfectam substituit perfectae: sed totam hanc in Christo monstrat. Vide sup. th. 9. & 11. Breviter, si Legem spectes, occurrit Apostolus, Hebr. 10. 30. Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei vivi. Atque ipse Christus, Matth. 5. 26. Amen dico tibi, nequaquam exibis illinc, usquedum reddideris ultimum quadrantem. Adde Jes. 33. 14. Psal 49. 8, 9 Si Euangelium acclamat Sospitator; Qui audit sermonem meum, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, &c. Johan. 5. 24. & Baptista; Iohan. 1. 16. Ex plenitudine ipsius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Confer Col. 2. 9, 10. Rom. 8. 1, 4. 1 Joh. 1. 7,-10.
units.tr: 3. From the consideration of the matter itself: for by the Law we owed punishments not only temporal but eternal, and to acquire a right to eternal life, a righteousness absolute in every respect was needed. But the Gospel covenant does not exchange eternal guilt for temporal punishment, nor substitute imperfect righteousness for perfect; rather it displays all of this in Christ. See above, theses 9 and 11. Briefly, if you look at the Law, the Apostle meets you: Heb. 10:30, "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." And Christ himself, Matt. 5:26: "Verily I say unto thee, thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing." Add Isa. 33:14; Ps. 49:8, 9. If the Gospel proclaims the Saviour: "He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life," etc. John 5:24; and the Baptist: John 1:16, "Of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace." Compare Col. 2:9, 10; Rom. 8:1, 4; 1 John 1:7, 10.

units.la: 4. Ex absurdis consequentibus: Nam si per Legem est justitia, igitur Christus frustra mortuus est; Gal. 2, 21. Et inanes facti dicuntur, separati à Christo, quicunque per Legem justificantur; & à gratia excidisse, &c. v. 4, 5. Rom. x. 3, 4, x) 6. iv, 2, - 5; 14, 15, 16. & alibi.
units.tr: 4. From the absurd consequences: "For if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain": Gal. 2:21. And those who are justified by the Law are said to be made void, severed from Christ, and to have fallen from grace, etc., Gal. 5:4, 5; Rom. 10:3, 4; 6:4; 4:2–5; 14, 15, 16; and elsewhere.

units.la: XXII. Obj. 1. In hac vitâ fideles multa patiuntur; quin & ipsa mors eorum temporalis poena est. Ergo. Resp. Istæ perpessiones, ipsaque mors temporalis, castigationis, probationis, vel etiam aliquando martyrii rationem habent; non autem poenæ strictè dictæ, vel satisfactionis. Vide sup. cap. 10. th. 12.
units.tr: XXII. Objection 1. In this life the faithful suffer many things; indeed their very temporal death is a punishment. Therefore [they make satisfaction]. Reply: Those sufferings, and temporal death itself, have the character of chastisement, of trial, or sometimes even of martyrdom; but not of punishment strictly speaking, or of satisfaction. See above, chap. 10, thesis 12.

units.la: Obj. 2. Deus rependit fidelibus secundum bona opera. Ergo. Resp. Non autem propter ea, tanquam causas meritorias.
units.tr: Objection 2. God renders to the faithful according to their good works. Therefore (the works merit). Answer: yes, but not on account of them, as meritorious causes.

units.la: Obj. 3. Beatitudo nonnunquam merces appellatur. Resp. Gratuita videlicet, seclusis meritis propriis: Rom. 4. 4.
units.tr: Objection 3. Blessedness is sometimes called a reward. Answer: namely, a free reward, apart from our own merits: Rom. 4. 4.

units.la: Obj. 4. Sic nostra bona opera inutilia censebuntur: quod absurdum. Resp. Neg. cum eorum praxis habeat rationem fructus consequentis, & gratitudinis; simulque fit conditio requisita ad actualem coelestis beatitudinis fruitionem, cujus jus nobis acquisivit Christus: Matth. 7. 17, 18. Joh. 15. 2, 5. Eph. 2. 10. Hebr. 12. 14.
units.tr: Objection 4. In this way our good works would be counted useless, which is absurd. Answer: I deny it, since their practice has the character of a consequent fruit and of gratitude; at the same time it is a condition required for the actual enjoyment of heavenly blessedness, the right to which Christ acquired for us: Matt. 7. 17, 18. John 15. 2, 5. Eph. 2. 10. Heb. 12. 14.

units.la: XXIII. Pro Praxi; Salutem plenissimam, à Christo nobis impetratam, agnoscamus; & in ipso reconciliationem ac pacem, viram æternam ac beatam, multamque fiduciam apud Deum apprehendamus: Hebr. 2. 3, 10. Rom. 5. 1, 2, 10, 18. Eph. 3. 12.
units.tr: XXIII. For the practice. Let us acknowledge the most full salvation obtained for us by Christ; and in him let us apprehend reconciliation and peace, eternal and blessed life, and much confidence before God: Heb. 2. 3, 10. Rom. 5. 1, 2, 10, 18. Eph. 3. 12.

units.la: 2. Admirandæ huic charitati pie respondeamus: 2 Cor. 5. 14, 15, 19, 20. 21. & alios quoque ad fidem permoveamus: ibid. 11. ut pariter in interiori homine, & praxi vitæ spiritualis, proficiamus: Rom. 7. 22. Phil. 3. 14.
units.tr: 2. Let us respond piously to this admirable love: 2 Cor. 5. 14, 15, 19, 20, 21; and let us also move others to faith: ibid. 11; so that we likewise make progress in the inner man and in the practice of the spiritual life: Rom. 7. 22. Phil. 3. 14.

units.la: Cap. XIV.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: De Vocat- ione, & Regeneratione.
units.tr: On Vocation and Regeneration.

units.la: Salutis applicatio. 1. In hac vitâ. Actus ejus varii. 2. Vocatio. 3. Ad unionem cum Christo: 4. Et S. S. Trinitate. 5. Actio gemina. Efficientia Verbi: & Spiritus S. 6. Operatio realis hyperphysica probatur. c. Pontif. Socin. Remonstr &c. Obj. solv. 7. Ministerium Legis. Euangelii. Actus nostep Vocationi respondens. 8. Consectaria. 9. Vocatio ista non universalis, Obj. solv. 10. Regeneratio. Vita spiritualis. 11. Electi adhuc irregeniti. 12. Regeniti quoad actum primum. 13. Conversi & sanctificati quoad actum secundum 14. Casus 15. Mortificatio veteris hominis, & Vivificatio novi. 16. Homo in primo momento habet se merè passive. Verbi usus. 17. Deinceps etiam activè. Conversio 18. Consectaria c. Pontif. & Remonstr. 19. Praxis. 20.
units.tr: The application of salvation. 1. In this life. Its various acts. 2. Vocation. 3. To union with Christ. 4. And with the Holy Trinity. 5. A twofold action: the efficacy of the Word and of the Holy Spirit. 6. The real hyperphysical operation is proved against the Papists, Socinians, Remonstrants, etc. Objections answered. 7. The ministry of the Law. The Gospel. Our act answering to vocation. 8. Corollaries. 9. This vocation is not universal. Objections answered. 10. Regeneration. Spiritual life. 11. The elect still unregenerate. 12. The regenerate as to the first act. 13. Converted and sanctified as to the second act. 14. Lapse. 15. Mortification of the old man, and vivification of the new. 16. Man in the first moment is purely passive. Use of the word. 17. Thereafter also actively. Conversion. 18. Corollaries against the Papists and Remonstrants. 19. Practice. 20.

units.la: I. Ergimus ad Salutis applicationem; per quam Christus hoc agit, ut electi & redemti sui actu fiant participes omnium bonorum beneficiorum salutarium. Beneficia ista nobis a Deo communicantur: a quo omnis donatio bona, & omne integrum donum, est descendens; Iac. 1. 17. Sed convenienter ordini Divinarum Personarum Applicatio ista interdum Patri tribuitur, tanquam personæ primæ in ordine operandi; Eph. 1. 3. interdum Spir. Sancto, tanquam cum vite.Quoniam membra sumus Corporis Ecclesiæ; Eph.5.30. cujus Caput est Christus; Col.1.18. Atque hinc ipse, Joh. 15.5. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites; is qui manet in me, & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructum multum; nam seorsum à me nihil potestis facere. Et Ecclesia; Dilectus meus, meus est; & ego illius; Cant. 2.16. Ex ista autem unione cum Christo, resultat pariter communio omnium bonorum spiritualium in ipso: Eph. 5 23. 1 Cor,1.30. Col.2 9,10. Joh. 1.16.
units.tr: I. We come now to the application of salvation, by which Christ brings it about that his elect and redeemed become, by his act, partakers of all the saving benefits. These benefits are communicated to us by God, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes down, James 1:17. But, in keeping with the order of the Divine Persons, this application is sometimes attributed to the Father, as the first person in the order of working (Eph. 1:3), and sometimes to the Holy Spirit, as the life-giving power. Since we are members of the body of the Church (Eph. 5:30), whose head is Christ (Col. 1:18), he himself says in John 15:5: I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me, and in whom I abide, bears much fruit; for apart from me you can do nothing. And the Church says: My beloved is mine, and I am his (Song 2:16). From this union with Christ there likewise results a communion in all spiritual good things in him (Eph. 5:23; 1 Cor. 1:30; Col. 2:9, 10; John 1:16).

units.la: V. Mediante vero unione & communione Christi Mediatoris, accipimus quoque unionem cum S.S. Trinitate; & consequenter communionem beneficentiæ Divinæ, ut reddamur consortes Divinæ naturæ, omniumque benedictionum spiritualium & cœlestium: simulque electi & redemti fruuntur quoque unione& communione inter se mutua, tanquam membra ejusdem corporis mystici. Sic 1 Joh.1.3. Ut & vos communionem habeatis nobiscum, & communio nostra sit cum Patre, & Filio ejus Jesu Christo. Et ipse Christus, Joh.17.21. Ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, & ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint. Atque iterum versu 23. Adde Eph. 4.3,-6. 1 Cor.12.13, &c.
units.tr: V. Through the union and communion with Christ the Mediator, we also receive union with the Holy Trinity, and consequently communion in the Divine beneficence, so that we are made partakers of the Divine nature and of all spiritual and heavenly blessings. At the same time the elect and redeemed also enjoy a mutual union and communion among themselves, as members of the same mystical body. So 1 John 1:3: That you also may have fellowship with us, and that our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. And Christ himself, John 17:21: That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us. And again in verse 23. Add Eph. 4:3–6; 1 Cor. 12:13, etc.

units.la: VI. Actio interim gemina occurrit externa, & interna: illa Verbo foris perficitur: hæc Spiritu intus. Verbum tum viva voce proponitur: sic audiendum: tum scripto; sic legendum est. De illo sic Divinitus ordinato, vide Rom. x.8.14,15,17. Et mandatum ipsius Christi. Marc. 16.15,16. Atque item Dei per Mosen, Deut.xi.19. De hoc Θεοπνεύστως exarato, Joh. 5.39. Rom. 15.4.2 Tim.3.16.17. & alibi. Efficientia autem Verbi sic propositi non nisi moralis est: atque hactenus Vocatio est Actio moralis. Cæterum cum actione illa externa in vocatione efficaci conjungitur actio interna Sp.Sancti, quæ est realis hyperphysica; non solum hoc agens, ut Verbum foris propositum sensu communi percipiatur, ejusque veritas moraliter duntaxat intellectui repræsentetur. tetur ac suadeatur: sed insuper ut homo de se ineptus, & spiritualiter mortuus, vivificetur; atque ita aptus fiat, ut possit Vocationem vitaliter spiritualiter percipere, & vocanti auscultare: quin imo velit percipere & auscultare; adeoque actu percipiat, auscultet, & credat. Sic Deus in hoc negotio ostendit, se eum esse, qui vivificat mortuos, & vocat ea quae non sunt tanquam sint; Rom. 4. 17. & qui splendet in cordibus nostris, ad praebendum nobis lucem notitiae, &c. 2 Cor. 4. 6. Adde 1. Thess. 1. 5. Rom. 1. 16.
units.tr: VI. Meanwhile the action is twofold, external and internal: the former is carried out outwardly by the Word, the latter inwardly by the Spirit. The Word is set forth both by the living voice, and so must be heard, and in writing, and so must be read. For that divinely ordained arrangement see Rom. 10:8, 14, 15, 17; and the command of Christ himself, Mark 16:15, 16; and likewise God's through Moses, Deut. 11:19. For this writing, divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος], see John 5:39; Rom. 15:4; 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; and elsewhere. But the efficacy of the Word so set forth is merely moral; so far the vocation is a moral action. Yet in effectual vocation that external action is joined with the internal action of the Holy Spirit, which is real and hyperphysical. This action does not merely bring it about that the Word set forth outwardly is perceived by common sense, and its truth is only morally presented to the understanding and urged upon it; but moreover it brings it about that man, who is unfit in himself and spiritually dead, is made alive, and so is made fit to perceive the vocation vitally and spiritually and to listen to the one calling; indeed, he is made willing to perceive and listen, and so actually perceives, listens, and believes. In this business God thus shows that he is the one who makes the dead alive, and calls those things which are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17), and who shines in our hearts, to give us the light of the knowledge, etc. (2 Cor. 4:6). Add 1 Thess. 1:5; Rom. 1:16.

units.la: VII. Veritatem istam de interna reali hyperphysica operatione Sp. Sancti in Vocatione efficaci, contra Pontificios, Socinianos, Remonstrantes, aliosque Pelagianizantes, pressius probamus:
units.tr: VII. We prove this truth, concerning the internal, real, hyperphysical operation of the Holy Spirit in effectual vocation, more closely against the Papists, the Socinians, the Remonstrants, and other semi-Pelagians:

units.la: 1. Quia ista efficientia in SS. Litteris diserte proponitur ut necessaria, quae accedat ad illam externam & moralem: 1 Cor. 3. 5. Quis igitur est Paulus? quis autem Apollos? nisi Ministri, per quos credidistis, &c. verf. 7. Itaque neque is qui plantat est aliquid, neque is qui rigat, sed Deus qui dat crescendi vim. Similiter 2 Tim 2. 24, 26. Joh. 6. 63; 45. Exemplum illustre est in Gentilibus, Act. 10. 44. & in Lydia; xvj. 14. Atque hinc preces Pauli pro aliorum conversione; Eph. 1. 17. 18. Deus det vobis spiritum sapientiae, illuminatis oculis mentis vestrae, ad sciendum quae sit spes illa vocationis ipsius, &c.
units.tr: 1. Because this efficacy is set forth plainly in the Holy Scriptures as necessary, and as added to that external and moral action: 1 Cor. 3:5, 7: What then is Paul? And what is Apollos? Only ministers through whom you believed, etc. So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase. Similarly 2 Tim. 2:24, 26; John 6:63, 45. A clear example is among the Gentiles, Acts 10:44, and in Lydia, Acts 16:14. Hence also Paul's prayers for the conversion of others: Eph. 1:17, 18: May God give you the spirit of wisdom, with the eyes of your mind enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, etc.

units.la: 2. Non sufficit objectiva solum Euangelii propositio, & suasio duntaxat moralis: propter humanae naturae corruptionem & ineptitudinem ad bona spiritualia salutaria. Vide sup. c. 10. th. 19, 30, 34. Consequenter necessaria est efficacia illa realis hyperphysica, ad auferendam corruptionem, restituendam aptitudinem, & actu in nobis producendam fidem ac respicientiam.
units.tr: 2. The objective proclamation of the Gospel, and merely moral persuasion, are not sufficient, because of the corruption of human nature and its unfitness for saving spiritual goods. See above, ch. 10, theses 19, 30, 34. Consequently that real, hyperphysical efficacy is necessary, to remove the corruption, to restore the fitness, and actually to produce faith and repentance in us.

units.la: 3. Quia variae phrases passim usurpantur, efficaciam istam satis emphatice exprimentes: nominatim, Apprehensio Christi activa; Phil. 3. 12. Tractio; Joh. 6. 44. Cordis mutatio, & Legis Divinae inscriptio; Ezech. 36. 25, 26, 27. Jerem. 31. 33. Conversio; Thren. 5.21. Circumcisio cordis ab ipso Deo facta, aut facienda; Deut. 30. 6. Nova Creatio; Eph. 2, 10. Pf. 51. 12. Regeneratio; Job. 3. 3, 5,-8. Resuscitatio ex morte spirituali Eph.2.5,6.
units.tr: 3. Because various phrases are used everywhere which express this efficacy quite emphatically: namely, the active apprehension of Christ (Phil. 3:12); drawing (John 6:44); change of heart, and the inscription of the Divine law (Ezek. 36:25–27; Jer. 31:33); conversion (Lam. 5:21); circumcision of the heart made, or to be made, by God himself (Deut. 30:6); new creation (Eph. 2:10; Ps. 51:12); regeneration (John 3:3, 5–8); resurrection from spiritual death (Eph. 2:5, 6).

units.la: 4. Ex ratione consequentiæ: Quia non crediderunt & resipuerunt carnales Israelitæ, eo quod iis non obtigerit gratia illa realiter efficax: unde Deut. 29. 5. Sed non dederat vobis Jehovah mentem ad cognoscendum, & oculos ad videndum, &c.
units.tr: 4. From the logic of consequence: because the carnal Israelites did not believe and repent, since that truly efficacious grace was not granted to them; hence Deut. 29:4: But Jehovah had not given you a mind to know, and eyes to see, etc.

units.la: Obj. 1. Efficientia moralis aliquoties proponitur, ut necessaria ad hominis conversionem. Ergo. Resp. A positione unius, ad negationem alterius, non valet consequentia.
units.tr: Objection 1. The moral efficacy is sometimes set forth as necessary for man's conversion. Therefore... Answer. From the positing of one thing, the negation of another does not follow.

units.la: Obj. 2. Passim occurrunt doctrinæ, præcepta, promissa, &c. Ergo ipsi homines suis viribus se possunt convertere, & credere. Resp. Ex illis recte colliguntur officia hominum, quibus ista proponuntur; non vero propria eorum facultas citra gratiam Dei realiter efficacem: quemadmodum pari ratione, ex reprehensionibus, querelis, &c. innotescunt peccata hominum, officia sua libere negligentium; non eorum aptitudo per se ad bona spiritualia salutaria.
units.tr: Objection 2. Doctrines, precepts, promises, etc. occur everywhere. Therefore men can convert and believe by their own powers. Answer. From these things we rightly gather the duties of the men to whom they are set forth, but not their own ability apart from the really effectual grace of God; just as, by the same reasoning, from reproofs, complaints, etc. the sins of men are made known, men who freely neglect their duties, but not their aptitude in itself for saving spiritual goods.

units.la: VIII. Attamen præcedere solet ministerium Legis, ad agnoscendum reatum, & gratiæ Evangelicæ necessitatem: Matth. 9. 12, 13. Rom. 3. 20. sequente deinceps Evangelio; & justitiam ac reliqua bona salutaria, in Christo, monstrante: Matth. xj. 28. Rom. 1. 16, 17.
units.tr: VIII. Nevertheless, the ministry of the Law usually precedes, to bring us to recognise our guilt and the necessity of evangelical grace (Matt. 9:12, 13; Rom. 3:20); then the Gospel follows, showing forth righteousness and the other saving goods in Christ (Matt. 11:28; Rom. 1:16, 17).

units.la: Vocationem istam deinde sequitur actus noster, quo ad vocantem Christum Mediatorem accedimus, & per ipsum ad Deum; sic ab ipso apprehensi, apprehendimus ipsum vicissim: Joh. vi, 45. Phil 1 1 1, 12.
units.tr: Our act follows this vocation, by which we come to Christ the Mediator who calls us, and through him to God; thus, having been apprehended by him, we in turn apprehend him (John 6:45; Phil. 1:11, 12).

units.la: IX. Ex dictis patet, 1. Vocationem istam ad unionem & communionem Christi, distinguendam esse à Vocatione ad munus, vel functionem aliquam insignem : cum illa omnium fidelium fit communis; hæc quorundam peculiaris, five electorum, five etiam reproborum:
units.tr: IX. From what has been said it is clear, first, that this vocation to the union and communion with Christ must be distinguished from the vocation to some office or special function: since the former is common to all the faithful, whereas the latter belongs to certain persons only, whether elect or even reprobate;

units.la: Atque item 2. à Vocatione duntaxat externa; vel etiam illuminante solum & persuadente,aut refrænante & cohibente,ac simul excitante ad quandam pietatis speciem; vel etiam conferente dona quædam extraordinaria, non salutaria. Sic enim Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi: Matth. 20. 16; xxij, 14
units.tr: And likewise 2. from the external calling alone, or from a calling that only enlightens and persuades, or restrains and checks while at the same time stirring up a certain appearance of piety, or even one that confers certain extraordinary gifts which do not save. For thus: Many are called, but few are chosen: Matth. 20. 16; 22. 14.

units.la: Nec non 3. Vocationem efficacem & verè salutarem, non esse ejusdem speciei cum externa solum; vel illuminante, persuadente, refrænante, &c. Quæ enim efficax, & salutaris est, à Christo, quâ Mediatore, in electis suis efficacia spirituali vivificante peragitur: altera non item; sed a Christo tantum procedit, ut Domino, omnium potestatem habente, & pro beneplacito suo, dona quædam, sine vera vita spirituali, quibusdam largiente.
units.tr: Nor, 3., is the efficacious and truly saving calling of the same kind as the external calling alone, or as the calling that only enlightens, persuades, restrains and so on. For what is efficacious and saving is carried out by Christ as Mediator, in his elect, by a spiritual and life-giving efficacy. The other is not so, but proceeds from Christ only as Lord, having all power, who at his good pleasure bestows certain gifts on some, without true spiritual life.

units.la: 4. Gratiam Dei & Christi in Vocatione electorum non esse resistibilem, nec effectum ejus a libero hominis arbitrio suspensum; sed obstacula omnia removere, difficultates superare, prorsus pertendere, atque efsectum salutarem certo sortiri: dum facit homines non solum posse; verum etiam velle, & incipere, imo insuper pergere ac perseverare; contra Remonstr.
units.tr: 4. The grace of God and of Christ in the calling of the elect is not resistible, nor is its effect suspended on the free will of man. Rather, it removes all obstacles, overcomes difficulties, altogether prevails, and surely obtains its saving effect, while it makes men not only able but also willing, and beginning, and moreover going on and persevering; against the Remonstrants.

units.la: X. Sed neque universalis est ista Vocatio: cum nec ipsa electio, cujus illa primum in executione medium est; nec ipsa fides, quæ formalis hujus Vocationis essectus est; nec ipsa denique Vocatio externa, plane fit universalis. Quod contra eosdem probè observandum, qui gratiam universalem sufficientem ad conversionem & salutem tam strenue propugnant; Deumque a sua parte paratum contendunt, sermonem reconciliationis omnibus & singulis proponere, quamvis re ipsa non proponat, propterea quod multi se eo indignos præstent.
units.tr: X. But this calling is not universal either. Neither election itself, of which it is the first means in execution, nor faith itself, which is the formal effect of this calling, nor finally the external calling itself, is plainly universal. This must be carefully noted against those who so vigorously defend a universal grace sufficient for conversion and salvation, and who contend that God on his part is ready to set forth the word of reconciliation to all and each, although in fact he does not set it forth, because many render themselves unworthy of it.

units.la: Obj. r.
units.tr: Obj. 1.

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui diserta omnium fit mentio; Marc. 16. 15. 1 Tim. 2. 4. Tit. 2. 11. Resp. Istic locutionem synecdochicam, de generibus singulorum, non de singulis generum, agnoscendam, satis obvium est.
units.tr: Obj. 1. But express mention is made of all: Marc. 16. 15; 1 Tim. 2. 4; Tit. 2. 11. Resp. That in these places there is a synecdochical manner of speaking, referring to the kinds of individuals and not to the individuals of each kind, is obvious enough.

units.la: Obj. 2. In Gentilibus, aliisque qui pereunt, multa praeclara dona atque opera reperiuntur. Ergo. Resp. Quae alicubi de donis naturae post lapsum, vel etiam de beneficiis quibusdam non salutaribus, occurrunt; haec cum iis quae sunt gratiae supernaturalis & salvificae, confundi non debent.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Among the Gentiles and others who perish, many excellent gifts and works are found. Therefore... Resp. Whatever passages occur somewhere concerning gifts of nature after the fall, or even concerning certain non-saving benefits, must not be confused with those that belong to supernatural and saving grace.

units.la: XI. Regeneratio est Actio realis hyperphysica, quae homini in Adamo spiritualiter mortuo, attamen electo & per Christum redemto, Vita spiritualis de novo inditur, ad ipsius salutem, & gloriosae Dei misericordiae demonstrationem.
units.tr: XI. Regeneration is a real, hyperphysical action, by which spiritual life is newly infused into a man who is spiritually dead in Adam, yet elect and redeemed through Christ, for his salvation and for the demonstration of God's glorious mercy.

units.la: Vita dupliciter spectari solet, tum in actu primo, ut est ratio formalis viventis, qua talis; tum in actu secundo, prout actiones ex isto principio reipsa procedunt. Priori modo vita spiritualis inditur per Regenerationem; & sic est facultas supernaturalis menti indita, per Spiritum Christi, ad producendas actiones spirituales salutares. Posteriore modo ipsae actiones vitales ex isto principio eliciuntur & imperantur.
units.tr: Life is usually considered in two ways: first, in the first act, as the formal reason of a living thing as such; second, in the second act, insofar as actions really proceed from this principle. In the first way spiritual life is infused through regeneration; and so it is a supernatural faculty implanted in the mind by the Spirit of Christ, for producing saving spiritual actions. In the latter way the vital actions themselves are elicited and commanded from this principle.

units.la: XII. Interim respectu diversorum subjectorum varia quoque de vita spirituali, & operationibus Dei circa ista subjecta, possunt observari. Sic autem occurrunt; 1. Electi adhuc irregeniti; 2. Regeniti quoad actum primum; 3. Converti & Sanctificati quoad actum secundum.
units.tr: XII. Meanwhile, with respect to different subjects, various things may also be observed about spiritual life and the operations of God concerning these subjects. They occur thus: 1. the elect not yet regenerate; 2. the regenerate as to the first act; 3. the converted and sanctified as to the second act.

units.la: Electi adhuc irregeniti sunt potissimum Electi nati & educati ab infidelibus, extra communionem Ecclesiae & Foederis Evangelici; quorum vita spiritualis per Christum impetrata, virtualiter est in Christo, & suo tempore ac ordine juxta Decretum Dei in ipsis producenda, quamvis ea formaliter hactenus sint deflituti; Quapropter Deus hoc agit, ut illi non moriantur riantur citrà regenerationem & conversionem; quin imò frequenter per gratiam reprimentem & coërcentem hoc efficit, ut ne in graviora flagitia contra communem honestatem proruant; aut si contingat eos Euangelio priùs vocari, curat omninò ut non peccent in Spir. Sanctum : sed suo tempore ac ordine regenerentur & vocentur salutariter. Vide Eph. 2. 1, 2, 3, 12. IV. 17–20. I Cor. 6. 9–11. Gal. 4. 8, 9. Joh. 10. 16.
units.tr: The elect not yet regenerate are chiefly those elect who are born and brought up among unbelievers, outside the communion of the Church and of the Evangelical covenant. Their spiritual life, obtained through Christ, is virtually in Christ, and is to be produced in them at its own time and order according to the decree of God, although hitherto they are formally destitute of it. Therefore God so acts that they do not die without regeneration and conversion. Indeed, often by a restraining and checking grace he brings it about that they do not rush into graver crimes against common decency; or if it happens that they are called to the Gospel earlier, he takes care altogether that they do not sin against the Holy Spirit, but are regenerated and savingly called at his own time and order. See Eph. 2. 1, 2, 3, 12; Eph. 4. 17–20; 1 Cor. 6. 9–11; Gal. 4. 8, 9; John 10. 16.

units.la: XIII. Regeniti quoad actum primum sunt Electi & redemti in quibus jàm est Spiritus Christi, tanquàm principium vitæ spiritualis; quamvis ab ipsis nondùm procedant operationes vitales spirituales: quales sunt Infantes electi & redemti, atque ex utroque parente, vel alterutro saltem fideli, nati in communione Fœderis Euangelici. Huc faciunt loca Gen. 17. 7, 11, 12; Pf. 22. 10, 11; Act. 2. 38, 39. I Cor. 7. 14. Marc. 10. 14. Exempla, in quibus adjuncta quidem fuerunt extraordinaria, sic tamen ut ipsum ordinarium interim involvatur, vide in Jeremiâ I. 5. Johanne Baptistâ, Luc. I. 15. Simsone, Jud. 13. 7. & in Paulo, Gal. I. 15, 16. Fidem habitualem multi appellant: Alii Spiritum, Semen, vel Radicem fidei. Nonnulli Gratiam, vel Regenerationem baptismalem. Alia est ratio eorum infantium, qui reprobati sunt; quemadmodum & adultorum: licet tales etiàm Sacramentorum & externæ communionis Ecclesiasticæ fiant participes; atque judicio charitatis pro electis habeantur, quatenùs non apparent indicia contraria.
units.tr: XIII. The regenerate as to the first act are the elect and redeemed in whom the Spirit of Christ already is, as the principle of spiritual life, although vital spiritual operations do not yet proceed from them. Such are elect and redeemed infants, born in the communion of the Evangelical covenant from both parents, or at least from one believing parent. To this point belong Gen. 17. 7, 11, 12; Ps. 22. 10, 11; Acts 2. 38, 39; 1 Cor. 7. 14; Marc. 10. 14. For examples in which extraordinary circumstances were added, yet so that the ordinary is meanwhile included, see Jer. 1. 5; John the Baptist, Luke 1. 15; Samson, Judg. 13. 7; and Paul, Gal. 1. 15, 16. Many call this habitual faith; others the Spirit, seed, or root of faith. Some call it grace, or baptismal regeneration. The case is different for those infants who are reprobate, as it is also for adults. Yet such persons too become partakers of the Sacraments and of outward ecclesiastical communion, and by the judgment of charity are held to be elect, insofar as no contrary signs appear.

units.la: In istis sic regenitis interim agnoscendum est Peccatum originale, tùm imputatum, quoad reatum in actù primo; tùm inhærens, quia destituuntur integritate imaginis Divinæ, & vitiositatem naturæ corruptæ habent, quamvis hæc per supervenientem gratiam vitæ spiritualis certò deinceps destruenda sit.
units.tr: In those thus regenerated, meanwhile, original sin must be acknowledged: both imputed, as to guilt in the first act, and inherent, because they lack the integrity of the divine image and have the viciousness of corrupt nature. Yet this is certainly to be destroyed afterwards by the grace of spiritual life that supervenes.

units.la: XIV. Sequuntur tandem Conversi & Sanctificati quoad
units.tr: XIV. Finally come the Converted and the Sanctified, as to the second act.

units.la: quoad actum secundum. Infantes electi, & in fœdere nati, vel in ejusdem communione educantur à fidelibus; vel extrà ejus communionem ab infidelibus ac profanis, & cum iis vivunt aliquamdiu. In prioribus dum inest intrinsecum vitæ spiritualis principium, accedente pariter exemplo fidei ac pietatis, atque item diligenti instructione de credendis & faciendis, in ipså sæpè pueritiâ eliciuntur & excitantur actûs quidam fidei & sanctitatis, licet initio incompleti; paulatim verò illi proficiunt, & vitam spiritualem plenius exerunt. Hùc spectant præcepta ista, Deut. 6. 6, 7. xi. 19. Prov. 22. 6. Eph. 6. 4. Exempla sunt in familiâ Abrahami, Gen. 18. 19. & in educatione Timothei, 2 Tim. 1. 5. iij. 14, 15. Qui autem ab infidelibus & profanis educantur, & adminiculis istis externis ad tempus destituuntur, tardius etiam & serius promoveri solent ad actûs secundos vitæ spiritualis: donec tandem Deus speciali quâdam efficaciâ Sp. Sancti eos moveat & excitet, adhibito foris Verbi sui ministerio. Exemplum tale obvium est in Paulo, qui in Judaïsmo educatus, & dogmata sectæ Pharisaïcæ edoctus, Christum in membris suis aliquamdiù persequebatur; donec ipsius Christi voce coelitùs demissâ prostratus, ad Ananiam de veritate salutari instruendus mitteretur. Act. 7. 58. ix. 1. & seqq. Similiter & in Augustino, qui matre fideli, patre autem infideli natus, & in educatione puerili variè agitatus, tandem per Ambrosium de veritate Christianæ religionis instructus, & ad communionem Ecclesiæ adductus est.
units.tr: Infants who are elect and born within the covenant are brought up either by the faithful, within its fellowship, or outside that fellowship by unbelievers and the profane, and live with them for some time. In the former case, while the inner principle of spiritual life is present, and the example of faith and piety is added, along with diligent instruction in what is to be believed and done, certain acts of faith and holiness are often drawn out and stirred up even in early childhood, though at first incomplete. Gradually these advance and put forth spiritual life more fully. To this belong the precepts Deut. 6. 6, 7; 11. 19; Prov. 22. 6; Eph. 6. 4. Examples are found in the household of Abraham, Gen. 18. 19, and in the upbringing of Timothy, 2 Tim. 1. 5; 3. 14, 15. But those who are brought up by unbelievers and the profane, and for a time are deprived of these external helps, are usually advanced more slowly and late to the second acts of spiritual life, until at last God, by a special efficacy of the Holy Spirit, moves and stirs them up, the ministry of his Word being applied from without. An example of this is Paul, who, brought up in Judaism and taught the doctrines of the Pharisaic sect, persecuted Christ in his members for some time, until, cast down by the voice of Christ sent from heaven, he was sent to Ananias to be instructed in saving truth. Acts 7. 58; 9. 1 and following. Similarly with Augustine, who, born of a believing mother and an unbelieving father, and variously tossed about in his childhood education, was at last instructed in the truth of the Christian religion by Ambrose and brought into the fellowship of the Church.

units.la: XV. Fieri tamen potest, ut Electi in Fœdere nati, & à fidelibus educati, diù in tenuibus quibusdam initiis subsistant; & ad quandam vitæ laxitatem, vel formalem subindè hypocrisin prolapsi, serius ad actuale & constans vitæ spiritualis exercitium promoveantur: in quibus valdè conspicua soler esse mutatio; quemadmodum modùm & in iis, qui ab infantiâ suâ regeniti; sed ab infidelibus aut profanis educati sunt. Maximè verò in illis adultis, ubi in intrinsecum istiusmodi principium non praeexistit; sed qui simul & semel vocantur, regenerantur; & convertuntur in actû secundo. Vide quae facta sunt in Israëlitis, die Pentecostes, Act. 2, 37, 41. In Paulo, Act. 9. 4, -9. & in Commentariensi, xvj. 25, -34. Adde 1 Cor. 14. 24, 25.
units.tr: XV. It may nevertheless happen that the elect, born within the covenant and brought up by the faithful, remain for a long time in some slight beginnings, and, having at times slipped into a certain looseness of life or formal hypocrisy, are only later advanced to an actual and constant exercise of spiritual life. In such people a very conspicuous change is usually seen, just as also in those who were regenerated from infancy but brought up by unbelievers or the profane. Most of all, however, it happens in adults in whom no such inner principle pre-exists, but who are called and regenerated at once and all together, and converted in the second act. See what happened among the Israelites on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2. 37, 41; in Paul, Acts 9. 4, 9; and in the jailer (the Commentariensis), 16. 25–34. Add 1 Cor. 14. 24, 25.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: In Regeneratione fit Mortificatio veteris hominis, & Vivificatio novi: prout scil. destruitur peccatum inhaerens ex Adamo; eâdemque operâ producitur vita verae sapientiae, justitiae; & sanctitatis, ex Christo. De utráque vide Col. 3. 3, 9, 10; & Eph. 4. 21, -24. utrobique interim distingui debet inter actum primum & secundum. Actû primo Mortificationis vetus homo lethaliter vulneratur: Actibus secundis vires ejus magis magisque franguntur. Sicut actû primo Vivificationis inditur principium vitale: actibus secundis ipsae operationes vitales ulterius exeruntur, & indies promoventur; donec tandem vita spiritualis complementum suum accipiat; quod in hoc saeculo non obtinetur perfectè.
units.tr: In regeneration there takes place the mortification of the old man and the vivification of the new: namely, the sin dwelling in us from Adam is destroyed, and by the same work the life of true wisdom, righteousness and holiness is produced from Christ. On both see Col. 3. 3, 9, 10 and Eph. 4. 21–24. In both cases, meanwhile, a distinction must be made between the first and the second act. By the first act of mortification the old man is mortally wounded; by the second acts his strength is more and more broken. Likewise by the first act of vivification a vital principle is implanted; by the second acts the vital operations themselves are further brought forth and daily advanced, until at last the spiritual life receives its completion, which in this age is not attained perfectly.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Sic igitur in primo momento habet se homo merè passivè; quod ex ejus conditione, & phrasibus in hac materiâ usurpari solitis, ac th. 7. §. 3. allegatis, manifestum est. Atque adeò ante Regenerationem suam non potest salutariter audire Verbum Dei; totali enim impotentiâ laborat ad bona spiritualia salutaria. Rom. 8. 7. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Consequenter nullae dispositiones praeparatoriae ad primam regenerationem in ipso fingendae; non magis quàm in quolibet mortuo ad vitam. Sic ante primam fidei ingenerationem in ipso supponi non debet, nec a parte ipsius praerequiritur pia quaedam docilitas; aut animi probitas: Pollutis enim & incredulis nihil est mundum, &c. Tit. 1. 15. Et sicubi forte de quibusdam tale quid praedicari videatur, ut de Eunucho, Act. 8. 27. &c. & Cornelio, x. 22, 24, &c. dicendum, quòd illi non fuerint irregeniti: sed jàm ante per Regenerationem & Sanctificationem eò usque producti, cùm essent Judæi Proselyti, licet poltea demum explicatam & applicatam de Jesû Christo instructionem acceperint.
units.tr: Thus, then, in the first moment man stands in a purely passive relation. This is plain from his condition, from the phrases customarily used in this matter, and from the passages cited in th. 7 §3. Therefore, before his regeneration he cannot hear the Word of God to salvation, for he labours under total inability toward the spiritual goods that save. Rom. 8. 7; 1 Cor. 2. 14. Consequently no preparatory dispositions for the first regeneration are to be imagined in him, no more than in any dead man for life. So before the first engendering of faith, no pious docility or uprightness of mind ought to be presupposed in him, nor required on his part in advance: "For to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean," etc. Tit. 1. 15. And if somewhere something of this kind seems to be asserted of certain people, as of the eunuch, Acts 8. 27 etc., and of Cornelius, 10. 22, 24 etc., it must be said that they were not unregenerate, but had already been brought by regeneration and sanctification thus far, since they were Jewish proselytes, although they afterwards received the instruction explained and applied concerning Jesus Christ.

units.la: Regeneratio per Verbum fieri dicitur, Jac. I. 18.
units.tr: Regeneration is said to take place "by the Word," Jas. 1. 18.

units.la: 1 Petr. I. 23. sed potissimùm tunc intelligendum est Verbum internum, cum externum habeat tantùm rationem causæ instrumentalis moralis in adultis, qui ejus capaces sunt.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1. 23. But chiefly the internal Word is to be understood here, since the external Word has only the character of a moral instrumental cause in adults, who are capable of it.

units.la: XVIII. Mortificatio igitur veteris hominis, & Vivificatio novi, in momento & actû primo sunt operationes solius Dei: sed deinceps in actibus secundis etiàm nostræ partes effectivæ sunt; quamvis dependenter à gratiâ Dei salutiferâ in Christo. Sic sedulò agimus, ut vetus homo magis ac magis mortificetur; novus autem jugiter incrementum capiat: quò pertinent adhortationes, Gal. 5. 24, 25. Rom. 6. 11.-14.
units.tr: XVIII. The mortification of the old man and the vivification of the new are therefore, in the moment and the first act, operations of God alone. But thereafter, in the second acts, our own parts are also effective, although dependent on the saving grace of God in Christ. So we diligently act, that the old man may be mortified more and more, and the new may continually grow; to this belong the exhortations, Gal. 5. 24, 25; Rom. 6. 11–14.

units.la: 2 Cor. 4. 16. Cùm interim alii minùs, alii magis in hâc praxi proficiant, pro diversitate graduum; de quibus alibi ex professo erit agendum.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 16. Meanwhile some make less progress in this practice, others more, according to the diversity of degrees, of which we shall treat expressly elsewhere.

units.la: Similiter de Conversione dicendum; quòd scil. primus ejus actus efficienter Deo, passivè nobis attribui debeat: sic Deo nos convertente, nos convertimur: Jerem. 31. 18. Cæterùm ex principio jàm indito, sed dependenter à gratiâ Dei, nos ipsos quoque convertimus ad Deum, & in viis ipsius piè ac sincerè ambulamus.
units.tr: Similarly, conversion must be spoken of: namely, that its first act is to be attributed efficiently to God and passively to us. So, God converting us, we are converted. Jer. 31. 18. Moreover, from the principle now implanted, but dependent on the grace of God, we also turn ourselves to God and walk in his ways piously and sincerely.

units.la: XIX. Ex superioribus tandem colligimus contrà Pontif. & Remonstr.
units.tr: XIX. From what has been said above we finally draw conclusions against the Papists and the Remonstrants.

units.la: 1. Vocationem salutarem à non salutari differre ipsâ intrinseca operatione vocantis, & effectu formali proximo; non verò tantùm adjuncto usû arbitrii humani, aut consequente fructû salutari.
units.tr: 1. The saving calling differs from the non-saving by the intrinsic operation of the one who calls and by its proximate formal effect; it does not differ merely by the adjunct of the use of the human will, or by the saving fruit that follows.

units.la: 2. Illuminationem salutarem distinguendam esse ab illuminatione qualicunque generali non salutari.
units.tr: 2. Saving illumination must be distinguished from any general non-saving illumination whatever.

units.la: 3. Veram Poenitentiam & Contritionem salutarem similiter differre ab attritione qualicunque, & tristitiâ secundum mundum, ex apprehensione irae Divinae, vel metû infamiae.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, true repentance and saving contrition differ from any attrition whatever, and from the sorrow of the world that arises from the apprehension of divine wrath or from fear of disgrace.

units.la: XX. Pro Praxi: 1. Vocationem nostram, ut & Electionem, firmam efficere studeamus: 2 Petr. I. 20.
units.tr: XX. For practice: 1. Let us take care to make our calling, as also our election, firm: 2 Pet. 1. 20.

units.la: 2. Quanta gratia nobis sit facta, quod Christus nos prior dilexerit, & efficaciam salutarem in nobis exerere coeperit, sedulò attendamus: Joh. 15. 16.
units.tr: 2. Let us carefully consider how great a grace has been shown us, that Christ loved us first and has begun to exert His saving efficacy in us: John 15. 16.

units.la: 3. Vitam spiritualem magis ac magis exeramus: Phil. 3. 12, 16, &c.
units.tr: 3. Let us bring forth the spiritual life more and more: Phil. 3. 12, 16, &c.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: De Justificatione, Reconciliatione, & Adoptione.
units.tr: On Justification, Reconciliation, and Adoption.

units.la: Justificatio. Actus judicialis. 1. Probatur. 2. Sententia Pontif. Obj. solv. 3. Judicium Dei. Justitia universalis, persona: non causa tantum. Articuli istius sententiae. 4. Causa efficiens prima, Procatarctica impetratoria. Causa efficiens altera. Finis. 5. Justitia Christi. Imputatio. 6. Objectiones solv. 7. Justitia propria rejicitur. Fidei usus organicus: c. Pontif. Socin. &c. 8. Sententia vera probatur. 9. Exceptiones solv. 10. Sententia Pontif. de Satisfactionibus humanis. 11. Objectiones solv. 12. Sententia eorum de Meritis humanis; quantum ad vocem. Obj. solv. 13. De re, obj. sol. 14. ac porrò, th. 15, 16, 17. De usu meritorum, secundum eosd. Cap.XV. eosd. 18. Sententia Socin. 19. Remonstr. 20. ac porrò, th. 21, 22. Aliæ objectiones solv. 23. Error Ofiandri. Obj. solv. 24. Distinctiones quædam. 25. Justificatio sub V. T. 27. Infantium electorum regenitorum. 28. Peccata quodammodò remissa, priusquàm commissa. 29. Justificamur unico actu, eoque immutabili: c. Pontif. & Remonstr. 30. Quomodò post hanc vitam aliqua peccatorum remissio, 31. Reconciliatio. Actus gratiosus. Termini. Quibus modis facta. 32. Pax. Cum Deo. Ejus fructus. 33. Amicitia. Cum Deo. 34. Adoptio. Filiatio. 35. Formaliter fit in tempore. Causa efficiens prima. Media. Quomodò virtualiter facta. Ejus testificatio. Confummata applicatio. Privilegia. 36. Libertas Christiana. primaria, etiàm sub V. T. 37. Secundaria, pro N. T. Obj. solv. Libertas conscientiæ à statutis humanis. Non tamen à Legibus civilibus. De Adiaphoris. Scandalum. datum. acceptum. sumtum. Non data carni occasio. Non permittenda quibusvis libertas prophetandi: c. Socin. Remonstr. &c. Filialis animi fiducia apud Patrem cœlestem. 38. Specialis conformatio cum Christo. Concio primogenitorum. Prophetæ. Sacerdotes. Reges. 39. Hæreditas. 40. Excellentia præ humanâ adoptione. 41. Praxis. 42.
units.tr: Justification. A judicial act. 1. It is proved. 2. The opinion of the Papists; objections answered. 3. The judgment of God. Universal righteousness belongs to the person, not merely to the cause. The articles of that opinion. 4. The first efficient cause: the procatartic, impetratory cause. The second efficient cause. The end. 5. The righteousness of Christ. Imputation. 6. Objections answered. 7. Our own righteousness is rejected. The organic use of faith: against the Papists, the Socinians, etc. 8. The true opinion is proved. 9. Exceptions answered. 10. The opinion of the Papists on human satisfactions. 11. Objections answered. 12. Their opinion on human merits, as to the word. Objection answered. 13. As to the thing, objection answered. 14. And further, the theses 14, 15, 16, 17. On the use of merits, according to the same authors. Chap. XV, the same authors. 18. The opinion of the Socinians. 19. The Remonstrants. 20. And further, the theses 20, 21, 22. Other objections answered. 23. The error of Osiander. Objection answered. 24. Certain distinctions. 25. Justification under the Old Testament. 27. Of elect infants who are regenerated. 28. Sins are in a certain manner remitted before they are committed. 29. We are justified by a single act, and that an unchangeable one: against the Papists and the Remonstrants. 30. How, after this life, there is some remission of sins. 31. Reconciliation. A gracious act. Its terms. In what ways it is brought about. 32. Peace, with God. Its fruit. 33. Friendship, with God. 34. Adoption. Sonship. 35. It takes place formally in time. The first efficient cause. The means. How it is brought about virtually. Its attestation. The completed application. Privileges. 36. Christian liberty: primary, and also under the Old Testament. 37. Secondary, for the New Testament. Objection answered. Liberty of conscience from human statutes, but not from civil laws. On things indifferent. Scandal: given, taken, and assumed. No occasion is to be given to the flesh. Liberty of prophesying is not to be permitted to everyone: against the Socinians, the Remonstrants, etc. The filial confidence of the soul before the heavenly Father. 38. Specific conformity to Christ. The assembly of the firstborn. Prophets. Priests. Kings. 39. Inheritance. 40. Its excellence above human adoption. 41. Practice. 42.

units.la: I. Uccedit Justificatio: Rom. 8. 30. Quos Vocavit, eos etiam Justificavit. Est autem Judicialis & gratiosus Dei actus, quo homo peccator, sed redemptus & credens, à reatu absolvitur, simul-que que vita æterna ei adjudicatur, juxta Euangelium; propter Justitiam Christi ipsi imputatam, & fide ab eo receptam.
units.tr: I. Justification follows: "Those whom he called, them he also justified" (Rom. 8:30). It is a judicial and gracious act of God, by which a sinner who is nevertheless redeemed and believing is absolved from guilt, and at the same time eternal life is adjudged to him, according to the Gospel, on account of the righteousness of Christ imputed to him and received by him through faith.

units.la: Actum judicialem dicimus; quia judicando statûs nostri mutationem relativam infert: non physicum, aut hyperphysicum; quasi realem qualitatum mutationem in nobis formaliter produceret. Sic enim Hebraicum הִצְדִּיק, & Græcum Δικαιῶν, vel Δικαιόω, quæ per Latinum verbum justificare reddi solent, passim in SS. Literis usurpantur. Atque ista significatio forensis in hac materia omnino retinenda est.
units.tr: We call it a judicial act, because by judging it brings about a relative change of our state, and not a physical or hyperphysical change, as though it formally produced a real change of qualities in us. For the Hebrew הִצְדִּיק [hitsdiq] and the Greek Δικαιῶν [dikaioun] or Δικαιόω [dikaioo], which are commonly rendered by the Latin word justificare, are used throughout the Holy Scriptures. And this forensic meaning must be wholly retained in this matter.

units.la: II. Huc pertinet 1. Inductio locorum V. T. utpote Deut. 25. 1. Si fuerit controversia inter aliquos, ideoque accesserint ad judicium, ut judices sententiam de eis ferant, tum justum pronunciaturi sunt; sive justificaturi, הִצְדִּיק) eum qui justus est: & Improbaturi sunt (sive Condemnaturi, וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ) eum qui Improbus est. Prov. 17. 15. Qui absolvit (sive justificat, מַצְדִּיק) Improbum, & qui Condemnat (sive Improbat, מַרְשִׁיעַ) justum, abominationi Jehovæ sunt æquè ambo. Adde Jef. 5. 22. 23. 2 Sam. 15. 4. Et confer Ezech. 16. 51, 52. Psal. 143. 2.
units.tr: II. To this belong: 1. The citation of passages from the Old Testament, such as Deut. 25:1: "If there be a controversy between men, and they come to judgment, that the judges may judge them, then they shall justify [הִצְדִּיק] the one who is righteous, and condemn [וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ] the one who is wicked." Prov. 17:15: "He who justifies [מַצְדִּיק] the wicked, and he who condemns [מַרְשִׁיעַ] the just, are both alike an abomination to the LORD." Add Isa. 5:22, 23; 2 Sam. 15:4. And compare Ezek. 16:51, 52; Ps. 143:2.

units.la: 2. Similis inductio locorum N. T. Rom. 8. 33, 34. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? Deus is est qui justificat. (ὁ Δικαιῶν.) Quis est qui Condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est, &c. v. 16. Reatus quidem est ex unâ offensâ (Adami) ad Condemnationem: (εἰς κατάκριμα.) Quod autem gratificatur Deus, est ex multis offensis ad justificationem, (εἰς δικαίωμα.) Vide etiam verf. 18. & cap. xi. 12. 13. Matth. 12. 37. Luc. 7. 29. 35. xvi. 15. In omnibus istis locis, ex subjecta materia, atque evidenti oppositione Justificationis & Condemnationis manifesta est forensis significatio æstimandi ac judicandi; non vero actionis realis physicæ, aut hyperphysicæ.
units.tr: 2. A similar citation of passages from the New Testament: Rom. 8:33, 34: "Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifies [ὁ Δικαιῶν]. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died," etc. v. 16: The judgment is indeed from one offence (of Adam) to condemnation [εἰς κατάκριμα]; but the gift is from many offences to justification [εἰς δικαίωμα]. See also v. 18, and chap. 11:12, 13; Matt. 12:37; Luke 7:29, 35; 16:15. In all these places, from the subject matter and the plain opposition of justification and condemnation, the forensic meaning of estimating and judging is evident, and not that of a real physical or hyperphysical action.

units.la: 3. Diligenter observanda est accuratissima huius negotii tractatio, Rom. 3. 19,--28. IV. 2,--8. & Gal. 2. 16. ubi clarissime agitur de reatu, per quem omnes sunt obnoxii condemnationi; atque interim Justificatio fit ex fide, & ex gratia, per redemtionem Christi, &c. ut peccata non imputentur, sed remittantur; & Justitia imputetur sine operibus, &c. ubi eadem forensis significatio necessario intelligenda est; non autem realis mutatio, & justitiæ inhærentis infusio.
units.tr: 3. The most careful treatment of this matter must be carefully observed in Rom. 3:19–28; 4:2–8; and Gal. 2:16, where it is most clearly dealt with the guilt by which all are liable to condemnation; and yet justification takes place by faith, and by grace, through the redemption of Christ, etc., so that sins are not imputed but forgiven, and righteousness is imputed without works, etc. Here the same forensic meaning must necessarily be understood, and not a real change or an infusion of inherent righteousness.

units.la: 4. Ipsi Adversarii in Justificatione agnoscunt contineri Remissionem peccatorum; quæ certe actio forensis & judicialis est.
units.tr: 4. The adversaries themselves acknowledge that justification includes the remission of sins, which is certainly a forensic and judicial act.

units.la: III. Pontificii aliter vocem accipiunt; & consequenter etiam in re significata errant gravissimè; quod patebit in progressu. Becanus in Manuali, lib. I. cap. 15. §. 1. "Justificatio nihil aliud est quàm mutatio, qua quis ex impio, seu peccatore, fit justus; sicut sanatio est mutatio, qua quis ex ægroto fit sanus. &c. Sed perperàm.
units.tr: III. The Papists take the word otherwise, and consequently they also err very gravely in the thing signified; this will become plain as we proceed. Becanus, in his Manual, book I, chapter 15, §1: "Justification is nothing other than a change by which someone passes from being impious, or a sinner, to being just, just as healing is a change by which someone passes from being sick to being well," etc. But this is wrongly said.

units.la: Obj. 1. Isef. 53. 11. Cognitione sui justificabit justus servus meus multos, &c. ibi forensis illa significatio non habet locum: sed realis mutatio, ad quam cognitio hominem disponit, intelligenda est. Resp. Imò Christus, ut Deus, & ut Judex, justos pronunciat fideles; pro quibus ipse, ut Sponsor, satisfecit, & salutem æternam meritus est. Sic, rectè ibi retinetur significatio forensis, seu judicialis.
units.tr: Objection 1. Isa. 53:11: "By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many," etc. There that forensic meaning has no place, but a real change, to which the knowledge disposes a man, must be understood. Answer: Rather, Christ, as God and as Judge, pronounces believers just, for whom he himself, as Surety, made satisfaction and merited eternal salvation. Thus the forensic or judicial meaning is rightly retained there.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dan. 12. 3. Erudientes splendebunt, --: & justificantes multos, ut stellæ, &c. Ibi forensis significatio non obtinet; sed realis, &c. Resp. Qui Euangelium prædicant, suoque ministerio alios ad fidem adducunt, quâ Christum ejusque justitiam amplectantur; deinceps etiam, quos credere deprehenduntur, dunt, minisserialiter declarant justos coram Deo. Vide 2 Cor. 5. 19,20. Joh. 20. 23.
units.tr: Objection 2. Dan. 12:3: "Those who teach shall shine... and those who justify many as the stars," etc. Here the forensic meaning does not obtain, but the real one, etc. Answer: Those who preach the Gospel, and by their ministry bring others to faith, by which they embrace Christ and his righteousness, then also, those whom they find to believe, they declare, ministerially, to be just before God. See 2 Cor. 5:19, 20; John 20:23.

units.la: Obj. 3. Apoc. 22. 11. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc, &c. Resp. Qui coram Deo justus est, dum praxin fidei continuat, subinde renovat, & pietati operam dat; in conscientiâ suâ magis percipit, ac dijudicat, se ab ipso Deo justificatum esse, & ab aliis hominibus talis agnoscitur.
units.tr: Objection 3. Rev. 22:11: "He that is righteous, let him be justified still," etc. Answer: He who is just before God, while he continues the practice of faith, renews it from time to time, and devotes himself to godliness, perceives and judges more within his conscience that he has been justified by God himself, and is acknowledged as such by other men.

units.la: Obj. 4. Jac. 2. 21. Abrahamus pater ille noster, nonne ex operibus justificatus est, &c. Resp. Sic ex operibus bonis, tanquàm fructibus verae fidei quâ coram Deo justi sumus, justi agnoscimur, & judicamur, in propriâ nostrâ conscientiâ; ac porro etiàm ab aliis, judicio discretionis.
units.tr: Objection 4. Jas. 2:21: "Was not Abraham our father justified by works?" etc. Answer: So by good works, as fruits of the true faith by which we are just before God, we are acknowledged and judged to be just, in our own conscience, and further also by others, by a judgment of discernment.

units.la: Obj. 5. Similia composita realem mutationem significant; ut Magnificare, Sanctificare, Glorificare, &c. Ergò. Resp. 1. Verba valent usu: sed alium usum verbi justificare, nos jam probavimus. 2. Verba Magnificare & Sanctificare etiàm in significatione aestimandi, declarandi, & celebrandi occurrunt: utpotè Luc. 1. 46. Magnificat anima mea Dominum. Matth. 6. 9. Sanctificetur nomen tuum. &c. Quemadmodùm 3. & simplex verbum Facio eâdem significatione quandoque usurpatur; ut cùm dicimus, Magni facio, Flocci facio, &c.
units.tr: Objection 5. Compound words of similar form signify a real change, such as magnify, sanctify, glorify, etc. Therefore... Answer 1. Words have their meaning from usage; but we have already shown the other usage of the word justify. 2. The words magnify and sanctify also occur in the sense of esteeming, declaring, and celebrating: as in Luke 1:46: "My soul doth magnify the Lord," Matt. 6:9: "Hallowed be thy name," etc. Just as the simple verb facio is sometimes used in the same sense, as when we say magni facio (I hold in high esteem), flocci facio (I think nothing of), etc.

units.la: IV. Facilè apparet, nunc judicium ipsius Dei proprie specûtari; non humanum qualecunque, nisi consequenter: atque itèm universalem justitiam personae, ut ea absolutè justa censeatur coram tribunali Divino; non verò justitiam causae tantùm, prout quis in particulari solùm casu vel facto infonsaut justus est. Vide Psal. 7. 4,5,9. de Davide respectu Saulis, & cvi. 31. de facto Pinchasi.
units.tr: IV. It is easily apparent that here we are looking properly at the very judgment of God, and not at any human judgment whatever, except consequently; and likewise at the universal righteousness of the person, so that he is absolutely judged just before the divine tribunal; and not merely the righteousness of the cause, in which someone is judged just only in a particular case or deed. See Ps. 7:4, 5, 9, concerning David with respect to Saul; and Ps. 106:31, concerning the deed of Phinehas.

units.la: Ista autem sententia gratiosa duos quasi articulos complectitur: prior est Absolutio ab omni nostro reatu, ob plenissimam Christi pro nobis Satisfactionem; Rom. 8. 33, 34. Quis intentabit crimina adversus electos Dei? &c. Sive Remissio peccatorum, h. e. reatus quoad actum secundum plena extinctio: Rom. 4. 6, 7, 8. „Sicut etiam David declarat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat Justitiam absque operibus: dicens Beati, quorum Remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum Obtecta sunt peccata: Beatus vir, cui non imputârit Dominus peccatum. Confer cap. 3. 24, 25, 26. Eph. I. 7.
units.tr: This gracious sentence, as it were, contains two articles. The first is absolution from all our guilt, on account of Christ's most full satisfaction for us: Rom. 8. 33, 34. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?" etc. Or it is the remission of sins, that is, the full extinction of guilt as to its consequence: Rom. 4. 6, 7, 8. "Just as David also declares the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works, saying: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin." Compare chap. 3. 24, 25, 26; Eph. 1. 7.

units.la: Alter est Adjudicatio vitæ æternæ, ob Christi Meritum pro nobis etiam consummatum: Rom. v. 17, 18, 19. „Multo magis ii, qui exundantiam illam gratiæ & doni Justitiæ recipiunt, in vita regnabunt per unum Iesum Christum. -- Per unam Justificationem (beneficium redundavit) in omnes homines ad Justificationem vitæ. -- Ita per unius Obedientiam justi constituentur multi. 21. „Ut, quemadmodum regnaverat peccatum ad Mortem; ita etiam gratia regnaret per Justitiam ad Vitam æternam, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: The second is the adjudication of eternal life, on account of Christ's merit, also accomplished for us: Rom. 5. 17, 18, 19. "Much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. ... Through one justification the benefit came upon all men to justification of life. ... So through the obedience of one many will be made righteous." 21. "So that, as sin reigned unto death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord."

units.la: V. Causa efficiens prima est Deus absolutè: Rom. 8. 33. Deus is est, qui Iustificat. III. 30. 2 Cor. 5. 19. Ies. 43. 25. Mich. 7. 18, 19. Confer Psal. 51. 6. Iac. 4. 12. Ei respondet proëgumena, ipsius Gratia: Rom. 3. 24. Ut qui Iustificentur gratis, ejus Gratia. Eph. I. 7.
units.tr: V. The first efficient cause is God absolutely: Rom. 8. 33. "It is God who justifies." 3. 30. 2 Cor. 5. 19. Isa. 43. 25. Mic. 7. 18, 19. Compare Ps. 51. 6; Jas. 4. 12. To this corresponds the antecedent cause, his grace: Rom. 3. 24. "Being justified freely by his grace." Eph. 1. 7.

units.la: Procatarctica impetratoria est Christus Sponsor ac Redemtor noster: Rom. 3. 24, 25. Per Redemtionem factam in Iesu Christo; Quem præstituit Deus Placamentum per fidem in Sanguine ipsius, &c. Eph. I. 7.
units.tr: The impetrating procatarctic cause is Christ, our Surety and Redeemer: Rom. 3. 24, 25. "Through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood," etc. Eph. 1. 7.

units.la: Causa efficiens altera est idem Christus, ut cui œconomicè traditum est omne Judicium: Ioh. 5. 22, 27. Istam potestatem Christus etiam in terra sibi competiffe, probavit miraculosa paralytici sanatione; Matth. 9. 2, -- 7.
units.tr: The second efficient cause is the same Christ, to whom all judgment has been committed in the economy of salvation: John 5. 22, 27. Christ also proved that he held this power on earth by the miraculous healing of the paralytic: Matt. 9. 2, ... 7.

units.la: Finis vero est demonstratio Gratiæ, & simul Justitiæ Divinæ: Eph. I. 6, 7. Ad laudem gloriosæ suæ Gratiæ, &c. Rom. 3.26. Ad demonstrationem Iustitiæ suæ præsenti tempore; ut sit ipse Iustus, & Iustificans eum qui est ex fide Iesu.
units.tr: The end, however, is the demonstration of grace and at the same time of divine justice: Eph. 1. 6, 7. "To the praise of the glory of his grace," etc. Rom. 3. 26. "For the demonstration of his righteousness at the present time, that he might be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus."

units.la: VI. In causa procatarctica propius hic spectari debet Iustitia Christi, quæ est formaliter impetratoria Justificationis nostræ; atque ita nobis imputatur: unde multi eam Iustificationis nostræ materiam appellant. Hanc vero ea amplitudine sumimus, ut passivam & activam pariter complectatur: sive omnem illam, quam Christus tum patiendo pœnas nobis debitas, tum agendo omnia ipsi mandata, pro nobis consummavit; h. e. Satisfactionem & Meritum ipsius, pro nobis præstita. Phil. 3. 8, 9. Ut Christum lucrifaciam: & comperiar in eo, non habens meam Iustitiam quæ est ex Lege; sed eam quæ est per fidem Christi, Iustitiam ex Deo per fidem. Confer 2 Cor. 5. 19, 21. Rom. 3. 30, 31. VIII. 3, 4, 5, 19. & sup. cap. 13. th. 9. & 11.
units.tr: VI. In the procatarctic cause, the righteousness of Christ must be considered more closely here; it is formally the impetration of our justification, and is thus imputed to us. Hence many call it the matter of our justification. We take it, however, in such breadth that it embraces both the passive and the active alike: that is, all that obedience which Christ accomplished for us, both by suffering the punishments we owed and by doing everything commanded him; that is, his satisfaction and merit performed on our behalf. Phil. 3. 8, 9. "That I may gain Christ, and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness from God through faith." Compare 2 Cor. 5. 19, 21; Rom. 3. 30, 31; 8. 3, 4, 5, 19; and above chap. 13, thes. 9 and 11.

units.la: Iustitiam illam Christi dicimus nobis imputari, λογίζεσθαι, vel ἐλλογεῖσθαι; h. e. cum præstita sit a Sponsore nobis conjunctissimo, censeri pro nostra, & in rationes nostras referri. Confer Philem. 18, 19. Vide sup. cap. 12. th. 30. Ac proinde Imputatio non debet exponi per Acceptilationem; quod velint Remonstrantes. Vide sup. cap. 13. th. 3.
