Differte autem Apostolus, Rom. 4. 3. ex Gen. 15. 6. Credidit Abraham Deo, & Imputatum est ei ad Iustitiam. Scil. prout fides organice justitiam Christi recipit & amplectitur. Vide porro vers. 5, 6, 9, 10, 11. Atque iterum 22, -25. „Quapropter etiam hoc Imputatum est ei ad Iustitiam. Non scriptum est autem propter eum solum, „quod hoc Imputatum fuerat ei: sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est ut Imputetur; Iis (nimirum) „qui credunt in eum, qui suscitavit Iesum Dominum „nostrum a mortuis, Traditum (morti) propter offen„sas nostras, & suscitatum ad nostri Iustificationem. Ubi objectum fidei, ejusque valor & habitudo ad nostri Justificationem clarè proponitur.
units.tr: We say that this righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, logizesthai [λογίζεσθαι] or ellogeisthai [ἐλλογεῖσθαι]; that is, since it was furnished by our Surety, who is most closely joined to us, it is reckoned as ours and credited to our account. Compare Philem. 18, 19. See above chap. 12, thes. 30. Therefore imputation must not be explained by acceptilation, as the Remonstrants wish. See above chap. 13, thes. 3. Moreover, the Apostle, Rom. 4. 3, from Gen. 15. 6: "Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness," that is, insofar as faith receives and embraces the righteousness of Christ instrumentally. See further verses 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, and again 22-25: "Therefore also it was imputed to him for righteousness. Yet it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him, but also for us, to whom it is going to be imputed, namely those who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered (to death) for our offences and raised for our justification." Here the object of faith, and its value and relation to our justification, is clearly set forth.

units.la: Æquipollentia etiam alibi occurrunt: ut Rom. 5. 19. „Sicut per contumaciam unius hominis, peccatores „ constituti sunt multi; ita per unius Obedientiam Justi „ constituentur multi. 2 Cor. 5. 21. „Fecit enim ut „ qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum esset; „ ut nos efficeremur Justitia Dei in eo. Utrobique satis „ manifesta est Imputatio. Atque hinc Christus dicitur, Jerem. 23. 6. Jehovah Justitia nostra. Et 1 Cor. 1. 30. nobis factus a Deo Justitia. Scil. per Imputationem.
units.tr: Equivalent expressions also occur elsewhere: as Rom. 5. 19. "As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be made righteous." 2 Cor. 5. 21. "For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him." In both places the imputation is quite plain. And hence Christ is called, Jer. 23. 6, "Jehovah our righteousness," and 1 Cor. 1. 30, made to us by God "righteousness." That is, by imputation.

units.la: VII. Obj. 1.
units.tr: VII. Objection 1.

units.la: Deus secundum veritatem judicat; ac proinde non judicat justum, nisi qui justitiam propriam & inhærentem habet; &c. Resp. Etiam secundum veritatem Deus judicat, hominem; credentem justum esse non quidem in se, sed in Christo; & justitiâ non inhærente, sed imputatâ.
units.tr: God judges according to truth; and therefore he judges no one to be just except the man who has a righteousness of his own, inherent in him; etc. Reply. God also judges according to truth when he judges a man to be just who believes that he is just, not in himself but in Christ, and by a righteousness that is imputed, not inherent.

units.la: Obj. 2. Nemo eruditus censeri potest, propter eruditionem alienam; aut probus, ob probitatem alienam. Ergò. Resp. Attamen propter personam bene meritam potest præmium etiam conferri in personas illi propinquas, secundum efficientiam virtualiter transitivam.
units.tr: Objection 2. No one can be called learned on account of another's learning, or upright on account of another's uprightness. Therefore, etc. Reply. Yet on account of a person who has deserved well, a reward may also be conferred on persons close to him, by a virtually transitive efficiency.

units.la: Obj. 3. Regeniti & sanctificati habent vitam spiritualem, & justitiam, & sanctimoniam sibi inhærentem. Ergò. Resp. Inde tamen non sequitur, istam vitam, justitiam, &c. esse formalem effectum justificationis: neque etiam, esse ejus causam impetratoriam.
units.tr: Objection 3. The regenerate and sanctified have spiritual life, and righteousness and holiness inhering in them. Therefore, etc. Reply. It does not follow from this, however, that this life, this righteousness, etc. is the formal effect of justification, nor even its impetratory cause.

units.la: VIII. Imò Justitia propria, ex operibus Legis, diserte rejicitur, tanquàm ἀσύκατ@ cum vero modo Justificationis Euangelicæ. Rom. 3. 9. 10. „Ante „ criminati sumus, & Judæos, & Græcos, omnes „ esse sub peccato. Sicut scriptum est: ( Psal. 14. 3. III: 3. ) Non est justus; ne unus quidem, &c. Ac porrò, 19. --. „Scimus autem, quæcunque Lex „dicit, iis qui in Lege sunt dicere; ut omne os obstruatur, & obnoxius fiat totus mundus condemnationi Dei. „Propterea ex operibus Legis nulla caro justificabitur in conspectu ejus: per Legem enim est cognitio peccati. „Nunc vero absque Lege Iustitia Dei manifesta facta est. &c.
units.tr: VIII. Indeed, proper righteousness, derived from the works of the Law, is expressly rejected as inconsistent [ἀσύμφωνον] with the true manner of Gospel justification. Rom. 3:9, 10: „We have already charged both Jews and Greeks that they are all under sin. As it is written (Ps. 14:3; 53:3): There is none righteous, no, not one, etc.” And further, verse 19: „We know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are in the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may become liable to the condemnation of God. Therefore by the works of the Law no flesh will be justified in his sight: for through the Law comes the knowledge of sin. But now, apart from the Law, the righteousness of God has been made manifest,” etc.

units.la: Sed Fides passim requiritur ad hanc Iustificationem. Rom. I. 16, 17. de Euangelio; Potentia est Dei ad salutem cuivis credenti, --. Iustitia enim Dei per illud revelatur ex fide ad fidem. &c. III. 22. Iustitia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi, in omnes & super omnes qui credunt; --. Vide etiam 25, 30. &c. Intelligenda vero est Fides Euangelica, specialis, salvifica, & justificans. Vide sup. cap. 2. th. 10, 11, 12. Eaque non absolute spectanda, ut est actus noster, ad quem (positis ponendis) etiam Lege obligamur; quasi specialis ista obedientia gratiose æstimaretur pro universa: neque ut est principium novæ obedientiæ, ac radix bonorum operum: contra Pontificios, Socinianos, & Remonstrantes, atque Anabaptistas quosdam. Verùm considerari debet organicè, ut est medium instrumentale ad unionem nostri cum Christo, & communionem beneficiorum; ac nominatim justitiæ ipsius. Ioh. I. 12. Quotquot Eum exceperunt, --qui credunt in nomen Eius. Hebr. XI. 13. Secundum fidem mortui sunt isti omnes, --postquam (promissa) ipsis fuissent persuasa, & ea amplexi fuissent. Confer ibid. verf. 1. Ioh. 6. 35, 56, 57. Eph. 3. 17. Gal. 2. 20.
units.tr: But faith is required throughout for this justification. Rom. 1:16, 17, of the Gospel: It is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, … For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith, etc. 3:22: The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe, etc. See also verses 25, 30, etc. But the faith to be understood is evangelical, special, saving, and justifying faith. See above, chapter 2, theses 10, 11, 12. And it is not to be regarded absolutely, as it is our act, by which (when the things to be done are done) we are also bound by the Law, as if that special obedience were graciously reckoned as the whole; nor as it is the principle of new obedience and the root of good works. This is against the Papists, Socinians, and Remonstrants, and certain Anabaptists. Rather it must be considered organically, as the instrumental means of the union of us with Christ and of communion in his benefits, and especially of his righteousness. John 1:12: As many as received him, … who believe in his name. Heb. 11:13: According to faith all these died, … after the promises had been persuaded to them and they had embraced them. Compare the same chapter, verse 1; John 6:35, 56, 57; Eph. 3:17; Gal. 2:20.

units.la: IX. Plenius autem probamus sententiam orthodoxam; 1. ex disertis SS. Literarum testimoniis. Negatur enim apertissimè Iustificatio ex operibus propriis: Rom. 3. 20. Ex operibus Legis nulla caro justificabitur in conspectu Ejus. Gal. 2. 16. Non justificabitur ex operibus ulla caro. III. 11. Nullum autem per Legem justificari apud Deum, manifestum est.
units.tr: IX. But we prove the orthodox view more fully, first, from the express testimonies of Holy Scripture. For justification by one's own works is most plainly denied. Rom. 3:20: Ex operibus Legis nulla caro justificabitur in conspectu Ejus. „By works of the Law no flesh will be justified in his sight.” Gal. 2:16: „No flesh will be justified by works.” 3:11: „Now that no one is justified before God by the Law is manifest.”

units.la: Asseritur contrà justificatio ex justitiâ Christi pro nobis præstitâ, & nobis imputatâ; adeòque respectu nostrî gratuita, & per fidem: Jerem. 23. 6. Nomen Ejus, Iehovah justitia nostra. Adde Rom. 5. 18,19.
units.tr: On the other hand, justification is asserted from the righteousness of Christ performed for us and imputed to us; and so, with respect to us, it is gratuitous and by faith. Jerem. 23:6: His name, Jehovah is our righteousness. Add Rom. 5:18, 19.

units.la: 1 Cor. I. 30. II. 5,21. Iterùm Rom. 4. 22,–25. de Abrahamo; Quapropter etiàm hoc imputatum est ei ad justitiam. Non scriptum est autem propter eum solum, quòd hoc imputatum fuerat ei: Sed etiàm propter nos, quibus futurum est ut imputetur, is nimirùm qui credunt, &c. III. 22. Iustitia Dei per fidem Iesû Christi, in omnes qui credunt. Adde, 24, 25, 26. v. 1. Ief. 53. 11. Item Luc. 5. 20. VII. 48,50. Ioh. 3. 14,15, 16,18,36. v. 24. Marc. 16. 15,16. Act. 10. 43.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1:30; 2:5, 21. Again Rom. 4:22–25, of Abraham: Therefore it was also imputed to him for righteousness. Yet it was not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him; but also for ours, to whom it is going to be imputed, those, namely, who believe, etc. 3:22: The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all who believe. Add verses 24, 25, 26; 1 Isa. 53:11. Likewise Luke 5:20; 7:48, 50; John 3:14, 15, 16, 18, 36; verse 24; Mark 16:15, 16; Acts 10:43.

units.la: Et conjunctim; Rom. 3. 28. Colligimus igitur fide justificari hominem, absque operibus Legis. IV. 5. Ei, qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Adde Gal. 2. 16. Eph. 2. 8,9. Phil. 3. 8,9. Tit. 3. 5. Act. 13. 38,39.
units.tr: And jointly: Rom. 3:28: We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith, apart from the works of the Law. 4:5: To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. Add Gal. 2:16; Eph. 2:8, 9; Phil. 3:8, 9; Tit. 3:5; Acts 13:38, 39.

units.la: 2. Ex consideratione Fœderis Euangelici, ejusque discrimine à Legali: Rom. 4. 3,–6. Quid enim Scriptura dicit? Credidit autem Abrahamus Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam (juxta promissionem Fœderis Euangelici.) Atque ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratiâ; sed ex debito; (juxta Fœdus Legale:) Ei verò qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui justificat impium, imputatur Fides sua ad justitiam. Sicut etiam David declarat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat justitiam absque operibus: &c. (secundùm Fœdus Euangelicum.) Porrò autem de Abrahamo verf. 11. Et signum accepit Circumcisionis, sigillum justitiæ fidei receptæ in præputio; ut effet pater omnium credentium in præputio, imputatâ etiàm ipsis justitiâ. &c verf. 16. Propterea ex Fide est hæreditas, ut fit per gratiam; ut firma fit promissio toti femini: id est, non solùm ei quod est ex Lege; verùm etiàm ei, quod est ex Fide Abrahami, qui est pater omnium nostrûm. Ideò neceffum est, ex fide, & per gratiam obtineri justitiam atque hæreditatem; ut promissio Fœderis Euangelici fit firma, & ad totum femen pertineat: hoc enim complectitur etiàm electos Gentiles: qui tamen Legem non itâ acceperunt, ut Israëlitæ post Abrahamum, sicut nec ipse Abrahamus eam itâ habuit; nedùm tunc cùm justificaretur. Vide etiàm Gal. 3. 5, 6, 7; 11,--. II. 21. v. 4, 5. Et confer Rom. 10. 3--.
units.tr: 2. From the consideration of the Gospel covenant and its difference from the Legal covenant. Rom. 4:3–6: For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness (according to the promise of the Gospel covenant). Now to him who works, the wage is not reckoned as grace, but as debt; (according to the Legal covenant). But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. Just as David also pronounces blessed the man to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works: etc. (according to the Gospel covenant). Further, concerning Abraham, verse 11: And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while still uncircumcised; so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, righteousness being imputed to them also, etc. Verse 16: Therefore the inheritance is by faith, so that it may be by grace, and the promise may be sure to all the seed: that is, not only to those who are of the Law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all. Therefore it is necessary that righteousness and inheritance be obtained by faith and by grace, so that the promise of the Gospel covenant may be sure and may pertain to the whole seed; for this also embraces the elect Gentiles, who nevertheless did not receive the Law as the Israelites after Abraham did, just as Abraham himself did not have it in that way, much less when he was justified. See also Gal. 3:5, 6, 7; 11, etc.; 2:21; verses 4, 5. And compare Rom. 10:3, etc.

units.la: 3. Ex consideratione eorum qui justificandi sunt; & operum ipsorum in ordine ad Legem: Rom. 3. 9; 10. Nam ante criminati fumus, &c. 19,20. Scimus autem quæcunque Lex dicit, &c. 23;24. Omnes enim peccaverunt, ac deficiuntur gloriâ Dei. Ut qui juftificentur gratis, &c. IV. 5;--8. Ei, qui non operatur, sed credit in Eum qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Sicut etiàm David declarat beatum, &c. Adde Gal. 3. 19;22. Itèmque confessiones & fupplicationes fidelium, Pfal.19.13. cxxx.3,4. cxliii.2. Prov. 20. 9. Eccl. 7. 20. 1 Reg. 8. 46. Matth. 6. 12. Jac. 3. 2. 1 Joh. 1. 8, 9, 10. Et confer Jac. 2. 10.
units.tr: 3. From the consideration of those who are to be justified, and of the works themselves in relation to the Law. Rom. 3:9, 10: For we have already charged, etc. 19, 20: We know that whatever the Law says, etc. 23, 24: For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; so that they are justified freely, etc. 4:5–8: To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. Just as David also pronounces blessed, etc. Add Gal. 3:19, 22. Likewise the confessions and supplications of the faithful: Pfal. 19:13; 130:3, 4; 143:2; Prov. 20:9; Eccl. 7:20; 1 Kings 8:46; Matt. 6:12; Jas. 3:2; 1 John 1:8, 9, 10. And compare Jas. 2:10.

units.la: 4. Omnis propria dignitas, atque in nobis ipsis gloriatio, à justificatione Euangelicâ prorsùs removeri debet. Rom. 3. 27;28. Ubi igitur Gloriatio? Exclusa est. Per quam legem? operum? Non: sed per legem fidei. Colligimus igitur, &c. IV. 2, 3. 4. Nam si Abrahamus ex operibus justificatus fuit, habet quod glorietur: at non apud Deum. Quid enim Scriptura dicit? Credidit autem Abrahamus Deo, &c. Eph. 2. 9, 10. Non ex operibus, ut ne quis glorietur. Nam ipsius sumus opus, conditi in Christo Iesu,--. 1 Cor. I. 29,30,31: Ut ne glorietur ulla caro in Ejus conspectu. Nam ex Ipso vos estis in Christo Iesu,--. Addi possunt testimonia antiquorum Ecclesiæ Doctorum. Imò etiàm sub densioribus tenebris Papatûs, hominibus ad mortem præparandis adhibitæ fuerunt Quæstiones nonnullæ, quæ Anselmo tribuuntur: earum postrema erat; ,, Gredis te non posse, nisi per mortem Christi salvari? Respondet infirmus: Etiam. Tum illi dicitur: Age, ergo dum superest in te anima, in hac sola morte fiduciam tuam constitue; in nulla alia re fiduciam habe! &c. Quin & ipse Bellarminus, post multa aliter disputata, de Justificat. lib. 5. cap. 7. proposit. 3. Propter incertitudinem propriae justitiae, & periculum inanis gloriae, tutissimum est, fiduciam totam in sola Dei misericordia, & benignitate reponere.
units.tr: 4. All proper dignity, and all glorying in ourselves, must be entirely removed from Gospel justification. Rom. 3:27, 28: Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. We conclude therefore, etc. 4:2, 3, 4: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of; but not before God. For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, etc. Eph. 2:9, 10: Not of works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus, etc. 1 Cor. 1:29, 30, 31: So that no flesh may glory in his presence. For of him you are in Christ Jesus, etc. The testimonies of the ancient teachers of the Church may also be added. Indeed, even in the thicker darkness of the Papacy, certain questions, which are attributed to Anselm, were used to prepare men for death. The last of them was this: „Do you believe that you cannot be saved except through the death of Christ?” The sick man answers: „Yes.” Then it is said to him: „Come, then, while there is still life in you, place your trust in this death alone; put your trust in nothing else!” etc. Indeed Bellarmine himself, after disputing many things otherwise, in De Justificatione book 5, chapter 7, proposition 3, says: Because of the uncertainty of one's own righteousness and the danger of vainglory, it is safest to place all trust in the mercy and kindness of God alone.

units.la: X. Exc. 1. Cum Paulus negat, hominem ex Lege justificari, de Lege Cerimoniali loquitur. Resp. Imo Moralem respicit potissimum, quae Gentilibus etiam naturaliter fuit cognita; Rom. 2. 12, 14, 15. per quam Judaei & Graeci pariter sub peccato sunt; 111. 9. & totus mundus condemnationi obnoxius; 19. per quam est cognitio peccati; 20. quae gloriationem inferret, siquidem homo per eam justificaretur; 27. quae iram efficit; IV. 15. & dicit; Qui praestiterit ea, vivet per illa; X. 5. Gal. 3: 12. nec non; Execrabilis est, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, &c. Gal. 3. 10. Ista sane Legi Morali omnino conveniunt, cui interim adjecta fuerunt Praecepta Cerimonialia, pro populo. V. Test. usque ad tempora correctionis.
units.tr: X. Objection 1. When Paul denies that a man is justified by the Law, he speaks of the ceremonial Law. Answer: Rather, he chiefly has in view the moral Law, which was known even to the Gentiles by nature; Rom. 2:12, 14, 15, through which both Jews and Greeks alike are under sin; 3:9, and the whole world is liable to condemnation; 3:19, through which comes the knowledge of sin; 3:20, which would produce boasting, since a man would be justified by it; 3:27, which works wrath; 4:15; and he says: "He who does these things shall live by them"; 10:5; Gal. 3:12; likewise: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things," etc., Gal. 3:10. These things surely agree altogether with the moral Law, to which, meanwhile, the ceremonial precepts were added for the people, until the time of reformation under the Old Testament.

units.la: Exc. 2. Apostolus illa solum opera a Justificatione exclusit, quae fidem antecedunt. Resp. 1. Exclusit omnia opera in universum, sine tali limitatione: fidei vero Justificationem adscripsit, quatenus ea promissionem Evangelicam respicit & amplectitur; atque ita ab operibus contradistinguitur; Rom. 3. 20, 28. IV. 16. Gal. 3. 17, 18, 21. Adeo quidem, ut per veram fidem statim obtineatur justificatio: sed bona opera postmodum ex fide, tanquam principio, sequantur; Rom. 4. 10, 11. Eph. 2. 8, 9, 10. R. 2. Generales etiam sunt rationes ab Apostolo productae, quod ex Lege sit cognitio peccati; quod totus mundus dus per eam sit condemnationi & execrationi obnoxius; quòd sic excludi debeat gloriatio; quòd alioquin Christus redderetur inanis, & homines gratiâ excidërent, &c. Rom. 3. 19,20,27. IV. 2. Eph. 2. 9. Gal. 3. 10, 11,12. v. 4. R. 3. Si Apostolus omninò probare solùm voluissret, hominem non justificari ex operibus fidem antecedentibus, nihil opus suisset tàm operosâ demonstratione, sed breviter indicare potuisset, ante fidem nulla opera esse verè bona: quemadmodùm Rom. 14. 23. Hebr. XI. 6. Tit. I. 15.
units.tr: Objection 2. The Apostle excluded from justification only those works which precede faith. Answer: 1. He excluded all works in general, without any such limitation; but he ascribed justification to faith insofar as faith looks to and embraces the Evangelical promise, and so is distinguished from works; Rom. 3:20, 28; 4:16; Gal. 3:17, 18, 21. Indeed, so that through true faith justification is obtained at once, but good works afterwards follow from faith as from a principle; Rom. 4:10, 11; Eph. 2:8, 9, 10. 2. The reasons which the Apostle brings forward are also general: that through the Law comes the knowledge of sin; that the whole world is thereby made liable to condemnation and curse; that boasting must thus be excluded; that otherwise Christ would be made void, and men would fall from grace, etc.; Rom. 3:19, 20, 27; 4:2; Eph. 2:9; Gal. 3:10, 11, 12; 5:4. 3. If the Apostle had wished only to prove that a man is not justified by works which precede faith, there would have been no need for so laborious a demonstration; he could have briefly indicated that before faith no works are truly good, as in Rom. 14:23; Heb. 11:6; Titus 1:15.

units.la: Exc. 3. Fides, de quâ Paulus loquitur, charitatem & bona opera includit. Resp. Fatemur, illam esse principium charitatis & bonorum operum; sed negamus, eam sic à Paulo considerari: hic enim nimis diserte Fidem à Bonis operibus contradistinguit; & quod de Fide affirmat, id de operibus in universum negat.
units.tr: Objection 3. The faith of which Paul speaks includes love and good works. Answer: We grant that it is the principle of love and of good works; but we deny that Paul considers it so: for here he distinguishes faith from good works very plainly, and what he affirms of faith, he denies of works in general.

units.la: XI Pontificii statuunt, Remissionem poenæ temporalis apud Deum impetrari per Satisfactiones humanas. Confer sup. cap. 13. th. 20. Satisfactio autem, juxta Bellarminum lib. 4. de Poenitentiâ, cap. 1. est actio, quâ is, qui alterum læsit, tantum facit, quantum satis est ad injuriam compensandam. Eaque præstatur ad æqualitatem imperfectam, intercedente aliquâ acceptatione aut donatione: non pro culpâ, & in ordine ad amicitiam; sed ut luatur poena, eaque temporalis, in ordine ad justitiam. Resp. 1. Christus pro suis absolutam satisfactionem præstitit; eamque Deus admisit, & fidelibus imputat: ergò neque satisfactionem ad æqualitatem imperfectam ab iis exigit Justitia Divina. 2. Absurda est distinctio inter reatum culpæ & poenæ: consequenter à quo non exigitur satisfactio pro culpâ, ab illo neque exigi potest respectu poenæ. 3. Christus totalem remissionem fidelibus suis impetravit, ut nulla nunc fit iis condemnatio; Rom. 8. 1. ut habeant vitam æternam, nec veniant in condemnationem &c. Joh. 5. 24. Ergo illis non retinetur pœna luenda, ne quidem temporalis, in ordine ad Justitiam vindicativam.
units.tr: XI. The Papists maintain that the remission of temporal punishment is obtained before God through human satisfactions. See above, chap. 13, th. 20. Now satisfaction, according to Bellarmine, De Poenitentia, book 4, chap. 1, is an action by which he who has injured another does as much as is enough to make amends for the injury. And it is rendered to an imperfect equality, with some acceptance or gift intervening; not for the guilt, and with a view to friendship, but so that punishment may be paid, and that temporal, with a view to justice. Answer: 1. Christ rendered complete satisfaction for his own; and God accepted it and imputes it to the faithful: therefore Divine justice does not demand from them a satisfaction to an imperfect equality. 2. The distinction between the guilt of sin and the penalty is absurd: consequently, from one for whom no satisfaction is demanded for the guilt, none can be demanded with respect to the penalty either. 3. Christ obtained for his faithful a total remission, so that there is now no condemnation for them; Rom. 8:1; that they may have eternal life and not come into condemnation, etc.; John 5:24. Therefore no penalty to be paid is retained for them, not even a temporal one, with respect to vindictive justice.

units.la: Idem ille contendit cap. 3. Pœnas temporales hujus vitæ interdum non posse redimi; sed necessario perpetiendas esse; & talem inprimis esse pœnam mortis: alias aliquando redimi posse, ac pro iis satisfieri, pœnas & flagella à Deo immissa patienter ferendo, opera laboriosa sponte assumendo, multam Sacerdotum arbitrio injunctam subeundo &c. Resp. 1. Quia Christus nobis impetravit plenam remissionem peccatorum, ista remissio nobis applicari debet certo quodam modo & ordine; ubi praxis fidei ac resipiscentiæ locum suum habet: sed jam nulla opera nostra formaliter pœnalia & satisfactoria ad consequendam remissionem exigi possunt, aut statui debent. Impetrare enim quod omninò impetratum est, nihil aliud est quàm actum agere, & à Justitia alienum. 2. Mortem quidem in hoc rerum statu nemo potest avertere: fideles tamen eam minimè subeunt ut pœnam strictè dictam. Vide sup. cap. 7. th. 45. §. 5. R. 3. Humilem ac piam afflictionum Divinitus immissarum tolerantiam, veram de peccatis pœnitentiam, vitæ emendationem, preces pro accipiendâ remissione, opera misericordiæ ac beneficentiæ erga alias: &c. commemorat & commendat S. Scriptura; sed minimè docet, ea esse satisfactoria.
units.tr: The same author contends, chap. 3, that the temporal penalties of this life cannot sometimes be redeemed, but must necessarily be endured; and that especially the penalty of death is such; otherwise, at times, they can be redeemed, and satisfaction made for them, by patiently bearing penalties and scourges sent by God, by voluntarily undertaking laborious works, by undergoing a fine imposed at the discretion of the priests, etc. Answer: 1. Because Christ has obtained for us full remission of sins, this remission must be applied to us in a certain manner and order; where the practice of faith and of repentance has its place. But now no works of ours that are formally penal and satisfactory can be demanded or ought to be set up to obtain remission. For to obtain what has already been wholly obtained is nothing but doing a thing over again, and foreign to justice. 2. Indeed, in the present state of things no one can avert death; yet the faithful by no means undergo it as a penalty strictly so called. See above, chap. 7, th. 45, §5. 3. Holy Scripture commends and recommends a humble and pious endurance of afflictions sent by God, true repentance for sins, amendment of life, prayers for receiving remission, works of mercy and beneficence toward others, etc.; but it nowhere teaches that these are satisfactory.

units.la: XII. Obj. 1. Claves Sacerdotibus datæ sunt non tantùm ad solvendum, ut pœnitentes à culpâ absolvant, & peccata remittant, quoad culpam & pœnam æternam; sed etiàm ad ligandum, ut possint ac debeant eosdem ad cætera pœnitentiæ opera alligare, & sic peccata retineant quoad pœnam tem-
units.tr: XII. Objection 1. The keys were given to priests not only for loosing, that penitents might be absolved from guilt and have their sins remitted as to guilt and eternal punishment; but also for binding, so that they may and ought to bind the same to the other works of repentance, and so retain sins as to temporal punishment. So God commanded his ministers that those who sinned after baptism should not be admitted to the divine indulgence without much enjoined penance, through the gate of reconciliation.

units.la: Oo poralem. Itâ Deus Ministris suis mandavit, ut peccantes post Baptismum non sine multâ injunctâ ad indulgentiam Divinam per januam reconciliationis admitterentur. Resp. Diversæ sunt actiones solvendi & ligandi pro diversâ conditione subjectorum: Matth. 16. 19. xviii. 18. cum Joh. 20. 23. Si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis; si quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Consequenter Ministri Evangelici (non Sacerdotes proprie dicti) ex præscripto Christi solvunt fideles & resipiscentes, h. e. ministerialiter iis peccata remittunt; infideles vero & impœnitentes ligant, h. e. eorum peccata retinent; itâ ut maneat ipsorum reatus, quamdiu illi tales sunt. Sed nihil istic, vel alibi in S. S. Literis, de pœnitentibus alligandis ad opera quædam pœnalia & satisfactoria; nihil de multâ injungendâ hominibus post Baptismum peccantibus, sine quâ illi ad indulgentiam Divinam non admitterentur: verum satis multa & diserta de gratuitâ justificatione, ejusque per Ministros annunciatione, citra imputationem ofsensarum; Rom. 3: 24. 2 Cor. 5. 19, 20.
units.tr: Answer: The acts of loosing and binding are different according to the different condition of the subjects: Matt. 16:19; 18:18, compared with John 20:23: "If you remit the sins of any, they are remitted to them; if you retain those of any, they are retained." Consequently, the Evangelical ministers (not priests properly so called), by Christ's prescription, loose the faithful and penitent, that is, they remit their sins ministerially; but they bind the unbelieving and impenitent, that is, they retain their sins, so that their guilt remains as long as they are such. But there is nothing there, or elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures, about binding penitents to certain penal and satisfactory works; nothing about much penance to be imposed on men who sin after baptism, without which they would not be admitted to the divine indulgence; but there is plenty, and plainly stated, about gratuitous justification, and its announcement through the ministers, without imputation of offences; Rom. 3:24; 2 Cor. 5:19, 20.

units.la: Obj. 2. Misericordia & Justitia Divina passim conjunctæ prædicantur; siquidem rationi maximè consentaneum est, ut Deus ex misericordiâ sic peccata condonet, ut etiàm justitiæ, quoad ejus fieri potest, satisfieri velit. Par erat ut nos ipsi, qui Deum offenderamus, eidem nostro labore satisfaceremus, postquàm per Christi gratiam idonei effecti sumus ad expiandam pœnam temporalem. Resp. 1. Conjunctæ prædicantur Misericordia & Justitia Dei: itâ videl. ut Misericordia in nobis demonstretur; Justitiæ vero per Christum satisfactum sit; non per nos ei satisfiat: Rom. 3. 24, 25, 26. Eph. 1. 7. Col. 1. 14. 2 Cor. 5. 18, 19, 21. R. 2. Gratia Christi non facit nos idoneos ad satisfaciendum Justitiæ Divinæ, & sic expiandam pœnam temporalem; sed quoniàm Ipse pro nobis plenè satisfecit, nos à satisfaciendi onere liberavit: 2 Cor. 5. 15. Ut qui hoc statuerimus, si unus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, nempe ipsos omnes fuisse mortuos. &c.
units.tr: Objection 2. The mercy and justice of God are everywhere proclaimed as joined together; for it is most reasonable that God, out of mercy, should forgive sins in such a way that he also wishes justice to be satisfied, as far as it can be. It was fitting that we ourselves, who had offended God, should satisfy him by our own labour, since through the grace of Christ we have been made fit to expiate the temporal penalty. Answer: 1. The mercy and justice of God are proclaimed as joined; namely, in such a way that mercy is shown in us, while justice has been satisfied through Christ, not satisfied by us: Rom. 3:24, 25, 26; Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14; 2 Cor. 5:18, 19, 21. 2. The grace of Christ does not make us fit to satisfy the justice of God, and so to expiate the temporal penalty; but since he himself has fully satisfied for us, he has freed us from the burden of satisfying: 2 Cor. 5:15, "that we who have concluded this, that if one died for all, then all were dead," etc.

units.la: Obj. 3. Poenitentia, quia medicamentum est animæ vulneratæ ac ægrotantis, id plane exigit, ut qui curatur, medicinales ustiones, incisiones, pharmaca amara, aliaque id genus multa sustineat. Ergò. Resp. Imò medicamentum ordinatur ad sanitatem ægro restituendam, non ad compendium Justitiæ. Sic poenitentia ad animæ sanitatem, per vitæ emendationem & sanctificationem referenda est. &c.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Repentance, since it is a medicine for the wounded and sick soul, plainly requires that the one being cured endure medicinal burnings, incisions, bitter drugs and many other things of that kind. Therefore... Resp. Indeed, medicine is intended to restore health to the sick person, not to serve as a shortcut to justice. So repentance is to be referred to the health of the soul, through amendment and sanctification of life. Etc.

units.la: Obj. 4. 1 Cor. 9. 27. Contundo corpus meum, &c. Resp. Ad subigendam carnem corruptam, & promovendam sanctificationem; non verò ad satisfactionem. Confer sup. cap. 9. th. 51. obj. 3.
units.tr: Obj. 4. 1 Cor. 9.27. I beat my body, etc. Resp. To subdue the corrupt flesh and advance sanctification, not to make satisfaction. Compare above, ch. 9, th. 51, obj. 3.

units.la: XIII. Pro Meritis humanis, & sic acquirendo jure beatitudinis æternæ, acriter etiam digladian- tur Pontificii.
units.tr: XIII. The Papists also fight fiercely for human merits, and thereby for acquiring a right to eternal blessedness.

units.la: Bellarminus lib. 5. de Justificat. cap. 1. probaturus, opera justorum recte vocari merita, producit 1. loca expressa (ut ipse quidem existimat.) Eccles. Sir. 16. 13. & Hebr. 13. 16. Resp. 1. Meritum proprie ac strictè dictum est opus indebitum ad acquirendam mercedem propter istius valorem debitam. Istud autem in nullâ creaturâ locum habet respectu Dei; propter omnimodam dependentiam ab Ipso, & obligationem ad Ipsum. Sed Meritum modificatum, laxè & improprie dictum, est opus debitum, cui tamen gratiosâ promissione merces constituta est, aut præmium: vel opus indebitum, cui merces constituta est supra ejus valorem; at verò supposito tali pacto, & præstito tali opere, propter pactum omninò debetur merces præstituta. Sic Deus in Fœdere Legali adjectâ promissione obligaverat se quidem Creaturis: (Vide sup. cap. 9. th. 119.) sed nunc
units.tr: Bellarmine, in book 5 On Justification, ch. 1, intending to prove that the works of the just are rightly called merits, produces first express passages (as he himself thinks): Sir. 16.13 and Heb. 13.16. Resp. 1. Merit, properly and strictly speaking, is an undue work by which a reward is acquired on account of its worth. This has no place in any creature with respect to God, on account of total dependence on Him and obligation to Him. But a modified merit, loosely and improperly speaking, is a due work to which a reward has nevertheless been fixed by gracious promise, or a prize; or an undue work to which a reward has been fixed beyond its worth. But once such a pact is supposed and such a work performed, the stipulated reward is wholly due on account of the pact. Thus God, in the Legal Covenant, by an added promise had indeed bound himself to creatures (see above, ch. 9, th. 119), but now

units.la: in homine lapso opera verè bona non præcedunt justificandum; verùm sequuntur justificatum; atque adeò jus vitæ æternæ, quod ex Christi merito credenti adjudicatur in justificatione, antecedit bona opera; non autem per ea, ut causam procatarcticam meritoriam, impetratur. Imò nec ea tàm persecta sunt, ut juxta promissionem Fœderis Legalis vitam æternam mereri possint. Ad promissionem vero Euangelicam quod attinet, hæc jus vitæ æternæ nequaquam suspendit à nostris meritis, sed in Christi merito constituit, & per fidem solummodò accipi docet. Alias etiàm latissimè & improprissimè mereri apud Patres idem valet, quod consequi, accipere, vel obtinere. Juxta illud, de peccato Adami; O felix culpa, quæ talem meruit habere Redemtorem! Qui usus in illis excusari quidem potest, ut evitetur κομματικία; tutius tamen ab eo abstinetur, ne verbum istud ab hominibus incautis accipiatur significatione primâ propriâ, aut saltem secundâ minùs impropriâ; quod in Papatû factum. 2. Locus Eccl. Sir. 16. 15. apocryphus est. Ac porrò Vulg. Versio quidem habet; secundùm meritum operum suorum: sed Græcus textus; κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς; secundùm opera sua; citra ullam meriti mentionem. 3. Hebr. 13. 16. Vulg. Versio admodùm vitiosè habet; Talibus enim hostiis promeretur Deus: cùm in Græco sit, εὐαρεστεῖται ὁ Θεὸς; delectatur Deus; aut benè placet sibi.
units.tr: in fallen man, truly good works do not precede justification; rather they follow the justified. And so the right to eternal life, which is adjudged to the believer in justification on the ground of Christ's merit, precedes good works; it is not obtained through them as a meritorious, procatarctic cause. Indeed, they are not so perfect that, according to the promise of the Legal Covenant, they could merit eternal life. As for the Evangelical promise, this does not make the right to eternal life depend in any way on our merits; it establishes that right in Christ's merit and teaches that it is received through faith alone. Otherwise, too, to "merit" in the broadest and most improper sense among the Fathers means the same as to "obtain," "receive" or "attain." Compare that saying about Adam's sin: "O happy fault, which deserved to have such a Redeemer!" This usage can indeed be excused in them, so as to avoid hair-splitting [κομματικία]; yet it is safer to abstain from it, lest the word be taken by incautious people in its first, proper sense, or at least in its second, less proper sense; which has happened in the Papacy. 2. The passage Sir. 16.15 is apocryphal. Moreover, the Vulgate indeed has "according to the merit of their works," but the Greek text reads "according to their works" [κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῆς], with no mention of merit at all. 3. Heb. 13.16. The Vulgate translation very faultily has "for with such sacrifices God is merited," whereas the Greek is "God is well pleased" [εὐαρεστεῖται ὁ Θεὸς], that is, God takes delight or is well pleased.

units.la: Obj. 2. Dignitas indicatur, 2. Thess. 1. 5. Apoc. 3. 4. xvi. 16. quæ Meritum infert. Resp. 1. 2 Thess. 1. 5. dicit Apostolus; Ut Digni habeamini Regno Dei. Et Christus, Apoc. 3. 4. Ambulabunt mecum albati; Digni enim sunt. Ubi Dignitas simpliciter notat convenientiam qualitatis; non æqualitatem quantitatis, aut valoris; neque antecedentem causam juris in eam rem, de quâ agitur. Quemadmodùm Eph.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Dignity is indicated in 2 Thess. 1.5 and Rev. 3.4, 16.6, and dignity implies merit. Resp. 1. In 2 Thess. 1.5 the Apostle says, "that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God." And Christ says in Rev. 3.4, "They shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy." Here "worthy" simply denotes fitness of quality, not equality of quantity or value, nor an antecedent cause of right to the matter in question, just as in Eph.

units.la: 4. I. Ut ambuletis ἀξίως τῆς κλήσεως; sicut convenit vocationi, quâ vocati estis. Jàm tùm vocati erant & convenienter isti suæ vocationi vivere debebant; non autem istâ suâ ambulatione merituri erant vocationem. Vide etiàm Phil. 1. 27. Col. 1. 10. 1 Thess. 2. 12. Matth. 3. 8. Deindè fideles digni habentur Regno Dei, &c. non propriâ dignitate operum suorum; sed gratiosâ Dei dignatione in Christo. Confer 1 Thess. 2. 11, 12. Et digni sunt ambulare cum Christo albati; postquàm laverunt stolas suas, ac dealbârunt in sanguine Agni illius; Apoc. 7. 14. R. 2. Apoc. 16. 6. dicitur; Quoniàm sanguinem sanctorum & prophetarum effuderunt, & sanguinem eis dedisti ad bibendum; Digni enim sunt. Ubi pro subjectâ materiâ istud nomen aliter accipiendum est: de peccato enim agitur, ejusque justâ poenâ, secundùm justitiam punitivam; undè non procedit consequentia ad bona opera, & quidem sub Fœdere Euangelico.
units.tr: 4.1, "that you walk worthily of the calling" [ἀξίως τῆς κλήσεως], that is, "as befits the calling to which you were called." They had already been called, and they ought to live in a way consistent with their calling; they were not going to merit the calling by their walk. See also Phil. 1.27, Col. 1.10, 1 Thess. 2.12, Matt. 3.8. Then, the faithful are "counted worthy of the kingdom of God," etc., not by the proper dignity of their works, but by God's gracious condescension in Christ. Compare 1 Thess. 2.11, 12. And they are "worthy" to walk with Christ "in white" after they "washed their robes and made them white in the blood of that Lamb," Rev. 7.14. Resp. 2. Rev. 16.6 says, "Because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you gave them blood to drink; for they are worthy." Here, given the subject matter, the term must be understood differently: the passage concerns sin and its just punishment according to punitive justice. Hence the inference to good works does not follow, and certainly not under the Evangelical Covenant.

units.la: Object. 3. Merces etiàm appellatur, Genef. 15. 1.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Reward is also called such in Gen. 15.1.

units.la: 2 Chron. 15. 7. Prov. xi. 18. Sap. 5. 16, Eccles. Sir. 18. 22. Isef. 40. 10. Matth. 5, 12. 1 Cor. 3, 14. Apoc. 22. 12. Ergò, Resp. 1. Merces in SS. Literis etiàm appellatur bonum utile aut jucundum, quod retribuitur pro aliquo opere, citra ejus dignitatem, aut rationem meriti: ut Ezech. 29. 18, 19, 20. Nebucadretzar Rex Babyloniæ exegit à copiis suis servitutem magnam contra Tyrum: merces autem non est ipsi, neque copiis ejus de Tyro, --. Idcirco sic ait Dominus Jehovi; Ecce ego trado Nebucadretzari Regi Babyloniæ terram Ægypti; --undè fit merces copiis ipsius. --Quia operati sunt mihi, dictum Domini Jehovi. Certè infideles illi nihil mereri potuerunt apud Deum. R. 2. Gen. 15. 1. dixit Deus Abrahamo; Ego clypeus sum tibi, merces tua ampla valdè. Sic vera ac perfecta beatitudo illi promittitur: sed jus istius mercedis non fundatur in operibus Abrahami, eorumve dignitate: imò impuimputata ei fuit ex gratia, non ex debito; ut Paulus distinctè docet. Rom. 4. 3, 4, 5. R. 3. Similiter accipienda sunt loca 2 Chron. 15. 7. Prov. xi. 18. Matth. 5. 12. 1 Cor. 3. 14. & Apocryphus locus Sap. 5. 16. R. 4. Sed Apoc. 22. 12. Merces tum ad poenas tum ad beatitudinem referri debet; sed diverso modo ac fundamento. Et Isef. 40. 10. retributio poenalis indicatur; cujus alia est ratio. 5. In Apocrypho autem Eccles. Sir. 18. 22, 23. Vulg. Interpres quidem habet; Merces Dei manet in aeternum. Sed in Graeco textu ista verba non exstant: atque etiam de poenis istic agitur.
units.tr: 2 Chron. 15.7, Prov. 11.18, Wisd. 5.16, Sir. 18.22, Isa. 40.10, Matt. 5.12, 1 Cor. 3.14, Rev. 22.12. Therefore... Resp. 1. "Reward" in Holy Scripture is also called a useful or pleasant good that is repaid for some work, apart from its worth or the reason of merit, as in Ezek. 29.18-20: "Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre... yet there was no wage for him, nor for his army, from Tyre... Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I give Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon the land of Egypt... because they worked for me, says the Lord God." Surely those unbelievers could merit nothing before God. Resp. 2. In Gen. 15.1 God says to Abraham, "I am your shield; your reward shall be exceedingly great." So true and perfect blessedness is promised to him; but the right to this reward is not founded on Abraham's works or their worth. Rather, it was imputed to him "by grace, not by debt," as Paul clearly teaches, Rom. 4.3-5. Resp. 3. The passages 2 Chron. 15.7, Prov. 11.18, Matt. 5.12, 1 Cor. 3.14, and the apocryphal Wisd. 5.16 are to be understood similarly. Resp. 4. But in Rev. 22.12 the reward must be referred both to punishments and to blessedness, though in a different way and on a different ground. And Isa. 40.10 indicates penal retribution, which has another rationale. 5. In the apocryphal Sir. 18.22, 23, the Vulgate translator indeed has "The reward of God remains for ever." But these words are not found in the Greek text, and moreover the passage there concerns punishments.

units.la: XIV. Deinde Bellarm. cap. 3. contendit, opera justorum vere esse meritoria vitae aeternae: & allegat Matth. 5: 12: 10. xx: 8. atque urget; Mercedem dari operibus, non soli promissioni. Et in Scripturis vitam aeternam non minus saepe, fortasse etiam saepius, dici mercedem, quam hereditatem, &c. Deum autem voluisse, ut Filii sui, qui usum rationis habent, propriis laboribus & meritis illam acquirant; ut duplici titulo iis vita aeterna deberetur, titulo scil. haereditatis, & jure mercedis: quoniam magis honorificum est, habere aliquid ex merito quam ex sola donatione, &c. Quemadmodum in ipso Christo etiam factum. Praeterea meritis operum reddi gradum aliquem gloriae sempiternae, ad quem non pertingant qui solo titulo haereditatis gaudent. Resp. 1. de loco Matth. 5. 12. modo diximus. Ibid. verf. 10. ait Servator, Beati, quos persequuntur homines justitiae causa: quoniam ipsorum est Regnum coelorum. Ista erit eorum merces; sed ex gratia. Cap. 20. 8. in parabola dicitur; Voca operarios, & redde eis mercedem, exorsus ab ultimis usque ad primos. Personis scil. datur retributio, ad opera, secundum promissionem: non tamen propter opera, eorumve dignitatem; sed propter justitiam Christi. Opus quodammodò nostrum intercessit; sed ex gratiâ Dei: sic præstita est conditio, non ad acquirendum jus beatitudinis; sed ad obtinendam fruitionem beatitudinis, cujus jus nobis acquisitum est merito Christi.
units.tr: XIV. Next, Bellarmine in ch. 3 contends that the works of the just are truly meritorious of eternal life. He cites Matt. 5.12 and 20.8, and urges that the reward is given to works, not to the promise alone. He adds that in Scripture eternal life is called "reward" no less often, perhaps even more often, than "inheritance," etc.; and that God willed that his Sons, who have the use of reason, should acquire it by their own labours and merits, so that eternal life would be owed to them by a double title: the title of inheritance and the right of reward, since it is more honourable to have something from merit than from donation alone, etc. This was also done in Christ himself. Besides, by the merits of works a certain degree of eternal glory is returned, which those who rejoice only in the title of inheritance do not attain. Resp. 1. We have just spoken about Matt. 5.12. In the same place, v. 10, the Saviour says, "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." That will be their reward, but it is given by grace. In Matt. 20.8 it is said in the parable, "Call the labourers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last even to the first." Retribution is given to persons, according to their works, by promise; yet not on account of the works or their worth, but on account of the righteousness of Christ. Our work has indeed intervened in some way, but by God's grace. Thus the condition was laid down, not to acquire the right to blessedness, but to obtain the enjoyment of blessedness, whose right has been acquired for us by the merit of Christ.

units.la: 2. Non est igitur Merces proprie dicta respectu operum nostrorum. Hæreditas vero frequenter appellatur: eaque in Adoptione fundatur: Rom. 8.17. & in Testamento; Heb. 9.15, 16, 17. R. 3. Filii Dei, usum rationis habentes, propriis laboribus non acquirunt jus vitæ æternæ; sed ad fruitionem ejus sic progrediuntur: Eph. 2.8, 9, 10. R. 4. Non spectandum est hîc, quid hominibus esset magis honorificum; unde ipsis nasceretur gloriatio: sed quid gloriæ Divinæ, & SS. Literis sit maximè consentaneum: Rom. 3, 27. iv. 2. Mirandum verò, Monachos Romanenses hominum donationibus usque adeò inhiare, vel etiàm ex mendicato vivere, ubi mercedem promereri possent; merita verò jactare, ubi meram gratiam agnoscere & sperare deberent. 5. Christus, ut persona Divina, ab æterno fuit Filius Dei, per æternam generationem: sic autem nihil sibi acquisivit. Sed humanæ naturæ alia est ratio, & sic specialis de Ipso constitutio; ut eatenùs gloriam & beatitudinem etiàm sibi merereturu, juxta pactum Legale. Sed à Christo ad nos non valet consequentia. 6. Gradùs distinctos gloriæ cœlestis admittimus; & quidem convenienter gradibus gratiæ in hoc sæculo: sed jus istud in merito Christi tantùm fundatur.
units.tr: 2. Therefore "reward" properly so called does not apply to our works. "Inheritance" is the term used more often, and it rests on adoption (Rom. 8.17) and on testament (Heb. 9.15, 16, 17). 3. The sons of God, once they have the use of reason, do not acquire a right to eternal life by their own labours; they advance towards its enjoyment in this way (Eph. 2.8, 9, 10). 4. Here we must not consider what would be more honourable for men, lest boasting should arise for them, but what best agrees with the glory of God and with Holy Scripture (Rom. 3.27; 4.2). It is indeed astonishing that the Roman monks gape so eagerly after gifts from men, and even live by begging, where they could earn a reward, yet boast of merits where they ought to acknowledge and hope for pure grace. 5. Christ, as a divine person, was from eternity the Son of God by eternal generation; in that respect he acquired nothing for himself. But the human nature stands on a different footing, and so there is a special arrangement concerning him, by which, to that extent, he would also merit glory and blessedness for himself, according to the legal covenant. But the inference from Christ to us does not hold. 6. We admit distinct degrees of heavenly glory, and indeed degrees corresponding to the degrees of grace in this age; but that right is founded only on the merit of Christ.

units.la: XV. Secundo ille argumentatur ex locis, ubi habetur; præmium cœleste dari hominibus secundùm mensuram & proportionem operum ac laboris; ut non solius promissionis habeatur ratio, vel liberalitatis; aut indulgentiæ Dei; sed etiàm dignitatis, & efficaciæ ipsorum operum: Psal. 61.13. Matth. 16.27. Luc. 6.38. Rom. 2.5.6.7. 1Cor. 3.8. Gal. 6. 7, 8. Apoc. 22. 12. Atque urget, omnes consentire, malis hominibus secundum mala ipsorum opera reddendam esse mortem æternam: &c. Resp. 1. In locis illis indicatur convenientia retributionis cum operibus; præmii cum bonis, & pœnarum cum malis. In pœnis quidem subesse rationem demeriti proprie dicti, aliunde constat. Vide sup. c. 4. th. 56. §. 3. Sed aliter se rem habere in præmio, patet item ex superioribus. Neque istud discrimen omnino latuit Bellarminum, lib. cit. cap. 17. Quin & præpositionem secundum, aliquando usurpari de re nullo modo meritoria, sed quæ solum est conditio quædam requisita, agnoscit idem lib. 1. cap. 21. R. 2. Sic ergo vita æterna redditur fidelibus & piis adultis, secundum opera, quæ sunt fructus & signa fidei, per quam illi organice ex Christo acceperunt jus vitæ æternæ; sed eadem quoque sunt conditiones requisitæ ad percipiendam ejus fruitionem, ut via regni, non causa regnandi; & quidem sic, ut interim quoque servetur proportio inter gratiam & gloriam.
units.tr: XV. Secondly, he argues from passages which say that heavenly reward is given to men according to the measure and proportion of their works and labour, so that account is taken not only of the promise, or of God's liberality and indulgence, but also of the worth and efficacy of the works themselves (Ps. 61.13; Matt. 16.27; Luke 6.38; Rom. 2.5, 6, 7; 1 Cor. 3.8; Gal. 6.7, 8; Rev. 22.12). And he urges that all agree that eternal death is to be rendered to wicked men according to their evil works, etc. Answer 1. Those passages indicate a correspondence of retribution with works: of reward with good works, and of punishments with evil ones. That in punishments there is a basis of demerit properly so called is established elsewhere (see above, ch. 4, th. 56, §3). But that the matter stands otherwise with reward is also clear from what has been said above. Bellarmine did not altogether miss this distinction (book cited, ch. 17). Indeed, the same man acknowledges in book 1, ch. 21, that the preposition "according to" is sometimes used of a thing in no way meritorious, but which is only a certain required condition. 2. Thus eternal life is rendered to believing and pious adults according to their works, which are the fruits and signs of faith, through which they have received the right to eternal life from Christ as its organ; yet these same works are also conditions required for receiving its enjoyment, as the way to the kingdom, not the cause of reigning; and indeed in such a way that, meanwhile, the proportion between grace and glory is also preserved.

units.la: Tertium argumentum sumit ex locis, quæ ita vitam æternam reddi testantur operibus bonis, utipsam rationem, cur detur vita æterna, in operibus ponant: Matth. 25. 34, 35. Apoc. 7. 14, 15. Ubi particulæ Enim, Quia, Ideo, sunt omnes causales. Stipendium peccati mors, &c. Rom. 6. 23. Et bona opera dicuntur salutem ipsam efficere, 2 Cor. 4. 17. Gal. 6. 8. Phil. 2. 12. &c. Resp. 1. In locis Matth. 26. 34, 35. Apoc. 7. 14, 15. agnoscimus ordinem & rationem consequentiæ a bonis operibus ad fruitionem gloriæ cœlestis, juxta Dei decretum, & promissionem gratiosam; sed rationem meriti non agnoscimus. 2. Apostolus quidem diserte, Rom. 6. 23. Stipendium peccati mors: sed aliter omnino de vita æterna; Donum autem Dei est vita æterna in Christo Iesu Domino Domino nostro. 3. 2 Cor. 4. 17. Gal. 6. 8. Phil. 2. 12. per afflictiones piè toleratas, praxin sanctimoniæ, & reverentiam Domini, dicitur salus nostra confici; quatenus ista sunt media Divinitus ordinata, & adhiberi solita, ad promovendam salutem nostram, & vitæ æternæ fruitionem; sed absque ratione meriti.
units.tr: The third argument takes from passages which testify that eternal life is rendered to good works in such a way that they place in the works themselves the very reason why eternal life is given (Matt. 25.34, 35; Rev. 7.14, 15). Where the particles "for," "because," and "therefore" are all causal. "The wages of sin is death," etc. (Rom. 6.23). And good works are said to bring about salvation itself (2 Cor. 4.17; Gal. 6.8; Phil. 2.12, etc.). Answer 1. In the passages Matth. 26.34, 35 and Rev. 7.14, 15 we acknowledge the order and reason of consequence from good works to the enjoyment of heavenly glory, according to God's decree and gracious promise; but we do not acknowledge the reason of merit. 2. The apostle indeed says expressly, "The wages of sin is death" (Rom. 6.23); but he says altogether otherwise about eternal life: "The gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." 3. In 2 Cor. 4.17, Gal. 6.8 and Phil. 2.12, our salvation is said to be accomplished through afflictions piously endured, through the practice of holiness and reverence for the Lord; insofar as these are means ordained by God and customarily used to advance our salvation and the enjoyment of eternal life; but without any reason of merit.

units.la: XVI. Quartò, argumentatur ex testimoniis, ubi præmium bonis operibus ex justitiâ dicitur esse reddendum: 2 Thess. I. 4. -- 7. 2 Tim. 4. 7. 8. Hebr. 6. 10. Jac. 1. 22. Apoc. 2. 10. Prov. 19. 17. 1 Cor. 9. 24.
units.tr: XVI. Fourthly, he argues from testimonies where a reward is said to be due to good works from justice (2 Thess. 1.4–7; 2 Tim. 4.7, 8; Heb. 6.10; Jas. 1.22; Rev. 2.10; Prov. 19.17; 1 Cor. 9.24).

units.la: 2 Tim. 1. 12. Resp. 1. Imò bonis operibus fidelium redditur præmium ex justitiâ; quatenus istam præmii redditionem antecedit jus, quod Christus iis acquisivit, ipsi autem fide acceperunt: hinc præstitâ conditione, quæ ad obtinendum reipsâ præmium, sive ad actualem ejus fruitionem, fuit proposita, Deus per justitiam & veracitatem suam, non potest non iis tribuere istud præmium.
units.tr: (2 Tim. 1.12.) Answer 1. Indeed, the reward is rendered to the good works of believers from justice, insofar as this rendering of reward is preceded by the right which Christ acquired for them and which they received by faith. Hence, once the condition proposed for actually obtaining the reward, or its actual enjoyment, has been fulfilled, God cannot but grant them that reward, through his justice and truthfulness.

units.la: Quintò, ex illis, quæ docent vitam æternam promissam esse operibus bonis: Matth. 19. 17, 29. 1 Tim. 4. 8. Jac. 1. 12. At promissio facta cum conditione operis, non solùm debitam facit rem promissam; sed etiàm facit, ut qui opus impleverit, meruisse rem promissam, eamque ut mercedem jure suo exigere posse, dicatur. Resp. 1. Matth. 19. 17. Christus dixit juveni Pharisæo; Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata; Fœdus Legale illi repetens; unde is suam impotentiam agnoscere debuit, ac porro ad Christum & gratiam Euangelicam confugere. Sed nequaquàm dixit fore, ut homines illo pacto consequerentur vitam æternam. 2. Quantum attinet ad reliqua; qui bene promisit, promissis stare debet ratione fidelitatis, quæ in justitiâ universali continetur; non tamen semper ratione justitiæ particularis: neque promissio hoc efficit necessariò, ut qui adjectam conditionem præstiterit, terit, rem promissam, tanquàm mercedem ex debito, jure suo exigere posse dicatur. Quid si enim pauperi promiserim, më ei daturum eleemosynam, ubi me domi meæ compellaverit; certè propter istam promissionem non desinet esse eleemosyna, neque fiet actus justitiæ particularis, aut retributio mercedis ex debito.
units.tr: Fifthly, from those passages which teach that eternal life is promised to good works (Matt. 19.17, 29; 1 Tim. 4.8; Jas. 1.12). But a promise made with the condition of a work not only makes the promised thing due, but also makes it so that one who has fulfilled the work is said to have merited the promised thing, and to be able to claim it by his own right as wages. Answer 1. Matt. 19.17: Christ said to the young Pharisee, "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments," thereby restating the legal covenant to him; whence he ought to recognise his own inability and afterwards flee to Christ and evangelical grace. But he by no means said that men would attain eternal life by that pact. 2. As far as the rest is concerned, one who has promised well ought to stand by his promises by reason of fidelity, which is contained in universal justice, yet not always by reason of particular justice. Nor does the promise necessarily bring it about that one who has performed the added condition is said to be able to claim the promised thing, as a wage owed, by his own right. For if I promised a poor man that I would give him alms, if he should call upon me at my home, certainly on account of that promise the gift will not cease to be alms, nor will it become an act of particular justice, or a repayment of wages owed.

units.la: XVII. Sexto ex illis, ubi fit mentio Dignitatis: nam Dignum esse præmio idem valet, quod Mereri præmium. Sic Luc. 10. 7. Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Huc ergo pertinent loca, Sap. 3. 5. 2 Theff. 1. 5. Luc. 20. 35. Apoc. 3. 5. Neque obstat illud Rom. 8. 18. Non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam. Loquitur enim Apostolus de substantia ipsorum operum; non de proportione absoluta: hæc autem datur, propter caritatis dignitatem, unde opera procedunt. Resp. 1. Dignum esse præmio interdum idem valet, quod Mereri mercedem: scil. cùm merces rectè proportionata refertur ad opus alias indebitum. Huc pertinet illud Luc. 10. 7. Dignus est operarius mercede sua: homo videl. respectu alterius hominis: at non respectu Dei. 2. Vide quæ de Dignitate dicta sunt sup. th. 13. obj. 2. Neque subsistit Bellarmini exceptio ad locum Rom. 8. 18. dum proportionem operum ad vitam æternam arcesset à dignitate charitatis: nam ipsa Charitas in hac vita imperfecta est; quemadmodum ex parte cognoscimus; 1 Cor. 13. 9. & in multis impingimus omnes; Jac. 3. 2.
units.tr: XVII. Sixthly, from those passages where mention is made of worthiness, for being worthy of a reward is the same as meriting a reward. Thus Luke 10.7: "The labourer is worthy of his wages." To this belong the passages Sap. 3.5; 2 Thess. 1.5; Luke 20.35; Rev. 3.5. Nor does Rom. 8.18 stand in the way: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come." For the Apostle speaks of the substance of the works themselves, not of an absolute proportion; and this proportion is given on account of the dignity of charity from which the works proceed. Answer 1. To be worthy of a reward sometimes has the same meaning as to merit a wage, namely when a properly proportioned wage is referred to a work that was otherwise not owed. To this belongs Luke 10.7, "The labourer is worthy of his wages," where the worthiness is that of one man with respect to another, but not with respect to God. 2. See what was said above, th. 13, obj. 2. Nor does Bellarmine's exception to Rom. 8.18 hold, when he derives the proportion of works to eternal life from the dignity of charity; for charity itself is imperfect in this life, as "we know in part" (1 Cor. 13.9), and "we all stumble in many things" (Jas. 3.2).

units.la: Septimò denique ex illis, ubi dicitur Deus judex justus, & non acceptor personarum: Rom. 2. 11. Gal. 2. 6. 1 Petr. 1. 17. Act. 10. 34. At acceptio personarum est vitium contrarium justitiæ distributivæ; cùm videl. judex dat præmium sine meritis, aut majus præmium minoribus meritis, vel contrà. Resp. Deus revera fidelibus tribuit præmium cœlestis gloriæ propter sufficientissimum Christi meritum, illis imputatum; quod justitiæ distributivæ satis convenit. Alioquin respectu nostri ipsorum, liberalitas, gratia, & misericordia celebrari solent.
units.tr: Seventhly, from those passages where God is called a just judge and not a respecter of persons: Rom. 2. 11; Gal. 2. 6; 1 Pet. 1. 17; Acts 10. 34. But respect of persons is a vice opposed to distributive justice, since a judge gives a reward without merits, or a greater reward for lesser merits, or the reverse. Reply: God truly gives the faithful the reward of heavenly glory on account of the most sufficient merit of Christ, imputed to them, and this agrees well enough with distributive justice. Otherwise, with respect to ourselves, liberality, grace and mercy are usually celebrated.

units.la: XVIII. Deinceps cap. 5: Ille contendit, merita hominum non requiri propter insufficientiam meritorum Christi; sed propter maximam eorum efficaciam: meruisse enim Christi opera apud Deum, non solum ut salutem consequeremur; sed etiam ut ea per merita propria consequeremur: sive non solum salutem æternam nobis meruisse, sed etiam virtutem merendi. Resp. 1. Si meritorum Christi non est insufficientia, sed maxima eorum efficacia, propter quam consequimur salutem æternam; certè Christi merita sunt causa totalis meritoria salutis nostræ æternæ, non partialis tantùm; & consequenter nostra bona opera non sunt formaliter ejus meritoria. 2. Si Christus nobis præter salutem æternam, etiam meritus esset virtutem merendi salutem æternam, sane meritus esset nobis virtutem actum agendi, &c.
units.tr: XVIII. Next, in chapter 5 he contends that the merits of men are not required on account of the insufficiency of Christ's merits, but on account of their very great efficacy. For Christ merited with God not only that we might obtain salvation, but also that we might obtain it through our own merits; that is, he merited for us not only eternal salvation but also the power of meriting it. Reply 1. If there is no insufficiency in Christ's merits, but a very great efficacy in them, on account of which we obtain eternal salvation, then surely Christ's merits are the total meritorious cause of our eternal salvation, not merely a partial one; and consequently our good works are not formally meritorious of it. 2. If Christ had merited for us, besides eternal salvation, also the power of meriting eternal salvation, then surely he would have merited for us the power of performing acts, and so on.

units.la: XIX. Socinani Satisfactionem ac Meritum Christi pro nobis præstita omninò negantes, verum Justificationis nostræ fundamentum prorsus subvertunt. Fidem quidem appellant, per quam servemur; sed eam describunt, quod fit in bonis operibus, quæ nobis Deus per Christum præscripsit, ambulare, &c. Resp. Fides ab operibus clarissimè & frequentissimè contradistinguitur: per illam justificari dicimur, quatenus sic justitiam Euangelio propositam agnoscimus & recipimus; per hæc nos justificari posse, diserte negatur.
units.tr: XIX. The Socinians, who utterly deny the satisfaction and merit of Christ offered on our behalf, entirely subvert the foundation of our justification. They do indeed speak of faith as that by which we are saved, but they describe it as walking in the good works which God has prescribed for us through Christ, and so on. Reply: Faith is most clearly and most frequently distinguished from works. We are said to be justified through faith insofar as we acknowledge and receive the righteousness proposed in the Gospel; that we can be justified through works is plainly denied.

units.la: Ofiorodus alibi: Dico, non esse verum, quòd cùm omnia fecerimus, quæ nobis mandata sunt, nihil tamen omninò mereamur: quoniam Christus, ejusque Apostoli, omnibus illis, qui præcepta ejus observant, vitam æternam isto nomine promiserunt. Resp. At minimè sic promiserunt, ut jus vitæ æternæ in noftris illis actibus, tanquàm in justitiâ propriâ, fundetur; ac proinde de nostro apud Deum merito nihil est præsumendum.
units.tr: Ostorodius elsewhere: I say it is not true that, although we have done everything that has been commanded us, we nevertheless merit nothing at all merit, since Christ and his apostles promised eternal life under this very name to all who observe his precepts. Reply: They by no means promised it in such a way that a right to eternal life is grounded in those acts of ours as in a righteousness of our own; and therefore nothing is to be presumed about our merit before God.

units.la: Idem iterùm: Luc. 17. 10. non dicitur, quid Deus de obedientiâ nostrâ judicet: sed tantùm quid nos de eâ judicare debeamus; fcil. ut semper nos ipsos humiliemus, &c. Si enim Deus nos servos inutiles judicaret, in æternum effemus perituri: quoniàm Dominus suo die inutilem servum vinćturus, atque in extimas tenebras abjećturus est, ubi fletus erit & stridor dentium; Matth. 25. 30. Resp. 1. Judicium Dei de nobis & operibus nostris procul dubio verum est: & nostrum judicium, ut verum fit, judicio Divino debet esse conforme. Quoniàm verò nos de nobis ipsis judicare debemus, quòd fimus fervi inutiles in nobis ipsis, qui Deo nihil conferre possimus, & quibus Deus prorsùs non egeat; similiter etiàm ipse Deus de nobis judicat, qui non nisi fecundùm rerum veritatem judicat. 2. Alio autem sensû servus inutilis dicitur Matth. 25, 30. qui prorsùs non dedit operam, ut suâ obedientiâ & sanctimoniâ gloriæ Divinæ illustrandæ, aut proximorum ædificatióni, suæque saluti promovendæ, inserviret; ac proinde foras ejiciendus est in tenebras extremas: non verò qui suæ in sese impotentiæ & indignitatis sibi conscius, Evangelio tamen credit; & fide justificatus, utilem gloriæ Divinæ illustrandæ, ac proximorum ædificationi, suæque saluti (quantum ad fruitionem) promovendæ, utilem operam navat ferio.
units.tr: Again the same author: Luke 17. 10 does not say what God judges concerning our obedience, but only what we ought to judge of it, namely that we should always humble ourselves, and so on. For if God were to judge us unprofitable servants, we would perish forever, since the Lord will bind the unprofitable servant on his day and cast him into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 25. 30). Reply 1. God's judgement concerning us and our works is undoubtedly true, and our judgement, if it is to be true, must agree with the divine judgement. But since we ought to judge of ourselves that we are unprofitable servants in ourselves, who can contribute nothing to God and whom God has no need of at all, so God himself judges of us in the same way, since he judges only according to the truth of things. 2. But in another sense the unprofitable servant of Matthew 25. 30 is one who has made no effort at all to serve, by his obedience and holiness, the illustration of the divine glory, the edification of his neighbours, or the promotion of his own salvation, and who is therefore to be cast out into utter darkness. It is not one who, conscious of his own impotence and unworthiness, nevertheless believes the Gospel, is justified by faith, and, as far as enjoyment is concerned, labours usefully to illustrate the divine glory, to edify his neighbours, and to promote his own salvation.

units.la: XX. Remonstrantes etiàm statuunt in Apol.cap.10.
units.tr: XX. The Remonstrants also maintain in the Apology, chapter 10.

units.la: Quòd per Fidem in negotio Justificationis intelligendus sit actus fidei, quatenùs includit in se totam obedientiam hominis Christiani, lege fidei, i.e. Evangelio præscriptam. Atque hanc controversiam, si rectè perpendatur, nil nisi Logicam aut Grammaticam litem esse. Quotquot enim sunt Ecclesiarum Reformatarum Confessiones, eas omnes consentientibus calculis agnoscere. Fidem vivam, non mortuam; fidem quæ conjuncta sibi habet bona opera; imo quæ sine operibus nec est, nec esse potest, esse fidem illam veram justificantem, &c. Meram vero Logicam pugnam esse, si disputetur, Utrum fides quæ est viva, an fides quâ est viva, requiratur ad justificationem? --. De respectu statuere, non esse nostrum; sed Judicis.--. Si dicatur, Fidem requiri ad justificationem, quatenus vel quâ est viva fides, necessitatem bonorum operum & pietatis Christianæ fortius adstringi. Neque particulam illam Quatenus efficientiam aliquam meritoriam tribuere fidei, ad consequendum remissionem peccatorum. Neque aliquam efficientiam (dummodo excludatur meritoria proprie dicta) fidei tributam in ordine ad justificationem, quicquam reale aut magni momenti addere ad voces necessariæ præsentiæ. Resp. 1. Fidem hic non esse spectandam, quatenus includit in se totam obedientiam hominis Christiani, &c. satis patet ex superioribus. 2. Remonstrantes contrarium statuentes, Euangelium, & doctrinam fidei, in novam Legem operum pervertunt; atque ex eâ hominem coram Deo justificari volunt. Sic non quæritur de termino aliquo Logico, vel Grammatico: sed de re gravissimâ controvertitur. 3. Fides, quâ Christum amplectimur cum omnibus suis beneficiis, ac specialiter prout nobis à Deo factus est justitia, necessariò viva est, non mortua; est principium & radix bonorum operum, sic virtualiter ea in se continens; nec fieri potest, ut consequenter ea non producat. Justificat autem organicè, quatenus Christum apprehendit, ut nobis factum à Deo justitiam; non verò formaliter quatenus viva est, & bona opera producit. 4. De usu & respectu fidei ex SS. Literis statuere, omninò eorum est, qui veritatem rectè æstimare volunt, & quid Salvatori suo debeant. 5. Si dicatur, Fidem requiri ad justificationem, quatenus viva est, necessitas bonorum operum non adstruitur fortius, quàm si dicatur, ad justificationem necessario requiri fidem quæ viva est; & Christum factum nobis à Deo justitiam; sic tamen ut ipsa bona opera in adultis etiàm sint requisita necessaria, ad accipiendam fruitionem vitæ æternæ: sed per illam Adversariorum assertionem erigitur justitia propria, homo inflatur temerè & à Christo abducitur. 6. Cùm dicitur, Fidem justificare quatenus viva est, seu totam obedientiam hominis Christiani in se includit, aperte opera prærequiruntur, ut antecedens causa ad justificationem hominis coram Deo; & quidem impetratoria istius juris, ac meritoria saltem laxè dicta: quod quàm alienum sit à Fœdere Euangelico, & SS. Literarum doctrinâ de Justificatione hominis coram Deo, patet ex superioribus.
units.tr: That by faith in the matter of justification is to be understood the act of faith insofar as it includes within itself the whole obedience of the Christian man, prescribed by the law of faith, that is, by the Gospel. And if this controversy is weighed rightly, it is nothing but a dispute about logic or grammar. For all the Confessions of the Reformed Churches, with one accord, acknowledge a living faith, not a dead one; a faith which has good works joined to it; indeed, a faith which without works neither is nor can be, that is the true justifying faith, and so on. That it is a purely logical battle, if it is debated whether faith which is living, or faith by which it is living, is required for justification... As to the respect, it is not for us to decide, but for the Judge... If it is said that faith is required for justification insofar as it is or is living faith, the necessity of good works and Christian piety is bound more strongly. Nor does that particle "insofar" attribute any meritorious efficacy to faith for obtaining the remission of sins, nor does any efficacy attributed to faith in relation to justification (provided that merit properly so called is excluded) add anything real or of great moment to the words "necessary presence." Reply 1. That faith here is not to be considered insofar as it includes within itself the whole obedience of the Christian man, and so on, is sufficiently clear from what has gone before. 2. The Remonstrants, maintaining the contrary, pervert the Gospel and the doctrine of faith into a new law of works, and want man to be justified before God by it. Thus the question is not about some logical or grammatical term, but a most weighty matter is in dispute. 3. Faith, by which we embrace Christ with all his benefits, and especially as he has been made by God righteousness for us, is necessarily living, not dead; it is the principle and root of good works, thus containing them virtually within itself, and it cannot happen that it does not consequently produce them. It justifies, however, instrumentally, insofar as it apprehends Christ as made righteousness for us by God; not formally, insofar as it is living and produces good works. 4. To determine concerning the use and respect of faith from the Holy Scriptures belongs entirely to those who wish to judge the truth rightly and to know what they owe their Saviour. 5. If it is said that faith is required for justification insofar as it is living, the necessity of good works is not asserted any more strongly than if one says that living faith is necessarily required for justification, and that Christ has been made righteousness for us by God; yet in such a way that good works themselves in adults are also required as necessary conditions for receiving the enjoyment of eternal life. But by that assertion of the Adversaries, one's own righteousness is raised up, man is rashly puffed up and is drawn away from Christ. 6. When it is said that faith justifies insofar as it is living, or includes within itself the whole obedience of the Christian man, works are clearly required beforehand as an antecedent cause of man's justification before God; and indeed as an impetratory cause of this right, and as a merit at least loosely so called. How foreign this is to the Gospel covenant and the doctrine of Holy Scripture concerning the justification of man before God is clear from what has gone before.

units.la: XXI. Instant iidem; Verissimum esse, quòd homo non ex fide tantùm, sed ex operibus etiàm justificetur: cùm totidem verbis id pronunciet Jacobus, 2.24. Nec istum locum intelligendum esse de declaratione justificationis: cùm nemo adeò vecors fuerit istò sæculo, qui cum Apostolo contendere voluerit, an homo justificetur, i. e. declaretur justus, ex fide tantùm; quia fides, quatenus fiducia est, distincta ab operibus pietatis, non est nisi in corde hominis. Addunt; Ne de operibus quidem ipsis constare posse, an bona sint; quia bona esse non possunt, nisi ex fide fiant: ex fide autem fieri, non modò non posse declarari alteri, sed ne illi ipsi quidem id constare posse qui ea facit; quia ipsi credamus, fieri posse ut reprobus opera eadem omnia faciat quæ electus, & sibi persuadeat se electum esse tali persuasione, quàm à persuasione electorum nullo certo signo, nullo characteristico indicio possimus distinguere. Vide Calvinum Institut. lib. 3. c. 2. §. 2. Resp. 1. Cum Jacobus ait, II. 24. Videtis igitur, quod ex operibus justificetur homo, & non ex fide tantum, non loquitur à priori & formaliter de justificatione hominis coram Deo; sed à posteriori eam considerat, quod ad declarationem & perceptionem, tùm in ipso justificato, tùm etiàm in aliis pro re natâ. Docet nimirùm, ad hoc, ut quis judicetur, vel agnoscatur justus esse coram Deo, non sufficere fidem qualemcunque, aut professionem oralem; sed requiri fidem vivam, quæ suis actibus vitalibus, etiàm imperatis, se manifestam faciat. Vide verf. 1: 14,--17,18, 19,20. & confer Gen.15.6. XXII. 1,2,3,9,10,12,16,17,18. R. 2. Multi Apostolorum sæculo, ac deinceps, adeò væcordes fuerunt, ut ex fide solùm historicâ fiduciam salutis conciperent; atque ex communione externâ in Ecclesia institutâ, ac professione Euangelii, voluerint justi reputari. Ipsa quidem fides in corde est: verùm illi per eam, cùm salvifica non esset, deceperunt se ipsos, & externâ professione orali alios in similem de ipsis opinionem adducere voluerunt. Hanc temeritatem ac deceptionem refutat Apostolus. 3. Opera non sunt verè ac spiritualiter bona, nisi ex fide salvificâ procedant: Rom.14.23. Tit.I.15. Hebr. 2.6. Atqui istius principii actuosi fidelis sibi conscius est: & ubi opera respondent professioni, aliis etiàm argumentum præbet pro judicio charitatis sufficiens. 4. Calvinus loco cit. nihil istiusmodi dicit, quale ab Apologistâ objicitur; sed §. 10. & 11. de fide historicâ ac temporariâ disserit: ubi inter alia; „Quamvis „magna sit similitudo & affinitas inter Dei electos, & „qui fide caducâ ad tempus donantur: vigere tamen „in solis electis fiduciam illam quam celebrat Paulus, ut „pleno ore clament, Abba, Pater. Ergò, ut solos „electos femine incorruptibili Deus in perpetuum re„generat, ut nunquàm dispereat femen vitæ eorum
units.tr: XXI. The same men insist that it is most true that man is justified not by faith alone but also by works, since James says exactly this in 2. 24. Nor is that passage to be understood of the declaration of justification, since no one in this age would be so mad as to want to argue with the Apostle whether man is justified, that is, declared righteous, by faith alone; because faith, insofar as it is trust, distinct from the works of piety, is only in the heart of man. They add that it cannot even be established concerning the works themselves whether they are good, since they cannot be good unless they are done from faith; and that it cannot be declared to another, nor even established to the one who does them, that they are done from faith, since we believe that a reprobate can do all the same works as the elect and persuade himself that he is elect by such a persuasion, which we cannot distinguish from the persuasion of the elect by any certain sign or characteristic mark. See Calvin, Institutes, book 3, chapter 2, §2. Reply 1. When James says, 2. 24, You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only, he does not speak a priori and formally of the justification of man before God, but considers it a posteriori, with respect to its declaration and perception, both in the justified person himself and in others as occasion arises.
