units.la: X. Sub Divinâ istâ gratiâ, ipsi fideles sanctificati perseverantiæ sedulò dant operam: 1 Joh. 3, 3, Quisquis habet hanc spem in Eo sitam, purum se conservat, sicut Ipse purus est. V, 18. Psal. 119. 112. 1 Tim. 4, 7, 8. Specialius verò constanter se exercent in Verbo Dei; quod efficax medium est ad perseverantiam: Psal. I, 2, 3. 2 Tim. 3, 14, -17. Consequenter abnegant se ipsos: hoc enim initio requirit Christus: Matth. 16, 24. 1 Cor. 9, 27. & sanctimoniæ incumbunt: Psal. 119, 43, 44. Imò etiam assumunt universam armaturam spiritualem, ut subsistant adversùs hostes spirituales: Eph. 6, 13, -18. Rom. 10, 13. 14. Matth. 26, 41. VI, 13. cum Joh. 16, 23. Item 1 Thess. V, 23, 24. 2 Thess. 2, 11, 12.
units.tr: X. Under this divine grace, the sanctified faithful themselves diligently labour for perseverance: 1 John 3:3, "Whoever has this hope set on him purifies himself, as he is pure"; ibid. 5:18; Ps. 119:112; 1 Tim. 4:7, 8. More specifically, they constantly exercise themselves in the Word of God, which is an effective means to perseverance: Ps. 1:2, 3; 2 Tim. 3:14-17. Consequently they deny themselves, for Christ requires this at the outset: Matt. 16:24; 1 Cor. 9:27. They also devote themselves to holiness: Ps. 119:43, 44. Indeed, they even take up the whole spiritual armour, so that they may stand against spiritual enemies: Eph. 6:13-18; Rom. 10:13, 14; Matt. 26:41; 6:13, together with John 16:23. Likewise 1 Thess. 5:23, 24; 2 Thess. 2:11, 12.

units.la: XI. Finis hujus conservationis summus & ulti- mus
units.tr: XI. The highest and ultimate end of this preservation

units.la: tem infirmi fumus in nobis ipsis : Matth. 26, 41. Rom. 8, 26. 2Cor. XII, 6.
units.tr: ...tem: that we, being weak, are in ourselves: Matt. 26:41; Rom. 8:26; 2 Cor. 12:6.

units.la: Similiter in precibus maximam apud se infirmitatem deprehendere solent sanctificati; in quâ tamen Sp. Sanctus iis mirum in modum succurrit. Rom VIII, 26, 27. Quid oremus ut oportet, non novimus : sed ipse Spiritus intercedit pro nobis suspiriis ineffabilibus. -.
units.tr: Likewise, in prayers the sanctified are accustomed to find in themselves the greatest weakness; yet in this the Holy Spirit wonderfully comes to their aid: Rom. 8:26, 27, "We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered."

units.la: Sed vita spiritualis robur acquirit, & virtutes Theologicæ incrementa capiunt: ità illi corroborati adversùs hostes subsistunt, & victoriam obtinent; atque in precibus potentes evadunt, Deo dante. Psal. 92, 13, 14, 15. Iustus ut palma florebit : sicut cedrus in Libano multiplicabitur, &c. Phil. 4, 13. Omnia valeo per eum, qui me corroborat, nempè Christum. Vide etiàm Isef. 40, 29, 30, 31. Zach. 12, 8. Mal. 4, 3.
units.tr: But the spiritual life gains strength, and the theological virtues grow; thus strengthened, they stand against enemies and obtain victory, and by God's gift they become powerful in prayer. Ps. 92:13-15, "The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon," etc.; Phil. 4:13, "I can do all things through him who strengthens me," namely Christ. See also Isa. 40:29-31; Zech. 12:8; Mal. 4:3.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Causa efficiens principalis est Deus omnipotens : Isef. 40, 29. 2 Thess. 3, 2. Sed juxta speciale œconomiam, Christus Mediator; idem Deus fortis, nos corroborans : Isef. 9, 5. Phil. 4, 13. Proximè autem quantum ad ordinem operandi attinet, Spiritus Sanctus : Rom. 8, 26.
units.tr: The principal efficient cause is almighty God: Isa. 40:29. 2 Thess. 3:2. But according to the special economy, Christ the Mediator, the same God, strong, strengthening us: Isa. 9:5. Phil. 4:13. Next, as regards the order of working, the Holy Spirit: Rom. 8:26.

units.la: Media sunt : 1. Adhortationes : Iof. 1, 6, 7, 9.
units.tr: The means are: (1) Exhortations: Josh. 1:6, 7, 9.

units.la: 2. Lectio, auditio, & meditatio Verbi Divini : 1 Petr. 2, 2. Hebr. 5, 14. cum 2 Tim. 3, 16, 17.
units.tr: (2) The reading, hearing, and meditation of the Divine Word: 1 Pet. 2:2. Heb. 5:14, with 2 Tim. 3:16, 17.

units.la: 3. Usus Sacramentorum, quæ obsignando Fœdus gratiæ, moraliter hanc corroborationem promovent: Rom. 4, 11. 1 Cor. 10, 16. cum Ioh. 6, 55.
units.tr: (3) The use of the Sacraments, which, by sealing the covenant of grace, morally promote this strengthening: Rom. 4:11. 1 Cor. 10:16, with John 6:55.

units.la: 4. Preces ac vota : 1 Petr. V, 10.
units.tr: (4) Prayers and vows: 1 Pet. 5:10.

units.la: 5. Exercitationes facultatum spiritualium, aliorumque donorum gratiæ : quò pertinet admonitio, 2 Tim. 1, 6. & querela. Isef. 44, 7.
units.tr: (5) The exercise of spiritual faculties and of the other gifts of grace: to which belongs admonition, 2 Tim. 1:6, and complaint. Isa. 44:7.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Finis summus est ipsius Dei & Christi gloria; Hinc Ipsi, 1 Petr. 5, 10, 11. gloria & robur in sæcula tribuitur. Subordinatus, redemptorum sanctificatorum salus. Psal. 84. 8. Ibunt de virtute ad virtutem, donec conspiciatur quisque eorum ante Deum in Tzijone. Phil. 4, 14.
units.tr: The highest end is the glory of God himself and of Christ; hence glory and strength are ascribed to him forever: 1 Pet. 5:10, 11. The subordinate end is the salvation of the redeemed and sanctified. Ps. 84:8. They go from strength to strength, until each of them is seen before God in Zion. Phil. 4:14.

units.la: XIX. Pro praxi; 1. Ne adversus praeclarum illud Dei & Christi nos conservantis beneficium prosana ingratitudine peccemus: 2 Cor. 7, 1. Sed serio expendamus, quae poenae maneant sanctimoniae expertes: Hebr. XII, 14, 16. Matth. VII, 23. XXV, 41. & quomodo ipsi sanctificati, ubi officia sua negligunt, & in graviora peccata labuntur, saepius affligantur graviter; tum animo, variis terroribus: Psal. 6, 4. tum corpore, morbis & cruciatibus: Levit. 26. 16. Psal. 6, 2, 3. XXXVIII, 2, 3, 4. 1 Cor. XI, 31, 32. tum denique bonis externis, per eorum jacturam: Levit. XXVI, 16, 17. Hos. 2, 8. Ista nos a defectione absterreant, & in veram sanctitatis viam redigant: Hos. 2, 13. VI, 1. 1 Cor. XI, 32. Hebr. 12, 10, -14.
units.tr: XIX. For practice: (1) Let us not sin against that remarkable benefit of God and Christ preserving us by profane ingratitude: 2 Cor. 7:1. But let us seriously consider what punishments await those who lack holiness: Heb. 12:14, 16. Matt. 7:23. 25:41. And how those who are sanctified themselves, when they neglect their duties and slide into graver sins, are often severely afflicted: in mind, by various terrors: Ps. 6:4; in body, by diseases and torments: Lev. 26:16. Ps. 6:2, 3. 38:2, 3, 4. 1 Cor. 11:31, 32; and finally in external goods, by the loss of them: Lev. 26:16, 17. Hos. 2:8. Let these things frighten us away from defection and bring us back into the true way of holiness: Hos. 2:13. 6:1. 1 Cor. 11:32. Heb. 12:10–14.

units.la: 2. Sincerum esto, ac perpetuum, sub hac Dei & Servatoris nostri gratia, studium Ipsi parendi ac placendi: Rom. 12, 1. 2 Thess. 2, 13. Sic methodum salutis obtinendae, Decreto Dei constitutam, Euangelio nobis revelatam, variisque Promissionibus confirmatam, observemus sedulo & constanter: Rom. VIII, 28. -. 1 Tim. IV, 7. -10. Hebr. X, 35, 36. Matth. XXIV, 13.
units.tr: (2) Let our zeal for pleasing and obeying him be sincere and perpetual, under this grace of God and our Saviour: Rom. 12:1. 2 Thess. 2:13. Thus let us diligently and constantly observe the method of obtaining salvation, appointed by the decree of God, revealed to us in the Gospel, and confirmed by various promises: Rom. 8:28. 1 Tim. 4:7–10. Heb. 10:35, 36. Matt. 24:13.

units.la: 3. Agnoscamus ordinariam illam methodum salutis applicandae: & necessitatem atque insignem utilitatem incrementi spiritualis: Eph. 4, 16. Psal. 84, 8. Phil. 3, 14.
units.tr: (3) Let us acknowledge that ordinary method of applying salvation, and the necessity and remarkable usefulness of spiritual growth: Eph. 4:16. Ps. 84:8. Phil. 3:14.

units.la: 4. Exploremus nos ipsos quousque modo pervenerimus; & quae sint nostrae vires spirituales: Zeph. 2, 1.
units.tr: (4) Let us examine ourselves, to see how far we have advanced and what our spiritual strength is: Zeph. 2:1.

units.la: 1 Cor. XI, 28. Profectui & corroborationi studeamus sedulo: Iof. I, 6, 7, 9. adhibitis potissimum mediis, quae indicata sunt sup. th. 17.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 11:28. Let us zealously strive for progress and strengthening: Josh. 1:6, 7, 9, employing especially the means indicated above, in chapter 17.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: De Obsignatione.
units.tr: On Sealing.

units.la: Obsignatio. Qualis actus. Effectus proprius. 1. Causa efficiens principalis. Media. Signa. 2. Sacramentum. Μυστήριον. 3. Illius definitio. 4. Auctor. Institutio. Promissio. 5. Subjectum. Objectum. 6. Forma. 7. Praedicationes Sacramentales. 8. Fines. 9. Efficientia realis Sacramentis non tribuenda : c. Pontif. 10. Sed obsignatio promissorum Euang. c. Anabapt. 11. Sacramenta. V. T. Ea non erant figurae Sacramentorum N. T. c. Pontif. Obj. solv. Duo Sacramenta N. T. 12. Baptismus. Βαπτισμὸν. Pluribus modis dicitur. 13. Administrandus aquâ verâ & naturali. Non consecratâ per adjurationem, &c. c. Pontif. Occasio. 14. Modus ablutionis. 15. Trina ablutio. Formula. 16. Aquae res significata. 17. Ritus triplex. Res significata. 18. Effectus. 19. Non ex opere operato: c. Pontif. 20. Causa efficiens princeps. Ministra. Mandatum: c. Socin. 21. Baptismus Johannis re ipsâ idem cum Baptismo Discipulorum Christi, &c. c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 22. Quinam baptizare debeant. 23. Aliqui nimis coartant istud jus. 24. Alii nimis extendunt: speciatim Pontificii. Obj. solv. 25. Objectum. Non baptizandae campanae: c. Pontif. Non mortui, &c. 26. Quales adulti. 27. Etiam infantes fidelium: c. Anabapt. 28. Objectiones solv. 29. Casus aliqui. 30. Necessitas praecepti: c. Socin. Ob. solv. 31. Non absoluta necessitas medii. c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 32. Locus. Tempus. 33. Baptismus non iterandus: c. Anabapt. 34. Sententia Pontif. Obj. solv. 35. Coena Dominica. Ejus institutio. Causa efficiens primaria. Ministra. 36. Subjectum. Panis. Non recte Pontificii adhibent, minutias farinaceas. An utendum azymis. Poculum vini. 37. Usus poculi necessarius: c. Pontif. Obj. solv. 38. Consecratio. Non fit per verba, Hoc est corpus meum, &c. c. Pontif. 39. Fractio. Distributio panis. 40. Missa privata. Panis in manus porrigendus. Non asservandus ad cultum: c. Pontif. 41. Ritus circa vinum. Actiones communicantium. De Genuflexione. 42. Res significata. 43. Forma. Praedicationes sacramentales. 44. Fines. 45. Comparatio Missa; in nomine, Auctore, Ministris. 46. In materia. Forma. 47. Transsubstantiatio refutatur, c. Pontif. 48. Objectiones solv. 49. Consubstantiatio refut. c. Luther. Obj. solv. 50. Sacrificium Missae refut. c. Pontif. 51. Objectiones solv. 52. Comparatio in fine, & adjunctis. 53. Falsa Sacramenta Pontif. Confirmatio. 54. Poenitentia. 55. Extrema unctio. 56. Ordo. 57. Matrimonium. 58. Sententia quae Anabapt. & Remonstr. de Lotione pedum. 59. Praxis. 60.
units.tr: Sealing. What kind of act it is. Its proper effect. 1. The principal efficient cause. The means. The signs. 2. Sacrament. Mysterion [Μυστήριον]. 3. Its definition. 4. Author. Institution. Promise. 5. Subject. Object. 6. Form. 7. The sacramental predications. 8. The ends. 9. A real efficacy is not to be ascribed to the sacraments: against the Papists. 10. But the sealing of the promises of the Gospel: against the Anabaptists. 11. The sacraments of the Old Testament. They were not figures of the sacraments of the New Testament: against the Papists, and the objection answered. The two sacraments of the New Testament. 12. Baptism [Βαπτισμόν]. It is said in several ways. 13. It is to be administered with true and natural water, not consecrated by exorcism, etc.: against the Papists. Occasion. 14. The manner of washing. 15. Threefold washing. The formula. 16. The thing signified by the water. 17. The triple rite. The thing signified. 18. The effect. 19. Not by the work worked: against the Papists. 20. The chief efficient cause. The minister. The command: against the Socinians. 21. John's baptism is in fact the same as the baptism of the disciples of Christ, etc.: against the Papists, and the objection answered. 22. Who ought to baptize. 23. Some restrict this right too narrowly. 24. Others extend it too far, especially the Papists; the objection answered. 25. The object. Bells are not to be baptized: against the Papists. Nor the dead, etc. 26. What kind of adults. 27. Also the infants of believers: against the Anabaptists. 28. Objections answered. 29. Certain cases. 30. The necessity of the precept: against the Socinians; the objection answered. 31. Not an absolute necessity of the means: against the Papists; the objection answered. 32. Place. Time. 33. Baptism is not to be repeated: against the Anabaptists. 34. The opinion of the Papists; the objection answered. 35. The Lord's Supper. Its institution. Primary efficient cause. Minister. 36. Subject. Bread. The Papists rightly use wafers of flour? They wrongly use crumbs of flour. Whether unleavened bread should be used. A cup of wine. 37. The use of the cup is necessary: against the Papists; the objection answered. 38. Consecration. It is not effected by the words, This is my body, etc.: against the Papists. 39. The breaking and distribution of the bread. 40. Private mass. The bread is to be put into the hands. It is not to be kept for worship: against the Papists. 41. The rite concerning the wine. The actions of the communicants. On kneeling. 42. The thing signified. 43. Form. Sacramental predications. 44. The ends. 45. Comparison of the Mass: in the name, author, ministers. 46. In the matter. Form. 47. Transubstantiation is refuted: against the Papists. 48. Objections answered. 49. Consubstantiation refuted: against the Lutherans; the objection answered. 50. The sacrifice of the Mass refuted: against the Papists. 51. Objections answered. 52. Comparison in the end and the accessories. 53. The false sacraments of the Papists. Confirmation. 54. Repentance. 55. Extreme unction. 56. Ordination. 57. Marriage. 58. The opinion of the Anabaptists and Remonstrants concerning the washing of feet. 59. Practice. 60.

units.la: I. Sequitur Obsignatio, de qua 2 Cor. I, 22. Qui (Deus) etiam obsignavit nos. Eph. I, 13, IV, 30.
units.tr: I. Next comes sealing, concerning which see 2 Cor. 1:22: "[God] who also has sealed us." Eph. 1:13; 4:30.

units.la: Est autem actus gratiosus moralis, quo certis quibusdam pignoribus & sigillis, in nobis confirmatur subjectiva certitudo mysticę communionis Christi & Ecclesiæ ipsius, atque adeò gratiæ salutaris.
units.tr: It is a gracious, moral act by which, through certain pledges and seals, the subjective certainty of the mystical communion of Christ and of his Church itself, and thus of saving grace, is confirmed in us.

units.la: Actum moralem dicimus: quia per eam subjectiva certitudo in nobis confirmatur, per quædam pignora & sigilla; quorum propria efficacia moralis est. Gratiosum addimus: quia singularis gratia sic nobis persuadetur, & quidem ex gratiâ ad salutem nostram ordinata.
units.tr: We call it a moral act because through it subjective certainty is confirmed in us by certain pledges and seals, whose proper efficacy is moral. We add gracious because a singular grace is thus made persuasive to us, and indeed a grace ordained from grace for our salvation.

units.la: Effectus proprius est subjectiva certitudo mysticæ communionis Christi & Ecclesiæ ipsius; atque adeò gratiæ salutaris.
units.tr: The proper effect is the subjective certainty of the mystical communion of Christ and of his Church itself, and thus of saving grace.

units.la: II. Causa efficiens proponitur tum Deus Pater; tum Christus Salvator; tum proximè respectu ordinis, Sp. S. 2 Cor. I. 21,22. Deus obsignavit nos, indiditque arrhabonem Spiritus cordibus nostris. Gal. iv. 6. Eph. I, 13. iv, 30. Aque ista est obsignatio interna.
units.tr: II. The efficient cause is set forth as God the Father, as Christ the Saviour, and most immediately, with respect to order, the Holy Spirit. 2 Cor. 1:21, 22: "God sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit into our hearts." Gal. 4:6; Eph. 1:13; 4:30. This is the internal sealing.

units.la: Media quædam externa accedunt à quibus etiam denominatur obsignatio externa: signa speciatim à Deo ad istum usum destinata.
units.tr: Certain external means are added, from which the external sealing is also named: signs, specifically appointed by God for this use.

units.la: Signum est ejusmodi res, quæ sensibus primùm percepta, & ad intellectûm delata, huic rem aliam cognoscendam offert. Hæc autem sunt alia naturalis; alia arbitraria. Arbitraria vel ex institutione Divinâ, vel humanâ, significant.
units.tr: A sign is a thing which, first perceived by the senses and conveyed to the intellect, presents another thing to be known. Signs are of two kinds: some natural, others arbitrary. Arbitrary signs signify either by divine institution or by human.

units.la: Ad nostram consideratione pertinent signa ex institutione Divina significantia: quæ, ratione rerum significatarum, sunt vel rememorativa rerum præteritarum; vel demonstrativa præsentium; vel præ〈nun〉ciativa futurarum; vel ex his tribus composita. Similiter ratione usûs, vel inserviunt intellectui; & sunt signa notificantia: vel memoriæ; & sunt commonefacientia: vel fidei; & sunt obsignantia: vel illis omnibus inserviunt simul. Atque hujusmodi sunt signa & sigilla sacra, quæ vulgò Sacramenta appellantur. Rom. iv, 11. Accepit signum Circumcisionis, sigillum justitiæ fidei receptæ in præputio. Confer Gen. 17. 7, 10, 11, Exod. 11, 11,-14.
units.tr: For our purpose the signs of divine institution are relevant. With respect to the things signified, these are either reminders of past things, or demonstrations of present things, or announcements of future things, or a combination of these three. Likewise with respect to use: either they serve the intellect, and are notifying signs; or the memory, and are admonishing; or faith, and are sealing; or all of these together. Such are the holy signs and seals which are commonly called sacraments. Rom. 4:11: "He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while still uncircumcised." Compare Gen. 17:7, 10, 11; Exod. 11:11-14.

units.la: III. Sacramenti vox origine Latina est; āverbo Sacro deducta. Notabat autem antiquitus oppignorationem pecuniæ, quæ à litigantibus fiebat in loco sacro, ea conditione, ut victor deinde pecuniam suam auferret, victus vero suam apud Pontificem relinqueret. Ita sacram quandam obligationem significabat. Specialis etiàm istius vocabuli usus erat in militia, de juramento, quo se milites, ad fidem & obedientiam Imperatori præstandam, obligabant. Hinc Antiqui Ecclesiæ Doctores videntur vocem illam ad militiam Christianam transtulisse.
units.tr: III. The word sacrament is Latin in origin, derived from the word sacred. Anciently it denoted the pledging of money which litigants made in a sacred place, on the condition that the winner would then take back his money and the loser would leave his with the Pontiff. Thus it signified a certain sacred obligation. The word also had a special use in the military, of the oath by which soldiers bound themselves to render faith and obedience to the Emperor. Hence the ancient Doctors of the Church seem to have transferred that word to the Christian warfare.

units.la: Græcè Μυστήριον appellatur; à verbo μύω, claudo, comprimo: unde μύστης, sacris initiatus, vel eorum peritus. In N. T. itemque in Græcâ Versione V. T. nec non in Libris apocryphis vox illa aliquoties occurrit: & quidem generalius de re arcana; Tob. 12. 7. Sir. 27. 16. 2 Thess. II, 7. vel minus generaliter, de re arcana aliquid significante, Dan. 2, 18, 19, 27, 28, 29, 30, 47. Apoc. 17, 7. aut de re arcana sacra; Matth. 13, 11. Rom. 16, 25. 1 Cor. XV, 51. 1 Tim. 3: 16. Col. I, 26, 27. Eph. 1, 9. v. 32. vel specialius, de re sacra aliquid significante; Apoc. I, 20.
units.tr: In Greek it is called mysterion [Μυστήριον], from the verb myō, to close, to shut up; whence mystēs, one initiated into the sacred rites, or skilled in them. In the New Testament, likewise in the Greek version of the Old Testament, and in the Apocrypha, the word occurs several times: more generally, of a secret thing, Tob. 12:7; Sir. 27:16; 2 Thess. 2:7; or less generally, of a secret thing signifying something, Dan. 2:18, 19, 27-30, 47; Rev. 17:7; or of a secret sacred thing, Matt. 13:11; Rom. 16:25; 1 Cor. 15:51; 1 Tim. 3:16; Col. 1:26, 27; Eph. 1:9; 5:32; or most specially, of a sacred thing signifying something, Rev. 1:20.

units.la: IV. Rem ipsam hic obviam, & vocabulo Sacramenti significari solitam, describimus, quòd sit, Sacrum & visibile signum ac sigillum à Deo & Christo in usum Ecclesiæ militantis institutum, & prædicationi Euangelicæ annexum, ad promissa Fœderis gratiæ amplius declaranda atque obsignanda, & fidem ac obedientiam Ecclesiæ confirmandam.
units.tr: IV. We describe the thing itself, which is met with here and is usually signified by the word sacrament, as: a holy and visible sign and seal, instituted by God and Christ for the use of the militant Church and annexed to the preaching of the Gospel, to declare and seal more fully the promises of the covenant of grace, and to confirm the faith and obedience of the Church.

units.la: Sacrum & visibile signum ac sigillum dicimus: quia ipsum sic in sensus externos incurrit, & speciatim oculis conspicitur, ut rem Deo insigniter gloriosam ac nobis salutarem intellectui offerat; eandem sc. quæ Verbo Euangelii prædicatur.
units.tr: We say a holy and visible sign and seal because it so falls under the external senses, and is especially seen by the eyes, that it offers to the intellect a thing gloriously remarkable to God and salutary to us: namely the same thing which is proclaimed in the Word of the Gospel.

units.la: V. Hujus Auctor necessariò Deus est; tum quia est pars Religionis, & signaculum Fœderis à Deo inter fe & electos vocatos erecti. Genef. 17,7, 9. - 14. Exod, 12, 2, 11, 13, 25, 26, 27. Matth. 3, 15. XXVIII, 18, 19. 1 Cor. XI, 20, 23, 24, 25, X, 16. Solus enim Deus partes Religionis jure suo constituere potest: Ezech. XX, 18, 19. Ief. XXIX, 13. Matth. XV, 9. Iac. IV, 12. Confer Deut. IV, 2, XII, 32. Prov. 30, 6. Et Omnis ἐθελοθρησκεία damnatur; Col. 2, 13. Levit. 10, 1, 2. Tum quia ipse solus beneficia promissa efficaciter praestare potest & vult: atque adeo solus eorum praestandorum certa signa & sigilla potest instituere.
units.tr: V. Its author is necessarily God: both because it is a part of religion and a seal of the covenant established by God between himself and the elect who are called. Gen. 17:7, 9-14; Exod. 12:2, 11, 13, 25-27; Matt. 3:15; 28:18, 19; 1 Cor. 11:20, 23-25; 10:16. For God alone can establish the parts of religion by his own right: Ezek. 20:18, 19; Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:9; James 4:12. Compare Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:6. And all self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] is condemned: Col. 2:13; Lev. 10:1, 2. Also because he alone can actually and willingly bestow the promised benefits, and so he alone can institute certain signs and seals of them.

units.la: Institutio complectitur mandatum erga homines, & promissionem beneficii Divini.
units.tr: Institution comprises the command laid upon men and the promise of divine benefit.

units.la: Hominibus mandata est administratio certo quodam modo peragenda, juxta auctoris placitum. Talem administrandi modum & finem intendere debet Minister: 1 Cor. 4, 2. Jerem. 48, 10. Perperam tamen Pontificii statuunt, efficaciam & essentiam Sacramentorum pendere ex Ministri intentione. Quicquid enim fuerit de intentione Ministri, cum solus Deus καρδιογνώστης, 1 Reg. 8, 39. si externa nobis conspicua administratio, sit institutioni Divinae consentanea, fideles Sacramentum recipientes bonorum promissorum procul dubio redduntur participes. Huc applicari potest illud Apostoli, Rom. 3, 3, 4. Quid tum, si infidi fuerunt quidam? Num ipsorum infidelitas fidem Dei cassam reddet? Absit: imo esto Deus verax; omnis autem homo mendax. Similiter 2 Tim. 2, 13. Confer de Ministris per invidiam & contentionem, ac non pure, Euangelium praedicantibus; Phil. I, 15, - 18.
units.tr: The administration is entrusted to men, to be carried out in a certain manner, according to the will of the author. The minister ought to intend this manner and end of administering: 1 Cor. 4, 2. Jer. 48, 10. Yet the Papists wrongly hold that the efficacy and essence of the sacraments depend on the minister's intention. For whatever the minister's intention may be, since God alone is the heart-knower [καρδιογνώστης], 1 Kings 8, 39, if the outward administration visible to us agrees with divine institution, the faithful who receive the sacrament are without doubt made partakers of the promised good things. To this may be applied the saying of the Apostle, Rom. 3, 3, 4: "What then, if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness make the faith of God void? God forbid; yea, let God be true, but every man a liar." Similarly 2 Tim. 2, 13. Compare those ministers who preach the Gospel out of envy and strife, and not purely, Phil. 1, 15-18.

units.la: Administrationi illi respondet aliorum perceptio; quae secundum institutionem quoque fieri debet: ita quidem ut ipsa signa, eaque integre, percipiantur; imo & eo modo ac fine, ut requirit Divina institutio.
units.tr: To that administration corresponds the reception of others, which must also take place according to the institution: in such a way that the signs themselves are received whole, and indeed in the manner and for the end that the divine institution requires.

units.la: Accedit promissio bonorum spiritualium ac salutarium, Fœdere gratiæ comprehensorum, cujus sunt ista signacula: Itâ sc. Verbo, tùm institutionis, tùm promissionis, accedente ad Elementum, fit Sacramentum. Verbum institutionis Divinæ efficit signum Divinum: Verbum promissionis efficit sigillum.
units.tr: To this is added the promise of spiritual and saving goods, contained in the covenant of grace, of which these are the seals. Thus, when the word of institution and the word of promise are added to the element, a sacrament comes into being. The word of divine institution makes the sign a divine sign; the word of promise makes it a seal.

units.la: Itâ statim hîc obvia est quædam mutatio, non substantiæ, aut essentiæ signi, in rem signatam: sed relativa mutatio, quâ talis res præter naturam suam, ex Divinâ institutione, fit signum ac sigillum rerum istiusmodi spiritualium.
units.tr: Thus there is at once a certain change, not of the substance or essence of the sign into the thing signified, but a relative change, by which such a thing, beyond its own nature, becomes by divine institution a sign and seal of such spiritual things.

units.la: VI. Subjectum & quasi materiam constituit, tùm substantia, metonymicè elementum appellata, & res terrena, vel etiàm species; tùm ritus, & actiones quædam solennes, circa substantiam illam observandæ, juxta institutionem Dei.
units.tr: VI. The subject, as it were the matter, consists both of the substance, called the element by metonymy, and the earthly thing, or even the species; and of the rites and certain solemn actions to be observed concerning that substance, according to the institution of God.

units.la: Objectum, sive res significata, est communio Fœderis Divini, & quidem Evangelici. Communio illa vel externa considerari potest, vel interna. Quantùm ad externam; hactenùs aliqui saltem externâ fidei & pietatis professione sese à mundi impuritate segregant, & cultui Divino in Ecclesiâ institutâ obstringunt: Deut. 26, 17, 18, 19. Exod. 20, 2. Psal. 81, 9, 11, 12, 14. Matth. 13, 41. VIII, 21.
units.tr: The object, or thing signified, is the communion of the divine covenant, and indeed of the Gospel. This communion may be considered either external or internal. As to the external, so far at least some separate themselves from the impurity of the world by an outward profession of faith and piety, and bind themselves to the divine worship instituted in the Church: Deut. 26, 17, 18, 19. Exod. 20, 2. Ps. 81, 9, 11, 12, 14. Matt. 13, 41. 8, 21.

units.la: Ad internam communionem quod attinet; Deus verè regenitis & fidelibus promittit, se ex gratiâ in Christo communicaturum iis omnia beneficia salutaria, quæ ad vitam & pietatem pertinent. Itâ Circumcisio sigillum justitiæ fidei appellatur, Rom. 4, 11. Vide insuper Job. 1, 16, 17. 2 Petr. 1, 4. Verùm etiàm Deus vicissim fidem & obedientiam sinceram stipulatur: Gen. 17, 1, 2. Ego Deus omnisufficiens; Ambula coram me, & esto perfectus. Ponamque pactum meum, &c. Marc. 16, 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, -. 1 Petr. 3, 21.
units.tr: As for the internal communion: God truly promises to the regenerate and faithful that, out of grace in Christ, he will impart to them all the saving benefits that pertain to life and godliness. Thus circumcision is called the seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4, 11. See further Job 1, 16, 17. 2 Pet. 1, 4. But God in turn also requires sincere faith and obedience: Gen. 17, 1, 2: "I am God Almighty; walk before me and be perfect. And I will establish my covenant," etc. Mark 16, 16: "He who believes and is baptized..." 1 Pet. 3, 21.

units.la: VII. Quasi forma Sacramenti consistit in speciali quâdam relatione talis signi ad talem rem signatam; ad visibilem significationem & obsignationem Fœderis gratiæ, & communionis etiam internæ mysticæ ac verè salutaris in isto Fœdere, pro verè fidelibus. Hæc unio sacramentalis quibusdam dicitur; quia inter duos terminos intercedit, eosque mutuo respectu quasi unit. Verùm res signata nobiscum potiùs unitur: Joh. 6, 56, 57. Qui edit Meam carnem, & bibit Meum sanguinem, in Me manet, & Ego in eo. &c. 1 Cor. 12, 13. Gal. 2, 20. Eph. 3, 17. Atque ista rei signatæ nobiscum unio, signis illis indicatur & confirmatur.
units.tr: VII. The form, as it were, of the sacrament consists in a special relation of such a sign to such a thing signified; in the visible signification and sealing of the covenant of grace, and also of the internal, mystical and truly saving communion in that covenant, for those who are truly faithful. This is called by some the sacramental union, because it lies between two terms and, by their mutual relation, as it were unites them. Yet the thing signified is united with us rather: John 6, 56, 57: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him," etc. 1 Cor. 12, 13. Gal. 2, 20. Eph. 3, 17. And this union of the thing signified with us is indicated and confirmed by those signs.

units.la: Unio illa Sacramentalis est relativa, partim posita in quâdam similitudine signi & rei signatæ: partim in certitudine rei obsignatæ, percipiendæ in legitimo signi usû, secundùm promissionem institutioni annexam. Sic autem signum & res signata simul percipiuntur in usû legitimo; ut patet de Circumcisione, Gen. 17, 7, 11. De Paschate, Exod. 12, 13. De Baptismo, Marc. 16, 16. Gal. III, 27. Rom. 6, 4. Et de S. Coenâ, 1 Cor. X, 16.
units.tr: This sacramental union is relative, partly placed in a certain likeness of the sign and the thing signified, partly in the certainty of the thing sealed, to be received in the lawful use of the sign, according to the promise annexed to the institution. In this way the sign and the thing signified are received together in lawful use, as is clear concerning circumcision, Gen. 17, 7, 11; concerning the Passover, Exod. 12, 13; concerning baptism, Mark 16, 16; Gal. 3, 27; Rom. 6, 4; and concerning the Lord's Supper, 1 Cor. 10, 16.

units.la: Neque tamen similiter, eodemque instrumento, percipiuntur signum & res signata: sed signum foris visibiliter per Ministrum offertur, & à fidelibus corporaliter accipitur; res verò signata ab ipso Domino intùs confertur; & à nobis spiritualiter per fidem recipitur: Matth. 3, 11. Col. 2, 11, 12. 1 Petr. 3, 21.
units.tr: Yet the sign and the thing signified are not received in the same way and by the same instrument: the sign is offered outwardly and visibly by the minister and is received bodily by the faithful; but the thing signified is conferred inwardly by the Lord himself and is received by us spiritually through faith: Matt. 3, 11. Col. 2, 11, 12. 1 Pet. 3, 21.

units.la: VIII. In ista, quam diximus, relatione, & unione Sacramentali, fundantur Prædicationes Sacramentales; quibus nomina & attributa signi & rei signatæ inter se permutantur. Hæc metonymia in aliis signis quoque usurpatur: sic Gen. 41, 26, 27. septem vaccæ dicuntur septem anni, cum annorum essent signa. Adde Dan. 4, 20, 21. VII, 17, 23, 24. Matth. 13, 37, 38, 39. Apoc. 17, 9, 12.
units.tr: VIII. On the relation and sacramental union which we have described are founded the sacramental predications, in which the names and attributes of the sign and of the thing signified are interchanged. This metonymy is used also in other signs: thus in Gen. 41, 26, 27 the seven cows are called seven years, though they were signs of years. Add Dan. 4, 20, 21; 7, 17, 23, 24. Matt. 13, 37, 38, 39. Rev. 17, 9, 12.

units.la: Nihil mirum igitur, si in Sacramentis quoque ufmodi locutiones metonymicæ usurpentur. Ità Circumcisio vocatur pactum, cùm esset signum pacti, Gen. 17, 13, 11. Rom. 4, 11. Similiter de Pasche, Exod. 12, 11, 12, 13, 27. Atque item in cæteris Sacramentis, quod est rerum signatarum tribuitur signis; contrà: 1 Cor. 10, 4. Act. xxii, 16, Tit. 3, 5. Luc. xxii, 19, 1 Cor. xi, 24, 25, 26. x, 16.
units.tr: It is no wonder, therefore, if such metonymical expressions are used also of the sacraments. Thus circumcision is called the covenant, though it was the sign of the covenant, Gen. 17, 13, 11. Rom. 4, 11. Similarly of the Passover, Exod. 12, 11, 12, 13, 27. And likewise in the other sacraments, what belongs to the things signified is attributed to the signs, and conversely: 1 Cor. 10, 4. Acts 22, 16. Titus 3, 5. Luke 22, 19. 1 Cor. 11, 24, 25, 26; 10, 16.

units.la: IX. Finis cujus proximus est significatio & obsignatio mysterii Fœderis gratiæ. Hùc pertinent, tum bona nobis à Deo promissa; tum fidei & obedientiæ nostræ confirmatio. Ex quibus significatio, oblivionem gratiæ; obsignatio verò, diffidentiam atque inobedientiam in nobis corrigit.
units.tr: IX. The proximate end is the signifying and sealing of the mystery of the covenant of grace. To this belong both the good things promised to us by God and the confirmation of our faith and obedience. By the signifying, forgetfulness of grace is corrected; by the sealing, distrust and disobedience in us are corrected.

units.la: Remotus, est Fœderatorum salus, dum per ea media moraliter fides & obedientia nostra excitantur & foventur. Hactenùs Sacramenta rectè dicuntur efficacia instrumenta gratiæ. Quia tamen salutem non præstant immediatè & per se, dicimus, eorum privationem non damnari, sed contemtum.
units.tr: The remote end is the salvation of those in the covenant, while through these means our faith and obedience are morally stirred up and nourished. In this respect sacraments are rightly called efficacious instruments of grace. Yet because they do not bestow salvation immediately and of themselves, we say that their privation is not condemned, but contempt is.

units.la: Summus, est gratiæ Dei in Christo gloria; dum illa his symbolis significatur & obsignatur: quo respectu etiàm metaphoricè Sacrificia eucharistica appellantur. Confer Hebr. 13, 15, 16. Rom. 12, 1.
units.tr: The highest end is the glory of God's grace in Christ, while that grace is signified and sealed by these symbols; in this respect the sacrifices are also metaphorically called eucharistic sacrifices. Compare Heb. 13, 15, 16. Rom. 12, 1.

units.la: Finis, cui sunt omnes Deo Fœderati in Ecclesiâ visibili ac militante: sed cum hoc discrimine, quòd vere fideles Sacramenta recipiant, ut sigilla justitiæ fidei ipsis imputatæ: Gen. 17, 1, 7. Rom. 4, 11. Marc. 16, 16. Act. 2, 38. viii, 37. 1 Cor. xi, 28. Cæteri non item; quoniam fide justificante carent; sed hypothetice tantum, si resipiscerent, & verè in Christum crederent. Vide Matth. 3, 7, 8. Act. 8, 13, 21, 22. Confer Isf. 66, 3. Hag. 2, 12, -15. Rom. 2, 25, 28. 1 Cor. xi, 20, 27, 29, 30.
units.tr: The end for whom are all those in covenant with God in the visible and militant Church; but with this difference, that the truly faithful receive the sacraments as seals of the righteousness of faith imputed to them: Gen. 17, 1, 7. Rom. 4, 11. Mark 16, 16. Acts 2, 38; 8, 37. 1 Cor. 11, 28. The others do not, since they lack justifying faith, but only hypothetically, if they should repent and truly believe in Christ. See Matt. 3, 7, 8. Acts 8, 13, 21, 22. Compare Isa. 66, 3. Hag. 2, 12-15. Rom. 2, 25, 28. 1 Cor. 11, 20, 27, 29, 30.

units.la: X. Ex superioribus patet, in excessu peccare Pontificios; dum Sacramentis realem efficientiam tribuunt: & eorum magis proprium dicunt sanctifica-re, re, quàm significare: nam 1. Signa diserte appellantur; Gen. 17, 11. Exod. 12, 13. Rom. 4, 11. Hactenùs autem eadem est ratio Sacramentorum V. & N. Test.
units.tr: X. From what has gone before it is clear that the Papists sin by excess, when they attribute a real efficacy to the sacraments and say that their proper function is to sanctify rather than to signify. For (1) signs are expressly so called: Gen. 17, 11. Exod. 12, 13. Rom. 4, 11. Thus far, indeed, the reasoning of the sacraments of the Old and New Testament is the same.

units.la: 2. Realis efficientia iis derogatur; quatenùs externè per Ministros conferuntur. Matth. 3, 11. 1 Petr. 3, 21. 1 Cor. 3, 6, 7.
units.tr: (2) Real efficacy is denied to them, insofar as they are conferred outwardly by ministers: Matt. 3, 11. 1 Pet. 3, 21. 1 Cor. 3, 6, 7.

units.la: 3. Sacramenta, cum sint corporea, non possunt reali efficientiâ, directè, & per se, agere in animam, substantiam immaterialem; ibique sic, effectus spirituales producere.
units.tr: 3. Since the sacraments are corporeal, they cannot act directly and in themselves upon the soul, an immaterial substance, by a real efficacy, and so produce spiritual effects there.

units.la: 4. Realis ista efficientia ad aliam causam refertur satis apertè; ad Christum scil. & Sp. S. qui realiter nobis applicat bona salutaria. Matth. 3, 11. Is qui post me venit, validior me est; -- Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu Sancto & igne. 1 Cor. 6, 11. Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed justificati estis, in nomine Domini Iesu, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Joh. 6, 63. Spiritus est id quod vivificat.
units.tr: 4. This real efficacy is clearly referred to another cause, namely Christ and the Holy Spirit, who really apply the saving benefits to us. Matt. 3:11: He who comes after me is mightier than I... He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 1 Cor. 6:11: But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. John 6:63: It is the Spirit who gives life.

units.la: XI. In defectû verò peccant Anabaptistæ; qualemcunque significationem gratiæ Divinæ, & mutuam fidelium confessionem quidem agnoscentes; non autem obsignationem promissorum Fœderis Evangelici: cum tamen, 1. Deus Circumcisionem instituens, diserte appellaverit Pactum inter se & Abrahamum ac posteritatem ejus; & Fœdus perpetuum, ut futurus esset Deus ipsorum; atque item Signum talis Pacti, Gen. 17, 7, 9, 10, 11. sicut & Paulus diserte Sigillum justitiæ fidei appellavit, Rom. 4, 11.
units.tr: XI. The Anabaptists err by defect, since they acknowledge some kind of signification of divine grace and the mutual confession of believers, but not the sealing of the promises of the Gospel covenant. Yet, (1) when God instituted circumcision, he expressly called it a covenant between himself and Abraham and his posterity, and an everlasting covenant that he would be their God, and likewise a sign of that covenant (Gen. 17:7, 9, 10, 11); just as Paul also expressly called it a seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11).

units.la: 2. Similiter Agnus Paschalis obsignavit liberationem, ac potissimum spiritualem: Exod. 12, 11, 12, 13. cum 1 Cor. 5, 7. Joh. 1, 29. xix, 33, 36. Addè Joh. 19, 33, 36. cum Exod. 12, 46. Num. 9, 12.
units.tr: (2) Likewise the Paschal Lamb sealed deliverance, and especially spiritual deliverance (Exod. 12:11, 12, 13), compare 1 Cor. 5:7; John 1:29; 19:33, 36. Add John 19:33, 36 with Exod. 12:46 and Num. 9:12.

units.la: 3. In Sacramento extraordinario, patres eandem escam spiritualem comederunt, & eundem potum spiritualem biberunt: 1 Cor. 10, 4. scil. obsignativè.
units.tr: (3) In the extraordinary sacrament, the fathers ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink (1 Cor. 10:4), namely in a sealing manner.

units.la: 4. Ubi de Sacramentis Novi Testamenti agitur, effectus spiritualis & salutaris iis metonymicè tribuitur, aut cum iis conjungitur; Marc. 16, 16. Act. 2, 38, 39. XXII, 16. Rom. 6, 4. 1 Cor. 12, 13. Gal. 3, 27. Eph. 5, 26. Tit. 3. 5. Unde ista obsignatio, & certitudinis subjectivæ in fidelibus confirmatio, iterum patescit.
units.tr: (4) Where the sacraments of the New Testament are discussed, a spiritual and saving effect is attributed to them by metonymy, or is joined with them (Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38, 39; 22:16; Rom. 6:4; 1 Cor. 12:13; Gal. 3:27; Eph. 5:26; Titus 3:5). Hence this sealing, and the confirmation of subjective certainty in believers, again becomes plain.

units.la: XII. De Sacramentis Fœderi Legali
units.tr: XII. On the Sacraments of the Legal Covenant

units.la: ante adjectis diximus sup. cap. 9, th. 120-. Fœderi gratiæ sub Euangelio promissionis & V. T. annexa etiam fuerunt Sacramenta, tum ordinaria, tum extraordinaria. Ordinaria autem erant vel initiationis, ut Circumcisio; vel corroborationis, ut Agnus Paschalis. Vide sup. cap. 2, th. 21, 22, 23.
units.tr: We have said above, in chapter 9, theses 120 onward, that sacraments, both ordinary and extraordinary, were also attached to the covenant of grace under the Gospel promise in the Old Testament. The ordinary sacraments were either of initiation, such as circumcision, or of confirmation, such as the Paschal Lamb. See above, chapter 2, theses 21, 22, 23.

units.la: Perperam dicunt Pontificii, Sacramenta V. T. differre à Sacramentis N. T. ut Typos à suis Prototypis, & Sacramenta V. T. fuisse figuras Sacramentorum N. T. Nam 1. fuit eadem gratia salutaris sub V. T. quæ est sub Novo; & consequenter, eadem bona salutaria Sacramentis illis obsignata fuerunt fidelibus istius temporis. Vide sup. cap. 2. th. 15,-18.
units.tr: The Papists wrongly say that the sacraments of the Old Testament differ from those of the New as types differ from their prototypes, and that the sacraments of the Old Testament were figures of the sacraments of the New. For (1) under the Old Testament there was the same saving grace as under the New, and consequently the same saving benefits were sealed to the believers of that time by those sacraments. See above, chapter 2, theses 15 to 18.

units.la: 2. Etiam in Sacramentis fuit eadem promissio Fœderis perpetui, & communionis cum Deo: Gen. 17, 7, 9. cum Act. 2, 38, 39.
units.tr: (2) In the sacraments there was also the same promise of the everlasting covenant and of communion with God (Gen. 17:7, 9), compare Acts 2:38, 39.

units.la: 3. Idem fuit effectus illorum Sacramentorum pro illis fidelibus, qui est nostrorum pro nobis. Sic Abrahamus diserte dicitur accepisse signum Circumcisionis; sigillum justitiæ fidei, in præputio ipsi imputatæ; Rom. 6, 11. Quod non debet putari solius Abrahami privilegium; cum ad semen ipsius idem quoque Fœdus perpetuum, eademque promissio, evidenter extendatur ibidem verf. 11, 12. Quin & ipsi Pontificii quandoque Circumcisionem appellant remedium adversus peccatum originale, &c.
units.tr: (3) The effect of those sacraments for those believers was the same as ours is for us. Thus Abraham is expressly said to have received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith, which was imputed to him while uncircumcised (Rom. 4:11). This ought not to be thought a privilege of Abraham alone, since the same everlasting covenant and the same promise are clearly extended to his seed in the same place (vv. 11, 12). Indeed the Papists themselves sometimes call circumcision a remedy against original sin, etc.

units.la: 4. Propterea etiam nostra Sacramenta transferuntur ad fideles V. T.; quòd illi eandem rem significatam habuerint sub aliis symbolis, 1 Cor. 10, 1,-4. Et vicissim Sacramenta V. T. transferuntur ad fideles N. T. quatenus sub aliis symbolis eandem rem spiritualem percipiunt; Col. II, 11, 12, 13. 1 Cor. 5, 7, 8.
units.tr: (4) For this reason our sacraments are also applied to the believers of the Old Testament, because they had the same thing signified under other symbols (1 Cor. 10:1–4). And conversely the sacraments of the Old Testament are applied to believers of the New Testament, inasmuch as under other symbols they receive the same spiritual thing (Col. 2:11, 12, 13; 1 Cor. 5:7, 8).

units.la: Obj. 1. Circumcisio nihil esse dicitur, 1 Cor. 7, 19. & in Christo nihil valere, Gal. 6, 15. Ergo. Resp. Istic manifeste agitur de ejus observantia citra fidem, & sub N. T. postquam Lex cerimonialis, unâ cum Sacramentis V. T. abrogata fuit.
units.tr: Objection 1. Circumcision is said to be nothing (1 Cor. 7:19), and to avail nothing in Christ (Gal. 6:15). Therefore... Reply: this plainly speaks of its observance apart from faith, and under the New Testament, after the ceremonial law was abrogated together with the sacraments of the Old Testament.

units.la: Obj. 2. Lex cerimonialis solum complectebatur umbras & typos rerum futurarum: Iob. I, 17. Col. II, 17. Hebr. 10, 1. 1 Petr. 3, 21. Ergo. Resp. Corpus sic adumbratum fuit Christus, in carnem venturus, & fundamentalem conditionem salutis reipsâ praestiturus. Verum ista non fuerunt signa nostrorum signorum, sive Sacramentorum: quanquam haec sunt signa analogice respondentia Sacramentis V. T.
units.tr: Objection 2. The ceremonial law embraced only the shadows and types of things to come (John 1:17; Col. 2:17; Heb. 10:1; 1 Pet. 3:21). Therefore... Reply: the body was thus foreshadowed, namely Christ, who was to come in the flesh and actually to furnish the fundamental condition of salvation. But these were not signs of our signs, that is, of sacraments, although these are signs analogically corresponding to the sacraments of the Old Testament.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Duo autem sunt Sacramenta N. T. Baptismus, & Coena Dominica: quę duo conjunctim proponuntur, 1 Cor. 12, 13, „Etenim per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, „& Judæi, & Græci, & servi & liberi: & omnes „potu sumus in unum Spiritum. x, 1,-4. Atque alibi „ista duo clare & distincte commemorantur; non „autem plura.
units.tr: There are two Sacraments of the New Testament, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. These two are set forth together in 1 Cor. 12, 13: "For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free, and have all been made to drink into one Spirit," and in 10, 1-4. Elsewhere these two are clearly and distinctly named, but no more.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Baptismus est prius N. T. Sacramentum; quo, juxta Verbum institutionis & promissionis Divinæ, per externam corporis ablutionem aquâ factam, infirmio in communionem Christi atque Ecclesiæ ipsius, & spiritualis ablutio peccatorum per Christi sanguinem ac Spiritum, fidelibus significatur atque obsignatur.
units.tr: Baptism is the first Sacrament of the New Testament, by which, according to the Word of Divine institution and promise, the external washing of the body with water signifies and seals to believers their incorporation into the communion of Christ and his Church, and the spiritual washing away of sins through the blood and Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Βάπτειν, & βαπτίζειν, unde βαπτισμός deducitur, notant mergere & tingere: quæ quia ad lotionem, vel ablutionem adhiberi solent, βαπτίζειν metonymicē etiam significat lavare, vel abluere. Ita Luc. xi, 38. Pharisæus admirabatur Christum non ablu-tum fuisse (ὁ δὲ ἰδὼν πρῶτον ἐβαπτίσθη) ante prandium. Confer Marc. 7, 2, 4. atque in Apocryphis, de Iudithâ, 12, 7.
units.tr: Dipping and dyeing are what βάπτειν and βαπτίζειν mean [βάπτειν, βαπτίζειν], and from these βαπτισμός is derived. Since these words are commonly used for washing or cleansing, βαπτίζειν by metonymy also means to wash or to cleanse. Thus in Luke 11, 38, the Pharisee marvelled that Christ had not washed himself [ὁ δὲ ἰδὼν πρῶτον ἐβαπτίσθη] before dinner. Compare Mark 7, 2, 4, and in the Apocrypha, Judith 12, 7.

units.la: Hinc I. magis proprie appellatur Baptismus aquæ, aut fluminis; juxta institutionem, Matth. 28, 19. III, 11.
units.tr: Hence, first, the more proper name is baptism of water or of a river, according to the institution, Matth. 28, 19; III, 11.

units.la: Ac porrò 2. improprie, Baptismus Flaminis, aut Sp. Sancti; de quo Johannes. Matth. III, 11. Baptizabit vos Sp. Sancto & igne. Act. 1, 5. Nam Spiritus Sanctus, ut animam ab inhærente peccato abluat, donisque spiritualibus imbuat, aquæ instar in eam effunditur: juxta Isai. xliv, 3. Ioël. II, 28. Act. II, 17. Zach. XII, 10.
units.tr: Secondly, improperly, there is baptism of the Wind or of the Holy Spirit, of which John speaks: Matth. III, 11. "He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." Acts 1, 5. For the Holy Spirit is poured into the soul like water, to wash it from indwelling sin and to imbue it with spiritual gifts, according to Isa. 44, 3; Joel 2, 28; Acts 2, 17; Zech. 12, 10.

units.la: Atque item 3. Baptismus sanguinis, sive martyrii, & afflictionum in negotio Christi: Luc. xii, 50. Baptismo oportet me baptizari: &c. Matth. 20, 22, 23. Confer Psal. 69, 1, 15, 16. XVIII, 17, XXXII, 6.
units.tr: Likewise, thirdly, there is baptism of blood, that is, of martyrdom and of afflictions suffered in the cause of Christ: Luke 12, 50, "I have a baptism to be baptized with," etc. Matth. 20, 22, 23. Compare Ps. 69, 1, 15, 16; 18, 17; 32, 6.

units.la: Nonnulli addunt 4. Baptismum lachrymarum, sive pœnitentiæ. Vide Luc. 7, 38.
units.tr: Some add, fourthly, the baptism of tears, or of repentance. See Luke 7, 38.

units.la: XIV. Ablutio ista aqua vera ac naturali peragi debet: sic administravit Johannes Christi præcursor, juxta mandatum ipsi factum: Ioh. 1, 33. Qui misit me, ut baptizarem aqua. Adde Matth. 3, 5, 6; 11; 13, 16. Ioh. 3, 23. Atque ita Baptismum administrandum docuerunt Apostoli ac Discipuli: Act. 8, 36. Ubi cùm Philippus & Eunuchus pariter in aquam descendissent, Eunuchus in eâ à Philippo baptizatus est. Adde Act. 10, 47. Eph. v, 26. Nequaquam igitur aqua rejicienda est, cum antiquis quibusdam hæreticis; sive ex vilitatis opinione; sive prætextu verborum Matth. 3, 11. Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu Sancto & igne. Obstat institutio ipsius signi.
units.tr: XIV. This washing ought to be done with true, natural water. So John, Christ's forerunner, administered it, according to the command laid upon him: John 1, 33, "He who sent me to baptize with water." Add Matth. 3, 5, 6, 11, 13, 16; John 3, 23. So too the Apostles and Disciples taught that baptism should be administered. Acts 8, 36: when Philip and the eunuch had both gone down into the water, the eunuch was baptized in it by Philip. Add Acts 10, 47; Eph. 5, 26. Therefore water is by no means to be rejected, as some ancient heretics did, either from an opinion of its lowliness or on the pretext of the words Matth. 3, 11, "He himself shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire." The institution of the sign itself stands in the way.

units.la: Sed & aquam illam vulgarem fuisse, constat ex allegatis; non consecratam adjuratione, signatione crucis, aut ejus immissione, & olei infusione: hæc enim utut antiquitatem aliquam habent, non tamen Divinitus sunt instituta, neque ab Apostolis ac Discipulis Christi usurpata. Quod contra Pontificios observandum.
units.tr: But that the water was ordinary is clear from the passages cited. It was not consecrated by exorcism, by the sign of the cross, or by its immersion and the pouring in of oil. However ancient these practices may be, they were not divinely instituted, nor were they used by the Apostles and Disciples of Christ. This is to be observed against the Papists.

units.la: Occasio, cur hoc elementum fuerit mandatum, statim est obvia: aptitudo ad externam corporis ablutionem, quae aquâ peragitur, & quidem mundâ; insignem ἀναλογίαν habens cum interna ablutione animae, quae sanguine & Spiritû Christi peragitur. Hebr. 10, 22, 23. Adspersione purgatis cordibus à conscientiâ malâ: & abluto corpore aquâ purâ. Non ergò hic utendum aquâ lutosâ, arenâ, lacte, &c.
units.tr: The reason why this element was commanded is immediately obvious: its fitness for the external washing of the body, which is done with water, and clean water at that. It has a remarkable analogy with the internal cleansing of the soul, which is accomplished by the blood and Spirit of Christ. Heb. 10, 22, 23: "Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water." Therefore muddy water, sand, milk, and the like are not to be used here.

units.la: XV. Ablutio per aquam, vel immersione ejus qui baptizandus venit peragi potest; vel infusione, aut aspersione, aquę in ipsum. De immersione satis clara sunt quaedam loca; utpote Matth. 3, 6. Baptizabantur ab eo in Iordane. 16. Baptizatus Iesus, ascendit ex aquâ. Ioh. 3, 23. Similiter Act. 8, 38. Descenderunt ambo in aquam, Philippus & Eunuchus, Confer Rom. 6, 3, 4; 5.
units.tr: XV. Washing with water can be accomplished either by immersion of the one to be baptized, or by pouring or sprinkling water upon him. Concerning immersion, some passages are quite clear, such as Matth. 3, 6, "They were baptized by him in the Jordan"; 16, "Jesus, when baptized, came up out of the water"; John 3, 23. Similarly Acts 8, 38: "Philip and the eunuch both went down into the water." Compare Rom. 6, 3, 4, 5.

units.la: Non tamen putandum est, immersionem ad Baptismi essentiam omninò requiri; cùm neque adspersio, aut perfusio, suis rationibus destituatur: hoc sc. modo vera lotio, sive ablutio, peragitur quoque; atque itâ verus etiam est Baptismus. Confer sup. th. 13. Et Scriptura rem significatam adspersionis voce etiam exprimit, Hebr. 10, 22. Adspersione purgatis cordibus à conscientia mala. XII, 24. Accessistis ad sanguinem aspersionis, -. 1 Petr. 1, 2. Ad sanctificationem Spiritûs, per obedientiam & adspersionem sanguinis Iesû Christi. Confer. Isef. 52, 15. Sic aspergct gentes multas. Ezech. 36, 25. Spargam super vos aquam mundam; & mundabimini. Zach. 13, 1. In quibus locis, licet ad caerimoniales adspersiones V. T. videatur spectari; ipsa tamen res significata emphaticè sic exprimitur: atque in hoc modo ablutionis conservatur ἀναλογία necessaria, ac proinde etiam hactenus Baptismi essentia.
units.tr: Yet it is not to be thought that immersion is wholly required for the essence of baptism, since neither sprinkling nor pouring is without its own justification. In this way a true washing or cleansing is also accomplished, and so baptism is true as well. Compare above, ch. 13. And Scripture also expresses the thing signified by the word sprinkling: Heb. 10, 22, "Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience." 12, 24, "To the blood of sprinkling." 1 Pet. 1, 2, "To sanctification of the Spirit, through obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ." Compare Isa. 52, 15, "So shall he sprinkle many nations." Ezek. 36, 25, "I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean." Zech. 13, 1. In these places, although the ceremonial sprinklings of the Old Testament seem to be in view, the thing signified is nevertheless expressed emphatically in this way. In this mode of washing the necessary analogy is preserved, and therefore so far also the essence of baptism.

units.la: XVI. Primis jam ab excesssu Apostolorum saeculis, in usu fuisse deprehenditur trina mersio, pro numero trium Personarum Essentiae Divinae; Matth. 28, 19. Alibi tamen, utpote in Hispania jam circa annum Ioc. semel duntaxat mergebant, ad significandam unam Deitatem, atque unam Christi mortem.
units.tr: XVI. From the first centuries after the Apostles it is found that threefold immersion was in use, corresponding to the number of the three Persons of the Divine Essence: Matth. 28, 19. Elsewhere, however, as in Spain already about the year 400, they dipped only once, to signify the one Deity and the one death of Christ.

units.la: Sed neque certa verborum formula, qua inter baptizandum necessario uti debeamus, praescripta est: Christus contentus fuit praecipere, ut Apostoli prosecti docerent omnes gentes baptizantes eos in nomine, vel in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Sp. Sancti; hoc est, eos isto Sacramento per ablutionem initiantes, aut consecrantes, in religionem Dei Patris, & Filii, & Sp. Sancti; ut illius arbitrio viverent, & salutem ab eo expectarent. Non autem praecepit hanc verborum formulam sic necessario pronunciandam; Ego te baptizo in nomine Patris, &c. Confer Act. II, 38. VIII, 16. XIX, 4. de Baptismo in nomine Domini Jesu Christi. Id vero cavendum necessario, ne quo pacto S. Trinitatis confessio aboleatur.
units.tr: But neither is a fixed form of words prescribed, which we must necessarily use in baptizing. Christ was content to command that the Apostles, once sent, should teach all nations, baptizing them in the name, or into the name, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. That is, by this Sacrament, through washing, they were to initiate or consecrate them into the religion of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that they might live under his direction and look to him for salvation. He did not, however, prescribe that this formula must necessarily be pronounced in this way: "I baptize you in the name of the Father," etc. Compare Acts 2, 38; 8, 16; 19, 4, concerning baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. This, however, must necessarily be guarded against, lest in any way the confession of the Holy Trinity be abolished.

units.la: XVII. Elementum aquae in isto usu aquam mysticam significat; sanguinem ac Spiritum Christi: ut enim naturalis aqua, corporis a sordibus mundandi facultatem & usum habet; ita sanguis ac Spiritus Christi, abluendae animae a spirituali impuritate peccatorum: 1 Joh. 1, 7. Hebr. 9, 14. Apoc. 1, 5. 1 Cor. 6, 11. Ezech. 36, 25, 27. Confer Psal. 51, 4, 9. Peccata sunt maculae, sordes, & immunditia spiritualis. Ista autem macula annexum habet reatum. Mundatio vero, sive ablutio, ratione reatus, fit per Justificationem; ratione ipsius maculae, per Regenerationem & Sanctificationem: quae beneficia Christus nobis impetravit, sanguine suo pro nobis fuso in oblationem vere expiatoriam. Atque istam virtutem perpetuam redem-
units.tr: XVII. The element of water, in this use, signifies mystical water: the blood and Spirit of Christ. For just as natural water has the power and use of cleansing the body from filth, so the blood and Spirit of Christ have the power of washing the soul from the spiritual impurity of sins: 1 John 1, 7; Heb. 9, 14; Rev. 1, 5; 1 Cor. 6, 11; Ezek. 36, 25, 27. Compare Ps. 51, 4, 9. Sins are stains, filth, and spiritual uncleanness. This stain carries guilt with it. Cleansing, or washing, with respect to guilt, takes place through justification; with respect to the stain itself, through regeneration and sanctification. Christ obtained these benefits for us, his blood having been poured out for us as a truly expiatory offering. And this perpetual virtue of redemption

units.la: * ptizo in nomine Patris redemtis efficaciter applicat per Spiritum suum.
units.tr: * ... he effectively applies to the redeemed through his Spirit.

units.la: XVIII. Ad Elementum accedit triplex Ritus; Immerfio in aquam, aut aspersio vel perfusio aquæ, per quam fit ablutio; 2. Mora aliqua sub aquâ; & 3. emerfio, aut aquæ diffluxus, vel abfterfio.
units.tr: XVIII. To the element three rites are added: first, immersion in water, or the sprinkling or pouring of water, through which the washing is effected; second, some pause under the water; and third, emersion, or the draining off or wiping away of the water.

units.la: In his conjunctim spectatis inest primò, quantum attinet ad præterita, commemoratio passionis, mortis, & sepulturæ Christi, atque item resurrectionis ipsius: Rom. 4. 25.
units.tr: In these rites, viewed together, there is, first, as regards past things, a commemoration of the passion, death, and burial of Christ, and likewise of his resurrection: Rom. 4, 25.

units.la: Secundò, quod ad bona præsentia attinet, immerfio in aquam demonstrat & obsignat, quemadmodùm & adspersio vel perfusio aquæ, conjunctionem & unionem mysticam cùm Christo, ut capite; & cum Ecclesiâ, ut corpore ipsius: 1 Cor. 12, 13. Per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus. Gal. 3, 27, 28.
units.tr: Second, as regards present benefits, immersion in water demonstrates and seals, as does sprinkling or pouring of water, the mystical conjunction and union with Christ as head, and with the Church as his body: 1 Cor. 12, 13, "For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body." Gal. 3, 27, 28.

units.la: Si verò magis distinctè consideremus, quomodò aquam subeamus, ac deindè iterùm ex eâ prodeamus, demonstratur & obsignatur peccati ac veteris nostri hominis mors ac sepultura cum Christo; quòdque vivificati, novi, justi, ac mundi, ipsius virtute reddamur: Rom. 6, 3,-6. Coll. II, 11, 12, 13.
units.tr: If we consider more closely how we go down into the water and then come up out of it again, the death and burial of sin and of our old man with Christ are shown and sealed, and we are made alive, new, righteous and clean by his power: Rom. 6:3-6; Col. 2:11, 12, 13.

units.la: Ablutio quæ interim peragitur, clarius designat gratiam justificantem, & simul renovantem ac sanctificantem: Act. 2, 38, 39. Baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomen Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum: & accipietis donum Spiritus Sancti. Vobis enim facta est promissio, &c. XXII, 16. Surgens baptizator, & abluitor à peccatis tuis. Eph. 5, 25, 26. Tit. III, 5. Hebr. 9, 14. X, 22, 23. XII, 24. 1 Petr. 1, 2. 1 Joh. 1, 7. Apoc. 1, 7.
units.tr: The washing that takes place meanwhile more clearly signifies justifying grace, and at the same time renewing and sanctifying grace: Acts 2:38, 39, "Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit; for the promise is to you, &c." Acts 22:16, "Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins." Eph. 5:25, 26; Tit. 3:5; Heb. 9:14; 10:22, 23; 12:24; 1 Pet. 1:2; 1 John 1:7; Rev. 1:5, 7.

units.la: Porrò, quia mundi ex aquâ prodimus, Justitiâ Christi & luce Sp. Sancti, ut veste splendidâ, circumfusi; hinc in Baptismo Christum induere, dicimur, Gal. 3, 26, 27. Confer Isai. 61, 10. Zach. 3, 4, 5. Itemque Eph. II, 22, 23, 24. 1 Joh. 1, 7.
units.tr: Furthermore, since we come up out of the water clean, clothed as it were in the splendid garment of Christ's righteousness and enveloped in the light of the Holy Spirit, we are therefore said in Baptism to "put on Christ": Gal. 3:26, 27. Compare Isa. 61:10; Zech. 3:4, 5; likewise Eph. 4:22-24; 1 John 1:7.

units.la: Tertiò, quod ad beneficia futura; sicut ex aquâ salvi prodimus, simul symbolicè nobis significatur & obsignatur liberatio & translatio nostrì ex hujus mundi calamitatibus in cœlestem gloriam: Marc. 16,16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur. 1 Petr. 3,20, 21. & speciališ resurrectio ad vitam æternam: Rom. 6,5. Nam sicut eo (Christo) plantati coaluimus assimilatione mortis ejus, nimirum etiam resurrectionis assimilatione coalescemus 8, 11. 1 Cor. 15,22.
units.tr: Thirdly, as to future benefits: just as we come up from the water saved, so deliverance and our transfer from the calamities of this world into heavenly glory are symbolically signified and sealed to us: Mark 16:16, "He who believes and is baptized will be saved"; 1 Pet. 3:20, 21; and especially the resurrection to eternal life: Rom. 6:5, "For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be in the likeness of his resurrection"; Rom. 8:11; 1 Cor. 15:22.

units.la: Quartò nobis ob oculos ponitur geminum officium;
units.tr: Fourthly, two duties are set before our eyes:

units.la: 1. Veteris hominis mortificatio, & studium sanctimoniæ: Rom. 6,3,4,6. Col. 3, 3,-5. .2. Quia in unum corpus, & in communionem ejusdem Spiritus, sumus baptizati, necessum est nos sub uno capite Christo, & per unum eundemque Spiritum, concordes vivere in charitate: 1 Cor. 12, 13, 14, 15. Per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, &c. Eph. 4, 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: (1) The mortification of the old man and the pursuit of holiness: Rom. 6:3, 4, 6; Col. 3:3-5. (2) Since we have been baptized into one body and into the fellowship of one and the same Spirit, we must necessarily live in harmony and love under the one head, Christ, and through the one and the same Spirit: 1 Cor. 12:13, 14, 15; "For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," &c.; Eph. 4:3, 4, 5.

units.la: XIX. Effectus Baptismi potissimum est receptio in Fœdus gratiæ, & quidem in Ecclesiâ institutâ, secundùm œconomiam N. T.; sic tamen ut ipsa communio mystica in legitimâ Sacramenti receptione simul significetur & obsignetur. 1 Cor. 12,13. Quemadmodum Circumcisio pactum Dei, & signum ejus appellatur, Gen. 17, 10, 11. ita nunc de Baptismo tenendum, qui in illius locum successit: inde nos spirituali Circumcisione dicimur circumcisi per Baptismum; Col. II, 10, 11. Confer 1 Joh. 5, 8. Ita Baptismus testificatur communionem Fœderis gratiæ.
units.tr: XIX. The principal effect of Baptism is reception into the covenant of grace, and indeed into the Church instituted according to the economy of the New Testament; yet in such a way that the mystical communion itself is at the same time signified and sealed in the lawful reception of the sacrament: 1 Cor. 12:13. Just as circumcision is called God's covenant and its sign, Gen. 17:10, 11, so we must hold the same of Baptism, which has succeeded to its place; hence we are said to be circumcised through Baptism with a spiritual circumcision: Col. 2:10, 11. Compare 1 John 5:8. Thus Baptism witnesses to communion in the covenant of grace.

units.la: Ista Fœderis communio 1. ponit gratiam Regenerationis: unde Lavacrum regenerationis appellatur, Tit. III, 5.
units.tr: This communion in the covenant (1) involves the grace of regeneration; whence it is called the "washing of regeneration," Tit. 3:5.

units.la: 2. Præstat gratiam Justificationis peccatorum Remissionem, & jus vitæ æternæ: Marc. 16, 16. Act. II, 38.
units.tr: (2) It bestows the grace of justification, the remission of sins, and the right to eternal life: Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38.

units.la: 3. Hinc fluit actualis nostri Renovatio; ac sanctificatio. Sic Tit. 3, 5. conjunguntur Lavacrum regenerationis, & Renovatio Sp. Sancti. Adde Act. 2, 38.
units.tr: (3) From this flows our actual renewal and sanctification. Thus Tit. 3:5 joins "the washing of regeneration" and "the renewal of the Holy Spirit." Add Acts 2:38.

units.la: 4. Comprehenditur etiam Adoptio in filios, atque adeò jus hæreditatis cœlestis: Gal. 3, 26, 27. Rom. 8, 17,
units.tr: (4) Adoption as sons is also included, and therefore the right of heavenly inheritance: Gal. 3:26, 27; Rom. 8:17.

units.la: XX. Non tamen realis, aut formalis, istorum beneficiorum efficientia ipsi externo huic Sacramento convenit; sed Sp. Sancto, quí quod sanguine Christi nobis partum est, applicat efficaciter, atque eadem ista bona hoc Sacramento significantur & obsignantur.
units.tr: XX. Yet the efficacy of these benefits, whether real or formal, does not belong to this external sacrament itself; rather it belongs to the Holy Spirit, who effectively applies to us what has been won by the blood of Christ, and these same goods are signified and sealed in this sacrament.

units.la: In excessû igitur hîc peccant Pontificii, qui Baptismo tribuunt realem efficientiam ex opere operato; atque itâ æquam supra naturam ad talem effectum elevari existimant. His opponimus:
units.tr: Therefore the Papists err in excess, who ascribe to Baptism a real efficacy ex opere operato, and think that it is thereby raised above its nature to such an effect. We oppose them as follows:

units.la: 1. Sacramenta communiter sunt signa & sigilla; undè similiter de efficientiâ Baptismi judicandum est.
units.tr: (1) Sacraments are in general signs and seals; so we must judge similarly concerning the efficacy of Baptism.

units.la: 2. Aqua Baptismi non potest gratiam spiritualem per se producere realiter; cùm sit materialis, & finitæ virtutis. Vide sup. th. 10.
units.tr: (2) The water of Baptism cannot by itself really produce spiritual grace, since it is material and of finite power. See above, thesis 10.

units.la: 3. Gratia spiritualis ad rectè ordinatum hujus Sacramenti usum præsupponitur: atque itâ statuendum saltem judicio charitatis. Sic de Baptismo diserte, Marc. 16, 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, &c. Fides ergò naturâ prior est. Act. 2, 39. ad liberos fidelium, etiam ante ipsorum Baptismum extenditur promissio. Vide porrò verf. 41, VIII, 37, 38. X, 36; 45, 47. Confer Rom. 4, 10, 11. cum Col. 2, 11, 12. iremque 1 Cor. 7, 14. Quin & latro pœnitens, Luc. 23, 42, 43. sine Baptismo salvatus est.
units.tr: (3) Spiritual grace is presupposed for the rightly ordered use of this sacrament, and so must be assumed at least by the judgment of charity. Thus concerning Baptism, plainly, Mark 16:16, "He who believes and is baptized, &c." Faith is therefore prior in nature. Acts 2:39: the promise extends even to the children of believers, before their Baptism. See further v. 41; 8:37, 38; 10:36, 45, 47. Compare Rom. 4:10, 11 with Col. 2:11, 12; likewise 1 Cor. 7:14. Indeed the penitent thief, Luke 23:42, 43, was saved without Baptism.

units.la: 4. Contrà verò, ad Baptismum externum non semper sequitur remissio peccatorum, & gratia salutaris: ut patet exemplo Simonis Magi; Act. 8, 13, 21.
units.tr: (4) On the contrary, external Baptism is not always followed by the remission of sins and saving grace, as the example of Simon Magus shows: Acts 8:13, 21.

units.la: XXI. Sacramenti hujus Causa efficiens princeps absolutè est ipse Deus; καθ' οικονομίαν vero Christus Mediator. Ministra primùm fuit Johannes Christi ἀγγελος; hinc Baptista dictus : deindè Apostoli, aliique ad docendum & baptizandum missi. Sic de Johanne illo extat, Joh. 1, 33. quòd ipse dixerit : Qui misit me ut baptizarem aquâ, &c. Confer Luc. 3, 2, 3. VII, 30. Matth. 21, 25. Itemque III, 5, 6, 13, - 17. Luc. 3, 21 22. Christus autem jam ascensurus in Coelum, Matth. 28, 18, 19, 20. accedens ad Apostolos locutus est eis, dicens : Data est mihi omnis auctoritas in cælo & in terra. Profecti ergo discipulos facite omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: XXI. The principal efficient cause of this sacrament is absolutely God himself; but according to the economy [καθ' οἰκονομίαν] it is Christ the Mediator. Its minister first was John, Christ's angel [ἄγγελος], hence called the Baptist; then the Apostles and others sent to teach and baptize. Thus concerning that John it is recorded, John 1:33, that he himself said, "He who sent me to baptize with water," &c. Compare Luke 3:2, 3; 7:30; Matt. 21:25; likewise Matt. 3:5, 6, 13-17; Luke 3:21, 22. Christ, however, about to ascend into heaven, Matt. 28:18, 19, 20, coming to the Apostles, "spoke to them, saying: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Rejiciendus igitur est error Socinianorum, quòd ex scriptis Apostolorum & Euangelistarum demonstrari non posiit, vel Johannem, vel Apostolos, à Deo, aut Christo, in mandatis accepisse ut baptizarent : quibus ex parte saltem præiverunt Pontificii, contendentes, Baptismum Johannis sic appellari, non quòd Johannes Minister tantùm ejus fuerit, sed etiàm Auctor : imò insuper, si ritum & effectum spectemus, Baptismum illum nihil habuisse, nisi humanum.
units.tr: The error of the Socinians must therefore be rejected, that it cannot be demonstrated from the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists that either John or the Apostles received a commission from God or Christ to baptize; in this they have been preceded, at least in part, by the Papists, who contend that Johnʼs Baptism is so called not because John was merely its minister, but also its author; indeed, moreover, if we look at the rite and the effect, that Baptism had nothing but a human character.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Nos contrà afferimus, 1. Baptismum Discipulorum Christi & Johannis convenire caus à efficiente principali, Deo. Idem planè de Johannis Baptismo probatum est modò ; nec dubitari potest de Baptismo Discipulorum Christi : Deus autem Pater locutus est per Filium ; Hebr. 1, 1. eique non ex mensurâ dedit Spiritum ; Joh. 3, 34.
units.tr: We, on the contrary, maintain first that the Baptism of Christ's disciples and that of John share the same principal efficient cause, God. The same has just been proved of John's Baptism, and there can be no doubt about the Baptism of Christ's disciples. God the Father spoke through the Son (Heb. 1:1), and God gave the Spirit to him without measure (John 3:34).

units.la: Obj. Atqui vocatur aliquoties Baptismus Johannis: Ergò. Resp. Ita tunc denominatur à Ministro : similiter ut Paulus dicit, Rom. 11, 16. Ex meo Euangelio.
units.tr: Objection. But Baptism is sometimes called "the Baptism of John." Therefore... Answer. It is so named only from the minister, just as Paul says, "according to my Gospel" (Rom. 11:16).

units.la: Afferimus 2. utrumque Baptismum convenire materiali; elemento aquæ. Vide sup. th. 14.
units.tr: We maintain, second, that both Baptisms agree in the material element, water. See above, thesis 14.

units.la: Atque etiam 3. formali relatione scil. ad rem significatam & obsignatam : uterque enim respexit resipiscentiam & fidem, tanquàm conditionem; & remissionem peccatorum, tanquàm fructum. Sic de Baptismo Johannis, Marc. 1, 4. & Luc. 3, 3. Venit prædicans baptismum resipiscentiæ, ad remissionem peccatorum. Similiter Actor. 19, 4. Confer Luc. 1, 76, 77. Atque Item de Baptismo Christi, Act. II, 38. XXII, 16.
units.tr: And third, they agree in their formal relation, namely to the thing signified and sealed. For both looked to repentance and faith as the condition, and to the forgiveness of sins as the fruit. So it is of John's Baptism: "He came preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins" (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3). Likewise Acts 19:4. Compare Luke 1:76, 77. The same holds of Christ's Baptism: Acts 2:38; 22:16.

units.la: Obj. 1. Baptismus Johannis vocatur Baptismus pœnitentiæ, aut resipiscentiæ: Ergò solùm genuit pœnitentiam; atque ita disposuit ad Baptismum Christi. Resp. Imò prærequirebatur resipiscentia, & sic administrabatur in remissionem peccatorum; præmisså etiam doctrinâ fidei in Christum: Marc. I, 4. Matth. III, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7. Luc. III, 3, 7, 8. Act. 19, 4.
units.tr: Objection 1. John's Baptism is called the baptism of repentance or of repentance-change; therefore it only produced repentance and so prepared the way for Christ's Baptism. Answer. Indeed repentance was required beforehand, and it was administered for the remission of sins, with the teaching of faith in Christ preceding it (Mark 1:4; Matt. 3:1, 2, 3, 6, 7; Luke 3:3, 7, 8; Acts 19:4).

units.la: Obj. 2. Johannes se aquâ baptizare dixit; Christum verò baptizaturum Spiritû & igne, Matth. 3, 11. Resp. Vox Baptismi istic sumitur diversimodè: in priori enim membro agitur de ipso Baptismo aquæ; in posteriori de Baptismo Spiritûs Sancti. Prius membrum ad externum morale ministerium pertinet; posterius ad internam rem signatam.
units.tr: Objection 2. John said that he baptizes with water, but that Christ will baptize with the Spirit and fire (Matt. 3:11). Answer. The word "baptize" is used in different senses here: in the first clause it refers to the Baptism of water itself, in the second to the Baptism of the Holy Spirit. The first clause pertains to the external moral ministry, the second to the inward thing signified.

units.la: Interim differt Baptismus Johannis à Baptismo Apostolorum, 1. ratione temporis: nam Johannes fuit Christi πρόδρομος, præiens ante faciem Domini, ut pararet ejus viam: Luc. 1, 76. Marc. 1, 2, 3, 4. Matt. 3, 11. cum Joh. 1, 29. Sic in Johanne fuit finis veteris dispensationis, & aliquod initium novæ. 2. Ratione auctoris; Baptismus Johannis à Deo quidem fuit institutus: non tamen à Christo Mediatore, ut in carne manifestato. Sed hoc modo à Christo mandatus est Baptismus Discipulorum. 3. Ratione adjunctorum; cum Baptismo Apostolorum uberior mensura Spiritûs conjuncta fuit: sæpè etiàm communicatio charismatum extraordinariorum: Act. 19. 3, 4.
units.tr: Yet John's Baptism differs from the Baptism of the apostles: first, in respect of time, for John was the forerunner [πρόδρομος] of Christ, going before the face of the Lord to prepare his way (Luke 1:76; Mark 1:2, 3, 4; Matt. 3:11), whereas John 1:29 belongs to the later period. Thus in John there was the end of the old dispensation and some beginning of the new. Second, in respect of its author: John's Baptism was indeed instituted by God, but not by Christ the Mediator as manifested in the flesh. The Baptism of the disciples, however, was commissioned by Christ in this way. Third, in respect of its accompaniments: a fuller measure of the Spirit was joined to the Baptism of the apostles, and often also the communication of extraordinary gifts (Acts 19:3, 4).

units.la: XXIII. Quantum ad Baptismum Discipulorum Chri- sti;
units.tr: XXIII. Concerning the Baptism of the Disciples of Christ;

units.la: Christus Mediator in carne manifestatus, ac munus suum jàm palàm obiens, discipulis suis Baptismum admiadministrandum præcepit ante extremam passionem suam, cùm eos solùm misit ad perditas oves domûs Israëlis: Matth. 10, 5, 6, 7. cum Joh. 3, 26. IV, 1, 2. Deindè verò post resurrectionem, jam in cœlum ascensurus, doctrinam Euangelii, ut & Baptismum, ad omnes gentes extendit: Matth. 28, 19, 20.
units.tr: Christ the Mediator, manifested in the flesh and already openly discharging his office, commanded his disciples to administer Baptism before his final passion, when he sent them only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 10:5, 6, 7; compare John 3:26; 4:1, 2). Then afterwards, after the resurrection, about to ascend into heaven, he extended the doctrine of the Gospel, and Baptism with it, to all nations (Matt. 28:19, 20).

units.la: Christus autem Baptismi administrationem non solùm Apostolis mandavit; sed & omnibus ordinariis Verbi Divini Ministris, per quos Apostolorum Ministerium quantum ad rem ipsam, continuatur: sic enim in Sacramenti hujus institutione, ejus administratio disertè conjungitur cum Verbi prædicatione. Quod autem Deus conjunxit, homo ne separet: Matth. 19, 6.
units.tr: Christ, however, did not entrust the administration of Baptism to the apostles alone, but also to all the ordinary ministers of the Divine Word, through whom the ministry of the apostles is continued as to the thing itself.
