units.tr: The faithful themselves will also judge, with and under Christ, acknowledging and approving his just judgement; which will pertain to their most intimate union with Christ, to their participation in his kingdom, and thus to their own glory; and at the same time to the fuller conviction of the damned. Hence Matt. 19:28: You also will sit on twelve thrones, judging, etc.; (1) 1 Cor. 6:2, 3: Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? (2) Do you not know that we are to judge the angels?

units.la: XXI. Judicandi autem venient, tum Angeli, tum Homines.
units.tr: XXI. Judgment will be carried out on both the angels and the human beings.

units.la: De Angelis patet ex loco proxime allegato. Specialius vero ad malos Angelos referetur judicium condemnatorium; 2 Petr. 2, 4. Deus Angelis, qui peccaverunt, non pepercit; sed in tartarum detrusos catenis caliginis tradidit, damnationi asservatos. Judae, 6. Angelos, qui non servarunt suam originem, sed reliquerunt suum domicilium, judicio magni illius diei vinculis aeternis sub caligine servasse. Matth. 25, 4. Dicet iis, qui ad sinistram erunt; Execrandi, abite a Me in ignem illum aeternum, paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus.
units.tr: That the angels are judged is clear from the passage cited just above. More particularly, the sentence of condemnation will apply to the evil angels: 2 Pet. 2:4, God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into hell, delivered them into chains of darkness, and reserved them for judgment. Jude 6: the angels who did not keep their first estate, but left their own dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under darkness until the judgment of the great day. Matt. 25:41: He will say to those on the left, Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

units.la: Sed Judicium de Hominibus magis est nostrae considerationis: quod communiter proponitur Eccl. III, 17. Justum & impium judicabit Deus. xII, 14. Matth. 25, 32,-. Et congregabuntur coram Eo (Christo) omnes gentes; & separabit eos ab aliis, ut pastor oves ab haedis, &c. Act. 17, 31. Rom. 2, 6, 16. xIV, 10, 12. 2 Cor. 5, 10. Apoc. 20, 12, 13.
units.tr: But the judgment of human beings is of greater concern to us. It is commonly set forth in Eccl. 3:17, God will judge the righteous and the wicked. Eccl. 12:14; Matt. 25:32, Before him (Christ) will be gathered all nations, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, etc.; Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:6, 16; Rom. 14:10, 12; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 20:12, 13.

units.la: Obj. 1. Joh. 5, 24. Qui credit,-non venit in judicium. Ergo fideles non judicabuntur. Resp. Istic fynecdochice intelligitur judicium condemnatorium.
units.tr: Objection 1. John 5:24, He who believes … does not come into judgment. Therefore believers will not be judged. Answer. There, by synecdoche, judgment of condemnation is meant.

units.la: Obj. 2. Pfal. 1, 5. Nonstabunt impii in judicio; &c. Ergo. Resp. H. e. non subsistent; sed causa cadent sive condemnabuntur.
units.tr: Objection 2. Ps. 1:5, The wicked will not stand in judgment, etc. Therefore. Answer. That is, they will not stand up; that is, they will fall in their cause, or be condemned.

units.la: XXII. Sententia duplex pronunciabitur; una de electis, altera de reprobis: prior erit justificatoria; posterior, condemnatoria.
units.tr: XXII. The sentence will be pronounced in two parts: one concerning the elect, the other concerning the reprobate. The former will be justifying; the latter, condemnatory.

units.la: Iustificatoria hominum electorum, feretur proprie juxta Euangelium: eritque nihil aliud, quam publica Justificationis Euangelicae promulgatio. Adeoque sententia gratiosa, attamen justitia Christi nixa; quemadmodum illi in hoc saeculo crediderint & speraverint, suamque fidem ac spem sincera pietate, sanctimonia, omnibusque bonis operibus demonstraverint; quod sic, remissis peccatis omnibus, habituri sint gloriam coelestem & beatitudinem aeternam.
units.tr: The justifying sentence on the elect human beings will be pronounced properly in accordance with the Gospel, and it will be nothing other than the public proclamation of evangelical justification. It will therefore be a gracious sentence, yet resting on the righteousness of Christ, just as they believed and hoped in this age and showed their faith and hope by sincere piety, holiness and all good works. Thus, with all their sins forgiven, they will receive heavenly glory and eternal blessedness.

units.la: Gratiam, sive Misericordiam, dixi: nulla enim erit hominum salvandorum ex seipsis, & in seipsis, talis dignitas; sed miseria satis est manifesta, unde perfecte liberabuntur ipso die. Hinc 2 Tim. 1, 16, 18. Praestet misericordiam Dominus Onesiphori familiae! - Det ei Dominus, ut inveniat misericordiam apud Dominum in die illo! Confer Rom. 4, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: I have said grace, or mercy, for there will be no such worth in human beings who are to be saved, considered in themselves and from themselves; their misery is plain enough, and on that very day they will be perfectly delivered from it. Hence 2 Tim. 1:16, 18: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus! and May the Lord grant him to find mercy with the Lord on that day! Compare Rom. 4:6, 7, 8.

units.la: Iustitiam Christi illis imputatam commemoravi: unde, dignitas, quae saepius appellatur. Ita Phil. 3, 8, 14. Ut Christum lucrifaciam; Et comperiar in eo, non habens meam justitiam; quae est ex Lege: sed eam, quae est per fidem: &c.
units.tr: I have mentioned the righteousness of Christ imputed to them, and hence their worth, which is often so called. So Phil. 3:8, 14: That I may gain Christ, and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith, etc.

units.la: Virtutes eorum & bona opera, ut fructus communionis Christi, ac verae fidei & spei; non ut causae meritoriae regnandi, sed ut via regni, adjiciuntur: juxta Matth. 25, 34, - 40. 2 Tim. 1, 16, 17, 18. Apoc. 14, 13. Atque haec omnia juxta decretum electionis, quo tota salutis nostrae methodus fuit definita. Unde Rex noster appellabit, Regnum nobis paratum à jasto mundi fundamento; Matth. 25, 34. Confer Apoc. 20, 12.
units.tr: Their virtues and good works are added, not as the meritorious cause of reigning but as the way into the kingdom, as fruits of communion with Christ and of true faith and hope: according to Matt. 25:34–40; 2 Tim. 1:16, 17, 18; Rev. 14:13. And all this is in accordance with the decree of election, by which the whole method of our salvation was determined. Hence our King will call the kingdom prepared for us from the foundation of the world, Matt. 25:34. Compare Rev. 20:12.

units.la: XXIII. Sententia condemnatoria feretur in improbos Angelos & Homines,
units.tr: XXIII. The sentence of condemnation will be pronounced on the wicked angels and human beings.

units.la: De malis Angelis satis evidentia sunt testimonia, 2 Petr. II, 4. Jud. 6. quia scil. peccarunt contra Legem sibi praescriptam.
units.tr: Concerning the evil angels the testimonies are sufficiently clear: 2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6, namely because they sinned against the law prescribed to them.

units.la: Similiter Homines reprobi, propter peccata sua, condemnabuntur, juxta Foedus Legale; sive Legem scriptam acceperint; sive Legis substantiam per naturalem conscientiam, vel qualemcunque insuper instructionem habuerint: Rom. II, 12, 14, 15. Quicunque absque Lege (scripta) peccaverunt, absque Lege quoque peribunt: & quicunque cum Lege peccaverunt, per Legem damnabuntur. Nam cum Gentes, quae Legem non habent, &c. Ita Lex dicitur iram operari; Rom. 4, 15. Et Ministerium mortis ac condemnationis appellatur; 2 Cor. III, 7, 9. Adde, 1 Tim. I, 9, 10. Gal. III, 10.
units.tr: Likewise, the reprobate human beings will be condemned for their sins according to the legal covenant, whether they received the written law or had the substance of the law through natural conscience or some other instruction. Rom. 2:12, 14, 15: Whoever has sinned without the (written) law will also perish without the law, and whoever has sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, etc. So the law is said to work wrath, Rom. 4:15, and is called the ministry of death and condemnation, 2 Cor. 3:7, 9. Add 1 Tim. 1:9, 10; Gal. 3:10.

units.la: Formam istius damnationis indicavit Christus, ipse Judex futurus; Matth. 25, 41, -45. Tunc dicet etiam iis, qui ad sinistram erunt; Execrandi, abite à Me in ignem illud aeternum, &c.
units.tr: Christ, who is to be the Judge himself, has indicated the form of this condemnation: Matt. 25:41–45, Then he will also say to those on the left, Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, etc.

units.la: XXIV. Tempus istius judicii consilio Dei definitum est; nobis vero sic minime revelatum. Hinc Ipse Christus, Matth. 24, 36, 37. De die autem illo, & hora, nemo scit: neque Angeli quidem coelorum: sed Pater meus solus. Nihil ergo curiose inquirendum; nec temere determinandum de isto tempore: Act. 1, 7.
units.tr: XXIV. The time of this judgment has been fixed by the counsel of God, but it has by no means been revealed to us. Hence Christ himself, Matt. 24:36, 37: But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only. Nothing therefore should be inquired into curiously, nor rashly determined about that time: Acts 1:7.

units.la: Praedictum est tamen fore, ut profani irrisores objiciant moram finis; atque inde concludant, illum diem nunquam esse venturum. Sed iis opponi debet historia creationis, à quo principio tempora hujus mundi labuntur, & ad finem tendunt; & veritas judicii universalis per aquas diluvii: tum quod Deus in sua aeternitate successionem non habens, propter se
units.tr: It has been foretold, however, that profane scoffers will object to the delay of the end, and from this conclude that that day will never come. But to them must be set against the account of creation, from which beginning the times of this world slip away and tend toward their end, and the certainty of universal judgment by the waters of the flood; and also that God, who has no succession in his eternity, does not delay that coming on account of himself,

units.la: non tardet adventum illum; sed quod patiente sit animo erga homines, atque universam electorum multitudinem ad resipiscentiam & salutem adduci velit:
units.tr: but that he is patient of mind toward human beings, and wishes the whole multitude of the elect to be brought to repentance and salvation:

units.la: 2 Petr. III, 3,-9. Quin & Christum praemonuisse, multa judicium hoc universale praecessura; Matth. 24, 4, --. Et Paulum noluisse, ut fideles essent in ea opinione, quasi jam illo tempore adventus ille Domini prope adesset: sed docuisse, futuram prius insignem apostasiam, & revelandum Antichristum; 2 Thess. II, 1, -- 12. Et vaticinatum de generali quadam Judaeorum conversione & restitutione, &c. Rom. XI, II,--. Confer 2 Cor. III, 14, 15, 16. Ac porro in Apocalypsi fata Ecclesiae N. Test. prophetice retegi. Semper interim observanda est salutaris illa Christi praemonitio, Matth. 24, 42. Vigilate ergo! Nescitis enim, qua hora Dominus venturus sit.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 3:3–9. Indeed Christ also forewarned that many things would precede this universal judgment, Matt. 24:4ff.; and Paul did not want the faithful to be of the opinion that as if that coming of the Lord was already near at hand at that time, but taught that a notable apostasy would come first and the Antichrist would be revealed, 2 Thess. 2:1–12. And he prophesied of a general conversion and restoration of the Jews, etc., Rom. 11:11ff. Compare 2 Cor. 3:14, 15, 16. Moreover, the fates of the Church of the New Testament are prophetically disclosed in the Apocalypse. Meanwhile that salutary warning of Christ must always be observed, Matt. 24:42: Watch therefore! For you do not know on what hour the Lord will come.

units.la: Locus autem indicatur futurus in Nubibus Coeli; Matth. 24. 30. nec determinamus specialius, vel aliter. Joel. III. 2, 12. commemoratur quidem judicium omnium gentium in valle Josaphati: sed vaticinium istud conferendum cum historia, 2 Chron. 20. & sic indicari videtur, judicium illud juste exercendum esse, inspectante Ecclesia.
units.tr: The place is indicated as being in the clouds of heaven, Matt. 24:30; nor do we determine more specifically or otherwise. Joel 3:2, 12 indeed recalls the judgment of all nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, but that prophecy should be compared with the history in 2 Chron. 20, and so it seems to be indicated that that judgment is to be exercised justly, with the Church looking on.

units.la: XXV. Ad Judicium istud extremum mox sequetur ejus executio; justis gloriosa ac beata, improbis vero miserrima & ignominiosa: Matth. 25,46. Et abibunt isti in supplicium aeternum; justi vero ad vitam aeternam. Unde 1. manifestum evadit improborum supplicium aeternum, & absque fine; non solum in genere damni, sed etiam in genere sensus. Apoc. 20, 10. Et torquebuntur die ac nocte in saecula saeculorum.
units.tr: XXV. This final judgment will be followed at once by its execution: glorious and blessed for the righteous, but most miserable and ignominious for the wicked. Matt. 25:46, And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. Hence, first, the eternal punishment of the wicked, and without end, is plainly evident, not only as to the kind of loss but also as to the kind of sensation. Rev. 20:10, And they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

units.la: 2. Idem emphatice docetur Matth. 25,41. Abite a Me; in ignem illum aeternum. Marc. 9,43-48. abire in gehennam, in ignem illum inextinguibilem: ubi vermis eorum non interit, & ignis non extinguitur. Similiter Isef. 66,24. 66, 24. Vermis autem rodens, & ignis urens, cruciatus denotant; quod interim vermis non interibit, nec ignis extinguetur, eorum æternitatem & durationem absque fine significat.
units.tr: Second, the same thing is taught emphatically in Matt. 25:41, Depart from me into the eternal fire. Mark 9:43–48, to go into hell, into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. Likewise Isa. 66:24. The gnawing worm and the burning fire denote torments; and the fact that the worm will not die nor the fire be quenched signifies their eternity and duration without end.

units.la: 3. Similis est phrasis, adjunctum æternum exprimens, Apoc. 14, 11. Fumus tormenti ipsorum afcendet in fæcula sæculorum: nec habebunt requiem die, nec nocte.
units.tr: Third, a similar phrase expressing the adjunct of eternity is Rev. 14:11, The smoke of their torment will go up for ever and ever; they will have no rest day or night.

units.la: 4. Hoc est consentaneum peccatorum demerito: cum enim ista adversùs infinitam Dei Majestatem commissa sint, eamque læserint; Justitia postulat, ut infinitis quoque pœnis luantur: quæ quidem infinitas, in subjectis finitis, esse debet infinitas durationis succeffivæ. Hinc Matth. 5, 26. Amen dico tibi; nequaquam exibis illinc, ufquedum reddideris ultimum quadrantem.
units.tr: Fourth, this agrees with the desert of sins: since these were committed against the infinite majesty of God and have offended it, justice demands that they be atoned for by infinite punishments as well; and this infinity, in finite subjects, must be an infinity of successive duration. Hence Matt. 5:26, Truly I say to you, you will by no means get out from there until you have paid the last penny.

units.la: XXVI. Gradus istarum pœnarum non erunt in omnibus omnino damnatis æquales; sed inæquales: atque in singulis apta proportione respondentes demerito peccatorum ipsorum: Luc. 12, 47, 48. Ille autem servus, qui novit voluntatem Domini sui, &c. Qui vero non novit, &c. Adde Matth. XI, 22. 24.
units.tr: XXVI. The degrees of these punishments will not be equal in all the damned, but unequal, and in each case fittingly proportioned to the desert of their own sins: Luke 12:47, 48. That servant who knew his lord's will, etc. But he who did not know, etc. Add Matt. 11:22, 24.

units.la: Causa efficiens principalis in genere sensûs proprie habebit locum: scil. Justitia Dei vindicativa, sic sese exerens in damnatis, ut Diaboli, & Homines reprobi in suis animabus, perferant cruciatus naturæ spirituali convenientes; ac porro etiam Homines reprobi in corporibus suis, juxta eorum conditionem.
units.tr: The principal efficient cause, in the sense-related sphere, will properly have its place: namely, the avenging justice of God, manifesting itself in the damned so that the devils and the reprobate humans suffer in their souls torments suited to a spiritual nature, and further that the reprobate humans also suffer in their bodies, according to their condition.

units.la: Societas Diabolorum, & Hominum damnatorum, pariter desperantium, & Judicem suum blasphemantium, augebit istam miseriam.
units.tr: The fellowship of devils and of damned humans, equally despairing and blaspheming their Judge, will increase this misery.

units.la: Locus proprius erit Infernus. Vide sup. cap. 7. th. 25.
units.tr: The proper place will be Hell. See above, chapter 7, thesis 25.

units.la: XXVII. Obj. 1. Apoc. 21, 8. appellatur mors se- cunda: ergo non erunt perferendi cruciatus positivi æterni.
units.tr: XXVII. Obj. 1. Rev. 21:8 calls it the second death; therefore the positive eternal torments will not have to be endured.

units.la: æterni. Resp. Vocatur mors secunda, non quasi futura esseт damnatorum annihilatio; aut omnimoda vitæ privatio: sed quia erit æterna abalienatio à vitâ Dei, & communione Ipsius gratiosa ac beata, dum absque fine durabunt etiam cruciatus positivi.
units.tr: Answer: It is called the second death not as if the damned were to be annihilated, or deprived of life altogether; but because there will be an eternal estrangement from the life of God and from his gracious and blessed fellowship, while positive torments also continue without end.

units.la: Obj. 2. Similiter 2 Thess. 1, 9. occurrit æternum exitium. Ergo. Resp. Iterum non personarum abolitio; sed privatio beatificæ communionis Dei, in personis pœnam sensus quoque sustinentibus.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Likewise eternal destruction occurs in 2 Thess. 1:9. Therefore, etc. Answer: Again this is not the abolition of persons, but the deprivation of the blessed fellowship of God, while the persons also undergo the punishment of sense.

units.la: Obj. 3. Actus peccaminosi finiti sunt: à justitia igitur alienum est, eos puniri cruciatibus æternis. Resp. Actus peccaminosi, ratione temporis interim labentis, finiti sunt: quia tamen adversus infinitam Dei Majestatem committuntur, inde emergit ratio demeriti infiniti.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Sinful acts are finite; it is therefore contrary to justice that they be punished with eternal torments. Answer: Sinful acts are finite in respect of the time that passes in the meantime; but because they are committed against the infinite majesty of God, from this arises the ground of infinite demerit.

units.la: XXVIII. Sic ergo Justi videbunt quoque Executionem sententiæ condemnatoriæ, in hostibus Dei, & Christi, & suis; in qua liberatione finali, sed duratura deinceps absque fine, ipsi non poterunt non exultare, Deique circa improbos justitiam celebrare. Huc pertinet illud, Apoc. 16, 5, 6, 7. Justus es, Domine, Qui es, & qui eras, & qui eris, quod hæc judicaveris. Digni enim sunt.
units.tr: XXVIII. Thus the just will also see the execution of the sentence of condemnation on the enemies of God and of Christ, and on their own; and in this final deliverance, which will nevertheless endure thereafter without end, they will not be able not to exult and to celebrate the justice of God concerning the wicked. To this belongs that passage: Rev. 16:5, 6, 7. You are just, O Lord, who are and who were, and who will be, because you have judged these things. For they are worthy.

units.la: Ipsi autem ibunt in vitam æternam. Matth. 25, 46. Confer 1 Cor. 2, 9. Beatissimam tunc habituri cum Deo communionem, qui erit omnia in omnibus: Psal. 36, 10. 1 Cor. 15, 28. Circa quam I. sic exercenda nunc est fides & spes, ut interim omnis curiositas evitetur: 1 Joh. III, 2, 3. - Nondum manifestum factum est quod erimus &c.
units.tr: But they will go into eternal life, Matt. 25:46. Compare 1 Cor. 2:9. They will then have the most blessed fellowship with God, who will be all in all: Ps. 36:10; 1 Cor. 15:28. Concerning which, first, faith and hope must now be so exercised that all curiosity is meanwhile avoided: 1 John 3:2, 3, It has not yet been made manifest what we shall be, etc.

units.la: 2. Non est statuenda corporalis Dei visio.
units.tr: 2. The bodily vision of God is not to be posited.

units.la: Neque 3. cognitio adæquata, sive comprehensiva. Vide sup. cap. 4. th. 22. & 32.
units.tr: Nor, 3, is adequate or comprehensive knowledge to be posited. See above, chapter 4, theses 22 and 32.

units.la: Neque 4. constituenda est illa beatitudo (cum impuris Muhammedanis) in voluptatibus corporeis: erimus enim ἰσάγγελοι; Matth. 22, 30. cum XVIII, 10.
units.tr: Nor, 4, is that blessedness to be established (with the impure Muhammedans) in bodily pleasures; for we shall be equal to the angels [ἰσάγγελοι]: Matt. 22:30, compared with 18:10.

units.la: v. 8. v, 8. 1 Cor. 13, 12. simili ergò cum Angelis beatitudine fruemur. Adde 1 Cor. 15, 44. Rom. 14, 17.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13:12. Therefore we shall enjoy a blessedness similar to that of the angels. Add 1 Cor. 15:44; Rom. 14:17.

units.la: XXIX. Ad communionem illam cum Deo, per cognitionem familiarissimam, ac fruitionem beatissimam in charitate perfectissima, & cum Christo Θεανθρώπῳ Capite nostro gloriosissimo, accedet Societas Angelorum sanctorum, omniumque Hominum electorum, pariter glorificatorum. Vide Heb. 12, 22, 23, 24.
units.tr: XXIX. To that fellowship with God, through the most intimate knowledge and the most blessed enjoyment in most perfect charity, and with Christ the God-man [Θεανθρώπῳ], our most glorious Head, will be added the fellowship of the holy angels and of all the elect humans, likewise glorified. See Heb. 12:22, 23, 24.

units.la: Locus proprius erit Cœlum supremum. Hinc Christus, Joh. 16, 2, 3. In domo Patris mei habitationes multæ sunt, Proficiscor paraturus vobis locum, --. Adde xvii, 24.
units.tr: The proper place will be the highest heaven. Hence Christ says, John 14:2, 3: In my Father's house are many dwelling places; I go to prepare a place for you, etc. Add John 17:24.

units.la: Duratio erit æterna; absque fine: Matth. 25, 46. Ibunt in vitam æternam, Rom. 11, 7.
units.tr: The duration will be eternal, without end: Matt. 25:46, They will go into eternal life; Rom. 11:7.

units.la: XXX. Aberit omnis molestia, calamitas, defectus: Apoc. 7, 16, 17. Non esurient amplius, neque sitient amplius; nec in eos cadet Sol, neque ullus æstus: & abstergsurus est Deus omnem lachrymam ab oculis eorum. xxi, 4, 5. Ex adverso aderit in tali communione & societate, in tali loco, cum plenissima certitudine æternitatis, gaudium perfectissimum. Matth. 25, 21, 23. Ingredere in gaudium Domini tui. Hinc David, Psal. 16, 11. Satietas lætitiarum est cum vultu Tuo; jucunditates sunt in dextera tua in sæculum. Hùc pertinent variæ locutiones metaphoricæ, de Paradiso; Luc. 23, 43. 2 Cor. 12, 2, 4. Nuptiis; Matth. 25, 1, 10. Apoc. 19, 7, 9. Regno; Matth. 5, 3: xxv, 34. Throno; xix, 20. Apoc. 3, 21. Potestate; Matth. 24, 47. Luc. 19, 17, 19.
units.tr: XXX. All annoyance, calamity and want will be absent: Rev. 7:16, 17, They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more; nor shall the sun fall on them, nor any heat: and God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes. Rev. 21:4, 5. On the other hand, there will be, in such fellowship and society, in such a place, with the fullest certainty of eternity, the most perfect joy. Matt. 25:21, 23: Enter into the joy of your Lord. Hence David, Ps. 16:11: In your presence is fullness of joys; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore. To this belong various metaphorical expressions about Paradise (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:2, 4), a wedding feast (Matt. 25:1, 10; Rev. 19:7, 9), a kingdom (Matt. 5:3; 25:34), a throne (Matt. 19:28; Rev. 3:21), and authority (Matt. 24:47; Luke 19:17, 19).

units.la: Admittendi tamen videntur gradus aliqui in gloria; sicut nunc dantur gradus in gratia; & gradus erunt in pœnis infernalibus. Dan. 12, 3. Intelligentes fulgebunt, ut splendor firmamenti: & justificantes multos, tanquàm stellæ in sæculum & in æternum. 1 Cor. 15, 40, 41, 42. Sunt corpora cœlestia, & sunt corpora terrestria: sed alius quidem cœlestium decor, -. Alius decor Solis, & alius decor Lunæ, & alius decor Stellarum: Stella enim Stellæ præstat decore. Itá erit & resurrectio, mortuorum. Sic illi, qui in parabolâ decem talentis rectè fuerat usus, dabatur potestas decem civitatum; qui verò quinque talentis, potestas quinque civitatum: Luc. 19, 17, 19.
units.tr: Nevertheless some degrees in glory seem to be admitted, just as degrees are now given in grace; and there will be degrees in the infernal punishments. Dan. 12:3: Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars forever and ever. 1 Cor. 15:40, 41, 42: There are celestial bodies and there are terrestrial bodies; but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. One glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also will be the resurrection of the dead. Thus, to him who had used the ten talents well in the parable, was given authority over ten cities; but to him who had five talents, authority over five cities: Luke 19:17, 19.

units.la: Obj. 1. Hinc fulcietur opinio de propriis meritis. Resp. Neg. Deus enim sua opera coronat in nobis; non nostra merita.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Hence the opinion about our own merits will be supported. Answer: Denied. For God crowns his own works in us, not our merits.

units.la: Obj. 2. Mercenarii, qui unam tantùm horam laborârant, eandem mercedem cum cæteris acceperunt; Matth. 20, 9, 10. Resp. Scopus parabolæ est, æquè ferò ac citò vocatos & conversos salvatum iri. Sic identitas salutis proponitur; non graduum æqualitas.
units.tr: Obj. 2. The labourers who had worked only one hour received the same wage as the others: Matt. 20:9, 10. Answer: The aim of the parable is that those called and converted late are saved as surely as those called early. So the identity of salvation is set forth, not an equality of degrees.

units.la: XXXI. Quæritur, Quid interim futurum sit de hac terra, & elementis reliquis, cœlisque visibilibus? Utrùm sint annihilanda, an verò relinquenda? Dicendum videtur; futurum, ut elementa magnâ ex parte cedant in corpora Hominum tùm beatorum, tùm damnatorum; prout ista resoluta fuerant in sua principia: reliqua autem mutentur in statum præstantiorem; quàm nunc habent, propter hominum peccata.
units.tr: XXXI. It is asked: what will meanwhile become of this earth, of the other elements, and of the visible heavens? Are they to be annihilated, or rather left in place? It seems to be said that it will come about that the elements will for the most part pass into the bodies of humans, both blessed and damned, according as these had been resolved into their principles; but the remaining things will be changed into a state more excellent than they now have, on account of human sins.

units.la: Hinc totus mundus dicitur sperare & expectare liberationem sui, ex servitute corruptionis & vanitatis, cui nunc subjectus est; Rom. 8, 19, -22. Atque ita erit novum cœlum, & nova terra; 2 Petr. III. 10,-13. Apoc. 21, 1.
units.tr: Hence the whole world is said to hope and to expect its deliverance from the bondage of corruption and vanity to which it is now subjected: Rom. 8:19–22. And so there will be a new heaven and a new earth: 2 Pet. 3:10–13; Rev. 21:1.

units.la: Obj. 1. Psal. 72, 7. Donec non sit Luna. CII, 27. Ipsi (Cœli) peribunt, &c. Matth. 5, 18. Usquedum præterierint Cœlum & Terra. Ergò annihilabuntur. Resp. Neg. Consequentia. Sic enim indicatur solùm finis, qui præsenti huic statui & ordini istarum creaturarum imponetur, cùm fiet insignis illa & gloriosa immutatio.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Ps. 72:7: until there is no moon. Ps. 102:27: They (the heavens) will perish, etc. Matt. 5:18: until heaven and earth pass away. Therefore they will be annihilated. Answer: Denied, the consequence. For these passages indicate only the end that will be set to the present state and order of these creatures, when that remarkable and glorious change takes place.

units.la: Obj. 2. Explicari non potest, qualia tunc ista omnia sint futura, & quem usum habitura: ergò potiùs statuenda annihilatio. Resp. In genere probavimus restitutionem in statum meliorem. Si quis in specie multa interroget, malumus doctam ignorantiam profiteri; quàm temerè quicquam determinare extra ea quæ scripta sunt. Nunc ex parte tantùm cognoscimus:
units.tr: Obj. 2. It cannot be explained what all these things will then be like, and what use they will have; therefore annihilation is rather to be posited. Answer: In general we have proved restoration into a better state. If anyone asks many things in particular, we prefer to profess a learned ignorance rather than rashly determine anything beyond what has been written. Now we know only in part:

units.la: 1 Cor. 13, 9. & nondùm manifestum factum est quod ipsi erimus: 1 Joh. III, 2. Quid mirum ergò, si ista speciatim explicare & asserere nequeamus?
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13:9; and it has not yet been made manifest what we shall be: 1 John 3:2. What wonder, then, if we cannot explain and assert these things in particular?

units.la: XXXII. Pro Praxi; 1.
units.tr: XXXII. For Practice; 1.

units.la: Glorificationem in hac vitâ inchoatam; & bona, quæ in eâ insunt, ritè æstimemus: 1 Joh. III, 1, 1, 1, 3, 4. Rom. 5, 5. Joh. 15, 15. 2 Pet. I, 8, 11. In eâ consolationem quæramus adversus omnes calamitates, labores, & miserias reliquas: 2 Cor. 1, 3, 4, 5. 1 Joh. 5, 4. Rom. 8, 37. Et exultemus gaudio spirituali: Joh. 16, 11. Phil. 4, 4. 1 Petr. 1, 8. 1 Joh. 1, 4.
units.tr: Let us rightly esteem the glorification begun in this life, and the good things that are present in it: 1 John 3:1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 4. Rom. 5:5. John 15:15. 2 Pet. 1:8, 11. In it let us seek comfort against all calamities, labours and remaining miseries: 2 Cor. 1:3, 4, 5. 1 John 5:4. Rom. 8:37. And let us exult with spiritual joy: John 16:11. Phil. 4:4. 1 Pet. 1:8. 1 John 1:4.

units.la: 2. Mortalitatis nostræ nobis conscii, temporis verò quo moriendum erit ignari, tantam interim expectationem habentes, juxta Euangelium; ritè nos præparemus semper; & piâ praxi spem istam confirmemus: Psal. 90, 12. Eph. 5, 16. 2 Cor. 5, 8, 9.
units.tr: 2. Being aware of our mortality, but ignorant of the time at which we must die, and having meanwhile such expectation, according to the Gospel, let us always prepare ourselves duly and confirm this hope by a pious practice: Ps. 90:12. Eph. 5:16. 2 Cor. 5:8, 9.

units.la: 3. Sedulò operam demus communioni cum Christo, per resurrectionem primam; quò magis corroboretur spes resurrectionis beatæ: Apoc. 20, 6. XIV, 13. 1 Joh. 3, 3.
units.tr: 3. Let us diligently labour for communion with Christ through the first resurrection, so that the hope of the blessed resurrection may be the more strengthened: Rev. 20:6; 14:13. 1 John 3:3.

units.la: 4. Sic meditemur Judicium extremum, ut quàm accuratissimè observemus atque instituamus singulas actiones nostras: 2 Cor. 5, 10, 11. Luc. 21, 34, 35, 36. Matth. 24, 42, 44, 1 Thess. V, 2, 6. 1 Petr. 4, 7: 2. III, 11. Terrorem illum Domini scientes tantò magis saluti nostræ studeamus, atque alios sedulò commonefaciamus: 2 Cor. 5, 11.
units.tr: 4. Let us so meditate on the final Judgment that we observe and order each of our actions as carefully as possible: 2 Cor. 5:10, 11. Luke 21:34, 35, 36. Matt. 24:42, 44. 1 Thess. 5:2, 6. 1 Pet. 4:7; 2 Pet. 3:11. Knowing that terror of the Lord, let us all the more earnestly strive for our salvation, and diligently admonish others: 2 Cor. 5:11.

units.la: 5. Quoniàm cognoscimus, qualis & quanta futura sit merces nostra in Cœlis, strenui simus & assidui in officiis nostris: Matth. 5, 12. 1 Cor. 15, 58. Phil, 3, 12, 13, 14, 20, 21. Tit II, 12, 13. 1 Joh. 3, 2, 3. Apoc. 20, 11, 12.
units.tr: 5. Since we know what and how great our reward in heaven will be, let us be eager and diligent in our duties: Matt. 5:12. 1 Cor. 15:58. Phil. 3:12, 13, 14, 20, 21. Titus 2:12, 13. 1 John 3:2, 3. Rev. 20:11, 12.

units.la: CAPUT XX. & ultimum,
units.tr: CHAPTER XX, and last,

units.la: De Ecclesia.
units.tr: Of the Church.

units.la: ECclesiæ synonyma. 1. Vocabuli usus varius in SS. Literis. Sed nusquam significat Pontificem Rom.
units.tr: Synonyms of the Church. 1. The varied use of the word in the Holy Scriptures. But nowhere does it signify the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: 2. Definitio. Ecclesia mystica. 3. Hujus Caput. Non Pontifex Rom. 4. Ecclesia militans, Triumphans. Errores tùm Pontif. tùm Socin. 5. Catholica. Invisibilis. Indefectibilis. 6. Ecclesia externa instituta. Distributiones quædam. 7. Quomodò constituatur Ecclesia particularis. 8. Ministri Ecclesiastici. Patriarchæ. Prophetæ, Ordinarii V. T. 9. Ministri N. T. Apostoli. 10. Prophetæ. 11. Exercitia prophetica. Revelationes extraordinariæ. 12. Euangelistæ. 13. Ordinarii. Pastores. 14. Vocatio. Ejus necessitas, c. Enthuf. Libert. &c. Obj. solv. 15. Electio. 16. Examen. 17. Approbatio. 18. Publica confirmatio. 19. Potestas vocandi & mittendi Pastores, tùm principalis, tùm ministerialis. 20. Praxis Ecclesiarum nostrarum. Jus Patronatûs. 21. Primorum Reformatorum vocatio legitima, &c. Dilemma Pontif. solv. 22. Necessitas muneris Pastoralis; c. Enthuf. &c. 23. Objectiones solv. 24. Pastorum æqualitas; c. Pontif. aliosque Hierarch. Obj. solv. 25. Petrus non superior reliquis Apostolis. Obj. solv. 26. Stipendium, c. Anabapt. Obj. solv. 27. Doctores. 28. Seniores gubernantes. Obj. solv. 29. Diaconi. 30. Opitulationes. 31. Reliqua multitudo fidelium. Male distinguunt Pontif. in Clericos, & Laïcos. 32. Itemque in Religiosos, & SaculaSaeculares, Religio quid illis. Refut. Obj, solv. 33. Functiones domatim obeundæ, 34. Publica S. Scriptura prælectio. 35. Psalmodia Ecclesiastica. 36. Preces Eccles. In iis Ministrum præire oportet clara voce; c. Anabap. & quidem lingua communiter notâ; c. Pontif. 37. Non conveniunt illis Antiphona, & Responsoria, c. eosd. Neque sufficiunt certæ quædam formulæ. 38. Conciones. Earum necessitas; c, Libert. 39. Textus. 40. Inventio. 41. Explicatio. Documentum. Usus. 42. Dispositio. 43. Exornatio. Actio. 44. Catechizatio: eaque varia. 45. Benedictio. Eleemosynarum collectio. 46. Administratio Sacramentorum. Excommunicatio. Reconciliatio. 47. Publica Ministrorum confirmatio. Jejunium publicum. Dies eucharisticus. Matrimonii Confirmatio. Exercitia Academica. 48. Presbyterium. Præses. Scriba. 49. Negotia ibi tractanda. Disciplina Eccles. Ejus necessitas. Obj. solv. 50. Partes Antecessorum Eccles. in eâ; c. Brown. 51. Excommunicatio major. Minor. Simplex abstentio. 52. Nemo excommunicandus sine prævia admonitione; aut jam resipiscens: c. Annapt. 53. Ea non extinguit obligationem naturalem, &c. Anathema. Excommunicatio illegitima. 54. Error Novat. Pœnitentes iterum admittendi. Reconciliatio apud Catholicos olim tarda. Occasio Indulgentiarum. Pœnitentes non satisfaciunt justitiæ Divinæ. 55. Electio Ministrorum. Dimissio Pastorum; & aliorum membrorum Ecclesiæ, &c. Conventus Diaconorum. 56. Unio & correspondentia plurium Ecclesiarum partic. 57. Classis. 58. Synodus Provincialis. cialis. Nationalis. Oecumenica. 59. Qui ad Synodum mittuntur, manent adstricti Verbo Dei; & consequenter suæ Ecclesiæ, atque Confessioni; c. Remonstr. Et juxta Verbum Dei rectè dicunt: Hoc firmiter & constanter credendum est. Sic etiam obligantur Adversarii. 60. Adjuncta Eccl. partic. Potestas ministerialis. 61. Visibilitas. Ecclesia nostra ante Lutherum. 62. Ecclesiæ partic. defectibilitas. etiam Romanæ. Obj. solv. 63. Nota. 64. Earum investigatio non inutilis; c. Socin. & Libert. 65. Sententia Pontif. 66. Contraria. Persecutiones. 67. Seductiones. 68. Antichristus. Magnus ille. 69. Est Papa Romanus. Ἀκτείνω. Efficacia Satanæ. Defectiones. Occasio patefactionis. 70. Hypocrisis. Scelerosus ille. ἀντικείμενος. Extollens se supra Deum, &c. 71. Illecebræ doctrinarum fallacium. Signa mendacia. Exempla vitæ impuræ. Crudelitas tyrannica. Effectus in aliis. Eventus ipsius. 72. Sententia Pontificiorum de Antichristo. Ecclesia Romana verè Antichristiana, & Babylon Apocalyptica. Deferenda. 73. Apostasia Muhammedica. Haretici: & errantes alii. 74. Praxis. 75.
units.tr: 2. Definition. The mystical Church. 3. Its Head: not the Roman Pontiff. 4. The militant and the triumphant Church. Errors both of the Papists and of the Socinians. 5. Catholic. Invisible. Indefectible. 6. The external institution of the Church. Certain distinctions. 7. How the particular Church is constituted. 8. The ecclesiastical ministers. Patriarchs; prophets; the ordinary ministers of the Old Testament. 9. The ministers of the New Testament. Apostles. 10. Prophets. 11. Prophetic exercises. Extraordinary revelations. 12. Evangelists. 13. Ordinary ministers; pastors. 14. The calling. Its necessity, against the Enthusiasts, Libertines, etc. Objections answered. 15. Election. 16. Examination. 17. Approval. 18. Public confirmation. 19. The power of calling and sending pastors, both principal and ministerial. 20. The practice of our Churches. The right of patronage. 21. The lawful calling of the first Reformers, etc. The Papists' dilemma answered. 22. The necessity of the pastoral office; against the Enthusiasts, etc. 23. Objections answered. 24. The equality of pastors; against the Papists and other hierarchs. Objections answered. 25. Peter was not superior to the other Apostles. Objections answered. 26. Stipend; against the Anabaptists. Objection answered. 27. Teachers. 28. Governing elders. Objections answered. 29. Deacons. 30. Assistance. 31. The rest of the multitude of the faithful. The Papists wrongly divide them into clergy and laity. 32. Likewise into religious and secular; what religion means for them. The objections are refuted. 33. The duties to be performed house by house. 34. The public reading of Holy Scripture. 35. Ecclesiastical psalmody. 36. Ecclesiastical prayers. In these the minister ought to lead with a clear voice, against the Anabaptists, and indeed in a language commonly known, against the Papists. 37. Antiphons and responsories are not suitable to them, against the same; nor do certain set formulas suffice. 38. Sermons. Their necessity, against the Libertines. 39. The text. 40. Invention. 41. Explanation. Teaching. Use. 42. Arrangement. 43. Ornament. Delivery. 44. Catechizing, and this in various forms. 45. Blessing. The collection of alms. 46. The administration of the sacraments. Excommunication. Reconciliation. 47. Public confirmation of ministers. Public fast. The Eucharistic day. The confirmation of marriage. Academic exercises. 48. The presbytery. The president. The clerk. 49. Business transacted there. Church discipline, and its necessity. Objections answered. 50. The parts of the elders of the Church in it; against Browne. 51. Major excommunication. Minor. Simple abstention. 52. No one is to be excommunicated without prior admonition, or if he is already repenting; against the Anabaptists. 53. Excommunication does not extinguish the natural obligation, etc. Anathema. Illegitimate excommunication. 54. The error of the Novatians. Penitents to be readmitted again. Reconciliation was formerly slow among the Catholics. The occasion of indulgences. Penitents do not satisfy the divine justice. 55. The election of ministers. The dismissal of pastors, and of other members of the Church, etc. The assembly of deacons. 56. The union and correspondence of several particular Churches. 57. The classis. 58. The provincial synod. National. Ecumenical. 59. Those who are sent to a synod remain bound to the Word of God, and consequently to their own Church and Confession; against the Remonstrants. And rightly, according to the Word of God, they say: "This is to be believed firmly and constantly." Thus the opponents too are bound. 60. The attributes of the particular Church. Ministerial power. 61. Visibility. Our Church before Luther. 62. Defectibility of particular Churches, even the Roman. Objection answered. 63. Marks. 64. The investigation of them is not useless, against the Socinians and Libertines. 65. The opinion of the Papists. 66. The contrary opinion. Persecutions. 67. Seductions. 68. The Antichrist. That great one. 69. It is the Roman Pope. Aktheino [ἀκτείνω]. The efficacy of Satan. Defections. The occasion of the revelation. 70. Hypocrisy. That wicked one. Antikeimenos [ἀντικείμενος]. Exalting himself above God, etc. 71. The allurements of false doctrines. Lying signs. Examples of an impure life. Tyrannical cruelty. The effect on others. His own end. 72. The opinion of the Papists about Antichrist. The Roman Church is truly Antichristian, and the Apocalyptic Babylon. To be rejected. 73. Muhammadan apostasy. Heretics, and other erring persons. 74. Practice. 75.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Ic fuerunt actus, per quos applicatur salus: sequitur ut videamus de objecto, circa quod isti actus versantur. Communi nomine Ecclesia appellatur; Græcè Ἐκκλησία, à verbo Ἐκκαλέω, evoco: est que Coetus hominum evocatus & convocatus; utpotè præconis voce. Similiter Concio dicitur, à concieido. Hebraicè קהל, à verbo קהל, congregagregavit; vel עָדָה à יָעַד, indixit, &c. Græci Interpretes utramque vocem transtulerunt Συναγωγὴν; sed & priorem aliquando 'Ἐκκλησίαν. Postea usus invaluit, ut Judæorum congregatio, atque item ejus locus, appellaretur Synagoga; Christianis autem servaretur nomen Ecclesiæ. Vide tamen Hebr. 10, 25. Jac. 2, 2.
units.tr: These were the acts through which salvation is applied; it follows that we should see about the object with which these acts are concerned. It is called by the common name Church; in Greek Ἐκκλησία [Ekklēsia], from the verb ἐκκαλέω [ekkaleō], to call out: it is an assembly of men called out and summoned together, as by the voice of a herald. Similarly it is called concio, from concieo. In Hebrew קהל [qahal], from the verb קהל [qahal], to gather; or עֵדָה [edah], from יָעַד [ya'ad], to appoint, etc. The Greek interpreters rendered both words by συναγωγή [synagōgē]; but sometimes they also rendered the former by ἐκκλησία [ekklēsia]. Later usage prevailed, so that the congregation of the Jews, and likewise its place, was called synagogue, while the name Church was kept for Christians. Yet see Heb. 10:25; Jas. 2:2.

units.la: II Ecclesia autem in SS. Literis quandoque sumitur generatim pro quolibet hominum coetû; etiam tumultuantium & malignantium: ut Act. 19, 31. Alii aliud clamabant; erat enim 'Ἐκκλησία confusa. Psal. 26, 5. in Versione Græca, & Vulgatâ Latinâ: Odivi Ecclesiam malignantium. Verùm ista significatio generalitate suâ excedit limites considerationis nostræ. Specialiter autem vel sic usurpatur, ut magis spectetur status interior; de corpore scil. mystico, ad æternam salutem electo, quod Christus summopere dilexit, & constanter in communione suâ conservat: Eph. 5, 25, 26. Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, &c. Hebr. 12, 22, 23. Matth. 26, 18. Vel etiam ut magis respiciatur status exterior.
units.tr: II. In Holy Scripture, however, Church is sometimes taken in general for any assembly of men, even a tumultuous and malicious one, as in Acts 19:31: "Some cried one thing, and some another; for the assembly (ἐκκλησία) was confused." Psalm 26:5 in the Greek version and the Latin Vulgate: "I have hated the Church of the wicked." But this meaning, by its generality, goes beyond the limits of our consideration. More specifically, however, the word is used in a way that looks rather at the inner state, namely of the mystical body, elect to eternal salvation, which Christ loved above all and constantly preserves in his fellowship: Eph. 5:25, 26, "Christ loved the Church, etc."; Heb. 12:22, 23; Matt. 16:18. Or again, it is used where the external state is in view.

units.la: Sic autem vel universaliter notat religiosam societatem eorum, qui ex universo genere humano per Verbi prædicationem collecti, eandem fidem salutarem profitentur: 1 Tim. 3, 15. Ut noris, quomodo oporteat in domo Dei versari, quæ est Ecclesia Dei vivi. Vel sumitur particulariter, prout talis societas exstitit in urbe, vico, simili loco particulari: 1 Cor. 1, 2. Ecclesiæ Dei, quæ est Corinthi. 1 Thess. 1, 1. Imò etiam 1 Cor. 16, 19. Salutant vos in Domino multum Aquila & Priscilla; cum Ecclesia, quæ est domi ipsorum: ubi intelligenda videtur societas fidelium, tùm in eâdem domo habitantium, tùm istùc ad exercitia sacra unà convenire solitorum. Similiter Rom. 16, 5. Col. 4, 15. Tales autem cœtûs distincti in aliquâ provinciâ, aut majori orbis tractu, pluraliter Ecclesiæ appellari solent; 1 Cor. 16, 1. Ordinavi Ecclesiis Galatiæ. 19. Salutant vos Ecclesiæ Asiæ.
units.tr: Thus it signifies either universally the religious society of those who, gathered from the whole human race through the preaching of the Word, profess the same saving faith: 1 Tim. 3:15, "that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God." Or it is taken particularly, as such a society existed in a city, a village, or a similar particular place: 1 Cor. 1:2, "the Church of God which is at Corinth"; 1 Thess. 1:1. Indeed, also 1 Cor. 16:19, "Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the Church that is in their house"; where the society of the faithful seems to be meant, both those living in the same house and those accustomed to assemble there for sacred exercises. Similarly Rom. 16:5; Col. 4:15. Moreover, such distinct assemblies in some province, or in a larger extent of the world, are usually called Churches in the plural: 1 Cor. 16:1, "I have given orders to the Churches of Galatia"; 19, "the Churches of Asia salute you."

units.la: Verum quandoque occurrit acceptio synecdochica; ut Multitudo fidelium pascendorum, à Pastoribus suis contradistincta, appelletur Ecclesia; quæ est pars major: sic Paulus Presbyteris Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ dixit, Act. 20, 28. Spiritus ille Sanctus vos constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, –. Interdum contrà magis spectatur Collegium ipsorum Pascentium; ubi est pars ratione ordinis potior: ita Christus de Disciplinâ Ecclesiasticâ agens, Matth. 18, 17. Quodsi neglexerit eos (testes à primo redarguente assumtos) audire; dic Ecclesiæ. Vulgò Ecclesia repræsentativa appellatur; quod Collegium illud in exercendo Regimine toti multitudini Ecclesiasticæ præeat, eamque quodammodò repræsentet. Paulus Πρεσβυτέριον vocat; 1 Tim. 4, 14.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, a synecdochical sense occurs, so that the multitude of the faithful to be fed, distinguished from their pastors, is called the Church, which is the greater part. Thus Paul said to the elders of the Ephesian Church, Acts 20:28, "The Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to feed the Church of God." At other times, on the contrary, the college of those who feed is regarded more, where it is the part more important by reason of order: so Christ, speaking of church discipline, Matt. 18:17, "If he refuses to hear them (the witnesses first taken to rebuke him), tell the Church." It is commonly called the representative Church, because that college, in exercising government, goes before the whole ecclesiastical multitude and in some measure represents it. Paul calls it πρεσβυτέριον [presbyterion], 1 Tim. 4:14.

units.la: Hactenus ergo semper significat in Scripturâ multitudinem; nunquàm verò unum quemcunque hominem; utpote Pontificem Romanum: quod volunt ejus sectatores. Hoc autem eo absurdius est, quòd ipsi cogantur fateri, fieri posse, ut ille ad Ecclesiam non pertineat; si videl. non fuerit baptizatus; vel propter Simoniam, aut hærefin occultam, ipso facto sit excommunicatus.
units.tr: So far, then, in Scripture the word always signifies a multitude, and never any single man, such as the Roman Pontiff, as his followers maintain. This is the more absurd because they themselves are forced to admit that it may happen that he does not belong to the Church, namely if he has not been baptized, or, on account of simony or a hidden heresy, is excommunicated by the very fact.

units.la: Ecclesia metonymicè etiam aliquando notat Locum, ubi Conventûs sacri solent haberi: sed in SS. Literis id non fit manifestè. Cùm enim dicitur, 1 Cor. xi, 18, 22. Cùm convenitis in Ecclesiâ, –. Aut Ecclesiam Dei contemnitis? intelligitur potius ipse Cœtus fidelium.
units.tr: Church also sometimes signifies, by metonymy, the place where sacred assemblies are usually held; but in Holy Scripture this is not clearly the case. For when it is said, 1 Cor. 11:18, 22, "when you come together in the Church…", or "Do you despise the Church of God?", the assembly of the faithful itself is rather to be understood.

units.la: III. Ad rem significatam quod attinet; Ecclesia est Cœtus hominum, ad communionem Fœderis salutaris cum Deo in Christo vocatorum, & assumtorum. Cœtum & Vocationem indicat ipsum nomen: Communionem Fœderis salutaris cum Deo in Christo, & Assumtionem in eam, indicat passim S. Scriptura. Ad Homines restringimus; quoniam Fœdus salutare in Christo intercedit inter Deum & Homines: ad Angelos istud non pertinet. Confer sup. 12. th. 27.
units.tr: III. As for the thing signified, the Church is the assembly and calling of men summoned to, and taken up into, communion in the saving covenant with God in Christ. Holy Scripture everywhere indicates the name itself and the communion in the saving covenant with God in Christ, and admission into it. We restrict the term to men, since the saving covenant in Christ is between God and men; it does not pertain to angels. See above, 12th thesis, 27th.

units.la: Quoniam verò Ecclesia à Vocatione nomen accepit, & per eam constituitur; ex hâc potissimùm cognosci debet. Primario igitur spectanda venit Ecclesia mystica: Cœtus hominum electorum, qui per vocationem efficacem ac verè salutarem adducti sunt ad interiorem, sive mysticam, unionem & communionem cum Capite suo Christo.
units.tr: Since the Church takes its name from calling and is constituted by it, it ought to be known chiefly from this. Primarily, therefore, the Church mystical comes under consideration: the assembly of the elect, who through effectual and truly saving calling are brought into inner, or mystical, union and communion with their Head, Christ.

units.la: IV. Itâ Caput hujus est Christus, qui ut per Spiritum suum ista membra spiritualiter vivificat; sic porrò eamovet, gubernat, & perficit ad veram æternamque beatitudinem. Eph. 1, 22, 23. Pater constituit Eum Caput super omnia Ecclesiæ: Quæ est corpus ipsius, & complementum ejus, qui omnia complet in omnibus, IV, 15, 16. V, 23. Col. I, 18. II, 9, 10, 19.
units.tr: IV. Thus the Head of this body is Christ, who, as he quickens these members spiritually through his Spirit, so also moves, governs and brings them to true and eternal blessedness. Eph. 1:22, 23: the Father "appointed him head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all"; 4:15, 16; 5:23; Col. 1:18; 2:9, 10, 19.

units.la: Neque tamen Christus putandus est proprie Pars Ecclesiæ: cùm omnis Pars proprie dicta ab aliis Partibus perficiatur in Toto, & Totum majus ac perfectius fit quàlibet suâ Parte; Christus autem à suis membris nullam accipiat perfectionem, ipse in Se persectionem infinitam habens.
units.tr: Yet Christ is not to be thought of as properly a part of the Church, since every part properly so called is completed by the other parts within the whole, and the whole becomes greater and more perfect by each of its parts; but Christ receives no perfection from his members, having in himself infinite perfection.

units.la: Pontificii suum Pontificem statuunt Caput Ecclesiæ veræ Catholicæ. Verùm I. S. Scriptura docet Christum esse Caput Ecclesiæ; atque hanc dignitatem ipsi peculiariter tributam: ut modò probatum est. Solus Ergò Christus talis agnoscendus est: plura Capita ejusdem Corporis, hoc monstrosum faciunt.
units.tr: The Papists set up their own pontiff as the Head of the true Catholic Church. But: 1. Holy Scripture teaches that Christ is the Head of the Church, and that this dignity is ascribed to him peculiarly, as has just been proved. Christ alone, therefore, is to be acknowledged as such; several heads of the same body would make it a monster.

units.la: 2. Huc etiam pertinent aliæ phrases, quibus eadem res, & eadem unitas, diserte exprimitur. Nempe quod Christus sit unus Dominus: Eph. 4, 5. Unus Doctor principalis: Matth. 23, 8, 11. cum Ephes. 4, 11. Unus Sponsus, & Vir Ecclesiæ: 2 Cor. XI, 2. Unicum Fundamentum hujus Spiritualis ædificii: 1 Cor. 3, 11. Unus Mediator·Dei & Hominum: 1 Tim. II. 5, 6. in quo solo salus: Act. 4, 12. cum Eph. 5. 23.
units.tr: 2. To this also belong other phrases by which the same reality and the same unity are expressly stated: namely, that Christ is the one Lord (Eph. 4:5); the principal one Teacher (Matt. 23:8, 11, with Eph. 4:11); the one Bridegroom and Husband of the Church (2 Cor. 11:2); the sole Foundation of this spiritual building (1 Cor. 3:11); the one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5, 6), in whom alone is salvation (Acts 4:12, with Eph. 5:23).

units.la: 3. Christus ita dicitur Rex Ecclesiæ, ut illa ἐξουσία illi soli tribuatur; imo etiam Divina ipsius Filiatio ipsi dignitati substernatur: Psal. II, 6, 7, 8, 12. Hebr. 1, 1, -9. Job. 5, 20, 23, 26, 27, 28. Phil. II, 6, -11.
units.tr: 3. Christ is called King of the Church in such a way that this authority [ἐξουσία] is given to him alone; indeed his divine Sonship itself is subordinated to that dignity (Ps. 2:6, 7, 8, 12; Heb. 1:1–9; John 5:20, 23, 26, 27, 28; Phil. 2:6–11).

units.la: 4. Actus isti interni spirituales, & efficaces, qui a Christo ut Capite Ecclesiæ procedunt, atque ex ipso in membris suis mysticis exeruntur, tales sunt ut a mera aliqua creatura proficisci minime possint; sed Personam Θεάνθρωπον requirant, ut per Spiritum Sanctum possit in iis vivere, eos movere, &c.
units.tr: 4. These inner, spiritual and effectual acts, which proceed from Christ as Head of the Church and flow out from him into his mystical members, are such that they cannot possibly arise from any mere creature, but require a God-man [Θεάνθρωπον], so that through the Holy Spirit he may live in them, move them, and so on.

units.la: V. Per veram fidem Evangelicam & salvificam, singula membra accipiunt hanc salutarem cum Christo Capite suo unionem & communionem; eademque opera accipiunt unionem & communionem inter se mutuam, tanquam Membra unius Corporis mystici.
units.tr: V. Through true, evangelical and saving faith, the individual members receive this saving union and communion with Christ their Head; and by the same means they receive mutual union and communion among themselves, as members of one mystical body.

units.la: Sic autem, ratione status distincti, Partes ejus sunt Ecclesia militans, & Ecclesia triumphans.
units.tr: Thus, according to the distinction of state, its parts are the Church militant and the Church triumphant.

units.la: Ecclesia militans in hoc sæculo, in Regno gratiæ, in virtute Christi, sub ipsius vexillo militiam gerit adversus hostes spirituales, ac per fidem victoria potitur: 1 Tim. 6, 12. De certa præclarum illud certamen fidei. 2: IV, 7, 8. Rom. 8, 37. In his omnibus amplius quam victores sumus. Militat ergo contra Diabolum. Ephes. 6, 12. Est nobis lucta -- adversus -- tenebrarum hujus sæculi Principes, adversus spirituales malignitates in sublimi. 1 Petr. 5, 8, 9. Diabolus - quærit quem devoret. Adversus Mundum: Joh. 14, 19. XVI, 33. 1 Joh. 5, 4. Fides nostra est victoria, quæ vincit mundum. Et adversus Carnem: Nam Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum, &c. Gal 5, 17. Col. 3, 5. 1 Cor. 9, 26, 27.
units.tr: The Church militant, in this age, in the kingdom of grace, by the power of Christ, under his banner, wages war against spiritual enemies and by faith obtains the victory: 1 Tim. 6:12, "fight the good fight of faith"; 2 Tim. 4:7, 8; Rom. 8:37, "in all these things we are more than conquerors." It therefore wages war against the Devil (Eph. 6:12: "our struggle is against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual wickedness in high places"; 1 Pet. 5:8, 9: the devil "seeks whom he may devour"). Against the World (John 14:19; 16:33; 1 John 5:4: "our faith is the victory that overcomes the world"). And against the Flesh: "for the flesh lusts against the Spirit," etc. (Gal. 5:17; Col. 3:5; 1 Cor. 9:26, 27).

units.la: Ecclesia triumphans est, quæ bello illo ad gloriosum finem virtute Christi perducto, cum ipso in Coelis beatum atque æternum triumphum agit; priùs secundùm animas separatas, deindè secundùm integras personas. Hebr. 12, 22, 23. Accessistis ad -- concionem primogenitorum, qui conscripti sunt in Coelis, -& Spiritus justorum consummatorum. Apoc 6. 9, 11. VII, 9, 14.
units.tr: The Church triumphant is that which, once that warfare has been brought to its glorious end by the power of Christ, celebrates with him in heaven a blessed and eternal triumph: first according to the souls separated from the body, and then according to the whole persons. Heb. 12:22, 23: "You have come to ... the assembly of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and to the spirits of just men made perfect." Rev. 6:9, 11; 7:9, 14.

units.la: In defectu hic peccant Sociniani; dum hinc ad extremum usque judicium nullam Ecclesiam actu triumphantem agnoscunt: in excessu vero Pontificii; qui insuper Ecclesiam aliquam laborantem in Purgatorio fingunt.
units.tr: In defect the Socinians err here, while they acknowledge no Church actually triumphant before the last judgment; in excess the Papists err, who moreover imagine a suffering Church in Purgatory.

units.la: Atque ità omnes vere fideles, dum sunt in hoc sæculo, ad Ecclesiam militantem; hinc autem translati, iidem ad triumphantem pertinent.
units.tr: And so all truly faithful, while they are in this age, belong to the Church militant; but once translated from here, the same belong to the triumphant Church.

units.la: VI. Ecclesia mystica recte dicitur catholica, invisibilis, & indefectibilis.
units.tr: VI. The mystical Church is rightly called catholic, invisible, and indefectible.

units.la: Catholica; quia omnes vere fideles, omnium locorum, omniumque temporum, sua amplitudine complectitur.
units.tr: Catholic, because it embraces, by its breadth, all truly faithful people of every place and every time.

units.la: Invisibilis; quia mystica unio & communio vere fidelium cum Christo, atque inter se mutuo, oculis omnino conspici non potest.
units.tr: Invisible, because the mystical union and communion of the truly faithful with Christ and with one another cannot be seen by the eyes at all.

units.la: Indefectibilis; quia fieri non potest, ut numero vere fidelium quicquam decedat. Huc pertinet illustre testimonium Christi, Joh. 10, 14, 15, 16. Ego sum Pastor ille bonus; & agnosco meas (oves.) - Habeo alias etiam oves, quæ non sunt ex hac caula: eas Me quoque oportet adducere: - fietque unus Grex, & unus Pastor. Ac porro, 26,-30. 2 Tim. 2, 19. 1 Petr. 2, 9.
units.tr: Indefectible, because it cannot happen that anything be lost from the number of the truly faithful. To this belongs the famous testimony of Christ, John 10, 14, 15, 16. I am that good Shepherd, and I know my (sheep). I have other sheep also, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and there shall be one flock and one Shepherd. And further, 26-30. 2 Tim. 2, 19. 1 Pet. 2, 9.

units.la: VII. Altera consideratio est Ecclesiæ secundum formam externam institutam, in suis Conventibus; ubi Verbum prædicatur, Sacramenta administrantur, Disciplina exercetur, aliaque similia peraguntur: sic tamen ut actusisti externi, tanquam signa & media, referantur ad statum interiorem; eumque promoveant.
units.tr: VII. The second consideration is of the Church according to its instituted external form, in its assemblies, where the Word is preached, the sacraments are administered, discipline is exercised, and other similar things are carried out; yet in such a way that the external acts, as signs and means, are referred to the inner state and promote it.

units.la: Citra istum respectum & usum media illa externa non constituunt Ecclesiam, aut Membra ejus; nisi æquivocè. Hos. 1, 9. Vos non eritis populus meus; &c. II, 2. Rom. 2, 25, 28, 29. Quod si transgressor Legis fueris, Circumcisio tua facta est Præputium. Non enim qui est in propatulo (Judæus,) Judæus est. 1 Joh. 2. 19. Non erant ex nobis.
units.tr: Apart from this respect and use, those external means do not constitute the Church or its members, except equivocally. Hos. 1, 9. You are not my people, etc. 2, 2. Rom. 2, 25, 28, 29. If you are a transgressor of the Law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly. 1 John 2, 19. They were not of us.

units.la: Sic autem ratione temporis atque œconomiæ statim occurrit distributio in Ecclesiam V. Test. & Ecclesiam N. Test.
units.tr: Thus, by reason of time and economy, the distinction between the Church of the Old Testament and the Church of the New Testament immediately presents itself.

units.la: Atque hæc porro considerari potest per sua Sæcula; priora, media, posteriora: deinde, secundum Plagas mundi; aut secundum Nationes, Regna, Provincias, Urbes, Vicos: atque adeo vel magis, vel minus universaliter; sive etiam particulariter. Potissimum vero spectari debent, ubi externam formam institutam consideramus, singulæ Particulares Ecclesiæ, secundum Urbes, Vicos, vel etiam Cœtus, distinctæ.
units.tr: This Church may further be considered through its successive ages: earlier, middle, and later; then according to the regions of the world, or according to nations, kingdoms, provinces, cities, and villages; and so more or less universally, or also particularly. Most importantly, however, when we consider the instituted external form, the individual particular churches, distinguished according to cities, villages, or even assemblies, ought to be regarded.

units.la: VIII. Ecclesia autem externa particularis instituta
units.tr: VIII. The instituted particular external Church

units.la: sic constituitur per Fidelium confœderationem & conjunctionem mutuam, ad communes actus religiosos, Verbi prædicandi, Sacramentorum administrandorum, Disciplinæ exercendæ, &c. præeuntibus Antecessoribus. Hinc Act. 13, 1, 2. Erant autem Antiochiæ, in Ecclesiâ quæ illic erat, quidam Prophetæ & Doctores, &c. Illis autem sacram suam functionem obeuntibus. Vide porro, XIV, 21, 22, 23. XV, 2, 3, 4, 6. XX, 17. 28. 1 Cor. 4, 17. XI, 16, 18 § 20, 22. XV, 1, 2. Phil. 1, 1. Tit. 1, 5. Apoc. 1, 20. Distinctè autem in Ecclesia instituta spectabimus deinceps Partes, Functiones obeundas, Adjuncta, & Contraria.
units.tr: is constituted in this way, through the confederation and mutual conjunction of the faithful for common religious acts: preaching the Word, administering the sacraments, exercising discipline, etc., their predecessors having gone before. Hence Acts 13, 1, 2: Now there were in Antioch, in the church that was there, certain prophets and teachers, etc. And when they were performing their sacred function. See further 14, 21, 22, 23; 15, 2, 3, 4, 6; 20, 17, 28. 1 Cor. 4, 17; 11, 16, 18, 20, 22; 15, 1, 2. Phil. 1, 1. Titus 1, 5. Rev. 1, 20. We shall next consider distinctly, in the instituted Church, the parts, the functions to be performed, the adjuncts, and the contraries.

units.la: IX. Partes Ecclesiæ institutæ sunt Ministri Ecclesiastici, & reliqua multitudo fidelium; qui pariter constituunt Exteriorem Politiam Ecclesiasticam.
units.tr: IX. The parts of the instituted Church are the ecclesiastical ministers and the remaining multitude of the faithful, who together constitute the external ecclesiastical polity.

units.la: Ministri Ecclesiastici dicuntur; Personæ, quibus ex ordinatione Christi, singularis aliqua functio demandata est, ad communem ædificationem. Hi confiderari possunt vel V. vel N. T. atque utrique in extraordinarios, & ordinarios, dispescuntur.
units.tr: Ecclesiastical ministers are called those persons to whom, by the ordinance of Christ, some particular function has been entrusted for common edification. These may be considered in either the Old or the New Testament, and in each they are divided into extraordinary and ordinary.

units.la: Extraordinarii vocatione & donis extraordinariis dignoscuntur. Tales sub V. T. fuerunt Patriarchæ, & Prophetæ.
units.tr: Extraordinary ministers are distinguished by an extraordinary call and extraordinary gifts. Such under the Old Testament were the Patriarchs and the Prophets.

units.la: Patriarchæ appropriato usu dicuntur ejusmodi Patres familiarum, iidemque Ministri extraordinarii, qui ante exaratas SS. Literas, & ante Sacerdotium Leviticum, Ecclesiam in suis familiis & in sua posteritate instituerunt, conservarunt, & propagarunt, tum ante, tum post Diluvium. Quantum ad nomen attinet, Jacobus Act. 7, 8. dicitur genuisse duodecim illos Patriarchas. Quantum ad rem, statim à lapsu Deus Adamo & Evæ Euangelium promissionis ipse revelavit; Gen. 3, 15. Nec dubitandum; quin modum sacrificandi porro docuerit: unde potissimum celebratur sacrificium Abelis per fidem oblatum, Gen. 4, 4. Hebr. xi, 4. Vide etiam Gen. 4, 26. Item v, 22, 24. cum Hebr. xi, 5. & Judæ, 14, 15. Porro autem tum ante, tum post diluvium, Patriarchæ fuerunt plures; de quibus per totam Genesin legere est.
units.tr: In a specially appropriate use, the Patriarchs are called those heads of families who were also extraordinary ministers, and who, before the Holy Scriptures were written and before the Levitical priesthood, instituted, preserved, and propagated the Church in their households and their posterity, both before and after the Flood. As to the name, Jacob (Acts 7, 8) is said to have begotten those twelve Patriarchs. As to the thing itself, immediately after the fall God himself revealed to Adam and Eve the gospel of promise (Gen. 3, 15). Nor is there doubt that he further taught the manner of sacrificing; whence chiefly is celebrated the sacrifice of Abel offered by faith (Gen. 4, 4; Heb. 11, 4). See also Gen. 4, 26; likewise 5, 22, 24, with Heb. 11, 5, and Jude 14, 15. Moreover, both before and after the Flood there were several Patriarchs, about whom one may read through the whole of Genesis.

units.la: Prophetæ V. T. dicuntur, qui citra respectum ad familiam ac posteritatem propriam, tamen ut Ministri extraordinarii, cum SS. Literæ exarari coeptæ sunt, & cultus œconomicus V. T. magis in ordinem redactus, ac deinceps, mysteria Divina Θεοπνεύστως revelarunt; vel etiam futura prædixerunt, ac potissimum de Messiâ venturo, ejusque vita, passionibus, gloriâ, officiis, & beneficiis: Act. 3, 21, -24. De quibus locutus est Deus à sæculo, per os omnium sanctorum suorum Prophetarum. x, 43. Huic (Christo) etiam omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant. Hebr. I, 1. 1 Petr. I, 10, 11, 12.
units.tr: The Prophets of the Old Testament are those who, without regard to their own family and posterity, yet as extraordinary ministers, when the Holy Scriptures began to be written and the economical worship of the Old Testament was brought more into order, thereafter revealed divine mysteries by divine inspiration, or also foretold future things, chiefly concerning the coming Messiah and his life, sufferings, glory, offices, and benefits: Acts 3, 21-24: Of whom God has spoken from of old through the mouth of all his holy Prophets. 10, 43: To him (Christ) all the Prophets also give testimony. Heb. 1, 1. 1 Pet. 1, 10, 11, 12.

units.la: Horum aliqui Spiritui Sancto servierunt, tanquam amanuamanuenses, in conscribendis SS. Literis. Tales fuerunt Moses, David, Salomon, &c. item Jesaias, &c. 2 Petr. 1, 19, 20, 21. 2 Tim. 3, 16. Alii valde etiam illustres fuerunt, variisque miraculis clari; neque tamen constat, libros aliquos sacros ab iis esse conscriptos: utpote Elias & Elisæus: 1 Reg. 17, -. 2, XIII.
units.tr: Some of these served the Holy Spirit as amanuenses in writing the Holy Scriptures. Such were Moses, David, Solomon, etc., likewise Isaiah, etc. (2 Pet. 1, 19, 20, 21; 2 Tim. 3, 16). Others were also very illustrious and renowned for various miracles; yet it is not established that any sacred books were written by them, as with Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 13).

units.la: Prophetis accensendæ sunt Prophetissæ; quales Debora; Jud. 4, Et Hulda; 1 Reg. 22, 14.
units.tr: To the Prophets are to be reckoned the Prophetesses, such as Deborah (Judg. 4) and Huldah (1 Kings 22, 14).

units.la: Ordinarii Ministri V. T. Primo quidem sub ductu Patriacharum fuerunt Patres singularum familiarum fidelium, eorumque Filii primogeniti; deinde vero, juxta præscriptum Legis cerimonialis, sed & à Prophetis, ubi exorbitarent, ad lineas revocandi, Sacerdotes & Levitæ.
units.tr: The ordinary ministers of the Old Testament: first, indeed, under the leadership of the Patriarchs, were the fathers of the individual families of the faithful, and their firstborn sons; then, however, according to the prescription of the ceremonial law, and also to bring back to the line by the Prophets wherever they went astray, the priests and Levites.

units.la: X. Ministri N. T. proponuntur, Eph. 4, 11. 12. & Rom. 12, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: X. The ministers of the New Testament are set forth in Eph. 4, 11, 12, and Rom. 12, 6, 7, 8.

units.la: In his extraordinarii sunt Apostoli, Prophetæ, & Euangelistæ.
units.tr: Among these the extraordinary ones are the Apostles, Prophets, and Evangelists.

units.la: Apostoli fuerunt Ministri extraordinarii, à Christo vocati & missi, ad Ecclesias in universum plantandas, propagandas, & reformandas. Tales initio, dum Christus vixit humilis, fuerunt duodecim; ab ipso immediate vocati, atque insignibus donis ad istam functionem instructi. Vide Matth. 4, 18, -22. IX, 9. Item X, 1. Tunc advocatis duodecim Discipulis suis, dedit iis auctoritatem adversus spiritus impuros, ut ejicerent eos; & sanarent quemvis morbum. Porro duodecim Apostolorum nomina, &c. Hos duodecim misit Jesus, & addidit eis mandata. Luc. 6, 13. In Judæ proditoris locum, qui unus illorum fuerat, postea suffectus est Matthias: Actor. 1, 21. 26. Accessit deinde Paulus: IX, 1, 6, 15, 16. Gal. 1, 1. Atque etiam Barnabas; ut nonnulli colligunt ex Act. 13, 2, 3. ac porro XIV, 14. ubi pariter appellantur Apostoli Barnabas & Paulus. Vide etiam verf. 12. & XV. 35.-. Sed officium illud universale, atque in docendo infallibile, ut constituendæ primùm œconomiæ N. T. serviit; sic post eam, per istas personas, constitutam desiit.
units.tr: Apostles were extraordinary ministers, called and sent by Christ to plant, propagate, and reform churches throughout the world. At first, while Christ lived in humility, these were the twelve, called immediately by him and equipped for this function with remarkable gifts. See Matt. 4, 18-22; 9, 9. Likewise 10, 1: Then, having called his twelve disciples to him, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease. Now the names of the twelve Apostles are these, etc. Jesus sent these twelve and gave them commands. Luke 6, 13. In place of Judas the traitor, who had been one of them, Matthias was afterwards chosen: Acts 1, 21, 26. Then Paul was added: Acts 9, 1, 6, 15, 16. Gal. 1, 1. And also Barnabas, as some gather from Acts 13, 2, 3, and further from 14, 14, where Barnabas and Paul are likewise called Apostles. See also verse 12, and 15, 35-. But that universal office, infallible in teaching, served to establish the economy of the New Testament at its beginning; after that economy had been constituted through these persons, it ceased.

units.la: XI. Prophetæ nunc intelliguntur extraordinarii Ministri N.T. singulari quodam dono, & revelatione Divinâ, arcana explanantes, & futura quandoque prænunciantes. Exempla occurrunt, Act. xi, 27, 28. Descenderunt Hierosolymis Prophetæ Antiochiam, inter quos Agabus, de quo etiàm, xxi, 10, 11. Adde xiii, 1.
units.tr: XI. Prophets are now understood as extraordinary ministers of the New Testament who, by a singular gift and divine revelation, explain hidden things and sometimes foretell future things. Examples occur at Acts 11, 27, 28: Prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch, among whom was Agabus, about whom also 21, 10, 11. Add 13, 1.

units.la: Prophetis annumerandæ Prophetissæ; quemadmodum Philippo Euangelistæ dicuntur fuisse quatuor filiæ virgines prophetantes, Act. xxi, 8, 9. Confer 11, 16, 17, 18.
units.tr: To the Prophets are to be reckoned the Prophetesses; just as the four virgin daughters of Philip the Evangelist are said to have been prophesying (Acts 21, 8, 9). Compare 11, 16, 17, 18.

units.la: Dùm verò Prophetæ & Doctores, pariter sua dona, ad mutuam, & communem Ecclesiæ ædificationem, conferebant; hinc enata sunt insignia quædam exercitia: quorum extat, Act. 13, 1, 2. Erant Antiochiæ, in Ecclesiâ quæ illic erat, quidam Prophetæ & Doctores.--Illi autem sacram functionem obeuntibus: &c.
units.tr: While Prophets and Teachers were contributing their gifts for the mutual and common edification of the Church, certain notable exercises arose from this; of which there is an example at Acts 13, 1, 2: There were in Antioch, in the church that was there, certain Prophets and Teachers.--And when they were performing the sacred function, etc.

units.la: Verùm etiàm alii, donis extraordinariis non instructi, illis sese adjunxerunt; expectantes, si forte Deo etiàm talia in ipsos conferre placeret: vel hoc agentes, ut saltem per istiusmodi media, ordinariâ Sp. Sancti gratiâ cooperante, proficerent in mysteriis fidei; deque iis ad mutuam ædificationem dissererent. Hinc 1 Cor. 14, 1. Affectate spiritualia, maximè verò ut prophetis. Vide porrò, 3, 4, 24, 25, 26, 29, 30, 32, 35. xi; 5.
units.tr: But others, not furnished with extraordinary gifts, also attached themselves to these men, hoping that God might perhaps be pleased to bestow such gifts on them as well, or doing so in order that, at least through such means and with the ordinary grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating, they might make progress in the mysteries of the faith and discuss them for their mutual edification. Hence 1 Cor. 14, 1. Desire spiritual things, but especially that you may prophesy. See further 3, 4, 24, 25, 26, 29, 30, 32, 35; xi, 5.

units.la: XII. Præclara fuerunt ista exercitia sub ductû Prophetarum extraordinariorum & Doctorum; magnæque utilitatis ad profectum in cognitione veritatis, quæ secundùm pietatem est. Hinc etiàm 1 Thess. v, 19, 20, 21. Spiritum ne extinguite: Prophetias ne pro nihilo habete: omnia explorate: quod bonum fuerit, retinete.
units.tr: XII. These exercises under the leadership of the extraordinary Prophets and Teachers were excellent and of great benefit for advancing in the knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness. Hence also 1 Thess. 5, 19, 20, 21. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast what is good.

units.la: Istiusmodi Collegia etiàm instituta fuerunt in Ecclefiis à Papismo reformatis, sub ductû ordinariorum Pastorum ac Doctorum.
units.tr: Collegia of this kind were also instituted in the Churches reformed from Popery, under the leadership of the ordinary Ministers and Teachers.

units.la: At si quid Extraordinariæ revelationis vel jactetur, vel deprehendi videatur, cavendum sedulò, ne quod opus Dei temeritate nostrâ contemnatur, aut blasphemetur: interim etiàm seriò cogitandum est de versutiâ antiqui illius serpentis, Diaboli, sese in Angelum lucis transfigurantis. Observandæ igitur cautiones duæ. Prior est: Deut. 18, 20. Quando loquetur Propheta in nomine Iehovæ, & non extiterit verbum ejus; per superbiam locutus est illud Propheta ille: ne metuas ab illo. Confer Num. 23, 19. Ier. 46, 9, 10. Nisi fcil. conditio aliqua fuerit vel expressa, vel intellecta. Vide Ierem. 18, 7, - 10. & confer Ion. III, 4. Altera est, Deut 13, 1, 2, 3. Cum surrexerit in medio tui Propheta, & dederit tibi signum vel portentum; eveneritque, quod locutus est tibi, dicendo: Eamus post Deos alienos, quos non nosti. Non obedies verbis Prophetæ illius; quia Iehovah Deus vester tentat vos. Confer Gal. I, 8, 9. 1 Joh. 4, 1, 2, 3. Rom. 12, 6. 2 Tim. II, 13. Jac. I, 17.
units.tr: But if any extraordinary revelation is either claimed or seems to be detected, we must take careful care that no work of God is despised or blasphemed through our rashness. Meanwhile we must also seriously consider the cunning of that ancient serpent, the Devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light. Two cautions are therefore to be observed. The first is Deut. 18, 20. When a Prophet speaks in the name of Jehovah and his word does not come to pass, that Prophet has spoken it presumptuously; do not fear him. Compare Num. 23, 19; Jer. 46, 9, 10, unless, namely, some condition was either expressed or understood. See Jer. 18, 7–10, and compare Jon. 3, 4. The second is Deut. 13, 1, 2, 3. If a Prophet arises in your midst and gives you a sign or wonder, and what he has told you comes to pass, saying: Let us go after other gods, whom you have not known, you shall not obey the words of that Prophet, for Jehovah your God tests you. Compare Gal. 1, 8, 9; 1 John 4, 1, 2, 3; Rom. 12, 6; 2 Tim. 2, 13; James 1, 17.

units.la: XIII. Euangelistæ sunt etiam extraordinarii Ministri N. T. Apostolis adjuncti auxiliares in ministerio Euangelico; qui ab iis assumebantur comites, alicubi post eorum discessum relinquebantur, vel etiam alio mittebantur ad Ecclesias particulares; ut constituerent necessaria ad spiritualem ædificationem. Isti diferte etiam appellantur Eph. 4, 11.
units.tr: XIII. Evangelists are also extraordinary Ministers of the New Testament, auxiliaries attached to the Apostles in the Evangelical ministry. They were taken on by the Apostles as companions, and were sometimes left behind after the Apostles' departure, or were sent elsewhere to particular Churches to arrange what was necessary for spiritual edification. These are expressly named in Eph. 4, 11.

units.la: Tales fuerunt Philippus Euangelista; Act. 21, 8. qui unus erat ex illis septem: scil. primus ordinatis Diaconis; VI, 5. Timotheus; ad quem 2, IV, 5. Opus perage Euangelistæ. Aliique plures, ut Titus, Marcus, Lucas, Silas, &c.
units.tr: Such were Philip the Evangelist (Acts 21, 8), who was one of those seven, namely the first ordained Deacons (Acts 6, 5); Timothy, to whom 2 Tim. 4, 5 says, do the work of an Evangelist; and several others, such as Titus, Mark, Luke, Silas, etc.

units.la: Alio significatû Scriptores historiæ Euangelicæ Euangelistæ communiter appellantur; cum tamen Matthæus & Johannes Apostoli fuerint; sed Marcus & Lucas in Euangelistarum ordine substiterint.
units.tr: In another sense the writers of the Evangelical history are commonly called Evangelists, although Matthew and John were Apostles, while Mark and Luke stood in the order of Evangelists.

units.la: XIV. Sequuntur Ordinarii; qui, juxta ordinem nomine Dei & Christi per extraordinarios constitutum, ad functionem Ecclesiasticam eliguntur & vocantur, atque alii aliis succedunt, usque ad consummationem sæculi & Ecclesiarum institutarum. Tales in Constitutionibus Ecclesiarum nostrarum recte recensentur Pastores, Doctores, Seniores gubernantes, & Diaconi.
units.tr: XIV.
