Next come the Ordinary Ministers, who, according to the order established by extraordinary Ministers in the name of God and Christ, are chosen and called to ecclesiastical function, and succeed one another until the end of the age and of the Churches instituted. Such are rightly listed in the Constitutions of our Churches as Ministers, Teachers, Governing Elders, and Deacons.

units.la: In N. T. ipse Christus καθ' ἐξοχὴν Pastor vocatur: Ioh. 10,11,14,16. 1 Petr. 11,25. qui Magnus Pastor: Hebr. 13,10. & Princeps Pastorum; 1 Petr. 5,4. Sed de Ministris, & quidem ordinariis, eadem vox usurpatur, Eph. 4, 11. iisque mandatum est, pascere Ecclesiam Dei; Act. 20, 28. Pascere gregem Dei, qui penes ipsos est; 1 Petr. 5,2. Confer Ioh. 21,15,16,17. cum 1 Petr. 5,1. Sed Act. 20,17,28. Presbyteri, & Episcopi appellantur. Confer 1 Tim. 5,17. Et Hebr. 13,17,24. Duˈtores, excubantes pro animabus populi, tanquam rationem reddituri. 1 Thess. 5,12. Laborantes, qui præsunt in Domino, & admonent.
units.tr: In the New Testament Christ himself is called Pastor [ποιμήν] pre-eminently (John 10, 11, 14, 16; 1 Pet. 2, 25), who is the great Shepherd (Heb. 13, 20) and the chief Shepherd (1 Pet. 5, 4). But the same word is used of Ministers, and indeed of ordinary ones (Eph. 4, 11), and they are commanded to feed the Church of God (Acts 20, 28), to feed the flock of God that is among them (1 Pet. 5, 2). Compare John 21, 15, 16, 17 with 1 Pet. 5, 1. In Acts 20, 17, 28 they are called Elders and Bishops. Compare 1 Tim. 5, 17, and Heb. 13, 17, 24, where they are Teachers, keeping watch over souls of the people, as those who must give an account. In 1 Thess. 5, 12 they are those who labour, who are over you in the Lord, and admonish you.

units.la: Pascunt igitur sermone & doctrinâ: quod est lac sincerum; 1 Petr. 11,2. & simul cibus solidus; Hebr. 5, 12, 13, 14. Unde Episcopum oportet esse διδακτικὸν 1 Tim. III, 2. Doctrinæ adjungitur Baptismus, Sacramentum initiationis: sic enim Christus ista conjunxit; Matth. 28, 19. Confer Eph. 5,26. Ac porro Cœna Dominica, Sacramentum nutritionis spiritualis; in cujus dispensatione satis etiam manifesta est pastio:
units.tr: They therefore feed by speech and doctrine, which is the sincere milk (1 Pet. 2, 2) and at the same time solid food (Heb. 5, 12, 13, 14). Hence a Bishop must be apt to teach [διδακτικὸν] (1 Tim. 3, 2). Baptism, the sacrament of initiation, is joined to doctrine, for Christ joined these together (Matt. 28, 19); compare Eph. 5, 26. Further, the Lord's Supper, the sacrament of spiritual nourishment, in whose administration the feeding is also quite plain:

units.la: 1 Cor. XI, 24,25. cum IV, 1. Disciplina Ecclesiastica huc quoque pertinet; atque adeo Claves Regni cœlorum, sive Potestas ligandi & solvendi; quam Christus in Ecclesiâ extare voluit: Matth. 16, 19. XVIII, 17, 18. Itemque Orationes publicæ: Act. II. 42, VI, 4. Ex quibus conficitur Descriptio; Pastores sunt Ministri ordinarii N. T. quibus in Ecclesia ministerium Verbi annunciandi, Orationem habendarum, Sacramentorum administrandorum, & Disciplinæ una cum Collegis suis pariter gubernantibus exercendæ, mandatum est. Nunc agamus de eorum Vocatione, Necessitate, Æqualitate, & Stipendio.
units.tr: (1 Cor. 11, 24, 25, with 4, 1). Ecclesiastical discipline belongs here too, and so also the Keys of the kingdom of heaven, or the power of binding and loosing, which Christ willed to exist in the Church (Matt. 16, 19; 18, 17, 18). Likewise public prayers (Acts 2, 42; 6, 4). From these a description is formed: Pastors are the ordinary Ministers of the New Testament, to whom it is committed in the Church to proclaim the ministry of the Word, to offer prayers, to administer the sacraments, and, together with their colleagues who govern alongside them, to exercise discipline. We now proceed to their Vocation, Necessity, Equality and Stipend.

units.la: XV. Vocatio hic ordinaria intelligitur: ea est Actio Ecclesiæ, vel Antecessorum ejus, qua nomine Christi, & juxta præscriptum Ipsius, talis persona eligitur & applicatur ad tale Ministerium.
units.tr: XV. Vocation here is understood as ordinary: it is the act of the Church, or of its predecessors, by which, in the name of Christ and according to his prescription, such a person is chosen and assigned to such a ministry.

units.la: Afferimus autem contra Enthusiastas, Libertinos, eorumque sequaces, Vocationem ad Ministerium Pastorale esse necessariam; non vero licitum esse cuivis idoneo, aut se idoneum putanti, sponte sua id capessere. Sententiam probamus istis Argumentis: 1. Necessitas illa satis diserte exprimitur in SS. Literis: utpote Rom. 10. 14, 15. Quomodo invocabunt eum, in quem non crediderint? quomodo autem credent ei, de quo non audierint? quomodo autem audient absque prædicante? Quomodo autem prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Missio igitur, quæ non differt realiter a Vocatione, necessaria est, ut quis prædicet Verbum; ex cujus auditu erit fides salutaris, ac fidelis invocatio. Similiter Hebr. 5, 4, 5. Neque sibi quisquam sumit hunc honorem; Sed qui vocatur a Deo, sicut & Aharon. Quæ propositio generalis est, licet ab Apostolo speciali usu applicetur. Munus autem Pastorale vere honorificum est; quapropter nemo illud ipse sibi sumere debet. Vide 1 Tim. 3, 1. cum 7, & 10. Item v, 17. cum 22.
units.tr: We maintain, however, against the Enthusiasts, the Libertines, and their followers, that vocation to the pastoral ministry is necessary, and that it is not lawful for anyone who is fit, or who thinks himself fit, to take up this office on his own initiative. We prove this opinion by these arguments. 1. That necessity is expressed quite plainly in the Holy Scriptures, as in Rom. 10, 14, 15: How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent? Therefore sending, which does not really differ from vocation, is necessary for anyone to preach the Word, from whose hearing comes saving faith and faithful invocation. Similarly Heb. 5, 4, 5: No one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. This is a general proposition, although the Apostle applies it in a special way. The pastoral office is truly honourable; therefore no one should take it to himself. See 1 Tim. 3, 1 compared with 7 and 10; likewise 5, 17 compared with 22.

units.la: 2. Reprehenduntur qui sine vocatione, aut missione, munus istiusmodi capessunt: Jerem. 23, 31. Non misi Prophetas illos; & ipsi currebant: non sum locutus ad eos; & ipsi prophetabant. Sic diserte redarguitur ille actus docendi, absque missione ad eum. Ut autem se habet vocatio extraordinaria ad functionem extraordinariam; sic vocatio ordinaria ad functionem ordinariam.
units.tr: 2. Those who take up such an office without vocation or sending are rebuked: Jer. 23, 31, I did not send those Prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. In this way that act of teaching without a sending to it is plainly condemned. Just as extraordinary vocation stands to extraordinary function, so ordinary vocation stands to ordinary function.

units.la: 3. Accedunt exempla & praxis perpetua; non solum in V. T. sed etiam in N. Johannes Baptista à Deo missus fuisse dicitur, Joh. 1, 6, 33. Apostoli à Christo, Matth. 10, 1-5. Septuaginta Discipuli etiam à Christo, Luc. 10, 1. Quæ quidem vocationes fuerunt immediatæ. Aliæ deinceps fuerunt mediatæ: ut saltem ex parte vocatio Matthiæ Apostoli; Act. 1, 21, -26. Atque amplius sic constituti sunt Presbyteri variarum Ecclesiarum; xiv, 23. xx, 28. Tit. 1, 5.
units.tr: 3. There are also examples and a perpetual practice, not only in the Old Testament but also in the New. John the Baptist is said to have been sent by God (John 1, 6, 33); the Apostles by Christ (Matt. 10, 1–5); the seventy Disciples also by Christ (Luke 10, 1). These vocations were indeed immediate. Others afterwards were mediate, as, at least in part, the vocation of the Apostle Matthias (Acts 1, 21–26). And moreover, Elders of various Churches were so appointed (Acts 14, 23; 20, 28; Titus 1, 5).

units.la: 4. Accedit ratio; quod sint Legati Dei & Christi 2 Cor. 5, 19, 20. Atqui Legatorum est a Principe missi. Confer 1, iv, 1, 2. cum 1 Petr. 4, 10, 11. Matth. 28. 19, 20. Ephes. 4, 11, 12, 13. 1 Cor. III, 10, -13. Eidem ergo Domino ministrant, & in eundem finem, ordinarii; ut ministrarunt extraordinarii.
units.tr: 4. There is also the reasoning that they are ambassadors of God and of Christ (2 Cor. 5, 19, 20). But ambassadors are those sent by a prince. Compare 1 John 4, 1, 2 with 1 Pet. 4, 10, 11; Matt. 28, 19, 20; Eph. 4, 11, 12, 13; 1 Cor. 3, 10–13. Therefore the ordinary Ministers serve the same Lord, and to the same end, as the extraordinary ones did.

units.la: Obj. 1. 1 Tim. III, 1. Si quis Episcopatum desiderat, præclarum opus desiderat. Ergo etiam licet personæ habili illud munus capessere. Resp. Non tamen licet absque vocatione legitimâ.
units.tr: Objection 1: "If anyone desires the office of a bishop, he desires an excellent work" (1 Tim. 3:1). Therefore it is also lawful for a suitable person to take up that office. Reply: Yet it is not lawful without a lawful calling.

units.la: Obj. 2. 1 Thess. 5, 11. Adhortamini alii alios; & ædificate singuli singulos; sicut & facitis. Singulis ergo licet alios docere & adhortari; atque adeo Pastoris munere fungi. Resp. Ex privato officio charitatis singuli singulos recte ædificant: sed hinc nihil adversus sententiam nostram conficitur.
units.tr: Objection 2: "Exhort one another, and edify one another, as you also do" (1 Thess. 5:11). Therefore each individual may teach and exhort others, and so may perform the duty of a pastor. Reply: Individuals rightly edify one another from a private duty of charity; but nothing against our position follows from this.

units.la: Obj. 3. Act. 8, 4, 5. agitur de fidelibus præter Apostolos, ex persecutione dispersis, qui dicuntur Evangelizasse sermonem Dei: ac nominatim Philippus in urbe Samariæ prædicasse Christum. Ergo. Resp. Philippus Evangelista fuit; Act. 21, 8. Nec dubitandum videtur, quin in ista multitudine fuerint plures Evangelistæ, & Doctores. Reliqui vero etiam ex privato charitatis officio privatim alios instituere & exhortari potuerunt. Sed hinc non sequitur, ad ordinarium Pastoris officium non requiri vocationem, aut missionem.
units.tr: Objection 3: Acts 8:4, 5 speaks of the faithful other than the apostles, who were scattered by persecution and are said to have preached the word of God; and in particular that Philip preached Christ in a city of Samaria. Therefore (the same follows). Reply: Philip was an evangelist (Acts 21:8). Nor does it seem doubtful that in that multitude there were many evangelists and teachers. The rest, indeed, could privately instruct and exhort others from a private duty of charity. But it does not follow from this that no calling or sending is required for the ordinary office of pastor.

units.la: Obj. 4. 1 Cor. 14, 3, -. loquitur Apostolus satis prolixè de libertate prophetandi singulis permittendâ. Ergò. Resp. Apostolus loquitur de variis donis in communem Ecclesiæ ædificationem conferendis, ac potissimum de dono prophetiæ; ubi etiam alii pio discendi ac proficiendi studio exercitia sua adjungebant; quamvis extraordinariam revelationem non habentes. Verum de iis adhuc præcipit Apostolus verf. 40. Omnia decenter & ordine fiant. Nedum cuicunque homini, quantumvis idoneo, vel idoneum se reputanti, liceat suâ sponte, sine vocatione, capessere Munus antecessorium administrandi Verbum, & Sacramenta, & Claves regni coelorum.
units.tr: Objection 4: 1 Cor. 14:3 and following, where the Apostle speaks at some length about the liberty of prophesying to be allowed to individuals. Therefore (the same follows). Reply: The Apostle speaks of the various gifts to be bestowed for the common edification of the Church, and especially of the gift of prophecy; where others also joined their own exercises with a pious zeal for learning and progress, although they did not have an extraordinary revelation. But concerning these very things the Apostle still commands in verse 40: "Let all things be done decently and in order." Much less is it lawful for any man, however fit, or however he may consider himself fit, to take up of his own accord, without a calling, the office that belonged to the first ministers: to administer the Word, the Sacraments, and the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: XVI. Ad legitimam Vocationem pertinent Electio, Examen, Approbatio, & publica Confirmatio.
units.tr: XVI. Electio, examen, approbatio, and public confirmation belong to a lawful calling.

units.la: Electio est personæ unius (si una tantum desideretur) ex pluribus discretio, & designatio, ad hoc munus, si omnia se in eâ & circa eam recte habeant, deinceps rite obeundum. Prius tamen, etiam cum unus tantum Minister requiritur, plures quandoque nominantur, & in consideratione veniunt; postea unus eligitur per suffragia. Huc analogicè pertinet illud, Actor. 1, 15, -- 26. ubi cum Petrus, in media multitudine fidelium exposuisset Judæ proditoris locum necessariò supplendum; duos nominarunt, Iosephum & Matthiam; ac porrò decisionem à Deo petierunt. Respondit autem Deus per sortem; atque ita locus ille suppletus est, omnibus pariter consentientibus. Similiter septem Diaconi, cap. 6, 2, -- 5. ab Ecclesiâ fuerunt electi. Propius autem hùc spectat, quod de χειροτονία, suffragiis protensâ manû datis, in eligendis Presbyteris, occurrit, cap. xiv, 23.
units.tr: Election is the discernment and designation of one person from among several (if only one is wanted) for this office, to be discharged thereafter duly, provided that everything in him and concerning him is in order. Yet first, even when only one minister is required, several are sometimes nominated and brought into consideration; afterwards one is chosen by vote. To this, by analogy, belongs Acts 1:15–26, where Peter, standing in the midst of the multitude of the faithful, set forth that the place of Judas the traitor had to be filled; they nominated two, Joseph and Matthias, and then asked God for a decision. God answered through the lot, and so that place was filled, with all consenting alike. Likewise the seven deacons were chosen by the Church (Acts 6:2–5). But more to the point is what occurs concerning the choosing of elders by cheirotonia, votes given with hands stretched out (Acts 14:23).

units.la: XVII. Examen est accurata observatio Personæ hactenus
units.tr: XVII. Examination is the careful observation of the person thus far chosen, and the testing of whether he is truly fit for this ministry.

units.la: haētenus electæ; & exploratio, nùm ea verè idonea sit ad istud Ministerium. 1 Tim. 5, 22. Manûs citò ne cui imponito: neque communicato peccatis alienis. Confer. 111. 10. Hi etiam explorentur priùs, &c.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 5:22: "Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in other men's sins." Compare 1 Tim. 3:10: "Let these also first be tested," etc.

units.la: Examen autem instituì debet non solùm ratione doctrinæ, & facultatis dicendi accommodatè ad spiritualem ædificationem; verùm etiàm ratione vitæ univers æ. Hinc 2 Tim. 3, 17. Ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfectè instructus. Tit. 1, 9, 10, 11. Oportet Episcopum esse tenacem fidei illius secundùm doctrinam sermonis; ut possit & auditores exhortari doctrinâ illâ sanâ, & contradicentes convincere. Adde 1 Tim. 3, 2, 6. Specialius de vitâ: verf. 2, 3. Oportet eum esse Irreprehensibilem, non vinosum, non percussorem, non turpem quæstum facientem, alienum à pugnis, alienum à pecuniæ amore. Tit. 1, 7. Pietate verò, modestiâ, omnibusque reliquis virtutibus ornatum: 1 Tim. 3, 2, 4, 5, 7. Unius uxoris virum, vigilantem, temperantem, compositum, hospitalem, æquum, &c. Tit. 1, 6, 7, 8.
units.tr: Examination ought to be conducted not only with regard to doctrine and to the ability to speak suitably for spiritual edification, but also with regard to the whole of life. Hence 2 Tim. 3:17: "That the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work." Titus 1:9–11: "A bishop must hold firmly to the faithful word as taught, so that he may both exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict." Add 1 Tim. 3:2, 6. More specifically concerning life, verses 2, 3: "He must be irreproachable, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy of base gain, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money." Titus 1:7 adds that he must be adorned with piety, modesty, and all the other virtues. 1 Tim. 3:2, 4, 5, 7: "the husband of one wife, watchful, temperate, orderly, hospitable, just," etc. Titus 1:6–8.

units.la: Atque itâ in Ecclesiis nostris receptum est, ut Theologiæ Studiosi, ad S. Ministerium aspirantes, examinentur priùs præparatoriè. Hinc, ut Ecclesiis innotescant magis, ad specimina publica admittuntur. Postquàm verò ad Ministerium electi sunt, iterùm instituitur examen; quod peremtorium appellatur.
units.tr: And so it is received in our Churches that students of theology who aspire to the sacred ministry are first examined in a preparatory manner. Hence, so that they may become better known to the Churches, they are admitted to public trials. But once they have been chosen for the ministry, the examination is held again; this is called the peremptory examination.

units.la: XVIII. Approbatio est, eorum, ad quos nego- tium istud pertinet, post examen sufficiens, judicium & consensus, ut talis persona deinceps ad Min- isterium istud admittatur.
units.tr: XVIII. Approbation is the judgment and consent of those to whom this business belongs, given after a sufficient examination, that such a person be thereafter admitted to this ministry.

units.la: Sic Act. 1, 26. de Matthiâ; Communibus calculis allectus est cum undecim Apostolis. Huc etiam pertinet illud de electis sex Diaconis, vi, 6. Quos statuerunt in conspectu Apostolorum; approbandos scil. atque porrò ordinandos. Finis nimirùm Examinis est, ut idonei approbentur; inepti reprobentur, aut relinquantur. In plerisque Ecclesiis Belgicis gicis accedit specialis Approbatio Magistratùs Religionem Reformatam profitentis; atque item Classis, ad quam Ecclesia ista pertinet.
units.tr: So Acts 1:26 of Matthias: "He was numbered with the eleven apostles by common votes." To this also belongs what is said of the six deacons chosen, Acts 6:6: "whom they set before the apostles," that is, to be approved and then ordained. For the aim of the examination is that the fit be approved and the unfit rejected or left aside. In most of the Belgic Churches there is added a special approbation by the magistrate who professes the Reformed religion, and likewise by the classis to which the Church belongs.

units.la: XIX. Publica Confirmatio est folennis admissio & introductio Pastoris electi, explorati, & approbati, ad Ministerium rite obeundum.
units.tr: XIX. Public confirmation is the solemn admission and introduction of the elected, examined, and approved pastor to the duly discharged ministry.

units.la: Antiquitus hic etiam usurpata fuit Impositio manuum: quo ritu tales personæ Deo veluti consecrabantur ad istud Ministerium, cum precibus ac benedictionibus. Confer Levit. 1, 4. Genef. 48, 17, 18. Itâ de septem primis Diaconis, Act. 6, 6. Adhibitis precibus, imposuerunt eis manus. xiii, 3. de Prophetis & Doctoribus Antiochenis, cùm Spiritus Sanctus iis mandaffet, ut sibi Barnabam & Paulum ad opus singularis Ministerii separárent; Cum jejunaffent, & orâffent, & imposuissent eis manus, dimiserunt eos. Iterùm 1 Tim. iv, 14. Ne negligito donum, quod in te est; quod datum est tibi per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum ordinis Seniorum. Et v, 22. Manus cito ne cui imponito.
units.tr: Anciently the laying on of hands was also used here: by this rite such persons were consecrated to God, as it were, for this ministry, with prayers and blessings. Compare Lev. 1:4; Gen. 48:17, 18. Thus of the first seven deacons, Acts 6:6: "With prayers offered, they laid hands on them." Acts 13:3, concerning the prophets and teachers of Antioch, when the Holy Spirit had commanded them to set apart for Him Barnabas and Paul for the work of a special ministry: "When they had fasted and prayed, and laid hands on them, they sent them away." Again 1 Tim. 4:14: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the body of elders." And 5:22: "Lay hands hastily on no one."

units.la: Istiusmodi ordinatio & confirmatio apud nos peragitur, adhibitâ publicâ χειροτονία, in iis qui primùm Ministerio Verbi consecrantur. In conventu Classis verò peragitur circa eos, qui mittuntur ad Ecclesias sub cruce latentes, aut valdè remotas; apud quas ordinatio non ita commodè posset peragi. Sed absque illo ritu fit confirmatio eorum, qui priùs etiam alibi munere Pastorali functi sunt, atque ita ordinati fuerunt.
units.tr: Such ordination and confirmation among us is carried out, with public cheirotonia employed, for those who are first consecrated to the ministry of the Word. In a meeting of the classis, however, it is carried out for those who are sent to Churches lying under the cross or very remote, where the ordination could not so conveniently be performed. But confirmation of those who have already served as pastors elsewhere, and have thus been ordained, takes place without that rite.

units.la: XX. Potestas vocandi & mittendi Pastores spectari potest vel principalis, vel ministerialis. Principalis competit Deo absolutè; aut Patri, tanquam primo ordine subsistendi & operandi. Hinc Christus Discipulis suis, Matth. 9, 38. Deprecamini Dominum messis, ut emittat operarios in messem suam. Confer 1 Cor. 1. 2: v, 20. Matth. xi. 25. Κατ' οἰκονομίαν verò compecompetit Christo Θεανθρώπῳ, qui tanquàm Rex Ecclesiæ Ministros instituit, ibique tanquàm supremo Prophetæ subordinat; juxta illud Ephes. iv, 11. Christus dedit alios Apostolos, -- alios Pastores & Doctores. Adde Ioh. 20, 21. Matth. 28, 18, 19. Secundùm aliam appropriationem tribuitur Spiritui Sancto, per quem Filius operatur, & docet intùs efficaciter. Sic enim Actor. 13, 2. Dixit Spiritus Sanctus; Separate mihi Barnabam & Saulum ad opus, ad quod eos advocavi. Adde xx, 28.
units.tr: XX. The power of calling and sending pastors may be considered either as principal or as ministerial. The principal power belongs absolutely to God, or to the Father, as to the first order of subsisting and working. Hence Christ says to His disciples, Matt. 9:38: "Pray the Lord of the harvest that He send out workers into His harvest." Compare 1 Cor. 12:5, 6 and Matt. 11:25. But by economy it belongs to Christ the God-man, who, as King of the Church, appoints ministers and subordinates them there as to the supreme Prophet, according to Eph. 4:11: "Christ gave some apostles, ... some pastors and teachers." Add John 20:21; Matt. 28:18, 19. According to another appropriation it is ascribed to the Holy Spirit, through whom the Son works and teaches inwardly and effectively. Thus Acts 13:2: "The Holy Spirit said, Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." Add Acts 20:28.

units.la: Ministerialis autem, quæ in Vocatione mediatâ locum habet, competit Ecclesiæ; præeuntibus tamen Antecessoribus, quos modò habet; juxta voluntatem Dei & Christi: haud secùs ac quælibet Respublica libera potestatem habet constituendi Rectores, qui præsint reliquæ multitudini; aut per Rectores, qui modò exstant, datâ occasione supplet defectum aliorum. Sic Apostoli ad multitudinem fidelium retulerunt de supplendo loco vacante, post interitum Iscariotæ, Act. 1, 14, 15. & Matthias communibus calculis dicitur allectus cum undecim Apostolis; verf. 26. Similiter ad multitudinem retulerunt de eligendis Diaconis; vi, 2, 3. Prophetæ autem & Doctores Antiocheni Barnabæ & Paulo manûs imposuerunt; xiii, 1, 2, 3. Timotheo in memoriam revocatur impositio manuum Presbyterii; 1 Tim. 4, 14. Iterùm Paulus & Barnabas, Lystram, & Iconium, & Antiochiam reversi, ad confirmandos fidelium animos, dicuntur per suffragia illis creâsse, per singulas Ecclesias, Presbyteros; Actor. 14, 23. Adde Tit. 1, 5. 1 Tim. 5, 22.
units.tr: The ministerial power, which has a place in mediate calling, belongs to the Church, though preceded by its present predecessors, in accordance with the will of God and of Christ; just as any free commonwealth has the power of appointing rulers to preside over the rest of the multitude, or, when an occasion arises, through the rulers who now exist, supplies the lack of others. So the apostles referred to the multitude of the faithful the filling of the vacant place after the death of Iscariot (Acts 1:14, 15), and Matthias is said to have been numbered by common votes with the eleven apostles (verse 26). Likewise they referred to the multitude the choosing of deacons (Acts 6:2, 3). The Antiochene prophets and teachers laid hands on Barnabas and Paul (Acts 13:1, 2, 3). Timothy is reminded of the laying on of hands by the presbytery (1 Tim. 4:14). Again, Paul and Barnabas, on returning to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, to strengthen the spirits of the faithful, are said to have appointed elders for them in each Church by votes (Acts 14:23). Add Titus 1:5; 1 Tim. 5:22.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Atque itâ in Ecclesiis nostris, juxta receptas Constitutiones, Electio Pastoris peragitur à Presbyterio, collegio Antecessorum Ecclesiasticorum: ubi verò Presbyterium nondùm est constitutum, peragitur à Classe, ad quam Ecclesia ista pertinet: quemadmodum etiàm ad Ecclesias sub cruce sic laborantes, ut ipsæ sibi Pastores vocare commodè non possint, aut ad Ecclesias de novo plantandas, vel colligendas, mittuntur Pastores à Synodo, aut Classe aliquâ propinquâ.
units.tr: And so in our Churches, according to the received constitutions, the election of a minister is carried out by the consistory, the college of ecclesiastical elders. Where a consistory has not yet been established, it is carried out by the classis to which that Church belongs. Likewise, ministers are sent by a synod or some neighbouring classis to Churches labouring under the cross, which cannot conveniently call ministers for themselves, and to Churches that are to be newly planted or gathered.

units.la: Quoniàm autem Magistratus in his Provinciis ferè Religionem Reformatam profitentur, observandum venit, ad Magistratum quâ talem pertinere, quinam sint cives in suâ civitate, vel territorio; ac potissimùm, quinam illic publico munere fungantur: dùm verò, & quatenùs iidem fideles sunt, & Ecclesiarum nutricii, eorundem consensus etiàm requiritur speciatim. Atque hùc pertinet Correspondentia, quam vocant.
units.tr: Since, however, the magistrates in these provinces mostly profess the Reformed religion, it must be observed that the magistrate, as such, is concerned with who are the citizens in his city or territory, and above all with who hold public office there. And insofar as these same faithful are also nurses of the Churches, their consent is also specifically required. To this belongs what they call correspondence.

units.la: Alicubi jus quoddam Patronatûs obtinet etiamnùm. Sub Papatû istud duplex fuit: unum Clericale, quod erat penes Clericos; alterum Laicale, quod penes Laicos, (ut isti appellant) ex ipsorum usurpatione, vel etiàm ex concessione Episcopi, ob insigne aliquod beneficium in Ecclesiam collatum: sic autem Patronum faciunt dos, ædificatio, fundum. Clericale per Reformationem abrogatum est: Laicale verò cùm tolli hactenùs omninò non potuerit, etiàm toleratur; sed conditionibus quibusdam limitatum. Vide Synodi Nationalis Dordracenæ Sessionem 157.
units.tr: In some places a certain right of patronage still holds. Under the Papacy this was twofold: one clerical, which lay with the clergy; the other lay, which lay with laymen (as they call them), arising from their own usurpation, or even from the bishop's grant, on account of some notable benefit conferred on the Church. In this way they make the patron out of dowry, building, or land. The clerical right was abolished by the Reformation; the lay right, since it could not hitherto be abolished altogether, is also tolerated, but limited by certain conditions. See Session 157 of the National Synod of Dort.

units.la: XXII. Videndum nunc de Legitimâ Vocatione Pa- storum in Ecclesiis Reformatis.
units.tr: XXII. Now we must consider the lawful calling of ministers in the Reformed Churches.

units.la: Hic autem initio occurrunt, qui primi Reformatores appellantur; ut Lutherus, Zuinglius, &c. iique habuerunt Vocationem legitimam, juxta ordinem tunc in Ecclesiâ Romanâ receptum; non quidem ἀνεγκλητον; talem interim, ut accedente Ecclesiæ cujusque particularis, ubi illi Ministerium obierunt, consensû & approbatione, essentialia censeri debeant integra.
units.tr: Here, at the outset, there come to mind those who are called the first Reformers, such as Luther, Zwingli, etc. They had a lawful calling according to the order then received in the Roman Church; not indeed [ἀνέγκλητον] faultless; yet such that, provided the consent and approval of the particular Church where they discharged the ministry is added, its essentials are to be considered wholly intact.

units.la: Vocati enim fuerunt, 1. ad Euangelium fideliter prædicandum: dùm autem hoc fecerunt magis fideliter, quàm illi à quibus fuerant ordinati, aut missi; sic in usu & exercitio magis legitimum fecerunt suum Ministerium; sed nequaquàm jure eo excidisse putandi sunt.
units.tr: For they were called, first, to preach the Gospel faithfully; and when they did this more faithfully than those by whom they had been ordained or sent, they made their ministry more lawful in use and exercise; but they are by no means to be thought to have forfeited that right.

units.la: 2. Cùm illi diù ante Concilium Tridentinum fuerint ordinati ac missi, non fuerunt in suâ ordinatione ac missione obnoxii illius Decretis, aut prohibiti docere adversùs ejus Canones.
units.tr: Second, since they were ordained and sent long before the Council of Trent, they were not bound in their ordination and sending by its decrees, nor forbidden to teach against its canons.

units.la: 3. Qualiacunque Decreta & Statuta Ecclesiastica nihil valent adversùs Verbum Dei.
units.tr: Third, whatever ecclesiastical decrees and statutes there are have no force against the Word of God.

units.la: Qui verò deindè secuti sunt in Ecclesiis Reformatis, legitimam Vocationem habuerunt, & habent, per Antecessores Ecclesiasticos, adstipulante Grege Ecclesiastico, juxta Verbum Dei.
units.tr: But those who afterwards followed in the Reformed Churches had, and have, a lawful calling through the ecclesiastical elders, with the assent of the ecclesiastical flock, according to the Word of God.

units.la: Ex his facilè solvitur Dilemma Pontificiorum; Primi Reformatores vel habuerunt Vocationem legitimam, vel non habuerunt: si non habuerunt, non licuit iis Ecclesiam reformare, tanquàm destitutis omni jure ac potestate ad eam rem: si verò habuerunt Vocationem legitimam, ergò Ecclesia Romana, in cujus communione Vocationem acceperunt, habet potestatem legitimè vocandi; consequenter est vera Ecclesia, non corrupta, aut Reformatione egens. Respondemus enim, eos habuisse Vocationem essentialiter legitimam; atque hactenùs valuisse Vocationem in Ecclesiâ Romanâ factam; non minùs quàm Baptismum in eâ administratum etiamnùm agnoscimus. Verùm inde nequaquàm sequitur, Ecclesiam Romanam esse incorruptam; sicut de ejus corruptione plurimi, etiàm diù ante Lutherum, merito fuerant conquesti. Homo æger, atque ex morbo periculosissimo morti propinquus, hactenùs tamen homo est, & actiones quasdam humanas edere potest; verùm inde minimè sequitur, nihil opus illi esse curatione.
units.tr: From these points the dilemma of the Papists is easily resolved. The first Reformers either had a lawful calling or did not. If they did not, it was not lawful for them to reform the Church, as being wholly destitute of any right or power for that purpose. But if they did have a lawful calling, then the Roman Church, in whose communion they received their calling, has the power of lawfully calling; consequently it is the true Church, not corrupt, nor in need of reformation. For we answer that they had a calling essentially lawful, and that the calling made in the Roman Church was valid up to that point; just as we still acknowledge the baptism administered in it. But it by no means follows from this that the Roman Church is uncorrupted; as very many, even long before Luther, had rightly complained of its corruption. A sick man, near to death from a most dangerous disease, is nonetheless still a man and can perform certain human actions; but it by no means follows that he has no need of treatment.

units.la: XXIII. Sequitur Necessitas muneris Pastoralis ad Ecclesiæ militantis collectionem, conservationem, &
units.tr: XXIII. There follows the necessity of the pastoral office for the gathering, preservation, and

units.la: propagationem. Ea autem probatur contra Enthufia-stas, Libertinos, & varios ἀπάχλης, 1. ex disertà ordinatione Divinâ: Matth. 28, 19, 20. Profecti ergò docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos, ---. Et ecce, Ego vobiscùm sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Sic Ministerium in Apostolis inchoatum, per eorum Successores continuari debuit usque ad finem mundi. Adde Joh. 20, 21. 2 Cor. 5, 18, 19, 20. Sic Ephes. 4, 11, 12. non minùs Pastorum & Doctorum, quàm Apostolorum, Prophetarum, & Euangelistarum constitutio, seu ordinatio ad opus Ministerii, & ad œdificationem Ecclesiæ, tribuitur Christo. Quemadmodùm Spiritui Sancto etiàm tribuitur constitutio Episcoporum, sive Presbyterorum: Actor. 20, 17, 28. Talis consequenter fuit Praxis Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ & primitivæ: Tit. 1, 5. Actor. 14, 23. xv, 2. Phil. 1, 1. 1 Tim. 4, 14. Apoc. 1, 20. cum Mal. II, 7.
units.tr: propagation of the militant Church. This is proved against the enthusiasts, the libertines, and various [ἀπάχλης], first, from the express divine ordinance: Matt. 28:19, 20: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them ... And behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Thus the ministry begun in the apostles ought to have been continued through their successors until the end of the world. Add John 20:21; 2 Cor. 5:18, 19, 20. Thus Eph. 4:11, 12 ascribes to Christ the institution or ordination of pastors and teachers, no less than of apostles, prophets, and evangelists, for the work of the ministry and the building up of the Church. Just as the institution of bishops or presbyters is also ascribed to the Holy Spirit: Acts 20:17, 28. Such, consequently, was the practice of the apostolic and primitive Church: Titus 1:5; Acts 14:23; 15:2; Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 4:14; Rev. 1:20; compare Mal. 2:7.

units.la: 2. Ex consideratione finium: Dan. 12, 3. Justificantes multos, &c. Joh. 20, 23. Si quorum remiseritis peccata (ministerialiter remissionem denunciando, postquam homines ad fidem & resipiscentiam fuerint adducti) remittuntur eis. Eph. 4, 11, 12, 13. Is igitur dedit alios quidem Apostolos; alios autem Pastores & Doctores: ad concinnationem integram sanctorum, ad opus ministerii, ad œdificationem corporis Christi: Donec deveniamus nos omnes in unitatem fidei, &c. Adde 1 Tim. 4, 16. Rom. 10, 13, 14, 15. Huc pertinent consequentia miseranda & noxia, ubi deest Ministerium: Prov. 29, 18. Am. 8, 11, 12. Tristis querela; Psal. 47, 9. & Christi commiseratio ac monitum; Matth. 9, 36, 37, 38.
units.tr: Second, from a consideration of the ends: Dan. 12:3: those who justify many, etc.; John 20:23: If you forgive anyone's sins (by ministerially declaring forgiveness, after men have been brought to faith and repentance), they are forgiven them. Eph. 4:11, 12, 13: He gave some to be apostles, and some to be pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith, etc. Add 1 Tim. 4:16; Rom. 10:13, 14, 15. To this belong the pitiable and harmful consequences where the ministry is lacking: Prov. 29:18; Amos 8:11, 12. The sorrowful complaint: Ps. 74:9; and the compassion and admonition of Christ: Matt. 9:36, 37, 38.

units.la: 3. Ex requisitis & conditionibus Ministrorum eligendorum; ac porro ex eorum officiis, tam accurate descriptis: 1 Tim. 3, 1, -13. Siquis Episcopatum desiderat, praeclarum opus desiderat. Oportet igitur Episcopum pum irreprehensibilem esse, unius uxoris virum, vigilantem, &c. Tit 1, 6,-9. 2 Tim. II, 2. Item Act. 20, 28. Attendite igitur animum ad vos ipsos, & totum gregem, in quo vos Spiritus ille Sanctus constituit Episcopos, ad pascendam Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo illo proprio sanguine acquisivit. Col. 3, 17. 1 Cor 4, 2. 1 Tim. 3, 15. IV, II,-16. 2. II, 24, 25. III, 17. IV, 2. Tit. II, 1,-.
units.tr: Third, from the requirements and qualifications of the ministers to be chosen, and further from their duties, so carefully described: 1 Tim. 3:1–13: If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a noble task. A bishop therefore must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, etc.; Titus 1:6–9; 2 Tim. 2:2. Likewise Acts 20:28: Take heed therefore to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. Col. 3:17; 1 Cor. 4:2; 1 Tim. 3:15; 4:11–16; 2 Tim. 2:24, 25; 3:17; 4:2; Titus 2:1.

units.la: 4. Ex mandatis, quomodo singuli Ministros debeant recipere, non rejicere, aut contemnere; sed audire, & in honore habere, &c. Matth. 10, 40, 41. Qui recipit vos, Me recipit: -. Luc. 10, 16. 1 Cor. 4, 1. Sic de nobis reputet homo, ut de Ministris Christi, & Dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei. 1 Thess. 5, 12,13. Rogamus autem vos, fratres, ut agnoscatis eos qui laborant inter vos, qui praesunt vobis in Domino, & admonent vos: 1 Tim. 5, 17. Hebr. 13, 17.
units.tr: Fourth, from the commands as to how individuals ought to receive ministers, not reject or despise them, but hear them and hold them in honour, etc.: Matt. 10:40, 41: He who receives you receives me; Luke 10:16; 1 Cor. 4:1: Let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 1 Thess. 5:12, 13: We ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labour among you, who lead you in the Lord and admonish you; 1 Tim. 5:17; Heb. 13:17.

units.la: XXIV. Obj. 1. Deus Ezech. 34, 11,-24. promisit, se in Christo quaesiturum & pasturum oves suas. Sic Ies. 54, 13. Joh. 6, 45. Erunt omnes docti à Deo. Confer Joh. 8, 47. x, 11. Nihil igitur opus est Ministris & Ministerio Ecclesiastico. Resp. Male sic separantur conjuncta; Causae secundae à prima, ministrae & instrumentales à principali. Paulus plantat, Apollos rigat; sed Deus dat crescendi vim: 1 Cor. 3, 6. Confer Act. 16, 14. Matth. 28, 19,20.
units.tr: XXIV. Objection 1. God promised in Ezek. 34:11–24 that he himself would seek out and pasture his sheep in Christ. So Isa. 54:13; John 6:45: They shall all be taught by God. Compare John 8:47; 10:11. Therefore there is no need of ministers and of the ecclesiastical ministry. Answer. Such things are wrongly separated that belong together: secondary causes from the first, ministerial and instrumental causes from the principal. Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the power of growth: 1 Cor. 3:6. Compare Acts 16:14; Matt. 28:19, 20.

units.la: Obj. 2. Christus Spiritum promisit, qui suos in omnem veritatem ductururs, Joh. 16, 13. cum Rom. 8, 9, 14. 1 Joh. II, 27. Resp. Sed non seclusso medio Ministerii. Diserte Joh. 16, 27. Spiritus testabitur de Me. Sed & vos testabimini.
units.tr: Objection 2. Christ promised the Spirit, who would lead his people into all truth: John 16:13; compare Rom. 8:9, 14; 1 John 2:27. Answer. But not with the means of the ministry excluded. Plainly John 15:26, 27: The Spirit will bear witness of me. But you also will bear witness.

units.la: Obj. 3. Christus est unus Mediator: 1 Tim. II, 5. & uno opus est: Luc. 10, 42. Ergo. Resp. Non tamen tolli debent media, quibus ad Christum, & studium salutis aeternae, ex Ipsius ordinatione, adducamur. Obj. Obj. 4. Fides est aliquid internum & spirituale; ut & Regnum Dei: Luc. 17, 20, 21. Apostoli erant Ministri Spiritus: 2 Cor. 3, 6. Ergo. Resp. Non tamen sequitur, fidem ordinarie produci sine ministerio prædicantium: Rom. 10, 14. & Ministri Spiritus discerni debent ab ipso Spiritu.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Christ is the one Mediator (1 Tim. 2:5), and only one thing is needed (Luke 10:42). Therefore... Resp. Nevertheless, the means by which we are brought to Christ and to the pursuit of eternal salvation, by His own appointment, must not be taken away. Obj. 4. Faith is something inward and spiritual, as is the kingdom of God (Luke 17:20, 21). The apostles were ministers of the Spirit (2 Cor. 3:6). Therefore... Resp. It does not follow, however, that faith is ordinarily produced without the ministry of preachers (Rom. 10:14), and the ministers of the Spirit must be distinguished from the Spirit himself.

units.la: Obj. 5. Abrahamus immediate ab ipso Deo fuit vocatus. Itemque Paulus non ab hominibus, neque per homines vocatus, &c. Ergo. Resp. 1. A factis quibusdam extraordinariis, ad ordinaria, non valet consequentia. 2. Abrahamus etiam familiam & posteritatem suam docere debuit: Gen. 18, 19. Et Paulus per Ananiam instructus & baptizatus est: Actor. 9, 10, 19. &c.
units.tr: Obj. 5. Abraham was called immediately by God himself. Likewise Paul was called not by men, nor through men, etc. Therefore... Resp. 1. The inference from certain extraordinary facts to ordinary ones is not valid. 2. Abraham also had to teach his household and posterity (Gen. 18:19). And Paul was instructed and baptized through Ananias (Acts 9:10, 19), etc.

units.la: XXV. Succedit Pastorum æqualitas:
units.tr: XXV. Next comes the equality of ministers

units.la: ut omnes & singuli Pastores Ecclesiastici eandem, sive æqualem, potestatem ministerialem habeant; juxta ordinem in Verbo Dei præscriptum. Pontificii magnam inæqualitatem statuunt: Episcopos enim Presbyteris dicunt majores, aut superiores, potestate ordinis, & jurisdictionis; h.e. ut illi, non hi, possint aliis conferre Sacramentum ordinis (quod vocant); & ut jurisdictionem spiritualem habeant. Quin imo Archiepiscopos, & Primates, & supra omnes Pontificem Romanum, agnoscunt iidem. Sed & alii Hierarchici similem fere inæqualitatem statuunt.
units.tr: that all and each of the ecclesiastical ministers have the same, or equal, ministerial power, according to the order prescribed in the Word of God. The Papists set up a great inequality: they say that bishops are greater or superior to elders in the power of order and of jurisdiction; that is, that the bishops, and not the elders, can confer the sacrament of order (as they call it) on others, and that they hold spiritual jurisdiction. Indeed, the same men acknowledge archbishops, primates, and above all the Roman Pontiff. Other hierarchical men also set up an almost similar inequality.

units.la: Verum 1. in SS. Literis Episcoporum & Presbyterorum appellationes inter se permutantur: sic enim qui Act. 20, 17. Presbyteri vocantur, iidem Episcopi appellantur, verf. 28. Sic Tit. 1, 5, 6, 7. 1 Petr. 5, 1, 2.
units.tr: But, first, in Holy Scripture the names of bishop and elder are interchanged. For the same men who are called elders in Acts 20:17 are called bishops in verse 28. So also in Titus 1:5, 6, 7, and 1 Peter 5:1, 2.

units.la: 2. Alibi in una Ecclesia particulari plures dicuntur fuisse Episcopi; cum tamen una urbs, quantumvis magna, plures simul Episcopos Hierarchicos non capiat. Sic autem Apostolus, Phil. 1, 1. Omnibus sanctis in Christo Iesu, qui sunt Philippi, una cum Episcopis Diaconis. Hoc igitur de Presbyteris intelligendum est necessario.
units.tr: Second, elsewhere in Scripture several bishops are said to have been in one particular church, although one city, however large, cannot hold several hierarchical bishops at once. Thus the Apostle, Phil. 1:1: "To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, together with the bishops and deacons." This must therefore necessarily be understood of elders.

units.la: 3. Presbyteris tribuuntur eadem officia, quæ Episcopis. Episcopis tribuitur præclarum opus; docere, & Ecclesiam Dei curare : 1 Tim. III, 1, 2, 3. Similiter etiam Presbyteris : v, 17. Adde Tit. I, 7. cum 1 Petr. 5, 2, 4. & Act. 20, 17, 28. Speciatim χειροτονία diserte ad Presbyterium refertur: 1 Tim. 4, 14.
units.tr: Third, the same duties are assigned to elders as to bishops. Bishops are given the excellent work of teaching and caring for the Church of God (1 Tim. 3:1, 2, 3). Likewise also for elders (5:17). Add Titus 1:7 with 1 Peter 5:2, 4, and Acts 20:17, 28. Specifically, ordination [χειροτονία] is expressly referred to the presbytery (1 Tim. 4:14).

units.la: 4. Dominationem vero, & superiorem potestatem spiritualem, quam sibi præ Presbyteris arrogant Episcopi Hierarchici, Christus aperte prohibuit: Matth. 20, 25, 26. Scitis, Principes Gentium in eas dominari. Verum non ita erit inter vos. XXIII, 8, -11. Unus vester Doctor; omnes autem vos fratres estis. -Qui maximus est vestrum, sit minister vester. 1 Petr. 5, 3. Non ut dominantes cleris; sed ut qui sitis exemplaria gregis.
units.tr: Fourth, Christ plainly forbade the domination and superior spiritual power which the hierarchical bishops claim for themselves over the elders: Matt. 20:25, 26: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. But it shall not be so among you." Matt. 23:8–11: "One is your Teacher, and you are all brethren." "Whoever is greatest among you, let him be your minister." 1 Peter 5:3: "Not lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock."

units.la: Obj. 1. 1 Tim. 5, 19. Adversus Presbyterum accusationem ne recipito, nisi sub duobus aut tribus testibus: Ergo Timotheus, tanquam Episcopus, habuit jurisdictionem supra Presbyteros, &c. Resp. Inde tamen non sequitur, Timotheum, tanquam Episcopum, potestatem de Presbyteris judicandi habuisse, ut superiorem de inferioribus: nam alii æquales de hoc vel illo, cætera æquali, delato, & testimoniis aliorum gravato, judicandi potestatem quoque habent: 1 Cor. 14, 29, 32.
units.tr: Obj. 1. 1 Tim. 5:19: "Do not receive an accusation against an elder except on the testimony of two or three witnesses." Therefore Timothy, as a bishop, had jurisdiction over the elders, etc. Resp. It does not follow from this that Timothy, as a bishop, had the power of judging the elders as a superior judges inferiors. For other equals also have the power of judging, when a case concerning this or that man is brought before them, the rest being equal and the man being burdened by the testimony of others (1 Cor. 14:29, 32).

units.la: Obj. 2. Ibidem verf. 22. extat hæc admonitio; Ne cui cito manus imponito. Episcopus ergo Presbyteris superior est potestate ordinis. Resp. Cum istud etiam ad Seniorum ordinem pertineat; 1 Tim. 4, 14. nihil probat.
units.tr: Obj. 2. In the same place, verse 22, there is this admonition: "Do not lay hands on anyone hastily." Therefore the bishop is superior to the elders in the power of order. Resp. Since this also pertains to the order of elders (1 Tim. 4:14), it proves nothing.

units.la: Obj. 3. Apoc. I, 20. appellantur Angeli septem Ecclesiarum in Asia. Consequenter, II, 1. Angelo Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ scribe, &c. Ex singulari ista appellatione patet, singulis istis Ecclesiis singulos Episcopos præfuisse. fe. Resp. Negamus, Angelum istic notare Episcopum unum cujusque Dioecesios, potestate jurisdictionis, aut dominatione aliquâ, cæteris præstantem. Intelligimus vero synecdochen numeri singularis pro plurali; qualis etiam occurrit Mal.II,7. Labia Sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, &c. cum tamen multi numero essent Sacerdotes. Confer Act. 20, 28, de pluribus Episcopis Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ.
units.tr: Obj. 3. In Rev. 1:20 the "angels of the seven churches in Asia" are named. Consequently, in 2:1: "Write to the angel of the Ephesian church," etc. From this singular designation it is clear that a single bishop presided over each of these churches. Resp. We deny that the angel here denotes one bishop of each diocese, excelling the others in the power of jurisdiction or in some kind of domination. We rather understand a synecdoche of the singular number for the plural, such as also occurs in Mal. 2:7: "The lips of the priest keep knowledge," etc., although there were many priests. Compare Acts 20:28, concerning several bishops of the Ephesian church.

units.la: XXVI. Quæ contra Episcopos Hierarchicos produximus, eadem quoque ad similes alias Dignitates superiores Ecclesiasticas applicanda sunt: speciatim vero adversus Pontificem Romanum hæc valent; qui omnes alios Antecessores Ecclesiæ sibi habere subordinatos dicitur à suis assentatoribus, tanquam Caput visibile Ecclesiæ catholicæ, Monarcha Ecclesiasticus, Christi in terris Vicarius, &c. Frustra autem hi provocant ad Petrum. Ille enim 1. reliquis Apostolis æqualis fuit; non vero iis superior, aut major. Hinc Paulus 1 Cor. 3, 21, 22, 23. Et Paulus, & Apollos, & Cephas, omnia vestra sunt; vos autem Christi. Ita hi omnes Christo pariter subordinantur. Vide etiam ibid. verf 5. & 1, 12. Atque iterum 2, xi, 5. Puto enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse summis Apostolis.
units.tr: XXVI. What we have brought forward against hierarchical bishops must also be applied to other similar higher ecclesiastical dignities. Especially against the Roman Pontiff, these points hold: he is said by his flatterers to have all the other predecessors of the Church subordinate to himself, as the visible head of the catholic Church, ecclesiastical monarch, vicar of Christ on earth, etc. But these men appeal to Peter in vain. For, first, he was equal to the other apostles, not superior or greater than them. Hence Paul, 1 Cor. 3:21–23: "Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, all are yours; and you are Christ's." Thus all of these are alike subordinate to Christ. See also verses 5 and 1:12, and again 2 Cor. 11:5: "For I consider that I am not in the least inferior to the most eminent apostles."

units.la: 2. Similiter Gal. II, 7, 8, 9. dicit Apostolus, sibi Evangelium Præputii, ac Petro Circumcisionis, creditum fuisse; & se à Jacobo, Cepha, (i.e. Petro,) & Johanne pro socio agnitum. Ac porro verf. 11, se Petro Antiochiæ in os restitisse, quod esset redarguendus.
units.tr: Second, likewise, in Gal. 2:7, 8, 9 the Apostle says that the gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to him, and that of the circumcision to Peter; and that he was recognized by James, Cephas (that is, Peter), and John as a partner. Moreover, in verse 11, he says he withstood Peter to his face at Antioch, because he was to be rebuked.

units.la: 3. Hoc ipsum etiam inde patet, quod Apostolis inter se de primatu certantibus, Christus litem non terminaverit, dicens; se illum Petro jam dedisse, vel decrevisse: sed contra; Inter vos non erit sic: Matth. 20, 26. Luc. 22, 26. Confer Matth. 23, 6-12.
units.tr: Third, this is also plain from the fact that when the apostles were contending among themselves about primacy, Christ did not settle the dispute by saying that he had already given or decreed it to Peter; but on the contrary: "It shall not be so among you" (Matt. 20:26; Luke 22:26). Compare Matt. 23:6–12.

units.la: 4. Consequenter Petrus, ut alios Presbyteros precatus est, ne dominarentur Cleris; itâ se συμπρεσ-βύτερον βύπεον appellavit, &c. nihil superioritatis sibi arrogans; I, V, I, 3,
units.tr: Fourth, consequently, Peter, when he begged the other elders not to lord it over the clergy, called himself a fellow-elder [συμπρεσβύτερος], etc., claiming for himself no superiority (1 Peter 5:1, 3).

units.la: Obj. 1. Atqui Christus dixit Petro, Matth. 16, 18, 19. Tu es Petrus; & super hanc petram, &c. Atque iterum; Tibi dabo claves Regni Coelorum. Ergò. Resp. 1. Petra illa, super quam aedificanda dicitur Ecclesia, non erat Petrus; sed ipse Christus: 1 Cor. 3, 11. x, 4.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Yet Christ said to Peter, Matt. 16:18, 19: "You are Peter, and upon this rock," etc. And again: "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Therefore... Resp. 1. That rock upon which the Church is said to be built was not Peter, but Christ himself (1 Cor. 3:11; 10:4).

units.la: 2. Ministerialis illa potestas clavium, & remittendi peccata, Petro quidem promissa & data fuit; sed non soli: Matth. 18, 18. Joh. 20, 21. 22, 23.
units.tr: 2. That ministerial power of the keys, and of remitting sins, was indeed promised and given to Peter, but not to him alone (Matt. 18:18; John 20:21, 22, 23).

units.la: Obj. 2. Petrus diserte primus appellatur; Matth. 10, 2, Resp. Istud fit ratione ordinis, quo Discipulus & Apostolus factus est: iv, 18, 19. unde nequaquam sequitur superior potestas.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Peter is expressly called "first": Matt. 10:2. Resp. This comes from the order in which he became a disciple and apostle (4:18, 19), whence it by no means follows that he had superior power.

units.la: Obj. 3. Ille saepius nomine omnium verba fecit, &c. Resp. Nulla iterum consequentia ad primatum, aut suprematum. Neque porro à Petro ad Papam: quod in superioribus quoque observandum.
units.tr: Obj. 3. He often spoke in the name of all, etc. Resp. Again, no inference follows to primacy or supremacy. Nor, indeed, does it follow from Peter to the Pope; which should also be observed in what has gone before.

units.la: Obj. 4. Idem postulat ratio ordinis atque unitatis. Resp. Ordo potest conservari per ea, quae ipse Christus instituit; atque etiam unitas.
units.tr: Obj. 4. The same is demanded by the reason of order and of unity. Resp. Order can be preserved through the things which Christ himself instituted, and unity as well.

units.la: XXVII. Nunc de Stipendio Pastorum agendum; potissimum propter Anabaptistas, qui Pastores nostros isto nomine criminari solent.
units.tr: XXVII. Now we must treat of the stipend of ministers, chiefly on account of the Anabaptists, who are accustomed to accuse our ministers on this score.

units.la: Stipendii nomine intelligimus hoc loco media honestae sustentationis, quae Ministris in Verbo laborantibus, & curae animarum omnino vacantibus, ab Ecclesiâ, aut ejus nutriciis, grato animo praebentur. Quod autem istiusmodi Stipendium praebere Ecclesiam deceat; idque accipere Ministris liceat, probamus;
units.tr: By stipend we mean here the means of decent support which is given with a grateful heart by the Church, or by its nursing fathers, to ministers who labour in the Word and are wholly free from the care of souls. That the Church ought to provide such a stipend, and that ministers may lawfully receive it, we prove as follows:

units.la: 1. Ex diserta ipsius Christi sententia, Ministris Evangelii, tanquam operariis, debentur sua alimenta; Matth. 10, 10.
units.tr: 1. From the express saying of Christ himself, that food is owed to ministers of the Gospel as to workmen: Matth. 10, 10.

units.la: 2. Paulus ex professo, & satis prolixe, hoc ipsum astruit, 1 Cor. 9, 4, 14. tum ex communi aequitate, tum ex jure Divinitus instituto.
units.tr: 2. Paul, professedly and at some length, asserts this very thing, 1 Cor. 9, 4, 14, both from common justice and from the right instituted by God.

units.la: 3. Confequenter hoc ipfum Ecclefiis mandatur : Gal. 4, 6. Communicet autem, qui inftituitur infermone, cum eo qui fe inftituit, omnia bona. 1 Tim. 5, 17, 18.
units.tr: 3. Consequently, this very thing is enjoined on the Churches: Gal. 6, 6. Let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches. 1 Tim. 5, 17, 18.

units.la: 4. Deus fub V. T. Sacerdotibus & Levitis, ordinariis Ecclefiæ Miniftris, de honefta fuftentatione profpexit: Levit. 27, 30. Num, 15, 20, 21. Deut. 26, 2, XVIII, 1, - 8. Levit. 6, 16, 17, 18. VII, 6, - 10, 14; 31, -34. VIII, 31. XXIV, 5, -9. Num. 35, 2, -. Jof. 21, 3, -. Unde analogice colligimus, nunc etiam Miniftris N.T. profpiciendum effe; quoniam in ipfa re fubeft eadem ratio æquitatis.
units.tr: 4. God, under the Old Testament, provided for the decent support of the priests and Levites, the ordinary ministers of the Church: Levit. 27, 30. Num. 15, 20, 21. Deut. 26, 2; XVIII, 1–8. Levit. 6, 16, 17, 18. VII, 6–10, 14; 31–34. VIII, 31. XXIV, 5–9. Num. 35, 2. Jos. 21, 3. Whence we conclude by analogy that provision must now be made for the ministers of the New Testament also, since the same reason of equity lies in the matter itself.

units.la: Obj. 1. Ezech. 34, 2, 3. reprehenduntur Paftores ic ipfos pafcentes. Hoc autem faciunt, qui ftipendium accipiunt. Refp. Jure merito iftic reprehenduntur carnales illi Paftores, qui propriis fuis commodis duntaxat intenti, gregem fuæ fidei commiffum negligebant. Inde autem minime fequitur, Paftoribus fidis, munus fuum fedulo obeuntibus, non deberi honeftam fuftentationem.
units.tr: Obj. 1. Ezek. 34, 2, 3. The shepherds are rebuked for feeding themselves, and those who receive a stipend do this. Resp. Those carnal shepherds are rightly rebuked there, who, intent only on their own advantages, neglected the flock committed to their faith. But it by no means follows from this that faithful ministers, who diligently discharge their office, are not owed a decent support.

units.la: Obj. 2. Matth. 10, 7. 8. Gratis accepiftis, gratis date. Ergo, &c. Refp. Chriftus ibi prohibet, ne bona fpiritualia, & dona gratiæ, pretio æftimentur; & quafi vendantur. Sed perperam inde colligitur, Miniftris, nullam deberi honeftam fuftentationem. Contrarium deinceps ibidem docuit ipfe Servator.
units.tr: Obj. 2. Matth. 10, 7, 8. Freely you have received, freely give. Therefore, etc. Resp. Christ there forbids that spiritual goods and gifts of grace be valued at a price and, as it were, sold. But it is wrongly inferred from this that ministers are owed no decent support. The Saviour himself taught the contrary in the same place afterwards.

units.la: Obj. 3. Paulus noluit à quibufdam Ecclefiis ftipendium accipere; fed potius labore manuum fuarum fibi victum quæfivit: Act. 20, 34, 35. 1 Theff. II, 9. Ergo Refp. Non, quafi non habuerit jus percipiendi ftipendium, five media honeftæ fuftentationis; fed ut calumniatoribus, qui ipfum quæftus gratia Euangelium annunciare vociferabantur, os occluderet; atque ita fcandalum averteret, & infirmis quibufdam fuccurreret; ut patet ex locis allegatis. Contra vero docet, fe illud jus habuiffe; 1 Cor. 9. 4, 5, 6, 12. &c. Et caufas explicat, cur à quibufdam Ecclefiis noluerit quicquam accipere; cùm tamen ab aliis etiàm acciperet; verf. 12, 15. 2: xi, 7, 8, 9, 12.
units.tr: Obj. 3. Paul was unwilling to receive a stipend from certain Churches, but rather sought his living by the labour of his own hands: Acts 20, 34, 35. 1 Thess. II, 9. Therefore, etc. Resp. Not as though he had not the right to receive a stipend, or means of decent support; but so that he might stop the mouths of the slanderers, who cried out that he preached the Gospel for the sake of gain, and thus avert scandal and help certain weak brethren, as is plain from the places cited. On the contrary, he teaches that he had that right: 1 Cor. 9, 4, 5, 6, 12, etc. And he explains the reasons why he was unwilling to accept anything from certain Churches, although he did accept from others: vers. 12, 15; 2 Cor. XI, 7, 8, 9, 12.

units.la: Obj. 4. Est species Simoniæ: Ergò. Resp. Non subest ratio Simoniæ; dùm ipsa bona spiritualia non æstimantur pretio; neque fidus Pastor spe lucri, & quæstùs ad functionem sui muneris inducitur. Verùm interim Ecclesia obligatur ad gratitudinem in Pastore sustentando demonstrandam, & Pastori jus est stipendium consequenter accipere.
units.tr: Obj. It is a kind of simony: therefore, etc. Resp. There is no ground for simony, since the spiritual goods themselves are not valued at a price, nor is a faithful minister induced to discharge his function by hope of gain and profit. Yet meanwhile the Church is bound to show gratitude in supporting its minister, and the minister has a consequent right to receive a stipend.

units.la: Inst. Vel acciperet stipendium pro labore in Evangelio; vel pro vacatione suâ ab aliâ quâcunque arte: prius videtur Simoniacum: posterius etiàm absurdum; sic enim omnibus otiosis deberetur stipendium pro suâ vacatione. Resp. Fidi Pastores minimè sunt otiosi; &, cùm ipsi alia sustentationis media omittant, Ecclesiæ ædificationi prorsùs invigilantes, æquum est illis hanc gratitudinem præstari.
units.tr: Inst. Either he would receive a stipend for his labour in the Gospel, or for his freedom from any other trade. The former seems simoniacal; the latter is also absurd, for on that reasoning a stipend would be owed to all idle persons for their idleness. Resp. Faithful ministers are by no means idle; and since they forgo other means of support, devoting themselves wholly to the building up of the Church, it is fair that this gratitude be shown to them.

units.la: XXVIII. Succedunt Doctores, quos Apostolus diserte ac distinctè etiàm appellat, Ephes. 4, 11. 1 Cor. 12, 28; 29. Et sunt Ministri ordinarii, in veritate fidei Christianæ, ex SS. Literis, accuratè explicandâ, inculcandâ, confirmandâ, & contra Adversarios defendendâ, laborantes. Hùc pertinent Catechistæ, qui circa rudiores occupantur: alii autem versantur in instructione eorum, qui ad Ministerium Verbi aspirant; & dicuntur Professores Theologiæ. Hi in Scholis & Academiis Christianis, SS. Literas methodicè interpretantur; Theologiam systematicè tradunt; Controversias accuratè tractant; Casus conscientiæ explicant, &c.
units.tr: XXVIII. There follow the Doctores, whom the Apostle also names expressly and distinctly, Eph. 4, 11; 1 Cor. 12, 28, 29. They are the ordinary ministers who labour to explain accurately, to inculcate, to confirm, and to defend against adversaries the truth of the Christian faith from the Holy Scriptures. To this office belong the Catechists, who are occupied with the more untaught; others are engaged in instructing those who aspire to the ministry of the Word, and they are called Professors of Theology. These, in Christian schools and academies, interpret the Holy Scriptures methodically, teach theology systematically, treat controversies carefully, explain cases of conscience, and so on.

units.la: Quoniam verò plurima requiruntur in istis Doctoribus, qui futuros Pastores informant ac præparant; hinc qui ad conditionem illam existimantur idonei, rectè priùs ab aliis Doctoribus examinantur; ac deinceps isto honoris titulo solenniter ornantur: quemadmodùm in aliis Facultatibus etiàm fieri solet. Istius promotionis Academicæ finis nequaquàm est, ut promoti illi Doctores titulo suo superbiant; sed ut publico isto testimonio constet, eos esse idoneos qui Theologiam itâ doceant, ut indicatum est modò.
units.tr: Since, however, very much is required of those teachers who form and prepare the future ministers, those who are judged fit for that office are rightly first examined by other teachers, and afterwards are solemnly adorned with this title of honour, just as is commonly done in the other faculties also. The purpose of this academic promotion is by no means that the promoted teachers should take pride in their title; rather, that by this public testimony it may be established that they are fit to teach theology in the manner just indicated.

units.la: Obj. Matth. xxiii, 10. Ne vocaminii Doctores : unus enim vester est Doctor, nempè Christus. Ergò. Resp. Verùm textum rite considerantì patet, non istum titulum absolutè prohiberi; sed saltum illi apud Pharisæos adjunctum. Similiter enim dicitur verf. 9. Et Patrem vestrum ne quenquam vocate in terrâ : unus enim est Pater vester qui in cœlis est. Confer Act. 13, 1. 1 Cor. 12, 28, 29. Eph. 4, 11. 1 Tim. II, 7.
units.tr: Obj. Matth. 23, 10. Do not be called teachers, for one is your teacher, namely Christ. Therefore, etc. Resp. On a proper consideration of the text it is plain that this title is not forbidden absolutely, but only the vain display attached to it among the Pharisees. For similarly it is said in vers. 9: And call no one your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Compare Acts 13, 1; 1 Cor. 12, 28, 29; Eph. 4, 11; 1 Tim. II, 7.

units.la: XXIX. Seniores gubernantes sunt etiam viri pieta- te, prudentia, & gravitate in Ecclesia conspicui, qui in ejus regimine, fideique & morum censura, Pastoribus adjunguntur.
units.tr: XXIX. The ruling elders are also men conspicuous in the Church for godliness, prudence, and gravity, who are joined to the ministers in its governance and in the oversight of faith and morals.

units.la: Itâ Apostolus in Ministeriis Ecclesiasticis gubernationes quoque recensèt, 1 Cor. 12, 28. Confer Rom. 12, 8. 1 Thess. 5, 12. Hebr. 13, 17. Evidentissimè verò distinctio horum Seniorum à Pastoribus patet ex loco 1 Tim. 5, 17. Qui bene præsunt Presbyteri, duplici honore digni habentur : maxime qui laborant in sermone & doctrinâ. Omnium ergò Presbyterorum, sive Seniorum, est bene præesse : sed aliquorum etiàm laborare in sermone & doctrinâ.
units.tr: So the Apostle also lists governments among the ministries of the Church, 1 Cor. 12:28. Compare Rom. 12:8, 1 Thess. 5:12, Heb. 13:17. The distinction between these elders and the ministers is most clearly shown by 1 Tim. 5:17: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and doctrine. It is therefore the task of all elders, or rulers, to rule well, but of some of them also to labour in word and doctrine.

units.la: Atque adeò Scripturaria & Apostolica est distinctio inter Pastores, sive Presbyteros gubernantes & docentes simul; & inter Seniores, sive Presbyteros gubernantes tantùm. Nec contemtim appellandi sunt Seniores Laici; quòd eligantur ex multitudine fidelium qui per Pastores docentur: Christus enim Discipulam Ecclesiasticam tribuit Ecclesiæ; Matth. 18, 17. nihil mirum igitur, si potestas hæc ministerialis, quæ radicaliter est penes Ecclesiam, exercenda committatur etiam quibusdam ex fidelium multitudine electis, qui simul cum Pastoribus Ecclesiam repræsentant. sentent, eique præeant; ut omnia decenter fiant & ordine.
units.tr: Thus the distinction between ministers, or elders who both rule and teach, and elders, or elders who only rule, is scriptural and apostolic. Nor should the latter be dismissively called lay elders, on the ground that they are chosen from the multitude of the faithful who are taught by the ministers. Christ gave the power of ecclesiastical discipline to the Church (Matt. 18:17), so it is no wonder that this ministerial power, which resides radically in the Church, is entrusted for its exercise also to some chosen from the multitude of the faithful, who together with the ministers represent the Church and preside over it, so that all things may be done decently and in order.

units.la: Exc. 1. Qui bene præsunt Presbyteri, sunt Episcopi Hierarchici. Resp. Absurdè istud dicitur; cùm illis Presbyteris non obscurè præferantur, & magis duplici honore digni pronuncientur alii, in Sermone & Doctrinâ laborantes.
units.tr: Exception 1. The elders who rule well are the hierarchical bishops. Answer. This is said absurdly, since the passage plainly sets those elders apart and pronounces others, who labour in word and doctrine, more worthy of double honour.

units.la: Exc. 2. Qui Laborant, &c. h. e. qui valdè seduli sunt, ac sese fatigant isto opere; illi maximè digni sunt duplici honore. Resp. Imò qui in re tantâ, ipsis etiam demandatâ, non sunt seduli, &c. nequaquàm dici possunt bene præesse: nec duplici honore digni: quin contrà eos ferit comminatio. Jerem. 48. 10.
units.tr: Exception 2. Who labour, etc., that is, those who are very diligent and wear themselves out in this work, are especially worthy of double honour. Answer. On the contrary, those who are not diligent in so great a matter, entrusted to them, etc., can by no means be said to rule well, nor are they worthy of double honour; rather, the threat of Jer. 48:10 strikes them.

units.la: Obj. Ex usu SS. Literarum Presbyteri iidem sunt qui Episcopi; & Episcopum oportet esse διδακτικὸν:
units.tr: Objection. By the usage of Holy Scripture, elders are the same as bishops, and a bishop must be apt to teach [διδακτικόν]:

units.la: 1 Tim. 3, 2. Nulli ergo Seniores debent esse gubernantes tantùm, & non etiàm docentes. Resp. 1. Apostolus, dùm istam conditionem requirit, speciatim respicit Episcopos, sive Presbyteros illos, quibus in cumberet munus docendi. 2. Seniores tantùm gubernantes etiàm debent apti esse ad docendum, quantum sufficit ad institutionem, exhortationem, correctionem, consolationem, &c. pro re natâ.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 3:2. Therefore no elders should be only rulers and not also teachers. Answer 1. In requiring this qualification, the Apostle has especially in view the bishops, or those elders for whom the office of teaching was a burden. 2. Elders who only rule ought also to be apt to teach, as far as is sufficient for instruction, exhortation, correction, consolation, etc., as the occasion requires.

units.la: XXX. Diaconi sunt viri pii, prudentes, ac fidi, quibus committitur collectio, conservatio, & dispensatio bonorum temporalium, quæ ad sustentationem pauperum in Ecclesiâ, & ad alios usûs Ecclesiasticos, conferuntur; atque in istis rebus Ecclesiæ ministrant. Hoc ministerium primitùs penes Apostolos quoque fuit: Act. 4, 34, - 37. v, 1, 2. Postea verò, cum Apostoli isti curæ non sufficerent, aliis ea necessariò mandari debuit. Hinc Act. 6, 1, - 5. septem viri, idoneo testimonio ornati, pii, & pleni Spiritu Sancto, in istam partem Ministerii eligebantur. Consequenquenter Paulus, ubi varia dona Spiritus Sancti, & distincta officia Ecclesiastica recenset, Rom. 12,7,8. dicit; Sive Ministerium, (Διακονίαν) versemur in ministrando. -- Tum is qui distribuit, cum simplicitate: tum qui miseretur, cum hilaritate. Et 1 Tim. 3, 8,13. ubi requisita Diaconorum enumerat, eadem opera docet, Diaconatum sic fuisse primitus ministerium distinctum, ut tamen gradatim ex eo facta fuerint promotiones ad Presbyteratum gubernantem, vel etiam in verbo laborantem. De Philippo Diacono nominatim vide Act. 21, 8.
units.tr: XXX. Deacons are men who are godly, prudent, and faithful, to whom is committed the collection, keeping, and distribution of temporal goods, which are contributed for the support of the poor in the Church and for its other ecclesiastical uses; and in these matters they serve the Church. This ministry was at first also in the hands of the Apostles (Acts 4:34–37; 5:1, 2). Later, when the Apostles could not sufficiently attend to it, it had to be committed of necessity to others. Hence in Acts 6:1–5 seven men, endowed with good testimony, godly and full of the Holy Spirit, were chosen for this part of the ministry. Accordingly Paul, when he lists the various gifts of the Holy Spirit and the distinct ecclesiastical offices, says in Rom. 12:7, 8: Or ministry (διακονίαν), let us wait on ministering; he who distributes, with simplicity; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. And in 1 Tim. 3:8, 13, where he enumerates the qualifications of deacons, he teaches at the same time that the diaconate was at first a ministry so distinct, and yet that from it advancement was made step by step to the ruling eldership, or even to the eldership that labours in the word. For Philip the deacon by name, see Acts 21:8.

units.la: XXXI. Hactenus satis de iis Ministrorum or- dinibus.
units.tr: XXXI. So much for these orders of ministers.

units.la: Verum Apostolus 1 Cor. 12,28. etiam opitulationes enumerat: quo quidem nomine Diaconi recte intelliguntur; attamen non soli videntur intelligendi. Olim in Ecclesia Apostolica fuerunt etiam Viduae Diaconissae, Diaconorum in quibusdam partibus adjutrices. Sic Rom. 12, 16. Phoebe appellatur Διάκονος, Ministra Ecclesiae Cenchreensis. Confer 1 Tim. 5, 9, 10.
units.tr: But the Apostle in 1 Cor. 12:28 also lists helps. Under this name deacons are rightly understood, but they do not seem to be the only ones meant. In the Apostolic Church there were also widows, deaconesses, who assisted the deacons in certain areas. So in Rom. 16:1 Phoebe is called a deaconess [Διάκονος], minister of the Church at Cenchreae. Compare 1 Tim. 5:9, 10.

units.la: Sed & opitulationes in nostris Ecclesiis praestant Praelectores & Praecentores, nec non Aegrorum Visitatores.
units.tr: But also in our churches readers and precentors render help, as do visitors of the sick.

units.la: Huc quoque pertinent Curatores, Quaestores, & Dispensatores bonorum Ecclesiasticorum. Quin & quomodo Apparitores, Ostiarii, Scopatores, &c.
units.tr: To these also belong curators, treasurers, and stewards of ecclesiastical goods. Indeed, so too attendants, doorkeepers, sweepers, etc.

units.la: XXXII. Agendum nunc de reliqua multitudine Fi- delium;
units.tr: XXXII. We must now speak of the rest of the multitude of the faithful;

units.la: qui etiam sunt Membra Ecclesiae instituta, & Deo in Christo insigniter chari, eodem sanguinis Christi pretio redemti, aeque pretiosam fidem sortiti, & ejusdem salutis consortes: 1 Cor. 6,20. VII,23. 1 Petr. 1, 18,19. 2:1, 1. Judae 3. 1 Joh. 1,3. Rom. 8, 16, 17. XII, 1. 1 Pet. II, 9, 10. Eph. 2,19,-22. Atque adeo cum Petrus, 1: v, 3. in sua exhortatione ad Presbyteros, scribit; Neque ut dominantes Cleris, sed ut quisitis exemplaria gregis, per Cleros itidem, ut per gregem, intelligi debet Populus Christianus; tanquam quàm verè sors, hæreditas, & peculium Domini: agnoscente etiàm Card. Cajetano.
units.tr: who are also members of the Church established by God, and remarkably dear to God in Christ, redeemed by the same price of Christ's blood, having obtained a faith equally precious, and partakers of the same salvation: 1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19; 2 Pet. 1:1; Jude 3; 1 John 1:3; Rom. 8:16, 17; 12:1; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10; Eph. 2:19–22. And so when Peter, in his exhortation to the elders (1 Pet. 5:3), writes: not as lording it over the clergy, but as examples to the flock, by the clergy the Christian people must likewise be understood, as well as by the flock*; since they are truly the lot, the inheritance, and the peculiar people of the Lord; as even Cardinal Cajetan acknowledges.

units.la: Minimè igitur Scripturaria est Pontificicrum distinctio in Clericos, & Laicos; quasi tota fidelium multitudo, seu populus Christianus, non pertineret ad hæreditatem, seu peculium Domini; sed soli Antecessores Ecclesiastici. Vide Deut. 7, 6. xiv, 2, xxvi, 18.
units.tr: The Papists' distinction between clergy and laity is therefore by no means scriptural, as if the whole multitude of the faithful, or the Christian people, did not belong to the inheritance or peculiar people of the Lord, but only the ecclesiastical leaders. See Deut. 7:6; 14:2; 26:18.

units.la: XXXIII. Neque admittenda est eorundem distinctio in Religiosos, & Seculares; quasi pro membris Ecclesiæ institutæ agnoscendi essent Sæculares Religionem non profitentes. Verùm Adversarii Religionis vocem strictius sumunt, & vitam Monasticam intelligunt: atque isto sensu Religionem definiunt, quòd sit Status hominum ad perfectionem Christianam, per paupertatis, continentiæ, & obedientiæ vota, tendentium. Verum 1. Christus & Apostoli tale vitæ genus non instituerunt; sed de Religione aliter docuerunt; Jac. 1, 26, 27 & alibi.
units.tr: XXXIII. Nor is their distinction between religious and secular to be admitted, as if secular persons who do not profess a religious order were to be acknowledged as members of the Church established by God. Rather, the adversaries take the word religion more narrowly, and understand by it the monastic life; and in this sense they define religion as a state of men tending toward Christian perfection through the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. But: 1. Christ and the Apostles did not institute such a way of life, but taught otherwise about religion; James 1:26, 27 and elsewhere.

units.la: 2. Absoluta perfectio, quam Adversarii intelligunt, à nemine post lapsum in hac vita acquiri potest. Vide sup. cap. 16. th. 18.
units.tr: 2. Absolute perfection, which the adversaries mean, can be acquired by no one in this life after the fall. See above, chapter 16, thesis 18.

units.la: 3. Vota Monastica superstitioni promovendæ satis apta sunt; non autem isti perfectioni, cui nos operam dare oportet.
units.tr: 3. Monastic vows are well suited to promote superstition, but not that perfection which we ought to strive for.

units.la: 4. Imò potiùs obsunt veræ pietati ac sanctimoniæ. Vide sup. cap. 9. th. 52.
units.tr: 4. Indeed they rather hinder true piety and holiness. See above, chapter 9, thesis 52.

units.la: Obj. 1. Tempore Enoschi cæptum est invocari nomen Domini: Gen. 4, 26. Ergò saltem præfiguratus Monachatus. Resp. Ille tamen in matrimonio vixit; sic filios & filias suscepit: cap. v, 9, 10. neque quicquam extat de ejus paupertate, vel cæcâ obedientiâ erga homines; aut tali voto.
units.tr: Objection 1. In the time of Enos men began to call upon the name of the Lord (Gen. 4:26). Therefore at least a monasticism was foreshadowed. Answer. Yet he lived in marriage and begat sons and daughters (Gen. 5:9, 10); nor is anything recorded of his poverty or of blind obedience to men, or of any such vow.

units.la: Obj. 2. Enoch ambulavit cum Deo: Gen. v. 22. Ergò. Resp. Sed & ille conjugatus, liberos genuisse commemoratur ibidem. Nihil de vitâ Monasticâ.
units.tr: Objection 2. Enoch walked with God (Gen. 5:22). Therefore, etc. Answer. But he too is recorded in the same place as married and as having begotten children. Nothing about monastic life.

units.la: Obj.3. Elias in monte Carmel vitam degit valde austeram, &c. Similiter Elisæus, &c. Ergò. Resp. Elias & Elisæus Prophetæ fuerunt; vitamque instituerunt juxta vocationem ac functionem suam extraordinariam, & ratione temporum istorum corruptissimorum: sed mons Carmel non fuit omnino desertus, aut habitatoribus destitutus: Ios. 12, 22. xv, 55.
units.tr: Objection 3. Elijah on Mount Carmel lived a very austere life, etc. Likewise Elisha, etc. Therefore, etc. Answer. Elijah and Elisha were prophets, and they lived in accordance with their extraordinary calling and function, and in view of the very corrupt times; but Mount Carmel was not wholly deserted or without inhabitants (Josh. 12:22; 15:55).

units.la: 1 Sam. 25, 2. &c. Ac porro nihil in illis de instituto Monastico.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 25:2, etc. Moreover, there is nothing in those passages about a monastic institute.

units.la: Obj. 4. Naziræi, &c. Resp. Nec illi fuerunt obligati ad cœlibatum, &c. sed ad observationes quasdam cerimoniales, œconomiæ V. T. convenientes, & ab ipso Deo præscriptas; Num. 6, 2, --21.
units.tr: Objection 4. The Nazirites, etc. Answer. Nor were they bound to celibacy, etc., but to certain ceremonial observances, suited to the economy of the Old Testament and prescribed by God himself (Num. 6:2–21).

units.la: Obj. 5. Rechabitæ, Ierem. 35, 2, --. &c. Resp. Etiam isti non ex Religione speciali, sed ex Patris sui præscripto, singularia quædam observârunt: at nec cœlibes vixerunt, nec omni possessione propriâ destituti.
units.tr: Objection 5. The Rechabites, Jer. 35:2, etc. Answer. These too observed certain particular practices not from any special religious order but by the command of their father; and they did not live unmarried, nor were they wholly without private property.

units.la: Obj. 6. Johannes Baptista vestitu, victu, loco habitationis, Monachatum, aut vitam Anachoreticam, præ-se tulit. Ergò. Resp. Ille extraordinarius Dei Minister, & Christi præcursor, frugaliter admodum vixit; sed nec de ejus voto cœlibatus, nec de spontaneâ paupertate, nec de cœcâ erga ullum hominem obedientiâ, quicquam legitur.
