Annal. ad A. 61. pag. 467., that bishops who came into another place were invited by that place's bishop to preach there), the following should be observed. (1) First and above all, consider what is most fitting to preach in that particular place. It sometimes happens that a church suffers from some notable evil, either in doctrine or in piety, and in such a case it often prefers to be instructed by someone else; and the sermon of a stranger is usually heard more attentively and is often more effective in moving people than one that is heard every day, however little inferior it may be. The preacher must attend to this above all, and with prudence, so that he chooses according to the condition of the place rather than considering only himself, preaching whatever sermon he has most readily at hand, or one from which he may hope for some greater honour, applause or advantage for himself. (2) But where this cannot be observed, or can hardly be observed in full, he should usually take a more practical text, because this defect is commonly found both in sermons and in our lives, that such things are taught too little practically. Thus he will be on safer ground and will achieve greater fruit. This is a common complaint. Abrenethy, in the preface to Medicina animae: Most books and sermons are filled with speculative and contemplative theology; very few with practical theology. See also what Telinghius learnedly and movingly argues on this point, Necessaria demonstratio, lib. 3, cap. 4 and lib. 4, cap. 2. Besides, what I have brought in on this matter elsewhere, disp. de Theologia, thes. 16., I have also cited here. Long ago Bernard began his eightieth sermon on the Song of Songs in this way: Some of you (as I have learned) bear it with less than equanimity that for several days now, while you delight to dwell on the wonder and astonishment of the sacraments, the sermon we offer has been either without any savour or seasoned with only a very little of moral salt.

units.la: III. Admodum e re Ecclesiae & Concionatoriae esset, ad arbitrarios textus explicare integram Theologiae praxin, quemadmodum dogmatica sic, & Catechesis tractari, etiam historica Christi solent. Inter Anglos (ut plurimi varia ad textus aliquos Practicae capita) feliciter hoc conatus est Thomas Hooker de vocatione & justific.; atque inter Germanos, egit id Johannes Arnd libris de vero Christianismo.
units.tr: III. It would be very useful for the Church and for preachers to explain, from freely chosen texts, the whole practice of theology, just as dogmatic and catechetical matter, and even the historical matter of Christ, are commonly treated. Among the English (as many do with various chapters of practical divinity from certain texts), Thomas Hooker has happily attempted this in his work on vocation and justification; and among the Germans, Johann Arndt did so in his books on true Christianity.

units.la: V. In textu quocunque, haec tenenda. I. Ne sumatur nimis brevis, ne ostentare velle ingenium videatur, nisi is vel copia sua, vel difficultate conspicua Concionatorem ab illa suspicione statim liberet; nihil enim aeque cavendum, quam ne in limine impingamus, & semper, ne ad ostentationem, vel propriae & vanae gloriolae captationem, agere videamur. Ἀπέχεσθαι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν. Gregor, in fine expos. in Job. tunc enim bene dicitur bonum: cum is qui dicit, sol iei, a quo accipit, per id appetit placere quod dicit. II. Neque etiam nimis longus fit, ne vel tempus lucrari velle, & singula, quae non minus emphatica, atque observari quoque merentur, tractare vel noluisse, vel non potuisse, videatur, quod vitium Postillatoribus commune est, iisque, qui non conciones ad textus, sed textus ad conciones habent, id est, aliquarum rerum, vel ut ipsi opinantur, quarumcunque locos communes quasi tenent, quas ad varios textus applicant, & repetunt, potius, quam ut ex textibus semper alia porro addiscant, doceantque; atque tales facile exhauriri compertum est. III. Ne dicis causa textus legatur solum, nihil autem minus quam ipse explicetur, ut qui ad illum & ab illo divagantur & excurrunt, alio, si non etiam quaquaversum. Quod vitium, judicii & eruditionis inopiam summam arguit.
units.tr: V. In any text whatsoever, the following should be kept. (1) It should not be taken too short, lest it seem that the preacher wishes to show off his talent, unless the text by its abundance or its conspicuous difficulty at once frees the preacher from that suspicion. For nothing must be guarded against more than stumbling on the threshold, and we must always avoid appearing to aim at display or at catching some vain little glory for ourselves. They have their reward [Ἀπέχεσθαι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν]. Gregory, at the end of his exposition of Job: For then a good thing is rightly said to be good when the one who speaks seeks through it to please the sun from which he receives it. (2) Nor should it be too long, lest it appear either that the preacher wished to gain time, or that he either would not or could not treat each single point, which deserves no less emphasis and attention. This fault is common to postillators, and to those who do not have sermons fitted to texts but texts fitted to sermons; that is, they hold, as it were, commonplaces of certain matters, or of whatever they think, and apply and repeat these to various texts, rather than learning and teaching ever new things from the texts themselves. It is well known that such men are easily exhausted. (3) The text should not be read merely for form's sake, while nothing at all is explained from it; for such men wander away from the text and run off from it, to some other subject, and even in every direction. This fault shows great lack of judgement and of learning.

units.la: VI. Textu jam electo, lustra primum, quid eo potissimum contineatur, meditatione soluta, sed attenta; atque, hinc ad preces: nempe hoc precare, ut Deus habituro, illa de re, ex verbo suo concionem, spiritus ejusdem gratia efficacissime adesse velit, & animum illustrare, sanctificare; movere etiam, quo digne & ad maximam Ecclesiæ ædificationem agas. Psalm 130: 18.
units.tr: VI. Once the text has been chosen, first survey what it chiefly contains, with a free but attentive meditation; and then turn to prayer, namely, pray that God, who is about to have the sermon on that matter from his word, may most effectively be present with the grace of his Spirit, and may enlighten and sanctify the mind, and also move it, so that you may act worthily and to the greatest edification of the Church (Ps. 130:18).

units.la: VII. Inde ad textum reverteris, quem jam iterum, sed meditatione presfiori, & ad methodum volvis, examinas, confers, atque ad singula attendis, præcipue ordinem.
units.tr: VII. Then return to the text, which you now turn over again, but with a more careful meditation and with method in view. Examine it, compare it, and attend to each part, especially the order.

units.la: VIII. Qui hic est, ut I. Videas textus tui cohærentiam, & connexionem cum antecedentibus, ac consequentibus: & II. Partes textus in se.
units.tr: VIII. This is done so that (1) you may see the coherence of your text and its connection with what precedes and what follows; and (2) the parts of the text in themselves.

units.la: IX. In cohærentia textus, nisi vel principium libri, seu σύνταξις sit, (ubi ex generali capitis vel libri divisione quoque commode exordiris,) vel textus abruptus, quales in Proverbiis & Ecclesiastæ plurimi, antecedentia deducunt animum in cognitionem sequentium, & vel convenit textus cum antecedentibus, vel ab iis differt: si convenit, vel in re, quæ tractatur: vel solum in contextu sermonis, & oratione: quomodo, quando una oratione, plura & varia proponuntur.
units.tr: IX. As to the coherence of the text: unless it is the beginning of a book or its σύνταξις (where one may conveniently begin from the general division of the chapter or book), or the text is abrupt, as are many in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, the preceding words lead the mind to a knowledge of what follows. The text either agrees with what precedes or differs from it. If it agrees, this may be either in the matter that is treated, or only in the context of the discourse and its wording, as when several and various things are set forth in one discourse.

units.la: X. Et hinc exordium (aliquando etiam hic, nisi quod quoque post reliqua, infine sæpe componi illud solet, & potest, quemadmodum præfationes ad libros, verum quandocunq; occurrit, notandum, locus tamen formado exordio proprior est vel hic, vel in fine (hinc, dico, exordium construitur, videlicet, omne exordium ad concionem se habet ut vestibulum ad atrium, ducitque ad rem; ideo propriissime sumitur ab eo; quod rem tractandam præcedit: idque alterutro modo quum solum fiat, vel præcedit in natura rei, vel contextu orationis, ex duobus etiam hisce capitibus petuntur optima exordia, quæ (quod in exordio ut diximus totum spectatur) ad rem commodissime & certissime ducunt: vel ex eo, quod rem tractandam præcedit, vel ex eo quod textum, ex quo hanc rem tractabis, in ordine contextus præcedit. Illud exordium Theologia indicat, hoc Logica; illud à re, hoc ab analysi petitur; vel illud ex analysi rei, hoc ex analysi sermonis. V. g. textus sit Luc. 1, 45. Et beata, quæ credidit; quia perficientur ea, quæ dicta ei sunt à Domino. Exordium concionis petam, vel ex eo, quod fidem proximè præcedit, quale ex objecto fidei (etiam ex aliis, quæ fidem antecedunt, peti potest, sed vide ut proprius antecedat) quod Deus homini plura offert, ac proponit, quæ ab eo credi vult, sive dicta simpliciter, sive quoque promissa: vel ex eo, quod in contextu orationis, & historiæ analysi, præcedit, ut ex verf. 39. sc. quomodo post acceptum de virginali conceptione nuncium, Maria ad domum Zachariæ profecta sit; Elizabetham salutatura, à quâ visa & audita, quid huic, quid infanti quoque in utero, contigerit, narratur, v, 41. sc. τὸ βρέφος ἐσκίρτησε, & mater spiritu f. repleta est. Unde tali acclamatione & concione Mariam excepit, quæ sequitur à verf. 42. I. Ad Mariam, de illâ, illiusque sobole, verf. 42. II. Desé, quam ipsa demiratur, & deprædicat ob hanc ei à Matre Domini sui factam visitationem, narrans insuper, quid sibi, ac infanti ad primam salutationem contigerit, verf. 42, 44. III. Ad Mariam sermonem iterum convertens, de illâ hoc dicit, quod textu nostro continetur.
units.tr: X. From this the introduction is also drawn (sometimes it is composed here, but often also after the rest, at the end, as prefaces to books are; whenever it occurs, this should be noted). Still, the proper place for forming the introduction is either here or at the end. From here, I say, the introduction is constructed, for every introduction stands to the sermon as a vestibule to a courtyard, and leads into the matter; therefore it is most properly taken from what precedes the matter to be treated. And since this is done in one of two ways, either by what precedes the matter in the nature of the thing, or by what precedes the text in the context of the discourse, the best introductions are drawn from these two heads. Introductions drawn from what precedes the matter to be treated, or from what precedes in the order of context the text from which you will treat this matter, lead most conveniently and most surely (since in an introduction, as we said, everything is aimed at the matter) to the subject. The former is taken from theology, the latter from logic; the former from the matter, the latter from the analysis of the discourse. For example, let the text be Luke 1:45: And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord. I may take the introduction for the sermon either from what immediately precedes faith, such as the object of faith (it may also be taken from other things that precede faith, but see that it precedes more closely), namely that God offers and sets before man many things that he wishes to be believed, whether simply stated or also promised; or from what precedes in the analysis of the context and history, as in verse 39, namely how, after receiving the message about the virginal conception, Mary went to the house of Zacharias to greet Elizabeth; when she was seen and heard by her, it is told what happened to her, and to the infant in her womb (v. 41), namely that the babe leaped [τὸ βρέφος ἐσκίρτησε], and the mother was filled with the Holy Spirit. Hence Elizabeth received Mary with such an acclamation and speech, which follows from verse 42. (1) To Mary, concerning her and her offspring (v. 42). (2) Concerning her faith, which she admires and extols because of this visitation paid to her by the mother of her Lord, relating moreover what happened to herself and to the infant at the first greeting (vv. 42, 44). (3) Turning her speech again to Mary, she says of her what is contained in our text.

units.la: XI. Non nego, etiam aliunde, præterquam è duobus hisce capitibus exordia peti, nempe, vel à re ipsâ tractandâ, & sic Patres plerumque suas conciones vel homilias incipiunt, quale tamen, potius propositio est, quam exordium; Chryfostomus celebrem illam concionem sic exorditur. Herodias denuò insanire, denuo commoveri, denuò saltare pergit, denuò caput Iohannis in disco accipere quaerit. Et illam etiam, cum de expulsione ipsius ageretur: Multi quidem fluctus, & undæ immanes, sed submergi non vereor: quia supra petram sto. Insaniat licet mare, petram non poterit commovere: insurgant quantumlibet fluctus, navis Iesu obrui non poterit. Sed quid putant? ne mortem verear, cui vivere Christus est, & mori lucrum. Ne exilium pertimescam, qui noverim Domini esse terram & plenitudinem ejus: sed bonorum proscriptionem metuam qui sciam, quod nihil intulerim in hunc mundum, sed neque auferre quid possim. Quidquid terroris habet mundus, contemno; quicquid delectabile habet, video. Divitias non cupio, pauperatem non horresco, mortem non timeo. Elegantissima concio, quæ ita incipit, in cujus initio describendo ut me vix temperare potuum, ita à nemine non legi eam oportere, judico. Vel à circumstantia ad rem ipsam, quæ tractabitur, non necessario faciente, ut temporis, loci, personarum, Actor. 24, 10. vel rei antea tractatæ, alteriusve alicujus introductione, quæ tunc adferre non omninò extra oleas videatur, exordia petuntur quoque, A circumstantia personarum, sive ejus, qui concionatur, Ambros. serm. 42. frequenter admonui vos, fratres, ut dum licet, dum tempus in spacio est, saluti vestræ omnibus modis consuleretis, & in hac vitâ brevi, vitam vobis prævideritis æternam. Gregorius Homil. xxii. in Evang. fractus longâ molestiâ stomachus, diu me charitati vestræ de lectionis Evangelicæ expositione loqui prohibuit. A personis Auditorum. Chrysosth. Homil. V. T. de fide Annæ; sic exorditur; equidem arbitror multos ex his, qui heri nos destituerant, & ad iniquitatis spectacula discesserant, hodie præsentes esse: optarem autem ipsos, qui sint, palam nosse, ut eos à sacris vestibulis arceam, non ut perpetuo fori maneant, sed ut correcti denuo redeant. A persona utriusque; Chrysosth. in Psalm. 41. Vos quidem nos nuper admirabamini, quando verba fecimus de Melchisedech, propter eorum, quæ dicta sunt prolixitatem, ego autem vos admirabar propter vestram in audiendo attentionem & sapientiam, & quod cum prolixior se obtulisset oratio, nos ad finem usque consequuti estis. Augustinus, de verbis Dom. serm. III. cum nobis pro officio competat dicere, vobis autem conveniat pro devotione audire. Videtis quoque a transitione rei, quam ante tractavimus, exordium fieri; Sic plerumque Ambrosii sermones a repetitione ejus, quod superiore Dominica dixisset, incipiunt. Superiore Dominica, vel etiam, hesterno die. vel, sicut ante dies prosecuti sumus. Bernardus serm. VI. in Cant. Ut precedenti sequens sermo cohæreat, & serm. LXXI. finis precedentis sermonis, principium hujus. Adde exordium Homil. Chrysosth. de Dav. & Saule. Sed accurate tamen agendo, vel illa duo exordii capita sola, vel saltem præcipua & optima sunt; sic Apostolus ad Romanos concionaturus de justificatione, exordiatur a statu peccati omnibus communi, & antecedente. Adde Iof. 24, 2. Iudic. 2, 1. A loco textui parallelo incipere, non adeo reprehendo: sed judicetur, annon hoc spectet potius ad textus tractationem, quam ut fit exordium ad textum tractandum? V.g. textus dati exordium fit ex loco parallelo, vel Psalm. 2, 12. vel Ierem. 17, 7. aut Luc. XI, 28. quæro de exacto judicio, annon potius illi textus & proprie spectent ad textus mei explicationem & tractationem, quam tractationis introductionem? atque item dico quando vel, à simili, vel à contrario petitur: nam iterum, vel est contrarium (& sic quoq; simile) vel rei, vel ejus, quod rem etiam antecedit: si hoc, exordium fit, quale volumus, ut si de gratia actutus, vel redemtione, à miseria incipias: vel ab infidelitate, quan-do dode fide : fi illud, redit quod dixi. Quintilianus Inftit. Orat. lib. 4. cap. 3. At nunc, omne quod coeperint, proœmium putant, & ut quicque succurrerit, utique si aliqua sententia blandiatur, exordium.
units.tr: XI. I do not deny that openings may also be drawn from elsewhere than these two heads, namely from the subject itself to be treated. The Fathers often begin their sermons or homilies in this way, though such an opening is really more a statement of the proposition than an introduction. Chrysostom begins his famous sermon thus: Herodias goes on raving again, is stirred up again, goes on dancing again, and again seeks to receive the head of John on a dish. He also begins another, when he was speaking of her expulsion, thus: There are many waves and huge billows, but I do not fear being submerged, because I stand upon a rock. Let the sea rage as it will, it cannot move the rock. Let the waves rise as high as they like, the ship of Jesus cannot be overwhelmed. But what do they think? I do not fear death, for to me to live is Christ and to die is gain. I do not dread exile, since I know that the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof; but I fear the confiscation of goods, since I know that I brought nothing into this world and can take nothing out. Whatever terror the world has, I despise; whatever pleasure it has, I see through. I do not desire riches, I do not shudder at poverty, I do not fear death. This is a most elegant sermon, which begins in this way; and while I could scarcely restrain myself from describing its beginning, I judge that it ought to be read by everyone. Openings are also taken from a circumstance that is not necessarily connected with the subject to be treated, such as the time, place or persons (Acts 24:10), or from the introduction of something treated earlier or of some other matter, which at that point may not seem entirely out of place. Openings are taken as well: from a circumstance of the persons, or of the one who preaches. Ambrose, Sermon 42: I have often admonished you, brothers, that while it is permitted, while there is time, you should look to your salvation by every means, and in this brief life provide for yourselves eternal life. Gregory, Homily 22 on the Gospels: My stomach, worn out by a long illness, has for a long time prevented me from speaking to your charity about the exposition of the Gospel reading. From the persons of the hearers: Chrysostom, Homily 5 on the Text concerning the faith of Anna, begins thus: I think that many of those who yesterday deserted us and went away to the spectacles of iniquity are present today. I would wish, however, to know openly who they are, so that I may keep them from the sacred porches, not so that they may remain outside forever, but so that they may return again once corrected. From the person of both: Chrysostom on Psalm 41: You lately marvelled at us when we spoke about Melchizedek, on account of the length of what was said; but I marvelled at you on account of your attentiveness and wisdom in listening, and because, although the discourse had become rather long, you followed us right to the end. Augustine, On the Words of the Lord, Sermon 3: Since it befits me by my office to speak, but it befits you by your devotion to listen. You also see that openings are made from the transition from a matter we treated before. Thus Ambrose's sermons often begin from a repetition of what he had said on the previous Lord's day: on the previous Lord's day, or even yesterday, or as we pursued in the days before. Bernard, Sermon 6 on the Song of Songs: So that the following sermon may cohere with the preceding one; and Sermon 71: the end of the preceding sermon is the beginning of this one. Add the opening of Chrysostom's homily on David and Saul. Yet, to act carefully, these two heads of an opening alone, or at least the chief and best, are the ones to use. Thus the Apostle, about to preach on justification in his letter to the Romans, begins from the state of sin common to all and preceding it. Add Joshua 24:2 and Judges 2:1. I do not greatly object to beginning from a parallel passage of Scripture, but let it be judged whether this pertains rather to the treatment of the text than to the introduction of the text for treatment. For example, if the opening of a given text is made from a parallel passage such as Psalm 2:12, or Jeremiah 17:7, or Luke 11:28, I ask, on careful judgement, whether those passages do not rather properly belong to the explanation and treatment of my text than to the introduction of the treatment. And I say the same when an opening is taken from a likeness or from a contrary: for again, either the contrary (and likewise the like) belongs to the matter or to something that also precedes the matter. If it is the latter, an opening arises of the kind we want, as when you begin at once from grace or redemption, from misery; or from unbelief, when you speak about faith. If it is the former, what I have said returns. Quintilian, Institutes of Oratory, book 4, chapter 3: But now they think that everything they begin is a prologue, and whatever occurs to them, especially if some sentence is pleasing, is an exordium.

units.la: XII. De hisce exordiis illa observanda.
units.tr: XII. Concerning these openings, the following points are to be observed.

units.la: I. Exordium, quod petitur ex antecedentia rei, præstare illi, quod ex sola oratio nis sumitur analysi; illud magis Theologicum, hoc Logicum, illud afficit magis, excitatque. Quare vitium est, semper, vel ut plurimum ex Logica analysi exordiri: facit enim vilescere exordia, & animos, qui in initiis erigi volunt & accendi, deprimit. Nisi quod tum hujusmodi exordia probanda, quando textus ita antecedentibus implicatus est, ut sine illis omnino non, vel etiam quid eum in re præcedat, intelligi non possit, quod sæpe etiam conjunctionis aliquâ, & relationis particulâ, in textu indicari solet; tum quoque Tyronibus, & primùm incipientibus, hæc exordia non concedenda solum, sed consulenda quoque sunt. II. Optimum est exordium, quod incipit ab antecedentia rei, & definit in analysin orationis: adeo hæc non omitti debet, sed statim subsequi. III. In antecedentia rei caute videndum, ne à quolibet rem quomodocunque antecedente inchoemus, sed quod proximè, & quo propius eo melius, ut à genere, quando de specie tibi agendum erit.
units.tr: I. An opening taken from the preceding context of the matter has an advantage over one drawn only from the analysis of the text: the former is more theological, the latter more logical; the former moves and kindles the hearer more. Hence it is a fault always, or for the most part, to begin from a logical analysis, for it makes openings cheap and depresses minds that want to be raised and inflamed at the beginning. Yet such openings are to be approved when the text is so entangled with what precedes that it cannot be understood at all without them, or without knowing what precedes it in the matter; this is often indicated in the text by a conjunction or a relative particle. And such openings are not merely to be allowed but even recommended to novices and to those just beginning. II. The best opening is one that begins from the preceding context of the matter and ends in the analysis of the text; so this analysis ought not to be omitted but should follow at once. III. In taking the preceding context of the matter, one must take care not to begin from whatever happens to precede the matter in any way, but from what immediately precedes it, and the nearer the better, as from the genus when you are to deal with a species.

units.la: XIII. Atq; hæc de exordio, quando illud necesse; non semper enim adhiberi, vel quoque adhibendum esse, constat, nimirum, quando vel brevis est habenda concio, vel materiæ copiâ prægravamur. Moses sine præfatione historiam creationis exponere aggreditur; Lucas autem Euangelium, non nisi præmisso exordio. Reliquas exordii (quas Rhetores dant) leges, addere supervacaneum, legi illæ suis locis apud eos possunt, immò quando observatur quod diximus, non facile peccari potest; si enim à proximo antecedente illud petatur, nec commune, nec vulgare, nec separatum erit, quæ exordii vitia ponit Cicero de Inventione lib. I. & post eum Quintilianus Institut. lib. IV. cap. I. Vitandam esse prolixitatem satis omnes norunt.
units.tr: XIII. So much for the opening, which is needed only when necessary; for it is evident that it is not always to be used, nor to be used in every case, namely when the sermon is to be brief or we are oppressed by an abundance of material. Moses sets out to describe the history of creation without any preface, whereas Luke begins his Gospel only after a prefatory introduction. To add the remaining rules of the opening that the rhetoricians give is superfluous; they can be read in their proper places among them. Indeed, when what we have said is observed, one can hardly go wrong: for if the opening is taken from the immediately preceding context, it will be neither common, nor commonplace, nor detached, which are the faults of an opening that Cicero lists in De Inventione, book I, and after him Quintilian in Institutio, book IV, chapter 1. That prolixity is to be avoided, everyone well knows.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: I. ADl exordium statim fit propositio, tum textus, tum rei in textu contentæ, & tractandæ, & judicatur simul, quale thema sit, quod tractabimus, (simplicis ad textum vix locus est, nisi forte in concionibus Catecheticis, ut ibi thema simplex proponatur, v.g. de Deo, scriptura &c.) an sit thema dogmaticum an historicum (ad historiam hic quoque Prophetias, & Parabolas refero) an utrumque, qualia per historiam alicujus, nominatim Christi, plurima. Basilius serm. 3. in divit. avar. quid igitur est, quod sermo vult nostER ostendere? suspensas enim tenet animas jamdudum audire cupientes, quo se vertat, dum, quod exspectatur, publicare cunctatur. Matth. 4, 17. & 23, 25. &c. Videndum hic, ut propositio sit. I. perspicua. II. brevis: Luc. 7, 40. Simon, habeo, quod tibi dicam. Gen 49, 1, 2. Psalm. 34, 12. Prov. 1: 1, 2, 3. Recte Quintilianus Orat. Instit. lib. 6. cap. ult. divisa & simplex propositio, quoties utiliter adhiberi potest, primum esse debet aperta atque, lucida (nam quid sit turpius, quam id esse obscurum ipsum, quod in hunc solum abhibetur usum, ne sint cætera obscura) tum brevis, nec ullo supervacuo onerata verbo.
units.tr: I. At the beginning of the exordium comes the proposition, both of the text and of the matter contained in and to be treated from the text. At the same time it is judged what kind of theme it is that we shall treat. (A simple theme has hardly any place in relation to the text, except perhaps in catechetical sermons, where a simple theme is proposed, for example concerning God, Scripture, etc.) Whether it is a doctrinal or a historical theme (here I also refer prophecies and parables to history), or both, as with the many themes drawn from the history of some person, especially Christ. Basil, Sermon 3 on the divisions of avarice: What then is it that the discourse wishes to show us? For it holds souls that have long wished to hear in suspense, as to where it will turn, while it delays to make public what is awaited. Matt. 4:17 and 23:25, etc. Here one must see that the proposition is (1) clear, (2) brief: Luke 7:40, Simon, I have something to tell you. Gen. 49:1, 2; Ps. 34:12; Prov. 1:1, 2, 3. Quintilian rightly says in the Institutes of Oratory, book 6, last chapter: A divided and simple proposition, whenever it can be usefully employed, ought first to be open and clear (for what is more shameful than for that very thing which is used only for this purpose to be obscure, so that the rest is not obscure), then brief, and burdened with no superfluous word.

units.la: II. Propositionem excipit textus ipsius Analysis. Bernard. serm. xxxix. in Cantic. sed oportet consequentiam sicut solemus, signare verbis, & sequentia prioribus copulare, & ita demum elicere suave quippiam, am, si possumus, quod prosit moribus instruendis. Analysis textum perscrutatur, & examinat methodicè, quid primo, quid secundo, & quo quodlibet ordine dicatur. Videt subjectum & prædicatum, antecedens & consequens: causam & effectum, argumentum & ejus probationem, &c. sed hic dum generaliter, & summa textus capita secat, & dislocata introspicit, necdum particulatim. Diligenter hoc præstitit in f. codices, at potissimum in N. Test. Analysi Piscator. Valde ea necessaria sunt, & conducunt ad animum Auditorum in textum intromittendum. אל בית היין Cantic. II. 4.
units.tr: II. The proposition is followed by the analysis of the text itself. Bernard, Sermon 39 on the Song of Songs: but it is necessary, as we are accustomed, to mark the sequence with words, and to join what follows to what precedes, and so at last to draw out something sweet, if we can, that profits in forming morals. Analysis examines the text in a methodical way and considers what is said first, what second, and in what order each thing is said. It sees the subject and the predicate, antecedent and consequent, cause and effect, argument and its proof, and so on. But here it cuts the chief parts of the text only in general and in summary, and looks into them as dislocated, not yet part by part. The Fathers did this carefully in the codices, but especially in the New Testament; among the analyses, that of Piscator is very useful. These are very necessary and contribute to bringing the hearers into the text. Hebrew: he brought me to the house of wine [אל בית היין] (Song 2:4).

units.la: III. Ex Analysi exsurgit textus partitio, immo jam analysis est partitio in actu exercito, liceat sic dicere, & hæc in actu signato: ibi fit anatome textus, & dislocatio, hic in capita distributio, & enumeratio, hæc illam perficit, & ut illa ad hanc tendit, ita hæc in concionem, & tractationem ex textu fœlicius aggrediundam ac perficiendam. Partitionem etiam videmus à Spiritu sancto nonnunquam observari, Genes. 2. 10. Et inde se dividit, fiturque in quatuor capita. Exod. 21, 11. Jerem. 2, 13. Duo mala fecit populus 1 Reg. 13, 11. Jesa. 47, 9. Jesa. 50, 1, 19. Matth. 13, 4. Joan. 16, 8. 2 Thess. 2, 2. Basilius in Psalm. 28. Vox Domini super aquas. Quæ vox? Super quas aquas? Homil. de gratiis Deo agendis: gaudete semper, inquit, sine intermissione orate, in omnibus gratias agite. Quid sibi velit hoc, gaudete, & quæ ex eo utilitas, & quomodo sine intermissione orare possimus, quomodo in omnibus Deo gratias agere oporteat, pro viribus paulo post declarabimus. Ita Chrysostomus in Rom. 1, 23. primum crimen, quod Deum non invenerunt, secundum, quod causas magnas & apertas habuerunt, tertium, quod se sapientes dicerent, quartum, quod non solum non invenerunt, sed quod venerationem illam in Dæmonas, in saxa ac ligna, dedeflexerunt. Leges partitionis observandæ, hæ sunt. I. Ne hic instituatur omnis textus analysis; sed tantum generalis in præcipua capita: particularior enim & ultima reservatur in explicationem singularum partium. Hic, ut bene Cicero, genera ipsa rerum ponuntur, neque permixte cum partibus implicantur. De invent. lib. I. v. g. Luc. 1,45. partes generales textus duæ sunt..1. beata illa, quæ credidit. II. quia erit consummatio &c. Prioris subdivisio est necessaria in subjectum, illa quæ credidit, & prædicatum, beata est; at cave dixeris, ideo textus hujus tres esse partes, nam hæc est subdivisio, & partitio partis, non textus generalis: si enim subdivisiones hic facerent æque partes cum generalibus, utique innumeras illas semper haberes. Ergo nec illa subdivisio hic instituenda, sed ad singulas demum partes, ubi illæ explicantur. II. Non debet, neque potest præscribi certa numero partitio, ut bimembris illa sit, vel trimembris: neque enim partitiones, ut Methodi (in quo tamen sæpe peccatur) rebus accommodandæ, vel adferendæ sunt: sed ex rebus ipsis promendæ & sequendæ, v. g. si tibi explicandum caput Genesis, non potes non istius facere sex partes, pro sex creationis diebus: si vero versus ejus primus, partes debent esse tres. Quis creavit, quid, quando, In principio, creavit Deus, cælum & terram. Creavit Deus, ibi iterum subdivides, in subjectum & prædicatum ut: in objecto quoque singulas illas partes distingues, terram & aquam. Vides partes dari à textu, non illi addi: deprehendi ibi, non introduci: quare non trahendus est textus ad aliquam Partitionem, sed ducendus, immo quam ipse ostendet, & offert, neque alia, arripienda est. III. Ne religio nobis sit ordinem textus invertere, & alio tractare, quam quo verba leguntur, id est, ordinem rei commutemus cum verbis, nam hæc illi inserviunt, & concio instituìstituitur tota in tractationem rei, propter quam textus est. v. g. Gal. 3,13. Christus nos redemit ex maledictione legis &c. Hoc primum quidem in textu legitur, at non est tamen prima textus pars, neque etiam secunda; sed prima est, Christus factus pro nobis maledictio. Secunda, quæ probatio illius est, scriptum enim est, maledictus omnis, qui pependit ex ligno. Tertia jam pars venit ex fructu illius, Christus redemit nos ex maledictione legis. Nempe præstat ordinem genesis sequi ad textum, quam contra ductum & naturam rei: ordinem verborum, 1. facit ad commodiorem, certiorem, & maxime genuinam rei intelligentiam. 2. tractationem, aliter enim non evitaveris obscuritatem, & tautologiam. IV. Hinc jam quoque illud sequitur, non semper easdem & totidem esse partes concionis ac textus, quia partes textus constituuntur juxta ejus primam & generalem analysin, concionis vero partes, juxta rei genesin. v.c. Rom. 3,28. Concludimus ergo, fide justificari hominem, sine operibus legis. Rationem conclusionis omitto, cæterum duas hic partes cernis. I. hominem justificari fide. II. sine operibus legis. Hæc textus sunt; at concionis commodius tres fecero I. Quid sit hominem justificari? quod tanti momenti in se est, & ad reliqua intelligenda tam necessarium est, ut distinctam partem jure faciat. II. Quomodo per fidem dicamur justificari? III. Quomodo opera omninò rejiciantur? sine operibus legis. Ita quidem est, ex textu hæc, & omnes partes petuntur etiam, at non ex prima textus Analysi, verùm rei ipsius natura, & genesi.
units.tr: III. From the analysis the division of the text arises. Indeed the analysis is already a division in active exercise, if one may so speak, and this is the division in marked form. There the text is anatomised and dislocated; here it is distributed and enumerated into heads. The latter completes the former, and as the former tends toward the latter, so the latter leads on toward the sermon and the treatment to be drawn from the text more happily and to be carried through. We see that the Holy Spirit sometimes observes division as well: Gen. 2:10, And from there it divides and becomes four heads. Ex. 21:11; Jer. 2:13, My people has committed two evils; 1 Kings 13:11; Isa. 47:9; Isa. 50:1, 19; Matt. 13:4; John 16:8; 2 Thess. 2:2. Basil on Psalm 28, The voice of the Lord is upon the waters. What voice? Upon what waters? In the homily on giving thanks to God: Rejoice always, he says, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. What this, rejoice, means, and what use comes from it, and how we can pray without ceasing, how it is fitting to give thanks to God in all things, we shall declare shortly, as far as our strength allows. So Chrysostom on Rom. 1:23: The first sin is that they did not find God; the second, that they had great and clear causes; the third, that they called themselves wise; the fourth, that they not only did not find him, but turned that reverence to demons, to stones and to wood. The rules of division to be observed are these. (1) Here the whole analysis of the text should not be instituted, but only a general one into the chief heads; for the more particular and final analysis is reserved for the explanation of the individual parts. Here, as Cicero well says, the kinds of things themselves are set down, and are not mixed up and entangled with the parts (De inventione, book 1). For example, Luke 1:45, the general parts of the text are two: (1) blessed is she who believed; (2) because there will be a fulfilment, etc. The subdivision of the first is necessary into subject, she who believed, and predicate, is blessed; but beware of saying that therefore this text has three parts, for this is a subdivision and division of a part, not the general text. For if subdivisions here made parts equal to the general ones, you would always have countless parts. Therefore that subdivision is not to be instituted here, but only at the individual parts, where those are explained. (2) A division of a certain number cannot and should not be prescribed, so that it is two-membered or three-membered. Divisions should not be fitted or brought to the matters, as in method (though this is often done wrongly), but drawn out of and followed from the matters themselves. For example, if you have to explain the chapter of Genesis, you cannot but make six parts, for the six days of creation; but if its first verse, the parts must be three: who created, what, when: In the beginning God created heaven and earth. In God created you will again subdivide into subject and predicate; in the object too you will distinguish those single parts, earth and water. You see that the parts are given by the text, not added to it; they are discovered there, not introduced. Therefore the text must not be dragged into some division, but led by the division it itself shows and offers, and no other should be seized upon. (3) Let us not scruple to invert the order of the text and treat it otherwise than the words are read, that is, to change the order of the matter from the words, for the words serve it, and the sermon is set up wholly for the treatment of the matter for which the text exists. For example, Gal. 3:13, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, etc. This is indeed read first in the text, but it is not the first part of the text, nor the second; the first is Christ made a curse for us; the second, which is its proof, for it is written, cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree; the third part now comes from its fruit: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Indeed it is better to follow the order of the matter in relation to the text than to go against the nature and course of the matter, the order of the words: first, it serves a more convenient, more certain and above all more genuine understanding of the matter; second, the treatment, for otherwise you will not avoid obscurity and tautology. (4) From this it also follows that the parts of the sermon and of the text are not always the same and equal in number, because the parts of the text are constituted according to its first and general analysis, but the parts of the sermon according to the genesis of the matter. For example, Rom. 3:28: We conclude, therefore, that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law. I omit the reasoning of the conclusion, but you see two parts here: (1) a man is justified by faith; (2) without the works of the law. These are the parts of the text; but for the sermon it is more convenient to make three: (1) What it is for a man to be justified? This is of such weight in itself, and so necessary for understanding the rest, that it rightly makes a distinct part. (2) How are we said to be justified by faith? (3) How are works wholly rejected? without the works of the law. So indeed it is: these and all the parts are sought from the text, but not from the first analysis of the text; rather from the nature and genesis of the matter itself.

units.la: IV. Ad propositionem atque partitionem, nonnunquam attentio ab Auditoribus, & benedictio à Deo peti iterum solet: sic & Bernard. serm. in Cantic. 67. Adsit ipse, ut digne ad gloriam ipsius, & nostram ipsorum salutem, sponsæ ejus possimus invcstigare
units.tr: IV. Before the proposition and division, it is customary to ask the hearers for attention and to ask God for a blessing, as Bernard does in his sermon on the Song of Songs 67: May he himself be present, so that we may worthily investigate his bride, to his glory and our own salvation.

units.la: B . fermisermones. Verùm nisi peculiare aliquid dicturi simus, ad quod specialiter velimus attentionem; quo loco illud serio inculcandum: qui aures habet ad audiendum, audiat. Quomodo & Gen. 49, 2. Deut. 32, 1, 2. Marc. 7, 14. audite me omnes, & intelligite. Actor. 2, 14. Basilius in Psalm. 33. Timor verò salutaris, qualis exsistat, si cupis audire, attende. Nisi illud sit, dico, non video eam illius hoc loco esse necessitatem, ut repeti iterum debeat. Ante concionem illud fieri ut debet, ita quoque solet. Prudentius sic Psychomachiam incipit.
units.tr: Yet unless we are about to say something special, to which we wish to draw particular attention, there is no need to urge it earnestly here: he who has ears to hear, let him hear. So also Gen. 49:2; Deut. 32:1, 2; Mark 7:14: hear me, all of you, and understand. Acts 2:14. Basil, on Psalm 33: But as for the fear that saves, what it is, if you wish to hear, pay attention. Unless that is the case, I say, I do not see the need for it to be repeated here. Before a sermon this is done as it should be, and it is usually done. Prudentius begins his Psychomachia thus, Sermones (speeches) of this kind:

units.la: Christe graves hominum semper miserate labores, &c. Dissere Rex noster, quo milite pellere culpas Mens armata queat,
units.tr: Christ, who always pitied the heavy labours of men, &c. Tell us, our King, with what soldier the armed mind may be able to drive out sins,

units.la: Plinius illum Panegyricum: Bene ac sapienter P.C. majores instituerunt, ut rerum agendarum, ita dicendi initium à precationib. caperetur.
units.tr: Pliny begins his Panegyricus: Well and wisely, conscript fathers, did our ancestors ordain that, just as actions begin, so speech should begin with prayers.

units.la: V. Ordo postulat, ut ad distinctam partium singularum tractationem concio pergat; quæ tractatio consistit. I. In partium singularum explicatione. II. Documentis, III. Vsibus, quæ documenta ex textu intime applicant, atque urgent, elaborandis.
units.tr: V. The order requires that the sermon proceed to a distinct treatment of each part; this treatment consists of: I. the explication of each part; II. the working out of doctrines; III. the uses, which press and apply the doctrines closely from the text.

units.la: VI. Explicatio textus ante & ad documenta, tria complectitur. I. Præfiorem partis, ac ultimam analysin, & subdivisionem. II. Expositionem, tam verborum, quam rei necessariam. III. Paraphrasin.
units.tr: VI. The explication of the text, before and in preparation for the doctrines, comprises three things: I. the preface of the part and its final analysis and subdivision; II. the exposition, both of words and of the matter, as far as necessary; III. the paraphrase.

units.la: VII. Primo loco venit strictissima analysis & subdivisio: qualis autem inter utramque hic concipiatur distinctio, modò dictum est: fermè quomodo Marc. 6, 38. quot panes habetis? ite, videte: illud analysis agit. Et cognoscentes, dicunt: quinque, & duos pisces. Hæc partitio, sive divisio. v. g. Rom. 8, 1. Duæ ibi partes, priorem hic iterum ἀναλύω in subjectum, iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, & prædicatum, nulla nunc est condemnatio. In subjecto, sunt in Christo, non in se, at extra se, & in quo; Christo. Hic iterum, Christo, tum Jesu. Si subdivisionem instituères, bipartitio foret. I. Qui non in se, sed extra se, in alio. II. In Christo Jesu, Hujusque iterum I. Christo. II. Jesu. In praedicato, condemnatio, nulla condemnatio, nunc. Bipartitio. I. nulla condemnatio. II. etiam nunc. Hic illa observes. Non semper instituendam, ultimam & omnem textus analysin, nempe quando textus prolixior est, & non omnis tractabitur: analysis enim tractationi inservit, & non ulterius necessaria est, quam haec requirit. II. At quando integrum textum, vel quodcunque ex textu integre tractabis, ejus immo omnem, & ultimam debes facere analysin: nam haec ad tractationem ex textu tam necessario se habet & praerequiritur, ac apertio Januae ad ingressum & egressum, quod hic est, textum analyticè explicare, & per genesin documenta inde elicere, atque tractare. Adeo ad omnia pulsandum hic, videndumque quid contineatur, uti aromata frangi ac fricari solent, quo copiosus ille & divinus sacrorum verborum fragror undique observetur: & sane tali exquisita & severissima analysi semper alia & alia offendi nobis, ac deprehendi, summa cum divinitatis in sacris admiratione, nemo negarit, nisi qui neglexerit. III. Non putandum, singula analysis membra, facere totidem partes: alioqui quot in textu voces, totidem & partes forent. Singula observanda & discutienda sunt: non in partes erigenda: partitio generaliora solum sectatur capita, vel membrorum classes. IV. g. in hoc praedicato nulla nunc condemnatio, non satis bene tres partes constituas, ubi tria tamen considero, condemnatio, nulla condemnatio, quod nulla nunc fit condemnatio: & similiter in subjecto. V. Commodissime, & ad explorandam hauriendamque textus integram cognitionem fit, si singula analyseos membra per quaestiones eruantur & proponantur sequuturæ statim explicationi, sub interrogatione, quomodo quæstiones proponi solent, videlicet, quid condemnatio? Quid nulla condemnatio? quid, nulla nunc condemnatio, & de subjecto hujus partis quid, esse in Christo? quid, & quorsum additur, Christo Jesu? hoc enim modo. 1. Animus in summam attentionem magis accenditur: Hoc enim omnis interrogatio præ simplici oratione habet, ut magis animum feriat, quomodo Rom. 8, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35. interrogationes efficacissimæ quis contra nos? quis accusabit? &c. 2. omnia quæ in textu diligentius & penitius evisceran-tur, ac perscrutantur, nihilque facile omittitur. Ut 1 Joan. 3, 12. Non sicuti Cain ex malo erat, & maactavit fratrem suum. Et quamobrem maactavit eum? 3, Veritas omnium certius eruitur, deprehenditur, tenetur. Hos. 9, 14. Da eis Jehova, quid daturus es? da eis vulvam aborientem, & ubera flaccida. Ps. 15, 1. Jes. 33, 15. Mich. 6, 6, 7.
units.tr: VII. First comes the strictest analysis and subdivision. How the distinction between the two is understood here has just been said. It is roughly as in Mark 6:38: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. That is the work of analysis; and when they knew, they said: five, and two fish. This is partition or division. For example, Rom. 8:1 has two parts. The first of these is again analysed [ἀναλύω] into a subject, those who are in Christ Jesus, and a predicate, there is now no condemnation. In the subject, are in Christ: not in themselves, but outside themselves, and in whom; Christ. Here again, Christ, then Jesus. If you were to make a subdivision, it would be a bipartition: I. those who are not in themselves but outside themselves, in another; II. in Christ Jesus, and this again into I. Christ and II. Jesus. In the predicate: condemnation, no condemnation, now. A bipartition: I. no condemnation; II. even now. Here you should observe these things. The full and final analysis of the whole text need not always be made, namely when the text is lengthy and not all of it will be treated; for analysis serves the treatment and is no more necessary than the treatment requires. II. But when you treat the whole text, or any part of it in full, you ought to make its complete and final analysis; for this stands in the same necessary relation to the treatment of the text, and is presupposed by it, as the opening of a door is to entering and leaving. To analyse the text in this way, knocking at everything here and seeing what it contains, is like crushing and rubbing spices, so that the rich and divine fragrance of the sacred words may be perceived on every side. Indeed, no one will deny, unless he has neglected it, that by such careful and strict analysis we always meet and discover something different and new, with the highest admiration for the divinity of the Scriptures. III. One should not think that each member of the analysis makes as many parts; otherwise there would be as many parts as there are words in the text. Each thing must be observed and examined, not raised into parts; partition pursues only the more general heads or classes of members. IV. For example, in this predicate, no condemnation now, it is not well enough to set up three parts, though I consider three things here: condemnation, no condemnation, and that there is now no condemnation; and similarly in the subject. V. It is most convenient, and serves to explore and draw out the full knowledge of the text, if the individual members of the analysis are elicited and put as questions, to be followed at once by the explication, under the form of questions as they are usually put, namely: What is condemnation? What is no condemnation? What is now no condemnation? And concerning the subject of this part: what is being in Christ? What, and to what end, is added, Christ Jesus? For in this way: 1. the mind is kindled to greater attention, since every question has this advantage over plain statement, that it strikes the mind more forcefully, as in Rom. 8:31–35, the most effective questions: who is against us? who will accuse? etc. 2. Everything in the text is disembowelled and searched more diligently and thoroughly, and nothing is easily passed over, as in 1 John 3:12: not as Cain, who was of the evil one, and slew his brother. And why did he slay him? 3. The truth of all things is more surely brought out, grasped and held. Hos. 9:14: Give them, O LORD, what will you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts. Ps. 15:1; Isa. 33:15; Mic. 6:6, 7.

units.la: VIII. Sequitur Analytica expositio, & duplex ea, tum verborum, tum rei. Ac verborum quidem, quæ est interpretatio.
units.tr: VIII. There follows the analytical exposition, which is twofold: of the words and of the thing. The exposition of the words is interpretation.

units.la: 1. Vocum, Grammatica est, quomodo Matth. 1, 23. Immanuel quod interpretatur, Deus nobiscum. Marc. 5, 41. & 7, 34. Matth. 26, 47. Matth. 2, 1. quid significet, magi? Gal. 3, 13. quid ἐξηγόρασεν? Phil. 2, 30. quid ταπεινοφροσύνῃ? Augustinus de verbis Domini serm. 35. Primum, quid est mammona? quod Hebræi dicunt mammona, latine divitiæ vocantur. Ut ergo latine totum dicamus, hoc ait Dominus noster Iesus Christus, facite vobis amicos de divitiis iniquitatis. Hoc quidam male intelligendo, rapiunt res alienas, & aliquid indepauperibus largiuntur, & putant se facere, quod præceptum est. 2. Vel ut ratio locutionis explicetur, sive 1. constructio grammatica, ut Psal. 1, 1. אשרי האיש Rom. 1, 1. Euangelium Dei. an significet, à Deo, &c. de Deo, vel utrumque? Marc. 2,22. fidem Dei baptizari in Mosem 1 Cor. 10,2,11. five figura Rhetorica, ut quid fit, ambulare secundum carnem Rom. 8,1. Marc. 9, 49. igne salietur, &c. Quo tropi, & schemata, Luc. 22,19. Hoc est Corpus meum. verf. 20. Hoc poculum, est Novum testamentum in meo sanguine. Explicatio prior petitur ex Grammatica; haec ex Rhetorica.
units.tr: 1. Concerning individual words, there is grammar, as in Matt. 1:23, "Immanuel, which is interpreted, God with us"; Mark 5:41 and 7:34; Matt. 26:47; Matt. 2:1, what does magi mean?; Gal. 3:13, what does ἐξηγόρασεν [exēgorasen] mean?; Phil. 2:30, what is meant by ταπεινοφροσύνῃ [tapeinophrosynē]? Augustine, on the words of the Lord, sermon 35: First, what is mammon? What the Hebrews call mammon is called riches in Latin. So, to say the whole thing in Latin, our Lord Jesus Christ said this: make for yourselves friends of the riches of iniquity. Some, understanding this badly, seize other people's goods and give something to the poor, and think they are doing what has been commanded. 2. Or the manner of speech is to be explained, either 1. by grammatical construction, as in Ps. 1:1, "Blessed is the man" [אשרי האיש]; Rom. 1:1, Gospel of God: does it mean from God, concerning God, or both? Mark 2:22, the faith of God to be baptized into Moses, 1 Cor. 10:2, 11; or 2. by figure of rhetoric, as to what it means to walk according to the flesh, Rom. 8:1; Mark 9:49, will be salted with fire, and so on; to which belong tropes and schemes, as in Luke 22:19, This is my body; v. 20, This cup is the New Testament in my blood. The former explanation is sought from grammar, the latter from rhetoric.

units.la: IX. Explicatio rei est, non ut ea ibi tractetur ex professo, sed obiter attingatur, neque diutius, quam textus expositio & intelligentia poscit. Marc. 9,10. atque illum sermonem in se retinebant, quaerentes, quid illud sit, ex mortuis resurgere. Hic quaeritur, quid sit amor, quid fides, spes, quid condemnatio, quid maledictio, quid beatum, esse in Christo? &c. non quid nominis, sed quid rei, & patet, quam late hujus explicationis Topica se diffundat, nempe ex Theologia, Philosophia, Philologia, Historia, Medicina, Jurisprudentia; & undiquaq; hanc peti; talia enim in sacris occurrere, quae eo faciant, notissimum est, & vel ex uno Alstedii Triumpho Biblico satis apparet. V. g. quid sit liber vitae? quid, anathema fieri pro fratribus? quid, aquę supra firmamentum? qualia illa ornamenta Jef. 3. de libro Henochi, lepra, judiciis, & multa ejusmodi? Observanda in explicatione Analytica haec sunt. 1. ne prolixior fit, neque huic concio extra necessitatem immoretur, cum dispendio reliquorum, unde contingere solet, ut ad necessaria omnino, eaque, quae animos magis tangunt & aedificant in documentis & usibus pertractandis, vix relicto tempore, inani postmodum excusatione Concionator culpam deprecari necesse habeat; sibi, nec Auditoribus satisfaciens. Hoc saepius Gregorius observat. In Euang. homil. 40. lubet fratres charissimi Euangelicae verba lectionis sub brevitate transcurrere; ut post diutius liceat in contemplatione tantae solemnitatis immorari. Et homil. 38. Textum tum lectionis Euangelicæ fratres charissimi, volo, si passim, sub brevitate transcurrere, ut in fine ejus valeam ad loquendum largius vacare. Alibi: In explanatione sua multa ad loquendum Sancti Euangelii lectio postulat, quam volo, si possum, sub brevitate perstringere, ne vos & extensa protensio, & prolixa expositio videatur onerare. II. Nec ea, quæ satis perspicua, & nota sint, diu volvantur, & quæsita expositione protrahantur, ac implicentur potius. Illud Augustinus sollicite observat. In Psalm. 30. concione tertia: In verbis enim ejus planioribus non est immorari necesse: ut ea nos tencant, quorum est necessitas expendendi. sic in Psalm. 33. & concione secunda in Psal. 48. Itaque hoc proloquor, & peto ne diuturnum sermonem in bis, quæ manifesta sunt, exspectetis. Gregorius quoque Homil. in Joan 4. est inter Homilias Patrum pag. 354 Lectio Sancti Euangelii quam modo fratres audistis, expositione non indiget. Sed ne hanc tacite præterire videamur, exhortando potius quam exponendo, in ea aliquid loquamur. Bernardus in Psalm. qui habitat, serm. XI. est autem verbis ipsius quantum nos capimus, facilis intelligentia, ad quam forte ex vobis jam aliqui prævolarint. Confer. Amesium Cas. conc. lib. I. cap. 26. qu. II, III. Ne in explicatione adferantur dubia, difficilia, obscura: quomodo enim alteri lucem attulerit, quod ipsum illustrari indiget? IV. Caveat, ne dum in applicatione, profana & exotica, etiam ex litteris, philosophia &c. licet attingere, divagetur & inhæreat illis, congerendo impotenter, quæ omitti possent, ac conveniret unde videatur lubentius profana sectari, quam sacra, vel laudem eruditionis inanem affectare. V. Neque terminos artis, & Logicos adhibeat, quando etiam citra illos commode se queat exprimere: vel saltem non nisi addita istorum sufficienti explicatione: quo pateat, ipsum necessitate adactum iis uti, non nisi ad commodiorem intelligentiam.
units.tr: IX. The explanation of the thing is not to treat it there ex professo, but to touch on it in passing, and not for longer than the exposition and understanding of the text require. Mark 9:10, and they kept that saying to themselves, questioning what it is to rise from the dead. Here one asks what love is, what faith, hope, condemnation, curse, or being blessed in Christ is, and so on: not what the name is, but what the thing is. It is evident how widely the topics of this explanation spread: namely from theology, philosophy, philology, history, medicine and jurisprudence, and that this material is drawn from all quarters. That such things occur in the sacred writings which bear upon this is well known, and it appears sufficiently from Alsted's Biblical Triumph alone. E.g., what is the book of life? What does it mean to become an anathema for the brothers? What are the waters above the firmament? What are those ornaments in Isaiah 3, the book of Enoch, leprosy, judgments, and many things of this kind? The following are to be observed in analytical explanation. 1. It should not be overly long, nor should the sermon linger on it beyond necessity, to the loss of the rest. From this it commonly happens that, when there is scarcely any time left for what is wholly necessary, and for what moves and builds up the hearts more, in the teaching and uses, the preacher must afterwards beg pardon with an empty excuse, satisfying neither himself nor the hearers. Gregory often observes this. In the Gospel homilies, 40: It pleases us, dearest brothers, to run briefly through the words of the Gospel reading, so that afterwards we may be allowed to linger longer in contemplation of so great a solemnity. And homily 38: The text of the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, I want, where possible, to run through briefly, so that at its end I may be free to speak more at length. Elsewhere: The reading of the holy Gospel in its exposition demands much to be said, which I want, if I can, to touch on briefly, lest extended length and a long exposition seem to burden you. II. Nor should things that are clear enough and well known be turned over for long, and drawn out or rather entangled by an elaborate exposition. Augustine carefully observes this. On Psalm 30, sermon 3: For it is not necessary to dwell on his plainer words; let us be held by those things which need weighing. So too on Psalm 33, and in the second sermon on Psalm 48: Therefore I say this beforehand, and ask that you not expect a lengthy discourse on things that are manifest. Gregory also, in his homily on John 4, among the homilies of the Fathers, p. 354: The reading of the holy Gospel which you, brothers, have just heard needs no exposition. But lest we seem to pass it over in silence, let us say something about it, exhorting rather than expounding. Bernard on Psalm "He who dwells", sermon 11: But the meaning of his words is easy, as far as we can grasp; and perhaps some of you have already flown ahead to it. Compare Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book 1, ch. 26, questions 2 and 3. Doubtful, difficult and obscure points should not be brought into the explanation: for how could that bring light to another which itself needs illumination? IV. Let him take care that, while in the application he may touch on profane and exotic matters, even from literature, philosophy and so on, he does not wander off and dwell on them, piling up without restraint what could be omitted. Otherwise it would seem that he pursues profane things more gladly than sacred ones, or that he affects an empty reputation for learning. V. Nor should he use technical and logical terms when he can express himself conveniently without them; or at least not without adding a sufficient explanation of them, so that it is clear he uses them only because necessity compels him, for easier understanding.

units.la: Quaer. 1. An in analytica explicatione locus sit elencho, ad vindicationem textus, & refutationem Adversariorum ? Resp. Est elenchus verborum, & rei, v. g. in verbis coenae: hoc est corpus meum, quaestio est de transsubstantiatione, & de verbis, quomodo illa explicanda ? quicquid ad explicationem verborum spectat, in explicatione analytica dicendum, elenctice etiam, nempe est Corpus, non significare, fit vel adest corpus; sed est sacramentum corporis, contra Pontificios, Lutheranos: at, in usu, post documentum, elenctico, disputari debet de re; & probandum, illud falsum esse, quod Adversarii ex illis verbis asseverare satagunt; & contrà, sententia orthodoxa confirmanda.
units.tr: Question 1. Is there room in the analytical explanation for elenchus, for vindicating the text and refuting the adversaries? Answer. There is elenchus of words and of the thing. For example, in the words of the Supper, this is my body, the question concerns transubstantiation, and how these words are to be explained. Whatever pertains to the explanation of the words is to be said in the analytical explanation, and elenctically too: namely that is the body does not signify "becomes body" or "body is present", but is the sacrament of the body, against the Papists and the Lutherans. But in use, after the teaching, one should dispute elenctically about the matter, and it must be proved that what the adversaries strive to assert from those words is false, and, conversely, the orthodox opinion must be confirmed.

units.la: Quaer. 2. An in explicatione textus dubia sint adferendae aliorum interpretationes, cum suis Auctoribus? Resp. Si necessario vindicandus est à perversa vel haeretica expositione adversariorum, illam adferendam constat, an nominandi sint Auctores, vel loca? definiemus, ubi agendum de usu doctrinae elenctico. Caeterum, quando certa textus & vera explicatio dari facile potest, non sunt Auditores grauandi aliorum expositionibus, multo minus omnibus. Aliud schola, aliud Ecclesiam decet. Neque sane is, qui in re certa aliorum sententias ibi adfert, Ecclesiae aedificationem unice intendit, sed vel tempus terere, vel quod non minus illicitum, se nomina populo ignota inaniter jactare. Aufert mercedem suam. Aliud est, quando incerta etiam inter Orthodoxos est interpretatio, & vix constat, quid certò sequendum; tum & eam quoque interpretationem addere licet, quae non minus probabilis, citra vanam tamen Auctorum citationem; sed illa ratione omnes quorumcunque, vel non necessarias, aut probabiles expositiones adferre est, difficultates non velle tollere, sed augere, & Auditores (quorum plurimi, si non omnes simplicissimi plicissimi) intricare. Talis sibi concionatur, 1Cor. 14, 4. immo nec sibi. Et neque Deo, neque officio, neque Ecclesiæ satisfacit. Hæc est regula Concionatoribus perpetua, & catholica: quod pro concione adfertur, & neque primò neque necessariò facit ad intelligentiam & ædificationem omnis Ecclesiæ, peccat. 1Cor. 14. Hic Concionator conscientiam suam judicem (ne de aliorum judicio dicam) constituere debet, in eo quod dicit, agitque, ut caste omnia & digne.
units.tr: Question 2. In the explanation of a text, when it is doubtful, should other people's interpretations be brought forward, with their authors? Answer. If the text must necessarily be defended against a perverse or heretical exposition of the adversaries, it is agreed that that exposition should be brought forward. Whether the authors or places should be named, we will define where we treat of the elenctic use of doctrine. Otherwise, when a certain and true explanation of the text can easily be given, the hearers are not to be burdened with other people's expositions, much less with all of them. A school suits one thing, the Church another. Nor indeed does one who there brings forward others' opinions on a matter that is certain aim solely at the edification of the Church; he either wastes time or, no less improperly, vainly brandishes names unknown to the people. "He forfeits his reward." It is otherwise when the interpretation is uncertain even among the Orthodox and it hardly is clear what must certainly be followed; then it is also permitted to add that interpretation which is no less probable, though without vain citation of authors. But to bring forward all the expositions of whatever authors, when they are not necessary or probable, is not to wish to remove difficulties but to increase them, and to entangle the hearers, most of whom, if not all, are very simple. Such a man preaches to himself, 1 Cor. 14:4; indeed not even to himself. He satisfies neither God, nor his office, nor the Church. This is the constant and catholic rule for preachers: what is brought forward for the sermon, and neither first nor necessarily contributes to the understanding and edification of the whole Church, is sin. 1 Cor. 14. Here the preacher must set his own conscience as judge (not to speak of others' judgment) in what he says and does, so that all things are done chastely and worthily.

units.la: X. Ultimo sequitur, & analyticam explicationem claudit loci explicati paraphrasis, quæ omnia iterum colligit, & complectitur, hactenus divulsa, & seorsim explicata; atque ut præcedentium summam dicit, & complementum, ita viam pandit & initium ad Documenta, simul ut sit analyseos finis, & genesin ostendat, protrudatque, sicque concionis summam habeat. In Paraphrastica Scripturæ explicatione commendant se Cartwrig. in Euangelia, Erasmus in N. Test. & Janfenius in Psalmos. V. c. Ex parte textus priori Rom. 8, 1, hæc exsurgit Paraphrasis: Non exigua est fidelium, eorum qui non in se, ac suo statu hærent, sed extra se spiritualiter jam Christi Jesu sunt, fælicitas: inde, quod dum in se nihil minus, quam justificari per opera sua possent, condemnari vero certissimè deberent, Christi in Christo justitiam adipiscantur, eamque suam faciant; ideoque, quum multiplex illos alias & omnis maneret condemnatio, cuncta jam evanescit, non sunt condemnandi ulterius, nunquam condemnabuntur, & vel jam extra statum sunt condemnationis. Basilius in Psalm. 61. Nonne Deo subjecta est anima? id ita Cur, inquit, pravorum affectuum animam facio servam: quæ à Deo & corporis & omnium ipsius sensuum dux atque princeps est creata? In paraphrasi, hæc duo spectanda. 1. Ut ad eam eruendam & inveniendam induamus animum illius, qui id dixit, quod paraphrasi volumus expositum: nempe ifthoc pacto verius & preffius dicti causam & rationem omnem deprehensuri. 11. Ut in promenda paraphrasi, omnium quæ textus habet, enarrationem faciamus; animis Auditorum quasi in apertum campum intromittendis, ubi singula spectent, legant, fruantur.
units.tr: X. Last comes the paraphrase, which closes the analytical explication of the passage. It gathers together again everything that was previously divided and explained separately. As it gives the sum and completion of what precedes, it opens the way and the beginning to the Doctrines, and at the same time marks the end of the analysis and shows and brings forward its origin, so that the sermon has its summary. For paraphrastic explanation of Scripture, Cartwright on the Gospels, Erasmus on the New Testament and Jansenius on the Psalms commend themselves. Take Romans 8:1 for the first part of the text. From it this paraphrase arises: The happiness of the faithful is no small thing, of those who no longer cling to themselves and their own state, but who are now spiritually outside themselves, in Christ Jesus. From this, since in themselves they could least of all be justified by their own works, yet most certainly ought to be condemned, they obtain the righteousness of Christ in Christ and make it their own. Therefore, although otherwise they would remain under manifold and universal condemnation, all of that now vanishes: they are not to be condemned any further, they will never be condemned, and they are already outside the state of condemnation. Basil on Psalm 61: Is not the soul subject to God? Yes, it is. Why, he says, do I make the soul a slave to depraved affections, when it was created by God as the leader and prince both of the body and of all its senses? In the paraphrase two things are to be considered. First, that in drawing it out and discovering it we put on the mind of the one who said what we wish to set forth in the paraphrase, namely that in this way we shall grasp the cause and the whole reason of the saying more truly and more precisely. Second, that in bringing forth the paraphrase we give an account of everything the text contains, bringing the minds of the hearers as it were into an open field, where they may look at, read and enjoy each thing.

units.la: Quær. An hinc ad reliquas textus partes explicandas progrediendum fit, ut sic simul omnibus primum explicatis, demùm documenta subjungantur, & tractentur: An verò cuilibet parti ita explicatæ: immediatè statim documenta istius sint annectenda? Diverfitas concionum hic fit manifesta, alii hoc, alii illo modo docent: utrumvis sece/s, mox/ò rectè doceas, τὰλὴν παντὶ τξόπῳ, Χριστὸς καταγγέλλετα. Ita Patres, & plerique. Augustinus duplicem in Psalmos sæpe facit enarrationem: priori textum verbotenus ac breviter explicans: altera quidem etiam, sed magis docet, & ad praxin applicat. Chrysostomus in epist. præmittit integram explicationem, tum subjungit ἠθικὸν Morale. Nobis tamen videtur, nisi partes textus adeo innexæ & implicatæ sint, ut solvi, neque secus explicari, quæant, ubi tum res ipsa jubet, ut sequamur id, quò ducimur, nempe pergamus ad alterius quoque partis explicationem: hoc ubi non est, præstare unicuique parti singulatim explicatæ connectere statim & conjungere sua documenta. Rationes, quare ita judicamus, hæ sunt. I. Quia sic manifestissimè liquet, quomodo documenta in textu continentur, quod postea non ita patet, nisi cum tautologia repetas jam ante dicta: & multum refert, tum ut documentum in animos operetur, tum ut concionis appareat forma, id ut quam maximè liqueat, te ex textu docere. Immò sæpe ea est connexio & consequentia textus explicati cum documento, ut trahi eo concio videatur, neque nisi invita alio iterum abstrahi possit; adeò proximè Auditoribus in paraphrasi documentum indicatur, & satis traditur, nisi quod forma desit. Hoc ex ratione concionis. II. Sic melius consulitur memoriæ, tum Concionatoris, tum Auditorum, quo filum tenes, secundum quod omnia ex se fluunt, & sequuntur. Aliter etiam quidni retineant concionem? sed præterquam de Concionatore, operosam ei fieri memoriam & difficilem, de Auditoribus certissimum id est, ut ut in genere multa alias recordentur, sola hac (quam docemus) methodo eos omnia retinere. Atque ita plus ædificationis hinc ad Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Question. Should one proceed from here to explain the remaining parts of the text, so that all are first explained together and only then the doctrines are added and treated? Or should the doctrines of each part, once so explained, be attached to it immediately? Here the practice of sermons is clearly divided: some teach in this way, others in that. Whichever way you teach, provided you teach rightly, only Christ is proclaimed in every way [τὸ ἀλλὰ παντὶ τρόπῳ, Χριστὸς καταγγέλλεται]. So the Fathers and most others. Augustine often makes a double explanation on the Psalms: the first briefly explains the text word for word; the second, though also explanatory, teaches more and applies it to practice. Chrysostom in his epistles first gives a full explanation and then adds the moral part. It seems to us, however, that unless the parts of the text are so closely interwoven and entangled that they cannot be untied or explained otherwise, and unless the matter itself requires us to follow where we are led, namely to go on to the explanation of the other part as well, it is better, where that is not the case, to connect and join the doctrines to each part explained separately, straight away. Our reasons for judging so are these. I. Because in this way it is most plainly clear how the doctrines are contained in the text. This would not afterwards be so evident unless you repeated what was said before, which is mere tautology. It matters greatly both that the doctrine should work upon the minds, and that the form of the sermon should appear, and that it should be as clear as possible that you are teaching from the text. Indeed the connection and consequence of the explained text with the doctrine is often so close that the sermon seems to be drawn along by it and could not be drawn away again to something else unless against its will. So near to the hearers is the doctrine pointed out and sufficiently handed on in the paraphrase, except that the form is lacking. This follows from the nature of a sermon. II. In this way the memory of both preacher and hearers is better served, since you hold the thread, and everything flows from it and follows on. Why would they not otherwise retain the sermon? But apart from the preacher, for whom the memory becomes laborious and difficult, it is quite certain for the hearers that, although in general they remember many other things, they retain everything only by this method, which we teach. And so there is more edification from this to the Church.

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR.

units.la: I. ✱ Actenus concio in textu dissolvendo, atque explicando occupata fuit, jam docebit ex textu: hactenus analysis, jam genesis. Duo supersunt, docere ex textu, & doctrinam intimare, applicare ad singulorum conscientiam & usum; Documenta, & Usus.
units.tr: I. Hitherto the sermon has been occupied with dissolving and explaining the text; now it will teach from the text. Hitherto has been analysis; now comes genesis. Two things remain: to teach from the text, and to impress the doctrine, to apply it to each person's conscience and use. These are the Documents and the Uses.

units.la: II. Documentum dicitur, doctrina, vel observatio doctrinæ, axioma nempe Theologicum, quod in textu observatum doceri, ex eo producitur, atque porro pro concione tractatur. Quomodo Basil. in Psalm. 37. Docet item nos hic sermo, ne mala nostra obticescere, aut velare velimus. Bernard. in Cantic. serm. 60. Mirum verò, si nec ficus, nec vineæ ista aliquid habent, quod mores ædificet. Ego hunc locum arbitror esse & moralem.
units.tr: II. A document is a doctrine, or an observation of doctrine, that is, a theological axiom, which is observed in the text to be taught, is drawn out of it, and is then handled further for the sermon. So Basil on Psalm 37: This passage also teaches us that we should not wish to keep silent about or conceal our evils. Bernard, Sermon 60 on the Song of Songs: It would indeed be strange if these fig trees and vines had nothing that builds up morals. I think this passage is also moral.

units.la: III. In documentis duo spectanda sunt. I. Documenti formatio. II. Tractatio: In priori judicium, in altero cœlestis sapientia præcipuè se ostendit, & requiritur, Matth. 13, 52. ideoque omnis scriba edoctus Ētus in regnum cœlorum, similis est homini œconomo, qui ex thesauro suo producit nova & vetera.
units.tr: III. In documents two things are to be considered: (1) the formation of the document; (2) its handling. In the first, judgement chiefly shows itself; in the second, heavenly wisdom, as Matthew 13:52 requires: therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.

units.la: IV. In priori, formando nempe documento, hoc agit. I. Ut genuinè eruatur. II. Recte proponatur.
units.tr: IV. In the first, that is, in forming the document, one aims at two things: (1) that it be genuinely drawn out; (2) that it be rightly set forth.

units.la: V. Documentum invenitur & eruitur, vel ex textus verbis expressis, vel ex textu per constructionem. Illud dicatur documentum magis apertum vel concinnatum; hoc constructum, vel elicitum, V. g. Matth. 4, 17. Resipiscite &c. Duæ textus partes sunt. I. Præceptum. II. Ratio præcepti. Documentum prioris est apertum, & textus: nisi quod explicatius proponatur & sub generali axiomate, nempe: quod homines debeant resipiscere. Posteriores documentum ex argumentatione Christi; quod & quia regnum Dei appropinquat, agenda est resipiscentia, constructum est documentum, vel instructum ex textus constructione. Hæc documentorum divisio est ex formâ, ex materiâ, alia sunt theoretica, de veritate, & fidei; alia practica, de moribus, quæ dividitur sumitur ex proximâ rerum differentiâ, non ex ultimo fine, & vel usu, nam in concione omnia omninò ad praxin referuntur.
units.tr: V. A document is found and drawn out either from the explicit words of the text, or from the text by its construction. The former may be called the more open or ready-made document; the latter constructed or elicited. For example, Matthew 4:17, Repent, etc. The text has two parts: (1) the command; (2) the reason for the command. The document of the first part is open and lies in the text itself, except that it is set out more fully and under a general axiom, namely, that men ought to repent. The document of the second part comes from Christ's argument: because the kingdom of God is at hand, repentance must be undertaken; this document is constructed, or built up, from the construction of the text. This division of documents is by form; by matter there are others, theoretical, concerning truth and faith, and others practical, concerning morals. This division is taken from the nearest difference of things, not from the ultimate end, or from use, for in a sermon everything is referred wholly to practice.

units.la: VI. Documenta formantur ex textu, at quomodo? & unde? I. Ex omni concionis parte; non ita necessario ex omni textus parte; quomodo illa aliquando distinguuntur, supra diximus. V. g. in historia Euangelica sæpius occurrit, tunc dixit Iesus, &c. ubi duæ in textu partes, quod dixerit Iesus, & quid dixerit, ex priori (quamvis textus parte) non ideo necessario documentum facies, sed ex sequentibus, quæ demum concionis partes instruunt, dabuntque illæ necessaria documenta. II. Documenta leguntur & fiunt ex iis quæ in textu ejusque explicatione notanda maxime, & observanda occurrunt, nihilque istorum temere omittendum. Quod si tempus non permittat ea omnia tractare, vel alio tempore id agas, vel saltem jam indices, ut constet te non neglexisse, quod observandum erat, & notari in documentum meretur. V. g. ex Rom. 8, 1. hæc fluunt documenta. Non est alicui salus in se, quin debet exire ex se, & illam non in, sed extra se quærere. II. Solum in Christo Jesu salus est, iisque, qui in illo sunt. III. Qui in Christo Jesu, vel Christi sunt, nulla ratione condemnari possunt. IV. Qui in Christo Jesu, jam etiam ab omni condemnatione liberati sunt. Ex illis hæc eliciuntur documenta, quæ in textu explicando maxime observabamus, & notabamus. Atqui id dicit, unde documenta formentur; jam, quomodo?
units.tr: VI. Documents are formed from the text, but how, and from where? (1) From every part of the sermon, though not necessarily from every part of the text, as we said above in how these parts are distinguished. For example, in the Gospel narratives it often occurs: then Jesus said, etc. Here there are two parts of the text: what Jesus said, and that he said it.
