From the first part (though it is part of the text) you will not necessarily make a document; rather from what follows, which finally furnishes the parts of the sermon, and these will supply the necessary documents. (2) Documents are read off and made from those things in the text and its explanation which are chiefly to be noted and observed, and none of these is to be carelessly omitted. If time does not allow all of them to be handled, either deal with them at another time, or at least indicate them now, so that it is clear you have not neglected what ought to be observed and deserves to be noted as a document. For example, from Romans 8:1 these documents flow: (I) No one has salvation in himself, so he must come out of himself and seek it not in himself but outside himself. (II) Salvation is in Christ Jesus alone, and in those who are in him. (III) Those who are in Christ Jesus, or are Christ's, cannot be condemned in any way. (IV) Those who are in Christ Jesus are already also freed from all condemnation. From these are drawn the documents which we were chiefly observing and noting in explaining the text. But this has said whence documents are formed; now, how?

units.la: VII. In Documentis expressis haud tanta difficultas: illa enim jam in textu occurunt, & non nisi paulo explicatius proponuntur, quasi in aciem axiomaticè. Constructa vel elicita Documenta hoc modo formantur. I. Sedulò attendatur res quælibet, quæ in textu tangitur, notatur, & exprimitur. II. Illa res extra nexum verborum trahatur, & liberetur, proponenda in thesin, & non constringenda ad textus eadem verba, sensus modò teneatur. III. formetur in axioma generale; non enim in textu sub formâ axiomatis occurrit: axioma dico, in ordine ad textus verba, quæ specialia & implexa, ideoque ut in documentum migrent, ac veritatem axiomaticam revocanda, & non nisi tali formâ proponenda sunt; generale dico, in ordine ad usus e documentis inferendos, & specialiter applicandos.
units.tr: VII. In open documents there is not so great a difficulty, for they already occur in the text and are only set forth a little more fully, as it were in the form of an axiom. Constructed or elicited documents are formed in this way: (I) Attentively consider whatever thing is touched on in the text, note it, and express it. (II) Draw that thing out of the connection of the words and free it, to be put forward as a thesis, and not confined to the very words of the text; only its sense is to be kept. (III) Form it into a general axiom. For it does not occur in the text in the form of an axiom. I say axiom in relation to the words of the text, which are particular and intricate, and therefore, if they are to pass into a document, must be brought back to axiomatic truth and set forth only in such a form. I say general in relation to the uses to be drawn from the documents and applied particularly.

units.la: V. g. 1 Pet. 4, 17. Nam tempus est &c. In hoc textu, subjectum de quo agitur, est judicium Dei, & de hoc judicio dicitur, illud incipere, & quod ei sit καιρὸς quando incipiat, incipiens vero, quod tum à domo Dei incipiat. Hic ergo omnia illa & singula, quæ ita emphatica, conside ro, neque omittere possum, quin in axiomata à textu nihil monstrata, extendam; Ergo documentum primum sit, ex primo subjecti prædicato: Iudicia Dei aliquando incipere, re. Secundum, ex secundo prædicato: Iudicia Dei habere suum proprium tempus, καιρόν quo incipiant. Tertium, ex eo quod sequitur: Iudicia Dei, quum incipiunt, à fidelibus primum incipere. Quid vero sit, res textus, quæ in axioma, vel documentum diducitur, ex nexu verborum, & dictionis schemate, ad id solvere, ex sequentibus magis patebit, ubi fit interrogatio. Si primum à nobis, quis finis non obedientium Euangelio! verf. seq. Si justus vix servatur, &c. ubi primo omnium solvenda res est, & in simplicem orationem exponenda: quis finis? i.e. admodum gravis profecto finis divini Judicii manet illos, qui Euangelio non obediunt, quoniam initia judiciorum Dei tam acria sunt, quæ suos tangunt! Versus seq. in syllogismum integrè disponendus venit, ut documentum constet, ita: si justus vix servatur, impius non habet quo subsistat (etenim ejus interrogationis, ubi apparebit? illa simplex enunciatio est, nullibi apparere, subsistere audebit (sed justus vix servatur.) Ergo. Similis locutio est Rom. 8, 31. & f. & alibi, atque idcirco eadem debet esse illorum quoque tractatio. Ubi, misso antecedente & consequente seorsim considerando, hoc documentum construitur. Difficultas salvandi in piis, ut illi salvantur, instruit de gravitate condemnationis in impiis. Scio in plura, si ita velis, documenta hæc distribui quoque posse, nempe si divisim antecedens, & consequens tractare etiam velis, ut I. In negotio salutis, instruendi veniunt homines, ex ratione status unius ad alium, quemadmodum Luc. 24, 31. II. Etiam justi, non nisi difficulter salvantur. III. Miserrimus improborum status, qui nusquam queant subsistere. Psalm. 1. Et IV. quod ex argumentatione construitur, ac solum in ejusmodi textibus aliquando satius est tractare, quia peculiarem, & omnes textus emphasin secum trahit, quare illud unicum modo proproposuimus: difficultas salvandi in piis, instruit de gravitate condemnationis in impiis. Unde jam quoque patet quartum hoc in formandis documentis observandum, nempe quod aliquando per extensionem documenta ex textu fiunt, aliquando per contractionem, id est, vel id quod textus habet extenditur, & expanditur, ut quando ex verborum connexione, vel relatione, veluti si ex versu statim dicto quatuor illa documenta fiant; vel contrahitur, si ex versu illo unum istud modo, & sic sæpe in textibus historicis, ubi plura comprehendimus in unam observationem, vel documentum. V. Axioma aut. jam illud, quod per attentam & sanctissimam textus observat. ex verbis (quorum constructu continebatur & implicabatur) solvisti, eruisti, & in formam talem axiomaticam redegisti, sive per extensionem rei, quæ in textu; sive per ejus contract. quale illud axioma esse debeat Theol. te docet, ut conveniat. sc. cum analogia fidei. Si quis loquitur, ὡς λόγια θεοῦ. 1 Pet. 4, 11. Rom. 12, 6.
units.tr: For example, 1 Peter 4:17, For the time is come, etc. In this text the subject under discussion is the judgement of God, and of this judgement it is said that it begins, and that for it there is a time [καιρός], and that, beginning, it begins at the house of God. Here, then, I consider all and each of these emphatic things, and I cannot omit them, but I extend them into axioms not shown by the text itself. So the first document is from the first predicate of the subject: the judgements of God sometimes begin, etc. The second, from the second predicate: the judgements of God have their own proper time, a kairos [καιρόν], at which they begin. The third, from what follows: the judgements of God, when they begin, begin first with the faithful. But what the thing of the text is, which is unfolded into an axiom or document, is to be solved from the connection of the words and the form of the expression; this will be clearer from what follows, where a question is asked: If judgement begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel? (verse following) If the righteous is scarcely saved, etc. Here first of all the thing must be solved and set out in plain speech: what will be the end? That is: indeed a very grievous end awaits the divine judgement for those who do not obey the gospel, since the beginnings of God's judgements are so severe, touching even his own! The following verse must be arranged fully as a syllogism, so that the document may be established, thus: if the righteous is scarcely saved, the ungodly man has nowhere to stand. For the question where will he appear? is equivalent to the simple statement that he will appear nowhere, and will not dare to stand. But the righteous is scarcely saved. Therefore... A similar form of speech occurs at Romans 8:31 and elsewhere, and so the handling of these passages ought to be the same. Here, setting aside the antecedent and the consequent considered separately, this document is constructed: the difficulty of the saved among the godly instructs us about the gravity of the condemnation of the ungodly. I know these documents can, if you wish, be distributed into several, that is, if you also want to treat the antecedent and the consequent separately, as: (I) In the matter of salvation, men are instructed by the reasoning from the state of one to another, as in Luke 24:31. (II) Even the righteous are saved only with difficulty. (III) The most wretched state of the wicked, who can nowhere stand. Psalm 1. And (IV) what is constructed from argument, which in texts of this kind it is sometimes better to treat alone, because it carries with it a particular emphasis and that of the whole text; for which reason we have set forth only this one: the difficulty of the saved among the godly instructs us about the gravity of the condemnation of the ungodly. From this it also now becomes clear that a fourth point is to be observed in forming documents: sometimes documents are made from the text by extension, sometimes by contraction. That is, either what the text contains is extended and expanded, as when from the connection or relation of the words, for example, four such documents are made from the verse just mentioned; or it is contracted, as when one such document is made from that verse; and so often in historical texts, where we gather several things into one observation or document. (V) An axiom, then, is that which you have solved, drawn out, and reduced to such an axiomatic form from the words through an attentive and most holy observation of the text, in which the words were contained and involved in their construction, whether by extending the thing in the text or by contracting it. What sort of axiom it ought to be, theology teaches you, so that it agrees, namely with the analogy of faith: if anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God [ὡς λόγια θεοῦ], 1 Peter 4:11; Romans 12:6.

units.la: VIII. In proponendo documento observandum,
units.tr: VIII. What is to be observed in proposing the Document

units.la: ut proponatur perspicuè, concinnè & solidè, i. e. quod sibi constet, non ambiguè, aut leviter. Deinde aliis quoque verbis repetatur, quo magis animis inhæreat; illud enim est, quod porro tractabitur, uti Christus Marc. 10, 23, 24. Directorium cultus publici anglicarum cap. de conc. verb. in eliciendis ex textu Documentis, potissima ejus cura esse debet primo, ut res sit vera, secundo, ut sit veritas textu contenta & fundata, quo Auditores queant dignoscere, quomodo id inde à Deo doceatur. Tertio, ut præcipuè insistat illis documentis, quæ maxime ex scopo textus fluunt, & plurimum faciunt ad ædificationem Auditorum. Et hæc de Documenti propositione, sequitur ejus tractatio, vel elaboratio, ubi tum concio est in ᾔκμῆ.
units.tr: It should be proposed clearly, neatly and soundly, that is, consistent with itself, and not ambiguously or superficially. Then it should be repeated in other words, so that it may cling more closely to the minds of the hearers, for this is what will be treated further, as Christ says in Mark 10:23, 24. The Directorium of the English public worship, in the chapter on the sermon, says: in drawing out Documents from the text, its chief care must be first that the matter is true; second, that it is the truth contained and grounded in the text, so that the hearers may be able to discern how God teaches it from there; third, that it dwell especially on those documents which flow most from the scope of the text and contribute most to the edification of the hearers. And this is what concerns the proposal of the Document; next comes its treatment or elaboration, where the sermon is in its prime [ἀκμῇ].

units.la: IX. In Documenti tractatione tria sunt. I. Ejus explicatio. II. Probatio. III. Amplificatio: quibus rite elaborandis illa consistit.
units.tr: IX. In the treatment of the Document there are three things: I. its explanation; II. its proof; III. its amplification. On the proper working out of these the whole matter depends.

units.la: X. In explicatione & illustratione Documenti hoc agitur, ut quemadmodum antea textus explicatus est, ita jam res, & documentum rei: nempe, verba sunt interpretata, ut res significaretur: in analytica explicatione tantum rei ibi dictum, quantum ad Documentum formandum requirebatur, Iam Documento posito, res explicari latius debet, ad generICAm ejus tractationem per rationes, & usus.
units.tr: X. In the explanation and illustration of the Document, the aim is that, just as the text was explained before, so now the matter and the document of the matter are explained. Namely, the words were interpreted so that the matter might be signified; in the analytical explanation only so much of the matter was said there as was needed to form the Document. Now that the Document is set down, the matter must be explained more fully, for its general treatment by reasons and uses.

units.la: XI. Probatio Documenti est duplex I. § ǒτι, quod ita sit veritas documenti, per locos parallelos. II. § διότι quare ita sit, per rationes ex verbo Dei deductas. In priori probatione haec tenenda. I. Ne multi scripturae loci adferantur, & accumulentur, sed pauci iique significantissimi, duo vel tres; ubi se tum ostendit Concionatoris judicium, si in scripturis divinis exercitatum sit, & quod Act. 18, 24. de Apollo dicitur, num potens sit in scripturis. Tria semper Ministro facienda, dixit Lutherus; revolvere Biblia, orare scrio, & semper discipulum manere. Et Musculus a pio ac venerando sene saepe se admonitum ait; Si bonus velis fieri Concionator, fac fis bonus Biblicus. Melchior Adamus in vitis Theol. pag. 165. & 350. Ita succum & sanguinem scripturae, quem imbibere jubemur omnes, ac praecipue Concionator, hic exprimimus, atque per id est, quod Spiritus Sanctus efficaciter operatur in animes hominum, nempe per suum ipsius verbum. II. Ne illi scripturae loci proferantur nudi, sed cum explicatione, & paraphrasi, at brevi, & quae ad rem faciat, hocque evidenter demonstret locum citatum convenire intentioni, & veritatem Documenti probare. Quomodo in citandis atque urgendis S. scripturae locis habere te debeas, docebit optime epistola ad Hebræos, five plura aliquando loca, unum post alterum adferas, ut cap. 2, 13. & 4, 5. istius epist. sive explicanda simul sint, cap. 3,16,17,18. sive applicanda. cap. 2,9. & 4,6. sive cum emphasi urgenda, & exprimenda, cap. 3,15. & 4,7. & 6, 13. & 7, 2,3,13. & 10,8,9,15,16. & 12,27. ex hoc scripto optime addiscas.
units.tr: XI. The proof of the Document is twofold: I. [ὅτι] that the Document is so true, by parallel passages; II. [διότι] why it is so, by reasons drawn from the Word of God. In the first kind of proof the following should be kept. I. Not many passages of Scripture should be brought forward and piled up, but a few, and those most significant, two or three; here the preacher's judgment shows itself, if he is practised in the divine Scriptures, and whether he is, as is said of Apollos in Acts 18:24, powerful in the Scriptures. Luther said there are three things the minister must always do: turn over the Bible, pray diligently, and always remain a learner. And Musculus says he was often reminded by a pious and venerable old man: If you wish to become a good preacher, see that you are a good student of the Bible. Melchior Adam, in the Lives of the Theologians, pp. 165 and 350. Thus we squeeze out here the sap and blood of Scripture, which we are all bidden to drink in, and above all the preacher; and through this the Holy Spirit works effectively in the souls of men, namely through his own Word. II. Those passages of Scripture should not be quoted bare, but with explanation and paraphrase, brief and to the point, and this should clearly show that the cited passage agrees with the intention and proves the truth of the Document. How you ought to conduct yourself in citing and pressing passages of Holy Scripture the Epistle to the Hebrews will teach you best: whether you sometimes bring forward several passages, one after another, as in chapters 2:13 and 4:5 of that epistle, whether they are to be explained together, chapters 3:16, 17, 18, or to be applied, chapter 2:9 and 4:6, or to be urged and brought out with emphasis, chapters 3:15, 4:7, 6:13, 7:2, 3, 13, 10:8, 9, 15, 16, and 12:27. You will learn this excellently from that writing.

units.la: Quær. An semper cum citatione loci, caput & versus exprimendus? Resp. Exprimitur Act. 13,33. quomodo etiam in secundo Psalmo scribitur. Alias non, & ut epistolam ad Hebræos iterum consulamus, nec exprimitur quis, vel ubi dicat, cap. 2,6. testatus est quis alicubi & cap. 4,4. at cap. 4,7. sicuti Spiritus Sanctus loquitur, & 10,15. ipse dixit, & cap. 13,5. & v, 6. Ergo judicamus, in locis, quæ adferuntur ad probandum Documentum & Usum, vel ad aliud quid notabile, sive in quorum emphasi situm, quodque ideo peculiariter urgemus ac notamus, commodè caput & versum indicari, & à populo inquiri. In reliquis, quæ passim citantur, non adeò id necesse esse.
units.tr: Question. Must the chapter and verse always be stated along with the citation? Answer. It is stated in Acts 13:33, as it is also written in the second Psalm. Otherwise not; and, to consult the Epistle to the Hebrews again, neither is it said who says it or where, in chapter 2:6, someone has testified somewhere, and in chapter 4:4; but in chapter 4:7, as the Holy Spirit says, and in 10:15, he himself said, and in chapter 13:5 and verse 6. Therefore we judge that in the passages adduced to prove the Document and the Use, or to some other notable matter, in whose emphasis the thing lies and which we therefore urge and note in particular, it is fitting to indicate the chapter and verse and to have them looked up by the people. In the rest, which are cited here and there, this is not so necessary.

units.la: Observandum hic & illud, quando locus adferitur, vel difficilis, vel admodum controversus, ut ille obiter, & breviter explicetur, vel si videatur ἐναντιοφανία, solvenda ea, neque enim alicubi remorandus est Auditorum animus, sed plananda omnia & apertissimè explicanda, amplificanda, inculcanda.
units.tr: Observe here also this: when a passage is cited that is either difficult or very controversial, it should be explained briefly and in passing; or if it seems to be an apparent contradiction [ἐναντιοφανία], that should be resolved. For the minds of the hearers must nowhere be detained, but everything should be made plain and explained, amplified and impressed most clearly.

units.la: XII. In probatione per rationes, hæc observan- da
units.tr: XII. In proof by reasons, the following is to be observed

units.la: I. Non semper rationes inquirendas, vel dandas esse; sunt, quorum ratio dari omninò nequit, & quorum non commodè ratio datur. Non vexandæ rationes, nisi resipsa eò ferat, invitetque. II. Dandæ sunt rationes propriæ, non communes, evidentes & certæ rationes. In hoc, ut priori etiam, plerumque peccatur, dum rationes adferuntur non satis tis congruç, quæ non dextrè & immediatè illud probandum venit, quales sunt, quæ longius petuntur, & generaliores sunt, vel abitrusiores; contra, si propriæ urgeantur, neque monendum tum erit, ne justò plures adferat, nam ipsa rei ratio numerum illarum cum iis satis dicet. III. Ne rationes nudæ adferantur, & enumerentur solum, sed explicatæ, & per scripturam probatæ, ac quovis modo amplificatæ, ut Jurisconsulti solent dicere: crubefcimus fine lege loqui. Vel ut Hieronimus ad Nepotian: totus sermo presbyteri scripturarum sale conspersus & conditus esse debet. Telingius ideò rationes scripturales appellat, Neceffi. demonstr. lib. 4. cap. 2. IV. Si textus ipse rationem contineat, & suppeditet, ut plurimum illam solam urgere, ac tractare convenit.
units.tr: I. Reasons are not always to be sought out or given; there are some for which no reason can be given at all, and some for which a reason is not conveniently given. Reasons should not be forced unless the thing itself leads to them and invites them. II. Reasons should be given that are proper, not common, evident and certain. In this, as in the former matter also, people commonly go wrong, when reasons are brought forward that are not sufficiently suitable, that do not bear directly and immediately on what is to be proved, such as those that are sought from further off and are more general or more obscure. On the other hand, if the proper ones are pressed, there will be no need to warn against bringing forward too many, for the nature of the matter itself will set their number well enough. III. Reasons should not be brought forward bare and merely listed, but explained, proved from Scripture, and amplified in every way, as the jurists are wont to say: we blush to speak without the law. Or as Jerome says to Nepotian: the whole discourse of a presbyter ought to be seasoned and flavoured with the salt of the Scriptures. Telinge therefore calls them scriptural reasons, Necessit. demonstr. book 4, chapter 2. IV. If the text itself contains and supplies the reason, it is usually fitting to press and handle that alone.

units.la: XIII. Ergò jam Amplificatio Documenti sequitur, quæ in eo consistit, utomnia quæ hic adferuntur, Documenti explicatio & probatio, dignè atque aptè amplificentur, quod ex omnibus fermè argumentorum locis fieri potest, maxime autem ex diffentaneis & comparatis. Prioris exempla vide, Psal. 1, 4. Jesa. 45, 10. 2 Cor. 4, 8, 9. 1 Petr. 1, 18, 19. vel quando κατ' ἀρσην & κατ' ϑεσιν quid asseritur. Rom. 8, 1. non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum. Joan. 3, 16. & 1, 20. Psal. 32, 5. Heb. 10, 9. tollit prius ut alterum ponat. & cap. 12, 18. Posterioris, nempe comparatorum exempla prope infinita sunt, huc Christi parabolæ spectant, Matth. 13. Joan. 4, 10. & 7, 17. Genes. 49. Psal. 58. 4. Jerem. 17, 2. Jacob. 2, 26. 2 Cor. 4, 8, 9. 1 Cor. 15, 4, 5, 47. Exemplar, ex quo discas, quomodo thema amplificandum sit, nullum præstantius epistola ad Hebræos, ubi judicio adhibito illud elegantissimè deprehendes, quo modo & ex locis scripturæ, citatis cap. 1. & explicatis, cap. 7. ac 9. & argumentis à simili cap. 7. & 12, 9, 24. & 13, 12. à contrario cap. 3. & 4. à minori cap. 2, 2. & cap. 10, 28. & 12, 25. à definitione, & exemplis cap. 11. restractanda sit.
units.tr: XIII. Next follows the amplification of the Document, which consists in this: that all the things brought forward here, the explanation and proof of the Document, should be amplified worthily and aptly, which can be done from nearly all the places of argument, but especially from contrasting and comparing things. For examples of the former see Psalm 1:4, Isaiah 45:10, 2 Corinthians 4:8, 9, 1 Peter 1:18, 19, or where something is asserted by way of negation and by way of affirmation [κατ' ἄρσιν, κατ' θέσιν]: Romans 8:1, not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit; John 3:16 and 1:20; Psalm 32:5; Hebrews 10:9, he takes away the first that he may establish the other; and chapter 12:18. Examples of the latter, namely of comparisons, are almost endless; here belong Christ's parables, Matthew 13, John 4:10 and 7:17, Genesis 49, Psalm 58:4, Jeremiah 17:2, James 2:26, 2 Corinthians 4:8, 9, 1 Corinthians 15:4, 5, 47. As a model from which you may learn how the theme is to be amplified, none is more outstanding than the Epistle to the Hebrews, where, with judgment applied, you will most elegantly perceive how it is to be handled: from the passages of Scripture cited in chapter 1 and explained in chapters 7 and 9; from arguments from likeness in chapters 7 and 12:9, 24 and 13:12; from the contrary in chapters 3 and 4; from the lesser in chapter 2:2 and chapter 10:28 and 12:25; from definition and examples in chapter 11.

units.la: XIV. Quaeritur. primò: An hic quoque exemplis locus? Resp. prout exempla quoque demonstrant quid verum sit, ita hic etiam adferenda; verùm prout dicunt, quid debeat fieri, vel omitti, ad usus pertinent. Jac. 2, 20. Vin scire, o vane homo, quod fides absque operibus est mortua? Abraham Pater noster &c. Hoc proprie est exemplum Documenti.
units.tr: XIV. Question. First: Is there room for examples here also? Answer. Just as examples also show what is true, so they are to be brought forward here too; but insofar as they say what ought to be done or omitted, they pertain to uses. James 2:20: Do you wish to know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Abraham our father etc. This is properly an example of the Document.

units.la: XV. Quae. II. An pro concione liceat adferre profana, & dicta, vel facta Gentilium? Resp. Vix, & quia facile hic & graviter à Junioribus & temerariò, atque per imprudentiam peccari solet, hasce damus cautiones. I. Non licet illa adferre ad merum ornatum, vel ostentationem, & applausum populi. Hieronymus epist. ad Nepotiam: nihil tam facile, quam vilem plebeculam & indoctam concionem, linguae volubilitate decipere, quae quidquid non intelligit, plus miratur. M. Tullius, in quem pulcherrimum illud elogium est: Demosthenes tibi praripuit, ne esses primus orator: tu illi, ne solus: in oratione pro Quinto Gallo, quid de favore vulgi, & de imperitis concionatoribus loquatur: attende, ut his fraudibus ludaris. Loquor enim, quae ipse nuper expertus. Vnus quidam Poeta nominatus &c. Nihil in Concionatore aeque reprehendo, quam ostentationem sui vanam, & aurae popularis captationem, ubi illam affectat potius quam ut animas Christo capter, ac lucretur, quum autem in id propendere populus soleat, & quoque Concionatoris animus, nihil tam enixè studere debet, quam ne hoc ullo pacto videatur agere. Optimè & cordatè Chrysosth. homil. ad Antioch. 28. Laudatis dictis, plausibus mihi non est opus, neque laudantium vocibus & tumultu. Vnum duntaxat volo, ut cum quiete & intelligentia audientes, quae dicuntur, faciatis. Hoc mihi pro plausu, hoc mihi pro laudatione. Lutherum (& quantus ille Concionator!) dicere solitum fuisse refert Melchior Adamus, in ejus vita: tres caniculas concionatori in suggestum adducendas minime esse, vid. superbiam, avaritiam, invidiam; illasque conciones probabat maxime, quæ puerliter, trivialiter, popula-riter, & simplicissime docerent. Contra dum Ecclesia detinetur profanis, & Gentilibus inaniter allatis, ab aliis, gravioribus & sanctis abducuntur, atque perit simul concionis sacræ vis, & efficacia. II. Ne Gentilia nimium adferantur, ne illa vel præferri vel saltem conjungi cum sacris videantur, & nos plus hisce, quam sacris illis studuisse: quod in concionibus Papicolarum notari potest, illis præcipue, quas ante reformationem habebant. Foxus in Martyrol. Anglico Vol. 1. sol. 517. narrat atque ridet merito concionem Episcopi, quam habuit in condemnationem beati Martyris Johann. Huffi, supra Rom. 6, 6. & ita incipiebat: Apparet authoritate Aristotelis libro de cælo & mundo &c. Ridiculas & profanas illorum conciones lepide & falsè perstringit ac refert Henricus Stephanus in erudito tractatu, Apologie pour Herodote: Ne de Erasmo dicam, cui obiter in omnibus pœne scriptis illi Concionatores vapulant, nominatim in Colloquiis, & Ecclesiaste. III. At præter illud, liceat pro concione adferre Gentilium quoque dicta & facta, verum non nisi ad convictionem, id est, ut per illorum consensum, de veritate aliqua, & per illorum exemplum, de praxi nostros homines convincamus; quod vim haud exiguam tum habet. Jer. 18, 13. idcirco sic ait Jehova, interrogate jam inter gentes, quis audierit talia: rem valde fedam fecit virgo Israelis. & cap. 2, 10, 11. Adde Matth. 12, 27. sic Augustinus de doctrinâ Christian. lib. 2. cap. 40. docet illa à Gentilibus, tanquam injustis possessoribus repetenda esse, sicuti Israëlitæ cum Ægyptiis egerunt. Nonne aspicimus quanto auro, & argento & veste suffarcinatus exierit de Ægypto Cyprianus doctor suavissimus, & martyr beatissimus, quanto Lactantius? Quanto Victorinus, Optatus, Hilarius? ut de vivis taceam, quanto innumerabiles Graeci? Clementis Alexandrini Stromata jam cogites. Ita inter scriptores N. Test. Paulus Apostolus ter Gentilium dicta citavit, nempe Act. 17, 28. 1 Cor. 15, 25, Tit. 1, 12. non ad ornatum, ut videtis, inanem, neque sæpius, sed ad convictionem & confusionem necessariam; quando enim vel de Gentili, vel cum Gentil. res nobis est, tum apte illos in testes adduci, est extra omne dubium. Hinc & de Poëtarum versibus ac dictis in concionem adducendis, quid judicemus, facile liquet. Hieronymi illud dictum est, epist. ad Eustoch. pag. 145. Adeo illis adulterium etiam linguæ placet. Quæ enim communicatio luci ad tenebras? qui consensus Christo cum Belial? quid faceret cum Psalterio Horatius? cum Evangelis Maro? cum Apostolis Cicero? & Gregorius: in uno ore se cum laudibus Iovis Christi laudes non capiunt, lib. 9. epist. 48. estque in jure Pontificio dist. 86. ca. cum multa. Quare audiendus relinquitur Amesius, Medull. Theol. cap. 35. §. 54, 55, 56, 57. quem vide.
units.tr: XV. Question. II. Is it permissible to bring forward profane sayings and deeds of the Gentiles in a sermon? Answer. Scarcely. Because young preachers often sin here, easily, seriously, rashly and through carelessness, I give these cautions. I. It is not permitted to adduce such things merely for ornament, display, or the applause of the people. Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus: Nothing is so easy as to deceive a common and unlearned congregation with fluent speech, since it admires all the more whatever it does not understand. Marcus Tullius, to whom belongs that most beautiful praise: Demosthenes snatched from you the chance of being the first orator; you took from him the chance of being the only one; in his speech for Quintus Gallius, speaks of the favour of the crowd and of unskilled preachers: note how you are mocked by these tricks. For I speak of things I have lately experienced myself. A certain poet, named ... In a preacher I find nothing so blameworthy as vain self-display and the hunting after popular breath, when he aims at this rather than at catching and winning souls for Christ. Since the people are usually inclined to this, and the preacher's own mind too, he ought to strive most earnestly of all not to seem to be doing it in any way. Chrysostom excellently and wisely, in homily 28 to the Antiochenes: I have no need of praise for my words, nor of the voices and uproar of those who praise. I desire only one thing: that you act upon what is said, with quiet and understanding. This is my applause, this is my praise. Melchior Adam, in his life of Luther (and what a great preacher he was!), reports that Luther used to say that three little dogs must by no means be brought up into the pulpit, namely pride, covetousness, and envy; and he especially approved those sermons which taught in a childlike, plain, popular and most simple manner. On the other hand, while the Church is occupied with profane matters and with the idle citing of Gentiles, it is drawn away from weightier and holier things, and at the same time the power and effectiveness of the sacred sermon perishes. II. Gentile material should not be cited too much, lest it appear to be preferred to, or at least joined with, the sacred, and lest we seem to have devoted more study to these things than to those sacred ones. This can be noted in the sermons of the Papists' adherents, especially those they gave before the Reformation. Foxe, in the English Martyrology, vol. 1, p. 517, relates and rightly laughs at a sermon of a bishop which he delivered in condemnation of the blessed martyr John Huss (see above on Romans 6:6), and which began thus: It is clear from the authority of Aristotle's book On the Heavens and the World, etc. Henri Estienne, in his learned treatise Apologie pour Herodote, wittily and truthfully lashes and reports the ridiculous and profane sermons of these men. I say nothing of Erasmus, whom those preachers are thrashed by almost everywhere in his writings, by name in the Colloquies and in the Ecclesiastes. III. But apart from that, it is permitted in a sermon to adduce also the sayings and deeds of the Gentiles, but only for conviction, that is, so that we may convince our people, by the agreement of the Gentiles, of some truth, and by their example, of practice. This has no small force. Jeremiah 18:13: Therefore thus says the LORD: ask now among the nations who has heard such things; the virgin of Israel has done a very horrible thing. And chapter 2:10-11. Add Matthew 12:27. Thus Augustine, in On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 40, teaches that such things are to be reclaimed from the Gentiles as from unjust possessors, just as the Israelites dealt with the Egyptians: Do we not see with how much gold, silver and clothing the most sweet teacher and most blessed martyr Cyprian went out of Egypt, and how much Lactantius did? How much Victorinus, Optatus, Hilary? to say nothing of the living, how much countless Greeks? You may now consider the Stromata of Clement of Alexandria. So among the writers of the New Testament, the apostle Paul cited the sayings of the Gentiles three times, namely Acts 17:28, 1 Corinthians 15:25, and Titus 1:12, not for empty ornament, as you see, nor more often than necessary, but for conviction and the necessary confutation. For when we have to do with a Gentile, or with the Gentile matter, it is beyond all doubt that it is fitting to bring them forward as witnesses. Hence it is easy to see what we should judge about bringing the verses and sayings of the poets into a sermon. That saying of Jerome is in his letter to Eustochium, p. 145: So much do they even take pleasure in the adultery of the tongue. For what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What would Horace do with the Psalter? Maro with the Gospels? Cicero with the Apostles? And Gregory: In one mouth the praises of Jupiter and the praises of Christ cannot fit together, book 9, letter 48; and it is in the Pontifical law, Distinction 86, chapter cum multa. Therefore Amesius, Medulla Theologiae, chapter 35, §§ 54, 55, 56, 57, remains to be heard, whom please consult.

units.la: XVI. Quær. III. An Theologorum, vel Patrum (quos appellamus) dicta; factaque adferre pro con- cione liceat? Resp.
units.tr: XVI. Question III. Is it lawful to bring forward in a sermon the sayings and deeds of theologians, or of the Fathers (as we call them)? Answer.

units.la: Uti in præcedenti quæstione diximus, ita hic. I. Ad ostentationem, quo animo sæpius id fieri solet, ei, qui nomini suo, non animis aliorum lumen affundere conatur, (inquit de talibus Verulamius in præf. Novi Organi) nefas est. II. Neque ad merum ornatum, quia ille quum humanus sit, obfuscat & adulterat vim verbi merè divinam, estque ἀσπίβλημα inconveniens Matth. 9, 16. III. Neque nimium illa adferenda. IV. Neque sentenzsententias ex illis communes, & nulla se emphasi commendantes: quorsum enim tum Patris alicujus nomen prætendatur, quum quivis Theologus idem dicere & melius forte posset? Unde simul patet qui & ubi hic peccent, nempe I. Qui nulla necessitate, vel causa quam proferre possint, quæve pateat, citant illa promiscue, quorum cum omnibus expensis, nulla ratio deprehendi potest, quam puerilis ostentatio, unde plus à junioribus, vel in scriptis Theologorum aut Patrum minus exercitatis peccari hic solet, quibus plus vanitatis, quam delectus & judicii saepe adest. II. Si judicemus, ac si concio non constet, nisi ejusmodi citationes interlabantur, & nos vel alios non bene concionatos æstimemus, nisi exotica talia audiantur; quasi concio non ex verbi Dei efficacissima & viva tractatione, sed humanorum dictorum & hujusmodi purpurei sæ commixtione æstimari debeat, contr. 1 Cor. 1, 1, 17, 19. & 11, 1. &c. III. Quando majori cura, expressione, & observatione videntur illa citari, quam loca scripturæ, & hæc non tam diligenter & presfim urgeri, ac quidem deberent, quod pæne est studio ædificationem Ecclesiæ, quam spiritus perscripturæ tractationem ἐνέργεια, impedire, & quasi velle suspendere ac divertere. Sic nempe patet, ut hic tum peccetur, I. In puritatem, sanctitatem & efficaciam verbi divini. Psalm. 19, 8. &c. II. In articulum illum religionis, de Auctoritate Patrum non nimium efferenda vel adorandā, etenim quā alias ratione putamus evenisse, ut ad tantam authoritatem, quam Pontificii illis indulgere videntur, pedetentim Patres pervenerint, nisi potissimum illa in concionibus doctrinis omnibus promiscua & crebra citatione? quod ideoque tam gnaviter adhuc Pontificii Concionatores observant. III. Peccant in populi attentionem & ædificationem, ignota dum & non canonica ita citra discrimen vel judicium jactantur, Licere tamen aliquo casu illa quoque pro concione adferre, non negaverim. Zanchius Tom. 8. orat. de conserv. puro Dei verbo, tres hosce casus constituit: I. Propter pervicaciam haereticorum. II. Propter malevolorum calumnias. III. Et infirmorum fratrum imbecillitatem, quibus casibus Patrum dicta citare concedit; eosdem iisdem verbis ponit Amesius caf. Confc. lib. 4. cap. 26. Nos ita respondemus, ut liceat. I. Quando paradoxum aliquod, vel quod videatur paradoxum, aut arduum & graviter controversum, sive in negotio fidei, sive praxi probandum nobis venit. Ita Chrysost. ferm. de anathematte (quod rarissime vel nunquam forte praeterea agit) in re difficiliori alium citat. Vultis discere, qualia de hoc sanctus quidam dixerit, qui & Apostolorum temporibus martyrium meruit? Monstraturus hujus verbi gravitatem tali utebatur exemplo, &c. Sive casus sit, qualis Basilii, calumniam ideo patientis, quod in doxologia dixisset: Gloria Patri per Filium, cum Spiritu Sancto quod dixisset cum Spiritu Sancto tali dico casu, optimo jure consensum Patrum adfert, ad Amphiloch. de Spir. sanct. cap. 29. tantum abest ut reprehendi illud debeat, vel possit. II. In disputatione contra haereticos, nominatim contra Pontificios ubi & Patres & Pontificios contra eos adferre maximi usus est, & sic contra alios, dum id demonstrare conamur, illorum doctrinam jam olim ab Ecclesia condemnatam fuisse & confutatam. III. In exempla, nempe haud exigui illud fructus, & efficaciae deprehenditur, exempla & facta aliorum in casibus conscientiae ac praxeos adferre, sive ex Patribus illa, sive ex historia Ecclesiastica infimae, aut cujusvis aetatis, immo ex Gentilibus, & undequaque ea adducantur, quae ad commovendum omnino multum valent. At cave exempla & facta incertæ fidei adferas, ut ex Prato spirituali, Vitis Patrum &c. Aliter quando vel dubitat Concionator, num proferre illa liceat, vel Auditores malunt unicè sacris Canonicis intenti hærere, cum minimâ mentis diversione, cautissimè talia adhibeat, vel potius omittat. Quando verò res postulare videtur, ut Patrum sententiæ etiam audiantur, præterquam quod ex propriâ lectione & observatione illa deceret expromere, varia ad id etiam adjumenta sunt, quæ vix sinent diligentiam tuam in conquirendis iis frustari, præter Commentaria, & Tractatus Theologorum, qui Patrum dicta quoque adferunt, & Florilegia, sive Polyantheas, consule ipsos Patrum in locum, quem velis commentarios. Scripsit quoque Jesuita Antonius Dauroultius flores exemplorum, sive Catechismum historialem, volumen satis crassum in quarto, nisi quod ut plurimum legendas & fabellas Papales congerat, præter Theat. historicum Hondorffii, ne de Theatro vitæ humanæ Zuingeri dicam, etiam Reinerus Bachovius in Catechesin Palatinam Patrum sententias annotavit, quod quoque post Harmoniam Confessionem factum, & jam nuperrimè à Cl. Forbeshio in Instruct. Historico-Theol. Ne de expositionibus Patrum conjunctis loquar, quales Catena Patrum in Jobum, Johannem, etiam Partem Psalmorum, & Jesaiam, Græc. Patrum in Pentateuchum, auctore Francisco Zephyro Florentino; in epist. ad Rom. Theoduli Coelesyrienf. qui extat in bibl. Patrum, vel de Ant. Monachi Melisses, sive loc. Comm. qui quoque in bibl. P. P. aut Euthymii Zigabeni Panoplia. Judicium de Patribus hic addere non necesse, præter id quod superiori thesi ex Augustt. citavimus de Doctr. Christ. lib. 2. cap. 40. eundem adi lib. 4. cap. 21. Hieron. Tom. I. epist. ad Paulinum pag. 104. Sidon. Apollinarem lib. 4. epist. 3. Cassiodorum Institut. cap. 18. ex veteribus. Adde his Erasm. in præf. ad Cyprianum. Et Ecclesiasticis lib. II. pag.2. 18. ubi illorum, & Patrum quoque judicia de Patribus reperies. Confer de citandis Patrum dictis pro concione, judicium Amesii cap. cit. qu. 4. & 5. Primerose in præf. la trombette de Sion. Director. Anglic. parce adferat dicta Ecclesiasticorum, aliorumve humanorum scriptorum, quantumcunque elegantia.
units.tr: As we said in the previous question, so here too: (I) it is wrong to do this for display, which is the usual motive for it. As Verulam says of such people in the preface to the New Organon, he who tries to shed light on his own name, and not on the minds of others, does wrong. (II) Nor should such material be brought in for mere ornament, since human ornament, however fine, dims and corrupts the purely divine force of the word, and is an ἐπίβλημα [patch] that does not fit (Matt. 9:16). (III) Nor should these things be cited too often. (IV) Nor should we bring forward sentences that are commonplace and recommend themselves by no distinction. For why should the name of some Father be put forward when any theologian could say the same thing, and perhaps better? From this it is also clear who sins here, and where. (I) They sin who, with no necessity or reason they can state or that is evident, cite such things indiscriminately. Once all the circumstances are weighed, no reason can be found for it except childish display. Juniors, or those less practised in the writings of theologians and Fathers, commonly sin in this way, since they often have more vanity than discernment and judgment. (II) They sin who judge that a sermon is not sound unless such citations are interspersed, and who think a preacher, or another, has not preached well unless such exotic things are heard. As if a sermon should be valued not by the most effective and living treatment of the Word of God, but by a mixture of human sayings and such purple patches. Compare 1 Cor. 1:17, 19, and 11:1, etc. (III) They sin when those citations seem to be made with greater care, precision and attention than the passages of Scripture, and when the latter are not pressed as diligently and vigorously as they ought to be. This is almost to hinder the edification of the Church, and to wish to suspend and divert the energy of the Spirit through the treatment of Scripture. Clearly, then, one sins here: (I) against the purity, holiness and efficacy of the divine Word (Ps. 19:8, etc.); (II) against that article of religion concerning the authority of the Fathers, which must not be exalted or adored too much. For by what other means do we suppose that the Fathers have gradually come to that great authority which the Papists seem to grant them, if not chiefly by this constant and indiscriminate citation of them in sermons on all doctrines? This is why the Papist preachers still observe it so zealously. (III) They sin against the attention and edification of the people when unknown and non-canonical things are thus bandied about without discrimination or judgment. Yet I would not deny that in some case it is lawful to bring such things forward in a sermon too. Zanchius, in the eighth volume of his orations, On the Preservation of the Pure Word of God, lays down three such cases: (I) on account of the obstinacy of heretics; (II) on account of the slanders of the malicious; (III) and on account of the weakness of brethren who are feeble. In these cases he allows the citation of the sayings of the Fathers. Amesius sets down the same cases in the same words in caf. Confc. lib. 4. cap. 26. We answer thus, that it is lawful: (I) when some paradox, or what seems a paradox, or a difficult and gravely controverted matter, whether in a question of faith or of practice, comes to be proved by us. Thus Chrysostom, in his sermon de anathemate (which he hardly ever or never treats otherwise), cites another in a more difficult matter: Do you wish to learn what a certain holy man, who earned martyrdom even in the times of the Apostles, said about this? Wishing to show the weight of this word, he used such an example, etc. Or let the case be like that of Basil, who suffered slander because in the doxology he had said Glory to the Father through the Son, with the Holy Spirit, where he had said with the Holy Spirit. In such a case, I say, he rightly brings forward the consent of the Fathers, to Amphilochius, On the Holy Spirit, chap. 29. So far is it from the case that this ought to be, or can be, blamed. (II) In disputation against heretics, especially against the Papists, where it is of the greatest use to bring forward both the Fathers and the Papists against them; and likewise against others, when we try to show that their doctrine was long ago condemned and refuted by the Church. (III) In examples. It is clear that there is no small fruit and efficacy in bringing forward examples and deeds of others in cases of conscience and practice, whether those examples come from the Fathers, or from ecclesiastical history of any age, lowly or otherwise, or even from the Gentiles. Wherever they are drawn from, such things are very powerful for moving the hearer. But beware of bringing forward examples and deeds of doubtful faith, such as those from the Spiritual Meadow, the Lives of the Fathers, etc. Otherwise, when the preacher doubts whether it is lawful to produce such things, or when the hearers would rather cling solely to the sacred canonical books with the least distraction of mind, he should use such material most cautiously, or rather omit it. When, however, the matter seems to require that the sayings of the Fathers also be heard, it would be fitting to bring them forth from one's own reading and observation. There are also various aids for this, which will hardly let your diligence in seeking them be frustrated: besides the commentaries and treatises of theologians, who also bring forward the sayings of the Fathers, and the florilegia or polyanthea, consult the Fathers themselves on the passage you wish, in their commentaries. The Jesuit Antonius Dauroultius also wrote Flores of Examples, or a Historical Catechism, a fairly thick volume in quarto, except that for the most part he heaps up Papal legends and fables. Besides the historical Theatre of Hondorff, not to mention Zwinger's Theatre of Human Life, Reinerus Bachovius also annotated the sayings of the Fathers on the Palatine Catechism, which was done also after the Harmony of Confessions, and has just now been done by the distinguished Forbes in his Historico-Theological Instruction. Not to speak of the joint expositions of the Fathers, such as the Catena of the Fathers on Job, on John, also on part of the Psalms and on Isaiah; the Greek Fathers on the Pentateuch, by Francis Zephyrus of Florence; on the Epistle to the Romans, by Theodulus of Coelesyria, which is in the Bibliotheca Patrum; or Antonius the Monk of Melissa, or his Common Places, also in the Bibliotheca Patrum; or the Panoplia of Euthymius Zigabenus. There is no need to add here a judgment on the Fathers, beyond what we cited in the previous thesis from Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chap. 40. Consult the same author, book 4, chap. 21. Jerome, vol. I, letter to Paulinus, p. 104; Sidonius Apollinaris, book 4, letter 3; Cassiodorus, Institutes, chap. 18, among the older writers. Add to these Erasmus in his preface to Cyprian, and the Ecclesiastical writings, book II, p. 2.18, where you will also find the judgments of these men and of the Fathers on the Fathers. On the citing of the sayings of the Fathers in sermons, compare the judgment of Amesius in the chapter cited, questions 4 and 5; Primerose in the preface to The Trumpet of Sion; the English Directory: let him sparingly bring forward the sayings of ecclesiastical or other human writers, however elegant they may be.

units.la: XVII. Quær. IV. An liceat allegorias sectari?
units.tr: XVII. Question 4: Is it lawful to pursue allegories?

units.la: Resp. I. integram concionem, vel concionis partem, facere continuatam allegoriam, vitium est, uti Origines solet, qui Homilia in Genef. 2. ubi de arca agit, concionum suarum hanc rationem exponit. Verum quoniam arca, quam describere conamur, non solum bicamerata, sed & tricamerata à Deo construi jubetur; operam demus & nos ad hanc duplicem, quæ præcessit, expositionem, secundum præceptum Dei etiam tertiam jungere. Prima enim, quæ præcessit, historica est, veluti fundamentum quoddam in inferioribus posita. Secunda hæc mystica, superior & excelsior fuit. Tertiam, si possimus moralem tentemus adjicere. Neque minus Bernardus in allegoriis sæpe luxuriat, vide ejus sententias, explicationes in Cantica, sermonem de tribus panib. &c. silvam illam umbrosam latebrosamque allegoriarum, inquit in Cantic. serm. 16. Hoc ergo caveatur. II. Ne allegoriæ sint inanes, incertæ, vel falsæ, contra certitudinem & analogiam fidei, quod peccatum facile committunt, qui verborum lusibus & figuris sæpe magis intenti sunt, quam rei. III. Sobriæ vero, & certæ ac perspicuæ allusiones, accommodationes, metaphoræ, sive allegoriæ probandæ veniunt, & etiam usurpare licet: Quemadmodum scripturam quoque idem facere videmus, Gal. 4,24. Rom. 10,18. Confer Amesium loc. cit. qu. 7.
units.tr: Answer: First, to make an entire sermon, or a part of a sermon, one continuous allegory is a fault. Origen is given to this, and in his Homily on Genesis 2, where he treats of the ark, he sets out this method for his sermons. However, since the ark we are trying to describe is ordered by God to be built not only with two chambers but with three, let us also, following the command of God, add a third to the twofold exposition that has gone before. For the earlier exposition is historical, lying as a kind of foundation in the lower parts. This second, the mystical, is higher and loftier. Let us try to add a third, the moral, if we can. Bernard likewise often indulges in allegories. See his opinions and his explanations on the Song of Songs, and his sermon on the three loaves, etc. He calls it that shady, hidden forest of allegories in Sermon 16 on the Song. This, then, must be guarded against. Second, allegories must not be empty, uncertain or false, contrary to the certainty and analogy of faith. Those who are more intent on plays of words and figures than on the matter itself easily commit this fault. Third, sober, certain and clear allusions, applications, metaphors, or allegories are to be approved, and it is also permissible to use them, just as we see Scripture doing the same, Gal. 4:24, Rom. 10:18. Compare Amesius, loc. cit., question 7.

units.la: XVIII. Quær. V. An Concionatori hoc spectare & studere liceat, quo delecter? Resp. simpliciter ut dele-
units.tr: XVIII. Question 5: Whether it is lawful for a preacher to aim and strive at this, that he may give delight?

units.la: delectet, atque in eo subsistat, neutiquam, 2 Tim. 4, 3, 4. Verum in docendo, vel severitatem, vel gratiam etiam pro re nata adhibere debet, 1 Cor. 4, 21. 2 Tim. 4, 2. sed ut moveat, atque aedificet ad fidem & pietatem. In Concilio Burdigal. Anno 1552. ita constitutum: caveant summopere Praedicatores, ne in suis concionibus fabulas, jocos, dicteria, & scommata, quibus risus excitetur, intermisceant; Concionatoris enim est, non risum movere, sed lachrymas auditoribus excutere. Bochell, lib. 1. decret. Eccles. Gallic. pag. 40. Adde Eraim. de rat. concion. lib. 2. pag. 224.
units.tr: Answer: Simply to delight, and to rest in that, is by no means permissible (2 Tim. 4:3–4). But in teaching he ought to use either severity or kindness as the occasion requires (1 Cor. 4:21, 2 Tim. 4:2), but so as to move and build up to faith and godliness. The Council of Bordeaux in 1552 decreed this: Preachers must take the greatest care not to mix into their sermons fables, jokes, witticisms and scoffing, by which laughter is provoked; for it is the task of a preacher not to move to laughter, but to draw tears from the hearers. Bochell, book 1 of the Decrees of the Gallican Church, p. 40. Add Erasmus, On the Method of Preaching, book 2, p. 224.

units.la: XIX. Quær. VI. An liceat concionem vel concionis partem exscribere, & mutuari ab alio? Resp.
units.tr: XIX. Question 6: Is it lawful to copy out a sermon, or part of a sermon, and borrow it from another? Answer.

units.la: Integram vel potissimam partem ab alio tacitè usurpare, arguit Concionatoris insciitiam, vel desidiam; quando vero illud abest, conceptus nonnullos aliorum elegantes suos facere, iisque uti, quia commodissimi videntur ad instruendam, movendam & aedificandam Ecclesiam, nostris quantum per Dei gratiam licet, additis, ne otio nostro plus, quam Ecclesiae usui videamur consuluisse, non video quid niji liceat. Audiamus Chrysostomum jam tum suo tempore conquierentem, lib. 5. de sacerdotio: Si quem forte ex Concionatoribus contigerit partem aliquam eorum, quae ab aliis elaborata fuerint, suis ipsius concionibus intertexere, certè pluribus opprobriis obnoxium se reddit, quam qui alienas opes suffurantur, quum aliqui etiam saepe fiat, ut concionator ne aliunde quidem mutuatus quidquam, sed ea dere tantum suspectus, instar furis alicujus in ipso furto deprehensi habeatur.
units.tr: To use another's whole sermon, or its chief part, secretly, shows the preacher's ignorance or laziness. But when that is absent, I do not see why it should not be lawful to make some of the elegant concepts of others our own and to use them, because they seem most suitable for instructing, moving and building up the Church, provided we add our own, as far as God's grace permits, lest we seem to have consulted our own idleness rather than the use of the Church. Let us hear Chrysostom, already complaining in his own time, in book 5 On the Priesthood: If it happens that some preacher weaves into his own sermons some part of those things that have been worked out by others, he certainly exposes himself to more reproaches than those who steal the wealth of others. Indeed, it often happens that a preacher who has borrowed nothing from elsewhere, but has only been suspected of having plagiarised, is regarded as a thief caught in the very act of theft.

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE.

units.la: I. POst Documentum, ejusque elaborationem, & amplificationem veniunt Vsus, sic dicti, quia quærunt, cui usui aut bono documentum illud fit: idque ex locutione Apostolica 2 Tim. 3, 16. scriptura divinitus inspirata, & ὠφέλιμος utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem illam quæ est in justitiâ. Hinc ratio Usuum venit, faciuntque ad penitiorem institutionem, admonitionem &c. Adde Rom. 14, 4. Potest etiam applicatio, & conclusio ad conscientiam dici: Perkinsus applicationem vocat, cap. 7. de unic. rat. conc. Applicatio est, qua doctrina recte collecta pro ratione loci, temporis, personæ varie accommodatur. Ezech. 34, 16 Amesius: usus est axioma Theologicum ex doctrinâ deductum, utilitatem, bonitatem, vel finem ejus ostendens. Medull. lib. 1. cap. 35. Consectarios usus vocat Strefo in Technol. Theol. Ita quod in Documento generaliter erat propositum, illud hic particularissimè, cuilibet, & ad quosvis conscientiæ casus applicatur, hoc est, quod dicitur. 2 Tim. 2, 15. ὀρθοτομοῦντα recte secantem verbum veritatis. 1 Tim 6, 17. Divitibus in hoc sæculo annuncia non superbire, &c. Patet differentia inter Documentum & Usum, quod Documentum in genere loquatur, Usus in specie; illud, quid debeat fieri; hoc, quid tu debeas facere. V. g. quod Psal. 118, 22. dicitur: lapis, quem ædificantes repudiarunt, à Petro Act. 4, 2. applicatur: hic est lapis à vobis ædificantibus, repudiatus. Usum applicationem, conclusionem facit & exprimit, dum ad Judæos, vobis inquit. Ita Hebr. 12, 5. num obliti estis consolationis, quæ vobis, ut filiis dicit: fili mi ne vilipende instructionem Domini &c. Jef.61,1,2, 3. Act.2,22. Job.5.27. Tit.2,1,2. Recte Alsted. lib.5. systems. Theol. cap. 9.: textus sit concionis radix centrum doctrinae, seu loci communes sint rami: usus, doctrinarum sint fructus: applicatio usus, sit fructuum decerptio & fruitio. Usus & applicatio Usus nobis idem sunt, ipse usus in applicatione consistit & proprie loquendo Documentum in usu applicatur, atque ita ulterius semper procedit, & pedetentim tandem fructus animae ingeruntur. Basil. Tom. 1. serm. in verb. Mos. attende tibi: magna profectio ex hoc verbo utilitas, non solum male habentibus, sed etiam valentibus provenit. Nam idem & hos a morbo liberat, & illos omnino perficit. Etenim quisque nostrum, qui hoc sermone erudiamur, unum hoc curandum habet, ex illis quae per Euangelium nobis praecipiuntur. Nam in Ecclesia, velut in magna domo vasa non solum aurea & argentea, sed lignea & testacea, & omnis generis artes exstiunt. Habet namque domus Dei, quae Ecclesia Dei viventis est, venatores, Viatores, architectos, aedificatores, agricolas, pastores, athletas, milites. Omnibus his coaptatur, & quadrat hoc breve verbum, cuilibet & agendi diligentiam, & propositi studium inculcans. Breviter & accurate Strefo in Technol. Theol. pag. 142. Inter Consectarios usus & ipsam doctrinam, concionis thema, non tantum ea differentia est, quod haec materialiter, illi tantum virtualiter in textu continentur, sed & haec, quod cum doctrinae absque affectibus mera theorica, procedant, usus e contra ad praxin tendunt, doctrinae explicant, usus applicant, doctrinae ferunt leges, usus exequuntur, elaboratio doctrinae est quasi qui tormentum aut bombardam instruit, ex qua deinde usus velut exploduntur, adeo ut inter doctrinas & usus fere interfit, quantum inter verbera & verba, & usus sint quasi reales & actuales argumentationes.
units.tr: After the Document and its elaboration and amplification come the Uses, so called because they ask what use or benefit the Document has. This is drawn from the apostolic words of 2 Tim. 3:16, "all Scripture is given by inspiration of God," and is [ōphelimos] "profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Hence comes the reasoning of the Uses, which serve for more inward instruction, admonition, and so on. Add Rom. 14:4. The application and conclusion may also be called the bringing home to conscience. Perkins calls it "application," in chapter 7 of De unica ratione concionandi: "Application is that by which doctrine, rightly gathered, is variously adapted according to the place, time, and person." Ezek. 34:16. Ames: "Use is a theological axiom deduced from doctrine, showing its usefulness, goodness, or end." Medulla, book 1, chapter 35. Strefo, in Technologia Theologica, calls them "consectarian uses." So what was stated generally in the Document is here applied in the most particular way, to each person and to every case of conscience. This is what is said at 2 Tim. 2:15, [orthotomounta], "rightly dividing the word of truth," and at 1 Tim. 6:17, "Charge those who are rich in this present age not to be proud," and so on. The difference between Document and Use is clear: the Document speaks in general, the Use in particular. The one says what ought to be done; the other says what you yourself ought to do. For example, what is said at Ps. 118:22, "the stone which the builders rejected," is applied by Peter at Acts 4:2: "this is the stone rejected by you builders." The Use makes and expresses the application and conclusion when he says "you" to the Jews. So too Heb. 12:5: "Have you forgotten the exhortation which speaks to you as to sons: My son, do not despise the chastening of the Lord," and so on. See also Isa. 61:1-3; Acts 2:22; Job 5:27; Titus 2:1-2. Alsted rightly says, in book 5, chapter 9 of his Systema Theologicum: the text is the root of the sermon and the centre of doctrine, or the common places are its branches; the doctrines are the fruits of the uses; the application of the use is the picking and enjoying of the fruits. For us, Use and application are the same thing: the use consists in the application. Properly speaking, the Document is applied in the Use, and so it always goes further, until at last the fruit is poured into the soul. Basil, Opera, vol. 1, sermon on the words "Take heed to yourself": "Great profit comes from this word, not only to those who are unwell but also to those who are well. For it frees the former from disease and brings the latter to perfection. Each of us who are instructed by this sermon has one thing to attend to, from among those things which are commanded us through the Gospel. For in the Church, as in a great house, there are vessels not only of gold and silver but also of wood and earthenware, and arts of every kind. For the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, has hunters, travellers, architects, builders, farmers, shepherds, athletes, soldiers. This short word fits all of them and suits them, urging on each both diligence in acting and zeal for his purpose."

units.la: Uti in Documentis formandis id requiritur, ut perspicue ostendatur quomodo illa ex textu fluant, ita in usibus idem patere debet, quomodo e Documentis deriventur: Ususque omnes sunt vel dogmatici, vel practici, (quemadmodum Documenta, nam similiter hic plane res se habet, nisi quod particularis fiat applicatio, sicuti jam dictum) illi fidem, hi mores, veritatem illi, hi pietatem & praxin spectant: Perkinsus dicit, Applicationem Noëticam, vel Practicam. Noëtica, quæ mentem respicit, estque vel διδασκαλία, vel ἐλεγχος. Quos ita Tertullianus in Apolog. conjungit, Certe fidem sanctis vocibus pascimus, spem erigimus, fiduciam figimus disciplinam præceptorum nihilominus inculcationib. densamus, ibidem etiam exhortationes, castigationes, & censura divina. Et Augustinus lib. de doctr. Christian. 4. cap. 4. debet igitur divinarum scripturarum tractator, & doctor, defensor rectæ fidei, ac debellator erroris, & bona docere, & mala dedocere: atque in hoc opere fermines conciliare adversos, remissos erigere, insicientibus quid agatur, quid exspectare debeant, intimare.
units.tr: As in forming Documents it is required that it be clearly shown how they flow from the text, so in the Uses the same should be evident, namely how they are derived from the Documents. All Uses are either dogmatic or practical, just as Documents are (here the matter stands in exactly the same way, except that the application becomes particular, as has already been said). The former look to faith, the latter to morals; the former to truth, the latter to piety and practice. Perkins calls them the noetic or practical application. The noetic application, which regards the mind, is either [didaskalia] teaching or [elenchos] refutation. Tertullian joins these together in his Apologeticus: "Surely we feed faith with holy words, we raise hope, we fix confidence; we also press home the discipline of precepts by repeated exhortation; in the same place there are also exhortations, rebukes, and divine censure." Augustine too, in De doctrina christiana 4, chapter 4: "The expounder and teacher of the divine Scriptures ought therefore to be a defender of the right faith and a fighter against error, to teach what is good and to unteach what is bad; and in this work he must reconcile the hostile, raise up the slack, and make known to the idle what is to be done and what they ought to expect."

units.la: III. Vius dogmatici sunt triplices, ita commodius omnia capita, quæ hic dari possunt, completi arbitramur. I. Ad veritatis alicujus certiorem & penitiorem instructionem, observationem, vel confirmationem. II. Vindicationem. III. Erroris Consutationem. Vel enim veritas solum observatur & confirmatur, vel ab exceptionibus Adversariorum vindicatur, vel error, atque argumenta Adversariorum refutantur. V. g. Gal. 3. 13. hoc documentum datur: Passione Christi maledicta redimimur ex maledictione legis. Hinc Usus dogmaticus. I. Ad confirmationem veritatis de satisfactione Christi, quam hinc probo & demonstro. II. Ad vindicationem, ejus ab expositionibus, quas V. g. in hunc locum dat Crellius, (cujus lectiones in hanc epistolam excepit, & edidit Schlichtingius) Nempe examinatur hic exceptio-
units.tr: III. The dogmatic Uses are threefold; we think it more convenient to gather in this way all the heads that can be given here. I. For a more certain and inward instruction, observation, or confirmation of some truth. II. Vindication. III. Refutation of error. For either the truth is only observed and confirmed, or it is vindicated against the objections of adversaries, or error and the arguments of adversaries are refuted. For example, at Gal. 3:13 this Document is given: "We are redeemed from the curse of the law by the passion of Christ." Hence the dogmatic Use: I. For the confirmation of the truth about Christ's satisfaction, which I prove and demonstrate from this passage. II. For its vindication against the expositions which, for example, Crellius gives on this passage (whose lectures on this epistle were taken down and published by Schlichting). Namely, here the exceptions are examined

units.la: {y} Cf. Schlichtingius, ad Gal. 3. exceptiones contra rem textus, ut exceptiones contra phrasim in expositione analytica, videlicet hic redemtionis veritas vindicatur, à figurâ illa, quam Sociniani faciunt. III. Hinc jam quoque arguo & disputo contra hæresim Socinianam ipsam, & offendo quam impia istorum sit, & execranda doctrina. Antea per ἀναστηδὴν jam per καθεστηκυῖαν, uti Christus ita quoque de resurrectione disputat ad Marc. 12,24,26. & Actor. 15,24. Distinctio Usus vindicatorii & refutatorii magis manifestus est in locis, quibus Adversarii ad errorem suum abutuntur; ibi enim vindicatio ut necesse, ita sufficit, nisi quoque ex loco contra illos disputatio concedatur.
units.tr: {y} Cf. Schlichting, on Gal. 3: the exceptions against the matter of the text, as the exceptions against the phrasing in the analytical exposition. That is, here the truth of redemption is vindicated against that figure which the Socinians make of it. III. Hence I also now argue and dispute against the Socinian heresy itself, and show how impious and detestable is the doctrine of these men. Earlier [anastasin] and now [kathestēkuian], just as Christ also disputes about the resurrection at Mark 12:24-26 and Acts 15:24. The distinction between the vindicatory and refutatory Use is more evident in those passages which the adversaries abuse for their error. For there the vindication is necessary and also sufficient, unless a disputation against them is also granted from the passage.

units.la: IV. Observanda in usu elenctico, & disputatione concionum hæc sunt.
units.tr: IV. What is to be observed in the elenctic use and in the disputation of sermons.

units.la: I. Ne hæreses, vel errores antiquos, ignotos, incertos referamus, aut illa, quæ nefanda & blasphema, neque sciri populo expediat, & horrore suo offendunt magis, quam ædificant, imprudenter proferamus. Neque etiam subtilia & obscura tractentur, ne moveamus quod auferre non possumus, uti concinnè monet Augustinus de Doctr. Christ. lib. 4. cap. 20. qualem agendi modum merito in suis Polyd. Virgilius, de invent. lib. 5. cap. 9. confutatio est inquit, argumentorum contrariorum dissolutio, qua nostri Theologi in suggestis sermocinando nonnunquam utuntur, magis ad ostentationem doctrinæ, quam ad utilitatem, & quæ addit, ibi vide. II. Ne nimium, vel per totam fermè concionem, & quotiescunque concionamur, neque etiam libenter disputemus, quidlibet in controversiam facilè arripientes; sed ut qui non nisi coacti ad pugnam descendunt: neque enim hoc officii nostri per se est, sed per accidens, & ut Amesius bene loquitur: controversiarum scientiam necessariam nobis fecerunt hæretici. sed studium pietatis, ut absolutè necessarium, Deus ipse mandavit. In paraenesi post casus Consc. quem locum, cum, ad rem hanc apprime facientem, omnino videas volo. III. Citra privatos affectus, odium, iram, vel contentionem disputatio sancte, pro veritate non pro gloria instituatur; nunquam acrius in hæreticos & errores, quam in morum vitia & peccatores invectus; videris alioqui non ita veritatis & conscientiæ, aliorumque convertendorum studio, quam quidem tui vindicandi, & explendi animi causâ egisse. Vide Amef. caf. cap. cit. qu. 14. & medull. cap. cit. §. 40. Director. Anglic. cap. cit.
units.tr: I. Do not raise old, unknown or uncertain heresies and errors, nor carelessly bring forward those that are wicked and blasphemous, which the people ought not to know and which offend by their horror more than they build up. Nor should subtle and obscure matters be handled, lest we stir up what we cannot put down, as Augustine neatly warns (de Doctr. Christ. lib. 4, cap. 20). Polydore Virgil rightly criticises this manner of proceeding in his work de inventione (lib. 5, cap. 9): refutation is, he says, the dissolving of contrary arguments, which our theologians sometimes use when preaching from the pulpit, more for the display of learning than for usefulness. He adds further points there, which see. II. Do not overdo it, either throughout nearly the whole sermon or every time we preach, and do not gladly engage in disputation, seizing on whatever comes to hand as a matter of controversy; rather, let us enter the fight only when compelled. For this is not in itself a part of our duty, but incidental to it, and as Amesius rightly says: heretics have made a knowledge of controversies necessary for us, but God himself has commanded the pursuit of piety as absolutely necessary. On this point, which bears most directly on the matter, I want you to look carefully at the paraenesis after the cases of conscience. III. Let disputation be conducted holily, free from private feelings, hatred, anger or contentiousness, for the sake of truth and not of glory. Never inveigh more sharply against heretics and errors than against the vices of morals and sinners; otherwise you will appear to have acted not so much out of zeal for truth, conscience and the conversion of others, as for the sake of avenging yourself and satisfying your own spirit. See Amesius, Casus conscientiae, the chapter cited, question 14, and Medulla, the chapter cited, §40; and the Director Anglicanus, the chapter cited.

units.la: Quær. An hæreses cum suis Auctoribus & scriptis semper distinĉte nominandæ sint? Resp. Non cum suis Auctoribus, & scriptis, nisi necessitas id poftulet, & illam eorum sententiam esse probari hoc pacto necesse fit: alioqui enim tantum illis, ut pro concione nominari mereantur, concedi nolim.
units.tr: Question. Should heresies always be named distinctly together with their authors and writings? Answer. Not together with their authors and writings, unless necessity requires it, and unless it must be proved in this way that such is their opinion. Otherwise I would not like to grant them, merely so that they might deserve to be named from the pulpit.

units.la: V. Sequuntur usus Practici, qui faciunt. I. Ad informationem, & directionem in praxi, ubi consulitur, quid agere hoc vel illo statu conveniat. Deinde, ad admonitionem, ut hoc agamus, & alterum caveamus: duplex ergo est, continetque adhortationem, & dehortationem, vel triplex potius, ut comprehendat quoque reprehensionem, quando officio in alterutro, vel utroque desumus. Tertio ad consolationem, voce consolationis generalius sumpta.
units.tr: V. There follow the practical uses, which are these. I. For information and direction in practice, where one asks what it is fitting to do in this or that state. Next, for admonition, that we should do this and beware of that. The use is therefore twofold, and contains exhortation and dissuasion, or rather threefold, so as to include also reproof, when we fail in one or both of these duties. Thirdly, for consolation, the word being taken in a more general sense.

units.la: VI. Primò Vsus informationis Practicæ, vel directionis est axioma vel conclusio ex Documento Theologica, dicens, quid ergo in vitæ praxi nos conveniat observare, & agere vel cavere, atque talis usus plerumque exsurgit ex Documento Dogmatico, vel (fi ita velis dicere) Theoretico, ante admonitionem, cujus fundamentum est hic usus, & ad illam via. Puta, documentum fit: Deus est ubique præfens, ex hoc Documento, præter usus dogmaticos, & elenĉticos, fluit primum hic practicus: ergo ubicunque fumus, Deum semper præsentem habere necesse est est instructio ad praxin. Neque ille est usus admonitionis accurate loquendo, sed is sequitur: Ergo id agamus sedulo, ut semper ita coram Deo præsenter ambulemus. Distincta illa sunt, illud instruit de officio, hoc excitat ad officium: neque est quod dicas, ejusmodi instructionem ad usus Dogmaticos spectare, quia judicium informant, non enim id, quod judicium informat, id eo omne ad dogmatica, ut Practicis contra distinguuntur: sed proximus finis, quo quidlibet spectat, differentiam hic facit, nempe si referatur ad informandum judicium de veritate aliquâ, an immediate de praxi. Illud discernet Usum hunc a Dogmaticis, & simul liquet, quo distinguatur ab usu admonitionis; nam admonitionem ducit, hancque continet pæne eo modo, quo de Documento diximus. Usus virtualiter & proximè in Documento contineri. Hoc enim semper hic videndum, ne saltus committatur, sed omnis progressus certò instituatur per conclusiones, quæ quot occurrunt, totidem quasi gradus fiunt. Nempe Deus est ubique præsens, hoc documentum. Ergo vera est doctrina, quam Ecclesia docet de divinæ essentiæ omnipræsentiâ. Hic usus est documenti dogmaticus ad Confirmationem. Porrò, Ergo male docent hæretici loca illa de omnipræsentiâ Dei non intelligenda esse de ipsa Dei omnipræsentia, vel hanc doctrinam calumniantur. Usus ad vindicationem. Ulterior Conclusio, & usus ad Confutationem: Improba ergò Hæreticorum est sententia, de omnipræsentiâ Dei solum secundum virtutem & imperium, exclusâ essentiâ. Nam &c. Usus ad praxin: Ergo ubicunque sumus, Deum præsentem habere necesse est, non aliter &c. Conclusio inde ulterior: Ejus ergo hoc agamus, & Deum sic semper præsentem gestemus, intueamur, &c. Viam ergo ad admonitionem proximam sternit Usus instructionis, quo instruimur ad praxin, ut illo admoneamur, estque usus, quem Apostolus vocat ἀρεῖς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, usus παιδεντικός. Sic, quando Documentum est de vitio aliquo V.g. Infidelitatem esse gravissimum peccatum Usus informationis practicæ est. cavendam maximè esse infidelitatem. Ad quod sequitur tum dehortatio. Quamvis sciam, plerumque hæc confundi, vel omitti solere, ob arctam utriusque communionem, vel temporis causâ: distinguí tamen patuit.
units.tr: VI. The first, the use of practical information, or direction, is an axiom or conclusion drawn from a theological doctrine, saying what in the practice of life it becomes us to observe, to do or to avoid. Such a use commonly arises from a dogmatic, or (if you like to call it so) theoretical, doctrine, and comes before admonition; this use is its foundation and the way to admonition. For example, let the doctrine be: God is present everywhere. From this doctrine, apart from the dogmatic and elenctic uses, there first flows this practical one: therefore, wherever we are, we must always have God present, which is instruction for practice. This is not, strictly speaking, the use of admonition, but what follows from it: therefore let us take care to walk always in this way, present before God. These are distinct: the former instructs about duty, the latter stirs us up to duty. Nor can you say that such instruction belongs to the dogmatic uses because it informs judgement; for what informs judgement is not for that reason all dogmatic, in contrast to practical things, which are distinguished in this way. Rather, the immediate aim to which anything is directed makes the difference here, namely whether it is referred to informing the judgement about some truth, or immediately to practice. That will distinguish this use from the dogmatic ones, and at the same time it will be clear how it is distinguished from the use of admonition, for it leads to admonition and contains it almost in the same way as we said of the doctrine. The use is virtually and most nearly contained in the doctrine. For here one must always see to it that no leap is made, but that every progress is securely made through conclusions, each of which, as they occur, becomes as it were a step. Thus: God is present everywhere, this is the doctrine. Therefore the doctrine which the Church teaches concerning the omnipresence of the divine essence is true. This use of the doctrine is dogmatic, for confirmation. Further: therefore the heretics teach wrongly, and calumniate this doctrine, when they say that those passages about God's omnipresence are not to be understood of God's omnipresence itself. This is the use for vindication. A further conclusion, and the use for confutation: therefore the opinion of the heretics is wicked, that God's omnipresence is only according to power and command, with his essence excluded. For &c. The use for practice: therefore, wherever we are, we must have God present, not otherwise &c. A further conclusion from this: let us therefore do this, and bear and behold God always thus present, &c. So the use of instruction, by which we are instructed for practice so that we may be admonished by it, prepares the way to the immediate admonition, and it is that use which the Apostle calls παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ [paideian tēn en dikaiosynē], the paedeutic use. So, when the doctrine concerns some vice, for example: unbelief is the most grievous sin, this is the use of practical information: unbelief above all is to be avoided. Dissuasion then follows from this. Although I know that these are commonly confused or omitted, because of the close fellowship between the two, or for the sake of time, it has nonetheless been shown that they are distinct.

units.la: VII. Usus Admonitionis (voce admonitionis latius sumtâ, ut illud Apostoli quoque ἀρεῖς ἐπι-νουθεσίαν) tria nobis, sicuti diximus, complectitur. I. Adhortationem, & hic ad virtutem, atque virtutis exercitium, homines excitantur. Hebr. 3, 13. Verum exhortamini vosmet, donec dies vocatur, &c. & cap. 10. 22. Ephes. 5, 17. Præter adhortationem duo hic potissimum consideranda veniunt. I. Motiva, quibus ut stimulis adhibitis quis acrius excitetur, & II. Media, quibus quis ad id pervenire studeat, & queat, ad quod adhortatur, quodque excitatus jam velit. Motiva quæcunque adhibentur, sunt duum generum, rationes, & exempla. Rationes judiciosè hic distingui debent ab iis, quæ allatæ sunt ad probandum documentum, & uti ibi diximus in illis assignandis plerumque peccari, ita hic adhuc magis, vixque nisi sedulâ attentione, exacto judicio & usu id addiscitur, quomodo & quæ rationes utrobique adferendæ sint & distinguendæ: ideoque cavendum, junioribus potissimum, ne hic nimium liberales sint, (uti fere solent quando ad hanc methodum concionari incipiunt) in adferendis rationibus, & motivis designandis. Hoc distinctionis inter utrumque est, licet motiva quoque rationes appellemus, (quia utraque argunt) quod rationes Documenti ex natura rei docendæ, & in Documento tractandæ ducuntur; motiva vero ex ratione nostri, & relatione, ac respectu quam res præstanda ad nos, quos adhortamur, proxime habet. v. c. illud est verum, vel bonum, ob rationes quas ipsa rei istius natura fundit, & dictat: Hoc vero nobis agendum, quia ita nobis id perquam necessarium est, & conducit: quare hic maximum usum habent argumenta ducta ex necessario, utili, decenti, honorifico, jucundo &c: ut mittam circumstantias temporis, Hebr. 10, 25. 1 Pet. 4, 3. loci, personarum, nos, & quos adhortamur, proprie tangentes.
