Vide Hebr. 3, 13, 14. Verum adhortamini vosmet &c. Nam participes facti sumus Christi, nempe si initium hypostasis usque ad finem firmum tenuerimus. Motivum ex decenti, & necessario, Phil. 4, 8. Heb. 12, 14. & 13, 13, 14, 16, 17. & 4, 14, 15, 16. Ephes. 5, 16. Deinde & exemplorum hic proprius locus est, ut quibus homines maxime percelli ac moveri solent. Heb. 2, & 13, 1, 2, 3. quæ exempla ex sacris, Ecclesiasticis, & Profanis etiam adferri possunt, ut maxime animos moveant, ac persuadeant. Non minor cautio in mediis proferendis adhiberi debet ac judicium, nempe ut sint I. Certa, quo qui illa observet, etiam virtutem assequatur: quorsum enim alias secerint? II. Proxima, quæ ad illam virtutem, proprium & specialem respectum habeant, ac causalitatem: ne proferas generalia illa, precari, audire Dei verbum, &c. bona quidem illa, sed nondistincte media sunt nisi communia, & si semper æquè adferri possunt, nisi quando de tali agitur virtute, quam propiori qua ratione spectant, & tangunt, tum rite ut media convocantur. Mediorum quoque usum Christus docet Joan. 6, 21. dixerunt autem ei, quid faciemus, ut operemur opera Dei? respondit Iesus, ac dixit illis: hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in illum, quem ipse misit. Adde Joan. 14, 5. Heb. 12, 15. Mich. 6, 6, 7, 8. Psal. 151, 2. &c.
units.tr: VII. The use of admonition (taking the word admonition more broadly, as in the Apostle's ἐπι-νουθεσίαν [epi-nouthesian]) embraces three things for us, as we have said. I. Exhortation, by which men are stirred up to virtue and to the practice of virtue. Heb. 3:13: But exhort one another while it is called "Today", &c.; and ch. 10:22; Eph. 5:17. Besides exhortation, two things chiefly need to be considered here. (1) Motives, by which, as spurs applied, a man may be more keenly stirred; and (2) means, by which a man may strive and be able to reach that to which he is exhorted, and which, once stirred, he now wishes to attain. The motives that are used are of two kinds, reasons and examples. Reasons must be carefully distinguished here from those adduced to prove the doctrine; and as we said there, mistakes are commonly made in assigning them, so here even more, and this is hardly learned except by diligent attention, exact judgement and practice: how and what reasons are to be brought forward and distinguished on each side. Therefore, young men especially must take care not to be too lavish here (as they usually are when they begin to preach in this method) in bringing forward reasons and assigning motives. The difference between the two is this: although we also call motives reasons (since both argue), the reasons of the doctrine are drawn from the nature of the thing to be taught and are treated within the doctrine, whereas motives arise from our own condition and from the relation and respect which the thing to be done has most closely to us whom we exhort. For example: this is true or good, on account of the reasons which the very nature of the thing pours forth and dictates; but this we must do, because it is most necessary and advantageous for us. Hence arguments drawn from what is necessary, useful, fitting, honourable, pleasant, and so on, have the greatest use here; not to mention circumstances of time, place and persons, which touch us and those whom we exhort most directly. See Heb. 3:13, 14: But exhort one another &c., for we have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end. A motive from what is fitting and necessary: Phil. 4:8; Heb. 12:14; 13:13, 14, 16, 17; 4:14, 15, 16; Eph. 5:16. Then, examples have their proper place here too, since men are chiefly moved and stirred by them. Heb. 2; 13:1, 2, 3. Such examples may be drawn from Scripture, from ecclesiastical history and even from profane writers, so that they may most powerfully move and persuade minds. No less caution and judgement must be used in putting forward means; namely, they should be (1) certain, so that whoever observes them also attains the virtue, for otherwise to what end would they be prescribed? and (2) proximate, having a proper and specific bearing on that virtue and a causal connection with it. Do not put forward those general things, to pray, to hear God's word, and so on: they are good, but they are undistinguished means, unless they are common means, and if they can always be brought forward equally, except when a particular virtue is in question, which they regard and touch by a nearer reason; only then are they rightly called as means. Christ also teaches the use of means, John 6:28–29: They said therefore to him, "What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?" Jesus answered and said to them, "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." Add John 14:5; Heb. 12:15; Mic. 6:6–8; Ps. 151:2, &c.

units.la: Præter motiva, & media veniunt hic quoque Modi, qui sunt qualitates & rationes, docentes quo modo & qualiter illas virtutes observare debeamus, petunturque ex virtutis, de quâ agitur, propriis affectionibus. Heb. 13, 3. memores sitis vinctorum, ac quomodo ? ut quoque vincti. Eorum, qui male habent, ut qui ipsi quoque in corpore adhuc estis, Ephes. 5, 15. Videte, ut accurate ambuletis non ut insipientes, sed sapientes.
units.tr: Besides the motives and the means, there are also here the Modes, which are the qualities and manners that teach how and in what way we ought to observe those virtues. They are drawn from the proper characteristics of the virtue under discussion. Heb. 13:3: "Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body." Eph. 5:15: "See that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise."

units.la: Observandum hic illud unicè venit, ut jam Concionator moveat, & ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων Matth. 7, 29. & ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως 1 Cor. 2, 4. loquatur, agat, concitetque. Nihil hic præterea attendat, nihil curet, ubi omnis concionis, & ejus quod ante dictum vis contracta, accensa, & in attentionem devota omnia, quam movere, & moveri. Isque optimè concionatus est, tum ex judicio Dei, tum Ecclesiæ, qui efficacius moverit. Huc facit I. Auditores jam crebrius interpellare, alloqui, attentionem & animos eorum iterum vellicare, pungere & erigere, cum omni instantiâ, efficaciâ, longanimitate, simul comiter & graviter ἵνα δῶ χάριν τῆς ἀκοῆς Eph. 4, 29. 2 Tim. 2, 25. & 4, 2. Ita & Bucholtzerus apud Keckermannum Rhetor. Eccles. pag. 49. judicat, modum conquerendi, obtestandi, gemendi, exorandi, idque ex animo, & omni sensu, hic optimum esse.
units.tr: The one thing to observe here is that the preacher should now move his hearers, and speak, act and stir them "as one having authority" (Matt. 7:29 [ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων]) and "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power" (1 Cor. 2:4 [ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως]). He should pay no attention to anything else and care for nothing else, since the whole force of the sermon, and of what has been said before, is gathered together, kindled and devoted to gaining attention, namely, to moving and being moved. That preacher has preached best who has moved most effectively, both by the judgment of God and by that of the Church. To this end serves: first, to interrupt the hearers more often, to address them, to pluck at their attention and their minds again, to prick and rouse them, with all urgency, efficacy and patience, and at once kindly and seriously, "that it may minister grace to the hearers" (Eph. 4:29 [ἵνα δῶ χάριν τῆς ἀκοῆς]; 2 Tim. 2:25; 4:2). So Bucholtzer, cited by Keckermann in his Ecclesiastical Rhetoric, p. 49, also judges that the manner of complaining, adjuring, groaning and entreating, and that from the heart and with every feeling, is here the best.

units.la: 2 Cor. 5, 20. Ut Dei per nos admonentis, precamur Christi causâ. Psal. 135, 9. contra te ô Ægyptus 1 Joan.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:20: "As though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead." Ps. 135:9: "Against thee, O Egypt." 1 John [...].

units.la: 2. II. Repetere, & sæpius inculcare adhortationem. Hos. 2, 2. Contendite cum Matre vestrâ, contendite. Marc. 13, 33. videte, vigilate, orate. 35. vigilate ergo. 37. quod vero vobis dico, vigilate. Aliis, atque aliis, verbis idem proponere, & urgere,
units.tr: 2. II. To repeat the exhortation and to inculcate it more often. Hos. 2:2: "Plead with your mother, plead." Mark 13:33: "Watch and pray." 35: "Watch therefore." 37: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." To propose the same thing in other and other words, and to press it.

units.la: Marc. xii, 14. Augustin. de verbis Dom. serm. 63. Tenete quod audistis, breviter replico, & rem utilissimam quantum existimo mentibus vestris collocandam committo. Bernardus: nam iteratio, affectionis expressio est. serm. 61. in Cantica.
units.tr: Mark 12:14. Augustine, On the Words of the Lord, sermon 63: "Hold fast what you have heard; I briefly repeat it, and I entrust a most useful matter, as far as I judge, to be lodged in your minds." Bernard: "For repetition is the expression of feeling," sermon 61 on the Song of Songs.

units.la: VIII. In Usu dehortationis eodem modo procedi- tur, nisi quod hic dehortemur homines à vitiis, & peccatis.
units.tr: VIII. In the use of dissuasion one proceeds in the same way, except that here we dissuade people from vices and sins.

units.la: Eph. 5; 18. Et ne inebriemini vino. Hebr. 10, 35, & 3, 13. videte fratres, ne quando in aliquo nestrum sit cor pravum infidelitatis. Hic similiter locum habent motiva per rationes Eph. 5, 18: vino, in quo est temulentia. Hebr. 10, 35, 36. Et per exempla Hebr. 12, 16. Ne quis sit scortator, aut profanus, sicut Esau. Verum, quod, in usu adhortationis sunt media, hic remedia dicuntur, quia de expugnando & repellendo male agitur, ut Marc. 12, 9. quid ergo faciet Dominus vineæ? adde Hos. 2, 5. Quo etiam faciunt cautiones, quibus sibi quis cavet ab iis, quæ in malum queant ipsum deducere. Jes. 7, 4. cave tibi ut sis quietus, ne timeto &c. Deut. 4, 9. tantum cave tibi, & serva teipsum valde. Luc. 21, 34. In cautionibus ejusmodi adhibendis diligens est, & eminet inter Concionatores Anglicos Thomas Gataker.
units.tr: Eph. 5:18: "And be not drunk with wine." Heb. 10:35 and 3:13: "See, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief." Here the motives by reasons likewise have place: Eph. 5:18, "wine, wherein is excess"; Heb. 10:35-36. And by examples, Heb. 12:16: "Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau." But since in the use of exhortation there are means, here they are called remedies, because the matter concerns driving out and repelling evil, as in Mark 12:9: "What shall the lord of the vineyard do?" Add Hos. 2:5. To this also belong the cautions, by which someone guards himself against those things that could lead him into evil. Isa. 7:4: "Take heed, and be quiet; fear not." Deut. 4:9: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently." Luke 21:34. In applying such cautions Thomas Gataker is diligent and stands out among English preachers.

units.la: Quær. Uter usus in tractatione debeat præcedere, an adhortationis, an dehortationis? Resp. si documentum sit de virtute, usus adhortationis, quia ille proximus est; si de vitio, dehortationis usus, ob eandem rationem. Non quod semper & ubique uterque usus adhibendus sit, sed quando consultum videtur utrumque tractari.
units.tr: Question. Which use should come first in treating a matter: that of exhortation or that of dissuasion? Answer. If the doctrine concerns a virtue, the use of exhortation should come first, since it is nearer; if it concerns a vice, the use of dissuasion, for the same reason. Not that both uses must always and everywhere be applied, but when it seems expedient to treat both.

units.la: IX. Usus reprehensionis est; ubi ex textu & docu- mento textus objurgantur homines de non præstito officio, sive erga virtutem, sive contra peccatum.
units.tr: IX. The use of reproof is that in which, from the text and the doctrine of the text, men are rebuked for failing in their duty, whether toward virtue or against sin.

units.la: 2 Tim. 4, 2, 3. Prædica verbum, insta opportunè, importunè: redargue, objurga &c. Et hic maxime usu convenit ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα ... neque cum nim accepimus [piritum timiditatis, sed potentiæ, & amoris & temperantiæ. cap. 1. 6. 7. Hebr. 5, 12. Matth. 3, 7. &c. & 23. Gal. 3,1. Vel in jure Canonico est 1. dist. 45. ca. sed illud: In populum ira Dei defcevit, cum Prædicator delinquentes palpat, & non corripit. & 1. dist. 86. ca. Inferiorum: Negligentiæ Rectorum imputantur culpæ inferiorum. Reprehensio debet fieri. I. Generaliter ἀνδ̀ συσσωπολἠψίας, in quoscunque peccantes, omnia vitia, vel in Regem 2 Sam. 12, 1. 1 Reg. 18, 18. &21, 20. Ambrof. lib. 5. epist. de Theodosio: Dilexi virum, qui magis arguentem, quam adulantem probaret, & orat. in Auxentium: Respondi ego quod sacerdotis est; quod imperatoris est, faciat Imperator. Prius est, ut animam mihi, quam fidem auferat. Vide de Mari episcopo Julianum increpante, Socratem histor. lib. 3. cap. 12. Et lib. 6. cap. 5. de Chrysostomo: & alium quoque ex Primoribus aliam ob causam multa cum libertate reprehendit, propter quam multis exosus erat. Gregorius in Pastorali par. 2. cap. 4. Sæpe namque Rectores improvidi, humanam amittere gratiam formidantes, loqui libere recta pertimescunt: & juxta veritatis vocem nequaquam jam gregis custodiæ pastorum studio, sed mercenariorum vice deserviunt: quia veniente lupo fugiunt, dum se sub silentio abscondunt. II. Reprehendi & notari debent vitia particularissimé; non quidem exponi, ut doceantur, sed castigari, ut omittantur; in generalibus hærere neutiquam sufficit, dum in specialibus se obducere homines, solent & vitia quo fuco palliant, eo excusant; atque pauciores gravia illa ac enormia peccata committere videri volunt, propterea que se nec tangi, quando de iis in genere sermo; magis τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης confundenda sunt, & peccatorum larvæ detegendæ, quo redargutio nostra certius & intimius pungat, moveat, corrigatque: & sanè, dum subtiliores quotidie peccandi viæ excogitantur, & patrocinia, profundiori examine & inquisitione opus hic esse quoque dubitare nemo potest: ipsam cordis arcem, peccati progressus, schematismos, exceptiones, defensiones subtiliores quasque maxime impetere necesse est, & curare Marc. 7, 6. Bene de vobis hypocritis concionatus est Isaias. Qui tamen sibi neutiquam videbantur hypocritae. Apoc. 2, 4. Verum habeo contra te &c. verf. 14. Lege & attendissime relege Ezhech. cap. 13. contra eos, qui leviter populo imponunt, dum non sincere corripiunt; atque adde, si placet gravissimam Boltoni contra tales dissertationem in Instruct. consol. Anglice. pag. 150. &c. Origenes in Genef. Homil. 10. asperior furtasse vobis videar, sed non possum limire parietem lapsantem. Tertullianus: nullis veternis parcor, nulli impetigini, de Pallio. Vide & Jus Canonic. 1. dist. 46. cap. sunt nonnulli. Mich. 2, 2. III. Reprehensio libera sit, ex animo non timido, non pusillo, sed virili, sancto, & coelesti, qui inferiora omnia despiciat. Ex Ambrosio id citat Hincmarus Rhemensis epist. 5. cap. 1. Non est Imperiale, libertatem dicendi negare: neque Sacerdotale, quid sentias, non dicere. cap.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 4:2-3: "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke," etc. And here most of all this use fits: "to stir up the gift" (2 Tim. 1:6 [ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα]), "for God hath not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind," chap. 1:6-7. Heb. 5:12. Matt. 3:7, etc., and chap. 23. Gal. 3:1. Or in the canon law, Dist. 45, c. sed illud: "The wrath of God falls upon the people when the preacher flatters the sinners and does not rebuke them." And Dist. 86, c. Inferiorum: "The negligence of rulers is imputed as the fault of their subordinates." Reproof ought to be done: I. In general, without respect of persons (ἀνευ προσωπολημψίας), against all sinners and all vices, or even against the king: 2 Sam. 12:1; 1 Kings 18:18; 21:20. Ambrose, Book 5, letter on Theodosius: "I loved the man who showed himself more willing to rebuke than to flatter." And in his speech against Auxentius: "I answered what belongs to a priest; let the emperor do what belongs to an emperor. It is better that he take away my life than my faith." See Socrates, History, Book 3, ch. 12, on bishop Marus rebuking Julian, and Book 6, ch. 5, on Chrysostom: "He also rebuked another of the leading men, with much frankness, for another cause, on account of which he was hated by many." Gregory, Pastoral Rule, part 2, ch. 4: "For often rulers, lacking foresight and fearing to lose human favour, shrink from speaking freely what is right; and, in the words of truth, they no longer serve the care of the flock with the zeal of shepherds, but in the manner of hired men, who flee when the wolf comes, since they hide themselves in silence." II. Vices ought to be reproved and marked most particularly. They are not indeed to be set forth so that they may be learned, but to be chastised so that they may be abandoned. It is by no means enough to remain in generalities, since men are accustomed to hide themselves under particulars and to excuse their vices by the veil with which they cover them, and they wish to seem to commit those grave and enormous sins less often, and so they do not feel touched when the discourse is about them in general. Rather, the hidden things of shame (2 Cor. 4:2) must be exposed, and the masks of sins uncovered, so that our rebuke may pierce, move and correct more surely and more deeply. And indeed, since ever subtler paths of sinning are devised every day, and no one can doubt that here a deeper examination and inquiry is needed, it is necessary to assail and to heal the very citadel of the heart, the progress of sin, its figures of speech, its excuses and its subtlest defences. Mark 7:6: "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites." Yet they did not at all seem hypocrites to themselves. Rev. 2:4: "I have somewhat against thee," etc., verse 14. Read with the closest attention Ezekiel chapter 13 against those who lightly impose upon the people while they do not rebuke sincerely; and add, if you like, Bolton's very serious dissertation against such men in his Instructions for Comfort, English, p. 150, etc. Origen, On Genesis, Homily 10: "I may perhaps seem harsher to you, but I cannot plaster a wall that is falling." Tertullian, On the Pallium: "I spare no old men, I spare no one with a sore." See also Canon Law, Dist. 46, c. sunt nonnulli. Micah 2:2. III. The reproof should be free, given from a heart that is not timid or faint, but manly, holy and heavenly, one that despises all lower things. Hincmar of Reims, letter 5, ch. 1, cites this from Ambrose: "It is not imperial to deny the freedom to speak, nor priestly not to say what you think." (ch.)

units.la: 2. Igitur dicamus liberè Domini Sacerdotes, quae dicuntur notabilia, & reprehensibilia de Rege nostro. Salvianus lib. 5. de provid. Nam aut tacent plurimi eorum, aut similes sunt tacentibus, etiamsi loquantur, & hoc multi non inconstantia, sed consilio, ut putant, atque ratione. Exertam enim veritatem proferre nolunt, quia eam aures improborum hominum sustinere non possunt: nec solum refugiunt, sed etiam odiunt & execrantur, IV. Prudenter tamen adhibeatur. 1 Tim. 5, 1, 2. in quem locum egregie Calvinus: Ubi objurgationes sunt faciendae, summa lenitas adhibenda est, ut intelligat auditor, agi de mera ejus salute. Nam qui acerbius increpat, videtur & odisse, & stomachum petulantius velle effundere; praeterea nihil difficilius est, quam ubi incaluimus, modum ponere nostro fervori: jam vero ubi nos capit impatientia, sine professu contendimus; præterquam enim quod ludibrio est nostra asperitas, etiam irritat populi animos. 2 Tim. 2, 24, 25. Hebr. 13, 22. 1 Joan. 2, 12, 13. Gregor. Pastoral. part. 2. cap. 10. Nonnulla autem vel aperte cognita, mature toleranda sunt, cum videlicet rerum minime opportunitas congruit, ut aperte corrigantur. Nam sœpta immature vulnera deterius infervescunt, & nisi cum tempore medicamenta conveniant, constat procul dubio quod medendi officium amittant. Et per totam tertiam partem hoc agit, ut doceat, quomodo aliter hi, aliter illi admonendi sunt: Ut enim longe ante nos, inquit in prologo, reverendæ memoriæ Gregorius Nazianzenus edocuit, non una eademque cunctis exhortatio congruit, quia non cunctis pars morum qualitas astringit. Sæpe namque alii officiunt, quæ aliis prosunt. Adde Bernard. serm. 44. in Cantic. Augustinum, vel quicunque Auctor. lib. de Ovibus cap. 8. Hinc & illud Zwinglii dictum, quod in concione nonnunquam usurpabat: frommer man, Nims dich nit an. Melch. Adamus in ejus vita. V. Quin & pro rei gravitate acrior fit reprehensio, atque cum sanctâ severitate haud leviter pungens. Jes. 58, 1. 1 Tim. 5, 20. & 2 Tim. 4, 2. Marc. 8, 17. Nec dum cognoscitis, neque scitis, adhuc cor vestrum habetis obduratum? 1 Cor. 3, 1, 3. Gal. 3, 1. &c. Ne adulatio verius videatur quam reprehensio, vel ut inquit Nilus Abbas in Asceticis: ne illis adulemur, qui ea complectuntur, quæ nos despicere professi sumus. Chrysosthomus advers. Judæos orat. 5. in fine. Adhæc vos singulis concionibus adhortari non cesso, sive mentem adhibeatis, sive non adhibeatis, ego dicere non desinam. Nam hanc legem nobis Deus præscripsit, ut sive audieritis, sive non audieritis, hoc ministerium impleamus. Etsi quidem audieritis ea quæ dicuntur, & quæ seq. Adde Ambros. serm. 86. n. jure Canonico 1. dist. 86. can. 5. Veniam à subditis non petat, qui in corripiendo modum excesserit. Vide & Cæsarii Arelat. homil. 8. in Bibl. P. P. & Nazianzeni Orat. in Julianum.
units.tr: 2. "Therefore let the Lord's priests speak freely about what is said of our king that is remarkable and worthy of reproof." Salvian, Book 5, On Providence: "For most of them either keep silent, or are like those who keep silent even when they speak; and many do this not from inconstancy but from design, as they think, and reason. For they are unwilling to bring forth the naked truth, because the ears of wicked men cannot bear it; and not only do they shun it, but they even hate and abhor it." IV. Nevertheless it must be applied prudently. 1 Tim. 5:1-2, on which passage Calvin writes admirably: "Where rebukes must be given, the greatest gentleness is to be used, so that the hearer may understand that the matter concerns his mere salvation. For he who scolds more bitterly seems both to hate and to wish to pour out his bile too wantonly. Moreover, nothing is more difficult than, once we have grown hot, to set a limit to our zeal. Indeed, when impatience seizes us, we contend without restraint; for not only is our harshness a mockery, but it also irritates the minds of the people." 2 Tim. 2:24-25; Heb. 13:22; 1 John 2:12-13. Gregory, Pastoral Rule, part 2, ch. 10: "Some faults, however, even when openly known, must be tolerated for a time, namely, when the opportunity of the circumstances does not agree with openly correcting them. For wounds that are prematurely cut open fester worse, and unless remedies are applied in due time, it is beyond doubt that they lose the office of healing." And through the whole third part he sets out how one should be admonished in one way and another in a different way: "For, as the Gregory of Nazianzus, of long-remembered name, taught long before us," he says in the prologue, "one and the same exhortation does not suit all, because one rule of conduct does not bind all. For often what helps some harms others." Add Bernard, sermon 44 on the Song of Songs; Augustine, or whatever author, On the Sheep, ch. 8. Hence also that saying of Zwingli, which he often used in the sermon: "Pious man, do not take it to heart." Melchior Adam in his life of him. V. Indeed, according to the gravity of the matter, the reproof becomes sharper, and with holy severity it pricks not lightly. Isa. 58:1; 1 Tim. 5:20; 2 Tim. 4:2; Mark 8:17: "Do ye not yet perceive, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened?" 1 Cor. 3:1, 3; Gal. 3:1, etc. Lest it should seem to be flattery rather than reproof, or as Nilus the Abbot says in his Ascetics: "Let us not flatter those who embrace what we have professed to despise." Chrysostom, Against the Jews, Homily 5, at the end: "Besides, I do not cease to exhort you in every sermon, whether you pay attention or not; I shall not stop speaking. For God has prescribed this law to us, that whether you hear or do not hear, we should fulfil this ministry. Although indeed you will hear what is said, and what follows." Add Ambrose, sermon 86. Canon law, Dist. 86, c. 5: "He who has exceeded the measure in rebuking should not seek pardon from his subordinates." See also Caesarius of Arles, Homily 8, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, and Gregory Nazianzen's Oration against Julian.

units.la: X. Usus Consolationis est, quo animus adversus mala hujus vitæ sive spiritualia, sive corporalia ex textu, vel Documento textus confirmatur, & bono contra recreatur, ac lætatur. Jes. 60, 1, 2. Consolamini, consolamini populum meum, dicit Deus vester. & cap. 1. 4. Dominus Jehova dedit mihi linguam eruditorum, ut sciam tempestive eloqui defessō verbum. Phil. 2, 1.
units.tr: X. The use of consolation is that, from the text or from the doctrine drawn from the text, the mind is strengthened against the evils of this life, whether spiritual or bodily, and is refreshed and rejoices in the good. Jes. 60, 1, 2. "Be comforted, be comforted, my people, says your God." And ch. 1, 4: "The Lord Jehovah has given me the tongue of the learned, that I may know how to speak a word in season to the weary." Phil. 2, 1.

units.la: 2 Thess. 5, 14. Hebr. 6, 19. Rom. 15, 4. Quâ autem ratione, & modo debeamus consolari, diximus disp. de consolatione.
units.tr: 2 Thess. 5, 14. Hebr. 6, 19. Rom. 15, 4. We have already discussed in the disputation on consolation in what manner and by what method we ought to console.

units.la: In hoc usu, ut quoque in usu observationis practicæ peculiarem locum habent Signa, quæ sunt argumenta status nostri spiritualis. Joann. 13, 35. In eo cognoscent omnes quod mei discipuli estis, si vos mutuò diligatis; & in epistola Joannis primâ eorum ratio ac usus satis fit manifestus. 1 Joann. 1, 6, 7. & 2, 3. In eo scimus, quod illum cognoscimus, si præcepta ejus servemus, verf. 4, 5, 9. cap. 3, 7, 10. In eo manifesti sunt filii Dei & filii Diaboli: quicunque non operatur justitiam, non est ex Deo, & qui fratrem suum non diligit, verf. 14. Nos scimus, quod ex morte transivimus in vitam, quia diligimus fratres. verf. 19. cap. 4, 2, 6, S. 13, 20. Si quis dixerit: Deum diligo, & odit fratrem suum, mendax est: qui non amat fratrem suum quem vidit, quomodo poterit Deum diligere, quem non vidit? cap. 5, 2, 3. Ita continuò ex amore mutuo & observantia præceptorum Dei ut certissimis signis, argumentum ducens ad veritatem status nostri spiritualis. Adde Marc. 13, 28, 29. Deut. 18, 21. Psal. 15, 1, 2. &c. & Luc. 1, 18. Illud unice & graviter hic monendum est, ut summo cum judicio, ac cautione signa adhibeantur, non facile, non negligenter: haud sanè sane levis illa res est, judicium ferre de alicujus statu & salute, ejusque signa adferre. Cave pecces hic, gravissimè enim in te, ac illos, quos instruis, delinqueres. Juniores hoc praecipuè moneo, qui communi indolis vitio ad difficiliora impotentius solent æstuare; ergò hanc partem omittas potiùs, quam non solidè & verè tractes, quæ maximè maturum judicium, ac praxin deposcit. Neque multa signa adferas, quum res tanta haud facilè multa ferat; neque semper, gravior enim res est, & sanctior, quam ut vulgò audiatur. Planè ut in Medicis, ita hic, signa vel ex rei naturâ petuntur, vel ex causis, vel ex effectis. Vide Sennertum Instit. Medic. lib. 3. part. 1. sect. 1. cap. 3. de signorum sontibus; ita & hic res se habet. V. g. fidei signa apud Practicos petuntur, vel ex naturâ fidei, vel causis fidei, quo pacto fides nobis ingeneretur, vel ex effectis; inter quæ, illa, quæ ex effectis manifestiora sunt, uti Verulamius in Novo Organo loquitur aphor. 73. Inter signa, nullum magis certum aut nobile est, quam quod ex fructibus. Quare hujus generis signa ut tutius, ita libentius premas, atque explices; sed vide, sint certa, ac reciproca, statum meum infallibiliter concludentia, ne sanguinis & animæ te imprudenter reum feceris.
units.tr: In this use, as also in the use of practical observation, the Signs have a special place. They are the proofs of our spiritual state. Joann. 13, 35: In that all men shall know that you are my disciples, if you love one another; and in the first epistle of John their reasoning and use are made sufficiently plain. 1 Joann. 1, 6, 7; 2, 3: In this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments, vers. 4, 5, 9; ch. 3, 7, 10: In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest: whoever does not do righteousness is not of God, and whoever does not love his brother, vers. 14: We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren. vers. 19; ch. 4, 2, 6, 13, 20: If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen? ch. 5, 2, 3. So continually from mutual love and the keeping of God's commandments, as most certain signs, he draws an argument to the truth of our spiritual state. Add Marc. 13, 28, 29; Deut. 18, 21; Psal. 15, 1, 2, etc.; and Luc. 1, 18. Here it must be stated above all and seriously that the signs are to be applied with the greatest judgment and caution, not lightly and not carelessly. It is by no means a slight matter to pass judgment on another's state and salvation, and to adduce his signs. Take care not to err here, for you would most gravely offend both against yourself and against those whom you instruct. I especially warn the younger men, who, by the common vice of their disposition, are wont to rush too headlong at more difficult things. Therefore you would do better to omit this part than to handle it unsoundly and untruly, since it demands the most mature judgment and practice. Nor should you adduce many signs, since so great a matter cannot easily bear many; nor always, for it is a weightier and holier matter than to be treated in the common way. Just as in medicine, so here the signs are sought either from the nature of the thing, or from its causes, or from its effects. See Sennertus, Institutiones Medicae, bk. 3, pt. 1, sect. 1, ch. 3, on the sources of signs; so here too the matter stands. For example, the signs of faith are sought among the practical writers either from the nature of faith, or from the causes of faith, by which means faith is engendered in us, or from its effects. Among these, those which are plainer from their effects, as Verulam speaks in the Novum Organum, aphorism 73: Among signs, none is more certain or noble than that which comes from fruits. Therefore signs of this kind you should press and explain as more safely, so also more willingly; but take care that they be certain and reciprocal, infallibly concluding your state, lest you unwittingly make yourself guilty of blood and of soul.

units.la: XI. Hic Documentorum & Usuum ordo, non eo facit, ut velimus, semper & pro quaque concione illa omnia isthac ratione adferenda esse, vel ut putemus quemlibet isti methodo alligatum esse, neutiquam, sed ut in genere, quæ nobis exactissima videatur concionandi ratio, doceamus, quam quivis sequatur prout status & ædificatio Ecclesiæ suæ videbitur potissimum postulare. Sunt qui de veritate, alii & plerique de praxi magis instruendi sunt, hi exhortandi, illi consolandi, & sic præcipuè attendendum, quid status Auditorum ferat, de quo sollicitè cavet Petkinf. de rat. conc, cap. 7. & Teling. neccess. demonstr. pag. 122. Solum caveatur, ne temere quaelibet confundamus, nihili pensitantes quo quid ordine dicatur, ubi neque conscientiae tuae, neque Auditoribus facis fatis, vel ne divagemur extra omnem textus aut methodi rationem, ne dicatur, quod Bernardus: at fortasse aliquis mihi dicat: bene admones, sed si ea diceres, quae tuo proposito convenirent, ferm. 13. in Cant. Nullibi hoc, minime autem in tam sancta actione probari potest. Vide Amcf. medull. cap. cit. §. 20. Teling. pag. 131. Director. Anglic. (quae tria scripta de ratione concionandi praestantissima sunt, & prae multis commendo,) cap. de conc. verbi inquit, quamvis id Concionatori videatur satis molestum esse, ut fc. Documenta ad usus referat rite, & conscientiis applicet: difficile agnoscens, ut sane est, quando non perfunctorie, sed digne illud instituitur.
units.tr: XI. This order of doctrines and uses does not mean that we wish all of them to be brought forward in this way every time and for every sermon, nor that we think anyone is bound to this method; by no means. Rather, we teach in general what seems to us the most exact method of preaching, which anyone may follow as the condition and edification of his own Church seems chiefly to require. Some must be taught more about the truth, others, and most, more about practice; the former must be exhorted, the latter consoled. Thus attention must be paid chiefly to what the state of the hearers requires, a point on which Perkins is anxiously careful (de ratione concionandi, ch. 7), as is Teling (Necessaria demonstratio, p. 122). Only let care be taken that we do not rashly confuse everything, caring nothing for the order in which things are said, where you neither satisfy your own conscience nor your hearers; nor that we wander outside every rule of the text or method. Lest someone say, as Bernard does: But perhaps someone will say to me: you admonish well, but if you were saying the things that suit your purpose... Sermon 13 on the Canticles. This can be approved nowhere, and least of all in so holy an action. See Amesius, Medulla, ch. cited, §20; Teling, p. 131. The Directorium Anglicanum (these three writings on the method of preaching are most excellent, and I commend them above many others), ch. "de concione verbi," says: although this may seem rather troublesome to the preacher, namely, to refer the doctrines properly to the uses and apply them to consciences; recognising it as difficult, as indeed it is, when it is undertaken not carelessly but worthily.

units.la: Quaer. An in concione ars occultanda, an vero omnium oculis aperte detegenda? Resp. Quum potiffima Ecclesiae pars, fi non omnis, fimplicior fit, & illiterata, quumque quo magis omnis concio retineri potest, eo magis quoque aedificet; judicamus, quo apertius hic constet concionis cum materia & forma, eo melius, contra Oratorum regulam, artis est clare artem, quod non ita hic & omnino verum, ubi concio a vanitate oratoria longius amat discedere, & discrepare. Et sic quod Telingius pag. 131. censet.
units.tr: Question: Should the art be concealed in a sermon, or rather laid openly before the eyes of all? Answer: since the greater part of the Church, if not all of it, is simpler and unlettered, and since the more a whole sermon can be retained, the more it also edifies, we judge that the more openly it is evident how the sermon agrees with matter and form, the better. This is contrary to the rule of the orators, "it is the art to make art clear," which is not wholly true here, where the sermon loves to depart from and differ from oratorical vanity. And so Telingius thinks at p. 131.

units.la: XII. Ad conclusionem, aliquando anacephalaiosis adhibetur, saepius non: neque etiam Rhetores semper eam necessariam arbitrantur. Pro rei pondere, ac Ecclesiae necessitate hic agendum. Heb. 8, 1. κεφάλαιον dictorum, talem habemus sacerdotem summum, qui sedet in dextra throni Majestatis in caelis, Augustinus serm. inter Homil. PP. pag. 24. Sed ut hæc, quæ suggessimus, sensibus vestræ charitatis tenacius inhæreant, breviter quæ dicta sunt, iteramus. Et Bernard. serm. de Clemente Papa: Ergo ut breviter repetam, prima &c. Alioqui abrumpere, nonnunquam cogimur, Bernard. ferm. 61. super Cant. Rumpamus sermonem, nec enim potest finiri modo: ne fit sine modo, si cuncta quæ adhuc ex proposito capitulo restant, uno isto velimus sermone completi. Vel aliquod dictorum summarium adhibemus modo, & sic concludimus, ut Joan. 20, 31. Et sic Ecclesiastes cap. 12, 13.
units.tr: XII. Finally, sometimes a recapitulation is used, more often not; nor do the rhetoricians always consider it necessary. It must be done here according to the weight of the matter and the need of the Church. Heb. 8, 1: the summary of the things said [κεφάλαιον]: we have such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. Augustine, sermon among the Homilies of the Fathers, p. 24: But so that these things which we have suggested may cling more tenaciously to the senses of your charity, let us briefly repeat what has been said. And Bernard, sermon on Pope Clement: Therefore, to repeat briefly, first, etc. Otherwise we are sometimes forced to break off; Bernard, sermon 61 on the Canticles: Let us break off the sermon, for it cannot be finished in this way; lest it be without measure, if we should want all that still remains of the proposed chapter to be completed in this one sermon. Or we may use some summary of the things said, and so conclude, as John 20, 31; and so Ecclesiastes ch. 12, 13.

units.la: XIII. Antiquissimus, & probatissimus ille mos est finiendi in doxologiam, quâ vel simpliciter Deo laus dicatur & honor, vel quoque à Deo petatur ejus gratia ad ea, quæ in concione edocti simus. Ita plerumque finiunt epistolæ Apostolicæ. Rom. 16, 24, 25, 26, 27. 1 Cor. 16, 23. 2 Cor. 13, 13. 1 Thess. 5, 23. 2 Thess. 3, 16, Hebr. 13, 20. 1 Pet. 5, 10. Neque aliter Patrum conciones. Origines Homil. 2. in Genef. Omnipotentis tamen Dei misericordiam deprecemur, qui nos non solum Auditores verbi sui faciat, sed & factores, & inducat super nostras quoque animas diluvium aquæ suæ, & dekat in nobis, quæ scit esse delenda, & vivificet, quæ judicat esse vivificanda, per Christum Dominum nostrum, & per Spiritum suum sanctum. Ipsi gloria in æterna sæcula sæculorum. Amen. Atque ita passim definit: cui gloria & imperium in sæcula sæculorum. Amen. Sic quoque Basilius, Augustinus, qui & votum sæpius addit, quam misericordiam faciat vobis Deus, Amen, aut simile. Cætera, quæ addenda sunt, ut superficiatur sensus vester, à Domino quærite. Bernardi formula est: qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula. Cæsarii Arelatensis: Qui cum Patre & Spiritu sanctovivit & regnat in sæcula sæculorum. Scilicet, ut Apostolus monet 1 Cor. 10, 31. sive quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Lutheri illud erat monitum, ut tum finiret Concionator, quando populum cerneret attentissimum, quo sc. alacrior postmodum iterum rediret.
units.tr: XIII. The most ancient and most approved custom is to end with a doxology, by which either praise and honour are simply given to God, or else his grace is asked of God for those things in which we have been taught in the sermon. Thus the apostolic epistles usually end. Rom. 16, 24–27; 1 Cor. 16, 23; 2 Cor. 13, 13; 1 Thess. 5, 23; 2 Thess. 3, 16; Hebr. 13, 20; 1 Pet. 5, 10. Nor do the Fathers' sermons differ. Origen, Homily 2 on Genesis: Let us, however, pray for the mercy of almighty God, who makes us not only hearers of his word but doers also, and who brings the flood of his waters upon our souls too, and destroys in us what he knows must be destroyed, and gives life to what he judges must be made alive, through Christ our Lord and through his Holy Spirit. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen. And so he ends everywhere: to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. So too Basil and Augustine, who also often adds a wish, may God grant you his mercy, Amen, or something similar. As for the rest, which must be added, that your sense may be made complete, seek it from the Lord. Bernard's formula is: who is God over all, blessed for ever. Caesarius of Arles: who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Clearly, as the Apostle admonishes, 1 Cor. 10, 31: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. It was Luther's advice that the preacher should then end when he saw the people most attentive, so that they might return the more eagerly afterwards.

units.la: Caput Sextum & Ultimum.
units.tr: Chapter Six and Last.

units.la: I. HActenus Concionem formavimus, & uti in initio dictum, omnem concionandi rationem consistere in recte formanda concione, & habenda, sic jam de eo agendum venit, quomodo ea, quam composuisti, ita quoque, id est, bene habeas. Duo autem maxime consideranda, quid observare Concionator debeat. I. Ante concionem. II. In concione. Addit Telingius tertium, quomodo & post concionem, quod ibi vide, necess. demonstrat. pag. 137. & Amef. Caf. loc. cit. qu. ult.
units.tr: I. Hitherto we have formed the sermon, and, as was said at the beginning, the whole method of preaching consists in forming a sermon rightly and delivering it. It now remains to deal with how one should conduct the sermon you have composed, that is, deliver it well. Two things chiefly must be considered, namely what the preacher ought to observe: I. before the sermon; II. during the sermon. Telingius adds a third, how one should conduct oneself also after the sermon, which you may see there; Amesius also (loc. cit., last question) necessarily sets this out, p. 137.

units.la: II. Ante concionem, quemadmodum de vita Concionatoris non necesse est iterum monere, sancta ut sit, ita nec de studiis, ut primum rite didicerit, quae alios doceat. 1 Tim. 5, 13, 15, 16. Ambrof. Offic. lib. 1. cap. 1. Vnus enim verus Magister est, qui solus non didicit, quod omnes doceret. Homines autem discunt prius, quod doceant, & ab illo accipiunt, quod aliis tradant. Ad hoc autem, quod jam unice agimus, illud magis facit ut se digne praeparet Concionator ad Concionem mox habendam.
units.tr: II. Before the sermon: as there is no need to advise again about the preacher's life, that it be holy, so neither about his studies, that he first properly learn what he is to teach others (1 Tim. 5:13, 15, 16). Ambrose, De officiis, book 1, chap. 1: For there is one true Teacher, who alone has not learned what he teaches to all. Men, however, learn first what they are to teach, and receive from him what they hand on to others. For the matter we are now treating, this consideration makes it more important that the preacher prepare himself duly for the sermon he is about to deliver.

units.la: III. Praeparatio haec post compositam concionem, ad eam habendam, consistit in tribus. I. Ut bene imprimat memoriae. II. Magis adhuc animae, id est, sibi primum illa applicet, quae alios docere studet. III. Maxime Deo commendet, id est precetur, & precibus id a Deo obtineat, ut sibi suisque que digne agat, & cum fructu, ad honorem Dei omnino & omnia.
units.tr: III. This preparation for delivering the composed sermon consists in three things: (1) that he impress it well on his memory; (2) that he impress it still more on his soul, that is, that he first apply to himself those things which he is eager to teach others; (3) that he above all commend it to God, that is, pray, and by prayer obtain from God that he may act worthily for himself and his own, and with fruit, entirely to the honour of God.

units.la: IV. Memoriae imprimat, sed non hoc solum, ne concionem videatur habere, ut pueri orationem, ex memoriâ magis, quam ex animo, quod est recitare, non agere; attamen & memoriâ probe teneat, quemadmodum Iudæi de Sacerdote M. referunt, qui se pridie & nocte ad diem propitiationis diligenter præparare soleret, ac perpetuâ cum studiosis super sacrificiorum negotio disputatione, & expósito ordine, quo vellet mane oblationes omniaque fieri, memoriam sic suam exercebat, ne (quod grave piaculum æstimabant,) in ipso die sacro alicubi erraret. Animo autem suo maturè & integrè docenda applicet, ne alios docens ipse ἀδόκιμος sit, ac seriâ & sanctâ meditatione sibi ante loquatur, quam aliis, se commoveat & tum reliquos. Rectissime Prosper Aquitanicus de vit. contemplat. lib. 1. cap. 33. Lachrymas, quas vult à suis Auditoribus fundi, ipse primitus fundat, & sic eos compunctione sui cordis accendat. Et Bernhardus serm. 59. in Cant. Exemplum sane tum in aliis multis, tum vel maxime hoc in negotio verbo efficacius est. Dabis voci tuæ vim virtutis, si quod suades, ipse tibi persuasisse cognoscaris. Inter Martini Dumiensis episcopi sententias, vel in libro ejus de moribus, in bibl. Patrum, & hoc est: Quicquid dicturus es, antequam aliis dixeris, tibi. Ideoque illud probatis Concionatoribus semper est in more, ut habendam coram populo concionem primum sibi, suoque animo funditus applicent, ac persuadeant, atque indeed populum agant, sicque melius observaturi illud Bucholceri, Concinatorem concionari debere ex praxi suâ, & auditorum: atque hinc maxima concioni venit efficacia, & Concionatori Zelus. Gregor. Non enim inflammare verba possunt, quæ frigido pectore proferuntur. Adde Amef.
units.tr: IV. Let him impress it on his memory, but not only this, lest he seem to be giving a sermon as boys recite a speech, from memory rather than from the heart, which is reciting, not acting. Yet let him also know it thoroughly by memory. The Jews relate of the high priest M. that on the day before and during the night before the Day of Atonement he would prepare himself diligently, and by constant discussion with students about the business of the sacrifices, and by rehearsing the order in which he wished the morning offerings and all the rest to be done, he so exercised his memory that he would not (which they judged a grievous sin) go wrong anywhere on the holy day itself. But let him apply what is to be taught to his mind early and thoroughly, lest, while teaching others, he himself be unapproved [ἀδόκιμος], and let him speak to himself by serious and holy meditation before speaking to others, moving himself and then the rest. Prosper of Aquitaine, De vita contemplativa, book 1, chap. 33, rightly says: The tears which he wishes to be shed by his hearers, let him first shed himself, and so kindle them by the compunction of his own heart. And Bernard, sermon 59 on the Song of Songs: Example, surely, is more effective than words, both in many other matters and above all in this business. You will give your voice the power of virtue, if you are known to have been persuaded yourself of what you urge. Among the sayings of Martin, bishop of Dume, in his book on morals, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, is this: Whatever you are going to say, say it to yourself before you say it to others. Therefore it has always been the custom of approved preachers to apply the sermon to be delivered before the people first to themselves and to their own minds thoroughly, and to persuade themselves, and indeed move themselves, and thus to observe more fully that saying of Bucholcer, that the preacher ought to preach from his own practice and that of his hearers. From this comes the greatest efficacy to the sermon, and zeal to the preacher. Gregory: For words cannot inflame when they are delivered from a cold heart. Add Amesius,

units.la: caf. [illegible, ~6 letters]af. cap.' cit. qu. 13. Teling. lib. cit. p. 124. quum [illegible, ~3 letters]ontra alias gravissima, & affectuosissima etiam sine [illegible, ~2 letters]ebitâ commotione & fructu sæpe abeant, quando [illegible, ~2 letters]ore, non animo dicentis veniunt, & non com-[illegible, ~2 letters]motum prius Doctoris animum arguunt. Hieronymus [illegible, ~2 letters]ist. ad Nepotianum egregiè: Delicatus magister est, [illegible, ~2 letters]ui pleno ventre de jejuniis disputat. Accusare avaritiam [illegible, ~2 letters]- latro potest. Sacerdotis Christi os, mens, manusque [illegible, ~2 letters]concordent.
units.tr: (chap. cit., question 13); Telingius, book cited, p. 124. Often sermons that are otherwise very weighty and very moving pass without emotion and fruit, when they come from the mouth of the speaker and not from his heart, and they reveal a teacher's mind that has not first been moved. Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, admirably: The teacher is a pampered one who discourses about fasting with a full belly. A thief can accuse avarice. The mouth, mind and hands of Christ's priest should agree.

units.la: V. At verò præcipue precatur, instantissime, & [illegible, ~1 letter]mni fervore, quemadmodum ante studia, ut dicen-[illegible, ~1 letter]a & componenda inspiraret ei Deus, sic jam ma-[illegible, ~1 letter]ne, ut quam concionem ei dedit recte formare, [illegible, ~1 letter]rro benedicat & perficiat, hocque largiatur, ut [illegible, ~1 letter]ebito modo, animo & gestibus, vi ac demonstra-[illegible, ~1 letter]ne spiritus ita agat ad Ecclesiam, ut omnes vivi-[illegible, ~1 letter]ssime sentiant, commoveantur, acsanctissimè ob-[illegible, ~1 letter]vent quod Deo per ministerium suum in con-[illegible, ~1 letter]ne placuerit exponere. Hoc precatur privatim, [illegible, ~1 letter]publicè; nam ipse duplicem personam quum [illegible, ~1 letter]nt, erudiendus ut fit juxta alios, illosque simul [illegible, ~1 letter]urus, tanto diligentius necesse habet hæc orare [illegible, ~1 letter]eo, & impetrare. Augustin. de doctr. Christ. [illegible, ~1 letter]4. cap. 30. five autem apud populum vel apud quos dicturus; five quod apud populum dicendum, vel [illegible, ~1 letter]is qui volucrint, aut potuerint legendum est dictatu- [illegible, ~1 letter]oret ut Deus sermonem bonum det in os ejus, Luthe-[illegible, ~1 letter]: bene orasse, est bene studuisse.
units.tr: V. But above all he should pray, most earnestly and with all fervour, just as before his studies, that God may inspire him in what he is to say and compose, so now too that God may bless and perfect the sermon he has given him to form rightly, and grant that he may act in the proper manner, with his mind and gestures, with the power and demonstration of the Spirit, towards the Church, so that all may feel most vividly, be moved, and most holily grasp what it has pleased God to set forth through his ministry in the sermon. He prays this privately and publicly; for since he bears a double person, being himself to be taught, as others are, and about to teach them at the same time, he must all the more diligently pray for and obtain these things. Augustine, De doctrina Christiana, book 4, chap. 30: Whether it is to be spoken before the people or before those to whom you are to speak; whether what is to be said before the people is to be read or dictated by those who have been willing or able... He prays that God may give a good word into his mouth. Luther: to have prayed well is to have studied well.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: I. In Concione, ubi actio, duo consideranda. I. [illegible, ~1 letter]cutio, pronunciatio, vel sermo. II. Gestus. In [illegible, ~1 letter]one, utloquatur recte Marc. 7, 35. Matt. 10, 19. [illegible, ~1 letter]ἡ τί λαλήσητε. De dicendi genere conciona-[illegible, ~1 letter]o agit Augustinus lib. 4. doctr. Christ. ferme [illegible, ~1 letter]torum. Si eloquenter vult dicere, inquit cap. 26. [illegible, ~1 letter]gre debet, ut intelligenter, ut libenter, ut obedien- [illegible, ~1 letter]diatur Sermo ejus. I. Sit clarus, perspicuus, & & distinctus. Ezr. 7, 9. Hab. 2, 2. Augustin. cap. 10. istius lib. quid enim prodest locutionis integritas, quam non sequitur intellectus audientis, &c. Qui ergo docet, vitabit omnia verba, quæ non docent. & cap. 12, 11. Patheticus, movens, penetrans. Augustinus d. lib. cap. 24. Non tamen egisse me aliquid putavi, cum eos audirem acclamantes, sed cum flentes viderem. Acclamationibus quippe se doceri & delectari: sletii autem lachrymæ indicabant. Hieronymus ep. ad Nepot. Docente te Ecclesia, non clamor populi, sed gemitus suscitetur. Lachrymæ auditorum, laudes tuæ sint. Elegantissima, & vere aurea sententia. Similiter Prosper de vit. contempl. lib. 1. cap. 23. non vocibus delectetur populi adclamantis sibi, sed sletibus, nec plausum à populo studeat exspectari, sed gemitum. Bernardus serm. 59. in Cantic. Illius Doctoris libenter audio vocem, qui non sibi plausum, sed mihi planctum moveat. Vere turturem exhibes, si gemere doceas. Etsi persuadere vis, gemendo id magis, quam declamando studeas oportebit.
units.tr: I. In Concione, where there is action, two things must be considered. I. The sermo, that is, the pronunciation or delivery of the words. II. Gestus, the gesture. In the sermo, one should speak rightly (Mark 7:35; Matt. 10:19, "take no thought how or what you shall speak" [ἡ τί λαλήσητε]). Augustine treats the kind of speech suited to the preacher in book 4 of On Christian Doctrine, nearly throughout. "If he wants to speak eloquently," he says in chapter 26, "he ought to speak so that he may be understood, so that he may be heard gladly, and so that he may be obeyed." His speech should be I. Clear, lucid and distinct (Ezra 7:9; Hab. 2:2). Augustine, in chapter 10 of the same book: "For what good is the correctness of speech if the hearer's understanding does not follow it?" etc. "Therefore whoever teaches will avoid all words that do not teach." And chapter 12, 11: moving, stirring, piercing. Augustine, in the same book, chapter 24: "I did not think I had accomplished anything when I heard them shouting their approval, but when I saw them weeping. For they are taught and delighted by applause; but sobs and tears show that they have been moved." Jerome, letter to Nepotianus: "While you are the Church's teacher, let there be raised not the shouting of the people but their groans. Let the tears of your hearers be your praise." A most elegant and truly golden saying. Similarly Prosper, On the Contemplative Life, book 1, chapter 23: "Let him not delight in the voices of the people shouting approval to him, but in their sobs; nor let him look for applause from the people, but for their groaning." Bernard, sermon 59 on the Song of Songs: "I gladly hear the voice of that teacher who stirs not applause in me but lamentation. You truly show yourself a turtledove if you teach me to groan. If you want to persuade, you will need to work at this more by groaning than by declaiming."

units.la: Quær. An liceat eloquenter, & oratorie dicere? Resp. Re neglecta, vel non ita attenta plus verbis & verborum ornatui studere, vel ita orationis flosculos, & sententiarum elegantias sectari, ut verba faciat præ rebus eminere, & attendi, est ἐν πει-θοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, vel ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγῳ inanem reddere crucem Christi, & sermonem crucis 1 Cor. 2, 4, 1, 17, 18. Viro captare flosculos turpe est, ait Seneca epist. 33. præcipue autem Theologo, & in tali actione. Prosper lib. cit. cap. 34. Denique alia est ratio Declamatorum, & alia debet esse Doctorum. Illi elucubratæ declamationis pompam totis facundiæ suæ viribus concupiscunt, isti sobrio nisitatoque sermone Christi gloriam quærunt, Illi rebus manibus pretiosa verborum induunt ornamenta: isti veracibus sententiis ornant, & commendant verba simplicia. Alioqui mascula illa, &
units.tr: Question: Is it lawful to speak eloquently and in the manner of an orator? Answer: If, the matter being neglected or not attended to closely enough, one takes more pains with words and the adornment of words, and pursues the flowers of rhetoric and the elegance of sentiments, so that one's speech stands out more than the things themselves and draws attention to itself, then it is in persuasive words of human wisdom [ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις], or in wisdom of speech [ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγου], and it makes the cross of Christ empty and the word of the cross (1 Cor. 2:4; 1:17, 18). "It is shameful for a man to hunt after flowers of speech," says Seneca, letter 33; this applies especially to a theologian, and to such an action. Prosper, in the book cited, chapter 34: "In short, the method of the declaimers is one thing, and that of the teachers ought to be another. The former covet the pomp of an elaborate declamation with all the powers of their eloquence; the latter seek the glory of Christ in a sober and restrained speech. The former clothe trivial matters with precious ornaments of words; the latter adorn and commend simple words with true sentiments."

units.la: nihil affectati vel vani habens, sed divina eloquentia, qualem in Iesaia, Iobo ac Paulo observare est, immo quali vel illustres mulieres induit Dei-spiritus, Deboram Iudic. 5. Abigalem: 1 Sam: 25. ne de Ma-ria dicam Luc. 1. cum rerum gravitate conveniens, eique subserviens, ut peculiare Spiritus S. charisma 1 Cor. 12, 10, 11. æstimanda est. Amef. caf. cap. cit. qu. 12. Adde Medull. cap. cit. §. 60. &c. Talis in Chrysostomo, Augustino; Vide huius lib. de doctr. Christ. 4. cap. 21. ubi de diverso loquendi genere quo usi fuerunt Cyprianus, & Ambrosius, loquitur. Veteres ut mittam, talis in Calvino, Farello; Vireto eloquentia, nisi quod in illo praeter eloquentiam ita summa eruditio eminuit, ut cui primas assignes, in ambiguo sit. Beza elegantí carmine trium iitorum in concionando dona ita expressit, ut si in unum daretur ea simul cadere, perfectus is Concionator esset futurus. Gallica mirata est Calvinum Ecclesia nuper, Quo nemo docuit doctius, Est quoque te nuper mirata, Farelle, tonantem, Quo nemo tonuit fortius. Et miratur adhuc fundentem mella Viretum; Quo nemo fatur dulcius, Scilicet aut tribus his servabere testibus olim, Aut interibis Gallia.
units.tr: Otherwise that manly eloquence, having nothing affected or vain, but divine, such as is to be observed in Isaiah, Job and Paul, or rather such as the Spirit of God clothed even illustrious women with, Deborah (Judg. 5) and Abigail (1 Sam. 25), not to mention Mary (Luke 1), agreeing with the weight of the matter and serving it, is to be esteemed as a peculiar gift of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:10, 11). See Amesius, Cases of Conscience, chapter cited, question 12. Add Medulla, chapter cited, §60, etc. Such was the eloquence of Chrysostom and Augustine; see this author's book On Christian Doctrine, book 4, chapter 21, where he speaks of the different manner of speaking used by Cyprian and Ambrose. Not to mention the older writers, such was the eloquence of Calvin and Farel; in Viret, apart from his eloquence, such great learning shone forth that it is doubtful to which of the two you should assign first place. Beza, in an elegant poem, expressed the three gifts of the preacher so well that, if they were all given together to one man, he would be a perfect preacher. The French Church recently admired Calvin, of whom no one taught more learnedly: "Farel, you were once also admired by the Church as a thunderer, of whom no one thundered more vigorously; and Viret, who still pours forth honey, is still admired, of whom no one speaks more sweetly." Doubtless, France, you will be preserved only by these three witnesses, or you will perish.

units.la: VII. Vitia sermonis ut plurimum haec sunt. I. Verbis plus attendere, quam rei; contra illud Augustini: in ipso etiam sermone malit rebus placere, quam verbis, lib. cit. cap. 16. II. μονότονον esse, vitium paene omnibus primum incipientibus commune, si modo illis vitium dici debeat: quum pro rei natura & concionis incremento sermo quoque se flectere, & augere debeat. Augustin. cap. 19,21. III. Si vel breviores faciat periodos, vel justo longiores. Basilius in verba Moisi, attende tibi: est enim ex natu-rā debeat; cui junge Gregorium Pastoral. part. 2. cap. 6. & lib. 26. in Iobum, cap. 1. In quorum commentariorum, sive librorum fine ingenue ita subjungit: Bona vero si qua divinitus accipiens dixi, meo videlicet vitio minus me dixisse profiteor. Nam ad me intrinsecus rediens, postpositis verborum foliis, postpositis sententiarum ramis, dum ipsam subtiliter, radicem meae intentionis inspicio: Deo quidem ex ea me summopere placere voluisse cognosco, sed eidem intentioni qua Deo placere studeo, furtim se, nescio quomodo, intentio humana laudis interserit.
units.tr: VII. The faults of speech are for the most part these. I. To pay more attention to words than to the matter; contrary to Augustine's saying, that in the very speech one should prefer to please with the matters rather than with the words (book cited, chapter 16). II. Monotony [μονότονον], a fault almost common to all who are beginning, if indeed it ought to be called a fault; whereas the speech too ought to bend and rise according to the nature of the matter and the growth of the sermon (Augustine, chapters 19, 21). III. Making the periods either shorter than they should be or too long. Basil, on the words of Moses, "take heed to yourself" (Deut. 4:9), ... ; join to this Gregory, Pastoral Care, part 2, chapter 6, and book 26 on Job, chapter 1. At the end of these commentaries or books he candidly adds the following: "If I have said anything good that I received from God, I confess that I have said it less well because of my own fault. For when I return inwardly to myself, set aside the leaves of words and the branches of sentiments, and carefully examine the root of my intention itself, I recognize that I have indeed greatly wished to please God by it, but that human desire for praise has somehow crept in secretly, mingling with that very intention by which I strive to please God."

units.la: VIII. In Gestibus haec observanda.
units.tr: VIII. What is to be observed in gestures.

units.la: I. Ut semper ac perpetuo sint graves, decori, sancti. II. Ad rem, quam tractas, convenientes; id est, quemadmodum, de voce dictum, ut non iidem semper, sed pro rei varietate alii atque alii, semper sint congrui. III. In exordio nulli vel paucissimi, paulatim aliqui, in fine omnes nempe quos adhiberi convenit. Plura de his addere supersedeo, quia facilia, & apud Rhetores, ubi de Pronunciatione agunt, copiose explicari illa solent. Cic. ad Herenn. lib. 3. & 4. Et de Oratore lib. 3. Quintil. Instit. Orat. lib. 10. & 11.
units.tr: I. They should always and throughout be serious, becoming, and holy. II. They should suit the subject matter, that is, as was said of the voice, they should always be appropriate, not the same throughout but varying with the nature of the matter. III. At the beginning there should be none or very few; gradually some; at the end, all those who ought to be used. I pass over adding more on these points, since they are easy, and the rhetoricians, where they treat of delivery, are accustomed to explain them at length. Cicero, Ad Herennium, books 3 and 4; and De Oratore, book 3. Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria, books 10 and 11.

units.la: IX. Hactenus de concionis qualitate quasi, jam & de quantitate aliquid addendum, sive quamdiu concionandum, & quoties. Ut nimium breves, ita quoque prolixiores conciones juste reprehenduntur. Brevis praedicatio, longa ruminatio, actio perpetua. Beatus Hussus in epist. ad quendam Sacerdotem, apud Foxum in Martyrol. pag. 817. Concionare perpetuo, sed breviter, & cum fructu, prudenter intelligens, & discrete dispensans S. Scripturas. Tempus haud idem & constans definiri nequit, quamdiu concionandum, sed pro re nata, & Ecclesiae usu agendum; videndumque ne nimia prolixitas taedium faciat, sed abrumpamus & differamus potius, quae concionem
units.tr: IX. So far on the quality of the sermon; now something must be added on its quantity, that is, how long one should preach, and how often. Sermons that are too short, as well as those that are too long, are rightly blamed. A short sermon, a long chewing over, a perpetual activity. Blessed Hus, in a letter to a certain priest, cited by Foxe in the Martyrology, p. 817: Preach continually, but briefly and with profit, understanding prudently and dispensing the Holy Scriptures with discretion. The time cannot be fixed as one and the same, how long one should preach; it must be done according to the occasion and the custom of the Church. Care must be taken that excessive length does not produce weariness, but we should rather cut short and defer whatever would keep the congregation beyond the customary and allowed time.

units.la: E ultra solitum & concessum tempus detinerent. Augustin. in Psal. 90. concione secundâ : sicut non dubito meminisse charitatem vestram, qui hesterno die sermoni adfuistis, Psalmum quem cæperamus exponere, ne ad terminum perveniret, angustia temporis impedivit, & dilata est pars ejus in hodiernum diem. Hoc qui hæri adfuistis, recordamini, qui non affuistis, agnoscite. Non minimam hic Auditorum quoque habendam rationem, significat Chrysosthomus orat. 4. adv. Judæos: Verum quoniam tantum est dicendum, quan-tum auditor possit capere, nec omnia simul, nec acervatim, illis in aliud tempus dispensatis, hic sermonem fi-niemus, exhortantes vestram charitatem, meminerit is eorum, quæ dicta sunt, & hæc illis, quæ prius dicta sunt, annectatis. Alioqui per horæ spatium concionari solitos Patres observamus. Basil. in Psal. 14. secundum distinctionem Latinorum, sive in reliqua, quæ super eodem Psalmo dicenda restabant, contra fæ-neratores, ita exorditur : Hesterna die super Psalmo decimo-quarto sermonem apud vos habuimus, quem sub horæ spatio absolvere nequivimus, nunc autem ut cer- ti debitores, reliqua quæ restabant, libentes exsoluturi venimus. Bernardus serm. 14. in Cantic. sed hoc quoque alias. Nam etsi in promtu nunc essent omnia, & neque vos oneràti, nec ego fatigatus essem, hora tamen finem inducit. serm. 46. Iam etiam, quid de sua consequenter charisma protestetur, bonum esset audire, sed hora non patitur. serm. 83. quantum quidem regularis hora permisit, quam nobis instituimus ad loquendum. Atque illud justum habendæ concioni tempus videtur: tantum enim unâ horâ facile dicitur, quantum totâ vitâ discitur.
units.tr: Augustine, on Psalm 90, second sermon: As I do not doubt that your charity remembers, you who were present at yesterday's sermon, the psalm which we had begun to expound did not reach its end, because the shortness of time hindered it, and part of it has been put off until today. Those of you who were present then, remember it; those who were not, take note of it. Chrysostom, in his fourth homily against the Jews, shows that the hearers also must not be left out of account: But since as much must be said as the hearer can grasp, and not everything at once or in a heap, having distributed those matters to another time, we will end the sermon here, exhorting your charity to remember what has been said, and to join these things to those that were said before. Otherwise we observe that the Fathers were accustomed to preach for the space of an hour. Basil, on Psalm 14, following the Latin division, or on the remainder of the same psalm which was still to be spoken, against usurers, begins thus: Yesterday we delivered to you a sermon on the fourteenth psalm, which we could not finish within the span of an hour; now, like debtors who are bound, we have come, gladly to pay what remained. Bernard, sermon 14 on the Song of Songs, but this also elsewhere: for even if everything were ready now, and neither you were burdened nor I wearied, the hour nevertheless brings the end. Sermon 46: Now also, what he consequently professes concerning his own gift would be good to hear, but the hour does not allow it. Sermon 83: as far as the regular hour permitted, which we have set for speaking. And that seems to be the just time for holding a sermon: for as much can easily be said in one hour as is learned in a whole life.

units.la: X. Similiter neque id certo & universaliter definiri potest, quoties sit concionandum, verum officii & Ecclesiæ ratio hic leges ferunt. Singulis præcipue Dominicis concionari, ut justissimum, ita in omni Ecclesiâ id apud Patres observatum videmus. Ambrofii conciones ita sæpius incipiunt, ab eo, quod superiore Dominica tractasset, serm. 2, 6, 15, 24, 29, 35, 43, 47, 85. &c. Idem de illo Augustinus in Confess. fatetur lib. 6. cap. 3. Et eum quidem in populo verbum veritatis rectè tractantem, omni die Dominico audiebam. Baron. Annal. ad Annum 375. num. 24. Atque hoc injungit can. 19. synodi 6. in Trullo, ad quem vide quoque Scholia Balsamonis pag. 380. Potissimum bis in hebdomade Antiochenis suis concionem habebat Chrysosthomus, patet ex Homil. 24. vel sec. al. cod. 25. in Joann. Pueri, singulis diebus ad scholas aguntur, ἀλλὰ δύο μόνον τῆς ἐκδο-μάδ᾽ ἡμέρας [?] ἀναγινωσκομένοις [?] περὶς βασιλεύ τῆς ἡμέρας μέρ᾽ quamvis etiam quotidie nonnunquam concionatum fuisse legimus, Homil. ad Antioch. 13. Ab eodem principio, & iisdem proœmiis, quibus heri & nudiustertius cœpi, & hodie incipiam. De quâ homilia quoque Baronius late agit ad Annum 388. num. 13. Homil. 4. de pœnitentia, inquit, quartum jam diem hunc ad pœnitentiæ modum gregem hunc pascimus, neque vel hodie digredi paramus, & Homil. 9. de pœnit. Atque idem plerisque Patrum observamus, illos ferme quotidie concionatos fuisse, Ambrosius ferm. 64. quoniam hesterno die de latrone fecimus mentionem. Basilius in Psal. 14. Hesternâ die super Psalmo decimoquarto sermonem apud vos habuimus &c.: immo, ut statim videbimus, quidem bis in die, Augustinus in Psal. 30. conc. secundam sic concludit: Iam sufficiat charitati vestræ, quod restat in nomine Domini crastina die ipso adjuvante reddemus. Conc. sec. in Psal. 33. Qui hesterno die affuistis non dubito meminisse pollicitationis nostræ. In Psal. 34. conc. sec. Quousque hesterno die disputatum sit, credo meminisse charitatem vestram, ex ipso loco hodie sumamus exordium. Similiter in Psal. 50, & 68. conc. sec. &c fec. & in 90. conc. item fecunda. De verbis Apostoli ferm. 5. Hesternam lectionem, de Sancti Apostol. Pauli epistola, qui sermoni adfuistis, audistis, illa lectio sequitur, quæ hodie recitata est. & ferm. 6. & 17. Bernardus ferm. in Cantic. 8o. Quidam vestrum (ut comperi) minus æquo animo ferunt, quod ecce jam per aliquot dies dum stupori & administrationi sacramentorum inhærere delectat, sermo quem ministramus &c. ferm. 14. tenete, in quo attentos vos reddidi, ut non sit cras necesse repetere. Serm. 38. quid igitur Dei ignorantia parturit? nam hinc incipiendum est, sicut recordamini hic heri fuisse terminatum. ferm. 68. Audite jam, quod heri distulimus. ferm. 83. biduum hoc in demonstranda verbi animæque affinitate expensum est. ferm. 8. in eundem Psalmum. Quin & bis sæpe in die concionabantur, ita Basilius, mane nempe & vesperi: Homil. 3. Hexaem, Opera diei primi &c. oratio nostra hesterno die in medium attulit. interpretationisque bipertito diversæ partem alteram matutinum alimentum, alteram vespertinam lætitiam animarum. Auditoribus obtulit, atque apposuit. Et ut scias coram populo illam habitam, subjungit: at me non præterit, cum plures operarios artifices ex opera quotidiana sibi victum comparantes, nos cingere, atque stipare, qui nostram orationem brevem esse percupiunt, ne suis ab officiis longo tempore distrahantur. Homil. 8. in fine: Verum hic finis sit hujusce nostri convivii matutini, ne satietas exuperans vos ad vespertinas sumendas epulas voluptatesque capiendas hebetiores efficiat. Et sic in initio 9. homil. Qualesnam ex vobis epulæ visæ sunt, quas in aurora vobis mea apposuit oratio? ferm. 2. in divit. avar. quæ dicta sunt hodie mane, fratres dilectissimi, diligens auditor facile reminisci poterit. Quæ omnia eo spectant, ut praxin Veterum cognoscamus, & diligentiam illorum in concionando observemus, ac simul æmulemur. Verbum Dei usque ad ipsam suam extremam ægritudinem impraetermisse, alacriter & fortiter, sana mente, sanoque consilio in Ecclesia prædicat, inquit de Augustino Possidonius, in ejus vita cap. ult. Neque aliter Calvinus, qui, ut in vitâ ejus testantur Beza, ac Melchior Adamus, indefessus in concionibus, quæ nobis divinos illos in Utrumque Testamentum commentarios dederunt. Alternis hebdomadibus totis concionabatur, triduo vero docebat; singulis diebus Iovis Presbyterii cognitionem regebat, diebus Veneris in communi collatione scripturæ, quam Congregationem ipsi vocant, justam pæne lectionem habebat &c. quare vel morti jam proximus, Amicis, ut saltem ægrotus ab omni scribendi vel dictandi molestia ulterius vacaret, ita vir maximus respondebat: quid ergo, vultis me otiosum à Domino deprehendi? atque ita de eo Thuanus lib. 36. cum septennium integrum variis morbis ac cruciatibus conflictatus esset, nec minus propterea in munere suo assiduus, aut a continua scriptione abstineret. &c. De Ivello, eruditissimo inter Anglos Theologo, idem in vita ejus narratur, quod Amico à concionando ipsum ob corporis imbecillitatem dehortanti, sic responderit: oportet episcopum concionantem mori, ad simile Vespasiani Imp. dictum procul dubio alludens. Marc. 10, 1: quemadmodum solitus erat, iterum docebat eos.
units.tr: X. Likewise, it cannot be fixed with certainty and universally how often one should preach; rather, the nature of the office and of the Church lays down laws here. That one should preach especially on each Lord's Day, as it is most just, so we see it observed by the Fathers in every Church. Ambrose's sermons often begin in this way, from what he had treated on the previous Lord's Day: sermons 2, 6, 15, 24, 29, 35, 43, 47, 85, etc. Augustine confesses the same about himself in the Confessions, book 6, chapter 3: And I used to hear him on every Lord's Day, handling the word of truth rightly before the people. Baronius, Annals, year 375, no. 24. The sixth Council in Trullo, canon 19, enjoins this too; see also the Scholia of Balsamon, p. 380. Chrysostom, at Antioch, mostly preached twice a week, as appears from his homily 24, or 25 according to other manuscripts, on John. Boys are taken to school every day, but only on two days of the week [ἀλλὰ δύο μόνον τῆς ἐκδομάδ᾽ ἡμέρας] ... read; although we also read that he sometimes preached even daily, Homily to the Antiochenes 13: From the same beginning, and with the same prefaces with which I began yesterday and the day before, I shall begin today as well. Baronius also treats this homily at length, year 388, no. 13. In homily 4 on repentance he says: For the fourth day now we are feeding this flock with the manner of repentance, and we are not preparing to depart even today, and in homily 9 on repentance. And we observe the same of most of the Fathers, that they preached almost every day. Ambrose, sermon 64: since yesterday we made mention of the thief. Basil, on Psalm 14: Yesterday we delivered a sermon to you on the fourteenth psalm, etc. Indeed, as we shall soon see, sometimes even twice a day. Augustine, on Psalm 30, second sermon, concludes thus: Now let it suffice your charity that what remains we will render tomorrow in the name of the Lord, with his help. Second sermon on Psalm 33: Those of you who were present yesterday, I do not doubt, remember our promise. On Psalm 34, second sermon: As far as the discussion went yesterday, I believe your charity remembers; today let us take our beginning from that same place. Similarly on Psalms 50 and 68, second sermon, etc., and on Psalm 90, likewise the second sermon. On the words of the Apostle, sermon 5: You heard yesterday the reading from the epistle of the holy Apostle Paul, you who were present at the sermon; that reading follows which was recited today. And sermons 6 and 17. Bernard, sermon 80 on the Song of Songs: Some of you (as I have learned) bear it with less than equal mind, that, behold, for several days now, while it pleases you to cling to wonder and the administration of the sacraments, the sermon which we are delivering etc. Sermon 14: Hold fast to that in which I have made you attentive, so that it will not be necessary to repeat it tomorrow. Sermon 38: What, then, does ignorance of God bring forth? For we must begin here, as you remember it was concluded here yesterday. Sermon 68: Hear now what we deferred yesterday. Sermon 83: This two days has been spent in showing the affinity between the word and the soul. Sermon 8 on the same psalm. Indeed they often preached even twice a day. So Basil: in the morning and in the evening. Homily 3 on the Hexaemeron: The works of the first day, etc. Our discourse yesterday brought forward the one part of the interpretation, which offered and set before the hearers the morning nourishment, and the other, the evening joy of souls. And so that you may know it was delivered before the people, he adds: But it is not unknown to me that many workmen and craftsmen, who earn their living by daily labour, surround and crowd us, wishing our discourse to be short, lest they be kept long away from their duties. Homily 8, at the end: But let this be the end of this our morning banquet, lest excessive satiety make you too dull to take up the evening feasts and pleasures. And so at the beginning of homily 9: What sort of feasts did my discourse seem to you to set before you at dawn? Sermon 2 on the rich man's avarice: What has been said this morning, beloved brothers, a diligent hearer will easily be able to recall. All these things point to our learning the practice of the Ancients and observing, and at the same time imitating, their diligence in preaching. He preached the Word of God in the Church, without intermission, even to his own last sickness, cheerfully and boldly, with a sound mind and sound counsel, says Possidius of Augustine, in his life, last chapter. Nor was Calvin otherwise, who, as Beza and Melchior Adam testify in his life, was tireless in sermons, which gave us those divine commentaries on both Testaments. He preached every other week in full, and on the third day he taught; each day on Thursday he presided over the examination of the presbytery, and on Friday he held nearly a lecture in the common assembly of Scripture, which they themselves call the Congregation, etc. Therefore, when he was already close to death, so that at least while sick he might be free from any further trouble of writing or dictating, that great man answered thus: What then? Do you want the Lord to find me idle? And so Thuanus writes of him, book 36: Although for a full seven years he had been struggling with various illnesses and torments, he was nonetheless no less constant in his office, nor did he abstain from continual writing, etc. Of Jewel, the most learned English theologian, the same is told in his life: when a friend urged him to give up preaching because of his bodily weakness, he replied thus: A bishop ought to die while preaching, undoubtedly alluding to a similar saying of the Emperor Vespasian. Mark 10. 1: As he was accustomed, he taught them again.
